US Democrats recruit 100 election observers over midterm interference fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:14 UTC
03:00:14 KST

US Senate Democrats have recruited and trained more than 100 congressional staffers to monitor voting and ballot counting in November's midterm elections, alleging possible interference from the administration.
The observers will be deployed across nine states with closely contested Senate races, including Ohio, Georgia and Michigan, Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and Senator Alex Padilla told reporters on Wednesday.
Their mission will be to document possible voter intimidation, threats against election workers and other irregularities, including during the counting and certification of ballots after the November 3 vote.
"Their role is very clear: to observe, to document, and report the facts," Schumer said.
"Donald Trump does not get to decide who votes. He doesn't get to decide which votes count," Schumer added.
Padilla, the senior Democrat on the Senate committee overseeing election rules, said the observers could remain deployed for days or even weeks after the election if necessary.
"I don't put anything past the Trump administration to try to interfere with the election," he said, warning that Democrats were preparing for possible challenges to the results.
The president has sought restrictions on mail-in voting and tougher proof-of-citizenship requirements, while his administration has pursued access to state voter records.
Other election-protection initiatives
The Justice Department says its election monitoring efforts are intended to ensure compliance with voting laws and protect election integrity.
Padilla stressed that the new Senate observers would have no role in administering elections or handling ballots.
"They're not there to interfere. They're not there to cause a scene," he said.
The programme, announced earlier this year, is an official congressional initiative rather than a campaign operation.
Padilla said Democrats hoped to deploy observers alongside Republican Senate staff where possible, following the example of a longstanding House of Representatives programme.
The effort comes as civil rights groups pursue their own election-protection initiatives, including Vote Safe, which has begun deploying trained community volunteers to polling locations in several battleground states.
Its organisers say their volunteers will help voters understand their rights, document possible intimidation and provide reassurance amid fears of immigration enforcement activity near polling places.
Schumer insisted American elections remained safe and safe and secure, saying the Democrats' preparations were intended to keep them that way.

Nord Stream trial opens in Germany, defense seeks dismissal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Nord Stream trial opens in Germany, defense seeks dismissal
October 14, 2026
The trial of a former Ukrainian special forces officer, Serhii Kuznietsov, opened in the northern German city of Hamburg on Wednesday amid considerable public and press interest.
Kuznietsov is accused of leading the September 2022 sabotage operation that put the undersea Nord Stream 1 and 2 gas pipelines linking Russian to Germany out of action. The pipelines remain inactive four years later, with no sign of plans to ever reactivate them as Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine heads into its fifth winter.
Prosecutors accuse the Ukrainian of participation in a war crime by targeting civilian infrastructure, but his defense lawyers on Wednesday argued that the case should be dismissed entirely on multiple grounds.
What did Kuznietsov's lawyers say on opening day?
A team of three lawyers representing Kuznietsov questioned the premise of the trial in court.
One of Kuznietsov's lawyers, Nicola Canestrini, argued that it was not valid to try the officer on war crimes charges for an attack on civilian infrastructure.
He argued that the pipeline, which provided half of Germany's natural gas imports prior to Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, was ultimately a "Russian weapon," given the importance of energy revenues for funding Moscow's military.
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked the court.
After the charges were read out, the judge asked Kuznietsov if he wanted to comment, and he said that he did not.
His lawyers argue that this silence extends beyond not speaking in court and say this should be the main grounds for dismissal.
They say Kuznietsov is sworn to secrecy by his home government in Ukraine and so is unable to discuss his case or potential exonerating evidence with anyone, including his legal representatives.
"He is not permitted to speak. His two immediate superiors told him that he does not have authorization to make any statements — not even to his lawyers," defense attorney Jes Meyer-Lohkamp told the court. In German law, Meyer-Lohkamp argued: "Anyone who cannot speak out cannot be convicted."
What was the mood in court in Hamburg?
DW's Matthew Moore was on hand in the court in northern Germany on Wednesday.
There is huge interest in this court case, Moore reported. No sooner had the court doors opened at 07:30 local time in Hamburg than the first journalists, observers and protesters began arriving.
A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist." One participant from Germany told Moore they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."
Inside, a Ukrainian student told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii Kuznietsov.
"Serhii Kuznietsov is a hero," the student said. In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, Kuznietsov faces a lengthy prison sentence.
Geramny's Wadephul: 'We will deal with any outcome'
The case has been highly politically awkward for Germany — a staunch supporter of Ukraine despite investigators pursuing a trail that led to Kuznietsov and other suspects.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has repeatedly denied any Ukrainian involvement in the operation, and had also resisted Kuznietsov's extradition to Germany after his arrest in Italy last year, arguing that there was no case to answer.
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul declined to comment on the trial on Wednesday, saying that the most important thing for now was for the case to proceed with no political interference or restrictions.
"We will deal with any outcome, and we will, of course, take it into account in our political calculations," he told a press conference in Berlin.
Court dates for the trial are currently scheduled through February of next year but this could be subject to change in either direction.
With additional reporting from DW's Matthew Moore in Hamburg.

This strange sea animal is on menus, but it is disappearing from our reefs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Sea cucumbers can live 100 years, but may not survive our hunger
The alien-looking sea cucumber is a delicacy eaten in soups or consumed for its perceived health and libido benefits.
But a boom in demand since the 1980s has led to overfishing and population collapses in parts of the world, including the Pacific.
Entire species are disappearing from remote Australian reefs, with illegal fishing pointed to as a key culprit.
And there are now concerns that regulators for Australia's legal sea cucumber fisheries are underestimating how long it takes fished stocks to recover.
A new "first-of-its-kind" genetic study, published in iScience, indicates at least one sought-after sea cucumber species lives longer than we thought.
Study lead author and molecular ecologist Sven Uthicke, from the Australian Institute of Marine Science, said the black teatfish (Holothuria whitmaei) could reach 100 years of age.
It was assumed the species, found in Australia's tropical waters but less so in other Pacific countries, only lived five to 20 years in the wild.
Dr Uthicke said the finding meant fishery management needed to revise whether current catch limits were sustainable.
"They're currently assuming that these animals are replaced, basically, 10 times more than they are likely to be,"
he said.
The age a marine species reaches is a major factor for calculating a fishery's environmental sustainability.
Dr Uthicke said the sustainable catch limit for black teatfish and similar species might be lower than we thought.
What are sea cucumbers?
Sea cucumbers are part of a large group of "spiny skin" animals that includes starfish and sea urchins.
Colours and patterns of their leathery skin range from plain browns to vibrant reds and yellows.
Sometimes they have alien-like mouth tendrils, which are actually modified "feet".
Sea cucumbers are believed to benefit the health of coral and seagrass meadows.
"We don't necessarily understand all the ecological services that sea cucumbers provide, but we do know that they are very important in aerating sediment," CSIRO marine ecologist John Keesing said.
Much is still unknown about these weird animals, with few studies into basic biology like how long they can live.
How old do sea cucumbers get?
In the new study, Dr Uthicke revisited a no-fishing zone near Lizard Island in the Great Barrier Reef 24 years after another study he did into the growth rates of black teatfish.
He was surprised to find 31 out of the 76 sea cucumbers from his earlier fieldwork in 2000.
"I'm pretty sure a few of those were over 50, 60 years old,"
Dr Uthicke said.
"We still don't know how fast they grow because the individuals in my study basically did not grow at all over the entire 25 years … and we didn't find any small ones."
As the research was only conducted in one location, Dr Uthicke said other locations and species could be looked at.
But, he said, regulators could use the current findings to manage stocks more conservatively.
Black teatfish stocks have previously collapsed at the Great Barrier Reef and Zenadh Kes (Torres Strait).
As black teatfish are considered globally endangered, the federal environment department has to sign off on any fishing regimes occurring in Australia.
The species is not caught in the regulated Western Australia or Northern Territory sea cucumber fisheries, but it is caught in Queensland fisheries.
A Queensland Department of Primary Industries spokesperson said a recent stock assessment for black teatfish indicated the species was being fished at sustainable levels.
"Future stock assessments will consider all new, relevant information."
An Australian Fisheries Management Authority spokesperson said the new research would be considered when advice was developed for future management settings in the Torres Strait.
They said a past CSIRO survey in 2019–20 found the black teatfish had significantly recovered from historic overfishing and was safe to be fished under a strict harvest strategy.
"Black teatfish is an important source of income supporting livelihoods and the traditional way of life in the Torres Strait," the spokesperson said.
"Torres Strait Islanders have exclusive access rights to black teatfish, which is estimated to be worth over half a million dollars to the local economy."
How much do sea cucumbers sell for?
Dried sea cucumbers can go for hundreds of dollars per kilogram in domestic markets like Hong Kong.
A similar price bracket to other high-end produce like Wagyu beef and foie gras.
Sea cucumbers move slowly, so they are easy to pluck from the water by the basket-load.
Once caught, a sea cucumber is gutted, cooked, salted and dried.
"There's very few other animals that eat them," Dr Keesing said.
"That's the reason why they don't bother hiding themselves too much."
This vulnerability is thought to have led to local extinctions at remote Australian reefs.
Where sea cucumbers are disappearing already
A study led by Dr Keesing last year suggested the golden sandfish (Holothuria lessoni), which was once common at Ashmore Reef, has gone locally extinct, with overfishing the most likely cause.
The reef is located about 200km from Indonesia and 300km from the Kimberley region of Australia.
"Reefs like Ashmore Reef to the north are now sort of fished out so they're [illegal fishermen] looking further south," Dr Keesing said.
At the next reef down, Scott Reef, black teatfish and white teatfish (Holothuria fuscogilva) have reportedly collapsed.
Illegal fishermen have been intercepted as far south as Rowley Shoals, islands west of Broome, in recent years by federal authorities.
Another study earlier this year suggested the white teatfish was no longer in Rowley Shoals and three other species, including the black teatfish, were close to dropping under a critical population threshold for remaining viable.
"That level of fishing just over quite short a period of time has had a very significant impact on those populations," Dr Keesing, one of the authors, said.
"If that can be prevented by greater surveillance, greater consequences for being intercepted, then those populations should recover.
"If that's just allowed to continue … then potentially you could have the Rowley Shoals in the same state as Ashmore Reef."

====================================================================================================

Chalmers and Frydenberg have more in common than they like to admit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

analysis
From GST to trusts, reform is almost impossible in this fraught political climate
Jim Chalmers and Josh Frydenberg have more in common than they like to admit.
The two former (and perhaps future) rivals are both sharp media performers. Both are highly energetic and ambitious. Both have also had complicated relationships with their respective prime ministers.
And this week both have been reminded of the difficulty of pursuing policy reform.
In the case of Frydenberg, it was the mere suggestion of revisiting the GST as part of broader reform to make the tax system more efficient.
"We need a considered but ambitious national debate about lifting the GST and removing some exemptions, with a significant portion of that additional revenue to fund a major reduction in income tax," he wrote in his memoir, A Grateful Son.
It's hardly an original or radical idea, having been floated over the years by everyone from the Liberal luminaries who brought the GST to life, John Howard and Peter Costello, to corporate leaders such as Matt Comyn and David Thodey, and economists Richard Holden and Saul Eslake.
But Frydenberg's attempt to revive the debate was shot down instantly by Angus Taylor.
"We will not be raising the GST in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis," the opposition leader told Insiders. "We won't be raising taxes," he declared more broadly, which suggests the Coalition will instead seek to fund its growing list of expensive promises through spending cuts alone.
Not that Frydenberg is deterred. His book, and various media interviews this week weighing a potential political comeback, have received a mixed response among Liberal MPs in a party room that has shifted to the right since he was last there.
But the former treasurer is upbeat about the broader public reception. If anything, he's even more energised. And after planting the flag on the GST, Frydenberg isn't walking away from his argument about the need to tackle difficult reform.
Chalmers's difficult week
As for Jim Chalmers, reminders have been coming thick and fast, ever since the May budget, of how bruising reform can be.
After months of blowback over negative gearing and capital gains tax changes that weren't taken to an election, now it's trusts.
Labor is confident it will ultimately win the support of the Greens to impose a 30 per cent minimum tax on discretionary trusts, but fears this could be an even tougher fight than the earlier tax battles, particularly when small business is already angry over a separate matter — the Tax Office decision to ban credit card payments.
The week became even more difficult for Chalmers after the prime minister appeared to suggest he'd been sidelined.
After trying to settle the nerves of anxious Labor backbenchers in Tuesday's caucus meeting, the prime minister then appeared on stage at an Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) dinner to claim credit for fixing the Tax Office problem.
"Andrew did text me last Thursday morning," Albanese said, referring to ACCI chief executive Andrew McKellar. "By Friday morning we had an announcement."
The comment not only created the impression Chalmers had been overruled, but it also suggested government positions could be quickly influenced by an industry group text message.
Chalmers, clearly, couldn't let that sit.
He then revealed he had in fact spoken to the prime minister a day earlier. "On the Wednesday I had discussions with the PM. We agreed it would be appropriate to find a better way through."
In other words, it was a joint decision taken between the two of them before the text message from Andrew McKellar.
Loading
Labor MPs divided on 'rift'
By Question Time yesterday, the prime minister was denying any rift, describing the decision as unanimous.
Tension between a prime minister and treasurer is nothing unusual, as Josh Frydenberg can attest. When it's publicly on show, that's a problem.
The opposition made the most of it, stirring both the prime minister and treasurer in parliament. Labor MPs, meanwhile, were divided.
Some reckon Chalmers should have seen the Tax Office troubles coming earlier. Others reckon it was a bit rich for Albanese to pass the buck after over-egging the benefits of removing credit card surcharges with a social media post suggesting "your morning coffee could be cheaper".
Either way, it's in the interests of neither to appear at odds.
Ultimately, Albanese and Chalmers agree on the big stuff. They both know the government is facing challenges. Both are confident Labor will be in a stronger position this time next year. And both agree sticking with the budget tax changes is the only course.
But delivering reform is proving more difficult by the day.
Late yesterday, the Coalition and Greens joined forces in the Senate to deliver a blow to the government on another front. They've sent Labor back to the drawing board on its plan to remove the more generous private health insurance rebate for over-65s.
That's another $3 billion savings measure up in the air.
As both Chalmers and Frydenberg would surely agree, there's no easy path to repairing the budget.
David Speers is national political lead and host of Insiders, which airs on ABC TV at 9am on Sunday or on iview.

Investing bonanza as younger Australians lean on AI advice
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

AI, crypto and ETFs see record number of Australians investing outside of superannuation
In short:
The stock exchange operator says market participation is at a record high among Australians.
An ASX survey found 54 per cent of Australian adults hold investments outside their super and primary home.
What's next?
The ASX estimates 950,000 Australians who do not currently invest plan to start within the next 12 months.
A record 11.5 million Australian adults now hold investments outside their superannuation and their main home, a new survey by the stock exchange operator finds.
The ASX Australian Investor Study 2026 has revealed an estimated 2.5 million Australians have joined the investor population since 2020.
Investors, the survey showed, now represent 54 per cent of the adult population.
"Australia is a nation of investors," ASX chief executive Anthony Attia said.
Who are Australian investors?
Most investors were middle-income earners and middle-aged, with a median gross income of $110,000 and an average age of 46.
Younger people, aged 18-29, made up 21 per cent of investors.
For the first time, the ASX survey looked at how investors are using AI tools for investment information and advice.
The bourse said investors continued to use professional advisers, brokers, online investment platforms, family and friends, social media, podcasts and other digital sources.
It found AI uptake was strongest among younger investors, used by 14 per cent of investors aged 18 to 29.
Mr Attia said Australia's public participation in share trading is among the highest in developed markets.
The survey, which polled roughly 4,500 people in January and February this year, found shares were the most widely held assets, followed by residential property, exchange-traded funds (ETFs), term deposits and cryptocurrency.
"What is particularly encouraging is the next generation of investors entering the market,"
Mr Attia said.
"Almost one million more Australians are looking to start investing.
"The rapid growth of ETFs, with ownership more than doubling since 2020, shows how innovation is opening new opportunities for investors."
ETF boom as money pours into stocks
Since the ASX survey, money has continued to increasingly flow into ETFs.
Data from investment firm Betashares showed the Australian ETF industry experienced $7 billion in cash flowing in during September after monthly inflows surpassed $7 billion for the first time in August.
The industry hit a record $388 billion in assets under management.
Recent tax changes appear to be behind the enthusiasm for stocks in general, but ETFs in particular.
The government announced in the May budget that it planned to replace the current 50 per cent capital gains tax (CGT) discount with a discount based on the actual rate of inflation.
It also said it would introduce a minimum 30 per cent tax on gains from July 1, 2027.
Forager Funds chief investment officer Steve Johnson said ETFs were popular under the new settings as net gains and losses were contained inside the investment, so a surge in an individual company that might attract capital gains tax could be offset by another loss-making stock.
Betashares agreed investors have paid more attention to the relative tax effectiveness of index-based investment strategies and ETFs following the CGT changes.
The firm also said the continued fall in Australian house prices was giving investors more reason to look at other asset classes like shares, bonds and commodities.
Global X ETFs senior strategist Marc Jocum said the scale of investing over the past quarter had been "significant".
"Australian ETFs have just delivered a record $21 billion quarter, demonstrating that they are becoming a core building block in Australian portfolios," Mr Jocum said.
"Investors are no longer using ETFs for one purpose.
"They are using them to build the foundations of their portfolios, access opportunities around the world and create more diversified sources of growth and income."
Regulator watching market evolution
As more Australians turn to investing, more are exposed to digital assets including cryptocurrencies.
Corporate watchdog ASIC is looking to firm up the regulation of digital assets, today beginning consultation on guidance and standards to accompany new laws which commence April 8, 2027.
ASIC wants digital asset platforms (DAPs) and tokenised custody platforms (TCPs) to hold an Australian financial services licence, provide customer disclosure documents and platform rules, and comply with asset holding standards, transactional and settlement standards, and net tangible asset requirements where relevant.
ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said that ASIC's proposal recognised the rapid evolution of global markets and "the increasing role of digital assets and tokenisation, including in traditional parts of the financial system".
"Our approach is based on the principle of 'same activity, same risk, same regulatory outcome' to align Australia with the approach of comparable overseas jurisdictions."
'Investors in waiting'
ASIC's job is only likely to get bigger with the pool of investors projected to keep expanding.
The ASX survey found an estimated 950,000 Australians who do not currently invest plan to start within the next 12 months.
Women, the survey showed, represented 61 per cent of this group.
Australians aged 18 to 29 account for almost four in 10 "investors in waiting".
The ASX said demand for financial advice is also increasing, with knowledge listed as the number one barrier to entering the market.

What to Know About Pope Leo's Lung Cancer Diagnosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:58:24 UTC
02:58:24 KST

After discovering a nodule in Pope Leo XIV's lung, surgeons at Gemelli Hospital in Rome performed surgery on Tuesday that revealed the Pope has cancer.
Dr. Stefano Margaritora, professor of thoracic surgery at the Catholic University of Sacred Heart, led the team that operated on the Pope at Gemelli, which has long provided care for Popes. The surgery was prompted after the Pope’s medical team, led by Dr. Luigi Carbone, found a suspicious nodule and performed tests that suggested it could be cancerous, according to a statement released by the Vatican. During the 90-minute operation, Margaritora removed the lower lobe of the Pope’s right lung, and further testing of the tissue confirmed adenocarcinoma.
What is lung adenocarcinoma?
Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer worldwide, accounting for 40% to 45% of lung cancer cases globally. Adenocarcinomas belong to a broader category of lung cancers known as non-small cell lung cancer, which tend to grow more slowly and spread less quickly to other parts of the body. Detecting adenocarcinomas early can help keep them from progressing to advanced disease.
How is lung cancer detected?
Current recommendations in the U.S. and most of the world advise low-dose CT scans to screen for lung cancer in high-risk people only: those 50 years or older who have smoked heavily in the past or who currently smoke. Many non-smokers are diagnosed with lung cancer when they get a chest CT for another reason, such as after an accident or other injury. Some advocacy and patient groups are pushing for expanded screening among those at higher risk so that more people can benefit from early detection, including those who are younger and may have been exposed to other factors that can increase lung cancer risk, like radon in the environment. “The best chance to cure lung cancer is when it’s Stage 1 and very early,” says Dr. David Jones, chief or thoracic surgery at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, who was not involved in the Pope’s care. “That’s what screening can help with.”
The Pope's smoking history is not publicly known, but lung adenocarcinoma occurs in both smokers and non-smokers, says Jones. “Lung adenocarcinoma is by far the most common type of lung cancer in non-smokers,” he says.
Why did surgeons remove part of the Pope’s lung?
Surgeons decided to remove part of the Pope’s lung “to ensure a radical resection,” according to the Vatican statement. That means doctors wanted to be sure they removed any tissue that might be cancerous, giving the Pope the strongest chance of avoiding any recurrence of disease.
How long will the Pope be hospitalized?
The Pope woke up from surgical anesthesia without any complications, and requested dinner while conversing with Vatican staff. He will be observed as additional tests are performed on his removed cancer tissue to guide doctors on what treatments might be needed next. The Vatican anticipates the Pope will remain at Gemelli for one week.
What are the treatments for lung adenocarcinoma?
The Pope’s treatment options depend on what additional tests on his tumor reveal. For some patients with Stage 1 cancer that has not spread to the lymph nodes, surgery and monitoring for recurrence may be sufficient, says Jones.
If the cancer is more advanced, a number of relatively new options for lung cancer are available, including targeted therapies designed to specifically attack certain mutations in cancer cells, or immunotherapy, which activates the immune system into destroying cancer cells. “The innovation in treatments for lung cancer have been profound,” says Karen Knudsen, CEO of the Parker Institute. Adenocarcinomas tend to have high numbers of mutations, which make them good targets for the immune system to recognize as foreign. That also makes them promising targets for checkpoint inhibitors, a new category of cancer therapy that releases the brakes on immune cells and allows them to better detect and destroy cancer cells. “Our knowledge base is improving, and there are better outcomes for non-small cell lung cancer because of immunotherapy,” says Knudsen.
Some patients can rely on targeted therapies alone and avoid chemotherapy, says Jones, while others may need chemo with immunotherapy, depending on how much of the cancer surgeons were able to remove and whether the cancer had spread to the lymph nodes.
Will Pope Leo be able to resume his papal duties?
The Vatican reports that prior to the surgery, the Pope was active, playing tennis and taking regular walks, and with the range of treatment options now available to treat his cancer, experts believe he should be able to return to his daily activities. “Advances in treatments all point to better prognosis and quality of life for patients with lung cancer,” says Jones. “And given his history of physical activity, even after removing one lobe of his lung, he should be able to do what he wants to do with very little limitation.”

Palantir, London mayor end legal battle over AI deal with metropolitan police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:57:23 UTC
02:57:23 KST

Aysu Bicer
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
US technology company Palantir and London Mayor Sadiq Khan’s office have withdrawn allegations against each other in a legal dispute over a £50 million ($65 million) police technology contract, heading off a High Court trial scheduled for January.
Palantir sued the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime (MOPAC) in June after Khan intervened to block a proposed two-year contract for the Metropolitan Police to use artificial intelligence to process intelligence in criminal investigations.
The system, known as unified operational analytics (UOA), was intended for use by Scotland Yard.
Khan’s intervention followed concerns about the company’s work with the Israeli military and the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. The mayor previously said Londoners wanted public money to go to companies that “share the values of our city.”
Palantir’s UK and Europe head, Louis Mosley, accused Khan of politicizing procurement, saying he was “putting politics above public safety.”
In a joint statement Wednesday, Palantir and MOPAC said the May 2026 decision to block the contract “was not based on Palantir’s values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company.”
MOPAC said media coverage of a statement by the mayor’s spokesperson before the decision could have created the impression that an assessment of Palantir’s values had influenced the decision.
It added that its assessment was based on its statutory responsibilities and relevant legal requirements concerning procurement, governance, affordability and value for money.
Khan said he was proud that leading software companies chose London as their home, and that Palantir contributed to jobs and investment in the capital.
The agreement comes one month after former Labour Party deputy leader Tom Watson was hired as a full-time lobbyist by Palantir. The company had raised concerns that excluding it from public contracts over objections to its leadership’s values could undermine its ability to operate in the UK.
Palantir also faces opposition to retaining its £330 million National Health Service medical data contract, amid calls from some members of the public and lawmakers for it to be replaced.
A new procurement process for the police contract is underway. MOPAC has agreed to treat Palantir “fairly and equally” if it submits a bid, although it is not obliged to award the contract to the company.

“The right to peaceful protest is a foundation of democracy and the state’s obligation to guarantee it. Advertisement

How Trump’s diesel deal with Russia will impact the United States and Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:55:00 UTC
02:55:00 KST

How Trump’s diesel deal with Russia will impact the US and Ukraine
October 14, 2026
Many Ukrainians and Europeans viewed news from Washington over the past weekend as a stab in the back by their US ally. First, President Donald Trump announced a deal to buy Russian diesel, which involves a temporary easing of US sanctions against Moscow.
And later Trump announced an allegedly agreed "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia. Kyiv said the idea had not been discussed with Ukraine, but that it was prepared to halt attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure if Moscow did the same.
'Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine'
Security expert Carlo Masala of the Bundeswehr University Munich said the developments showed that "Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine at all, but that domestic US politics and relations with Russia are far more important to him than supporting Ukraine."
He added that the president aims to sway the outcome of the US midterm elections on November 3 through an agreement with Russia.
All seats in the House of Representatives and a regularly scheduled portion of the Senate will be contested in the midterm elections. Polls suggest that Trump's Republican Party could lose its majority in the House. A loss of the Republicans' Senate majority is also possible. Surveys indicate that American voters are unhappy with high fuel prices, and the US president apparently hopes to influence prices through diesel shipments from Russia.
Observers, however, consider Trump's hopes that Russian diesel shipments could affect prices in the US illusory.
"The volume is so small that it will have absolutely no effect on prices," Thomas Jäger of the University of Cologne told German public broadcaster ARD.
The political scientist added that shipments planned before the midterm elections would not even cover US diesel demand for a single day.
"The same applies to any shipments that may arrive afterward, if they materialize, they will have no effect on prices either," he said.
Trump's goal, Jäger said, is simply "the story" — showing voters that he is trying to solve a problem that matters to them.
'No concrete military benefits for Russia'
The main criticism from Kyiv and EU countries is that Russia will use the revenue from diesel sales to finance its war against Ukraine.
Carlo Masala, however, does not foresee the agreement with the US having "any concrete positive military effects" for Russia.
He points out that Washington had already temporarily suspended sanctions on Russian oil exports in March this year, shortly after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran.
"Despite the money Russia has and has received, it has no military strategy for making further advances in the Donbas. The issue is more about the political impact and the symbolism of the Americans striking separate deals with the Russians at Ukraine's expense," the expert said.
Another cause for concern in Kyiv could be US threats to suspend intelligence sharing with Ukraine and block the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) program unless Ukraine halts its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Under the PURL program, European countries procure US weapons for Ukraine.
European alternatives to US intelligence
A possible US decision to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine for strikes on Russian territory would have "dramatic" consequences for Kyiv, Masala said, but European intelligence, particularly from France, could help mitigate the impact.
While French intelligence is "not as comprehensive as American intelligence," the Ukrainian military already uses it to carry out strikes in Russia with French weapons systems.
As for the weapons European countries procure from the US for Ukraine under the PURL program, Masala noted that the program's most important component — interceptor missiles for air defense — has barely been available to Ukraine since the start of the war with Iran.
Support for Ukraine across both US parties
Ahead of the US midterm elections, experts point out that Ukraine enjoys broad support not only among Democrats but also among Republicans. One example is the bipartisan passage this summer of legislation to tighten US sanctions against Russia, known as the "Lindsey Graham Act," named after its Republican congressional sponsor, who has since died.
Signed by Trump in September, the law gives the president a broad range of tools. He can impose sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions and Russia's shadow fleet, which is used to circumvent restrictions on oil exports. He can also impose punitive tariffs on buyers of Russian energy products.
"Trump may resist, but political forces, particularly after the US midterms, may push the administration in the direction of trying to seek an end to the war by using the tools available," former US diplomat Daniel Fried told DW.
He added that the "Lindsey Graham Act" and the 2022 law banning US imports of Russian oil are "not absolute, but strong barriers against dumb ideas like a unilateral unrequited diesel deal with Russia."
Several Democratic and Republican senators cited this legislation in a joint statement in which they described the diesel deal with Russia as illegal, calling on the US government to "immediately correct" its decision.

Helsinki Celebrates Grazia Deledda 100 Years After Her Nobel Prize
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:53:22 CEST
02:53:22 KST

One hundred years after Grazia Deledda was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, a seminar hosted at the University of Helsinki traced the work and success in Finland of the Sardinian-born writer, the first and only Italian woman to receive this highest literary honor, and the second in the world after the Swedish author Selma Lagerlöf.
                                    
At the heart of the event—which inaugurated the program of initiatives in Helsinki for the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World—was Deledda’s original poetic style, which allowed the self-taught author to establish herself among the great female voices of 20th-century Italian and European literature. Her popularity in Finland dates back to the 1920s, when the Nobel Prize and Jalmari Hahl’s translations introduced her novels to the public of the young Finnish nation.
                                    
Organized by the Helsinki committee of the Dante Alighieri Society, with the support of “La Dante - Roma” and in collaboration with the Italian Cultural Institute and the University of Helsinki, the seminar featured presentations by Professor Giovanni Capecchi, an associate professor of Italian literature at the University for Foreigners of Perugia, in dialogue with Professor Outi Merisalo, full professor of Romance philology at the University of Jyväskylä, and with linguist Professor Enrico Garavelli of the Department of Italian at the University of Helsinki.
                                    
“Grazia Deledda’s greatness lies in her extraordinary ability to transform the ancestral roots of her homeland’s civilization into a universal narrative capable of deeply resonating with the imagination of the Nordic peoples, thereby contributing significantly to the dialogue between Italian and Finnish cultures.” These were the words of the Italian Ambassador to Finland, Nicola Todaro Marescotti, as he kicked off the celebrations at the historic Italian Residence, which was acquired as part of the national heritage in 1926.

Both failures came right after the US struck a diesel deal with Russia, letting low volumes of fuel into global markets and America while pressure grew on Ukraine to stop hitting the Russian oil refineries that raise the cost of the war.
"Reports of Starlink failing in Ukraine are deeply alarming— potentially crippling air defense against Russia’s murderous missiles & drones. Trump & Musk must be held accountable," he says.
When the network falters, the war feels it
The alarm rests on how completely Ukraine leans on the system. SpaceX has reportedly throttled the StarShield military package Ukrainian drones use, with connections dropping once the drones move at speed, and breaking a series of missions.
Ukraine neither owns nor controls Starlink, and the latest limits revived long-running fears that its battlefield lifeline can be dialed down from outside the country.
Blumenthal’s demand sits inside a broader revolt in Congress. A bipartisan group of 12 senators wrote Trump on 13 October urging him to rescind his deal letting Russian diesel back to market, calling the Treasury’s General License No. 135 a gift to Moscow that should be withdrawn.
They pressed him instead to use the Graham-Leach-Bliley Act he signed in September to squeeze Russia and its enablers, above all, China.
"If there's one lesson from Trump's mindless warmongering, it's that we need to break our dependence on foreign imports of fossil fuels & embrace alternate sources of energy," he said.

The Beersheba District Court on Wednesday sentenced Shahadeh Abu Alqian, a resident of an unrecognized Bedouin community in the Negev, to 24 1/2 years in prison after he was convicted under a plea agreement of assisting the enemy in wartime, terrorism offenses and weapons violations. Abu Alqian acted on behalf of a terrorist organization based in the Gaza Strip and even enlisted in the Israel Defense Forces on his handlers' instructions to gather intelligence. He also stole a weapon from an IDF soldier and later transferred weapons to the West Bank for the terrorist organization.
According to the amended indictment filed by attorney Hofit Kantrowitz of the Southern District Attorney's Office, Abu Alqian decided in 2019 to take revenge against Israel and harm its security after an administrative demolition order was issued for his father's home. In September of that year, he stole an M4 assault rifle, a magazine and a laser sight from an IDF soldier in the Yatir area, then buried them near his home.
Beginning in 2021, Abu Alqian contacted terrorist operatives in the Gaza Strip through social media and Telegram, expressed support for the struggle against Israel and sought to join Hamas' military wing. He later began operating on behalf of the terrorist organization Kataib al-Mujahideen, providing his handlers with information and photographs of IDF bases, train stations, government-owned companies and shopping centers. He also reported on the movements of soldiers and helicopters near his home.
In March 2022, an operative from the terrorist organization known as "Abu Suleiman" contacted him and asked to purchase weapons. Abu Alqian offered to sell him the rifle he had stolen from the IDF and insisted on delivering the weapons directly to the West Bank. In May 2022, he recruited his cousin to help him, and the two loaded an M4 rifle, thousands of rounds of ammunition and five hand grenades into a vehicle and drove to the West Bank. There, they left the weapons in a hiding place for the terrorist organization.
At the same time, acting on his handler's instructions, Abu Alqian enlisted in the IDF on May 22, 2022, intending to gather information from within the military about Bedouin soldiers, army bases and military positions and pass it to the terrorist organization. About eight days after enlisting, he was arrested by Israeli security forces, thwarting his activities.
In December 2025, Abu Alqian was convicted after admitting to the charges in an amended indictment as part of a plea agreement. The offenses included assisting the enemy in wartime, active membership in a terrorist organization, aggravated theft, weapons offenses involving carrying and transporting firearms and handling weapons for terrorist purposes.
During sentencing arguments, prosecutors sought a lengthy prison term, a suspended sentence and a substantial fine. They also emphasized the severity of Abu Alqian's ties to Mujahideen Brigades, which was involved in the murder of members of the Bibas family during the war that began with Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.
A three-judge panel consisting of Daniel Ben Tolila, Tal Lahiani Shoham and Yoav Atar sentenced Abu Alqian to 24 1/2 years in prison, a suspended sentence and a fine of 25,000 shekels.
Kantrowitz, who prosecuted the case, said after the hearing: "This is an exceptionally serious case in which an Israeli citizen chose to act against his country, maintain ties with a terrorist organization and even enlist in the IDF on behalf of a terrorist organization, with the aim of gathering information from within the military and harming national security.
"It is worth noting that, alongside the criminal proceedings, the defendant's details were also forwarded to the interior minister for consideration of revoking his citizenship. The sentence reflects the severity of his actions, the harm to national security and the need for significant deterrence," she added.
"The prosecution will continue to pursue the full extent of the law against those who choose to act on behalf of and assist terrorist organizations, endangering the security of the state, its soldiers and its citizens."

Kuznetsov, a former soldier, was accused of leading the sabotage group, involving six other people. German investigators claim that he commanded the yacht "Andromeda," from which a team of divers allegedly carried out the attack against the pipelines.

The trial — the first held in connection with the Nord Stream sabotage — is expected to run until February.
Kuznietsov was arrested in August 2025 near the Italian town of Rimini under a European arrest warrant before being extradited to Germany.
Another Ukrainian suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravliov, was detained in Croatia in August 2026 and awaits extradition. Zhuravliov was first detained in Poland in September 2025, but a Polish court refused to extradite him to Germany and instead released him a month later.
The Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never became operational, had long been a flashpoint in European energy politics.
Even before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, critics said it deepened Germany's dependence on Russian gas and undermined European energy security.

He was allegedly contacted by an FSB officer who offered him money in exchange for cooperation.
Within days of being recruited, the suspect registered 15 Starlink terminals using the passport details of relatives and acquaintances. He then prepared personal information belonging to other individuals to register another 133 devices.
SBU officers detained the suspect near a post office, where he allegedly planned to activate another batch of terminals.
The 15 previously registered Starlink terminals, whose details had already been sent to his Russian handler via a messaging app, were also blocked.
The suspect remains in custody without the possibility of bail. If convicted, he faces life imprisonment and confiscation of property.
The case adds to a growing number of incidents in which Russia allegedly recruits Ukrainians to carry out assignments on Moscow's behalf, including a recent case on Oct. 12, when Ukrainian authorities detained a 19-year-old suspected of plotting a bomb attack on a bus carrying soldiers in Rivne.

Pope's cancer prognosis may depend on these factors, doctors say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:47:04 UTC
02:47:04 KST

Pope Leo's lung cancer prognosis could depend on these factors, doctors say
Pope Leo XIV was recovering Wednesday, a day after having a lobe of his right lung removed and confirming a diagnosis of lung cancer.
Leo had blood tests and a chest X-ray that showed a "normal post-operative course," the Holy See Press Office said. "The values are within the expected range for the type of procedure performed."
The surgery removed what the pope and Vatican described as a localized nodular lesion.
"Those types of lesions can actually be removed and even cured just by surgery alone," CBS News chief medical correspondent Dr. Jon LaPook said.
But the Vatican has not shared the stage of cancer, or whether it has spread, which would help determine if Leo needs further treatment.
Here's what multiple doctors, who are not involved in the pope's treatment, told CBS News about his possible prognosis.
What type of cancer does Leo have?
Leo was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, a common type of non-small cell lung cancer, doctors say.
"It's very common and also generally a very good prognosis when found early on," Dr. Kalvin Lung, a thoracic surgeon at the Northwestern Medicine Canning Thoracic Institute, told CBS News 24/7 on Tuesday.
The surgery Leo underwent "is also something we commonly do, and it's a very successful surgery and people can recover very quickly from it," Lung said.
What stage is the cancer?
The Vatican has not said what stage the cancer is. "They may not know yet," LaPook said Wednesday morning.
But the information that has been provided suggests the cancer may have been caught early.
"The fact that he can have a successful surgery so quickly is all a very good prognosticators of probably an early-stage lung cancer," Lung said.
If there had been evidence that the cancer had spread elsewhere in the body, Leo may have had treatment before the surgery like chemotherapy or immunological therapy, LaPook said.
"But the fact they went right in and tried to take it all out might say to you, well, they think maybe that's it," he said.
If that is the case, Leo likely would not need further treatment, Lung and LaPook said.
Is there lymph node involvement?
If the cancer spread to the lymph nodes, which filter fluid in the body, that would change the prognosis and possible treatment plan, doctors said.
"Sometimes it looks like on all the tests beforehand that it's just localized, and it turns out the lymph nodes are involved," LaPook said.
Further testing would determine the treatment, he said.
"There are all these special tests you do. Look at the genetic makeup of it. Are there any special markers? Are there any special things on it that are driving it to multiply?" LaPook said.
What is the recovery?
Doctors have said the recovery from the surgery is typically a few weeks. Leo is expected to stay at the hospital for a week, according to the Vatican.
The pope's recovery was "proceeding as expected," the Holy See Press Office said Wednesday.
"The Holy Father has carried out respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room," they said. "He has resumed a regular diet, having both breakfast and lunch."
Leo may have some pain from the surgery "for the first couple of days up to the first one to two weeks," Lung said.
"I think he'll be back to doing what he wants to do around three to four weeks," said Dr. David Jones, chief of thoracic surgery at the Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. "Maybe a little slower, but he'll be fine."

How Azerbaijan is building its next chapter in tourism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:45:25 UTC
02:45:25 KST

Florian Sengstschmid, CEO of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board, tells the Travel and Tourism Summit how direct flights, regional investment and a 2030 plan are shaping the country’s future.
Florian Sengstschmid first set foot in Baku in 2001. After a career working in destinations around the world, the Austrian-born CEO of the Azerbaijan Tourism Board might be hard to surprise. Yet he says the country still has surprises in store.
A crossroads with European roots
Sengstschmid believes the South Caucasus is underrated. Its countries are often lumped together under a post-Soviet label, he says, without their individual histories and cultures being fully understood.
Azerbaijan sits where Europe meets Asia, and he points to a European thread that few visitors expect. Bridges built by the Siemens brothers can still be crossed. German heritage villages such as Helenendorf remain. Across the country, a mosque, a church and a synagogue sit side by side. With its distinctive red-tiled roofs, the country’s largest Jewish settlement is believed to have been the only entirely Jewish settlement outside Israel and the United States, as well as the world’s last surviving shtetl.That mix of cultures and faiths, he says, is part of everyday life in Azerbaijan.
He also sees the regional peace process, including the initial deal signed in Washington in August 2025, opening the door to multi-country journeys. That could make the South Caucasus easier to visit for long-haul travellers and raise the region’s profile.
A city that knows how to host
Just days before the summit, Baku hosted a Formula 1 weekend that drew more than 17,000 international visitors, alongside the Azerbaijan Investment Forum. Hospitality, Sengstschmid says, is deeply rooted in the country’s culture, with visitors treated as guests.
Baku’s profile has grown since Eurovision in 2011, and COP29 in 2024 tested its capacity further.
“Who can host a COP can host any other meeting and conference,” he said.
Beyond the capital
Still, Sengstschmid urges visitors not to stop in Baku.
Along the Silk Road lie side valleys, ancient heritage villages and the UNESCO-listed town of Shaki, set in the Greater Caucasus and known for its Khan palaces. There is also a wine route, while wellness cluster includes unique natural resources such as naftalan oil, which has been used for skin treatments for centuries.
The country spans a vast range of climate zones, from desert landscapes to peaks reaching 4,000 metres.
Winter tourism is another focus. A five-year partnership with the International Ski and Snowboard Federation (FIS) will bring races and World Cups to Azerbaijan, including FIS World Cup finals in freestyle moguls and dual moguls in the mountains of Shahdag in March.
Connectivity is improving too. Baku airport holds a five-star Skytrax rating, while Azerbaijan Airlines is taking delivery of new aircraft this year. From 8 May 2027, the carrier will fly four times a week between Brussels and Baku.
Entry is also straightforward. For major events such as F1, a passport and a valid ticket are enough, while other travellers can use the e-visa system, with standard processing within three days and urgent visas issued within three hours.
“Connectivity and accessibility are the key bottlenecks in tourism,” Sengstschmid said.
Building tourism with the people who live there
Behind the growth sits a new state program running to 2030. It aims to stimulate demand through incentives for charter airlines, new routes and tour operators. On the supply side, it encourages quality, green-built accommodation in the regions and supports micro and small entrepreneurs. It also asks transport, customs and other parts of the visitor journey to pull together.
Sengstschmid says protecting local life comes first. He cites Basgal, a mountain village on the Silk Road and a historic centre of silk printing that had been largely abandoned.
After investment in infrastructure, families returned. Today, the village has small tea houses and food stalls, while women practise traditional silk printing. Visitors can experience the village’s traditions alongside the people who live there.
In 2025, tourism contributed 7 billion manat, around €3.5 billion, or 5.4% of GDP. The target is 12 billion manat by 2030. Sengstschmid says the plan centres on longer stays and greater economic impact, with visitor numbers, currently just under three million, rising only modestly.
A village that feels like a secret
Asked to share a secret, he chose Sim, a village in the south of the country that he describes as a fairytale.
Moss covers the old wooden buildings and their balconies, water runs through the village, waterfalls tumble nearby and a UNESCO-listed forest begins at its edge. It feels like a jungle, he says, yet you are in Azerbaijan.
Asked to sum up the country in three words, he did not hesitate: real, warm and uplifting.
Warm, because of its people. Real, because he believes development has left much of the country genuine and intact. And uplifting, because Azerbaijan still has new things to show him.
For someone who first set foot in Baku in 2001, still being surprised 25 years later may be the strongest endorsement of all.

​World's oldest shipwreck found off Turkey's coast, archaeologists say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:44:53 UTC
02:44:53 KST

World's oldest shipwreck found off Turkey, archaeologists say: "Time capsule at the bottom of the sea"
Archaeologists have discovered the world's oldest shipwreck off the coast of Turkey, dating it to between 4,400 and 4,700 years old.
The structure of the ship has not survived the nearly five millennia underwater, but its contents of clay jars have been preserved surprisingly well, with some still containing traces of what they transported over 4,000 years ago.
The archaeologists who found the vessel said that it was a nearly 33-foot-long trade ship transporting goods across the Mediterranean Sea and originated somewhere on the eastern Mediterranean coast.
The wreck dates back to the same time period as when the Pyramids of Giza were being built, and will "offer insights into ancient trading connections and the everyday lives of seafarers," according to Turkey's Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy.
"The shipwreck is a time capsule at the bottom of the sea," Hakan Öniz, an associate professor at Turkey's Akdeniz University who oversaw the expedition to uncover the ship, told CBS News' partner network BBC News.
Alongside the 30 ceramic storage jars in the wreckage, called amphorae, three stone anchors were also discovered.
Öniz told CBS News that when his team first found the wreck four years ago, the amphorae only appeared to be a century or two old.
"However, we later became excited when we saw the same amphora forms in a publication on Egyptian archaeology and returned to the site," Öniz said. "Indeed, they were similar to those found at the Giza pyramids in Egypt. We were incredibly excited."
The design of these amphorae — with two handles, a flat base and a ridge in the middle — was distinctive to pottery from that period of history.
Karin Sowada, an archaeologist at Australia's Macquarie University, examined the pots after they were brought to the surface. She told the BBC that there was still a viscous, glossy residue inside some of the amphorae.
"I looked inside and nearly fainted. I could not believe how much [residue] was visible. It wasn't just like spots … a lot of this material was still remaining," she said.
Analysis of the clay used to make the jars suggests that they were produced in workshops in the Middle East's Jordan Valley, located along Jordan's border with Israel and the West Bank.
"It appears the vessel sank while transporting olive oil or wine from that region westward — perhaps to Troy or to the Minoan civilization in Crete," Öniz told CBS News.
Similar examples of amphorae have also been found in Egypt, Troy and Crete, according to Ersoy.
Öniz told the BBC that when he was diving for the wreck, his first thoughts were on the lives of the many people connected to the ship.
"We are the first humans who [have] touched these objects after 5,000 years," he said.
"We are always thinking of the sailors ... the producers of the amphora and the person who carried the amphora on their shoulders to the ship, and the women who were waiting for their husbands, and they unfortunately couldn't go back."
The discovery has taken the record of the world's oldest shipwreck from the previous holder in the Aegean Sea located near Greece, which was dated to 4,200 years ago.

Attacks in Strait of Hormuz reach highest level since start of war: Security data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:43:29 UTC
02:43:29 KST

Attacks in Strait of Hormuz reach highest level since start of Iran war: Security data
LONDON - At least ten vessels have been attacked in or near the Strait of Hormuz since Oct 11, a high since war broke out between the United States, Israel and Iran, security data showed on Oct 14.
Four vessels were struck on Oct 13 and six on Oct 11 – the highest number of attacks in a single day since the start of the conflict – according to data from security firm Vanguard, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) and the British maritime agency UKMTO.
Two seafarers have been reported missing and a container ship reportedly sank as a result of recent attacks, according to the maritime sources.
Merchant vessels transiting the vital passage were first targeted by Iran in March in retaliation for US-Israeli strikes on its territory, and Tehran has continued to strike vessels passing through the strait via routes it has not approved.
The attacks have disrupted shipping through the strait, which is normally one of the busiest routes for exporting oil and other commodities from Gulf countries.
Twenty-three attacks have been recorded since the start of October, almost double the average monthly number of incidents since the start of the war.
The United States said on Oct 10 that it had struck a cargo vessel as part of its embargo on Iranian ports, but the incident was not listed by the IMO.
The recent uptick in energy exports, which almost returned to pre-war levels at the start of October but have since fallen back, may be behind the latest increase in attacks, according to Vanguard analyst Barun Gupta.
“Gulf oil flows have been recovering, with traffic through Hormuz recently returning to around 80 per cent of pre-war levels despite the conflict.
“Increasing the tempo of attacks therefore gives Tehran a way of demonstrating that it can still disrupt that recovery and impose costs on commercial shipping and global energy markets,” Gupta told AFP on Oct 14.
He said Trump’s promise last week not to launch further attacks on Iran before the midterm elections in the US could also be a factor, giving Tehran “a perceived window to increase pressure with a lower immediate risk of US military escalation”.
Some 24 seafarers have died as a result of incidents in the area near the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the conflict, according to the IMO. AFP

From first to 22nd: How world’s former №1 plunged in global broadband rankings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

17:43:14 UTC

From first to 22nd: How world’s former №1 plunged in global broadband rankings
South Korea's fixed broadband speed has plunged to 22nd place, once ranked first in the world, according to an analysis by Seattle-based network intelligence platform Ookla, AJU Press reports.
Ookla, which tracks internet speeds worldwide, said South Korea's median fixed broadband download speed stood at 251.33 Mbps in August, ranking 22nd among 149 countries, behind Viet Nam in eighth place and Thailand in ninth.
Singapore topped the ranking at 462.50 Mbps, followed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) at 382.40 Mbps.
By city, Seoul ranked 34th, behind Bangkok in sixth place and Ho Chi Minh City in 14th. Valparaíso, Chile, topped the ranking at 416.81 Mbps, followed by Abu Dhabi in the UAE at 408.67 Mbps.
But South Korea's mobile internet download speed remained high, ranking sixth globally at 250.56 Mbps.
Ookla compiles its rankings from data collected when users visit websites or apps and tap the "go" button. However, results may be skewed if more users repeatedly click the button when their connections feel slow or unstable. Critics also say that differences in subscription plans and access environments across countries make the rankings unreliable for direct comparisons.

Return to war with Iran after US midterm elections may be increasingly likely - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:40:12 UTC
02:40:12 KST

A return to war between the United States and Iran is far from a certainty, and an ongoing tense standoff is still the most likely scenario, but there is no question that the chances of renewed conflict between Washington and Tehran will jump after America’s midterm elections on November 3.
Many have misinterpreted Iran’s latest additional moves to better defend the Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility as a sign that the Islamic Republic is possibly trying to rush out to a nuclear weapon.
The Jerusalem Post has confirmed that Iran has no significant active nuclear operations currently at Pickaxe Mountain and that Israeli concerns there are more about the future.
The Post was also told by numerous sources that it is unclear that even American mega bunker busters such as the 30,000-pound Massive Ordnance Penetrator bomb could fully penetrate the Pickaxe Mountain nuclear facility – even prior to any of the recent new defenses.
Iran may be trying to deter US, Israeli ground operations
In that sense, the new defenses are likely an attempt to deter the US and Israel from staging a ground operation at the mountain.
The US staged a successful temporary ground operation in Iran at the height of the war in early 2026 to rescue shot-down pilots, and Israel staged a ground operation to destroy a major underground Iranian-built Syrian nuclear facility in Masyaf, Syria, in September 2024.
Iran wants to convince both Washington and Jerusalem that pulling off such an operation at Pickaxe Mountain would be much harder, more costly, and therefore not worth the risk.
In that sense, all of Iran’s efforts currently show it is preparing for war in the near future and will try to strike America and its allies’ weak underbellies: energy facilities, slow and large ships, and other economically damaging targets.
Despite constant warnings from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz, there is still little inclination from Iran to get caught up in another war with Israel.
Iran’s regime saw that Israel’s war-fighting was more merciless than America’s in the sense of targeting top Iranian officials and that Jerusalem was more ready to continue attacking Iran indefinitely as compared to Washington, which was worried about a drawn-out conflict.
In that sense, all of the warnings about Iran seeking to pick a fight with Israel are mostly about lower-grade hostilities, such as attempting terror attacks against Israelis, or Jews globally, or small targeted attacks on Israel which would fall short of requiring a massive Israeli response.
Iranian threats potentially intended to force US concessions
Such Iranian threats against Israel are more about forcing the US into making concessions out of fears that an Iranian attack, which would bring Israel back into the war, would lead to Washington losing control and creating greater regional instability.
In August, the US’s military power achieved a shift vs Iran in which the harm to the West’s economy was regularly reduced while the harm to Iran’s economy continually worsened.
All of this led US President Donald Trump to bet that Iran would blink before the US midterm elections. In that scenario, he could declare victory leading into those elections and potentially even regain some of the nuclear concessions ceded earlier, in the summer.
Trump’s error was projecting Western rationalism onto the IRGC and religious fanatics running Iran, who believe their regime is aided by divine messianic currents.
The president and his team have alternated between proclaiming that a deal with Iran is imminent after the midterm elections and threatening a return to full war with the regime after the midterms.
Iran believes that when Trump’s Republican Party loses the midterms, he will make more concessions to extract himself from this otherwise potentially endless conflict, which appears to sap his popularity daily.
And if Trump does not give in after the midterm elections, the Islamic Republic may escalate to cause enough chaos to bring him back to those concessions.
None of this is a grand strategy in which Iran could badly hurt the US or Israel in any deep or strategic way.
Iran has more ballistic missiles left over, around 1,600, than the US and Israel expected in April, but the number is so much lower than the around 6,000 it had expected to reach by now. Further, its future production has been slowed by about as much as 90%.
Most importantly, the regime cannot fire more than a few dozen rockets in a day vs the several hundred it was able to fire daily in early 2026.
Iran’s preparations are therefore more about either deterring the US from launching a new massive attack, being better prepared to outlast such an attack if it happens, or carrying out a limited Iranian offensive to try to get some more concessions from the US.
For months, America’s midterms have been viewed as a turning point in the conflict.
Developments in recent weeks suggest that turning point could mean more conflict. The whole world will be watching closely after November 3.

The ministers asserted that the delay would “once again deprive Palestinians of the opportunity to vote and will further erode public confidence in democratic institutions.”
They additionally highlighted the importance of the elections in light of Abbas and the PA’s earlier commitments to reform, accountability, and democratic renewal.

Hezbollah exploits EU terror distinction to launder money through human trafficking, JCFA claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:39:58 UTC
02:39:58 KST

Hezbollah has exploited the European Union’s failure to designate its political wing as a terrorist organization to launder money raised through human trafficking in South America and Africa, according to a new analysis published by the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs (JCFA).
Ella Rosenberg, a senior research fellow at the JCFA and a member of the Dvorah Forum, argued in her analysis that the EU’s failure to designate Hezbollah’s political wing has allowed the Iran-backed group to operate more freely in its fundraising activities.
She said the distinction between Hezbollah’s political and military wings has enabled proceeds from human trafficking in Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East to be laundered through front companies, charitable organizations, and trade networks in Europe.
Hezbollah's documented fundraising through crime
Although Hezbollah, as an Iranian proxy, receives much of its weaponry and resources from Tehran, it also maintains a documented criminal network that relies heavily on human trafficking to finance its activities.
Although Lebanon criminalized human trafficking in 2011 under Law 164, enforcement has frequently been undermined by state corruption and Hezbollah’s influence, Rosenberg argued. The law covers the sexual exploitation of women, yet reports dating back to 2016 have highlighted prostitution rings allegedly operated in cooperation with Hezbollah-affiliated officials.
The terrorist organization has reportedly protected these rings, using its influence to prevent state security agencies from intervening in their illicit activities in exchange for an unknown share of the profits.
According to Rosenberg, the protection money generated by the sex trafficking rings was reportedly directed toward Hezbollah’s social welfare programs and used to cover the living expenses of terrorists killed in action.
Outside Lebanon, Hezbollah-affiliated logistical hubs have become deeply entwined with human traffickers, she continued. In Latin America, particularly Argentina, Brazil, and Paraguay, cartel members have reportedly supported Hezbollah operatives.
Victims trapped in debt bondage are coerced into forced labor or illicit activities to repay exorbitant transit fees charged by Hezbollah-aligned facilitators. Reports also indicate significant cooperation with violent drug cartels, including Los Zetas, generating substantial proceeds that are subsequently laundered through trade-based mechanisms.
Questions over the origins of Hezbollah's funds
In West and Central Africa, Hezbollah has a “deep financial footprint,” Rosenberg wrote. Hezbollah operatives are said to systematically exploit both the Lebanese diaspora living in the region and local populations.
Rosenberg also described Hezbollah’s alleged involvement in trafficking blood diamonds and narcotics across Africa. The group can reportedly organize bulk-cash smuggling operations and use schemes involving real estate and vehicles to facilitate transactions that leave little trace and transfer funds to Beirut while circumventing sanctions.
The origins of Hezbollah’s funding have come under increased scrutiny in recent weeks after reports that the group received $200 million from Iran to support people displaced by its war with Israel. The US State Department dismissed the initial report as a fabrication. However, days after Reuters reported on the alleged transfer, Hezbollah announced financial assistance of up to $14,000 for displaced families.
The origins of the funds have seemingly caused some confusion in Beirut. Lebanese MP Fouad Makhzoumi said that there were “serious questions about the sources of these funds, how they were brought into Lebanon, and how they were transported and distributed outside official financial frameworks.”
“Assisting our affected people is a national duty, but their suffering cannot serve as a cover for parallel financial systems or a pretext for circumventing Lebanese laws…,” he said.
“There can be no sovereignty for a state that does not monopolize arms nor assert its authority over the movement of money. Nor can we accept a state within a state, neither militarily nor financially. Lebanon needs one state, one legitimate weapon, and a law applied to all without exception.”

An unidentified group set fire to Starlink satellite communications antennas in Bulgaria. Ivaylo Mirchev, a local lawmaker from the Yes, Bulgaria! party, was the first to report the incident.
Mirchev said 11 of the site’s 17 Starlink antennas were damaged at the facility, which is located near the Bulgarian capital, Sofia. On his Facebook page, Mirchev published a video of the fire. The footage shows a facility resembling a Starlink ground station — a key piece of terrestrial infrastructure that links satellites in orbit with the internet network.
It is unclear exactly when the fire was set. The first post about the incident was published on the evening of Oct. 12.
Mirchev said two unidentified people set the station on fire. He accused Bulgarian authorities of keeping quiet about the incident.
“It is obvious that these antennas were not chosen as a target by chance, because they provide the main communications link with the satellites. In late September, similar Starlink antennas were also attacked in Poland. How did the Polish state respond? It informed citizens and the public and took swift action.”
The exact location of the incident was not initially disclosed. Mirchev said only that the fire occurred at a “secret facility” near Sofia. Surveillance footage he posted shows a distinctive antenna and a sign reading “Plana Earth Station.”
The site appears to be the Plana satellite communications station, located south of Sofia. Satellite imagery reviewed by The Insider shows spherical structures at the site characteristic of Starlink ground stations.
Bulgaria’s parliament held a hearing about the incident on Oct. 14. Prime Minister Rumen Radev confirmed the incident and said an investigation was underway, though he declined to comment on the details.
Plamen Tonchev, head of Bulgaria’s State Agency for National Security, said the Starlink antenna site had been scheduled for expansion and that part of the fencing had therefore been removed. That appears to have made it easier for the perpetrators to gain access to the facility.
The station also provides service used by the Ukrainian military.
It remains unclear who was behind the fire. Mirchev suggested Russian intelligence services could have been responsible, though there is currently no evidence to support that claim.
A similar incident occurred in Poland in late September. Two suspects in that arson attack were detained in Germany earlier this week. Polish authorities have said they suspect Russian intelligence services of organizing the attack.

Iranian Cinema Day to be held during 3rd Toji Somon National Film Festival in Tajikistan

Simultaneously with the 3rd edition of the Toji Somon National Film Festival in Dushanbe, “The Gambler,” a production of the Farabi Cinema Foundation, will be featured in the event’s Iranian Cinema Day, Mehr reported.
In each edition of the festival, the screening of works from one or more specific countries is highlighted. In this edition, Iranian Cinema Day is being held to expand cultural and artistic interactions between the two countries.
A social-mystery thriller, “The Gambler” features a cast composed of Kourosh Tahami, Armin Rahimian, Shabnam Qorbani, Amir Norouzi, Roshan Rostampour, and Emad Emami.

International distribution for “The Gambler” is handled by the International Affairs Department of the Farabi Cinema Foundation. Previously, the film received the Special Jury Prize at the Across the Lake Film Festival in North Macedonia, and Shabnam Ghorbani won the Golden Crane award for Best Actress for her performance in the film at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Film Festival in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
In the second edition of the Toji Somon National Film Festival last year, the feature film “Knight,” directed by Hossein Namazi, was screened in the festival’s competition section.

The third edition is scheduled for October 15 to 20, marking the 35th anniversary of Tajikistan's independence. The 2026 theme is "Celebrating True Art." The second edition, held October 15 to 20, 2025, screened more than 40 films from 15 countries under the theme "The History of the Development of the Tajik People."
The festival is part of the Cinema Development Program of the Republic of Tajikistan for 2023 to 2027, a state-backed initiative to strengthen the national film industry, support young creative talent, and expand international cooperation in filmmaking.
