Tehran puppet theater festival to open with public ceremony
TEHRAN- The 21st Tehran-Mobarak International Puppet Theater Festival will open on Saturday with a ceremony at the open-air grounds of Tehran’s City Theater Complex, bringing together puppetry artists and members of the public in a celebration of the art form.
For the ceremony, festival secretary Poopak Azimpour Tabrizi has invited artists, students, university professors, theater practitioners and other interested participants to attend with their own puppets, the public relations office of the City Theater Complex announced on Wednesday.
The invitation extends to citizens of all ages, highlighting the festival’s effort to encourage public participation and bring puppetry beyond the stage.
The opening event will mark the beginning of the six-day festival, which will run in Tehran from October 17 to 22, featuring puppetry performances and activities dedicated to the art form.
The Tehran-Mobarak International Puppet Theater Festival is one of Iran’s major cultural events dedicated to puppetry, bringing together Iranian and international artists to showcase different traditions, techniques and approaches to puppet theater. Named after Mobarak, a traditional Iranian glove-puppet character known for his humor and lively exchanges with audiences, the festival celebrates the country’s rich heritage of traditional puppetry while providing a platform for contemporary forms of the art. Its programs highlight puppetry as a medium for storytelling, cultural expression and communication across generations.
Over the years, the festival has sought to promote innovation in puppet theater, encourage interaction among artists and introduce younger audiences to the art form. Productions presented at the event range from traditional Iranian performances to experimental works incorporating different puppetry techniques, visual design, music and movement. By bringing together performers, theater practitioners and audiences, the festival also supports professional exchange and helps expand the role of puppetry within Iran’s performing arts scene.

Kiarostami’s “Where Is the Friend’s House?” selected for Tokyo festival
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:35:35 UTC
02:35:35 KST

Kiarostami’s “Where Is the Friend’s House?” selected for Tokyo festival
TEHRAN- The 1987 Iranian film “Where Is the Friend’s House?” by the late acclaimed filmmaker Abbas Kiarostami will be screened at the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival in Japan as part of a special program celebrating films cherished by legendary Japanese director Akira Kurosawa.
Produced by the Institute for the Intellectual Development of Children and Young Adults (Kanoon), the film is scheduled to screen on October 26 at TOHO Cinemas Chanter in Tokyo, according to Kanoon’s public relations and international affairs department.
The film will be presented alongside three other works in the program “Akira Kurosawa’s Favorite Films”: Charlie Chaplin’s “The Circus” (1928), and Kurosawa’s own films “Sanshiro Sugata” (1943) and “Ikiru” (1952).
The special program brings together works associated with Kurosawa’s cinematic legacy, placing Kiarostami’s landmark Iranian film in conversation with major works from the history of world cinema.
“Where Is the Friend’s House?” follows Ahmad, a schoolboy who discovers that he has accidentally taken home his classmate’s notebook. Determined to return it before his friend faces punishment for failing to complete his homework, Ahmad sets out to find the boy’s house in a neighboring village. His search becomes a journey through rural Iranian life, exploring childhood, responsibility, kindness and the challenges children encounter in a world governed by adult rules.
With its understated storytelling, naturalistic performances and close attention to everyday life, the film became one of the defining works of Kiarostami’s career and helped introduce Iranian cinema to wider international audiences. It also established themes that would recur throughout the director’s work, including the moral complexity of ordinary decisions and the relationship between children and adults.
The film has won several awards since its release, including the Bronze Leopard at the Locarno International Film Festival in Switzerland and the Critics' Prize at the Sao Paulo International Film Festival, and the Pasinetti Award at the Venice Film Festival.
“Where Is the Friend’s House?” is one of Kiarostami’s landmark works and the first installment of his Koker trilogy, which also includes “And Life Goes On” (1992) and “Through the Olive Trees” (1994).
The film has been screened at numerous international film festivals and cinematheques over the decades and continues to feature in retrospectives and programs dedicated to world cinema.
Kiarostami was a film director, screenwriter, poet, photographer, and film producer. An active filmmaker from 1970, he was involved in the production of over 40 films, including shorts and documentaries. He attained critical acclaim for directing “Close-Up” (1990), “The Wind Will Carry Us” (1999), and “Taste of Cherry” (1997). In later works, “Certified Copy” (2010) and “Like Someone in Love” (2012), he filmed for the first time outside Iran: in Italy and Japan, respectively.
He was part of a generation of filmmakers in the Iranian New Wave, a Persian cinema movement that started in the late 1960s and emphasized the use of poetic dialogue and allegorical storytelling dealing with philosophical issues. He is known for his use of Persian poetry in the dialogue, titles, and themes of his films. His films also contain a notable degree of ambiguity, an unusual mixture of simplicity and complexity, and often a mix of fictional and documentary elements. The concepts of change and continuity, in addition to the themes of life and death, play a major role in Kiarostami's works.
Kiarostami, the winner of the Palme d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival in 1997 for his “Taste of Cherry”, died of cancer on July 5, 2016 at the age of 76.
The screening in Tokyo offers another opportunity for international audiences, including younger generations of filmgoers, to discover Kiarostami’s work and revisit a film that remains an enduring reference point in Iranian cinema.
The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival will run from October 26 to November 4 under the theme “Connecting — Cinema Connects Us to the World Beyond.” The festival will present more than 200 films across its various sections, with screenings and related events taking place in Tokyo’s Hibiya, Yurakucho, Marunouchi and Ginza areas.

Ex-UK army chef jailed for ‘terror’-related offence
The former British Army member harboured ‘extreme right-wing’ views and was ordering explosives components, say police.
A British court has handed a former army chef a nearly four-year jail term for possessing weapons for “terrorist purposes”.
Mark Broadhurst, 28, was given the sentence on Wednesday at Sheffield Crown Court in England, two years after police uncovered online messages in which he expressed racist views and an intention to sell homemade firearms to right-wing groups.
Police found a stockpile of weapons at Broadhurst’s home address when they took him into custody in September 2024, including knives and crossbows, black powder, ammunition, air pistols and what officials described as “an improvised homemade cannon”.
The former British Army member was also found to be part of an online chat group with three other men who last year were jailed for planning to carry out a “terrorist” attack at mosques or synagogues as part of what they believed to be a coming “race war”.
Frank Ferguson, head of the special crime division of the UK’s public prosecution agency, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), said Broadhurst was “clearly interested in violence and developing weapons that had the ability to cause untold harm to innocent people”.
Detective Chief Superintendent James Dunkerley, who heads “counterterror” policing in the northeastern region, said Broadhurst was found to be harbouring an “extreme right-wing mindset” and was “proactively ordering components to make explosives”.
Broadhurst pleaded guilty to firearm possession and possessing an explosive under suspicious circumstances, but denied they were for “terrorism” purposes. A judge, however, ruled that Broadhurst’s offences were connected to “terrorism”.
His conviction comes against a backdrop of rising racial tensions and hate crimes in the UK, with marginalised communities increasingly targeted.
British police in July arrested 12 people in connection with an “extreme right-wing terrorism threat” targeting an Islamic gathering in eastern England.
Six months earlier, UK prosecutors said they were handling the highest number of hate crime cases referred by police in its history.

UN envoy says Libya's political progress 'milestone,’ significant challenges remain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:30:37 UTC
02:30:37 KST

Merve Aydogan
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The UN's special envoy for Libya said Wednesday that the Smaller Convening Agreement signed in Tripoli marks a break in the country's prolonged political deadlock, but warned that disinformation and rejection of dialogue by some parties continue to threaten progress.
Hanna Tetteh, who also heads the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL), told the Security Council that "since my last briefing, we have seen encouraging progress on the UNSMIL-facilitated political process."
She said the parties to the Smaller Convening Agreement signed it on Aug. 30 after four months of deliberations, and that it "has received broad support from national and international actors."
Tetteh stressed that elections cannot be separated from wider institutional problems, including the fragmentation of the judiciary.
"The electoral process cannot be isolated from wider institutional challenges which impact the holding of elections, including the fragmentation of the judiciary," she said.
On security, she described the situation as "fragile" but welcomed "positive steps toward enhanced military cooperation between Eastern and Western military and security institutions."
Drawing attention to southern Libya, she said that "strengthening state presence, improving border management, as well as addressing local grievances related to access to services, can contribute positively to stability in these areas."
Tetteh warned of a continuing wave of "misinformation, disinformation, hate speech and incitement" targeting refugees, migrants, humanitarian actors and UN personnel in Libya.
"Legitimate public concerns regarding migration must be addressed through responsible policy, dialogue and verified information, not through hate speech, intimidation or violence," she said.
She cautioned that the continued rejection by some parties to engage constructively, together with inflammatory rhetoric, risks "hardening political positions, eroding willingness to compromise, and seeking to justify unilateral actions that would undermine the political process or lead to violence."
Calling on the council to back the parties with "positive incentives and guarantees," Tetteh said that "the council should hold spoilers accountable."
"I appeal to this council to urge all parties to move forward quickly given the political, economic and security fragility of the situation in Libya and its impact on the overall stability of the region," she said.
Tetteh also said that "the path to a stable, unified, and prosperous Libya remains long, but our destination remains within reach."

Smart use of Hormuz Strait
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

Smart use of Hormuz Strait
The Iran newspaper analyzed the increasingly complex regional environment and argued that careful strategic judgment is essential. According to the paper, the convergence of multiple crises, including the Gaza war, tensions in the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the Iran-Israel rivalry, the US military presence, and competition among regional powers, has made security in West Asia more fragile than ever. One of the clearest examples of this fragile balance is the Strait of Hormuz.
The geopolitical value of the strait for Iran lies primarily in its deterrent capability. Although a complete closure of the waterway has long been discussed in strategic circles, such a move could trigger broad international consensus against Iran, increase the legitimacy of intervention by external powers, and diminish Iran's geopolitical capital. Consequently, the paper suggested that in the event of escalating tensions, Iran is more likely to rely on limited, gradual, and reversible measures rather than fully employing this strategic tool.
Sharq: Iran at the Trump-Putin table
Shargh discussed the reported agreement between Putin and Trump regarding diesel fuel. Although details of the conversation between the two presidents have not yet been released, questions remain over whether they also reached understandings concerning Iran. For Tehran, the issue is sensitive. On one hand, Iran considers Russia a strategic partner; on the other, it sees that same partner, only hours after discussing regional developments with the Iranian president, sitting down with the US president and reaching an agreement. The visible outcome of the call was an announced deal for supplying Russian diesel fuel to US and global markets. For Putin, the agreement represents both an economic and political achievement. For Trump, it provides an opportunity to demonstrate to voters, ahead of the Congressional midterm elections, that he is taking steps to reduce living costs and curb rising fuel prices. In Tehran, however, the issue goes beyond diesel fuel. What raises concern is the timing of the agreement amid continuing tensions between Iran and the United States and uncertainty about the political content of the conversation between the two leaders.
Kayhan: Trump trapped in an Iranian quagmire
Kayhan wrote about Trump's inability to escape a predicament created by Iran. The economic situation of ordinary Americans continues to deteriorate under the shadow of the war with Iran. It also cited the Hebrew-language newspaper Calcalist as reporting a decline in America's financial strength. The impact of the Iran conflict is weighing heavily on US Congressional midterm elections. Analysts allegedly believe voters may punish Trump and his Republican supporters by backing Democrats in the Nov. 3 elections. Proposals such as keeping the Strait of Hormuz open, distributing financial assistance to citizens, and reaching a diesel agreement with Putin are among the measures Trump is pursuing to avoid electoral defeat.
Siasat-e-Rooz: Iran's new initiative to end the Yemen war
Siasat-e-Rooz highlighted Iran's announcement that it is prepared to facilitate dialogue between Yemen and Saudi Arabia. As fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen intensifies, and while Western countries and Israel are accused of fueling the conflict in an effort to regionalize it, Iran says it is ready to help create conditions for negotiations between the two sides. Tehran has consistently sought to play a constructive role in regional security. Although Iran itself is currently engaged in confrontation with the United States and Israel, it maintains that it remains committed to responsible regional behavior and is actively pursuing a political solution to the Yemen crisis. Analysts believe that ending regional conflicts and including a halt to Yemeni attacks in any future agreement involving Iran could reduce pressure on Riyadh.
Ettelaat: How would China benefit or suffer from Iran-US war?
Ettelaat published an interview with Morteza Firouzi, a professor of international relations, comparing Russian and Chinese positions regarding the Iran war. Firouzi argued that China gains little economically from such a war. Unlike Russia, which he believes would benefit from confrontation between Iran and the United States, China would suffer economically. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, he said, would also be detrimental to Beijing. China is currently drawing on its energy reserves and therefore faces economic challenges. He added that both Russia and China understand that the United States has focused much of its strategic planning on moving beyond the Middle East and concentrating on China. Washington has strengthened political and military cooperation with countries such as Japan, South Korea, and Australia in preparation for long-term competition with Beijing. From China's perspective, Firouzi argued, it is preferable for the United States to remain deeply engaged in Middle Eastern crises rather than redirect its full attention toward China. Therefore, while a conflict harms China economically, continued US involvement in the Middle East could provide strategic advantages for Beijing.

The Guardian view on Trump’s deal with Putin: grim and grubby, but not gamechanging | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:30:08 UTC
02:30:08 KST

When Donald Trump pledged to end the war in Ukraine within 24 hours of re-entering the White House last year, no one with any depth of insight into the conflict believed him. But Mr Trump took his own words seriously enough to feel the lack of a ceasefire as an affront to his self-image as a master dealmaker. After a period when it seemed that Kyiv’s European allies had steered the US president away from pro‑Kremlin partisanship, he has reverted to the grotesque view that Ukrainian capitulation is a necessary precondition for peace.
These are the perilous circumstances in which President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met Andy Burnham on Wednesday in Downing Street. In recent days, the US president has called for a change of government in Ukraine. He claimed that a partial ceasefire had been agreed, while Russia escalated its bombardments. According to Mr Zelenskyy, the latest missile strikes have come without the intelligence warnings from the US that have, in the past, facilitated self-defence. There have been reports of Ukrainian soldiers losing access to the Starlink satellite network, controlled by Elon Musk, the US tech oligarch. This raises suspicion of coordinated pressure to tip the scales in Russia’s favour after many months when Mr Putin’s forces have failed to deliver significant advances and his country’s economy has been suffering from the effect of Ukrainian missile and drone counterstrikes.
Mr Trump is unhappy with Ukraine targeting Russian oil refineries. He claims that this is the cause of high energy prices afflicting American consumers and threatening Republican prospects in next month’s midterm elections. The domestic imperative to keep pump prices down led Mr Trump to do a grubby deal to import diesel from Russia, in flagrant breach of international sanctions.
The real driver of global energy prices is not Ukraine defending itself from Russian attack, but Mr Trump’s failing war against Iran. However, the US president is incapable of admitting any fault. Blaming Mr Zelenskyy enables him to deny his own culpability and, with malevolent encouragement from Mr Putin, to revive the preposterous notion that Ukrainian intransigence rather than Russian aggression is the reason why his promise to broker a peace deal remains unfulfilled.
Disrupting Mr Trump’s pro-Russian delusions is not easy, but it has been done before. It is not a gratifying diplomatic task to indulge the monstrous vanity of the US president by trying to impress upon him a view of his country’s national interest, that Mr Putin is not an ally of his country or his personal friend, which is self-evident to any rational observer.
Mr Burnham rightly resists invitations to denounce the US president in public. He recognises that Ukraine’s cause and, by extension, also the cause of European democracy more widely, is better served by making the case in private. The best response to Mr Trump’s perfidy is for Mr Zelenskyy’s friends to reaffirm their support, as Mr Burnham has done, thereby signalling that Ukraine will not be beaten by deals between the Kremlin and the White House.
Russia is failing to achieve its war aims because the invasion was conceived in delusional hatred for the very idea of independent Ukrainian nationhood, which routinely underestimates that country’s will to resist. That is a flaw in Mr Putin’s plans that no amount of collusion with Mr Trump can fix.

Three Russian artistic gymnasts — Angelina Melnikova, Viktoria Listunova, and Anna Kalmykova — have been denied visas to the Netherlands ahead of the Oct. 17-25 World Championships, the Russian Gymnastics Federation said on Telegram earlier today. Two have publicly backed Russian government policies, while a third is believed to have ties to Rosgvardiya, Russia’s National Guard, a separate internal-security force that reports directly to Vladimir Putin.
The federation said the three leading Russian gymnasts were denied visas four days before the start of the competition in Rotterdam, where the first team qualification spots for the 2028 Olympics will be awarded. It quoted the reason given for the refusals:
“One or more Schengen-area member states consider the athletes a threat to their international relations.”
Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev said the Russian Olympic Committee would appeal to the International Olympic Committee and World Gymnastics, the sport’s international governing body, demanding that the Rotterdam event be stripped of its Olympic qualifying status.
Kyiv has accused all three gymnasts of either supporting Russia’s full-scale invasion or having links to Russian security institutions.
In Melnikova’s case, in 2025 Ukraine’s Ministry of Youth and Sports called for the 2020 Olympic champion to be stripped of her neutral status, saying she had posted photos featuring the letter Z, a symbol widely used in support of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. The ministry also said she held “charity” training sessions for the children of Russian occupation forces and helped raise money for the daughter of a Russian serviceman.
Ukrainian authorities also noted that Melnikova represents CSKA, a sports club subordinate to Russia’s Ministry of Defense, which they said means she has a contractual relationship with the Russian Armed Forces. In addition, in 2025 Melnikova ran for a seat on the Voronezh City Duma as a candidate for the ruling United Russia party.
Viktoria Listunova took part in a March 2022 rally-concert attended by Vladimir Putin shortly after the start of the full-scale invasion. The event marked what the Kremlin calls the “anniversary of Crimea’s reunification with Russia” (its euphemism for the illegal invasion and subsequent annexation of the Ukrainian peninsula in 2014). Listunova appeared at the event wearing a jacket emblazoned with the letter Z; she was 16 at the time. According to Ukraine’s Sports Ministry, she also raised money for the family of a Russian serviceman killed in the war.
According to Ukraine’s Sports Ministry, Anna Kalmykova competes for Moscow’s Dynamo club and is under contract with Rosgvardiya, whose units have taken part in the invasion and occupation of Ukraine.
Other Russian gymnasts from both the women’s and men’s teams also applied for Dutch visas. The Russian Gymnastics Federation said three of the six Russian women — Alyona Glotova, Lyudmila Roshchina, and Milana Kayumova — were granted entry documents by the Netherlands. Elizaveta Us, who was listed as an additional reserve, also received a visa.
Five of the six male gymnasts who applied received visas as well. The federation said 47 of the 61 members of Russia’s delegation were granted permission to travel to the world championships in Rotterdam.

Bulgaria expects to join a NATO anti-drone initiative by the end of October, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov has said, as drone attacks on cargo vessels in the Black Sea intensify concerns over maritime security near the alliance’s southeastern borders.
Wednesday’s announcement came a day after a drone strike sank a cargo ship off Bulgaria’s coast for the second time in a week, highlighting the risks facing commercial shipping as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues to affect Black Sea trade routes.
“Bulgaria will be part of this project as soon as possible,” Stoyanov said during a parliamentary hearing, according to local media. He added that the country was expected to join by October 30.
Two ships hit, 11 sailors missing
Two cargo vessels were struck by drones off the Bulgarian coast on October 13. One, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity, sank, leaving 11 sailors missing at sea and prompting Sofia to summon Russia’s ambassador.
Drones had struck two other cargo ships in the same waters on October 6.
Bulgaria’s transport ministry announced on Wednesday afternoon that rescue operations for the missing sailors had been halted because of strong winds, reduced visibility and high waves.
Although Bulgarian authorities have stopped short of directly accusing Moscow of carrying out the attacks, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Tuesday that their outcome “benefits the Russian Federation”.
Russia’s ambassador to Sofia, Eleonora Mitrofanova, said she had received no information from Russia’s defence ministry about attacks on commercial vessels. She also suggested that a third party could have carried them out as a provocation, according to the Bulgarian government.
War at sea raises risks for NATO’s Black Sea coast
The attacks have added to concerns that drone warfare linked to the Russia-Ukraine conflict could threaten commercial vessels operating close to NATO members Bulgaria and Romania.
Russia has been bombing Ukrainian Black Sea ports, forcing Kiev to rely increasingly on Danube river ports and shipping routes running close to NATO territory.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has stepped up attacks on Russian grain-exporting vessels in other parts of the Black Sea and near the mouth of the Don River in the Sea of Azov.
Bulgaria’s planned participation in the NATO initiative reflects its push for stronger alliance defences against drones as the conflict’s maritime risks extend beyond the immediate combat zone.

German newspaper Die Zeit vows legal fight over seized interview files
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:28:16 UTC
02:28:16 KST

Ayhan Simsek
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Weekly German newspaper Die Zeit said it will use every legal means available after a Hamburg court ordered it to hand over interview recordings, a step journalist groups condemned as an assault on press freedom.
Prosecutors and officers from the Hamburg State Criminal Police Office visited Die Zeit’s offices on Monday and threatened a search of the editorial rooms. The Hamburg Regional Court had issued a warrant covering audio recordings of an interview on a high-profile kidnapping case. The editor who did the interviews handed over the files, sealed, to avoid an immediate search.
Die Zeit editors-in-chief Giovanni di Lorenzo and Jochen Wegner said protecting sources is essential for media that report independently. “As part of press freedom, the protection of sources, which is of vital importance for independent media, is particularly indispensable. That is why we will use every legal means available to defend ourselves,” they said in a statement.
Mika Beuster, chairman of the German Journalists’ Association (DJV), criticized the authorities’ approach. “At the start of Hamburg Press Freedom Week, the attitude shown by the authorities raises serious questions about the protection of journalistic work,” he said. Beuster added that journalistic conversations must not be turned into tools for criminal investigations.
Reporters Without Borders called the move a serious attack on press freedom. The trade union known as Ver.di demanded the immediate return of the seized material, saying research material is not a depot for evidence for the judiciary and that such coercion undermines editorial secrecy.
Alleged kidnapping
A court spokesperson said the recordings concern conversations done roughly two weeks after the alleged kidnapping of Christina Block’s two children from Denmark on New Year’s Eve 2023-2024. The interviews involved the children’s father, Stephan Hensel, his wife Astrid Have, and the children. The court argued the files could hold evidentiary value in the trial of Block and six co-defendants, potentially illuminating events not yet examined in the main hearing.
The long-running custody battle between restaurant chain heiress Block and her former husband Stephan Hensel became a criminal case after their two younger children were taken from Denmark on Jan. 1, 2024 by people linked to an Israeli firm and brought to Germany. Prosecutors allege Block ordered the operation. Her partner, former TV presenter Gerhard Delling, is accused of aiding the offense. Block has denied the charges.
During the investigations, prosecutors also examined August Hanning, formerly head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service, the BND, over alleged involvement in the kidnapping.
Thousands of filed seized
In a recent television interview, Hanning rejected any role in the alleged kidnapping or related accusations. He said that, as a legal expert, he had given only advisory support and had advised Block in 2022 on legal options under international custody rules. He insisted he had no knowledge of later operations and described the Hamburg investigation as baseless.
About 2,000 confidential BND files seized during searches of Hanning’s premises in September 2025 led to a separate inquiry and his arrest. He was taken into custody this Oct. 7. Federal prosecutors accuse Hanning of obtaining and using the classified documents in his private consulting work, including for a foreign intelligence service, and of maintaining intensive contact with another foreign intelligence official. They charged him with espionage, researching state secrets, and attempted treason. His lawyer rejected the accusations, saying Hanning is being unjustly prosecuted.

Tokyo decries arrest of Japanese journalist in Russia
October 14, 2026
Japan's Foreign Ministry on Wednesday summoned Russia's ambassador after a Japanese journalist was arrested by Russia's FSB security agency on suspicion of espionage.
What do know so far?
The journalist's arrest comes amid a dispute in a dispute between Russia and Japan over the four southernmost islands of the Kuril Island chain, which are controlled by Moscow and claimed by Tokyo. The archipelago in the northwest Pacific is near the Russian island of Sakhalin where the man was arrested.
Russia's Federal Security Service announced the arrest on Tuesday and claimed the journalist, who works for the northern Japanese Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was gathering information about Russian defense capability on behalf of Japanese intelligence.
In a statement, Japan's Foreign Ministry lodged a "strong protest" against Russia for "detaining this Japanese national and issuing unilateral statements regarding the matter, while the Japanese government has not received any explanation concerning the detained national as yet."
On Wednesday, Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said Tokyo called for Russia to treat the detainee fairly and humanely, while asking Russian authorities for more information about his arrest.
Kihara added that Japanese officials have been unable to contact the man, his condition is unknown, and Moscow had not responded to Tokyo's requests for access.
"We'll do everything we can for the protection of the Japanese citizen," he said.
Russia claims Japan using journalists as spies
Russian authorities identified the journalist as Yuki Imai. The Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper has not yet confirmed the journalist's identity, saying it is still gathering details of what could have led to the arrest.
The newspaper said the man had been reporting in Russia on a journalist visa and was supposed to leave on Monday.
In footage on Russian state television, a man is seen being placed in handcuffs by three masked men in black uniforms, and then being accompanied by FSB agents onto a plane. The man is then seen in a cage in a Moscow court, which ordered him detained for two months.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova claimed that Japan is using accredited journalists in Russia to gather sensitive security information.
Kimitake Nakamura, head of the European Affairs Bureau at Japan's Foreign Ministry, said he has asked Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to quickly arrange a meeting between the detained journalist and the Japanese government.
Japan-Russia Kuril Islands dispute
The Soviet Union seized the Kuril Islands from Japan in the final days of World War II. The territorial dispute has prevented the two countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending their hostilities.
Bilateral tensions were aggravated by Japan joining Western sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine.
The dispute reignited in August after Russian President Vladimir Putin visited one of the Kurils for the first time, with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi calling the visit "absolutely unacceptable." Putin was only the second Russian leader to ever visit the islands
Russia has also increased its military presence on the islands in recent years, including by deploying missile systems, expanding air fields, and using the islands for live fire drills.
In Wednesday's Foreign Ministry statement, Nakamura reiterated Japan's territorial claims over the four southernmost Kuril Islands, which Tokyo calls the "Northern Territory."

Strikes on three combined heat and power plants did not cause a total blackout in Kyiv: what to expect in winter
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:27:53 EEST
02:27:53 KST

Strikes on three combined heat and power plants did not cause a total blackout in Kyiv: what to expect in winter
Kyiv • UNN
An expert explained why the attacks did not leave Kyiv without electricity and what determines the duration of repairs. Disruptions to heating are possible in winter.
Russian forces are attempting to damage Kyiv’s energy infrastructure, including combined heat and power plants and substations that ensure the transmission of electricity. Energy expert Mykhailo Honchar told a UNN journalist more about how critical the damage to all three of the capital’s CHP plants is and whether prolonged outages should already be expected.
Why Kyiv was not left without electricity after the strikes on the CHP plants
According to the expert, Russia is attempting to carry out comprehensive strikes on energy facilities, seeking to disrupt the city’s electricity and heat supplies simultaneously. However, he notes that the enemy has not carried out such attacks for the first time; in particular, attempts to destroy the energy system began as early as 2022.
In such massive combined attacks, the calculation is always that “that’s it—now we’ll strike once and for all,” but that is not how it turns out. Of course, we have more damage, but the situation here depends on how quickly our repair crews respond
In addition, Mykhailo Honchar emphasizes that the mere fact of a strike on one energy facility does not automatically mean that the entire city will be de-energized. The consequences depend on the facility that was hit and the nature of the damage. Kyiv is the largest electricity consumer in Ukraine.
Kyiv has an energy deficit in terms of the generation available within the city. The issue of the energy deficit was finally resolved with the commissioning, at the end of 2015, of the 750 kV Rivne Nuclear Power Plant–Kyivska substation transmission line. Together with the power flow from the Khmelnytskyi Nuclear Power Plant, this made it possible to balance the needs of Ukraine’s largest electricity consumer—Kyiv and the Kyiv metropolitan area
In addition, according to the expert, Russian attacks are aimed not only at the city’s combined heat and power plants, but also at Ukrenergo substations through which electricity flows from nuclear power plants toward the capital; damage to such facilities complicates the supply of electricity and forces energy workers to change its transmission schemes. At the same time, the extensive structure of the energy system makes it possible to create alternative routes, although this does not rule out disruptions in the operation of the grid.
The enemy’s main efforts are aimed not only at striking Kyiv’s CHP plants. This is specifically intended to make it impossible to generate heat for city residents. Other strikes target substations that carry power from nuclear power plants toward Kyiv. These strikes have periodically been effective, but as we can see, although the situation is problematic, they have not achieved the expected result—namely, leaving Kyiv in darkness
Why restoring electricity and heat supplies may take different amounts of time
Mykhailo Honchar explained that the duration of repairs after shelling depends on exactly what equipment was damaged and whether a replacement is available. The availability of backup equipment and the security conditions under which repair crews can begin work are also important.
It varies greatly. It depends on what you have to replace. Figuratively speaking, it is one thing when you need to replace severed wires—this can be done quickly; but if, for example, a transformer has been hit, then it takes a long time. It also depends on whether backup equipment is available and where it is located. So it is impossible to say exactly how long it will take. Each case is separate
Moreover, Russian forces may carry out repeated strikes on the same facilities, forcing repair crews to take additional risks into account.
Before repair crews begin repair work, the State Emergency Service must inspect the area to determine whether any dangerous objects remain in the affected zone. In addition, we see that they have already done this many times: a subsequent strike follows the first impact. Therefore, unlike before—even last year—when repairs began immediately after the impact and the fire was extinguished, if there was one, the process is now being slowed down for security reasons
Also, due to the specific features of the city’s power grid, the consequences of attacks may differ even in neighboring districts of the city, Mykhailo Honchar noted. He explained that this is related to the configuration of the distribution network, its technical condition, and the ability to redistribute the load. This leads to the uneven application of outage schedules.
The networks are operating in an abnormal mode. Therefore, one district may be without electricity for half a day or even a full day, while somewhere else things may be more or less normal — the power was switched off for several hours, and that’s it. There is no malicious intent here whatsoever. You never know what will be hit and where, how long restoration will take, or how to set up a bypass route if the direct one is not functioning
Does Kyiv face a prolonged lack of heat in winter?
Strikes on all three of the city’s main combined heat and power plants pose risks to getting through the heating season, since the primary purpose of these facilities is heat production. At the same time, damage to them does not mean that all residents of the capital will necessarily be left without heating. According to the expert, the city has boiler houses to which consumers can be reconnected if necessary, although the feasibility of such a solution depends on the specific district and the condition of the infrastructure.
A combined heat and power plant, that is, a cogeneration plant, has the primary task of generating heat. Electricity is produced in parallel, and that is task number two. The enemy’s main efforts are aimed at making heat generation impossible. Heat and heating are not yet needed now, so the enemy is working with the winter outlook in mind
In addition, the expert recalled that in winter, after the combined heat and power plants were hit, some districts of Kyiv also experienced heating problems, but in some cases heat supply was restored by reconnecting buildings to boiler houses. According to him, this shows that even significant damage does not always mean that restoring heat by the next heating season is impossible.
Let’s recall how we dealt with the situation in January–February this year, when they also hit all these combined heat and power plants and there was no heat supply. Yes, entire districts of the capital were left without heat. I remember someone writing in a closed chat: "That’s it, we probably won’t be able to repair anything, even by the start of the next heating season." But imagine our surprise when heat supply was restored literally in just under three weeks. It turned out that they had reconnected them to a boiler house
However, Mykhailo Honchar believes that residents of the capital should nevertheless prepare for possible disruptions, but should not draw conclusions about an inevitable large-scale blackout after every enemy attack.
Hoping for the best, we need to be prepared for the worst-case scenario. I think that, with the experience of the past four winters, our people are more prepared than usual. At the same time, when you look out at night and see that the lights have gone out somewhere in the building opposite, and someone immediately writes falsely on a Telegram channel that Kyiv is experiencing a blackout, this is stoking passions and operating as the enemy’s useful idiot
Thus, strikes on Kyiv’s combined heat and power plants and substations may complicate the operation of the energy system and cause localized disruptions to electricity and heat supplies. At the same time, the further development of the situation will depend on the extent of the damage, security conditions, and the speed of repairs. The expert urges people to prepare for possible difficulties, while assessing the situation based on verified information.

Palestine said Wednesday that Colombia’s opening of an embassy in West Jerusalem violates international law and UN resolutions, Anadolu reports.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry said the opening constituted “a flagrant violation of international law and relevant UN resolutions, and an assault on the Palestinian people and their just and legitimate national rights.”
It stressed that all measures and decisions to change the legal and historical status of Jerusalem are “null and void and have no legal effect.”
It said that “opening an embassy to Israel in occupied Jerusalem violates international legitimacy resolutions, particularly UN Security Council Resolutions 476 and 478.”
The two resolutions that were adopted in 1980 affirm the illegality and invalidity of Israeli measures intended to alter the character and legal status of Jerusalem, amid Israel’s enactment of a law annexing East Jerusalem.
The ministry said Colombia’s move also “undermines the international consensus on the city’s legal status and infringes on the Palestinian people’s inalienable rights.”
It warned that the step encourages Israel to continue its “colonial policies and attempts to impose illegal realities on the ground.”
READ: Colombia opens embassy in West Jerusalem despite city’s disputed international status
In addition to Colombia, the US, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Papua New Guinea, Paraguay, Fiji, Nauru and Somalia’s breakaway region have moved their embassies to West Jerusalem or opened embassies in the city, a move that runs counter to international resolutions concerning the status of Jerusalem.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry urged Colombia to comply with international law and respect relevant UN resolutions, calling on it to “reverse this step to preserve prospects for achieving a just and comprehensive peace.”
Earlier Wednesday, Colombia opened the embassy in West Jerusalem. The move follows the restoration of its diplomatic relations with Israel in August, after Colombia severed ties with Tel Aviv in May 2024 under a previous government.
Jerusalem remains at the heart of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and is widely regarded as one of its most sensitive issues.
While Israel claims the entire city as its capital, Palestinians view East Jerusalem, occupied by Israel since 1967, as the capital of a future Palestinian state, in line with longstanding international consensus and UN resolutions.

Europe risks becoming mere tourist attraction – Polish FM
Europe risks becoming little more than a tourist attraction unless it dramatically expands its military capabilities, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has warned, calling for an increasingly confrontational stance against Russia and refusing to return its frozen assets.
Speaking at the Warsaw Security Forum on Tuesday, Sikorski argued that Europe must translate its economic power into military strength to avoid being sidelined as the US, China, and Russia compete for global influence.
”What’s at stake is not whether we will be occupied,” referring to speculation of a Russian invasion, which Moscow has dismissed as nonsense. The main question, according to Sikorski, is Europe’s “status in the global division of power.”
“The triumvirate that divides the world into spheres of influence” will either be composed of the US, China, and Russia, while Europe serves as “suppliers of data and tourist attractions,” or Europe will be the “third leg” of the group instead of Russia, he said.
Sikorski called for a more assertive military posture toward Russia, including the creation of a European army that Russia would never attack.
Moscow has denied that it has any intention of attacking Europe, warning that the continent’s accelerating military buildup could instead provoke a direct confrontation. Russian officials have cautioned that the conflict could be “very short” and potentially nuclear.
The Polish foreign minister also rejected the idea of returning Russia’s frozen sovereign assets, declaring that Moscow will recover the assets “over our dead bodies.”
Around $300 billion in Russian central bank reserves have been frozen by Western countries since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. The EU has already begun channeling proceeds generated by the assets to Kiev but has stopped short of confiscating the principal, amid legal and financial concerns.
Belgium – which hosts Euroclear, the clearinghouse that holds most of the frozen assets in the EU – has resisted outright confiscation. Officials warn that doing so could undermine confidence in Europe’s financial system and send “a very bad signal to other countries worldwide” that hold assets in the EU.
Russia has denounced the proposals to seize the assets as outright theft, warning that doing so would trigger legal action and retaliation against Western assets in Russia.

The Guardian view on Spain’s snap election: high stakes for Europe as Pedro Sánchez gambles again | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:25:08 UTC
02:25:08 KST

When it comes to risk-taking, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has a formidable track record. In 2018, the Socialist party leader swept to power by triggering a no-confidence vote that unexpectedly ousted his centre-right predecessor Mariano Rajoy. He held on to it against the odds after calling a snap election in 2023, at a time when the popularity of his own party had plummeted and the far right was on the rise.
As he endures another rocky period in office, Mr Sánchez has once more rolled the dice. Last week, he announced a snap poll for November after his minority government was blocked from passing measures to ease Spain’s chronic housing crisis. The eviction of 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal from her Madrid home sparked nationwide protests over soaring rents and prices. The outrage grew with news of her death last Wednesday. Mr Sánchez clearly hopes that campaigning on a national cause célèbre gives him a chance of winning a stronger progressive mandate next month.
It would be rash to bet against one of Europe’s great political survivors. But the wider context suggests an uphill struggle and a potentially disastrous outcome. The poll lead enjoyed by the conservative Partido Popular (PP) over the Socialist party is substantial, while the far-right Vox party is polling close to 20% – enough to make it an indispensable partner in a PP-led coalition.
Both parties have exploited public anger at a damaging wave of corruption allegations involving senior Socialist figures in Mr Sánchez’s inner circle. The recent border chaos in Ceuta, when an influx of tens of thousands of migrants temporarily overwhelmed the Spanish exclave, has also damaged the government’s reputation.
The stakes for Spain and the rest of Europe are alarmingly high. A PP-Vox government would hand national power to the far right for the first time since the return of democracy after Franco’s death. As well as making life more difficult for migrants and minorities, that could have significant and destabilising constitutional implications. One achievement of Mr Sánchez’s tenure has been the defusing of tensions in relation to the Catalan separatist movement, albeit through agreeing a controversial amnesty deal in exchange for parliamentary support. Vox’s ultranationalist programme includes incendiary proposals to outlaw regional governments and parties, and centralise power in Madrid.
More broadly, defeat for Mr Sánchez would end a period in which Spain has acted as a much-needed counterweight to the rightwards lurch in European politics. His Socialist-led government has resisted Fortress Europe rhetoric and made the necessary case for the benefits of migration, while presiding over an economy that has comfortably outperformed France and Germany. Madrid has also stood apart from the continental rush to prioritise defence at the expense of social spending, while forthrightly opposing Donald Trump’s reckless war in the Middle East and the conduct of Israel’s war in Gaza.
During his eight years in power, Mr Sánchez has proved a master at spotting political opportunities in the midst of crises. By going to the polls as the issue of affordable housing dominates political debate, he has given his party the chance to play to its traditional social democratic strengths. But against strong headwinds, political brinkmanship may not be enough this time round. European progressives can only wait and hope that the prime minister’s biggest gamble yet comes off.

Why your cat is the best philosopher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:24:09 UTC
02:24:09 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
A young girl looks out of the classroom window. It’s the end of the day, and she’s bored. She spots a goldfinch land on the ground outside. It hops about and twitches for whatever reasons goldfinches do that, and then takes off. It swoops and dives around the playground, as if doing it all for the girl. Oh, how she would like to fly.
Humans have long looked to the animal kingdom for inspiration. We envy their skills and talents: flight, speed, strength, sociability, and so on. Religions almost always feature animal imagery, and flags will often blazon a lion, an eagle, a wolf — something bold or heroic. And philosophers are in on the game as well.
Even in the earliest historical records, people were exploring the philosophical side of animals. What can this animal teach me? What virtues does it embody? What can I learn about myself by studying this creature?
Joining in an ancient line is John Gray’s book Feline Philosophy. In the book, Gray examines what we can all learn about life from spending more time around cats. His conclusion: We should all be a bit more feline.
Mo the Philosophical Cat
A cat does not do philosophy, and that makes it a better philosopher than anyone else. Gray argues that for humans, philosophy acts as a kind of medicine. We are full of doubt and anxiety about how to live, yes, but most of all we are filled with the existential dread that comes from knowing that we will die.
To combat this, we create systems like religions and ideologies. We try to soothe our death-terror with stories. We become obsessed with “the good life,” “the examined life,” and “time well spent.” We have turned the word “happiness” into a multi-billion-dollar industry, but as a species we are no happier than we ever were. We are sick, craving a cure, but the medicine we have isn’t working.
Cats, though, have no such sickness. Imagine a cat called Mo. Mo does not search for meaning in her life, and she is not trying to become a better cat. She does not experience her life as a project that could fail, and she doesn’t wake up with the imagined burden of a thousand cats’ expectations.
Mo hunts, she sleeps, and she sits in the sunlight. When she suffers, she does not add to her suffering by asking why. She does not need to invent systems or stories because the world is as the world is. Gray’s point is not that Mo is wise; Mo wouldn’t write books even if she could. The point is that Mo is not sick. Humans are.
Be more cat
Gray starts his book by saying that we cannot become a cat. We can try to transfigure if we want, but you’re mostly running up against the immovable wall of cellular biology. Still, we can mimic a cat. We can do more cat things and try to see things like a cat. Gray leans on a point that Blaise Pascal makes about ritual and religion: If you do something enough, it changes you. If you force your mind a certain way, it stays like that.
As the philosopher Mark Vorobej pointed out, it’s not entirely clear why Gray has singled out cats. What’s true here of cats is true of dogs, birds, rats, squirrels, moles, badgers, or mongooses. Should we be more mongoose? It’s a fair critique, but it is somewhat pedantic. I’m sure Gray is not some feline exceptionalist. I take his book to be a lesson in intentionality. We can try to become more like a cat, rat, or badger, and I think he chose cats because they’re both cute and far more present in our lives. We see cats at home or on social media. All over social media. It’s just much easier to talk about something so available. Yes, he could have chosen dogs, but hey — take your pick.
So, how can we be more cat? Well, we need to distance ourselves from this sick and broken human way of seeing things. Stop seeing your lives in terms of some huge, overarching metanarrative. Don’t try to find meaning in your suffering. Stop seeing the world in terms of puzzles to solve. Don’t try to persuade other people to be more reasonable. Recognize that you are who you are, and it is what it is. Sometimes life just happens. So climb trees, play with a ball, sleep a lot more, and lie by the fire when things get cold and dark. Cherish life and think only as much as you want.
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.

British Premier Andy Burnham on Wednesday ruled out a partnership between the Labour Party and the Green Party following the Greens' controversial motion declaring that "Zionism is racism."
Burnham was asked during the Prime Minister's Questions whether he would rule out a pact with the Greens.

The Green Party passed a motion defining Zionism as "a political ideology which called for the creation – and, now it exists, the continuity – of an ethnonationalist Jewish State in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population."

"A Labour government who apologized over their actions over Gaza is demonstrating that it was all performative," said Polanski. "Andy Burnham still stands with Israel whilst it kills innocent people."

Estonia Backs Finland’s Call for EU-Wide Ban on Russian Tourist Visas
Estonia has joined Finland’s call for the European Union to suspend tourist visas for Russian citizens and impose broader entry restrictions while Russia continues its war against Ukraine, Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna stated in a post on X on October 13.
Tsahkna was responding to Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen, who called on EU member states to support a letter to the European Commission seeking a complete ban on Russian tourist visas for the duration of Russia’s war.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia has also intensified sabotage, espionage, cyberattacks, and other hybrid operations across Europe since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In October, Ukraine’s military intelligence warned that Russian intelligence services were preparing further operations across EU and NATO countries aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and weakening allied capabilities.
“Estonia joins Finland’s call to suspend tourist visas for Russian citizens across the European Union,” Tsahkna wrote.
“As Russia continues its relentless assault on Ukraine, bombing cities, destroying civilian infrastructure, and killing innocent people, it is unacceptable that Russian citizens can still enjoy unrestricted leisure travel within the Schengen area,” he added.
Tsahkna argued that EU visa policy should reflect the scale of Russia’s aggression and called for further pressure on the Kremlin.
“Visa policy must reflect the gravity of Russia’s ongoing aggression. The EU should continue to strengthen pressure on the Kremlin through all available means,” he wrote.
The Estonian foreign minister also urged the EU to adopt the measures needed to establish what he described as “a comprehensive entry ban on Russian combatants.”
In her original post, Valtonen called for a complete EU-wide ban on Russian tourist visas, noting that Finland had already stopped issuing visas for non-essential travel to Russian citizens in 2022.
“We must stop issuing tourist visas for Russian citizens across the EU,” Valtonen wrote. “I am calling for a complete EU ban on Russian tourist visas for as long as Russia continues its war of aggression.”
“It is not right that Russians can travel to Europe to enjoy the way of life and freedoms here while their country bombs the homes of Ukrainians,” she added.
Valtonen also called for a Schengen visa ban targeting the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin’s inner circle, tighter restrictions on Russian athletes, and stronger enforcement of existing visa restrictions on Russian combatants.
Finland has maintained stricter visa rules for Russian citizens since 2022, and Valtonen is now seeking to extend that approach across the EU. Her proposal would require coordinated action by member states and the European Commission.
In September, US prosecutors charged five alleged members of a Russian intelligence network accused of recruiting operatives for assassinations, arson attacks, and other violent plots in the US and Europe. Investigators linked the network to planned operations in Lithuania and Prague, while stating that countries supporting Ukraine were among its targets.

Russia’s Newest Drones Are Still Full of Western Tech—Ukraine Just Put the Evidence on Display
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:22:54 UTC
02:22:54 KST

- Category
- World
Russia’s Newest Drones Are Still Full of Western Tech—Ukraine Just Put the Evidence on Display
Ukraine displayed a captured Russian Geran-2 drone and Western-made components recovered from Russian UAVs at the Warsaw Security Forum, highlighting how foreign technology continues to reach Russia’s weapons industry despite years of sanctions and export controls.
The exhibition was organized by Ukraine’s Independent Anti-Corruption Commission, or NAKO, with support from the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry, the organization told UNITED24 Media on October 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The display was intended to show that Russia’s dependence on Western technology has not disappeared as its weapons production expands. Experts continue to identify electronics from the US, Switzerland, Germany, the UK, Japan, and Taiwan inside Russian drones, including newer jet-powered models that Moscow began deploying on a much larger scale in 2026.
According to NAKO, the components cannot simply be explained as old inventories accumulated before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Investigators are finding relatively recent electronics, indicating that Russia continues to acquire restricted technology through sanctions-evasion networks and third countries.
“Why should Western countries reconsider their approach to sanctions policy? This is a matter of Ukraine’s survival and the security of the entire democratic world. And we want to raise it to the political level,” NAKO Executive Director Olena Tregub said.
NAKO also organized a panel at the Warsaw Security Forum focused on sanctions and export controls. Opening the discussion, former US presidential special envoy Gen. Keith Kellogg said Western technology remains one of the factors sustaining Russia’s war effort.
Every foreign component that reaches a Russian defense factory, he argued, represents a failure somewhere in the supply chain and raises questions about enforcement.
EU sanctions envoy David O’Sullivan acknowledged that there is no simple solution.
Russia continues obtaining Western components through third countries that are not required to follow EU sanctions, making cooperation with those governments increasingly important if Europe wants to close the remaining routes into Russia’s defense industry.
Russia’s dependence is also not limited to microelectronics. Its military-industrial complex still relies on imported raw materials, machine tools, and other industrial equipment needed to manufacture advanced weapons.
“Even despite its rich natural resources, Russia still purchases a great deal of raw materials abroad, including rare-earth metals. It also purchases machine tools and other equipment. We have to approach this problem comprehensively,” Ukraine’s Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk said.
The Warsaw Security Forum brings together government officials, international institutions, and security experts from roughly 90 countries each year.
Previously, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate revealed new details about Russia’s Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile, identifying 58 Russian companies involved in its production, 22 of which remain outside international sanctions.

Iran sets out defense modernization plans as officials stress deterrence and domestic arms productio
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Iran sets out defense modernization plans as officials stress deterrence and domestic arms productio
TEHRAN — Iran is seeking to accelerate the modernization of its armed forces, expand domestic weapons production and strengthen its defense-industrial infrastructure, according to plans presented by defense minister nominee Mehrdad Akhlaqi, as senior military officials stress the importance of deterrence and preparedness amid continued tensions with the United States and Israel.
Addressing the Iranian Parliament, Akhlaqi outlined six-month and 22-month implementation programs designed to build on existing defense initiatives while adapting them to changing technological and operational requirements. His priorities include expanding the production and supply of military equipment, upgrading advanced weapons systems, developing missile and air defense capabilities, and reinforcing cyber infrastructure.
The proposed agenda places particular emphasis on domestic scientific and industrial capacity, with greater participation by private companies and knowledge-based firms expected to help accelerate research, improve production capabilities and meet the Armed Forces’ requirements.
The plans come as senior commanders of Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) have reiterated their emphasis on indigenous defense capabilities, describing sustained weapons production and technological development as essential to military preparedness and deterrence.
In a separate meeting with Akhlaqi, IRGC Commander Major General Ahmad Vahidi stressed the strategic importance of maintaining Iran’s defense production chains and expanding cooperation between the Armed Forces’ operational and industrial sectors.
Together, the statements outline a defense agenda centered on technological development, domestic manufacturing, and military readiness, while reflecting Tehran’s stated position that its capabilities are intended to deter aggression and enable a forceful response to any renewed attack.
A timetable for military modernization
Presenting his plans to parliament, Akhlaqi said the Defense Ministry would continue existing programs with appropriate revisions while introducing six-month and 22-month implementation frameworks to advance its objectives.
He identified the production and supply of weapons required by the Armed Forces as a central priority, emphasizing the need to mobilize the country’s industrial, scientific and technological resources.
The nominee also highlighted targeted research projects capable of producing practical results in the near term. He said cooperation with domestic industries, private-sector companies and knowledge-based firms could accelerate technological development, increase production capacity and improve the military’s ability to respond to operational requirements.
Maintaining combat readiness, Akhlaqi said, would require the continuous upgrading of advanced weapons and equipment, the expansion of intelligent systems and investment in emerging fields of warfare.
He called for defense planning and force architecture to evolve alongside technological advances and regular assessments of operational needs. The broader objective, according to his presentation, is to align military requirements with the country’s scientific and industrial capabilities while improving the efficiency of defense-related investment.
Missile capabilities are another priority. Akhlaqi said Iran’s missile capacity should be strengthened in line with the level of regional threats.
His proposed program also includes strengthening air defense, developing ground combat capabilities, pursuing the development of a heavy multirole fighter aircraft and reinforcing cyber infrastructure.
The nominee called for the reconstruction and modernization of defense facilities and infrastructure, stressing that commanders’ assessments should be consolidated to establish priorities and guide the allocation of resources.
IRGC head stresses domestic production and industrial coordination
In a meeting with Akhlaqi, IRGC Commander Major General Ahmad Vahidi emphasized the contribution of specialists and employees in Iran’s defense industries during ‘the US-Israeli wars of aggression.’
Vahidi said domestic knowledge, the determination of technical specialists and the continuity of defense equipment production were essential to maintaining the Armed Forces’ readiness and countering potential threats.
He called for the fuller use of national scientific and industrial capabilities, arguing that closer coordination between operational units and defense manufacturers could strengthen military preparedness and deterrence.
Vahidi also stressed the need to develop strategic technologies, reinforce production infrastructure and mobilize domestic expertise to address both current and future defense requirements.
Akhlaqi, for his part, said the Defense Ministry was prepared to prioritize support for the Armed Forces while ensuring the continuity of production chains and advancing technological development, particularly in strategic weaponry.
He also highlighted the potential for expanded cooperation between the ministry’s industrial sectors and corresponding IRGC divisions in the design, manufacture, supply, and maintenance of military equipment.
IRGC Navy commander issues warning over Strait of Hormuz
IRGC Navy Commander Rear Admiral Ali Ozmaei, in his first televised interview, challenged US forces to approach the waterway if Washington believed the strait was open and secure.
“If the Americans think the Strait of Hormuz is open, let them come closer. We are impatient to sink American warships,” Ozmaei said.
He stated that a US warship worth $13 billion had been rendered ineffective and had moved approximately 700 kilometers away from the strait because it did not dare approach the waterway.
“We are waiting for US warships to approach the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz so we can sink them. We are counting down every moment until this happens,” he added.
Ozmaei also accused the United States and its regional partners of imposing a media blackout to prevent international audiences from learning about vessels penalized for violating rules governing passage through the strait.
He said the IRGC Navy had released footage of two incidents involving vessels that had violated the rules and faced consequences.
IRGC spokesman says Iran has acquired more advanced weapons
IRGC spokesperson Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi has separately said Iran has acquired substantially more advanced weapons since the 40-day war of aggression imposed by the United States and Israel, arguing that the country’s military capabilities have continued to develop since the conflict.
Mohebbi described a renewed US attack as an illogical course of action but said the possibility could not be ruled out. He suggested that the Trump administration might seek a military or political achievement ahead of the US midterm elections.
He warned that Iran was prepared to respond forcefully to any renewed aggression.
“This time, the consequences for the US will be far more painful,” Mohebbi said.
According to the IRGC spokesperson, Iran relied mainly on older-generation weapons during the 40-day conflict but has since gained access to considerably more advanced weaponry.
Mohebbi also criticized US media coverage of foreign military campaigns, arguing that mainstream outlets were concealing the realities and consequences of military aggression from the American public.
He rejected allegations by US officials that divisions within Iran’s leadership were undermining coordination among the country’s authorities. Describing those allegations as “completely false,” he said they were intended to justify Washington’s failures during the war.
The spokesperson’s remarks reinforce the message conveyed by Akhlaqi’s proposed plans: that military modernization and the development of domestic weapons production remain central priorities following the conflict.
A World War, in the view of the global public
Brigadier General Yadollah Javani, deputy for political affairs of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), also underscored the full combat readiness of the Iranian Armed Forces to counter potential threats, saying any miscalculation by the enemy will prompt a crushing response.
Speaking at the Administrative Council of the northern province of Golestan on Wednesday, General Javani addressed the regional and global consequences of the US-Israeli aggression, stating that the war imposed on Iran is not labeled a world war, but global public opinion considers it one.
He explained that the US-Israeli war on Iran had the same nature and characteristics as World Wars I and II, which impacted the global order, the geometry of power, and the shifting power equation—creating new realities.
Referring to Iran's evolving capabilities, he said new technologies, weaponry, and equipment have bolstered the country's defense—a reason the US was forced to move its aircraft carriers some 700 to 800 kilometers away. "Today, the Persian Gulf region—which previously hosted over 100 military vessels and warships—is free of foreign military forces."
Iran will dictate terms for ending the war
The advisor to the chief commander of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC), Brigadier General Ramezan Sharif, has also argued that Iran’s geopolitical position and military response would ultimately compel the United States to accept conditions set by the Islamic Republic to end the war.
Speaking in Mashhad on Wednesday in a book unveiling ceremony in Razavi Khorasan Province, Sharif said there was no prospect of a US victory in a war against Iran.
He praised the performance of the Iranian Armed Forces in confronting US-Israeli aggression and said Washington had mobilized its regional and European resources to weaken the Islamic Republic.
According to Sharif, those efforts had failed to achieve their objectives.
He also argued that the United States and Israel had miscalculated the consequences of targeting Iran’s senior leadership and military commanders, believing that such actions could bring about the collapse of the Islamic Republic or overturn the Islamic Revolution, which is approaching its 48th anniversary.
Sharif said the two countries had assumed direct responsibility for the confrontation after their regional allies proved unable to carry out the objectives expected of them. He portrayed Iran’s response as a demonstration of the country’s strategic resilience and its ability to challenge a militarily superior adversary.
The IRGC adviser further stated that Iran’s defense operations had neutralized US capabilities at 17 bases surrounding the country, and the outcome was one that Washington had not anticipated.

“Our Defense Forces received no warning about these restrictions, and this led to the disruption of a number of missions. It is obvious that this decision cannot be a coincidence and is connected to the current political situation.”
The new limit means the service can no longer be used on jet-powered drones or other high-speed unmanned aircraft.
Georgy Trishkin, a missile-launch analyst and commentator on spaceflight and rocketry, told The Insider that standard Starlink service on drones traveling faster than 160 kph had stopped working in 2025, while StarShield continued to function until Oct. 13.
“Military StarShield is physically a different system and a different service. It is available only to defense and government customers. Starlink stopped working under these conditions last year and never worked on Russian territory in the first place. Drones using it would lose their connection when crossing zones near the border and switch to other methods, including mobile networks using Russian SIM cards.
The decision was not made by SpaceX, but by the customer in the United States [meaning the Pentagon — The Insider]. That does not absolve the company of responsibility, but it is important to understand who made the decision and which service it concerned.”
Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski also commented on the move.
“Hey, Elon Musk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you,” he wrote on Musk’s X platform.
A day earlier, on Oct. 13, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with NPR that the Trump administration had threatened to stop sharing intelligence with Kyiv unless Ukrainian forces halted long-range drone strikes on oil refineries inside Russia.

Student protests in Albania turn violent as demonstrators clash with police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:21:21 UTC
02:21:21 KST

Tens of thousands of students have taken to the streets of Tirana, the Albanian capital, setting alight a government building and two banks and hurling stones at police during a protest over rising education costs and corruption.
Police responded with water cannon and teargas to disperse protesters who started a fire at the ministry of education building, overturned bins and smashed the fronts of local businesses. A branch of Raiffeisen Bank near the education ministry also caught fire.
The protests are the most violent outburst yet against Edi Rama, the prime minister, who won a fourth term in office in May last year but has since faced growing discontent at perceived graft surrounding top officials. Protesters also dismiss opposition figures as unpalatable alternatives.
The unrest caps a summer of peaceful protests against Rama, triggered by the proposed development of a luxury resort along Albania’s pristine southern coast backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, which has been caught up in legal disputes.
“This is a revolution. We are tired of peaceful protests. We will not stop until Rama resigns,” said Lora, a student who declined to give her last name as she threw rocks at the police.
Others chanted “resignation” and “police of crime”.
Student organisers said the protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, a lack of financial support and employment prospects after graduation.
The unrest is part of a broader wave of student activism sweeping Europe over education and living conditions. In France, high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education.
Albanian media reported that Wednesday’s protests had spread to universities at Elbasan and Shkodër.
The government condemned the violence.
Albana Koçiu, the deputy prime minister of Albania, said on Facebook: “Protesting is a legitimate right, but it cannot be used as an excuse for violence, city destruction or ugly fighting in the middle of the road. I call on students and every honest citizen who believes in the right to protest: distance yourself from violence and vandalism!”
The police issued a statement calling for calm. “Any person who uses violence, burns or destroys property, or attacks police officers, bears individual responsibility and will face the law, in accordance with the offences committed,” they said.
Meanwhile, the EU, which the Balkan nation aspires to join, voiced concern over what it called the “violent escalation at the protest in Tirana”.
A statement by the EU delegation in Tirana said: “We take note of the allegations of excessive violence by the police against protesters and journalists,”
Calling for a prompt investigation, the delegation encouraged “all sides to de-escalate the tension”.
