Cooperation Project on Agricultural Innovation Launched in Colombian Regions
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:20:54 CEST
02:20:54 KST

In the presence of the Italian Ambassador to Colombia, Giancarlo Maria Curcio, the LabInnova Latin America 2026 project was launched in Bogotá. Promoted by the International Italian-Latin American Organization (IILA) and the Italian Trade Agency (ICE), the project is supported by the Italian Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation.
                                    
The initiative involves Colombian agri-food companies—particularly those in the fruit and vegetable sector—based in four departments in the country’s central region and in Cauca (in the southwest). These companies will participate in a knowledge exchange with Italian counterparts and experts, with the aim of improving internal innovation and production processes and fostering technology transfer, all with a view to strengthening trade relations between Bogotá and Rome.
                                    
“Italy and Colombia continue to strengthen their ties. We are complementary nations: Italy offers a high level of industrialization and technology, while Colombia boasts a highly significant agricultural sector,” observed Ambassador Curcio, also noting the agricultural support and development initiatives currently underway in various areas of the country through the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS).
                                    
“We continue to work to ensure that Italy and Colombia remain united and prosper together in their respective roles,” the diplomat stated during the event held at the “Casa del Huila” headquarters; the department of Huila, along with Boyacá, Cundinamarca, Tolima, and Cauca, is among those participating in the initiative. Following the presentation, the project will get underway tomorrow in Popayán, the capital of Cauca, with the launch of a training program that will continue through October 17. The program will take place at the Regional Agricultural Center of the SENA (National Learning Service)—the country’s leading public agency for free technical, technological, and complementary training, which is also a partner in the initiative.
                                    
In a message sent from Rome on the occasion of the project’s launch, Giorgio Silli, Secretary General of IILA, described it as an “excellent example of Italian institutional cooperation in the service of innovation and development.” Silli then emphasized that the project aims to enhance the “knowledge and skills” of Colombian entrepreneurs in order to “strengthen innovation and technology transfer processes for SMEs in the agro-industrial sector and foster commercial relationships and opportunities with the Italian market.” 
   “We cannot tackle the major challenges of the agro-industry on our own. We need innovation, cooperation, and partnerships that transcend borders. Italy and Colombia have the opportunity to build a more sustainable future together, and IILA plays a strategic role in this journey,” concluded the IILA Secretary General.

Editorial: Donald Trump is helping Russia win the war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:19:29 UTC
02:19:29 KST

Editorial: Donald Trump is helping Russia win the war
U.S. President Donald Trump in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 13, 2026. (Samuel Corum / Sipa / Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The Kyiv Independent
It's already been said many times that the U.S., under President Donald Trump, was turning its back on Ukraine.
But the past few days show something worse than abandonment: Trump is now actively helping Russia win the war.
Many media and commentators have been far too careful in their phrasing, saying that Trump is "squeezing Ukraine" or putting pressure on it. We all need to do the responsible thing and call it what it is, as ugly as it sounds: Trump is not trying to reach a deal — he is trying to "end the war" by simply helping Russia win.
Since last week, the Trump administration has been in a downward spiral of betraying Ukraine and embarrassing the U.S.
It started when Trump announced that he had reached a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia. By doing so, he went against the sanctions bill he himself had signed less than a month ago, which sought to penalize countries buying energy from Russia.
The deal is not going to help bring down fuel prices for regular Americans, but it sends a tremendously harmful signal: That it's alright to make deals that pump cash into Russia, despite its brutal ongoing invasion of Ukraine.
That move was followed by Trump announcing a surprise energy ceasefire that Kyiv didn't know about. When Russia ignored it and continued to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure, Trump said nothing about it.
It only got worse from there. For the past two nights, Russia has hit Ukrainian cities with ballistic missiles that came without any warning. That is, the early warning alerts that Ukraine typically receives about missile and drone launches from its partners — chiefly, the U.S. While there is no confirmation yet, there is a strong possibility that the U.S. has limited some intelligence data sharing.
If true, it would mean more Ukrainians killed. No warning means there is no time to get to the shelter. At least three people were killed in such an attack in Kyiv last night — civilians in their homes.
Finally, this morning, we learned that Ukraine's military use of Starlink had been restricted without warning, undermining Ukraine's middle-strike capabilities that are critical for its front-line operations against Russia. In the rear, it hurts Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian drones targeting civilians.
This betrayal comes after one of the deadliest weeks for Ukrainian civilians. Last week, Russia killed more than 150 civilians in Ukraine. Just one of the strikes, on a bus stop in Kramatorsk, killed 33 people. In another Russian attack, in Pryluky, three one-year-old children were among the dead.
Most strikingly, Trump has repeatedly condemned Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries — Moscow's largest source of revenue to fund its war effort — but remained silent on Russia's slaughter of Ukrainian children.
The most recent time we found Trump publicly condemning Russian strikes on Ukrainian civilians was in 2025.
While Trump has shown his disdain for Ukraine on many occasions (you will remember the Oval Office episode, surely), his latest cynicism should shock even his most ardent supporters.
But what may come as a surprise to the American president is that giving a boost to Russia’s war effort, while a big help, cannot force Ukrainians to stop fighting. That is not up to the U.S. What is up to it, and to its president, is whether it wants to uphold the values of democracy by supporting a country under siege from its aggressive neighbor that wants to determine its future.
Because helping Russia to win the war won't stop it. It will simply give it the ability to cause more death and more destruction. In other words, it will help prolong the war.
And the danger isn't confined to Ukraine — the rest of Europe is at risk. U.S. intelligence last month warned that Russia could launch a limited attack on a NATO country as early as this fall.
An emboldened Putin makes that more likely. Trump is endangering the security of the entire European continent in an attempt to score short-term political points. It's difficult to name a time when a U.S. president has acted so recklessly on the international stage.
We all need to start calling it what it is:
Trump indeed wants the war to end quickly. He’s just choosing to end it with a Russian victory.

Escalating Yemen conflict cuts off food aid to 800,000 people: UN food agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:17:38 UTC
02:17:38 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Escalating conflict in Yemen has cut off life-saving food assistance to 800,000 people, as insecurity, blocked roads and shifting frontlines severely restrict humanitarian access, the World Food Program (WFP) warned Wednesday.
The UN agency said in a statement that more than 600,000 people in Taiz city, including over 200,000 women and children, are now beyond its reach.
Taiz faces particularly severe food insecurity, with 10 of its 16 districts previously classified at emergency levels. Wheat flour stocks are nearly exhausted, while remaining market supplies could run out soon, WFP warned, calling the situation "alarming."
"This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most," said WFP's Yemen representative El-Khidir Daloum.
Across Yemen, more than 18 million people face acute food insecurity, while 2.2 million children under the age of 5 suffer from acute malnutrition, including 500,000 severely malnourished.
Recent monitoring found 74% of households in accessible areas cannot meet their basic food needs.
WFP also reported that 72 UN personnel remain detained by Houthi authorities, including 37 of its staff.
The agency warned that without additional funding, assistance would be significantly reduced beginning in November.
WFP needs $268 million to sustain food assistance and other humanitarian operations in Yemen through 2027, according to the statement.

Russian drone debris damages 'Cosmogony,' world's largest painting, in Lutsk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:16:00 UTC
02:16:00 KST

Russian drone debris damages 'Cosmogony,' world's largest painting, in Lutsk
According to Ukrinform, the museum announced the incident on its Facebook page.
"Debris from a Russian drone fell on the Korsaks Museum late in the evening of October 13, causing a fire. Emergency Service rescuers arrived promptly, contained the fire, and extinguished it, limiting the extent of the damage," the statement said.
The damaged work was Cosmogony, a large-scale philosophical and artistic project. The canvas covers an area of more than 2,000 square meters and set a national record in Ukraine in 2024.
The project consists of six parts and addresses three questions: Where did we come from? Who are we? What will happen to us? The sixth section, titled "The Future," was partially destroyed.
"War destroys not only what exists today. It destroys what could have emerged tomorrow: human lives, dreams, discoveries, and opportunities. At the same time, the future is not predetermined. We create it through our own decisions and actions," said Viktor Korsak, the museum's founder and the creator of the painting's concept and philosophical vision.
The museum is considering two options: fully restoring the damaged section or preserving the fire damage as a reminder to future generations of the consequences of war.
"Sometimes scars tell us more about history than a restored surface," Korsak remarked.
A final decision will be made after an assessment of the canvas's condition and consultations with the painting's author, artist Petro Antyp, and restoration specialists.
The other exhibition halls and the artworks displayed in them were not damaged. The museum team continues to work on exhibition, educational, and cultural projects.
"We will continue working, creating new projects, and developing Ukrainian art. After all, the future is not something that awaits us. It is something we create today," Korsak emphasized.
As Ukrinform previously reported, on the evening of October 13, debris from a Russian drone fell on the grounds of the Adrenalin City shopping and entertainment center in Lutsk, causing a fire on the roof.

The exercise will include computer-assisted simulation and field training with opposing forces to enhance the capabilities of AFBiH command structures and units in planning and conducting peace support operations.
The ministry described the exercise as the largest and most complex AFBiH exercise in 2026 in terms of scale, organizational complexity and international cooperation, and one of the key priorities for operational capability training and evaluation. ■

KINSHASA, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) shows early signs of slowing, but new hotspots are complicating response efforts, authorities said Wednesday.

The outbreak's epicenter was gradually shifting from Ituri Province, where the epidemic is believed to have first emerged in the country's east, toward neighboring North Kivu Province, Kaseya noted.
Despite the encouraging trend, Kaseya stressed that significant gaps remain in disease surveillance and contact tracing, hampering efforts to break chains of transmission.
International pledges to support the Ebola response have reached 3.045 billion U.S. dollars, up from 1.656 billion dollars in June, figures presented by Kaseya showed. However, only 962.66 million dollars, or 31.6 percent of the total pledged, has been disbursed.
Kaseya also called for greater transparency in the use of the funds.
Declared on May 15, the outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo ebolavirus, is the deadliest ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak worldwide, after the epidemic that struck West Africa between 2014 and 2016.
According to the latest epidemiological report released Wednesday by Congolese health authorities, the DRC had recorded 9,144 confirmed cases, including 4,410 deaths, as of Oct. 12, representing a case fatality rate of 48.2 percent. ■

====================================================================================================

Roundup: Chinese green technologies revitalize South African cement plant
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
01:13:08 CST
02:13:08 KST

DURBAN, South Africa, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- In South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal Province, a cement plant that has operated for more than four decades is taking on a new look.
At the Simuma cement plant, acquired by Huaxin Building Materials Group Co., Ltd. in December 2023, aging equipment is being upgraded, waste heat is being turned into electricity, and electric mining trucks are replacing diesel ones. At the same time, local employees are gaining technical skills through training and hands-on exchanges with Chinese colleagues.
TARGETED UPGRADES
Simuma was previously a major production base of Natal Portland Cement (NPC), one of South Africa's established cement producers. While the plant had an established production system and distribution network, some equipment had been operating for decades, pushing up production costs and limiting efficiency and capacity.
After acquiring NPC, Huaxin made Simuma a key site for technological upgrading and capacity expansion.
"The operations here started in 1984, which is quite a while back. And so it was in dire need to be upgraded, modernized and made efficient," said Simuma Plant Manager Rory Govender. "When Huaxin took over the plant and started the expansion and upgrading, we were very excited. It is something that we wanted for a long time."
Rather than replacing the entire equipment of the plant, Huaxin has focused on targeted upgrades, making use of existing infrastructure while addressing key production bottlenecks.
"We are not simply taking a solution from China and applying it here. We are looking at the existing equipment and the actual conditions in South Africa and carrying out targeted upgrades," said Wang Dongdong, the plant's maintenance manager.
Key facilities, including the preheater tower and clinker cooler, have been upgraded, alongside improvements to the limestone quarry and other parts of the production line, Wang added.
According to Govender, daily clinker output from Kiln 2 has risen from about 1,500 tons to 4,000 tons, while Kiln 1, which has been operating for more than four decades, has increased from about 1,500 tons to 2,200 tons a day.
"The plant now has an annual clinker production capacity of about 1.8 million tons and annual cement production capacity of around 2.5 million tons," said Govender, adding that this gives the plant a much stronger ability to supply the cement market not only in KwaZulu-Natal, but across South Africa.
GREEN TRANSFORMATION
The production-line upgrades have been accompanied by changes in how the plant uses energy.
Cement production is an energy-intensive industrial process that generates substantial amounts of heat. At Simuma, waste heat that would otherwise be lost is now recovered and converted into electricity.
The waste heat recovery system, introduced as part of Huaxin's efforts to improve energy efficiency and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, has allowed the plant to generate part of its own power, Govender said.
"At the moment, around 30 percent of our power is generated internally," Govender said, adding that the system reduces the plant's dependence on the national electricity grid while improving energy efficiency and helping cut emissions.
The green transition has also reached the limestone quarry. Huaxin has introduced electric mining dump trucks using new-energy equipment technologies from China, gradually replacing conventional diesel-powered vehicles.
NPC is the first cement company in South Africa to use electric mining trucks at its quarry, said Govender. "Compared with traditional diesel trucks, the electric trucks reduce operating costs, noise and carbon emissions."
BUILDING SKILLS
The transformation is not only visible in machinery and production figures. It is also changing the skills and career paths of local employees.
Following the acquisition, Huaxin retained the plant's local management structure while sending Chinese technical specialists to work alongside local teams on the plant's expansion and upgrade. On-site guidance, job-specific training and day-to-day technical exchanges have become part of the process.
Eugene Bray, the plant's expansion project manager, said the training had strengthened local employees' technical capabilities and confidence.
The company's mentor-apprentice approach, introduced in 2024, pairs Chinese technical specialists with South African employees and provides opportunities for employees with potential to advance into technical and management positions, he added.
"Chinese experts are paired with local employees according to their different positions," said Lungelo Mthalane, who was paired with Wang as mentor. He has risen from frontline worker to deputy maintenance manager after six years at the plant.
Some local employees have also had opportunities to travel to China and to Huaxin's operations in Tanzania and Zambia for further training and exposure to different production and management practices, he added.
"Through continuous learning, our technical skills and our ability to solve problems ourselves have improved," Mthalane said.
GROWING TOGETHER
Huaxin's investment also offers the opportunity for the surrounding communities to grow together along with the company.
Bray said the expansion and upgrade project created about 800 temporary jobs, benefiting communities within five to 50 kilometers of the plant.
Local contractors and small businesses have also gained new opportunities through their involvement in the project, Bray said. "Local contractors are also able to work very hands-on with the Chinese skills and experience, and they gained from that."
The transformation of Simuma offers a glimpse of how existing industrial assets can be upgraded through new investment and technology rather than replaced entirely.
By combining existing infrastructure and local expertise with Chinese technology, management experience and green solutions, the project is improving productivity while creating opportunities for skills development and local businesses.
For South Africa, which is seeking to revitalize manufacturing and strengthen industrial competitiveness, the experience shows how technological upgrading can help renew traditional industries. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: 84 years on, Doolittle Raiders' descendants and Chinese volunteer researchers honor wartime friendship
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
01:12:54 CST
02:12:54 KST

HANGZHOU, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Holding a photo frame embedded with a fragment of a bomber, Beverly Daigle wiped away tears. The piece of metal came from the B-25 flown by Crew No. 13 of the Doolittle Raid -- the plane her father, Sergeant Robert Bourgeois, served aboard as bombardier.
"Getting a piece of the plane has really touched me," said Daigle, standing beside Zheng Weiyong, vice president of the Quzhou Doolittle Historical Research Association, in whose home the emotional handover took place on Wednesday.
"I'm so thankful for the gentleman who found this. The history is very important. Our journey is very important on both sides."
On April 18, 1942, a group of 16 U.S. bombers carried out a surprise raid on Japan in retaliation for the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor. After the mission, 15 planes heading to a friendly airport in Quzhou in China's Zhejiang Province ran out of fuel and crashed in various localities in east China. Of the 75 airmen aboard, 64 were rescued by the Chinese people.
Their rescue came at a tremendous cost. Some locals were tortured or killed by the Japanese soldiers who came to hunt for the Americans. After the rescue, the airport in Quzhou was subjected to intense bombing by the Japanese, who also waged biological warfare by spreading cholera, plague and other diseases.
In China, the Doolittle story has long been regarded as a symbol of the friendship forged between the Chinese and American peoples during their joint fight against fascism.
All members of Crews No. 13 and No. 14 came down in east China's Jiangxi Province. With help from Chinese civilians and military personnel, they eventually regrouped in Quzhou and arrived safely at the home front. Daigle's father was one of them.
On Tuesday, Daigle and four other representatives of the Children of the Doolittle Raiders arrived in Quzhou.
At the air-raid shelter where her father had once rested, she fell silent. She reached out and touched the shelter's stone wall, where the names of two Doolittle Raiders remained legible after more than 80 years.
"Luckily, they're still here," she said, her fingers tracing the carvings.
Since World War II, and particularly since the 1990s, descendants of the Doolittle Raiders have visited Quzhou repeatedly to trace where their fathers once stayed. In Quzhou, a group of volunteer researchers has worked to preserve this history. They have dug through archives and trekked through mountains and villages to help the Doolittle Raiders' descendants retrace their fathers' footsteps.
Zheng Weiyong is one of them. In his study, a hand-drawn map, 1.2 meters high and 2.4 meters long, records about 20 years of his fieldwork, with more than 100 crash sites and villages where pilots landed marked on it.
Zheng has visited the United States four times at the invitation of surviving Doolittle Raiders and their families. "We need to tell the world clearly how the Chinese rescued them," he said. "If the Chinese don't dig into these good deeds, who will?"
The descendants stood before the map for a long time, trying to read from the markings where their fathers' planes fell, where parachutes drifted, and the difficult routes they took under the protection of Chinese civilians.
"You need to understand the geography of the entire flight route -- where these pilots jumped and where the planes landed," said John Thomas Johnson, son-in-law of John Hilger, commander of Crew No. 14. "Without that geographic information, you can't tell the full story."
The markings on the map helped bring the fragments home. This time, Zheng returned five pieces from Crews No. 13 and No. 14 to the descendants. The fragments are mounted in frames noting the discovery location, finder and date, along with the following text:
"This fragment witnessed the Sino-American joint fight against Japanese militarists. The bravery, humanitarianism and selflessness demonstrated by the American and Chinese people during the Doolittle Raid and the rescue operations will be eternally remembered by posterity."
In return, Johnson Kimberly Jane, granddaughter of commander John Hilger, presented a model plane to the association. The inscription said her grandfather owed his long and fulfilling life to the Chinese people's "courage, kindness, and sacrifice," and that his family would be "forever grateful."
John Thomas Johnson, a journalism professor at the University of San Francisco, said the full story of the Doolittle rescue owes much to the dedication and collaboration of many people in both countries.
He hopes to do more research on the selection, formation and training of the crews after returning to the United States to "add more detail to that aspect of the story."
Hugs were the most common gesture between the descendants and members of the Quzhou research association, suggesting that, after more than 80 years, the bond between the Chinese and American peoples is still going strong.
Before leaving, John Thomas Johnson wrote a line for the journey: "Friendship today and tomorrow." ■

NAIROBI, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Kenya confirmed a second case of the Ebola disease caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which is linked to the first case, with no evidence of wider community transmission, the Ministry of Health said Wednesday.
"Kenya has now recorded two confirmed cases and one death," said Patrick Amoth, director-general for health in Kenya's Ministry of Health.
The patient, a 39-year-old male, is a close family contact of the index patient and was already undergoing mandatory quarantine and daily medical surveillance when he presented with symptoms on Tuesday, health officials said.
After he developed a fever, fatigue and joint pain, the quarantine response team isolated him and collected clinical specimens for laboratory testing.
According to the Ministry of Health, diagnostic evaluations returned matching positive results from both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute-CDC facility, confirming the infection.
"He is now in a designated treatment center where trained teams are giving him supportive care. Because he was already in quarantine, his illness was detected early," the ministry said in a statement issued in Nairobi.
"Early supportive care improves his chances of recovery, and isolating him at the first symptom limits the chance of passing the virus to others. This is the response working as designed," it added.
The latest case comes after Kenya confirmed on Oct. 6 its first case of Ebola linked to the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
The index case, a Kenyan citizen who had resided in the DRC for seven years, recently returned to the country via regional transit routes.
The World Health Organization said the individual had sought medical evaluation at healthcare facilities in the DRC before traveling by road on Oct. 2 through Beni to Kampala, Uganda.
On Oct. 3, he boarded a commercial flight operated by Jambojet to Nairobi, where he initially underwent standard health screening upon arrival at the airport. He was then transported by a family member to Nairobi Hospital, where attending medical personnel immediately placed him in isolation.
Despite receiving supportive care, the patient died on Oct. 5 and was buried the following day in accordance with the country's safe and dignified burial protocols for viral hemorrhagic fevers. ■

Interview: Egyptian young actor hopes Chinese film gives voice to children of war
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
01:12:48 CST
02:12:48 KST

CAIRO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- For Egyptian young actor Omar Sherif, playing Seif in the Chinese film "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East" was more than an acting experience. It was an opportunity to draw attention to the suffering of children caught in war and remind the world that they deserve to live in peace and choose their own futures.
"When I read the script, what touched me the most was how it talked about children caught up in war and showed care for them," Sherif said in a recent interview with Xinhua.
At the time, the war in Gaza was raging, making the story particularly meaningful to him.
"I wanted to play this role to show people that children of war struggle just to survive and live their own lives," he said.
Against the backdrop of continuing conflicts across the Middle East, the film's message carries particular weight. Beyond the destruction and displacement that dominate news coverage, it draws attention to the ordinary needs of children whose lives have been disrupted by violence: food, safety, someone they can trust, and the freedom to decide who they want to become.
"I wish this film makes people care more about war children and stop seeing them as just numbers," he said.
In the film, Seif is a kind-hearted person who sometimes struggles with anger. For Sherif, however, the character's real strength lies not in his ability to fight, but in his capacity to control his anger and prevent it from destroying his future.
The character's needs, the actor said, are universal, transcending nationality, language and political boundaries. His Egyptian background helped him connect emotionally with the story of conflict in the Middle East, even though he had never personally experienced war in Egypt.
Much of his understanding of war came from television and social media. To portray Seif convincingly, he relied on the script and the director's guidance, drawing on his own emotional responses to the suffering he had witnessed from afar.
For Sherif, the film's most moving moment comes when Seif bids farewell to Xu Fu, a character who has become especially important to him.
Having lost his colleagues, Seif faces the departure of one of the few remaining connections in his life. The farewell captures the loneliness and emotional loss that accompany conflict, reminding audiences that the consequences of war extend far beyond physical destruction.
"It was the most emotional scene for me," Sherif recalled, adding that he cried so intensely that it took him some time to return to himself even after the director called "cut."
The experience also left a lasting impression on the young actor personally. After spending months working with the cast and crew in China, he found it difficult to say goodbye to the people with whom he had built close relationships and shared unforgettable memories.
His journey to China had begun long before the film. With Chinese roots on his father's side, he had grown up watching Chinese action films featuring actors such as Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan.
But his first visit to China came when he was barely a teenager, after he was selected for the role from a huge pool of young actors who auditioned for the film.
Preparing for the role required him to learn Chinese and cook in Egypt for three months before continuing his training in China.
"I thought it would be easy to speak Chinese, but it was so hard and required a lot of practice," he said.
Yet the difficulties also brought him closer to the film and the people behind it. Returning to Egypt, he felt that China was no longer simply a country he had known through movies, but a place associated with people and personal memories.
Sherif hopes Seif's story will resonate with audiences far beyond the screen. For him, the character's name carries a final, deeply personal message: Seif means "sword" in Arabic, but he would rather use his hands to cook than to fight.
"I want children to live their lives, become what they want to be and choose their own futures," he said. "I want them to live in peace." ■

Irish novelist Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in Britain over her plans to use her royalties to support Palestine Action, a pro-Palestine group banned as a terrorist organisation in the country, Rooney and her publisher said on Wednesday.
The bestselling author, known for novels including "Normal People" and "Conversations with Friends", has been a vocal supporter of Palestine Action, including after it was proscribed by the British government under terrorism laws last year.
Rooney previously said in a witness statement submitted to London's High Court, in support of a legal challenge over the ban on Palestine Action, that her plans could lead to her books being withdrawn from sale in Britain.
Her publisher Faber said on Wednesday that it had agreed with Rooney that "we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format", though it would sell her works elsewhere.
"Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work," Faber said in a statement.
"To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher."
Rooney said in a statement: "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."
Palestine Action, which had increasingly targeted Israel-linked defence companies, was banned shortly after a June 2025 break-in at the Royal Air Force's Brize Norton base.
Last year, Palestine Action's co-founder Huda Ammori challenged the ban and the High Court ruled in her favour in February, before the Court of Appeal overturned that decision in June. The Supreme Court is due to hear an appeal next month.
More than 3,000 people have since been arrested for holding signs in support of Palestine Action and its proscription has been criticised by civil liberties groups.

Iran, Azerbaijan seek to turn bilateral agreements into concrete action

Iran, Azerbaijan seek to turn bilateral agreements into concrete action
TEHRAN — Iran and the Republic of Azerbaijan are seeking to translate bilateral agreements into practical measures to expand passenger and commercial traffic, improve border cooperation and strengthen coordination in disaster prevention and response, following a visit to Baku by Iranian Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni.
The one-day visit brought Momeni into talks with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and senior officials responsible for interior affairs and emergencies. Discussions focused on implementing agreements reached by the two countries’ presidents and identifying practical ways to deepen cooperation between the neighboring countries.
Expanding passenger and commercial movements and strengthening joint efforts to prevent and respond to emergencies and disasters were among the principal outcomes of the talks.
The visit also highlighted the role of provincial diplomacy, with the governors of Iran’s Gilan and Ardabil provinces presenting proposals and practical recommendations for expanding cooperation with Azerbaijan.
Momeni had traveled to Baku on October 12 at the head of an Iranian delegation. In an interview with Azerbaijan’s Trend news agency, the minister emphasized the importance of implementing existing agreements and said the two sides had agreed to establish joint working groups to follow up on bilateral commitments and address issues of mutual interest.
From political agreements to practical cooperation
During his meeting with Aliyev, Momeni followed up on agreements reached between the presidents of Iran and Azerbaijan, seeking to advance their implementation through closer coordination between the two governments.
The discussions reflected a shared interest in strengthening cooperation at international, regional, national and border levels. Economic and trade relations, security and border management featured prominently in the agenda, alongside cooperation between the two countries’ interior ministries.
In his interview with Trend, Momeni described relations between Tehran and Baku as rooted in shared history, culture, religion and social interests. He said these common bonds provided a solid foundation for further developing bilateral ties.
The minister also noted that relations had moved in a positive direction over the preceding two years, citing constructive engagement between the two presidents as an important factor in advancing cooperation. He described the talks in Baku as constructive and stressed that the implementation of agreements, rather than the conclusion of additional commitments alone, was a key objective of the visit.
The planned joint working groups are intended to provide a mechanism for following up on commitments, addressing outstanding issues, and identifying further opportunities for cooperation.
Passenger traffic, trade and border management
Facilitating passenger and commercial traffic was among the central priorities discussed during Momeni’s visit. Closer coordination between border authorities and relevant government agencies could help improve cross-border movement and support economic and commercial exchanges between the two countries.
The talks with Azerbaijan’s minister responsible for emergencies also addressed security and border cooperation, alongside efforts to improve the prevention of and response to disasters and emergencies.
These areas of cooperation fall within the responsibilities of the two countries’ interior ministries and have direct implications for border communities, travelers, businesses and the management of cross-border emergencies.
The discussions also underscored the importance of maintaining coordination at several levels of government. While presidential agreements establish the political direction of bilateral relations, their implementation depends on practical arrangements among ministries, border authorities and provincial administrations.
Provincial diplomacy opens additional avenues
The participation of the governors of Gilan and Ardabil added a regional dimension to the visit.
The two governors presented proposals and operational recommendations aimed at expanding cooperation with Azerbaijan, highlighting the potential contribution of provincial authorities to advancing bilateral ties.
Regional engagement can complement national-level agreements by identifying practical areas for cooperation and facilitating coordination between local administrations. In this context, provincial diplomacy was presented as an additional channel for translating political commitments into concrete initiatives.
For Iran and Azerbaijan, closer engagement between provincial authorities and central government institutions offers a way to pursue cooperation across multiple levels while maintaining coordination with national priorities.
A focus on implementation
Momeni’s visit comes as Tehran and Baku seek to consolidate bilateral relations through more systematic follow-up on existing agreements.
The Iranian interior minister’s remarks to Trend, as reported by Tehran Times, placed particular emphasis on the implementation of commitments and the establishment of joint working groups. The discussions in Baku also highlighted the importance of economic and trade cooperation, border management, passenger movements and disaster response.
The immediate significance of the visit lies in its focus on practical implementation. Expanding cooperation will require the relevant institutions on both sides to follow up on the proposals discussed, coordinate their responsibilities and develop workable arrangements in areas of mutual interest.
By combining high-level political consultations with ministerial coordination and provincial engagement, Iran and Azerbaijan are seeking to give their bilateral agreements a more practical dimension and strengthen cooperation between the two neighboring countries.

The scope of the proposed changes remains unclear. Their eventual effect will depend on the final wording approved by lawmakers and how the legislation is implemented.

Around 40% of accounts amplifying Mario Nawfal’s X posts show bot-like signals, CAM study shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:04:26 UTC
02:04:26 KST

Around 40% of the unique accounts amplifying the most-shared posts by news aggregator Mario Nawfal exhibit strong signals of being bots, fake profiles, or inauthentic accounts, according to a study by the Antisemitism Research Center of the Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM).
The study, released on Tuesday, is titled “Bot-Like Amplification on X: Findings from CAM’s Study of the @MarioNawfal Amplifier Network,” and was conducted between August 29 and October 12, analyzing 10,015 unique X/Twitter accounts that amplified 230 of the most-shared original posts published by Nawfal.
Nawfal is a Lebanese-Australian entrepreneur, business influencer, podcast host, and political commentator who co-founded NFT Technologies and serves as CEO and founder of IBC Group.
Nawfal runs a news-aggregation account on the platform with roughly 3.95 million followers. Using public data from the official X API, 4,054 of these accounts showed strong bot-like signals, the report stated.
Nawfal accused of spreading hateful narratives about Ukraine, Israel
The analysis said that, “Nawfal’s team does not vet posts for accuracy, and since 2025 he has given long-form, largely unchallenged platforms to the Russian foreign minister and the president of Belarus, among other heads of state.”
The report added that “his content leans pro-Russian and hostile to Israel,” and noted that Conspiracy Watch describes him as “spreading false and hateful narratives about Ukraine, Jews and Israel.”
The report addressed the reach of the account, stating that “Elon Musk interacts with the account almost daily, regularly pushing its posts to millions of views.”
Combined with an amplifier network where roughly two in every five accounts behave like automated or fake profiles, this dynamic created “a ready-made distribution system that can push unverified claims and state-aligned narratives, including against Israel, to millions of users while appearing to reflect genuine public interest.”
The report noted that coinciding with the timing of the study, between October 8 and 11, Ukrainian drones struck three Yandex data centers in Russia, and Cloudflare radar showed automated traffic from Yandex’s network dropped by roughly 94%.
The report said that simultaneously, Israeli observers reported that accounts posting aggressive political comments in Russian and Hebrew fell silent, occurring ahead of Israel’s October 27 election and against a documented record of Russian bot operations targeting Jewish and Israeli audiences.
To evaluate the accounts, researchers used CAM’s detection model, known as X model v1.4.0, which measures each account against 32 signals across account behavior, profile characteristics, coordination patterns, and language.
The model is designed to ensure that “post content and ideology are not inputs, so an account is never scored as a bot for what it says.”
Bot-like activity differs from human-run account activity
Furthermore, the report noted that “any one measurable human behavior, such as original varied text, real conversations, or a daily sleep gap, pulls a borderline account out of the bot-like group.”
The signals of bot-like activity include specific automated patterns such as high posting rates and activity bursts, posting during odd hours, repetitive or duplicate text, default or placeholder avatars, digit-suffixed handles, abnormal follower patterns, and generic or repetitive replies.
Illustrating these behaviors, the report highlighted examples such as an account that accumulated 105,800 posts since October 2025 at a rate of about 280 posts a day using a placeholder avatar, another with 40,200 posts since April 2026 using a default avatar, and accounts created recently with minimal followers maintaining heavy, automated posting volumes.
Out of the 10,015 accounts evaluated in the final audit, 4,054 accounts (40.5%) displayed strong bot-like signals, 244 accounts (2.4%) showed moderate bot-like signals, 3,460 accounts (34.5%) exhibited some inauthentic signals without bot-like behavior, and 2,240 accounts (22.4%) were consistent with human activity.
The data also revealed that bot-like signals increase with user loyalty, rising to 54.6% among accounts that amplified three or more of the sampled posts.
The report also stated that “cross-account tests found a dense core of repeat amplifiers but no evidence of a centrally operated network: no copy-paste text across accounts, no sustained sub-minute synchronized reposting, and no clusters of accounts created in batches.”
Instead, the pattern indicated “a loyal, heavy-reposting audience in which a large share of accounts behave like automated ones.”
Pointing out that X’s authenticity policy prohibits “any activity that attempts to manipulate our platform or disrupt our services through inauthentic accounts, behaviors or content,” and that its platform manipulation policy forbids artificial amplification, CAM argued that enforcement is not keeping pace with platform rules.
CAM is calling on X to apply its platform manipulation policy to amplifier networks around high-reach accounts and to grant independent researchers necessary data access.

Cairo ‘not serious’ about joining Mecca pact, offer to help Saudis is symbolic, expert tells ‘Post’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:03:58 UTC
02:03:58 KST

Cairo has no real intention of joining the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement and its offer to send support to Riyadh, though significant, is symbolic and unlikely to be called upon, Jonathan Hessen, a senior fellow at the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security (JISS), told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.
His comments came a day after Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said in an interview with Bloomberg on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting that Egypt was both considering joining the pact and willing to provide whatever support Riyadh requested in its ongoing war against the Houthis.
“Whatever is being asked by the Saudis, of course we will respond,” Abdelatty said. “Without any reservation, we are providing all kinds of support.”
Hessen explained that on the same day Cairo said it was considering the pact, the defense ministers of Cyprus and Greece held a trilateral meeting in Cairo with their Egyptian counterpart, which “does not necessarily bode well for the Turkish narrative that Egypt would soon join.”
Each Mecca pact member focused on combating specific power
Beyond the issue of Cairo navigating the conflict between Cyprus and the Turkish occupation, Hessen highlighted that each member of the Mecca pact had a power they were fixated on, motivating their membership. For Saudi Arabia, it is the Houthis; for Pakistan, it is India and Iran; and for Turkey, it is Israel.
Notably, Article 6 of the 1979 Egypt-Israel Peace Treaty requires Cairo to carry out the peace terms unconditionally, regardless of outside political pressures or external treaties, and restricts it from signing future international agreements that contradict or undermine the peace treaty.
Under the Mecca agreement, an attack on one country must be considered an attack on all, which could potentially pave the way for future complications given the state of Ankara-Jerusalem relations, as explained in an analysis by Institute for National Security Studies senior researcher Ofir Winter.
“It’s about strategic autonomy. On the one hand, it’s about hedging against the US-based security architecture in the region. More importantly, it’s about having an integrated military-industrial base that can address deficiencies in the West’s ability to shore up support for these countries, particularly Saudi Arabia and Turkey,” Hessen said.
“I do not think we will see a significant alliance emerge between Turkey and Saudi Arabia. I believe this is a form of alignment aimed at deterrence, with no real intention of implementing long-term strategic goals that could involve deploying entire military divisions to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. I just don’t see that happening.”
Egypt preoccupied with other challenges
Though he maintained such regional alliances could materialize in the distant future, he maintained Egypt was too preoccupied with other challenges to focus on supporting Riyadh.
“We will not see a reenactment of the 1950s and 1960s, when Egypt joined Saudi Arabia in the fight in Yemen. This is a new reality in which Egypt sees a whole host of challenges surrounding it,” he said, noting the issues posed by the Muslim Brotherhood, tribal tensions, and disagreements with Ethiopia over the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, which Ethiopia built on the Blue Nile River, potentially threatening water supply.
With conflict-rife Sudan sharing a border with Egypt, Hessen reasoned that Cairo’s plate was also simply too full to accept any support that would require significant resources being sent abroad.
However, he admitted that it was in Egypt’s interest to ensure the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains as open as possible, given its potential to impact the Suez Canal, which is now just starting to recover after the Houthis began targeting Red Sea shipping in 2023.
“They’re talking about a net loss of some $20 billion resulting from Houthi belligerence, which has disrupted freedom of navigation through that very important strategic strait,” he said. “While the Saudis have asked for Egyptian support, and we saw MBS [Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman Al Saud] travel to Cairo to meet with President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on September 15 – despite the joint statement issued at the time and Egypt’s pledges to stand by Saudi Arabia as a founding member of the Saudi-led naval operation to ensure freedom of navigation through the Red Sea and the adjacent strategic waterways – Egypt has yet to send any naval assets in that direction.”

A fatwa (a legal ruling on a point of Islamic law) against buying olive products from settlers was issued by the grand mufti of Jerusalem and the Palestinian Territories and head of the Supreme Fatwa Council, Sheikh Muhammad Ahmad Hussein, in response to the rise of settler attacks on the olive industry.
The legal ruling was given on Tuesday in response to escalating settler violence, specifically against olive trees this harvest season, Hussein’s office published.
“The basic principle is the prohibition of buying something stolen, because its seller does not own it, nor does he have the right to dispose of it; Buying it encourages theft, cooperates in sin and aggression, and endorses wrongdoing,” Hussein said.
“The sin is magnified if buying stolen goods encourages the enemies to seize the lands of the Palestinians, plunder their resources, and displace their people from them.”
Based on this ruling, the Grand Mufti insisted it was forbidden to purchase olive products “stolen from Palestinian trees and sold by settlers, due to the great evils involved.”
Olives are the backbone of Palestinian agriculture
“Among these evils is that it empowers the usurping occupier of our land, which necessitates concerted official and popular efforts to reject the sale and purchase of usurped and stolen goods,” he said.
His ruling came weeks after Israeli military bulldozers allegedly bulldozed olive groves near Ramallah.
Though the IDF has not issued a statement on the alleged destruction of the groves, the military has previously cited the need to clear land of olive trees to prevent security threats or ambushes on troops.
The olive harvest usually begins in the first week of October. Olives are the backbone of Palestinian agriculture, a sector that accounts for around 8% of GDP and more than 60,000 jobs, according to the Palestinian Authority’s Agriculture Ministry.
It has also reported that more than 45,000 trees, including more than 26,000 olive trees, were cut down or damaged across the West Bank during the first half of 2026.
The National has also reported that Palestinian farmers have been killed in recent weeks by extremist settlers, including an individual named by the Palestinian Health Ministry as 44-year-old Ali Hassan Yusor al-Bazzari.
Notably, the official account for the Palestinian Authority deleted an AI-generated video showing multiple Israeli bulldozers destroying an olive grove, and the images have been shared widely across pro-Palestinian social media accounts.

Kenya’s health ministry confirms second Ebola case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:03:19 UTC
02:03:19 KST

Kenya’s Health Ministry confirms second Ebola case
A relative of the first case, 39-year-old man’s infection raises concerns of a cross-border spread.
Kenya has reported a second Ebola infection, about a week after confirming its first-ever case of the disease when a citizen who had been living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) travelled to Kenya and died two days later at a Nairobi hospital.
The second patient, a 39-year-old man who is a close family member of the first case, fell ill on Tuesday and was already in quarantine when he came down with symptoms of fever, fatigue and joint pain, the Ministry of Health said in a statement Wednesday.
‘Leave Uganda out’
Last week’s case raised concerns about deficiencies in border screening systems in the region after the patient drove from the DRC to Uganda and flew to Nairobi from there.
Given the closure of the border between the DRC and Uganda since May because of the outbreak of the virus, it is not clear how he was able to enter the country.
Alan Kasujja, executive director of the Ugandan government’s media centre, questioned how Kenya allowed the man to enter via its airport.
“Leave Uganda out of this conversation. We don’t have Ebola here,” he wrote on X.
When asked how the patient was able to travel through three countries undetected, Kenya’s Director-General for Health Patrick Amoth said last week that a meeting was scheduled with officials from the DRC and Uganda and the Africa CDC to investigate.
Stepped-up response
Kenya has intensified its national response to the disease since the country recorded the first case. At the time, Kenya traced everyone who came in contact with the patient and reported at least 57 people, with 10 immediately quarantined, Health Minister Aden Duale told journalists on October 7.
Kenya is the fourth country to record a case linked to the Ebola epidemic in the DRC, the second-largest on record globally with more than 9,000 cases and more than 4,000 deaths.
Uganda reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in the year but was declared Ebola-free in August. A doctor who returned to France in June from the DRC tested positive, but there was no further spread of the virus.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected people, whether living or dead. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding.
The second patient is currently at a designated treatment centre, where he is receiving the appropriate care, the Health Ministry said. It will continue to share information on his progress, the ministry added.

Ukraine accuses US of helping Russia as Starlink restrictions disrupt drone attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:02:55 UTC
02:02:55 KST

Senior Ukrainian officials accused the United States on Wednesday of imposing restrictions on Kyiv's ability to use the Starlink satellite network, owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, for military operations in its defense against Russia's invasion. The satellite communications network is critical to the Ukrainian military, and officials in Kyiv now report restrictions on its use at high speeds, disrupting drone attacks against Russian forces, among other operations.
Musk and his company have not commented on the allegations, which come amid intense pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump, a close ally of Musk, on Kyiv to halt its attacks on oil facilities deep inside Russia. According to reports, Trump has even threatened to suspend intelligence assistance or weapons deliveries to Ukraine.
Musk allowed Ukrainian forces to use Starlink's internet satellites in the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, the communications and navigation capabilities they provide have become critical on the battlefield.
Starlink is also considered more resistant to electronic jamming, making it useful for drone attacks carried out by Kyiv, particularly in Russian-held areas of eastern and southern Ukraine. According to Reuters, Ukrainian drones do not use Starlink when entering Russian territory, relying instead on other communications systems.
But senior Ukrainian officials now say restrictions on military use of Starlink are severely hampering Ukrainian operations, particularly along the front lines. The New York Times reported that officials in Kyiv were stunned by the restrictions.
Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky, said Wednesday morning that no advance warning was given before the restrictions were imposed, disrupting several "missions."
According to Beskrestnov, the restrictions cut off access to the military version of the service at speeds exceeding 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph). He added that Starlink is also crucial to air defense systems Kyiv is using to intercept the fast jet-powered drones Russia has begun deploying in attacks on Ukrainian cities in recent months. These faster drones are more difficult to intercept.
Beskrestnov suggested the move was deliberate. "It is clear that this action cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation," he said.
Ukraine's military said the restrictions had also caused disconnections during drone flights at lower speeds of 110 to 120 kilometers per hour (68 to 75 mph).
"The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," said the 7th Rapid Response Corps, a Ukrainian air force unit operating in the country's southeast.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry also told Reuters that the restrictions significantly complicate logistics and the operation of several types of drones.
The Starlink restrictions come alongside allegations made in recent days by Zelensky and his aides that Kyiv had, on several occasions, failed to receive advance warnings from Western allies about Russian missile attacks.
Western intelligence is also critical to Kyiv's preparations for such attacks, and no warnings were issued in the Ukrainian capital on either of the past two nights when Russian missiles were launched toward the city.
According to the Ukrainian air force, Russia launched another 39 ballistic and cruise missiles overnight Tuesday into Wednesday, along with 128 drones. Only four missiles and 115 drones were intercepted.
At least four people were killed and about 20 others wounded in the overnight attack on Kyiv. Two other civilians were killed in the Dnipropetrovsk region and a third was killed in the Zaporizhzhia region.
"A Russian ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. Once again, no early warning from our partners," Zelensky said Wednesday morning.
A U.S. official told Agence France-Presse that Washington "has not changed its policy on intel-sharing" with Ukraine. However, a senior official in Kyiv told the news agency that the United States had threatened to suspend intelligence assistance unless Ukraine stopped attacking Russian oil refineries.
According to the Ukrainian official, Washington had in fact failed to warn Kyiv about ballistic missile launches on two occasions.
"And on top of that they've throttled Starlink speeds," the Ukrainian official said on condition of anonymity. "It's obvious they [the United States] are helping Russia for some reason."
Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries, arguing that they have caused a surge in global diesel prices. Experts, however, say the war in Iran is the main reason for the increase, which is hurting Republicans' chances of retaining control of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections.
After stunning Kyiv and its European allies by lifting sanctions on Russia late last week to allow it to export diesel to global markets, Trump also announced an "energy ceasefire" on Sunday, supposedly with the agreement of both sides. In reality, however, no such agreement had been reached.
Zelensky revealed Tuesday that Ukraine had indeed suspended its attacks on Russian oil facilities for two days, but said Russia had continued attacking energy facilities in Ukraine throughout that period.
He said the latest overnight strikes also targeted Ukrainian energy infrastructure, particularly in the Kyiv and Kharkiv regions, leaving 600,000 people without electricity.
"We ask America and everyone in the world who does not close their eyes to reality to react and react harshly. Russia missed the opportunity for de-escalation and clearly chose to continue its insane war of destruction," Zelenskyy said following the overnight Russian attack.
Zelenskyy called on Trump to renew pressure on Moscow, invoking the approach of former Republican President Ronald Reagan. "Peace can only come through strength, and we ask America to remember this principle of Reagan's," he said.

Families of Iran's terror victims call on Pakistan to act against militants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:02:10 UTC
02:02:10 KST

Families of Iran's terror victims call on Pakistan to act against militants
TEHRAN — Families representing Iran's 23,000 victims of terrorism have sent an open letter to the government of Pakistan urging decisive action against terrorist groups operating along the southeastern border, following a recent escalation of attacks in Sistan and Baluchestan Province.
The letter, issued Tuesday by the Habilian Foundation, which represents families of terror victims in Iran, specifically names the Takfiri group Jaish al-Adl, now operating under the title People's Strugglers Front. It accuses the group of exploiting border conditions to move freely into Pakistan, reside and find shelter in some areas.
Such a sustained pattern, the families wrote, could not occur without the knowledge of some local and central officials in Pakistan, citing Pakistani media reports and interviews with members of the groups.
The letter frames the issue not only as political and human rights concern but as a matter of legal obligations. It cites the Island of Palmas arbitration of 1928 and the International Court of Justice ruling in the Corfu Channel case of 1949 on the duty of states not to knowingly allow their territory to be used against the rights of other states.
It also invokes U.N. Security Council Resolution 1373 (2001), adopted under Chapter VII and binding on all members under Article 25 of the U.N. Charter, which requires states to refrain from supporting terrorists, deny them safe haven, prevent use of territory against other states, bring perpetrators to justice and ensure effective border controls, as well as to exchange operational information and cooperate bilaterally. It further cites Resolution 1566 (2004) on full cooperation with victim states and the principle of extradite or prosecute.
The families also refer to the General Assembly's 1970 Friendly Relations Declaration, its 1994 Declaration on Measures to Eliminate Terrorism and its 2006 Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy, while distinguishing those instruments from binding Council decisions.
On bilateral frameworks, the letter cites the 1960 Iran-Pakistan border administration agreement, the 1960 extradition treaty noted in the April 24, 2024 joint statement, and that statement's pledges on cooperation against terrorism, hostage-taking and kidnapping.
The families, acknowledging these are duties of due diligence rather than absolute guarantees, say the continued, open movement of militants is incompatible with any reasonable standard of care. They call on Islamabad to dismantle safe havens, secure the border, share intelligence, prosecute or, where treaty conditions are met, extradite suspects, establish a joint security and judicial mechanism, issue a formal written response, and create a permanent channel to receive documents from victims' families and inform them of proceedings.
The letter stresses that Iran-Pakistan ties have been uniquely fraternal since Pakistan's independence and warns that terrorists seek to undermine that bond.

Trump was ready to offer Ukraine enhanced security guarantees before the diesel deal with Putin - media
Kyiv • UNN
The President of the United States was ready to offer Ukraine expanded security guarantees. The talks reached an impasse over territorial concessions and a deal with Putin regarding diesel.
US President Donald Trump was ready to offer Ukraine expanded security guarantees as part of a new peace plan. However, the territorial issue brought the negotiations to a deadlock, UNN reports, citing The Telegraph.
In addition, further dialogue became impossible after the unexpected agreement between the American leader and Russian dictator vladimir putin on easing restrictions on the export of Russian diesel fuel
Details
According to the publication, on October 9, during six-hour negotiations in Miami, the US president’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed an updated plan to end the Russian-Ukrainian war with representatives of Ukraine and European countries. One of the key issues at the meeting was providing Kyiv with enhanced security guarantees that would prevent another Russian invasion.
In particular, the American side made it clear that Trump was prepared to consider more extensive security commitments than those discussed previously. This involved potentially expanding support for Ukraine beyond the patrolling of its airspace by American aircraft and the provision of satellite intelligence data. At the same time, official Washington expected that strengthened security guarantees would help persuade the Ukrainian side to agree to a compromise on the territories (in particular, the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the Donetsk and Luhansk regions) as part of a future peace agreement.
Ukrainian representatives generally viewed the discussion of additional guarantees positively. However, Kyiv and European capitals immediately began to fear that Ukraine would be asked to make territorial concessions to russia in exchange for support and guarantees.
The situation became more complicated after Trump announced an agreement with putin to ease US restrictions on the export of Russian diesel fuel.
According to the publication, the US president’s decision came as a surprise to some participants in the negotiation process. In particular, Björn Seibert, head of the office of the President of the European Commission, told European diplomats during a closed briefing that the announcement of the diesel deal had been unexpected for the meeting’s participants. As a result, the negotiations in Miami ended without final agreements on security guarantees and the terms for ending the war.
Context
As Reuters previously reported, citing sources, the US administration viewed the diesel deal with moscow as a way to bring the Russian dictator back to peace talks. According to Washington’s plan, economic concessions were intended to demonstrate to the kremlin the potential benefits of ending the war. However, the Ukrainian side was skeptical of this approach, as russia continues to put forward territorial demands and shows no readiness to end the hostilities.
What preceded this
On October 9 US leader Donald Trump announced an agreement providing for the easing of restrictions on the supply of approximately 300,000 tonnes of Russian diesel fuel. The American president explained the decision by the need to stabilize fuel prices.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the agreement, calling it unfair, and stressed that easing sanctions against russia would be possible only if moscow took genuine steps toward ending the war.

Access to Public Lands Should Unite All Americans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:00:26 UTC
02:00:26 KST

Experiencing wild, open, and natural spaces is part of what it means to me to be American, and I know I'm not alone in that belief.
Our shared connection to nature crosses geography, generations, and political beliefs. From a neighborhood trail to a national park or a stretch of open desert, the outdoors gives us places to come together, find perspective, and experience something larger than ourselves.
At a time of growing loneliness, division, and stress, being outside can improve physical and mental well-being, strengthen community, and reconnect us with one another. For millions of Americans, public lands make that possible.
But the places that sustain that connection are under growing pressure due to decisions made by elected leaders. That is why, as we head into this year’s midterm election, voters must ask every candidate a simple question: How will you protect our public lands?
The answer will help determine what we leave future generations.
Consider Bears Ears National Monument in Utah. A presidential proclamation issued this summer reduced the monument’s boundaries from roughly 1.36 million acres to about 131,000, removing monument protections from more than 90% of the landscape. Bears Ears is a living cultural landscape and sacred ancestral homeland of deep significance to Tribal Nations.
Similar decisions are unfolding across the country. Congress rolled back protections for the Boundary Waters, opening the door to mining in its headwaters. The Trump Administration is also considering transferring a parcel of Yosemite National Park to a private developer. Pristine roadless backcountry may also be opened to development and extraction. These decisions will have lasting consequences.
There is room for honest debate about how public lands should be managed. Recreation, conservation, grazing, timber, energy development, and local economies all deserve consideration. Responsible stewardship requires balancing those interests while protecting the places that generations of Americans have worked to preserve.
That debate matters because public lands are not only a conservation legacy—they are also an economic engine.
Outdoor recreation generates $1.3 trillion in economic output and supports 5.2 million American jobs. Communities and businesses across the country depend on the forests, rivers, trails, parks, and open spaces that draw people outdoors.
The meaning runs deep. Public lands are among the few places in American life that connect all of us. The rock climber in Yosemite and the hunter in Montana may not share the same politics, but they share a stake in keeping these places healthy, accessible, and protected. Public lands remind us that our common ground is more than an idea—they’re real places beneath our feet.
The decisions made today will outlast this administration and this Congress. Once public lands are permanently altered, fragmented, or developed, there’s no going back.
One of the best ways to protect these places is to help connect more people to experience them. People protect what they know. They fight for places that become part of their lives. The future of our public lands will be decided by whether Americans still believe they are worth protecting, and whether we elect leaders who believe it too.
As candidates ask for our vote, we should ask where they stand. Look at the choices they have made. Look at the policies they support and listen carefully to their answers. For generations, Americans of every political persuasion have chosen to safeguard extraordinary places for everyone who would come after them. The forests, rivers, and mountains we enjoy today exist because of those choices.
Now, the choice is ours.
We can treat public lands as another political issue, or we can recognize them for what they are: places that make us healthier, bring us together, and connect us to something larger than ourselves.
This November, we must elect leaders who believe that public lands are worth protecting.

City attended the trade delegation alongside several other northern sports and leisure organisations, including Lancashire cricket club and Visit Lake District. While in India, the football club took part in an event in Delhi promoting British tourism.
The Great North – a coalition of mayors from the north of England which organised the India event – said its aim was “to shine a spotlight on the great tourism products across the north of England”.
The Greater Manchester mayoral authority said on Tuesday that representatives of Greater Manchester sporting clubs would “routinely join business delegations” on international visits during Burnham’s time as mayor.
Burnham’s defence of City and its owners has focused attention not only on his links to the club but on how reliant he was on investment from Abu Dhabi to power Manchester’s strong growth rates when he was mayor.
Other senior politicians on this week’s trade delegation include Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, Douglas Alexander, the Scotland secretary, and Angela Eagle, the environment secretary.
Reynolds took part in a Premier League event on Tuesday, where he met schoolchildren being taught by British-trained coaches. He denied afterwards that the charges against City had tainted the league’s reputation. It is otherwise one of Britain’s most successful cultural exports.
“The brand of the Premier League – one of the UK’s most important brands … that is incredibly powerful,” he said.
Asked whether it was appropriate for City to have been invited, given the charges it faced, he said: “That’s a Greater Manchester issue, and obviously they are a major participant in the economy in Greater Manchester.
“I understand the interest – the relationship between Manchester and Manchester City – but in terms of the allegations, their appeal, that is a football matter.”
