Plan unveiled to increase share of land farmed organically in England to 10%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:49:15 UTC
01:49:15 KST

The government has set an ambition to increase the share of English land farmed organically to 10% by 2036, but concerns remain over how the transition will be funded.
Currently, just 3.4% of England’s agricultural land is farmed organically, one of the smallest shares in Europe. France, for example, farms 10.4% of its land organically, and aims to increase this to 18% by 2027.
Rob Haward, the chief executive of organic veg box company Riverford, said it was a reflection of organic farming having political backing in the EU. Whereas in England, the last organic farming plan was published more than two decades ago.
The government’s new plan, which has been more than three years in the making, sets out a vision for growth in the organic sector, with public procurement – in schools and hospitals, for example – cited as a significant opportunity. The government already has a long-term ambition for 10% of public sector food spend to meet higher environmental production standards. The plan states that the organic sector can play a vital role in achieving this.
The environment secretary, Angela Eagle, said the plan was about “opening up opportunities across the sector, from backing farmers already producing organic food to helping others decide whether it could work for their businesses”.
She added: “Organic farming should not be treated as a niche. More people are looking closely at where their food comes from, how it is produced and whether it meets standards they value.”
Haward said public procurement was “impenetrable” for small organic farms, but hoped the plan would be a “catalyst for growth”. However, he said the sector now needed proper backing from the government, including grant funding.
In September, thousands of farmers were left empty-handed after the government’s sustainable farming incentive 2026 (SFI) funding was spent in just six hours. This meant that some farmers who might have been planning to use the funding to transition to organic farming may have missed out.
“SFI needs to be reliable, successful and secure to enable this transition,” said Haward. “It’s hard for any farm to invest in their business if things change, we need some consistency.”
Gareth Morgan, the head of farming policy at the Soil Association, said there had been a lot of discussions with Defra about funding, but in the end “there has been a compromise”.
“There is now an urgent need to reopen SFI to enable farms to move to organic farming,” he said.
Morgan added that increasing the share of land farmed organically could bring down the price of organic food for consumers. “Currently the price of food is subsidised and we don’t pay for the environmental impact. If organic food becomes more mainstream, the price difference will become less,” he said.
Martin Lines, the chief executive of the Nature Friendly Farming Network, said farmers could not rely on government funding alone to make this transition, and said there needed to be “real investment from the supply chain and the private sector, along with fairer prices for farmers for their goods and stronger domestic markets for homegrown produce”.
The National Farmers’ Union, whose members include organic and non-organic farms, said the plan signified a “really positive step forward … for the wider supply chain”.
“Supporting domestic production will strengthen the resilience of our food supply chains and ensure British farmers and growers benefit from opportunities, rather than increasing our reliance on imports,” said Paul Tompkins, the deputy president of the union.
In the plan’s foreword, Eagle said: “Across England, organic farmers, growers and food businesses play an important role in producing high-quality food while caring for soils, wildlife and the rural communities they are part of. In doing so, they also help advance wider goals for nature recovery, cleaner water and greater climate resilience.”
This year has been challenging for farmers because of crop-destroying heat and drought alongside soaring fertiliser costs tied to the war in Iran. Organic farms have been found to be more resilient in the face of these extreme weather conditions and are also not affected by rising fertiliser costs.
“Organic farmers are much less exposed to these risks,” Morgan said, adding that the plan was a sign that the government was thinking hard about the pathway for food security.

'Unprecedented': Global Palestine movement vows to drive change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:47:46 UTC

Breadcrumb
'We are driving change': Global Palestine movement hails growing influence worldwide
The global Palestine solidarity movement has reached unprecedented levels of influence, with growing public anger over Israel's genocide in Gaza putting governments under mounting pressure to translate support for Palestinian rights into meaningful political action.
Speaking exclusively to The New Arab, Global Alliance for Palestine (GAFP) secretary-general Anas Altikriti said the movement was gaining momentum worldwide, as hundreds of organisations mobilised across more than 80 countries to mark three years of Israel's war on Gaza.
"This momentum around the world that we've seen build and reach a level was never ever expected – totally unprecedented," he said.
But Altikriti warned that growing international recognition of Palestinian statehood would remain "superficial" unless governments adopted policies to hold Israel accountable for its actions.
"We saw how in late 2025, a catalogue of countries recognised the state of Palestine, how there were Palestinian embassies opened throughout the world – but we insisted then and we insist now that all of this is superficial if not followed with actual policies that first of all hold Israel to account and those who took part in the war crime that we saw and we witnessed."
His comments follow a three-day global solidarity campaign held from 9 to 11 October, which brought together pro-Palestine organisations and campaigners for demonstrations, vigils, cultural events and community gatherings.
The coordinated actions demanded an end to Israel's genocide in Gaza, its decades-long occupation, ongoing settler violence and settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, as well as accountability for governments accused of enabling Israeli war crimes.
Altikriti said the mobilisation reflected growing frustration not only with Israel's military offensives in Gaza, Lebanon and elsewhere, but also with the international community's failure to stop them.
"People are angry beyond what we've known in terms of the crimes committed incessantly and with impunity by Israel and the Israeli government. But also the silence and the tacit complicity of the entire world and here in the UK," he told TNA.
He also urged Britain's government under Prime Minister Andy Burnham to match its changing rhetoric on Israel and Palestinian rights with concrete policies.
"And whilst this new government under Andy Burnham has adopted a new narrative in regards with Israel and the Palestinian rights, we still need to see actual policies being put in place to reflect that kind of anger and frustration that the streets, not only of the UK, but the entire world, feel."
'Of course, we're vilifying Israel'
The growing international movement has also faced criticism from pro-Israel voices, including Israel's Foreign Ministry, which condemned GAFP's global campaign and highlighted a Fox News report describing the activism as "the protest playbook to vilify Israel".
Asked about the Israeli government's criticism, Altikriti responded defiantly.
"Of course, we're vilifying Israel," he said. “Israel is an occupying terrorist state. We made that proclamation time and time and time again, not just myself, not just the Global Alliance of Palestine, but countless Israelis who have themselves seen the poison that Israel creates, not only in Palestine, but throughout the entire world.”
Altikriti argued that Israel's own policies, rather than the activities of solidarity campaigners, were responsible for the growing international anger towards the country.
“The vilification has actually come from Israeli policies itself. Israel has created this. Israel has created the momentum that we see around the world. The anger that people feel, the questioning of American people as to why their tax dollars are being shipped to Israel for them to then kill Palestinian children.”
His comments come as pro-Palestine campaigners seek to sustain international pressure on governments over their diplomatic, military and economic ties with Israel.
Global solidarity reaches new heights
GAFP hailed its three-day mobilisation as a major success, saying it demonstrated the growing reach and influence of the international Palestine solidarity movement.
“Hundreds of organisations and campaigns in over 80 countries around the world do all sorts of activities, whether there are demos, marches, vigils, stands, flag waving or balloon settings,” Altikriti told TNA.
“We count this as a tremendous success, not only for ourselves, the Global Alliance for Palestine, but also all the activist groups and all the campaigns that took part in this, whether under our umbrella or whether independently, we regard this as being an inspiration from the people of Gaza.”
The campaign culminated in a Global Day of Action on Saturday, 10 October, when tens of thousands of pro-Palestine protesters marched through central London.
GAFP estimates that more than 250,000 people joined coordinated actions organised by established groups, including the Muslim Association of Britain (MAB), Palestinian Forum in Britain (PFB), Palestine Solidarity Campaign (PSC), Stop the War Coalition (STWC), Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND) and Friends of Al-Aqsa (FoA).
The mobilisation came as Palestinians marked three years since Israel launched its devastating military assault on Gaza in October 2023.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since then.
Despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreed in October 2025, which envisaged the eventual reconstruction of the devastated territory, little progress has been made towards implementing the agreement.
At least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire since the so-called ceasefire took effect.

China’s drone modem pipeline: How mesh technology helps Russian UAVs penetrate deep into Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:45:29 UTC
01:45:29 KST

The Insider's correspondent in Ukraine examined a mesh modem — one made by China’s Xingkai Tech — that was found in a Russian Gerbera drone. Then, posing as a Russian military supplier, they obtained evidence that the Chinese company is knowingly willing to sell its modems to the Russian drone factory in Alabuga. Several banks, including DBS Bank, China Merchants Bank, and Ping An Bank, are actively facilitating these sales. Mesh networks are the most practical technology for controlling Russia’s long-range drones over Ukraine. They allow operators to control drones manually and send commands in flight, exploiting gaps in Ukrainian air defenses. According to The Insider’s estimates, Xingkai Tech accounts for about half the market for high-power mesh modems used in Gerbera and Geran drones, making its supplies critical to Russian military manufacturers.
In February 2026, the Russian military lost access to the Starlink terminals it had previously used to facilitate attacks on Ukraine. As a workaround, it has since turned to the use of Geran and Gerbera drones equipped with Chinese-made mesh modems.
A typical attack involving Geran and Gerbera drones works as follows: some drones flying near the border connect to Russian or Belarusian signal repeaters and relay signals to drones operating deeper inside Ukraine. Each relay node is equipped with a powerful mesh modem.
Gerbera drones are becoming increasingly important. They are significantly cheaper than Gerans and have a similar radar signature, allowing them to serve as decoys for Ukrainian air defenses.
In 2024 Ukraine’s military intelligence agency (HUR) reported finding Xingkai Tech modems in Gerbera drones. Later, the use of these modems and the role of Gerberas in combat operations in 2026 were discussed on a major pro-Russian website. However, there was no evidence that Xingkai Tech was knowingly and openly supplying modems directly to the Russian Alabuga plant where the drones are assembled.
In an earlier investigation, The Insider found that Chinese company Shenzhen Xingkai Technology, also known as Xingkai Tech, had issued an invoice for 30 mesh modems destined for Vladivostok as part of a supply chain supporting Russian drones.
In 2026, The Insider examined a mesh modem obtained privately in Ukraine that had been found in an upgraded Gerbera drone fitted with a vertical stabilizer. This variant first appeared this past summer.
An investigator from the Nordsint project then posed as a Russian military supplier based in Alabuga, where Geran and Gerbera drones are manufactured. Xingkai Tech confirmed that the model was available and that Xingkai Technology was its sole manufacturer. The journalist also obtained an invoice for 500 mesh modems that were identical to the one examined in Ukraine — a shipment worth approximately $2.87 million.
How the modems are sold
Posing as a Russian military supplier, The Insider and Nordsint contacted Xingkai Technology through its official WeChat account to request a quote for modems “similar” to the one shown in a photograph from Ukraine. The undercover investigators made clear that the end user needed exactly the same version, with an identical casing.
A company employee who introduced himself as “Jack Jiang” (his actual name is Jiang Qin (蒋钦), and he is the director and owner of the company) confirmed that Xingkai Technology manufactured the modems; he even provided the investigators with the XK F-359 user manual. Some sources, including the Ukrainian military intelligence agency’s War and Sanctions portal, had previously misidentified the device as a separate but similar model, the XK F-358.
To make sure the end user would receive an identical device, the investigators asked Jiang to take photographs and video of the modem at the production facility. He complied.
The modem examined by The Insider in Ukraine proved identical to the device described in the manual and shown in the warehouse video. It differed only slightly from the models featured in Xingkai Technology’s online catalog. Jiang explained that other versions of the F-359 had different casings but retained the same internal layout.
The Insider and Nordsint then ordered 500 modems for delivery to Alabuga, home to a factory that produces most of Russia’s long-range drones. Jiang responded with an invoice for 19.5 million yuan, offering the “client” two payment options: U.S. dollars to Xingkai Tech’s account at DBS Bank in Hong Kong, or yuan to Jiang’s personal account at Ping An Bank in China.
Jiang also confirmed that identical modems were available through Shenzhen Sinosun Technology (although Xingkai Tech itself manufactured the devices). In their correspondence, Nordsint explicitly stated that the end user was a military production facility. Xingkai Tech’s director raised no objections.
Nordsint explicitly stated that the end user was a military production facility. Xingkai Tech’s director raised no objections
In another message, Jiang asked whether his Russian customer had “won” the “project,” apparently referring to a tender.
After being asked to “update the address,” Xingkai Tech issued a slightly revised invoice. This time, the company spelled “Alabuga” in Latin characters, making it harder to claim later that it had been unaware of the end user’s identity.
The Chinese bank account listed on the revised invoice was in the name of Huang Qiuping, who may also use the name Fanny Huang (she is listed under that name as a contact in the mesh modem’s user manual). According to Tesari records, Huang Qiuping left her management position at Xingkai Tech in 2025.
The revised invoice directed payments to an account at the Hongling branch of the China Merchants Bank in Shenzhen.
The key component of a mesh modem is a field-programmable gate array (FPGA). It enables the modem to make decisions about network topology and optimize communications. This “intelligent” component configures the mesh network linking a swarm of drones.
The Xingkai Tech director who corresponded with an undercover Nordsint investigator said the company uses the XC7Z020-2CLG4001 FPGA made by U.S.-based company AMD. When asked to provide an AMD licensing agreement (ostensibly to meet Russian bureaucratic requirements), Jiang refused, saying Xingkai Tech obtains its FPGAs through an intermediary.
The Insider contacted AMD, which provided the following statement:
“Xingkai Technology is not an AMD customer or authorized partner, and AMD has not sold products to the company. AMD complies with all applicable U.S. export control and sanctions laws and strictly prohibits the export or reexport of AMD products to Russia in violation of those requirements.”
What this little box can do
The XK F-359 modem can maintain line-of-sight communications over distances of 100–300 km. This means that an attack on Kyiv theoretically may require just a couple of Gerbera or Shahed drones acting as relay stations to provide a stable radio link for the entire attacking drone group, allowing the drones to receive updated commands in flight and maneuver to evade air defenses. The technology is also crucial for providing live video feeds from operator-controlled drones equipped with cameras and guidance systems, such as those recently reported by Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov.
Mesh modems can autonomously establish and manage network topology in real time.
The XK F-359 manual states:
“The network operates on a single frequency and uses multi-hop relaying. Each node can move rapidly and freely, while the network topology can change and update rapidly without disrupting data transmission. The network is easy to deploy, flexible to use, and simple to operate and maintain. It provides reliable, timely, efficient and secure integrated IP services, including voice, broadband data, high-definition video, visual command and dispatch, and other multimedia services in challenging conditions, such as rapid movement and the absence of a direct line of sight.”
In other words, the mesh network reconfigures itself automatically, freeing drone operators from having to manage it manually and allowing them to focus on military tasks.
Notably, the manual’s opening line lists military and police operations among the intended applications of mesh technology:
“Broadband self-organizing networks can be widely used in the military, public security agencies, armed police, fire services, civil defense, electric power, the oil industry, mining, transportation, water management, forestry, radio and television, medicine, maritime and aviation communications, and other fields.”
Given these capabilities, the Xingkai Tech XK F-359 is almost ideally suited to Gerbera and Geran drones.
The specific XK F-359 variant documented by The Insider in Ukraine does not appear in Xingkai Technology’s public catalogs. The manual for this version became available only after The Insider established direct contact with the company.
Some online sources, meanwhile, identified Shenzhen Sinosun Technology as the modem’s manufacturer. The company’s website features a photograph of an identical modem, sometimes found among drone wreckage bearing the HX-50 label. When asked about this, Jack Jiang of Xingkai Technology confirmed that his company was the modem’s sole manufacturer.
Who bought them in Russia
The Insider examined Russian customs data and found that Xingkai Technology had shipped its products to Russia, declaring them simply as “antennas” and “remote control equipment.”
One Russian recipient was Atlant-Engineering, a trading company that does not manufacture drones. The company is owned by the family of Rafik Zagrutdinov, a mid-level official in the Moscow city government. Another recipient was LT Global Forwarding.
Both companies filed declarations of conformity, apparently for Xingkai Technology equipment; however, for reasons unknown, Quanzhou Yunzhuo Technology was listed as the manufacturer.
What’s new with the Gerberas
Gerbera drones were initially inexpensive decoys, as their radar signature resembled that of older Geran models without turbojet engines.
Later, Gerberas were fitted with warheads and began carrying out reconnaissance missions. During the summer of 2026, upgraded versions began to appear, distinguished primarily by a vertical stabilizer. Some variants were also equipped with cameras.
Gerberas have been shot down in European countries. Recently, one such drone flew into Lithuanian airspace.
The Insider analyzed a sample of 30 listings for parts from downed Russian drones on Ukraine’s largest online auction site for war trophies. At least nine lots featured easily recognizable Xingkai Tech mesh modems. One listing offered 10 modems at once. Identical Xingkai Tech mesh modems have also been found in Banderol loitering munitions (drone missiles).
Equipping a drone — even one that once served as a decoy — with a modern mesh modem turns it into a weapon capable of threatening Europe. Recently, the Spanish publication El Mundo reported that the CIA had warned European countries that Gerberas could be launched against Europe from vessels belonging to Russia’s “shadow fleet.”
Many of Xingkai Tech’s drone components are available on the popular Russian online marketplace Wildberries.
The Insider contacted the press offices of DBS, Ping An, and China Merchants Bank, and also reached out to DBS by phone. None of the three banks responded.
Another mesh modem
The Insider identified another mesh modem widely used in Shahed drones that had not previously been publicly identified. Comparing listings on Reibert with the manufacturer’s website, it established that the modem is made by China’s Xi'an Sihou Network Technology Co., Ltd.
Xi'an Sihou Network Technology is another major player in the market for captured equipment sold at auction. It accounts for roughly half of the listings for captured mesh modems examined by The Insider. The company’s owner and director is Li Li.
Geran drones, along with Banderol loitering munitions, have become Russia’s main weapons in its campaign of terror against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, as well as in attacks on railway locomotives. The survival of Ukraine’s civilian population through the coming winter will depend largely on whether the West can use sanctions and diplomacy to quickly halt large-scale sales of mesh modems to Russia.

Israel’s warnings of a PA attack shifts focus from the unresolved Hamas threat - analysis
Netanyahu and Katz warn Palestinian Authority forces could turn their weapons on Israel, but security sources report no concrete threat, raising questions about the timing ahead of elections
As Israel marks three years since the multi-front war launched by Hamas and other Palestinian terror groups on October 7, the various fronts remain open: the IDF continues to conduct near-daily strikes in Lebanon and in the Gaza Strip, where Hamas is still in power; Israeli forces are still deployed in Syria; and the Iranian and Houthi fronts are on pause, but far from resolved.
Last week, the Israeli public was suddenly presented with a new threat. "The IDF is preparing for a scenario in which the Palestinian Authority's security apparatus turns its weapons against Israeli settlers and IDF forces in Judea and Samaria and in communities along the Seam Zone," Defense Minister Israel Katz declared at the weekly cabinet meeting.
"In such an event, we will declare war against the Palestinian Authority, and the IDF will launch a full-scale offensive in accordance with a structured plan formulated and approved by Prime Minister Netanyahu and myself—based on the principles outlined for the IDF."
That's quite a bombshell. Just think about it: tens of thousands of armed Palestinian Authority security personnel deployed throughout the West Bank decide one day to launch an October 7-style attack on dozens of Israeli communities and military bases in Judea and Samaria. The results would be disastrous.
Yesterday, Netanyahu added his own warning. "Our enemies are considering testing us during this period leading up to the elections; we are prepared for any scenario, including a sudden turning of the guns. The IDF has presented a robust plan to me and the Ministry of Defense for such an eventuality; I would advise our enemies not to put us to the test," he said, speaking from the West Bank.
In a post-October 7 reality, Israel's security bodies must be prepared for any scenario, and it's good to know that the country's top leaders are aware of the threat. There is only one problem: there is no indication that such a threat exists. Security sources I've spoken with say the IDF has no intelligence pointing to such an attack, and Shin Bet sources told Israeli media they know of no concrete threat from the PA.
So why the sudden scare, when there is no apparent threat and Israelis have nothing in their power to do about it? There are other possible explanations, from instability within the PA to plain deterrence signaling. But none of them explain the timing. The public first heard of this new threat on October 6, the day before the anniversary of the worst security failure in Israel's history.
Talking about how Hamas is still in power three years after it massacred some 1,200 people and kidnapped 251 more, on their watch, is inconvenient, to say the least, for leaders seeking reelection. So why not shift the conversation to other armed Palestinians, who, apart from a few rogue security personnel, pose no actual threat to Israelis?
Beyond the political cynicism, presenting the PA security forces as an emerging threat is divorced from reality. As you read these words, PA security forces are helping protect Israeli communities in Judea and Samaria. Their contribution to combating Palestinian terror in the West Bank is minimal at best, but their presence and ongoing coordination with the IDF are a net gain for Israel's security.
Could they one day turn on Israel and endanger it? Potentially, yes, and Israel must be prepared for that, especially after October 7. But nothing points to it. The threat posed by Hamas, which is still in power and refuses to disarm, is very real. Talking about that two weeks before the first elections since October 7, however, is politically dangerous. It's far easier to inflate a new threat and divert attention from the failure in Gaza.

Palestine has said that Colombia’s opening of an embassy in West Jerusalem violates international law and UN resolutions.

It stressed that all measures and decisions to change the legal and historical status of Jerusalem are “null and void and have no legal effect".
It said that “opening an embassy to Israel in occupied Jerusalem violates international legitimacy resolutions, particularly UN Security Council Resolutions 476 and 478.”
The two resolutions that were adopted in 1980 affirm the illegality and invalidity of Israeli measures intended to alter the character and legal status of Jerusalem, amid Israel’s enactment of a law annexing occupied East Jerusalem.
The ministry said Colombia’s move also “undermines the international consensus on the city’s legal status and infringes on the Palestinian people’s inalienable rights.”
It warned that the step encourages Israel to continue its “colonial policies and attempts to impose illegal realities on the ground".
The Palestinian foreign ministry urged Colombia to comply with international law and respect relevant UN resolutions, calling on it to “reverse this step to preserve prospects for achieving a just and comprehensive peace.”
Jordan 
In a statement issued following the embassy’s opening, the Jordanian foreign ministry said the kingdom condemns and rejects the move.
The ministry stressed that any measures or decisions aimed at changing the status or legal standing of Jerusalem are “null and void, illegitimate and without legal effect.”
It said the only way to achieve a just and comprehensive peace is to establish an independent, sovereign Palestinian state along the June 4, 1967, lines, with East Jerusalem as its capital.
Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia’s foreign ministry condemned and denounced the move, describing it as a “blatant violation of international law and relevant international resolutions.”
It said the move contradicts the established international position on Jerusalem’s legal and historical status.
Riyadh renewed its demand for the international community, including the UN Security Council and all concerned parties, to fulfil their “legal and moral responsibilities” and act urgently to halt “illegal Israeli policies aimed at imposing a new reality by force and undermining prospects for a just and lasting peace.”
Jerusalem remains at the heart of Israel’s dispossession of Palestinians and subsequent occupation of Palestinian lands and is widely regarded as one of its most sensitive issues.
While Israel claims the entire city as its capital, Palestinians view East Jerusalem, occupied by Israel since 1967, as the capital of a future Palestinian state, in line with longstanding international consensus and UN resolutions.

The UK energy secretary is flirting with a bad idea for bills – the ‘rising block tariff’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:43:15 UTC
01:43:15 KST

‘My mark of failure or success is whether I can get bills down or not. That’s the only thing I’m in this job to do.” So said Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, recently, bracing for the hike in energy bills that looks inevitable in January. Industry projections suggest £400-ish on an annual basis is on the way, with “stubbornly high” levels for the rest of decade even if wholesale gas prices cool down.
So, yes, one can understand why “affordability” is Fahnbulleh’s “top priority”. And, as this newspaper reported last week, there is likely to be an intervention in that direction in chancellor John Healey’s budget this month: £1bn of extra support for poorer households this winter.
But the chat in energy-land is about what comes after that – and what Fahnbulleh’s other remarks about covering the costs of the energy system in a “fairer” way seem to be hinting at.
Will the government finally get round to designing a co-called “social tariff” for energy – a way to get financial support to the most needy on a more targeted basis than the clunky warm homes discount, the mechanism Healey will be obliged to use?
Will Healey, after chopping VAT from electricity for six months, do so permanently and then shift more green levies and other “hidden taxes” of energy transition into general taxation?
And is Fahnbulleh also contemplating something very different? Welcome to the idea of the “rising block tariff” (RBT), the unwieldy name for the proposal to give every household an initial block, or allowance, of cheaper gas and electricity to cover “essential” use and then make subsequent blocks more expensive. In other words, heavier energy consumers would pay higher rates for their extra units.
Fahnbulleh has got officials in her department to explore an RBT model. And, note, the New Economics Foundation, the thinktank she used to lead, is a proponent.
The Joseph Rowntree Foundation is another backer: in its version, the government could fund an RBT with, say, £5bn of public money, allowing bills to fall for most households – but, critically, the biggest savings would flow to light users, who tend to be low-income households. “An RBT would produce greater reductions in bills lower down the income distribution,” it says.
What’s not to like? Plenty. There are at least three reasons why an RBT has few fans elsewhere, not even among charities and thinktanks that focus on fuel poverty.
First, Citizens Advice regards low energy use as a poor proxy for low income in practice. Traditional electric heaters, with high electricity usage, “are more common in social or private rented homes, where people can’t change their heating system”, it argues.
Quite: a progressive-sounding policy could end up being nothing of the sort, especially if second-home owners, by spreading their usage, are winners. If the reply is that an incomes overlay could address tricky cases in both directions, why not just do the data modelling work to design a proper social tariff in the first place?
Second, a rigid RBT would be an awkward fit with a renewables-heavy system where the most interesting innovations are “flex” tariffs to exploit very windy or sunny hours when wholesale power prices are dirt cheap. There is a danger of baffling consumers by making them mix their blocks with their flexes.
Third, a core aim of the energy transition is to drive take-up of electric vehicles, heat pumps and so on. That becomes harder if the message to consumers is that “the more electricity you use, the more you’ll be charged per unit”.
Lobby group Electrify Britain calls block tariffs “hugely counterproductive” for electrification: “You can’t ask families to go electric and then pursue a policy that would charge them more for doing so.”
That feels the killer point: an RBT model cuts across too many other goals. Fahnbulleh should keep things simple: go for a serious social tariff or discount scheme that effectively identifies “vulnerable” energy users. That idea has enjoyed wide support for years. Block tariffs are too complicated and fiddly to administer.

（By Eddy Chang, Taipei Times／台北時報張迪）

With the crowd chanting his name, a fired-up Freddy Peralta on Tuesday pumped one fastball after another past hitters all night long.
Peralta threw six innings of four-hit ball and Liam Hicks lined a two-run single after Jose Ramirez’s fielding error as the Tampa Bay Rays beat the Cleveland Guardians 3-1 to even the American League Championship Series (ALCS) at 1-1.
Peralta threw the hardest pitch of his big league career at 159.97kph and relied on his four-seam fastball on 71 of 99 pitches — his 71.7 percent usage was his highest since June 11, 2019.
Photo: Kim Klement Neitzel-Imagn Images
“It’s no secret that I trust in my fastball a lot and it’s my best pitch,” Peralta said.
Peralta’s 155.95kph average fastball velocity was 4.18kph above his season average.
“It plays a big role, the adrenaline,” Peralta said. “And also I define myself as a competitor, and I like these kind of games. I’ve always said in the past, that I enjoyed this as a Dominican pitcher. I grew up watching the games in DR [Dominican Republic], and that’s the game that you see.”
Peralta pumped a fist and screamed joyfully walking off the mound in the sixth after fanning Petey Halpin swinging at a 3-2 changeup.
“I just enjoyed the moment because it was a really good at-bat,” Peralta said. “It wasn’t an easy game since the first pitch that I threw until the last one. It was a lot of competition between me and the hitters... I think that was why I was fired up like that.”
Ramirez — whose two-run homer in Game 5 of their AL Division Series against Chicago helped the Guardians become the 11th team to overcome an 0-2 deficit in a best-of-five series — misplayed a grounder in the fourth inning that led to three unearned runs against rookie lefty Parker Messick.
Junior Caminero walked to start that inning and Victor Mesa Jr grounded into a force out originally ruled a double play. The Rays challenged the calls at both first and second and Mesa was ruled safe when a video review overturned the out decision by first base umpire Mark Ripperger.
After Jonny DeLuca struck out, Chandler Simpson beat out a high chopper to shortstop, and the Mesa reached third standing up when Ramirez failed to cover the bag.
Ben Williamson followed with a grounder that scooted underneath Ramirez’s glove and between his legs after the ball hit the edge where the artificial turf met the infield dirt. The third baseman played back rather than charging.
“It’s a little bit faster here this type of surface,” Ramirez said through a translator. “It’s frustrating. I feel bad because I wasn’t able to make that play and after that the runs came in.”
Williamson reached second and Simpson went to third. Hicks drove the next pitch to right-center for a 3-0 lead, electrifying the towel-waving, cowbell-ringing crowd of 32,125 fans at Tropicana Field.
Peralta and three relievers did not need any more support.
Kevin Kelly got two outs in the seventh, retiring Ramirez on a fly ball to center with two runners on.
Lefty Ian Seymour replaced him and Chase DeLauter lined an RBI double to the right-field corner.
Seymour struck out Jo Adell swinging at a changeup, leaving runners at second and third. Seymour pitched a 1-2-3 eighth and Bryan Baker finished with a perfect ninth for his fourth post-season save.
Acquired by the Rays from the Mets at the trade deadline, Peralta turned around his season in Tampa Bay going 5-2 with a 3.25 ERA in 10 starts after posting a 4.99 ERA for New York.
He pitched his latest gem in front of Mets owner Steve Cohen, who was in attendance.
“We have a good relationship,” Peralta said of Cohen. “I think he’s awesome, and I’m happy that he was here watching, not watching me, watching the Rays.”

Airport proposals need care, officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:43:03 UTC
01:43:03 KST

Any plans to remove Taipei International Airport (Songshan airport) need to be carefully assessed, government officials said yesterday, adding that international artificial intelligence (AI) firms might not find the site ideal for building computing centers.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) on Thursday last week said that airport should cease operations, with part of the vacated site turned into an AI park.
He said yesterday that he is willing to discuss issues related to the proposal with the central government, adding that the timing is right and the conditions are ideal.
Photo:George Tsorng, Taipei Times
Chiang’s proposal was scrutinized at a meeting of the legislature’s Transportation Committee later yesterday, with Minister of Digital Affairs Lin Yi-ching (林宜敬) asked whether he supported having an AI park built in the capital if Songshan airport was removed.
An AI park at the site would accommodate varied operators in the AI ecosystem, including software, hardware and IC design firms, Lin said.
Some firms might want to have their headquarters there, he said.
“However, companies such as Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電), Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海), Quanta Computer (廣達) and Wistron Corp (緯創) are not likely to build factories at a prime location in the capital,” he said.
IC design firms generally built their facilities near hardware or wafer plants, which are not typically near major urban centers, he said.
The most likely scenario is that companies would have their international headquarters in an AI park. For example, Nvidia is building its Taiwan headquarters at Beitou Shilin Technology Park (北投士林科技園區) in Taipei, Lin said.
Building AI data centers on the site would not be ideal either, Lin said, adding that the ministry favors Changhua Coastal Industrial Park (彰化濱海產業園區) or Asia New Bay Area (亞洲新灣區) in Kaohsiung for such facilities.
At a meeting of the legislature’s Foreign and National Defense Committee, Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) and Deputy Minister of Transportation and Communications Lin Kuo-hsien (林國顯) cautioned that proposals to remove Songshan airport would need careful evaluation.
“Songshan airport is an important facility for Taiwan’s defense resilience in peacetime or at war,” Koo told reporters on the sidelines of the meeting. “It is an important hub for domestic air transport as well. Residents of outlying islands and the east coast seeking emergency healthcare need to land at Songshan airport to access hospitals in Taipei. It is also the rescue operation base for the National Air Service Corp.”
“We need to assess whether the functions of Songshan airport could be effectively replaced by a similar facility elsewhere,” he said. “We would provide professional opinions should the government begin evaluating the possibility of moving the airport to a different site to ensure that defense capabilities would not be compromised.”
Lin Kuo-hsien said that Songshan airport handles about 50 percent of Taiwan’s domestic air traffic, while 92 percent of domestic travel at the airport being to or from outlying Kinmen, Lienchiang or Penghu counties.
Demand for air transportation services during major national holidays are 1.5 times higher than normal, he said.
Songshan is also an airbase for private jets, he said.
As of last month, the airport had facilitated 1,185 private aircraft arrivals and departures so far this year, Lin Kuo-hsien said.
The nine hospitals designated for critical emergency care in Taiwan that are within a 10-to-15-minute drive of an airport are near Songshan airport, he said.
“Taiwan’s aviation safety and resilience are enhanced with two airports in northern Taiwan, providing greater flexibility for flight diversions and operational scheduling in case of inclement weather and other situations,” he said.
“Large metropolitan areas in other countries, such as those surrounding Tokyo, Osaka, Seoul, London and New York, have two or more airports to meet demand,” he said.
Pegatron Corp (和碩) chairman Tung Tzu-hsien (童子賢) said that he is against removing Songshan airport, instead favoring expanding it to facilitate regional partnerships with neighboring countries.
An AI park should be built in Danhai New Town (淡海新市鎮) in New Taipei City’s Tamsui District (淡水), Tung said.
“If the Guosheng Nuclear Power Plant in New Taipei City’s Wanli District (萬里) can be reactivated, what it generates could power an AI park,” he said.
“Danjiang Bridge opened this year to complement Guangdu Bridge,” he said. “Along with the Danhai light rail system and new highway projects, there will be multiple transport links serving Danhai New Town.”
“Songshan airport is needed to facilitate the development of the area,” he said.

Boasting South Korea footballers spark rethink of military service exemptions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:43:02 UTC
01:43:02 KST

For South Korea’s gold medal-winning footballers, victory at the Asian Games came with a reward beyond sporting glory: exemption from mandatory military service.
But the way some players celebrated that benefit has sparked a public backlash, prompting Seoul to reconsider a decades-old system originally designed to reward athletes for bringing prestige to the nation.
The controversy erupted after Asian Games football captain Lee Gi-hyuk proclaimed with a smile “I’m not going to the military” after beating hosts Japan in the men’s final this month.
Photo: AFP
He said he would have had to report for duty just nine days later had his team lost, interrupting a lucrative career at its peak.
A video of Newcastle United’s 19-year-old Park Seung-soo wearing a military discharge cap tilted to one side and giving a smiling salute further fueled the outcry.
Both players later apologized.
Their actions contrasted with the cautious approach traditionally taken by South Korean athletes towards exemptions, long a sensitive subject in a country where most young men are required to serve.
Former Tottenham captain Son Heung-min, who earned his exemption after leading South Korea to gold at the 2018 Asian Games, was famously measured.
Asked about the exemption, Son said: “Rather than thinking about that, we came here to win this tournament.”
South Korea requires most able-bodied men to perform between 18 and 21 months of military service, as it faces off against nuclear-armed North Korea, with which the country technically remains at war.
But under a system introduced in 1973, athletes who win an Olympic medal of any color or an Asian Games gold are eligible for an exemption for “enhancing national prestige and promoting culture.”
Artists who win prizes at designated competitions can also get an exemption.
UNFAIR?
For some, the latest controversy has laid bare the perceived unfairness of a set-up that rewards only a select few while hundreds of thousands of young men report for duty every year.
“What has become clear from this controversy is that military exemptions have come to be regarded as a reward, even though only just a few dozen people every year benefit from them,” an official with ties to the draft process said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
When a select few openly boast about their exemptions, “it symbolically turns military service into a punishment for around 180,000 young men who enlist every year to serve,” the official said. While prize-winning classical musicians and dancers have at times also qualified for an exemption, pop stardom has famously not met the bar.
All seven members of supergroup BTS served out their military obligations, despite supporters noting the act generated billions of dollars for the South Korean economy.
Those who qualify for an exemption are still required to undergo three weeks of basic military training and complete 544 hours of community service related to their speciality over a 34-month period.
Responding to the recent controversy, Defence Minister Kang Shin-chul has pledged to gradually scale back the benefits, with the ultimate goal of abolishing them altogether.
The interviewed official suggested replacing full exemptions with shorter periods of military service.
“We need an alternative in which elite athletes get a reduced military term instead of getting a full pass around it,” they said.
PRODUCT OF BYGONE ERA?
With pressure mounting for reform, the Military Manpower Administration is conducting a review of the system, including eligibility criteria and public service requirements.
The study is expected to be completed by mid-November.
The debate also reflects how much South Korea has changed since the system was introduced more than half a century ago, said Kim Seong-sheen, a professor at Hanyang University.
“The exemption system introduced in 1973 was a product of an era when success at international sporting events was closely tied to national prestige,” he said.
The controversy underscores how times have changed, he said. “More than 50 years later, South Korea is grappling with a shrinking pool of military recruits, the commercialization of sports and growing public demands for fairness.”

Vietnam buries remains of dead from mass grave
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:43:00 UTC
01:43:00 KST

Thousands carrying white flowers lined the roads in Vietnam’s Ho Chi Minh City yesterday as the remains of 731 people believed to have been killed during the 1968 Tet Offensive were taken for burial nearly six decades after their deaths.
Vietnamese Prime Minister Le Minh Hung attended the memorial services at Le Thi Rieng Park, where the remains were recovered from mass graves after over three months of excavations.
They were laid to rest at Ho Chi Minh City Martyrs’ Cemetery in the city previously known as Saigon.
Photo: AFP
Generations in Vietnam have spent decades searching for loved ones who never returned from war, hoping to recover their remains, give them a proper burial and find some measure of closure.
The Tet Offensive began on Jan. 31, 1968, when North Vietnamese communist forces launched coordinated surprise attacks across South Vietnam during the Lunar New Year holiday, known in Vietnam as Tet.
One of the largest campaigns of the Vietnam War, it sparked fierce fighting and heavy casualties, including in the southern capital, Saigon, where communist fighters attacked the US embassy, military installations and government buildings.
Photo: AP
Although the communist forces suffered a military defeat, the offensive shocked Washington, undermined US public support for the war, and became a turning point in the conflict.
“The resultant conflict has changed the pattern of the war,” The Associated Press reported in February 1968.
The South Vietnamese government collected the bodies of communist fighters and civilians, and buried them in mass graves during and after the fighting, according to Vietnamese government news.
The remains at Le Thi Rieng Park, which was previously the site of Do Thanh Cemetery, were discovered during excavations that began on June 23 at the park.
Over weeks, excavators painstakingly unearthed bones and fragments, along with weapons, ammunition, military hammocks and personal belongings, the Vietnamese government’s official news portal reported.
They discovered a wallet containing a faded military document bearing the name Huynh Van Quen, which helped authorities identify one of the dead as a soldier from the 1st Long An Battalion, a communist unit that fought a fierce seven-day battle at Saigon’s Y-shaped Bridge.
Among the mourners yesterday was Vo Huy Thinh, 70, who remembered watching bodies being buried there when he was 12.
“The memory of that burial pit has stayed with me,” he told Vietnamese state media.
For years, architect Nguyen Xuan Thang pored over photographs from the Vietnam War, searching for clues to the location of the burial site.
A breakthrough came when he found a color photograph taken by an AP photographer on Feb. 12, 1968, with a caption describing three large burial trenches that each contained about 300 bodies, he told state media.
The photograph shows two men carrying a body as two others look on. Three boys stand nearby, one of them wearing shorts and a short-sleeved shirt and looking directly at the camera. A water tower is visible in the background, providing a crucial clue to the site’s location.
The image was shot by a French photographer credited as Gautron.
Thang told state media that he spent months riding his motorbike through Ho Chi Minh City, comparing old military maps with present-day landmarks, including the water tower.
His research was part of a nearly eight-year effort, from November 2018 to May, involving his team and the military, which helped authorities narrow their search to the park.
Investigators worked with researchers, historians, journalists and witnesses to piece together the location of the mass graves.
They examined other photographs, satellite images, military maps and archival records from Vietnam and abroad, comparing them to field surveys and accounts from people who witnessed the burials, the Vietnamese government’s official news portal reported.
The recovery is part of a nationwide 500-day campaign running through July next year to locate the remains of about 7,000 war dead and identify them.
More than half a century after the war ended in 1975, many Vietnamese families are still searching for relatives who never returned home.
Of the 731 sets of remains recovered in Ho Chi Minh City, 307 were found with personal belongings, state media reported.
Most have not yet been identified.
Similar memorial and burial ceremonies were planned for today in three other parts of Vietnam, with the remains of what are believed to be 93 people to be buried in Tuyen Quang Province.
Another 65 are to be buried in Hai Phong and 120 in Can Tho.

Book review: Why people are having fewer babies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:43:00 UTC
01:43:00 KST

“Don’t be weird about this,” representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez laughed into the camera as she prepared to jab a hormone-filled needle into her midsection, adding that she knew full well that, yes, people were definitely going to be weird about it. At 36, the congresswoman had begun freezing her eggs, and was making a point of bringing her online audience along with her as she did, stepping directly into the fraught question of how an ambitious woman should manage her fertility.
It’s a live concern: around the world, birthrates are falling sharply.
“Only the Black Death in the 14th century is comparable to what is happening now,” Financial Times journalist Camilla Cavendish notes in a new book examining why.
‘NOT THE WHOLE STORY’
Setting aside the most toxic gender-war narratives, “the standard explanation is that as women get educated, they choose freedom and autonomy over family.” As Cavendish explains, however, that is “not the whole story.”
Drawing on a wealth of reporting, her book seeks to present a more nuanced picture. Cavendish begins with the “fertility gap” — the official name for the difference between the number of children people say they want and the number they actually go on to have — and works her way backwards, focusing on the lived experience of men and women who find themselves with fewer children than they expected. What stopped them?
For some, the main barrier is finding the right partner in time. For others, it comes down to the increasing costs of raising a family (where housing specifically can be a factor) and the enormous difficulty of balancing a career with caregiving, particularly when it takes longer to establish a professional foundation in the first place.
There’s more: a “rational pessimism about prospects for the next generation” in an unstable world, the stigma of embracing motherhood, the shortage of stories glorifying fatherhood, a pressure to perform “intensive parenting,” the lure of well-compensated but all-consuming “greedy jobs,” and so on. There’s also the sheer exhaustion that comes with caring for a small child. The headwinds are strong.
‘DAUNTING, LONELY AND EXPENSIVE’
Taken together, “the joyous, messy, life-giving task of raising a family has become something that feels more like a daunting, lonely and expensive chore,” Cavendish observes. “We’ve shifted, slowly but surely, into treating parenthood like a self-indulgent lifestyle choice. The onus is on you to cope.”
These aren’t abstract observations. Cavendish herself is a working mother of three, well acquainted with the difficulties of supporting a family and managing a career. She has no illusions about how hard it can be, and no interest in pretending otherwise.
“I am struck by how little has changed in the workplace in the last 20 years, despite the rhetoric about flexibility,” she notes. “What has changed, I think, is how grimly realistic young women now are about the trade-offs.”
“Reproduction is kind of the whole ballgame,” the trailblazing feminist Gloria Steinem told David Remnick in a 2015 interview, “and who controls it is the most fundamental question.”
Generation Maybe charts how authoritarian governments in China, Russia, Iran and elsewhere have responded to falling birthrates with a variety of repressive pronatalist policies — sanctioning child marriage, making divorce more difficult and denying abortion access. The Trump administration’s attacks on reproductive rights and federal childcare funding follow this trend, conscripting women into domestic roles. A simple solution to the problem of birth deficit is to force women to breed.
It may not be easy to create effective pronatalist policy interventions that encourage, rather than entrap — but it’s not impossible. Cavendish looks at what’s worked and what hasn’t in Singapore, Scandinavia and France, and outlines just shy of a dozen ways to help people choose children, from building more housing to offering parents benefits and even giving children themselves the vote: “Almost all policies which may help to lift birthrates are also ones which could enable human flourishing,” she notes.
There is no hectoring or finger-wagging in this book. What’s offered instead is an empathetic and curious approach to an entirely rational ambivalence. In so doing, Generation Maybe illuminates the enormous gulf between popular talking points about fertility and the actual conversations potential parents are having. For Cavendish, the real goal isn’t to persuade anyone to have kids; it’s simply “to make children a genuine choice.”

As a young practitioner, he focused on speed and strength. “I trained that way for many years without becoming still enough to search within myself,” said Yuan, who founded a kung fu academy in central China in 2004. “But as you gradually settle into stillness, you begin to understand what the scriptures mean by spirit,” he added. “You can begin to rediscover yourself.” That process is known as “entering the Dao” in martial arts. Taiwanese pineapples are expected to be exported to the US next year, after the US Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service in March announced importation requirements, the Ministry of Agriculture said yesterday.
The ministry has completed all necessary administrative procedures, the public comment period has closed and it is now waiting on Washington to give formal notification to begin exports, Minister of Agriculture Chen Junne-jih (陳駿季) told the Legislative Yuan’s Economics Committee.
The US is concerned about the oriental fruit fly and mealybug caterpillar, but said that pineapples with more than 50 percent Cayenne genetics do not host the insect, he said.
Photo: Wu Chun-feng, Taipei Times
Accepted varieties include golden diamond and mango pineapples, which would not require special quarantine treatments, he added.
Golden diamond pineapples account for 90 percent of Taiwanese pineapple production, while mango pineapples, a newer variety, have a total cultivation area of 50 hectares, the ministry said.
The government has also helped prepare 50 hectares for pineapples that would be exported to the US, including the two varieties, it added.
The ministry highlighted Taiwan’s recent success in expanding its overseas markets for pineapples: 15,700 tonnes of pineapples were exported to Japan this year, while shipments to Canada, South Korea and Australia rose by nearly 409 percent, 171 percent and 29 percent respectively.
New markets also include New Zealand, Singapore and Malaysia, it added.
Taiwan’s peak pineapple season runs from February to May, so notification might arrive before February next year, it said.
Golden diamond pineapples, the primary variety, would be the first to be exported, although the government would gradually encourage farmers to switch to mango pineapples, which are more suited for storage and transportation, and are better for high-end markets, it added.
As for exports of other fruits, Taiwan’s first shipments of mangoes, dragon fruit and lychees arrived in France in June and are expected to subsequently reach the UK, Austria, the Netherlands and other markets, the ministry said.
The EU approved imports of Taiwanese mangoes and guavas last year, followed by jujubes, dragon fruit and lychees in February.
The government is seeking to resume pork exports to Japan, as well as secure approval for the export of all varieties of mangoes to Japan and South Korea, and Taiwanese guavas to Australia, the ministry said.

The US and other wealthy nations need to urgently tackle mounting global debt levels that are weighing most heavily on low-income countries and straining the global financial system, IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva said yesterday.
US Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent and other US leaders recognize that the federal deficit and national debt are too high, but economic growth alone would not be enough to address the country’s more than US$40 trillion in national debt, Georgieva said.
Meanwhile, rising bond yields, reflecting higher premiums demanded by investors for taking on greater risk, have been disrupting financial markets, she said.
Photo: EPA
“We believe that growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments,” Georgieva said at the autumn meeting of the IMF and the World Bank in Bangkok.
“There is no magic,” she said, adding that other measures would be needed.
“You have to go in a direction of tightening, bringing it down, bringing the deficit down,” she said.
Rising debt levels and global inflation have pushed interest rates to multidecade highs, adding to the burdens of the world’s poorest nations.
Efforts to bring debt under control with what Georgieva and other experts call “fiscal consolidation” have suffered setbacks from heavy spending during the COVID-19 pandemic and since.
“Fiscal risks are rising and a proper reaction is largely absent in many countries,” said Rodrigo Valdes, director of the IMF’s Fiscal Affairs Department.
“And in major advanced economies, the effect of fiscal indiscipline does not stop at the border. It travels to the rest of the world,” Valdes added.
“Among the world’s poorest countries, interest payments have reached historic highs relative to revenue, and declining amounts of aid are creating gaps that some countries have been unable to finance,” the IMF’s latest Fiscal Monitor said.

Make the right to disconnect workable
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:58 UTC
01:42:58 KST

Imagine a teacher sitting down to dinner with their family. A parent’s message arrives: a question about tomorrow’s homework. Answering takes only a moment, and not answering risks seeming uncaring. The teacher replies, another question follows, and the school day quietly resumes.
Taiwan’s discussion of teachers’ right to disconnect asks whether professional commitment should be measured by constant availability.
In “Protecting teachers, improving education” (Oct. 3, page 8), teacher Lee Chi-fu (李基福) welcomed efforts to protect educators from after-hours demands. His argument invites a wider discussion about how schools should organize care, responsibility and trust.
Teaching depends on relationships. Families need confidence that teachers understand their children. Teachers need confidence that parents and administrators respect their professional judgement.
Expecting instant access can distort these relationships. Teachers become service providers whose commitment is judged by response time, while parents become customers monitoring performance.
Japan offers a useful comparison. Japan’s education ministry reported that 7,087 public-school educational personnel, including teachers and principals, were on formal sick leave for mental illness in 2024. The figure does not show that parental communication caused their difficulties. However, it does underscore the importance of examining how educational responsibilities accumulate.
Some Japanese local education authorities have introduced automated telephone responses outside designated school hours. Closing a telephone line achieves little if teachers still feel obliged to monitor personal messages.
The deeper issue is control over time. A message takes seconds to send, but its recipient must decide whether to interrupt dinner, postpone rest or risk appearing indifferent. The sender’s convenience can become the recipient’s obligation. Without clear rules, teachers must repeatedly defend boundaries that their institutions should establish.
A formal right to disconnect means little if teachers fear that delayed replies would damage their evaluations or provoke complaints. That right needs administrative backing.
Parents also face constraints. Those working irregular hours might only be able to contact schools at night. Families dealing with bullying, disability-related needs or school refusal need support. Restricting communication without offering alternatives would merely shift the burden from teachers to families.
Community psychology offers a useful way to understand this dilemma: An interaction between a parent and a teacher is shaped by conditions beyond either person’s control. Staffing, school leadership, parents’ work schedules and the availability of support services all matter.
The goal should be to distribute responsibility fairly.
First, schools should establish predictable response periods. Being able to send a message is not the same as being entitled to an immediate answer.
Second, schools should identify clear routes for urgent concerns. Those routes need adequate resources.
Third, teachers, parents and, where appropriate, students should help develop communication rules. Accessible complaint procedures must remain available, so that boundaries do not become barriers to accountability.
For Taiwan, the task is to make the right to disconnect workable. Parents should know when to expect a reply and where to turn for urgent help. Teachers should know that following agreed communication rules would not count against them.
Toshiaki Sasao is professor emeritus of psychology and education at International Christian University in Tokyo and a community psychologist.

World Medical Association pledges to support Taiwan’s WHO bid

16:42:53 UTC

The World Medical Association (WMA) last week reaffirmed a resolution passed in April to support Taiwan’s participation in all WHO programs and mechanisms related to the International Health Regulations (IHR).
The association held its 77th annual general assembly from Wednesday last week until Saturday in Rotterdam, the Netherlands.
The assembly considered the resolution, passed by the WMA Council in Belgrade in April, the Taiwan Medical Association (TMA) said in a news release yesterday.
Photo: Reuters
The WMA in April also sent an open letter to WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, calling for the meaningful participation of Taiwan in the World Health Assembly.
“The continued exclusion of Taiwan is counterproductive and potentially dangerous for future global health security. Taiwan has consistently proven to be one of the WHO’s ‘best students’ in implementing public health measures, prevention strategies, and Universal Health Coverage,” it said in the letter.
It also said that “Taiwan possesses significant expertise and material resources that offer valuable support to the international community.”
The WMA’s assembly last week reaffirmed the resolution without objection, drawing applause from attending delegates, it said.
Under WMA regulations, a resolution that has been reaffirmed cannot be submitted for reconsideration within the next five years.
The assembly’s formal reaffirmation of the resolution demonstrated the international medical community’s support for Taiwan’s participation in the global health system and would allow the resolution to remain in effect over the coming years, the TMA said.
TMA secretary-general Chang Pi-cheng (張必正) represented the association at the assembly.
Chang launched a multilayered lobbying strategy ahead of the meeting, coordinating with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs to enlist Taiwan’s representative offices in like-minded countries to help promote the resolution, the TMA said.
He engaged with delegates from Europe, the US and across the Asia-Pacific region, it added.
Chang was further invited to a dinner hosted by the American Medical Association, which was attended by current and former presidents, it said.
He also consolidated resources from the World Organization of Family Doctors to ensure the strongest possible support from Taiwan’s diplomatic allies, it added.
TMA president Chen Hsiang-kuo (陳相國) said the WMA had long supported Taiwan’s participation in the global health system.
The reaffirmation also demonstrated the international medical community’s core values that health has no borders and no one should be left out of global health, he said.
The TMA said it would continue to strengthen exchanges with international medical associations through the WMA and other international medical organizations, while also advocating for Taiwan’s meaningful participation in the World Health Assembly, the WHO and IHR-related mechanisms.

Notes from Central Taiwan: Annexation could sever Taiwan’s chip lifeline
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:49 UTC
01:42:49 KST

The South China Morning Post (SCMP) article from earlier this month on how Beijing would govern a post-annexation Taiwan (Amber Wang, “Beijing’s policy advisers map out how post-reunification Taiwan could be governed,” Oct. 6, 2026) is a reminder that even “peaceful” (coerced) occupation by the People’s Republic of China (PRC) will beggar Taiwan.
The “scholars” cited in the SCMP piece argued that Taiwan would be governed in a manner similar to Hong Kong. As I observed in my piece for Monday (“Beijing’s intimidation tactics in Taiwan and beyond,” Oct. 12, 2026), that claim is simply a form of cognitive warfare. One of the functions of “One country, two systems” is to conceal the profound changes to Taiwan’s economy and to the global trade system that would occur if Taiwan were forced inside the PRC.
SEMICONDUCTOR INDUSTRY
Photo: Hung You-fang, Liberty Times
Consider Taiwan’s semiconductor industry, currently driving Taiwan’s world-beating economic growth and stock market performance. What would happen to this industry if the PRC occupied Taiwan peacefully? For starters, it would become subject to US export controls.
Many governments, led by the US, at present are conducting a coordinated campaign to prevent the PRC from gaining access to critical semiconductor manufacturing technology, chips, materials and personnel. These include bans on exports of advanced chips. The US, the Netherlands (home to ASML) and Japan restrict exports of critical chipmaking machinery, especially Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV) and advanced Deep Ultraviolet (DUV) lithography systems.
Further, US investment rules under the Outbound Investment Security Program prohibit US venture capital, private equity and joint ventures from financing PRC firms in the fields of “semiconductors and microelectronics, quantum information technologies and artificial intelligence.”
Photo: AFP
Another US initiative is the Foreign Direct Product Rule. First promulgated in 1959, it was intended to control the trade in US technologies. It says that if a product is made using US technology, the US government has the right to forbid the sale of that product. This includes products made outside the US, if the production technology came from the US.
Under these rules, the flow of technology required to keep the semiconductor industry running and up to date would halt. The industry would begin falling behind the technological frontier as production technology continued to advance outside Taiwan. Moreover, the US, which currently permits Taiwan to export semiconductor products made with US technology, would rescind that permission for factories in Taiwan. US investment in Taiwan technology firms, including Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) would cease.
This ripple effect would cascade across many other firms, firms that are not as famous as TSMC, but are nevertheless key industry players, such as Powertech Technology Inc (PTI, 力成科技), a semiconductor testing and assembly firm, or King Yuan Electronics Co (KYEC, 京元電子), a semiconductor testing company, which recently committed to a US$1.4 billion investment in the US. These firms are also powered by materials and technologies from Japan and the US.
Many observers have noted Taiwan’s paradoxical “K-shaped” economy, with its electronics industries experiencing soaring growth while its traditional industries shrivel. In an occupied Taiwan, with the electronics industry under US sanctions, those traditional industries would be much of the economy. Not for long, though, as competition from the PRC would almost certainly wipe them out.
In other words, even if we assume that all goes as the pro-PRC shills would have it, and occupation proceeds smoothly, Taiwan is finished as an industrial power. The PRC is well aware of the US sanctions regime and will simply loot Taiwan for what it can get.
What will happen to the migrant workers who are a crucial part of the electronics industry, and who care for Taiwan’s aged? In a 2023 survey the PRC doesn’t even appear on top 10 lists of preferred work destinations for Filipino overseas workers.
TAIWAN-PRC ANSCHLUSS
Note too that the PRC has its own restrictions on technology and on the people who make it. As Inquirer.net has pointed out, a law took effect last month gave PRC officials the power to stop engineers, founders and other specialists from leaving the country if their expertise is in batteries, rare earths or artificial intelligence (AI). When Taiwan becomes part of the PRC its technologists will come under these rules. For decades Taiwanese technology researchers have circulated out to western countries to absorb the latest technology. All of that motion, an important source of information and technology, will be cut off.
Moreover, many technology workers in Taiwan probably think that a PRC-Taiwan Anschluss won’t affect them since, they figure, they can easily get a job elsewhere. They won’t realize how wrong they are until they try to leave for the US or Europe, and find they cannot. How then will major Taiwan firms run their investments in the US?
The joint effect of US and PRC restrictions sheds new light on criticisms of President William Lai (賴清德) by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) over the semiconductor industry’s investments in the US. When the wave of investment first began, KMT politicians immediately attacked it. Former president Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九) said Lai was “selling” TSMC to the US. KMT heavyweight Fu Kun-chi (傅崑萁) was quoted in the Taipei Times as saying “Where would Taiwan’s safety be when it no long has its ‘sacred mountain protecting the nation’ (護國神山)?”
A Voice of America (VOA) piece by William Yang (“Taiwan lauds TSMC investment as ‘historic moment’ for US relations” March 6, 2025) quotes wise words from Taiwan-based scholar Lev Nachman, who observed that critiques of the semiconductor industry’s investments abroad appear only in relation to the US, never to Japan or other countries. That indicates, Nachman noted, that they are really attempts to drum up skepticism of America in Taiwan.
That is true. But the KMT maintains these criticisms even though many of its leading members must know that if Taiwan’s electronics firms do not have factories outside Taiwan they will soon cease to function if Taiwan is occupied, whether coercively or violently. They must also know that there is no “silicon shield.” Is it just an attempt to drive skepticism of the US? Or are the KMT’s criticisms one with the party’s quiet opposition to nuclear power and more open opposition to renewables, part of a larger program to hem in the nation and reduce its options in the face of PRC threats?
For the global economy, whether TSMC and its supply chain is seized coercively or violently, the end result will be the same: the flow of high-end chips will stop almost immediately as Taiwan begins to fall under US sanctions. Recall that before Nancy Pelosi’s trip to Taiwan in August, 2022, US commerce secretary Gina Raimondo warned that the loss of US access to Taiwan’s semiconductor industry production would cause “a deep and immediate recession” in the US. Hundreds of millions in products and investments would be lost. In the near term there is no replacement for TSMC production. Instead, it will take years to rebuild that capacity.
Somewhere else, of course, someplace not under PRC control.

Address the shortage of teachers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:42:49 UTC
01:42:49 KST

According to the Ministry of Education’s latest International Comparison of Education Statistical Indicators, Taiwan has a lower proportion of teachers under the age of 40 in elementary and junior-high schools than its neighbors Japan and South Korea — in fact, Taiwan’s share stands at only about half that of the two countries. In other words, the nation’s teaching workforce is clearly aging and faces a growing generational gap.
As the saying goes, with age comes wisdom — teachers that have accumulated more years of experience tend to have developed a deeper understanding of teaching, and are better able at identifying key curriculum priorities and communicating with parents, making them less likely to make mistakes. However, as technology advances rapidly, some older teachers are slower to adapt to new teaching methods and integrate artificial intelligence into the classroom. They tend to be less receptive to these changes, making it more difficult for them to adapt to today’s educational environment.
Furthermore, a significant generational gap between older teachers and their students can make it harder for teachers to understand the younger generation’s perspectives and language, increasing the likelihood of misunderstandings and ultimately undermining teaching quality.
Taiwan might experience an education crisis over the next five to six years, as the retirement of senior teachers leaves schools facing a severe staffing gap with too few younger teachers to fill their places. Young people today are generally reluctant to enter the teaching profession because salaries and benefits are not attractive enough to compensate for the heavy responsibilities. Without early preventive measures, schools could find themselves relying increasingly on substitute teachers, creating further instability and potentially jeopardizing the quality of education in elementary and junior-high schools.
To prevent this, the ministry must take action on several fronts. First, it must find ways to retain experienced teachers so they can pass on their knowledge and expertise to their less experienced colleagues; it must offer greater incentives to attract younger people to teaching; and it must urgently assess potential teacher shortages in elementary and junior-high schools across the nation, project future staffing needs amid falling student numbers caused by a declining birthrate and prepare well in advance to ensure that future students are not left without teachers.
To avoid sacrificing students’ rights to education and falling behind Japan and South Korea in educational quality, the ministry can no longer turn a blind eye to these stark figures. It must act swiftly to develop effective measures to address the looming teacher shortage.
Lee Chi-fu is a teacher.
