Exclusive: Draft EU summit conclusions reveal what leaders will and will not say on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:20:40 UTC
01:20:40 KST

Draft EU summit conclusions reveal what leaders will and will not say on Ukraine
A red carpet and European Union (EU) flags in the Europa building ahead of a European Council meeting in Brussels, Belgium, on Thursday, Oct. 23, 2025. (Simon Wohlfahrt/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Leaders of the EU's 27 member states have a Ukraine-packed agenda when they meet in Brussels Oct. 15-16, according to the latest draft conclusions of the upcoming meeting seen by the Kyiv Independent.
The 25-page document contains six-and-a-half pages of comments specifically on Ukraine, three-and-a-half pages on defense and security, where Ukraine features prominently, and a page on the future of enlargement.
Those hoping for a long list of decisions from the European Council will be left disappointed, as the document mostly consists of leaders noting developments since they last met in June and issuing calls for what should happen next.
But some of those calls can lead to concrete outcomes further down the line.
For example, the draft conclusions say that the European Council "calls for the swift and effective implementation of the measures concerning Russian ex-combatants, and for further (sanctions) measures."
A visa ban for Russian soldiers was pushed for in the bloc's previous sanctions package, but ultimately fell through after France and Italy railed against it.
Since Russia's drone attack on Leipzig, Germany, the conversation has shifted, and EU diplomats from three countries said France had begun to budge when foreign ministers met in Luxembourg on Oct. 12.
Finland also upped the pressure by issuing a letter arguing against issuing visas to Russians and outlining five key demands.
The draft conclusions signal that concrete action is due to land soon.
In a similar vein, the Council conclusions state that it "underlines the EU's readiness to step up its engagement" on "diplomatic efforts to bring Russia's war of aggression to an end."
The week before, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's right-hand man discussed peace with the U.S., NATO, and Ukraine.
But those talks were overshadowed by U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement of a likely-illegal diesel deal with Russia — a development that the conclusions note with "regret."
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told journalists on Oct. 12 that the U.S.' approach shows that "Europe should take its future in its own hands, speak with one voice, and restore peace," and the conclusions' readiness to do so suggests that the EU agrees.
Shouting into the wind
On other topics, the draft conclusions expose the EU's seeming inability to tackle Ukraine's most pressing issues.
With Kyiv being pummeled by ever more jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles, the call for "further intensified efforts and coordination to strengthen Ukraine's air and missile defense capabilities, the resilience of its critical infrastructure, and its energy system," rings especially hollow.
Similarly, the call for "immediate restoration of safe passage for grain cargo ships in the Black Sea," after weeks of Russian blockade, and the sinking of ships — which has also led to the loss of life — reads as weak in the absence of any accompanying measures.
However, the European Council "stresses the need to prevent grain stolen by Russia from temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories from being exported via the EU," read the conclusions, which suggests support may be gathering for a Russian grain transit ban, as proposed by Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania the week before.
Likewise, support may be brewing for future EU action to prevent Russia's re-entry into international sports and cultural events, which the conclusions say should not be allowed to happen, three days after EU Sports Commissioner Glenn Micallef met with EU foreign ministers for the first time to discuss the issue.
The result of Micallef's meeting was the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, announcing that her team "will put forward proposals on how to sustain Russia's isolation in global sports."
And in the meantime, some countries take unilateral action, such as the Netherlands, which has denied visas to Russians due to compete at an international gymnastics event in Rotterdam, even as the world body for gymnastics has again allowed Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete under their own flag.
Other mentions in the conclusions can be seen as messages to other allies of Ukraine, in Europe and beyond.
That the EU "strongly condemns the deployment of North Korean military forces in the war against Ukraine" is a useful reminder to South Korea of what is at stake for them, just as relations between Kyiv and Seoul reach a new low.
And the renewed call for "international partners to swiftly step up their support to help meet Ukraine's pressing financing and military needs," likewise points to the fact that since the EU adopted its 90 billion euro loan ($100 billion) for Ukraine in April, third countries appear to have slowed down on their own contributions to Kyiv.
read also
Conspicuously absent: Russia's immobilized assets
One word missing from the draft conclusions: "assets." This is despite a renewed push from various directions to revive discussions about how to use 200 billion euros ($224 billion) of immobilized Russian wealth to directly support Ukraine.
Four EU countries reopened the topic with an open letter in August, and it came up prominently during the Oct. 12 meeting of foreign ministers.
Sybiha spoke about the idea to journalists, published an opinion piece the same day with news website Politico, and had strong support from his Swedish colleague Maria Stenergard, who even brought along visual aids for the discussion.
But the lack of a mention is because the EU is still by no means united on what approach to take.
Belgian newspaper De Morgen reported on Oct. 13 that President Volodymyr Zelensky wants to meet with Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever bilaterally around the EU leaders' summit, which he will also attend on Oct. 16.
De Wever led resistance to the use of Russian assets in December 2025, the last time it was seriously discussed, and as the vast majority of immobilized Russian government assets are in Belgium, a solution that does not work for De Wever will go nowhere.
read also
In response to a question from the Kyiv Independent about the Russian assets, Kallas said "I think this discussion will continue because eventually it is about sharing the risks between member states."
"It is important that it is not off the table. We are thinking about different tools to fill that financing gap," Kallas said.
Alternative options do exist: Russian assets could be invested more profitably to create new funds for Ukraine, as suggested by a plan called the Windfall Optimization Loan Framework, or the EU could simply agree to create new loans.
What is clear is that the topic is not set to disappear just yet, with one senior EU official telling the Kyiv Independent they expect it to dominate EU leaders' December meeting.
read also
Don't forget the future
The October meeting of EU leaders was supposed to have the future of EU enlargement as a main topic, to which end the European Commission issued proposals for consideration on Oct. 6.
Instead, with a new multi-year budget to discuss, energy prices, migration issues, the Middle East, and all the other Ukraine topics on the agenda, enlargement risks being overshadowed, and it only accounts for one page in the 25-page Council conclusions draft.
Even so, that one page contains a potentially big shift, if the conclusions are adopted as written.
"The European Council ... looks forward to the opening of all the other clusters as soon as possible, in line with the merit-based approach," read the draft conclusions.
What looks like an innocuous enough sentence takes on new meaning when one has in mind the last leaders' meeting in July, in which Hungary lobbied hard to remove the words "as soon as possible" because it wanted Ukraine to pass a law bolstering the rights of its Hungarian-speaking minority first.
Ukraine passed that law on Oct. 12, unlocked two further enlargement clusters on Oct. 13, and may have no further obstacles to overcome.
France and Poland were expected in some quarters to make it difficult to unlock the remaining cluster covering agriculture due to fears of Ukrainian competition, but they publicly ruled this out on Oct. 13.
A high-ranking EU official and a European minister told the Kyiv Independent that they expect the last two clusters to open in December 2026, as several EU countries must follow their own political procedures at home to give a formal green light.
For example, Slovenia needs to vote on the decision through its parliament, even if the vote itself is not expected to cause any problems, and has never done so for Ukraine so far.
But that does not mean Ukraine has nothing still to do.
Both for the EU's financial support to be greenlighted, and for Ukraine to join the bloc one day, the Council conclusions "recall the importance of Ukraine continuing its reform efforts and upholding the rule of law."

New York Seeks to Ban Horse-Drawn Carriages

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

New York Seeks to Ban Horse-Drawn Carriages
Kyiv • UNN
Mayor Zohran Mamdani supported banning horse-drawn carriages in New York starting in June 2028. The Council may vote on the bill on October 22.
Mayor Zoran Mamdani and the speaker of the New York City Council have agreed to ban horse-drawn carriage rides in the city, a popular tourist attraction that has drawn widespread criticism, UNN reports, citing The Guardian.
Details
Mamdani agreed to support a bill backed by Julie Menin, the speaker of the New York City Council, that bans the operation of horse-drawn carriages starting in June 2028, Politico reported on Tuesday. The City Council is expected to vote on the legislation next week.
"The horse-carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will ensure that workers and owners are protected, and that the horses are safe," Mamdani wrote on X on Tuesday.
A person familiar with City Hall confirmed that an agreement had been reached.
Although carriage rides are ubiquitous in Central Park, animal advocates have long raised concerns about the treatment of the horses. Since 2020, several horses have died, at times collapsing during carriage rides.
The push for a ban intensified over the summer after 18-year-old tourist Romanch Mahajan died after being thrown from a carriage.
In a statement, Menin said that horse-drawn carriages had "become a growing public-safety concern."
"We can honor our city's traditions while recognizing that it is time to move forward in the interests of public safety, protecting workers and strengthening the economic vitality of our city," Menin said.
A spokesperson for Menin said that the City Council speaker would bring the bill to a vote on October 22.
In addition
Despite broad support for a ban on horse-drawn carriages, officials have struggled to advance the legislation because the Transport Workers Union of Greater New York, which represents carriage drivers, has raised concerns about the drivers' livelihoods.
Mamdani had previously indicated that he would support a bill banning horse-drawn carriages; however, he expressed concerns about the bill as drafted because it contained insufficient protections for carriage workers.
A copy of the bill sent to The Guardian contains language requiring the city to create a workforce-transition program providing carriage drivers with counseling and referrals to other jobs in the private and public sectors.
The bill also requires the city to "consider" creating a compensation program for carriage owners based on the value of their businesses.
John Samuelsen, the international president of the Transport Workers Union, told Politico that the bill does not provide "significant economic relief for workers."
"This is shameful political opportunism, and Zoran should not simply go along with it, especially when the livelihoods of immigrant families are being destroyed," Samuelsen said. "This entire situation is reprehensible."
It is unclear whether Mamdani plans to sign the bill in its current form or whether additional changes will be made.
Sneha Chowdhury, a spokesperson for City Hall, said in a statement: "We are working closely with the City Council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal-protection advocates and community leaders to ensure a just transition that protects workers while ending the use of horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all."
The bill also requires the city to introduce a program to help drivers humanely relinquish their horses—prohibiting them from selling the horses, transporting them for slaughter or selling them for use in horse-drawn carriage operations elsewhere.

To unlock Britain’s innovation potential, Labour needs to think outside the box | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:19:16 UTC
01:19:16 KST

Gordon Brown wants Britain to invent, invest in and own the future (British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents, 9 October). But invent what, and for whom? His hunt for “lost Einsteins” rests on a narrow vision: a lone genius invents, commercialisation scales, the problem is solved.
That may suit a cancer drug, but not the wicked problems of our time – social care, education, climate – which demand not silver bullets but new technologies and practices for collaboration, distributed ownership and collective innovation.
The current struggle to retrofit governance, accountability and benefit on to AI exposes the fiction of genius-engineered “solutions”. Nor do trillion-dollar companies make every household £5,000 richer. They concentrate short-term gain in a narrow founder-investor class; the rest of us carry the work and cost of long-term cleanup.
It’s a vicious cycle: the government worries about big tech yet incentivises more of it, competing with Silicon Valley by doing the same – just not quite as well. My organisation is a community interest company with an asset lock, built for competitive innovation in the public interest.
Labour created this structure in 2005 to enable a new generation of public-good companies, but innovation policy has yet to back it. UK Research and Innovation is closed to us: we aren’t a research organisation. Innovate UK now deems our community interest company ineligible for a knowledge transfer partnership, despite previous success with the University of Edinburgh. The Advanced Research and Invention Agency backs lone inventors. The Seed Enterprise Investment Scheme and the Enterprise Investment Scheme reward only uncapped shareholder returns.
Much is made of Palantir and the NHS, yet current policy doesn’t let a competitive British alternative emerge: one that tackles systemic data problems while letting trusts and communities retain ownership and agency. With funding, that is five years away, not a fantasy. If the government wants innovation that tackles the hardest problems, benefits all citizens, and competes globally, it must look beyond the models it rewards today.
Kate Fleming
Director, IDEMS
Gordon Brown’s analysis of Britain’s innovation ecosystem is largely correct. We do have world-class universities, rigorous research and a track record of discovery, and he’s right to highlight the gap between these strengths and their commercial returns. It’s no doubt a defining challenge of our time.
But there’s one word conspicuously absent from his argument: creativity. In making the case for innovation, Brown has fallen for a common trap, defaulting to a vision of research and development (R&D) that begins and ends with Stem (science, technology, engineering and mathematics). This vision leaves no place for the creative advantage that in many cases makes true innovation possible.
The UK’s creative industries contribute £145bn to the economy annually, growing at four times the national rate. Research by the Creative Industries Policy and Evidence Centre shows that nearly two-thirds of creative micro-firms have engaged in R&D in the past three years, outstripping every other industrial strategy priority sector. Brown might be surprised to learn that the UK university producing the most student startups is actually University of the Arts London (UAL).
UAL startups are using lateral thinking to develop biodegradable alternatives to plastic, building tools that decarbonise supply chains, pioneering food waste fermentation technology, and creating new materials from agricultural byproducts that could transform the construction industry.
They are engaging in real-world R&D to solve major global problems that transcend the creative sector, yet as creative businesses with arts graduates at the helm, they are consistently excluded from the narrative and the wider policy framing.
If we are serious about innovation driving good growth, we cannot afford a definition that excludes one of our most dynamic, inventive and internationally competitive sectors. Unlocking Britain’s full innovation potential means recognising that creativity and science are partners, not opposites.
Jenny Haigh
Head of policy for creative economy, University of the Arts London

Build-it-yourself housing project was a huge success in 1970s Lewisham | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

01:19:08 KST

An uplifting article by Phineas Harper about plans for self-build houses by Lewisham council in London (Free land for those who will build social homes on it. Is this the radical solution to the UK’s housing problem?, 8 October).
The original 1970s Lewisham self-build scheme that he mentions, using methods developed by the German architect Walter Segal, was proposed by a friend of mine, Brian Richardson, who was a Lewisham council architect at the time.
Brian persuaded the local authority to offer people on the council house waiting list the materials to build their own homes, with advice from him. They had no building skills, but they worked evenings and weekends, and built homes and a community.
Brian often said that the most successful outcome was the changes to the builders themselves in terms of pride and self-confidence.
Just search for “Walter’s Way Lewisham” online for contemporary and more recent videos and the views of the builders themselves.
John Banks
Ledbury, Herefordshire
Phineas Harper is right to highlight Lewisham council’s proposals to make publicly owned land available for community-led social housing. From a valuation perspective, the most interesting aspect to me is viability. Land value is often a significant barrier to delivering social housing, particularly on smaller sites that can involve almost as much time, effort and cost as larger schemes, and are therefore difficult for developers and housing associations to justify taking on.
This will not replace established affordable housing delivery, and there will still be challenges around building costs, funding, planning and delivery. But it could provide a practical way to unlock smaller, community-led schemes.
Sometimes improving viability is not about increasing development value, but reducing the cost of the land itself. I will be interested to see whether other local authorities follow suit.
Jonathan Pearson
RICS registered valuer, Residentially Chartered Surveyors

The problem with living in a rich man’s world | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:19:01 UTC
01:19:01 KST

The idea that the departure of the super-rich is a problem ignores a historical fact (Apparent exodus of super-rich suggests UK is no longer billionaires’ playground, 7 October). Capitalism works better without them. The most successful countries today are states where redistributive taxation has empowered the working masses and provided a better and more stable market for business people.
How do today’s complaining uber-rich explain the postwar decades, when the top rate of income tax was commonly 80% or 90%, and yet the period is known as a golden age of capitalism? Then Margaret Thatcher lowered the top rate to 60% and the country tilted into a massive recession. The rich get to a point where they simply become wealth extractors, using their money to buy assets and raising the cost of them for the rest of us – housing being a good example today.
A good story from 1969 comes from a music writer who was embedded in the Rolling Stones’ tour of America. Earwigging the band talking about becoming tax exiles, if not on main street, then maybe in France, he hears Charlie Watts (a non-songwriter, so less affluent) say that he rather likes his land and his house and his horses, and he wouldn’t want to leave. Isn’t that rich enough for most of us? It’s appropriate that John Maynard Keynes is now on stage in the West End. People might remember what he said about the dangers of wealth disparity and the bubbles of speculation that they bring.
David Redshaw
Saltdean, East Sussex
Your report (‘I reside in Monaco’: billionaire said to have quit UK over potential wealth tax had already left, 7 October) exposes something far more troubling than billionaires fleeing Britain: the extraordinary power of the super-rich to hold an entire country hostage to the threat of their departure.
Ordinary working people cannot relocate their tax obligations to Monaco. They pay their taxes, fund public services and shoulder the consequences of a system increasingly tilted towards those who need its protection least. Yet we are expected to tremble at the prospect of billionaires taking their fortunes elsewhere. Why? Wealth does not exist in a vacuum. It is built on a society’s workers, infrastructure, institutions and opportunities.
If the wealthiest can enjoy the fruits of that society while escaping their fair share of its responsibilities, the scandal is not that they leave. It is that successive governments have allowed them to make the rules. A country that cannot afford to lose its billionaires should ask itself why it can apparently afford to impoverish everyone else.
Fernando Quintana
London

Nigeria elected to UN Human Rights Council seat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:17:48 UTC
01:17:48 KST

Kabir Adeniyi
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Nigeria has been elected to the United Nations Human Rights Council for a three-year term beginning in January, the government said Wednesday.
Nigeria was among 15 countries elected to the 47-member council for the 2027–2029 term during Tuesday’s vote in New York.
The country received 172 out of 181 votes, placing third among the four African countries elected. Zambia received 177 votes, Ghana 173 and Burundi 160, according to the results.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs thanked UN member states for supporting Nigeria’s candidacy and reaffirmed the country’s commitment to international cooperation, dialogue and the promotion of human rights.
“Nigeria’s election reflects international confidence in its commitment to advancing human rights and improving human rights conditions across the world,” Foreign Affairs spokesperson Oluwafemi Adeniyi said in part.
The government said Nigeria looked forward to working with other council members to strengthen global efforts to protect fundamental freedoms and uphold human dignity and justice.
The Human Rights Council, based in Geneva, is the UN body responsible for promoting and protecting human rights worldwide. It addresses alleged violations, makes recommendations to member states and conducts the Universal Periodic Review, through which the human rights records of all UN member states are assessed.
The council has 47 members elected by the General Assembly, with seats allocated among regional groups. Members serve three-year terms and are expected to uphold high standards in the promotion and protection of human rights.
Nigeria’s term will begin Jan. 1 and run through Dec. 31, 2029.

Spanish NGO postpones Mediterranean rescue mission over fuel costs
MADRID, Oct 14 - Spanish humanitarian rescue charity SMH has postponed its next mission in the central Mediterranean until 2027 due to soaring fuel costs, the group said on Wednesday, highlighting the financial pressures facing humanitarian efforts along one of the world's deadliest migration routes.
SMH, which operates the Aita Mari, a former fishing vessel converted into a rescue ship in 2017, said on X the doubling of fuel prices had forced it to suspend operations in the central Mediterranean and shift activities to waters around Spain's Valencia coast, and the islands of Mallorca and Menorca.
It also launched a crowdfunding campaign to cover the extra costs.
The central Mediterranean crossing from North Africa to Italy and southern France is one of the world's most dangerous migrant routes, used by migrants from Africa and the Middle East seeking to reach Europe, often in overcrowded or unseaworthy boats.
Spanish NGO Open Arms said it had also scaled back its central Mediterranean missions in recent years because of rising fuel costs and Italy's policy of assigning rescue vessels ports in northern Italy. The practice can require ships to sail for two or three days from their operating area, increasing costs and reducing time available for search-and-rescue work.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's right-wing, anti-immigration government has repeatedly argued that humanitarian rescue vessels encourage migrants to attempt the crossing. REUTERS

“The energy truce proposed by Trump was not specified, so it cannot be said that Russia is not complying with it,” Peskov said according to the Russian news outlet Astra.
Moscow names Kyiv, Kharkiv power plants as targets
Russia’s Defense Ministry said that its forces used ground-based precision weapons and long-range attack drones against energy and communications facilities it claimed were serving Ukraine’s military and defense industry.
The ministry listed the Darnytsia CHP-4 and CHP-5 combined heat and power plants in Kyiv, as well as CHP-6, the Trypillia thermal power plant and a major electrical substation in Kyiv region.
In the Kharkiv region, the ministry named the Kharkiv CHP-5 and the Zmiiv thermal power plant.
It also claimed to have hit an Ukrssibbank data center, alleging without evidence that it was used to gather intelligence on Russian forces.
Ukrainian authorities confirmed that Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv’s CHP-4 power plant and a nine-story residential building late Tuesday, Oct. 13, killing at least three people and injuring 26, including an eight-year-old child.
Russia to Sign Diesel Contracts With Washington Soon, Putin’s Money Man Says
According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russia launched 39 missiles and 128 drones in the attack, which began at 6 p.m. local time. Air defenses downed four missiles and 115 drones.
Zelensky continues pressing Washington for sanctions
Zelensky called the strike deliberate, saying it damaged 26 sites in Ukraine’s power system and four oil and gas facilities, and warned of further outages.
“Russia does not view the US President’s statements as strong,” Zelensky said.
He urged Trump to impose “STRONG sanctions” on Moscow under the sanctions law named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, and asked for more Patriot interceptors; the only weapons system that can successfully deter Russia’s ballistic missiles.
Strains between Kyiv and Washington have continued to grow throughout this week.
For the second night in a row, Ukraine received no early warning from Western partners about incoming ballistic missiles.
The lapse followed reports that US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner warned Ukraine’s delegation at talks in Miami on Friday, Oct. 9 that Washington could cut off intelligence sharing if Kyiv kept striking Russian refineries.
Trump’s administration reportedly also warned it could suspend the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) – a mechanism that enables European purchases of US weapons for Ukraine, the main channel for buying Patriot interceptors.
US Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker denied the claims, saying that no change has been made.
Meanwhile, Trump has denied that the US stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv and Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha confirmed that cooperation with Washington continues, although neither disclosed whether the scope of intelligence sharing had changed.
How the truce claim unfolded
Following a telephone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday, Oct. 9, Trump announced that the US struck a diesel arrangement with the Kremlin.
Shortly after, the US Treasury Department issued a license authorizing the sale and import of Russian diesel through April 7, 2027.
On Sunday, Oct. 11, Trump announced that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop striking each other’s energy infrastructure, without an official response from neither Ukraine nor Russia.
Although Ukraine signalled willingness to abide by the truce and refrained from striking Russia’s facilities, Russia continued its attacks on Ukraine nationwide.
Trump insisted that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an energy ceasefire because he told them to, despite neither government confirming such a deal. “They agreed. You know why? Because I said, ‘You agree’ – that’s why,” he told reporters on Monday.
On Tuesday, 12 US senators – six Republicans and six Democrats – signed a joint letter urging Trump to rescind the diesel deal and enforce the new Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which grants him the power to sanction Russia and buyers of its energy with tariffs of up to 500%. The senators called the deal “a betrayal” of Ukraine and argued it only helps Russia’s aggression.
The bill was signed into law by Trump just three weeks before he struck the deal with the Kremlin leader.
On the same day that Trump announced the deal, a bipartisan US delegation was in Kyiv, backing expansion of Ukraine’s access to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network and urging an effort to win over the company’s owner, Elon Musk.
However, Musk did the opposite and imposed speed restrictions on Starshield, the military version of Starlink used by Ukraine’s military, without prior warning overnight on Oct. 13-14. The cap cuts connections for terminals moving faster than 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour).

NYC moves to ban Central Park horse carriages after 150 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:14:00 UTC
01:14:00 KST

New York City lawmakers are preparing to ban horse-drawn carriages from Central Park, potentially ending a 150-year tourism tradition amid longstanding animal welfare concerns and renewed scrutiny following the death of a teenage tourist last spring.
The City Council is expected to approve a bill next week that would end the rides by 2028. Three consecutive mayors had called for an end to the carriage rides because of safety concerns, only to have lawmakers yank back the reins.
A spokesperson for Julie Menin, the council speaker, confirmed the incoming vote and said the proposal had enough support to pass. Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office said he had reached a deal with the speaker on the legislation.
"The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City,” Mamdani said in a social media post.
The latest push for a ban started in June, when 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan, visiting the city from India, died after jumping from a runaway horse carriage during a ride with family members. His death, which appeared to be the first fatality in a horse carriage accident since they were introduced in Central Park, reignited the debate over whether carriages, a romantic throwback to the city's past, have a place in a modern metropolis.
Mahajan's family has appeared at City Hall, in person and through videoconference calls from India, begging the city to finally end the rides.
"We are shattered, our whole family shattered. The pain does not go away,” his father, Deepak Mahajan, told city council members via a videocall during a hearing for the bill last summer, saying his son leapt from the carriage to try and help his mother, who was flung from her seat, after the horse bolted. "Every morning we wake up and think of nothing but the loss of our son.”
For decades, animal welfare activists and other critics have decried the carriage industry, arguing horses shouldn't be hauling tourists around busy streets and Central Park while having to navigate bustling traffic and gawking passersby. In the past, horses have collapsed, gotten startled and run off, hitting cars or other objects, with each accident resulting in fresh calls for a ban.
"The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable. Horse-drawn carriages have long been part of New York City’s history, but in an increasingly busy Central Park, this tradition has become a growing public safety liability,” Menin said in a statement.
The industry and its supporters have long cast the rides as a way for visitors to experience the New York they know from classic movies and television.
Fred Astaire and Cyd Charisse danced into one of the carriages in "The Band Wagon.” Robert Redford and Jane Fonda rode one in "Barefoot in the Park.” Macaulay Culkin escaped bandits in a carriage in "Home Alone 2: Lost in New York.”
"Taking a horse and carriage ride in New York City is one of the most iconic things to do in New York City and people from all over the world know about us and travel to New York to go to a carriage ride in New York,” Conor McHugh, a longtime carriage driver, told the Council earlier this year.
Efforts to close down the industry have been met with pushback from unions and influential supporters, often resulting in tiresome political fights that have seen mayors throw up their hands over nagging worries about putting carriage drivers out of work and what to do with the horses if they can no longer work.
Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen said the Council's bill has "no meaningful economic relief for workers” and that Menin "used the tragic death of a tourist to contrive a public safety crisis.”
"This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families’ livelihoods are being destroyed. This entire situation is reprehensible,” he said in a statement.
The proposal as written would require the mayor's office to develop a workforce transition plan for drivers, and includes a measure that would allow the city to consider some kind of compensation for industry workers. Carriage owners could not sell their horses off for slaughter, according to the bill's language, which requires that horses be disposed of in a "humane manner.”
"I think we have a civic responsibility to ensure that we are not leaving anybody out to dry,” Mamdani told reporters Wednesday.
The mayor's predecessor, Eric Adams, called for ending the industry during the waning days of his administration, but the proposal went nowhere. The mayor before that, Bill de Blasio, had pledged to eliminate the rides on day one of his administration but abandoned the crusade after heavy opposition from unions and a media blitz involving actor Liam Neeson.
Over the years, the city has placed various safety regulations around the industry, including a requirement that the horses get at least five weeks of vacation a year outside of city limits with daily access to a pasture. The horses are inspected by a veterinarian twice a year, and the maximum age they can work at is 26, according to city regulations. And they don't work when it is hotter than 89 degrees.

UK’s ‘incoherent’ approach to China plagued by lack of expertise, report says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:13:49 UTC
01:13:49 KST

The UK’s approach to China is “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of senior expertise, according to a report warning of the risks inherent in misjudging the bilateral relationship.
An audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), an international grouping of China-sceptic legislators, says past engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised.
“Successful UK engagement with China must always be framed by an understanding that the PRC (People’s Republic of China) is an inherently hostile authoritarian state that does not share our values,” an underlined sentence in the audit, published on Wednesday, reads.
The inherent power imbalance in the relationship with the world’s second largest economy is “further compounded by muddled policy and weak engagement”, it says.
It cites the example of a visiting Chinese delegation who had noted that no one who engaged with Beijing at a senior level in government was a Mandarin speaker, or had significant experience of living in China.
Although British expertise exists, it is often siloed and “not translated into capability”, Ipac, which counts members from all the UK’s major parties, says.
In an endorsement, the former security minister Tom Tugendhat said the report was “a clear-eyed and realistic take on the defining foreign policy problem of this century, filling a gap left by years of policy neglect”.
While the report accepts that “disengagement was not an option”, it advocates for clearly defined red lines around issues such as critical infrastructure, frontier technologies and human rights.
The document offers several recommendations, including better institutional coordination, the strengthened use of national security tools, and diversification of supply chains.
It identifies emerging technologies such as AI as posing new challenges, in terms of disinformation and surveillance capabilities.
The climate crisis is identified as a low-risk area for cooperation and alignment.
“Climate targets as set will not be met without cooperation with China, and accepting medium-term dependence. This means accepting supply chains tainted by forced labour and unfair trade practices,” the audit says.
The Guardian has contacted the UK government and the Chinese embassy in London for comment.
It was “very welcome” that there was an understanding that better language skills were needed to deal with China, said Kerry Brown, a former diplomat and director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London.
However, he said, “the critical issue now is lived experience” in China.
“Some of the members of Ipac … are really keen on promoting this very security-oriented idea that going to China is in some ways opening you up to exposure,” he said.
“You can’t teach really important things in a classroom; you can only go and learn them through daily life … and that is the thing that is very difficult to do now, and it’s also the thing that doesn’t seem to be supported.”

Burnham’s ‘Russia did Brexit’ ruse crumbles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:11:13 UTC
01:11:13 KST

Burnham’s ‘Russia did Brexit’ ruse crumbles
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s attempt to blame Russia for the Brexit vote is a crude attempt to undo the referendum and tie the UK back to Brussels. It’s also imploding dramatically.
In an appearance on the ‘The Rest is Politics’ podcast on Sunday, Burnham said that he sought answers about alleged meddling in the 2016 Brexit referendum after taking office this summer.
“I asked the question coming to Downing Street: Well, was there interference in the 2016 referendum from Russia? I’ve had the clear answer that yes, there was.”
Burnham did not identify who had provided the assessment or present any evidence to back it up. Nor did he say whether the alleged interference actually affected the result of the referendum. However, he insisted that anti-establishment movements in Britain, France, and Germany – where Chancellor Friedrich Merz has claimed that the right-wing AfD are “Russian-backed” – are “instigated via our enemies, namely Russia.”
Haven’t we heard this all before?
On June 23, 2016, Britain voted to leave the EU by a margin of 51.89% to 48.11%. The vote was largely driven by a public desire to reclaim sovereignty, control immigration, and humiliate the country’s political elites, the majority of whom favored continued EU membership.
Six months later, Labour MP Ben Bradshaw announced in parliament that Russia “probably interfered” in the vote. Bradshaw conceded that “we do not have the evidence for that yet, but it is highly probable.” His claims were picked up by media outlets in Britain and the US, where the ‘Russiagate’ hoax was taking root in Washington.
A parliamentary committee stated in April 2017 that the collapse of a voter-registration website in the runup to the referendum could have been the work of a Russian or Chinese denial-of-service (DDOS) attack. In November of that year, City University alleged that 13,000 bot accounts – some of them Russian – were tweeting about Brexit before and after the referendum.
X, then called Twitter, rejected the City University study, stating that it found no evidence linking the bot accounts with Russia; separate research tying Russia to the ‘leave’ campaign was found to be fabricated by an anti-Brexit group funded by liberal billionaire George Soros; and in 2020, a parliamentary report found “no evidence of successful interference in the EU referendum.” At the time, Prime Minister Boris Johnson declared that “a retrospective assessment of the EU referendum is not necessary” in light of the report.
All of this begs the question: ten years after the Brexit vote, why is Burnham conjuring up the specter of “Russian interference” again?
Burnham’s big break
Burnham’s political maneuvering is obvious here. The British PM has repeatedly said that he would like to see the UK rejoin the EU, and two weeks before appearing on ‘The Rest is Politics’, he opened his speech at the UN General Assembly with a reference to Brexit, lamenting that “my country has lived through the disruption it brought.”
Speaking at his Labour Party’s annual conference a week later, Burnham argued that “Brexit has done more harm than good.” The following day he pledged to forge closer relations with Brussels and, if politically feasible, “go all the way” and rejoin the union.
Burnham has refused to say whether he intends to run his next election campaign on a platform of EU membership. However, he has promised to have “a serious dialogue about the different options for our relationship in the long-term” when he meets EU leaders in Brussels next month.
With the UK and EU both embroiled in a proxy war with Russia, there is no more effective way to delegitimize the Brexit vote at the moment than by tying it to Moscow. Burnham made this explicit in an address to Parliament on October 12, arguing that it would be “a dereliction of duty” not to pursue closer relations with the EU, given Russia’s alleged interference in the referendum.
The hoax crumbles
The prime minister’s confidence began to crumble under questioning. Asked by Conservative MP Julian Lewis “exactly how he thinks Russia was able to alter the result of the referendum,” Burnham replied that Moscow’s interference in British elections was “a matter of record,” without elaborating further.
Responding to Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch, Burnham claimed that he never implied that the result of the referendum was invalid, before repeating the same “matter of record” line.
Burnham’s lack of evidence became clear when his foreign secretary, Stephen Doughty, appeared on ITV’s ‘Good Morning Britain’ the same day.
“What did Russia do during that Brexit referendum?” host Susanna Reid asked Doughty, who responded that he was “not going to get into the specifics.”
“Why are you not getting into specifics when the Prime Minister has just got into the specifics on the podcast?” Reid pressed.
Asked repeatedly about Russian interference in the Brexit vote, Doughty gave a variation on “Russia attempts to interfere in all of our democratic processes. They’ve been doing this for many, many years” every time.
“This is embarrassing,” co-host Ed Balls interjected. “It’s really bad for politics when you just blatantly don’t answer the question on something so important and go back to a nonsensical line, which is contradicted by what the prime minister just said.”
The final nail in the coffin came from MI5 Director Ken McCallum. McCallum is no stranger to anti-Russian opportunism, having pushed for mass internet surveillance to prevent Russia causing “mayhem on British and European streets.” However, he warned on Tuesday against exaggerating “Russian influence” on Brexit, arguing that debating the influence of “Russian trolls” on the vote “play[s] into our adversaries’ hands by making these trolls look 10ft tall.”
The Burnham playbook
Burnham has a habit of making extraordinary claims without the extraordinary evidence to back them up. After five Londoners were arrested outside RAF Fairford in an apparent terror bust last month, the British PM told the BBC that there are “strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened.”
The five men – plus two more suspects arrested afterwards – have all been released on bail. No explosives were found in their vehicles, and no link between the men and the Iranian government has been established, according to all available information. However, Burnham told the BBC that “we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part,” before telling Parliament that the supposed terror plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).
Tehran has described the incident as “a clumsy false-flag operation,” aimed at “advancing an anti-Iran campaign and evading accountability for Britain’s involvement in the US-Israeli military aggression against the Iranian people.”
Likewise, Moscow has repeatedly denied interfering in the Brexit referendum. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described Burnham’s allegations as “the latest baseless accusations made without any proof.”
One final irony
Burnham’s claim would never have been torn apart in parliament, in the media, and by his own domestic intelligence agency had ‘The Rest is Politics’ host Alastair Campbell pushed back and demanded evidence or elaboration. However, Campbell has a track record of embellishing facts to suit political narratives, with disastrous consequences.
Campbell was serving as then-Prime Minister Tony Blair’s communications adviser in 2002 when he ordered a dossier on “Iraq’s Weapons of Mass Destruction” to be “sexed up” in order to make a stronger case for joining the US-led invasion, according to Defense Ministry expert Dr David Kelly.
An inquiry found that Campbell changed multiple lines within the dossier to make Iraq appear more threatening. Among them was a line stating that Iraqi forces “may be able to deploy” chemical weapons against British troops within 45 minutes of receiving an order, which became “are able to deploy.”
Campbell then compiled a second dossier, now known as the “Dodgy Dossier.” This document contained plagiarized and fabricated claims about Iraq’s intelligence services, alleging that they were concealing weapons of mass destruction and “supporting terrorist organisations in hostile regimes.” None of these claims were true.
The second dossier was published in February 2003. Five weeks later, Parliament held a vote to join the invasion, with Burnham one of 139 Labour MPs voting in favor of the war. Burnham has since said that, if he could go back to 2003, he “wouldn’t have voted for it.”
More than two decades later, Burnham is once again making “dodgy dossier”-tier accusations in service of two foreign conflicts, and in aid of his own political ambitions.

US Social Security benefits to rise by 3.6 percent in 2027

US Social Security benefits to rise by 3.6 percent in 2027
Retired Americans will see a $75 boost in monthly cheques as benefits rise amid widespread inflation challenges.
United States Social Security benefits will increase by 3.6 percent beginning in 2027, marking one of the largest cost-of-living adjustments (COLAs) of the decade.
On Wednesday, the Social Security Administration announced the hike after the Bureau of Labor Statistics published the Consumer Price Index for September. The alteration represents a four-year high, boosting average monthly cheques by $75 for older adults and people with disabilities.
The benefit bump will roll out in January for 72 million Social Security recipients, and on December 31, for nearly 73 million Supplemental Security Income (SSI) beneficiaries.
Starting in 2027, the maximum limit for a taxable wage base, or income cap, is slated to increase to $192,300, up from $184,500 in 2026.
The social security programme is the largest federal social insurance framework in the country. The entitlement programme provides financial support for older adults and disabled people, as well as benefits for survivors of families of workers who have passed away. Funded through dedicated payroll taxes, it serves primarily as a federal pension system that replaces a portion of an individual’s pre-retirement income upon leaving the workforce.
The agency bases the annual increase, closely watched by retirees and others receiving benefits, on the average of the annual increase in the CPI for urban wage earners and clerical workers, also known as the CPI-W index. That index rose 3.9 percent in September and averaged about 3.6 percent for the three months of July, August and September. For 2026, the increase was 2.8 percent.
The announcement comes as high US inflation continues to remain a persistent economic headwind, fuelled primarily by energy shocks from the ongoing wars in Ukraine and Iran, which have caused global energy market turmoil that has sent crude oil prices above $100 a barrel.
More recently, refined petroleum products like diesel fuel have climbed to record highs and have contributed to a widening of inflationary pressures.
Most older adults in the US believe the COLA isn’t adequately keeping up with inflation, according to an AARP poll from September. That poll found that about three-quarters of those 50 or older disagreed with the idea that a 3.5 percent COLA in 2027 would be enough to keep up with rising prices.

how the spectacular set design of alejandro g. iñárritu’s digger unveils a wild masterpiece
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:10:14 UTC
01:10:14 KST

how the spectacular set design of alejandro g. iñárritu’s digger unveils a wild masterpiece
a story about the most powerful man in the world and the environmental catastrophe he unleashed turns out to be something else entirely, and with every shift the disaster moves a little closer to the audience watching.
[FEATURED]
Spoiler alert! We are about to delve into what Digger spends its first half hour hiding – if you have not seen the film yet, save this piece for afterwards.
A CLOSER LOOK AT THE SCENOGRAPHY in ALEJANDRO G. IÑÁRRITU’S DIGGER
About thirty minutes into Alejandro González Iñárritu’s Digger, a model tree falls over, a section of what had looked like a hillside opens up, and a giant man steps out to pick it up while the rest of the crew floods the frame behind him. The director starts shouting instructions, Tom Cruise drops the Texas accent, and everything you have watched so far turns out to have been a technical rehearsal for the 25th anniversary of a stage play called Fossil Fools.
Cruise has been playing Curtis Markson, an actor cast as the oil baron Digger Rockwell in a play about the massive global environmental and climate catastrophe that Rockwell, the most powerful man in the world, has caused: a Greenland drilling operation that releases an enormous ice shelf toward Europe and drowns the coastlines of the world.
It is a plot twist, and a designer’s one, because it first arrives not in dialogue but as a stage technician walking into the shot to deal with a fallen tree. That is the first of four positions the film puts its audience in, each one first arranged by the scenery rather than announced by a character: a mansion that holds the disaster at a safe distance, a play with an audience sitting in front of it, a play that turns out to be a reconstruction of something real, and finally no distance at all. The sets are not a structural game but a measuring instrument for the distance between spectator and spectacle, and across two hours they shorten that distance to nothing.
SET DESIGN AS A STORYTELLING DEVICE
Digger’s world was built by production designers Dennis Gassner and Richard Johnson. Gassner, nominated seven times for the Academy Award for Best Production Design and a winner once, for Bugsy, has a filmography that runs through Barton Fink, Road to Perdition, Blade Runner 2049 and the Craig-era Bond films among many others. The credit that matters most here, though, is The Truman Show, where he built a town that turns out to be a set. The difference in Digger is who is kept in the dark. Truman does not know he is living inside a set while the audience is told in the opening minutes, and Digger reverses that completely, since every actor on screen knows exactly where they are standing and we are the ones who have not yet been told.
That first world is Digger Rockwell’s lavish mansion, where he wakes beside a bedroom window framing a view that could have been painted by Albert Bierstadt, where taxidermied alligators are pinned to the ceiling, and where full-body mirrors lined with antlers repeat him into infinity. Everything in that house builds the portrait of a monstrous man, and of a monstrousness a long way from your own life. It is the oldest arrangement cinema has: a villain in his lair, a disaster he has caused unfolding somewhere cold, and a fourth wall holding the whole thing at arm’s length. The design here is doing what spectacle has always done, making a catastrophe watchable by placing it somewhere else.
COLOR PALETTE AND PROPS REINFORCE THE NARRATIVE
Then the tree falls over, and for a few minutes the film hands you an alibi. Once you know you have been watching a stage production, the artifice of the previous half hour stops being a flaw and becomes a signature. Maggie, Digger’s one-eyed geriatric cat, is a conspicuously obvious animatronic in a film with the money to make a cat look like a cat. Miniatures appear with their seams showing, and clouds and aircraft cross the sky on sticks. None of it was careless, because all of it was intentionally designed.
The palette is running the same argument, and, speaking to Dazed, Iñárritu explains where it comes from. He names Vermeer and the Danish painter Vilhelm Hammershøi for color, with Hopper and Rembrandt for contrast. Hammershøi is the one you can clearly see on screen: a career spent on near-empty grey interiors, two or three notes of color permitted and never more, doorways opening onto further doorways. Iñárritu describes that grey as an instrument rather than a mood, saying that as Digger takes over the narrative, the color is vanishing. So the play looks drained and the backstage looks alive, and the contrast is reassuring in a way that is almost physical. Grey is where the fiction lives, color is where reality is, and reality appears to be holding.
A MOVIE PLOT TWIST IN STAGES
The third reveal takes the alibi back. Fossil Fools is not an invention, Digger Rockwell was a real man, the disaster genuinely occurred, and the character bankrolling the production turns out to be his nephew, staging his own family’s catastrophe for a paying audience. Nothing in the design changes here, and yet all of it changes meaning.
The grey chamber where Digger addresses a tribunal of European politicians, its councillors dressed to match the walls until they nearly disappear against him, stops reading as caricature and starts reading as testimony. The visible seams on the miniatures stop saying this is only a play and start saying this is a reconstruction, the way a museum diorama is openly a model of something that really took place.
This is the part that explains why the film exists at all. Iñárritu spent roughly a decade on it, and during that decade the things he was inventing kept arriving on their own. When the first drafts were written there was no ice shelf detaching and methane was a technical term rather than a headline. In an interview with Letterboxd, he put it plainly: reality was chasing fiction and passing us by.
FICTION AND REALITY COLLAPSE into one
The play ends with Digger diving from his rig to his death, the theater audience inside the film rises to applaud, there is a curtain call, and then an intercom announces Level 4. Every person in that theater reaches for a breathing mask and files out into a flooded, militarized street, past debris and the remains of machines, into the world the play had spent the evening describing, while Melanie’s 1970 song What Have They Done to My Song, Ma plays them out.
The backstage color, it turns out, was never reality, it was a slightly later stage of the same collapse. Then the film ends, and about ninety seconds into the credits the Level 4 announcement sounds again, in the cinema where you are sitting. I heard it, and several people around me got up to leave on exactly that cue.
Stepping outside afterwards into an ordinary sunny afternoon produced an unexpected sense of gratitude,
followed immediately by an understanding of how thin the margin is between that afternoon and the street the audience in the film had just walked out to.
That is the entire film delivered in a single sound cue, and it is why the set designs matter as much as the story. Asked by the New York Times whether the bleakness represented his own outlook, Iñárritu said this is a disaster movie in which the disaster is us, and then added: ‘If we can get together in the same room, in the same reality, and understand where we are in the narrative, I think it’s hopeful.’ Which is precisely what the film’s design has spent two hours arranging. Four sets, four distances, until everybody is in the same room, in the same reality, being asked to understand exactly where they stand in the story.
project info:

director: Alejandro G. Iñárritu
cast: Tom Cruise, Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Sandra Hüller, Michael Stuhlbarg, Jesse Plemons, Sophie Wilde
screenplay: Alejandro G. Iñárritu, Alexander Dinelaris, Nicolás Giacobone, Sabina Berman
story: Sabina Berman, Alejandro G. Iñárritu and Jez Butterworth
production design: Dennis Gassner and Richard Johnson
costume design: Jacqueline West

duration: 128 minutes
release: October 2026, Warner Bros. Pictures

The IDF and Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) conducted a joint raid operation on the offices of the Addameer Charity Association in Ramallah on Tuesday, as well as the Islamic Association for the Care of Orphans in Yatta, near Hebron, the military confirmed on Wednesday.
According to the military, the "illegal charities" acted as fronts for terrorist organizations, including Hamas and the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP).
Five terrorist collaborators were arrested in the West Bank operations, while evidence including computers, documents, and checkbooks bearing markers associated with Hamas was seized.
The Addameer Charity Association, according to the military, is funded by terror funds in order to provide legal assistance to PFLP terrorists held in detention.
Terrorists who participated in the Danny Spring bombing of 2019, which resulted in the death of 17-year-old Rina Shnerb, were working at the association at the time of the raid.
Hamas financial front raided in West Bank
In Yatta, wanted individuals were arrested during the raid on the Islamic Association for the Care of Orphans, and Hamas funds were seized before being transferred to security forces for further investigation.
The organization served as an organizational hub and financial arm of Hamas that transferred funds directly to the terrorist organization as well as to family members of Hamas terrorists. The military said that it "serves as infrastructure for entrenching the Hamas terrorist organization’s standing in Yatta, while exploiting its purportedly civilian activities."
According to the IDF statement, the director and other senior officials at the association have been imprisoned in the past.
Eyal Zamir strengthens forces in West Bank to maintain security
Meanwhile, IDF Chief of Staff, Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir said the IDF must remain vigilant on all fronts and act swiftly to thwart threats, while deploying the 98th Division to the West Bank to "strengthen security and stability in the area."
In a situational assessment held in coordination with IDF Central Commander Maj.-Gen. Avi Bluth and senior leadership within the Central Command, Zamir reviewed operational challenges during a tour of the West Bank region. According to the IDF, Zamir approved plans for continued operational activity in the area.
“In light of the increased number of alerts across all fronts and the sensitivity of this period, the potential for escalation has grown... The IDF is at a high level of readiness to launch extensive offensive operations against anyone who attempts to harm Israeli civilians," the military chief said.

Irish author Sally Rooney's books no longer sold in UK over support for banned Palestine Action

Irish novelist Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in Britain over her plans to use her royalties to support Palestine Action, a pro-Palestinian group banned as a terrorist organization, Rooney and her publisher said on Wednesday.
The bestselling author, known for novels including Normal People and Conversations with Friends, has been a vocal supporter of Palestine Action, including after it was proscribed by the British government under terrorism laws last year.
Rooney previously said in a witness statement submitted to London's High Court, in support of a legal challenge over the ban on Palestine Action, that her plans could lead to her books being withdrawn from sale in Britain.
Her publisher Faber said on Wednesday that it had agreed with Rooney that "we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format," though it would sell her works elsewhere.
"Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work," Faber said in a statement.
Palestine action banned after break-in at Royal Air Force base
"To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher."
Rooney said in a statement: "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences."
Palestine Action, which had increasingly targeted Israel-linked defense companies, was banned shortly after a June 2025 break-in at the Royal Air Force's Brize Norton base.
Last year, Palestine Action's co-founder Huda Ammori challenged the ban, and the High Court ruled in her favor in February, before the Court of Appeal overturned that decision in June. The Supreme Court is due to hear an appeal next month.
More than 3,000 people have since been arrested for holding signs in support of Palestine Action, and its proscription has been criticized by civil liberties groups.

Hezbollah cannot buy back Shia support as group promises $14,000 to displaced families

Hezbollah’s financial assistance to displaced families in southern Lebanon, capped at $14,000, is only the first step in a long process if the Iran-backed group hopes to regain the trust and support of Lebanon’s Shia community, Lieutenant-Colonel (res.) Moran Levavoni, a researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.
Levavoni spoke with the Post a day after Hezbollah announced it would provide up to $14,000 in financial assistance to families whose primary homes were destroyed during this year’s war with Israel.
Under the plan presented by Hezbollah Executive Council chairman Ali Damoush, eligible families in Beirut and its southern suburbs will reportedly receive $14,000, namely $8,000 for furniture and $6,000 for rent. Families elsewhere in Lebanon will reportedly receive $12,000, comprising $8,000 for furniture and $4,000 for rent. The amounts maintain the same rates as in 2024.
The assistance is not extended to families who lost their homes during war in 2006
The assistance has not been extended to those families who lost their homes during Hezbollah’s 34-day war in 2006 and have still not been compensated, Levavoni noted. The war, triggered by a Hezbollah cross-border raid, displaced around one million Lebanese. The Lebanese government estimated direct war damage at $2.8 billion and lost output and income in 2006 at $ 2.2 billion.
While there may have been anger toward Hezbollah at the time, Levavoni argued that the “rift” between Lebanon’s Shia community and Hezbollah widened in 2023, when the terror group decided “to support Gaza on the back of the local population.”
Majority of Lebanese support a deal with Israel, poll says
According to a poll conducted by Statistics Lebanon, a Lebanese public opinion research organization, and published last week, Hezbollah’s standing among the country’s Shia population has weakened significantly. Of the 800 Shia adults surveyed in September, 42.1% expressed disappointment, anger, or concern over Hezbollah’s leadership and conduct.
A majority of respondents, 67.4%, also said they did not believe Hezbollah had achieved any or all of its objectives in the war. Reflecting this apparent lack of confidence, 63.3% supported some form of agreement with Israel, whether through direct negotiations, mediation, or a comprehensive regional deal to end the conflict. Meanwhile, 71.1% said decisions on war and peace should be made solely by Beirut.
Most respondents, 66.4%, also said they would support Hezbollah transferring its weapons to the state, while only around a third said the terrorist group should retain its arsenal.
Hezbollah’s first step toward rebuilding trust should be to compensate those affected by the war, Levavoni said.
“They can try to minimize [the damage] by starting to pay refunds to the population, the people, the families that were away from their homes, and for the damaged villages,” he said. “And only after that, they can start thinking about regaining the trust.”
Despite the damage to Hezbollah’s standing, the organization retains some support among Lebanon’s Shia population. The poll found that 37.1% of respondents still had a high level of trust in Hezbollah, while another 22.4% expressed some trust. Meanwhile, only 38.5% admitted there was some level of distrust.

UN official warns of looming food crisis as Hormuz fertiliser plan stalls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:08:09 UTC
01:08:09 KST

UN official warns of looming food crisis as Hormuz fertiliser plan stalls
Without a quick deal to move fertiliser through the strait, agricultural productivity would ‘significantly drop’.
A senior United Nations official has warned that parts of Asia and Africa could face a food security crisis unless Iran and the United States quickly agree on a UN-backed plan to move fertiliser through the embattled Strait of Hormuz.
UN Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said on Wednesday that it was “absolutely critical” that the two countries agree to the proposal within weeks as planting season approaches. It calls for a UN-staffed coordination centre in Oman to help register vessels and oversee their safe passage in the waterway, through which a large portion of key global fertiliser inputs traditionally flow.
“If we miss that planting season, the productivity of agriculture would significantly drop and the impact on prices will significantly increase,” Moreira da Silva told Reuters on the sidelines of International Monetary Fund and World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Thailand.
Farmers operate strict crop calendars, and even slight delays could severely affect yield.
‘Negligible’ fertiliser shipments
Traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has been severely disrupted since the start of the US-Israel war on Iran, with Iran targeting vessels in the strait and the US and Iran exchanging fire in and around the waterway.
The disruption has hit global supplies of urea, the world’s most widely used nitrogen fertiliser, as well as seaborne sulphur, a key input. Before the war, roughly a third of global urea shipments and nearly half of seaborne sulphur passed through the strait.
Although some ships have been able to sail through amid the crisis, fertiliser products have made up a “very negligible” share of moving cargo, according to the Washington-based International Food Policy Research Institute.
Moreira da Silva said the UN-backed fertiliser mechanism, drawn up in March, could be activated within seven to 10 days if both Iran and the US agree.
Under the plan, UN monitors would work alongside local authorities at Gulf ports to verify cargo loading. Ships would be tracked during transit, and additional inspections could be carried out if countries raised concerns about a vessel or its cargo, said Moreira da Silva. He did not say why the US and Iran have not yet agreed.
The passage of only five vessels per day through the Strait of Hormuz could keep fertiliser supplies flowing to countries in critical need, he added.
‘Let us do our job’
The UN mechanism could work alongside negotiations for a “comprehensive deal” to restore freedom of navigation in the strait, Moreira da Silva said.
Iran and the US have exchanged proposals through intermediaries since a June interim ceasefire collapsed. Efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled over Tehran’s conditions and Washington’s insistence on addressing Iran’s nuclear programme from the outset.
“What we are telling them is, while you continue your discussions towards a comprehensive deal, let us work, let us do our job,” said Moreira da Silva.
His plea comes amid growing concern that fertiliser shortages could hit global food supplies.
In May, the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization warned that fertiliser scarcity could tighten food supplies from late 2026 into 2027, and would likely hit countries facing climate or other crises much harder.
In South Asia, where most rely on imported fertiliser, farmers are already struggling because of soaring costs and fertiliser scarcity. On Wednesday, farmers in Spain took to the streets to protest rising production costs amid high oil and fertiliser prices.

Turkey: Government raids, takes over top news channel
October 14, 2026
Turkish authorities took control of Halk TV on Wednesday — raiding the outlet's Istanbul studios, cutting all broadcasts and appointing a government trustee to oversee the company during an investigation into alleged corruption.
"Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee [manager] has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted," posted the popular news channel on X as police guarded the building, financial crimes agents searched offices and computers, and technicians cut live news channel feeds and YouTube broadcasts.
Footage posted online showed the moment the channel's live broadcast feed was cut — during an interview about a huge investment-fund scandal — and replaced with a classic Turkish film from 1973.
In a statement, the Istanbul Prosecutor's Office announced that Halk TV owner Cafer Mahiroglu is under investigation for "bribery, tender-rigging, and laundering of assets derived from crime."
Government trustees were installed at Halk TV and other companies owned by Mahiroglu.
In all, prosecutors say 17 detention warrants were issued, with 11 individuals taken into custody.
Mahiroglu, who lives abroad and is being sought by authorities, decried what he called "a dark day for Turkey" and blasted the allegations against him as "baseless" in a video posted on X. The pro-opposition broadcaster said seven of his relatives had been detained by authorities.
"The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons," he said. "Using the judiciary as a weapon is the greatest harm inflicted on Turkey."
Erdogan smothering all press dissent in Turkey
Press freedom groups and opposition parties joined Mahiroglu in condemning the government takeover as the latest step by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to silence his critics.
Ozgur Ozel, leader of the main opposition New Party, said the raid was an abuse of government power.
Ozel called the raids "weak and cowardly," saying it was no coincidence they occurred just as jailed Erdogan opponent, Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, was set to make headlines delivering his defense in a sprawling graft trial.
"Raiding a television channel at dawn and appointing a trustee is an act only dictators would commit," Ozel wrote on X. "Unfortunately, this is the state to which they have reduced our country."
Press freedom has suffered dramatically during Erdogan's 22 years in power.
In the most recent Reporters Without Borders world press freedom index Turkey ranked 163 of 180 countries.
Similar pattern as Erdogan government eats up one media outlet after another
Ankara-based Contemporary Journalists Association decried the action against Halk TV, stating: "The appointment of a trustee at Halk TV and the suspension of its broadcast constitute a grave intervention against press freedom and freedom of expression. This decision, which disregards constitutional rights and the public's right to access information, is unacceptable."
Halk TV's takeover made it the fifth major Turkish news outlet forcefully put under trusteeship, following similar situations at Flash TV, Eko Turk, Haberturk and Tele1.
Veysel Ok, co-director of media-rights watchdog MLSA, said the intervention against Halk TV was "one of the most significant steps in the government's efforts to monopolize the flow of information."
"Halk TV's position as the most-watched news channel also reveals the real target of this intervention: Depriving the public of its right to access news from different sources," Ok told French news agency AFP.
"Defending press freedom means defending the public's right to learn the truth, hold the government to account and freely decide its own future."
The European Parliament's Turkey rapporteur Nacho Sanchez Amor criticized the move on X, saying the government was clearly "not happy with controlling 90% of media" and was instead "aiming for the 100%."
"Amidst detentions of journalists & broad online censorship, freedom of media & expression will soon be just a memory."
