Retrouvez le compte rendu du Conseil des ministres du mercredi 14 octobre 2026 :
14 octobre 2026 - Compte-rendu
Compte rendu du Conseil des ministres du 14 octobre 2026.
PROJETS DE LOI
DISPOSITIONS RELATIVES AU SECTEUR NUCLEAIRE
La ministre déléguée auprès du ministre de l’économie, des finances et de la souveraineté industrielle, énergétique et numérique, chargée de l’énergie, a présenté un projet de loi visant à accompagner la relance du nucléaire français. Complémentaire de la loi adoptée en 2023, ce texte va faciliter la réalisation des grands projets de la filière, notamment le renouvellement des installations de traitement et de recyclage des combustibles nucléaires, tout en préservant les plus hauts standards de sûreté.
Le 10 février 2022, dans son discours à Belfort, le Président de la République fixait un cap ambitieux : faire de la France la première grande nation à sortir de sa dépendance aux énergies fossiles, en réduisant sa consommation d'énergie tout en accroissant sa production d'électricité décarbonée. Au cœur de cette stratégie figure la relance du nucléaire français, avec la prolongation des réacteurs existants lorsque les exigences de sûreté le permettent, la construction de nouveaux réacteurs EPR2 et le renforcement de l'ensemble de la chaîne industrielle. Cette orientation a été confirmée et confortée par la troisième programmation pluriannuelle de l'énergie (PPE3) présentée par le Premier ministre le 12 février dernier.
La loi d'accélération du nucléaire du 22 juin 2023 a permis de simplifier et d'accélérer les procédures nécessaires à la construction de nouveaux réacteurs EPR2, notamment sur les sites existants.
Un peu plus de trois ans après son adoption, l'avancement des projets et les premiers retours d'expérience ont mis en évidence la nécessité de compléter ce cadre législatif. À l'approche du lancement formel du programme de nouveau nucléaire français, le Gouvernement s’engage pour lever les derniers obstacles identifiés et donner à la filière les moyens de concrétiser ses projets.
Le projet de loi présenté en conseil des ministres a été construit autour de quatre objectifs :
- Accélérer la modernisation des installations du cycle du combustible nucléaire.
Les mesures de simplification prévues par la loi de 2023 seront étendues aux installations de l'aval du cycle, notamment au projet « Aval du futur » porté par Orano. Ce programme vise à renouveler les installations industrielles de La Hague, essentielles au traitement et au recyclage des combustibles nucléaires.
- Clarifier les règles applicables aux installations nucléaires pour garantir la priorité à la sûreté.
Le texte vise également à assurer la primauté des exigences de sûreté nucléaire et de radioprotection lorsque l’application de certaines dispositions du code de la construction et de l'habitation aggraverait des risques en matière de sûreté ou de radioprotection ou s’avèrerait techniquement impraticable.
- Faciliter l'organisation des grands chantiers industriels, sans réduire les exigences de contrôle.
Sous réserve d'une autorisation préalable de l’Autorité de sûreté nucléaire et de radioprotection (ASNR), les exploitants pourront confier la surveillance d'intervenants extérieurs à certaines sociétés de leur groupe. Cette organisation resterait placée sous la responsabilité, la direction et le contrôle de l'exploitant nucléaire.
- Faire de la relance du nucléaire une réalité industrielle et économique.
Avec ce nouveau texte, le Gouvernement donne les moyens à la France de passer des orientations stratégiques à la réalisation concrète des projets, en donnant aux industriels un cadre adapté à l'ampleur des investissements et des chantiers à venir.
RATIFICATION DE L’ORDONNANCE DU 27 JUILLET 2026 PORTANT DIVERS AJUSTEMENTS DU CODE DES IMPOSITIONS SUR LES BIENS ET SERVICES
Le ministre de l’économie, des finances et de la souveraineté industrielle, énergétique et numérique et le ministre de l’action et des comptes publics ont présenté un projet de loi ratifiant l’ordonnance n° 2026-671 du 27 juillet 2026 portant divers ajustements du code des impositions sur les biens et services (CIBS).
Cette ordonnance prolonge le chantier de modernisation et de simplification du droit fiscal engagé par le Gouvernement en 2019. Ce travail a conduit à la création du CIBS au 1er janvier 2022, puis à son enrichissement progressif, notamment avec l’intégration de plusieurs taxes au 1er janvier 2023 et, par une ordonnance du 17 décembre 2025, avec le transfert des dispositions relatives à la taxe sur la valeur ajoutée (TVA).
Une entrée en vigueur du nouveau régime de TVA reportée au 1er janvier 2027
À la suite de la consultation publique menée sur la recodification de la TVA dans le CIBS, le Gouvernement a pris en compte les attentes exprimées par les entreprises et les praticiens du droit.
L’entrée en vigueur du transfert des dispositions relatives à la TVA dans le CIBS est ainsi reportée au 1er janvier 2027, afin de permettre aux acteurs concernés de préparer plus sereinement la transition vers ce nouveau cadre juridique, notamment dans le contexte de la mise en œuvre de la réforme de la facturation électronique à compter du 1er septembre prochain.
L’ordonnance répond également à une demande importante de simplification : elle regroupe désormais, au sein d’une subdivision unique du livre II du CIBS consacré à la TVA, l’ensemble des dispositions relatives au droit à déduction de la TVA pour améliorer la lisibilité du droit applicable.
L’ordonnance intègre par ailleurs les mesures relatives à la TVA adoptées depuis l’ordonnance du 17 décembre 2025, notamment celles issues de la loi de finances pour 2026. Elle prend ainsi en compte plusieurs évolutions récentes du droit fiscal, comme l’harmonisation à 5,5 % du taux de TVA applicable aux services liés à la gestion des déchets.
L’ordonnance met également à jour les références rendues nécessaires par l’entrée en vigueur de la partie législative du nouveau code des douanes au 1er mai 2026.
Elle poursuit aussi l’harmonisation des catégories fiscales utilisées pour identifier les régimes de contrôle, de recouvrement et de contentieux : les « taxes sur le chiffre d’affaires » deviennent par exemple les « taxes sur les biens et services ».
Une sécurité juridique renforcée pour les opérateurs
L’ordonnance confirme explicitement que la doctrine administrative opposable aux redevables demeure inchangée lors de l’entrée en vigueur du CIBS. Cette garantie, déjà prévue par l’ordonnance du 17 décembre 2025 et précisée dans un rescrit publié le 18 février 2026 au Bulletin officiel des finances publiques – Impôts, est ainsi réaffirmée.
L’ordonnance prend également en compte plusieurs demandes de clarification formulées lors de la consultation publique, notamment afin de rapprocher certaines formulations de la jurisprudence et procède enfin à diverses corrections d’erreurs matérielles identifiées dans l’ordonnance du 17 décembre 2025.
DECRET
ACCELERATION DES PROCEDURES LIEES A LA CONSTRUCTION DE NOUVELLES INSTALLATIONS NUCLEAIRES A PROXIMITE DE SITES NUCLEAIRES EXISTANTS ET AU FONCTIONNEMENT DES INSTALLATIONS EXISTANTES
Le ministre de la ville et du logement a présenté un décret relatif à la détermination des modalités d’application de l’autorisation d’urbanisme spéciale pour les constructions, installations ou aménagements temporaires nécessaires au logement, à l’hébergement ou aux déplacements des personnes participant aux travaux de construction d’un nouveau réacteur électronucléaire ou à la logistique et aux activités de préfabrication du chantier de ce même réacteur. Il est pris pour l’application de l’article 9-1 de la loi n° 2023-491 du 22 juin 2023, créé par la loi n° 2025-1129 du 26 novembre 2025 de simplification du droit de l’urbanisme et du logement (« Huwart »).
Ce décret vient préciser ce régime spécifique des autorisations d’urbanisme qui permet, compte tenu du caractère temporaire des constructions, installations ou aménagements concernés, de les autoriser à déroger aux règles d’urbanisme, tout en les soumettant à une autorisation délivrée par le préfet après accord du maire de la commune concernée. L’autorisation fixe le délai, qui ne peut excéder vingt ans, à l’expiration duquel le terrain doit être remis en son état initial.
Le décret détaille la liste des pièces supplémentaires à fournir dans les dossiers de demande d’autorisation et les modalités particulières d’instruction de ces demandes.
En outre, il fixe les modalités relatives aux garanties financières qui peuvent être exigées lorsque les caractéristiques du terrain d’assiette ou l’importance du projet le justifient. Il précise les critères permettant au préfet d’en fixer le montant, ainsi que les conditions de consignation et de déconsignation. Sont également précisées les conditions de remise en état des terrains à respecter, ainsi que les mesures permettant d’en assurer le respect.
Enfin, le décret prévoit que lorsque l’autorité compétente pour délivrer l’autorisation ne répond pas à la demande dans les délais qui lui sont impartis, son silence vaut décision implicite de rejet. En effet, compte tenu de l’objet de l’autorisation, qui doit notamment mentionner la durée d’implantation temporaire et, lorsque cela se justifie, le montant des sommes à consigner, le décret prévoit qu’une décision expresse de l’administration doit intervenir.
Ces mesures, particulièrement attendues par les acteurs du secteur nucléaire et ciblant des projets déjà identifiés, notamment sur le chantier EPR2 de Penly (76), seront applicables aux demandes d’autorisations d’urbanisme déposées à compter du lendemain de la publication du texte au Journal officiel.

Pope Leo recovering well after cancer surgery, Vatican says

Pope Leo recovering well after cancer surgery, Vatican says
The 71-year-old pontiff is recovering in Rome’s Gemelli hospital after surgery to remove a cancerous growth on his lung.
Pope Leo XIV is out of bed, walking, eating and has undergone respiratory physiotherapy, according to a doctor’s note published by the Vatican a day after his lung cancer surgery.
A blood test and chest X-ray revealed “normal post-operative” progress, doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora said, adding that values were “within the expected range for the type of procedure performed”.
“The Holy Father underwent respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking in his room”, they said, adding that “he resumed his regular diet and had breakfast and lunch.”
“Recovery is proceeding as planned,” the doctors said.
Part of lung removed
The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with cancer after an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, according to a medical bulletin published by the Vatican on Tuesday.
Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican added, noting the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests. It did not provide details on the recovery outlook or course of treatment.
The Vatican said the procedure lasted 90 minutes and that the surgery “was successful, and there were no complications”.
A medical statement shared by The Holy See’s press office, following the surgery, noted the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in the hope of eliminating any lingering traces of the cancer.
After the procedure, Pope Leo returned to his room at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where he is expected to recover for a week, with all his audiences through October 20 cancelled.
The Vatican said doctors are not currently discussing chemotherapy or other therapies pending the results of other tests.

Internationals lose right to IND payouts under new asylum law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:09:47 UTC
00:09:47 KST

Internationals lose right to IND payouts under new asylum law
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
International workers, students and family migrants will no longer be entitled to penalty payments when the immigration service IND misses its deadlines, the asylum ministry has said after a new law was passed by the senate on Tuesday.
The change was presented as an asylum measure, but a ministry spokesperson told Dutch News the law applies to applications for regular residence permits, including highly skilled migrants, students and family members.
The IND is supposed to make a decision on a residence application within 6 months. If it misses that deadline, applicants can go to court to demand a payment for every day it remains late. Once the new law takes effect, judges will only be able to order the IND to reach a decision within a set period.
The government abandoned plans to axe penalty payments for regular residence applicants in 2024, saying it could conflict with EU law. The ministry told us it could not yet say what had changed.
Asylum minister Bart van den Brink told MPs in September the IND had paid out close to €100 million in penalties, noting that some asylum applicants had ended up receiving over €100,000. The IND also insists these penalties do nothing to speed things up.
A spokesperson from the IND told Dutch News the service does not currently know how much in penalty payments is paid for regular permit applicants, but it will calculate the figures in the coming weeks.
D66, which voted against the asylum package in April, backed the new law. In April, D66 senator Boris Dittrich told Dutch News the party opposed the package because it would have made living in the country without valid papers a criminal offence. That measure is not part of the new law.
A D66 spokesperson acknowledged that the IND’s failure to meet deadlines “is not resolved by this amendment”, but told us on Tuesday the penalties “no longer provide an incentive to work more efficiently and have therefore outlived their purpose”.
“In our view, abolishing the penalty payments must go hand in hand with measures aimed at the ultimate goal: faster procedures, so that everyone who comes here receives clarity as quickly as possible,” the spokesperson said.

The ex-OpenAI employee allegedly wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and inserted it into a television located in an "executive conference room".
OpenAI said it has alerted the FBI after it found a hidden recording device in an executive conference room in its San Francisco office, which led to the firing of an employee.
The suspect was identified as employee Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, who was arrested on October 9, about a week after OpenAI discovered the surveillance device. He made an initial appearance in a US court on Tuesday.
He was charged with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. Alfozan joined OpenAI as an engineer in July 2025.
Prosecutors said the device was wrapped in toilet paper and inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
He was allegedly spotted near the executive conference room in CCTV footage on multiple dates before the device was discovered, according to the Justice Department.
Conversations in the conference room "frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information," the Justice Department said.
The allegations come as the US and China race to become the leader in AI, which the Trump administration has pushed to be rebranded as "superintelligence".
“We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier,” OpenAI said in a statement posted on X.
The ChatGPT maker said it had “no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data”.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (€200,000) fine, followed by three years of supervised release.

UK’s only naval icebreaker breaks down – Telegraph
The British Navy has been left without its only icebreaker after HMS Protector suffered double engine failure at sea, The Telegraph reported on Tuesday. The breakdown adds to mounting concerns about Britain’s readiness for a major war and persistent funding problems.
HMS Protector, which was originally built in Norway in 2001, suffered simultaneous engine defects while departing Britain and had to be towed back to the Devonport naval base in Plymouth, the report says.
Maintenance failures are suspected, according to The Telegraph, although the full extent of the damage is unclear. If it cannot be repaired, a replacement may not arrive until the 2030s, the paper said.
One Navy source cited by The Telegraph described the incident as a “catastrophic failure.” Former HMS Endurance Commander Tom Sharpe warned that losing the icebreaker would undermine Britain’s presence in the South Atlantic amid renewed tensions with Argentina over the Falkland Islands (Malvinas, as they are known in Argentina) and the Sea Lion offshore oil project, as well as growing competition in the Arctic. 
“These ships cost a tiny fraction of the defense budget yet deliver an outsized effect in presence and soft power,” Sharpe said.
HMS Protector typically deploys to the South Atlantic and Antarctic, conducting hydrographic surveys, supporting scientific stations, and carrying personnel for inspections under international agreements. The vessel, which has a crew of around 88, does not have any heavy weapons but can carry machine guns and embark specialist Royal Marines.
The UK relies on the ship to project its influence in the Antarctic, where its territorial claims overlap with those of Argentina and Chile, though they have effectively been frozen under the 1959 Antarctic Treaty. Britain also operates a separate civilian icebreaker, RRS Sir David Attenborough, but it cannot replace HMS Protector’s naval patrol role.
The reported incident comes after the UK Navy announced in July the retirement of two more Type 23 frigates, leaving the fleet with just five frigates alongside six destroyers. Around the same time, retired Naval Staff chief Lord Alan West suggested that the British fleet has been reduced to the worst state in history.
In March, First Sea Lord General Sir Gwyn Jenkins acknowledged that the Navy is not ready for war, saying it aims to reach that level of preparedness by the end of the decade.
Officials have also sounded the alarm over the hollowed-out military budget, with the Treasury struggling to find £4.7 billion ($6.2 billion) for its multi-year military investment strategy.

Israeli satire show takes jab at far-right's vehement opposition to NAZA documentary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:07:07 UTC
00:07:07 KST

Israel's SNL-style satire show Eretz Nehederet portrayed NAZA co-directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor alongside far-right firebrand Tally Gotliv as mythical sirens spouting conspiracy theories and accusations from opposite ends of the political spectrum in an episode aired Tuesday.
The four-minute sketch, a parody of Christopher Nolan's summer blockbuster "The Odyssey," follows an Israeli soldier trying to return home after three years of war in the Gaza Strip. It opened the first episode of the show's special pre-election season.
Warning: Spoilers for "The Odyssey" ahead:
מסע החזרה של אודי סאוס מהמילואים הביתה בימוי: גדי פורטנוי אמן ai: דניאל קוץ
The sketch features an Israeli soldier named "Udi Seus" – a play on "Odysseus" – trying to return to his wife and son after 500 days of reserve duty.
Along the way, he encounters Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who continues promising "total victory" and urges him to keep fighting in Gaza, Lebanon and Turkey; a Cyclops-like figure modeled on United Torah Judaism leader Yitzchak Goldknopf, who refuses to support drafting Haredi men into the military; and blocked roads caused by traffic that Transportation Minister Miri Regev, portrayed as a goddess, has failed to manage.
The sketch reaches its climax at what it calls "the most difficult obstacle": the mythical sirens. As they approach, the main character has himself tied down while the other two soldiers block out the voices with headphones.
The three sirens are modeled on Gotliv, who recently left Netanyahu's Likud party to join Itamar Ben-Gvir's far-right Otzma Yehudit party, and NAZA co-directors Abraham and Szor.
The Gotliv character, who in real life is notorious for repeated disruptions during legal and state proceedings, rattles off conspiracy theories, including claims that the IDF chief of staff had prior knowledge of Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack and that Israeli pilots who threatened to stop volunteering for reserve duty during the government's 2023 judicial overhaul were "traitors."
On the other side, Abraham and Szor tell the soldiers: "The pilots are murderers, and you are NAZA criminals" – pronouncing "NAZA" in Hebrew in a way that sounds similar to "Nazi criminals."
As the tied-down soldier screams, Gotliv yells: "That's not impressive; I can scream louder. Now I can scream with Jewish Power!" – a reference to the English translation of Otzma Yehudit.
As the NAZA filmmakers applaud, the screaming soldier asks them to stop. Another soldier references the film's record-breaking standing ovation at last month's Venice Film Festival and says, "We have at least 20-25 more minutes."
Israeli human rights lawyer Snir Klein accused Eretz Nehederet of McCarthyism and said its writers were taking part in a "witch hunt" against the NAZA directors.
"There must be a special place in hell for the group of comedians who are serving Tally Gotliv and her friends under the guise of criticism…" he wrote on X.
"They are just an instrument that allows the Israeli mainstream to feel like it is being critical while it is actually unable to move away from the consensus dictated by the government."
Nir Wolf, TV critic for the right-leaning Israel Hayom newspaper, wrote that the season premiere showed how much Eretz Nehederet caters to the mainstream despite frequent criticism from the right that it is "too leftist."
Wolf said the show had played a major role in "normalizing the insanity" of Netanyahu's coalition by often turning figures such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Tally Gotliv into entertainment.

NGO: Brussels confirms Czech PM’s agri business conflict of interest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:06:52 UTC
00:06:52 KST

NGO: Brussels confirms Czech PM’s agri business conflict of interest
Babiš placed Agrofert in a trust fund before returning to power in an effort to preserve its eligibility for EU farm cash — but Brussels remains unconvinced.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš’ links to the agro-chemical giant Agrofert represent a conflict of interest and EU subsidies could be withheld as a result, according to an NGO’s account of a letter it received from the European Commission.
Ahead of his return to power in December 2025, Babiš placed Agrofert in a trust fund in an effort to preserve its eligibility for EU farm cash. However, that appears not to have convinced Brussels. Transparency International Czechia quotes a letter from DG AGRI Director-General Elisabeth Werner, confirming that “the Commission concluded that Mr Babiš’ situation constitutes a conflict of interest” under EU financial regulations.
The trust fund and “measures currently being implemented and notified to the Commission are insufficient” to resolve it, she adds, according to the watchdog NGO, which said it was not allowed to publish the letter.
Advertisement
Babiš has been under renewed scrutiny over Agrofert — a large agro-chemical conglomerate and a major recipient of EU funds — as well as other companies since his return to power last year. Babiš placed the company in a trust fund in a bid to avoid a conflict of interest, but the arrangement has raised questions from both the Commission and the Czech opposition, partly because his children would benefit from it after his death.
Babiš has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing. “I don’t own Agrofert, I never will again and I don’t benefit from it in any way. I don’t know what else I’m supposed to do,” he told Czech media last month. “Apparently, even if I shot myself, it still wouldn’t be enough.”
Babiš’ office did not immediately reply to POLITICO’s request for comment about the contents of the letter.
Werner warned in the letter that Brussels would take all necessary steps to protect EU funds, “including the possible interruption of payment deadlines, suspension of payments or application of financial corrections,” according to TI Czechia.
TI Czechia Executive Director David Kotora told POLITICO that he received the letter in September. A follow-up letter from Werner dated Oct. 5 gives the NGO permission to share the contents of the letter without publishing it.
The conflict-of-interest dispute echoes Babiš’ first term as prime minister, when a Commission audit found he still controlled Agrofert. That left Czech taxpayers to foot the bill for EU subsidies deemed to be erroneously paid.
History could now repeat itself as Brussels last month froze €3.18 million in reimbursements to the Czech state for farm subsidies paid out to Agrofert. That followed its earlier May decision that it would not reimburse any paid-out subsidies until doubts about his involvement in the business could be put to rest.
Commission spokesperson Louise Bogey confirmed it had sent a letter to TI Czechia in September, but would not comment on its content. However, she pointed to her remarks at a Sept. 8 midday briefing, during which she said Babiš was in a “potential conflict of interest” and that “the Commission considers the trust fund set up by Mr. Babiš does not sufficiently mitigate this situation.”
Czechia’s agricultural paying agency, which earlier decided that the conglomerate is eligible for EU subsidies despite the Commission’s warning, said Tuesday it had sent clarifications to the Commission this week.
Agrofert spokesperson Pavel Heřmanský said neither Agrofert nor any of its subsidiaries were involved in the communication between the Commission and Czech authorities.
“The cited letter from DG AGRI expresses the opinion of one of the European Commission’s departments. It does not constitute an official position of the European Commission,” said Heřmanský in a statement, adding that “only the Court of Justice of the European Union can provide a binding interpretation of European Union law.”
He added: “We remain convinced that we have received and continue to receive subsidies in compliance with both Czech and European law.”

Croatia's wartime grievances threaten Montenegro's hopes of joining EU by 2028
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:06:30 UTC
00:06:30 KST

Croatia's list of grievances with Montenegro include missing persons, war crimes, prison camps, property seizures and borders. Podgorica has closed 21 of 33 chapters, but Zagreb is blocking progress unless bilateral issues are resolved.
Croatia has warned that a series of unresolved disputes with neighbouring Montenegro, including wartime abuses, property claims and contested borders, could stand in the way of the country's ambition to join the European Union by 2028.
In a document sent to other EU governments on Monday and seen by Euronews, Zagreb set out eight demands it wants Montenegro to address before completing its accession to the bloc.
Montenegro is widely regarded as the frontrunner among countries seeking EU membership, with hopes of becoming the bloc's 28th member by 2028. But its long-running disputes with Croatia, many dating back to the breakup of Yugoslavia in the 1990s, threaten to derail that timetable.
“Croatia sincerely wishes to turn the page on this painful chapter of shared history and build a forward-looking relationship with Montenegro. Yet mutual trust and genuine, lasting reconciliation cannot be built without resolving these issues,” the document reads.
Montenegro made further progress towards EU membership on Monday, completing negotiations in three more policy areas – statistics, economic policy and employment – bringing the total to 21 out of 33.
However, Croatia is blocking progress in four other areas, covering transport, foreign relations, fundamental rights and home affairs. Because every existing EU member has a say over the accession process, Zagreb has considerable leverage over its neighbour's membership bid.
The document expands on grievances previously outlined by Croatia's Foreign Ministry in July, many rooted in the wars that accompanied Yugoslavia's collapse.
Among the most sensitive is Zagreb's demand for compensation for around 300 Croatian nationals detained and mistreated at the Morinj prison camp in Montenegro between October 1991 and August 1992. Croatian civilians and prisoners of war were forcibly transferred to the camp during the conflict.
Croatia also wants a memorial plaque at the former camp to remain permanently visible. A large metal frame was installed around it following protests by Montenegrin nationalist groups.
Another demand concerns the fate of 14 people still missing from Croatia's war of independence. Zagreb wants Montenegro to help locate their remains, describing the issue as a “major humanitarian issue that has yet to be resolved.”
A further point concerns war crimes: Croatia wants command responsibility for the crimes against civilians committed at Morinj to be considered in the cases of already convicted war criminals.
Croatia also expects Montenegro to resolve long-standing property disputes dating back to the early 1990s, involving Croatian families unlawfully deprived of their property without adequate compensation.
The paper points out that a 2021 law enabled the restitution of land in a region predominantly inhabited by the Albanian minority, “raising concerns about unequal treatment in comparable cases.”
Zagreb is also calling for the return of the Jadran, a sail training ship which has been under Montenegrin control since Yugoslavia dissolved in 1991.
Finally, Croatia wants the territorial disputes with its neighbour settled, over both the land and maritime border, in line with the Arbitration Commission of the Conference on Yugoslavia.
Croatia itself has an unresolved border dispute with Slovenia, although this did not prevent it from joining the EU in 2013.
“Croatia has consistently encouraged Montenegro to resolve outstanding bilateral issues while actively supporting its EU accession,” the paper continues. “Despite Croatia’s sustained efforts and constructive approach, none of the outstanding issues has yet been resolved.”

Renewed fighting risks ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ in Yemen, aid groups warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:06:18 UTC
00:06:18 KST

Renewed fighting risks ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ in Yemen, aid groups warn
Almost one million people cut off from food aid as health infrastructure overwhelmed by war-wounded.
The humanitarian groups the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the World Food Programme (WFP) have sounded the alarm over the worsening humanitarian situation in Yemen amid ramped-up fighting.
An estimated 800,000 people have been cut off from life-saving food assistance as front lines have rapidly shifted between Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government and the Iran-aligned Houthis, according to the WFP.
“This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe,” said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP’s country director in Yemen.
The crisis is worst in Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, where an estimated 600,000 people have no access to food assistance, including 200,000 women and children, the United Nations agency said in a statement.
Taiz has been the focus of recent clashes and is hemmed in by Houthi forces, imperiling aid deliveries.
The WFP said that the loss of access is especially alarming given that Taiz has some of the country’s highest levels of food insecurity.
Across Yemen, more than 18 million people do not have enough to eat, it added, while the latest monitoring shows a record 74 percent of households in accessible areas cannot meet their daily food needs.
Casualties flood hospitals
Meanwhile, “overwhelmed” health facilities in Marib, Taiz and along the Red Sea coast were bearing the brunt of the fighting in those areas, according to a statement released by the ICRC, with some receiving more than 700 cases in a single week,
Firas Abu Samra, the ICRC’s health services coordinator, said only a handful of facilities operating in Yemen can provide comprehensive care for the injured.
Front-line hospitals are taking in large numbers of wounded while running short of surgical supplies, anaesthetics, oxygen and medicines, he said.
“Additional pressure on hospitals can mean fewer beds, fewer supplies and less capacity to treat people with conditions unrelated to the conflict”, said Eduardo Toro, an ICRC surgeon at Marib General Hospital.
Christine Cipolla, the ICRC’s head of delegation in Yemen, said the country’s battered health system is ill-prepared to cope with any more fighting.
“Our concern is that the system may have little capacity left to absorb a major surge in casualties,” she said.

Trump says massive oil, gas exploration set to begin in 'our Greenland'

Unknown Publisher

Trump says massive oil, gas exploration set to begin in 'our Greenland'
COPENHAGEN, Oct 14 - US President Donald Trump said on Wednesday that "massive oil, gas and mineral exploration" was set to begin on Greenland, a contentious statement on a territory that has resisted his efforts to control it and has banned new drilling for crude.
Trump described the Danish Arctic island which is run by a semi-autonomous government as "our new and beautiful Greenland" in a social media post that hailed what he said were US gains from a security deal signed in September.
The Greenlandic prime minister's office declined to comment on Trump's statement.
The Danish foreign ministry and Greenland's ministry of mineral resources did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
TRUMP HAILS US SECURITY GAINS
Greenland has been caught up in a confrontation with Trump who has been saying since 2019 the US should buy or take the strategically located and mineral-rich island for security reasons. On several occasions, he refused to rule out force.
Along with Denmark, the US and Greenland reached an agreement last month to allow the US to boost its military presence on the island - a deal that had appeared to settle the standoff.
The agreement did not allocate any rights for mining or drilling.
"Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social platform.
"There are Experts that are saying that the amount of easily available Oil is far greater than that of almost any land, anywhere in the World," he added without naming any specific deals or specific development.
Greenland banned uranium mining in its territory along with all future exploration of oil in 2021.
The government has said it is reviewing whether a Texas firm, Greenland Energy, can use permits predating that prohibition.
The company said in August this year it had plans to drill for oil in 2027 at an untested basin on Greenland's east coast, although it lacked its own permit to do so. The previous owner, ARCO, spent heavily on seismic work in the 1970s but never drilled.
Independent Danish security policy advisor Jacob Kaarsbo said Trump's comments could be seen as a sign that his desire to control Greenland remained unchanged.
"It is extremely dangerous to view this agreement between the Trump administration and Denmark as something that has altered Trump’s intentions," he said.
The 10-page deal between the US, Denmark and Greenland paved the way for two new military bases and Trump's "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.
"Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived," Trump said in his post on Wednesday.
"It gives us time, location, and sightline, like nowhere else in the World!" he added. REUTERS

The eyes have it: Reform politician’s ‘smart glasses’ prompt calls for ban in Westminster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:05:53 UTC
00:05:53 KST

It was a flowing speech packed full of precise statistics – but Jason O’Connell, a Reform UK Senedd member, was not quite the gifted orator he had first appeared. The periodic flashing in his spectacles seemed to give the game away as he spoke for five minutes in the Senedd chamber without a glance at his notes.
“Cardiff reviewed 192 roads, following 933 requests, and only four routes have returned to 30mph,” he said as he led the party’s charge to abolish 20mph traffic zones. “£38.3m wasted to implement this policy and up to £8.9bn in an act of economic self-harm.”
It was probably no feat of memory – rather, the Reform member for Pontypridd Cynon Merthyr was suspected of using smart glasses that turned his lenses into tiny teleprompters.
In the days afterwards, Senedd members said the issue of smart glasses – popularised by Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta – needed to be dealt with at pace, with explicit guidance developed on their use.
There was no suggestion that O’Connell’s glasses were recording. But it has prompted a fresh debate about the increasingly popular technology, with the House of Commons facing calls to ban smart glasses at Westminster.
The Liberal Democrats wrote to Lindsay Hoyle, the Commons speaker, on Wednesday urging him to act amid the “increasing use of smart glasses” on the parliamentary estate. They warned that with Christmas coming, even more people could start using the AI-enabled devices in 2027.
The technology has myriad implications. Anna Sabine, the Liberal Democrat spokesperson for culture, media and sport, said smart glasses could lead to debates becoming increasingly “managed”.
“How much is the quality of what an MP is saying actually down to what they’re getting through the AI glasses?” she said. “It’s a really interesting question.”
She said she had not yet identified anyone wearing smart glasses in parliament but added: “This is the problem: I wouldn’t necessarily know.” A law would help to keep the estate and the work MPs did “private and secure”.
Sabine added: “Smart glasses can record video and take photographs discreetly … creating a particular risk to the existing rules on the parliamentary estate [limiting recording and photography].
“I am regularly in meetings with documents or talking about important, private matters on behalf of my constituents. I am sure you will agree that the details of such cases should never be at risk of being shared because someone is filming or taking pictures discreetly.
“Because smart glasses look like ordinary glasses, and increasingly their recording indicator lights can be covered or disabled, filming could easily go unnoticed by security teams, putting private information at risk.”
A spokesperson for the UK parliament said it was reviewing its policy on the use of camera-equipped smart glasses, as well as other forms of wearable technology, on the parliamentary estate.
The senior deputy speaker of the House of Lords, Lord Ponsonby, told parliament last month that the review “is considering the implications of these emerging technologies and whether additional guidance is required”.
He added: “This work will bring together expertise from those responsible for filming and photography policy, physical and information security, privacy and data protection compliance and accessibility and reasonable-adjustment requirements, ensuring that any future approach appropriately balances security, privacy, operational needs and accessibility considerations.”
O’Connell has been contacted for comment. On Sunday he posted a picture on X of himself wearing a pair of comedy large pink glasses for a breast cancer charity, with the message: “Trialling some new glasses for the chamber this week. Apparently my last ones caused quite a stir.”

German leader insists Ukraine aid is not reducing social spending at home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:04:14 UTC
00:04:14 KST

Ayhan Simsek
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday defended his government's financial and military support for Ukraine, rejecting opposition party claims that the aid comes at the expense of social spending at home.
Addressing lawmakers in parliament, Merz said continued support for Ukraine is essential to safeguard peace and security across Europe as Russia’s threats intensify. He argued that military assistance to Kyiv does not reduce funds available for domestic priorities.
“Not a single euro flowing to Ukraine is being diverted from social or educational spending in our country. Not a single euro is missing," Merz said. He added that they had introduced an exception to Germany’s constitutional debt rule to allow defense-related spending to be financed through additional borrowing.
Merz warned that the danger is concrete rather than theoretical. "We see that Russia's readiness to escalate is rising toward Ukraine, toward our Eastern European neighbors, but also toward our own country," he said.
He slammed the right-wing AfD and the socialist Left Party for downplaying threats and fueling division.
"It is incomprehensible to me how those on the far left and far right continue, to this day, to play down the situation,” he said, accusing them of deliberately driving divisions, uncritically spreading disinformation. "One gets the impression you want the chaos because you want to gain party-political advantages from it."
Opposition lawmakers from the AfD and the Left Party have repeatedly argued that billions of euros in support for Ukraine should instead go to domestic priorities such as pensions and infrastructure.
Merz's conservative CDU/CSU alliance is facing pressure as it trails in opinion polls while the right-wing AfD leads. An INSA survey published this week put the AfD at 30%, the CDU/CSU at 18.5%, the environmentalist Greens at 14%, the center-left SPD at 13.5%, and the Left Party at 10%.

On Wednesday, the Japanese foreign ministry said European Affairs Bureau official Kimitake Nakamura summoned the Russian ambassador, Nikolay Nozdrev.

Territorial dispute

The FSB published a video showing masked officers storming a hotel room, pushing a man to the floor and handcuffing him.
He was flown to Moscow, where a court ordered he be held in pre-trial detention.
It did not say when the arrest or court hearing occurred.
In 2023, US journalist Evan Gershkovich was arrested in Russia on espionage charges, later sentenced to 16 years in prison before being released in a 2024 prisoner swap.
Moscow and Tokyo have been locked in a territorial dispute for decades over the status of a string of islands in the Pacific Ocean, off the northeast coast of Japan and to the southwest of Russia’s Sakhalin region.
The Kuril Islands – called the Northern Territories in Japan – have been under Russia’s control since the end of World War II, when they were seized by the Soviet Union.

The Chinese foreign ministry meanwhile said a delegation visited Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, the capital of Sakhalin Oblast in Russia, which is not on the disputed islands.

Ukraine hits two Russian refineries despite Trump’s demands – Moscow
Ukraine targeted two Russian oil refineries on Wednesday, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Aleksandr Novak has said.
The facilities are in Russia’s Saratov and Ryazan regions, Novak said on the sidelines of the Russian Energy Week forum. He did not specify whether either refinery sustained damage.
“We can see that the Ukrainian side is making no moves towards an energy ceasefire,” Novak said, referring to a limited ceasefire between Moscow and Kiev proposed by US President Donald Trump.
On Sunday, Trump claimed that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate energy ceasefire. Neither Moscow nor Kiev, however, has confirmed the truce, sending out mixed messages on the matter.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky said the announcement “was news” for him, but expressed readiness to stop attacking Russian refineries should Moscow halt strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also declined to confirm the deal, stating that contacts were still ongoing. Peskov also reiterated Moscow’s longstanding position that Russia seeks a long-term peace agreement rather than a temporary truce.
The US president has also accused Zelensky of seeking to “make problems” for the US and the whole world by ignoring demands to stop its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
“Russia supplies a large portion of the diesel fuel throughout the world. And we told him, do whatever you want, but don’t hit the diesel fuel,” Trump said last week. “And what does he do? He goes and hits the diesel fuel. He can do whatever he wants, but he can’t do that. He’d better damn well stop.”
On Friday, the US eased its restrictions on Russia’s diesel trade, allowing it to be sold, delivered, and imported into the US until April 7, 2027.
According to Trump, Moscow agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 metric tons in November, and 1 million more shortly thereafter. Novak confirmed the figures, saying Russia will move to lift its own export restrictions immediately.
According to US media reports, Trump struck the deal after Zelensky repeatedly ignored demands to stop attacking Russian oil refineries. The US president accused the Ukrainian leader of exacerbating the global fuel crisis.
Kiev reportedly asked the US what it would get for stopping its attacks on Russian refineries. The Trump administration suggested that Kiev is receiving enough help and is in no position to demand more.

Bulgarian authorities are investigating the arson of Starlink satellite communications antennas at a site near Sofia.

Bulgarian parliament member Ivaylo Mirchev first reported the arson. According to him, 11 of the 17 antennas used to connect to SpaceX’s Starlink satellite network were deliberately set on fire at a restricted site near Sofia.

Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said police had taken additional measures to protect similar sites across the country after the incident, although their owners remain directly responsible for security.
The incident comes amid another suspected act of sabotage targeting Starlink infrastructure in Europe.
In late September, Militarnyi reported a fire at a Starlink ground station in Poland that provided satellite connectivity to users across Europe, including Ukraine. Polish investigators later determined that the fire had been deliberately set.
Polish prosecutors were investigating the possibility of sabotage on behalf of Russian intelligence services. On October 12, two suspects in the arson were detained in Germany. The Polish government said it considered the incident an act of hybrid warfare and linked it to Russia.

‘The Mind is a Computer or LLM’: We Need to Talk About the Effect of this Simplistic View on our Relationships to our Own Minds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:00:39 UTC
00:00:39 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
We repeatedly encounter claims that the brain is an LLM, or a computer, or very like one of these things. What effect does repeatedly encountering this debate have on how we understand ourselves? I think it’s worth asking, because, in my view, the debate isn’t one we would be having were it not for the historical circumstances.
I’ve argued against this view plenty. Today, I dig deeper. What effect is it having that many of us believe this view is true? Or, even if we do not believe it, what effect is it having that everywhere we read articles about it, suggesting it is at least possibly true?
My classrooms are tech free this term and I am witnessing more palpably than ever the effect that LLMs are having on our students, but really on our society. As someone who has spent over a decade being nothing short of fascinated with the human mind —yes, I went to undergraduate to enthusiastically pursue psychology only to take a somewhat winded path into Columbia’s philosophy halls for my PhD— I want to bring this theoretical work into a shared practice of exploring and exercising our own cognitive capacities, our own minds. After almost 10 months on Substack experimenting with how to turn my philosophy practical, that day has come.
In this post, I am going to preliminarily sketch my decade+ thinking on brains and minds, and how I think we can use this knowledge to examine our relationships to our own minds in this AI-obsessed age.
Here is my hypothesis: being told on repeat that the brain is a computer of some form (whether in the traditional sense of a something like a digital computer, or, an LLM, see a breakdown here on these views) is having an impact on our relationship to our own cognitive capacities, to our own minds.
There has been much talk about cognitive de-skilling and cognitive decline. These topics are incredibly important, but the question I am asking is a different one.
I’m asking — holding constant whether de-skilling and cognitive decline is a problem for you, and to what extent — whether how we conceive of our minds is impacted, the more we are required to use AI at work, or the more we default towards using it in other aspects of our lives.
Another way to motivate the question is this: most of our mental lives happens below conscious awareness. Assuming this, what kinds of assumptions might we be harbouring about our own minds in the face of how we are told to think about human brains today?
Have we started to believe that LLMs really are better at thinking than us? That they really are more creative than us? Have we started confusing speed, with intelligence? Confident sounding sentences, with knowledge? I think that these are not just questions for research, but conversations we need to be having together and with ourselves.
Let me tell you my unique reasons for believing we desperately need to have these conversations, because it’s rooted in years of thinking about human brains.
I’ve been writing on Substack now for almost 10 months. When I first started out, I did not know what I was doing —I still don’t, obviously — but I did have two general goals. I wanted to share my work in accessible ways, and I wanted to figure out how to turn my insights into something that could make a difference.
I started with the first goal —substantially more achievable — which included writing articles that argued the brain is not a computer, that it’s not an LLM, that mainstream philosophy of mind is also wrong, imho, in how it frames questions of mind, that LLMs do not have language, as well as building a framework that shows why current efforts to understand AI consciousness are, I think, completely off the mark.
Detecting a pattern in any of this? My astute Substack subscribers sure did. Everything I wrote was about what the mind isn’t, what the brain isn’t, and what LLMs don’t have. All my work is showing what’s wrong with the current frameworks.
But what about a positive proposal, Ellen?! Let me explain.
I stand by all of the intellectual arguments I’ve made. And I stand by my decision to only argue negative proposals in theoretical terms (for now, at least). However, today I am in a place where I can explain what the positive proposal might have to look like. All of my thinking here is preliminary of course, but many of you have asked me to push my work into a positive proposal space, and I’m trying to do just that.
Because here’s the thing: There’s a reason that all my intellectual work is about showing where we go awry in our thinking about brains/minds.
It’s because I think there are limits to what we can theoretically or scientifically understand about the mind. Human judgement, human creativity, human thought, I believe we can study aspects of these things scientifically, but I also think that a lot of it escapes scientific frameworks. They are things we have to understand in different ways, through novels, art, or music, for example, or through exercising those capacities for ourselves. Some things about the mind we can only know through experience.
Experiencing these kinds of intellectual moments for myself, for instance, has helped me come to terms with the limits of scientific understanding of minds (though of course, so have the years of study I have done on these topics).
I think back to when I wrote my dissertation, for example, and how there was no way that an LLM could have ever produced it.
The ideas were too sparse in existing literature, the connected thoughts across fields were not well-trodden paths, the intuitions I used to decide what to read, and what not to read, what to focus on, and what not to focus on, could never have been identified by an LLM. I can’t systematise the intuitive knowledge I worked on myself, how could I have even begin to tell an LLM how to do it for me?
And I don’t say these things to toot my own horn. I think every single human being is just like me—infinitely creative and exploratory if given the opportunity, though not infinitely capable of articulating, let alone developing a scientific understanding, of what those intuitive processes look like, or how they work.
But these intuitions and creative urges can be suppressed, if, for example, we never think to exercise them, because —oh, I don’t know — everyone is telling us that LLMs are bigger and better than our own brains… You see where this is going.
With that said, here are some questions I invite you to ask yourself, either by yourself or with others, to see if a broader conversation could happen around these kinds of questions in ways that might help us better relate to AI.
(1) Do I ever think my own mind is inadequate in comparison to an LLM? Why might I think this? This could look like having an idea, plugging it into an LLM, and deciding based on the LLMs response that you don’t want to pursue the idea.
Why exactly might this happen? Why think the LLM is any kind of authority in this situation? What would you have done with the idea prior to the existence of LLMs?
In my view, we shouldn’t compare the ourselves to LLMs, especially not when it comes to our relationship to our own minds and cognitive capacities vs that of LLMs. The human brain should be appreciated on its own terms. Secondarily, we can decide what we think LLMs are good at doing and not doing, where it can help and where it can hinder.
(2) How do you think of the human brain if you were asked about it? Do you think of it as one big computer as you’ve likely seen a lot in the media the last few years? Do you have no conception at all? Whatever ideas you have about the brain, where did you get them? Do you think any of this impacts how you view your own mind?
Sometimes I worry that the simplistic narratives making the headlines will impact our relationship to our minds in daily small ways. For example, the generative capacities of human brains are not understood, though we know the mind is generative from work on language, for instance, and we recognize it intuitively.
The ‘generative’ capacities of LLMs, on the other hand, are well-understood, and the technology produces outputs in an instant. But humans generating ideas can take time. Sitting with an idea. Reading another book that stimulates your mind further and helps you sharpen an idea. Going for a walk, etc.
In the case of our own generative minds, we need patience, we need exposure to an array of ideas, we need reading, we need writing, we need time, and ideally, we need to talk to other humans interested in the same ideas. Being exposed to LLMs that spit out ideas in seconds, might mean that we need to work harder than ever to remember that our brains work differently, and that that’s not a bad thing.
(3) What do you do with inchoate ideas, ideas that are not yet well-formed? Do you let yourself have fragments of ideas, intuitions, or thoughts, and sit with them before being able to clearly articulate what you mean by them? How does your relationship to LLMs influence this process? Does using an LLM help you articulate your ideas more clearly, or does it just give you a thought that feels acceptably like what you were sitting with? Do you hold enough awareness around your thinking to know?
(4) Are there parts of your life that shape your thinking and beliefs in valuable ways that you might not necessarily get from an LLM? Do you pay enough attention to those things? The thought your friend mentioned to you the other day, your child’s curiosity, your partners musings?
(5) Are there things you value about your cognition that you want to preserve for just you, i.e., that you don’t want to outsource to an LLM? Things that give you joy even if the finished product isn’t ‘as good’ or as polished as if you put it through an LLM? Exercising our cognitive capacities as human beings is a good in and of itself. That’s something to bear in mind.
One of the main ideas I keep coming back to in my work is that today, we keep confusing models of the mind with what minds are. One of the deepest consequences of this mistake is that we systematically erase all those parts of our minds that we do not understand, that we cannot neatly fit into the latest, ‘model’ of the mind. Consequently, I am increasingly concerned, we do not pay enough attention to those parts of our mind, and in doing so subconsciously undermine them, through for example not exercising those capacities.
I hope these questions can serve as a way to generate a broader conversation between yourself and others in thinking through these issues.
Thank you for being here. If you found this article valuable, consider a free or paid subscription. You’ll be helping support the existence of rigorous independent philosophical writing on AI consciousness, something we all desperately need today.

Todd Haynes at Lumière Festival: 'It is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:00:37 UTC
00:00:37 KST

"It is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms, and our ability to speak freely." Euronews Culture sits down with celebrated filmmaker Todd Haynes during this year's Lumière Film Festival.
One of the guests of honour this year at Lyon’s Lumière Film Festival is none other than Todd Haynes, one of the most important and singular voices in contemporary American cinema.
The celebrated director and screenwriter of Far From Heaven, I’m Not There, Carol, and May December is known for his pioneering work associated with the New Queer Cinema movement of the early 90s. He then gained acclaim for his films exploring the emotional repercussions of social repression and the unspoken desires revealed by marginalized experiences.
He attends the Lumière Film Festival to present the restored versions of his directorial debut Poison (1991), a provocative exploration of AIDS-era perceptions. He also presents the Julianne Moore-starring psychological drama Safe (1995), marking the first time that these two films have screened in French cinemas since their initial releases.
Euronews Culture sat down with Todd Haynes during the festival to discuss the enduring timeliness of Poison and Safe, his thoughts on the evolving Hollywood ecosystem, as well as his upcoming film De Noche.
Euronews Culture: How does it feel to be at the Lumière Film Festival in Lyon, the birthplace of cinema?
Todd Haynes: Pretty thrillingly natal! No, really, it's a festival I've been hearing so much about for so long. And it really is such a celebration of movies of all kinds, of every genre, of every era. Restorations are presented, artists are attributed, and it's a really remarkable place and atmosphere, and it's so much about just the filmmaking and the films.
There's a retrospective of your films, including two newly restored versions of Poison and Safe. How do you look back on these films, and how do you feel about the fact that there are going to be audiences at this festival who are seeing these two films for the very first time?
I was there for the introduction of Poison. People were asked in the theater who were seeing it for the first time and almost every hand went up! And it was a completely full theatre, so that just demonstrates a kind of interest and curiosity about what's being shown in Lyon, and an audience that is very enthusiastic about it.
So, it's incredibly meaningful. These are my first two features. They are very, very different. Poison came out in the height of the AIDS era and it was among the first couple of films that would join other films in being categorised as the New Queer Cinema. None of which, I don't think, would have been possible outside of that political and socio-economic crisis - the public health crisis of AIDS. In certain times, those kinds of conditions make creating film and documentary, and protest and organised resistance, essential. They drive a kind of urgency that we don't always feel in our medium or our market. That was absolutely true for Poison. And then I made a film [Safe] that also is, in my mind, inconceivable without the AIDS era as a framework. It's a film that takes the place about as far away from the battlefield, if you will, but still engaged. A lot of the themes and issues deal with illness, and the body, and feeling alienated from the world around you...
I had the pleasure of re-watching both films, and that sense of isolation in Safe still feels incredibly prescient.
That’s always surprising and encouraging to hear. I understand how that might be what people could say about Safe. The film was watched again during Covid. There was a lot of discussion about the film and articles that came out were sent to me. And sadly, these issues remain relevant when we're hit by things that are overwhelming and that challenge every single aspect of the way we lead our lives, and the assumptions about how to live our lives that we take for granted.
Both explicitly and implicitly about the AIDS crisis, do you find it heartening or disheartening that Poison and Safe still feel timely? After all, Poison was made at a specific time, and there are many members of the gay, trans, queer communities who continue to feel threatened and continue to express fears...
Absolutely. One does feel at times like we’re in a replay, if not crashing backwards in battles we’ve fought. Battles around reproductive rights, around tolerance and acceptance over queer communities and trans communities. Poison in particular addressed very much that sense of vulnerability that the community was feeling under the siege of AIDS and HIV.
Jean Genet, who's a writer and thinker and poet and playwright who I've always loved - but also derived a certain energy from his attitude about how important it is to remember that being defined marginal... The goal to that is not necessarily to find your way back to the table and become just like everybody else. For him, his queerness, it came out of a criminal background. He liked that homosexuality had this criminal aspect to it. He used that as a way of weaponising his critique of dominant culture. Poison was made at the very end of the 80s and we needed a voice like that.
I'm heartened to see that some of Jean Genet’s books are displayed next to DVDs of your films at the Lumière marketplace...
Oh, I didn’t see that. That’s awesome!
From a European perspective, when you look at present day Hollywood, it’s hard not to see a sense of regression. For instance, to take a recent example, the Paramount-Warner merger feels like it threatens the financing of films from a plurality of voices. What are your thoughts on the evolution of the studio system and Hollywood at the moment?
It's distressing when you see the conglomeration of huge media organizations that one might imagine would provide enough revenue and foundation for risk-taking to still occur. But sadly, that is rarely what you end up seeing. I don't feel it, particularly in the moment, among some of the big streaming companies. There's a sense of wanting to repeat what worked the last time, and keep replicating what the audiences seem to crave. And that's tough.
For my last couple films, we've really gone elsewhere. I mean, we did sell May December, my last feature, to Netflix - and they were a fantastic company, full of incredibly smart people who really believed in the film. But the way we made the film was through the limited amount of investment that we absolutely had to have to get it done so we could all retain our creative freedom and identity. That's how we put together the financing for my current film that I'm finishing now, De Noche. And in that case, I really do want a company fully committed to theatrical release.
Discourse around film and the creation of film feels in jeopardy at the moment. For example, we saw it this year at the Berlinale with the controversy surrounding Tricia Tuttle and the pro-Palestinian speeches made by invited filmmakers. Do you fear or foresee that cultural institutions will become increasingly threatened by political pressure, like in Berlin?
Sure. I think Germany has a unique, specific, and at times contradictory attitudes or laws around how we discuss Israel, for instance. There's this happening on the one hand where speech is kind of being watchdogged and limited, and people have a hard time of just saying that it doesn't have to be about Jewish people to have problems with the policies of Netanyahu, or whoever it may be.
But at the same time, the AfD is rising in Germany... So you have that complete sort of disconnect between these two forces - one trying to make remedy after an incredibly horrific past in history, and then all of a sudden, wanting such extreme change to come into place from completely the opposite direction.
So, Germany is a unique case, but I think we're feeling similar things about a crackdown on content and what is called ideology or point of view in the United States. It's targeted at the media, it's targeted at the news industries, and it's targeted at universities... So it is a time to remember how important it is to protect our freedoms, and our ability to speak freely.
To temporarily move away from the doom and gloom, I wanted to share with you that the first film of yours that I saw was Velvet Goldmine (1998), which had a profound impact on me. I remember seeing the trailer for the first time, watching Brian Slade in his feather outfit on stage, hearing the gunshot followed by the needle drop of T. Rex’s '20th Century Boy', and... it still gives me goosebumps.
(Laughs) Awww....
The film turns 30 very soon... How do you look back on Velvet Goldmine and please tell me there’ll be a resotration?
Oh, it's another film that sort of realised or completed a phase of my creative life that was very profound and deep in that whole era of music and the early 70s. And the very interesting relationship between the UK and the US in how that music came to be. Criterion Collection is working on the release of Poison that will coincide with that 30th anniversary. I'm very, very excited about that.
Music plays a big part in your filmography – whether it’s Karen Carpenter, Bob Dylan, The Velvet Underground... I read somewhere that you’re working on a documentary about The Cure...
You know, that was news to me! (Laughs) Somebody brought it up... I mean, I love The Cure and they were formative in my life. Their music and evolution as a band from record to record... But no, it's not something I'm doing, and I'm not exactly sure where that came from! (Laughs)
Can you blame people for trying to manifest this project into existence?
(Laughs) Exactly!
Well, glad we got that cleared up! You mentioned your upcoming film, De Noche... You’ve wrapped, right?
We've wrapped the film and we're in post-production. We're moving from the picture cut to the sound. The whole production was based in Mexico. And this film was a particular struggle to get to this place, so I'm very proud of it.
You mention struggles...
Oh well, it began with the relationship with an actor [Joaquin Phoenix] who came to me for it and we moved forward. We got very close to production two years ago, and then he had a very abrupt or unexpected change of heart and walked away. And so De Noche 1 fell apart. But it was remarkable how the financiers and the investors who were there for that version came back, and demonstrated loyalty to the project and a film that means so much to all of us.
I’m glad De Noche 2 happened, with Danny Ramirez and Pedro Pascal starring. You also worked with Jon Raymond, who you’d previously collaborated with on the miniseries Mildred Pierce. I’m a huge fan of his work with Kelly Reichardt, especially on Old Joy and First Cow, which is a masterpiece in my book.
I couldn't agree more. Jon is a novelist first and has become a screenwriter. I’m so proud to have played even the smallest part in introducing Jon to Kelly when I moved to Portland, Oregon. They met each other, and they really hit it off. Many of his short stories were the first places that she went to in order to resuscitate a career in feature filmmaking that she had kind of put aside. And amazingly, well before she ended up even settling down in the Pacific Northwest, she and Jon really became the chroniclers of that region, its history, of Portland and beyond. So that unexpected move in my life to Portland from New York City... There have been so many rewards from it. And Jon is one of my dearest, closest friends. He's the most fabulous human being.
I can't wait to see De Noche. Is there anything else you can tell us about the film?
I don't know if I've ever quite seen anything like it before as a concept. It sort of begins as a detective story in the late 30s in a very corrupt Los Angeles, and through circumstances and the corruption that these two characters have become embroiled in, they're forced to leave Los Angeles and flee to Mexico. A very inexplicable, unexpected relationship begins to form between the two of them. To get to that point, a lot of dynamics of divisions between them in terms of power and race are overcome bit by bit, step by step, through the exploration of each other as lovers. It ultimately becomes a love story that that leaves you, I hope, longing and wondering what will happen between these two men.
To wrap up, at the opening ceremony of the Lumière Festival, you shared with me that the first film that had a profound impact on you was Mary Poppins. What was it about that film that marked you?
For one thing, it was the sort crown jewel of the Disney experiment, in terms of the films that came out of Disney at that time. The score is so exquisite, the two actors who take the leads are just perfection, it's so beautifully produced... I think for a three-year-old's imagination, there’s something about a maternal subject who comes with unique powers, and also discipline. Just a curious combination of various aspects of that character. I think seeing a movie on the big screen for the first time can't be overstated. The sheer power of that... I think all of those things conjoined to make it a sort of escapable moment of introduction to this medium.
This year has been a very good one in terms of cinema attendance and that being mirrored at the box office. Still, there are cinemas struggling and many fears expressed about the threat that artificial intelligence represents for the creative arts. As broad a question as this is, are you optimistic about the future of cinema?
I have to be optimistic. Because it's a medium I just love. I wasn't able to shoot De Noche on film, as we couldn't afford it, but it will always be my starting point on any film that I make. And what you are seeing among young people is an incredible desire to go out of their houses and leave their home screens and their phones behind and join in the experience of watching a movie on the screen.
You know how we all thought vinyl was going to go away with the introduction of CDs and MP3 and there was a sort of counter movement that was like ‘No, I want to hold it in my hand'... The desire to actually experience it and the warm resonance of hearing vinyl play with a needle on... Sometimes the simplest technology remains the best and the most profound. I hope that continues and I hope we can see that still being played out. It is about younger people and exposing them to what that experience means, and what that's like to share communally in a theatre in the dark.
On that note, Mr Haynes, thank you very much for your time.
The Lumière Film Festival takes place until 18 October in Lyon, France. The restored versions of Todd Haynes' Poison and Safe are being screened, as well as Far From Heaven and I'm Not There. Safe is out now on Criterion 4K UHD Blu-ray.
Todd Haynes' new film, De Noche, finished shooting in April 2026. No release date has yet been announced.

Trump convinces Putin to restart diesel exports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:00:11 UTC
00:00:11 KST

Trump convinces Putin to restart diesel exports
The first result of the US reengaging in talks over Ukraine has arrived: yet another easing of sanctions against Russia. On Friday, Donald Trump spoke with Vladimir Putin and then announced that Russia would supply more than 2 million tons of diesel fuel to the global market before the end of the year, possibly rising to up to 3 million tons a month after that. The US Treasury has already lifted restrictions on its sale.
- On Friday — late in the evening in Russia — Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that he had held an “extremely successful” conversation with Vladimir Putin, who had agreed to deliver Russian diesel “to the American and Global marketplace.” According to Trump, and later confirmed by Russia’s Deputy PM Alexander Novak, Russia will immediately ship more than 300,000 tons, followed by another 500,000 tons in November, and 1 million tons right after that. Then, “based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries”, another 3 million tons shortly after, Trump said. Shortly afterward, the U.S. Treasury Department issued a general license suspending sanctions on Russian diesel fuel through April 2027.
- Putin and his administration were quick to confirm that the call with Trump had been successful and that Russia was ready to supply oil and petroleum products to U.S. and global markets. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak promptly announced the immediate lifting of a ban on diesel exports by Russian companies that had been in place since July. He added that Moscow could eventually increase supplies to 3 million tons a month — roughly the volume Russia exported before the war.
- The lifting of U.S. sanctions is unlikely to have a major impact on Russian diesel exports. Until the summer of 2026, sanctions had not prevented Russia from supplying global markets with volumes just 10% below prewar levels. Brazil and Turkey were traditionally the main buyers. Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries have proved a much more serious obstacle to exports. In July 2026, after the attacks triggered a fuel crisis in Russia, the government introduced a ban on diesel exports as part of a broader effort to protect the domestic market. Shipments immediately fell sixfold. But as seasonal demand began to ease, Russian officials had already started discussing lifting the ban for selected producers in early October.
- A resumption of Russian supplies would not be a panacea for the U.S. or global markets either. Analysts doubt that Russia will be able to ramp up exports quickly in the wake of Ukrainian attacks. In September, three of the country’s six largest diesel-producing refineries were forced to cut output following drone strikes.
- It remains unclear whether Trump and Putin discussed any agreement to de-escalate the war in Ukraine alongside the diesel deal. Judging by the Kremlin’s comments, however, if they did, the discussion produced no results. “By attempting to disrupt our elections with an extremely massive drone attack on Moscow, the Kyiv regime effectively derailed the possibility of immediately resuming the negotiation process. And now, as the president said, we will consider when those talks can be resumed,” Putin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Friday evening.
Why the world should care
Ukrainian and US officials were due to meet in Miami on Friday in a bid to restart talks on ending the war, just as Trump announced the lifting of sanctions on Russia. It is clear that anyone who expected Russia and Ukraine to reach some kind of de-escalation agreement before the US midterms should not hold their breathe. “We will burn [Russian] refineries,” a Ukrainian official told the FT right after the Trump-Putin call. The Russian leader has even less reason to stop his own attacks on Ukraine’s energy sector. Every winter gives him hope of breaking Ukraine’s will by attacking the infrastructure that supplies power and heating to its largest cities.
