====================================================================================================

France’s students are angry about more than crumbling classrooms and missing teachers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:29:13 UTC
23:29:13 KST

Say what you will about France’s high schools, they still produce world-class slogan writers. Here’s a brief selection spotted during three weeks of blockades and marches over chronic teacher shortages, overcrowded classes and crumbling buildings:
“Pas d’avenir, pas de calme” (No future, no calm). “Diplômés aujourd’hui, précaires demain” (Graduates today, insecure tomorrow). “Vous détruisez notre futur, on bloque votre présent” (You destroy our future, we block your present).
A couple more: “Nos lycées tombent en ruines, comme nos espoirs” (Our schools, like our hopes, are falling into ruin”). “On n’est pas mal éduqués, on n’est pas écoutés” (We’re not badly brought up, we’re just not being listened to).
Spot the common theme? The protests, which continued this week with more than 160,000 on the streets on Tuesday, might be over very material problems – but beneath them there clearly lies an altogether more existential worry.
This generation fears its future will be one of diminishing prospects, poorly paid, unstable jobs, unaffordable living costs and steadily decaying public infrastructure – the end, in short, of the basic socioeconomic security their parents, mostly, enjoyed.
That was the central theme of a 30-second Instagram post I recorded last week with the Guardian’s social media team and that, at time of writing, had been watched almost 540,000 times – with young people in France the largest single group of viewers.
The same core concerns underlie youth protests elsewhere – notably, ongoing mass housing demonstrations in Spain, where the twentysomethings of Madrid and Barcelona are in revolt at the monthly rental on a one-bed flat costing an entire monthly median salary.
In France, teenagers in Seine-Saint-Denis, a low-income area in the north of Paris, show reporters pictures of broken chairs and desks, holes in walls, leaking ceilings, mould, shattered toilets and defective audiovisual equipment. Some have gone months without key teachers.
The consequence, here, is protest.
As Kitty Sayers, who went to school in France, explained, France’s republic “was born of insurrection and has never forgotten it … The language of rights, citizenship and collective power is woven into French education.”
This means that in French schools protest is “taught as a legally framed, fundamental right and a civic responsibility”. But the government’s response has also been arguably very French: riot police, teargas, baton charges and stun grenades.
More than 250 pupils have been injured, along with about 100 school staff and 750 police. One teen has lost a hand from a stun grenade, another the sight in one eye, a third his teeth. More than 6,000 people – almost all minors – have been detained.
After a public outcry, the interior minister last week suspended the use of stun grenades. But as Alexander Hurst observed, when pupils complain about the state of their schools “and the response is riot police, the government has lost the plot”.
Wider public support
If the government hoped public opinion would be on its side, it miscalculated. Teachers’ and other unions, parents and university students have marched with the pupils, and a poll this week showed 57% of the public approved of the protests, with 33% opposed.
They come at a particularly delicate time for France’s political establishment. Presidential elections to replace Emmanuel Macron are due next spring, and without a parliamentary majority his government is caught in legislative deadlock.
Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally and the radical-left La France Insoumise of Jean-Luc Mélenchon are weaponising the protests, the former castigating an out-of-control youth, the latter an out-of-control police, and both blaming centrist incompetence.
Above all, the government’s financial room for manoeuvre is all but nonexistent. As Philip Inman pointed out, with a debt-to-GDP ratio and a budget deficit both among the highest in the EU, France has no cash to spare – and the markets are watching.
So while cost-cutting will only provoke more unrest, the absence of it could trigger a boycott of French bonds, or even a default and bailout (although as the economist Paul Krugman says, France “may have crossed from too big to fail to too big to save”).
Ultimately, there seems little doubt France will have to make some of the same painful adjustments to bring its debt back under control that Italy, Spain and Greece made a decade or more ago – and to which French public reaction could be dramatic.
We began with slogans; let’s end with some. The best-known French youth protest – a revolution, more or less – was, of course, May 1968. Comparing its iconic posters with those of today’s demonstrating school pupils is instructive.
In 1968, there was “Sous les pavés, la plage” (Beneath the cobblestones, the beach); “L’imagination au pouvoir” (Put imagination in charge); “L’ennui est contre-révolutionnaire” (Boredom is counter-revolutionary).
Those, you can see, were slogans born out of infinite possibility: a generation that, in overthrowing the old social hierarchies, never doubted its material survival. May 68 was about blowing open the doors of a rigid, outmoded society to grasp a bright future.
Today’s students are fighting to stop the doors slamming shut on them altogether.
Guardian live-streamed event – Hacking Tech
Big tech and AI pose immense challenges for our societies and democracies. EU summit: Leaders tackle energy prices, spar over budget and unite on Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:28:11 UTC
23:28:11 KST

The two-day summit of EU leaders comes with a packed agenda topped by energy prices, the long-term budget and Russia's war on Ukraine. Hybrid warfare, enlargement and migration will also feature prominently.
Spiralling energy prices, the EU's long-term budget and support for Ukraine in the wake of Donald Trump's latest overture to Vladimir Putin will dominate the conversation as the leaders gather for a two-day summit in Brussels.
Enlargement, hybrid warfare, economic stagnation, rising borrowing costs, trade imbalances and irregular migration will also feature in the talks.
The meeting will start early on Thursday with a hotly anticipated discussion on energy prices, which hostilities in the Middle East have sent skyrocketing. Oil remains above $100 per barrel despite a coordinated G7 release, while gas trades at its highest level since winter 2022, with underground storage running below average.
The market shockwaves have rattled EU leaders, who are under mounting pressure to deliver tangible relief for households and industries, especially as temperatures cool down and the heating season begins.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis have led the charge, asking Brussels to relax the bloc's fiscal rules to allow governments to finance "temporary and targeted measures" to cushion the energy crunch.
Other countries, however, worry that excessive flexibility will promote fossil fuel consumption and discourage investments in the green transition.
Meanwhile, six member states (Austria, Germany, Italy, Poland, Portugal and Spain) have proposed an EU-wide windfall tax to capture excess profits from energy companies amid high prices. But the idea remains divisive and has not gained enough traction.
Energy will be followed by another pressing economic challenge: China.
With a €1 billion trade deficit every day, Brussels threw down the gauntlet by imposing a deadline on Beijing to deliver "tangible results" by October at the latest.
Those results emerged last week in Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič's trip to Beijing, where he secured preliminary concessions on hybrid and plug-in hybrid cars, rare earths and permanent magnets, and market access for European companies.
"We're satisfied with the results, but for us, it's only a first step because imbalances are not specific to one sector – there are across the board," a senior diplomat said, cautioning implementation will be key to show whether Beijing is serious.
"Why is China agreeing to something that China has never agreed before? (Because) they're starting to realise they're killing their customers. We're not naïve."
The concessions avert, for now, an all-out trade war. Leaders are expected to call on the Commission to continue "results-oriented dialogue" with China and "urgently enhance" trade tools to retaliate if needed, according to the draft conclusions seen by Euronews.
In a sign of exasperation, Germany and France have pitched a "kill switch" to cut off China's access to the EU market if the deficit remains unsustainable.
Money talks, but does anyone listen?
The summit's most contentious moment will arrive on Thursday afternoon when the next seven-year EU budget is put on the table. The wrangle will take place against the backdrop of steep borrowing costs, particularly alarming in France.
European Council President António Costa has appealed to member states to move away from their red lines and reach an agreement by the end of the year so that the complex legislative work can be fully completed before January 2028.
Ireland, the country holding the rotating presidency, has tabled a proposal that cuts the original draft by €141 billion. But the knife mostly spares agriculture and cohesion funds and falls instead on research, technology, climate action, security and foreign policy.
The Irish "nego-box" has made everyone unhappy.
The so-called "frugals" (Austria, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Sweden and Germany) say the cuts need to go much deeper and across the board. The 17 "Friends of Cohesion" say the opposite, that the cuts have gone far too deep. The European Commission warns its vision of a modernised, flexible budget is in real danger.
On top of that, nobody agrees which EU-wide taxes should be approved to collect additional revenue for the common pot.
The clash of opinions and the unwillingness to compromise bode ill for Costa's ambition to have a unanimous deal in December. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's shock decision to call snap elections adds yet another layer of uncertainty.
"I don't think there will be blood on the wall, but it's important in these sorts of negotiations that leaders feel where the contradictions are," another senior diplomat said. "We are not in a hurry. We need a good deal. We don’t feel any time pressure."
The first day will end with a strategic debate on how to prepare the 27-strong bloc for the admission of new member states and reform its internal decision-making. Montenegro, the frontrunner in the accession race, aims to close all chapters this year.
Backing Zelenskyy, rebuking Trump
Friday will be dedicated to Ukraine in the presence of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The peace talks took a dramatic turn after US President Donald Trump blindsided Europeans by cutting a deal with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to bring tens of thousands of Russian diesel into the US market. Washington issued a sanctions waiver until April 2027 to enable what would until now have been a forbidden sale.
The news jolted Europeans and prompted a scramble to close ranks and rally behind Ukraine to control the fallout from a unilateral, uncoordinated decision that has revived memories from the Trump-Zelenskyy showdown in the White House.
Although the diesel deal is likely to have a limited impact on the prices at the pump, which Trump wants to lower ahead of the midterm elections, there is greater concern over the diplomatic implications of providing relief to Russia at a time when it escalates its attacks to decimate the Ukrainian economy ahead of the winter.
The summit's conclusions have been changed to add a rebuke: "The European Council regrets the United States' decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel."
Trump has spent the last few days calling on Zelenskyy to stop attacks on Russia's oil refineries and abide by his energy ceasefire. Zelenskyy says he is ready for the truce as long as Russia complies, but Russia keeps bombing Ukraine's power facilities.
Europeans are reluctant to endorse Trump's petition because the long-range strikes are Kyiv's greatest leverage over Moscow. Giving it up would further tilt the war.
"It's not the first time that we're going through divergences with the US in what the Ukraine war is concerned, but I would disagree with the idea that we're ignored," a senior EU official said.
"We have seen that dialogue with the US doesn't always lead to full agreement in the way the EU and the US see things, but it's always better than not having dialogue," the official added. "This is what needs to continue to be done. It's the normal thing."
The last item on the summit will be a strategic debate on migration poised to pit Sánchez against the Meloni-led majority in the room. In the aftermath of the Ceuta border crisis, Italy introduced border checks with Spain, and Spain retaliated in kind.
The checks, which are conducted randomly at airports, last to this day.

DeepMind co-founder warns AI hacking incidents are ‘early warning shots’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:28:03 UTC
23:28:03 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis on Wednesday warned that hacking incidents involving artificial intelligence are “early warning shots,” urging companies and governments to strengthen security as autonomous systems become more powerful.
Speaking at the International AI Summit 2026, Hassabis said AI agents capable of acting on users’ behalf increase both the technology’s usefulness and its risks.
“But also that means that increases also the risks involved with what those systems might do, and we've seen that recently earlier this year with some of these hacking incidents. I think these are early warning shots for us,” he said.
“The systems aren't that powerful yet, so the incidents aren't that major,” he added, warning that incidents could become more serious over the next few years without additional security efforts.
Hassabis said ensuring that systems follow their assigned goals and remain within established safeguards becomes harder as they gain autonomy.
“And that gets increasingly difficult the more automation there is in the systems,” he said.
He also warned that AI “can also be repurposed by bad actors for harmful ends.”
Hassabis called for testing systems in secure environments, initially disconnected from the internet, and drawing on containment practices from biology and nuclear technology.
“I think there's a lot of lessons that can be learned about containment systems, and I think we need to start taking that seriously and bring experts in from those areas,” he said.
He advocated giving trusted defenders, including banks and governments, access to advanced AI tools before wider release to identify and repair software vulnerabilities before attackers could exploit them.
“So we've got to kind of asymmetrically power up our defensive side to keep ahead of the attackers,” he said.
Hassabis also called for an international standards body capable of adapting to technological developments.
“It's going to affect everyone in the world,” he said, urging safeguards that reflect emerging risks while preserving innovation.
“If you legislate for something three years ago, it will be out of date today, and actually probably won't even address what the real problems are,” he said.
He also called for “10 times or more resources” for AI safety and security, including research and computing capacity.

Climate change and drone attacks exacerbate the humanitarian crisis in war-torn Sudan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:25:00 UTC
23:25:00 KST

Climate change, drone attacks exacerbate Sudan's humanitarian crisis
October 14, 2026
In Sudan, clashes between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have intensified in North Kordofan and parts of Blue Nile state. The fighting has forced thousands of civilians to flee amid the planting season.
Since war broke out between the two factions and their allied militias in April 2023, both sides have fought for power. However, neither has managed to establish control over the entire country.
The SAF, the nation's official army, is in control of Sudan's north and center, including the capital, Khartoum, while the RSF maintains its presence in the western Darfur region and parts of the south.
The brutal war has plunged Sudan into one of the world's worst humanitarian and displacement crises, according to the United Nations and international aid organizations. The estimated death toll ranges from 40,000 to 250,000 people as reliable figures remain difficult to obtain amid the ongoing fighting. More than 12.4 million Sudanese have also been displaced, both within Sudan and to neighboring countries.
This week, the aid organization Action Against Hunger sounded the alarm.
"24.6 million people are experiencing high levels of acute food insecurity," Jan Sebastian Friedrich-Rust, executive director of the German section of the NGO, told DW.
Friedrich-Rust added that an estimated 825,000 children younger than 5 suffer from severe acute malnutrition in 2026, while a total of 4.2 million children and pregnant or breastfeeding women are thought to be acutely malnourished.
In October, the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET) — which monitors food insecurity and uses the internationally recognized Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) system — also warned that several areas including camps for internally displaced people in Greater Darfur and Greater Kordofan, are expected to face Catastrophe (IPC Phase 5), the most severe classification of acute food insecurity.
"The situation in Sudan continues to deteriorate and humanitarian needs are growing, even as the resources to respond are shrinking," Fabrizia Falcione, the Sudan representative of the United Nations Population Fund, the UN agency for sexual and reproductive health, said.
"I recently visited the displacement camp Tawila and I am still struggling to find the words to describe what I witnessed," Falcione told DW. "Imagine a population larger than that of Frankfurt, Germany, forced to flee their homes and seek refuge in one place in less than three years."
She added that more than 700,000 people there rely on just one hospital capable of performing Caesarean sections.
Despite repeated warnings about the deteriorating humanitarian situation, the 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which calls for $2.9 billion (€2.59 bn), is just 41% funded, with $1.2 billion (€1.07 bn) received from international donors so far.
Climate shocks exacerbate Sudan's humanitarian crisis
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) recently warned that extreme heat and heavy flooding are worsening the crisis in Sudan.
"This year, a massive heatwave brought power cuts of up to 12 hours per day in some regions," Hager Ali, a Sudan researcher at the German Institute for Global and Area Studies (GIGA), told DW. "Riverbeds and dried-out fields are barren, which comes on top of the damage from combat, the RSF's scorched-earth tactics and environmental destruction."
While the drought is affecting roughly half the country, heavy rains and localized flooding have worsened conditions in other areas of Sudan.
"As if that wasn't enough, there is also a massive shortage of fertilizer and diesel," Ali told DW.
Sudan relies on imported fertilizer and diesel shipped from the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. However, amid the wider Iran war, Iran has been blocking shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, while the Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen have threatened and at times disrupted shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
"Fertilizer supply collapsed from 450,000 metric tons to only about 50,000" in 2026, Ali said, adding that a similar diesel shortage and the soaring cost of diesel compound the situation in two ways.
"Agricultural equipment uses diesel and the transportation of humanitarian and agricultural goods within the country is getting a lot more expensive," Ali said.
In October, the International Food Policy Research Institute warned that staple food- and fuel prices in Sudan rose sharply in September 2026.
Limited arms embargo curbs hope for an end to the war
Observers have long pointed out that the war in Sudan will not end until foreign backers stop supplying arms. The SAF is officially supported by Egypt, Turkey, Russia and Iran while the United Arab Emirates is alleged to be the RSF's main backer, a claim Abu Dhabi denies.
However, in October, the UN Security Council extended the existing arms embargo only on Sudan's Darfur region until December 11, dropping calls for a nationwide embargo.
"To expand the UN embargo across Sudan would have included drones in particular," Hager Ali said, noting that Sudan is one of the biggest theaters for drone warfare: As of 2026, the leading cause of civilian casualties in Sudan are drone strikes.
She also told DW that Al-Harith Idriss al-Harith Mohamed, Sudan's permanent representative to the United Nations, opposed the extention of the embargo over concerns that it would disproportionately limit the Sudanese Armed Forces on the battlefield.
"An arms embargo would deter potential backers from cooperating with the Sudanese Armed Forces, whereas the Rapid Support Forces don't necessarily source their weapons through official ways," Hager Ali said.
"The RSF rely on trafficking with other militias, private military contractors and traders in the region," she said, adding that because the RSF obtains supplies from numerous sources and actors, it is difficult to target the group through a single embargo.

Iran's 'soft war': How Tehran turned antisemitism into a weapon against the West
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:23:36 UTC
23:23:36 KST

Antisemitism and anti-Israel rhetoric across the Western political spectrum are being amplified by a decades-long Iranian campaign designed to erode trust in American institutions and forge alliances across ideological divides, according to a report published on Wednesday by the Simon Wiesenthal Center (SWC).
The report, titled “The War on Western Minds: Iran’s 30-Year Campaign to Divide the West,” said that the Islamic Republic has weaponized antisemitism in its ideological “soft war” against the West, exploiting nationalism, religious narratives, and anti-imperialism to spread anti-American and anti-Israel rhetoric.
Unable to match US military power, particularly under decades of sanctions, Iran has instead focused on undermining Western social cohesion and trust in democratic institutions, the report said.
Antisemitism predates the Islamic Revolution, but the SWC said that it provides Iran with a narrative that crosses ideological boundaries. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has exploited this by presenting the regime as an ally against the “Antichrist,” an anti-imperialist force resisting Western hegemony, or a nationalist partner opposing alleged Jewish and Israeli manipulation.
Iran brought conspiratorial claims to the mainstream
The report said Iran has helped accusations of Jewish control over American foreign policy become mainstream, allowing such narratives to spread without continued Iranian involvement. It compared this strategy to methods first developed in the Soviet Union.
Using narrative intelligence (NARINT) to track Iranian influence campaigns, the SWC found that the objective was not simply to spread false information but also to shape how audiences interpret events, assign blame, and identify enemies. Once established, narratives of Zionist conspiracy, Jewish financial control, or Israeli manipulation of US foreign policy can become resistant to conventional fact-checking, the report said.
Iran tailors these narratives to different audiences.
Among religious Christians, it uses apocalyptic language and biblical prophecy to frame geopolitical conflicts as battles against the Antichrist, hoping to manufacture Christian-Muslim religious convergence, weakening the perceived Judeo-Christian affinity that underpins American support for Israel.
The report cited Russian political philosopher Aleksandr Dugin, who consulted Athonite monks before Russia’s 2012 intervention in Syria. According to the report, the monks encouraged Moscow’s participation in the civil war as part of a “final battle” against the Antichrist. Dugin later credited Russia and Iran with saving Syria from destruction allegedly sought by the West and Dajjal, an Islamic term associated with the Antichrist.
Iran has also sought to exploit grievances in other communities.
The report highlighted the January 1996 World Friendship Tour by Nation of Islam leader Louis Farrakhan, a prominent antisemite who visited countries hostile to the United States. The SWC said Iran recognized an opportunity to capitalize on Pan-African grievances while presenting itself as a defender of the mustad’afin, or oppressed and dispossessed.
In February 2001, Tehran hosted a regional preparatory meeting for the United Nations World Conference against Racism, culminating in the Tehran Declaration. The declaration accused Israel of committing “a new kind of apartheid, a crime against humanity, a form of genocide and a serious threat to international peace and security.”
The report said that these forums enabled Iran to combine anti-imperialism, left-wing anti-Americanism, Black internationalist organizing, and antisemitism under the banner of international legitimacy.
Iranian-linked media apparatus amplified 9/11 conspiracies
Iran also used its media apparatus to amplify conspiracy theories. In the weeks following the September 11, 2001, attacks, the Hezbollah-affiliated Lebanese television network al-Manar promoted the false claim that 4,000 Jewish employees had been warned to stay away from the World Trade Center that day.
Although initially confined to fringe circles, such claims helped attract conspiracy theorists and anti-establishment figures who could carry Iranian narratives into Western media, the report said.
It cited former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke and political writer Michael Collins Piper as examples of Western voices aligned with Tehran’s messaging.
In 2007, Iran launched Press TV to reach Western audiences directly. The report highlighted programming such as Zero Degree Turn, which portrayed Iranians as saviors of Jewish victims of Nazism while comparing Zionism to Nazism and delegitimizing Israel’s founding.
Iranian filmmaker Nader Talebzadeh helped develop programming designed to influence international audiences through polished, emotionally engaging storytelling, the report said.
The SWC also identified MintPress News as an example of an American-facing outlet that presents itself as an independent progressive watchdog but allegedly relays Iranian and Russian narratives.
The outlet’s mix of left- and right-wing contributors, the report said, helps it mimic progressive investigative journalism while promoting positions aligned with Iranian foreign policy. The United Kingdom-based Institute of Contemporary Islamic Thought was cited as another platform promoting Iranian narratives while presenting itself as an intellectual hub for the global Islamic movement.
The report said that this media ecosystem can have real-world consequences. It pointed to the manifesto of Payton Gendron, the perpetrator of the May 2022 Buffalo supermarket massacre, which referenced a 2016 MintPress News article titled “Thousands of Israelis Take to the Streets Calling For Palestinian Genocide.”
By 2026, Iran’s influence operations had expanded to include fake news websites mimicking American media, fabricated online personas posing as American activists, and campaigns designed to simulate grassroots support.
The report said these operations use wire-service material and plagiarized articles to appear credible and embed Iranian narratives within broader coverage. Additionally, they manipulate Wikipedia, which, by extension, manipulates the majority of AI algorithms and allows the network to exploit social media algorithms.
IRGC used cyberattacks to target US institutions
Iran has also conducted hacking operations targeting American institutions. During the 2024 US presidential campaign, an IRGC-linked group sent spear-phishing emails to a senior campaign official using a compromised former adviser’s account, attempting to infiltrate county-level government accounts in swing states, according to Microsoft’s Threat Analysis Center.
OVER THE past year, the SWC identified over 340 influencers, media outlets, organizations, and affiliated entities that it said formed an interconnected influence network with shared amplification channels and consistent information flows.
The report named Dugin, Jackson Hinkle, Max Blumenthal, The Grayzone, and the account GodivaGoddess97 among central figures. It also identified CODEPINK, Jewish Voice for Peace (JVP), and the Party for Socialism and Liberation.
The SWC outlined a six-stage cycle through which these narratives spread.
First, humanitarian organizations publish legitimate reports with appropriate caveats.
Second, academics and credentialed figures provide intellectual frameworks that, according to the report, delegitimize rather than merely criticize Israel.
Third, alternative media outlets such as The Grayzone and MintPress remove caveats, add inflammatory framing, and cite the original organizations as authorities.
Fourth, commentators, such as Andrew Napolitano, Candace Owens, Jackson Hinkle, and Jimmy Dore, repackage the content for left- and right-wing audiences.
Fifth, activist organizations translate online rhetoric into campus organizing and direct action, creating environments hostile to Jewish students.
Finally, conspiracy theorists cite The Grayzone and MintPress as evidence of alleged Jewish conspiracies.
Jewish-affiliated voices and organizations, including JVP and Norman Finkelstein, are also invoked to deflect accusations of antisemitism, the report said.
Several recommendations were offered to combat this threat: mandatory coordinated-threat disclosure for platforms; mandatory AI-generated-content labeling; a congressional review of Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act to remove immunity for content that can be attributed to designated foreign adversaries or their proxies.
“For more than 30 years, Iran has been building an infrastructure designed to exploit the divisions within American society,” said Jim Berk, CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center. “What makes this campaign so dangerous is that Iran doesn't need Americans to support its regime to succeed. It only needs Americans to lose trust in their institutions and in one another. Antisemitism has been central to that strategy, giving a hostile foreign government a way to turn existing grievances into deeper divisions. This is a threat not only to Jewish communities, but to the foundations of American democracy itself.”
“This is not about the Jews. It has never been only about the Jews,” said Jim Berk, CEO of the Simon Wiesenthal Center. “Antisemitism is the tool. The real target is Western civilization itself: the Judeo-Christian values, democratic institutions, and shared sense of citizenship that hold free societies together. Palantir settles dispute with Sadiq Khan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:23:11 UTC
23:23:11 KST

LONDON — The Mayor of London Sadiq Khan and U.S. tech company Palantir have agreed to drop legal proceedings relating to a blocked £50 million police contract.
Palantir brought a claim against the Mayor’s Office for Policing and Crime in the High Court in June after Khan’s deputy mayor refused to sign off on the £50 million contract with the Metropolitan Police for the provision of an AI and data analysis service.
In July, lawyers working on behalf of MOPAC in turn accused the Met Police and Palantir of coordinating to fix the outcome of the procurement process in breach of the rules. Palantir claimed Khan’s office had unlawfully blocked the contract over the company's “values and ethics,” based on media reporting.
Advertisement
A full trial was expected in January but on Wednesday both sides agreed to “settle their differences” and drop the allegations without admitting liability. They will each cover their own legal costs.
In an agreed statement, the two sides said MOPAC’s decision to block the Palantir contract was “not based on Palantir’s values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company,” though MOPAC said it “recognizes Palantir’s concerns that media reporting of a statement from the Mayor's spokesperson before the decision was taken could have incorrectly created the impression that an assessment of the company’s values had been a factor in that decision.”
“MOPAC’s consideration was based upon its statutory role of examining spend proposals, against the appropriate legal tests and the relevant guidance on procurement, governance, affordability and ensuring value for money for Londoners and in doing so it focussed on the available information at the time,” the statement said.
The settlement also notes that MOPAC is working with Metropolitan Police Service to re-run a competitive procurement for the relevant service, which Palantir will be eligible to bid for.
“MOPAC does not have, and has never had, any policy of not contracting with Palantir,” the statement confirms, while noting the mayor’s duty is to ensure “all procurements are lawful, fair, transparent and deliver value for money.”
“London is the technology capital of Europe, and I am proud that leading software firms choose the city as their home. Palantir makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital, employing a large number of Londoners whose services have been procured legally by organizations across the U.K. and beyond,” Khan said.

Israeli judoka Raz Hershko, one of the country’s top athletes, missed a major opportunity in 2025 when the 12-day war between Israel and Iran closed Israeli airspace, preventing her from traveling to Budapest. Earlier this year, she withdrew from the Tashkent Grand Slam after the Shin Bet ordered the Israeli team to leave Uzbekistan.
But nothing could keep Hershko off the podium this weekend, when she won a bronze medal at the World Judo Championships in Baku, Azerbaijan.
Hershko, 28, burst into tears after winning the bout that secured her medal.
Hershko dedicates her win to IDF soldier killed in Oct. 7 massacre
“Representing Israel has always been something that moves me, but at this moment, it carries so much more meaning,” Hershko told JTA. “At the end of the day, I step onto the mat alone, but I feel like I have an entire country behind me.”
Hershko dedicated her victory to the memory of Yonatan Gutin, an Israeli soldier killed on October 7, 2023, as well as his family and the people of Israel.
According to his official memorial page, Gutin, a 20-year-old Israel Defense Forces officer, was killed fighting to rescue civilians during the battle for Kibbutz Be’eri. Judo was a central part of his life. He had trained in the sport for about 14 years and was a member of Israel’s cadet national team. Even during his military service, he occasionally returned to his judo club to coach.
'I was aiming for gold'
Despite the achievement, Hershko made clear that bronze was not the result she had hoped for.
“I’m pretty disappointed that the day ended with a bronze medal, because I was aiming for gold,” she said. “But now it’s time to look ahead to the next goals.”
Hershko has established herself in recent years as one of the world’s leading judokas and one of Israel’s most prominent athletes. She won an individual silver medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics and a gold medal at the 2024 European Championships. She competes in the women’s heavyweight division.
Her latest achievement came just days after Israel marked the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas-led attacks, a date that has continued to shape the country’s public life and weigh heavily on its athletes competing abroad.
“Knowing that I was able to give people back home even a few moments of happiness, a smile, a sense of pride — that means so much to me. Especially during the times we’re going through, these are the moments that remind me why I do what I do,” she added.
The judoka said that “everything has felt different since Oct. 7” and that she can’t “disconnect” herself from the Israeli reality.
“Before that, I would go into competitions feeling immense pride in representing my country,” she said. “Today, that pride is even stronger. I’m much more aware of what the flag I wear represents, and of the fact that I stand for something far bigger than myself.”
Hershko, however, has little time to dwell on the medal. She told Channel 13 that she would take two days off before returning to training ahead of another competition next week. Asked by JTA how she has managed to stay hungry and focused after achieving so much, the Israeli athlete said she simply enjoys the journey.
“I really love what I do. I love judo, I love competing, I love the challenges, and I think that’s what keeps me hungry,” she said. “Of course, I’m proud of everything I’ve achieved, but I never feel like I’m done or that there’s nothing left to strive for. At the end of the day, the medals are incredible moments, but the journey is what builds me as an athlete, and I’m still enjoying that journey.”

Ethiopian troops mass heavy weapons near Eritrean border amid war fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:22:29 UTC
23:22:29 KST

Andrew Wasike 
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Ethiopian government forces have deployed tanks and heavy weapons toward the Eritrean border after advancing through northern Tigray, according to the latest conflict-monitoring reports on Wednesday.
The move has raised fears that renewed fighting could escalate into a confrontation between the neighboring countries, said the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), an independent organization that monitors armed conflicts worldwide.
“Eyewitnesses observed a substantial convoy of tanks and heavy weaponry advancing from Adigrat toward Fatsi and Zalambessa,” according to ACLED, referring to two key strategic towns on the Eritrean frontier.
ACLED reported that the movement began overnight Monday and continued Tuesday, following the capture of the towns by Ethiopian troops and allied Tigray Peace Force (TPF) fighters.
Eritrea has rejected Ethiopian accusations of military incursions, with Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel accusing Addis Ababa of pursuing “an unprovoked war of aggression.”
The Eritrean government has also urged international intervention, with Foreign Minister Osman Saleh urging the UN Security Council to “take the requisite deterrent measures against it in accordance with Chapter VII of the UN Charter.”
The Critical Threats Project, a US-based security research organization, said in its Tuesday assessment that Ethiopian troops had advanced approximately 37 kilometers (23 miles) north from Adigrat to Zalambessa without encountering substantial resistance.
It also reported that Eritrean troops had established defensive positions north of Zalambessa, citing open-source military monitoring, although the extent of Eritrea's deployment could not be independently confirmed.
ACLED said Eritrean forces previously stationed along the Zalambessa-Fatsi corridor withdrew across the border Monday, while rival Tigrayan fighters retreated toward Debre Damo and Irob.
The withdrawal does not establish that all Eritrean troops have left Ethiopian territory, with the situation along other sections of the border remaining unclear.
The military advances are part of an Ethiopian counteroffensive against forces linked to the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), whose renewed campaign has destabilized northern Ethiopia.
The TPF is aligned with Ethiopia's federal government, while the rival Tigray Defense Forces are associated with the TPLF.
The latest fighting has also brought Ethiopia and Eritrea into an increasingly hostile diplomatic confrontation.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of sending troops into Tigray and supporting armed opposition groups, allegations Asmara denies.
In a letter to the UN Security Council, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos warned that his country had "no option but to defend itself against Eritrea."
Eritrea responded by accusing Ethiopia of threatening its sovereignty and attempting to justify military action against its territory.
The dispute is further complicated by Ethiopia's longstanding demand for access to the Red Sea, which Eritrea views as a potential threat to its territorial integrity, particularly regarding the strategic port of Assab.
Landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993, Ethiopia has repeatedly described maritime access as essential to its economic development.
The two countries fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 before restoring diplomatic relations in 2018. Eritrean troops later supported Ethiopia's federal government during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, but relations deteriorated after the Pretoria peace agreement.
The renewed military buildup threatens to undermine that agreement and raises concerns that fighting inside Ethiopia could spread across the border.

When a drone outruns its own signal
The cap bites exactly where Ukraine’s drones do their work. The StarShield package had previously carried no data speed limit, and the change directly affected drones that use Starlink to steer in flight, the 7th Air Assault Corps said.
“During flights, the connection could drop for 10 to 20 seconds at speeds of just 110 to 120 kilometers per hour. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control,” the corps said, describing problems that now start well below the new ceiling.
A dependence Kyiv has feared for years. The limit revives an old worry. Ukraine neither owns nor controls Starlink, and the restriction follows fresh fears of a shutdown after Musk backed US President Donald Trump’s call for Zelenskyy to resign.

Nuran Erkul Kaya
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
- Middle East crude oil, petroleum, and LNG exports collapse amid sharp escalation in maritime attacks
- Strait of Hormuz traffic down to 6 vessels on Monday
- Low of 6.7M barrels of crude transited per day this week
Crude oil and petroleum exports from the Middle East sharply dropped over the past week as Iranian-backed Yemeni Houthi militias intensified their attacks on commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting regional shipping lanes.
Maritime transit in the region suffered drastically since the US and Israel’s pre-emptive joint strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, followed by Tehran’s effective closure of the vital waterway and a subsequent American naval blockade.
Attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz reached a new peak this year over the past week.
At least 14 incidents of attacks, attempted strikes, and obstructions were recorded in and around the Strait of Hormuz on Oct. 5-12, while six ships were attacked on Monday alone, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations and global maritime security sources.
Commercial vessel traffic via the strategic chokepoint fell to its lowest since July 22, affecting outward energy flows.
Oil, petroleum, and liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports from the Middle East plummeted in the wake of the war, and while there have been signs of partial recovery, intensifying security risks sparked concerns.
Houthis increased their attacks on Saudi Arabia, threatening transit through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. 
Vessel transits through Bab el-Mandeb, Hormuz hit new low
Middle Eastern crude oil, petroleum, and liquid chemical exports — including shipments from the Gulf of Oman and the Red Sea — fell from 21.1 million barrels per day on Oct. 8 to 6.7 million barrels on Oct. 11, 10.4 million barrels on Monday, and 8.3 million barrels on Tuesday, according to Kpler.
The weekly average of 17 million barrels remained below the pre-war volume of around 23.3 million barrels per day.
Only six commercial ships were able to transit the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, while previously 32 ships passed through on Oct. 8, 24 on Oct. 9, 11 on Oct. 10, and 12 on Oct. 11.
Meanwhile, vessel transit through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait also dropped, with 35 vessels passing through on Oct. 8, 39 on Oct. 10, 46 on Oct. 11, and 32 on Monday.
The attempts by the Houthis to establish a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia to seize control of the Bab el-Mandeb corridor added a new volatile dimension to the wider conflict.
Large-scale supply disruptions across both the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait could pressure global energy supplies and market stability even further, analysts say.

Hong Kong extends smart fire alarm scheme to another 6,000 old buildings
Fire service says no installations have been completed so far although the policy was rolled out over five months ago for 3,600 blocks
Hong Kong’s Fire Services Department has extended a scheme allowing property owners to install smart fire alarm systems rather than traditional safety equipment to another 6,000 old buildings, but conceded that no installations had been completed although the policy was rolled out over five months ago for 3,600 blocks.
Lai Kin-mo, acting deputy chief fire officer for building improvement, said on Wednesday that while 300 buildings had expressed interest in installing the system, which can send alerts within 10 seconds of detecting smoke, owners were still trying to reach a consensus on related issues.
“Different service providers will provide different installation plans that involve work fees. I think it’s mostly prices that they are negotiating as the technology is already there and space is not a concern,” Lai said.

Pope Leo XIV's post-operative recovery is proceeding normally after he had the lower part of his right lung removed to remove a malign tumour, the Vatican said Wednesday. 
"This morning, the Holy Father underwent the blood tests and chest X-ray scheduled following the surgery. The results confirm a normal post-operative course: the readings are within the normal range for the type of procedure performed," said a medical bulletin released by the Vatican.

Bruni said the pope's estimated hospital stay remains, for the time being, "about a week from the time of admission," as had been anticipated from the start.

Former Groningen mayor loses appeal against indecency conviction
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The former mayor of Groningen, Koen Schuiling, has lost his appeal against a conviction for offending public decency that led to him being forced to take early retirement two years ago.
Judges upheld a €250 fine imposed by a court in Zwolle after he was found guilty of masturbating in his car on the A7 motorway in the city.
He was reported to police by a passing lorry driver, but insisted when questioned that he had stopped to relieve stomach complaints caused by a medical condition.
The court found that the driver had a clear view of Schuiling’s car and had given an detailed and consistent account of what he saw. His testimony was corroborated by an audio recording made in the cab in which he could be heard angrily challenging Schuiling about his behaviour.
Schuiling stepped down from his post in September 2024, a year before his term of office was due to end. At the time he said he lacked energy after an “extraordinarily intense period” that included the coronavirus lockdowns and the rollout of compensation to homeowners in Groningen who were affected by earthquake damage.
But it soon emerged that home affairs minister Judith Uitermark demanded his resignation after she was briefed by the police and public prosecutor about the allegations against Schuiling, arguing it exposed him to blackmail.
Police had received two earlier complaints in the previous six months about the mayor behaving inappropriately at the wheel of his vehicle.

Burnham rules out partnership with Greens after Zionism row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:17:42 UTC
23:17:42 KST

LONDON — Andy Burnham appeared to rule out cooperating with the Green Party on Wednesday, after the left-wing force passed a motion declaring that Zionism is a form of racism.
At prime minister’s questions in the House of Commons, Burnham condemned the motion approved at the Greens’ annual conference earlier this month, which defines Zionism as supporting “an ethnonationalist Jewish state.” Party members also backed a “single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine.”
Asked by Conservative Shadow Paymaster General Harriett Baldwin if he would rule out cooperating with the Greens, Burnham said: “We will always take the right response when it comes to any partnerships we have with other parties. We cannot support a partnership with a party that holds a position that has recently been adopted.”
Advertisement
On the motion, he said: “It is wrong. It is antisemitic, and this side of the house will have nothing to do with it.”
Burnham currently has a House of Commons majority, but a seat model by YouGov published last month suggests Labour would be the largest party in a hung parliament at the next general election — not due until the middle of 2029.
The Greens currently have five MPs in the Commons after winning their first by-election in Greater Manchester from Labour in February. Zack Polanski, the Green Party leader, failed to take the Holborn and St Pancras constituency from Labour in a by-election early this month, days after the party conference motion was passed.
A Labour party official was unable to immediately clarify what Burnham’s stance means for local government partnerships between Labour and the Greens.
Polanski said he wouldn’t have supported the motion but did not vote because he was campaigning in the contest. Senior party figures, including former leaders Caroline Lucas and Adrian Ramsay and Westminster leader Ellie Chowns, opposed the motion. Co-Deputy Leader Mothin Ali supported the motion.
In a joint statement after the vote, Polanski, the co-deputy leaders and party MPs said the Green Party “will never tolerate any form of discrimination or harassment.” It said, “there is no conflict between supporting the rights of Palestinians and the rights of Jewish people.”

Southeast Asia's VIP prison scandal exposes inequality behind bars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:17:00 UTC
23:17:00 KST

Indonesian VIP prison scandal exposes inequality across Southeast Asia
October 14, 2026
Air-conditioned apartments, flat-screen televisions and even a golf simulator are hardly what most people would associate with life behind bars. Yet these luxuries were among the facilities uncovered last month at Indonesia's Cibinong Prison, near Jakarta, during a surprise inspection by the country's Ombudsman.
Investigators discovered more than 10 apartment-style units equipped with refrigerators, sofas and private living areas. A gym was also reportedly under construction.
The revelations prompted an investigation into whether inmates had paid for preferential treatment.
Five prison officials were initially suspended, while the prison's warden was dismissed on October 5. Authorities demolished 10 unauthorized buildings and took further disciplinary action against prison staff.
It wasn't Indonesia's first luxury prison scandal. In 2018, investigators from the Corruption Eradication Commission discovered that wealthy inmates at Sukamiskin Prison in Bandung enjoyed accommodation resembling private apartments.
Similar controversies have emerged elsewhere in Southeast Asia. Last November, authorities in Thailand investigated allegations that Chinese prisoners at Bangkok Remand Prison received special privileges, including access to an executive lounge.
In Malaysia, allegations of preferential treatment for politically connected prisoners have repeatedly surfaced. The latest Indonesian scandal prompted renewed calls for independent inspections of Malaysian prisons.
Why do VIP prison scandals in Southeast Asia keep recurring?
"Just like in the outside world, money and influence act as capital within the prison system. Powerful inmates generally do not lose their wealth and often maintain strong connections with influential people," Iwa Maulana, a senior researcher at Indonesia's Center for Detention Studies (CDS), told DW.
"When certain inmates receive different treatment based on their resources and influence, it demonstrates that, much like in the outside world, a person's identity affects how they are treated, even within prison walls," he added.
Overcrowded and poorly resourced prison systems also create opportunities for corruption.
Indonesia's detention facilities held approximately 279,000 people in late September, despite having an official capacity of around 154,000, according to government data.
Thailand's prisons are also severely overcrowded. At the end of 2025, they held approximately 301,000 inmates, around 21% above official capacity, according to the World Prison Brief.
Corruption within prison administrations also reflects wider governance problems, with Southeast Asian states routinely appearing at the bottom of Transparency International's annual Corruption Perceptions Index.
Where bribery and patronage already influence public services, prison officials may face similar incentives to exchange preferential treatment for money or favors.
"Corruption and political interference may explain particular cases," Nasrul Ismail, senior lecturer in criminology at the University of Bristol, who recently conducted a major study of prison governance in Malaysia, Thailand and the Philippines, told DW.
"When decisions are made behind closed doors, with limited transparency about who receives what and why, there are opportunities for personal connections and financial resources to influence treatment."
However, he argues the problem extends beyond a relatively small number of wealthy inmates enjoying extraordinary privileges.
Across Southeast Asia, many prisoners depend on financial support from their families for everyday necessities that prison administrations do not provide.
Ismail said poorer inmates often rely on money deposited by relatives into prison canteen accounts to purchase food, clean water and hygiene products.
"This is distinct from wealthy prisoners receiving luxury accommodation, but both illustrate how broader inequalities can be reproduced within prisons through different institutional arrangements. Where minimum standards are not consistently guaranteed, access to decent conditions becomes dependent on the resources and connections prisoners possess," Ismail told DW.
"The fundamental issue is not simply whether wealthy prisoners receive special privileges, but why access to basic welfare and humane treatment can be so unequal in the first place."
Can prison systems be reformed?
Repeated scandals suggest that dismissing officials and demolishing unauthorized facilities achieve little without broader institutional reforms.
Independent inspections are one possible solution. The UN's Nelson Mandela Rules call for regular internal inspections and external monitoring by bodies independent of prison administrations.
Greater transparency over inmate accommodation, transfers, medical treatment and disciplinary decisions would also make preferential treatment harder to conceal.
Reducing overcrowding, improving staff training and protecting whistleblowers could further limit opportunities for corruption.
But CDS researcher Maulana believes meaningful reform requires a more fundamental change in how criminal justice systems operate.
"The current system primarily treats imprisonment as the main form of punishment, leading law enforcement to frequently resort to incarceration for all types of legal violations," which leads to overcrowding and creates opportunities for corruption.
"It is essential to intensify efforts to implement non-custodial penalties and alternatives to detention," Maulana said.
Although prison authorities cannot eliminate the social inequalities outside their walls, Ismail argued that Southeast Asian governments have previously shown a "considerable capacity" to respond to emergencies inside prisons.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, governments quickly contained outbreaks in detention facilities and prevented infections from spreading into the wider population. Yet such interventions rarely translate into lasting improvements in prisoners' living conditions.
Ismail described this as "selective state capacity," whereby "governments demonstrated considerable ability to act when prison outbreaks threatened public health beyond prison walls, yet failed to sustain comparable improvements in prisoners' everyday welfare."
A similar pattern emerges whenever luxury prison scandals attract public attention.
"Investigations are announced, officials may be suspended or dismissed, and new procedures introduced. All of these measures can be necessary and important, but they do not necessarily change the institutional arrangements that enabled preferential treatment," said Ismail.
"The danger is that prison systems become better at responding to scandals than preventing the conditions that allow them to recur."
Edited by: Karl Sexton

Russia cracks down on AI bears as real attacks spread fear
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:15:51 UTC
23:15:51 KST

Russia cracks down on AI bears as real attacks spread fear
- A woman in Russia’s Amur region was fined 15,000 roubles after a ChatGPT bear image went viral and caused panic, police calls, and a wildlife hunt.
- Russia is facing more real bear attacks in 2026, with at least 26 deaths since spring. Experts blame larger bear numbers and poor berry and pine nut crops.
- The government is planning urgent action to control brown bears, now estimated at 308,000. More than 3,440 threatening bears have been killed this year, TASS said.
AI generated
A woman in Russia’s Far East was fined this week after an AI-generated image of a bear, created to prank a friend, went viral and triggered a real-life hunt, the regional courts said.
The Russian authorities are on high alert in 2026 due to a spate of deadly attacks in several regions, where growing bear populations and a poor crop of berries and pine nuts have increased the chances of encounters with humans, experts say.
The resident of Magdagachi settlement, in the Amur region, used ChatGPT to generate the picture of a large brown bear seemingly strolling down a local street and sent it to her friend in September.
“The joke quickly got out of control. The photograph of the bear spread through messaging apps, and police began receiving alarmed calls from residents,” the Amur courts’ press service said in a statement, describing how the district head dispatched wildlife rangers to deal with the phantom animal.
The woman called police and confessed to creating the image. A court this week ordered her to pay a fine of 15,000 roubles (S$230), it said.
In mid-September, another woman in the eastern Transbaikal region was fined 30,000 roubles for posting a fake image of a bear in a village, Russian legal news agency RAPSI reported.
In 2026, at least 26 people have been killed in bear attacks since spring, when hungry bears emerge from hibernation, news agency RIA Novosti said on Oct 12.
In response to the attacks, the government said in September that it was drawing up urgent measures to control the brown bear population, which has more than doubled in the last three decades to 308,000, in part due to shorter and milder winters.
Since the start of the year, more than 3,440 bears that were deemed to pose a threat to humans have been killed, according to a tally compiled by state news agency TASS and published on Oct 10. REUTERS

Announcement of the 2015 Defence Employer Recognition Scheme Gold winners.
Update to Defence Employer Recognition Scheme silver and bronze award holders.
The Defence Employer Recognition Scheme (ERS) encourages employers to support defence and inspire others to do the same. The scheme encompasses Bronze, Silver and Gold awards for employer organisations that pledge, demonstrate or advocate support to defence and the armed forces community, and align their values with the Armed Forces Covenant.
The ERS is designed primarily to recognise private sector support although public sector organisations such as the emergency services, local authorities, NHS trusts and executive agencies are also eligible to be recognised.
Pledge your organisation’s support via the Bronze award or express your interest in applying for Silver or Gold award, contact us to find out more.
Privacy policy
You can read our Privacy policy to find out more about how we process data.
Bronze award
Bronze award holders must have:
Signed the AFC and registered their interest for a Bronze award (via the ERS website).
Confirmed their understanding of the AFC and ERS and what it means to be a supporter of the Armed Forces community with the appointed DRM.
Informed their workforce of their positive support for the Armed Forces community.
Desirable Criteria. Factors which add value to an application. Note that the description of these allows for an assessment of evidence in the context of the scale, business model and market sector of the employer. The employer is willing to consider:
How to develop a suitable HR framework to enable Reserve mobilisation for members of their work force.
Provide additional leave for Reservists (i.e. Part Time Volunteer Reserves) to conduct training.
How they would promote volunteering and support to the Cadet movement through official Cadet Force channels.
How they ensure that Service personnel/Armed Forces community are not unfairly disadvantaged as part of their recruiting and selection processes.
Silver award holders in addition to Bronze Criteria must have:
ERS Bronze Award status and have held it with sufficient time to have put in place the necessary essential policies and evidence to support their application. It would be unusual for an organisation to achieve Silver status within 12 months of gaining Bronze.
Proactively demonstrate that Service personnel and Armed Forces community are not unfairly disadvantaged as part of their recruiting and selection processes.
Actively ensure that their workforce is aware of their positive policies towards the Armed Forces community. E.g. Internally publicised positive HR policy on Reserves in their workforce. In the case where no HR policy exists this should be demonstrated by specific references in job descriptions/organisation’s website.
Support Active Reservists (PTVRs) by:
Having Policy in place to support mobilisations or have made a commitment evidenced by their DRM that they understand the mobilisation process and would support a mobilisation if practicable. E.g. Employers of reservists must be aware of the role of Unit Employment Support Officers (UESO) and how they support the Reservists in their work forces.
Demonstrated support to their training by providing at least 5 days additional annual leave (ideally paid).
A proactive relationship with their DRM, which can be demonstrated through various interactions, including but not limited to personal contact, automated communications, and engagement with supporting products or resources.
The employer must allow flexibility for employees who are Cadet Force Adult Volunteers to fit their working hours in with their volunteering.
Desirable Criteria. Factors which add value to an application. Note that the description of these allows for an assessment of evidence in the context of the scale, business model and market sector of the employer. The employer is willing to consider:
Scoping opportunities to support the Cadet movement (via official Cadet Force channels) through the following example activities: sponsorship, supporting the development of cadets’ wider skills to enhance their future opportunities; or providing employment advice and guidance.
Employ at least one individual from the Armed Forces community .
Hosting a Reserve recruiting event on their premises in partnership with a local Reserve Unit or Military Command recruiting teams.
Have inclusive policy in place to support Strategic Reserves (those with an Ex-Regular and Callout liability).
Gold award holders in addition to Silver Criteria must have:Hold ERS Silver Award and have held it with sufficient time to have put in place the necessary essential policies and evidence to support their application. It would be very unusual for an organisation to achieve Gold status within 12 months of gaining Silver.
Be an exemplar within their sector, advocating for the AFC and or ERS to partner organisations, suppliers and customers with tangible positive results. E.g. demonstrate proactive steps/activity and clear success in encouraging partner organisations and their supply chain to engage with and sign the AFC, and or mentor others in progressing through the ERS.
Actively encourage a positive workplace environment for Active Reservists (Part Time Volunteer Reserves) by ensuring that positive policies in support of Reservists within the workforce are communicated to line managers and support their training by providing at least 10 days additional paid leave annually.
Demonstrate support to the Cadet movement by committing resources to improving the outcomes for cadets. This is to be achieved by verifying they deliver one or a combination of the following through official Cadet Force channels:
1) Sponsorship (e.g. for additional resources, competitions, events and specific activities such as overseas expeditions);
2) Supporting the development of cadets’ wider skills to enhance their future opportunities;
3) Providing employment advice and guidance.
Promote volunteering with the Cadet Forces by having policies in place that cater to offer additional paid or unpaid leave to employees who are Cadet Force Adult Volunteers.
Engaged with CTP to support recruitment of Service leavers and have registered with the Forces Families Jobs website.
Desirable Criteria. Factors which add value to an application. Note that the description of these allows for an assessment of evidence in the context of the scale, business model and market sector of the employer. The employer is willing to consider:
Support to Reserve Service and the wider Armed Forces community through internal and external communications, amplifying DRM social media messaging around Armed Forces Week, Reserves Day, ERS Gold /Silver announcements etc.
Actively finding out the numbers of Reservists employed and have a declared target for the number of Reservists within their workforce. Ideally, they will have relationships with the relevant Unit Employment Support Officers (UESO) for reserve units in their local area.
If there are Reservists within the workforce, the employer has positively engaged with them on how the company would support their mobilisation.
Host a Reserve recruiting event on their premises in partnership with a Reserve Unit or Military Command Recruiting Teams.
Where scale and business models permit, the employer should actively encourage and support an internal Armed Forces community network within their organisation.
Nominations will be validated to determine the level of defence personnel employment within the nominated organisation and to check that the organisation has signed the Armed Forces Covenant.
Once the nomination has been validated it will be considered by a selection board at national level for gold awards and regional level for silver awards. The selection boards will be a panel chaired by a senior military officer and they will consider each nomination against the award criteria. Lithuania expects to make progress toward restoring diplomatic representation with China by the end of the year, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Wednesday, expressing confidence in Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys’ efforts to improve ties.
“The work is ongoing, it is happening,” Sinkevičius told reporters. “With Eastern countries, perhaps less background noise is needed, and quiet cooperation is required instead.”
He said the government had prepared an action plan setting out specific steps and deadlines for restoring diplomatic representation, with December identified as the target for a breakthrough.
“I hope it will succeed,” Sinkevičius said, adding that the outcome depended on both countries and that diplomatic matters took time.

He also neither confirmed nor denied whether talks had resumed over the name of Taiwan’s representative office in Vilnius. Sinkevičius said he was not involved in negotiations with Beijing, which are being handled by Budrys.
Earlier, the prime minister said he expected progress toward restoring diplomatic relations before Lithuania assumes the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union in the first half of 2027.
Sinkevičius said he was satisfied with Budrys’ performance, arguing that the foreign minister’s work should be assessed more broadly than by progress on a single issue.
“We are visible, heard, and new partnerships are being forged,” he said, adding that he saw potential for progress on other issues, including labour migration.
The ruling coalition has increasingly voiced support for normalising relations with China to the level of diplomatic representation maintained by other EU member states. The goal is also included in the government’s program.
Relations between Lithuania and China deteriorated in 2021 after Vilnius allowed Taiwan to open a representation under the name “Taiwanese Representative Office”. Similar offices in other countries generally operate under the name Taipei.
China responded by downgrading its diplomatic representation in Lithuania from ambassador to chargé d’affaires. Chinese diplomats have been absent from Lithuania since May 2025, after Vilnius declined to issue new accreditations to them.

Trump's diesel deal with Russia is unlikely to significantly lower global fuel prices despite expectations of rapid relief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:15:00 UTC
23:15:00 KST

Trump's diesel deal with Russia unlikely to bring down fuel prices
October 14, 2026
With or without a deal with Russia, diesel prices on global markets are unlikely to fall significantly anytime soon.
That is the assessment of experts interviewed by DW regarding the latest fuel-supply agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"The main reason for high diesel prices is the war in Iran and the simultaneous disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," said Samina Sultan, a foreign trade expert at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne.
The situation has led to production outages and made fuel shipments "more expensive, less secure and more difficult," she said.
Trump's deal with Russia also has an additional geopolitical dimension, Sultan said: "It causes the wars in Ukraine and Iran to become completely intertwined."
Wars reducing refinery output
Things are looking up, though. Roughly 13.5 million barrels of crude oil are once again flowing through the Strait of Hormuz a day, according to shipping and commodities analytics firm Kpler.
But for refined products such as diesel, volumes remain far lower at around 677,000 barrels per day, compared with 3.6 million barrels before the war.
Carsten Fritsch, a commodities analyst at Commerzbank, also attributes the price increases to the wars.
"If nothing changes in Ukraine and the Middle East, I see very few ways to resolve these supply bottlenecks," he said.
Trump expects prices to fall at record speed
In a social media post on October 9, Trump announced that he would temporarily suspend some sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel.
He wrote "diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" in a mix of lowercase and all caps.
Russia confirmed the arrangement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS on October 13 that supplying diesel fuel was "in the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets."
Diesel prices in the US and many EU countries have risen sharply over the past 12 months.
According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), prices in the US have climbed by about 60% and now stand at $6.30 per gallon, equivalent to $1.66 (or €1.49) per liter of diesel.
Diesel — Made in the USA
But even if Russia were able to flood global markets with cheap diesel, prices would not fall nearly as much as they recently rose, something all of the experts contacted by DW agree on.
Many refineries around the Gulf region have suffered disruptions or damage, while transporting fuel via shadow fleets and securing insurance remains costly, cumbersome and risky.
Another key shift is that Russia is no longer the world's largest diesel exporter. In fact, it is facing its own fuel shortages at home.
The US is now the world's biggest diesel exporter. In 2025, it exported an average of 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day, accounting for roughly 15.4% of global diesel exports.
At the same time, Russia fell to second place with a 9.5% share, and that was before major Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries.
Debates over export restrictions continue
Besides the new US-Russia diesel agreement, Trump also recently floated the idea of US diesel export restrictions. But the idea was abandoned because it could lead to even higher diesel prices in the country, according to Samina Sultan.
"There simply is not enough diesel storage capacity in the United States," Sultan said. "Production would have to be reduced, and then prices would rise again."
If the US were to impose export restrictions on diesel, buyers in Latin America and the European Union would be hit particularly hard. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, EU countries have increasingly imported diesel from the US instead of Russia because of sanctions.
"An export ban merely redistributes the shortage; it does not solve it," said ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski.
"Global prices would continue to rise, while refineries would scale back production as margins shrink," he added.
Limited impact on US diesel demand
Export restrictions aside, few people consider that the US-Russia diesel deal will have any big impact.
According to calculations by the platform The World Data, the promised shipment of 2.2 million barrels of diesel from Russia would not even cover a single day's US diesel demand of roughly 4 million barrels.
Even if all of the diesel volumes announced by Trump were combined, totaling 35.8 million barrels, they would only cover about nine days of US domestic demand.
"I CANNOT OVERSTATE HOW MUCH OF A NOTHING BURGER THIS IS," Canadian oil market analyst Rory Johnston wrote in an all-caps post on X shortly after the announcement.
Russia would normally export almost 10 times that volume if its refinery fleet was not being targeted by Ukrainian drone attacks, he added.
Canada also supplies diesel to the United States. Roughly 80% of all US diesel imports come from its northern neighbor.
Given Trump's verbal attacks on Canada and the ongoing trade dispute, analysts view the prospect of Canada supplying significantly more diesel to the US as highly unlikely.
This piece was originally published in German.

Germany moves to ban social media for children under 13
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:14:45 UTC
23:14:45 KST

Ayhan Şimşek
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Germany’s Cabinet on Wednesday approved policy guidelines to better protect children and young people online, including a national ban on social networks for those under 13 until European rules take effect.  
The planned measures focus on shielding children from online dangers, building their skills to use digital tools competently and supporting their participation in the digital world. They follow the final report of an independent expert commission that presented 56 recommendations last month.  
“The analysis is over, now it is about implementation: With the new framework, we as the federal government create the basis so that children and young people can also grow up safely and self-determined in the digital world,” Education and Family Affairs Minister Karin Prien said in a statement.  
“Protection, empowerment and participation – that is our mandate. The internet has long been everyday life especially for young people – that is why we do not want to lock them out of the digital world, but to make them strong and weatherproof,” she added.  
Under the new rules, children under 13 would generally be barred from social networks such as TikTok, Snapchat or Instagram. Only platforms that are clearly designed for children would be permitted. For teens between 13 and 18, the rules would set different limits depending on age. The government also plans reliable age verification from 2027 via the German implementation of the EU Digital Identity Wallet, called “d-you.”  
Germany will also press platforms to stop addictive designs by default. In talks on the EU Kids Act, Berlin wants algorithmic recommendation systems switched off automatically and measures to prevent features that encourage endless scrolling or compulsive use.
