New York City moves to ban horse-drawn carriages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:14:20 UTC
23:14:20 KST

Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the leader of the New York City council have agreed to ban horse-drawn carriages from the city, a popular tourist attraction that has faced widespread scrutiny.
Mamdani has agreed to back a bill supported by Julie Menin, the speaker of the New York city council, that would make it illegal to operate horse-drawn carriages beginning in June 2028, Politico reported on Tuesday. The city council is expected to vote on the legislation next week.
“The horse carriage industry is coming to an end in New York City. Our administration will make sure workers and owners are protected and the horses are safe,” Mamdani wrote on X on Tuesday.
A person familiar with the mayor’s office confirmed a deal had been struck.
While horse-drawn carriage rides are ubiquitous in Central Park, animal rights activists have long expressed concern over the treatment of horses. Multiple horses have died since 2020, occasionally collapsing in the middle of carriage rides.
The push for a ban increased over the summer after an 18-year-old tourist, Romanch Mahajan, died after being thrown from a carriage.
In a statement, Menin said horse-drawn carriages had “become a growing public safety liability”.
“We can honor our city’s traditions while recognizing when it’s time to move forward in the interest of public safety, protecting workers, and strengthening our city’s economic vitality,” Menin said.
A spokesperson for Menin said the city council speaker would bring up the legislation for a vote on 22 October.
Though there has been broad support for a horse-drawn carriage ban, officials have struggled to push legislation forward because the Transport Workers Union, a New York transport union that advocates for carriage drivers, had raised concerns about the carriage drivers’ livelihoods.
Mamdani had previously signaled he would support legislation banning horse-drawn carriages; however, he expressed concerns about the bill as written because it contained insufficient worker protections for carriage drivers.
A copy of the bill, shared with the Guardian, includes language requiring the city to create a workforce transition program that provides carriage drivers with career counseling and referrals to other job opportunities in the private and public sector.
The bill also requires the city to “consider” establishing a program to compensate the carriage owners for the value of their businesses.
John Samuelsen, the international president of the Transport Workers Union, told Politico the bill gave “no meaningful economic relief for workers”.
“This is disgraceful political opportunism, and Zohran should not simply go along with it, particularly when immigrant families’ livelihoods are being destroyed,” Samuelsen said. “This entire situation is reprehensible.”
It is unclear if Mamdani plans to sign the bill as is or if there will be further changes.
Sneha Choudhary, a city hall spokesperson, said in a statement, “We have been working closely with the city council, union partners, carriage drivers, animal welfare advocates, and community leaders to deliver a just transition that protects workers while ending horse-drawn carriages in Central Park once and for all.”
The bill also requires the city to implement a program to assist drivers in getting rid of their horses humanely – prohibiting the horses from being sold or transported for slaughter or sold for horse-drawn carriage industries elsewhere.

CNN: Russia is attacking American businesses in Ukraine, while the Trump administration remains silent
Kyiv • UNN
Russian strikes have damaged Coca-Cola, McDonald’s, and PepsiCo facilities in Ukraine. The American Chamber of Commerce is calling on the White House to respond.
Amid President Donald Trump and his administration’s stepped-up pressure on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, citing harm to American consumers, they have "remained silent about recent Russian strikes on American businesses in Ukraine." This is stated in a CNN report published on October 14, UNN writes.
Details
Over the past few months, the outlet writes, "russia has intensified its attacks on facilities linked to American corporations and on civilian infrastructure in Ukraine in general."
According to Andy Hunder, president of the American Chamber of Commerce in Ukraine, Russian missiles and drones have damaged facilities belonging to some of the best-known American brands, including Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, McDonald’s, and Oreo.
Although russia has tried to deter successful American businesses in the past, "we have not seen anything like this in recent months," Hunder told CNN.
"This is a direct strike by drones and missiles, and they continue attacking them. It sends a signal that they are targeting American businesses. We are not seeing any response from the White House," he said.
"We need this to stop because these are American interests, American money, American investors who are being hit and targeted," he noted.
When a Russian drone struck a Coca-Cola plant near Kyiv in early September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the attack was a "clear signal" to the United States.
Later that month, the Russians used a "strike drone" to destroy a warehouse used by McDonald’s, Zelenskyy said in a post on X. McDonald’s Ukraine confirmed in a statement that "a warehouse operated by one of our logistics partners in the Kyiv region was damaged as a result of a drone attack on September 25." McDonald’s Ukraine said that, as a result of the damage, its restaurants were offering a limited menu.
PepsiCo acknowledged in a statement at the end of August that a production facility in the Mykolaiv region had been damaged, but there were no casualties.
There is no consensus among American companies on the ground about how openly they want to speak publicly about having been struck, "or disclose the fact that they have repeatedly been targeted," a former senior U.S. State Department official told CNN.
"Some companies want us to raise this issue," Hunder reiterated, but others "are acting very cautiously."
However, several Democratic U.S. lawmakers have publicly called on the White House to do more to protect American businesses in Ukraine and condemn moscow’s actions. Ukraine has highlighted these attacks as another reason to increase defense support so that they can adequately protect American companies on the ground, the outlet notes.
The Chamber of Commerce meets with American lawmakers from both parties who visit Kyiv, and Hunder told CNN that they asked them to raise this issue with the White House.
U.S. President Donald Trump spoke publicly when asked in August 2025 about a Russian strike on an American electronics plant, saying that he had told kremlin head vladimir putin that he was "not happy about it."
A White House official said that Trump "wants the war to end completely, so that the senseless killings stop."
"The President and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we will ultimately reach a peace agreement," the official said, asserting that the United States is the "only country in the world" that can "play a constructive role in talks with both sides, working to end the war."

An increasing number of European companies are using artificial intelligence (AI) and algorithmic management systems, with 42% of small and medium-sized enterprises and mid-cap companies surveyed already adopting the technologies, according to a Eurobarometer survey published on Wednesday.
The survey found that a further 21% of the companies plan to introduce AI and algorithmic management systems in the future, although most current applications remain limited or experimental.
AI and algorithmic management are primarily used in customer service and client relations, with 47% of surveyed companies reporting applications in this area.
Monitoring employee performance and productivity ranked as the second most common use, at 36%, followed by logistics, planning and staff scheduling at 30%.
Meanwhile, 61% of the companies said AI helps them make decisions, while 75% believe the technologies will improve job quality.
Despite the growing adoption of AI, human oversight remains widespread, with 90% of companies saying people make the final decisions.
Only 2% reported fully automated decision-making processes.
The survey also identified several obstacles to wider adoption, including high investment costs (50%), legal uncertainty (49%), and a lack of expertise (48%).
Nearly half of the surveyed companies (49%) said they do not trust AI or automated systems to make decisions concerning workforce and staff matters.

America has sided with Russia against Ukraine. Europe should stop pretending and build a coalition against Russia, China, and even the US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:11:59 UTC
23:11:59 KST

On 11 October, Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine. It binds only Ukraine. In the two days that followed, Kyiv held its fire while Russia kept hitting Ukrainian energy and critical infrastructure across 19 regions. A Russian strike collapsed an apartment stairwell in Kharkiv and killed three. And before Russia’s latest ballistic missile strike, five missiles and more than 100 drones, Ukraine received no early warning at all. Washington then said both sides were to blame.
This is what one of Trump’s decisions looks like on the ground. There were four of them, in three days, 9 to 11 October.
Three days that further weaken the West and undermine liberal democracies. Three days that encourage Putin to continue his war against Ukraine and his hybrid war against Europe. Like China, the US has sided with Russia against Ukraine and Europe. Whatever the motives in Washington—diesel prices before the midterms, a long feud with the court—the effect is the same.
International law
On 9 October, the Trump administration announced new sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), an institution crucial for holding Putin and the Kremlin responsible for the war of aggression and its atrocities. The sanctions came hours after the Nobel Peace Prize went to Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge.
"We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said. "Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC." He expects allies, many of them ICC members that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court.
The ICC exists to investigate, prosecute, and try individuals accused of the world's gravest international crimes. Washington wants to end it. The court called the measures an assault on the rule of law and the foundations of the international legal order.
What if Russia uses nuclear weapons? Can we say Ukraine brought peace to world? Norwegian professor who nominated Zelenskyy and Ukrainians for 2026 Nobel Peace Prize takes on tough questions
Funding Russia's war
On 9 October, Trump also lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports. The deal comes less than a month after he signed the sweeping Russia sanctions law dedicated to the memory of Sen. Lindsey Graham, which allows tariffs on buyers of Russian oil. Multiple US lawmakers argue the move violates federal law. Congress banned Russian energy imports in 2022, and a bipartisan group of seven senators, including Republicans Thom Tillis and Lisa Murkowski, stated that the decision "runs directly counter to that law." They also argue that the administration failed to consult Congress or justify its decision as the statute requires.
Western sanctions and Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries—its own "sanctions"—aim at the same effect: making the war unaffordable for Russia. Trump's decision does the opposite: it helps Russia pay for the war. It also breaks with the principle of unity of effort, further undermining Western cohesion.
Zelenskyy said the deal showed US weakness, as Washington had secured no concessions in return: "What did [Trump] get? That he will have more diesel? For whom? More Russian diesel for Americans? ... It looks like Alaska No. 2. You know, it looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible."
Stability and sovereignty
On 10 October, Trump said of the elected president of a country fighting off Russia's full-scale invasion: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president... I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal, because he could have made many deals and, for some reason, he never does." He claimed Zelenskyy could have ended the war many times, and insisted that Zelenskyy "wants to make problems for the world" by authorizing strikes on Russian refineries.
The Trump Administration conspicuously ignores the Swiss Summit on Peace in Ukraine, President Zelenskyy’s 10-point peace plan based on international law, and not least, the international effort to establish unity of efforts to enforce a just peace.
Zelenskyy has repeatedly proposed talks and shown willingness to compromise for a peace that guarantees Ukraine's sovereignty. On 18 July, he said: "This year alone, we have reached out to Russia dozens of times with proposals to stop this war—but all we got in return were refusals."
The "deals" Trump alludes to would not have secured peace or guaranteed Ukraine's future existence, nor safeguarded Europe against future Russian aggression. They were not rooted in international law, but in the prospect of great wealth for Trump and his associates—business deals dressed up as "peace plans”. Ukraine and its European partners instead proposed amendments and defined red lines to bring the drafts up to the standards of international law.
The Kremlin itself exposed the absurdity of Trump's claim. In a phone call with Trump, Putin categorically ruled out resuming peace talks, his aide Yuri Ushakov said, and sought to convince Trump that Ukrainian resistance has "no prospects whatsoever."
Supporting Russia
On 11 October, Trump announced: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
He gave no details. Zelenskyy had no prior knowledge, but said Ukraine would agree if Russia did. He had already offered to stop striking Russian refineries if Russia stopped attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
It was not an energy ceasefire. It was a gift to Putin. A White House official told Axios that, as Trump understands it, the term means only that Russia and Ukraine stop attacking each other's oil refineries—and that this is what Washington expects Ukraine to do. Ukraine has one refinery, while Russia has 38, of which 21 have been targeted by Ukrainian drones.
Three days after Washington announced an energy ceasefire, Russia fires 39 ballistic missiles at Ukraine’s grid
To most of the world, an energy ceasefire covers the whole energy sector: nuclear power, oil refineries, power plants, the grid down to local transformers. But not in Trump's world. The official said a deal on power plants and grids could come next—if Ukraine first stops striking the refineries fueling Russia's war.
Axios wrote that White House officials see Ukraine's refinery strikes as doing more damage to Zelenskyy's relationship with Trump than to Russia. The administration has reportedly threatened to cut Ukraine off from US intelligence if the strikes continue.
Forcing Ukraine to halt its refinery strikes, while Russia keeps hitting not only power plants and the grid but heating and water systems, hospitals, schools, railways, ports and civilians, does not motivate Russia to stop. Within hours of Trump's announcement, Russia struck a power plant in Kharkiv. Trump's one-sided pressure encourages Russia to continue.
Enabling Russian aggression
Moscow paints Ukraine as the intransigent party, though Russia has offered no concessions and rejected numerous compromise proposals from the US and Ukraine. Still, Trump insists that Ukraine, not Russia, is the problem.
In three days, Trump has sanctioned the court that could hold Russia accountable, called on Zelenskyy to step down, secured revenue for the Kremlin's war, and declared an "energy ceasefire" that only asks Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries, while Russia goes on turning winter into a weapon.
The call for Zelenskyy to step down led Marie-Agnes Strack-Zimmermann, chair of the European Parliament's Committee on Security and Defence, to say: "If Trump calls on Zelenskyy to step down, he is clearly siding with a murderer. Only the Ukrainian people can decide who leads Ukraine in free elections, not the White House, and certainly not the Kremlin." Her conclusion: "By once again attacking allies and democratic institutions, Trump is weakening the West and undermining democracy. [...] Europe must therefore remain firmly on course and support Ukraine, because the US can no longer be relied on."
The US's latest National Security Strategy does not merely shift America's foreign policy priorities. It aligns them with Moscow's on seven separate issues, while explicitly calling for Washington to "cultivate resistance to Europe's current trajectory" by backing nationalist parties against sitting EU-aligned governments.
Europe has 11 ways to choke Russia’s war. It doesn’t need Trump’s permission for any of them
Europe must stand on its own
The last three days demonstrate that the US is no longer an ally, but a strategic adversary. None of Trump's recent decisions helps end the war on Ukrainian or European terms. On the contrary, they encourage Putin and push any realistic hope of peace years away. They undermine international law and support the notion that might makes right.
Worse still, they help explain why war between Russia and Europe by 2029 is becoming more likely. Trump—Putin's close ally—leaves office on 20 January 2029.
Europe must stress its support for continued Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries unless the Kremlin agrees to a comprehensive energy ceasefire in line with Ukraine’s demands.
Europe urgently needs to distance itself from the US and its foreign policy. Heads of state must join Canada's efforts to unite middle and small powers in common defense against increasingly aggressive great powers. As this series has repeatedly argued, Europe must build a Coalition of Like-Minded countries strong enough to confront Russia, China and, sadly, the US.

Nord Stream May Have Been Lawful Target, Argue Lawyers for Ukrainian Accused of Bombing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:09:00 UTC
23:09:00 KST

Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany on Wednesday that "an aggressor's infrastructure" may have been a lawful target.
Serhii Kuznetsov is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents including divers and an explosives expert that blew up Russia's largest gas pipeline to Europe in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times.
The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the bombing.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Kuznetsov's lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany's imports of natural gas before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a "Russian weapon."
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked.
Right to remain silent
Prosecutors have alleged that Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant in Italy last year, worked with members of the Ukrainian military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.
Kuznetsov, 50, who prior to Wednesday was referred to publicly only as Serhii K. under German legal rules, has denied any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile)-long Baltic Sea pipeline.
Wearing a grey suit and with a shaved head, he exercised his right to remain silent in court but did not cover his face. His lawyers said he could not mount a proper defense because he was obliged to withhold Ukrainian state secrets.
The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military aid. Russia said on Monday it expected a "just verdict" that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.
Kuznetsov's legal team had tried reaching out to Ukraine for information that might assist the defense but heard nothing, according to another defense lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp.
Attacking civilian targets is considered a war crime
German prosecutors say the actions Kuznetsov is accused of — attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services — would amount to a war crime.
Kuznetsov is the only person on trial, but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers.
The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's longstanding dependence on Russian natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Nord Stream's supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, already built, but Berlin canceled approval to open it just prior to Russia's invasion.
Plumes of methane gas
The trial, expected to continue into February next year, could have domestic political implications.
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in opinion polls for more than a year, has called for an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ties with Moscow.
Although German state parliaments have no role in foreign policy, the AfD filed a motion in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Wednesday calling for an end to support for Ukraine, noting the "historical parallel" with the start of the trial.
The Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 meters under the Baltic and built by Russian gas concern Gazprom to supply up to 110 billion cubic meters of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries.
The Sept. 26, 2022, blasts that ruptured three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines created a giant whirlpool at sea as huge plumes of methane gas rose into the atmosphere.
Prosecutors allege that Kuznetsov traveled to Germany through Poland some three weeks before the attack, using a forged Ukrainian passport. He and his group then used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialized military-grade explosives to the sea floor.
The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on Sept. 6 and returned on Sept. 23, 2022.

Colombia inaugurates embassy to Israel in Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:08:45 UTC
23:08:45 KST

Colombia inaugurates embassy to Israel in Jerusalem
Palestinian officials condemn move by Colombia’s new government that marked a major shift after former President Petro had severed ties with Israel.
Colombia has opened its embassy to Israel in Jerusalem, joining a small group of countries in taking the controversial step of backing Israel’s claim to sovereignty in the contested city.
Palestinian officials swiftly denounced the inauguration on Wednesday that came as Israel is facing mounting international pressure over the genocidal war on Gaza, where three years of attacks have killed more than 74,000 people.
The move by the administration of new Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella is a major shift from his left-wing predecessor Gustavo Petro, who in 2024 severed ties with Israel over the war on Gaza.
De la Espriella, who was sworn in in August, has also restored a free trade agreement between Israel and Colombia that Petro terminated.
Colombian Minister of Foreign Affairs Omar Bula Escobar said on Wednesday that relations between the two countries “should never have been broken” and that Bogota was taking “taking a concrete step towards restoring diplomatic relations”.
“Israel is a strategic partner. It always has been, and from now on, it will be an even stronger one,” he said during a ceremony that marked the embassy’s opening.
The opening made Colombia the 10th country to establish its embassy in Israel in Jerusalem – most countries keep their formal diplomatic missions in Tel Aviv.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar welcomed the move during the ceremony. “This is an important date for the State of Israel. It’s also an important date for the city of Jerusalem,” he said while signing the Colombian embassy’s guest book.
Colombian Ambassador Tania Gilinski said Israel had always been a “strategic partner” and that moving forward it “will be so with even greater determination and strength”.
‘Violation of international law’
The Palestinian Authority condemned Colombia’s embassy move, calling it “a violation of international legitimacy resolutions” that undermines “the international consensus on the legal status of the holy city”.
Jordan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also criticised the move as a “violation of international law and relevant international resolutions”.
United States President Donald Trump moved the US embassy to Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem during his first term in 2018, angering Palestinians and sparking international condemnation. Previous US presidents, as well as nearly every other country, refrained from opening embassies in Jerusalem, arguing that the city’s final status should first be resolved in negotiations between Israelis and Palestinians.
The status of Jerusalem remains one of the core unresolved issues of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, with Israel claiming the undivided city as its capital while Palestinians view occupied East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state.
Israel occupied East Jerusalem and annexed it in 1967, in a move not recognised by the vast majority of the international community.
Since Trump relocated the US embassy to Jerusalem, only a handful of small, US-aligned countries have followed suit, namely Fiji, Guatemala, Honduras, Papua New Guinea, Paraguay and Nauru. Kosovo and Somaliland, which are not member-states of the United Nations, have also opened what they consider their embassies in Jerusalem.

When the man living at the property asks the man filming for his ID he briefly shows him a lanyard. It is unclear what information it shows.

When challenged, often by private security outside hotels, some have attempted to confuse the issue by quoting supposed “common law” principles, which have been taken up by members of the far right as a legal recourse that supersedes statutory laws.
However, the increasing use of houses of multiple occupancy (HMOs) as part of the government’s plans to phase out the use of hotels to house asylum seekers has given some of these activists a new target, with some obtaining addresses from publicly available documents and sharing details with one another in online groups.

A YouTube spokesperson said: “Harassment and cyberbullying are not allowed on YouTube and as part of this, we do not allow content that reveals someone’s personally identifiable information. Upon review, we have removed the flagged video for violating our harassment and cyberbullying policies.”

The audacity and sense of entitlement is breathtaking.

The end of UNIFIL: What next for south Lebanon?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:07:46 UTC
23:07:46 KST

Breadcrumb
The end of UNIFIL: What next for south Lebanon?
Beirut, Lebanon - As the UN's longest-serving presence on the Blue Line between Lebanon and Israel counts down to its exit, a European replacement is being floated as the answer.
The real choice facing Beirut, however, is between a security arrangement written in Washington and one it builds itself.
For 48 years, the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) has been deployed across the country's southern border villages.
It never deterred the wars fought across the Blue Line - a 120-kilometre (75-mile) temporary demarcation boundary established by the United Nations on 7 June 2000 to confirm the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon.
What they did, consistently, was watch, record, and report, and in a region where every side contests every account, that act of witnessing carried weight of its own.
Few in Lebanon expect the UN body's exit to change the balance of force. “UNIFIL was merely an eyewitness,” retired Brigadier General Saeed Qazah, a military expert, told The New Arab.
Operating under Chapter VI of its mandate, it could only record violations and report them to the UN. Its absence, he argued, “will not change the military reality on the ground as much as it will leave a logistical and economic vacuum”.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun's push for an extension was blocked by a US-Israeli veto, and he had welcomed a French-Italian idea for a European Union force to take UNIFIL's place. On Monday, the contours of that EU role took a more concrete shape.
European Union foreign ministers agreed to establish a new support mission in Lebanon to advise and train the country's military and internal security forces. It would have an initial mandate of three years.
But the European option still lacks the mandate, consent, and the American backing it would need.
UNIFIL's real successor is being negotiated elsewhere, and what awaits Lebanon after December is less a handover than a test of whether the state can do alone what it has long outsourced.
A European force without a shape
The new European mission "will advise and assist the Lebanese Armed Forces and Internal Security Forces to strengthen territorial control, border security, and internal security," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a statement on Monday.
Over 10 EU members are reportedly willing to contribute people and resources to it, but more operational planning is required before it is launched. An EU official told Reuters this week that the mission hoped to deploy personnel in the coming months.
But retired Brigadier General Saeed Qazah sees a deeper flaw.
“UNIFIL could not prevent the Lebanese-Israeli conflict or control the land and the border, and European forces will have no effective role there either,” he said.
Enforcing peace would require a Chapter VII mandate, which a Russian and Chinese veto would block. “No country is willing to send its soldiers to fight or sacrifice their lives on behalf of the Lebanese army,” he added.
Consent is the other wall. Political analyst Ali Sbeiti says Israel refuses to give Paris any role, given their disputes over regional files and the Gaza war. Qazah agrees that no foreign force can deploy on the border without the approval of both Lebanon, Israel, and a UN resolution.
The one exception, he said, “is a mission limited to training and logistical support for the Lebanese army, away from the border. The only feasible European mission, in other words, is the one that does least of what UNIFIL did”.
UNIFIL's real successor is being negotiated elsewhere
Writer and political analyst Nader Hijaz points to the "third party" under discussion in talks between Beirut and Israel, a body that would verify implementation of the framework agreement.
“That is, in practice, the field replacement for UNIFIL,” he said. Whether it would merely monitor or hold broad powers, such as searching homes and seizing weapons, is unresolved, and a deal has been deferred until after Israel's elections.
On one point, Hijaz is categorical. “Washington will never accept any force that is not under direct American command,” he told The New Arab. The US and Israel, he said, are open to a specific Italian role but not a French one.
Sbeiti adds that the Europeans lack the nerve to act in the south without explicit American blessing. The successor, in short, is being decided in a US-brokered process, on a timetable set by Israeli politics.
Beirut and Hezbollah's calculations
The Lebanese state and army would welcome almost any arrangement that averts a vacuum, and President Joseph Aoun immediately expressed backing for the EU’s announcement this week of a security support mission.
Hijaz notes that military cooperation with France and Italy is already established, and Sbeiti describes an official welcome for any friendly presence, even as a mere eyewitness.
Hezbollah, however, is harder to read. Its secretary-general, Naim Qassem, has called the US-sponsored framework agreement a red line and a surrender of sovereignty, holding up instead the US-Iranian memorandum signed in Islamabad.
Qazah expects the party to reject any foreign force, since it does not want a witness to its breaches, “just as Israel does not want neutral forces bearing witness to its violations”.
Sbeiti, however, disagrees. “Hezbollah can no longer block a plan the state backs, and has no fundamental problem with France, given shared understandings between Paris, the party and Tehran,” he told The New Arab. “The main knot remains with the American and Israeli sides,” he noted.
Hijjaz, meanwhile, says the party's stance will hinge on whether a force operates south of the Litani or beyond it, and whether it pursues the group's weapons. Either way, the decisive veto lies outside Lebanon.
What south Lebanon loses
The mission is exiting in its worst hour. It has recorded a sharp escalation between Israel and Hezbollah, with hundreds of projectiles on some days. It still fields more than 7,400 troops from 46 countries, its backbone European, and seven peacekeepers have been killed in hostile attacks in 2026 alone.
Ceasefires have collapsed in succession, from April's arrangements to the US-sponsored Trilateral Framework in June, and Israeli forces still hold positions inside Lebanon that Beirut says block the army's full deployment.
Washington led the push to end the mission, favouring arrangements outside the Security Council, as in Gaza. Prime Minister Nawaf Salam warned of a vacuum, arguing the UN offers a neutrality no other actor can match, and more than two-thirds of parliament petitioned for UNIFIL to be strengthened, not withdrawn.
Since 1978, and especially after its reinforcement following the 2006 war, UNIFIL has been an economic engine for the border villages.
At its peak, Qazah said, more than 15,000 soldiers in a narrow area drove spending, services, and procurement. Their departure will cut “a vital economic artery” in a region already devastated by Israeli strikes.
Three roads after December
The first is direct military coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli armies, favoured by Washington and Israel and signalled by US envoys' talk of opening crossings once the weapons file is closed. Lebanon rejects it as security normalisation.
The second is a multinational force with European troops under American command, which depends on a wider regional deal and US-Iranian understandings and Israel's elections.
The third is self-reliance: Qazah argues the government can declare the border villages a military zone under National Defence Law No. 102 of 1938, placing all security forces under army command and allowing curfews, closures and searches.
A European coalition will remain ink on paper without a UN mandate, the consent of both parties and an American guarantee against escalation. None of these is in Beirut's gift. The world is not handing the south to a new guardian; it is handing it back to the Lebanese state. Lebanon can assert its sovereignty through its own army or risk a vacuum that turns the border strip into an open front once more.
For Qazah, the choice is already clear. Imposing security, he said, is the exclusive responsibility of Lebanon's political leadership, which must give the army firm orders “to impose security by military force, not by begging for it or imposing it by consensus”.
Alaa Sarhal is a Lebanese journalist

Edited by Charlie Hoyle

The Best Way to Respond to Passive-Aggressive Comments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:07:29 UTC
23:07:29 KST

Have you ever left work at 5 p.m., only for a colleague to not-so-sweetly ask, “Going home already?”
If so, you’ve probably been the target of a passive-aggressive comment. The two halves of the very phrase “passive-aggressive” spell out the familiar dynamic, says Laurie Weingart, a professor of organizational behavior at Carnegie Mellon University who has studied how people express conflict at work. Someone is expressing opposition or anger—the aggressive part—but doing so indirectly. The words leave room for an innocent interpretation. The tone? Not so much.
That ambiguity puts you in an awkward position: Do you respond to what was said or what you think the other person meant—or give in to the urge to snip right back? We asked experts what to say when someone seems to be taking a dig at you but won’t quite say what they mean.
Why people default to passive-aggressive communication
Sometimes it feels safer to hint at a feeling than to say it directly. Admitting you feel some sort of way calls for a kind of vulnerability that a sarcastic remark does not. “Some people just haven’t learned how to say or don’t feel comfortable saying, ‘I’m hurt. You hurt my feelings,’” says Melissa Gluck, a psychologist in New York City. If you grew up around people who rarely said what they meant, the indirect approach might even feel normal.
There can also be something more specific behind a partner’s pointed comment. In research on romantic relationships, Levi R. Baker, a psychology professor at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro, found that people sometimes express displeasure indirectly because they’re unsure how much their partner cares. “People are really doing this to kind of test their partner,” he says. They’re signaling, “I’m upset with you, I’ve got some hurt feelings,” then waiting to see whether their partner notices and tries to find out what’s wrong. Underneath it all, Baker says, they may be wondering: “Do they care about me? Do they value me?”
Still, understanding where a comment might come from doesn’t make it feel any better to hear. It can leave you wondering whether you’ve been insulted—and how to answer an accusation the other person never quite made.
How to respond to a passive-aggressive comment
Weingart’s advice is to make your response “more direct and less intense” than the comment you just heard. Start by giving your friend a chance to be direct. If someone says, “Must be nice to have that much free time,” Brook McKenzie, a licensed chemical dependency counselor in Dallas who often helps families work through indirect communication and resentment, suggests responding: “I’m not sure how you meant that. Can you say it another way?” Another option: “It sounds like there might be something you want to say to me directly. Is there?”
The question should be an invitation, not an accusation. “Why are you being so passive-aggressive?” may be tempting, McKenzie says, but you’ll likely end up arguing about their tone instead of whatever is actually bothering them. Returning the sarcasm tends to cause the same problem, with two people annoyed instead of one.
If you’re talking to someone you’re especially close to, Gluck suggests a gentle opening: “I feel like something’s off. Do you want to talk about it?” That lets them tell you what’s wrong without requiring you to guess. If they say everything’s fine, you can take them at their word for the time being. “It’s not our job to become the feelings detective,” Gluck says.
If you have a good idea of what's underneath the comment, you can acknowledge that, too. Say your partner responds to your plans with friends by remarking that you certainly have time for everyone else. Baker suggests reassuring them that you want to spend time together and proposing a plan: “I’m going out tonight, but I’d really like to have dinner with you tomorrow.” You don’t need to cancel your plans to show that you care.
At work, clarity may serve you better than a conversation about feelings. If your boss says, “Leaving already?” when your workday is over, Weingart suggests asking: “Is there something else you need me to do before I leave?” A coworker’s jab may warrant even less: “Yep, the workday’s over. Have a great weekend.” Either response avoids assuming you know what the other person meant.
And sometimes the best response is no response. If a friend makes one out-of-character comment on a rough day, Gluck says, you can let it pass. If it keeps happening, that’s a different conversation.
What to do when someone is repeatedly passive-aggressive
A pattern deserves a more direct approach. If a friend repeatedly jokes that you never make time for them, Gluck suggests naming both what you’ve noticed and how it lands: “This isn’t the first time you’ve made that comment. It’s starting to hurt my feelings, and I’d like to know if something’s bothering you.”
The same pattern can emerge in families. Say you tell your mother it upset you when she criticized you in front of relatives, and she replies, “I guess I’m just a bad mom.” Gluck suggests saying: “That’s not what I said. I was trying to tell you how I feel, and it hurts when you put those words in my mouth.” That brings the conversation back to what she said in front of your relatives, instead of turning it into a debate about whether she’s a good mother.
What if they insist they were just joking? Weingart recommends separating their intention from the effect: “You may not have meant it to be hurtful, but that’s how it sounded to me.” You don’t have to prove what was in their head to explain what happened on your end.
It’s also fair to be clear about what you’re willing to do next. Consider borrowing McKenzie’s go-to line for recurring comments: “I’m willing to have difficult conversations with you. I’m not willing to keep guessing what you mean.”

Documents
Details
If consultation is to be undertaken on an amendment to the regulations or the implementation of new regulation, the MAA will issue an NPA. The NPA will explain the rationale behind the amendment, the possible impact on the regulated community (developed into an impact assessment (IA)) and set the deadline for comment/feedback. Feedback is important to further develop the IA.
Comments or enquiries on any NPA are to be sent to DSA-MAA-MRPEnquiries@mod.gov.uk by the date stated in the NPA. Please use the NPA Response Form template provided below to return your consolidated comments.
After the comments closure date, the NPA will be removed from the website.
NPA comment response sheets contain the collated MAA responses to individual NPA publications.
In the final preparation for publication similar Regulated Community comments have been consolidated into one response.
Some of the MAA responses to the Regulated Community comments may have been superseded by further internal review prior to the official publication of the new issue.

France records 4% rise in women killed by partners or ex-partners in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:06:47 UTC
23:06:47 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The number of women killed by their current or former partners in France rose 4% in 2025, reaching 111 victims, according to figures released Wednesday by the Interior Ministry.
Police and gendarmerie recorded 136 violent deaths involving current or former partners last year, compared with 138 in 2024, a decrease of 1%, the ministry said in its annual study.
Of the victims, 25 were men, down 19% from the previous year.
On average, one person died every three days in a case involving a current or former partner, according to the report.
Authorities also recorded 445 attempted homicides involving current or former partners in 2025, accounting for 10% of the 4,365 attempted homicides recorded nationwide.
The share was up from 9% in 2024, the study said.
The northern department of Nord recorded the highest number of victims, with eight, followed by Bouches-du-Rhone with seven.
Alpes-Maritimes and Herault each recorded five victims, while Aisne, Gironde and Marne each reported four.
In France’s overseas territories, Reunion recorded three victims, while French Guiana and New Caledonia each recorded two, according to the ministry.

Louvre could be forced to close without major overhaul, director warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:06:40 UTC
23:06:40 KST

A year after thieves made off with €88 million of crown jewels that have never been found, the new man in charge says leaking pipes and crumbling galleries mean security fixes alone won’t save the Paris landmark.
The Louvre could eventually have to shut its doors to the public unless France’s next government backs a sweeping transformation of the world’s most-visited museum, its director has warned.
Christophe Leribault told Le Figaro on Wednesday that the museum would seek private funding for the work, but that a major injection of public money would have to be approved after France’s national elections next year.
“Whoever forms the next government must keep in mind that if the Louvre is not repaired, updated, and transformed, it will very quickly fall behind and will eventually have to close its doors to the public. That would be a disaster,” he said.
Successive minority governments have struggled for years to pass annual budgets, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is trying to rein in public spending to reduce France’s vast deficit.
A year on from the heist
Leribault, an art historian who previously ran the Musée d’Orsay, took over in February after Laurence des Cars resigned in the fallout from last year’s jewel theft.
On 19 October 2025, a four-man gang used a lorry-mounted lifting platform to break into the Apollo Gallery and, in broad daylight, took eight pieces of the French Crown Jewels worth an estimated €88 million. A Senate inquiry later found that only one of two cameras covering the break-in point was working. The jewels have never been recovered.
Speaking to AFP ahead of the anniversary, Leribault said an €83 million security masterplan was “moving forward at speed”. Measures include a new head of security post, an upgraded camera network – found to have old cameras and major gaps – and better surveillance around the perimeter and at access points.
No ‘miracle’ solution
Leribault argued that lasting improvements could only come as part of a wider overhaul of the museum, which welcomed around nine million visitors last year.
"The operations needed to secure the museum require work on the historic building and its infrastructure," he wrote. "There is no easy, miracle ‘surface’ solution. Everything is interconnected, everything is linked."
The museum first opened its doors the public in 1793 and celebrated it 233rd birthday this summer.
The museum’s problems include old plumbing, badly insulated galleries and cramped public areas. A leaked memo from des Cars in January 2025 said some areas "are no longer watertight" and that "visiting the Louvre is a physical ordeal". In February, a burst heating pipe damaged a ceiling painted by Charles Meynier in 1819.
The scale and cost of the work have become highly political. President Emmanuel Macron has championed the "Louvre – New Renaissance" project, which includes a new entrance and has been estimated by the government at €700–800 million over ten years, partly funded by a 45% rise in ticket prices for most non-European visitors.
Trade unions have criticised Macron and des Cars for prioritising grandiose plans for an architectural overhaul instead of more modest changes that would improve the visitor experience.

Foreign minister: No sign of Russian forces massing at NATO borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:05:00 UTC
23:05:00 KST

Foreign minister: No sign of Russian forces massing at NATO borders
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte told Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna (Eesti 200) there are no signs of Russian preparations for an imminent confrontation with NATO, Tsahkna said Wednesday.
Tsahkna said Russia is nonetheless testing allies through sabotage and cyberattacks, and that NATO remains ready to defend every inch of allied territory.
The NATO chief was in Tallinn Wednesday and met with the foreign minister. The two discussed implementation of decisions taken at the NATO summit in Ankara in July, continued support for Ukraine, regional security, and Russia's acts of sabotage against allies.
"During today's visit, the NATO Secretary General emphasized what Estonia has consistently said: there are no Russian forces or other signs of preparations for an imminent military confrontation with NATO at NATO's borders," Tsahkna said. "At the same time, Russia is testing NATO allies through acts of sabotage and cyberattacks, but the alliance remains vigilant and united," he continued, via a ministry press release.
According to Tsahkna, NATO has taken highly practical measures in recent years demonstrating its readiness to defend allies decisively and in line with NATO plans.
"The Secretary General confirmed that NATO is ready and able to respond to any threat and defend every inch of allied territory. Article 5 of the NATO Treaty, which states that an attack against one ally is an attack against all Allies, remains in force," said Tsahkna. "NATO has demonstrated this repeatedly in recent years. It has responded to airspace violations and damage to critical infrastructure with concrete measures, confirming that the Alliance is ready to act."
NATO has consistently demonstrated its readiness to defend every inch of Allied territory. To ensure this remains true in the years ahead, we discussed today in Tallinn with @SecGenNATO Mark Rutte how to turn growing defence investments into real capabilities and keep NATO's deterrence and defence strong. We also discussed support for Ukraine. A just and lasting peace must be the goal, and Ukraine needs continued military assistance to defend itself against Russia's aggression. @NATO's PURL mechanism remains crucial, and Estonia will contribute an additional €10 million to Ukraine through this initiative.
— Margus Tsahkna (@Tsahkna) October 14, 2026
Tsahkna said the two also discussed how NATO can ensure it remains capable of countering future threats. "Increasing defense investment by European Allies and Canada will enable NATO to meet its capability targets more quickly and strengthen its deterrence and defense posture," he said.
The discussions also covered expanding defense industry production capacity, applying lessons from Russia's war against Ukraine, and further support for Ukraine.
"It is in the long-term security interests of all NATO Allies that Russia's aggression against Ukraine ends with a just and lasting peace. For now, the priority is to equip Ukraine ahead of its fifth winter of war so that it can effectively protect its population and civilian infrastructure from Russia's increasingly brutal aerial terror and continue fighting for its independence and sovereignty," Tsahkna said.
He added that NATO support, including through the PURL mechanism, remains crucial to providing military assistance to Ukraine. "Estonia has so far contributed €21 million to Ukraine through the PURL initiative and will soon provide an additional €10 million through this mechanism."
"Estonia will continue to provide military assistance to Ukraine amounting to at least 0.25 percent of GDP each year, and our own defense investment already exceeds 5 percent of GDP," Tsahkna said.

New Language Board chief to focus more on prevention than on fining businesses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:03:00 UTC
23:03:00 KST

New Language Board chief to focus more on prevention than on fining businesses
Minister of Education and Research Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200) has appointed Martin Eessalu as director general of the Language Board.
Eesalu was proposed by the Government Office's senior appointments committee and replaces Ilmar Tomusk, who recently stepped down.
Eessalu's five-year term begins on January 1, 2027. The board needs to focus more on prevention and support, and less on fines, which the board can issue for instance in the case of customer-facing businesses failing to meet language requirements.
Eessalu also noted strengthening the board's capacity is the task for the coming years, and the rise of artificial intelligence (AI) will also be in focus.
"Alongside supervision, there is an increasing need to focus on prevention and support. The state's aim is not to issue fines, but to promote the use of Estonian and increase its vitality," he said.
"Second, I consider the use of language technology and artificial intelligence very important. A third significant direction is a greater contribution to Estonian language reputation activities and communication. Finally, it is important to take a fresh look at what institutional form can fulfill the expectations set. The team is small and the task is large, and there is also great potential for more substantive cooperation with other agencies, above all the Institute of the Estonian Language," Eessalu went on.
Since 2023 Eessalu has worked as director of R&D at the Institute of the Estonian Language (EKI). Prior to that he spent nine years at the Ministry of Education and Research in various language and research roles, most recently as head of the research infrastructure field, and served as acting director of the Estonian Literary Museum (Eesti kirjandusmuuseum) 2020-2021.
Eessalu takes over from Ilmar Tomusk, who had led the Language Board and its predecessor, the Language Inspectorate, for over 30 years. Tomusk did not apply for a new term when his previous one expired.
The Language Board (Keeleamet) is a government agency under the Ministry of Education and Research. Its main task is implementing Estonian language policy and state supervision of compliance with the Language Act and other legislation governing language use.

OPEC+ countries boost oil output by 2.31 mln bpd in September but miss targets — IEA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:02:48 UTC
23:02:48 KST

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. OPEC+ countries participating in the oil production restraint agreement increased output by 2.31 million barrels per day (bpd) in September 2026, yet still fell significantly short of their targets, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA).
According to IEA data, the target level for OPEC+ countries voluntarily limiting oil production was 34.45 million bpd in September, while actual output stood at 29.03 million bpd. Thus, the underproduction relative to the target amounted to approximately 5.42 million bpd.
In September, according to the IEA, among seven key OPEC+ nations, Kuwait cut production by 550,000 bpd, Iraq increased it by 520,000 bpd, Saudi Arabia raised output by 2.33 million bpd, Oman increased it by 20,000 bpd, and Russia increased it by 70,000 bpd.
Meanwhile, Kazakhstan and Algeria kept production levels unchanged from the previous month.
Total production across all OPEC+ nations rose by 2 million bpd in September, reaching 34.8 million bpd.

German economy loses momentum as energy costs, shipping disruptions weigh: Government
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:02:32 UTC
23:02:32 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Germany’s economy temporarily lost momentum in the third quarter but remains on a recovery path, with high energy costs and shipping disruptions weighing on activity, the Economy and Energy Ministry said Wednesday.
In its October economic report, the ministry said growth likely slowed following a recovery in the first half as global stockpiling of energy-intensive goods eased and low water levels restricted inland shipping.
Domestic demand is unlikely to provide much support in the near term as higher energy prices erode purchasing power, uncertainty persists and financing costs rise.
Production in the goods-producing sector increased 2% in August from July, adjusted for prices, calendar and seasonal effects. Construction output jumped 9.3%, partly reflecting the completion of a major energy infrastructure project, while industrial output rose 0.6%.
However, industrial production averaged 1.4% below its second-quarter level in July and August, with energy-intensive industries particularly weak.
Manufacturing orders fell 10.6% in August from the previous month, largely reflecting fluctuations in large contracts, including defense procurement. Excluding large orders, the decline was just 0.1%.
Nominal exports of goods and services dropped 2.7% in August, their second consecutive monthly decline, although they remained 6.9% above a year earlier.
Despite weaker activity, business sentiment improved. The ifo business climate index rose for a fifth consecutive month in September to its highest level since May 2023, with companies assessing both current conditions and their outlook more favorably.
Energy inflation weighs on consumers
Annual consumer inflation accelerated to 3.3% in September, driven by an almost 15% increase in energy prices. Core inflation, excluding food and energy, remained at 2.4%.
Food prices rose 0.4%, while services prices increased 2.7%.
The ministry said higher energy costs were increasingly being passed on to consumers, with price pressures expected to persist into winter.
Retail sales rebounded 1.3% in August after falling 3.2% in July, but consumer confidence weakened again. The GfK consumer climate indicator fell to a five-month low for October.
Labor market conditions also deteriorated. Seasonally adjusted unemployment rose by 12,000 in September, while employment declined by 29,000 in August.
With hiring prospects still subdued, the ministry said neither a decline in unemployment nor an increase in employment was expected in the coming months.

Netflix cuts about 6% of jobs in biggest layoff since 2022, WSJ reports
Netflix is cutting about 6% of its workforce, or roughly 1,000 jobs, in its biggest round of layoffs since 2022, the Wall Street Journal reported on Oct 14, citing an e-mail sent to employees.
The streaming giant’s layoffs come as it faces intense competition for users’ time in a consolidated media market.
The bulk of the job cuts would be in the streaming giant’s product, tech, legal and human-resources teams, the report said, citing the e-mail to employees by co-chief executives Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos on the morning of Oct 14.
Netflix did not immediately respond to Reuters’ request for comment.
The company had about 16,000 full-time employees at the end of 2025.
The streaming company has been expanding beyond its subscription business, investing in advertising, live programming and gaming to diversify its revenue sources.
Netflix lost out to Paramount Skydance in the bidding war for Warner Bros Discovery’s streaming and studio assets earlier in 2026.
Paramount completed its US$110 billion (S$141.44 billion) acquisition of Warner Bros earlier in October to form Skydance, a media giant with a portfolio of leading news and film studios. REUTERS

Banks, buildings burn as Albania's capital Tirana erupts into student violence
TIRANA, Oct 14 - Tens of thousands of students stormed the streets of Tirana on Wednesday, setting alight a government building and two banks and hurling stones at police during a protest over rising education costs and corruption.
Police responded with water cannons and tear gas to disperse protesters who started a fire at the ministry of education building, overturned garbage cans and smashed the fronts of local businesses, Reuters footage showed.
A Raiffeisen Bank branch near the education ministry also caught fire, a Reuters witness said.
The protests represent the most violent outburst against Prime Minister Edi Rama, who won a fourth term in office in elections in May last year but has since faced growing discontent at perceived graft surrounding top officials. Protesters also dismiss opposition figures as unpalatable alternatives.
The unrest caps a summer of peaceful protests against Rama, triggered by the proposed development of a luxury resort along Albania's pristine southern coast backed by US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner which has been caught up in legal disputes.
"This is a revolution. We are tired of peaceful protests. We will not stop until Rama resigns," said Lora, a student who declined to give her last name said as she threw rocks at the police.
Others chanted "Resignation" and "Police of crime."
WIDER PROTESTS
Student organisers said the protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, a lack of financial support and employment prospects after graduation.
The unrest is part of a broader wave of student activism sweeping Europe over education and living conditions. In France, high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education.
Albanian media reported that Wednesday's protests spread to universities at Elbasan and Shkodra.
The government condemned the violence.
"Protesting is a legitimate right, but it cannot be used as an excuse for violence, city destruction or ugly fighting in the middle of the road," Deputy Prime Minister Albana Kociu said on Facebook. "I call on students and every honest citizen who believes in the right to protest: Distance yourself from violence and vandalism!"
The police issued a statement calling for calm.
"Any person who uses violence, burns or destroys property, or attacks Police officers, bears individual responsibility and will face the law, in accordance with the offences committed," it said. REUTERS

Full train service between Fredericia and Odense to resume Monday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:00:47 UTC
23:00:47 KST

The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

Signal fault disrupts trains between Copenhagen and Næstved until evening
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:00:44 UTC
23:00:44 KST

A signal fault near Kildebrønde in eastern Zealand is disrupting train services between Copenhagen Central Station and Næstved via Køge.
On Wednesday morning, DSB said passengers should expect longer travel times until 1 p.m. But about an hour before that deadline, the railway operator announced that disruptions would continue until 7 p.m., according to its website.
Banedanmark, which operates and maintains Denmark’s state-owned railway network, told DSB that repair work would not take place until Wednesday night, leading into Thursday.
However, a solution has been found that will allow trains to run normally on the affected section after 7 p.m., even though the fault will not yet have been repaired.
Some trains that usually run via Køge Nord are being diverted through Roskilde instead. These services will not stop between Copenhagen Central Station and Ringsted.
Additional replacement buses were introduced between Køge and Næstved on Wednesday morning to ease pressure on train services. The buses stopped running at noon, and DSB is advising passengers to take the S-train from Copenhagen toward Køge. Trains between Køge and Næstved are running once an hour.
Banedanmark told the Danish news agency Ritzau that a severed cable caused the signal fault. DSB advises passengers to check Rejseplanen, Denmark’s public transport journey planner, before setting off.
Meanwhile, fewer trains are running between Odense and Fredericia through Sunday, October 18, according to DSB. The date is provisional, and services could return to normal earlier or later than expected.
