Excluding UK from ‘Made in Europe’ law will hurt entire EU car industry, Mercedes boss warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:57:03 UTC
22:57:03 KST

Locking the UK out of the EU’s flagship industrial “Made in Europe” legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc, the head of Mercedes-Benz has said.
Speaking in his capacity as president of the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), Ola Källenius said such a move would “weaken the industry on both sides”.
He was speaking just weeks before political leaders hope to reach agreement on the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), potentially keeping the UK car industry out of key contracts in the EU.
The act, known as the Made in Europe law, aims to protect local industry by countering competition from outside the EU.
It is mainly aimed at China, which is now enjoying a £1bn a day trade surplus with the EU, but could cause problems for the EU’s close allies including the UK, Norway, Turkey and Switzerland.
“It does not make any sense … We would hurt our industry in the UK and the EU. That would be a deliberate choice to worsen the competitiveness of your own [EU] industry,” Källenius said at an annual briefing in Brussels on the state of the car industry.
“We are talking about how we industrialise more in Europe, how we build local supply chains, that is what the IAA is all about,” he added.
Andy Burnham has been lobbying hard to get the UK included in the Made in Europe legislation but is hitting resistance, particularly from France.
The prime minister intends to raise it at the UK-EU summit on 20 November and is hoping it is not too late, even though EU leaders are aiming for political agreement on the current text by December.
Last month, the EU urged the UK to follow the bloc and impose tariffs on imported Chinese vehicles, which it introduced in 2024. It argued this would help the UK’s case to be included in Made in Europe as it would align more closely with the EU on key trading sectors.
But the UK business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said on a trip to India that this was not on the cards at the moment.
The ACEA is also lobbying for an urgent suspension of plans to introduce 10% tariffs on UK electric vehicles (EVs) imported to the EU, and EU EVs exported to the UK.
“We are getting very anxious about it. The deadline is in less than three months’ time. We have our feet to the fire in terms of the tariffs. All our manufacturers are worried,” said Jonathan O’Riordan, the ACEA’s international trade director.
The tariff schedule is written into the post-Brexit Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA) as a way of incentivising the industry on both sides of the Channel to speed up the production of batteries, which can represent about 45% of the cost of a new car.
Under the TCA, car exports on both sides are tariff-free if they are mainly made in Europe, but with the EU and the UK unable to produce sufficient electric batteries to compete with China, cars exported to each other’s market would be subject to a 10% tariff from next year.
The tariff was originally due to come into force in 2024 but was suspended for three years to give the car industry more time.
The car industry says it needs a further two- or three-year suspension urgently.
Meanwhile, concern has intensified in the EU in the last three months over China’s trade surplus with the bloc, with a threat of trade barriers leading to an agreement on Friday between Beijing and Brussels to reduce sales of hybrid electric cars by half over four years.
One official said the time to rebalance trade by increasing EU exports was gone. “No amount of champagne [exports] is going to revitalise the relationship [with China],” a senior EU official told a separate trade policy briefing in Brussels.

Two veterans who each lost a lower leg while defending Ukraine have summited Mera Peak in Nepal, reaching an altitude of 6,476 meters (21,247 feet) and dedicating their ascent to Ukrainian service members fighting Russia’s full-scale invasion and those who have died in the war.
Christopher John Park-Greenwood, a former British soldier who served in Ukraine’s military, and Roman Havryliak, a Ukrainian veteran, completed the climb using prosthetic legs as part of an expedition organized with Second Wind, a Ukrainian community supporting service members and veterans with limb loss through adaptive mountain sports.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The expedition began on Oct. 1, Ukraine’s Defenders Day. The climbers dedicated their ascent to those continuing to defend the country and to the memory of those who have given their lives.
According to Second Wind, the team faced demanding high-altitude conditions, including temperatures below freezing, up to three meters of fresh snow and avalanches in close proximity. The multi-day expedition required gradual altitude gain and acclimatization before the final push to the summit.
For Greenwood and Havryliak, Mera Peak marked another milestone in a mountaineering journey that began after their combat injuries. The climb followed their ascent of Mount Ararat in Turkey, which stands at 5,137 meters (16,854 feet), in the summer of 2026.
From combat injuries to high-altitude mountaineering
Both climbers spent more than a year preparing for the expedition through regular training, climbing-gym sessions and increasingly challenging routes in Ukraine’s Carpathian Mountains.
Russian Drones Kill Six in Lutsk, Injure Five in Rivne
Greenwood, originally from Yorkshire, England, is a career soldier who previously served in the British Army and the French Foreign Legion.
Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, he joined the Armed Forces of Ukraine’s (AFU) 73rd Naval Special Operations Centre. He sustained a severe combat injury in 2023 that resulted in the loss of his lower leg.
                                                                                                                                                                         Two veterans summited Mera Peak in Nepal with the support of the Second Wind Foundation team. (Photo courtesy of the Second Wind Foundation)                             
Havryliak, known by the call sign “Hava,” is from the Lviv region. He volunteered to join the AFU following the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion and served as a drone operator with the 80th Separate Air Assault Brigade. He also sustained a severe combat injury that led to the loss of his leg.
After more than a year of treatment and multiple surgeries, Havryliak set himself a new goal: returning to the mountains.
Both veterans subsequently became active members of Second Wind, a charitable foundation and community that brings together Ukrainian service members and veterans who use prostheses, taking part in its training sessions and mountain programs.
The expedition was accompanied by Gennady Gazin, Anna Vozna and Oleksii Aleksieienko, the founders of the organization.
Second Wind grew out of the documentary project Second Wind, which followed five Ukrainian service members who climbed Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa’s highest mountain. The foundation currently runs regular adaptive mountain sports programs in Ukraine and organizes mountain expeditions for its community members.
Ukrainian veterans turn to mountain climbing for rehabilitation
Ukrainian veterans are increasingly taking on mountain-climbing challenges at home and abroad as part of their rehabilitation after severe combat injuries.
Many of these expeditions involve service members who have undergone amputations and climb using prosthetic limbs, demonstrating how adaptive mountaineering can help veterans return to physically demanding activities.
In early 2025, five Ukrainian veterans completed a group ascent of Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa’s highest peak, at 5,895 meters (19,341 feet). The expedition was described as a world first for a group of veterans with combat-related injuries.
The participants included Roman Kolesnyk, known by the call sign “Dobriak,” a veteran of the 3rd Assault Brigade who underwent an amputation after a severe injury; border guard Vladyslav Shatilo, known as “Shatia,” who lost a limb; and Mykhailo Matviiv, or “Grizzly,” a member of the Omega Special Forces Detachment of the National Guard of Ukraine who was injured by a landmine near Vuhledar.
The group also included Oleksandr Mikhov, known as “Ragnar,” an Omega special forces fighter who uses a prosthesis, and a servicewoman known by the call sign “Vysota” (“Height”), who sustained severe injuries twice while serving at the front.
In May 2025, Ukrainian military intelligence veterans Ivan Taran and Oleksandr Dashko, both of whom had undergone major amputations, reached the Everest Base Camp in Nepal at an altitude of approximately 5,400 meters (17,717 feet), using prosthetic limbs. The expedition was organized by Ukrainian mountaineerc Tetiana Yalovchak.
Veterans have also taken on mountain challenges within Ukraine. Volodymyr Voropai, a veteran of the 73rd Naval Special Operations Centre who lost a leg during the war, helped pioneer climbs of Mount Hoverla (2,061 meters, or 6,762 feet) for veterans with amputations.
In October 2026, service member Maksym Bashynskyi, who was wounded near Huliaipole, climbed Mount Vysokyi Verkh in the Carpathians, which stands at 1,176 meters (3,858 feet), as part of the Travel Therapy project. Volunteers assisted him using a specialized all-terrain mobility cart known as “Julietta.”
Group ascents of Mount Hoverla have also brought together dozens of veterans. Among the initiatives reported in late 2025 and 2026 were a climb involving 50 veterans from the Kyiv region and an ascent by Special Operations Forces (SSO) personnel who carried a fellow veteran with an amputation to the summit of Ukraine’s highest mountain.

EU's new Lebanon security mission explained, and what's next
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:56:41 UTC
22:56:41 KST

Breadcrumb
EU's new security mission to Lebanon explained, and what's next
The European Union has agreed to establish a new security mission in Lebanon as the country faces mounting uncertainty over the future of UN peacekeepers amid continued Israeli attacks and its occupation of parts of the south.
Approved on Monday at the request of Lebanese authorities, the mission will operate under the EU's Common Security and Defence Policy, with an initial mandate of three years.
The move comes as the United States opposes extending the mandate of the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), which expires on 31 December 2026, raising concerns about a potential security vacuum along Lebanon's southern border.
While the European mission is intended to strengthen Lebanon's army and security institutions, it will not replace UNIFIL or carry out peacekeeping operations.
So what exactly will the new mission do, when will it begin, and what does it mean for Lebanon's security?
What is the EU's new mission in Lebanon?
The mission is a European initiative designed to strengthen Lebanon's security institutions, improve border management and support the Lebanese state's ability to exercise authority across its territory.
It was established by the Council of the European Union following a formal request from Lebanese authorities and will operate under a unified political mandate.
Unlike a conventional peacekeeping force, the mission will not deploy troops to patrol Lebanese territory or monitor ceasefire violations.
Instead, it will provide technical assistance, specialised training and strategic advice to the Lebanese Armed Forces and Internal Security Forces.
Its work will extend beyond southern Lebanon, with a broader focus on strengthening state institutions and improving security capabilities nationwide.
EU sources told The New Arab that the initiative is separate from ongoing discussions about UNIFIL's future.
When will the mission begin and how long will it last?
The mission could begin operations in late 2026 or early 2027, according to EU sources who spoke to TNA.
However, no final start date has been agreed, and the number of personnel who will participate remains undecided.
The EU is expected to announce further details as decisions are finalised.
The mission has been granted an initial three-year mandate, although the precise arrangements for its deployment and activities have yet to be confirmed.
Unlike UNIFIL, which operates under UN Security Council resolutions, the European mission does not require Security Council approval because it was established through a bilateral agreement between Lebanon and the EU.
What will the European mission actually do?
The mission will have two main components, military and civilian, working under a single political mandate.
The military component will support the Lebanese army through training and advisory assistance in several areas, including border security, maritime operations, intelligence gathering, surveillance and reconnaissance.
It will also help strengthen the army's ability to monitor and control land borders, combat smuggling and improve coordination between security units.
The civilian component will focus on Lebanon's Internal Security Forces, providing specialised training to improve operational capabilities and establish sustainable training programmes.
These will cover areas such as cybercrime investigations, anti-smuggling operations and internal security.
The mission will also help improve security management at Lebanese ports, including the Port of Beirut.
The broader objective is to strengthen Lebanon's state institutions and contribute to long-term stability in line with UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
Will the EU mission replace UNIFIL?
No. European officials have explicitly ruled out the mission replacing UNIFIL or serving as the alternative international force currently under discussion.
The two missions have fundamentally different responsibilities.
UNIFIL was established in 1978 under UN Security Council Resolutions 425 and 426, with its mandate expanded following the 2006 war between Israel and Hezbollah under Resolution 1701.
Its responsibilities include monitoring the cessation of hostilities, supporting the Lebanese army and helping the government extend its authority across southern Lebanon.
UNIFIL peacekeepers maintain a physical presence throughout the south, including along the Blue Line separating Lebanon and Israel.
They conduct patrols, monitor military activity and work alongside Lebanese forces.
The EU mission, by contrast, will not carry out operational deployments, patrol borders or monitor ceasefire violations.
EU sources said the missions would also have different geographical areas of focus, with the European initiative extending beyond southern Lebanon.
EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas emphasised the distinction during her visit to Beirut last week, while stressing the importance of avoiding a security vacuum if UNIFIL withdraws.
Why is UNIFIL's future under threat?
UNIFIL's mandate is due to expire on 31 December 2026, amid US opposition to extending the peacekeeping operation.
Washington and Israel have criticised UNIFIL's performance, arguing that it failed to prevent Hezbollah from building its military infrastructure in southern Lebanon.
The United States has also pushed for new security arrangements, including direct military coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli armies.
Lebanon has resisted such proposals, instead calling for UNIFIL's mandate to be extended or for a replacement international force to operate under UN authority.
Lebanese MP Najat Aoun Saliba told The New Arab that 14 of the Security Council's 15 members were prepared to support extending UNIFIL's mandate, but Washington remained opposed.
Saliba is among 86 Lebanese MPs who submitted a legal memorandum calling on the Security Council to reconsider Resolution 2790, particularly the timing and mechanism of UNIFIL's withdrawal.
She warned that implementing the resolution under current conditions would be extremely difficult because Israeli forces continue occupying Lebanese territory.
One particular concern involves the transfer of UNIFIL positions and facilities to the Lebanese army.
Saliba argued that where these positions remain under Israeli occupation, transferring them to Israeli forces instead would effectively consolidate that occupation.
What happens to southern Lebanon if UNIFIL leaves?
The potential withdrawal has raised serious concerns about border monitoring, civilian protection and the ability of the Lebanese army to fill the gap.
Saliba warned that more than 10,000 residents of three southern Lebanese villages, Debel, Ain Ebel and Rmeish, could become completely isolated without an alternative to UNIFIL.
The peacekeeping force currently helps maintain a humanitarian corridor serving these communities, which have faced increasing pressure as Israeli occupation expands around their villages.
Residents are also dealing with the weakening presence of Lebanese state institutions and limited access to essential services.
Saliba warned that UNIFIL's departure would leave important border positions along the Blue Line without international observers.
"UNIFIL is responsible for the border points demarcated by the Blue Line," she said.
"If it leaves the south, these points that safeguard Lebanon's borders will be left open and unattended."
She stressed that the central concern was the absence of international monitors to help protect Lebanon's borders.
Could another international force replace UNIFIL?
Discussions are continuing over the possibility of establishing an alternative international force, although no agreement has been reached.
Lebanon wants any replacement to operate under the United Nations, maintaining international oversight of the southern border.
Washington has not ruled out an alternative force, according to Saliba, but the negotiations remain complicated by US and Israeli demands for new security arrangements.
Among the proposals is direct coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries, an arrangement Beirut opposes.
The EU mission will operate independently of these negotiations and will not assume the responsibilities of any future international peacekeeping force.
For Lebanon, the European initiative could provide valuable long-term assistance to its military and security institutions.

Who met Egypt's intelligence chief? Israeli security officials all deny receiving pre-Oct. 7 warning

2026-10-14

One by one, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the former head of the National Security Council and senior Israeli security officials all denied Wednesday any involvement in a meeting with whoever arrived at Ben Gurion Airport aboard an Egyptian aircraft on September 26, 2023, just 11 days before the October 7 massacre. According to reports, Egypt's then-intelligence chief Abbas Kamel was the man on the plane and he came to warn those he met of "a major attack being planned by Hamas."
In an interview with Channel 14 on Tuesday night, Netanyahu acknowledged, contrary to his previous statements, that Kamel had indeed arrived in Israel. However, he insisted that the Egyptian intelligence chief "did not meet with me because I was at a memorial ceremony for fallen IDF soldiers."
Former Mossad chief David Barnea and former Shin Bet director Ronen Bar also said they had not met with Kamel. Both said they believed reports of the visit were fake news, arguing that it would have been unlikely for Kamel to visit Israel without meeting them.
The Mossad said no representative of the agency had met with Kamel.
Ghassan Alian, who was then coordinator of government activities in the territories and was heavily involved in efforts to maintain calm in Gaza, also denied meeting Kamel that day. Former National Security Council head Tzachi Hanegbi similarly said he had not met with the Egyptian official.
Israel's embassy in Egypt, another body that maintains contact with the Egyptian intelligence chief, was excluded from the meeting.
Two days after the October 7 massacre, Ynet journalist Smadar Perry reported, following an Associated Press report about an Egyptian warning, that Kamel had contacted the Prime Minister's Office and conveyed a message warning of "something unusual, a massive operation" expected to originate from Gaza.
The Prime Minister's Office denied the report at the time. Yet, at least as things appear now, it made no urgent effort over the following three years to establish whether any messages had indeed been conveyed by the Egyptian side, even if not directly to Netanyahu.
As for Netanyahu's claim that he could not have met whoever arrived on the aircraft because he was attending a ceremony marking the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War at Mount Herzl, The Atlantic reported that the ceremony took place about two hours after Kamel's arrival.
Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana suggested Wednesday morning that "it was one of the heads of the security establishment." However, the IDF chief of staff, Mossad director, Shin Bet chief and police commissioner were all seated alongside Netanyahu and President Isaac Herzog at the ceremony.
'Reinforcing the deep state narrative'
A former senior Israeli official commenting on the reports Wednesday said: "It is unlikely that Abbas Kamel would come to Israel to meet with anyone below the level of prime minister. Netanyahu has met him before, contrary to what he said on Channel 14. He also met his successor, Hassan Rashad, last year.
"In any case, it is clear that when the Egyptian intelligence chief arrives, a minister and President el-Sissi's No. 2, he meets at the very least with the prime minister and also with the president. It is unlikely that Abbas Kamel did not meet the prime minister. You cannot hide something like that."
The former official continued: "When a senior foreign official arrives, his aircraft enters a special route managed by the Israel Airports Authority. There are cameras and digital location records. Bibi is manipulating things here and laying the groundwork for his continued portrayal of himself as a victim: 'Why wasn't I informed?'
"Netanyahu is reinforcing the deep state narrative. But it is not difficult to check these things. The prime minister is claiming there was a breach of trust. He says a plane arrived. For years, I didn't care. Now I'm saying it happened.
"So the attorney general can order all the digital evidence to be seized, examine the computer records and see who was in a restricted area that day. A plane lands, and its crew is supposed to be registered. Did anyone get off the plane? Did anyone come to meet them?"
Netanyahu's son, Yair Netanyahu, responded with a post on X.
"To all the 'left-wing journalists,' stop your propaganda already! My father was referring to the fact that a prime minister does not meet the intelligence chief of another country 'alone,' as the blood libel against him claimed.
"The meeting they showed from 2021 with the Egyptian intelligence chief also included his Israeli counterparts, such as the head of the National Security Council, Israel's intelligence minister and others.
"During the Egyptian intelligence chief's one-hour visit to Ben Gurion Airport in 2023, 11 days before the massacre, my father was at a ceremony commemorating the Yom Kippur War."
Yair Netanyahu concluded: "Now the question is: Who did meet with the Egyptian intelligence chief at the time? And why has this been concealed from the prime minister and the public for three years? Why are they still refusing the prime minister's request to reveal who met the Egyptian intelligence chief in Israel?"
'We do not dismiss any threat'
Last month, The Atlantic reported that Kamel had arrived in Israel for an exceptionally brief visit on September 26, 2023, during which he "warned that Hamas was preparing a major attack and urged Israel to introduce economic relief measures to prevent escalation."
According to the magazine's investigation, a chartered aircraft linked to Egyptian intelligence services landed at Ben Gurion Airport and remained in Israel for just 67 minutes before departing for Cairo.
A former Israeli official who spoke to the magazine said the Egyptian intelligence chief's decision to make such a short and unusual visit should itself have conveyed the urgency of the warning.
"The messenger was the message," the official said.
Approximately two hours after the Egyptian aircraft landed, Netanyahu attended a ceremony in Jerusalem marking the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War. "As a central lesson from that war, we do not dismiss any threat," Netanyahu said at the time.
The Wall Street Journal separately reported that Kamel called Netanyahu in early October 2023 to warn him of an impending attack from the Gaza Strip, after two earlier Egyptian warnings had gone unheeded.
"Kamel began to grow concerned," the newspaper reported, lending further support to Smadar Perry's reporting in Ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth in the days following the massacre about an Egyptian warning.
Netanyahu, however, continues to deny that he spoke with Kamel.

A North Korean Missile Already Supplied to Russia Just Got a Much Longer Reach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:55:18 UTC
22:55:18 KST

- Category
- World
A North Korean Missile Already Supplied to Russia Just Got a Much Longer Reach
North Korea launched a KN-30 ballistic missile more than 910 kilometers during an October 12 test, demonstrating substantially greater range than in the weapon’s earliest known trials.
The same missile type has previously been transferred to Russia and could potentially be used in strikes against Ukraine, according to Militarnyi on October 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
North Korea’s state-run KCNA released images from the launch but did not publicly identify the missile or disclose its range.
Based on photographs of the five-axle mobile launcher, the secretary general of the Korea Defense and Security Forum identified the weapon as the Hwasong-11Da-2.5, also known in Western reporting as the KN-30.
The KN-30 is a solid-fueled short-range ballistic missile and an enlarged member of North Korea’s Hwasong-11 family. Pyongyang has claimed that the weapon can carry a 2.5-ton warhead, although that figure has not been independently confirmed.
At least two ballistic missiles were launched toward the Sea of Japan on October 12. Japan’s Defense Ministry said one traveled roughly 220 kilometers, while the second flew more than 910 kilometers and reached an altitude of about 70 kilometers.
KCNA said the test was intended to verify improvements made to key components of the missile system. North Korea did not specify which components had been upgraded, leaving open the question of whether the longer flight reflected changes to propulsion, guidance, payload configuration, or another part of the weapon.
The reported 910-kilometer flight is particularly notable compared with earlier KN-30 tests. When North Korea first tested the missile in March 2021, Pyongyang claimed a range of 600 kilometers, while Japanese and South Korean military assessments placed the actual distance at roughly 420 to 450 kilometers.
The KN-30 was first publicly displayed during a military parade in Pyongyang on January 14, 2021. It is launched from a mobile transporter on a five-axle wheeled chassis and uses a solid-fuel motor, allowing it to be prepared and fired more quickly than liquid-fueled ballistic missiles.
Russia has already received KN-30 missiles from North Korea. Their presence in Russian stocks has raised concern that Moscow could add the weapon to the growing inventory of North Korean ballistic missiles used or available for strikes against Ukraine.
Earlier, reports emerged that more than 50% of the identified electronic components in North Korean Hwasong-11 (KN-23) ballistic missiles recovered in Ukraine were found to be fake.

A New Report Sheds Light on the Secretive Race to Build Self-Improving AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:55:01 UTC
22:55:01 KST

For months, Anthropic and OpenAI have warned that AI may be on the verge of improving itself.
This tipping point, known as “recursive self-improvement,” or RSI, could mean that new AI capabilities arrive faster than ever. But the advent of RSI might also be highly perilous for humanity, potentially marking the stage at which developers lose control of AI systems entirely.
Even as AI companies warn about the potential dangers of RSI, they have shared remarkably little about how they’re pursuing it. A new report, published Wednesday by the firm Gladstone AI, attempts to change that. It gives one of the most detailed pictures yet of how RSI could work and how AI companies are progressing toward it. The report is based on what the authors say are conversations with half a dozen researchers inside the top AI companies.
The report, exclusively shared with TIME ahead of its publication, emphasizes that AI companies are “actively working on” automating all parts of the AI development pipeline, including generating new ideas, running experiments to test those ideas, and interpreting the results. Most of the insiders Gladstone spoke to “believe RSI will start within the next 3 to 12 months, and possibly sooner, assuming there’s no U.S. government intervention or slowdown,” the report states.
Read More: Inside the Race to Make AI Build Itself
“There's a fair amount of [disaster] prepping and bio-bunker purchasing going on” among these researchers, says Edouard Harris, Gladstone’s chief technology officer.
The aim of the report, Gladstone’s executives tell TIME, is to give lawmakers a better understanding of how RSI works, and, in turn, a greater ability to regulate it.
“Our goal here was to define recursive self-improvement well enough that people can have a sane conversation about it, especially in Washington,” says Jeremie Harris, Gladstone’s CEO. (The pair are brothers.) “There are all these bills proposed to ban superintelligence, which are really interesting attempts to grapple with this problem. But what we're more interested in is: what is the process that needs to be regulated?”
How RSI could work
The report gives a simplified outline of how the AI research pipeline currently operates inside AI companies—and how those companies are beginning to automate the process.
For the first phase of training an AI model, known as pretraining, much of the emphasis is on finding ways to squeeze more intelligence out of a model with less and less computing power, known in the industry as “compute.”
The AI companies take a portfolio approach to testing these ideas. Researchers allocate a small amount of compute to each idea, using it to train a series of models. The models that reliably perform better as they scale up are selected for another round of training, using larger amounts of compute.
Companies don’t have infinite compute, which limits the number of promising ideas they can test at larger scales. This means that even if AI companies can train an AI that is able to generate ideas that seem promising, it matters greatly how many bad ideas it generates simultaneously. If companies need to spend huge amounts of time or compute filtering good AI-generated ideas from bad ones, it might make sense to continue to rely on human researchers with sound intuition.
Conversely, AI companies with access to more compute are able to test more ideas—potentially allowing them to reach RSI first. With more compute to throw at experiments, companies may also be likelier to catch ideas that the Gladstone report describes as the rarest and most desired by AI companies: those that perform better as more compute is thrown at them, even if they appear to be duds at smaller scales.
Being able to tell when those ideas are found—and particularly whether AI is helping find them—“is just such a critical part of this process that right now legislators have essentially zero visibility into,” says Jeremie Harris.
One of the traits that makes regulating RSI tricky is that it is a gradual process. “This is actually one of the reasons why we went to pains to describe it in so much detail,” says Edouard Harris. “So that it is possible to point to a part of this process and say: a human needs to be there.”

Janonis noted that the court was co-operating with police officers and had provided them with the video recordings they had requested.

The minister welcomed the man's arrest but criticised the officers over his escape.

22:53:59 KST

Russian forces attacked Epicentr’s hub in Khmelnytskyi, a city in western Ukraine, 10 times on 13 October, starting five large fires that destroyed about 85% of the goods stored inside, the company said.
Epicentr is a Ukrainian chain of home-improvement and household-goods stores. The attack adds pressure to Ukraine’s logistics network, already damaged by Russian strikes. On 10 September, Ukrainian entrepreneur Ruslan Shostak, co-owner of the popular retail chains Eva and Varus, said that 2.1 million square meters of Ukraine’s modern warehouse space had been destroyed since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. He put the country’s total modern warehouse space at approximately 5 million square meters. The strike on the hub came the same day Russia opened a barrage of 39 ballistic missiles on Ukraine’s power grid.
About 30 drones in the sky kept the fire from being put out, and the hub burned down completely overnight, Epicentr said. None of its people were hurt, the company said.
“The most important thing is that all our people are alive,” Epicentr wrote.
Russia had earlier completely destroyed Epicentr’s two largest logistics complexes, in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast, the company said. The Khmelnytskyi hub had remained effectively its only surviving large warehouse complex. Goods were sent from there to the company’s shopping centers, and people worked there every day “so that millions of Ukrainians could buy what they need,” it wrote. Epicentr described every such attack as a blow to Ukrainian businesses’ ability to operate, pay wages, preserve jobs, and support the country’s economy.
Epicentr’s earlier losses
Epicentr said in August that 10 of its shopping centers had been completely destroyed since February 2022. Another 13 retail sites had been damaged, and one in Melitopol remained under Russian occupation, it said. At the time, the company operated 70 shopping centers, down from 80 at the end of 2021.
Earlier, during a Russian missile attack overnight on 5 August, Epicentr’s logistics center in Kyiv burned down completely, Epicentr’s Yulia Chudnovets said. The company’s ceramic tile plant in Kalynivka, one of the largest in Ukraine, was effectively lost, she said. One employee was killed and three were injured, she added.
A fourth Ukrainian pharmaceutical warehouse has burned in a Russian strike since the start of the month
On 25 May 2024, Russian airstrikes on an Epicentr hypermarket in Kharkiv killed 19 people, Interior Minister Ihor Klymenko said.
Attacks across Khmelnytskyi Oblast
Fires broke out at enterprises in Khmelnytskyi and Shepetivka districts on 13 October, Serhii Tiurin, head of the Khmelnytskyi Oblast Military Administration, reported. He did not name the enterprises. On 14 October, Tiurin said one of the fires had been put out, and crews were still fighting the other. Khmelnytskyi Mayor Oleksandr Symchyshyn said six people were injured in Khmelnytskyi district that day, where Russian strikes damaged private enterprises, a gas station, and a medical facility.

Van Essen dismisses farmers’ alternative nitrogen emissions plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:53:58 UTC
22:53:58 KST

Van Essen dismisses farmers’ alternative nitrogen emissions plan
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen has dismissed an alternative plan to solve the nitrogen pollution crisis presented by farmers’ organisations, arguing it would lead to legal challenges.
Four organisations under the banner of the Landbouw Alliantie (“Agricultural Alliance”) called for the cabinet to adopt its more limited programme of reforms as a basis for negotiations.
The farmers want the Netherlands to implement a German-style system with exclusion zones of 250m around protected nature areas rather than 500m or 1,000m, so that fewer farmers would have to reduce their cattle herds.
But Van Essen said the plans were not a realistic route out of the crisis. “The Netherlands will not end the impasse by weakening measures in places where nature needs it most and at the same time relaxing the rules for permits.”
He said the package of measures announced by the government in June remained “the basis” for discussions with the agriculture sector. The left-wing opposition party Pro, whose support is key to passing the legislation, has also warned that the plan “must not be weakened”.
“Paper problem”
Sieta van Keimpema, of the Dutch Dairy Board (DDB), one of four organisations that make up the Landbouw Alliantie, said the government should rewrite the rules to allow more generous limits, as in Germany. “It is a paper problem, so we should be able to come up with a paper solution,” she said.
But farmers also face the prospect of legal challenges from environmental groups such as Mobilisation for the Environment, which has raised cases in 10 provinces against 130 farms that have breached nitrogen deposition limits.
Van Essen’s plans aim to reduce nitrogen compound emissions from farming by up to 46% and by 50% for other high-polluting sectors such as heavy industry and transport.
The most vulnerable conservation zones will be protected by 1km exclusion zones, where farmers will have to abide by strict pollution limits, while another 85 nature areas will be surrounded by 500m zones.
The reforms were triggered by a Council of State ruling in 2019 that struck down the system for issuing nature permits for large construction projects such as roads, suburbs and extensions to farms.
Until then permits were issued if applicants could show that the nitrogen generated during construction would be offset by efficiencies made by the finished project. But the Council of State said nitrogen limits had to be adhered to during building work as well.

Microsoft, OpenAI executives call for AI safety laws, says warnings alone are not enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:53:15 UTC
22:53:15 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Microsoft Vice Chair and President Brad Smith on Wednesday called for new artificial intelligence safety laws, saying tech companies must prevent harm rather than simply warn of risks.
Speaking at the International AI Summit 2026 in Ireland, Smith said AI capabilities had advanced faster than protections.
“The world here in Europe or anywhere does not expect our industry simply to warn about what could go wrong. They expect us to prevent it. They expect us to take action,” he said.
“And if we need to slow down, then it is up to each company and each leader to slow down.”
Describing 2026 as “a sobering year for AI safety,” Smith cited reports of rogue AI agents hacking networks and AI worms targeting connected homes.
“There are more safety rules for a carton of milk than for AI. There are more safety rules for your oven than for AI,” he said.
He urged the industry to overcome resistance to regulation and to back incident reporting, notification of victims of AI-enabled breaches, and independent evaluations with findings shared with governments and customers.
“But we need law. We need regulation. It needs to be sensible. It needs to be balanced. It needs to take into account innovation,” Smith said.
“We need to recognize that the power of AI has moved faster than the safety for it. Safety needs to catch up.” 
'We need to make sure the defenders have the tools'
Also speaking at the event, OpenAI Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar supported cooperation among leading AI developers, saying the company had called for global regulation.
Friar said OpenAI is withholding an unreleased model while doing further safety and alignment work, but cautioned against slowing development so sharply that cyber defenders lose ground.
“So the folks with malicious intent have the tools. So we need to make sure the defenders have the tools,” she said.
She said OpenAI had used AI to identify vulnerabilities in its own infrastructure.
“We found the vulnerabilities, we patched them at machine speed,” Friar said.
“Selling fear is not a good way to come to the world. We have to sell solutions and solutions that feel transparent, open, honest, and so on.”

Ukrainian Il-76 spotted leaving Saudi airport near Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:53:03 UTC
22:53:03 KST

- A Ukrainian Air Force Il-76MD flew from Sharurah, near Saudi Arabia’s border with Yemen, toward Istanbul on Oct. 12, flight-tracking data shows.
- Neither Ukraine nor Saudi Arabia has explained the flight, which follows Ukraine’s deployment of counter-drone specialists to Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states.
A Ukrainian Air Force Il-76MD heavy transport aircraft was tracked on Oct. 12 flying out of Sharurah, a Saudi town in Najran Province near the border with Yemen, in a rare appearance of a Ukrainian military cargo plane in the south of the kingdom.
Flight-tracking data shared by the open-source account Egypt’s Intel Observer shows the four-engine jet, registration 76661, heading north over the Red Sea at about 10,350 m (33,975 feet) at 17:28 UTC on its way from Sharurah to Istanbul’s Sabiha Gökçen airport, roughly an hour and 48 minutes after takeoff. The account said the aircraft had earlier flown to Sharurah from Lviv in western Ukraine, a leg not visible in the published screenshot.
Neither Kyiv nor Riyadh has said what the aircraft carried or why it landed at Sharurah. The open-source account speculated that it may have delivered Ukrainian interceptor drones or military specialists, possibly to support Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, and described Sharurah as their main supply hub, a claim that has not been confirmed by any government.
Sharurah’s airport serves both civilian and military traffic and sits close to the Yemeni frontier. It was one of seven southern airports Saudi Arabia shut to civilian flights in March 2015, when the kingdom began its air campaign against the Iran-aligned Houthi movement in Yemen.
Ukraine already has a documented military footprint in the Gulf. After Iran launched drone and missile strikes on Gulf states during the war that began in March 2026, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had sent more than 200 counter-drone specialists to the region, and later put the number at 228 across five partners, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Jordan. Zelensky signed a defense agreement with Saudi Arabia during a Gulf visit in the spring, and Ukrainian officials have offered partners interceptor drones built to bring down Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones.
According to information obtained by The Defence Blog, Ukrainian specialists are helping Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region defend against hostile drone strikes, and are also training local forces in new tactics for employing attack drones.
That work has drawn threats from Tehran. In March, an Iranian member of parliament said Ukraine’s support to Gulf states made it Iran’s “legitimate war target.”
The Il-76MD is a Soviet-designed strategic airlifter able to carry about 40 tonnes (88,000 pounds) of cargo, and the Ukrainian Air Force operates only a small number of them. Ukrainian military Il-76 flights abroad are usually tied to cargo pickups, equipment deliveries or the movement of personnel.
The routing through Istanbul fits a flight path north over the Red Sea and Turkey back toward Ukraine, though the tracking data does not show the aircraft’s final destination after Sabiha Gökçen or whether it returned empty.
What the aircraft unloaded or picked up at Sharurah, and whether the flight was linked to Ukraine’s counter-drone mission in Saudi Arabia or to the conflict in Yemen, remains unconfirmed.

Russia’s internet shutdowns push state firms back to landline phones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:52:44 UTC
22:52:44 KST

State procurement of landline telephones tripled in the first eight months of 2026 as mobile internet outages hit nearly 80% of the country. Rostelecom’s chief urged Russians to keep one at home “like a fire extinguisher".
Russian state-owned companies spent more than three times as much on landline telephones in the first eight months this year as in the same period in 2025, as mobile internet shutdowns affecting nearly 80% of the country push ministries and businesses to seek alternatives to disrupted networks.
Procurement data cited by the Russian business daily Vedomosti show spending at 118 million roubles (€1.26 million) from January through August, with the number of purchase tenders up 12.5%.
Purchases are concentrated in the country’s largest business and infrastructure hubs.
Market participants told Vedomosti that the surge was driven by the restrictions, a shift by Russian ministries and companies to domestically produced software-based PBX systems after Western vendors withdrew from the Russian market following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and demand for secure communications channels.
Russia began systematically shutting down mobile internet access in May 2025, when services went offline in more than 40 regions ahead of Victory Day celebrations. What were initially episodic outages quickly became routine.
An independent monitoring project recorded 655 mobile internet outages in June 2025, rising to 2,099 in July, a figure that exceeded the worldwide total for the entire previous year, according to analysts.
The disruptions have hit banking, taxi services, food delivery and navigation, particularly in rural areas.
The authorities have justified the shutdowns as a defence against Ukrainian drones, which they say are guided via mobile internet signals.
Experts have disputed this, saying drones can fly preset routes without a network connection, and the shutdowns have reached regions far from the front line.
In March, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the presidential administration “uses landline telephones” when asked how restrictions in central Moscow affect the work of the president’s office.
Shortly after, head of state telecoms company Rostelecom Mikhail Oseyevsky urged Russians to return to fixed lines.
“Like a fire extinguisher, there should be one in every home," Oseyevsky said.
Russia has approximately 12.2 landline telephones per 100 residents. In Moscow, around 2 million households use fixed lines provided by MGTS, the city’s main telephone operator.
Across the country, there are about 17.4 million urban household landline connections.
The Ministry of Economic Development forecasts that the number of all landlines will fall to between 8.2 and 8.5 per 100 residents by 2029.

"This is incredible. I never expected a robot to do kung fu so well, almost like a real person," the university student from Ecuador told Xinhua in an interview.
Valarezo and her friends also planned to have afternoon tea at a nearby restaurant, where nearly 20 robots of different types work together to provide services, from greeting guests to cooking, serving and cleaning up after meals.
"We just couldn't wait to try," Valarezo said. "Everything here feels so futuristic!"
The three were among a growing number of global tourists drawn to China not only by the country's ancient wonders and culinary delights, but also by its futuristic intelligent robots, as the country's artificial intelligence (AI) boom turns cutting-edge technology into a new tourist hook.
During the week-long National Day holiday in early October, multiple Chinese cities rolled out robot-themed events and AI-powered experiences that became unexpected hits among visitors.
In east China's Shanghai, a street fair dedicated to embodied AI drew crowds, with foreign tourists seen posing for photos with humanoid robots. In tech hub Shenzhen in south China, the Huaqiangbei electronics market attracted overseas shoppers eager to try AI translation glasses and flying devices. Similar scenes played out in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, where robot shop managers greeted customers and introduced products.
Official data shows that foreign nationals made almost 61.29 million border crossings in the January-August period this year, up 19.5 percent from the same period in 2025. Over the National Day holiday week, visits by foreign tourists also maintained an upward trend, increasing 5.4 percent from last year.
For Anna Seferta and Thomas Drayton, a young couple from the United Kingdom aged 24 and 29, Robot Mall in Beijing was a must-stop. Drawn by online clips of humanoid robots running a half marathon in Beijing in April, they decided to see it for themselves.
"We think it's very advanced. We've never seen anything like this in the U.K.," Seferta said, highlighting that she was mostly impressed by the hospital section. "The robot arm helps cut surgery down by five hours, and the exoskeletons for old people would be very good. All these applications are rewarding."
Launched in 2025 in the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area, also known as E-Town, the mall is the world's first 4S store for embodied AI robots.
It displays more than 100 of China's most advanced robot products across fields like medical care, elderly care, entertainment, logistics and industry, turning sci-fi fantasy into an experience within arm's reach.
Inside the mall's exhibition hall, visitors can interact with a wide range of robots. They can grab a cup of robot-made latte with their own image printed in the foam, ask a humanoid robot resembling Albert Einstein questions about almost any topic, or join a tabletop drift car race in which speed depends on their brainwaves.
"International visitors are a common sight here," said Yang Song, an on-site technical supporter at the mall. "They enjoy robot boxing and soccer the most. Many find it interesting to control robot players in competitive games."
The mall did not land in E-Town by chance. Home to over 300 leading robotics companies, E-Town has put the whole district to work as a testing ground: self-driving cars, robot restaurants, robot elderly care stations and the world's first humanoid robot half marathon have all taken root there, alongside Beijing's largest public AI computing platform.
The area is working to build a global AI hub, with its core AI industries projected to surpass 200 billion yuan (about 29.74 billion U.S. dollars) in scale by 2030.
E-Town's rise mirrors the country's broader momentum. China's robotics industry has developed a complete industrial chain covering key chips, components and complete machines. By the end of June, China had completed or brought into operation more than 70 robot training facilities, with over 40 others under construction or on the drawing board.
This growing network is preparing more machines for roles beyond the factory floor, and beyond the country's borders. In the first half of 2026, Chinese manufacturers accounted for 97 percent of humanoid robot shipments worldwide, according to a report released at the 2026 World Robot Conference.
Among the visitors to E-Town was Phillip Sepulveda, a 34-year-old photographer from New York. The young man has since childhood suffered from a neurological condition caused by a tumor. Touring the exhibition hall in a wheelchair, he was drawn to a hiking exoskeleton on display.
"The exoskeleton is the sort of thing that would help me a lot," he said. "There are many products now, devices for the hips, for the knees, but we are looking for something for the whole leg."
His father, Jorge Sepulveda, a physician, photographed the product information and said the family was interested in further research.
"We came to see medical devices for mobility, like exoskeletons. It seems China is investing a lot in AI," the father noted, stressing the importance of global cooperation in this rising industry. "AI could be dangerous, as agreed by the CEOs of some AI companies. But if governments and the world cooperate, maybe we can prevent the dangers of it and use it to benefit more people."
For the family, the visit was about more than sightseeing. They left the mall hoping that somewhere in China's expanding robotics industry, they might find a device that could help Phillip walk more easily.
It is a hope that speaks to something broader. Technology is ultimately about changing lives for the better. ■

Two scenarios for the Yemen war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:50:28 UTC
22:50:28 KST

Two scenarios for the Yemen war
What comes next is either a retreat for the Houthis or a war of attrition.
The attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi Arabia have pushed the war in Yemen to a new level. The targeting of civilian infrastructure, including airports, which has killed at least a dozen people and injured hundreds, has left no room to maintain the “red lines” that previously outlined the limits of escalation.
This is a reckless gamble by the Houthis which is not in their interest. They are aware that the retaliation will be fierce, yet they continue to attack Saudi Arabia to fulfil Iran’s agenda that seeks heightened tensions before the United States midterms.
Given the motivation to escalate, the present situation has the potential to develop into two scenarios: A major region-wide operation against the Houthis or a war of attrition.
Scenario one: A united front against the Houthis
In response to the Houthi escalation, Saudi Arabia is striving to garner maximum international support while deepening its regional and international alliances. The aim is to come up with a united front capable of taking on what has become a regional threat.
Riyadh is certainly looking to its Gulf neighbours who, themselves, are impacted by the continuing conflict in the region. There is a collective realisation that everyone is in grave danger, not just Saudi Arabia.
Therefore, Gulf states – perhaps with the exception of Oman – will support Riyadh both directly and indirectly in the fighting in Yemen.
Pakistan and Turkiye are also likely to join the front, having signed with Saudi Arabia a defence agreement known as the Mecca Pact. The pact is to be ratified by the Turkish parliament in the next few days, opening the way for Turkish military deployment in support of Saudi Arabia. Meanwhile, indirect involvement by Turkiye and Pakistan, along with logistical and intelligence support, appears to be already well under way.
A US intervention is also possible, although it seems unlikely before the US midterms, as military engagements in the Middle East remain unpopular among US voters.
A region-wide coalition can help support the counteroffensive of the forces loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government already under way. This could give the necessary push to retake the western coastal region, including areas beyond Bab al-Mandeb and Dhubab.
Such gains could ease pressure on Red Sea shipping and potentially shift the military balance in favour of the government. The opening of additional fronts across other Yemeni cities and governorates could stretch Houthi forces, disperse their resources, and increase the likelihood of further government advances.
Retaking Sanaa could also be on the horizon. The primary obstacle delaying the Yemeni government’s recapture of the city is internal discord among the various factions within the government itself, compounded by negative external interference that exacerbates these rifts and weakens the collective effort to confront the Houthis.
Recent measures taken by the government, specifically efforts to unify its decision-making and consolidate its military operations command, have yielded noticeable progress on the ground. However, achieving the ultimate objective of retaking Sanaa requires sustained effort and focused determination.
If government forces make substantial gains, that could force the Houthis to offer concessions in exchange for a pause in fighting. They have done that before. Their purpose would not be to seek peace but to get enough breathing room to regroup and eventually go back to fighting. Negotiators should keep that in mind when approaching talks with the Houthis.
Scenario two: A war of attrition
If the Saudi-led coalition and the Yemeni government succumb to internal divisions and disagreements, this may slow progress against the Houthis. This would allow the Houthi fighters to hold on to their positions while increasing their pressure on the strategic town of Taiz and maintaining the campaign against civilian targets in Saudi Arabia.
Such a development could further complicate the conflict, increase civilian casualties and displacement, and prolong the war without producing a decisive military outcome.
This will have a significant economic impact on Saudi Arabia and complicate the implementation of its development goals, as it would have to prioritise defence spending.
The rest of the Gulf economies will also be negatively impacted because Saudi Arabia plays such a central role in the region. What is more, losing ground to the Houthis would mean that the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz would also continue, disrupting energy exports from the region.
In this scenario, there will be “no victor, no vanquished” deadlock in Yemen, but Iran would emerge as winner. A war of attrition along the Red Sea coast would provide Tehran with significant breathing room, allowing it to alleviate pressure on its own war efforts.
This would enable Iran to use the Houthi card as leverage in the intermittent negotiations it conducts with the international community, emboldening it to raise the bar regarding its conditions and demands during those talks.
This means that the only way to resolve the crisis in Yemen is decisive military action led by the Yemeni government and supported by a region-wide coalition. For that to happen, the government has to get its internal affairs and its relations with allies in order.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Chinese premier stresses continued pursuit of high-quality development, expansion of high-standard opening up
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:50:18 CST
22:50:18 KST

Chinese Premier Li Qiang delivers a keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the 140th China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Ding Haitao)
GUANGZHOU, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Wednesday emphasized that China will continue to promote high-quality development, expand high-standard opening up, and take proactive and practical actions to add more impetus to the world economy.
Li made the remarks while delivering a keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the 140th China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province.
Noting this year marks the 70th anniversary of the establishment of the Canton Fair, Li said that President Xi Jinping specially sent a congratulatory letter, fully affirming the achievements made by the Canton Fair and reaffirming China's determination to expand high-standard opening up.
Through the Canton Fair, the world has witnessed the tremendous vitality in China's economy and society, seen the magnificent journey of hundreds of millions of Chinese people striving forward all the way, and felt the increasingly deep connection between China and the world, Li said, adding that an increasingly open, continuously innovative and trustworthy China brings new opportunities, provides new impetus and injects certainty into the world.
Li pointed out that the Canton Fair has stood the test of shifting international circumstances and kept brimming with fresh vitality, embodying plain yet profound inspirations.
"Market connectivity is not a tool for playing games, but an effective means to generate incremental growth. China is committed to promoting the continuous integration and common growth of its domestic market and the international market, and building an open world economy," the premier said.
Li said China is willing to import more high-quality products, especially high-value-added products. "We hope that more countries will work with China in the same direction, lift restrictions and actively promote the optimized and balanced development of trade," he added.
"As the largest developing country, China has always been committed to promoting common development," said the premier. "China will always be a trustworthy and reliable good friend of developing countries, and is willing to join hands with the vast number of developing countries on the journey to modernization," he added.
He said China stands ready to share more market opportunities, expand more mutually beneficial cooperation, and firmly safeguard the international economic and trade order with all parties.
WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala delivered a video address, noting that China has achieved remarkable development and provided rare opportunities for the world.
Noting that the Canton Fair is an important platform connecting China with the world, Okonjo-Iweala said that against the backdrop of increasing global uncertainties, it is hoped that all parties will jointly advance WTO reform and build an open, rules-based global trading system.
More than 700 representatives from nearly 90 countries and regions attended the opening ceremony.
This edition of the Canton Fair brought together more than 30,000 exhibiting companies and about 340,000 overseas buyers. ■

The 2027 state budget provides for spending restraint, a smaller government deficit and a lower nominal amount of new government debt compared to 2026 and 2025, Prime Minister Rumen Radev announced at the beginning of the cabinet meeting. The draft budget also envisages increased support for families and children, as well as additional funding for healthcare, education and defence, alongside measures to stimulate investment and support businesses.

NEW DELHI, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- An Air India flight from Frankfurt to New Delhi was diverted to Rajasthan and made an emergency landing at Jaipur International Airport on Wednesday after the pilot issued a hijacking alert, multiple local media reports said.
The scare, however, turned out to be a hoax.
Reports said the pilot of flight AI 2030 was squawking transponder code 7500, the internationally recognized aviation code for hijacking or unlawful interference. The alert was received by air traffic control, following which the flight was diverted to Jaipur, a local newspaper, Hindustan Times, quoting its sources, said.
At Jaipur airport, the aircraft landed safely and was moved to a designated isolation bay for security checks. However, nothing objectionable was found in it.
Air India described the incident as a "perceived security concern" and said the aircraft was cleared after the required security check. The aircraft was allowed to take off and landed safely at New Delhi airport.
Reports said India's civil aviation watchdog, the Directorate General of Civil Aviation, has ordered a probe into the incident. ■

LISBON, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Portugal's government on Wednesday selected Lufthansa Group as the winner of the partial privatization of national carrier TAP Air Portugal, in a deal valuing the airline at 2.55 billion euros (2.83 billion U.S. dollars) in total.
Prime Minister Luis Montenegro announced the decision following a cabinet meeting, saying Lufthansa's financial proposal was 16 percent higher than the competing bid from Air France-KLM and carried a lower degree of uncertainty.

The prime minister said the deal guarantees the growth of TAP's fleet, passenger numbers, destinations, routes, investment and employment.
The decision will be followed by a final negotiation phase and the required regulatory approvals before the transaction is completed. ■

BRATISLAVA, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The Slovak parliament on Wednesday passed the state budget draft for 2027, which projects a general government budget deficit of 4.94 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), up from an expected 4.37 percent this year.
According to the News Agency of the Slovak Republic (TASR), of the 78 MPs present for the vote, 76 voted in favor of the budget, while two abstained.
State budget revenues are projected to reach 27.91 billion euros (31.18 billion U.S. dollars) in 2027, while expenditures are expected to total 35.66 billion euros (39.84 billion dollars). This would result in a deficit of 7.75 billion euros (8.66 billion dollars).
General government revenues are forecast at 63.34 billion euros (70.77 billion dollars) next year, against expenditures of 70.78 billion euros (79.08 billion dollars). This would leave a deficit of 7.44 billion euros (8.31 billion dollars), equivalent to 4.94 percent of GDP.
The government aims to reduce the deficit to 4.5 percent of GDP in 2028 and 4 percent in 2029, a plan that will require additional fiscal consolidation measures, according to the Slovak Finance Ministry. ■

Batalhadzhin community linked to international terrorist organizations — FSB
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:49:20 UTC
22:49:20 KST

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. The "Community of Followers of Batal Hajji Belkhoroev - Batalhadzhins," which Russia's Supreme Court tagged as a terrorist organization today, has been linked to international terrorist organizations and illegal armed groups since the 1990s, the FSB and the Interior Ministry said.
On Wednesday, the Supreme Court recognized the community as a terrorist organization and banned its activities in Russia.
"The court took into account the materials indicating that members of the wird, as a closed pseudo-religious movement, have been interacting with participants in illegal armed groups and international terrorist organizations since the 1990s and up to the present day, adopting their methods and providing assistance to terrorist and extremist structures," the FSB noted.
The Interior Ministry said the community members help other international terrorist organizations and illegal armed groups, and participate in terrorist and extremist activities.
Terrorist acts
The Supreme Court ruled to recognize this organization as terroristic based on evidence of its terrorist activities collected by the FSB in coordination with the Prosecutor General’s Office, the Investigative Committee, and the Interior Ministry.
"Within the framework of criminal cases investigated by the Investigative Committee, data was obtained on the involvement of members of this organization in terrorist crimes," the Investigative Committee noted.
According to the FSB, the Interior Ministry, and the Investigative Committee, in 2004, several members of the community participated in an armed attack on government bodies in Ingushetia killing 78 people and wounding more than 100. Sixty·eight defendants in the criminal case were convicted in the crime, while law enforcement continues to try to track down those who were able to flee and escape justice. In 2019, terrorist attacks were carried out in Moscow, resulting in the deaths of Ibragim Yeldzharkiyev, head of the Center for Countering Extremism of the Interior Ministry for the Republic of Ingushetia, his brother, and an employee of the National Guard. The Investigative Committee established that followers from the organization were also involved in these crimes.
In 2009, the Kartoyev brothers, members of the Belkhoroev community, assisted terrorists in the bombing of the Nevsky Express train, which killed 27 people.
As part of the investigation into a criminal case concerning the terrorist attack at the Crocus City Hall, it was established that the individuals who provided weapons to the perpetrators of the crime belong to the religious movement associated with Batal Hajji Belkhoroev, including Dzhabrail Aushev and Husen Medov, who are serving life in prison.
Russian general's death
The Batalhadzhins were involved in a terrorist attack organized by Ukraine’s special services, in which the head of the radiation, chemical and biological protection forces (RCBZ) Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov was killed.
"Wird members Ramazan Padiyev and Batukhan Tochiyev assisted the special services of Ukraine in the terrorist act committed against the head of the RCBZ of the armed forces of the Russian Federation, Lieutenant General I. Kirillov," the FSB said. The Investigative Committee added that Padiyev and Tochiyev helped the perpetrator of this terrorist act. "This crime was prepared for a long time on the territory of Ukraine. The accomplices are serving long prison terms," the Investigative Committee said.
Assistance to Ukrainian militants
The FSB and the Interior Ministry said that the Batalhadzhins actively assisted Ukrainian armed groups engaged in combat operations against the Russian army. "Members of the community participated in supporting terrorist and extremist groups engaged in combat operations against the armed forces of the Russian Federation on the territory of Ukraine," the FSB said. The Interior Ministry also said that "there is reliable information about the active assistance provided by the organization to the activities of Ukrainian armed groups that oppose the armed forces of the Russian Federation."
Ongoing investigation
The Investigative Committee, the Interior Ministry, and the FSB said that criminal groups belonging to the community continue to commit various crimes, including murders, robberies, and property theft. "Thus, in Moscow, a criminal case is being investigated against several followers of the movement who are involved in murders, extortion, and kidnapping," the Investigative Committee said. In Ingushetia, a local resident supplied forged documents to the wanted members of the community.
"In this regard, law enforcement agencies are carrying out measures to identify, suppress, and solve all crimes committed by members of the ‘Community of Followers of Batal Hajji Belkhoroev -- Batalhadzhins,’" the FSB said.
Warning
The Investigative Committee said that "the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation contains a separate article that establishes liability for participating in the activities of an organization recognized as terrorist under the legislation of the Russian Federation."
The Interior Ministry said this concerns Article 205.5 of the Criminal Code (organizing the activities of a terrorist organization and participating in the activities of such an organization).
Thus, as explained by the Investigative Committee, the Interior Ministry and the FSB actions related to financing, managing, or providing any other assistance to the leaders and participants of the community entail criminal liability and punishment, up to and including life imprisonment.
Batalhadzhins
Batal Hajji is an offshoot of the Qadiri order, one of the influential Sufi brotherhoods. It got its name after its founder, Batal-Hajji Belkhoroev, an (Ingush) Sufi sheikh of the late 19th - early 20th century. It is a closed organization with strict discipline. Although its direct ties to organizations such as Al·Qaeda and the Islamic State (terrorist organizations banned in Russia) were not established, the so·called "combat wing of the Ingush wird (brotherhood) of the Batalhadzhins was put on the federal list of terrorist organizations under a November 28, 2022 decision of the Southern District Military Court. The charges included blood feuds, arms smuggling, extortion, and corruption. According to some legal experts, the community is more reminiscent of a criminal·clan structure with a religious veneer and motives driven by revenge than an ideological jihadist movement.
Several leaders of the Batalhadzhin group were convicted (Yakub Belkhoroev, ten years for embezzlement and misappropriation) or are on the federal wanted list, such as Akhmed Belkhoroev, who, according to law enforcement officials, is one of the leaders of the combat wing. Another active member of the group, Ilyas Belkhoroev, according to open sources, left for Ukraine in 2015, and joined the Dzhokhar Dudayev Volunteer Battalion in 2021. In August 2026, it was reported that he died in prison in Poland, where he was accused of supplying weapons to that country. Poland never confirmed this.

Police have launched a major search in the western city of Essen after two masked men attacked prison officers taking an inmate to a doctor's appointment and freed him.
They overpowered and tied up the prison staff in the building lobby leading into the doctor's office on the Kennedyplatz in the city center, shortly before 1 p.m. local time (11 a.m. UTC).
The assailants and the inmate then split up and fled in different directions using e-scooters, police said. The prisoner was serving a custodial sentence for drug offenses and assault charges.
"The 34-year-old inmate with German citizenship and the two men suspected of freeing him are on the run. Police are searching for the men with numerous officers and has published a photo of the prisoner," Essen police wrote in a statement.
Police warned that it "could not be ruled out" that the suspects were armed, and asked anybody who thought they saw them not to approach or speak to them, but to call the emergency services immediately.
The operation also briefly involved a bomb scare that turned out to be a false alarm. Specialists deployed after a call from a concerned member of the public but it transpired the item was a wooden mock hand grenade.
Police did not immediately comment on whether the prisons officers accompanying the prisoner sustained injuries in the attack.

Nord Stream defendant's lawyers challenge war crime charge
Lawyers for the Ukrainian man accused of organizing the Nord Stream pipeline attack have challenged the evidence and the war crime charge as his trial opened in Hamburg.
Serhii Kuznietsov, a 50-year-old former Ukrainian special forces officer, is accused of planning and supervising the September 2022 sabotage. Prosecutors say the attack targeted civilian infrastructure using prohibited methods of warfare.
Defense lawyer Jes Meyer-Lohkamp said there were no fingerprints, DNA traces or witness statements placing his client aboard the Andromeda, the yacht allegedly used in the operation.
Prosecutors allege Serhii Kuznietsov boarded the vessel on the German island of Rügen with six accomplices: a skipper, an explosives expert and four divers. The group allegedly attached four explosive devices fitted with timers to the pipelines.
His lawyers argued that Russia used the pipelines as a weapon of economic pressure, making them a legitimate target. They also said Italy had approved his extradition on sabotage allegations, rather than a war crime charge, and sought dismissal of the case.
The defense sought to have the case dismissed, also arguing that military secrecy obligations prevented Serhii K. from discussing potentially exonerating evidence, even with his lawyers.
The explosions ruptured three of the system's four pipelines near Denmark's Bornholm island. Russia had already halted supplies through Nord Stream 1, while Nord Stream 2 had never entered service.

Fat-fingered cockpit error likely triggered Nuremberg hijack alert
A pilot's apparent mistake when entering a transponder code triggered the hijack alert that led to a major police operation at Nuremberg airport, German police said.
Investigators believe the pilot intended to report a radio failure but accidentally entered 7500, the code signaling a hijacking.
The Boeing 737-800's radio was defective, leaving the crew unreachable after takeoff from the Greek island of Corfu, police said.
Police spokesperson Michael Petzold said the pilot apparently did not realize the mistake. The pilot is not under investigation because police believe he acted unintentionally.
Military aircraft accompanied the plane in Croatian airspace, and Austrian interceptors were alerted. Two German Eurofighters then escorted it to Nuremberg.
A police team trained to negotiate with hijackers and a Bavarian support unit were deployed at the airport during the alert.
Officers had less than an hour between the emergency signal and landing to prepare, Petzold said. Police later gave the all-clear.

Social justice and Christian references: DW's Berlin bureau chief weighs in on Merz's speech
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's overriding message was one of justice, especially between generations.
That was for the home crowd, trying to explain the governing coalition's reform plans of the social systems. Interestingly he also sprinkled in some Christian references, something he seems to be doing more recently.
Most likely the German chancellor is trying to show more empathy and a more positive vision of the future.
His own conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party colleagues have increasingly been demanding this after losses in three state elections this fall.
Merz warns of growing injustice between generations
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned that Germany faces a growing gap in fairness between generations unless it undertakes major reforms of its social security systems.
"A justice gap has opened up between the generations in our country, and this gap will grow unless we act," Merz told the Bundestag.
He said children and young people risked being forced to shoulder a greater burden than could reasonably be justified under principles of fairness.
Merz acknowledged that successive governments had paid insufficient attention to the long-term consequences of their decisions, explicitly including governments led by his own center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
The chancellor said his government had developed a broad reform program covering pensions, care, the labor market, economic competitiveness and the modernization of the state.
He argued that justice should mean equal opportunities, fair rewards for achievement and fairness between generations, rather than redistribution at the expense of those contributing to the economy.
Merz said the reforms were necessary to preserve Germany's prosperity and ensure that younger generations were not left carrying an unfair share of the costs.
Merz accuses political extremes of seeking chaos
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has accused political forces on the far left and far right of deliberately dividing society, spreading disinformation and downplaying the threat posed by Russia.
Speaking in the Bundestag, Merz said he could not understand why politicians at both ends of the political spectrum continued to minimize Russian aggression.
"One gets the impression that you want chaos because you hope to gain political advantage from it," he told lawmakers.
Merz warned that extremism was increasingly making its presence felt in Germany's national and regional parliaments, as well as everyday life.
However, he acknowledged that extremist movements could draw support from legitimate dissatisfaction and feelings of injustice, arguing that constructive political action was the only effective response.
"Justice for us does not come through the exclusion of minorities," Merz said, calling for policies that promote equal opportunities and fairness between generations.
He contrasted what he described as the destructive politics of division and exclusion with the responsibility of democratic parties to address genuine grievances and govern for everyone in Germany.
