Merz says Ukraine aid does not come at welfare's expense
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has rejected accusations from the far right and far left that support for Ukraine comes at the expense of social spending.
"Not a single euro is missing from social spending," he told parliament, speaking ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.
Merz said an exemption from Germany's constitutional borrowing limits allows spending on defense and assistance for Ukraine to be financed through additional credit.
He accused the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the socialist Left Party of seeking to divide Germany
AfD and BSW join forces against Ukraine support
In the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany Party (AfD) won recent elections in a landslide, a new alliance has flexed its muscle.
The AfD put forward a motion to halt arms deliveries to Ukraine and lift sanctions against Russia. Instead, they argue, peace talks with Russia should be initiated.
The Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), which holds five seats in the state parliament, again teamed up with the AfD to ensure a majority for the motion. The BSW combines left-leaning economics with right-wing populist positions on immigration and relations with Russia.
AfD and BSW also called for an immediate halt to financial support for Ukraine, to the extent that it goes beyond humanitarian aid.
The motion by the AfD and BSW has no more than symbolic value, as decisions regarding sanctions against Russia and aid to Ukraine are made not by the federal states, but by the federal government and the European Union.
But the new alliance of AfD and BSW has a wider significance. It is seen by observers as a sign of longer-term and closer cooperation between the two parties, which originate from very different ideological camps.
Although the AfD emerged as the clear winner of the state elections in September 2026, it lacks a majority to form a government. It has been searching for partners in the state legislature. So far, the BSW is the only party officially negotiating with the AfD on forming a government.
Merz to set out EU priorities after urging reforms
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is expected to outline Germany's priorities on Ukraine, European defense and economic competitiveness in a parliamentary address ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.
His government statement is scheduled for 14:05 local time (12:05 UTC), followed by a 90-minute debate. EU leaders meet on Thursday and Friday, with the Middle East, the bloc's next long-term budget and EU enlargement also on the agenda.
After the speech, the opposition Greens are set to put forward two motions calling for faster bloc enlargement and stronger measures to counter economic coercion and protect the bloc's market.
Merz's address follows a more domestic-focused speech on planned reforms at an employers' conference in Berlin on Tuesday. There, he said he would press ahead with changes to Germany's welfare system even at the expense of his own popularity, arguing that younger generations stood to benefit.
Energy prices push German inflation to 3.3%
Germany's annual inflation rate rose to 3.3% in September, its highest level since December 2023, as fuel and heating oil prices surged.
The Federal Statistical Office confirmed its preliminary estimate, up from 2.9% in August and 2.8% in July.
The increase was again driven by energy prices, said the office's president, Ruth Brand, highlighting higher costs at gas stations and for heating oil.
Energy prices rose 14.9% compared with September last year, their steepest annual increase since February 2023. That followed increases of 10.5% in August and 8.3% in July.
Motor fuel prices jumped 37.1%, while heating oil rose 74.9%. Firewood, wood pellets and other solid fuels became 15.6% more expensive.
However, electricity prices fell 5.5%, natural gas prices dropped 2.8% and district heating cost 1% less.
The office attributed those declines partly to government measures implemented since the start of the year.

Sally Rooney halts book sales in Britain and even cancelled a trip due to fears of arrest — what happened
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

22:47:37 KST

Sally Rooney halts book sales in Britain and even cancelled a trip due to fears of arrest — what happened
Kyiv • UNN
Faber will no longer supply Sally Rooney’s books to Britain because of her support for the banned Palestine Action. The author fears criminal prosecution.
Writer Sally Rooney said she was forced to stop selling her books in the United Kingdom because of her support for the proscribed organisation Palestine Action, reports UNN, citing The Guardian.
Details
The Irish writer, author of such works as "Normal People" and "Conversations with Friends," said that because of her public support for the direct-action group, she could no longer receive royalties from sales in the United Kingdom.
After Palestine Action was proscribed last year, Rooney said she would direct proceeds from the sale of her books to support it. Supporting organisations proscribed under the Terrorism Act is an offence; the writer later cancelled a trip to the United Kingdom to accept an award, fearing arrest.
In a statement provided to The Guardian, the bestselling author said: "In July 2025, the direct-action group Palestine Action was designated a terrorist organisation in the United Kingdom. The following month, I wrote an article expressing my intention to continue supporting Palestine Action — an organisation that is neither proscribed nor deemed unlawful here in the Republic of Ireland."
"As a result, fulfilling contracts for the publication of my work in the United Kingdom may now be considered a serious criminal offence. Therefore, following consultations and discussions, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has decided that it can no longer supply my work to the United Kingdom market. I have made every effort to be open with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am entirely prepared to accept the consequences."
In a statement to the High Court supporting a legal challenge against the organisation's proscription — and warning of its impact on freedom of expression — Rooney said that her books could disappear from the shelves of British bookshops and that publishing new works in the country could become impossible.
Her books have received critical acclaim (she has been called "the voice of a generation") and achieved huge commercial success in the United Kingdom. Sales of the novel "Normal People" exceeded one million copies, while "Conversations with Friends" and "Beautiful World, Where Are You" each sold more than 500,000 copies. The BBC created television series based on "Normal People" and "Conversations with Friends"; the former attracted 62.7 million views, making it the broadcaster's most popular series of 2020.
Last year, Rooney said that the independent producer of the television adaptations had warned her that any payments for the series (both of which had aired before the proscription was introduced) would breach counter-terrorism legislation if the producer knew or suspected that she was using the money received to fund Palestine Action.
Under Section 15 of the Terrorism Act, it is an offence for a person to "provide money or other property, knowing or having reasonable cause to suspect that it will or may be used for the purposes of terrorism." The maximum penalty is 14 years' imprisonment. Faber, which publishes the author's work in the United Kingdom and Ireland, said: "The current law in the United Kingdom has created circumstances in which Faber cannot transfer to Sally Rooney funds earned by her in the country. For a publisher, a situation in which a writer's works are being sold but the resulting income cannot be passed on to her is untenable. Therefore, with Sally's full agreement, we have decided to stop supplying her work to the United Kingdom in any format. We are proud to publish her significant body of work and will continue to sell it in other territories."
We would add
It is believed that more than 3,700 people have been arrested in the United Kingdom for allegedly supporting Palestine Action since it was proscribed last July; most of them were detained over placards reading: "I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action."
Approximately 2,500 people have been charged, but none of them has yet appeared in court, as a legal challenge to the ban is ongoing and will be heard by the Supreme Court next month. Most of the arrests and charges concerned Section 13 of the Terrorism Act, which carries a maximum penalty of six months’ imprisonment.

Berlin can’t deport migrants due to broken police cars – Welt
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Berlin can’t deport migrants due to broken police cars – Welt
Berlin police have been unable to carry out planned migrant deportations because of a shortage of functioning vehicles, Welt has reported, citing a police union warning about the German capital’s deteriorating fleet.
Several operations could not proceed as planned because officers simply did not have enough vehicles to collect people scheduled to be returned to their home countries, Frank Teichert, Berlin chairman of the German Police Union, told the newspaper.
The shortages have caused considerable frustration, turning every promised “deportation offensive” into “real-life satire” on the ground, he said.
Some 159 of Berlin’s 3,304 police vehicles have been unavailable because of workshop work, according to a parliamentary inquiry. Teichert also said more than half the fleet meets at least one criterion for replacement.
The problems stem from years of underfunding, Benjamin Jendro, a police union spokesman, said. Officers regularly encounter worn brakes, seat belts, buckles and interiors, while the vehicle budget remains at 2016–17 levels despite higher prices and increased demand.
The problems also extend to the fire service, where vehicle shortages force neighboring stations to cover calls, increasing travel distances and response times, according to the firefighters’ union. External repair costs have also risen from around €4.7 million in 2024 to nearly €8 million last year.
Berlin’s interior administration maintains that reserve vehicles ensure operational readiness, while acknowledging that limited funding and rising procurement costs are hampering efforts to replace aging equipment.
The failures come despite Germany’s promises to tighten migration controls, expand border checks and accelerate deportations. Growing public frustration over immigration, housing shortages, and subsequent pressure on public services has continued to fuel mass protests in recent months both in Germany and across the EU.
European governments have pledged faster removals, but implementation has continued to lag. EU countries issued around 110,000 deportation orders in the second quarter of 2026, while fewer than 37,000 people were actually removed from the bloc, according to Eurostat. Missing documents, legal challenges and receiving countries’ refusal to cooperate have remained obstacles to deportation.

IMF chief warns growth alone cannot bring US debt under control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:47:07 UTC
22:47:07 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Economic growth alone will not bring US public debt under control, International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said Wednesday, urging additional measures to cut fiscal deficits.
Speaking at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Georgieva said stronger growth could help improve public finances but would not deliver the necessary adjustment quickly enough.
She said US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recognized that federal deficits and debt had become too high and needed to return to a more sustainable path.
US authorities, however, were relying heavily on strong economic growth to reduce those imbalances, she added.
Bessent has argued that sustained growth above 3%, combined with spending restraint, could lower the debt-to-gross domestic product ratio. The administration has pointed to artificial intelligence investment, manufacturing expansion and tax cuts as drivers of economic activity.
Georgieva’s warning underscored the IMF’s broader demand for governments to strengthen public finances as repeated shocks erode their capacities to respond to new crises.
In opening remarks published by the IMF, she said the global economy remained resilient despite frequent shocks and uncertainty, but that resilience was approaching its limits as energy and fiscal buffers were depleted. Inflation also remained persistently high in many economies.
She urged policymakers to increase revenues, rationalize spending and improve public financial management, while ensuring that assistance amid rising energy and food prices protected vulnerable people.
Georgieva said the global outlook was being pulled in opposite directions by an energy supply shock stemming from the Middle East war and stronger demand associated with artificial intelligence.
Economies closely integrated into AI supply chains were generally performing better, while low-income countries and fragile states faced particularly severe pressures, especially those dependent on energy imports or excluded from the technology boom.

How Australia’s Gambling Lobby has Successfully Avoided Any Reform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:47:00 UTC
22:47:00 KST

Gambling businesses in Australia have a long history of effectively influencing and controlling government policy and regulation over a national pastime that makes Australians the world’s biggest gamblers per capita. The gambling industry can wield that level of control because it turns over AU$244.3 billion (2022–23) and generates more than AU$10 billion a year in gambling tax revenue to financially stretched state governments. This substantial financial contribution from gambling provides access to government decision-makers.
Meanwhile, gambling businesses have adopted parts of the tobacco industry’s “corporate playbook” to resist regulation. These tactics have allowed the gambling industry to effectively avoid regulation and instead allowed them to expand their highly profitable commercial activities.
Gambling businesses are well resourced because the products they sell are extremely profitable, and they have worked hard over many years to ensure gambling remains deeply embedded in Australian social life. A key development toward that came with the introduction of gambling machines, known as poker or “pokie” machines, into suburban social clubs from 1956 onward, and later into pubs and hotels. This helped make gambling seem like a normal part of community life. In most Australian states and territories (except Western Australia, which restricts poker machines to a single casino), poker machines are widespread and operate largely without question in venues that are also used for family meals and social and sporting activities.
The development of these social clubs in New South Wales was particularly important. They helped provide sporting and recreational facilities in new postwar suburbs at a time when governments were unable to provide enough financial support for community infrastructure. This gave the clubs a strong community image and helped make their gambling activities more acceptable.
This approach continues today. It is not unique to Australia. Gambling businesses around the world use similar strategies, sometimes described as the “alibi model.” Clubs NSW, the largest gambling network in Australia, has carefully maintained this tradition and uses it whenever possible to promote the image of these social clubs as organizations that give generously to their communities. The close connection between local community clubs, sporting organizations, and some of Australia’s largest commercial gambling operators makes it harder to challenge the normalization and influence of the gambling industry.
Gambling operators are also among Australia’s biggest political donors, according to research. Political donations can provide access to decision-makers, which can then give gambling businesses greater influence over policies that affect them. Australia has also developed a strong “revolving door” between politics and the gambling industry.
There are some restrictions on politicians taking jobs after leaving office, but the definition of a “lobbyist” is narrow. It generally excludes people working directly for companies or industry associations to influence government. As a result, many people involved in lobbying are not subject to the same rules. Former senators, premiers, ministers, political advisers, and senior public officials have taken jobs with some of Australia’s largest gambling companies, sometimes soon after leaving public office.
Hospitality is another form of influence. This can range from MPs given private boxes at major sporting events, or the sports minister attending football grand finals and tickets for MPs attending the Melbourne Cup racing carnival, to “policy briefing” lunches and dinners for the minister responsible for oversight of the gambling industry at expensive restaurants.
These benefits may have to be declared, but the conversations that take place are not made public. The access provided by hospitality can be significant. A politician may spend several hours with an industry representative at an event, giving the host much more time and access than they would normally have during a visit to a parliamentary office.
Some states have introduced new rules that limit political donations from certain businesses, including gambling operators. The federal government has weaker rules around political transparency and integrity, with limited enforcement and relatively weak penalties. In practice, this means that Australia has a political system in which powerful interests can influence governments while making that influence difficult for the public to see.
Recent experience suggests they can be extremely effective. In 2010-11, the minority Gillard government sought to introduce a system that would allow poker machine players to set limits on how much they could spend. ClubsNSW, representing clubs with poker machines across New South Wales, launched a highly effective campaign to block the change. It targeted Labor politicians in marginal seats in New South Wales and Queensland.
Although Clubs NSW remained the public face of the campaign, partly because of the positive community image created by the “alibi” of community benefits, it brought much of the gambling industry together behind the campaign and had access to almost unlimited financial resources. Nervous backbenchers became increasingly concerned, and Prime Minister Julia Gillard eventually found a way to abandon the commitment. No major reform followed.
More recently, a 2023 federal parliamentary inquiry into “online gambling and its impacts on those experiencing gambling harm,” chaired by MP Peta Murphy, concluded that “enough is enough.” It recommended major reforms to online gambling in order to reduce its harm to Australians. The recommendations included banning gambling advertising across all media, developing a national strategy for gambling regulation, and establishing a new national gambling regulator. Once again, the gambling industry responded quickly, with wagering companies taking the lead.
Sporting organizations and broadcasters, which now receive significant revenue from gambling, were among those most strongly opposed to the proposed reforms. They successfully stymied the changes. The reforms eventually announced by the government in 2026 fell well short of those recommended by the parliamentary committee.
In both cases, the gambling industry organizations successfully utilized their enormous lobbying powers to influence government. In both cases, those methods worked. And the Murphy inquiry’s important reform proposals were weakened or abandoned.
The gambling industry provides a clear example of how the corporate playbook can be used to prevent reforms that could significantly reduce gambling harm. The reason is simple: the all-powerful gambling industry knows only too well that effective regulation could reduce their revenues and profits.

US blasts case against Lebanon DC envoy over 'Israel contact'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:46:56 UTC
22:46:56 KST

Breadcrumb
US blasts case against Lebanon DC envoy over 'Israel contact'
A legal complaint against Lebanon's ambassador to Washington over an alleged contact with her Israeli counterpart has been referred to the military judiciary, drawing strong criticism from the United States and dividing opinion in Lebanon.
Lawyer Hassan Adel Bazzi filed the complaint against Ambassador Nada Hamadeh Moawad after Lebanese and Israeli media reported that she had contacted Israeli Ambassador Yechiel Leiter following an attack in the occupied West Bank in which his son was injured.
The reports said Moawad expressed sympathy with Leiter and condemned the attack.
Moawad has neither publicly confirmed nor denied that the conversation took place. Lebanese media have cited sources denying the call, while official Lebanese sources told The New Arab they had no comment.
Lebanon's public prosecutor has referred the complaint to Judge Claude Ghanem, the government commissioner at the Military Court, for review.
The step does not itself constitute charges against Moawad or a formal referral for investigation.
The US State Department nevertheless condemned the move.
"It is shameful that a military court is considering a complaint against Lebanon's ambassador in Washington simply for implementing her legitimate government's policy and participating in US-led negotiations," a spokesperson said.
Washington said the military judiciary should instead focus on Hezbollah members it accused of plotting against the Lebanese government and called for an end to laws and practices it said enabled the politically motivated targeting of civilians and diplomats.
The case has also reignited debate over Lebanon's longstanding law banning dealings with Israel, which has faced renewed scrutiny since Beirut began direct US-mediated negotiations with Israel earlier this year.
Several Lebanese politicians opposed to Hezbollah rallied behind Moawad.
Kataeb Party leader Samy Gemayel described the referral as "unacceptable" and "a dangerous precedent".
"Lebanese diplomacy must not be subjected to political calculations," he said. "What is needed is to protect institutions, not intimidate them."
Bazzi, however, told The New Arab that the complaint raised a legitimate issue requiring judicial scrutiny.
"We have no vindictive objective," he said. "There is an incident that requires investigation."
He argued that prosecutors could have dismissed the complaint if they considered it without merit, and said any evidence of contact outside Moawad's authorised negotiating role could raise questions under Lebanon's boycott legislation.
Bazzi also criticised the US response as interference in Lebanon's judiciary and sovereignty.
Moawad is a central member of Lebanon's negotiating delegation with Israel, led by former ambassador Simon Karam.
She and Leiter met at the US State Department in September as part of talks on implementing the framework agreement signed on 26 June.
The negotiations have been politically contentious in Lebanon, particularly as Israel continues military operations and maintains forces in parts of southern Lebanon despite months of diplomacy.

"The joint Russian-Indian cross-branch exercise Indra 2026 has begun in the Chelyabinsk Region and the Far East. Units of the ground forces of the two countries, warships of the Russian and Indian Navy, as well as aircraft of the Russian Aerospace Forces are participating in the maneuvers," the ministry said in a statement. The ministry noted that the crews of the Russian corvette Aldar Tsydenzhapov and the Indian Navy frigate INS Sahyadri, which arrived in Vladivostok several days ago, participated in the opening ceremony of the maritime part of the Indra 2026 joint exercise at the Pacific Fleet's main base.
The ministry specified that the active phase of the land part of the exercise will continue until October 23. The core of the Russian military contingent consists of servicemen from the 90th Guards Tank Division of the Central Military District. At the training ground, the military contingents will practice unit command and control and conduct a joint operation to destroy illegal armed groups.
The practical phase of the maritime part of the exercise will take place in the Sea of Japan on October 16-17. The ships in the joint detachment will practice tactical maneuvering, conduct artillery fire exercises against sea and air targets, conduct an inspection operation, and free a vessel simulated to have been seized by terrorists.
One of the episodes of the naval phase will include practicing joint actions to repel attacks by unmanned aerial vehicles and unmanned boats.
In addition, as part of the exercise, crews of the Russian Aerospace Forces and the Indian Air Force, operating joint Su-30SM tactical aircraft, will practice combating small, low-flying targets, destroying short-and medium-range airborne weapons carriers, and practicing maneuverable air combat at medium and low altitudes.
The ministry added that crews of the Russian Aerospace Forces and the Indian Air Force, using Mi-8 army aviation helicopters, will land special forces units and practice search and rescue of crews in distress in remote areas.

Entire Swedish reality show season lost weeks before premiere amid disputed AI claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:46:12 UTC
22:46:12 KST

The project could not be restored, wiping out hundreds of days of work, according to Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet.
An AI agent reportedly deleted an entire edited season of a Swedish reality show just five weeks before its planned premiere, forcing the broadcaster to postpone its release until next year.
Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet, citing unnamed sources, reported that the production company behind a reality show named The Challenge Sverige had given an AI agent access to its server, where it deleted the completed season.
The project could not be restored, wiping out hundreds of days of work, according to the report.
Swedish commercial broadcaster TV4 confirmed to Aftonbladet that a “technical failure” had caused the loss, pushing the planned 22 November premiere back to 2027.
Its news division initially repeated the newspaper’s account of AI involvement, but in an update on Wednesday afternoon, TV4’s head of programmes Mia Lindqvist denied that an AI agent was responsible, saying “that is not true”.
Adapted from the American show The Challenge, the series is billed by TV4 as the world’s toughest reality contest, combining physical challenges, mental endurance and strategic alliances.
How can AI agents go wrong?
Although the Swedish TV channel has rejected the AI explanation in this case, other incidents have exposed the risks of systems that can act on users’ behalf.
AI agents use software tools to carry out tasks, such as drafting and sending emails, rather than simply generating responses. Depending on their permissions, they can make changes to real files, websites and computer systems.
Problems can arise when a system misunderstands instructions, misjudges an action’s consequences or works around an obstacle instead of stopping.
In a report published on Friday, Anthropic said models given impossible tasks could pursue “unintended and sometimes misaligned strategies to achieve their goals”.
In July, its Claude Haiku 4.5 model submitted fabricated information about an unsolved homicide to the US police website while performing example tasks.
TV4 said all the original footage of the show remains available but the season must be edited again from scratch.

The Israel Allies Foundation (IAF) launched two new parliamentary caucuses in Greece and Cyprus this week, seeking to strengthen ties with Israel and expand cooperation on regional security, energy, and technology.
The Greek Parliamentary Israel Allies Caucus was inaugurated at the Hellenic Parliament in Athens on Tuesday, followed by the launch of the Cyprus Israel Allies Caucus at the House of Representatives in Nicosia on Wednesday.
The new caucuses aim to build on the existing trilateral partnership between Israel, Greece, and Cyprus, with a particular focus on security challenges in the Eastern Mediterranean, including tensions with Turkey.
“The new Israel Allies Caucuses in Greece and Cyprus will help translate these commitments into parliamentary action,” said Leo van Doesburg, executive director of IAF Europe.

Cyprus, Greece, Israel ties 'more vital than ever'

Tsiaras said the initiative comes amid growing regional security challenges and proves the three countries' shared strategic interests and historical ties.
In Cyprus, the new caucus will be chaired by Democratic Party MP Chrysis Pantelides and will include six lawmakers from three political parties.
The launch followed a meeting between the IAF delegation and Cypriot President Nicos Christodoulides at the Presidential Palace. The delegation was also hosted by House of Representatives President Annita Demetriou.
Pantelides emphasized the importance of strengthening relations between Cyprus and Israel in light of regional security threats.
“The strengthening of relations and the development of alliance ties between Cyprus and Israel is more vital than ever,” he said, citing the security challenges facing both countries.
Israeli ambassadors attended the launches in their respective host countries, while the US ambassador to Cyprus also attended the ceremony in Nicosia.
Reinstein welcomed the establishment of the two caucuses, saying they would help strengthen parliamentary cooperation and support for Israel.
“Through faith-based diplomacy, we are building a bridge between parliamentarians who understand that Israel's security, and the security of the free world, depend on strong alliances rooted in shared Judeo-Christian values,” he said.

Dublin hotel cancels 70 rooms booked for antisemitism conference delegates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:45:57 UTC
22:45:57 KST

The Herbert Park Hotel in Dublin canceled a reservation for 70 rooms intended for delegates attending an international conference on combating antisemitism after learning the purpose of their visit, according to Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland.
In his speech at the opening event at the Irish Foreign Ministry – sent to The Jerusalem Post – Cohen recalled meeting with hotel management after the booking was completed, and being questioned about whether the gathering was connected to the Israel Defense Forces.
Cohen also remembered the manager’s demeanor changing and becoming tense after he mentioned that the delegates would be Jewish leaders.
“There is an uncomfortable irony in organizing an international conference to discuss antisemitism and finding that, before the conference has even begun, you have already encountered something that forces you to ask exactly the questions the conference was created to address,” he said.
“How quickly does the word ‘Jewish’ change a conversation? How easily does a gathering about antisemitism become associated with the Israeli army?”
He noted that the question about the IDF was not an innocent misunderstanding, as it instead “revealed how quickly Jewish identity can be collapsed into Israel, how quickly Israel can be collapsed into suspicion, and how quickly suspicion can become discrimination because contemporary antisemitism does not always arrive wearing the language of the past.
“It does not always announce itself with a slur, a threat, or a placard. Increasingly, it can present itself as a question, a precaution, a policy, a request for clarification. It begins by treating Jewish identity as evidence of political allegiance,” he said.
Resetting the conversation between Jewish groups and governments
The European Jewish Congress called the incident “deeply disturbing.”
“That a hotel would cancel accommodation for participants in a conference dedicated to combating antisemitism, while raising questions about supposed links to the Israeli military, reflects precisely the kind of prejudice and suspicion that such gatherings seek to confront,” the EJC noted.
“It is profoundly troubling that those working to combat antisemitism should themselves encounter such treatment. Jewish organizations and those standing against hatred must never face exclusion or discrimination because of their work,”
Israel’s Foreign Ministry said. “The Irish government cannot use the fight against antisemitism as a diplomatic PR exercise while failing to confront it at home.”
The conference in question was the 15th meeting of the Special Envoys and Coordinators Combating Antisemitism (SECCA) Forum, organized by the World Jewish Congress in partnership with the European Commission, and convened as an Associated Event under Ireland’s rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union.
Jewish community leaders from across the world joined government envoys, representatives from international organizations, and technology company executives in Dublin from October 12 to 14.
Leaders representing the J7 Large Communities’ Task Force Against Antisemitism – connecting the Delegación de Asociaciones Israelitas Argentinas, Executive Council of Australian Jewry, Canada’s Center for Israel and Jewish Affairs, the Representative Council of French Jewish Institutions, Central Council of Jews in Germany, and Board of Deputies of British Jews, alongside the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) and the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations from the United States – also joined the forum following a series of high-level meetings in London earlier in the week.
Statements, condemnations only go so far
The gathering included a meeting with Ireland’s Taoiseach or government leader, Micheál Martin; visits to the European headquarters of TikTok and Meta; and other discussions.
“Our meeting in Dublin is a much-needed opportunity to reset the conversation between Jewish organizations, governments, and technology companies,” Maram Stern, WJC executive vice president, said. “Statements and condemnation of antisemitism only go so far. Practical solutions must urgently be put in place to protect Jewish life globally.”
The delegates were officially welcomed by Irish ministers despite the current Ireland-Israel tensions.
At the start of Tuesday’s agenda, Colm Brophy, a member of the Irish parliament, said he was “very pleased to welcome Jewish community leaders” and was particularly happy to see that the event has a focus on AI and on the regulation of online platforms, given the “troubling increase in antisemitism and other forms of racism online in recent years.”
The incident comes amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Ireland and Israel, with Jerusalem accusing Dublin of fostering an increasingly hostile environment toward the Jewish state.
Tensions have escalated following Ireland’s recognition of a Palestinian state, its legal and diplomatic moves against Israel, and controversy over Dublin City Council’s proposal to remove the name of former Israeli president Chaim Herzog from Herzog Park in Rathgar and replace it with “Free Palestine Park.”
The attempt was eventually condemned by Irish officials, and the J7 representatives visited the park for a photo-op this week during the conference.

INTERVIEW - ‘You’re not alone, the truth will come out’: Nobel winner Navi Pillay on global support for Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:45:10 UTC
22:45:10 KST

Nobel Peace Prize laureate Navi Pillay said Palestinians seeking justice are not alone and the truth will emerge, urging the international community to draw lessons from the collective action and economic sanctions that helped end apartheid in her native South Africa.
In an exclusive interview on Wednesday, Pillay, judge at the International Court of Justice and a former UN human rights chief, reflected on her experience fighting apartheid and the importance of international support for Palestinians amid continuing concerns over accountability for violations in the Gaza Strip.
"I imagine I'm correct in saying that even though Palestinians are struggling for their freedom for more than 90 years now, attention by the international community and support by the international community would be of great significance for them," she told Anadolu.
"The message being, you're not alone. That with information and correct information, the truth will come out."
Pillay, 85, who was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize for her contributions to international justice, chaired a UN commission of inquiry, which concluded last year that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Recalling her experience under apartheid, she said South African lawyers fought a lonely struggle with little international attention. "We really had very little relief. And honestly, the rest of the world didn't pay attention to us," she said.
The rights lawyer said a UN commission gathering evidence and presenting its findings internationally would have greatly helped Black South Africans at that time.
Pillay stressed the importance of identifying the root causes of Palestinian suffering, and reiterated her commission's finding that Israel's unlawful occupation was the root cause of the longstanding conflict.
She criticized governments for increasingly prioritizing their political and regional interests over their responsibilities to maintain international peace and justice.
She said the UN Security Council already possessed mechanisms to respond to violations, including peacekeeping operations, investigative commissions, mediation and economic sanctions.
"The principal tool they have is to impose sanctions, economic sanctions against governments that are violating international human rights law, international humanitarian law, they've used this before," she said.
Questioning the international community's response to Gaza, Pillay said: "So, the question that civil society is asking: 'Why are you sitting back and doing nothing in the face of huge violations that we, the people, can see daily? We can see genocide being committed on our television screens'."
"And I am as unhappy as most people that there has been so little action," she added.
Drawing on South Africa's experience, where apartheid ended in 1994, Pillay emphasized the decisive role of international economic pressure.
"Apartheid came to an end mainly because of the economic sanctions imposed by the Security Council, by the United Nations against the apartheid government," she said.
"I never thought apartheid will end in my lifetime, but it's this collective action by governments, by businesses, and civil society all over the world that brought an end to apartheid."
Pillay said she had been hoping for similar international cooperation in response to the situation in Gaza.
"I've been hopefully looking for and calling for that level of cooperation, that level of condemnation of the huge violations and killings of Palestinians," she said.
Asked whether Israel's growing international isolation and sanctions targeting settlers in the occupied West Bank could help end its impunity, Pillay said such developments could contribute to broader collective action.
"The one thing we cannot accept is doing nothing," she said.
Recalling Nelson Mandela's position that South Africans could not fully enjoy freedom while Palestinians remained oppressed and occupied, she said Palestinians were seeking measures similar to those used against apartheid.
"Palestinians are calling for the kind of action that was taken to end apartheid. They see the value of economic boycotts," she said.
She also referred to protests by Israelis against efforts to weaken the country's Supreme Court, urging governments to respect civilians' right to protest and cooperate with international criminal investigations.
She stressed that international legal principles must be applied consistently, without selectivity or bias, particularly when civilians are suffering.
Pillay emphasized that governments, rather than international organizations alone, bear responsibility for preventing genocide.
"The Genocide Convention is very clear. The duty is on every state to prevent genocide," she said. "That's a purpose; it's not to react to genocide and to punish the alleged perpetrators. The main reason is to prevent, because it's an intolerable crime when a whole group is being destroyed in whole or in part."
About the potential legal responsibility of governments supplying weapons, intelligence or political support despite warnings of serious violations, Pillay said the states themselves established international conventions and treaties.
"They set the standards. Now they must implement them without selection," she said, arguing that governments were failing to apply their own commitments because of political interests.
Pillay recalled that her UN commission had urged the General Assembly to seek an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice (ICJ) concerning Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory.
She welcomed the court's opinion in 2024, which found Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful, and outlined obligations concerning Palestinian rights.
She, however, acknowledged that legal proceedings offered limited immediate relief to people suffering on the ground.
"I agree; they're not very helpful to relieve their immediate dire situation," she said. "Let's use international law to assert and realize the rights of people who are oppressed everywhere in the world."
On shortcomings of the international system and its eroding credibility, Pillay pointed to the dominance of governments within the UN and the shrinking space for civil society.
"Certainly, the system is very skewed. Who controls the United Nations? It's member states, it's governments," she said, urging UN members to conduct their affairs in closer cooperation with civil society organizations.
Turning to Washington's measures against the International Criminal Court (ICC), Pillay called on governments, including those outside the Rome Statute, to oppose the campaign.
"I would like to see states of the world, the member states, whether they're parties to the Rome Statute or not, to condemn the unlawful measures and sanctions that the United States is imposing on this court," she said.
"We should say roundly that it's unacceptable, and then we all have the responsibility to help the court to overcome these obstacles."
The former ICC judge expressed confidence that the court's staff would continue their work despite mounting political pressure.
"They're not going to stop doing what they are doing because they are working out of commitment. They believe that it is possible to realize justice for all," she said.
Reflecting on receiving the Nobel, Pillay described the recognition as unexpected and deeply meaningful. "This award was a huge surprise to me, but a wonderful surprise," she said.
She expressed gratitude that the Nobel Committee had recognized different aspects of her decades-long career, from challenging apartheid to advancing international justice.
"You don't win a case all the time. You win some. You lose many, especially under apartheid South Africa," she said.
Pillay described the committee's recognition of her work as a "memorable moment," saying she appreciated its efforts to examine her contributions to international peace and justice.

France’s Mélenchon sees Spain’s Sánchez as inspiration for fixing public finances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:44:43 UTC
22:44:43 KST

Jean-Luc Melenchon attends a press conference on the sidelines of the debates on the draft state budget for 2027 at LFI's headquarters in Paris, France on October 14, 2026. | Lou Benoist/AFP via Getty Images
PARIS — Jean-Luc Mélenchon pointed to Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez as proof that greater public spending can boost the French economy and repair its strained public finances.
“Ever since Spain adopted a budget focused on ecological and social growth, it has experienced steady growth and a decline in its debt,” said Mélenchon, the leading left-wing candidate for next year’s presidential election in France.
In a press conference focused on the budget on Wednesday, the 75-year-old radical doubled down on his calls for a positive demand shock driven by billions in new state spending. He also reiterated his proposal to write off billions of euros in French debt held by the European Central Bank, which has drawn strong criticism, including from ECB President Christine Lagarde.
Advertisement
Polls show Mélenchon neck and neck with center-right candidate Édouard Philippe in the race to qualify for a second-round runoff against Marine Le Pen, the far-right frontrunner who presented her own budget plans last week.
Under Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, Spain has significantly reduced its budget deficit, while public debt is projected to fall below 100% of GDP in 2026. His government has raised the minimum wage and supported investment in green energy, alongside other sectors. Although inflation is a major concern and economic growth is expected to moderate in 2027, Spain remains one of Europe’s fastest-growing major economies, with the IMF on Tuesday forecasting 2.5% growth in 2026.
Spanish deficit fell significantly under Sánchez, and became one of the Eurozone’s fastest-growing economies after the pandemic.
Spain’s debt-to-GDP ratio dropped below 100% — while France’s raised to 119% — as the government invested heavily in sectors such as green energy and raised the minimum wage. But the cost of living remains a major concern in the country, particularly housing — one of the issues that led Sánchez to call a snap election earlier this month.
More money, less problems?
Mélenchon wants to boost growth by increasing purchasing power through higher salaries — including a higher minimum wage, a 10% raise for public-sector workers and a nationwide round of collective bargaining — as well as higher benefits for welfare recipients and a monthly payment of €1,337 for every French student intended to lift them above the poverty line.
Together, these measures form what his campaign calls an €82 billion “emergency spending” package.
Advertisement
Eric Coquerel, a Mélenchon ally who heads the French National Assembly’s powerful finance committee, argued in the same press conference that the new spending would drive GDP growth and increase tax revenue.
He also outlined ways to fund it, including a 2% wealth tax on households worth more than €100 million, popularized by French economist Gabriel Zucman, and higher taxes on large inheritances, which would be capped at €12 million under a Mélenchon presidency.
Fiscally conservative think tanks such as Institut Montaigne have argued that Mélenchon significantly underestimated the cost of his proposed spending and the potential tax revenue in previous campaigns. Critics also warn of capital flight if he is elected president, as occurred after his political mentor François Mitterrand was elected in 1981 on a platform of mass nationalizations.
In a statement, Edouard Philippe’s campaign called Mélenchon’s budget proposal “dangerous.”
Mélenchon blamed the current state of France’s finances on President Emmanuel Macron’s decision to cut several taxes early in his presidency, a move Macron said was intended to attract more investment.
“There are no other causes [of the deficit] than the systematic depletion of the state orchestrated by Macronism,” Mélenchon said.
Advertisement
“We are pitting the virtuous cycle of ecological and social recovery … against the vicious cycle of Macronist budgets and the dismantling of the state,” he added.
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu’s government has presented a budget with €43 billion in spending cuts, aiming to reduce France’s deficit to 5% of GDP without raising taxes. This year’s deficit is expected to reach 5.4% of GDP, missing the initial 5% target.
The counter-proposal from Mélenchon’s France Unbowed includes €106.4 billion in additional revenue and €81.7 billion in further spending, according to Coquerel, leaving about €25 billion to reduce the deficit.
France’s current center-right government is expected to pass its budget through the country’s hung parliament either by invoking a constitutional mechanism that allows the executive to pass legislation without a vote or by executive order. Mélenchon said his first order of business if elected in May would be to draft a new budget, which he hopes to pass in summer 2027.
France Unbowed advocates for a reduction of France’s contribution to the European Union, which presidential frontrunner Le Pen also wants to cut by €11 billion, though Coquerel clarified that he had not included a potential rebate in his economic forecasts.
Mélenchon intends to use the contribution as leverage to push for revised EU treaties, including scrapping the 3% deficit target for member countries and allowing national governments to adopt protectionist policies.
Critics, including Lagarde, said Mélenchon’s debt proposal was “dangerous” and potentially illegal because it could amount to direct financing of member countries by the ECB, which is prohibited by European treaties.

US judge blocks sanctions against 2 human rights groups engaging with international court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:43:09 UTC
22:43:09 KST

Yasin Gungor
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
A US federal judge blocked the Trump administration from penalizing two human rights organizations communicating with the International Criminal Court (ICC), ruling that the measures unconstitutionally restrict free speech.
US District Judge Jesse Furman granted a preliminary injunction, determining that the federal prohibition against providing services to sanctioned ICC personnel constitutes a content-based regulation of speech that fails strict scrutiny.
The ruling bars federal agencies from enforcing civil fines of up to $377,700 or criminal penalties of up to 20 years in prison under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act against plaintiffs Democracy for the Arab World Now (DAWN) and the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (TAAG). DAWN had routinely submitted war crimes evidence filings under Article 15 of the Rome Statute. TAAG was formed to prepare similar submissions but had withheld filing out of fear of prosecution.
The rights groups welcomed the victory and announced they will immediately resume submitting evidentiary documentation to the tribunal, restart formal coordination with UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese and re-engage with Palestinian human rights bodies Al-Haq, Al Mezan, and the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights.
ICC measures
The litigation challenged Executive Order 14203, issued in February 2025, which directed federal agencies to impose tangible consequences on entities tied to investigations targeting the US or allies such as Israel that have not consented to ICC jurisdiction.
The order targeted former ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan, six judges and UN personnel.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced last Friday that Washington imposed sanctions on the court, warning that the US would dismantle the tribunal if member nations fail to rein in its authority.
US pressure intensified after the court issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes in the Gaza Strip. The ICC has 125 member states, while neither the US nor Israel is party to the tribunal.

Ivan Kuritsyn, from Citizens’ Initiative Vilni De Ua, a non-profit organisation set up by Ukrainians displaced by the war, said the demonstrators had come to show their solidarity with Serhii Kuznietsov.
The 50-year-old defendant, identified by German prosecutors as Serhii K., is accused of helping organise the operation that damaged Nord Stream 1 and 2 on 26 September 2022. Prosecutors allege that he led a team of divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.
He faces several charges, including offences linked to the explosions, property damage, disruption of public services and an alleged war crime involving civilian infrastructure. He has not been convicted.
The pipelines were designed to carry Russian gas to Germany. The trial is expected to run for several months, with hearings scheduled until February.

US inflation rises to 3.7 pct as fuel costs climb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:41:24 UTC
22:41:24 KST

Higher gasoline prices drove over half of September’s monthly inflation increase.
U.S. annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September, exceeding forecasts as higher fuel prices drove the increase, while core inflation also topped expectations, official data showed on Oct. 14.
The consumer price index climbed 0.6 percent on a seasonally adjusted basis from August, when prices rose 0.4 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics said.
The monthly increase matched the average estimate from a broad survey of forecasters. The annual rate, up from 3.4 percent in August, beat the 3.6 percent prediction.
Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3 percent on the month, matching August’s pace but exceeding the 0.2 percent forecast. The annual rate climbed to 2.6 percent from 2.4 percent, above expectations of 2.5 percent.
Gasoline prices jumped 9.1 percent, accounting for more than half of the overall monthly increase. The broader energy index rose 5.2 percent, accelerating from 2.1 percent in August.
Shelter costs increased 0.4 percent, compared with 0.3 percent the previous month. Food prices were unchanged overall, with grocery prices falling 0.1 percent and the cost of eating out rising 0.2 percent.
Other categories recording increases included used vehicles, airfares, medical care and clothing. Communication prices were among the few major categories to fall.
The figures follow the Federal Reserve’s decision in September to raise its benchmark interest rate by a quarter percentage point to a range of 3.75 to 4 percent.
The central bank said inflation remained elevated and that the move would support a return to its 2 percent goal.

MOD Guard Service
The MGS (MOD Guard Service) plays a vital role in supporting MOD security.
What we do
The Ministry of Defence Guard Service (MGS) has guarded the defence estate since 1992 and provides security services at more than 135 sites across England, Scotland and Wales, including high-profile locations such as MOD Main Building in London and His Majesty’s Naval Bases in Portsmouth, Devonport and the Clyde.
The MGS was formed as a result of a security review of all British military bases following the bombing of the Royal Marines School of Music at Deal Barracks by the Provisional Irish Republican Army in 1989. Over the years, the MGS has evolved into a dynamic organisation that takes great pride in the services it delivers.
The MGS works closely with its security partners: Ministry of Defence Police (MDP), Security Services Group (SSG) and Military Provost Guard Services under Standing Joint Command (SJC) GUARDIAN and the wider MOD to protect the homeland and defend Defence.
The MGS prides itself on delivering a high-quality customer-focused service and will continue its mission to protect Defence from threats including crime, terrorism, espionage and sabotage by providing the highest quality of security services through professionalism and excellence. Working to become a technical authority on security, its vision is to be recognised as an outstanding provider of security services.
It strives to ensure its standards are maintained through external accreditation, holding the National Security Inspectorate (NSI) Gold standard.
The MGS employs more than 2,700 operational and support staff as civil servants. They are managed by a Head Office team, dispersed strategically around the country according to requirements.
MGS officers are often the first point of contact with the MOD for employees, visitors and contractors. They pride themselves on their inclusive, customer-focused culture, working to the Civil Service Code of Conduct and MGS core values of honesty, integrity, professionalism and efficiency.
MGS services
MGS offers a range of services to meet customer needs.
These include:
- control of access and egress
- security searches
- reception management
- event security co-ordination
- incident cordon and control
- control room management including CCTV and alarm monitoring and response
- emergency first aid
- patrolling, including dog patrols
Working for MGS
To achieve our goals, we need dedicated, highly-motivated people with diverse backgrounds, experience and skills, who can adapt to meet a complex range of threats and challenges in a rapidly-changing world.
Our staff come from a variety of backgrounds and professions and bring a wealth of customer service and security experience. We take the time to understand our customers’ values and security needs, and our highly-trained officers must be equipped to deliver services which reflect our culture and underpin the security mission.
We offer a broad range of interesting and challenging jobs, with a variety of working patterns, contributing directly to the UK’s Defence Mission. We enable our people to work at the right place, with the right people, at the right time. We believe that if we look after our people, they will be passionate about delivering great things for our customers.
Training and development
The MGS is committed to investing in its people through structured training and development. All officers receive role‑specific initial training to ensure they are prepared for operational duties, supported by regular continuation and refresher training to maintain skills, confidence and professionalism throughout their career.
We align our training with Defence standards and best practice, supporting both operational effectiveness and personal development. There are opportunities to develop specialist skills, progress into supervisory and management roles, and build long‑term careers while contributing directly to the UK’s Defence Mission.
New entrant requirements
All new entrants will be subject to security vetting and must pass a selection interview.
The MOD Guard Service is currently undertaking a review of grade structures, pay and conditions, aimed at improving employee experience, wellbeing, and career progression. This review may result in future changes to terms and conditions; however, the requirement for this role remains unchanged.
Working hours and leave
Most staff work on average 48 hours per week. Further benefits include:
- day and shift working for operational staff
- flexitime scheme upon completion of 6 months service (dependent on role)
- alternative working practices
- 25 days paid annual leave rising (1 day per year) to 30 days upon completion of 5 years’ service
- in addition to 8 public holidays per year, you will also receive leave for HM The King’s birthday
- generous maternity and paternity package
- highly competitive pension scheme
How to apply
Please visit Civil Service Jobs and look at our for more information.
If you have any questions, please email MGS-RH@mod.gov.uk

The Uyghurs Who Fought in Syria’s Civil War
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:41:00 UTC
22:41:00 KST

The Diplomat author Mercy Kuo regularly engages subject-matter experts, policy practitioners, and strategic thinkers across the globe for their diverse insights into U.S. Asia policy. This conversation with Emily Feng – author of “Our Hearts Burned for Home: Uyghur Militants in Syria’s Civil War” (Columbia Global Reports 2026) and award-winning correspondent for NPR – is the 530th in “The Trans-Pacific View Insight Series.”
What was the impetus behind your reporting on Uyghur militants in Syria’s civil war?
For years, I had been reporting on the ground on the Xinjiang region and the sweeping detention campaign that began in early 2017. And one of the reasons cited in rare official comments from Beijing about why authorities were detaining and arresting hundreds of thousands Uyghur people mentioned the presence of Uyghur “terrorists” in Syria and Afghanistan, but offered no evidence and since these places were nearly impossible to access, no one had done interviews with any of these supposed Uyghur militants.
In late 2024, it suddenly became possible to go to Syria after the surprising collapse of the Assad regime there and the end of a terrible civil war. Coincidentally, I was in nearby Lebanon when the Assads fled to Russia, and I ended up spending much of the beginning of 2025 in Syria.
Imagine my surprise when I saw Uyghur fighters milling about Syria! Indeed, there were thousands of Uyghur fighters in Syria, and I was later to discover, their role in the civil war had been much more impactful than anyone expected.
But I sensed there was much more to the story about these Uyghur fighters than Beijing’s narrative – that these were masterminds behind fatal attacks on Chinese civilians who were now hellbent on destroying China. I wondered what had made them leave their families and livelihoods behind to live in an active war zone, and how they had transformed themselves from hairdressers and engineers and teachers into hardened militant fighters, working in alliance with Arabic-speaking, Syrian rebel groups.
I was also sensitive to the possible implications of reporting on Uyghurs. In no way is their existence in Syria justification for the detention and arrests, mostly without real due process, of so many Uyghur citizens of China. I resolved to find a way to contact the Syrian Uyghurs and interview them – a difficult task, as they had operated as a secretive and highly-disciplined force for more than a decade – and learn more about why they had come to the Middle East.
Analyze the factors propelling Uyghur militants to join the civil war and how they contributed to the overthrow of the Assad regime.
I don’t want to give too much away here! The details are in the book. But in short, many Uyghurs who ended up in Syria had initially hoped to put down roots in Turkey, where a sizeable Uyghur diaspora already exists. However, Turkey does not want these Uyghurs, and it has stymied their ability to get residence documents and even aided in their deportation back to China.
Turkey happens to share a long, mostly unfortified border with northern Syria, however, where a rebel-held swath of territory had been established in a growing civil war. And so that’s where a lot of Uyghurs headed, because Syria was not checking documents or asking for visas, frankly. All of them were also looking for a constructive way to help Uyghurs back in Xinjiang, or East Turkestan as the Uyghurs call it, and they hoped Syria would become a base to fight back politically or militarily against the Chinese Communist Party.
A good number of Uyghurs had also already heard of the possibility of Uyghur fighters in Syria, and they were eager to train militarily. An active war, one Uyghur commander later told me, was free practice.
The Uyghurs’ wholehearted embrace of violence for the sake of establishing an independent Uyghur state is controversial, I should mention, among the Uyghur diaspora globally. But of the five dozen or so interviews I did with Uyghur fighters and their families, all of them described experiences where they felt diplomacy or political activism had failed them, and they felt they had nothing left to lose anymore by taking up arms.
The deadly race riots that began July 5, 2009 in Urumqi, which left scores of both Han Chinese and Uyghur Chinese dead, was a real turning point for many Uyghurs I met. The mob violence they witnessed from all parties that week and the ensuing crackdown and racism Uyghurs experienced in the aftermath convinced the majority of the fighters I spoke to to seek their fortunes in Turkey and later Syria.
What surprised me the most after weeks on the ground in Syria with Uyghur fighters was discovering the reach and breadth of the Uyghurs’ role in the Syrian civil war. The participated in major battles, played a key role in helping rebels with Hayat Tahrir Al-Sham (HTS) take Aleppo, and eventually marched into Damascus to establish the new government. HTS’ Ahmed Al Sharaa, now Syria’s president, privately credits the Uyghurs with being a consistently loyal, effective fighting force, and for that reason, the Uyghurs now have an unusual political purchase in the new Syria.
Explain the difference between the Turkestan Islamic Party (TIP) and East Turkmenistan Islamic Movement (ETIM) and how China views their respective identities.
Both of these entities are part of a broader movement of Uyghurs who have taken up arms and seek to establish an independent Uyghur homeland in the Xinjiang region. I found evidence that members of both groups still maintain communication links, and some of the earliest TIP fighters in Syria initially tried to train with ETIM officials along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border.
But to call ETIM in particular an organization would be a stretch, based on what I was able to find. The ETIM-linked fighters I met said there were never many Uyghurs along the Af-Pak border, many were killed in American bombings, training was nearly impossible due to the difficult geography of the place, and there were ideological differences between the more relaxed Uyghurs and the more conservative al-Qaida-linked and Taliban fighters there.
TIP, the Syria branch of this nationalist Uyghur militant movement, was much more successful. They became highly disciplined and managed to remain organized, sharing scarce financial resources in self-sustaining communities in Idlib, in northern Syria, and setting up robust social services for a growing Uyghur population that has now reached 20,000 men, women, and children.
While TIP also maintained substantial links to al-Qaida affiliated groups, including with HTS, for years, these links later became problematic and internally divisive as TIP and HTS tried to brand themselves as politically more mainstream and welcoming to Syrians and Uyghurs of all castes. Yet TIP remains controversial within Syria, and also within much of the Uyghur diaspora community, who view their militant past with distaste.
Why are Uyghur militants controversial in Syria?
The Syria Uyghurs find themselves in an awkward position. At home, they were the oppressed. In Syria, they are widely viewed as oppressors, in the eyes of Syria’s many minority communities.
Foreign fighters, including the Uyghurs, are viewed with fear and suspicion, as the civil war quickly devolved into a proxy war for various nation states and Islamist groups. Many remain in Syria in peacetime, creating resentments among Syrians who wish for the foreigners to return to their home countries. All the time, Uyghurs are confused with Uzbek fighters, and so many Syrians also do not know why the Uyghurs came to Syria in the first place, and do not understand why they cannot simply return to China.
During the civil war, the Sunni Uyghurs were active in besieging Shiite Syrian villages. They were frequently attacked by Hezbollah proxy forces and retaliated against Shiite populations in response. And for many years, the Uyghurs occupied and lived in several Shiite and Christian villages whose residents had fled in advance of Sunni Islamist groups like TIP arriving, which sowed more distrust and fear among Syrian minority communities who are increasingly on edge under the Sunni HTS-dominated government in Damascus. The Uyghurs maintain they are friendly neighbors and open to Syrians of other faiths and have tried to moderate their religious beliefs somewhat, but there are often significant cultural and linguistic gaps between them and Syrians, which the Uyghurs themselves sometimes do not even fully grasp.
Finally, there were also reports that the Uyghurs were among the perpetrators, alongside Syrian government soldiers, of horrific massacres of mostly Alawi Syrians in 2025. I found no evidence to suggest Uyghurs were involved, and they have no interest in doing so, as involvement would certainly imperil their still uncertain and vulnerable status as stateless refugees in Syria.
Assess the role of Uyghur militants in China-Syria relations and the implications for China-U.S. relations.
In some ways, the Uyghurs are not very important to China-Syria, or broader China-Middle East, relations. Syria has made it clear that it will not let groups on its soil threaten China, even though they also have made it clear they will not send the Uyghurs to China, as Beijing has demanded.
For China however, the Uyghurs are the top issue for them in Syria, and successive diplomatic delegations to Damascus have always mentioned TIP and the Uyghurs as the dominant concern Beijing has for the new government.
The result is that Gulf states, notable Saudi Arabia, have become major investors in Syria’s post-war reconstruction. China was once one of Syria’s top economic partners before the civil war, and it does not look like it will regain that position.
It will be interesting to see how the Uyghurs navigate their future in Syria. Will they buy land and build houses — setting up a much more permanent community in Syria? Will their children born in Syria still maintain strong Uyghur identity links and a commitment to set up a Uyghur state, when they feel more and more wedded to their Syrian upbringing as the years go by?

How much does public transport really cost in Denmark? And is it cheaper than owning a car?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

A few days ago, we broke down how much it costs to own a car in Denmark, and, well, it is not cheap. Nonetheless, public transport is also fairly expensive. And while for a single person living in a city the choice may be clear, for a family the story can be different.
We broke down how much public transport costs in Denmark and what the cheapest option is.
Public transport in the city
Monthly commuter passes are generally cheaper in Denmark’s other major cities than in Copenhagen. In 2026, a 30-day Pendlerkort, or commuter pass in English, in Copenhagen costs DKK 530 for two zones, rising to DKK 600 if Metro access is included. In Aarhus, Odense and Aalborg, the lowest adult commuter fare is DKK 435 for one or two zones, while three zones cost DKK 585 and four zones DKK 810. All four cities use zone-based systems, so the final price depends on how many zones a commuter crosses rather than on the city alone.
Families can reduce public transport costs in Denmark because an adult with a valid ticket or pass can generally bring up to two children under 12 free of charge in Copenhagen, Aarhus, Odense and Aalborg. Children who need their own commuter pass usually pay about half the adult fare, with a 1-2 zone Pendlerkort costing around DKK 218 a month in Aarhus and DKK 217.50 in Odense and Aalborg, while Copenhagen also offers roughly half-price commuter passes for children.
Children aged 12 to 15 must pay for public transport even when travelling with an adult, but they generally qualify for child fares of around half the adult price.
Using trains
For regular train commuters, DSB offers a Pendlerkort covering a specific route or set of zones, with unlimited travel during the validity period. The pass can also be used on buses, metro and light rail within the zones included.
Adults with a valid ticket or commuter pass can generally bring up to two children under 12 for free, while older children can qualify for reduced child fares.
For regular train commuters, the effective cost can be around DKK 1.1 per kilometer when a monthly pass is used five days a week. A Copenhagen-Roskilde Pendlerkort costs about DKK 1,410 for 30 days, which works out at roughly DKK 1.17 per kilometer for someone commuting both ways 20 days a month. A comparable Aarhus-Skanderborg commute costs about DKK 990 for a 30-day pass, or roughly DKK 1.13 per kilometer under the same assumption.
The pass also covers local public transport within the zones included, such as buses and, where relevant, metro or light rail, so commuters can use it for the urban part of their journey as well. Because the passes allow unlimited travel within those zones, the effective cost per kilometer falls further if they are also used outside the daily commute.
Deduction
Denmark’s transport deduction can reduce the cost of commuting for people who travel more than 12 kilometers each way between home and work, meaning more than 24 kilometers in total per working day. In 2026, there is no deduction for the first 24 kilometers, while travel between 25 and 120 kilometers qualifies for a deduction of DKK 3.17 per kilometer, and distances above 120 kilometers qualify for DKK 1.59 per kilometer.
For example, a person travelling 60 kilometers in total each working day can deduct 36 kilometers, which, at the 2026 rate, amounts to about DKK 114 per commuting day. Over 203 commuting days, that would give a deduction of around DKK 23,200, worth roughly DKK 6,000 in lower taxes. The deduction only applies to days when the person actually travels to work, so holidays, sick days and days spent working from home must be excluded, but it applies regardless of whether the journey is made by car, train, bus, bicycle or another form of transport.
Lower-income workers can receive an additional benefit: people earning less than DKK 391,500 before the labour market contribution in 2026 may qualify for an extra transport deduction of up to DKK 30,800, with the additional amount gradually reduced for incomes between DKK 341,500 and DKK 391,500.
The commuting deduction in Denmark is individual rather than family-based. If both partners work and each travels more than 24 kilometers in total between home and work on a working day, both can claim their own deduction based on their personal commute and the number of days they actually travel to work. Having children does not increase the deduction, and extra distance driven to drop off or pick up children cannot be added to the home-to-work journey. If family members share a car, each eligible worker can still claim their own commuting deduction, while lower-income workers may also qualify individually for an additional deduction.
A comparison: car vs. public transport
For a single commuter, public transport is clearly cheaper on both routes. Travelling between Copenhagen and Roskilde 20 days a month costs about DKK 1,410 with a Pendlerkort, compared with around DKK 3,732 in an electric car or DKK 4,200 in a petrol car, using FDM’s total ownership costs. Between Aarhus and Skanderborg, the monthly cost is about DKK 990 by public transport, DKK 2,737 by electric car and DKK 3,080 by petrol car.
For two adults travelling together, the gap narrows because they can share one car, while public transport requires two passes.
Even then, two commuter passes cost about DKK 2,820 on Copenhagen-Roskilde and DKK 1,980 on Aarhus-Skanderborg, still less than sharing either type of car. These figures are before tax deductions, but Denmark’s commuting deduction is calculated in the same way per kilometer regardless of whether someone travels by car, train, bus or bicycle, so applying it would reduce the effective cost of both options rather than giving cars a special advantage.
