====================================================================================================

From Protest to Procedure
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:10:56 EEST
22:10:56 KST

Oleksandr Larin, Founder of ‘Idealist Media’ platform, General Secretary of the Basketball Federation of Ukraine (2011-2015), Deputy Minister of Sport of Ukraine (2010)
Recently Ms. Stella Zakharova, Olympic champion and Vice President of the Ukrainian Gymnastics Federation submitted a report to the Gymnastics Ethics Foundation, the body responsible for ethical and disciplinary matters within the World Gymnastics system. The report is based on documented actions by Russian gymnastics structures in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. It was prepared not as a political declaration, but as a legal case: facts, documents, federation rules, procedure, and a request that the competent body provide an assessment.
At first glance, this is a story about gymnastics. To me, it is much more than that. It tests whether Ukraine is capable of moving from the model of “we object your decision” to a different one: “here are your rules, here are the actions of your member — explain whether the two are consistent.” And it brings us back to a broader question: why has Ukraine still not built a systematic legal mechanism for protecting its interests in international sport?
Several years ago, we already proposed a different approach: not to wait for an unfavorable decision and not to start looking for lawyers after the problem has already emerged, but to work proactively — through statutes, regulations, disciplinary procedures, the rights of national federations, and, when necessary, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS).
In 2023, after the Ms.Olga Kharlan case, Mr.Taras Samborskyi said it directly: the rules of international federations must be worked with before a conflict, not after one. In December of that same year, the NGO Sports Context presented the Office of the President and the Ministry of Youth and Sports(Ministry) with a concept for reforming the system: the state should stop merely reacting to consequences and instead create mechanisms that function regardless of who happens to occupy the minister’s office.
The problem was visible, and an alternative was proposed, but it never became a system. That is why the principle we proposed to the state of Ukraine is now being implemented, together with the lawyers and experts of Sports Context, in our work with Ms.Stella Zakharova. There is a concrete case, a procedure, and eventually there shodw be a result.
The State and International Sport Use Different Tools
The state operates through diplomacy, political statements, sanctions, intergovernmental relations, and decisions by public authorities. International sport operates through its own statutes, disciplinary codes, ethical rules, appeals procedures, membership rules, and dispute-resolution mechanisms.
Even if Ukraine is one hundred percent right politically, an international federation is not legally obligated to act the way we demand. A minister of Youth and Sports can make a statement, the Foreign Ministry can send a diplomatic note, partners can support Ukraine — but in the end, the federation will open its own statute. If we do not speak the language of that statute, political legitimacy risks remaining nothing more than a statement.
A Different Strategy Could Have Been Chosen Earlier
After the start of the full-scale invasion, the focus on the political and diplomatic isolation of Russian sport was logical and produced results. But over time, the limitations of that strategy became clear: “neutral status,” the return of Russian athletes, and the gradual rollback of restrictions. And each time, Ukraine was reacting to a decision that had already been made.
Mr.Matvii Bidnyi has been part of the leadership of the Ministry of Youth and Sports since 2020 — long enough to see the weak points of the existing strategy and to hear an alternative. That alternative existed: move from a reactive model to a systemic one — work through law, procedures, the internal mechanisms of international federations, and support Ukrainian national federations as full-fledged actors in international sport.
That transition never happened. First, an international institution makes a decision; then Ukraine looks for a way to stop it, change it, or appeal it. At this point, the problem is no longer a single decision. It is the architecture of the policy itself.
The Difference Between Protest and a Legal Problem
A political statement can be ignored. A properly framed legal question is much harder to ignore.
“Do not allow Russian athletes to compete because Russia is waging a war” is a strong moral and political position, but it still leaves a federation room to choose. A very different question is: “Do the actions of your member comply with your own rules?” At that point, the federation no longer has to be persuaded to support Ukraine; it has to explain how it applies its own rules.
That is the logic behind Ms.Zakharova’s case: not “support us,” but “here is the fact, here is the document, here is the action of your member, here is the relevant rule — now provide an answer.” Political volume is replaced by a legally structured contradiction.
And This Is Where Sports Context Has to Be Mentioned
The evidentiary and strategic architecture of this case is being developed with the participation of experts from the NGO Sports Context — the same organization that previously proposed this kind of work to the Ministry.
In January 2025, as head of the NGO, I signed a memorandum of cooperation with Mr.Matvii Bidnyi. We saw it as an opportunity to move from conversations about reform to joint professional work. A permanent mechanism for that cooperation never took shape.
We were ready to cooperate, but not to serve as expert decoration, not to endorse decisions that had already been made, and not to participate in a process where an expert is expected to agree rather than maintain an independent position. We were ready to work on changing the rules. That model turned out not to be needed.
The work moved outside the Ministry. We are now implementing the same approach directly within sport. Ms.Stella Zakharova’s case is one example — and, at the same time, an experiment: political reaction after a problem emerges versus a legal sequence of fact, evidence, rule, and procedure.
What a “Legal Approach” Means in Practice
First, the fact is established. The evidence is verified. The applicable rule is identified, along with the competent body, the applicant’s procedural standing, and the relevant procedure. Only then does political and diplomatic support come into play.
If a Russian sports structure is operating in occupied Ukrainian territory, the first question should not be, “What statement will the Ministry make?” It should be: what rule may have been violated, who has standing to submit a complaint, to which body, within what deadline, under what standard of proof, and with what documents?
That is when politics strengthens the law instead of replacing it.
The State Should Not Do the Federation’s Job
This should be part of the state’s sports infrastructure. Today, we see two extremes: either the state treats federations as if they were its own administrative departments, or it suddenly remembers the autonomy of sport and says, “that is your problem.” Both approaches are wrong.
The state should not draft an appeal to an international federation on behalf of a national federation. It should provide access to sports lawyers, an evidence base, systematic monitoring, diplomatic support, and, where necessary, funding for complex international proceedings. Its role is not to manage the federation, but to strengthen its capacity.
The responsibility of the relevant minister is not to produce the best statement after the latest decision by World Gymnastics, the IOC, or another international federation. It is to make sure the system is working before that decision is made.
Developments should be monitored continuously, documents should be collected, and a legal team should immediately determine whether there is a potential violation, whether a procedure exists, who has standing, and what further action is available. A national federation should not have to start from scratch every single time.
That is exactly what we proposed. So the question is not whether the minister knew about another approach. He did: there were meetings, proposals, a concept, and even a memorandum of cooperation.
Why did this approach never become part of state sports policy?
What Such a System Should Actually Do
It should monitor not only the eligibility of Russian athletes, but deeper processes as well: which Russian sports federations incorporate organizations from occupied territories into their structures; where Crimea, Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, or Kherson regions appear in official Russian sports documents; who participates in competitions; who is included on judging lists; which regional organizations are recognized; which appointments are made; and what changes are introduced into statutes.
Every fact should pass through a legal filter: what is legally significant here, what rule may have been violated, which body has jurisdiction, and what procedure is available? That is what professional policy looks like.
We are Not Saying the Ministry and the NOC Did Nothing
There were statements, diplomatic efforts, and legal steps. The question is why they never became a permanent system. Why does law usually appear only after a crisis? Why is there no unified evidence infrastructure? Why are Ukrainean national sports federations so often left alone with the problem? Why were the experts who proposed such a model several years ago never integrated into a permanent mechanism?
Against that background, Ms.Zakharova’s case is particularly revealing: a concrete legal process is now being prepared with the same expert team whose potential for systematic cooperation the Ministry failed to recognize.
The NOC Could Also Play a Different Role
The National Olympic Committee of Ukraine can be an important institution precisely because it is not a government body, yet it operates inside the international Olympic movement. It could accumulate legal practice across sport federations, maintain expertise in international procedures, and create an early-response mechanism. But the Ukrainean NOC should not turn into a second Ministry. Its strength lies in its autonomy.
A Strong Sport Federation Is a Resource, Not a Problem
The state does not need a weak sport federation that is easy to control. It needs a strong one — one that knows its rights, has the necessary expertise, and is capable of acting within its international federation.
A government official often has no procedural standing there, while a national federation does. A minister can send a letter; a federation, under certain conditions, can initiate a procedure. That is why sports autonomy is not a threat to the state, but an additional channel for protecting the national interest.
The Most Important Part of Ms.Zakharova’s Story Is Still Ahead
I do not know what decision the GEF will make, and no one has the right to guarantee the outcome: legal results are not announced in advance.
But already today, a small team of athletes, lawyers, and experts is doing what we proposed several years ago should become part of a state system: gathering evidence, verifying facts, identifying rules, determining procedures, working with a person inside the sports system who has the appropriate standing, and building a legal case instead of merely creating a media event. To a significant extent, this is happening outside the state system.
So my question to the Ministry — and personally to Mr.Matvii Bidnyi — is not whether they support Ms.Stella Zakharova’s report. That is secondary. The real question is why an expert resource capable of building cases like this never became part of the system for protecting Ukrainian sports interests, especially when this very approach had been proposed to the Ministry in advance.
From Asking for Support to Becoming a Legal Actor
Ukraine has already learned how to explain to international sport why its decisions are unfair. The next step is to learn how to work with the system itself: its statutes, regulations, procedures, competencies, disciplinary bodies, and CAS.
And to move from the position:
“Support us because we are right”
to another:
“Here is the fact. Here is the evidence. Here is your rule. Here is the procedure you created. Now apply your own rules.”
To me, that is what real agency means.
For the Ukrainian state, the principle is simple: do not manage sport in place of sports institutions; create the conditions in which those institutions are capable of professionally defending both their own rights and Ukraine’s national interests.
This is the logic we have been advancing for several years at Sports Context. The Ministry had the opportunity to use this expertise; at one point, we even formalized our cooperation, but no lasting working relationship emerged. The expertise did not disappear. It simply began to be implemented directly through actors within sport.
After the Ms.Stella Zakharova case, I would leave two questions.
First: what is more effective for the state — to control an independent expert community, to distance itself from it, or to learn how to use it as a normal part of a modern sports ecosystem?
And second: if the approach we proposed to the Ministry several years ago is now beginning to work without the Ministry, perhaps it is finally time to look not at who proposed it, but at the approach itself.

UVision moves beyond loitering munitions with sensor-to-strike network
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:10:44 UTC
22:10:44 KST

WASHINGTON – UVision unveiled new launch and ISR integrations at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting & Exposition in Washington, DC, expanding its portfolio beyond loitering munitions with a networked sensor-to-effect architecture built around its CORTEX mission-management system.
The company displayed an eight-canister launcher for the Hero120 alongside new airborne intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) links designed to tie sensing and strike nodes into a single operational loop.
The Multi-Canister Launcher, shown in an eight-round configuration, is designed for remote operation and can be deployed on mobile, fixed, or containerized platforms across land and maritime environments. Itzik Huber, general manager of UVision, told Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post at AUSA that the containerized solution can hold up to 20 Hero-120 or Hero-400 loitering munitions.
Integrated with CORTEX, the launcher operates as part of a distributed network connecting surveillance assets, decision tools, and precision-strike capabilities.
At the exhibition, UVision promoted persistent border defense as one application with launch nodes positioned along extended border areas and tied into CORTEX with ISR platforms, enabling continuous monitoring and rapid response across multiple sectors.
“We have changed the concept to a multi-layer, multi-solution instead of a single solution for a single soldier,” Huber said, explaining that one soldier can now strike several targets rather than just one.
At the exhibition, the company also demonstrated an expanded sensing layer through the integration of Wayland Autonomy’s IRIS airborne ISR payload with Tactical CORTEX.
IRIS is a compact, platform-agnostic airborne ISR payload that provides wide-area surveillance and onboard target generation, including in GPS-denied environments, allowing UVision to fuse airborne sensing with its growing portfolio of launchers and effectors across the Hero, Viper, and Peregrine families.
“It’s not just about having more effects in the field. It’s about having them where you need them, when you need them, and giving forces the flexibility to use the right capability for the mission,” said Dr. Ran Gozali, CEO of UVision. “That’s what we’re focused on: bringing sensing, mission management, and a broader range of effects together in a way that gives forces more options and greater operational flexibility.”
Expanding global footprint
Headquartered in Emek Hefer, UVision has a strong foothold in Israel, India, and the United States, where it is continuing to expand its footprint. The company’s Hero-120 is supporting the army’s Lethal Unmanned Systems program, and Hero-90 is participating in the Low Altitude Stalking and Strike Ordnance effort. The company is also building out domestic manufacturing, integration, and training capacity as it moves toward a more comprehensive mission-solutions role.
The war in Ukraine has forced European governments, that for years have neglected their defenses, to recognize that major conflict on the continent remains a reality. That has led European nations to accelerate their investment in autonomous weapons and unmanned systems.
And the wars that have been raging in Europe and the Middle East have fundamentally altered battlefield requirements. Huber argued that autonomy and artificial intelligence will be among the most consequential technologies shaping future conflicts.
"AI and autonomy will be more influential on future battlefields," he said.
And with that, UVision sees a future battlefield built around layered, networked capabilities rather than single platforms. According to Huber, "It's a different way of thinking. It's a more complex, holistic solution."

UK Green Party gambling on anti-Israel politics, former deputy leader warns 'Post' - exclusive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:10:41 UTC
22:10:41 KST

The UK Green Party has undergone an ideological transformation that has accelerated under leader Zack Polanski, with antisemitism, Islamist influence, and electoral opportunism increasingly shaping its political direction, its former deputy leader Shahrar Ali told The Jerusalem Post in an interview on Tuesday.
Ali warned that the changes are no longer simply an internal Green Party matter, but pose a danger to wider British society.
“When a political party, any political party that has de facto power, gets into positions of influence, and that gets subverted and corrupted beyond recognition, it’s a danger to society.”
Ali has been a member of the Green Party for “the best part” of 20 years. He served as deputy leader of the Green Party of England and Wales from 2014 to 2016, and as the party’s policing and domestic safety spokesperson in 2021.
Ali has a history of disciplinary disputes with the party. In 2022, he launched legal action against the Greens over alleged discrimination concerning his gender-critical beliefs, later securing a ruling that his dismissal had been procedurally unfair and that he had been subjected to “unlawful discrimination.”
He was excluded from the party for two years in September 2024 over comments on the same issue, and was suspended again on October 7, 2026, following his condemnation of the “Zionism is racism” motion and his calls for voters not to support the Greens.
For Ali, these “weaponized disciplinary processes” indicate increasing extremism within the party. “I was criticizing the motion long before the time it was passed, way back in spring, when it first reared its ugly head at the Spring conference,” he told the Post.
A party transformed under Polanski
Ali told the Post that the current radical approach taken by the Greens has “accelerated to devastating effect, particularly since Polanski became leader of the party.”
While he said it was “in gestation, even prior to that,” the culture of the party has predominantly shifted since autumn 2025, when the Jewish leader took over.
“The authoritarian drift and the rot, it’s set in more deeply from Polanski’s tenure as leader. Now we’re seeing the old guard like Caroline Lucas and Adrian Ramsay, and also some of the MPs, notably Ellie Chowns, getting far more agitated around the direction of the party. But it’s too little too late, unfortunately.”
Ali attributed much of this transformation to the rapid expansion of the party’s membership and what he described as a failure to scrutinize the political beliefs of those joining.
“During the last 12 months, the party’s seen a huge increase in membership but a corresponding lack of control regarding who is entering the party and why. There are a lot more pro-Palestine campaigners, Corbynista types who were kicked out of the Labour Party because of antisemitism.”
Ali said he thinks the shift to more overt antisemitism in the Green Party is two-pronged: one is the actual ideologues of the party who are strongly anti-Israel and often antisemitic; the other is a political ploy to take voters from the Labour Party and to secure support from Muslim voters, including those he believes hold Islamist views in the UK.
He cited the example of Hannah Spencer, who won the Greens’ first-ever parliamentary by-election in Gorton and Denton earlier this year, with major Muslim support. Her winning campaign was heavy on Gaza messaging.
However, Ali thinks the issue is more endemic than that.
“Unfortunately, the membership and the activist base has also changed,” he told the Post.
“I do think we’re dealing now with ideological zealotry of a very ugly sort, where members, some of whom may self-identify as Muslim, have extreme views around Israel and the right of Jews to a homeland.”
While he said it is difficult to put a figure on it, he thinks a large number of members and councilors have been resigning or threatening to resign as a result.
The controversy has also raised questions about Polanski’s own position on Israel.
Asked by the BBC on Friday whether he believed Israel has a right to exist, Polanski refused to say.
Other members have been more overt, calling for the end of the Jewish state. “They’re not going to get disciplined, I’m sure. Whereas I’ve been disciplined for criticizing the motion,” Ali said.
He said this is no longer a purely party-related issue but a much bigger issue involving wider politics and society.
“The Green Party has had an absolute blind spot; I think I’ve been quite vocal about it, including Polanski, around the exponential rise of antisemitic hatred in this country, in the UK, which is horrific. They hardly say anything about it, or next to nothing about it. I think they’re in complete denial about the impact of their campaign upon the rise of antisemitic hatred.”
Islamism and the Green Party's changing identity
Ali also spoke about the issue of Islamism in the party, which is now in the strange place of “both attracting Muslims and targeting Muslims.”
He argued that the problem extends beyond the party’s stance on Israel, describing what he sees as an erosion of its traditional eco-focused secular identity.
He cited Mothin Ali, the Green Party’s deputy leader.
“I’ve never once heard him criticize Islam. And that’s a problem. I think that is the beginnings of Islamism. The reason it’s Islamism is because it means the religion is beyond reproach, irrespective of the fact that it keeps popping up in the news cycle in ways which are directly relevant.”
“So what we’re ending up with is a party which is no longer occupying a secular space – where all religions and the non-religious are equal. It now seems to be promoting a Muslim agenda.”
Ali said that this is evident with respect to the Middle East.
“The Greens are going out of their way to target Muslim voters on Palestine issues, who have a kind of visceral reaction to the suffering of the Palestinian people, but this is to the exclusion of the suffering that’s happened to Israelis and Jews on and since October 7”
“The complete absence of sympathy, empathy, or compassion for innocent Jews is just staggering.”
Can Gaza-focused campaigning continue to deliver votes?
The key question here is, will the Greens’ strategy of Gaza-centric politics pay off? The party didn’t win the by-election seat in Holborn and St. Pancras on October 8 (just days after the controversial motion passed), but nevertheless made gains compared with previous years.
Ali told the Post that “it could go either way.”
“Many traditionally-Green voters will recoil at voting for the Greens. So they will lose a lot of support. And I can think of a couple of MPs who probably at the moment would lose their seats.”
“But what the party’s gambling on is that there are enough young cosmopolitan activists who are sufficiently misguided in various cities and towns, and students who will still vote for this antisemitic party. And so that’s just profoundly dangerous. So the extremists in the party are probably calculating that they actually want to carry on with this strategy.”
The Post pointed out that only around 1% of the party’s membership voted in the conference last week, and suggested that it is possible that the other 99% would have voted down the “Zionism is racism” motion.
Despite this, Ali does not believe the result necessarily misrepresents the wider party.
He argued that the party’s membership had increased dramatically under Polanski and that the motion could still pass if put to a wider membership vote.
“I do think the activists often represent the critical mass of the membership. For every activist, there’ll be other voters who are influenced by those activists.”
Why did senior Greens wait to speak out?
Ali also expressed skepticism over why, only after the failure to secure the by-election seat, did several senior Greens come out to voice their concerns about the “Zionism is racism” motion, as well as extremism in their party.
He suggested that the timing of their criticism reflected political calculations rather than principled opposition to the motion.
“If Polanski had won the by-election, it’s unlikely that there would have been furore around the motion. I interpret it more as they’re only objecting strongly now because they can see it can cause the party electoral damage. That is very concerning.”
When reached for comment, a spokesperson for the Green Party told the Post that “Mr. Ali is entitled to his views but is no longer a member of the party. We are proud to be a party that bravely stands up for some of the most vulnerable people in the world.”

The remains of around 30 Ukrainians killed in 1944 have been discovered in Poland

The remains of around 30 Ukrainians killed in 1944 have been discovered in Poland
Kyiv • UNN
Around 30 remains of Ukrainians killed in March 1944 were discovered at an Orthodox cemetery in Lasków. The search and research will continue.
A Ukrainian search expedition discovered the remains of approximately 30 people at an Orthodox cemetery in the Polish village of Lasków. They are Ukrainians who died during an attack by units of the Home Army and Peasant Battalions in March 1944. This was reported by the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance, writes UNN.
Details
Search operations began on October 6 on the grounds of the Orthodox cemetery in Lasków. They are being carried out by the Lviv Regional Council’s municipal enterprise "Dolya" commissioned by the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance. The Polish side granted the relevant permit on August 31, 2026.
The research uncovered both individual and mass graves. Sviatoslav Sheremeta, head of the municipal enterprise "Dolya," said that the preliminary results confirm the accounts of former village residents who managed to survive the events of March 1944.
We plan to continue searching for burial sites, and the next stage will be to conduct exhumation research, rebury the victims, and honor their memory with dignity
Oleksandr Alfyorov, Head of the Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance, emphasized the importance of honoring the victims with dignity. He also thanked the Polish side for granting permission to conduct the research.
Our shared task is to ensure that the memory of all those who died is honored with dignity, regardless of their origin or nationality. After all, true reconciliation begins with respect for the memory of everyone, acknowledging the pain of the other side, and a shared commitment to understanding
Historical background
According to various historical sources, more than 300 people were killed during the mass murder of Ukrainians in Lasków on March 10, 1944. Research by historians and experts from Ukraine and Poland has established data on 327 residents of Lasków who died in 1944.
At the same time, some historians cite a higher number of victims—approximately 350 people. The final number of victims may be established as a result of further historical and search research.

Bomb disposal experts recover 90-kg Russian drone warhead from premises of house in Kyiv – photo, video
Law enforcement officers have recovered an unexploded warhead from a Russian drone from the grounds of a house in Kyiv's Desnianskyi district.
Source: Kyiv Main Directorate of the National Police
Details: A 14-year-old resident of a neighbouring house alerted police to the dangerous find.
The Geran-5 drone damaged the roof and brick walls of a single-storey building, while its warhead, weighing around 90 kg, became lodged in the ground.
"The munition was also equipped with pre-formed fragmentation elements. Experts estimate that, had it detonated, the explosion could have destroyed this building and neighbouring properties within a radius of around 50 m," the police said.
Bomb disposal experts defused the warhead and transported it to a temporary demolition site for subsequent destruction.
Background:
- On 11 October, bomb disposal experts recovered the warhead and non-explosive debris from a ballistic missile at the site of a Russian strike in the Obolonskyi district of Kyiv.
- On 8 October, it was reported that bomb disposal experts had defused two unexploded ballistic missiles used by Russian forces to attack Kyiv on 7 October.

Starlink Restrictions Strip Ukraine of One of Its Few Defenses Against Jet-Powered Shaheds
Ukraine risks losing one of its few effective defenses against Russian jet-powered Shahed drones following new restrictions on Starlink satellite communications, Ukrainian presidential technology adviser Serhii Beskrestnov, known as “Flash,” warned on October 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Beskrestnov’s Telegram channel, Starlink is used in interceptor drones that currently provide one of Ukraine’s most effective solutions for countering high-speed Russian attack drones. The restrictions could therefore affect not only Ukrainian long-range operations and frontline logistics but also the country’s ability to protect its airspace.
While much of the discussion has focused on disrupted military missions, Beskrestnov said the implications for air defense could be even more serious.
“Starlink is used in what is currently the most effective solution—interceptors—for protecting our skies from jet-powered Shaheds,” he wrote.
“In effect, through their actions, our partners are depriving us of one of the few chances we have to defend the country against jet-powered Shaheds,” Beskrestnov added.
His warning suggests that the communications restrictions could undermine Ukraine’s efforts to counter a growing threat from faster Russian attack drones, which present additional challenges for conventional drone interception systems.
Earlier on October 14, SpaceX introduced new speed restrictions on Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian forces, reportedly without prior notification.
The limitations affect the military-grade Starshield service, with connections dropping when terminals travel faster than approximately 100 mph (160 km/h). Beskrestnov said the changes had already disrupted several military missions.
Separately, Zelenskyy raised concerns about Ukraine not receiving advance intelligence warnings from Western partners ahead of recent Russian missile attacks, adding to questions about the reliability of critical US support.

US agrees to drop foreign agent prosecution against former CIA analyst
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:07:33 UTC
22:07:33 KST

Yasin Gungor
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
US federal prosecutors in New York agreed to pause and ultimately dismiss criminal foreign agent charges against prominent foreign policy expert and former CIA analyst Sue Mi Terry, according to a court agreement made public Tuesday.
"After a thorough investigation, it has been determined that the interest of the United States of America and your own interest will be best served by deferring prosecution in this District," the 12-month deferred prosecution agreement filed in the US District Court for the Southern District of New York said, adding that proceedings will remain deferred during a period of "good behavior and satisfactory compliance."
Under the terms of the settlement, the US Attorney's Office will drop the case after one year if Terry adheres to several strict conditions. The pact explicitly bars her from knowingly communicating with employees of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, requires pretrial approval for any planned interactions with South Korean government officials, prohibits foreign gifts exceeding $100, and restricts her travel outside the continental US.
The resolution arrives weeks before Terry was scheduled to face trial in Manhattan federal court on charges of conspiracy and substantive violations of the Foreign Agents Registration Act.
2024 indictment
Terry was originally arrested in 2024 following an indictment alleging that she covertly advanced Seoul's policy positions, disclosed non-public American government information to South Korean handlers, and facilitated access for foreign officials to US personnel over more than a decade. Prosecutors claimed that intelligence operatives rewarded her with luxury goods, high-end dinners, and more than $37,000 in funding for a Korean affairs policy initiative under her control.
Terry, who previously worked as an East Asia analyst at the CIA and served on the White House National Security Council between 2001 and 2011, maintained her innocence throughout the proceedings.

US inflation rises to 3.7% as fuel costs climb ahead of midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:07:23 UTC
22:07:23 KST

Higher petrol prices and airfares pushed US inflation to 3.7% in September, adding pressure on households and the Federal Reserve weeks before the midterm elections.
US inflation accelerated last month as petrol, clothing and airfares became more expensive, adding pressure on households just a few weeks before the midterm elections.
The consumer price index rose 3.7% in September compared with a year earlier, the US Department of Labor said on Wednesday, up from 3.4% in August. On a monthly basis, prices jumped 0.6%, up from 0.4% the previous month.
The annual figure was above the 3.6% forecast by economists surveyed by data provider FactSet.
The figures underscore the lingering impact of the Iran war on petrol prices and the persistence of inflation, which fell sharply from a 9.1% peak in 2022 but has risen since the war began in late February.
Excluding the volatile food and energy categories, core prices rose 2.6% from a year earlier, up from 2.4% in August. Monthly core inflation held at 0.3%.
“CPI came in at 3.7%, slightly above expectations, and similarly core inflation was above predictions, suggesting that prices are feeding into the wider economy,” said Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot.
Elevated inflation has posed political problems for Republicans in Congress and complicated the Federal Reserve’s efforts to bring price rises under control.
A poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that just 17% of US adults approve of President Donald Trump’s handling of the cost of living. Only 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall, a new low.
Markets react: Will the Fed raise rates again?
Following the higher-than-expected inflation figures, major US stock indices turned negative. Gold fell more than 1.7% to $4,105.50 an ounce, while silver was down more than 4% at $56.91 an ounce.
Oil prices were mixed, with international benchmark Brent trading just above $105.70 a barrel, close to its opening level. US benchmark WTI rose 1.4% to $95.50 a barrel.
Bond yields jumped following the news. The policy-sensitive two-year US Treasury yield rose 13 basis points to 4.93%, as traders increased bets on further Fed rate rises. The benchmark 10-year yield climbed about eight basis points to around 5.3%.
Inflation moving further away from the Federal Reserve’s 2% target was the “last thing” global bond markets needed, according to Robin Brooks, a former Goldman Sachs economist and a senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution.
Carter warned that persistent inflation could push US government borrowing costs higher. “It is not inconceivable that ten-year Treasury yields continue to march higher,” he said.
The figures add pressure on the Fed as it weighs whether to raise rates again at its next meeting on 27–28 October.
Last month, the central bank raised rates for the first time in three years, to a range of 3.75%–4%. Fed chair Kevin Warsh said inflation was not falling quickly enough towards its target.
“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Warsh said at a news conference last month. He added that summer inflation reports “do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved”.
Some Fed officials have since suggested they can wait before raising rates again, although their latest projections point to one more increase this year.
Higher borrowing costs can slow spending and growth, helping to ease inflation. But they cannot resolve supply disruptions such as those caused by the Iran war, leaving the Fed trying to prevent higher energy costs from feeding into broader price rises.
Higher fuel costs feed through to other prices
Warsh has said his goal is to keep the petrol price spike from spreading to other areas of the economy. Higher fuel costs have already helped push airfares up by about 23% from a year ago.
Petrol prices jumped about 9% from August to September, driving much of the overall increase in inflation.
Prices at the pump have eased in recent weeks, though they remain higher than a month ago. Petrol averaged $4.34 a gallon nationwide on Tuesday, up a few cents from a month earlier.
Higher fuel prices also raise shipping costs for businesses, some of which pass those costs on to consumers. Last week, PepsiCo said it would raise prices for some snacks and soft drinks to offset higher costs for fuel, aluminium and food ingredients.
The expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure has also sharply increased the cost of semiconductors, computer equipment and electrical components, feeding through to prices for consumer electronics such as gaming devices, laptops and smartphones.

Sally Rooney says she can no longer sell books in UK due to Palestine Action support
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:06:08 UTC
22:06:08 KST

Sally Rooney has said she is being forced to withdraw her books from sale in the UK because of her support for the banned organisation Palestine Action.
The Irish novelist, whose books include Normal People and Conversations With Friends, said her public support for the direct action group meant she could no longer receive royalties from UK sales.
After Palestine Action was banned last year, Rooney said she would use proceeds from her sales to support Palestine Action. Supporting organisations banned under the Terrorism Act is an offence and she subsequently cancelled a trip to the UK to pick up an award, for fear of arrest.
In a statement provided to the Guardian, the bestselling author said: “‘In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland.
“As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence. After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK. I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences.”
In a high court statement in support of the legal challenge to proscription, warning against its impact on freedom of expression, Rooney said her books could disappear from UK stores and the publication of new works in the UK could be prevented.
Her books have been critically acclaimed – she has been described as the voice of a generation – and hugely commercially successful in the UK. Normal People has sold more than 1m copies, while Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You have each sold more than 500,000. Normal People and Conversations With Friends were adapted by the BBC, and the former racked up 62.7m views, becoming the broadcaster’s most-streamed series of 2020.
Rooney said last year that she had been advised by the independent producer of the TV dramatisations that any payment to her for those series, both broadcast before the ban, would be a breach of terrorism laws if it knew or suspected that she was using the royalties to fund Palestine Action.
Section 15 of the Terrorism Act makes it an offence if a person “provides money or other property, and knows or has reasonable cause to suspect that it will or may be used for the purposes of terrorism”. It carries a maximum sentence of 14 years in prison.
Her UK and Ireland publisher, Faber, said: “Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. To sell a writer’s work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher.
“As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format. We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories.”
More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK for alleged support of Palestine Action since it was banned in July last year, most for holding placards saying: “I oppose genocide, I support Palestine Action.”
About 2,500 people have been charged, although none have been tried as a legal challenge to the ban is continuing and will be heard by the supreme court next month. Most arrests and charges have related to section 13 of the Terrorism Act, which carries a maximum jail term of six months.
Huda Ammori, a co-founder of Palestine Action who has brought the legal challenge against the ban, said: “Sally Rooney being unable to publish her work in the UK marks a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action …
“[She] took a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced. She has refused to compromise her convictions, even at considerable personal and professional cost. Her work should be celebrated and widely available, not driven off the shelves of British bookshops because she refuses to be complicit in the suppression of solidarity with the Palestinian people. No author should have to choose between their principles and their freedom to publish.”
Kerry Moscogiuri, the chief executive of Amnesty International UK, said: “Whatever one’s views on Palestine Action, we should all be concerned when laws intended to combat terrorism end up silencing artistic freedom and the ability to engage in peaceful political dissent.
“Writers should not find their books disappearing from shelves because of their political beliefs. Nor should people have to choose between expressing their conscience and pursuing their livelihoods.
“Sally Rooney’s willingness to accept the personal consequences of her convictions deserves recognition. There is a real danger that others, seeing the price she has paid, will decide they cannot afford to speak out.”
Rooney’s books were still on sale in central London on Wednesday afternoon, and Waterstones said that existing stock could still be sold.
Gian Carlo, a bookseller at Henry Pordes Books, said the same, adding: “Nothing goes to Sally Rooney in this case. We sell books of all types, they’re not connected to the author. I can’t say I don’t agree with her.
John Clegg, a bookseller at London Review Bookshop, said: “I ordered more as soon as I saw the news. I saw the number go down to zero, so I hope they go through. People are going to want them and we’re not going to be able to get them through Faber.
“Good on her for taking a stand, it seems a ridiculous law. If this thing convinces the Home Office to move faster to get rid of it, I’m all for it.”

AI worms, ‘major’ incident fears spur safety calls at industry summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:05:00 UTC
22:05:00 KST

AI worms, ‘major’ incident fears spur safety calls at industry summit
- AI safety dominated the Dublin summit, as experts warned of “major” incidents and possible AI worms. Demis Hassabis said current problems are “early warning shots”.
- Brad Smith urged urgent regulation, saying there are more safety rules for milk and ovens than AI. He backed “safety brakes” and mandatory incident reporting.
- The EU said firms must test models more and keep control, while OpenAI warned rules must not slow innovation too much. The AI Act now gives the Commission new powers.
AI generated
DUBLIN – From the spectre of refrigerator-infecting AI worms to warnings of “major” security incidents at the horizon, calls to prioritise safety in the development of artificial intelligence dominated an industry summit on Oct 14.
Concerns about AI guardrails have soared after models developed by OpenAI and Anthropic were involved in security incidents during testing, piling on pressure to regulate the technology.
Google DeepMind chair Demis Hassabis warned AI capabilities were growing fast, telling the conference in Dublin such instances were “early warning shots” fired by systems that “aren’t that powerful yet”.
“So the incidents aren’t that major,” he said.
“But they could be, looking into next year and the next couple of years, if we don’t do more work as an industry and individually as companies and governments on securing these systems,” Hassabis warned.
New AI models should likely first be tested in offline “sandboxes”, after other companies’ models escaped the closed environments used to assess their capabilities, he added.
Milk and worms
Microsoft president Brad Smith called for regulation saying industry and governments must “act with urgency” to create “real and effective safety standards” to contain the risks linked to artificial intelligence.
“There are more safety rules for a carton of milk than for AI. There are more safety rules for your oven than for AI,” he told the conference.
“We need to recognise that the power of AI has moved faster than the safety for it. Safety needs to catch up. And we’re going to need some new AI safety laws and rules.”
AI agents should be equipped with “safety brakes” that users could activate in the event of an incident and AI providers should face mandatory incident-reporting obligations, he said.
Highlighting worries about the technology, Smith pointed to a recent Anthropic report suggesting small AI models may be only months away from behaving like computer worms, copying themselves from one internet-connected device to the next.
As tech companies race to build ever more powerful AI directly into phones, laptops, cars and household devices rather than running it in distant data centres, Anthropic said such AI might eventually autonomously hop from device to device.
“I mean, seriously? I don’t want AI worms in my refrigerator.” Smith told the Dublin conference. “I just don’t want any worms of any kind in my refrigerator. And I think most of the public feels that way too.”
Speed and control
A self-replicating AI worm would be hard to stamp out, because there would be no central switch to turn off, Anthropic said.
The European Union’s tech chief, Henna Virkkunen, told the conference AI firms needed to invest more time into testing their systems to retain control over them.
“The competition is so hard globally that it seems that all the companies, they are not investing enough time and resources really to test their models,” Virkkunen told reporters upon arrival.
“They have to be able to control... these systems,” she said, noting that the European Union has sent information requests to all major AI companies asking what safety and security measures they have in place.
The European Commission gained new regulatory powers in August under the AI Act, the world’s most far-reaching rules to curb potentially dangerous uses of the technology.
But OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar warned a “balance” needed to be struck so that safety rules did not pull the brakes on innovation.
“We want to be open, we want to make sure the right people can review models, but again we need to make sure that doesn’t slow us down to the extent that we then end up behind the folks who are on the malicious side of deployments,” she said. AFP

Lebanon united on keeping UN peacekeeping mission in south: Official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:04:29 UTC
22:04:29 KST

Wassim Seifeddine and Ikram Kouachi
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Lebanese Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri said Wednesday that there is an official consensus in Lebanon on keeping the UN Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) and continuing its mission in the south in accordance with UN Security Council Resolution 1701.
During a meeting in Beirut with Jean-Pierre Lacroix, the UN under-secretary-general for peace operations, Berri said Lebanon would continue its efforts at all levels “to safeguard its sovereign rights, protect its borders and liberate every last inch of its land from Israeli occupation.”
In a statement, Berri said Resolution 1701 tasks UNIFIL with monitoring the international border along the Blue Line, helping identify disputed points over which Lebanon has reservations, and monitoring and documenting daily Israeli violations of Lebanese sovereignty.
Adopted by the UN Security Council in August 2006, the resolution established the international framework for ending hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah at the time.
Berri said UNIFIL’s role “extended beyond security and military matters to include humanitarian, social, cultural and economic activities.”
He said there was an official Lebanese consensus on “maintaining the presence of the international forces and their mission,” pointing to parliamentary efforts to engage the international community and the UN on the issue. 
According to the statement, Berri and Lacroix also discussed the general situation in Lebanon, particularly developments on the ground in UNIFIL’s area of operations in the south, amid continued Israeli attacks and violations of Resolution 1701.
They also discussed Lebanon’s unified position calling for an extension of the international force’s mandate in southern Lebanon in a way that serves the interests of Lebanon and the region.
UNIFIL was established in 1978 following Israel’s invasion of southern Lebanon. Its mandate was significantly expanded after the July 2006 war under Security Council Resolution 1701.
In August 2025, the UN Security Council decided to end UNIFIL’s mandate on Dec. 31, 2026, after which a gradual, safe and coordinated drawdown and withdrawal is to begin over the course of a year.

Thales is now building Lightweight Multirole Missiles at its Belfast site at four times the rate it managed in 2022, and has committed £100 million to expanding that capacity further, the company told the UK Defence Journal after the Prime Minister announced accelerated deliveries of the weapon to Ukraine.
Phil Siveter, chief executive of Thales in the UK, said: “We are proud that the Prime Minister continues to see Thales in the UK as a trusted partner of the UK Government. Our Lightweight Multirole Missiles are designed and built at our site in Belfast, which has been supplying complex weapons to the UK for more than 70 years. With the support from Government, we have been able to quadruple our production to meet the global demand, and we are committed to investing £100m to expand this capacity further.
“The work carried out in Northern Ireland helps to sustain 1,100 direct jobs and supports around 700 more across our UK supply chain, giving the UK a sovereign capability it can rely on when it matters.”
Andy Burnham hosted Volodymyr Zelensky in Downing Street on Wednesday, pledging faster deliveries of air defence missiles alongside further military aid and tighter sanctions on Russia, with Britain pressing international partners to restrict Russian liquefied natural gas exports and to lean harder on Moscow over its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The Prime Minister said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.”
All of that rests on a single production line in Belfast, a site that has built complex weapons for Britain for more than seventy years, through Shorts and then Thales, and it is the home of the Starstreak family from which LMM descends. Starstreak and LMM share the launcher and much of the surrounding equipment, which is part of why the line has been able to grow quickly.
LMM is a laser beam riding missile weighing around thirteen kilograms, with a range of about six kilometres. It is fired from shoulder launchers, from lightweight multiple launchers on vehicles, and from the Royal Navy’s Wildcat helicopters, where it carries the name Martlet. Against drones it is substantially cheaper than the surface to air missiles that would otherwise be expended on them, which is the characteristic that has driven demand since 2022.
The Belfast expansion is the kind of industrial response the Strategic Defence Review and the Defence Investment Plan have both called for, with onshore capacity that can be surged when a war consumes stock faster than peacetime contracts replace it.

Newcomers face tougher Dutch standards, but some see opportunity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:03:33 UTC
22:03:33 KST

Partner content
Newcomers face tougher Dutch standards, but some see opportunity
The Netherlands has raised the level of Dutch it expects from newcomers. For those who reach B1, the payoff goes beyond the paperwork. We spoke with experts at language school Language Corner about how the change in requirements is both a challenge and an opportunity for the international community.
Foreigners in the Netherlands are increasingly expected to speak Dutch at an intermediate level, as the government moves the standard from the basic A2 level to the more advanced B1.
For those who have to meet it, that means more time and money spent in the classroom. But learners and teachers say the higher level also brings people closer to working and living in the Netherlands.
For many, B1 is already the norm. Since January 1, 2022, people covered by the Civic Integration Act 2021 – mainly refugees and family members joining a partner here – have had to aim for B1 as part of their integration (inburgering) programme.
They can drop down to A2 only after making what the rules call “significant effort”, including 600 hours of lessons, according to municipal social services association Divosa.
Citizenship next
Citizenship is the next step; for now, people who want to naturalise can still do so with an A2 integration diploma. EU, EEA and Swiss nationals are largely exempt.
But the coalition of D66, the VVD and CDA has written a B1 requirement into its January coalition agreement, as part of a new route to citizenship for people on temporary residence permits.
The pledge is not new. The Rutte III, Rutte IV and Schoof cabinets all promised to raise the language bar for naturalisation to B1, and none put it into effect.
A2 versus B1
Both levels come from the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, the scale used across Europe to measure language skills.
At A2, a “basic user” can handle simple, routine exchanges on familiar topics such as shopping, family and directions. At B1, an “independent user” can follow the main points of clear, standard speech about work, school and leisure, and deal with most everyday situations.
B1 speakers can also write simple connected texts, describe experiences and give reasons for their opinions. In practice, that means considerably more study than A2.
The opportunities 
The rules are not the only reason to aim higher. Carlos Blasco, a design engineer from Valencia who has taken two courses at Amsterdam language school Language Corner, said he has noticed a shift in the job market.
“When I moved here three years ago, Dutch wasn’t really a requirement,” he said. “Nowadays, I see it in almost every job offer, so I think it makes professional sense to improve my Dutch.”
Blasco is now on a B1 course. He said he is learning to integrate into local life as much as for work.
Exam preparation
Language Corner, which teaches Dutch at two locations in Amsterdam and online, said many of its students switch to private lessons once they reach A2, to prepare for the B1 exams.
“Private lessons can really focus on an individual’s situation,” said Eric van Heesen of Language Corner. “In addition to prepping for the B1 exams, private lessons can help students improve where they need to, whether it’s speaking, listening or grammar.”
Teacher Daniel Vis said some students need B1 for a specific goal. “Some want to learn something specific, like studying for a master’s degree, in which case you need to be at the B1 level,” he said. “For such specifics, private lessons are better, because we do intensive course work with them.”
Edward Blake, an American experience designer, took group classes before moving to one-to-one lessons. “We had conversations, gave presentations, played games, wrote short papers and even watched a bit of broadcaster NPO,” he said.
Outside the classroom
The school also runs social gatherings outside lessons. Vis said he took his students to watch the recent eclipse, and they spoke Dutch together.
Blake, who said he chose classroom lessons over online or AI-based learning, is measuring his progress in daily life. “I’m faultless in an ice cream shop, but that skill has become less useful as the weather turns,” he said. “I try reading the Dutch newspapers but to mixed success (for now). I’m getting there.”
For Blasco, the turning point came at the Lowlands festival this summer, where there were few internationals. “I got to practise a lot of Dutch, and people – contrary to before – didn’t switch to English,” he said.
He said he can now follow conversations on the street and the news. “I might still miss some nuances, but that’ll come with time.”
If you’re just starting your language journey or need to pass your B1 levels, check out the Dutch course offerings at Language Corner.

At least 38 people were killed and dozens injured in a Russian drone strike on an ammunition depot in the Bucha district near Kyiv, triggering a massive fire and hours of explosions in a residential area, CNN reported. The attack in the Bucha district came amid near-constant Russian airstrikes, which continued into Sunday, the outlet reported.
Russian forces were likely seeking to exhaust Ukraine’s air defenses, disrupt civilians’ daily lives, and increase the scale of destruction, analysts at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said, citing CNN’s reporting.
On 8 September, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte stressed the urgent need to strengthen support for Ukraine, particularly by providing air defense systems. Delays in delivering assistance cost human lives, he said.
On 1 October, a Russian drone struck a school in Kyiv’s Solomianskyi district while 104 children were inside, Suspilne reported. Students and school staff took shelter, so no one was injured, the report said.
Russian attacks continue after Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire
Following US President Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire, Russia continued striking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, including in Kyiv. On 13 October, Russian ballistic missiles struck Kyiv, hitting a thermal power plant in the second attack in 24 hours without advance warning from Ukraine’s allies, Zelenskyy said. The evening and morning strikes killed four people in Kyiv, three of them women in a high-rise in Desnianskyi district, Kyiv prosecutors said.
Russia attacked energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv with 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 14 October. At least 600,000 people were left without electricity, he said. Later that day, an accident on the grid cut power to part of Kyiv’s right bank, energy company DTEK said.

Meet the 76-year-old Kazakh traveller on a mission to walk around the world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:00:38 UTC
22:00:38 KST

Sarsenbay Kotyrashov began travelling on foot in his 70s. After walking across Kazakhstan and through parts of Asia and Europe, he is now preparing to cross the US.
It is hot and noisy inside the blacksmith workshop. Sarsenbay Kotyrashov, a 76-year-old blacksmith, wipes the sweat from his forehead as he works with a piece of hot iron.
“There is a Kazakh verse that goes: ‘I’m as soft as iron and as white as coal,’” Kotyrashov says with a laugh.
There is something of the iron he works with in his own character. Kotyrashov was introduced to blacksmithing at an early age and has practised the craft ever since. Years of hard physical work seem reflected in the strength and endurance that now take him far beyond his workshop.
“I had never travelled far in my life. But it is never too late to travel. Age doesn’t matter,” Kotyrashov says.
In 2022, he finally set out on his first long-distance journey. Starting in his native Ulytau region, Kotyrashov crossed Kazakhstan entirely on foot. His route took him through the south of the country, then east and north, before finishing in the west, on the shores of the Caspian Sea in Aktau.
The 8,000-kilometre journey took him six months. By the end of it, Kotyrashov realised he could go even further. He decided to push himself beyond Kazakhstan’s borders and, for the first time in his life, set foot in another country.
Later, setting off from Atyrau in western Kazakhstan, Kotyrashov crossed into Russia and continued through the Caucasus, eventually reaching Türkiye and Istanbul. Along the way, he met people from different cultures and saw places he had never visited before. The experience only fuelled his appetite for more.
By then, Kotyrashov had adopted the nickname Ulytauman, a reference to his native region. His distinctive look — a lean but strong figure in a hat, pulling a suitcase covered with stickers from the places he had visited — became increasingly recognisable. People began posting photos and videos of him on social media and stopping him for selfies along the way.
His next destination was China. Setting off from Oskemen in eastern Kazakhstan, Kotyrashov made his way through Russia’s Altai region and Mongolia before reaching Beijing. The journey eventually brought him to one of China’s most famous landmarks, where he posed for a photograph on the Great Wall.
On his latest journey, in 2026, Kotyrashov secured funding, obtained a Schengen visa and walked through five European countries. He started in Belgrade, Serbia, then continued through Hungary, Austria and Germany before reaching Paris, France, covering around 3,000 kilometres in 53 days.
Kotyrashov recounts the long list of countries he has crossed on foot almost like a tale, moving from one place to another and drawing his listener into the journey.
But as he retraces his journeys from memory, he also recalls some of their most difficult moments. “Once, I spent three and a half days out in the wilderness without food or water. It turns out a person can endure it. If you have the will and desire to live, you can endure anything,” he says.
Then the conversation takes a lighter turn as Kotyrashov shifts to one of his most recognisable travel companions — his signature leather hat.
“I’ve travelled through five European countries wearing this. Now, God willing, I’ll conquer America next,” he says.
Now, Kotyrashov is preparing to walk across eight US states in 2027, travelling from the Atlantic to the Pacific coast. The journey is part of a bigger ambition. Kotyrashov says he hopes to enter Guinness World Records by covering more than 40,000 kilometres on foot after the age of 75.
With a mischievous smile, Kotyrashov adds: “I don’t consider myself old. Until I complete this plan and make it into the Guinness World Records, I won’t consider myself old.”

Delfi faces 1.5 million euro lawsuit over alleged unpaid advertising fees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:00:37 UTC
22:00:37 KST

Riga City Court opened civil proceedings in late September over a claim seeking to recover 1.5 million euros from Latvian media company AS Delfi. The lawsuit was filed by SIA Ekis & Co-Positioning and Consulting, the owner of news portal LA.LV, according to LA.LV.
The claim concerns an alleged failure to fulfil obligations under a cooperation agreement signed between the two companies in February 2024.
According to LA.LV, Delfi approached Ekis & Co-Positioning and Consulting in 2023 with a proposal to become the exclusive advertising sales provider for the LA.LV news portal.
However, LA.LV alleges that Delfi subsequently failed to meet the sales targets it had established under the agreement. The portal attributes this failure to what it describes as a lack of professionalism on Delfi’s part. Rather than addressing the situation, Delfi allegedly stopped fulfilling its contractual obligations by discontinuing the agreed payments.
LA.LV claims that Delfi has offered conflicting and, in some cases, mutually exclusive explanations for its failure to fulfil the agreement.
 According to the portal, Delfi initially argued that the contract had caused it excessive financial losses. LA.LV disputes this argument, maintaining that such a claim is legally untenable because Delfi itself had determined the sales targets.
Delfi also allegedly argued that the cooperation agreement was entirely invalid.
LA.LV points out that Delfi raised this argument more than a year after the agreement was signed, at a time when the company allegedly began experiencing difficulties making the required payments. Despite the emerging legal dispute, Delfi continued selling advertising space on LA.LV and retaining the revenue generated from those sales, the portal claims.
“At one point, they simply stopped paying the invoices while continuing to place advertisements on LA.LV. It was a rather strange situation – the service was being used, but no money was being paid,” said LA.LV Chief Financial Officer Normunds Kalniņš.
LA.LV believes the underlying cause of the dispute is poor business management at Delfi. 
According to the portal, Delfi was forced to borrow money from an affiliated company to avoid insolvency proceedings. LA.LV also alleges that Delfi went as far as proposing to use funds allocated under media support programmes and held in the State Treasury to fulfil its contractual obligations. The portal argues that such funding cannot legally be used to settle private contractual liabilities.
LA.LV stated that several circumstances suggested Delfi was not only unwilling to meet its obligations but potentially unable to do so. Consequently, the company decided to pursue the dispute through the courts. LA.LV expects lawsuit to set precedent for Latvian media market LA.LV believes the proceedings should be public and could establish a lasting precedent in Latvia’s media industry.
The portal has announced that it will continue informing the public and other media market participants about developments in the court case. The allegations presented in the report are those of LA.LV. The article does not include Delfi’s response to the claims, and the court has not yet ruled on the dispute.

Germany urges Russia to halt Black Sea attacks threatening grain supplies
Unknown

Ayhan Simsek
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Germany on Wednesday called on Russia to halt attacks in the Black Sea and agree to a ceasefire for civilian shipping, warning that continued strikes would deepen hunger in Africa and erode Moscow’s remaining standing in the Global South.
Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul made the appeal at a joint news conference with his Bulgarian counterpart, Velislava Petrova-Chamova, after talks in Berlin focused on regional developments and Black Sea security.
“If Russia continues these attacks, it does so at the expense of people in the Global South — primarily people in Africa,” Wadephul said. “These people are suffering as a result, and they face the threat of hunger.”
Germany’s top diplomat said recent attacks on civilian ships, especially those carrying grain, endangered food security and lives in vulnerable regions while further isolating Moscow.
“Russia will need to be very careful not to lose what remains of its reputation in this region by once again expanding the theater of war in the Black Sea,” Wadephul said. “That is why I reiterate the clear appeal: we need a ceasefire in the Black Sea for civilian shipments, particularly of grain.”
The official stressed that Black Sea coastal states were ready to hold talks with Russia and Ukraine on a ceasefire to guarantee safe passage for civilian vessels and uninterrupted grain exports to countries that rely on them.
“It is now up to Russia to show whether it is willing to weigh its relations with the countries of the Global South — and its own interests — in a way that can save lives,” he said.

Exploring Dubrovnik: Lilly’s epic Adriatic adventure of history and thrills

13:00:16 UTC

Dubrovnik welcomes more than a million visitors a year. Join Lilly Douse as she explores its historic Old Town, tries traditional Croatian cooking, and heads out onto the Adriatic Sea.
Her journey begins in the heart of the Old Town, where she joins the CEO of Rewind Croatia to explore Dubrovnik’s cobbled streets and uncover the stories behind its medieval defensive walls. The Old Town has been a UNESCO-World Heratige site since 1979. Along the way, she learns how Dubrovnik became one of the Adriatic's most important trading centres.
Leaving the historic centre behind, Lilly joins X-adventure for a kayaking trip along the coast, taking in views of the fortified walls from the water. Stretching for almost two kilometers, the walls include five fortresses and 16 towers.
She then takes a boat trip to the island of Lopud, one of three inhabited Elaphiti Islands of the coast of Dubrovnik, before exploring the city’s famous Blue Caves, and stopping for a swim in the Adriatic.
At Restaurant Konoba Pjatanca, Lilly learns how to prepare a traditional peka, a slow-cooked dish prepared beneath a bell-shaped iron lid. She joins in the cooking and learn about this Croatian tradition.
During her time in Dubrovnik, Lilly stays at the Hilton Imperial Dubrovnik, a historic five-star hotel just outside the historic city centre. Its building dates back to 1897 and is a short walk from the gates of the Old Town.
To end her trip on a high note, Lilly takes on an exhilarating zipline adventure with Panorama Zip Line Dubrovnik. Set on Mount Srđ, the course has two line, each 250 meters long. Despite being afraid of heights, Lilly embraces the challenge, and enjoys the views across the city and coastline.

What does the historic Bank of America fine mean for US-China capital streams?

What does the historic Bank of America fine mean for US-China capital streams?
Analysts say penalties signal tighter scrutiny over cross-border financial flows
As the US Treasury imposed historic fines on Bank of America over compliance failures involving Chinese money-laundering networks, analysts see the action as a signal that could prompt Western banks to tighten scrutiny of Chinese clients and cross-border transactions.
The penalties, announced on Tuesday and totalling more than US$1.21 billion, included what the US Treasury described as its third-largest penalty on record and the largest in the history of the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.
Bank of America had failed to report more than US$5 billion in suspicious transactions in a timely manner, including more than US$1 billion involving national security-related and other priority risks such as “suspicious transactions indicative of Chinese money-laundering networks, fraud and potential trade-based money-laundering with a substantial nexus to the southwest border”, according to a Treasury statement.
The bank had also processed millions of dollars in payments “in apparent violation of sanctions programmes”, including those targeting Russia, Iran and narcotics and global terrorism networks, the Treasury added.
