In Gaza, even cash comes at a cost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Muhammad Hussam thought the 200 shekels (approximately 65 USD; 1 shekel equals 0.3253 USD) he had received in cash from a humanitarian organization would bring a little joy to his children. The 38-year-old father, who was displaced from Shuja’iyya to Tel al-Hawa in western Gaza City, was struggling to provide food for his family, who were living in a tent.
Delighted by the cash assistance, he went to a grocery store near the displacement camp to buy some fruit. But when he handed over the 200 shekels to pay for two kilograms of apples, the shopkeeper refused it. He told Hussam that he only accepted bank transfers — Cash was no longer welcome.
Hussam tried another seller and received the same answer, with one exception: this shopkeeper would accept his cash only if he agreed to a 10% commission. He could then buy goods with whatever remained.
Hussam’s struggle to make ordinary financial transactions with cash — a predicament that would have once been unthinkable in Gaza, a society that until recently ran mostly on cash transactions — represents a new financial emergency facing Palestinians in Gaza.
Financial transactions in Gaza have been upended since the early stages of the Israeli war on the enclave. In the height of the genocide, Palestinians once paid commissions of up to 50% to withdraw cash from their own bank accounts. Now, as electronic payments spread and the banknotes in circulation deteriorate, some depositors are being charged for adding cash to their bank accounts, while others are charged for spending the cash they already have.
With bank branches either closed or bombed, residents have limited ways to withdraw their money, with many resorting to cash dealers. These dealers receive electronic transfers from customers’ bank accounts in exchange for physical banknotes. However, they charge heavy commission fees that could reach up to half of the original transfer.
Today, financial applications, including Jawwal Pay wallet and Bank of Palestine’s banking app, have become widely used for buying and selling. Even taxi drivers receive fares through electronic transfers. Cash, meanwhile, has become increasingly unwelcome, largely because the notes are aged and damaged. In addition to this, Israel has prevented new banknotes from entering the Strip since the beginning of the war.
Hussam, and many others in Gaza, see this shift as part of an Israeli effort to tighten control and track Palestinians’ access to money.
Palestinians, he says, have no choice but to use whatever means are available. When obtaining cash meant losing 50% of their money, they accepted the deduction because they had no alternative. Now, he says, they are being pushed toward electronic payments for the same reason. And if a place like Gaza becomes wholly dependent on electronic payment infrastructures, it means that those in control — in this case, Israel — will have even more power over the society.
A financial siege
Ismail al-Thawabta, director general of Gaza’s Government Media Office, describes Israel’s actions as a deliberate economic and financial war, no less dangerous than its military campaign. Its direct aim, he says, is to undermine the government and paralyze its ability to provide basic services.
“This financial siege involves preventing cash from entering Gaza, destroying banks and banking infrastructure, freezing accounts and clearing funds, and targeting vehicles transporting money,” al-Thawabta said. He argues that these measures are intended to bring about a complete breakdown in administration and services and push Gaza into social chaos as part of Israel’s broader policy of genocide.
He calls the financial restrictions “collective punishment directed at the population as a whole, with ordinary residents bearing the greatest harm.”
Sami al-Khaldi, a financial and economic expert based in Ramallah, paints a more detailed picture. He attributes a large part of the crisis to traders who exploited conditions in Gaza and now need to replenish their bank balances to pay suppliers outside the Strip.
“Israel indirectly controls payments in Gaza by imposing specific policies on Bank of Palestine, the largest Palestinian bank, which implements those policies out of fear of further restrictions,” he said. “Under these policies, banks will not accept cash deposits without knowing the source of the money. This has pushed traders away from cash and toward electronic transfers because they cannot deposit the cash they hold. In this way, Israel can exert control over society through electronic payments.”
The banknotes circulating in Gaza are also deteriorating, he said. According to al-Khaldi, around 17% of the cash in circulation needs to be replaced each year. With no such replacement taking place in Gaza since the war began in 2023, he said, a substantial share of the banknotes now circulating is worn out and unfit for use. Al-Khaldi also pointed to Israeli restrictions on cash transactions, describing a limit of 6,000 shekels (approximately 1,950 USD) after which payments must be made electronically. He said these measures are intended to “strengthen oversight of financial transactions and curb tax evasion.”
Government employees are part of that same social fabric, al-Thawabta added. Whatever cash salaries the government can provide from its severely limited resources are spent immediately in local markets, helping keep the economy moving. The siege, he says, seeks to choke everyone without exception and impose “starvation and submission.”
According to al-Thawabta, the lack of cash strikes at the heart of the local economy. It prevents residents from collecting money transfers and stops families of those killed or wounded, as well as recipients of cash assistance, from withdrawing funds to meet their basic needs.
The lack of cash also paralyzes trade. Al-Thawabta says that the committee overseeing government affairs in Gaza is taking steps against traders who accept worn banknotes in exchange for electronic balances while charging commissions that have risen to 10%.
“The committee views these practices with the utmost seriousness and considers them an economic crime and a vile exploitation of our people’s blood and sacrifices during the genocidal war,” he said. “We will not allow any party to profit unlawfully from citizens’ suffering.”
Al-Thawabta told Mondoweiss that the Ministry of National Economy, supply police, and public prosecution have pursued and arrested people accused of manipulating exchange rates and hoarding cash. Authorities have also confiscated money received through financial extortion and referred offenders to the courts on charges of exploitation and harming the national economy during a state of emergency.
Government authorities have issued binding directives requiring traders and retailers to accept circulating banknotes, including damaged notes, provided they retain their legal value under the Palestinian Monetary Authority’s standards, he says. Refusing these notes or charging a commission to accept them has been criminalized.
Consumer protection teams and supply police conduct regular market inspections to monitor compliance, al-Thawabta explains.
“Authorities have opened direct channels for residents to report traders who refuse banknotes or exploit the crisis. Enforcement measures include closing shops, imposing fines, and, in some cases, detention and prosecution.”
Civilian employees under pressure
For Abu Ibrahim, a 43-year-old civilian employee of the Hamas-run government, the cash crisis compounds restrictions he says have affected his access to banking services since the first month of the war. ‘Abu Ibrahim’ spoke to Mondoweiss using a pseudonym for his protection.
He previously received his salary through the National Bank or the Palestinian Production Bank, both of which were destroyed by the Israeli military early in the war. He says he still has money in the bank that he cannot access.
Abu Ibrahim previously received 2,000 shekels every 30 to 35 days. Now, he receives 1,500 shekels every 45 to 50 days, paid in worn banknotes that are difficult to spend.
He says transferring his salary through banks is not an option. He fears that whoever transfers the money could be targeted in an airstrike once identified, while his own account could be frozen or closed because he is a government employee.
Abu Ibrahim says the Bank of Palestine blocked his account in the first months of the war without giving a reason. He believes Israel exercises control over Palestinian banks.
His difficulties spending cash began during the famine. When he went to buy something, shopkeepers would tell him he had to spend the full value of the note he handed over because they had no cash to give him change. Otherwise, he had to pay by bank transfer.
“Now, some sellers demand 120 shekels in cash for goods worth only 100 shekels.”
“Just as we struggled to get cash at the beginning of the famine, we now face the same struggle to deposit money into our bank accounts and turn cash into a bank balance,” Abu Ibrahim said.
One of his greatest difficulties is finding a seller who will give him change. If he hands over a 200 shekel note, he may have to spend the entire amount, sometimes buying things he does not want to use.
At other times, he leaves the full amount with the shopkeeper and spends from it over several visits.
“I give the seller 200 shekels and buy with it in stages,” he said. “Today I buy 50 shekels’ worth, then I come back tomorrow to spend the rest, or part of it, until I have used it all.”
Even then, the shopkeeper deducts a commission for accepting the payment in cash.
Abu Ibrahim also believes that militias affiliated with the Israeli military are draining cash from Gaza. For instance, the gangs who control the trade of cigarettes only accept cash payments. With cigarette prices soaring, he believes a substantial share of Gaza’s cash has left the strip through this trade and has not been replaced.
These challenges are on top of other economic pressures that Abu Ibrahim sees as part of Israel’s effort to choke Gaza’s economy and its population. Before the war, he says, 100 shekels bought enough vegetables, fruit, and meat to feed his family for a week. Now, the same amount does not cover a single day’s food.
He sees these practices as “part of an Israeli effort to empty Gaza of banknotes, leaving electronic payments as residents’ only option. Once that happens, Israel can track who sends and receives money, making it easier to identify and cut off funding for Gaza’s government and its employees.”

The lack of cash also paralyzes trade. Al-Thawabta says that the committee overseeing government affairs in Gaza is taking steps against traders who accept worn banknotes in exchange for electronic balances while charging commissions that have risen to 10%.
“The committee views these practices with the utmost seriousness and considers them an economic crime and a vile exploitation of our people’s blood and sacrifices during the genocidal war,” he said. “We will not allow any party to profit unlawfully from citizens’ suffering.”
Al-Thawabta told Mondoweiss that the Ministry of National Economy, supply police, and public prosecution have pursued and arrested people accused of manipulating exchange rates and hoarding cash. Authorities have also confiscated money received through financial extortion and referred offenders to the courts on charges of exploitation and harming the national economy during a state of emergency.
Government authorities have issued binding directives requiring traders and retailers to accept circulating banknotes, including damaged notes, provided they retain their legal value under the Palestinian Monetary Authority’s standards, he says. Refusing these notes or charging a commission to accept them has been criminalized.
Consumer protection teams and supply police conduct regular market inspections to monitor compliance, al-Thawabta explains.
“Authorities have opened direct channels for residents to report traders who refuse banknotes or exploit the crisis. Enforcement measures include closing shops, imposing fines, and, in some cases, detention and prosecution.”
Civilian employees under pressure
For Abu Ibrahim, a 43-year-old civilian employee of the Hamas-run government, the cash crisis compounds restrictions he says have affected his access to banking services since the first month of the war. ‘Abu Ibrahim’ spoke to Mondoweiss using a pseudonym for his protection.
He previously received his salary through the National Bank or the Palestinian Production Bank, both of which were destroyed by the Israeli military early in the war. He says he still has money in the bank that he cannot access.
Abu Ibrahim previously received 2,000 shekels every 30 to 35 days. Now, he receives 1,500 shekels every 45 to 50 days, paid in worn banknotes that are difficult to spend.
He says transferring his salary through banks is not an option. He fears that whoever transfers the money could be targeted in an airstrike once identified, while his own account could be frozen or closed because he is a government employee.
Abu Ibrahim says the Bank of Palestine blocked his account in the first months of the war without giving a reason. He believes Israel exercises control over Palestinian banks.
His difficulties spending cash began during the famine. When he went to buy something, shopkeepers would tell him he had to spend the full value of the note he handed over because they had no cash to give him change. Otherwise, he had to pay by bank transfer.
“Now, some sellers demand 120 shekels in cash for goods worth only 100 shekels.”
“Just as we struggled to get cash at the beginning of the famine, we now face the same struggle to deposit money into our bank accounts and turn cash into a bank balance,” Abu Ibrahim said.
One of his greatest difficulties is finding a seller who will give him change. If he hands over a 200 shekel note, he may have to spend the entire amount, sometimes buying things he does not want to use.
At other times, he leaves the full amount with the shopkeeper and spends from it over several visits.
“I give the seller 200 shekels and buy with it in stages,” he said. “Today I buy 50 shekels’ worth, then I come back tomorrow to spend the rest, or part of it, until I have used it all.”
Even then, the shopkeeper deducts a commission for accepting the payment in cash.
Abu Ibrahim also believes that militias affiliated with the Israeli military are draining cash from Gaza. For instance, the gangs who control the trade of cigarettes only accept cash payments. With cigarette prices soaring, he believes a substantial share of Gaza’s cash has left the strip through this trade and has not been replaced.
These challenges are on top of other economic pressures that Abu Ibrahim sees as part of Israel’s effort to choke Gaza’s economy and its population. Before the war, he says, 100 shekels bought enough vegetables, fruit, and meat to feed his family for a week. Now, the same amount does not cover a single day’s food.
He sees these practices as “part of an Israeli effort to empty Gaza of banknotes, leaving electronic payments as residents’ only option. Once that happens, Israel can track who sends and receives money, making it easier to identify and cut off funding for Gaza’s government and its employees.”

Voyager 1 is nearly one light-day from Earth. What’s out there?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Voyager 1 is nearly one light-day from Earth. What’s out there?
The spacecraft is finding the sun’s reach extends farther than expected
This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)
NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft has been breaking distance records for decades. Launched almost 50 years ago, it became the farthest human-built object from Earth when it overtook the pathfinding Pioneer 10 probe in 1998. It was the first spacecraft to leave the solar system’s protective bubble, and it will be humankind’s first emissary to the stars.
The cameras on Voyager 1, along with those on its twin spacecraft, Voyager 2, captured powerful megastorms in the outer solar system, the first images of dozens of moons and never-before-seen details of the gossamer rings around Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune and Uranus. The images and data sent home have shaped theories of how the solar system formed and evolved, inspired subsequent missions and posed enough new questions to keep space scientists busy for decades.
And this month, Voyager 1 will set another big record. On November 18 at 5:16:07 a.m. Eastern Standard Time, it will become the first spacecraft to reach one light-day from Earth: the distance light travels in 24 hours. That’s a journey of 25.9 billion kilometers, or more than four times the distance from the sun to Pluto. At that point, signals from Earth will take a full day to reach Voyager 1; it will take another day to hear back.
“I just never imagined [the mission] would last that long,” says Linda Spilker, a planetary scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., who began working on Voyager shortly before the probes launched in 1977. Spilker was in Cape Canaveral, Fla., for the first launch. She even planned the births of her children, now in their 40s, around mission milestones. After stepping away to lead another mission, she is now back as Voyager head scientist.
Two other scientists have been with Voyager since the beginning. Others weren’t yet born when the spacecraft launched. “Voyager, to this day, is a multi-generational mission,” Spilker says. But it isn’t a mission of nostalgia. There’s still a world of discovery out beyond the solar system’s edge.
“Every piece of data, every day that goes by that we get data from the Voyagers, tells us something new,” says physicist Jamie Rankin of Princeton University, who started her Ph.D. in August 2012, the same month that Voyager 1 left the solar system for the cold, calm seas of interstellar space. “Every day, it’s in places nobody’s ever explored before.”
Exploring our neighborhood
The original mission of the Voyager probes was to explore the outer parts of our solar system, which until then had remained largely mysterious. A rare planetary alignment meant that a spacecraft launched in the late 1970s could swoop past Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, getting a gravitational boost from each planet that it passed. With these gravitational assists, the spacecraft could complete the tour in less than 15 years. Such an alignment won’t happen again until the 2150s.
The project was a bold step for its time. When work began in the early 1970s, no spacecraft had gone farther than Mars. NASA set a conservative goal for the mission: flybys of Jupiter and Saturn. In 1972 and 1973, NASA launched two Pioneer probes, which made sure the trek was possible and gathered data along the way. As with Voyager, there were two spacecraft in case one failed.
After nail-biting launches and a wait of nearly two years, the Voyagers began uncovering many of Jupiter’s and Saturn’s long-held secrets, including the volcanoes on Jupiter’s moon Io, details of Jupiter’s Great Red Spot and hints of geologic activity on Saturn’s moon Enceladus.
Mission accomplished, Voyager 2 went on to pass Uranus and Neptune. It took the first images of the planets’ rings and discovered more than a dozen moons along the way. The spacecraft also spotted a perpetually churning storm on Neptune and erupting geysers on Neptune’s moon Triton.
“The highlights of Voyager were clearly the planetary encounters,” said Ed Stone, the mission’s original head scientist, in a NASA interview before his death in 2024. “We had a lifetime of discovery packed into each one.”
The uncontested stars of these encounters were the images shared in news reports and TV broadcasts as the planets and their moons came into view. Jupiter’s moon Io turned out to be a shocking splotchy orange color that looked like a pizza.
A humble navigation image of that moon led to one of the most surprising discoveries of the entire mission. Four days past Voyager 1’s closest approach to Jupiter, after the excitement had died down, project astronomer Linda Morabito of the Jet Propulsion Laboratory started processing additional images of Io. These images had been taken after the flyby, when Voyager was looking back over its shoulder.
As Morabito enhanced one image’s brightness, she spotted an odd bulbous formation protruding from Io’s edge. “What’s that?” she asked herself. Her supervisor had the same reaction: “Jesus, what’s that?” she later recalled him saying.
The bulb turned out to be a volcanic plume — an erupting fire fountain extending 250 kilometers above Io’s surface. It was the first discovery of active volcanism anywhere other than Earth, and it transformed our view of the outer solar system. Instead of a cold, inert icebox, this was a bubbling and dynamic region.
The findings inspired many future missions. While visiting Jupiter from 1995 to 2003, the Galileo probe found that Europa may have a subsurface ocean that could be hospitable to life. When the Cassini probe orbited Saturn from 2004 to 2017, it discovered that the moon Enceladus also has a potentially habitable ocean that spews icy geysers into space.
In 1990, with Voyager 1 about 6 billion kilometers from the sun, astronomer Carl Sagan convinced mission leaders to turn the spacecraft backward for one last look at the planets. Voyager 1 took a family portrait in which Earth appeared faintly as a “pale blue dot,” Sagan said. “Everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives … on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam,” he wrote in the 1994 book Pale Blue Dot.
To save power, Voyager 2’s cameras were shut off in 1989. After the family portrait, Voyager 1’s cameras were also turned off. Where the spacecraft were headed, there wouldn’t be much to see.
The edge of nowhere
The probes were now on their way out of the solar system along their own separate paths, both headed toward a mysterious boundary that no human emissary had ever crossed. In this next phase of their voyage, no one knew what to expect. How long would the spacecraft keep communicating? How far would the powerful forces that drive the sun reach? And what would it be like to taste interstellar space?
For its first 35 years in space, Voyager 1 was swaddled in the solar wind. This stream of hot, charged particles flows constantly from the sun, forming a vast bubble called the heliosphere. The bubble surrounds the solar system, protecting it from cosmic radiation; it extends billions of kilometers past the planets up to a boundary called the heliopause. Heliophysicists consider this boundary, where the solar wind bumps into interstellar space, the edge of the solar system, although the sun’s gravitational influence extends much farther.
Scientists expected the Voyagers to cross the heliopause, but they didn’t know when — or what the spacecraft would find when they did. Rankin had just started her Ph.D. at Caltech when in August 2012 Voyager 1 detected an abrupt jump in the number of high-energy cosmic rays alongside a drop in solar particles, hinting that the spacecraft had crossed the boundary. But magnetic field measurements suggested otherwise. Instead, those measurements indicated that the sun still exerted some influence. The interstellar magnetic field diverted around the heliosphere like a river around a rock.
A Voyager instrument that could have settled the question of whether the probe had passed the heliopause was no longer working. But scientists got a lucky break in April 2013 when an eruption on the sun sent a pressure wave rippling outward. It set the electrons around Voyager 1 vibrating, which allowed scientists to estimate the density of charged particles nearby.
The results showed that Voyager 1 had in fact crossed the heliopause on August 25, 2012, when it was about 18 billion kilometers away, or 120 times Earth’s distance from the sun. Data from Voyager 2 later backed up that finding. “This is the beginning of a new era of exploration for us,” Stone told Science News in 2013.
The space beyond
But the line between our solar system and interstellar space isn’t solid. The sun’s reach extends farther than anyone expected, and “this boundary is not very sharp or very thin,” says physicist Jeewoo Park of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Md.
With Voyager on the other side of the heliopause, particle speeds and gas temperatures have dropped. The magnetic field is weaker. Even dust particles are about half as abundant compared with inside the heliosphere. “For the most part, it’s been very quiet and very consistent,” Rankin says.
But it’s not entirely silent. In four instances, scientists saw spikes in the magnetic field strength and particle density measurements around the probe. After the fourth, in mid-2020, those numbers have remained high. No one knows why. Perhaps Voyager 1 continues to ride the aftershocks of solar eruptions, says Park, who reported on the events in June in the Astrophysical Journal.
Where pure interstellar space begins is still an open question. So is the heliosphere’s shape. Most scientists think it is elongated, like a comet, but others think it is a sphere or even a croissant.
Space telescopes launched in 2008 and 2025, the Interstellar Boundary Explorer and Interstellar Mapping and Acceleration Probe, could help answer that question.
Meanwhile, the Voyager probes are silently sailing onward. Scientists estimate that the onboard power sources that keep the crafts’ instruments running will dry up in 10 to 15 years, preventing them from sending data back to Earth. Our conversation will come to an end. But the journey goes on.
Voyager 2 will approach a red dwarf star known as Ross 248 in about 42,000 years, coming within 700 light-days. It will be 44,000 years before Voyager 1 next encounters another star, Gliese 445, at a similar distance. “The Voyagers become our silent ambassadors, a little bit of us that continues into space,” Spilker says.
They carry a message, should anyone find it, contained on the Golden Record. A copy of the phonograph record, which is plated in gold, rides on each of the probes. The long-distance dispatches feature sights and sounds of Earth, including a map of the solar system; images of Earth’s monuments; greetings in dozens of languages; and the sounds of whale song, laughter, classical composers and Navajo chants.
That time capsule captures the optimism and promise of the mission, Spilker says. “It may well outlast humanity.”

Formlabs Has a 3D Printer for Normies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Fourteen boxes are piled in front of my desk, stacked around me like a cardboard fort. Inside one is a Form Studio 1, the new, affordable, consumer-focused 3D printer Formlabs just announced.
David Lakatos, chief product officer at the 3D printer manufacturer, assured me that the Form Studio 1 has a very economical size. “It doesn't take a lot of space,” Lakatos said. “If you have a desk, then I think you should be good to go.” I have a desk. It’s covered in boxes sent by his company.
Formlabs is one of the biggest 3D printer producers, with nearly 200,000 printers in service. The company’s customers are primarily professional businesses, like assembly shops or dentists, able to shell out $2,500 or more for a printer. (Its last affordable printer was $2,300.)
But the Form Studio 1 is Formlabs’ first consumer-oriented device. It prints with SLA (stereolithography) resins—a common 3D printing material that hardens into solid plastic when exposed to ultraviolet light—and can use Formlabs-branded products or third-party resins. It costs $699 and is now on sale; individual resin bottles start at $29.
The Studio 1 takes up roughly the same space as a minifridge. You’ll also likely need a wash and cure unit, sold separately for $199 with a similar footprint (it removes uncured liquid resin from the surface of models). Then you’ll need room for all the tools and resin cartridges. Getting all that stuff can pile up. Or at least it did when Formlabs sent more than a dozen boxes to the WIRED office for testing. Your pileage may vary.
The front touchscreen lets you troubleshoot and ready prints. When the printer starts, it’s relatively quiet and odor-free. 3D printing with resin can be stinky, but Formlabs-branded Alpha resins are UL GreenGuard-certified—the same standard used to ensure baby products aren’t harmful from skin contact or off-gassing—when used with a Formlabs VOC Extractor. Lakatos says the idea is that the Studio 1 can be used anywhere without the room being overwhelmed by resin stank.
“We know that some people are going to put it in their bedrooms,” Lakatos says. “I don't sleep with my printers, but you could if you really wanted to.”
After going through the stack of boxes, I set up the Form Studio 1 and the Form Studio Wash+Cure. They’re stylish, with translucent orange cases that conjure old-school iMac aesthetics. The printing process itself is supposedly quick. Lakatos says you can print a casing for a Raspberry Pi setup in around eight minutes.
I’ve only printed a couple of things so far, but have had a good experience with the orders. (Full review coming soon.) I printed a clear cover for the toolbox that comes with the Studio 1. It took about 17 minutes and came out clean and intact. The process was relatively quiet. The resin smell was there, but really only when lifting the hood after the process was done. I’m excited to use it more and see what kind of very detailed unholy abominations I can make.
The SLA printing enables very detailed constructions. In Formlabs’ internal testing, the company says it has had a roughly 2 percent failure rate for its prints. If that holds in the real world, it’ll be a big jump over competitors. That’s if you use its own resins, though.
“You can use any material,” Lakatos says. “If you want to use the toxic resin on Amazon, you can do it. We don't recommend it, but you can do it.”
Formlabs also has an app called Form Mobile that can control prints or send designs to the Form Studio 1. The overall printer experience feels surprisingly straightforward.
“It’s great if you want to mess around with some stuff,” Lakatos says. “For serious, beautiful things and projects that really require better material properties, beautiful resolution, stuff like that—it's hard to compete with it.”
Correction on 12 pm on October 14, 2026: We've clarified that you likely need the “wash and cure” unit, and specified that Formlabs' Alpha resins are UL GreenGuard-certified when used with a Formlabs VOC Extractor.

Kazakhstan seeks Antwerp-Bruges partnership to boost trade via Middle Corridor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:59:41 UTC
21:59:41 KST

Kazakhstan is seeking closer cooperation with Belgium on the Middle Corridor, including a potential partnership between the Port of Antwerp-Bruges and the Caspian ports of Aktau and Kuryk, as King Philippe and Queen Mathilde make their first state visit to the country.
Kazakhstan is seeking a partnership between the Port of Antwerp-Bruges and its Caspian ports of Aktau and Kuryk as the country looks to expand trade along the Middle Corridor, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said.
Speaking at the Belgium-Kazakhstan Business Council in Astana, attended by King Philippe and Queen Mathilde of Belgium, Tokayev said Kazakhstan was investing heavily in railways, roads, seaports and terminals along the route.
“In this context, Belgium’s rich experience as a major European logistics center is particularly valuable to us. We anticipate a concrete partnership linking the ports of Antwerp-Bruges, with the ports of Aktau and Kuryk. This could open wider markets for our metals, petrochemicals and agricultural products,” he said.
King Philippe also expressed Belgium’s support for the Middle Corridor, calling for closer links between the route and European ports, railways and logistics hubs.
The Middle Corridor, also known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, connects China with Europe through Kazakhstan, the Caspian Sea and the South Caucasus, providing an alternative to traditional east-west routes.
A day earlier, Nurlan Zhakupov, CEO of Samruk-Kazyna, Kazakhstan’s sovereign wealth fund which manages some of the country’s largest transport, energy and industrial companies, told reporters on the sidelines of the official welcoming ceremony for King Philippe and Queen Mathilde at Akorda that talks with the Port of Antwerp-Bruges were underway.
He said Kazakhstan was interested in drawing on the Belgian port’s expertise and eventually reaching concrete agreements and logistics contracts.
Speaking later to Euronews, Zhakupov said the route's viability would ultimately depend on its economic case.
“For the Middle Corridor, it has to make economic sense and deliver an economic benefit. That is why negotiations are ongoing — it is a large and complex process,” he said. “I think concrete results are not far off.”
Challenges along the road
The Port of Antwerp-Bruges was not represented at the business council, but the discussion focused on the practical challenges facing the Middle Corridor.
Speaking to Euronews after a session on new trade routes between Europe and Central Asia, Ahlers Logistics CEO Dave van den Bos said that while investment in physical infrastructure was already under way, one of the biggest challenges was coordinating handovers between the numerous companies and authorities involved along the route.
As many as 15 different companies or authorities can be involved in a single shipment from Europe to Kazakhstan, van den Bos said.
“Digitisation is the most important,” he said. “Even if the capacity is there, if you’re standing at the border with your document and waiting for someone to give a green light or a stamp, that’s still going to delay quite a bit. Infrastructure is easier to fix than the whole digitisation of it.”
Van den Bos said transit times from Europe to Kazakhstan had fallen from around 80 days to roughly 40–60 days, although port congestion and weather on the Caspian Sea still cause delays.
According to Kazakhstan Temir Zholy, the country’s national railway company, the Middle Corridor transported around 44,000 TEUs in the first eight months of 2026, up 58% from the same period last year.
Kazakhstan is seeking to increase overall freight volumes along the route to 10 million tonnes, a target Tokayev previously announced.
Investment and critical raw materials
Belgium is among Kazakhstan’s ten largest investors, with more than $15 billion invested in the country over the past two decades, according to Tokayev.
The forum's sidelines saw 17 agreements covering logistics, agriculture and food processing, artificial intelligence, energy, healthcare and manufacturing.
Tokayev also highlighted critical raw materials, stating Kazakhstan already produced 21 of the 34 raw materials considered critical for European industry and supplies Belgium with titanium and molybdenum products.
“By combining our resource potential with Belgian investment, technology and expertise, we can build a strategic partnership in this critically important area,” Tokayev said.
Belgium and Kazakhstan deepen ties
King Philippe and Queen Mathilde's visit is the first state visit by a Belgian monarch to Kazakhstan and the wider Central Asian region. President Tokayev welcomed the royal couple with an official ceremony at the Akorda presidential palace in Astana, followed by talks between the two sides.
The visit comes ahead of the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations between Kazakhstan and Belgium next year.
“Your visit gives new impetus to preparations for this important anniversary and opens up opportunities to fill our cooperation with concrete results,” Tokayev said, describing Belgium as a long-standing and reliable partner for Kazakhstan in Europe.
“We are convinced that we can take our cooperation to a new level,” King Philippe said. “The delegation accompanying me includes representatives from a wide range of promising, forward-looking sectors.”
As part of the state visit, Tokayev and the royal couple visited Kazakhstan’s National Museum, the National Children’s Rehabilitation Centre and the Alem.ai International Centre for Artificial Intelligence in Astana.
The programme also included a rectors’ forum and a roundtable on critical minerals. King Philippe and Queen Mathilde are due to continue their visit in Almaty.

Another storage tank exploded at an oil terminal in Russia’s southern city of Rostov-on-Don late Tuesday, as a fire sparked by a drone attack continued to burn for a fourth day, monitoring channels reported.
The blaze at the Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery’s terminal has spread to eight of its 12 storage tanks, the independent news outlet Astra reported. The Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ said another tank exploded late Tuesday.
Footage from the site showed tanks engulfed in flames beneath columns of black smoke. The local Telegram channel Rostov Glavny reported a bright flash on the city’s left bank at 11:50 p.m. Tuesday.
Drones struck the terminal, formerly known as Yug Rusi, in Rostov’s Zheleznodorozhny district overnight on Oct. 10. NASA’s FIRMS satellite monitoring system detected a fire at the site.
Authorities had not announced that the blaze had been extinguished as of Wednesday morning.
The terminal’s storage tanks have a combined capacity of 60,000 cubic meters. The facility can handle 3.5 million metric tons of petroleum products a year, loading sea and river tankers for export. It has also been used to supply fuel to the Russian military.
Separately, Rostov region Governor Yury Slyusar said the region came under a large-scale drone attack overnight Wednesday. More than 160 drones were shot down over the city of Kamensk-Shakhtinsky and eight districts, he said, without providing information on casualties or damage on the ground.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he had ordered his military to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries from Oct. 11 at U.S. President Donald Trump’s request as part of an “energy ceasefire.”
Moscow has yet to confirm that it is observing the arrangement. The strike that sparked the terminal fire preceded the announced halt.

Katy Perry’s ex-husband appeared in court on sex offense charges, prosecutors call him a “true predator”
Kyiv • UNN
Prosecutors accused Russell Brand of rape and sexual assault against six women. He denies all the charges.
Actor and comedian Russell Brand, who was once one of the United Kingdom’s best-known television presenters, acted as a ruthless predator: to satisfy his insatiable sexual appetite, he raped women or sexually assaulted them, ignoring their protests. Prosecutors said this, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The 51-year-old Brand, the former husband of American singer Katy Perry, is on trial on charges of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of engaging in sexual activity without the complainant’s consent; the charges concern six women and events that took place between 1999 and 2009.
He denies all the charges and will present his defence later in court.
"Today I feel blessed," he said as he arrived at London’s Southwark Crown Court. "Of course, I am nervous, but I hope this trial will lead to positive outcomes for everyone involved."
Opening the case, prosecutor Riel Karmi-Jones said that some of the six women who brought the allegations had resisted, while others had been unable to respond to his advances. According to her, this made no difference to Brand.
"His appetite — a strong desire for sexual contact — was indiscriminate and insatiable," the prosecutor said.
Although he could be funny, charming and pleasant to talk to, when he wanted something he also displayed a childish conviction that any desire of his should be satisfied, she added.
"He was ruthless, calculating, manipulative and, the prosecution contends, a sexual predator," Karmi-Jones said.
According to her, the alleged offences were committed over a decade while he was building his career — from performing stand-up comedy to working as a television presenter, actor and star of Hollywood films.
In addition
The first of these incidents allegedly occurred in 1999, when he was performing a show on the sidelines of a Labour Party conference in Bournemouth. The first complainant, who watched the show and believed Brand was gay, said that he raped her in a hotel room; she had invited him there because she thought he was interested in the matter she had discussed with him.
According to the prosecutor, one of the fellow performers who appeared with him at that show said that Brand boasted of wanting to sleep with 5,000 women over the course of his life.
He is accused of trying to drag a woman into a toilet cubicle at the MTV Europe office where she worked in 2001. Three years later, another woman said that he pulled her into a toilet cubicle in a bar and then committed an act of oral rape.
Around the same time — in 2004 or 2005 — a woman who worked for a media company reported that he engaged in sexual activity with her without her consent in her office.
The fifth complainant — one of his fans — said that in 2009 she had consensual sex with him at his home, but that he then raped her anally, the prosecutor said. The sixth complainant, who worked for Channel 4, alleges that Brand demanded a massage from her that same year and then pressed his face against her groin.
During police questioning, Brand refused to answer questions but provided a written statement in which he said that he did not remember the incidents and had never engaged in sexual activity without his partner’s consent, although he admitted having sex in toilet cubicles during parties, Karmi-Jones said.
According to the prosecutor, the women involved in the case did not know one another and had not reported the matter to police at the time for various reasons, but decided to make their complaints after a television programme aired and a newspaper article was published in 2023, in which other women made anonymous allegations.
Brand sat in the dock wearing a dark suit and a thin white scarf, staring intently ahead.
The trial, which is expected to last around six weeks, has attracted enormous media attention: an additional courtroom was opened to accommodate more journalists, and numerous media outlets launched daily podcasts.
The comedian, known for his outrageous style and appearance, rose to popularity in Britain before he began appearing in films—including the 2010 movie "Get Him to the Greek"; that same year, he married Perry. They divorced in 2012.
Recently, Brand has taken part in online broadcasts discussing U.S. politics, religion, and freedom of speech.

Louvre boss warns of closure risk without major renovations

Louvre boss warns of closure risk without major renovations
- The Louvre risks closure unless lawmakers approve major renovations, as boss Christophe Leribault warns the museum is “creaking and over-capacity” and needs urgent repair.
- Leribault wants private funding too, but says major public money may only come after the 2027 elections. He warned delay would be a “disaster”.
- The museum is also upgrading security after a 2025 jewel heist worth US$100 million. Plans include new security leadership, better cameras and stronger perimeter checks.
AI generated
PARIS – The Louvre Museum risks having to close its doors to the public unless lawmakers approve a major overhaul of the creaking and over-capacity institution, its head told a French newspaper on Oct 14.
Speaking to Le Figaro, Christophe Leribault said that the museum intended to tap private sources of funding for its transformation, but that a major injection of public money would need to be approved after national elections in 2027.
“Whoever forms the next government must keep in mind that if the Louvre is not repaired, updated and transformed, it will very quickly fall behind and will eventually have to close its doors to the public. That would be a disaster,” he said.
Successive minority governments in France have struggled for years to pass annual budgets and current Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is struggling to rein in public spending to reduce the country’s vast deficit.
Leribault was appointed in February in the aftermath of an embarrassing Oct 19 heist in 2025 which saw a gang of thieves raid the Louvre to steal crown jewels worth an estimated US$100 million (S$128.3 million).
He has made tackling the problems highlighted by the theft a priority, with the roll-out of an €83 million (S$118.9 million) security masterplan “moving forward at speed”, he told AFP ahead of the one-year anniversary of the crime.
Measures include creating a new head of security position, upgrading the security camera network – which was found to have old cameras and major gaps – as well as improved surveillance around the perimeter and at access points.
No ‘miracle’ solution
Leribault argued that long-term improvements could only be made as part of the larger overhaul he has planned for the institution, which welcomed around nine million visitors in 2025.
“The operations needed to secure the museum require work on the historic building and its infrastructure,” he wrote.
“There is no easy, miracle ‘surface’ solution. Everything is interconnected, everything is linked,” he added.
The world’s most-visited museum is widely seen as facing structural problems from its old plumbing, badly insulated galleries and cramped public areas.
The extent of the work and the cost have become extremely political, with President Emmanuel Macron championing a €600 million overhaul that would include a new entrance.
Trade unions criticised Macron and Leribault’s predecessor, Laurence des Cars, for prioritising grandiose plans for an architectural overhaul instead of more modest changes that would improve the visitor experience. AFP

Colombia opens embassy in Jerusalem
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:57:32 CST
21:57:32 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Colombia inaugurated its embassy in Jerusalem on Wednesday as its new president Abelardo de la Espriella moved to restore full diplomatic relations with Israel, reversing his predecessor's decision to sever ties over Israel's military operations in Gaza.
The ceremony was attended by Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar and his Colombian counterpart, Omar Bula Escobar.
Under de la Espriella, the two countries reached an agreement on July 15 to restore full diplomatic and economic relations, which took effect after the new Colombian president took office in August. On Tuesday, Colombia and Israel formally reinstated their free trade agreement.
In May 2024, then-Colombian President Gustavo Petro announced that Colombia would sever its ties with Israel, accusing its government of committing genocide in Gaza, an allegation Israel rejects.
In October 2025, after Israel intercepted a Gaza-bound flotilla and detained two Colombian nationals, Petro expelled Israel's remaining diplomats and terminated the free trade agreement between the two countries.
Colombia's embassy, previously located in Tel Aviv, is the tenth foreign embassy in Jerusalem.
The Palestinians see East Jerusalem as the capital of their future state. Israel annexed East Jerusalem after the 1967 Middle East war and declared the whole city as its "eternal and indivisible capital" in 1980.
The United Nations Security Council declared the move "null and void" in Resolution 478 in 1980, stating that it violates international law and does not alter the status of East Jerusalem as occupied territory under the Fourth Geneva Convention.
The United States recognized Jerusalem as the capital of Israel in December 2017 and relocated the U.S. embassy in Israel to the city in May 2018.
As the city's status remains disputed, most countries maintain diplomatic relations with Israel but keep their embassies in Tel Aviv or elsewhere. ■

Namibia embarks on compulsory mass vaccination drive to contain FMD outbreak
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:57:22 CST
21:57:22 KST

WINDHOEK, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Namibia has launched a compulsory vaccination drive in the Karasburg State Veterinary District, the epicenter of an ongoing foot and mouth disease (FMD) outbreak, a government official announced Wednesday.
In an update, Romeo Muyunda, deputy director for public relations at the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform, said the exercise will begin on Wednesday and run in three rounds over three months.
"Animal owners must present their animals as instructed by the District State Veterinary Office, at the time and place to be communicated by the Office," he said, noting that the campaign covers all farms south of the B3 and C10 roads up to the Orange River, plus a band of two farms north of those roads.
Veterinary officials will conduct the campaign and livestock owners are not allowed to vaccinate their animals.
To further contain the virus, Muyunda said that authorities will construct a new animal disease control fence stretching from Klein Manasse to Naute Dam and onward to the Fish River Canyon. Construction will commence after the official notification to affected landowners, in accordance with the Animal Health Act.
Surveillance figures indicate that a total of 63,011 animals have been inspected, with 131 testing positive for FMD across 18 confirmed infected farms. The outbreak in the Kharas Region remains confined to the Karasburg State Veterinary District, he highlighted.
Addressing the recent detection of FMD in the northern Zambezi Region on Oct. 11, Muyunda stressed that there is no epidemiological link between the southern outbreak in Kharas and the northern cases.
As of Oct. 13, active surveillance had detected no new clinical cases or additional lesions in the Zambezi Region since the 12 positive cases reported on Oct. 7.
"The Zambezi Region remains at high risk of FMD introduction due to the presence of resident buffalo populations in protected areas, which are known carriers of the FMD virus, as well as ongoing FMD outbreaks in neighboring countries," Muyunda said.
He said the ministry is monitoring the situation closely and urged the public and the livestock industry to report any suspected unauthorized movements of meat and meat products violating containment measures. ■

EU proposes one-year delay to methane import rules
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:57:18 CST
21:57:18 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The European Commission on Wednesday proposed postponing certain obligations for fossil fuel importers to ease pressure on them due to high energy prices and supply concerns.
The obligations under the European Union (EU) Methane Regulation would be postponed for one year, it was announced.
The proposal came as the conflict in the Middle East has put further strain on global energy markets, driving up prices and raising the risk of reduced availability of oil and gas, the Commission said.
The proposed amendment to the regulation would delay monitoring, reporting and verification obligations for importers of natural gas, oil and coal, as well as methane-intensity reporting requirements for both importers and EU producers.
The Commission said the postponement would give importers additional time to comply with the rules, while helping avoid further pressure on security of supply of imported fossil fuels.
Nevertheless, it added that the amendment would not change the overall ambition, integrity or scope of the regulation, reaffirming the bloc's commitment to reducing methane emissions.
The proposal will now be submitted to the European Parliament and the Council of the EU for adoption.
Adopted in 2024, the EU Methane Regulation introduced phased requirements to increase transparency on methane emissions. It covers domestic energy production, transportation and processing, as well as imports of oil, gas and coal.
According to the Commission, methane is the second-largest source of greenhouse gas emissions after carbon dioxide. ■

Maldives tightens foreign investment rules
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:57:05 CST
21:57:05 KST

MALE, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The Maldives has tightened foreign investment rules in several sectors, requiring at least 25 percent Maldivian ownership for certain construction, real estate, auditing and information technology investments, while reserving some activities entirely for Maldivians, state media PSM News reported on Wednesday, quoting a minister.
Minister of Economic Development, Transport and Trade Mohamed Saeed said that, under the revised framework, foreign investors may participate in construction projects valued below 15 million U.S. dollars and real estate projects valued below 100 million dollars only if Maldivians hold at least a 25 percent stake.
The same local ownership requirement applies to auditing and information technology services, he said. Residential real estate projects valued below 100 million dollars and general sea transport services have been reserved for Maldivians.
Saeed said 150 foreign investments are required to comply with the new conditions introduced under a policy developed in line with the Foreign Investment Act, which came into effect in 2024.
Saeed said 29 foreign investments operating in sectors now reserved for Maldivians had already been discontinued, while 17 foreign investors had submitted applications to comply with the revised requirements.
The policy also covers wholesale and retail trade, logistics, general sales, and passenger and cargo sales agencies representing airlines operating in the Maldives.
Saeed said 17 businesses previously operating in wholesale and retail trade had expressed interest in bringing Maldivian shareholders into their operations.
Existing foreign investors operating in newly reserved sectors will be given time to restructure their businesses or withdraw from those activities, while joint ventures and partnerships with Maldivian shareholders will remain possible in certain sectors.
The Economic Ministry said the revised framework is intended to expand opportunities for Maldivian businesses while retaining foreign investment in areas where international expertise can contribute to economic development. ■

Herent Mayor Luk Draye must answer to the governor of Flemish Brabant on account of an automatic out-of-office email. Mayor Draye drafted an out-of-office message in Belgium’s three national languages, Dutch, French and German. An act of basic courtesy, says Draye, although in doing so he breached Belgian language legislation.
The disputed out-of-office message was sent whilst the mayor was away on a work trip to Guatemala. Draye drafted the message in Dutch, French and German. “Purely out of courtesy,” he explains. “I do occasionally receive emails in German or French. It therefore seemed only natural to me to draft my out-of-office message in the three national languages, especially as it was not a policy decision.”
Language legislation in administrative matters
Nevertheless, an anonymous complaint was lodged with the Flemish interior department. According to the complainant, Draye had allegedly breached the language legislation governing administrative matters. This legislation stipulates that a local authority in the Dutch-speaking region may only communicate in Dutch.
Provincial Governor Jan Spooren is investigating the alleged breach of the law. Draye has already promised to cooperate fully with the investigation. “The governor has asked for a motivation of the trilingual message. We will be happy to provide him with one,” he says.
A strange country
The whole affair is a storm in a teacup, says Draye. “I assume that far worse offences are committed, and that any penalty will therefore be proportionate to the offence,” he explains. “In some respects, we are quite a strange country. In the meantime, surely we shouldn’t need to be afraid of dispatching a message in a language that is not our mother tongue?”
The Flemish nationalist party N-VA, on the opposition benches on Herent council, takes a slightly different view. “At first glance, this might seem like a minor issue, but in Brussels and the Vlaamse Rand, the Flemish borderlands, we can see where this leads when language legislation is relaxed,” says councillor Esther Deroo. “Think of medical procedures where patients are not assisted in their own language, or citizens who cannot file a police report in Dutch. Language legislation is there for a reason!”

Economic Watch: China's foreign trade maintains sound momentum as new drivers power exports
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:56:58 CST
21:56:58 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's foreign trade maintained sound momentum in the first three quarters of 2026, with both exports and imports growing rapidly and the overall growth rate reaching its highest level for the same period in five years, official data showed Wednesday.
The country's total imports and exports rose 18.8 percent year on year to 39.94 trillion yuan (about 5.94 trillion U.S. dollars) in the January-September period, according to the General Administration of Customs (GAC).
Growth accelerated through the year, with the expansion rate rising from 15.3 percent in the first quarter to 18.3 percent in the second quarter and 22.3 percent in the third quarter.
Foreign trade growth in the first three quarters was the fastest for the same period in the past five years, with both quarterly and monthly growth rates generally accelerating, said Wang Jun, GAC's deputy head.
"Latest international data show that such a growth rate ranks among the top among major economies, and China remains the world's largest trader of goods," the official told a press conference on Wednesday.
Wang said the performance could be summed up in four words: "fast, new, quality and open." Describing the "new," he noted that trade in industrial robots, electronic components, computer parts and electrical equipment exceeded 10 trillion yuan in the first three quarters, up 58.9 percent and driving overall import and export growth by 11.3 percentage points.
Exports increased 16.4 percent year on year to 23.2 trillion yuan, while imports expanded by 22.3 percent to 16.74 trillion yuan, GAC data showed.
In September alone, China's total imports and exports reached 5.16 trillion yuan, up 27.5 percent from a year earlier and crossing the 5-trillion-yuan mark for the first time. This figure also marked the sixth consecutive month of double-digit monthly growth.
Exports rose 29.6 percent year on year to 3.03 trillion yuan, while imports grew 24.6 percent to 2.13 trillion yuan for the month.
Exports continued to shift toward smarter and greener products. Integrated circuit exports surged 99.1 percent year on year in the first three quarters, while exports of electric vehicles, lithium batteries, and wind power generating sets and their parts rose 72.3 percent, 36.4 percent and 22.4 percent, respectively.
In east China's Anhui Province, robotics manufacturer EFORT Intelligent Robot Co., Ltd. has continued to see growth in overseas orders this year. After completing simulated spray-painting tests on vehicle bodies, a batch of its spraying robots will be exported to Italy.
The company's overseas revenue increased by more than 50 percent year on year in the first half of 2026. "We provide well-known automakers like Maserati and Volkswagen with integrated robotics solutions for smart production, covering painting, welding, precision assembly and the handling of materials," said You Wei, EFORT's chairman and CEO, adding that EFORT's overseas robot business has grown at a compound annual growth rate of nearly 100 percent over the past three years.
Foreign-invested enterprises in China remained active players in the trade expansion. Their total imports and exports rose 19 percent to 11.69 trillion yuan, a record high for the same period, with intermediate goods trade up 27.4 percent to 7.9 trillion yuan and high-tech product exports up 42.1 percent. Wang said more foreign firms are embracing "China Opportunity 2.0," deepening their integration into China's industrial and innovation chains.
"The global AI investment boom has kept overseas demand firm, and rising prices will continue to drive rapid growth in chip exports, which is currently the main driver of China's export expansion," said Wang Qing, chief macro analyst at Golden Credit Rating. He added that China's manufacturing upgrading has continued to boost exports of new energy vehicles and high-tech products.
The country's trade with more than 180 countries and regions expanded during the first three quarters. Trade with free trade partners reached 19.55 trillion yuan, up 30 percent and contributing over 70 percent of the total trade increment. Meanwhile, trade with other APEC economies rose 23.9 percent to 24.07 trillion yuan.
Trade with ASEAN grew 22.7 percent to 6.84 trillion yuan, that with the European Union rose 8.4 percent to 4.78 trillion yuan, and trade with the United States increased 4.1 percent to 3.18 trillion yuan.
Exports continued to shift toward new and higher-quality growth drivers. The equipment manufacturing sector contributed nearly 90 percent of the export increment, while intermediate goods accounted for more than half of total exports, underpinning global industrial and supply chains, according to the GAC. ■

Xinhua Headlines: China's energy push set to fuel long-term global energy resilience
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:56:56 CST
21:56:56 KST

* China appears to be somewhat shielded from Middle East conflict-driven price shocks by its significant energy reserves, diversified energy supply and rapidly expanding renewable energy sector, which together reduce its dependence on Middle Eastern oil.
* China's commitment to and pursuit of peaking carbon dioxide emissions before 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality before 2060, coupled with rapid advances in wind, solar and new energy vehicle technologies, is fundamentally compressing oil demand.
* China's exports of batteries, wind turbines, electric vehicles and, above all, solar panels helped avoid 374 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions globally in 2025, which is more carbon dioxide emissions than Britain produced last year.
BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- As the world confronts what the International Energy Agency (IEA) has described as the most severe energy crisis in its history, China, the world's largest crude importer, has chosen restraint over panic, helping stabilize global oil markets.
Rather than scrambling to secure supplies after the Strait of Hormuz, one of the planet's most critical oil choke points, was thrown into turmoil in late February, China has reduced its crude purchases, released strategic reserves to meet domestic needs, and drawn on its increasingly diversified supply channels and expanding renewable energy capacity.
The result, according to IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol, has been a meaningful cushion for a market reeling from the largest supply disruption in modern history.
On the demand side, China has played an important role in stabilizing markets by reducing its crude oil imports by nearly 50 percent compared with pre-war levels, Birol said in a statement, while noting that significant supplies from Gulf producers and increased exports from the United States, Brazil, Venezuela and Kazakhstan have also helped offset some of the losses from the Gulf.
China's restraint has not been accidental. It reflects a viable, multi-layered energy strategy that has been quietly reshaping the country's role in the global energy order: from a passive price-taker vulnerable to geopolitical tremors to an anchor of stability with domestic policy choices now rippling outward, resulting in tangible, positive outcomes for the world economy.
OIL PURCHASE RESTRAINT
Customs data tell a striking story. In the first nine months of 2026, China's crude oil imports totaled 358 million tonnes, a year-on-year decline of 15.3 percent. This contraction deepened sharply in June, when imports fell to 29.27 million tonnes -- down 41.3 percent from a year earlier and 11.5 percent from May, marking the lowest monthly figure since October 2016.
Chen Shouhai, director of the oil and gas policy and law research center at China University of Petroleum in Beijing, anticipates a short-term rebound in imports as restocking demand kicks in during the early stages of any de-escalation, but he cautions that this would represent only a cyclical inventory correction, not a reversal of the underlying demand trend.
Over a three-to-five-year horizon, China's total crude imports are likely to decline gradually, according to Chen.
The logic is structural, with China's oil consumption having already passed its peak, seeing refined product demand falling year by year since 2024. Petrochemical feedstock demand continues to grow modestly, but nowhere near enough to offset the erosion in transport fuel consumption. Meanwhile, domestic exploration and production have strengthened steadily, with output rising and the import dependency ratio of roughly 70 percent expected to ease.
China's commitment to and pursuit of peaking carbon dioxide emissions before 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality before 2060, coupled with rapid advances in wind, solar and new energy vehicle (NEV) technologies, is fundamentally compressing oil demand.
China's decision not to hit the panic button has drawn international attention. Nicholas Wagner, manager of energy initiatives at the World Economic Forum, observed in an analysis of how the war in the Middle East is reshaping Asia's energy transition: "China appears to be somewhat shielded from Middle East conflict-driven price shocks by its significant energy reserves, diversified energy supply and rapidly expanding renewable energy sector, which together reduce its dependence on Middle Eastern oil. This lesson will not be lost on policymakers."
STRATEGIC ENERGY PUSH
Domestic scholars argue that China's composure amid this global energy tsunami is no accident. It is the product of a strategic architecture first articulated in 2014 -- promoting revolutions in energy consumption, supply, technology and institutions while strengthening international cooperation across the board.
Data from the National Energy Administration revealed that in 2025, China's primary energy production had reached 5.13 billion tonnes of standard coal equivalent, with domestic crude oil output hitting 216 million tonnes and natural gas production exceeding 260 billion cubic meters, all record highs. China's energy self-sufficiency rate climbed to 84.4 percent in 2025 and is expected to rise further in 2026.
Alongside this domestic expansion, China has constructed a "land-sea linkage, multi-corridor parallel" energy import architecture, with crude oil imported from 49 countries and natural gas from more than 20 countries.
Xiao Hongwei, a research fellow at the National Development and Reform Commission, sees the first half of 2026 as a period of multiple breakthroughs in supply security and green transition.
China's oil and gas production continued to set records in this period: industrial crude oil output reached 109.43 million tonnes, while natural gas production hit 133 billion cubic meters, both all-time highs for the period.
Installed power generation capacity surpassed 4 billion kilowatts, up 10.8 percent year-on-year, maintaining the country's position as the world leader, with non-fossil energy accounting for 62 percent of installed capacity. For the first time, coal-fired power generation fell below 50 percent of total electricity output, while renewable sources exceeded 40 percent, a signal that wind and solar are playing greater roles in China's power mix.
Energy efficiency has continued to improve as well. Preliminary calculations show energy consumption grew 2.7 percent in the first half of 2026, with the growth rate decelerating by 1.2 percentage points from the first quarter. Coal's share in the consumption mix held steady, oil's share declined by one percentage point, and clean energy's share rose by one percentage point, serving as evidence that green and low-carbon energy use is becoming an increasingly automatic choice across industries and households.
The most visible transformation, however, is in transportation. According to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers, NEV production and sales both exceeded 10.6 million units in the first eight months of 2026, with year-on-year growth of more than 10 percent, while NEVs accounted for 52.4 percent of all new vehicle sales.
Zhao Qibo, an economist based in Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in northwest China, said China's long-standing efforts to diversify its energy transport routes, sources and types have clearly paid off. As a stabilizing anchor for national energy security, Xinjiang has abundant oil and coal resources in the traditional energy sector, providing solid support for the country's energy supply. At the same time, Xinjiang's vast land has irreplaceable advantages in wind and solar resources, supplying strong support for sustainable energy development.
POTENTIAL BOOST TO WORLD ENERGY FUTURE
In June, China released its first-ever five-year plan for building a new energy system, targeting the initial establishment of a clean, low-carbon, safe and efficient energy architecture by 2030.
This month, meanwhile, China issued a set of guidelines aimed at accelerating the development of new quality productive forces. The energy revolution has been elevated to an unprecedented level, and nuclear power, photovoltaics, energy storage and hydrogen energy have received clear policy endorsement.
Hu Ming, Party secretary of China Electric Power Planning and Engineering Institute, describes the coming five years as a period of overlapping security risks and accelerating low-carbon transition. International instability will continue to test the resilience of energy systems, while China's own commitments, including a 17-percent reduction in carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP and a 10-percent decline in energy consumption per unit of GDP, will demand an intensification of the green transition.
Under the plan, China will strengthen new energy infrastructure construction, pursue a diversified portfolio spanning wind, solar, hydropower and nuclear power, and expand non-fossil energy supply at scale. This includes steadily advancing coastal nuclear power, offshore wind and distributed new energy development, while actively promoting clean energy bases and transmission corridors in its northern regions and integrated hydro-solar-wind projects in the southwest.
Michal Meidan, head of China energy research at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, argues that the U.S.-Iran conflict has demonstrated the efficacy of China's energy strategy.
"China's dependence on imported oil remains substantial, but the geopolitics of energy are shifting from control of oil flows to control of electrified industrial systems," she wrote in a signed article, noting China's clear head start in this transition.
Hu also sees the current period as a critical window for speeding up international cooperation in China's energy industry. The present circumstances, he argues, favor leveraging China's industrial strengths in energy technology to expand green industry collaboration and help shape a new pattern of global energy governance.
From grid interconnections and clean energy supply chains to technology transfer and joint standards development, opportunities for partnership are expanding just as the global demand for energy resilience has never been more urgent.
Lauri Myllyvirta, co-founder of the Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, noted that China's exports of batteries, wind turbines, electric vehicles and, above all, solar panels helped avoid 374 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions globally in 2025, which is more carbon dioxide emissions than Britain produced last year.
Calculated over the full lifecycle of these products, China's clean technology exports shipped in 2025 are projected to avoid a total of 6.9 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions over their operating lifetimes. This is a 31-percent increase compared with the 2024 estimate and equivalent to roughly twice India's carbon emissions in 2025, according to the expert.
(Video reporter: Su Chuanyi; Video editors: Zhou Yang, Zhao Xiaoqing, Li Qin, Zhang Mocheng and Hong Liang) ■

China-Africa research center inaugurated in South Africa
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:56:48 CST
21:56:48 KST

PRETORIA, South Africa, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The inauguration ceremony of the China-Africa Institute -- the South Africa China-Africa Research Center and a seminar on "The Global South Working Together to Build a Community with a Shared Future for Humanity" were held Tuesday at South Africa's National School of Government (NSG) in Pretoria, the country's administrative capital.
Vice President of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences Peng Jinhui, NSG Acting Principal Phindile Mkwanazi, and Chinese Ambassador to South Africa Wu Peng jointly unveiled the plaque of the center.
Peng highlighted the inauguration of the center as a concrete step to implement the outcomes of the 2024 Forum on China-Africa Cooperation Beijing Summit and an important achievement in deepening academic cooperation between China and South Africa and between China and Africa.
He called on both sides to leverage the center to strengthen joint research, academic exchanges, policy dialogue, personnel exchanges and cooperation among young scholars, and to continuously produce solid research outcomes.
The center should become an important platform rooted in South Africa, serving Africa and connecting China, providing intellectual support for deepening China-South Africa and China-Africa cooperation and advancing common modernization among the Global South, Peng added.
Mkwanazi said the inauguration marks a new starting point for deepening cooperation and translating the center's research into tangible outcomes, adding that the NSG looks forward to further strengthening exchanges and cooperation with its Chinese partners through the center and contributing more to public governance and national development.
Wu noted that amid profound changes in the global landscape, China and Africa should strengthen research and academic exchanges to better safeguard the common interests and legitimate development rights of developing countries.
He expressed hope that the center would facilitate mutual learning on governance and development, respect and support African countries in exploring development paths suited to their national conditions, and leverage its platform to produce high-quality research, contributing to closer China-South Africa and China-Africa cooperation.
Following the inauguration ceremony, participating experts and scholars held discussions on topics including modernization among the Global South, exchanges of governance experience between China and Africa, and the development of manufacturing in the era of artificial intelligence. ■

Chinese premier attends symposium with representatives of overseas buyers,  exhibitors at Canton Fair
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:56:48 CST
21:56:48 KST

Chinese Premier Li Qiang attends a symposium marking the 70th anniversary of the establishment of the Canton Fair in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Ding Haitao)
GUANGZHOU, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Wednesday attended a symposium with representatives of overseas buyers and exhibitors at the Canton Fair in Guangzhou, calling on Chinese and foreign enterprises to actively promote global supply-demand matching and lead international innovation cooperation.
About 70 business representatives from nearly 30 countries and regions participated in the symposium in Guangzhou, capital of south China's Guangdong Province, where the Canton Fair will be held from Oct. 15 to Nov. 4.
After hearing remarks from representatives of overseas buyers and exhibitors, Li said that over the past 70 years since its launch, the Canton Fair has grown along with China's opening up and development. "It has become not only a bright business card of China's opening up to the outside world, but also an important window for the world to observe China," Li said.
As one of the world's one-stop trade platforms boasting a complete range of goods and high efficiency, the Canton Fair brings together cutting-edge products and technologies, Li said, adding that it serves as a grand stage for traditional goods trade and a barometer for the development of new types of trade.
In recent years, the enterprises participating in the Canton Fair have engaged in more diversified business exchanges and are gradually upgrading to all-round partners, Li said. He noted that China will continue to foster an open and innovative ecosystem, strengthen the protection of foreign-related intellectual property rights, and actively address the concerns of enterprises.
"China will continue to optimize the investment environment for foreign investors, expand market access and support foreign enterprises in local production," the premier said. "It will also accelerate the building of a modern industrial system and promote the planning and construction of new power grids, computing power networks and new-generation communication networks," he added.
"We welcome enterprises from all countries to invest more in China, deepen their presence in the Chinese market, strengthen mutually beneficial and practical cooperation in the industrial and supply chains, and promote the building of open and inclusive global industrial and supply chains," Li said.
Li also called for enhancing the digital and intelligent content of the Canton Fair, introducing more green products and exhibition areas and promoting green trade, and highlighting the humanistic elements of the fair.
Noting that global production and supply chains are undergoing profound restructuring, business representatives said the competitiveness of "Made in China" is increasing day by day, making significant contributions to promoting the development of the world economy.
They said the Canton Fair is the most reliable global business platform and that the Chinese government has been continuously implementing precise policies, constantly optimizing the business environment, and helping enterprises from all countries achieve leapfrog development.
The foreign representatives said they are fully confident in China's development prospects and are willing to cooperate with China, share innovation, promote mutual growth and achieve mutual benefit and win-win results. ■
