India's wholesale inflation rises to 11.39 pct in September
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:56:41 CST
21:56:41 KST

NEW DELHI, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- India's wholesale price index (WPI) rose to 11.39 percent in September, according to data released by the federal Ministry of Commerce and Industry on Wednesday.
"All India WPI inflation for September 2026 is 11.39 percent on year-on-year (YoY) basis, compared to 9.92 percent in August 2026," reads a statement issued by the ministry.
According to the ministry, YoY inflation rates for major groups, namely, primary articles, fuel and power, and manufactured products are 8.67 percent, 25.85 percent, and 9.76 percent, respectively, in September, compared to 7.76 percent, 22.93 percent, and 8.37 percent, respectively, in August 2026.
WPI inflation, an indicator of prices in the wholesale market, rises or falls mainly due to a steep increase or decrease in commodity prices globally.
The food index observed a YoY inflation of 8.66 percent in September, compared to 7.05 percent in August 2026, the ministry said. ■

Lithuanian Minister proposes banning self-employed status for foreign students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:56:12 UTC
21:56:12 KST

Lithuania's Interior Minister has proposed banning foreign students from working as self-employed individuals, noting that some use student visas to obtain residence permits rather than to pursue an education.
Tanjid, a second-year student at Vilnius College who came from Bangladesh, told LRT that he combines his studies with work. He knows his lecture schedule, and if there are only one or two lectures a day, balancing the two is easy. At the same time, it is quite difficult to find a job with a standard employment contract while studying. Tanjid worked a full-time warehouse job over the summer, but found it hard to juggle once classes resumed, so he quit. However, he emphasized that he came to Lithuania to study and works only to earn extra money.
According to data from the Lithuanian Migration Department, temporary residence permits have currently been issued to more than 230,000 foreign nationals. Only 5%—or 12,000 individuals—came to study. The majority of international students come from Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Morocco, and Belarus.
Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas noted that some students seek entry into Lithuania primarily to work rather than to study. Foreign students reportedly exploit the system, attending only enough lectures to maintain their residence permits. Employers and universities also benefit from the current arrangement, as higher enrollment numbers generate additional revenue for educational institutions. Meanwhile, lecturers report that some migrants show up only to take exams and demand passing grades to avoid having their residence permits revoked. The minister aims to bar foreign students from obtaining self-employed status, which allows for more flexible working arrangements than standard employment contracts.
He stated that while European Union directives prevent Lithuania from completely banning foreign students from working, the regulation of self-employed status falls within national jurisdiction.
Last year, the Migration Department inspected higher education institutions and identified instances where students were absent from classes they were required to attend. It was also revealed that educational institutions had failed to report in a timely manner when a student suspended their studies—a circumstance that can serve as grounds for revoking a residence permit.
Lithuanian Member of Parliament Eugenijus Gentvilas questioned whether the restrictions imposed on foreign students were justified, given that international students make up a very small fraction of the total immigrant population. Gentvilas stated that the educational institutions where violations were found should be named. He argued that applying such restrictions to students was unnecessarily harsh on higher education institutions, especially considering that these institutions are required to admit foreign students.
Indrė Gasperė, Director of the Migration Department, said that educational institutions have begun reporting student violations more diligently. The Migration Department must be notified of any changes affecting students, including instances where a student has stopped studying or failed to earn the required number of credits; failure to report such matters carries the risk of a fine.
Universities also report that the situation has improved.
At the private Kazimieras Simonavičius University, approximately two-thirds of the students are foreign nationals. University representative Edgaras Genys stated that attendance has improved and the number of violations has decreased following the tightening of regulations. Such incidents had occurred in previous years when rules were more lenient and admission criteria lower. However, Genys warned that restricting employment opportunities could make Lithuania less attractive to international students.
The Lithuanian University Rectors' Conference also opposes the restrictions proposed by the Minister of the Interior. Alvidas Šarlauskas, a representative of the association, stated that they do not want students in Lithuania to be at a disadvantage compared to international students in other countries.
Katelynas insisted that if the changes are implemented, students will still be able to work under standard employment contracts. In practice, however, this would be nearly impossible, as employers are reluctant to sign standard employment contracts with students or to hire them for part-time work.

President Volodymyr Zelensky called on G7 leaders – including the US, which recently struck a dieseldeal with Russian President Vladimir Putin – to force Moscow to stop its war after a Russian Shahed strike killed six people and injured 13 in Lutsk on Wednesday, Oct. 14.

“This is exactly why Moscow must not be persuaded but forced to stop – through increased pressure, sanctions and assistance to Ukraine that makes it possible to protect people from such attacks,” Zelensky said in a statement on Telegram.

Lutsk death toll rises to six
The death toll rose to six killed and 13 wounded according to the latest statement by Zelensky.
“There must be action,” the President said. “Because as long as Russia does not feel enough pressure, it continues to bring death.”
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (SES) raised the death toll in Lutsk to six, with 12 people injured, including a child, in its previous update.

Woman rescued from rubble in Rivne
In Rivne, five people were wounded, including a child born in 2012, according to the SES.
Rescuers pulled a woman from beneath the rubble and handed her over to medical workers.
Four privately owned cars and the roof of a three-story residential building caught fire. Windows were blown out and a neighboring residential building was also damaged.
Firefighters extinguished the blaze. Emergency crews continued clearing rubble and dousing damaged structures.

Repeated attacks on western Ukraine
The latest attack on Rivne came one day after a Russian drone attack on the Rivne State University of Humanities wounded 30 people and severely damaged premises used by its music department. The university moved students to remote learning.
Russia also launched 39 missiles and 128 drones across Ukraine overnight, according to the Ukrainian Air Force. Attacks were recorded at 22 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight others.

Defense minister: Estonia should consider acquiring light jet fighters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:56:00 UTC
21:56:00 KST

Defense minister: Estonia should consider acquiring light jet fighters
Estonia should consider acquiring light fighter jets to counter Russia's increasingly fast and sophisticated long-range attack drones, Defense Minister Martin Herem told Postimees in an interview.
Speaking to Postimees after visiting Ukraine, Herem said Estonia must improve its air surveillance, command systems and multilayered air defenses, including machine guns, cannons, interceptor drones and potentially aircraft. He suggested that Estonia could explore arming its existing L-39 training aircraft with machine guns or small cannons, emphasizing that the aim would be to intercept drones rather than engage enemy fighter jets.
According to Herem, Ukraine's interception rate for Russian Shahed-type long-range drones has fallen from approximately 90 percent to 70 percent, significantly increasing the damage caused by Russian attacks.
The minister said Estonia should strengthen military cooperation with Ukraine by systematically collecting battlefield data, purchasing Ukrainian-made equipment and exploring joint defense production. Priority areas include electronic warfare, air defense, surveillance systems, drones and digital command-and-control capabilities.
Herem warned that Russia's defense industry shows no signs of slowing down despite economic difficulties and could continue expanding even if the war ends.
During a roughly 30-minute meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Herem learned that Ukraine's most pressing air defense problem is a shortage of interceptors capable of destroying Russian ballistic missiles. He also stressed the importance of protecting critical infrastructure and providing adequate shelters for civilians, drawing on Ukraine's experience of surviving Russian attacks.
Herem warned that advances in drone warfare mean Estonia must prepare for a conflict in which the entire country could become an operational zone, with no safe rear areas.

Can the China-US Detente Last?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:56:00 UTC
21:56:00 KST

The recent thaw in China-U.S. relations – highlighted by reciprocal visits by President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping – raised the prospect of a more stable relationship between the world’s two largest powers. After years of escalating tariffs, technology restrictions, and strategic mistrust, both governments appear willing to step back from the brink. The emerging language of “constructive strategic stability” suggests that Washington and Beijing may be converging on the need to manage their rivalry rather than allow it to define every aspect of their relationship.
But agreement on the need to manage competition is not the same as agreement on its terms. The two sides may have reached a shared conclusion that escalation is too costly without resolving the underlying disputes that drove them toward confrontation in the first place. If so, the current detente could prove less a turning point than a temporary adjustment in a much longer strategic contest.
The history of Soviet-U.S. detente offers a useful way to understand this possibility – not because the China-U.S. relationship is destined to follow the same trajectory, but because it highlights a central problem of great power relations: the conditions that encourage rivals to seek restraint may also make that restraint difficult to sustain.
Why Now?
The current thaw cannot be understood in isolation. It is the latest stage in more than a decade of intensifying strategic competition between China and the United States.
The Obama administration’s “Pivot to Asia” signaled a stronger U.S. commitment to the region as China’s power grew. Washington presented its policy as an effort to sustain regional order, while Beijing increasingly viewed U.S. initiatives through the lens of strategic containment. Yet competition remained partly bounded by the hope that economic interdependence and diplomatic engagement could prevent rivalry from overwhelming the relationship.
The first Trump administration marked a more decisive turn. The 2018 trade war transformed economic grievances into a central instrument of strategic competition. The Biden administration subsequently retained much of the competitive framework while expanding restrictions in areas such as advanced technology. Across successive administrations, Washington’s approach increasingly treated China not simply as a difficult partner but as a long-term strategic competitor.
The escalation of 2025-26 exposed the limits of this approach. Tariffs and countermeasures, particularly China’s leverage over rare earths and other critical supply chains, demonstrated that both countries possess vulnerabilities the other can exploit. But the ability to impose costs does not necessarily translate into a sustainable strategic advantage. Escalation can inflict damage on the opponent while simultaneously disrupting domestic industries, unsettling markets, and narrowing the room for diplomatic maneuver.
This gave both governments incentives to pursue a pause. Washington wants to stabilize trade, reduce supply chain exposure, and avoid a prolonged confrontation that complicates its broader economic and strategic priorities. Beijing has reasons to ease external pressure, preserve access to important markets and technologies, and secure a more predictable environment for economic development.
Their objectives for the detente, however, might not be identical. Washington may see a truce as an opportunity to rebuild leverage and reduce dependence on Chinese inputs. Beijing may see it as an opportunity to protect its economic position, limit U.S. pressure, and consolidate gains made during the confrontation. Each side can welcome stability while preparing for the possibility that competition will intensify again.
The significance of “constructive strategic stability” therefore lies less in whether it signals a fundamental reconciliation than in what the two governments understand it to mean. Does stability imply shared limits on competition, or merely a shared interest in preventing competition from becoming unmanageable? The distinction will determine whether the current thaw can endure.
What Detente Can – and Cannot – Do
The Soviet-U.S. experience is instructive in this regard. During the Cold War, detente emerged not because Washington and Moscow overcame their ideological rivalry, but because both recognized the dangers and costs of unconstrained confrontation. Arms control negotiations and diplomatic engagement could reduce the risks of escalation even while the two superpowers continued to compete for strategic advantage.
Yet detente never eliminated the underlying sources of rivalry. Disputes over regional conflicts, military competition, and divergent conceptions of international order repeatedly strained the Soviet-U.S. relationship. Changes in strategic calculations and domestic political environments also affected the willingness of leaders to sustain restraint. Detente could manage competition, but it could not make incompatible interests disappear.
The lesson for Washington and Beijing is not that their relationship will inevitably reproduce the Soviet-U.S. trajectory. Their economic interdependence, technological competition, and regional strategic dynamics differ substantially from those of the Cold War. Rather, the historical comparison directs attention to the conditions under which detente becomes self-reinforcing – or begins to unravel.
First, relative power matters. If either side believes that time is working decisively in its favor, it may view restraint as an unnecessary concession. Conversely, if leaders conclude that neither side can impose its will without incurring prohibitive costs, compromise may become more attractive. But a temporary balance of leverage can be unstable, especially when both governments are racing to reduce their dependence on the other.
Second, detente is vulnerable to miscalculation. Measures intended as defensive preparations may be interpreted as offensive moves, prompting countermeasures that gradually erode trust. Washington’s efforts to diversify critical supply chains and strengthen technological resilience may reduce its exposure to Chinese coercion. Beijing’s efforts to insulate itself from American economic pressure may serve a similar purpose. Such measures can make future crises less costly to withstand, but they can also weaken the mutual vulnerabilities that currently encourage restraint.
Third, domestic politics can narrow the space for compromise. Leaders must defend their policies against critics who regard accommodation as weakness or believe that strategic competition requires sustained pressure. Electoral cycles, economic pressures, and leadership changes can alter the political value of engagement. Even when leaders reach an informal understanding, they may struggle to preserve it if their domestic coalitions interpret restraint differently.
These dynamics suggest that detente is not simply a one-time choice between confrontation and cooperation. It is an ongoing contest over the boundaries of acceptable competition.
From a Pause to a Durable Arrangement?
The central question is therefore not whether the current China-U.S. detente will last, but what would make it more resilient.
One indicator is whether diplomatic engagement produces mechanisms that can survive political shocks. Regular communication, crisis-management procedures, and clear expectations about military interactions would matter more than the symbolism of leader-level meetings alone.
Another sign is whether both sides develop a more consistent understanding of the limits of competition. They need not agree on the ultimate distribution of power, but they must have some shared sense of which actions risk turning rivalry into a crisis.
A third indicator is how each government uses the breathing room created by detente. If restraint primarily enables both sides to prepare for a more intense confrontation, the thaw may postpone rather than resolve the next crisis. If it creates incentives to preserve communication, contain disputes, and cooperate where interests overlap, it may gradually acquire a more durable foundation.
Washington and Beijing may be learning that neither can easily defeat the other without paying an unacceptable price. But recognizing the costs of escalation is only the beginning of strategic stability. Competition can generate incentives for restraint, and restraint can create opportunities for further competition. The same reduction in tensions that makes diplomacy possible can also give both sides time to reduce their vulnerabilities and reassess their strategic positions. That is the paradox of the current moment.
The immediate thaw should therefore be welcomed without being mistaken for a permanent settlement. The ultimate significance will depend on whether the two powers use restraint to establish more predictable rules for managing rivalry – or simply to prepare for the next round of confrontation.

Houthis will respond ‘eye for an eye’ to Saudi attacks – foreign minister (VIDEO)
Yemen’s Houthis will continue retaliatory strikes against Saudi airports and oil facilities as long as Riyadh continues its military operations in Yemen, the Houthi administration’s acting foreign minister, Abdulwahid Abu Ras, has told RT. 
He said the fighting could end if Saudi Arabia lifted its blockade and withdrew its forces from Yemeni territory. 
Recent Houthi-claimed strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport have killed at least 14 people and injured more than 300 over the weekend. On Tuesday, the Saudi-led coalition struck a fuel depot near Yemen’s capital, Sanaa. 
The minister described the group’s approach as “an eye for an eye,” saying Houthi forces were targeting Saudi oil facilities, infrastructure, and military positions in retaliation.
“Siege for siege, airport for airport, ports for ports, and escalation for escalation,” Abu Ras told RT India Managing Editor Ashok Bagriya in an exclusive interview. 
The renewed confrontation began in July when strikes on Sanaa airport were followed by Houthi missile attacks on Saudi Arabia, breaking years of relative calm following a United Nations-brokered truce in 2022. United Nations envoy Hans Grundberg warned last week that Yemen had returned to full-scale war. 
“Our red lines are that the blockade on Yemen, our airports, and our ports must not continue,” Abu Ras said. He also demanded access to the country’s oil and gas resources.
He said the Houthi administration remains prepared for direct negotiations with Riyadh despite Saudi Arabia allegedly failing to implement earlier humanitarian agreements. “We invite the Saudi regime to sit at the negotiation table to implement what was agreed upon,” Abu Ras said, calling for humanitarian facilities to be kept out of the fighting. 
Abu Ras, however, ruled out Sanaa imposing tolls or fees on commercial vessels using the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which its forces now control after recent advances along the coast. “This is out of the question… Sanaa is keen to keep the shipping lane and commercial traffic in Bab el-Mandeb completely normal in every sense of the word.”
The minister also sought to separate the fighting in his country from the conflict between the US and Iran, the Houthis’ main backer. “The Yemeni position is a declared position regarding its internal cause, its national cause… which have nothing to do with any external agenda.”
“Whether the brothers in the Islamic Republic of Iran reach solutions with the American side or not, this is a completely separate issue,” he said.
Abu Ras accused the UK of adopting hostile positions in the UN Security Council, providing cover for Saudi actions, and legitimizing them in international forums.
“Such interventions further complicate the conflict and drag the region towards a potentially larger conflict, which could lead to repercussions and consequences that affect everyone,” the minister warned.

Trump's diesel deal means little for the global economy but promises political gain for the Kremlin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:55:07 UTC
21:55:07 KST

Trump's Russian diesel deal isn't about economic relief
Russian President Vladimir Putin delivers a speech during the 23rd Annual Meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow, Russia, on Oct. 1, 2026. (Sefa Karacan / Anadolu via Getty Images)
When U.S. President Donald Trump announced Oct. 9 that Washington had agreed to buy millions of tons of Russian fuel, he pledged that the deal would mean lower gas prices for ordinary Americans.
"Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" he said.
The statement is far from reality, experts warn. The initial shipments, as announced by Trump, are small and unlikely to significantly lower prices in the long term.
Although Trump is hoping for a midterm boost, the only winner is the Kremlin.
The deal is putting new strain on Kyiv-Washington relations, as Ukraine is forced to press pause on one of its most successful war tactics.
Meanwhile, Moscow is buoyed by the prospect of weakened sanctions, which could boost its economy, its war chest, and its global image.
Lower prices unlikely to last
Global diesel prices are soaring. In its most recent report on Oct. 5, the U.S. Energy Information Administration put the cost of U.S. diesel at $6.20 per gallon — a rise of $2.49 in just 12 months.
The main factor driving those soaring prices is the U.S.-Iran war. The conflict has not only disrupted the flow of oil tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz but has also driven up security costs for those ships making the journey.
A study by Ukraine's KSE Institute, shared with the Financial Times, assessed that the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran had a far bigger impact on global diesel and gasoil supplies than Ukrainian drone strikes, estimating that exports from the Persian Gulf fell by 152 million barrels between March and August, compared with a 68 million-barrel drop in Russian exports over the same period.
But Ukrainian drone strikes against Russia’s oil refineries have also made their mark.
In a report published in September, the International Energy Agency said that the amount of crude oil moving through Russia’s refineries had fallen to a 20-year low, with diesel production down by nearly 30%.
Global energy markets operate on a razor-thin balance between supply and demand, meaning any drop in output will affect prices, says Jeff Krimmel, founder of consulting firm Krimmel Strategy.
He says that Trump's deal could trigger a small drop in diesel prices, but that those changes are unlikely to last.
While the numbers in Trump's announcement are impressive at first glance, they are a small drop in the global energy market.
In October 2026, the U.S. Energy Information Administration reported that the country was using 493,000 tons of distillate fuel oil — a category that includes diesel and certain heating oils — in a single day. If that rate continues, the total of Russia’s first two deliveries, or 800,000 tons, would supply U.S. needs for less than 48 hours alone.
Real change would need a much wider shift, says Krimmel.
"The U.S. administration wants some visible demonstration that they're responding to this diesel supply crunch and the price rise that comes with that crunch," he says.
"(But) there is no single deal that the U.S. president can make with any foreign leader to change the shape of diesel markets in the near term."
Tension for US-Ukraine relations
Meanwhile, the planned diesel shipments place increasing pressure on Ukraine.
Kyiv's long-distance drone strikes against Russia’s oil infrastructure have become one of Ukraine's most effective weapons, slowly eating away at the Russian economy. Russia was plagued by fuel shortages throughout the summer, with some regions suspending civilian sales. Notably for world leaders such as Trump, the shortages also led the Russian government to place a temporary ban on diesel exports in July.
A lack of available data from Russia means that it's difficult to know how quickly the country has been able to repair its drone-damaged refineries. But the fall in Russia’s refinery output has been great enough for experts to express doubt that Moscow would be willing or able to fulfill the export numbers outlined by the U.S. president.
However, with his eyes now focused on U.S. opinion polls rather than global affairs, Trump has started to intensify his criticism of Ukraine for carrying out such strikes.
"The relationship with the U.S. (and Ukraine) is right now probably as bad as it was on Feb. 28, 2025, when we had this massive bust-up between Trump and Zelensky in the Oval Office," says Stefan Wolff, professor of international security at the U.K.'s University of Birmingham.
Shortly after the diesel deal was announced, Kyiv halted strikes on Russian refineries, following the terms of a unilateral, U.S.-led "energy ceasefire." Moscow has continued its attacks.
Even so, Trump threatened Kyiv with the withholding of intelligence and other assistance in a bid to protect Russian oil refineries, Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent.
President Volodymyr Zelensky later shared that several missile strikes on Ukraine took place with "no early warning from our partners" — a suggestion that the U.S.-Ukraine intelligence sharing had been, at least partly, disrupted.
Ukraine's Starlink access was also restricted without warning on Oct. 14, severely disrupting "several" military missions, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," Beskrestnov said.
Ukraine could keep exerting pressure on Russia’s energy infrastructure without targeting refineries, says Wolff. In particular, oil tankers in Russia’s shadow fleet are among the potential targets.
But Kyiv will be pressured to keep Washington onside to keep receiving vital aid, such as air defenses, to protect civilians under Russian bombardment.
“Air defences are clearly depleted,” says Wolff. “There's not a lot that the Europeans can put in to backfill what the Ukrainians have used. So, I mean, in that sense, they still very much depend on the U.S., as do the Europeans.”
While Russia won't make large amounts of money from the small shipments outlined by Trump, the shift signals new possibilities for further sales down the line — greater revenues to fund Russia’s war machine.
read also
A symbolic victory
But the real win for Russia is not only the breathing space to bring its refineries back online, but the outsized political statement that Trump's deal sends.
The U.S. Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 7 to make Trump's deal happen. That decision from a powerful global player such as the United States — a country that has, until recently, publicly pledged to support Ukraine — may prompt other countries to rethink their own stance on sanctions.
It could also open the door for countries buying Russian oil products at lower prices to start paying more, says Daniel Spiro, a professor at Uppsala University specializing in resource and political economics.
"The fact that Trump is now saying it's okay to buy from Russia, that could mean that those buying that oil and diesel are going to think, now it's safe, so we can pay full price for it," he says.
While Russia won't make large amounts of money from the small shipments outlined by Trump, the shift signals new possibilities for further sales down the line — greater revenues to fund Russia’s war machine.
"From Russia's perspective, it's symbolic. It shows that Russia can negotiate with others. It gives a green light; it shows that the world is reliant on Russia," says Spiro. "I do think it's mainly symbolic. But, sometimes, symbolism matters."

NAD and CDS want capability delivered faster as DSEI 27 launched
The National Armaments Director and the Chief of the Defence Staff urge faster capability delivery, greater innovation, and improved readiness.

- National Armaments Director Rupert Pearce has warned the UK and its allies have until “the end of 2030, at best, to deter and be ready to fight”.
- DSEI UK, the flagship biennial defence exhibition, is expected to attract 65,000 visitors and up to 1,700 exhibiting companies to ExCeL London in September 2027.
National Armaments Director Rupert Pearce, and Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton KCB, Chief of the Defence Staff, have jointly launched DSEI UK 2027: Delivering the Integrated Force.
Mr Pearce, who is responsible for defence acquisition and industrial capability, warned that the UK and its allies have just over four years to prepare for conflict.

That is the perfect discussion to have at DSEI UK with all the stakeholders together: military, industry, procurement agencies, innovators and the finance community… If we get that right at DSEI UK we will position the UK Armed Forces in a vanguard of being the most innovative armed forces in the world.

Swedish prisoners in Estonia: No motivation to strive for a more law-abiding life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:55:00 UTC
21:55:00 KST

Swedish prisoners in Estonia: No motivation to strive for a more law-abiding life
An unannounced inspection of Tartu Prison by the chancellor of justice's advisers has revealed concerns among Swedish inmates over detention conditions.
One of the chancellor of justice's duties is to regularly inspect detention facilities and the conditions in which prisoners are held. On August 27, advisers to the chancellor of justice therefore made an unannounced inspection visit to Tartu Prison to examine detention conditions for inmates, including Swedish prisoners.
At the time of the inspection, Tartu Prison was holding 15 Swedish inmates. The chancellor's advisers interviewed eight inmates, spoke with prison officials, toured the prison facilities and reviewed selected documents.
"The inmates confirmed that no restraints were used on them during their journey to Estonia and that they were able to drink, eat and use the toilet during the trip," according to a report prepared following the inspection. Upon arrival at the prison, the inmates agreed to undergo medical examinations and were satisfied that they were promptly provided with the medication they needed.
Inmates did not agree to be transferred to Estonia
Most of the inmates who spoke with the chancellor of justice's advisers said they had opposed their transfer to Estonia. According to the inmates, they were given very little advance notice of the transfer — in some cases about two weeks and in others just a few days.
The inmates had an opportunity to raise objections, but they felt the responses they received were vague and brief, in some cases consisting of just a few sentences. They believed they had not been given a genuine opportunity to defend their positions and that their personal circumstances had not been taken into account when the decisions were made.
The inmates explained that they had reportedly been well-behaved and motivated prisoners in Swedish prisons. They therefore believe that the purpose of transferring them to Estonia is not to support their reintegration into society, but to portray the prison rental arrangement as a success story.
They see their transfer to Estonia as a double punishment and say they have lost their previous motivation to work toward a law-abiding life. Concerns were raised that dissatisfaction among inmates could lead to more serious problems at the prison, particularly if the number of prisoners transferred from Sweden increases.
All the inmates who spoke with the chancellor of justice's advisers claimed that, while in Swedish prisons, they had received information about detention conditions in Estonia primarily through an information brochure. They believed that the information provided in Sweden differed significantly from the actual conditions at the Estonian prison.
Some inmates claimed they had been assured in Sweden that they would continue serving their sentences at Tartu Prison under Swedish law. They also said they had been told that inmates at Tartu Prison would enjoy at least the same privileges as those in Swedish prisons, if not more. According to the inmates, this is not the case.
In addition, the inmates were unclear about what types of requests and complaints they were entitled to submit while at Tartu Prison, to whom they should address them and how to do so.
"The chancellor of justice does not know and cannot confirm what information was provided to the inmates in Sweden or how it was communicated, but all the inmates had similar impressions and understandings of the information they had received," the report stated.
Language barrier a problem
According to information gathered during the inspection, the inmates had not been given sufficient information about detention conditions and prison rules at Tartu Prison before being brought to Estonia. Once at Tartu Prison, language barriers have made it difficult for them to understand the information they receive and communicate with prison officers and other staff.
The inmates who spoke with the chancellor of justice's advisers had some command of English. The report noted that language barriers could become particularly significant when discussing more complex matters.
The inmates said they believed not all prison officers spoke fluent English, which meant they had little communication with the officers and that officers had struggled to answer their questions. This increases the risk of misunderstandings, which the inmates said could lead to unnecessary conflicts.
For example, one inmate was prohibited from using an item that some other inmates were allowed to use. The inmate perceived this difference in treatment as hostile and believed it was due to his skin color and ethnic background.
However, subsequent discussions with prison officers revealed that the inmate had not been allowed to take the item into his cell because security stickers first needed to be attached to it. The allegation of discriminatory behavior by prison officers was not substantiated. The situation and the unnecessary tension it caused could have been avoided if the inmate had received a timely explanation in a language he understood.
The report also noted that prison officers had not yet used translation apps when communicating with inmates. Although an interpreter was present during medical examinations, the interpreter translated explanations from Estonian into English rather than Swedish.
For example, one inmate was found to have a heart-related health condition during a medical examination. The inmate said he would like to receive more information about his condition in Swedish and have the opportunity to ask questions about the complex medical issue and receive answers he could fully understand.
Fees to high to keep in touch with family
Based on information gathered during the inspection, the chancellor of justice's advisers questioned how thoroughly the family ties of Swedish inmates transferred to Tartu Prison in August, as well as the rights and interests of their children, had been assessed.
Several inmates who spoke with the advisers said their loved ones lived in Sweden and that they had maintained regular contact and visits with them before being transferred to Estonia. According to the inmates, the transfer has made communication with their loved ones considerably more difficult and in-person visits impossible.
One younger inmate said he was very close to his mother and two younger sisters, both minors. He said the transfer to Estonia had been extremely difficult for both him and his family, as they had been a major source of support and had encouraged him to lead a law-abiding life.
Another inmate said he had a child around 10 years old in Sweden and that, before his transfer to Estonia, he had hoped to reach an agreement with the child's mother that would allow the child to visit him in prison. According to the inmate, his transfer to Estonia has made such visits impossible.
A third inmate said his approximately 2-and-a-half-year-old child lived about 20 minutes from the Swedish prison where he had been serving his sentence. He had received regular weekly visits from his child since the child was 3 months old. The inmate was deeply concerned that his relationship with his child would be irreparably damaged and that the child would become estranged from him.
The inmates who spoke with the chancellor of justice's advisers said they believed calling their loved ones from Estonia was more expensive than calling from Sweden. As a result, they may no longer be able to maintain contact with their families as frequently as before. At the time of the inspection, inmates transferred from Sweden to Estonia were not yet able to make video calls.
All the inmates who spoke with the chancellor of justice's advisers said their loved ones could not afford to travel to Estonia because of travel and other costs associated with visits. Most inmates said neither they nor their family members had been informed whether financial assistance was available to cover travel and other visit-related expenses or, if so, how to apply for it. Only one inmate interviewed mentioned having heard that such assistance might be available.
Wrong placement of TVs
The inmates were also dissatisfied with the placement of two televisions side by side in cells at Tartu Prison. In Swedish prisons, televisions are mounted on the walls opposite the beds, allowing cellmates to watch television without disturbing each other.
Although inmates are allowed to use headphones, they find it distracting to watch two different programs simultaneously on adjacent screens. The inmates believed this arrangement could easily lead to conflicts.
Several inmates also raised concerns about the safety of sleeping in the upper bunk because it has no guardrail. They said they were afraid of falling out of bed while asleep and acknowledged that their sleep had been disrupted as a result.
The inmates explained that they had raised their concerns with prison officers and had subsequently been placed in cells on their own, allowing them to sleep in the lower bunk. However, they said the problem could arise again when more inmates arrive at the prison and two people are assigned to each cell.
No privacy while showering
The inmates who spoke with the chancellor of justice's advisers pointed out that the shower room in their prison unit has three showerheads positioned close together, intended to serve approximately 40 inmates. The inmates felt their privacy was not adequately protected while showering because there were no partitions between the showers. As a result, they currently shower one at a time.
The inmates explained that showering individually is manageable when there are seven or eight inmates in the unit, but becomes very difficult as the number increases. It is unrealistic to expect approximately 40 inmates to be able to use the shower room individually every day.
Muslim inmates noted that they had not yet had an opportunity to meet with an imam or participate in communal prayers. Prison officers acknowledged that inmates must be given the opportunity to practice their religion. However, it remained unclear whether arranging access to Muslim religious leaders was the responsibility of Estonia or Sweden.
The report stated that the problems could only be resolved through cooperation between Estonia and Sweden and that the findings would therefore also be forwarded to the relevant Swedish authorities.

Editor: Marcus Turovski

Iran mulls tactical shift in Hormuz attacks before key US vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:55:00 UTC
21:55:00 KST

Iran is using new tactics to target ships in the Strait of Hormuz to maintain high oil prices and influence the U.S. midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.
Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran on Feb. 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.
Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit.
The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.
The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the U.S. vote, they said.
"The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices," one of the two officials said.
The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials said.
A U.S. military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Iran had changed tactics in one significant way: after the U.S. destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including U.S. naval vessels, the official said.
Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the U.S. military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. U.S. forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the U.S. official said.
Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran had been unable to prevent a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official said, particularly after U.S. strikes devastated its navy.
The war – and its $3 billion monthly price tag – has become a key issue on the U.S. campaign trail for November's midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress.
U.S. President Donald Trump has been weighing next steps against Iran, but has said he will not attack again before the vote.
The U.S. has meanwhile been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports and extending sanctions as it tries to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict.
The standoff over Hormuz has left global energy markets exposed to further disruption, with the threat of attacks and high shipping and insurance costs complicating efforts to restore normal traffic.
In recent days, attacks on commercial ships still sailing through the strait have surged to their highest level since the war began, according to independent data.
There have been at least five incidents in the past 48 hours involving tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area, including drone strikes, according to data analysis from maritime security sources and incidents reported to British navy-affiliated agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
That approximately mirrored the rate of attacks on Oct. 3-5, pointing to a new escalation, according to data from the U.N. shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization.
"There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate," one maritime security source said.
As part of the new strategy, Tehran will also expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, the officials said.
Analysis by maritime security sources based on attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security companies in the region suggest this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the Strait of Hormuz, including waters off the coast of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days.
The second Iranian official added that Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices before the November elections.
"Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the second official said.
"Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz."
The Pentagon and Iran's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Both Iranian officials said Tehran is moving towards a situation in which no vessel violating its restrictions would be able to pass through the strait. "It will be complete closure soon," one of the officials said.
In its latest report on Sunday, the U.S. Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) said the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained "severe," the second-highest level.
"IRGC attacks, attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing," JMIC said.

Taiwan cannot afford a US retreat from Indo-Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:54:41 UTC
21:54:41 KST

CODEPINK: Women for Peace’s open letter to the Jamestown Foundation on Oct. 1 offers a dangerous blueprint for the Indo-Pacific: unilateral US de-escalation as a path to peace.
The peace group portrays Western commitments to Taiwan as militarism that raises the risk of war. That argument mistakes wishful thinking for strategy. It ignores how authoritarian powers respond to weakness, leaving Taiwan exposed to coercion or subjugation.
CODEPINK argues that independent intent shields a position from being called propaganda. In statecraft, however, motive matters less than strategic effect.
One need not be a Chinese Communist Party agent to advance Beijing’s goals. Lobbying to cut defense budgets, dismantle alliances and end military aid to democracies such as Taiwan serves outcomes Beijing seeks.
The group invokes the security dilemma, urging unilateral de-escalation to prevent defensive measures from triggering conflict. But against an expansionist power, a lack of credible military capability signals vulnerability, not reassurance. US retreat would lower the cost of aggression, subsidize Beijing’s gray-zone pressure and embolden the People’s Liberation Army’s daily air defense zone incursions and naval blockades.
Replacing active deterrence with a strategic vacuum invites the conflict such prescriptions claim to prevent. As President Lai Ching-te warned in his National Day address, peace cannot rest on wishes alone and tolerance cannot become a pretext for aggression.
Repeat same error
History shows the danger of failing to extend deterrence to allies. The Korean War followed a collapse of deterrence, not a military buildup.
In January 1950, US Secretary of State Dean Acheson defined the US’ Pacific defense perimeter in a speech that excluded the Korean Peninsula and Taiwan. Sensing a security vacuum, North Korean leader Kim Il-sung, backed by Soviet leader Joseph Stalin and Chinese leader Mao Zedong, invaded the South five months later. The war forced President Harry Truman to deploy the Seventh Fleet to the Taiwan Strait, halting Mao’s planned amphibious invasion of Taiwan.
Beijing has repeatedly exploited power vacuums. The PLA invaded Tibet in 1950 after the region was left isolated and without defense guarantees. It seized the Paracel Islands from South Vietnam in 1974 amid the US withdrawal from Indochina.
In 1979, it launched a punitive invasion of Vietnam, calculating that the Soviet-Vietnamese defense pact would not be enforced. And after the US military left Subic Bay and Clark Air Base in 1992, Chinese forces occupied Mischief Reef in the Philippine exclusive economic zone. What Beijing then called shelters for fishermen is now a fortified air and naval base.
The 2016 South China Sea arbitration ruling tested the legalistic approach CODEPINK favors. The Obama administration encouraged the Philippines to pursue its claims under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
But when an international tribunal rejected Beijing’s nine-dash-line claims, Washington offered rhetorical support rather than deterrent force. Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte set aside the victory and pivoted toward Beijing, while the PLA accelerated island-building at Mischief, Subi and Fiery Cross reefs. Manila later reversed course under President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., reinforcing its alliance with Washington.
Effective deterrence
Effective deterrence requires both credible costs for an adversary and firm assurance for allies. CODEPINK ignores the self-determination of regional populations. Asia’s security architecture rests on mutual defense treaties and laws such as the Taiwan Relations Act and Reagan’s Six Assurances, which regional democracies demanded to counterbalance US-China diplomacy. Pulling back that umbrella would shatter allied confidence and push some partners toward nuclearization or accommodation with Beijing.
Lai has directly rejected the isolationist narrative, saying Taiwan’s defense investments are meant to deter war, not provoke it, and to create conditions for cross-strait dialogue based on parity and dignity.
CODEPINK also relies on a false choice between defense spending and social welfare. Domestic prosperity depends on international stability.
Roughly one-third of global maritime trade passes through the South China Sea, and Taiwan supplies more than 90% of the world’s advanced semiconductors. Eroding that security architecture would threaten supply chains, fuel inflation and damage economies far beyond Asia.
Absent enforcement
Beijing’s record makes the stakes clear. The subjugation of Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia, followed by the political crushing of Hong Kong, shows how little international commitments constrain the CCP when enforcement is absent.
The 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration promised Hong Kong a high degree of autonomy until 2047. Beijing dismantled that promise 27 years early with its 2020 National Security Law.
The lesson applies to Taipei as well as Washington. Taiwanese politicians who advocate appeasement or unilateral de-escalation to pacify Beijing repeat the same error.
Democratic concessions and weakened defenses will not earn goodwill from an expansionist regime. Whether advanced by US activists or Taiwanese politicians, preemptive concession does not buy peace. It rewards coercion and invites the next act of aggression.

Lai backs closer Taiwan-Canada ties in critical industries

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) said Wednesday that Taiwan and Canada should build on their complementary strengths to expand cooperation in key industries.
Lai made the remarks while meeting a Canadian parliamentary delegation led by Judy Sgro, chair of the Canada-Taiwan Parliamentary Friendship Group, per CNA. He said Taiwan excels in semiconductors and IT while Canada has strengths in AI, energy, and critical minerals.
Lai thanked Canada’s parliament for a motion countering China’s interpretation of UN General Assembly Resolution 2758. He also praised Sgro’s efforts to advance a trade cooperation framework agreement and noted expanding ties in supply chains and maritime security.
Lai thanked Canada for sending a warship through the Taiwan Strait in May and for emphasizing cross-strait peace and stability at the Group of Seven summit in June. He said the country would strengthen its self-defense capabilities and work with Canada and other partners to uphold the rules-based international order and Indo-Pacific stability.
Lai noted that Taipei is Canada’s sixth-largest trading partner in Asia and said closer cooperation could create opportunities for businesses and people on both sides as AI transforms industries.
Sgro, making her sixth visit to Taiwan as a delegation leader, said Canada regarded the country as a valued friend and partner. She cited shared democratic values and close ties in trade, education, and culture.

Taiwan university builds cancer treatment and imaging center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:54:25 UTC
21:54:25 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Hsinchu-based National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University said Wednesday that it has begun construction on a boron neutron capture therapy and imaging center, CNA reported
NYCU and Heron Neutron Medical Corporation held the ceremony at its Hsinchu Boai Campus, hosted by NYCU President Lin Chi-hung (林奇宏), and Heron Neutron Chair Hsu Chin-jung (許金榮). The 3,073-square-meter facility is located next to Jumin Hospital and will have one story and two basement levels.
NYCU said the center offers boron neutron capture therapy and 7 Tesla magnetic resonance imaging. It will be the hospital’s core installation for providing precision diagnosis.
Boron neutron capture therapy is a two-step radiation treatment method that destroys cancer cells while avoiding surrounding healthy tissue, per Taipei Veterans General Hospital. Selected cancer cells are injected with Boron-containing drugs and then exposed to thermal neutron beams to trigger heavy particles that create DNA strands to destroy cancer cells from within.
Magnetic resonance imaging is a non-invasive scanning technique that uses radio frequency waves and computing to generate high-definition 2D or 3D imaging for clinical diagnosis. Regular hospitals typically use 1.5 to 3 Tesla levels, whereas specialized facilities use 7 Tesla levels for extremely high resolution to identify conditions such as early-stage brain tumors, hints of seizures, or microbleeding.
NYCU said the project aims to complement the school's medical expertise with the tech firm's advancements and advanced equipment. Both aim to combine capture therapy with imaging and clinical research data to research new applications.
NYCU said the building is part of the school's broader initiative to rejuvenate the campus. It added that the school has also renovated its ShuTien biomedical engineering building and dormitories.

Cheap weapons, growing fears: Inside the Taliban’s drone campaign against Pakistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:52:44 UTC
21:52:44 KST

Cheap weapons, growing fears: Inside the Taliban’s drone campaign against Pakistan
Pakistan says it intercepted 23 suicide drones launched from Afghanistan into Pakistani airspace in September alone. Since the conflict began in February 2026, the Taliban have increasingly used drones to attack Pakistan, raising concerns in Islamabad.
The Pakistani army on September 23 said it had shot down at least eight fixed-wing drones in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, less than 1,000 metres from the Afghan border. It was the latest reported attempt by the Taliban to target Pakistani forces using this type of drone.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Since the conflict between Pakistan and the Taliban began in February of this year, the Taliban have deployed armed first-person-view (FPV) drones – small quadcopters carrying munitions such as mortar shells – to attack Pakistani positions near the border. They have also used larger, fixed-wing suicide drones equipped with more powerful engines, potentially capable of flying hundreds of kilometres.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
On September 28, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said it had delivered a diplomatic protest note to the Taliban over what it described as "provocative incursions", citing 23 drones launched from Afghanistan into Pakistani airspace since the beginning of the month.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
From friends to foes
Once close allies, Pakistan and the Taliban entered into open conflict about eight months ago when Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Mohammad Asif publicly declared that “relations with the Taliban had deteriorated into an ‘open war’.”
The conflict escalated after Pakistan began targeting positions of the Pakistani militant group Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) inside Afghanistan. Also known as the Pakistani Taliban, the TTP is officially recognised as a terrorist organisation by multiple countries and international bodies, including the United Nations, Pakistan and the European Union.
The TTP has carried out attacks in Pakistan for nearly two decades and has long-standing ties with the Afghan Taliban, which Pakistan accuses of sheltering and supporting the group.
When Pakistan, which has aerial military superiority over Afghanistan, has struck suspected TTP positions deep inside Afghanistan, the Taliban has retaliated with ground attacks and drones.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
'Making a fixed wing drone is not that complicated anymore'
UAV expert Mark Grozel explains:
 These drones are roughly two metres in size and could carry between half a kilogram and one kilogram of explosives. They have a very limited military effectiveness and are easy to intercept. They are slow and fly at low altitude. The difficulty is detecting them: they are hard to spot, but once detected, they are easy to shoot down.
There are multiple scenarios. One is that a foreign government supplies them. Or they could be, to some extent, homemade. Today, making a fixed-wing drone is not that complicated anymore.
Autopilot software that controls a drone’s trajectory is widely available.
On [the e-commerce site] Alibaba, you can easily buy components such as the engine and battery. The body could be made with a 3D printer, or from polystyrene or even balsa wood…
After examining photos and videos of drones that Pakistan’s army said it had intercepted, FRANCE 24 identified what appear to be DLE55 engines fitted to each of the suicide drones shown. These 55cc single piston engines and are commercially available online.
Despite their basic engines, small explosive payloads and simple radio navigation systems, these drones have a heavy psychological impact.
'Their main power is their psychological impact'
According to Grozel:
 The strength of this kind of fixed-wing drones is that they are cheap to make. Any group with the resources, including the Taliban, can now produce them.
They allow you to tell your adversary: ‘I can threaten your infrastructure at any moment.’ If one hits a school or a fuel facility, the consequences could be catastrophic. Their main power is their psychological impact.
The Taliban’s drone attacks come amid a broader conflict between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban, fueled by the activities of the TTP.
Direct engagements between the TTP and Pakistani security forces have increased significantly since the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, rising from 98 incidents in 2021 to 470 in 2024. Throughout 2025, regular clashes along the border reportedly resulted in approximately 4,000 deaths.
On September 18, 2026 a TTP suicide car bomb attack on a mosque killed 21 people in the Pakistani border city Kohat .
The roots of the Taliban–TTP alliance
Mukhtar Wafaei, an expert on the Taliban who specialises in Afghan affairs, explains how relations between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban deteriorated into military conflict.
 To understand the current situation, we have to go back to the Soviet-Afghan war in the 1980s.
During those years, Afghan and Pakistani fighters were sent from religious schools in Pakistan to participate in the “jihad” against Soviet forces in Afghanistan.
These relationships were forged during that period and remained largely unquestioned until the September 11 attacks and the subsequent US invasion of Afghanistan.
After the collapse of the Taliban’s first government in 2001, Taliban leaders and members dispersed, with many seeking refuge in Pakistan’s border regions, including Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Waziristan and Balochistan.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
 They maintained these long-standing cross-border relationships. In 2008, the Afghan Taliban expanded their presence across various parts of Afghanistan. Around the same time, several jihadist organisations operating in Pakistan, originating from the same tribal regions and carrying out violent attacks, came together under the TTP.
Another turning point came in 2021, when the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan. Taliban leaders who had been sheltered in safe houses in Pakistan belonging to the TTP, left for Afghanistan. Their Pakistani friends, allies and associates accompanied them to Kabul and also took refuge there.
Between late 2021 and mid-2022, Pakistan attempted to negotiate with the TTP. But after the group refused to disarm or accept Pakistan’s constitutional framework, it ordered its fighters to launch nationwide attacks on November 28, 2022. The Taliban claim the TTP is a Pakistani internal issue and deny any responsibility.
When diplomatic ultimatums failed to halt cross-border militant operations, Pakistan resorted to air strikes inside Afghanistan, prompting the Afghan Taliban to retaliate with attacks on Pakistani territory.
To display this content from , you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Pakistan also launched a mass expulsion campaign, with 2.39 million Afghans returning from Pakistan to Afghanistan over a period of more than two years.
To display this content from , you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
 There is a very deep ideological relationship between the Afghan Taliban and the TTP rooted in the extremist Islamist religious schools in Pakistan. They share the same ideology, come from the same religious tradition and follow the same teachings. They can no longer be separated. They are effectively one group.
A few months after the Afghan Taliban returned to power, the TTP leader stated very clearly in Pashto that Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan and the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, meaning the Afghan Taliban, were one group. He said: “We are not two groups. We are one group, following one programme, one ideology and one method.”
This is particularly revealing because the TTP leader himself explicitly described the two movements as one.

Returning to Gaza after two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:52:18 UTC
21:52:18 KST

When I entered Gaza through the crossing, I was shocked and stunned by what I saw. Looking to my right and left, all the houses were destroyed, leaving no trace. The streets were unrecognizable. Every street had a name, but I couldn’t identify them, there were no landmarks. The destruction was utter and unnatural.
I returned to Gaza in May after two years of living in Egypt. I don’t regret going back to Gaza. But I’m still in shock, unable to accept life and the situation people are living in. The situation is terrible, unnatural.
Since the genocide began in October 2023, things have been extremely difficult. We were deeply shocked by the reality of what was happening in Gaza: the destruction, the displacement, and the killing of people.
This war, of course, had a grave impact on us and changed the course of our lives. This also affected our work and changed the nature of our role as women leaders and advocates in the field of women’s rights.
Carrying out our work in Rafah at the beginning was difficult. During the first three months, I refused to ask the social workers and lawyers to work inside the shelters out of fear for their safety. But little by little, we began working, knowing this war could last a long time. It is extremely difficult to be responsible for your team, to ask your own team to put themselves at risk, when, at any moment, they could be exposed to bombardment or death.
Then our office was destroyed, and its assets and resources were lost, so I had to start managing and directing the association from my home. I lived in a two-storey house in Rafah and I hosted between 35 and 40 displaced people there, yet I still managed to use part of the ground floor for work. We were able to continue providing services from my home despite the serious risks, because the Israeli occupation was targeting us, targeting anyone trying to help people, whether through offices, warehouses, or vehicles used for humanitarian response.
The area where I lived in Rafah was sheltering almost 1.2 million people, due to the mass displacement from the north to the south. We distributed hygiene and food assistance packages to displaced families in tents and UNRWA school shelters at a time when government shelters were not yet operating. At the time, we had a kitchen in Rafah allowing us to cook regularly for people. That was an important part of our work in addition to distributing fresh water to the tents. We also built women’s restrooms among the tents in informal shelters.
I had two main reasons for going to Egypt. I was scheduled for surgery in November 2023, but I ignored it. I thought that being in the middle of a war was not the right time for surgery. But eventually, my condition worsened, and I became more ill and exhausted. I decided I had to undergo treatment.
It was also because I felt I was in real danger. I had a feeling that Rafah was nearing its end. I was terrified for my children. I was having nightmares that made my fear for them even stronger and that led me to decide to go to Egypt.
It was not an easy decision. It is not easy to leave your home, your family, and your work, and even my entry into Egypt was not guaranteed.
I was not granted a medical referral for medical evacuation. If I had waited for medical evacuation for my turn to come and had been lost in the bureaucracy, only God knows whether I would have survived. So I decided to pay for my treatment out of pocket. I paid $7,500 (£5,580) to be able to leave and that was only for me to pass through the Rafah crossing into Egypt. I also paid $3,000 (£2,230) for my daughter to be allowed to leave with me.
Thankfully, I was financially able to afford leaving and receiving treatment. Sadly, most people in Gaza were not and this left many patients, especially women and children, at risk of death.
It was a very difficult journey. All my children were with me when I was at the Rafah crossing. I was crying so hard, thinking I might never see them again, afraid that while going to Egypt, I might lose them, because the possibility that I or they may die or never seeing each other was real.
I thought I would go for a couple of months and register my children so they could come to Egypt while I received treatment, and then I would return to Gaza, to my home, my husband, and my work. I wanted to return to my life in Gaza once I knew my children were safe.
Then what I feared most happened. I travelled on the 29th of April 2024, and on the 5th of May, the Rafah crossing was permanently closed. It remained closed until February 2026.
I found myself stranded, separated from my kids. Those were two very difficult years for me. I was constantly trying to ensure their safety, as they were in danger while I was safe and this was an agonizing guilt. I was given sedatives so I could sleep, instead of staying awake with worry. Whenever there was shelling near them in Al-Mawasi, Khan Yunis, my daughter and I were gripped by terror. We couldn’t enjoy life, we couldn’t feel any sort of safety or mental peace. We lived in a state of constant tension.
Then came the news that my home had been completely destroyed. I hadn’t even finished paying for it yet; I still owed the half amount in installments and outstanding checks and I had lived there for less than two years. All the toil and hardship of a lifetime spent building a home for ourselves and our children to settle down, it vanished in the blink of an eye. It was devastating news; I fell ill for a week after hearing it and seeing the images of the house’s total destruction.
Things were extremely difficult; the suffering and hardship were very real. Yet I remained fully engaged in my work on a daily basis, around the clock. Sometimes I worked normal hours, other times, the internet was so poor in Gaza that I had to communicate at night. We spoke whenever possible, at any time, even on weekends. I did not have a single day off to rest. God helped Wefaq remain standing, continue working, and keep helping people.
The decision to return to Gaza was inevitable. What should I do in Egypt? Just live in a safe house? Of course not. I had to return to my Homeland, to my children, my family, my home, my work, my friends, my colleagues, and everyone.
Honestly, as soon as the crossing opened, I registered on the embassy’s website to return. What delayed me a bit was completing my medical treatment to ensure my health. I didn’t feel safe in Egypt, and I did not feel joy in Egypt during my two years because, truly, the land, the homeland, and the family are the only safe havens.
The days leading up to my return were filled with anxiety. My name was on the lists, but no one knew when the approval would come. I was in a terrible hurry and wanted to go back and see the children. I was afraid the crossing might close again before I could return. I was constantly stressed, anxious, and making calls, desperately wanting someone to help me get back quickly.
Then I returned to Gaza on May 13th, 2026. The journey back was incredibly tiring, it’s inhumane. We sat in the sun for three or four hours to be checked waiting for the Israelis to tell the Europeans and the Palestinian side that “it’s ok, send their group”. There are no toilets. It was very hot that day and you could not drink water, so that you would not have to go to the bathroom and in the end when I arrived at the [Israeli crossing] and we were searched and we got on the buses, I got dizzy from sunstroke, where I fainted.
At the Israeli crossing there was humiliation and inspection. I saw people who were harassed and had many of their belongings confiscated. There was disrespect. We remained on the bus waiting after we were searched and checked, sitting in the bus, locked up and suffocating, and there was no air conditioning. We remained waiting on the bus from 5:30 PM until 2:30 AM, when the buses finally set off.
It was a shock to me after I entered Gaza and the bus started moving. People began to cry at the sheer scale of the devastation we had witnessed in Rafah city and along our route from the crossing to Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis.
I now live in a tent in the Al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis in the Sultan Mahmoud camp, which houses no fewer than 200 families. The situation is terrible, unnatural. I’m still honestly in shock and I can’t accept life at its natural rhythm
Imagine living in a tent, just a tarpaulin, on sand. I am considered much better than others: I have a large tent for my children and a room roofed with corrugated zinc. I have a bed, and I bought a wardrobe. I’m trying to cope. Other people’s situation is extremely bad. I’m still in shock at how people can bear this and live normally.
Daily life in Gaza is very difficult. There’s no water and people have to wait for a water tanker to come so they can fill up. Goods are available now, but it’s very expensive and not everyone can afford it; most people rely on charities but even many charities have stopped operating.
The health situation is dire; garbage is everywhere and basically there’s no sewage system. The pipes could burst in some streets, making them impassable. There’s also a widespread infestation of rodents and fleas in most of the tents and not everyone can afford pesticides or rodent control products, which could lead to the spread of epidemics. Most people go to hospitals knowing beforehand that there is no treatment, no medicine, and no equipment. The most important thing Gaza needs now is the rehabilitation of hospitals and the establishment of various medical points to provide health services.
We at the Wefaq Foundation are working on a humanitarian response to meet people’s needs, providing hygiene kits, dignity kits, food parcels, vegetable baskets, hot meals, children’s clothing, women’s clothing, and tents. We are also doing our basic work of providing multi-sectoral services to women who are victims of violence, and women and children at risk. We provide psychological support, consultations, psychotherapy also, health services, social services, legal services, and consultations, even representation through referrals. We have also implemented many economic empowerment projects to develop businesses such as bakeries, mills, spice shops, restaurants, food products, and sweets.
Buthaina, pictured back in Gaza this month
Gaza needs everything. But first, Gaza needs an end to the Israeli occupation and its reconstruction, so that people can live a dignified, protected, and honorable life, far from the humiliation and degradation that people are currently living in and the restoration of rights to their owners.

Failure to activate Hormuz fertilizer plan could trigger food crisis, UN official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:51:09 UTC
21:51:09 KST

Failure to activate Hormuz fertilizer plan could trigger food crisis, UN official says
BANGKOK, Oct 14 - A failure by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertilizer through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday.
The United Nations set up a taskforce in March to facilitate passage of fertilizers through the strait. It is yet to implement the mechanism it drew up, but United Nations Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said this could be activated within 7-10 days of an agreement between Washington and Tehran.
"It's absolutely crucial to get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting season," he said in an interview in Bangkok, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings.
The White House, US State Department and Iran's Embassy in Bangkok did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Iran has sought to tighten its grip on the Strait of Hormuz since US and Israeli strikes on February 28, using the chokepoint to pressure Washington, which has been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Before the war, the waterway handled roughly a third of globally traded urea — the world's most widely used fertilizer — and nearly half of seaborne sulphur, a key input. It is also a major conduit for global oil supplies.
Fertilizer shipments out of the Gulf region remained largely halted more than six months after the start of the conflict, the Washington-based International Food Policy Research Institute said in a note last month. Fertilizer products accounted for a "very negligible" share of the resumption of some shipping during a ceasefire between mid-June and mid-July, it said.
FIVE VESSELS A DAY
If the Hormuz disruption continues, commodity prices could rise by up to 81% for cereals, 66% for oil crops and 30% for animal products, according to an August report by the International Chamber of Commerce.
"If we miss that planting season, the productivity of agriculture would significantly drop and the impact on prices will significantly increase," Moreira da Silva said.
The proposed operation would use a coordination centre in Oman to register vessels and coordinate safe passage, with UN monitors working alongside local authorities at Gulf ports to verify cargo loading.
The passage of only five vessels per day through Hormuz could keep fertilizer supplies flowing to countries in critical need, Moreira da Silva said.
Ships would be tracked during transit, and additional inspections could be carried out if countries raised concerns about a vessel or its cargo, he added.
MULTIPLE SHIPPING CHOKEPOINTS
Iran and the United States have exchanged proposals through intermediaries since a June interim ceasefire collapsed, but efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled over Tehran's conditions and Washington's insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset.
The proposed UN mechanism could operate alongside negotiations on a comprehensive deal aimed at securing lasting peace and freedom of navigation, Moreira da Silva said.
"What we are telling them is, while you continue your discussions towards a comprehensive deal, let us work, let us do our job," he said, declining to specify the exact bottlenecks to a deal as discussions continue with both sides.
Beyond the Hormuz crisis, a deteriorating situation in the Black Sea region, where cargo vessels have come under attack, and an offensive by Iran-backed Houthi militants along a key Red Sea shipping route are compounding the threat to global food security.
"What we are witnessing now is a concentration of factors," Moreira da Silva said. "Climate crisis, simultaneous disruption of maritime chokepoints on the Black Sea, on the Red Sea and on Hormuz." REUTERS
