Elections delayed: A generation of Palestinians is being denied its right to choose - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:01:40 UTC
21:01:40 KST

What pains me most about the postponement of the Palestinian elections is that I know the faces of those who were waiting for them. I spoke with them, heard their dreams, and saw how the prospect of voting restored some of their confidence in themselves and their country. They were not expecting a miracle. They wanted a simple right: to choose their representatives and have a say in their future. Then the door was closed.
Based on my close observation of the political process leading up to the decision, I hold Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh and Jamil Mezher primarily politically responsible for pushing for this postponement. This does not absolve others of responsibility. But it prevents those who drove the decision from hiding behind vague phrases about “national consensus” and “creating the right conditions.” Palestinians have the right to know who closed the door, and why. Those responsible have a duty to answer.
In my assessment, Sheikh worked persistently to prevent the election decree from being issued last July. Once it was issued, he continued his efforts to cancel the date it had set. He succeeded in securing the postponement. The painful irony is that his success in closing the path to elections followed a series of failures in areas that should have opened a way out of the crisis.
Postponement of the elections
Internal dialogue within Fatah and national dialogue were used to justify the postponement. Yet these are two processes the vice president helped lead over many years. Numerous capitals hosted lengthy meetings without achieving reconciliation or ending the division.
How does the failure of dialogue become a reason to deny people elections? Why should citizens pay the price for their leadership’s failures and then be denied the democratic means to hold it accountable?
As for Palestinian-American relations, where is the breakthrough ordinary citizens can see? And as for civilian coordination with Israel, ask the worker cut off from his job, the student arriving late to university, or the employee who leaves home before dawn without knowing when he will arrive.
The occupation bears direct responsibility for the checkpoints, restrictions, and humiliation. But the Palestinian official entrusted with coordination must also be held accountable for the results he has achieved in protecting people’s interests. It is not enough for the office to remain in place while citizens’ lives become harder every day.
Holding leadership accountable
I have known Sheikh since his release from prison in the early 1990s, after many years of detention. At the time, I headed Fatah’s youth movement in Jerusalem and served in its leadership across the West Bank and Gaza Strip. He was a member of Fatah’s Higher Movement Committee: well liked, cheerful, and close to ordinary people and the youth movement’s activists. We had a strong relationship, as he did with many leaders of our generation.
I do not know what these long years have done to the leader we once knew. But I know that the young man who once defended his generation’s right to participate has now become, in my assessment, one of the leading figures denying that same right to a new generation.
These young people are present within Fatah, too. In recent weeks, I saw its members and activists eager to stand as candidates and participate. According to the information I followed, more than 430 people in Hebron alone applied for a place on the movement’s electoral list, including many young grassroots leaders. This was a clear expression of a desire to take part in political life, and of talent waiting for an opportunity, even within the organization to which the vice president belongs.
As for Mezher, deputy secretary-general of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine, who holds a leading role while Secretary-General Ahmad Sa’adat remains imprisoned, his responsibility raises a question no less painful: How can an organization with such a substantial political history and popular following accept a role in closing the path to political renewal?
For me, that question has a face and a name: Nidal al-Rabadi.
He was my friend and schoolmate, and a supporter of the Popular Front. During a demonstration in Jerusalem in 1988, a bullet struck him and he fell beside me. We were 15. Lying on the ground, he looked at me and spoke his last words: “Don’t leave me.”
I have never left him behind in my memory. To this day, I keep his photograph in my home beside those of my children, and I cannot hold back my tears whenever his name is mentioned.
When I think about Mezher’s position on the elections, I remember Rabadi and ask: How do we honor that generation by denying its children the right to choose? What future do we preserve for their sacrifices if young people remain outside our institutions, waiting for permission to participate from those who have held their positions for decades? I invoke Rabadi because politics, to me, means responsibility toward people’s lives and toward those who died believing their sacrifices would open a better path for future generations.
The Popular Front was once the second-largest force in the Palestine Liberation Organization, with a clear grassroots presence during the First Intifada. In my assessment, that presence has diminished considerably over the years. Recently, I have witnessed young people and activists moving from its ranks to other political groups and electoral lists, including Masar Jadid.
This phenomenon extends beyond any single organization. Many of my colleagues in Masar Jadid and I came from other political movements. We brought our history and convictions with us, but we sought a space where we could work, make a difference, and participate. When organizations fail to make room for their members’ abilities, people look for other doors. Postponing elections will not resolve this alienation. It will deepen it.
The cost of delay
The cost of waiting is visible in almost every Palestinian household. Employees receive delayed portions of their salaries, workers have lost their incomes since October 2023, and families borrow money to pay rent and buy food. I have met people overwhelmed by loans, checks, and obligations they can no longer meet. Fear of creditors and the courts has become part of their daily lives.
In education, the financial crisis affects both regular schooling and teachers’ lives. When a teacher must seek additional work or sell goods on the street to support a family and afford the journey to school, the future of all our children is at risk.
In Gaza, families – many displaced into tents – are approaching a third winter since the war began. Mothers and fathers spend their days searching for the bare minimum of food, water, and medicine for their children.
Amid these conditions, I spoke for hours every day with young men and women from Gaza by phone, Zoom, and social media. Their education, knowledge, and capacity to think and act impressed me. I was moved by the hope in their voices simply because a political organization existed that allowed them to express their views and participate.
For them, elections offered a chance to become decision-makers in a society accustomed to treating them as recipients of aid. How painful it is to see these abilities buried once again beneath a closed bureaucracy and leaders who refuse to make room for them.
There are Palestinians approaching 40 who have never once voted in a national election. There are leaders who have held their positions for most of these young people’s lives. This imbalance cannot be corrected through more waiting or through dialogue that continues for years without restoring people’s rights – especially when the cost of postponement extends beyond our internal affairs.
French President Emmanuel Macron invested significant political effort in supporting recognition of Palestinian statehood and advancing an international path toward a two-state solution. Those efforts were linked to Palestinian commitments to reform, renew democratic legitimacy, and hold elections.
When we postpone this vote again, we confront our partners with a difficult question: How can they defend support for Palestinian institutions that deny their own people the opportunity to choose their representatives?
I cannot say with certainty that donor countries will freeze their assistance. But I fear this decision will weaken their willingness to honor their commitments and make it harder to defend support for us before their parliaments and taxpayers.
When our institutions and public services depend on that support, international trust becomes a direct Palestinian interest. Squandering it places an additional burden on citizens who are already suffering. Even so, I still see an opportunity to correct course, and I place cautious hope in it.
President Mahmoud Abbas has the authority on the Palestinian side to bring the date forward. Macron can use his diplomatic influence to support that correction and link the reform process to a clear electoral timetable in the near future.
We may have missed the opportunity to hold elections on November 28, 2026, but that does not justify waiting until September 11, 2027. I call for presidential and legislative elections to be brought forward to no later than March 2027, with preparations beginning immediately and conditions created that allow all Palestinian lists and political forces wishing to stand to carry out their preparatory work and activities on the ground.
Elections alone will not solve all our crises. But they give people a peaceful means of demanding accountability, open institutions to new talent, and rebuild trust between citizens and their leadership. Every day we postpone this opportunity makes it harder to recover.
At Masar Jadid, we will continue reaching out to everyone who can help. We will use the political, administrative, and legal means available to advocate for an earlier date. We will participate in every serious national dialogue that leads to a clear outcome: returning the decision to the people.
I hold Sheikh and Mezher politically responsible for pushing for the postponement. I call on Abbas to correct the decision he signed, and I urge Macron to help protect the opportunity that remains.
Thirty-eight years ago, Rabadi told me: “Don’t leave me.”
Today, in those words, I hear the voice of an entire Palestinian generation waiting for someone to open the door.
We have a duty not to leave them behind.
Samer Sinijlawi is a Palestinian political figure from Jerusalem and the founder and president of Masar Jadid (New Path), a Palestinian political movement advocating democracy, nonviolence, reform, and regional peace.

Iran's stock market climbs despite US blockade, energy shortages, collapsing currency

Iran’s stock market has recently rallied despite its plummeting economy.
Iran International reported on Tuesday that the Iranian stock market has seen an influx of Investments, despite increasing power outages, a shortage of foreign currency, and the rate of the rial tanking.
The report noted that this could mean one of two things: either investors believe Tehran and Washington will reach a peace deal soon, or they have no other way to stop their savings from losing value.
Iran International points to a few competing analyses of the situation to better explain investors’ choices.
One analysis from Farau indicates that a lack of foreign exchange currency in the country, energy shortages, and uncertainty over the war are the primary stressors for Tehran’s economy.
Why is Iran's stock market rallying?
Iranian oil exports have effectively stopped under the US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, leaving Iran with a dwindling supply of foreign currency.
The report noted that Khabar Online cited a 35,000-toman rise ($.003495) in the free-dollar market in the last month alone.
Additionally, energy shortages in Iran are exacerbating the problems. Iran's energy sector was already underfunded before the war began, and strikes on Iranian energy infrastructure have further strained production.
On top of that, Iranian investors are unsure what comes next. The economic effects of a third round of war would be disastrous, but diplomatic efforts continue.
Businesses that rely on imported goods are feeling these effects, as they face higher operating costs with less access to foreign currency, Iran International added.
These factors significantly complicate long-term investment and leave Iranians seeking assets that will preserve their value.
Some analyses indicated that investors are optimistic about a deal.
Rouydad24 argued that investors expect a deal and believe more access to international markets is on the horizon.
However, Iran International noted that other analyses show a different picture.
Just because the market is rising does not mean that investors in Iran are optimistic about the country’s economic prospects. Instead, it might indicate that Iranian’s lack alternatives for preserving their wealth.
The rial’s value has tanked, property is losing value, and bank deposits are losing purchasing power, making domestic equities more attractive to investors, the report noted.
This could offer a more stable assessment than the first: investors may be buying domestic stocks out of fear that cash will lose value in the country.
This comes as the International Monetary Fund forecasted that Iran’s economy would contract by 7.6% in 2026, as compared to the rate of 5.4% projected in July.
Notably, Iran International noted that the Middle East and Central Asia were expected to contract by 0.3%.

Kraków’s new mayor withdraws patronage of LGBT+ equality march

Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march.
Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall.
His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city.
Łukasz Gibała: Nie obejmę patronatem Marszu Równości. Polityka progresywna nie zawsze się sprawdza https://t.co/vIw8ZsSPQK
— Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) October 12, 2026
Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people.
In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”.
However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.
Kraków's new mayor has announced that he will attend the city’s LGBT parade next week, something his long-serving predecessor never did.
"I want to build a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone," says @OlekMiszalski, who took office this week https://t.co/ZQ9SzZiHp4
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 9, 2024
The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”.
“I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.”
Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments.
Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch).
During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed.
When asked if that meant that, as mayor, he would continue the city’s practice of transcribing foreign same-sex marriages into the civil registry – as Poland was ordered to do last year by the Court of Justice of the European Union – Gibała said that he would.
However, he added that he was doing this as a “legalist” who respects the current legal situation. “If a different political party wins [parliamentary elections] next year and changes the law in Poland, it [recognition of foreign same-sex marriages] won’t happen,” he told Radio Kraków.
In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union.
The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries.
Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue.
Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46).
The Polish government has granted same-sex couples who married abroad the same tax rights as other married couples

In the same interview this week with Radio Kraków, Gibała was asked if he would “return to your political roots” and be a “progressive mayor”. He responded by saying that, while “there are some issues where progressive policies actually work, there are others where they don’t”.
Asked for an example of the latter, Gibała said that, “if we look, for example, at what’s happening in western European cities, there are entire neighbourhoods in which there is a fear of entering for people of our skin colour”.

Italian Language Week at the National Library of Georgia
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:01:26 CEST

The first event celebrating the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World took place at the historic National Library of Georgia. This initiative, launched in 2001 through an agreement between the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation and the Accademia della Crusca, with the subsequent support of the Swiss Confederation, which takes place annually under the High Patronage of the President of the Italian Republic and aims to promote Italy’s linguistic and cultural heritage abroad. Each Week is dedicated to a different theme, which serves as the central thread for a rich program of conferences, exhibitions, and meetings. The 26th edition of SLIM, dedicated to the theme “A Brilliant Language: Conceiving, Designing, and Creating with Italian,” aims to explore the deep connection between our language, culture, and creativity.
                                    
In Georgia, the Week of the Italian Language in the World began with a symposium conceived by the Italian Embassy, supported by Silk Hospitality, and organized in coordination with the Committee of the Dante Alighieri Society of Tbilisi to mark the 800th anniversary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi. The symposium, titled “The Roots of Universal Humanism and the Great Precursors of the Renaissance” and inaugurated by Italian Ambassador Massimiliano D’Antuono and the Director of the National Library of Georgia, Konstantine Gamsakhurdia, featured as speakers, among others, Davide Rondoni, an Italian poet, writer, and playwright; David Magradze, Knight of the Order of the Star of Italy, a renowned Georgian poet and winner of various literary awards who is well-known and beloved in Italy; and Pierluigi Vercesi, an Italian journalist and author of historical essays.
                                    
“We decided to dedicate the symposium to two important anniversaries: the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World and the 800th anniversary of the death of St. Francis of Assisi,” said Ambassador D’Antuono. “The idea to organize this event arose during the visit to Tbilisi by the Secretary General of the Dante Alighieri Society, Prof. Alessandro Masi, who presented the Georgian audience with the keynote lecture ‘Italian Triptych: Giotto, Francis, Dante, and the Birth of Italian Humanism.’ To explore these themes further, we have brilliant speakers here today who will speak to us about the great Italian and Georgian figures who have profoundly shaped the history of Humanism, paving the way toward modernity.”
   The true highlight of the event—attended by Giorgi Gabunia, Chairman of the Cultural Committee of the Parliament of Georgia; Monsignor Giuseppe Pasotto, Apostolic Administrator of the Caucasus for the Latins; and numerous enthusiasts of the Italian language and culture, was the priceless 1481 incunabulum of the Divine Comedy, housed at the Book Museum of the National Library of Georgia—the only 15th-century edition printed in Florence, the homeland of the Supreme Poet. This extremely rare edition (of which approximately 180 surviving copies are held in major libraries and collections around the world) was displayed specifically for the symposium held at the National Library of Georgia.

Business warns that the new reservation rules could damage the defense industry, energy sector, economy, and food security
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:01:16 EEST
21:01:16 KST

Business warns that the new reservation rules could damage the defense industry, energy sector, economy, and food security
Kyiv • UNN
The government plans to review the limits on reserving employees of critical enterprises. Businesses forecast losses of personnel, production, and budget revenues.
The changes proposed by the government to the rules for reserving conscripts and determining critically important enterprises may lead to the loss of qualified employees, a reduction in production, disruptions to defense contracts, and decreased tax revenues to the state budget. Business representatives warn that another tightening of restrictions does not guarantee a significant increase in the mobilization pool, but instead creates additional risks for the economy and defense financing, UNN writes.
The government is preparing new restrictions for critically important enterprises
On October 13, the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine considered amendments to Resolution No. 76, which regulates the procedure for reserving conscripted employees. According to Forbes Ukraine, during the meeting the government did not make a final decision on reducing the reservation quotas for critically important enterprises.
The draft resolution proposed reducing the percentage quotas for reservations for enterprises in the defense-industrial complex and energy sector—from 100% to 85%, and for the utilities sector—from 75% to 60%. The relevant amendments are planned to be finalized within five days.
The provision excluding employees who have a deferment (students, parents of many children, and others) from the calculation was removed from the document.
The government decided to establish a Coordination Center involving the Security Service of Ukraine, the Main Directorate of Intelligence, the Foreign Intelligence Service, and the National Police, with the relevant decision to be further finalized.
At the same time, business representatives pointed out that the proposed changes had not been discussed with them and that businesses had not received official explanations regarding the decisions adopted.
Although the final changes have not yet been approved, the prospect of another review of the rules has itself caused concern among entrepreneurs. The issue concerns not only the number of employees companies will be able to reserve, but also the ability of enterprises to fulfill contracts, maintain production processes, and ensure the uninterrupted operation of critical infrastructure.
The issue is particularly acute for the defense industry and related sectors, the energy sector, and enterprises that ensure the population's basic needs.
Business warns of the risks of production cuts and employee losses
The Union of Ukrainian Entrepreneurs (SUP) opposed tightening the restrictions without a preliminary assessment of the economic consequences of the proposed changes and comprehensive discussions with business representatives.
The Union of Ukrainian Entrepreneurs opposes another tightening of restrictions on reservations without assessing the consequences and discussing them with business. We call on the Government not to introduce decisions that could weaken enterprises' ability to fulfill defense contracts, ensure the operation of critical infrastructure, and support the economy
The SUP emphasizes that enterprises have only recently completed procedures to confirm their critical status and re-reserve their employees. Another review of the rules complicates the planning of operations, contracts, and investments, while the repeated submission of documents creates an additional burden on businesses and government agencies.
Qualified specialists are difficult to replace quickly. This is particularly important for the energy and utilities sectors on the eve of the heating season and amid attacks on infrastructure. For the defense-industrial complex, the loss of employees could disrupt production cycles and contract fulfillment, while replacing them requires checks and access to sensitive information
The proposal for the defense-industrial complex to fix the number of employees as of the date on which an enterprise's critical status is determined is a separate cause for concern. Such an approach could create obstacles to expanding production and recruiting new specialists, even if an enterprise receives additional defense contracts.
Among other things, the SUP calls on the government to preserve the possibility of reserving up to 100% of conscripted personnel at defense, energy, and other critically important enterprises when there is a substantiated production need, and to hold relevant consultations with business.
A strong army needs a strong economy. The task of the state and business is to combine mobilization needs with preserving the ability of enterprises to manufacture products, restore infrastructure, and ensure Ukraine’s economic resilience
Restrictions on deferments from mobilization may pose a threat to food security
The All-Ukrainian Bakers’ Association (ABA), in a comment to UNN, warns of threats to food security related to restrictions on deferments from mobilization.
For the baking industry, the loss of key employees creates risks for uninterrupted production and the daily supply of bread to the population. Recognizing the priority of the needs of the defense forces, the ABA emphasizes the need to preserve the capacity of enterprises that ensure the state’s food security
The All-Ukrainian Bakers’ Association, like the Union of Ukrainian Entrepreneurs, calls on the government to hold discussions before adopting changes to the procedure for granting deferments from mobilization and to take into account the possible consequences for uninterrupted bread production and ensuring Ukraine’s food security.
Instead of strengthening mobilization, weakening the economy
Andriy Dlihach, founder of the Advanter Group of companies and the Board community, and co-founder of the Center for Economic Recovery, believes that the proposed changes do not address the systemic problems of mobilization. Instead, they could cause significant harm to businesses.
We view the proposed changes to the deferment rules negatively. First, this is not a solution that would significantly improve the state’s mobilization potential. These changes would affect tens of thousands of people, whereas, according to available estimates, around 1.5 million people are wanted. In other words, the scale of these phenomena is incomparable
According to him, the problem also lies in the constant changes to the rules under which enterprises operate. Companies plan production, enter into long-term contracts, invest in development, and hire employees based on the rules in force. And when the state changes them, enterprises lose the ability to forecast their activities.
The state is effectively changing the rules of the game retroactively once again. Businesses, particularly those in the defense and energy sectors, which are currently at the center of ensuring the state’s resilience, need predictable operating conditions. It is already extremely difficult to find qualified specialists. And this approach signals to businesses that conditions may only get worse
In his view, this approach creates a risk that Ukrainian companies will move their production facilities and engineering teams abroad. For the state, this would mean more than just the loss of jobs. Along with relocation outside Ukraine, tax revenues to the budget, investment, and added value could decline.
"We have already seen similar processes due to bans on weapons exports and other state decisions," Dlihach recalled.
At present, companies in Ukraine are operating amid constant Russian shelling, a shortage of personnel, high production costs, limited access to financing, and the additional uncertainty surrounding deferments from mobilization will have a negative impact on the economy.
We have repeatedly modeled the consequences of worsening the conditions for deferments from mobilization. This does not necessarily lead to increased mobilization; instead, it may result in staff reductions, lower economic activity, and reduced revenues to the state budget
Thus, the state may lose part of the funds that are currently directed toward supporting the Armed Forces and the functioning of the economy, which is particularly dangerous amid a budget deficit.
In Andriy Dlihach’s view, the state should focus not on yet another reduction in quotas, but on creating a system that would make it possible to support mobilization while simultaneously ensuring economic resilience. He names the introduction of a model of economic deferments from mobilization for critically important employees as one possible solution.
As early as 2024, it could have provided additional resources to finance defense by bringing wages out of the shadow economy. According to our estimates, potential revenues could have amounted to approximately UAH 250 billion per year. However, in our view, the refusal to introduce such a system contributed to the preservation of large-scale corruption risks in the reservation system
Dlіhach also proposes reviewing approaches to the use of human resources in government bodies, including assessing the possibility of reallocating them in favor of the Armed Forces.
According to him, business representatives plan to communicate with the Minister of Economy and the Prime Minister, and are also preparing a joint statement by think tanks and the business community with alternative proposals for the relevant order.

German startup tests RDX 1 tracked ground drone with troops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:00:27 UTC
21:00:27 KST

- Reactive Dynamics says combat troops tested its RDX 1 unmanned ground vehicle for logistics, casualty transport, reconnaissance patrols and leading manned vehicles.
- The German company lists the electric tracked RDX 1 at 80 km/h top speed, 150 km range and 1,200 kg payload.
German startup Reactive Dynamics says combat troops have put its RDX 1 tracked unmanned ground vehicle through its first tactical trials, using it to haul supplies and carry soldiers, evacuate casualties and run reconnaissance patrols by day and night.
The company said the tests took place last week with frontline units and also covered using the vehicle as a lead element ahead of manned systems, a role that sends the uncrewed platform first into ground where mines or ambushes are a risk. Reactive Dynamics did not identify the units, the country whose troops took part, or where the trials were held.
The company said it plans to add more payloads over the coming weeks and keep testing with the same units.
“Their feedback goes directly into the next RDX1 iterations,” Reactive Dynamics wrote.
Registered in Eching, just north of Munich, Reactive Dynamics describes the RDX 1 on its website as a fully electric tracked platform running on rubber tracks with full suspension. The company lists a top speed of 80 km/h (50 mph), a range of 150 km (93 miles) and a payload of 1,200 kg (about 2,650 pounds), along with the ability to climb a 60% gradient. Its 400-volt electric drivetrain gives off little heat or noise, which makes the vehicle harder to pick up with thermal cameras and acoustic sensors.
For now the RDX 1 is driven by remote control, with Reactive Dynamics planning to push autonomy features to the fleet through over-the-air software updates until the system can operate on its own. The company’s longer-term concept is a “Reactive Squad,” in which several vehicles carrying different payloads move together under the command of a single operator.
Payloads plug into an open architecture, and the company names German drone maker Quantum Systems and turret specialist Valhalla Turrets as partners. Its website shows mission modules for combat and reconnaissance, alongside supply, protection and casualty evacuation versions, although the LinkedIn post described no armed configuration in last week’s trials.
Unmanned ground vehicles have moved from experiments to daily use in Ukraine, where both sides rely on them to move ammunition and food to frontline positions and to pull wounded soldiers out under drone and artillery fire. Several European firms are now chasing the same market, among them Munich-based ARX Robotics, which also builds tracked UGVs and partners with Quantum Systems.

High smartphone dependency linked to altered time allocation in teens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:00:13 UTC
21:00:13 KST

Adolescents who exhibit problematic smartphone use tend to reallocate their daily hours away from studying and toward screen-based entertainment, which ultimately hinders their ability to manage their own learning. While heavy smartphone use also goes hand in hand with heightened academic stress, this stress appears to be a pre-existing condition rather than a direct consequence of digital habits. The research was published in Behavioral Sciences.
As smartphones have become central to modern life, psychologists have debated how excessive use impacts adolescent development. Past research has consistently linked problematic smartphone use to depression, anxiety, and poorer school performance. Problematic use refers to a pattern of overdependence that interferes with daily life, rather than a clinical addiction diagnosis.
Despite these known associations, the specific ways in which screen habits alter teen development remain a subject of active debate. Joungmin Kim, a researcher at Soonchunhyang University in South Korea, designed the current study to test two complementary ideas regarding how digital habits influence growing teenagers.
The first idea is a stress-activation theory. This proposes that excessive smartphone use interferes with offline socializing and healthy sleep routines. When teenagers lose these coping resources, they may feel overwhelmed by schoolwork, which then erodes their general well-being.
The second idea focuses on time displacement. This theory suggests that passive screen activities simply consume the finite hours in a day. During adolescence, the brain’s reward-seeking systems mature faster than its cognitive control systems. High-reward digital entertainment captures an adolescent’s attention, leaving less time and mental energy for effortful tasks like studying.
To explore these two pathways, Kim analyzed data from the Panel Study on Korean Children. The research tracked 1,116 adolescents across three consecutive years, starting when the participants were 14 years old. The researchers controlled for background factors like sex, household income, and average sleep duration to isolate the role of digital habits.
The adolescents completed surveys measuring their smartphone dependency, daily schedules, and emotional states. The survey also tracked four distinct developmental outcomes to see if smartphones affect different areas of life in different ways. These outcomes included school adjustment, self-regulated learning, ego resilience, and subjective happiness.
School adjustment measures how well a student behaves and relates to others in a classroom environment. Self-regulated learning reflects an adolescent’s ability to independently plan, monitor, and complete their academic work. Ego resilience refers to a person’s capacity to adapt their emotions and behavior in response to environmental demands. Subjective happiness is a broad evaluation of one’s own life satisfaction.
Kim first looked at the adolescents at age 14 to establish baseline measurements for their smartphone habits, stress levels, and developmental outcomes. At age 15, the survey recorded the participants’ daily hours spent gaming, watching videos, and studying independently, alongside their perceived academic stress. Gaming and video watching were measured separately because gaming is highly interactive, while video watching is generally a passive experience. At age 16, the survey assessed the four final developmental outcomes.
The initial analysis revealed that problematic smartphone use at age 14 predicted lower scores in school adjustment, self-regulated learning, and ego resilience two years later. Smartphone use did not have a direct statistical association with subjective happiness, but the data initially hinted at an indirect link.
When Kim mapped out the intermediary steps at age 15, two distinct patterns emerged. For self-regulated learning, the relationship flowed largely through how the teens spent their time, although smartphone use also retained a direct association with this outcome. Higher smartphone dependency at age 14 predicted an increase in gaming and a decrease in independent studying at age 15. This reallocation of time then predicted poorer self-regulated learning at age 16.
For the other three outcomes, time displacement played a minimal role. Instead, the initial models suggested that school adjustment, ego resilience, and subjective happiness were linked to smartphone use through heightened academic stress. Adolescents who reported higher smartphone dependency at age 14 also reported greater academic stress at age 15. This elevated stress then predicted lower resilience and happiness at age 16.
The most prominent detail in the research emerged when Kim adjusted the statistical models to account for the adolescents’ initial stress levels at age 14. Once this baseline stress was factored in, the apparent pathway connecting smartphone use to subsequent academic stress completely vanished. The statistical results for this pathway were not statistically significant after the adjustment.
This adjustment indicates that problematic smartphone use does not prospectively increase a teenager’s academic stress over time. Rather, high stress and heavy smartphone use are concurrent vulnerabilities. The adolescents who exhibited high smartphone dependency were already experiencing elevated academic stress from the very beginning of the study.
In contrast, the time-displacement pathway remained robust even after baseline adjustments. The data supported the idea that smartphone overdependence actively shifts a teenager’s future schedule. It draws time away from studying and into gaming or video watching.
This shift in habits appears to be the primary mechanism hindering an adolescent’s ability to manage their own learning. Self-regulated learning depends on the sustained allocation of time and attention, which are exactly the resources that digital entertainment consumes.
Because the data relies entirely on self-reported surveys, the responses may be influenced by personal reporting styles or a lack of objective self-awareness. Unmeasured factors, such as family dynamics, prior mental health conditions, or parental monitoring, could also influence both smartphone habits and developmental outcomes.
The initial baseline data was collected in 2021, during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic. The disruptions caused by the pandemic may have jointly elevated both screen time and academic stress for this specific group of adolescents. While the baseline adjustments help account for this, the unique historical context means the findings should be generalized cautiously.
These findings offer guidance for school-based interventions. Because high smartphone dependency and high academic stress often occur together, stress-reduction programs could serve as an important tool for vulnerable students. Meanwhile, time-management training and study-skill workshops might help protect students from the behavioral shifts caused by digital distractions.
Future research might benefit from incorporating objective measurements of digital behavior, such as screen-time tracking applications. Tracking actual app usage could help identify exactly how digital task-switching disrupts attention. Additional studies could also evaluate whether time-management training helps protect adolescents’ learning habits against the pull of digital entertainment.
The study, “Problematic Smartphone Use and Adolescent Developmental Outcomes: A Three-Wave Longitudinal Analysis of Prospective Associations Through Academic Stress and Time-Use Pathways,” was authored by Joungmin Kim.

How to use stale bread to make a classic British pudding – recipe | Waste not
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

We have a family tradition of making our daughter a fruit pie of some sort for her first day of school each September. Last year, it was a simple apple pie, but we intend to make our way through the myriad heritage desserts, from crumbles and crisps to cobblers, buckles, pandowdys, grunts, slumps and sonkers. This year, we made a brown betty, a wonderful, crumble-like dessert made with stale bread. We kept things seasonal with apples and blackberries from the garden, but any combination of fruit works really. I sweetened this one with maple syrup, but use your sweetener of choice: each adds its own unique flavour.
Apple, maple and blackberry brown bread betty
A brown betty is easier to make than crumble; it’s also arguably even tastier, and it saves waste, too. I used three brown bread crusts left over from my wholemeal bread taste test, which, when stale, make perfect and flavourful breadcrumbs. The topping should be good enough to eat even before cooking – totally delicious, salty sweet with maple syrup, and crunchy with seeds – so taste and adjust as you see fit with more salt, sweetener, nuts and seeds. The addition of sea salt is a gamechanger that really brings out the sweetness of the maple syrup.
Serves 4-6
4 apples 
100g blackberries
70-80g maple syrup, or brown sugar or another sweetener
1 tsp vanilla essence
50ml water, or brandy
75g butter, 50g of it melted, or extra-virgin olive oil
3 slices wholemeal bread (about 85g), torn into pieces
50g mixed seeds, or roughly chopped nuts (optional)
½ tsp sea salt
1 tsp ground cinnamon
Yoghurt, or cream, ice-cream or custard, to serve
Cut the cored apples into rough cubes (compost the cores, or turn them into pectin jelly) and toss with the blackberries, 40g of the maple syrup (or other sweetener), the vanilla essence and 50ml water (or brandy; the alcohol will cook off, and leave behind a lovely, complex flavour). Tip into a roughly 20cm-wide skillet or ovenproof dish, then dot with 25g of the butter (or extra-virgin olive oil).
Tear the bread into pieces, then pulse-blend into chunky breadcrumbs. Stir in the remaining 30-40g sweetener, the melted butter (or extra-virgin olive oil), the mixed seeds or nuts, if using, the sea salt and ground cinnamon. Scatter this mix over the top of the fruit, then bake in a 200C (180C)/390F/gas 6 oven for 40-45 minutes, until golden brown and bubbling.
Remove, leave to rest on the counter for 10 minutes, then serve with yoghurt, cream, ice-cream or custard.

Yemen: WFP warns of potential ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ as fighting blocks aid delivery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Yemen: WFP warns of potential ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ as fighting blocks aid delivery
Intensifying fighting in Yemen has cut off life-saving assistance to 800,000 people as shifting frontlines, blocked roads and growing insecurity severely restrict access to the city of Taiz and other conflict zones, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) said on Wednesday.
“We are critically concerned about the escalating conflict, but even more so about the growing number of people we can no longer reach because of it,” said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP country director in Yemen.
He noted that many of the affected families have been displaced multiple times and were already struggling to afford even basic food items.
“This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most,” he warned.
Trapped families, rising needs
Taiz is Yemen’s third largest city and capital of an eponymous governorate in which some districts have hosted the largest numbers of people displaced by the mounting violence between Saudi-supported Government troops and Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Many of the displaced are now inaccessible due to ongoing fighting and imminent road closures around the governorate.
WFP said the situation is especially alarming as Taiz has some of the highest levels of food insecurity, with 10 out of 16 districts already classified at emergency levels.
Dwindling food stocks
The latest monitoring indicates that wheat flour stocks are nearly depleted while local markets are running out of food, according to the UN agency.
WFP and partners cannot access more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance, including more than 200,000 women and children.
Some 800,000 people are now out of reach nationwide, taking into account communities affected by access losses on the West Coast.
Millions going hungry nationwide
The UN continues to sound the alarm over the crisis in Yemen, where more than 18 million people face acute food insecurity. Some 2.2 million children under five are acutely malnourished, including 500,000 suffering from severe acute malnutrition, the most life-threatening form of the condition.
Recent WFP monitoring in accessible areas found that nearly 75 per cent of households were unable to meet their basic food needs – a record number for this year and a sign that food security is significantly deteriorating.
WFP said the escalation has also severely disrupted its operations, with offices breached, assets and food stocks lost and critical supply chain routes cut off.
Disrupted operations, detained personnel
Meanwhile, 37 of its staff are among 72 UN personnel who remain detained by Houthi de facto authorities. WFP has joined UN Secretary-General António Guterres in repeatedly calling for their immediate and unconditional release.
The agency continues to uphold the critical need for safe and sustained humanitarian access in Yemen along with immediate funding. Teams have provided emergency assistance to more than 115,000 newly displaced people are preparing to expand to include 1.5 million people when access is restored.
WFP stressed that it requires $268 million to sustain operations through 2027, which include emergency food assistance, nutrition programmes, school meals, resilience activities and critical humanitarian logistics services.

WHO calls for urgent health action across the Eastern Mediterranean

Unknown Publisher

WHO calls for urgent health action across the Eastern Mediterranean
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) has called for promoting, providing and protecting health in the Eastern Mediterranean region, home to some of the world’s top humanitarian crises such as Sudan, Yemen and the Occupied Palestinian Territory.
Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus was speaking on Wednesday to health leaders and senior officials attending the WHO regional committee meeting underway in Cairo, Egypt.
“Over the past year, Member States have continued to advance the health and wellbeing of their people, often under the most difficult circumstances,” he said in remarks on the annual report for the region, which spans 22 countries and territories.
He highlighted numerous achievements, including strengthened response to noncommunicable diseases – such as cardiovascular disease, cancer and diabetes –which account for roughly two thirds of all deaths in the region, with more than 2.8 million lives lost every year.
Millions displaced, healthcare attacked
Yet, the report was also a reminder that the Eastern Mediterranean continues to face a multitude of challenges.
“This region remains the epicentre of global humanitarian need, with more than 117 million people in need of humanitarian assistance,” he said. It is also home to some of the world’s largest displacement crises.
“Conflict continues to affect millions of people across several countries and territories,” he said.
“We continue to see an appalling number of attacks on healthcare and climate-related shocks continue to place additional pressure on already fragile health systems.”
These developments are unfolding amid a sharp fall in international funding for both healthcare and humanitarian operations and increasing fiscal constraints at the national level.
“At the very moment when needs are increasing, resources are declining,” he said.
Investment and preparation
Tedros urged leaders to continue measures that promote health, such as reducing tobacco use and other risk factors for noncommunicable diseases and ensuring that all children are vaccinated.
Governments should also continue to invest in strong, equitable and resilient health systems and in health workers.
“Make every primary healthcare facility a place where a woman can receive quality care during pregnancy, where every newborn and child can get a healthy start in life and where hypertension, diabetes and cancer can be detected and managed early,” he said.
The WHO chief called for protecting health by strengthening preparedness, security and resilience.
“The threats facing this region are evolving,” he warned, noting that conflicts and outbreaks continue while climate risks continue to grow.
“Preparedness cannot be an afterthought. Preparedness saves lives before emergencies begin,” he said, underlining the need for continued investment in surveillance, laboratories, emergency workforces, resilient health facilities and supply chains.

Artist of the month: Steph Huang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:58:56 UTC
20:58:56 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – When picking up a bottle of olive oil at the supermarket, few consumers consider the complex geographic landscapes and global capital networks it crossed before reaching the table.
For London-based Taiwanese artist Steph Huang (黃麗音), food serves as a primary lens through which to dissect the globalized economy and contemporary labor systems. Following prestigious accolades including top honors at the Taipei Art Awards in 2022 and the Mark Tanner Sculpture Award in 2023, alongside exhibitions at Tate Britain and Perrotin, this year marks another career pinnacle for the 1990-born artist.
In October, Huang teams up with curator Liao Chuan-ya (廖釧雅) for her solo exhibition, "The Glittering Grove," at TKG+ gallery in Taipei. Meanwhile, a British iteration of her signature project, "Lili Deli," debuted at Frieze London.
As the featured artist of the month, Huang reflected on her creative path, tracing global food systems from memories in Taiwan to the olive groves of southern Spain.
Huang’s practice frequently centers on micro-objects from everyday life. In "Grafting," presented at Art Basel Hong Kong, she layered mangoes, shoji screens, and Taiwan’s colonial histories to explore family memory and identity.
In "The Glittering Grove," her field research shifted to olive groves and industrial assembly lines in southern Spain. Huang explained that while both projects started with specific agricultural products, olive oil operates on a planetary scale that shapes our fundamental relationship with food and nature.
Immersing herself in Spanish olive orchards, Huang witnessed the stark realities of agricultural economics firsthand. She was surprised by how small a fraction of the market price actually returns to the farmers for their fruit.
She said that while advertisements promote ultra-processed foods, fresh produce rarely receives such attention because it carries no brand and generates no outsized profit margins. The remote, off-grid experience also reshaped her personal outlook, leading her to realize that much of the modern convenience people pursue is not strictly necessary.
Inside the exhibition space, visitors hear the subtle sounds of olive harvesting, while wallpaper featuring field photographs of fallen olives and branches frames the room.
Blown glass plays a crucial role in Huang’s material vocabulary, where its delicate, translucent, and fluid quality contrasts sharply with mass-produced olive oil. Huang explained that the fragility of blown glass serves as a metaphor for the vulnerability of the global food system.
For Huang, using readymades is an act of assemblage rather than a desire to provoke. She said that readymades carry their own history and weight, allowing her to utilize their material forms and textures to reveal hidden social relations.
By highlighting discarded olives and branches, Huang elevates systemic remnants into visual focal points. Unharvested pods, fish bones, fallen figs, discarded shells, and old shoji screens have all taken center stage in her recent work as part of an effort to subvert conventional perspectives and flip hierarchical relationships.
"The Glittering Grove" observes that while an olive's economic value shifts across production stages, the fruit itself remains unchanged while the surrounding institutional framework transforms.
When asked if this mirrors the market fate of artworks, Huang offered a candid view on the dual reality of art.
She explained that while a piece accumulates layers of commercial value and class signifiers upon entering art fairs and collections, art ultimately exists for the public to engage with, criticize, and view. She added that when standing in front of a work with friends, the discussion revolves around personal affinity rather than market value.
Huang’s cross-cultural experience living in London sharpens her view of global supply chains. She attributed her curiosity about food systems to her Taiwanese background, saying that being an outsider makes it natural to question local dining habits and cultural traditions.
Looking ahead, Huang remains eager to explore new media, including an upcoming project incorporating a collection of vintage ties. Through poetic assemblages, Huang translates global capital into tangible form, encouraging viewers to look at everyday items on supermarket shelves with a renewed sense of awareness.

Military sources said the exercises are strategically important for securing the southwest maritime corridor. Waters are deep and have complex currents, making them a key area for submarine operations and a potential route for Chinese submarines seeking to pass through the First Island Chain and enter the Pacific Ocean.
Frequent exercises in the area allow surface ships and submarines to practice defensive tactics under realistic conditions and build a database of local underwater conditions, according to Liberty Times. This knowledge could help Taiwan improve its underwater warfare capabilities and deter Chinese submarines from infiltrating nearby waters or imposing a maritime blockade, the sources said.
The exercises will also test coordination among naval and air force units, which must share information to detect and track underwater threats. During the drills, the Hai Lung is expected to serve as a simulated adversary or a key component of underwater defense scenarios involving P-3C aircraft, S-70C helicopters, and Navy surface vessels.

Researchers use genome sequencing to study tuberculosis transmissions in Kaohsiung
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:58:27 UTC
20:58:27 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Researchers have used whole-genome sequencing to trace how tuberculosis bacteria spreads in Kaohsiung and understand the role of older adults in the chain of transmission.
“As many countries face rapidly ageing populations, reading the genetic code of TB bacteria can show us where the disease is really spreading and help us act earlier,” said Lin Hsien-ho (林先和), a co-corresponding author of the study and the director of the Institute of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine at National Taiwan University.
In a study published in The Lancet Microbe, researchers read the complete genomes of tuberculosis bacteria collected from close to 4,000 patients diagnosed over five years in Kaohsiung and compared the samples to identify links between infections.
Taiwan recorded 5,742 tuberculosis cases last year, the lowest number on record, but more than half of the patients were aged 65 or older, according to data from the health ministry. The study sheds light on the role older adults may play in transmission, suggesting they are not only vulnerable to the disease but may also contribute to its spread.
“We often think of older people with tuberculosis as patients who need treatment, not as part of the chain of transmission,” Lin said. “Our results suggest they may be both.”
The researchers found that adults aged 65 and older accounted for about four in 10 patients whose samples were genetically linked to those from at least one other patient, suggesting relatively recent transmissions.
The study also identified distinct patterns of transmission among different strains of tuberculosis bacteria. One strain spread readily in rural and mountainous areas but did not reach urban areas, where another group of strains predominated.
“Combining bacterial DNA with information about patients and where they live can reveal where tuberculosis is spreading and which groups of people need closer attention,” according to a press release.

A state-funded school renovation project in Helsinki has become the centre of a labour exploitation scandal involving unpaid wages, false employment records and a subcontractor allegedly managed from an Estonian prison by a man convicted of involvement in organised crime.
Finland's Construction Union (Rakennusliitto) identified the suspected violations at the Valteri Ruskis school in Ruskeasuo, which serves children and young people requiring special educational support.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
The union said its investigation uncovered 30 workers classified as self-employed despite working under conditions resembling regular employment. Several foreign workers received wages below collective agreement rates, while the authorities had not properly verified the right of some workers to work in Finland.
State property agency Senaatti Properties commissioned the renovation, with Mirlux Oy acting as the main contractor. The allegations concern subcontractors Varatek Oy and Kore Metal Oy.
According to the union, Varatek registered 36 people to work at the site, although only three were its direct employees. Others worked through an invoicing service, raising concerns that the company had disguised employment relationships to avoid labour obligations.
The union also identified unpaid overtime and Sunday work allowances. Some workers received trainee-level wages despite working extended hours.
Finnish newspaper Helsingin Sanomat reported that three employees worked 122 hours across 13 days within a two-week period. Union calculations indicated that each had lost nearly €1,500 in wages.

Rakennusliitto placed Varatek under a union boycott on Tuesday after the company allegedly failed to resolve the wage disputes.
Toni Malmström, senior expert at the union, criticised the oversight failures, warning that companies violating labour agreements gain an unfair advantage over employers following the rules.

Cornell scientists identify rare human genetic disorder in two unusually long-legged cats

Cornell scientists identify rare human genetic disorder in two unusually long-legged cats
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Cornell University
- Summary:
- Two unusually long-legged cats have helped scientists uncover the first genetically confirmed cases of Marfan syndrome in domestic felines. Researchers at Cornell University discovered that the brothers carried two altered copies of a gene linked to the rare connective tissue disorder, which can affect the eyes, heart, and blood vessels. Surprisingly, the cats survived into adulthood because their genetic mutation still allowed some normal function.
- Share:
Two brothers named Gary and Shaggy have helped Cornell University researchers make a rare genetic discovery. In a study published in Scientific Reports, scientists reported the first molecular characterization of Marfan syndrome in domestic cats, a condition primarily recognized in humans.
Gary and Shaggy first stood out as kittens because of their unusually long limbs. As they grew older, veterinarians also identified abnormalities in their eye structures and an enlarged aorta, the body's main artery. Together, these symptoms suggested Marfan syndrome, an inherited condition that weakens connective tissues throughout the body. The disorder affects approximately 1 in 4,000 people, but these brothers represented the first known documented feline cases.
"The findings provide a foundation for improved veterinary diagnostics," said senior author Dr. Jacquelyn Evans, assistant professor in the College of Veterinary Medicine and at the Baker Institute for Animal Health. "It can help veterinarians recognize similar cases in the future and may help develop genetic tests."
Scientists Uncover a Surprising Genetic Twist
To determine what caused the brothers' unusual symptoms, researchers from multiple disciplines conducted thorough medical examinations and analyzed their DNA. Their investigation identified changes in a gene called FBN1, which provides instructions for producing fibrillin-1. This protein is essential for healthy connective tissue, helping support structures throughout the body, including blood vessels, bones, ligaments, skin, and eyes.
Genetic testing revealed that Gary and Shaggy each had two altered copies of FBN1, having inherited one from each parent. This was especially notable because, in humans, a mutation in just one copy of the gene can be enough to cause Marfan syndrome. Having two altered copies is exceptionally uncommon and can severely disrupt the production of normal fibrillin-1.
Yet the brothers' genetic changes had an unexpected effect. Further analysis showed that their particular variant did not completely disable the gene. Instead, it interfered with how the gene's instructions were processed while still allowing some normal activity to continue. That remaining function helps explain why Gary and Shaggy were able to survive into adulthood, even though carrying two copies of such a mutation could otherwise have resulted in a much more severe form of the disorder.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Cornell University. Original written by Teresa Griffin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Shawna R. Cook, Jessica J. Hayward, Soon Hon Cheong, Linda Impe, Ian R. Porter, Brian Lamendola, Gavin R. Hitchener, Urs Giger, Philip R. Fox, Jacquelyn M. Evans, Bart J. G. Broeckx. A homozygous hypomorphic FBN1 splice region variant in domestic cats with Marfan syndrome. Scientific Reports, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-70702-3

Wie Maroš Šefčovič der Durchbruch im Handel mit China gelang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Wie Maroš Šefčovič der Durchbruch im Handel mit China gelang
Europas Handelskommissar hat ein erstes Zugeständnis aus Peking errungen. Nun muss er die EU-Spitzenpolitiker davon überzeugen, dass der Dialog noch mehr bewirken kann.
Als Maroš Šefčovič im Juli den EU-Botschaftern seine Strategie für den Umgang mit China vorstellte, richtete er eine Warnung an die Regierungen, die auf strengere Handelsmaßnahmen gegen Peking drängten.
„Manchmal ist es sogar populär, einen Handelskrieg zu beginnen, aber es ist sehr schwierig, ihn zu beenden“, erinnerte sich der EU-Handelskommissar später in einem Interview mit POLITICO.
Drei Monate später ist Šefčovič ein erster Durchbruch gelungen: Letzte Woche wurde in Peking eine Vereinbarung erzielt, die Importe chinesischer Hybridautos drastisch zu reduzieren. Dieser symbolische Erfolg ist ein kleiner Schritt zur Stabilisierung der Handelsbeziehungen, die nach Ansicht Brüssels einen gefährlichen Wendepunkt erreicht haben.
Für Šefčovič, der im vergangenen Jahr mit Donald Trump einen Zollwaffenstillstand ausgehandelt hatte, deutet die Vereinbarung darauf hin, dass sich seine Strategie des Engagements, gestützt durch die Androhung härterer Handelsmaßnahmen, allmählich auszuzahlen beginnt.
Šefčovič hatte sich bei einem Treffen mit dem chinesischen Handelsminister Wang Wentao Ende Juni in Brüssel darauf geeinigt, den Handelsdialog aufzunehmen.
Der slowakische Kommissar hoffte, wenn er sich zuerst auf den Automobilsektor konzentrieren würde – einem Bereich, in dem die EU als einer der wenigen großen Märkte, die chinesischen Herstellern noch offenstehen, über Einfluss verfügt – einen vertrauensbildenden Erfolg zu erzielen. Erst später will er sich den schwierigeren Fragen zuwenden: den kritischen Rohstoffen bis hin zu Chinas enormen industriellen Überkapazitäten.
Gleichzeitig bemühte er sich darum, die europäischen Regierungen parallel hinter einer Initiative zur Stärkung der Handelsschutzmaßnahmen der EU zu vereinen. Šefčovič untermauerte seine Verhandlungsposition mit der Androhung härterer Maßnahmen, um das Handelsdefizit der EU gegenüber China in Höhe von einer Milliarde Euro pro Tag zu senken.
Der Hybrid-Deal ist jedoch nur der erste Schritt in einem weitaus größeren Wettstreit.
Advertisement
Die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU treffen sich am Donnerstag in Brüssel, um Bilanz zu ziehen. Sie müssen abwägen, ob sie die Forderungen nach aggressiveren Maßnahmen zum Schutz der europäischen Industrie durchziehen.
Das Treffen wird zeigen, ob ein Kommissar, der seine Karriere darauf aufgebaut hat, Kompromisse mit schwierigen Partnern zu finden, die Unterstützung Europas für eine Strategie aufrechterhalten kann, deren Erfolg alles andere als sicher ist.
„Man hat es mit demselben Partner am Verhandlungstisch zu tun“, sagte Šefčovič im August in einem Interview mit POLITICO über die Risiken eines Handelskriegs. „Wenn man das also vermeiden kann, wäre das viel besser.“
Marktmacht
Šefčovičs erster Schritt bestand darin, sich auf einen Bereich zu konzentrieren, in dem Europa noch Einfluss hat: den Zugang zu seinem Markt mit 450 Millionen Menschen.
Chinas Hersteller haben sich zu globalen Kraftzentren entwickelt, kämpfen jedoch mit einer schwachen Nachfrage im Inland. Ein anhaltender Einbruch auf dem Immobilienmarkt belastet den Privatkonsum, während der gnadenlose Wettbewerb Preiskämpfe ausgelöst hat. Die Inlandsverkäufe von Pkw gingen im September gegenüber dem Vorjahr um 28 Prozent zurück.
Dadurch gewinnen die Märkte in Übersee zunehmend an Bedeutung. Da die USA chinesische Importe ausschließen, bleibt Europa einer der lukrativsten Märkte, der chinesischen Herstellern noch offensteht.
Advertisement
Šefčovič setzte darauf, dass Peking lieber Exportbeschränkungen akzeptieren würde, als den Zugang zum europäischen Markt gänzlich zu riskieren.
Er richtete sein Augenmerk auf den Automobilsektor, in dem chinesische Hersteller sehr schnell Fuß gefasst haben. Im Jahr 2024 hatten chinesische Autohersteller einen Anteil von lediglich 2 Prozent sowohl am europäischen Hybrid- als auch am Plug-in-Hybrid-Markt; bis zur ersten Hälfte des Jahres 2026 waren die jeweiligen Anteile laut Branchenzahlen auf 14 Prozent beziehungsweise 25 Prozent gestiegen.
Die Kommission bereitete sich darauf vor, die Einfuhr von Hybridfahrzeugen auch ohne ein Abkommen zu beschränken. Eine Verhandlungslösung bot Šefčovič jedoch auch einen politischen Mehrwert: den Beweis, dass der Dialog mit Peking zu greifbaren Ergebnissen führen kann.
Die Verhandlungen verliefen intensiv, wie eine mit den Gesprächen vertraute Person auf chinesischer Seite berichtete.
„Es war sehr, sehr hart“, sagte die Person, die anonym bleiben wollte, um offen über die hinter verschlossenen Türen stattfindenden Verhandlungen zu sprechen. „Beide Seiten hatten seit langem keine solche Intensität mehr erlebt. Keine Sommerpause, keine Feiertage. Sie arbeiteten rund um die Uhr, sogar noch ein oder zwei Tage vor Šefčovičs Reise nach Peking.“
Während Brüssel den Dialog suchte, wollte es Peking gleichzeitig davon überzeugen, dass es bereit sei, härtere Maßnahmen zu ergreifen, sollten die Verhandlungen scheitern.
Advertisement
Šefčovič hatte zuvor Pläne für ein neues „Diversifizierungsinstrument“ angekündigt, das Unternehmen in kritischen Sektoren dazu verpflichten würde, wesentliche Vorleistungen von mindestens drei Lieferanten zu beziehen – ein Schritt, um Chinas Fähigkeit einzuschränken, Europas Abhängigkeit von seinen kritischen Rohstoffen auszunutzen.
Dann, nur drei Tage vor Šefčovičs Reise nach Peking, erhöhten Frankreich und Deutschland den Druck.
Präsident Emmanuel Macron und Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz forderten eine wirkungsvolle neue Handelswaffe, die es Brüssel ermöglichen würde, Ländern, denen unlautere Wettbewerbsvorteile vorgeworfen werden, innerhalb weniger Tage den Zugang zum europäischen Markt zu beschränken – oder sogar ganz zu sperren.
Der Vorschlag nannte China zwar nicht ausdrücklich, doch Peking war das offensichtliche Ziel.
Den Zusammenhalt wahren
Mehreren Diplomaten zufolge werden die EU-Staats- und Regierungschefs die Einigung voraussichtlich begrüßen, die Kommission jedoch gleichzeitig dazu drängen, rasch zu handeln, um die Handelsschutzmaßnahmen der Union zu stärken. Die in Peking erzielte Einigung hat Zeit gewonnen, aber noch nicht geklärt, wie weit Brüssel gehen sollte, falls die chinesischen Exporte weiter steigen oder die Verhandlungen ins Stocken geraten.
„Wir verlieren Tausende von Arbeitsplätzen in der Industrie; Olivenöl und Eiscreme werden das Kernproblem nicht lösen“, sagte ein EU-Diplomat, nachdem Šefčovič die Botschafter am Sonntag informiert hatte, und bezog sich dabei auf die gemeldeten Ergebnisse der Gespräche.
Advertisement
Ein hochrangiger deutscher Beamter begrüßte das Abkommen von Peking als einen ersten Schritt in die richtige Richtung. „Es ist ein positives Zeichen – das natürlich das Problem des Handelsdefizits mit China nicht vollständig löst“, sagte der Beamte.
Doch Berlins Unterstützung für eine härtere Linie könnte sich als kurzlebig erweisen.
Alicia García-Herrero, Senior Fellow beim Thinktank Bruegel, argumentierte, dass Pekings Zugeständnisse darauf ausgelegt gewesen seien, Berlin zu beschwichtigen, angesichts der Bedeutung der Automobilindustrie für die deutsche Wirtschaft.
„Ich hoffe nur, dass Merz nicht von dem Brief abrückt, den er an die Kommission geschickt hat“, sagte sie. Da der deutsche Bundeskanzler im eigenen Land politisch geschwächt ist, befürchtet García-Herrero, dass er zögern könnte, eine langwierige Konfrontation zu riskieren: „Ich mache mir Sorgen, dass Merz diesen schnellen Erfolg nutzen und sich aus dem Staub machen wird.“
Damit steht Šefčovič vor einem Balanceakt: Er muss die EU-Regierungen bei der Fortsetzung des Engagements mit China an Bord halten und gleichzeitig die glaubwürdige Drohung mit härteren Maßnahmen aufrechterhalten, falls die Gespräche scheitern sollten.
„Ich gehe davon aus, dass [die Staats- und Regierungschefs] der Kommission grünes Licht geben werden, weitere handelspolitische Schutzmaßnahmen voranzutreiben. China könnte dies als Verrat auffassen. Sollte das der Fall sein, könnten wir sehr schnell wieder in einen Konflikt geraten“, sagte Noah Barkin, Senior Advisor im China-Team der Rhodium Group.
Advertisement
Der bevorstehende Kampf
Für Šefčovič besteht die Herausforderung nun darin, einen begrenzten Durchbruch bei den Autos in eine umfassendere Neuausrichtung des Handels mit China umzumünzen – und Europa gleichzeitig Zeit zu verschaffen, seine Abwehrmaßnahmen zu stärken, falls die Verhandlungen scheitern sollten.
„Es spricht einiges dafür, China das anzutun, was China Europa jahrelang angetan hat – Peking in Dialogen und Verfahren zu verzetteln, während Europa seine Instrumente bereitstellt. Aber die EU muss die Zeit, die diese Gespräche bieten, voll ausschöpfen“, sagte Barkin von Rhodium.
Der Handelskommissar wird voraussichtlich im Januar ein Videogespräch mit Wang führen, bevor sich die beiden im kommenden März erneut treffen. Diese Gespräche werden zeigen, ob Peking bereit ist, weitere Zugeständnisse in Sektoren zu machen, in denen die europäische Industrie zunehmend in die Defensive gerät, darunter die Chemieindustrie.
Eine weitere Priorität sind kritische Rohstoffe, bei denen China zugestimmt hat, weiterhin Ausfuhrlizenzen für Seltene Erden zu erteilen. Pekings Kontrolle über deren Versorgung verschafft dem Land erheblichen Einfluss auf europäische Hersteller, was die Grenzen von Šefčovičs Verhandlungsposition deutlich macht.
Die Kommission bereitet zudem zwei Vorschläge für Dezember vor: das Diversifizierungsinstrument, das darauf abzielt, die Abhängigkeit von chinesischen Lieferungen zu verringern, und einen Mechanismus zum Schutz europäischer Industrien und Regionen vor Vergeltungsmaßnahmen.
Das Ausmaß der Herausforderung ist gewaltig: Chinesische Importe von Hybridautos beliefen sich im ersten Halbjahr 2026 auf 6,7 Milliarden Euro, während das Handelsdefizit zwischen der EU und China im vergangenen Jahr bei 360 Milliarden Euro lag. Das Abkommen verschafft den europäischen Automobilherstellern zwar eine gewisse Erleichterung, trägt aber kaum dazu bei, das zugrunde liegende Ungleichgewicht zu beheben.
Advertisement
Brüssel hofft, dass die Schutzmaßnahmen für Hybridfahrzeuge als Blaupause für den Schutz anderer Branchen dienen können, die mit einem Anstieg chinesischer Importe konfrontiert sind.
„Wir hören auf unsere Industrie. Dazu gehören die chemische Industrie, die Windkraftbranche und die Möbelindustrie. Wir wissen, wo es zu einem Anstieg kommt, und wir wissen, was uns im Hinblick auf unsere Deindustrialisierung am härtesten trifft“, sagte ein hochrangiger Kommissionsbeamter am Montag.
Šefčovič räumte in seinem Interview im August die Grenzen des Dialogs ein und warnte, dass Verhandlungen ohne greifbare Fortschritte immer schwieriger aufrechtzuerhalten seien.
„Es wäre sehr wichtig, zurückzukommen und zu sagen, dass das Problem anerkannt wird und es bereits einige Pilotprojekte gibt, die wir testen wollen, um zu sehen, ob sie funktionieren“, sagte er.
„Aber wenn einfach nichts geschieht, dann wird es für uns natürlich viel schwieriger sein, nur über diese Themen zu sprechen.“
Jordyn Dahl in Brüssel und Hans von der Burchard in Berlin haben zu diesem Artikel beigetragen.
