In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:54:34 UTC
03:54:34 KST

In Ukraine the situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns.
Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued.
Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph).
Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate.
The immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal with Russia.
However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental.
Even Serhii Beskrestnov, Zelenskyy’s high-profile military technology adviser, has expressed public doubts about whether the US had paused the sharing of missile detection. “Friends, this is not the first time that the launch of an S-400 has not been detected,” he posted on Monday. “We should not jump to conclusions.”
However, there has now been an absence of incoming warnings for two days in a row. The second of these was in tandem with the unexpected throttling of Starlink, a system supplied by Musk with the approval of the US military.
So it is hardly reassuring against the backdrop of White House threats, which have emerged every time a flailing Trump has tried to end the war in Ukraine.
The last time Trump paused intelligence-sharing – which is, in effect, valuable information about Russian positions and movements – was in March 2025, shortly after Zelenskyy’s infamous dusting down in the Oval Office.
“You don’t have the cards,” Trump said, as he took another away. Ukraine rapidly lost a chunk of territory it had occupied in Russia’s Kursk region before sharing was restored.
A confirmed pause this time would mark a serious breach when Ukraine is more than holding off its larger neighbour on the frontline, even as the situation on the home front is worsening.
Russia has bombed two bridges in Kyiv, gas stations, city centre buildings and out-of-town warehouses, showing little restraint as it aims to harm Ukrainian civilians while it struggles to win the conventional war.
The effect of a more permanent halt to Starlink for Ukrainian drones or anything military that moves faster than 50mph is a little more complex. Starlink is how Ukraine directs many of its mid-strike (or mid-range) drones accurately towards their targets into occupied areas behind enemy lines, critical for helping the defenders maintain the rough balance on the front.
Yet, ironically, Starlink is not used for the long-range missions that target the Russian oil refineries about which Trump is so concerned, because it has long been disabled by the company inside Russia’s internationally recognised borders.
“There’s no meaningful effect on deep-strike operations,” one Ukrainian soldier said, while conceding there could be as much as a 30-fold drop in mid-strike operations because the alternatives are 30 times more expensive. Commanders are “replanning everything”, the soldier added, and aiming to find ways to carry on missions using different technologies and techniques.
Starlink is also, more importantly – as Beskrestnov emphasised on Wednesday – used by air-defence interceptors in the most effective system to down Russia’s deadly new jet-powered Shahed drones. These are at least twice as fast as traditional piston-engined Shaheds, and Ukraine’s rate of interception had dropped to 60% in September, before recovering to 75% according to the country’s air force.
The reality, then, is that the Starlink manoeuvre may not have much impact on oil prices, and only a limited effect on Ukraine’s frontline position, while putting the country’s civilians in greater danger.
As the Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk put it: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.”
Meanwhile, diplomatically, the situation is more finely poised. It was already the case that the Trump White House had proved to be a difficult and unreliable partner. What Zelenskyy, on a visit to London on Wednesday, needs from the likes of the UK prime minster, Andy Burnham, is pressure on the US to ensure the Starlink pause and whatever is happening with intelligence-sharing does not metastasise into a deeper crisis.

Injury toll after Russian attack on Rivne rises to eight
The regional police reported this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.
“Eight injured people, including a 14-year-old boy, have now been taken to hospital. Four of them have been admitted,” the statement said.
1 / 10
The strike on Rivne. / Photo: National Police of Ukraine
Rescue workers, police officers, medical personnel and other relevant services are working at the scene. Investigators from the Security Service of Ukraine (SSU) are documenting the consequences of the attack as part of a pre-trial investigation launched under Article 438 of Ukraine’s Criminal Code, which covers war crimes.
According to police, on October 14, Russian forces launched another attack on Rivne, striking a residential area.
The attack damaged residential premises, nine vehicles and an outbuilding.
Rescue workers are conducting emergency operations and dealing with the aftermath of the Russian strike. Police are securing the scene, restricting access to the hazardous area and assisting residents.
Explosive ordnance specialists are inspecting the impact site and surrounding area for unexploded ordnance and debris.
Law enforcement officials warn that anyone who finds suspicious objects or fragments of munitions should not approach or touch them and should immediately call the emergency numbers 101, 102 or 112.
As Ukrinform reported, overnight and morning attacks in the Rivne region struck residential infrastructure and two agricultural enterprises.

Putin Convenes Top Russian Officials to Discuss Cybersecurity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:54:39 UTC
20:54:39 KST

Russian President Vladimir Putin will discuss cybersecurity with top officials on Wednesday, the Kremlin said, describing it as an increasingly pressing issue but denying the meeting was prompted by a spate of Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian data centers.
"Artificial intelligence technologies bring many benefits and advantages, boosting efficiency. But at the same time, of course, attempts by various states to weaponize these new technologies... pose threats to entire sectors of any country's economy," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
"Naturally, we are no exception, and we must be prepared for these challenges. That is why the president is holding this meeting today."
Peskov said the meeting was not connected with Ukrainian drone strikes in the past week on four Russian data centers — three belonging to tech group Yandex and one to Sberbank.
"No, this is a much more systemic meeting. It is not connected to those specific, isolated attacks," he said.
The participants will include government ministers, top security officials, the head of Sberbank and Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina, Peskov added.

Uvision shows remote kamikaze drone launcher at AUSA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:54:37 UTC
20:54:37 KST

- Uvision is showing an eight-canister HERO 120 launcher at AUSA 2026, designed for remote operation in mobile, fixed and containerized configurations.
- The HERO 120 is already on contract with the U.S. Army under a Lethal Unmanned Systems deal worth up to $982 million.
Israeli loitering munition maker Uvision is showing an eight-canister launcher for its HERO 120 at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, pitching the remotely operated system as a way to spread strike capacity across land and maritime platforms and tie it to the company’s AI-enabled CORTEX mission management software.
The Multi-Canister Launcher holds up to eight HERO 120 loitering munitions and is designed for remote operation, according to the company’s Oct. 13 announcement. Uvision says it can be fielded in mobile, fixed and containerized configurations, and that CORTEX, which the company describes as an AI-enabled battle intelligence and mission management system, links the launcher with sensors and decision-makers in what it calls a sensor-to-effect network.
Loitering munitions, often called kamikaze drones, can circle over an area while an operator searches for a target and then dive onto it with a warhead. The HERO 120 is a mid-range design aimed at armored vehicles and other high-value targets, combining reconnaissance and strike in one airframe with a built-in camera that lets the operator abort an attack and re-engage.
Uvision singled out border defense as one use for the multi-canister setup, with launch nodes spread across long stretches of border in mobile and fixed positions and connected through CORTEX to surveillance assets, so that a threat spotted in one sector can be answered from the nearest launcher. The company did not name any customer that has ordered the launcher or say whether it is being offered to the U.S. Army.
At the same show, Uvision is demonstrating Wayland Autonomy’s IRIS airborne surveillance payload running with Tactical CORTEX, a version of the software for forward units. The company says the pairing adds wide-area surveillance and onboard target generation, including in areas where GPS signals are jammed or unavailable.
“It’s not just about having more effects in the field. It’s about having them where you need them, when you need them, and giving forces the flexibility to use the right capability for the mission,” said Dr. Ran Gozali, CEO of Uvision.
The HERO 120 already has a foothold in the U.S. Army, and in October 2025 the service awarded Mistral Inc. and Uvision a multi-year contract worth up to $982 million under the Lethal Unmanned Systems program to buy, field, train on and sustain the weapon, with Mistral as prime contractor and Uvision as design authority. Production systems passed their first lot acceptance tests in August 2026, and the companies then received an additional order worth more than $50 million to increase the number of HERO 120 systems and support equipment going to soldiers.
The smaller HERO 90 supports the U.S. Army’s Low Altitude Stalking and Strike Ordnance effort, known as LASSO, which tests soldier-portable, tube-launched loitering munitions for infantry units. The U.S. Marine Corps fitted HERO 120 munitions on one of its Long-Range Unmanned Surface Vessels in 2023, an early example of the maritime launch role Uvision now advertises for the multi-canister launcher.
Beyond the HERO line, Uvision markets the VIPER encapsulated multi-mission systems and the PEREGRINE tactical kinetic systems, and says CORTEX is meant to manage effectors across all three families.

Ghalenoei targets improved Iran performance at AFC Asian Cup 2027
Unknown

Ghalenoei targets improved Iran performance at AFC Asian Cup 2027
TEHRAN - Iran head coach Amir Ghalenoei has expressed confidence that Team Melli will deliver a stronger performance at the 2027 AFC Asian Cup, insisting that the national team are determined to improve on its showing at the previous edition in Qatar.
Iran have been drawn in Group C alongside China, Syria and Kyrgyzstan for the continental tournament, where they will aim to challenge for the title and bring joy to millions of supporters.
At the previous Asian Cup, held in Qatar, Iran reached the semi-finals but suffered a defeat against the host nation, missing out on a place in the final. Ghalenoei believes the experience gained from that campaign will help his players approach the next tournament with greater determination and improved quality.
“The national team will prepare for the Asian Cup with extra determination, and our performance in the tournament will be better than at the previous Asian Cup and the World Cup,” Ghalenoei said.

US dollar’s rally pauses as markets brace for inflation report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:52:53 UTC
20:52:53 KST

Ali Canberk Ozbugutu, Burhan Sansarlioglu, and Emir Yildirim
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The US Dollar Index paused its upward rally and traded flat on Wednesday, ahead of the key US inflation data expected to shape the Federal Reserve’s future policy roadmap.
The US dollar closed Tuesday after a 0.4% decline to 102.2, while retreating slightly from a recent peak of 102.6 that was its highest since April 2025.
The index stood relatively flat at 102.2 as of 1100GMT, as currency markets are bracing for the inflation report.
The US headline inflation is expected to rise 3.4% on an annual basis to a range between 3.6-3.7%, while core consumer inflation is expected to rise from 2.4% to 2.5%.
The Fed’s hawkish expectations could rise with higher-than-expected inflation, while money markets expect the bank to maintain rates this month with an 80% probability and to hike rates in December with a 92% likelihood.
New York Fed President John Williams’ remarks cooled the dollar’s immediate momentum after he said further tightening after a singular rate hike this year will likely be unwarranted, noting that the disinflationary factors remain and that the US inflation will decline next year.
The US dollar is expected to sustain its broader dominance over other currencies due to deep structural weaknesses and political turmoil pressuring the euro, analysts say.
Jane Foley, senior foreign exchange strategist at Rabobank, told Anadolu that the US’ strong economic growth allowed markets to overlook the country’s fiscal deficit but similar fiscal indiscipline is currently pressuring the euro.
“The same is not true for France — in both late 2024 and 2025, tough budget negotiations in France led to government instability and an underperformance of French government debt. By the end of last year, the 10-year Oat-Bund yield spread was trading at levels significantly wider than those in early 2024, before President Macron called a snap election,” she said.
Foley stated that the European economy showed some resilience but other factors continue to weaken the currency.
“Factors such as the region’s energy importer status, concerns about hybrid Russian warfare and political worries concerning growing far-right support in both Germany and France are likely undermining the EUR,” she said.
“These worries are reflecting kindly on the USD, given its safe haven status. We expect the dollar index to remain well supported in the coming months,” she added.
Kit Juckes, head of foreign exchange strategy at Societe Generale, told Anadolu that the Middle East conflict beginning in late February drove the US dollar’s rise from its lowest levels since 2022.
“The US is a major energy producer now and higher oil prices, as well increased global uncertainty, are dollar supportive,” he said.
He noted that the developments in artificial intelligence (AI) supported the American economy’s growth than other countries, which was evident when growth forecasts for the US were upwardly revised in the first quarter.
He mentioned that the reshaping of monetary policy expectations after the Fed’s Jackson Hole summit also supported the dollar, as Fed chair Kevin Warsh emerged “not afraid” to raise rates.
“The shift in market pricing of Fed Funds since then, has taken the dollar to current levels,” he said. “The fourth (factor driving up the US dollar) has been the rise in global bond yields, which has caused concern about the European bond market and underpinned the dollar.”
“Now, the question is, with a peak level of rates at 4.7% priced into the market, whether that will prove excessive — the key to expectations about where rates will peak, will be sensitive to tomorrow’s US CPI data, where the market expects core CPI inflation to rise from 2.4%, and headline inflation to increase from 3.4% to 3.6%. Further near-term dollar strength may be predicated on a higher-than-expected inflation print, or increased strain in global bond markets,” he added.

Thousands of sources about Golden Horde and Kazakh Khanate found in Eastern countries

Addressing the international scientific and practical conference “Historical, cultural, political and economic relations between Kazakhstan and the Eastern countries: History, Present and Development Trends,” he highlighted the importance of studying Kazakhstan’s historical, cultural, and economic ties with Eastern countries.
He emphasized, after gaining its independence, Kazakhstan began establishing diplomatic relations with Western and Eastern countries, creating a need for systematic academic research in both directions. One of the Institute’s key tasks has been to search foreign archives for historical sources related to Kazakhstan and introduce them into scholarly circulation.
He also highlighted studying the history, culture, languages and religions of Eastern countries, as well as their socio-political and economic development, is not just a matter of academic interest; it is an important task linked to our strategic interests.
“During two and a half centuries of the colonial period, we lost part of our historical memory. Eastern sources can help us rediscover information about our forgotten language and civilization,” he said.
The scientist added work at the archives of the Eastern countries helped discover substantial materials shedding light on various periods of Kazakhstan’s history. In particular, the point at issue is thousands of studies and historical sources related to ancient times, the Middle Ages, the Golden Horde and the Kazakh Khanate.
Duken Masimkhanuly said thirty years is a significant milestone. This conference will show the public the achievements Kazakhstan has made over three decades of studying the East, as well as the discoveries and findings that have emerged from this work.
The conference also focuses on Kazakhstan’s political, economic and cultural cooperation with Eastern countries, regional security issues, and interaction within international organizations.
Special attention is being paid to the historical significance of the Great Silk Road, the religious landscape of Central Asia, and integration processes among Turkic-speaking states.
A presentation of the photo album book Ordaly otyz jyl dated to the 30th anniversary of the Suleimenov Institute of Oriental Studies and a collection of conference papers will be held as part of the conference.
Besides, an exhibition of scientific publications has also been organized.
It should be noted, a Kazakh-language edition of French historian Marie Favereau’s book Altyn Orda. Dala imperiasy älemdı qalai özgerttı (Golden Horde. How the steppe empire changed the world) was presented in Almaty.

She is stepping away from her role as an observer to make herself "useful" to her country, denouncing a France mired in "chaos", amid a debt crisis, "tragic" unrest in secondary schools and a "total lack of prospects."
The list of candidates for the 2027 French presidential election continues to grow.
Speaking on France Inter radio on Wednesday, Natacha Polony, a 51-year-old journalist and essayist, announced that she would run for president, saying she wanted to "shake up the political landscape."
'The situation leaves me no choice'
Former editor-in-chief of Marianne magazine, Polony denounced what she describes as France's "complete loss of standing".
She advocates economic, energy and food sovereignty and calls for a reindustrialisation policy to "revive economic activity" and "bring money into the state's coffers."
In a video posted on her social media accounts shortly after her radio appearance, the newly announced candidate outlined her vision of a more sovereign France.
"A nation that no longer produces what it needs is no longer truly free to fund our schools and hospitals, preserve our social model, create skilled jobs and prepare for artificial intelligence," Polony said.
"We must produce...We must produce at home, on our own terms," she insisted.
A decision months in the making
At the end of August she launched her movement "Nous sommes la France" aimed at "all those orphaned by politics", saying she wanted to bring together "those who no longer feel represented by the current political options."
Speaking on France Inter, Natacha Polony claimed that her movement had 60,000 members who wanted to "fight against France's decline".
Often described as a "sovereigntist", she rejects the label, calling it the system's "favourite anathema".
In late September, during a heated televised debate with French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, Polony accused him of seeing France as a "small country".
In her view, under Emmanuel Macron, Paris "fantasises" about European unity and seeks "at all costs" to be "Europe's star pupil", even if that means sacrificing the country's "vital" interests.
She points in particular to the cancellation of the Franco-German fighter jet project, as well as decisions she considers detrimental to French interests regarding European preference in the defence sector, while Germany continues to favour purchasing American weapons systems.
Crowded field of candidates
Besides Natacha Polony, nearly 30 public figures have already announced their candidacy or are being tipped to run in the 2027 presidential race.
Among the main contenders are Marine Le Pen of the National Rally (RN), Jean-Luc Mélenchon, leader of La France insoumise, and former prime ministers Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal.
On the centre-left, Raphael Glucksmann, who won the first round of the social-democratic primary, hopes to position himself as an alternative to Jean-Luc Mélenchon's radical left.
Meanwhile, former Socialist president François Hollande, Dominique de Villepin, a former prime minister under Jacques Chirac, and Bruno Le Maire, who served as economy minister from 2017 to 2024, have yet to reveal whether they intend to run.
The list remains provisional: to officially stand in the first round of the presidential election, scheduled for 18 April 2027, candidates must secure at least 500 sponsorships from elected officials.

French navy chief sees no threat to US catapult supply for future carrier
PARIS, Oct 14 - The US has not yet decided whether to abandon the electromagnetic launch system for aircraft carriers, France's navy chief said on Wednesday, two months after President Donald Trump ordered the US Navy to drop the technology that France has chosen for its next carrier.
Trump ordered the Navy in August to revert to the older steam-powered catapults, calling the electromagnetic system unreliable. The move raised doubts over the future supply of the technology, which is used for launching jet fighters from the ships.
"The American decision has not yet been taken," Admiral Christophe Cluzel, chief of France’s naval staff, told a parliamentary hearing. "I do not see our contract threatened."
The US Embassy in France did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The situation highlights France's reliance on US technology for the vital component of its next-generation aircraft carrier, the France Libre, due to replace the ageing Charles de Gaulle around 2038. European dependence on US defence technology has come under growing scrutiny as the continent seeks greater strategic autonomy.
Cluzel added that he had a meeting scheduled with his American counterpart next week, and that he thought the topic would be discussed.
The Admiral was answering a question from a member of parliament about the dependency of the French aircraft carrier, a key part of its nuclear deterrence, on an American technology, and the possibility that it could be left without supply if the US turned to steam catapults.
"It’s a dependency that within the framework of the programme was accepted and considered to be under control", the navy chief said. He added that France would buy a substantial stock of spare parts from the beginning of the programme. Naval Group is leading the construction of the carrier.
However, Cluzel also said that a study was planned to examine France’s capacity to design such catapults, its potential costs and delivery times, with conclusions expected in 2028.
"I think we would be able to do it, but on timelines that go far beyond the service-entry horizon of the France Libre, and at a unit cost that would obviously be considerably higher", he said. REUTERS

EXPLAINER - Why is a 1988 privacy law before the US Supreme Court?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:49:55 UTC
20:49:55 KST

- US Supreme Court is set to hear arguments in a case on whether subscribers to non-video services qualify for protection under a 1988 federal video privacy law
-  Dispute arose after a sports newsletter subscriber accused Paramount of sharing his video-viewing history with Facebook through an online tracking tool
-  Expected later this year, a ruling could determine who can sue over the sharing of viewing data, with implications for digital publishers, streaming platforms and targeted advertising
The US Supreme Court will hear arguments on Wednesday in a case that could determine how far a nearly 40-year-old federal privacy law extends to users of modern websites, streaming platforms and other digital services.
The case, Salazar v. Paramount Global, centers on the Video Privacy Protection Act (VPPA), a 1988 law originally designed to prevent video rental stores from disclosing customers’ viewing histories.
At issue is whether people who subscribe to a company’s non-video services, such as email newsletters, are protected when that company shares information about the videos they watch online.
The outcome could affect how media and technology companies collect and share viewing data, potentially exposing them to lawsuits over practices commonly used in targeted advertising. 
What is the case about?
The dispute began in 2022 when Michael Salazar filed a proposed class-action lawsuit against Paramount Global, the owner of 247Sports, a website covering US college sports and recruitment.
Salazar subscribed to a free newsletter from the website and watched videos while logged into his Facebook account.
He alleged that Paramount used a tracking tool known as the Facebook Pixel to send information about his viewing activity to the US social media platform without his consent.
The information allegedly included the titles and web addresses of videos he watched, along with his Facebook identification number, which could be used to identify him.
Pixel is a small piece of computer code that websites can install to collect information about visitors’ activities and share it with advertising platforms.
Such tools are widely used to measure advertising performance, track user behavior, and deliver targeted advertisements.
Salazar argued that disclosing his viewing history violated the VPPA, which restricts video providers from sharing personally identifiable information about their customers without consent.
Paramount disputed his interpretation of the law, arguing that subscribing to a sports newsletter did not make him a protected consumer of audiovisual services.
A federal district court in Tennessee dismissed his lawsuit, and the US Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit upheld that ruling in April 2025.
The appeals court concluded that the law protects people who rent, purchase or subscribe to audiovisual products or services, not everyone who subscribes to an unrelated offering from a company that also provides videos.
Federal appeals courts in New York and Chicago had previously adopted broader interpretations of the law in separate cases, creating a legal disagreement that prompted the Supreme Court to intervene. 
Why does a 1988 law matter today?
Congress enacted the VPPA after the video rental history of Robert Bork, a Supreme Court nominee, was obtained and publicized during his controversial 1987 confirmation process.
The episode raised concerns that viewing records could expose sensitive information about people’s political beliefs, religious interests and personal lives.
The resulting law prohibited video providers from knowingly disclosing information identifying customers and the specific videos they requested or obtained, subject to certain exceptions.
It also allowed individuals to sue over violations and seek damages of at least $2,500, along with potential punitive damages and legal costs.
Although Congress amended the law in 2013 to update consent requirements for electronic services, much of its original language remains unchanged.
The statute still refers to “video tape service providers,” even as video consumption has shifted from physical rental stores to websites, streaming platforms and mobile applications.
That shift has created disputes over whether modern online users qualify for protections originally written for people renting or purchasing videotapes. 
What are the competing arguments?
Salazar argues that the law’s definition of a consumer includes anyone subscribing to goods or services from a video provider, regardless of whether the subscription itself involves videos.
His lawyers maintain that Congress could have explicitly limited the definition to audiovisual services but did not do so.
Paramount argues that the law must be read in its original context, which was to protect customers engaged in video-related transactions.
Under its interpretation, subscribing to an unrelated service does not establish the customer relationship necessary to bring a privacy claim.
The case has attracted attention from privacy advocates and major technology and media organizations.
The Electronic Privacy Information Center and other privacy experts support Salazar’s broader interpretation, warning that a narrower definition could leave users’ viewing histories vulnerable when companies bundle video content with newsletters and other digital services.
Meta Platforms, which owns Facebook, and several media and business organizations have filed briefs supporting Paramount.
Industry groups argue that expanding the law could expose websites to substantial financial liability and undermine advertising-supported business models.
News organizations have also warned that a broader interpretation could discourage the use of free video content or force changes to digital advertising and analytics practices. 
What could the Supreme Court decide?
A ruling favoring Salazar could allow more website users to bring lawsuits over disclosures of their viewing histories, even when their subscriptions are not specifically for video content.
A ruling favoring Paramount would reinforce a narrower interpretation, limiting protection to consumers who have a qualifying relationship involving audiovisual goods or services.
However, the case does not directly ask the justices to decide whether tracking tools themselves are unlawful or whether Paramount ultimately violated the VPPA.
Those questions involve separate legal requirements, including whether the information disclosed identifies viewers and their video activity.
The Supreme Court’s decision could nevertheless establish an important boundary for privacy protections in an online environment where written content, video, advertising and data collection are increasingly interconnected.
A ruling is expected before the court’s current term concludes in 2027.

20:46:23 KST

The job does not give the holder age-old perks such as the right to drive sheep across the great structure, but the title “bridge master” does have a certain ring to it.
“I don’t tend to say I’m the bridge master when I’m at a party,” said Tristan Ralph, the current holder of the title. “But people do seem to know and bring it up. It’s a job less ordinary, isn’t it? It’s a Victorian sounding title and people are really, really interested.”
There is, however, nothing ceremonial about the title. Ralph is in charge of maintaining and running the Clifton Suspension Bridge, a UK feat of engineering, without any public money.
“It does feel a big responsibility,” said Ralph. “When the chairman of the trustees rang to say we’d like you to do it, you suddenly feel the pressure. It’s so famous and people in Bristol, quite rightly, are proud and almost possessive of it. Bristolians think: ‘It’s our bridge.’”
The bridge master – and the not-for-profit charity the Clifton Suspension Bridge Trust – have the task of maintaining the bridge “in perpetuity”. “I’m a temporary custodian,” Ralph said. “When I’m finished, I have to make sure it is handed on in just [as] good a condition or better than I inherited it.”
Ralph, a bridge engineer by profession, was speaking to mark the conclusion of a large refurbishment project that has taken two and a half years and involved hand-painting more than 4,000 original iron chain links and installing an energy-efficient lighting system. It has cost about £7.5m. “It’s been a big job,” he said. “But it’s come pretty much bang on budget, which is rare these days.”
That is important because, to many visitors’ surprise, the bridge does not receive public funding. “The upkeep of the bridge, the running of it, the salary costs and everything are all paid only by our toll money,” said Ralph. “People think that we might get something from local or central government. But, no, it’s just the toll money.”
Motorised vehicles – including motorcycles – pay £1 to cross the bridge. There is no charge for pedestrians, cyclists or horse riders. As well as being a beautiful structure, it is also a vital part of Bristol and North Somerset’s transport system.
Ralph said: “It draws the tourists in. We get visitors from hundreds of countries every year but primarily, it’s still a vital piece of local infrastructure. If the bridge wasn’t here, the difference it would make to Bristol traffic would be incredible. We average over 8,000 vehicles a day still. Maintaining it as a transport link is utterly vital.”
The end of the refurbishment does not mean Ralph can rest on his laurels and spend more time hobnobbing with members of the Bridge Owners Forum.
“In a few years, we’ll need to paint the underside of the bridge. The under-bridge gantry unit itself will be replaced over the coming years. So there’s always something. We need to keep on top of things. It’s like your house or your car. If you just ignore it, don’t do things for a couple of years, they start breaking down.”
As in most walks of life, the climate emergency is a challenge Ralph and the trust are having to face. “We were monitoring the bridge daily in the summer with the very hot weather. And maybe if the bridge was being designed today, there would be a little bit more robustness around wind.”
The prevailing south-west wind is not usually a problem and the bridge rarely has to close but if it blows directly through the Avon Gorge it can be more difficult. “We need to keep an eye at both the magnitude of any wind events but also their frequency,” Ralph said.
The engineer admires the bridge’s designers, including Isambard Kingdom Brunel. “It’s remarkably advanced for its time.”
And there is no sign that its days are numbered, largely because the Victorians did not skimp. Ralph said: “There are three layers of chains. The original Brunel design only had two, but because it went from a timber design to a cast-iron deck, they upped it to three.
“There’s a little bit of comfort in there. Today there might be pressure to say, well, can you keep it to two, but in Victorian times they did like to add a little bit of meat on the bones.
“It doesn’t have a finite life. There’s no end date in our plans. We all just keep it going in the highest standards as we can. It’s in really good condition as long as we keep doing what we need to do, keep our attention on it and don’t let things drift. Forever is a long time but there’s no reason why we have any need to worry at the moment.”

Israel now treats US as ‘declining power’ and war as permanent condition, says former intelligence chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:46:15 UTC
20:46:15 KST

A former head of Israeli military intelligence has said that since 7 October 2023, Israel has been run by an unwritten security doctrine that writes off the US as a declining power, rejects peace as a strategic goal and makes war a permanent feature of national life.
Major General (res.) Tamir Hayman, who now heads Tel Aviv’s Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), sets out the doctrine in a paper the think tank published this week.
Hayman says the new concept has never been written down or presented to the public. Even so, it now “inform[s] decision-making and dictate[s] Israel’s approach to security”. He argues the shift goes beyond military planning and points to “a change in Israel’s national identity”.
The most striking principle is the doctrine’s view of Washington. Hayman says it treats the US as a “declining power” and holds that “excessive adherence to restrictions imposed on Israel by a US administration is dangerous”.
Under this thinking, the US, “given its ongoing social and political shifts, will soon abandon Israel in any event”. Dependence on Washington is also seen as exposing Israel “to the influence of a progressive American value system that is incompatible with Israel’s Jewish character”. Cutting ties with the US is therefore “not only inevitable, but essential to Israel’s independence and the resilience of its Jewish national identity”.
Hayman rejects that view. He points out that Israel is a small country with few natural resources and depends heavily on trade with the rest of the world. For that reason, he says, the country’s security chiefs have always believed it needs a major power on its side, because Israel “cannot sustain an autarkic defence economy isolated from the world”. In other words, Israel is incapable of producing everything it needs for its own defence.
Hayman questions whether a relationship with Washington based only on mutual interest would be enough to protect Israel. He also asks whether cutting Israeli science and arms industries off from international partnerships, such as the EU’s Horizon research programme, would leave Israel facing “technological stagnation and diplomatic isolation”.
Throughout the Gaza genocide, Israel has relied on American weapons and on US diplomatic protection at the UN.
READ: Axios: Netanyahu discussed joint strike on Iran with Trump before Israeli election
Hayman identifies four other major principles behind the new doctrine. Taken together, they describe a state that puts ethnic identity before democracy, sees peace as a trap and treats war as normal.
The first is that Israel’s Jewish identity comes before its democracy. Under the doctrine, the state must stay Jewish “even at the cost of eroding its democratic values”. Hayman asks whether Israel can still call itself “Jewish and democratic” if it pursues a policy of curbing the civil rights of its Palestinian citizens, who make up about a fifth of the population.
The second principle rejects peace altogether. The doctrine holds that “a meaningful peace agreement is unattainable in the Middle East” and assumes that “any arrangement with Arab actors is temporary and deceptive”.
The doctrine treats peace deals as “merely technical and temporary arrangements”. Peace has no value of its own and is only “a means of achieving other policy objectives”. Peace itself is dismissed as “a naive concept” belonging to the left-wing “peace camp”, and set against “security”, which belongs to the right.
The third is contempt for Israel’s Arab neighbours as states. The doctrine views most of them as “not genuine nation-states, but collections of tribes and ethnic groups lacking a shared history”. It therefore sees their collapse as “a natural process” that Israel can manage and “should even encourage”.
The fourth is that war is Israel’s normal condition, not an exception. Preventive war is preferred, and the “constant presence” of war is considered “an asset to national security”. The paper quotes the slogan “Silence is filth” to sum up the view that seeking peace is a sign of weakness.
The doctrine goes further on territory. It calls for “forward defence” zones and civilian settlements in the occupied West Bank and in security zones inside Syria, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip. It rules out a Palestinian state and dismisses the Palestinian national movement as “an inauthentic Western narrative”.
Hayman says the doctrine draws its power from never being stated openly. It works “as an unwritten concept revealed through practice, rather than as a government’s declared policy”. He calls for a public debate on whether it is “a necessary adaptation” to Israel’s security situation or “an expression of a fundamental, unchecked shift in the state’s identity”.

Peacekeeping and dividing: The US intervention in Sudan takes a familiar path
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:41:32 UTC
20:41:32 KST

Peacekeeping and dividing: The US intervention in Sudan takes a familiar path
At the end of September, the US refused to issue a visa to Sudanese Armed Forces leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, just days before his scheduled speech at the UN General Assembly in New York City. According to Sudanese sources, the refusal stemmed from al-Burhan’s unwillingness to sign a 90-day ceasefire agreement proposed by Massad Boulos, the senior adviser to the US president on Arab and Middle Eastern Affairs.
When civil war broke out in Sudan on April 15, 2023, the US refused to support either side of the conflict. Washington officially maintained a neutral stance toward both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), and pushed for a transfer of power to a civilian-led government.
However, US policy has recently become tougher with regard to the SAF and al-Burhan, who also heads the Transitional Sovereignty Council recognized by most countries. Besides denying al-Burhan a visa, Washington is also pushing the UN to expand the existing arms embargo (which currently targets only the Darfur region, largely controlled by the RSF) to encompass all of Sudan.
Visa scandal
The US decision to deny al-Burhan a visa drew sharp criticism from the UN and various international observers. A spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, Stephane Dujarric, said Guterres is “deeply concerned that a visa has reportedly not yet been issued to the President of the Transitional Sovereign Council of Sudan.”
A few days before the planned trip, Sudan’s permanent representative to the UN, al-Harith Idriss al-Harith Muhammad, sent a letter requesting UN intervention to allow al-Burhan to attend the meeting.
The US State Department, however, declined to comment on the visa controversy. Spokesperson Tommy Pigott stated that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces nor the RSF and their leaders represent the legitimate, constitutional government of Sudan.
“The United States and President Trump stand ready to work with anyone who is a serious partner for peace in Sudan,” Pigott added.
In accordance with the 1947 UN Headquarters Agreement, the US is committed to facilitating visa issuance for representatives of UN member states, including political opponents. However, the US has frequently deviated from these obligations in practice. Notably, the Obama administration denied entry to former Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir in 2013, preventing him from attending the UN General Assembly.
Al-Burhan, who was scheduled to speak at the General Assembly on September 24, ultimately canceled his trip to New York City. Instead, the Sudanese delegation was led by the foreign minister.
The Boulos plan
Massad Boulos’ proposal, initially presented in February, consists of five key elements: establishing an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, ensuring access for humanitarian organizations and protecting civilians, establishing a permanent ceasefire, transitioning to a civilian government, and post-war reconstruction.
As part of the American initiative, a nationwide 90-day humanitarian ceasefire is meant to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid and safeguard civilian populations; a coordinating committee will also be created to oversee the implementation of the ceasefire. The plan also calls for establishing a UN mechanism involving the African Union and the League of Arab States in order to monitor a limited withdrawal of troops and deploy international observers.
In July, the Sudanese government expressed doubts regarding the political aspects of this plan but generally supported the humanitarian initiatives. The RSF, on the other hand, agreed to a three-month humanitarian ceasefire but rejected the demand for troop withdrawals from captured territories.
In September, Boulos confirmed that the US continues to collaborate with partners – including the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, and European nations – to achieve a humanitarian ceasefire in Sudan. Nevertheless, both sides remain skeptical: The army fears that a pause would allow the RSF to regroup, while the Rapid Support Forces are reluctant to lose ground in Darfur and Kordofan.
US sanctions and allegations of the use of chemical weapons
In Washington, many view al-Burhan as the more favorable partner compared to his rival, RSF commander Muhammad Hamdan Daglo. However, despite the numerous war crimes committed by the RSF – especially following their takeover of El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur State – Washington has officially maintained an equidistant stance toward both sides and positioned itself as a mediator.
The US has repeatedly imposed sanctions on both the armed forces and the RSF, but the primary focus has been on Sudan’s Armed Forces and General al-Burhan. The first round of sanctions was announced on June 26-27, 2025. At the time, the US State Department declared that the armed forces used chemical or biological weapons (reportedly chlorine) against their own population during clashes with the RSF in 2024. Washington called this a violation of the Chemical Weapons Convention and international law.
The Sudanese government adamantly rejected the accusations, calling them baseless and politically motivated, asserting that Sudan neither produces, stores, nor uses chemical weapons, and expressed willingness to cooperate with the US in a technical investigation of the claims.
The sanctions severely restricted the export of sensitive American goods and technologies to Sudan, and imposed an outright ban on Sudan’s access to loans, guarantees, and any form of financial assistance from the US government.
A second package of sanctions was implemented in June-July 2026, further restricting the government’s access to international financing, banning the export of certain American goods to Sudan, and preventing Sudanese airlines from using US airspace. According to the US State Department spokesperson, these sanctions will remain in effect until Sudan eliminates “all chemical weapons and production facilities under international verification.”
In regard to the RSF, the US has applied individual measures. In April, at Washington’s initiative, the UN Security Council imposed sanctions on four RSF leaders, including Muhammad Hamdan Daglo’s brother, citing war crimes and crimes against humanity in El Fasher. Nevertheless, the main economic pressure points are directed against Sudan’s Armed Forces.
Critics argue that while the aim of these sanctions is to penalize violators of international law, they could exacerbate the humanitarian crisis by limiting supplies not only of arms but also of essential goods, as all resources will be diverted toward military operations, leading to the worsening of living conditions.
Does US policy legitimize the divide?
Following the fall of El Fasher – the last stronghold of the army in Darfur – the RSF solidified control over the entire region. In July 2025, they announced the formation of a parallel government in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur State. The presidential council, made up of 15 members, was headed by RSF commander Muhammad Hamdan Daglo himself.
The US has not officially recognized the structure, but is effectively engaging with it as a legitimate political actor, even in the wake of UN sanctions against its members. Washington continues to view the RSF as a potential participant in peace talks; however, this stance inadvertently legitimizes Sudan’s fragmentation by acknowledging the RSF as a parallel political entity with its own administration and agenda. The proposals risk leading to a de facto division of the country, with the Sudanese Army controlling the north, east, and center of the country, and the RSF controlling Darfur and parts of the south.
Russia’s veto
On September 11, 2026, the UN Security Council unanimously voted to extend the existing arms embargo on the Darfur region for another month, a measure initially implemented in 2004 amid the brutal ethnic War in Darfur. However, US efforts to broaden these restrictions to encompass all of Sudan have met with strong opposition from Russia and China. Russian Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN Anna Evstigneeva questioned why the council was being asked to expand the embargo at this particular moment, pointing out that similar concerns were not raised in 2023 when the Rapid Support Forces posed a threat to Khartoum and other major cities.
“The Sudanese government and its armed forces now have an undisputed advantage on the ground and serve as guarantors of state institutions, national unity, and civilian protection,” she said, noting that all available resources are necessary for achieving these goals.
The US argues that the current sanctions framework is outdated and no longer reflects the realities of the ongoing conflict. Russia’s potential veto has effectively blocked a US resolution aimed at extending the embargo to all of Sudan and increasing sanctions pressure on both sides of the conflict.
However, the US is not backing down. On October 8, the UN Security Council extended the arms embargo on Sudan’s Darfur region for another two months, until December 11, unanimously adopting a draft resolution tabled by the US. Once again, the renewal period is as short as possible – essentially a technical rollover. Over the course of these two months, member states will continue negotiations on broader amendments to the sanctions regime. China, Russia, as well as the DR Congo, Somalia, Liberia, and Pakistan, oppose the US initiative, favoring instead a sanctions regime strictly limited to Darfur without expanding its scope.
Campaign in the US media
Just days before the Security Council vote, the US media again started talking about the Sudanese Army’s alleged use of chemical weapons – a key factor influencing the US initiative to broaden the embargo. In early September, The New York Times and Washington Post published findings from a joint investigation based on a supposedly leaked confidential dossier, which included videos, photographs, blueprints, and intercepted communications – totaling around 150 files.
Massad Boulos, while presenting his initiative to the UN Security Council, explicitly cited the use of chemical weapons as one of the justifications for the need to extend the embargo.
Russia and China oppose this proposal, even though there was no formal vote on the US resolution. According to Evstigneeva, Moscow “will not allow even a hint of broadening the restrictions.” China’s representative to the UN, Sun Lei, stated that expanding the embargo could worsen the humanitarian situation and lead to the further fragmentation of Sudan.
The Boulos initiative comes amid an apparent shift in the dynamics of the war in Sudan. The Rapid Support Forces have been affected by a new wave of desertions; meanwhile, the Sudanese Army is ramping up operations in Darfur and the Blue Nile region. It has also achieved significant gains in North Kordofan by capturing several strategic locations in recent months. This offensive ensured the safety of the National Export Highway linking Khartoum (via Omdurman) to El-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, and intensified pressure on RSF supply lines.
The risks of US intervention
Despite its stated peacekeeping intentions, US involvement in Sudanese affairs risks complicating an already challenging situation. Firstly, tying visa issuance to specific ceasefire conditions sets a dangerous precedent for using access to international institutions as leverage.
Secondly, US initiatives effectively reinforce Sudan’s division by recognizing the RSF as a legitimate power alongside the official army. This could drive both sides toward a permanent split rather than fostering compromise within a unified state.
Lastly, expanding sanctions and embargoes without considering local realities may trigger an even greater humanitarian disaster, limiting supplies of not just weapons but also essential goods. History shows that unilateral pressure seldom leads to peace; more often, it prolongs conflict and fuels radicalization. The US policy toward Sudan risks deepening the country’s divisions and extending the conflict, potentially turning Sudan into yet another ‘frozen’ hotspot on the African map.

Russia’s Supreme Court on Wednesday outlawed the Batal Hajji brotherhood, a closed Sufi Muslim order originating from the North Caucasus republic of Ingushetia.
The court granted a request from state prosecutors to designate the order as an “extremist” organization for “providing material support for bandit insurgents of the North Caucasus.”
The Prosecutor General’s Office said Batal Hajji members were linked to numerous attacks on Russian police and military in the North Caucasus and orchestrated the deadly 2009 Nevsky Express train bombing claimed by Chechen rebel leader Doku Umarov.
The prosecutor also said that Batal Hajji affiliates aided the deadly March 2024 attack on the Crocus City Hall concert venue near Moscow and the assassination of Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov the same year by selling weapons and ammunition to the perpetrators.
“More than 100 members of the order have been convicted of the illicit trafficking of means for committing acts of terror. Leaders and members of the community organized illegal channels to supply foreign-made firearms from abroad,” the prosecutor’s office said in a statement published Wednesday.
Russian authorities designated the brotherhood’s so-called “military wing” a “terrorist” organization in 2023.
The Batal Hajji brotherhood was founded in the 19th century by Ingush Sheikh Batal Hajji Belkhoroev, a pupil of the Chechen Muslim mystic Kunta-Hajji (Kunta Kishiev).
Membership in the closed order, which numbers around 20,000 members, is passed down strictly by birthright.
The order’s members held a handful of key government roles and a near monopoly on Ingushetia’s construction industry in the 1990s and early 2000s before a clash with the republic’s new Kremlin-appointed leadership led to their fall from power.
Around 100 of its members allegedly joined the Russian military in 2022 as part of the Batal Hajji Rapid Response Unit, a part of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov's Akhmat military unit within the Russian army, according to the exiled news website Meduza.

Andy Lord appointed Interim Chair of NAD Group Advisory Board

The appointment comes as the NAD Group continues to establish a simpler, more integrated governance model designed to support effective decision-making, clearer accountability and stronger management of performance and risk across the Group.
National Armaments Director Rupert Pearce said of the appointment:
  I am delighted to welcome Andy as Interim Chair of the NAD Group Advisory Board. Andy brings extensive experience both within our organisation, having served as a DE&S Board member and trusted critical friend for eight years, and in leading large, complex organisations.
His insight, challenge and independent perspective will be invaluable as we continue to build the NAD Group into an integrated, mission-focused organisation.
The new Advisory Board’s role is to provide independent support and challenge to the NAD and senior leadership, helping to ensure that the Group is well run and manages its strategy, performance and risks effectively.
On taking up the role, Andy said:
  I am delighted to be appointed the Interim Advisory Board Chair. I have seen first-hand the expertise and commitment that exists across the organisations that now make up the NAD Group, and the vital contribution they make to Defence.
The opportunity now is to build on those strengths, bringing together expertise from across the Group to deliver even greater impact. I look forward to supporting the leadership team as it continues to drive integration, transformation and operational excellence in support of its mission.
The Board provides a strategic, Group-wide perspective, testing whether the organisation is moving in the right direction and identifying where further support, challenge or intervention may be valuable.
These contributions support the NAD Group’s ambition to create a high-support, high-challenge environment, in which leaders are empowered to deliver while remaining accountable for results.
Alongside Andy, the NAD Group’s Non-Executive Members (NEMs) are Robert MacLeod, Tony Meggs, Tracy Sheedy, Carolyn Battersby, Claire Hawkings and Sarah Albon.
NEMs are not part of the NAD Group’s executive management structure. Their value comes from their independence and the breadth of experience they bring.
The Board will be supported by three specialist committees covering nominations and remuneration; audit and risk assurance; and safety and security.

Former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar has filed a NIS 3 million (almost $1 million) defamation lawsuit against Prime Minister Netanyahu, alleging that the premier falsely accused him of knowing in advance about the October 7 attack and deliberately withholding that information.
The lawsuit, filed in the Central-Lod District Court, centers on a post Netanyahu published on X accusing Bar of “failures and crimes” on the night of the Hamas-led massacre.
Bar alleges that the post forms part of a coordinated campaign to shift responsibility for the October 7 failures away from Netanyahu and onto him and the security agencies.
According to the lawsuit, Netanyahu accused Bar of knowingly failing to inform the political leadership, warn IDF troops and local security teams, or evacuate the Nova music festival. Bar calls the allegations a “blood libel” and says the prime minister’s military secretariat received updates in real time that night.
The filing also details warnings Bar says he delivered to Netanyahu throughout 2023 about Hamas’s growing strength, the erosion of Israeli deterrence and the risk of war on multiple fronts. Bar says he issued a “strategic war alert” several months before October 7.
Bar further alleges that Netanyahu disregarded Shin Bet assessments, blocked proposals for offensive operations and the targeted killing of Hamas leaders, and pursued a policy of “quiet at any price,” including allowing Qatari funds to continue flowing into Gaza.
The lawsuit cites a November 7, 2022, meeting at which Bar says he recommended killing Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar. According to the filing, the recommendation was not advanced.
Bar also links the alleged campaign against him to his opposition to using the Shin Bet as a “secret police” force against political protesters. The filing references his previous statement raising security concerns about advisers in the Prime Minister’s Office who were also connected to an influence campaign on behalf of Qatar.
Bar resigned in June 2025 after accepting responsibility for the Shin Bet’s role in the intelligence failure. He has repeatedly called for an independent state commission of inquiry into October 7.
In the lawsuit, Bar asks the court to order the disclosure of relevant documents and meeting records held by Netanyahu. He alleges that the prime minister’s opposition to establishing a state commission of inquiry is intended to keep the facts from the public.
Responding to Bar, Netanyahu accused the former Shin Bet chief of failing to contact him despite seeing warning signs on the night of October 7. He rejected Bar’s claim that he did not have his phone number, saying Bar could have used his “red line” or reached him through the Shin Bet agents assigned to his security detail. “How many lives could we have saved if only you had called in time?” Netanyahu said.

Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi missile launched towards Riyadh

Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi missile launched towards Riyadh
Saudi civil defence says danger passed after it issued two warnings through its national early warning platform.
The Saudi-led coalition says it intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile launched towards Saudi Arabia’s capital, Riyadh, as the Yemeni armed group said it carried out more attacks on the kingdom.
Coalition spokesman Major-General Turki al-Maliki on Wednesday announced the thwarted attack on X, days after two separate strikes hit Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport, killing 14 people and injuring hundreds.
The General Directorate of Saudi Civil Defence also issued two alerts through its national early warning platform, later saying the danger had passed. One alert was for the Al-Kharj governorate in Riyadh province, and the other for the capital.
The Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for supporters of God), issued a statement saying they targeted facilities of Saudi Arabia’s national oil company Aramco in Dhahran, an Aramco refinery in Riyadh, and the capital’s King Khalid international airport.
Overnight, the Saudi Ministry of Energy confirmed that the administrative building belonging to Aramco in Dhahran was hit.
Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi, reporting from the Qatari capital Doha, said any notion that the Saudi-led coalition could contain the conflict to Yemen had been shattered over the last 10 days, which saw the targeting of several sites in Saudi Arabia.
Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid international airport over the weekend killed 14 people and wounded more than 300 others. Houthi attacks have also been reported on other airports, including the Abha international airport, where two people were killed, and on Aramco facilities.
Meanwhile, Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces have launched a counteroffensive in Yemen to retake coastal territory from the Houthis near the Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea, a vital maritime trade chokepoint.
Fighting in Yemen between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces escalated sharply last month, shattering a United Nations-brokered ceasefire that had largely held since 2022.
The Houthis have controlled Yemen’s most populous areas, including the capital Sanaa, since seizing the city in 2014, forcing the internationally recognised government to flee to southern Yemen.
The Muslim World League on Wednesday condemned the continued Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, saying they deliberately target civilians and civilian sites. The league’s secretary-general, Sheikh Mohammad bin Abdulkarim Al-Issa, said their nature confirms “the criminal approach of this terrorist militia in deliberately targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure”.
Meanwhile, Yemen’s Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah television reported that four air strikes hit the Harib district in the country’s Marib governorate. The results of the attacks were not immediately clear.
Nawaf Obaid, a security and intelligence analyst and senior research fellow at King’s College London, told Al Jazeera that while air strikes are intensifying, the “actual ground war hasn’t really begun” for the Saudi-led coalition.
Obaid broke down the phases in which such an operation could unfold, saying the first phase would be “to hit at basically the power and the energy source that’s allowing the Houthis to operate … tanks, armoured vehicles, trucks”.
Phase two would be to look at the “systematic increase of Houthi control in the region, which is critical,” he said.
Phase three would involve a discussion on how “to start taking back these territories that the Houthis have gained since the beginning of the war”.
Obaid said these “multipronged phases” would include “extra-specialised” troops, especially in mountain warfare, because the Houthis are taking the battlefield into difficult terrain.

EU allocates $188.2M to boost defense production under new program

Melike Pala
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The European Commission allocated Wednesday €168.2 million ($188.2 million) to eight projects aimed at boosting Europe's defense production capacity under the European Defense Industry Program.
The projects are expected to mobilize €1.26 billion in industrial investments to accelerate and expand the production of energetic components used in missiles, drones, and ammunition, according to a statement.
The projects, which will become operational from 2027, are expected to reduce manufacturing times by up to 90% and enable annual production of more than 20,000 tons of energetic materials, 3,500 drone and missile propulsion systems, 200,000 loitering munition warheads, and 60 million rounds of ammunition.
The investments will cover 17 production sites across 14 member states and Norway, while also strengthening their protection against growing physical and cyber threats.
The initiative builds on the EU's Act in Support of Ammunition Production, an emergency instrument introduced to address production bottlenecks and increase ammunition manufacturing capacity following the start of the war in Ukraine.

IEA warns diesel prices in Europe could rise as global crunch lasts into 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:37:32 UTC
20:37:32 KST

Europe could face renewed wholesale diesel price rises in the coming weeks, the International Energy Agency warned on Wednesday, as disrupted supplies leave markets tight well into 2027 despite recovering Gulf oil output.
Diesel markets will remain tight well into 2027, and wholesale diesel prices in Europe could rise again in the coming weeks, the International Energy Agency (IEA) warned on Wednesday.
In its monthly report, the Paris-based energy watchdog said recovering Gulf oil supplies had failed to resolve the fuel squeeze, with global output still falling short of consumption.
Supply rose by 2.5 million barrels a day (mb/d) to 102.3 mb/d in September on a Saudi-led jump in Gulf crude exports to more than three-quarters of pre-war levels, but remains slightly below global demand of around 103.5 mb/d, the IEA estimated.
The war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February is far from over.
Iran has choked the Strait of Hormuz, the route for about a fifth of the world’s oil, and recently stepped up attacks on ships there, while Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels are striking Saudi oil sites.
"Renewed attacks in the Gulf leave the recovery fragile," the IEA stated.
On Tuesday, Britain’s maritime security agency UKMTO said projectiles of unknown origin had hit a tanker and a container ship in the strait.
Early on Wednesday, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said a container ship carrying more than 2,500 containers sank south of the strait after hitting a naval mine and catching fire, claiming it took an unauthorised route and warning others of continued dangers in the maritime chokepoint.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose around 1%, spiking above $107 per barrel in early trading on Wednesday, but it later pared gains and is hovering around $106 at the time of writing.
Meanwhile, the US benchmark, West Texas Intermediate, has traded flat at roughly $94.75 per barrel.
Diesel crunch
Diesel prices have retreated from September’s records above $200 a barrel, but benchmarks "remain nearly double the price of crude oil and their pre-crisis levels", the IEA stated.
With Middle Eastern fuel exports below half of their pre-war levels and Russian refineries hit by Ukrainian drones, diesel supplies remain under pressure.
Rising shipping costs could add to that pressure.
"As tensions in the crude freight market have spread to other tanker categories, delivered diesel prices in the dominant gasoil importing markets – Europe, Africa and Latin America – could rise again in the coming weeks," the IEA said.
The IEA said lost diesel stocks were unlikely to be replenished beyond normal seasonal changes before the second half of 2027.
The G7 pledged on 2 October to release up to 100 million barrels of emergency stocks through the IEA, diesel first.
However, an internal document seen by Euronews shows this would cover barrels still owed under March’s 400 million pledge, 326 million of which have been released, rather than add to it.
Diverging demand views
The IEA now expects high prices and weaker growth to cut global oil demand by 2.6 mb/d this year to 102.4 mb/d, slightly more than the 2.5 mb/d drop it forecast last month.
It also trimmed next year’s rebound to 2 mb/d from 2.6 mb/d, meaning 2027 demand would stay 0.6% below 2025 levels instead of edging above them.
On the other hand, OPEC, the oil exporters’ group, is more upbeat.
It lowered its forecast for 2026 demand growth for a sixth month running on Tuesday, to 180,000 barrels a day from 380,000, but raised its 2027 estimate to 2.55 mb/d from 2.36 mb/d, expecting stocks drained by the war to be rebuilt.
Crude output from OPEC+, which includes Russia, rose by about 900,000 barrels a day to 39.07 mb/d in September, OPEC said.
Seven core members kept November targets unchanged on 4 October, with most pumping below quota due to the war, and will meet again on 1 November. The UAE quit both groups in May.
Unless the conflicts in the region are resolved, "oil markets may experience more turmoil in the months ahead before any eventual surplus emerges in 2027", the IEA warned as its board meets on Thursday.

Behind the scenes in Europe, plans to push out Starlink are being discussed - media
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:37:06 EEST
20:37:06 KST

Behind the scenes in Europe, plans to push out Starlink are being discussed - media
Kyiv • UNN
In the EU, there are calls for leading European players to create a new “alliance” to strengthen collective satellite capabilities. The EU is considering preferences in frequency allocation.
European players are joining forces to curb the dominance of the American giant in the satellite communications industry. Politico reported on how "Europe plans to push Starlink out," writes UNN.
Details
"Taking the stage at the International Space Summit in Paris, French President Emmanuel Macron called on leading European players to create a new 'alliance' to strengthen collective satellite capabilities. The real target of the 'let's unite' message? Elon Musk's Starlink," the publication says.
Macron's speech last month, the publication notes, "was a public endorsement of behind-the-scenes efforts that would see the bloc's major telecommunications companies make an aggressive push for direct-to-device connectivity—mobile signals transmitted directly from satellites to phones."
On Tuesday, communications ministers from EU national governments gathered in Ireland to discuss a legislative proposal that could make it easier for leading European operators to access satellites.
According to the publication, the initiative "envisages Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Vodafone and Telefónica joining forces to secure critical and desirable frequencies that will become available next year, as the European Commission considers a new allocation procedure that would reserve frequencies for European players." The plan, reported by Bloomberg before Macron's September 10 speech, was confirmed by two sources familiar with the negotiations.
"We are looking at this issue," said Mikael Trabbia, a senior executive at French telecommunications group Orange, in an interview, declining to comment further on the plans. "As a leading, innovative telecommunications group, we want to be able to offer this service to our customers. We do not want to have one dominant player."
Vodafone declined to comment, while Deutsche Telekom and Telefónica did not respond to requests for comment.
The future of space, the publication writes, is attracting attention in Europe as geopolitical conflicts increase its strategic importance, while security requirements and technological advances create business opportunities.
Musk has made it clear that Starlink seeks to deepen its dominance in low Earth orbit, where satellites fly close to Earth to provide faster connectivity. The company hopes to obtain these valuable frequencies in order to offer mobile services without having to cooperate with local telecommunications providers.
SpaceX, Starlink's parent company, did not respond to a request for comment, it was reported.
The question of control
As noted, amid the EU's need to reallocate the 2 GHz satellite communications band in 2027, the proposal under discussion envisages a licensing process that would favor European operators.
A group of members of the European Parliament submitted amendments to the European Commission's May proposal aimed at raising the barrier to non-European players' access to strategic radio frequencies.
"Starlink is not sitting idle. Musk's company has stepped up its lobbying in Brussels over the past two years, holding more meetings with the European Commission and lawmakers ahead of policy initiatives that could delay its expansion," the publication notes.
Earlier this year, the American company warned that the EU plan would leave Europeans without reliable direct-to-device connectivity services. "Starlink Broadband and Starlink Mobile [SpaceX subsidiaries focused on consumers] have done more to achieve the European Commission's connectivity objectives than any other satellite operator," the company's four-page submission obtained by the publication says.
It also warned that the plan could create "global interference problems, particularly for emergency services, such as those in Ukraine."
"Starlink may not be trying to make countries dependent on it, but it is trying to make itself indispensable," said Célestine Rabouam, a researcher at the French Institute of Geopolitics (GEODE). "Right now, they are the only ones that can deploy so quickly and adapt so easily."
What was said at the EU meeting
"We must also have our own technological sovereignty when it comes to satellites," EU Perspectives quotes Henna Virkkunen, Executive Vice-President of the European Commission, as saying at a meeting of ministers responsible for telecommunications on Tuesday, October 13.
She wants the Digital Networks Act to simplify the rules and strengthen the European telecommunications market.
Against the backdrop of Europe's desire for reliable satellite communications and faster broadband access, governments, as reported, put forward different priorities: Germany sought reliable satellite services and competition, while the Czech Republic emphasized opportunities for European companies. Finland warned against giving Brussels greater control.
Thomas Jarzombek, Parliamentary State Secretary at Germany's Federal Ministry for Digital Affairs, advocated satellite services that Europe could rely on even under difficult circumstances. He also called for competition between at least two providers, arguing that this would foster innovation.
Asked about allocating frequencies to Starlink, Thomas Jarzombek "pointed to Ukraine as evidence of the dependence that such technology can create," the publication writes. Access to frequencies should be accompanied by obligations to provide a reliable service, particularly at critical moments, he argued. Satellite connections will complement terrestrial networks, not replace them. "They need a partner on the ground," he said.
Opening the roundtable, Ireland's Minister for Communications Patrick O'Donovan emphasized protection against extreme weather, cyberattacks and hybrid threats, including the protection of undersea cables. "Greater security, diversity and redundancy can help reduce strategic vulnerabilities," he said. However, the talks in Limerick were interrupted when chair Patrick O'Donovan was taken to hospital by ambulance.
Ireland, which holds the presidency of the EU Council, wants the discussions to produce a first compromise on the legislation by December, when the EU Telecommunications Council will meet in Brussels, the publication writes.
