The secret to easier exercise as an adult may start in childhood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:36:23 UTC
20:36:23 KST

The secret to easier exercise as an adult may start in childhood
A surprising new study suggests that staying active while growing up could make exercise easier and less exhausting for the rest of your life.
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Penn State
- Summary:
- Exercise during childhood could have a surprising lifelong benefit, potentially making physical activity less exhausting in adulthood. In a study involving guinea fowl, researchers discovered that birds accustomed to carrying weights while growing up could carry those weights as adults without using extra energy, while untrained birds burned 23% more.
- Share:
How much energy your body needs to move as an adult could be influenced by how active you were during childhood. A new study led by researchers at Penn State suggests that physical activity early in life may have lasting effects on movement efficiency. Using birds as a model, the scientists provided the first direct evidence that experiences during development can change how much energy animals expend when moving as adults.
According to Jonas Rubenson, a professor of kinesiology at Penn State, the ability to move efficiently could play an important role in animal evolution. Animals that spend less energy getting around may have more resources available for essential activities such as finding food, hunting, and reproducing. The findings, published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, Biological Sciences, suggest that the energy demands of movement are more adaptable than scientists previously believed.
To investigate, the researchers attached small weights to one leg of young guinea fowl, birds closely related to chickens that walk on two legs like humans. They wanted to determine whether carrying extra weight during development would change how efficiently the birds moved once they matured.
The results revealed a striking difference. Birds that grew up carrying the weights could walk with the added load without expending additional energy. By comparison, birds raised without weights required 23% more energy when the same load was attached to their legs.
"This study showed how limb loading -- the application of mechanical stress on arms or legs, typically through weights or exercise -- during development can help an animal save energy during movement throughout its lifespan," said Rubenson, senior author of the study. "This is one of the first studies to indicate that animals' behaviors and environments in youth can affect how effortful moving is as adults."
Why Childhood Exercise Could Matter for Lifelong Health
Although the experiment involved birds, the findings raise important questions about human physical activity. One widely accepted scientific hypothesis proposes that people tend to avoid movement when it feels physically demanding or requires substantial energy.
If early activity influences movement efficiency in humans as it does in these birds, people who were less active during childhood might need to expend more energy to perform the same movements as adults. That additional effort could make them less inclined to exercise, potentially reinforcing a pattern of inactivity.
Rubenson believes the discovery could have broad implications for public health, particularly as children today are generally less physically active than those in earlier generations.
"Overall, children in the U.S. today are much less active than previous generations," Rubenson said. "This study suggests that more exercise through play and exercise during childhood could make it easier for people to remain or become more active as adults. If people do not need to exert as much energy to move as adults, then exercise -- and all its health benefits -- will be more accessible to them. This could have implications for many aspects of our nation's well-being, from heart health to mental health."
How Researchers Tested the Effects of Early Exercise
The experiment followed 12 guinea fowl from two weeks of age until they reached 16 weeks, when the birds were approaching their full adult size.
Half of the birds wore lead bands on one leg, with each band weighing 4% of the bird's body weight. The remaining six birds developed without any added weight. Apart from this difference, all 12 animals experienced the same living conditions and exercise routines.
When the birds reached nine weeks of age, the researchers began training them to walk on a treadmill.
At 16 weeks, the team assessed their energy expenditure using a flow-through metabolic chamber fitted to the treadmill. This equipment measured the oxygen each bird consumed, along with the carbon dioxide and water vapor it released. According to the researchers, this approach is considered the gold standard for determining how much energy an animal uses during a particular activity.
Each bird was tested under three conditions: standing still, walking on the treadmill without added weight, and walking while wearing a weight band on one leg. By comparing oxygen consumption and carbon dioxide production across these conditions, the scientists could determine how the additional load affected energy use.
Early Training Produced a Surprising Energy-Saving Effect
The researchers found no differences in energy consumption when the birds were standing still. However, their responses changed considerably once they began walking with weights.
Birds that had not carried weights while growing up experienced a 23% increase in energy expenditure when walking with the added load compared with walking without it.
The birds that had worn weights throughout development showed a remarkably different response. Their bodies had adapted so effectively that walking with the extra load required slightly less energy than walking without it. This unexpected result surprised the research team.
"The birds became so efficient that they were not using any more energy to carry the weight than they needed to walk without the weight," Rubenson said.
Another unexpected finding emerged when the researchers compared the two groups. On average, birds accustomed to carrying weights throughout development used no more energy while walking with their bands than ordinary birds used when walking without any added weight.
Together, these observations suggest that experiences early in life can substantially influence how efficiently animals move as adults.
"This shows that animals -- and this probably includes humans -- can become more efficient based on their life experiences. So, when humans exercise regularly throughout our childhood and adolescence, it could build our capacity for exercise throughout our lives."
The findings provide new evidence that physical activity during development can have lasting effects on the energy required for movement. Whether the same adaptations occur in humans remains to be established, but the research suggests a potential mechanism through which childhood exercise could help support physical activity later in life.
Research Team and Funding
Stephen Piazza, a professor of kinesiology at Penn State, also participated in the research, along with several current and former graduate students working with Piazza and Rubenson.
The study's two co-first authors were Talayah Johnson and Kavya Katugam-Dechene. Johnson completed her master's degree at Penn State and is now pursuing a doctorate at the University of Pennsylvania. Katugam-Dechene received her doctorate from Penn State and currently serves as a research assistant professor of biomedical and rehabilitation engineering at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.
Other contributors included Ian Dechene, who worked as research staff on the project and is now a software engineer, and Roberto Castro, a Penn State doctoral student jointly advised by Piazza and Rubenson.
Funding was provided by the National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases, part of the National Institutes of Health, through awards R21AR071588 and R01AR080711. The researchers are solely responsible for the study's content, which does not necessarily reflect the official positions of the National Institutes of Health.

Journal Reference:
- Talayah A. Johnson, Kavya Katugam-Dechene, Ian Dechene, Roberto Castro Jr., Stephen J. Piazza, Jonas Rubenson. Chronic limb loading results in remarkable load carriage economy in growing fowl. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences, 2026; 293 (2074) DOI: 10.1098/rspb.2026.0199

British troops training to ‘recapture’ Falklands – Times
Unknown

British troops training to ‘recapture’ Falklands – Times
British troops have practiced retaking the disputed Falkland Islands in the event of another Argentine attempt to take over the territory, The Times has reported.
The exercise comes as tensions rise between Britain and Argentina over a British-Israeli oil project near the islands, known in Argentina as the Malvinas. Buenos Aires claims sovereignty over the territory and surrounding waters.
The drills, held from September 27 to October 2, included amphibious landings for the first time in years, according to the newspaper. During the exercise, Argentina announced international arbitration proceedings against Britain in an effort to block the $2.2 billion oil project.
British forces regularly hold exercises with local troops on the islands. The latest Cape Upholder drills involved around 150 British paratroopers from the 2nd Battalion, Parachute Regiment (2 PARA), and 100 members of the Falkland Islands Defense Force.
The exercise took place in several locations on East Falkland, including near San Carlos where British troops landed during the 1982 war with Argentina. According to The Times, the drills included amphibious operations to retake the islands, rather than the usual focus on defending them.
Argentine President Javier Milei, an ally of US President Donald Trump, has renewed his country’s claim to the islands and opposed the Sea Lion oil project. British firm Rockhopper and Israeli company Navitas plan to begin oil production about 220 km (137 miles) north of the islands in early 2028.
Britain has also urged Interpol to reject Argentine requests to arrest people involved in the Sea Lion project, including British nationals, The Guardian reported. London argues that the requests are politically motivated.
In early September, Milei announced plans to revive a naval base project in Ushuaia, southern Argentina. He called British plans to extract oil claimed by Argentina a threat to its sovereignty and reaffirmed Buenos Aires’ goal of regaining control over the Falklands.
Trump has also questioned whether Britain retains the military capabilities it had under Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher during the 1982 Falklands War, while declining to give a clear commitment of US support in the event of another conflict.
“You went there and you just took it back very quickly,” Trump said in a September interview with GB News. “I just don’t know if you have the capacity to do it.”
The Times quoted the commanding officer of the 2 PARA contingent as saying the exercise “gave us the opportunity to walk in the footsteps of our forefathers” while also exploring “how the cyber and space domains could affect missions like this in the modern era.”
The islands had no permanent indigenous population before European settlement. France, Britain, Spain, and Argentina subsequently established settlements or asserted authority over the archipelago before Britain took control in 1833.
The Russian government supports neither side’s territorial claim, advocates for peaceful resolution of the dispute, and opposes possible militarization of the South Atlantic.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP: Speech at the 2026 LGBTQ+ Defence Awards.
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:35:49 BST

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP: Speech at the 2026 LGBTQ+ Defence Awards.
Transcript of the speech given by Defence Secretary, Wes Streeting MP, at the 2026 LGBTQ+ Defence Awards.
Tonight we stand on the shoulders of giants.
In defiance of those who do not accept who we are, or who we love, or how we present ourselves to the world.
In defence of the values of freedom, equality, and democracy – the things that make this country great.
In celebration of our LGBTQ+ community in all of its diversity – and particularly this evening those of you whose stars have shone most brightly and whom we all look to as role models.
We are able be here this evening because of Jeanette Smith and Graeme Grady, and Duncan Lustig-Prean and John Beckett.
Jeanette and Graeme, dismissed from the Royal Air Force in 1994 after being outed as lesbian and gay.
Duncan and John discharged from the Royal Navy in 1995 and 1993 respectively for the same reason.
All of them removed in accordance with the policy of the department I now lead, the Ministry of Defence – a policy that was deemed unlawful thanks to the cases brought to the European Court of Human Rights by Jeanette, Graeme, Duncan and John.
They did not fail their country. Their country failed them.
Their courage in bringing those cases changed laws, hearts and minds.
And because of them, there are now more than 2,500 openly LGBTQ+ people serving in our Armed Forces today.
We owe them an enormous debt of gratitude for not only making our Armed Forces more equal but also making them stronger.
But I don’t want to sanitise our history, or the harm that it caused, because it teaches us something about how we meet the challenges we face today.
Take Dawn, who was outed while serving at sea in 1994.
When she was just 20 years old – roughly about the same age I was when I came out – someone – anonymously, obviously – reported her as a lesbian.
She was investigated.
Questioned for hours.
Had her personal belongings and letters taken.
Was removed from her ship.
And told to leave the Royal Navy that she loved and had served with distinction for three years.
Dawn has since received restorative measures, including recognition of her service, a beret, an apology and the Etherton Ribbon.
She says that she now feels ‘validated’ and ‘valued’.
But ultimately, she was denied the career she dreamed of and worked so hard to get into.
And the indignity of the ban is hard to wash away.
To this day, some people who were prepared to fight for their country are still having to fight for the justice they are owed.
And so I know that there is still lots that we – that I – need to do.
I think about the experiences of that generation in the context of trans people serving in our Armed Forces today.
Of our collective responsibility – but also of my personal responsibility – to make sure that they can do so feeling valued, respected, and equal in worth and dignity.
We do not exist in a vacuum in the Ministry of Defence or in our Armed Forces.
As society finds its way on navigating the law and protecting the rights and dignity of trans people, I want to be clear about some fundamental things as we do.
I want trans and non-binary people in our country to be able to live their authentic lives and be themselves.
I want all of them to live with dignity and freedom, independence, and quality of life and respect.
And I especially want them to be able to do that if they choose to wear the uniform.
No one should face persecution, or have to hide who they are, or battle for acceptance whilst serving their country.
We cannot change the past.
But we can confront it honestly – and learn from it.
And, perhaps most importantly, we can make certain that the generations who follow never have to endure what previous generations endured.
So you have my commitment to work with our LGBT networks, Fighting with Pride and the Royal British Legion to make sure that we live up to our responsibilities to our people today and to future generations.
In the space of a single generation, we have gone from a Britain where gay people could be dismissed from the Armed Forces simply for being who they are, to a Britain where a gay man can lead the Ministry of Defence.
But my social media feeds demonstrate on a daily basis that there will always be those who would prefer to cling on to the prejudices of the past.
The prejudice that says that to be gay or lesbian or bisexual or trans or non-binary is to be weak.
We, in this room, and those like us beyond, know all too well how much courage and strength it can take to be your authentic self.
At home.
At school.
At work.
What is weak about those who served their country with extraordinary loyalty, of being prepared to give their lives for that country, even when that same country denied them the dignity of being themselves?
That wasn’t weak. That was strong and courageous.
Courage isn’t simply the absence of fear.
Courage is looking fear in the face and refusing to let it define you.
It is the determination to do what is right, even when doing so comes at a personal cost.
It is standing your ground when others would rather you disappeared.
It is having the confidence to say, in the words of that great political philosopher, Gloria Gaynor: ‘I am what I am. And what I am needs no excuses.’
For generations, LGBTQ+ people in our Armed Forces have demonstrated precisely that courage.
The courage to serve.
The courage to endure injustice.
The courage to challenge prejudice.
And, increasingly, the courage to serve openly and proudly, without apology and without compromise.
Your sexuality does not determine your strength.
Your gender identity does not determine your courage.
And neither has ever diminished your capacity to serve your country with distinction.
Real strength is not about how loudly you speak, how tough you look, or how closely you conform to somebody else’s idea of what a soldier, a sailor, a marine or an aviator should be.
Real strength is found in character. In loyalty. In integrity. In the willingness to stand up for others. In the quiet determination to keep going when everything around you tells you to stop.
I want young LGBTQ+ people in our cadets, and other young people who might be considering serving in our Armed Forces or working in the Defence industry, to know that our country wants their talent, their commitment, and their courage.
I’m glad that that generation has, in this room, role models to look up to.
People who have served with distinction.
People who have made their units stronger, their colleagues prouder, and their country safer.
People whose example reminds us that progress is not simply something we celebrate in speeches.
It is something we create through the lives we lead, the barriers we break, and the example we set for those who follow.
So thank you to the organisers and sponsors for bringing us together tonight.
To our winners – in and out of uniform – congratulations.
To all of our LGBTQ+ service personnel here tonight and throughout our Armed Forces, let me just end by saying:
Thank you for your courage. Thank you for your service.
And thank you for helping our country become a better reflection of the values that those who came before us always stood ready to defend.
Because of you, generations yet to come will never have to ask whether they belong. They will simply know.
Thank you.

EU seeks to raise cash for Ukraine at IMF and G7 meetings, Dombrovskis says
BANGKOK, Oct 14 - Ukraine faces a funding gap for 2027 and the European Union is trying to raise extra cash for the country at the meetings of the International Monetary Fund and G7 finance ministers this week in Bangkok, European Economic Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said.
Ukraine's 2026 funding is already covered, with some €31 billion from the EU waiting for disbursement as soon as Kyiv votes through the agreed reforms.
But despite another €45 billion ($50 billion) already promised from the EU for 2027, Ukraine's needs will be much higher and the EU is scrambling to organise the cash from countries such as Norway, Switzerland, Canada, Japan or Britain.
"This is one of the topics being discussed during the IMF and G7 meetings, where we are seeking to mobilise support from other partners," Dombrovskis told Reuters on the sidelines of the IMF meetings in Bangkok.
"From the beginning, we have emphasised that the European Union aims to cover roughly two-thirds of Ukraine's financing needs, and we would expect other partners to cover the remainder," he said.
To gain time for others to chip in, the EU plans to front-load the disbursement of the €45 billion it has for Ukraine next year, but the issue is complicated by the fact that the EU is still working out how much Ukraine will need next year.
"It is worth noting that there is a gap between what a number of NATO member states have pledged in military support for Ukraine and what has actually been delivered. Narrowing that gap would go a substantial way towards addressing Ukraine's military financing needs," Dombrovskis said.
Dombrovskis singled out Norway as a positive example of substantial help. "Norway has pledged another €9 billion for next year. It provided a similar amount this year, which is a very substantial sum," he said.
Asked if others were helping, but not enough, he said:
"To put it bluntly, yes." REUTERS

Rada passes law implementing international property valuation standards
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:35:33 EEST
20:35:33 KST

The Verkhovna Rada has approved in the final reading the law "On Property Valuation" (bill No. 13435), which provides for a systemic update of legislation on valuation activity and implementation of European and international property valuation standards (IVS and EVS).
The approved law fully replaces the law "On Valuation of Property, Property Rights and Professional Valuation Activity in Ukraine" in force since 2001 and is aimed at fulfilling commitments under the Extended Fund Facility (EFF) program with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and at receiving the European Union's macro-financial assistance, the Ukraine Support Loan. The bill is also an indicator under the Ukraine Facility.
According to an Interfax-Ukraine correspondent, the decision was backed by 272 MPs.
The law abolishes the separate expert monetary valuation of land plots, introducing a single valuation of real estate together with the land plot in line with international rules and the principle of unity of legal fate. In addition, the document clearly defines the main types of value, distinguishes between independent and standardized property valuation, and separately regulates valuation for determining the amount of damage caused by the war.
It also changes the regulatory model and the professional status of market participants. The document introduces an open-ended valuer's qualification certificate, updates flexible conditions for confirming professional development every three years at the specialist's choice, and creates a Unified Register of Valuers of Ukraine. In addition, the law provides for creating a single self-regulatory organization of valuers, introducing a three-tier regulation system involving the State Property Fund and a Qualification and Disciplinary Commission, and sets a simplified procedure for acquiring qualifications for foreign specialists.
At the same time, the law regulates the review of reports, introduces an effective system of disciplinary liability with fines and a procedure for pretrial appeal of disputes through an appeals committee, and extends the requirements of the valuation methodology to forensic experts, introducing disciplinary liability for them for violations of property valuation rules.
The innovations are expected to reduce cases of undervaluation or overvaluation of property, increase tax revenues and cut state budget spending on administering the sector.
As reported, in May parliament sent bill No. 13435 for a repeat first reading.
Although in September 2025 the Rada Committee on Economic Development recommended that parliament adopt the bill as a basis, the document received a number of objections. In particular, the Ministry of Economy and the Ministry of Finance supported the draft only on condition of its substantial revision. The Ministry of Justice pointed to inconsistency of some provisions with procedural legislation and violation of the principle of legal certainty. Objections were also voiced by the State Property Fund, the National Securities and Stock Market Commission (NSSMC) and the Main Scientific and Expert Department of the parliamentary staff.

Robot allegedly used to grope teen girl seized by German police
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

German police seize humanoid robot that allegedly groped teen girl, and phones of young men who had it
Berlin — German police have seized a humanoid robot after it allegedly touched a 16-year-old girl in an indecent manner and made sexually suggestive gestures toward her. Investigators were trying to determine Wednesday whether the robot's actions were deliberately controlled by two young men who apparently livestreamed the incident in the western city of Cologne on social media.
The unusual incident occurred on Oct. 10, shortly before midnight near a fast-food restaurant on a bustling nightlife strip in Cologne, according to a police statement released Monday.
Videos shared online appear to show the teenage girl standing with two friends, aged 17 and 18, when a red-and-gold robot in athletic wear, about 4 feet tall, approaches her from behind. According to police, and as the videos appear to show, the robot touches the 16-year-old's buttocks and repeatedly makes thrusting movements toward her.
The owner of the robot, a 16-year-old male, and his 19-year-old companion are said to have recorded and livestreamed the encounter themselves, while commenting on it live on social media.
Police officers alerted to the incident encountered the two young men nearby shortly after it was reported. At that point, the robot was already in the trunk of a Volkswagen, but the police say they seized both the robot and the two suspects' smartphones as evidence.
German media identified the robot as a commercially available humanoid model that costs around 5,000 euros, or about $5,600.
One of the individuals involved later claimed on TikTok that the robot had accidentally collided with a woman while trying to avoid another passerby. But longer videos circulating online appear to show the robot performing sexually suggestive movements after the contact with the girl.
Investigators are analyzing surveillance video and online recordings to reconstruct the exact sequence of events, the police said. They also hope to determine whether the robot's actions were controlled remotely, whether specific movements were programmed, or whether the machine acted on its own.
The incident raises some unusual legal questions. Under German law, the criminal offense of sexual harassment generally requires direct physical contact between people. Legal experts told the television network RTL that the use of a robot could therefore make it difficult to prosecute the robot's owners under existing harassment laws.
Instead, police are investigating the case on suspicion of a sexually motivated insult. Possible violations involving the unauthorized publication of images may also be examined.
No charges have been filed against either of the two suspects so far.
The case highlights new challenges for law enforcement agencies as increasingly powerful humanoid robots become more accessible to private individuals, bringing new questions about where responsibility lies when machines are used to commit potentially criminal acts.

Tallinn City Archives restore historical goods hoist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:35:00 UTC
20:35:00 KST

Tallinn City Archives restore historical goods hoist
Tallinn's Old Town now boasts a working historic freight hoist.
The historic freight hoist was restored and brought back into working order in the attic of the Tallinn City Archives building on Tolli tänav.
The wheel, which measures 3.4 meters in diameter, is believed to be the only functioning historic hoist in Tallinn. In the Middle Ages, however, almost every building had one.
Juhan Kreem, a researcher at the Tallinn City Archives, said every medieval building needed a hoisting mechanism in its attic because storage areas were located on the second and third floors.
"This particular example is much more recent. The building was in ruins in the 17th century and was not renovated until the 18th century when it was converted into a warehouse for the customs authorities. They needed a hoisting mechanism again, so they began assembling one from various components, the oldest of which may have come from a shipwreck or leftover materials at the harbor," Kreem said.
The freight hoist preserved at the City Archives dates back to the 19th century and has a 34.5-meter-long lifting rope.
During reconstruction work carried out in 2025, access to the historic hoisting mechanism was improved, making it possible to demonstrate how it works to visitors and conduct lifting demonstrations in the future.

Germany’s wholesale inflation hits 8.7% in September, highest since February 2023
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:34:34 UTC
20:34:34 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Germany’s annual wholesale inflation accelerated to 8.7% in September, its highest level since February 2023, as surging energy prices drove up costs, official figures showed Wednesday.
The rate increased from 6.8% in August and 5.3% in July, according to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis). Wholesale prices also rose 1.9% month-on-month.
Destatis attributed the increase to the conflict in Iran and the wider Middle East, which pushed up prices for energy products and intermediate goods, particularly metals.
Mineral oil products were the main driver, with prices surging 48.8% annually and 10.5% from August.
Prices for non-ferrous ores, metals and related semi-finished products climbed 24.9% year-on-year, while grain, unmanufactured tobacco, seeds and animal feeds rose 19.3%.
Chemical products became 16.4% more expensive, while prices for computers and peripheral equipment increased 12.1%.
By contrast, live animal prices fell 15.1% annually. Prices for milk, dairy products, eggs, edible fats and oils declined 9.7%, while meat and meat products dropped 6%.

‘Heartbreaking’ elephants and wily coyotes: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 – in pictures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:32:49 UTC
20:32:49 KST

‘Heartbreaking’ elephants and wily coyotes: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 – in pictures
This year's winners showcase powerful stories from the natural world and the urgent need to protect it.
A poignant photo of a female elephant carrying a deceased calf has won the Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition 2026.
Titled ‘The Aftermath’, it was taken by Italian wildlife photographer Federico Veronesi while he was tracking elephants in Huab River Valley in Namibia.
After noticing an unusual pattern of drag marks in the sand of a dry riverbed, he caught up with a family of elephants, one of whom had the calf wedged between her tusk and trunk.
It isn’t the first time possible displays of grief have been witnessed in elephants, with previous behaviours including vocalisations, guarding the dead, and inspecting and handling bones.
The black-and-white image has been described by Kathy Moran, Chair of the Wildlife Photographer of the Year Jury, as an emotional “gut punch” and “heartbreakingly poignant” proof of the animals’ consciousness.
As well as the Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, a further 19 category winners were selected from a record-breaking 65,403 entries from 121 countries and territories.
Who won Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026?
Oscar Whitfield, who was 14 when he captured his prize-winning photo, took home the main youth award this year for a shot of a dung beetle at work in Zambezi National Park, Zimbabwe.
Though small, these powerful insects play their part in curbing the Earth’s greenhouse gases by breaking up and burying dung, preventing it from producing planet-heating methane. This also helps it decompose faster, reducing the number of pests affecting livestock and wildlife.
There are more than 5,000 species of dung beetle found around the world.
Prize-winning photographers capture urban wildlife
From coyotes roaming the hills of San Francisco to giant lizards hunting in Bangkok, this year’s winning photographs also revealed how animals are adapting to life alongside humans.
In his award-winning portfolio, ‘Wily Coyotes of San Francisco’, US photographer Loren Elliott documents a resident pack living among the city’s more than 800,000 inhabitants.
Around 100 coyotes are thought to live in the city, where attitudes towards the animals are mixed. While they sometimes prey on domestic animals, they also help control populations of disease-carrying rodents. Elliott’s photographs invite viewers to reconsider these often-misunderstood animals and their place in an increasingly urban world.
Another urban encounter by UK photographer Seth Forestson won the Urban Wildlife category.
Capturing a common monitor lizard carrying its prey through Bangkok’s Lumphini Park, Seth lowered himself onto the muddy ground to frame the creature against the city skyline.
Common water monitors have successfully adapted to the Thai capital’s urban environment, taking advantage of readily available food, including catfish and koi in Bangkok’s park lakes.
Underwater encounters reveal what’s hidden in the depths
Human impacts on wildlife are not confined to land. Beneath the surface, photographers are documenting both intimate animal encounters and the growing pressures on marine ecosystems.
Animal Portrait-winner Aaron Sanders had been diving off a Cornish beach when he noticed the footprints of octopus suckers through a thin blade of kelp. As a single eye emerged, “We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity,” he recalls.
The encounter is a glimpse of a wider story brewing in the waters off southwest England, where sightings of common octopuses have increased dramatically. While the carnivorous predators are more commonly found in the Mediterranean, above-average spring sea temperatures have expanded their territory, with devastating impacts on local fishing industries.
In another show of humans’ impact on marine life, US photographer Alex Lindbloom snapped a whale shark investigating the catch of a ‘bagan’, or mobile net-fishing platform, in the inky waters off Papua, Indonesia.
The species has declined sharply over the past 75 years mainly due to ship strikes, fishing gear entanglements and illegal fishing.
A watering hole brings wildlife together
Some of the winning images reveal the unexpected interactions that take place when different species gather in the same habitat.
In ‘The Meeting Place’, UK photographer James Lewin captures a young bull elephant spraying a group of zebras as they congregate around a waterhole in Kenya’s Chyulu Hills. Lewin used an infrared-converted camera to soften the harsh light, giving the scene a dreamlike quality.
Waterholes can become vital lifelines during severe droughts, bringing together animals that might otherwise keep their distance.
Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London. The winning photographs will be on display at the Natural History Museum from 16 October 2026 until July 2027.

Amateur astronomer harnesses AI to find a possible hidden exoplanet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:32:26 UTC
20:32:26 KST

An amateur astronomer harnessed artificial intelligence agents to find a previously undiscovered exoplanet lurking in publicly available data.
Pavel Rabtsevich, a Spain-based product manager and a space science hobbyist, was poring over data collected by NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), an exoplanet-hunting space telescope, when he noticed something odd.
TESS looks for the subtle dimming caused by planets transiting, or passing in front of, their stars. Of the more than 126,000 target stars that Rabtsevich was examining with a custom-built AI algorithm, his machine-learning assistant directed its focus toward one in particular: TIC 4206066. The star was located around 116 light-years away from Earth in the Orion constellation, and the data indicated it dimmed for about two hours every three days.
With his curiosity piqued, Rabtsevich dug through the TESS archives for more data on the same star and found an additional 22 instances of dimming. If the signal were to be confirmed to represent an exoplanet, that world would a super-Earth with a radius around 1.4 times as large as that of our planet. Although such an exoplanet would likely be a rocky world, its three-day orbit of TIC 4206066 would mean it had an estimated surface temperature of 1,000 degrees Fahrenheit (540 degrees Celsius).
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
But stars can dim for many other reasons. In this case, for instance, Rabtsevich noticed the dips in TIC 4206066's light in 2018 tended to align with moments where TESS fired its thrusters, which may have skewed the results. For now, while Rabtsevich hopes this may be a new exoplanet, he acknowledges that all that can be confirmed is a “repeating transitlike signal in open data, with a plausible planetary explanation and alternatives that aren’t yet ruled out.”
“Models agreeing with each other isn’t evidence,” he says. “What I rely on is a signal anyone can measure, calculations anyone can rerun, control samples and rules published before the next [datasets] arrive.”
The search couldn’t have been done without AI, Rabtsevich adds, noting that he used multiple agents and that the models “wrote the code, ran it and checked each other's work.” Even so, he maintains, “the research itself was mine: the question, the plan, the rules, the computing, the decisions on every candidate and what to publish.”
The potential for at least one exoplanet orbiting TIC 4206066 seems “solid,” says astronomer Greg Laughlin of Yale University, who now works in the AI industry. Rabtsevich’s analysis is “a great example of human-AI teamwork,” he adds: large language models such as Claude and Codex have proven effective at combing astronomical literature for overlooked discoveries.
If there is indeed an exoplanet circling TIC 4206066, Rabtsevich may not actually be the first to have seen it. Pablo Mercader Perez, a Ph.D. student at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and a member of the TESS team, says the signal was picked up by a detection filter in 2020 but was ultimately rejected because of a lack of conclusive evidence. Since then TESS has conducted many more observations of that part of the sky.
“Thanks to this, we got much more data than we had before for this particular star system, and the signal became a lot clearer,” Mercader Perez says. In terms of statistical significance, “this planet candidate became effectively detectable only in January of this year.”
A deep-learning model developed by Mercader Perez’s team has also flagged the potential exoplanet, he says.
“Independently but also not public yet, a search performed by [astronomer] Michelle Kunimoto using her software called LEO-Vetter had also selected this planet candidate already back in early 2026, which is another way in which it would almost certainly have been alerted in the official list in the next few months,” Mercader Perez says.
Other amateurs, either acting entirely independent of or taking cues from Rabtsevich's exciting candidate, are now pursuing additional AI-assisted dives into public datasets from TESS and other NASA missions. And some have reported promising early results.
In the meantime, Rabtsevich's calculations have prompted NASA’s TESS team to reexamine the star once the spacecraft’s orbit around the sun brings the target into position in November. He’s also recruited several other astronomers to look at the star and critique his findings, which include a speculative additional exoplanet in a more distant orbit around the star.
Regardless of who might claim the discovery, “it’s exciting that the parent star has been put on TESS’s high-cadence list, which should elevate the confidence in the detection,” Laughlin says. “There’s every reason to expect that this candidate super-Earth will pass further tests and make it into the official census.”

French viewers shocked by Israeli soldiers’ accounts of Gaza in ‘NAZA’ documentary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:31:41 UTC
20:31:41 KST

French viewers who attended screenings of “NAZA,” a documentary exposing Israel’s killing of civilians in Gaza, said they were shocked by Israeli soldiers’ accounts that reduced Palestinian victims to numbers rather than recognizing them as human beings.
Produced by British newspaper The Guardian and directed by Oscar-winning filmmaker Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the documentary was screened in French cinemas on Oct. 12-13.
The film drew considerable interest in Paris on its opening day, with most tickets sold.
French viewers who watched “NAZA” at two cinemas in the capital shared their reactions with Anadolu. 
‘I think the filmmakers are very courageous’
A French viewer, Kenzi, said the documentary explained the meaning of NAZA, a term referring to civilian casualties, and left him deeply shocked.
He said Israeli soldiers repeatedly discussed numbers and calculations, almost all of which represented people killed in Gaza.
“We know what is happening, we talk about it, we see it, but not to this extent. And here, it was really shocking to see Israeli soldiers talking about it. Sometimes you could sense regret, sometimes not so much. They spoke quite coldly. So, it really disturbed me. And, I think it was very well made. It went by very quickly,” he said.
Noting that the soldiers compared their actions in Gaza to a video game, Kenzi said: “They talk about artificial intelligence to identify people to kill. At a certain point, you see that they no longer measure the number of people they are going to kill, the collateral damage, the NAZAs.”
He said the soldiers frequently referred to a “system.”
“It seemed as though they had been brainwashed and made to believe that they were on the right side, until they realized for themselves that what they were doing was vile,” he said.
Kenzi recalled the soldiers repeatedly saying they “just wanted to eliminate the enemy.”
“They clearly said that the enemy was children aged 3 to 6, women who had done nothing to deserve this. Often, they wanted to eliminate an enemy leader, and in the end, they killed his entire family except that person,” he said.
Praising the Israeli directors, he added: “I think the filmmakers are very courageous to have initiated a project like this.” 
‘It affected everyone in the theater’
Iona, a 23-year-old French viewer, said: “I think the film is extremely important. It is extremely important to have this perspective because we often hear testimonies from victims, but here we have testimonies from the attackers, who put the situation into concrete words.”
She said the documentary could help people understand what was happening and stand on the right side of history, adding that the language used and the questions asked deeply affected her.
“He was not afraid to use the word ‘genocide.’ He asked directly whether it was genocide, and they said yes,” she said, referring to the interviewer.
Iona said she found it shocking that the soldiers did not regard the victims as people.
She also highlighted scenes showing people living normally in Tel Aviv while people in Gaza were dying.
“Everything was extremely striking,” she said.
Emphasizing the importance of making such films and allowing everyone to speak, she added: “There was everyone in the theater — young people, older people. You could see that it affected everyone in the theater. There was silence at the end. It was extremely moving.”
She urged people to watch the documentary, ending her remarks with: “Free Palestine.” 
‘Reducing human beings to numbers shocked me the most’
Adam, a 27-year-old French viewer, said the documentary left him speechless throughout.
“I was aware of the history and the political issues behind it, of the massacre and genocide taking place in Palestine,” he said.
But hearing testimony from people within the system was still shocking, he added, saying it gave concrete substance to the atrocities.
“Overall, I think the documentary is very well made and presented, because it raises several questions, particularly about the dehumanization of victims through the term NAZA.
Ultimately, the victims, the ‘collateral damage,’ as they like to call them, become nothing more than numbers. Reducing human beings to numbers was what shocked me the most,” he said.
Adam said the massacre in Palestine did not begin in October 2023 and praised the directors’ courage despite pressure from the Israeli government.
‘An interviewer who recognized the disastrous situation in Gaza’
Another French viewer, Yacine, said the repeated emphasis on numbers was among the documentary’s most striking elements.
“They had an interviewer who appeared objective, who had some distance and recognized the disastrous situation unfolding in Palestine and Gaza,” he said, referring to Abraham.
By contrast, he said, the soldiers interviewed appeared conditioned by war.
“There is a real contrast between the images we saw of Tel Aviv, where people seem safe and appear to lead fairly peaceful daily lives, and the images of Gaza at the end of the film, which embody war and destruction themselves,” he said.
“When you see the images, you get the impression that there is almost no life left. People are surviving.”

Zelensky arrives in UK as London vows to speed up anti-drone missile deliveries for Ukraine
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in the U.K. on Oct. 14 to meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III, as London pledges missiles to help Ukraine counter Russia's jet-powered drones.
The visit comes at a tense moment for Ukraine, with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration pressuring Kyiv to halt strikes against Russian oil refineries and threatening to cut off intelligence sharing and arms shipments.
Ahead of Zelensky's visit, Burnham vowed that the U.K.'s support for Ukraine remains "rock-solid."
The Ukrainian president was first welcomed by King Charles at Buckingham Palace before meeting Burnham.
"I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience. It is important for me to have the opportunity to personally thank him for his unwavering support for Ukraine," Zelensky said on X.
The British prime minister then welcomed Zelensky at 10 Downing Street in the company of a military ceremonial guard, the first such honor granted to a foreign leader, according to the BBC.
The British government has announced an air defense missile package worth 45 million pounds (around $60 million) for Ukraine, as the country faces an intensifying onslaught of Russian missiles and drones.
"The U.K. will accelerate deliveries of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), which have proven extremely effective against jet-powered drones that are being used to strike far beyond the front lines in Ukraine, including Kyiv and beyond," the British government said in a press release on Oct. 13.
Russia has been increasingly deploying jet-powered drones that are faster and more difficult to intercept than older Shahed models, posing a new threat as Ukraine braces for massive strikes against energy infrastructure in winter.
Of the 45-million-pound package, the U.K. will expedite the delivery of 10 million pounds ($13 million) worth of LMMs to meet the most urgent winter needs.
"I’m announcing that we're accelerating the delivery of British-made air defenses for (Ukraine)," Burnham told the press while meeting Zelensky. The British leader also said he would seek to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the U.S.
Burnham's office said earlier that he had instructed his cabinet to prepare additional military and financial assistance packages for Ukraine, as well as fresh sanctions against Russia.
The U.K. further reiterated that it stands by its plans to ban maritime services for Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.
London said last year it would implement the phased ban over 2026 "in lockstep with our European partners."
The EU plans to ban Russian LNG imports by January 2027 but has failed to agree on a full ban on maritime services, with Greece securing a carve-out for Russian LNG exports to non-EU countries.

She Remains a Stranger: Motherhood, memory and the loss of home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:31:09 UTC
20:31:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Rasha Hilwi's She Remains a Stranger: On motherhood, inherited exile and the meaning of home
In the opening pages of her recently published literary memoir Dhalat Gharibeh (She Remains a Stranger), Palestinian author, storyteller and journalist Rasha Hilwi offers a lexicographical meditation on the word ghurba.
"Ever since I crossed those seas, I’ve tried to translate the word ghurba into other languages. I came to the same conclusion as others before me: some things cannot be translated.
Ghurba derives from the root gharaba.
Ghurba (noun). The verbal noun of gharuba.
“His ghurba lasted long”: his separation from his homeland and family lasted a long time.
Ghurba is nawā or being far away.
“He lived for a long time in ghurba”: he lived for a long time in lands of displacement.
“I found him in a state of ghurba”: he was found in loneliness and desolation.
“The loss of loved ones is itself a ghurba”: whoever loses someone dear becomes like a stranger among people, even if they have never left their homeland."
Published in July 2026 by the Berlin-based Arabic bookshop and publisher Khan Al Janub, She Remains a Stranger is an intimate autobiographical narrative about motherhood, Palestine, and what it means to inhabit several forms of ghurba all at once.
For Hilwi, the impulse to write this book was an old one. But it was motherhood, and the estrangement born of it, that ultimately gave form to the story.
"Before motherhood, writing about culture was a major part of my life. Then motherhood came and severed me from that world. This is characteristic of how motherhood functions more generally: It imposes a particular kind of isolation, separating you not only from your former self, but also from the outside world," Hilwi tells The New Arab.
"But more than that, motherhood put me face to face with so much I had left unresolved: my relationship with myself, with places, with my family’s heritage, and that of my ancestors. It forced me to deal with feelings of pain, loss and, above all, ghurba," she adds.
Together with the realisation that she was battling postpartum depression, this confrontation set Hilwi on a journey of healing.
So, in 2022, she returned to her most familiar form of expression: writing.
She began chronicling her life as a new mother of twins in Amsterdam, far from her first home, Palestine, and the coastal city of Akka, where she grew up.
Writing became a way of making sense of it all.
"It shielded me from a heaviness I hadn’t yet realised I was carrying," she asserts.
Hilwi writes of the weight she was carrying, which was never hers alone. It comprised the histories of the women who had moulded her, particularly her mother and grandmother, and all they had passed down to her.
It was an inheritance imbued with both pain and love.
She also writes of the weight of becoming a mother abroad: of her attempts to root her children in a heritage that is geographically remote yet intimately present.
Sometimes, this means something as ordinary as encouraging them to enjoy her familiar spreads of labneh, za’atar and olive oil on their Amsterdam dining table.
At other times, it means insisting they pronounce helwe properly with the Arabic ‘ḥ’ rather than the ‘h’ of a foreign accent.
As Hilwi navigates everyday life, the book's bigger question begins to take shape. What can a mother give her children of a home they have not known as she has?
But just as writing offered Hilwi a way through this question, the devastation unfolding in Gaza rendered the very act of writing meaningless.
For Hilwi, motherhood made the distance between Amsterdam and Gaza unbearable.
She found herself comparing her children’s safety against the reality of Palestinian mothers struggling to keep theirs alive, or "how one child could be playing on an actual slide while another slides down the wall of a destroyed house in Gaza."
Yet, with time, Hilwi realised she could not abandon writing. However modest, it was a contribution she could make, "a small piece in a much larger mosaic through which Palestinians continue to affirm their continued existence, whether in academia, theatre, cinema, literature, or elsewhere."
Making a home from fragments
Hilwi’s She Remains a Stranger contributes to that mosaic, her act of remembering offering some relief from a deepening sense of ghurba.
As she takes the readers with her through the daily rhythms of motherhood in Amsterdam, Hilwi journeys back through memory, revisiting the life she once shared with her family in Palestine, from Haifa, where her grandparents rebuilt their lives after being forcibly displaced from their village of Iqrit in the Upper Galilee in 1948, to Akka, her hometown, where she was born and raised.
As a third-generation Nakba woman, she imagines the life that might have been. She writes of a ghurba that did not begin with her departure from Palestine to Berlin, or her subsequent move to Amsterdam.
It is a ghurba that was already part of her inheritance.
"There is a ghurba that I know: that of Palestinians in their own country, in their own cities, especially those who stayed. I am one of them. I did not witness the Nakba, but I have lived with its direct impact on my grandparents, who became strangers on their own land, constantly reminded by an entire system that they were strangers and refugees in their own country."
But if ghurba can be inherited without ever leaving home, what happens when one does leave? This question also runs through Hilwi’s account of her journey from Akka to Berlin, a city she sought out in search of a life she had been denied.
"I did not go to Berlin for Berlin. I went for Arab Berlin, a city that had taken in so many of our people because of our catastrophes."
There, she found glimpses of the life she might have known in Akka had the Nakba never happened. Surrounded by friends from Beirut and Cairo, she could eat Syrian food, attend an Egyptian show, or listen to Lebanese music.
In Berlin, she found a home assembled from fragments of other homes, brought together by people whose different journeys had directed them to the same city.
"There was still alienation, of course, much of it arising simply from being in a new city, with a new language and a new way of life. Despite all that, Berlin gave me a sense of home. I needed it because I had been denied that in my own hometown. Israel had taken that right from me."
But finding something of home elsewhere did not mean that Hilwi’s ghurba disappeared. When she eventually moved from Berlin to Amsterdam, to be with her husband and raise her family, it followed her, taking on new meanings.
"It was in Amsterdam that motherhood truly put me face to face with all these forms of estrangement: from Palestine, from the experience of creating a life in two new cities; and from the heritage I was carrying."
With time, however, Hilwi came to see that her ghurba was not necessarily something to overcome, but something to understand.
"I don’t think there will ever be a moment when I stop feeling estranged. Ghurba will always accompany me, and perhaps that is important because it gives rise to questions as well as a constant search for meaning."
As it acknowledges the persistence of ghurba, Hilwi’s text is equally concerned with the life that remains possible after rupture, whether after motherhood, displacement or the devastation of genocide.
For Hilwi, this possibility materialised in motherhood, which offered "a sense of home" and, as she writes in the book, became "the vital force that stirs the muscle of imagination."
For her, motherhood was not only another site of estrangement, but a way of imagining life beyond it. And storytelling, in turn, became Hilwi’s way of insisting on that life’s continuation.
"The fact that we are still able to tell the story, that the story continues to be told, is itself an answer to genocide."
A Dutch Translation of She Remains a Stranger, titled Ze blijft een vreemde and translated by Djuke Poppinga, is scheduled for publication in November 2026 by Uitgeverij Jurgen Maas in Amsterdam.
The book excerpt featured at the beginning of this article was translated from Arabic by Nourhan Tewfik.
Nourhan is a London-based arts journalist specialising in the Middle East. She is also an Arabic TV/film consultant and researcher
Follow her on Instagram: @nourhantewfik

Bank of America Fined $1.21B Over AML Failures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:29:00 UTC
20:29:00 KST

Reported by
U.S. authorities imposed more than $1.21 billion in penalties on Bank of America on Tuesday over failures in its anti-money laundering controls and apparent violations of U.S. sanctions, in what the Treasury Department called the third-largest enforcement penalty in its history.
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed a $1.2 billion penalty, saying the bank failed to adequately detect and report financial activity involving priority national-security and illicit-finance risks, including Chinese money-laundering networks and activity along the U.S. southwestern border. Regulators said Bank of America failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, including more than $1 billion linked to such priority risks.
As part of the FinCEN resolution, Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act, including by failing to maintain an adequate anti-money laundering program, conduct required due diligence on correspondent accounts for foreign banks, and file suspicious activity reports. The bank must also use an independent third party to identify and report suspicious activity its systems previously missed.
Separately, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) imposed a $750 million penalty — the largest in the regulator’s history. That amount is credited toward FinCEN’s $1.2 billion penalty rather than added to it. The OCC said the bank’s compliance program remained “deficient and ineffective” despite a 2024 cease-and-desist order and that weaknesses in transaction monitoring caused late suspicious activity reports involving billions of dollars.
The Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) also reached an $11.66 million settlement with the bank over 475 apparent violations of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Myanmar, Somalia, narcotics trafficking and global terrorism. OFAC cited payments involving blocked banks, failures to properly prioritize sanctions alerts and delays in updating watchlists.
Bank of America said it worked with regulators to resolve the cases and was addressing the deficiencies.
“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” a spokesperson said, adding that the bank has invested billions of dollars in technology and assigned thousands of employees to combat financial crime. The bank said its remediation work is well advanced and that it remains committed to completing the measures required by regulators.

Hundreds of generators, mobile boiler houses and backup power plants: Klitschko spoke about how Kyiv will get through the most difficult winter
Kyiv • UNN
Kyiv has prepared nearly 700 generators, 70 mobile boiler houses and three diesel power plants. The capital's hospitals have 480 generators.
Kyiv’s city authorities have prepared hundreds of generators, mobile boiler units, and other backup power sources to ensure the operation of critical infrastructure. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko stated this from the parliamentary rostrum after being invited to the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine on October 14, reports UNN.
Details
The mayor said that throughout the full-scale war, the capital had been increasing the number of backup power sources intended to ensure the operation of critical infrastructure in the event of possible prolonged power outages.
In particular, nearly 700 generators of various capacities and 70 mobile boiler units have been prepared for heat and water supply facilities. In addition, three diesel power plants have already been built in the capital, and a backup water intake has been arranged.
Currently, Kyivvodokanal has 103 generators. At the same time, the utility is awaiting additional high-capacity generator systems being manufactured abroad for Kyiv
According to him, the mayor’s office paid particular attention to providing residential buildings with backup power. Under the city’s energy resilience programs, more than 6,000 pieces of equipment have been purchased for residential buildings, including generators, inverters, and batteries.
Ensuring the provision of hospitals and educational institutions
According to the mayor, all educational institutions in the capital are equipped with generators of various capacities. Among them are 285 high-capacity generators.
In the medical sector, additional capabilities are also being created to enable institutions to operate autonomously in the event of disruptions to centralized electricity, water, and heat supplies. In particular, hospitals in the capital currently have 480 generators
He added that their own wells for water supply had already been installed at 15 medical institutions, while six more are under construction.
In addition, eleven hospitals have autonomous heating supplied by their own boiler houses. By the end of 2026, the city authorities plan to increase the number of such medical institutions to 21
Klitschko emphasized that these measures are aimed at maintaining the operation of vital institutions even if centralized networks are damaged.

Ukraine Cancels Drone Missions as Starlink Restrictions Disrupt Battlefield Communications
Ukrainian forces have been forced to cancel drone missions after new restrictions on SpaceX’s Starlink satellite communications disrupted connections during flight, with some unmanned aircraft losing contact for up to 20 seconds at speeds as low as 110–120 km/h.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to hromadske on October 14, Ukraine’s 7th Air Assault Corps confirmed that its units operating in the Huliaipole sector of the Zaporizhzhia region began experiencing connectivity problems overnight. The disruptions affected Starshield, the military-oriented satellite communications service used to control drones in flight.
Military personnel reported that connections could disappear for 10–20 seconds when drones reached speeds of approximately 110–120 km/h. Although the aircraft continued flying, the interruptions made remote control more difficult and increased the risk of losing them during operations.
The restrictions also create additional risks for Ukrainian drone operators. Reducing flight speeds to maintain connectivity makes unmanned aircraft easier targets for Russian forces, while faster drones may be unable to complete their missions under the new conditions.
The 7th Air Assault Corps warned that the problem is particularly serious for medium-range strike drones, which must accelerate rapidly during launch. Unstable communications at those speeds could prevent certain aircraft from taking off successfully or carrying out their intended missions.
The operational consequences have already emerged. According to the corps, one Ukrainian drone unit operating in the Huliaipole sector was forced to cancel several missions on October 14 because of the connectivity disruptions.
Separately, a source within Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense told hromadske that overnight testing identified restrictions preventing Starshield from functioning at speeds exceeding 160 km/h.
The source said the limitations were complicating military logistics, unmanned systems operations, and medium-range strike missions. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry is investigating what caused the restrictions.
Earlier, sources in Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense told UNITED24 Media that overnight testing had identified new restrictions affecting StarShield terminals moving at speeds above approximately 160 km/h.
The reported restrictions came a day after SpaceX owner Elon Musk publicly supported US President Donald Trump’s criticism of Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries. Musk wrote on X that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had gone too far.

Ukraine Gains Ground Near Sumy as Russian Offensives Fail to Break Through Elsewhere
Ukrainian forces have made a confirmed advance in the Sumy region while disrupting a series of Russian offensive operations across several other sectors of the front, according to the Institute for the Study of War’s (ISW) October 13 assessment.
Geolocated footage published on October 12 shows Ukrainian troops advancing southeast of Yunakivka, northeast of Sumy, confirming recent gains in the area.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
ISW also found no evidence of meaningful Russian progress in several sectors where Moscow continued offensive operations over the previous two days.
In northern Kharkiv region, Russian forces continued attacks on October 12 and 13 without making confirmed gains. Near Kupiansk, Russian troops were also reported to be using Ukrainian civilians as human shields while withdrawing, an action that would violate international humanitarian law.
Russian sources separately claimed attacks southeast of Borova, but ISW found no evidence that those operations resulted in territorial advances.
The same pattern was visible farther south. Russian forces attacked Lyman and areas north of the city toward Kolodiazi, but Ukrainian counterattacks prevented them from consolidating new positions.
Near Chasiv Yar, Russian troops recently attempted to infiltrate Ukrainian positions northwest of the city, while geolocated footage later showed Ukrainian strikes against Russian positions in eastern Klynove.
Russian assaults around Kostiantynivka also failed to produce confirmed gains. Moscow’s forces attacked inside the city, west of it, and southwest of Druzhkivka on October 12 and 13, but ISW recorded no advances. Farther west, Russian troops attempted additional infiltration south of Dobropillia, prompting Ukrainian strikes against positions around Matiashove and Svitlle.
On the Oleksandrivka axis, Russian forces continued offensive operations without confirmed success as Ukrainian troops counterattacked toward Fedorivka.
Russian attacks around Huliaipole on October 11 and 12 similarly failed to produce verified territorial gains.
Earlier, Ukrainian forces regained control of another 101 square kilometers (39 square miles) of territory and liberated three villages in the Donetsk region, bringing the total area recovered during Operation Vivaldi to 277 square kilometers (107 square miles).
Ukraine’s Third Army Corps commander Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi reported that Ukrainian forces had restored full control over 16 settlements during the four-stage operation.
Biletskyi said Russian forces suffered approximately 3,000 personnel losses during the latest phase, raising their estimated total losses throughout the operation to 8,000. These figures have not been independently verified.

Ukraine says it frees more territory in Donetsk region counteroffensive
KYIV, Oct 14 - Ukraine has freed 16 villages from Russian forces in the eastern Donetsk region in its latest counteroffensive, a senior commander said on Wednesday, part of what he called a major frontline pushback amid increased Russian air attacks elsewhere.
Kyiv's Third Army Corps has waged an operation, announced last month, to dislodge Russian troops north of the strategic city of Sloviansk, one of the two main bastions in Ukraine's so-called "fortress belt" anchoring its eastern defences.
Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said recent Ukrainian assaults had liberated three more villages in the area of the counteroffensive - some 30 km (19 miles) north of Sloviansk - bringing the total of freed territory to 277 square kilometres (107 square miles) and the number of settlements to 16.
Russia, whose pace of battlefield gains has slowed this year, has demanded that Ukraine cede the 20 percent of the Donetsk region it still controls before it stops fighting.
"The Kremlin's plan to seize the Donetsk and Luhansk regions will not be implemented in the foreseeable future," Biletskyi said in a video address. Donetsk and Luhansk, which Russia almost entirely occupies, make up Ukraine's mineral-rich Donbas.
The highly publicised operation, dubbed "Vivaldi", comes as Ukrainian forces aim to seize the ground initiative from Russia in the fifth year of fighting, in part by embracing technology and new tactics.
Russia regularly reports seizing frontline villages. Reuters could not immediately verify the battlefield reports.

Aramco executives' offices damaged in Houthi attack, regional officials say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:24:58 UTC
20:24:58 KST

An overnight Houthi strike damaged executive offices at Saudi oil giant Aramco's headquarters in Dhahran, two regional officials told The Associated Press on Wednesday, as fresh explosions shook Riyadh and the Iran-backed rebels intensified their missile and drone campaign against Saudi Arabia.
The reported damage to one of the kingdom's most important economic institutions came amid renewed attacks on airports, military installations and oil infrastructure, raising concerns about Saudi Arabia's ability to withstand sustained strikes and the potential consequences for global energy markets.
Residents of Riyadh reported hearing additional explosions Wednesday. The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said its air defenses had intercepted cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and drones targeting the capital, as well as a ballistic missile aimed at Dhahran and a cruise missile targeting Al-Kharj.
Dhahran is home to Aramco's headquarters, while Al-Kharj houses Prince Sultan Air Base and Saudi Arabia's state-owned Military Industries Corporation.
The attacks have increased pressure on US President Donald Trump, who has said he is considering whether American forces should join Saudi strikes against the Houthis.
Saudi officials have reported repeated attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh over the past week, with strikes killing at least 18 people and injuring more than 300.
The Houthis described the latest attacks as retaliation for what they called Saudi aggression against Sanaa, Yemen's rebel-held capital, and other areas under their control.
Russia and China involved in ceasefire efforts
Despite the escalation, diplomatic efforts to halt the fighting are underway.
Mohamed al-Bukhaiti, a senior member of the Houthis' political bureau, told AP that Oman had attempted to bring the warring sides back to negotiations, while Russia and China had also pursued contacts through Iran.
"We're welcoming any mediation that leads to an end of the war and the blockade between Sanaa and Riyadh," al-Bukhaiti said.
"We're ready for a comprehensive end of the war and the blockade from both sides, not just a temporary ceasefire."
The Houthis nevertheless continued threatening Saudi airports and oil installations.
The attacks have severely disrupted air travel across the kingdom. More than 3,000 flights scheduled to depart from Saudi airports over the past week were canceled or listed as not operating, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium.
The campaign has also highlighted the Houthis' ability to inflict significant disruption despite Saudi Arabia's advanced Western-supplied air defenses.
Saudi air defenses under growing pressure
Saudi Arabia, one of the world's largest purchasers of American weapons, has sought additional military support from allies as it confronts daily missile and drone attacks across a vast territory.
Regional officials have warned that the kingdom is running low on missile interceptors, while military analysts say completely preventing Houthi strikes is virtually impossible.
Saudi Arabia covers an area approximately three times the size of Texas, and Houthi weapons are capable of reaching targets more than 1,600 kilometers, or 1,000 miles, away. Some missiles can also change course during flight, complicating interception efforts.
Even successful interceptions can cause casualties and damage on the ground.
Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense said debris from two intercepted Houthi ballistic missiles fell on residential neighborhoods in Riyadh overnight, injuring four people, including a child, and damaging 15 homes.
The escalating attacks have revived concerns about the vulnerability of Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure and transportation networks, with repeated strikes threatening facilities central to the kingdom's economy.
Saudi strikes intensify inside Yemen
Saudi Arabia has responded with its own military operations against Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen, supporting the country's internationally recognized government.
The latest confrontation erupted after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of attacking an airport in Sanaa, reigniting tensions over the longstanding Saudi blockade of rebel-held territory.
The Houthis subsequently announced their own blockade against Saudi Arabia, while the Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive approximately a week and a half ago.
On Wednesday, the Houthi-run Health Ministry said two people had been killed and two wounded in a Saudi airstrike Tuesday on an oil facility in the Ras Isa port area of Hodeida province.
The Saudi-led coalition also struck an oil facility in Sanaa.
Ahmed Nagi, a senior Yemen analyst at the International Crisis Group, said the attacks on fuel storage facilities in Houthi-held areas represented a new phase in the conflict.
He warned that a prolonged war of attrition could significantly weaken the Houthis' military capabilities.
"The Houthis are betting on pressure, while the Saudis are betting on time," Nagi said.
"The Houthis are trying to strike critical infrastructure in Saudi Arabia to raise the cost of continued military intervention and support for the Yemeni government."
Humanitarian crisis deepens
The renewed fighting has also threatened to plunge Yemen deeper into the civil war that devastated the country before four years of relative calm.
The International Committee of the Red Cross reported an unprecedented increase in people suffering weapons-related injuries along Yemen's front lines, particularly in Marib, Taiz and areas near the Red Sea.
Hospitals are struggling to cope with the surge in casualties, with increasingly frequent incidents involving large numbers of wounded patients.
The World Food Program also warned that it could no longer reach more than 600,000 people dependent on humanitarian assistance in the besieged city of Taiz.
With Saudi Arabia and the Houthis continuing to exchange strikes, the diplomatic efforts involving Oman, Russia and China have yet to produce a breakthrough, leaving both the kingdom's critical infrastructure and Yemen's civilian population exposed to further escalation.

European Commission allocates nearly €2.9 bln more to Ukraine for drones, air defense and missiles
According to Ukrinform, this is said in a press release published on the Commission’s website.
“As Russia stalls on the frontlines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks - cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies and save lives. With today's €2.86 billion disbursement, we keep addressing Ukraine's most urgent operational needs, including drones and missiles vital to its defence,” Ursula von der Leyen, President of the European Commission, said.
The Ukraine Support Loan totals €90 billion for 2026–2027, including €60 billion for defence needs and development of Ukraine’s defence‑industrial base, and €30 billion for budget support.
During 2026, €28.3 billion is expected to be directed to support Ukraine’s defence industrial capacity. The Commission said further disbursements under the 2026 defence leg of the instrument will continue in the coming weeks.
By the end of 2026, Ukraine will still have access to €29.64 billion available in EU financial assistance. This includes €25.24 billion under the Ukraine Support Loan (with €12.54 billion for defence‑industry support and €12.7 billion for budget financing) and €4.4 billion in remaining budget support under the initial Ukraine Facility.
In total, more than €17 billion is earmarked to ensure the stability of Ukraine’s budget for the remaining months of 2026. Disbursement depends on meeting conditions set out in the Ukraine Plan and the Memorandum of Understanding.
As reported, since 2022 the European Union and its Member States have provided €231.5 billion in assistance to Ukraine, including €3.8 billion from the proceeds of immobilised Russian assets.
In February 2026, the European Parliament and the Council adopted Regulation (EU) 2026/467, establishing the Ukraine Support Loan. The Regulation provides for up to €90 billion in support to Ukraine. The support is designed to strengthen Ukraine’s defence capabilities and ensure the uninterrupted functioning of the state, delivery of essential public services and economic resilience amid Russia’s aggression.
