Trump blamed Islam for France's protests. Students want teachers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:15:28 UTC
19:15:28 KST

Breadcrumb
France's students demand better schools as Trump turns protests into an Islam debate
At a demonstration in Paris’s 13th arrondissement on 10 October, high school students sang the national anthem and chanted "Macron démission." Their placards read "Nous avons besoin de plus de professeurs," "We need more teachers." Some urged others to stay calm and not to run, warning that this was what the CRS, France’s riot police, wanted. Before long, officers moved in to disperse the crowd.
For three students aged 16 to 18 from the 13th and 19th arrondissements, interviewed that day, the problems are concrete: overcrowded classrooms, no computer room, a shortage of teachers in their final year, and a canteen so packed that they have about 10 minutes to eat.
Meals must be booked in advance, and many end up buying food elsewhere. One week, they said, food had cost them €170. All three asked not to be named because of tensions around the protests.
When they sat their exams, the students said, they were sent to other sites, in rooms so stifling that some left for the toilets just to breathe. They took their concerns to a meeting at another high school with school leaders and officials, but the answers were disappointing.
Some issues were passed on to other authorities, including the education authority and Valérie Pécresse’s regional council, and the agreed changes won't take effect until next year. The students want them now.
On 6 October, as demonstrations spread across France, US President Donald Trump offered a different explanation.
"This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!" he wrote on Truth Social.
The students reject that. The protests have nothing to do with religion or immigration, they said. High school students come from every background, and there should be no shortcuts. None of them wanted their origins or religion mentioned. They wanted, they said, to be judged on what they were saying.
The movement began in September in disadvantaged suburbs of Paris and has since spread across the country.
More than 250,000 people took part in protests nationwide, according to the Interior Ministry, while organisers put the figure at 450,000.
'They tend to infantilise us'
A 23-year-old Arab medical student of North African heritage from Seine-Saint-Denis, the department north of Paris where the movement has deep roots, described classrooms not built for more than 30 pupils, broken furniture, and rooms that are hard to bear in winter. He asked to remain anonymous because of upcoming exams.
"Instead of trying to understand our difficulties and find solutions, they tend to infantilise us," he said. "We are capable of identifying the problems in our schools and saying what needs to change."
He is used to Trump’s provocations, he said, and pays them little attention. "What he said has, as usual, nothing to do with reality," he said, adding that he saw it as political point-scoring ahead of the US midterm elections.
What worries him more is that young people from immigrant families have their grievances read through assumptions about their identity, rather than their experience. "Our demands risk being reduced to questions of origin or religion," he said.
Many young people, he said, refuse to speak to channels such as CNews and BFMTV, which they see as portraying people from immigrant backgrounds in racist and Islamophobic terms.
"We want the media to talk about why we are mobilising, rather than turning our demands into a debate about our identity," the young student added.
A 21-year-old woman who went to school in Seine-Saint-Denis before moving to a Paris high school, and who also asked not to be named, said the protesters’ demands were legitimate.
She was stunned, she said, that students asking for better conditions had been met with violence. As for Trump, she said, "he should keep quiet."
The crackdown has been heavy. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted over alleged offences linked to the unrest, including 1,483 minors, according to the Justice Ministry.
Inequality built into the system
The staffing crisis is national. According to the Education Ministry’s statistics directorate, DEPP, 9.8 percent of teaching hours in public secondary schools went undelivered in 2024–2025: 7.5 percent because absent teachers were not replaced, and 2.3 percent because schools were closed.
In Seine-Saint-Denis, two-thirds of schools had unfilled teaching positions, according to a union survey cited by Reuters.
Louise Paternoster, a representative of the CGT education union in the department, told Reuters the area did not receive resources to match its needs.
"In a period of budgetary restraint, it is more difficult to reduce inequalities," said Clémence Cardon-Quint, a professor at Paul-Valéry University Montpellier who studies education funding.
The problems start long before high school. A primary school teacher in her fifties, who asked not to be named, said her biggest challenge was supporting pupils with autism, ADHD and dyslexia.
"Inclusion is a very good thing, but we need the resources to welcome these children properly," she said.
Teachers sometimes have to make or buy materials themselves, which multiplies preparation time, and other children get less attention.
"Unfortunately, the die is very often cast as early as the first year of primary school," she said. A child who struggles to read needs help from speech therapists or psychologists, or support through France’s disability service, the MDPH, and that depends on families pushing for it. Some children, she said, reach secondary school without the level they need.
A concession, not a solution
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu acknowledged that young people’s anger did not come out of nowhere, while condemning violence and accusing outside groups of exploiting the protests. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot rejected Trump’s reading, saying France should tell its own story.
On 8 October, Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced that around 3,000 qualified teachers who had not yet started work would be sent to schools facing staffing shortages.
It was a stopgap, not 3,000 new permanent posts. Student unions welcomed it as a first victory but vowed to keep mobilising.
Student unions have called a new national day of protest for 17 October. Asked about Trump’s claim that the protests were about Islam, the primary school teacher did not hesitate.
"It’s completely absurd and has absolutely nothing to do with it."

Iran executed mountaineer and musician Ali Sina Mostafavi, 38, on Wednesday, according to state sources, continuing the Islamic Republic’s use of executions as punishment against protesters. The judiciary said he carried out armed attacks during the six-week war with Israel and the United States earlier this year, supported exiled Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, and maintained links with Israel.
Mostafavi, from Bam in Kerman province, was executed after the Supreme Court upheld a death sentence handed down by a Revolutionary Court in Kerman, the judiciary-affiliated Mizan news agency reported.
Human rights groups had warned less than 24 hours earlier that he had been moved to solitary confinement and his family summoned for a final visit. Pahlavi’s communications team then issued an urgent appeal, saying he had been tortured into confessing and convicted in a sham trial.
Mizan said Mostafavi carried out a series of shootings in Kerman during the war, which Iranian authorities call the Ramadan War. It said he opened fire in Azadi Square on March 24, wounding a civilian and a young girl. On April 21, it said, he fired at conscript soldiers and passing vehicles, injuring several people. It also accused him of two failed shooting attempts targeting police on the Kerman-Mahan road.
Authorities said a search of his hideout turned up a scoped Brno rifle, two shotguns, 246 rounds of ammunition and 30 Molotov cocktails.
The judiciary also said Mostafavi sent photographs and videos of sites struck during the war to Persian-language opposition media abroad. It said he expressed willingness to carry out an operation at Kerman airport. According to the authorities, messages on his phone included exchanges with Persian-language broadcasters and messages to Israel’s official Persian-language account.
Mizan said he took part in the nationwide protests that began in December 2025 and continued into January, and sent footage of the unrest to media outside Iran.
The judiciary said the case was heard with a defense lawyer present. It said the conviction rested on investigative findings, security reports, and Mostafavi’s confessions. The public account did not include the defense’s arguments or independently verifiable evidence. Iranian authorities have not released evidence that he acted under the direction of Pahlavi or Israeli officials, while human rights groups have raised concerns about his treatment in detention and the circumstances of his conviction.
'A political prisoner and young athlete'
Pahlavi’s team described him as “a political prisoner and young athlete” in “immediate danger of execution.” The account said in Persian that he was a patriotic mountaineer and alleged his conviction followed “forced confessions under torture” and a “show trial.”
The League for the Defense of Human Rights in Iran said armed security officers arrested Mostafavi at his home in the early hours of April 25. The group alleged he was beaten during the arrest.
Branch 1 of the Kerman Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Hadi Aghaei, sentenced him to death on charges including moharebeh, or waging war against God, acting against national security, and gathering and colluding. Branch 41 of the Supreme Court upheld the sentence on September 28, according to human rights reports.
On Tuesday, rights groups reported his transfer to solitary confinement at Kerman prison.
Iran sees sharp rise in the use of the death penalty
Before his arrest, Mostafavi was an experienced mountaineer. IranWire and Human Rights for Sports said he climbed Island Peak in Nepal and attempted Ama Dablam, reaching about 6,600 meters. Records in Kerman mountaineering club archives show he joined a 2016 expedition to Alam-Kuh, one of Iran’s highest mountains. Human rights reports also describe him as a musician.
The execution follows a sharp rise in the use of the death penalty against people accused of involvement in the January protests, opposition activity and war-related security offenses.
On Tuesday, Amnesty International condemned the executions of five men between September 30 and October 5 who had been convicted in connection with the January uprising. “The arbitrary executions of these five young men serves as another chilling reminder of how the Iranian authorities weaponize the death penalty to render the cost of dissent so high that it terrorizes the population into silence,” said Diana Eltahawy, the group’s deputy regional director for the Middle East and North Africa.

Marrakech Airshow showcases building blocks of Israel-Morocco defense ties - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:15:10 UTC
19:15:10 KST

The recent Marrakech Airshow showed that Israel and Morocco are moving toward closer defense ties. Israel’s Defense Ministry said last week that Israel has opened a national pavilion at the show and that the ministry had led an Israeli delegation to Morocco to participate.
“This marks Israel's first official participation in the defense exhibition held in Morocco since the signing of the Abraham Accords, and the first time the Israel Ministry of Defense (IMOD) International Defense Cooperation Directorate (SIBAT) has opened an Israeli national pavilion and headed a delegation of Israeli defense industries at the show,” the ministry said.
Eight Israeli companies came with the delegation, including ASIO Technologies, Orbit Communication Systems, SHILAT Optronics, UVision Air, and XTEND Systems. Israel’s big three defense giants, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, Elbit Systems and Israel Aerospace Industries, were also present.
This was an important opportunity for Israel’s large companies as well as the smaller and midsize ones to showcase various systems. The ministry highlighted “advanced, combat-proven technologies at the show, including loitering munitions, AI-powered robotic systems, autonomous navigation capabilities for UAVs, laser guidance for FPV drones, satellite communications, and more.”
The ministry is seeking greater defense cooperation with countries abroad. This includes numerous Israeli companies taking part in AUSA this week.
It also includes the recent major Israeli defense deal with Greece for Achilles Shield. In that deal, valued at around €3 billion, Israel will help Greece build a multi-layered air defense array based on Israeli systems. These systems include David’s Sling and Spyder, made by Rafael, as well as the Barak system, made by IAI.
As such, a trend is clear. Israeli ties with Morocco are not just about Morocco but part of a larger story of Israeli ties with Greece and the US. Morocco is seeking to acquire several Israeli defense systems, and reports indicate it has already acquired several. For instance, we reported in January 2026 that Morocco had deployed IAI’s Barak air defense system.
The Economist also reported last year that Morocco was producing drones in cooperation with an Israeli company. “Morocco is Africa’s new military tech hub,” an op-ed at The Jerusalem Post said in April.
Israeli-Moroccan friendship goes back years
The building blocks of Israel-Morocco relations include a friendship going back years. Morocco is part of the Abraham Accords. A small number of Israeli troops joined a US-backed exercise called Africa Lion in Morocco in 2025. Calcalist reported on October 12 that “Moroccan Military Industry (MMI) will begin delivering armored vehicle turrets to the Moroccan army in March 2027, the company's general manager said on the sidelines of the Marrakech Air Show.”
The report added that “sources at the air show and earlier media reporting have said MMI is closely linked to Israel's Elbit Systems and uses its technology. MMI itself told Reuters it is a Moroccan defense company, a characterization that leaves the precise nature of the relationship with Elbit unaddressed on the record.” A separate report at Calcalist also said that Morocco was interested in IAI’s Lora missile.
The Lora missile has been around for years. Back in 2020, IAI said that a “complex trial included two scenarios to test and demonstrate LORA’s advanced capabilities. The first scenario involved a short-range launch to 90 km and the second to a long range of 400 km.” The German Navy completed a successful dual operational firing trial with IAI's Naval Lora ballistic missile, IAI said in September.
On October 12, Morocco World News also noted: “Morocco and Israel are holding advanced talks over the possible integration of the Israeli David’s Sling air defense system into the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces, according to the German defense publication Europäische Sicherheit & Technik (ES&T).”
Several reports from the Marrakech show highlighted Morocco's search for more advanced defense equipment. For instance, Le360 reported that Morocco’s MMI unveiled a system called Spear, an “autonomous mortar system designed for light combat vehicles.”
The same site highlighted Israel’s pavilion at the air show. Le360 also noted that an Israeli officer “held a one-on-one meeting with the commander of the Royal Air Force. The two officials discussed strengthening strategic ties and continuing cooperation between the two air forces, according to reports.” The goal of these reports is to illustrate growing Israel-Morocco cooperation.
Morocco has been welcoming of Israel cooperation
The air show was a key part of publicly showcasing Israel-Morocco cooperation. At a time when Israel has sometimes faced challenges abroad and controversy, Morocco has been welcoming. It has been more welcoming than France, for instance. Morocco’s drive to increase its capabilities, especially in air defenses and precision fire, is important. It would knit Morocco into a regional defense architecture that brings together countries with advanced systems. These could include Israeli systems that are being sold in Europe, such as to Greece.
As such, one could imagine a link between Morocco, Greece, Israel, and other countries that share various advanced systems. This would also position Morocco as an advanced, capable military power at the head of the Mediterranean. This matters because Morocco and Algeria are rivals, and Algeria is hostile to Israel. A recent UAE-Algeria diplomatic crisis also adds to the complexity. Libya, divided by civil war, also plays a role.
With so much at stake in today's regional shifts from the Horn of Africa to the Sahel, Morocco-Israel ties likely matter more than ever. The recent air show symbolized these ties and showcased practical military technology.

Opposition bloc leaders condemn Deri's statements
Opposition leaders in the bloc seeking to replace Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in the upcoming elections condemned Deri’s statements, sharply criticized the premier’s partnership with the haredi parties, and warned of the IDF’s enlistment crisis.
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett, who leads the B’Yachad party, said that “Netanyahu will continue funding draft dodgers, and in return, Deri will give him the reins of power, all at the expense of those who serve.”
“The IDF chief of staff is raising 10 red flags over the army’s collapse, while Deri, a member of the Security Cabinet, tells him: ‘We intend to continue down the same path and institutionalize draft evasion,’” Bennett added.
“A vote for Netanyahu, [Finance Minister Bezalel] Smotrich, or Deri is a vote for draft evasion, 150 days of reserve duty a year, and billions of shekels every year transferred from the pockets of those who serve to those who evade service,” he said.
Leader of the Yisrael Beytenu party MK Avigdor Liberman noted that Deri had “admitted in his own words that he will agree to forming a government only if his puppet, Netanyahu, agrees to permanently exempt all haredim from military service.
“What does this mean in practice? Voting for the draft-dodgers’ government led by Bibi [Netanyahu] and Deri means an even greater burden on those who serve, hundreds more days of reserve duty, and further extensions of mandatory service for active-duty soldiers,” he said.

Uzbekistan to host European Film Festival
The European Film Festival will be held in Tashkent between October 23 and 25, and for the first time, in Urgench on 27 October, Qazinform News Agency cites UzA.
The film festival program includes 11 films featuring thought-provoking dramas and biographical stories, as well as documentaries and animated films.
The films will be screened at the National Palace of Cinematic Arts of Uzbekistan.
Besides, a program of short films for students will be presented on 28 October by the British Council in Uzbekistan in partnership with Uzbekistan State World Languages University.
The embassies of Cyprus, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, Romania and Slovenia, with support from the Alliance Française in Tashkent and the Goethe-Institut, contributed to the festival’s program.

Kazakhstan forecasts nearly 3.8 tn tenge in oil revenues for 2027
Members of Kazakhstan’s Qurultay have approved the draft law on the republican budget for 2027–2029 in its first reading, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the Qurultay’s Finance and Budget Committee, Kazakhstan’s National Fund is expected to receive 3.78 trillion tenge from oil sector companies in 2027, down 342 billion tenge from the 2026 estimate.
The forecast assumes oil production of 96 million tons, a global oil price of $70 per barrel, and an exchange rate of 480 tenge to the US dollar.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Kazakhstan had narrowed its oil production shortfall by 4 million tons.
In the first nine months of 2026, oil production at the Tengiz field reached 26.7 million tons (88% of the previous year's level), followed by Kashagan at 12.8 million tons (94%) and Karachaganak at 7.5 million tons (82%).

Spain’s King Felipe VI said on Tuesday that Ceuta and Melilla in North Africa were “an integral part” of Spain and that its sovereignty and territorial integrity “are not up for negotiation”, during a historic visit to the two cities claimed by Morocco.
The Spanish monarch also stressed the importance of maintaining good neighbourly relations with Morocco, amid tensions between the two countries following a large influx of migrants into Ceuta last July.

Ohio's working-class voters rethink support for Trump and the Republican Party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:11:05 UTC
19:11:05 KST

Ohio's working-class voters rethink support for Trump and the Republican Party
WARREN, Ohio, Oct 14 - A decade after Republican Donald Trump peeled away working-class and union voters who had long been a cornerstone of Democratic support in Ohio, Democrats and labor leaders see an opening to win back some of them in the November 3 US elections.
Now midway through his second term, the president's magic appears to be losing at least some of its luster with blue-collar men and women as rising prices, the Iran war and concerns about his rhetoric prompt some voters to reconsider their support.
The state's reputation as a leading swing state began to fade in 2016 when Trump won strong support from working-class voters who felt their economic concerns were being heard, helping turn Ohio into a reliably Republican state.
Almost overnight, Ohio became rock-solid Republican. Ohio voted for the eventual winner in 14 straight presidential elections from 1964 until 2020 when Democrat Joe Biden won nationally but Ohio backed Trump.
A shift in Ohio toward Democrats could matter in elections that will help determine whether Republicans retain control of Congress during Trump's final two years in office or hand new leverage to Democrats over his agenda.
The stakes are high in Ohio, where Republicans are defending a US Senate seat and the governor's office. Two House races are rated "toss-ups." One, in northwestern Ohio, has long been held by a Democrat and the other, in northeastern Ohio, is Republican-held.
Trump is not on the ballot this time but has told supporters to act as if he is. It remains to be seen whether that could end up helping or hindering Republicans running in tough races.
Republican Senator Jon Husted is in a tight competition with Democratic former Senator Sherrod Brown, while Democrat Amy Acton is challenging Republican Vivek Ramaswamy for an open governor's seat.
Trump campaigned with Husted and Ramaswamy in Youngstown on Monday to try to energize the Republican base.
'GOD KNOWS WE DIDN'T VOTE FOR THIS'
Paul Ringold, a 48-year-old steel hauler and pastor of the mostly Black congregation at the Shalom Church of God and Christ in the city of Warren, embodies the uncertainty that Democrats hope could help them make inroads with working-class voters.
Ringold voted for Trump for president in 2016, Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 and Trump again in 2024, but said he remains undecided about whom to support for the US Senate, governor and other offices this year.
"I'm in the wilderness trying to find a place," he said.
Ringold said rising fuel and food prices and Trump's combative style have left him questioning some of the choices made by a president he once strongly supported.
"God knows we didn't vote for this," he said of inflation.
Like several voters interviewed by Reuters, Ringold also cited Trump's rhetoric. "I wish he would just tone down that rhetoric ... that old New York in-your-face 'I got you sucker'" persona, he said.
EARLY TURNOUT FAVORS DEMOCRATS
In early voting that began in Ohio last week, Democrats appeared to be more motivated than Republicans.
In Trumbull County, home to the city of Warren and many blue-collar jobs, a strong turnout during the first three days brought 1,224 Democrats to the polls, 559 Republicans and 453 with no known political affiliation, according to county data.
Paul Sracic, an Ohio-based senior fellow with the right-of-center Hudson Institute, said "working-class voters, if they are moving at all away from Trump, Brown is a safe landing spot for them" because of the former senator's populist record.
"Trump has done a good job of basically focusing on social issues with our guys," said Jose Arroyo, a United Steelworkers official who engages in contract negotiations and labor relations for the sprawling labor union.
Trump "seemed to latch on sort of to the dissatisfaction of where the working man has gone. Pensions go away. Plants close. Livelihoods they've always known disappear."
The problem, he said, is that focusing primarily on hot-button social issues ignores advancing policies that would "improve the lives of working people" and actually turn them into law.
The 50,000 manufacturing jobs in 1990 in the Youngstown-Warren area fell to about 20,000 in 2026, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.
In recent years, the Mahoning Valley, long a powerhouse of the steel and automotive industries, has attracted a few new manufacturing plants. Arroyo said the Iran war has boosted domestic oil industry exploration, creating more demand for equipment made of steel. But he acknowledged that the war had also brought higher consumer prices.
NLRB 'DISMANTLING'
When Trump began his second term in January 2025, he promptly fired two Democratic officials at the National Labor Relations Board and left the agency without the quorum required to take actions. That paralysis lasted for nearly a year.
Ohio AFL-CIO President Tim Burga cited what he called Trump's "dismantling" of the NLRB as having hindered union organizing efforts and made it harder to contest unfair labor practices and secure work contracts with companies.
"We were on a path for the first time in my lifetime, under the Biden administration, for having a national industrial policy," Burga said, but the Trump administration rolled much of it back. Biden and Congress enacted programs to spur investment in such industries as clean energy and semiconductors.
Trump's trade battles with Canada also were unhelpful to labor, he said.
OHIO VOTERS REMAIN DIVIDED
Bill Callahan, 75, a self-described Democrat from Cortland, said some relatives who once backed Trump "are traveling back" toward Democrats because "they don't like (politicians) taking money out of their pockets."
A part-time warehouse worker from Cortland after a career at General Electric, he said he considered voting for Trump in 2016 but was put off by ethical concerns.
Others interviewed by Reuters said higher prices were not enough to change their vote.
Joe Scarabino, who co-owns a bait-and-tackle business with his wife Kathryn near Cortland, said the couple responded to higher fuel costs by raising delivery charges rather than product prices, thus having an impact on fewer customers and small business owners.
"We believe our Christian values are more than gas prices," he said. The couple declined to say who they support.
Retired coal-fired power plant worker Chuck Burns, 67, of Wellsville, credited Trump with reducing illegal immigration and boosting the value of his retirement investments. "He's done a good job ... he's got balls," Burns said.
Burns praised Trump's immigration restrictions at the southern border and said his retirement savings have increased in value since Biden left office.
Asked what issues worry him in this election season, Burns said, "It's just that Democrats – it's unbelievable some of the stuff that they want to do."
Asked to explain, Burns raised transgender issues. "Those poor people, they feel that way, that's fine, that's their business," he said. "They (Democrats) don't need to incorporate our young kids into that stuff." REUTERS

Nvidia, worth $5.5tn, donates $250m to UK for AI safety research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:10:37 UTC
19:10:37 KST

The $5.5tn (£4.1tn) US chipmaker Nvidia is donating $250m worth of computing power to the UK to support AI safety research.
The donation from the world’s most valuable company comes as the UK government confirmed its AI Security Institute (AISI), which tests advance AI models, will be able to examine cutting-edge technology developed by companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google before they are released.
Nvidia said the donation, which spans five years, would “support agentic safety and security research across the UK”.
Safety concerns about AI agents – highly capable computer programs that are able to design and perform sequences of tasks autonomously – have risen since the summer, when OpenAI confirmed that a “swarm” of agents had attacked Hugging Face, a tech startup.
Nvidia did not reference AISI in its statement but said most of the money would “support the wider UK AI safety and security research community”, with a proportion of the cash going to the British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab, the Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab – run by the Edinburgh, Cambridge, Oxford and University College London universities – and Imperial College London.
The computing power will be delivered via UK-based datacentres using Nvidia chips.
“The UK brings world-class scientific rigour to this essential engineering challenge,” said Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive. “With this $250m commitment, Nvidia will put accelerated computing in the hands of UK researchers to develop, test and strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI.”
Kanishka Narayan, the UK’s AI minister, said the announcement was a “vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research”.
On Monday Narayan confirmed that AISI was conducting tests on US-developed AI models before they are released, after reports that the White House had restricted access.
The AI minister also warned that the UK faces agentic attacks similar to the one carried out by OpenAI agents on Australia’s healthcare system this year.
“It seems likely, if not inevitable, that our own cyber defences will be breached,” said Narayan.
Anthropic, the developer of the Claude chatbot, warned of a new AI safety threat on Monday after it published a blogpost stating its models could soon become self-replicating. They find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart ovens and lawnmowers, the company said.
Under such a scenario the models could power themselves without datacentres, and instead could use a “botnet” of interconnected devices, Anthropic said, adding that the world should prepare for a future where such botnets were here to stay.
“A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down since there’s no centralised point to shut off,” Anthropic’s researchers wrote.

Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg to build anti-drone factory in Poland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:10:08 UTC
19:10:08 KST

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support.
Norwegian defence firm Kongsberg has announced plans to build a new factory in Poland producing counter-drone systems. The firm will invest over 200 million zloty (€46 million) in the facility, creating more than 100 long-term jobs.
“The new facility will support Polish industry and defence capabilities and strengthen Kongsberg’s presence in Poland,” declared CEO Eirik Lie alongside Polish defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz at the Warsaw Security Forum, where Norway is this year serving as the official partner nation.
In January, Kongsberg signed an agreement to supply a new anti-drone system to Poland in partnership with Polish state defence group PGZ. The project comes in response to growing fears over the threat of Russian drones, around 20 of which violated Polish airspace on one night in September last year.
Norwegowie inwestują w Polsce. Duża inwestycja #Kongsberg na Pomorzu ogłoszona właśnie na #WSF2026. Szybka budowa fabryki i nowe miejsca pracy. pic.twitter.com/msI2FWGym8
— Beata Górka-Winter (@BeataGWinter) October 12, 2026
Kosiniak-Kamysz thanked Kongsberg for its investment and emphasised that Polish-Norwegian relations are at their highest point in history, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP).
The announcement of the counter-drone plant came as Poland and Norway’s prime ministers, Donald Tusk and Jonas Gahr Støre, signed a declaration on strategic partnership that pledged to deepen security ties, including joint defence production and strengthening NATO’s northern and eastern flanks.
While the exact location of the plant has not been revealed, Kongsberg stated that it would be in northern Poland, near the Tricity area (consisting of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Sopot) on the Baltic Sea coast.
Construction of the facility is scheduled to begin this year, with production at the site scheduled to commence in the first half of 2028.
Counter-drone technology has become an increasing priority for Poland following Russian airspace violations and also the growing use by Moscow of jet-powered drones to strike targets in Ukraine close to the Polish border, including recently a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw.
Polish spending on drones and counter-drone systems combined rose from 100 million zloty in 2023 to 26 billion zloty in 2026, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced in August, quoted by news website Interia.
The summary report of this week’s Warsaw Security Forum suggested the use of counter-drone systems to create a “controlled fly-zone” over the Suwałki Gap, a strategically important choke point along the Polish-Lithuanian border that sits between the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and Russia’s ally Belarus.
Poland has signed an agreement for a new anti-drone system that it claims will be the first of its kind in Europe.
The network is intended to protect Poland’s eastern borders, where last year around 20 Russian drones crossed in an unprecedented incursion https://t.co/WhWhJxDwXA
— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 30, 2026
Poland has in recent years moved to strengthen its defence ties with countries around the Baltic Sea. In January, it was announced that Poland will manufacture missiles for rocket artillery systems that Norway is purchasing from South Korea. Norway has already bought Piorun air-defence systems from Poland.
In 2024, Poland and Sweden signed a strategic partnership. The two countries subsequently held their first bilateral military exercises in the Baltic, and Poland this year ordered three submarines from Swedish manufacturer Saab.
Saab this year also signed a strategic collaboration agreement with PGZ that will see them cooperate on naval production, servicing and technology.
On Monday this week, Norway’s defence ministry announced that Poland will join an initiative recently launched by 11 European countries and Canada to cooperate more closely on security in the North Atlantic, Arctic and Baltic Sea.

Israeli air strike kills Palestinian woman in Gaza City

An Israeli air strike on an apartment block in Gaza has killed a woman and wounded two other people, hospital officials said.
Reem Asaad Awad, 33, was killed in the attack early on Wednesday in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood of Gaza City, the Turkish state news agency Anadolu reported, quoting a source at Al Shifa hospital.

Everything we know about Lebanon's seized explosives shipment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:06:54 UTC
19:06:54 KST

Breadcrumb
Everything we know about Lebanon's seized explosives shipment
Lebanese security agencies have launched an expanded investigation into a substantial shipment of explosives, with sources telling The New Arab that the materials seized were of a type previously used in political assassinations in the country.
Sources familiar with the investigation said army intelligence and the Internal Security Forces' Information Branch had been tasked by the public prosecutor with identifying those behind the shipment, amid growing fears of renewed political violence in Lebanon.
"The case is sensitive, and the quantity of materials seized was not small. These materials have been used in political assassinations in Lebanon," the sources told The New Arab.
They said investigators had already taken statements and would pursue further leads to identify individuals named during questioning.
The sources stressed that authorities would not tolerate any wrongdoing but warned against rushing to conclusions or exploiting the case politically, given Lebanon's fragile domestic situation.
The revelations came as Interior Minister Ahmad Hajjar disclosed new details on Tuesday about the discovery of the explosives at the Dahr al-Baidar checkpoint, which connects Beirut with the Bekaa Valley.
Hajjar said security personnel became suspicious of a grey Dodge Caravan on Monday because it appeared to be carrying an unusually heavy load.
A search uncovered explosive materials, prompting officers to arrest the driver and his passenger. Both suspects, along with the seized materials, were handed over to military police on the instructions of the judicial authorities.
The discovery has revived fears of political assassinations, with suspicion quickly falling on Hezbollah, although investigators have yet to publicly establish who was responsible for the shipment or its intended purpose.
Hajjar confirmed that army intelligence and the Information Branch had been instructed to expand their inquiries to establish the full circumstances and hold anyone found responsible accountable.
The minister also ordered tighter security at checkpoints, increased inspections and patrols, and a stronger security presence across the country.
He praised officers at Dahr al-Baidar for intercepting the vehicle, saying their vigilance had helped prevent a potential threat to Lebanon's security and stability.
Further explosives discovered near Syrian border
The investigation has also drawn the attention of Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, who discussed the case with army commander General Rodolphe Haykal.
Salam praised Lebanese security forces for discovering an additional quantity of explosives in the Qasr-Hermel area near the Syrian border.
He called for investigations to continue until all those involved in the smuggling operations, including the parties behind them, were identified and referred to the judiciary.
The prime minister reiterated his support for the Lebanese army and emphasised the need to strengthen its capabilities to secure the country's borders and extend state authority across Lebanese territory.
Justice Minister Adel Nassar, meanwhile, said on Monday that he would seek to refer the explosives case to the Judicial Council, a special court responsible for cases involving serious threats to national security.
He insisted that such a referral would not delay or obstruct the ongoing investigation.
Nassar also warned that the regional situation could encourage Hezbollah to take actions that might drag Lebanon into another devastating war.
He raised concerns over reports that explosives had been transported from the Bekaa Valley towards Beirut's southern suburbs, warning that storing such materials in densely populated areas would itself constitute a serious crime, regardless of their intended use.
According to Nassar, experts had warned that the reported quantity of explosives could destroy an entire neighbourhood.
The case comes as Lebanon faces mounting pressure to implement decisions aimed at placing all weapons under state control and extending the authority of its security institutions across the country.
US links reconstruction aid to Hezbollah disarmament
The developments coincide with renewed US pressure on Hezbollah, with Washington declaring that billions of dollars in reconstruction assistance for Lebanon would depend on the group's disarmament.
In remarks circulated by the US embassy in Beirut on Wednesday, a State Department spokesperson dismissed claims that Hezbollah had received substantial Iranian funding and accused the group of using criminal activities to compensate for its financial difficulties.
The spokesperson alleged that Hezbollah was involved in drug smuggling and maintained links with drug cartels in Latin America.
Washington also dismissed Hezbollah's recently announced financial assistance programme for displaced Lebanese families as an attempt to restore its reputation rather than genuinely help those affected by the war.
The State Department spokesperson said the US was working with Gulf and European partners on a plan to release billions of dollars in reconstruction assistance, but insisted that Hezbollah must surrender its weapons first.
The spokesperson also said Washington would continue supporting the trilateral framework agreed by Lebanon and Israel on 26 June, describing it as the only viable route towards long-term peace and security for both countries.
The comments followed Hezbollah's announcement on Tuesday of a financial assistance programme for families displaced by Israeli attacks or whose homes had been destroyed or rendered uninhabitable.
Under the programme, eligible households in Beirut and its southern suburbs could receive up to $14,000 in housing and furniture assistance, while those elsewhere could receive up to $12,000.
The payments would include a standard $8,000 furniture allowance, alongside rental assistance of $6,000 in Beirut and its southern suburbs and $4,000 in other areas.
Hezbollah said the assistance would be distributed in four instalments over one year, subject to available resources, with the first payments set at $3,500 in Beirut and its southern suburbs and $3,000 elsewhere.
The programme would also cover eligible families displaced by Israeli attacks in September 2024 and March 2026.
The announcement followed media reports that the group had received $200 million from Iran to support displaced Lebanese families.
Hezbollah sources did not deny the reports when contacted by The New Arab, but said its funding came from several sources, including the group's own resources, supporters and donations from Lebanon and abroad.
US diplomatic sources told The New Arab that Washington would continue imposing sanctions on Hezbollah and its financial networks to prevent the group from rebuilding its military and financial capabilities.
The sources said that even if Hezbollah secured additional Iranian funding, it would not be sufficient to restore its capabilities, and Washington would continue targeting individuals and networks accused of financing or facilitating its activities.
The pressure comes as Lebanon struggles with the devastation caused by Israel's continuing military campaign, with preliminary estimates putting losses at more than $27 billion.
Israeli forces have continued demolishing buildings and damaging infrastructure and agricultural land in southern Lebanon, while maintaining occupation or military control over parts of the border region.

Climate change is putting Europe’s brain health at risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:06:41 UTC
19:06:41 KST

Rising temperatures, poor air quality and the spread of infectious diseases could increase the burden of neurological disorders, with the most vulnerable communities facing the greatest risks.
Climate change is emerging as a growing threat to brain health, as rising temperatures and other environmental pressures add to the burden of neurological health conditions.
Neurological disorders, ranging from migraines to dementia and Parkinson’s disease, affect around one in three people over their lifetime, according to estimates cited by neurologist Ulf Kallweit, who is also a co-chair of the environmental influences task force at the European Academy of Neurology. Combined with mental health conditions, they accounted for an estimated global economic burden of €1.5 trillion in 2019.
“Everybody is somehow affected or knows somebody who is affected by a neurological disorder,” Kallweit told Euronews Health on the sidelines of the European Health Forum Gastein.
As climate change drives temperatures higher, the situation could deteriorate further, he warned, worsening existing conditions and potentially increasing the risk of developing neurological disorders.
But the trajectory is not inevitable. Policymakers can help limit the risks through measures that reduce exposure to heat and pollution and improve the environments in which people live.
Heat puts the brain under pressure
One of the clearest concerns is the relationship between high temperatures and stroke.
The number of stroke cases rises as temperatures climb above 30°C, Kallweit said, warning that heat-related strokes, which he said currently account for around 1% of all stroke cases, could represent 5 to 8% within the next 20 to 30 years.
Heat can also affect brain health indirectly by disrupting sleep.
Tropical nights, when temperatures remain above 20°C overnight, make it harder for the body to cool down. This can interfere with deep sleep and prevent people from recovering properly overnight.
“Everybody who experienced the last summer knows that sleep gets worse in these kind of heat nights,” Kallweit said.
Prolonged sleep disruption may have more serious consequences than a few restless nights.
“If you don't sleep well, not maybe one night, but for a longer time, there's a huge increase, let's say, for the risk of getting a stroke or also becoming demented,” he said.
Rising temperatures are also changing the geographical range of some infectious diseases, including those transmitted by ticks and mosquitoes. Some of these infections can affect the nervous system. Lyme borreliosis, for example, is transmitted by infected ticks and can cause neurological complications.
Malaria, meanwhile, remains a concern in discussions about the future spread of mosquito-borne diseases in Europe.
“Malaria is still not fully on yet there, but maybe in five or 10 years it may also affect us in southern parts of Europe,” Kallweit said.
Where you live matters
The risks are not shared equally.
Children, pregnant women, older people and those with pre-existing health conditions can be particularly vulnerable to extreme heat and other environmental pressures.
If they live in deprived neighbourhoods, their health risks rise further. Recent research has found that people living in socioeconomic deprivation have poorer indicators of brain health, including lower total brain volume and more signs of vascular damage.
Climate change could compound these existing inequalities.
“If you have heat and you cannot afford an AC, then you are more bothered,” Kallweit said. Access to healthy food, housing conditions and the surrounding environment can also shape people's health, he added.
Urban environments are particularly important. Noise, pollution and stressful living conditions can all affect wellbeing, while access to green spaces may offer some protection.
Therefore, improving access to green spaces is one potential way to support brain health.
“Going out to the forest one hour per week decreases your stroke risk by 3% or dementia risk by 4%,” Kallweit said.
Kallweit urged people to spend time in green surroundings and to protect their sleep by limiting exposure to light, noise and other disturbances.
But individual measures are only part of the answer. Public policy can help determine whether people have access to cooler homes, quieter neighbourhoods and cleaner air.
Kallweit called for safeguards against pollution and toxic substances, as well as changes to the way buildings are designed.
“How buildings are constructed should be reconsidered because they're still looking very much to the south, where the sun is entering,” he said, adding that such architecture “may be changed in the future.”

Nicaraguan families beg for answers as dissenters vanish into state custody
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:05:40 UTC
19:05:40 KST

Nicaraguan families beg for answers as dissenters vanish into state custody
MEXICO CITY, Oct 14 - Thelma Brenes grew worried when her father in Nicaragua did not return her messages.
Retired Army Colonel Carlos Brenes, 71, lived with his wife, Salvadora Martinez, 69, on a rural property south of the capital Managua. Brenes' daughter Thelma, living in the Netherlands, asked a neighbor to check on the couple. He found the house empty.
Local residents later told her they’d seen the police escorting the couple away in a patrol car.
That was August 2025. Since then, the Brenes family have pleaded with the authorities for information about the couple’s whereabouts, health and status, but they have heard nothing, not even if they are in custody.
What they do know is that Carlos Brenes is one of President Daniel Ortega's most outspoken critics. Martinez is a homemaker with no known political involvement.
"For us, as family members, this is a form of torture," said Thelma Brenes.
She is one of growing number of Nicaraguans who say their loved ones have been forcibly disappeared by the government of Ortega. The leader rose to prominence in the leftist Sandinista movement in the 1970s, battling to overthrow the Somoza dictatorship that itself arrested and forcibly disappeared suspected dissidents.
One of those who fought alongside Ortega was Carlos Brenes.
After Somoza's 1979 ousting, Ortega ruled the country, first as provisional government leader and then as president. He returned to office in 2007, and has ruled Nicaragua continuously since then. During this time, the United Nations, international human rights groups and regional leaders say, he has consolidated an increasingly authoritarian system, especially since anti-government protests in 2018.
The Nicaraguan government did not answer detailed questions regarding the Brenes and Martinez case. The Interior Ministry, Attorney General's Office and the Nicaraguan Army did not respond to requests for comment.
TOOL 'TO SOW FEAR'
Human rights groups like Memoria y Justicia, led by Nicaraguans in exile, and relatives of political prisoners said that at least 68 people were imprisoned in Nicaragua for political reasons as of the end of September, including 31 victims of enforced disappearance.
The UN defines enforced disappearance as the deprivation of liberty by agents of the state, followed by concealment of the person’s whereabouts.
Family members told Reuters that the Nicaraguan authorities offer no justification for the detentions: they rarely confirm an arrest, schedule court hearings, or provide information to families. People simply vanish.
Last month, three UN experts asked to investigate human rights in Nicaragua said they had documented imprisonment, torture and persecution on political grounds as part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians.
According to the UN experts, at least eight people detained for political reasons have died in state custody since the political crackdown began in 2018. They said they have verified 161 cases of enforced disappearance since April 2018, ranging from a few days to several years.
The Ortega government has dismissed critics as "fascists" and "coup mongers" and has not commented on the accusations of disappearances. The UN said it has received no official response from Managua to requests for comment sent since 2018.
"The government uses enforced disappearance as a deliberate strategy: to sow fear not only among the detained person, but also among their family members, and to warn the entire society: ‘This could happen to you,’" said Reed Brody, a member of the UN Group of Human Rights Experts on Nicaragua.
The tactic is not new to Latin America. In previous decades, military dictatorships in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, and other countries carried out enforced disappearances as part of widespread repression to keep the regimes in power.
'NO ONE HAS SEEN HIM IN MORE THAN TWO YEARS'
As a student, Carlos Brenes joined the protests against Anastasio Somoza, the last of a family clan that ruled Nicaragua for four decades. Brenes enlisted in the revolutionary Sandinista National Liberation Front and helped plan the insurrection that overthrew the dictatorship in 1979.
But around 1992, he became disillusioned with Ortega and retired from the Army. In 2018, he once again joined mass protests — this time against the Sandinista government. He was jailed on terrorism charges and released after 10 months. Then, in 2025, he disappeared.
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights said in an April report that it had been informed unofficially that Brenes and his wife were tried for treason and sentenced to 15 years in prison. The family said they were not informed of the proceedings and feared for Brenes' health because he suffers from diabetic neuropathy.
The Court called on the Nicaraguan government to protect the lives of the couple and other political prisoners and provide information about their whereabouts. The Nicaraguan government has not replied.
Brenes is not the only ex-Sandinista who has disappeared.
Victor Boitano, 65, the son of an Italian father and a Nicaraguan mother, joined the guerrilla movement at the age of 12, inspired by the example of his mother, who was tortured by the Somoza dictatorship for her political activism. During the revolution, he trained at military academies and rose to the rank of colonel in the Army, but retired in 2007 and began to accuse the Sandinista government of corruption and political crimes.
In April 2024, armed police and plainclothes officers arrested him without a warrant at his home in Managua, said his wife, Eugenia Valle, who witnessed the event and says she was hit by an officer during her husband's arrest. He disappeared into the prison system. Valle went from one prison to the next trying to find him, but said the guards always directed her elsewhere.
The Nicaraguan Presidency, Interior Ministry, Attorney General's Office and the Army did not respond to a series of detailed questions regarding Boitano's case.
Six months after his disappearance, Valle fled the country after her housekeeper called her and told her there were some 30 police officers surrounding her house.
Now in exile in Italy, she said she barely sleeps three hours a night and is racked by worry over the fate of her husband, who suffers from hypertension and diabetes.
"We don't know what's happening, how he is, or where he is," said Valle. "No one has seen him in more than two years." REUTERS

(DHA Photo)
Turkish authorities on Oct. 14 appointed a state trustee to the pro-opposition news channel Halk TV, with the police raiding its headquarters and halting its live broadcasts.
Officers from the Financial Crimes Investigation Board (MASAK) searched the building in Istanbul’s Zeytinburnu district for evidence, while riot police cordoned off the surrounding area.
A statement from the Istanbul Chief Prosecutor’s Office said an investigation was launched into Halk TV chairman Cafer Mahiroğlu over allegations of bid rigging, bribery and money laundering.
Detention warrants were issued against 17 suspects and 11 of them were taken into custody, the statement said.
Mahiroğlu was not among those detained as he lives abroad.
Citing financial records obtained from MASAK, confidential witness testimony and suspect statements, the prosecutors said an analysis of the financial data found that companies linked to Mahiroğlu as a shareholder or executive had a combined transaction volume of 30.35 billion Turkish Liras.
Prosecutors also alleged that Mahiroğlu had used his connections at the İzmir Municipality to facilitate the establishment of BUSTECH Vehicle Maintenance and Repair Services Inc., appointed individuals to run the company and secured illicit gains through transactions related to municipal tenders.
Authorities seized companies co-owned or managed by Mahiroğlu and placed them under the administration of government-appointed trustees, the prosecutor’s office said.
He had previously come under scrutiny over alleged interference in public procurement procedures. Prosecutors subsequently opened a separate investigation into him following statements by Turkish businessman Aziz İhsan Aktaş and further inquiries.
“Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted,” the channel wrote on X shortly before 7 a.m. (04:00 GMT).
Halk’s news channel and the live broadcasts on its YouTube site were both offline.
“Today is a dark day for Türkiye. The public’s right to information is being seized for political reasons,” said Mahiroğlu in a video on X in which he said seven of his family members were among those detained.
The move drew a furious reaction from the main opposition New Party and press groups.
New Party leader Özgür Özel lashed out against a TV channel “watched by millions,” describing the action as “weak.”
The Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party) co-chair Tülay Hatimoğulları called for the decision to be “immediately” reversed.
The Halk TV chair, meanwhile, held the opposition Republican People’s Party (CHP) leader Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu responsible for the operation.
Özel had resigned from the CHP and founded a new party in August after being removed from the party leadership through a court ruling that reinstated Kılıçdaroğlu as chairman.
Halk TV sided with Özel in the aftermath of the split, airing programs that sharply criticized Kılıçdaroğlu.
In an interview four days ago, Kılıçdaroğlu criticized Mahiroğlu for living abroad despite operating a television channel in Türkiye.
In response to Mahiroğlu’s allegations, the CHP said its commitment to the rule of law did not vary depending on the individuals or institutions involved.
“Halk TV must be allowed to continue broadcasting; you cannot put an end to its broadcasting operations. Legal scrutiny must be carried out, but restrictions imposed on press freedom are unacceptable,” the party said.

AI generated
LONDON – British actor and comedian Russell Brand, once one of Britain’s most high-profile broadcasters, was a ruthless sexual predator who raped or abused six women despite their protestations to satisfy his voracious sexual appetite, prosecutors said on Oct 14.
Brand, 51, the former husband of US singer Katy Perry, is on trial facing three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault relating to six women from 1999 to 2009.
He denies all the accusations and will set out his defence in court at a later date.
“Today I feel blessed,” he said as he arrived at London’s Southwark Crown Court. “I feel of course concerned but hopeful that this process will lead to good outcomes for everybody involved.”
Desire was indiscriminate, prosecutor tells court
Opening the case against him, prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones said some of the six women who had made the allegations had protested against, while others had no opportunity to react to his advances. It had made no difference to Brand, she said.
“His desire, his strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious,” the prosecutor said.
Although he could be funny, charming and likeable when he wanted something, he also had a childlike expectation that his every desire should be met, she added.
“He was ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative and, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator,” Karmy-Jones said.
The alleged offences took place over a decade as he progressed from gigs as a stand-up comedian to a TV presenter, actor and Hollywood movie star, she said.
Brand says never engaged in non-consensual activity
The first is alleged to have occurred in 1999 when he was performing in a show on the fringe of the Labour Party Conference in Bournemouth.
The first complainant, who had watched the show and had assumed Brand was gay, said he had raped her in her hotel room where she had invited him because she thought he was interested in a cause she had been talking to him about.
One of his co-performers at that show said Brand had bragged that he had wanted to bed 5,000 women in his lifetime, the prosecutor said.
In 2001, he is accused of trying to drag a woman into a toilet cubicle at MTV Europe where she worked. Three years later, a woman said he had dragged her into a toilet cubicle in a bar before orally raping her.
Around the same time in 2004 or 2005, a woman working at a media company said he indecently assaulted her at her office.
The fifth complainant, a fan, had consensual sex at his home in 2009 but then he anally raped her, the prosecutor said. The sixth complainant, who worked for Channel 4, alleges Brand had demanded a massage and then pressed his face into her groin area, in the same year.
When interviewed by police, Brand declined to answer questions but provided written statements in which he said he did not remember the incidents, had never engaged in non-consensual activity and accepted that he had had sex in toilet cubicles during parties, Karmy-Jones said.
Woman came forward after TV programme
The women involved did not know each other and had not taken the matter to the police at the time for various reasons, but came forward with complaints following a TV programme and a press report in 2023 in which anonymous allegations were made by other women, the prosecutor said.
Brand sat in the dock wearing a dark suit and thin, white scarf, staring forward intently.
His trial is expected to last about six weeks, has attracted huge media attention, with a second court opened to allow more journalists to attend and many outlets running daily podcasts.
The comedian, known for his flamboyant style and appearance, became famous in Britain before starring in a number of films including Get Him To The Greek in 2010, the same year he married Perry. They divorced in 2012.
More recently, Brand has mainly appeared in online broadcasts, with content often focused on US politics, religion and free speech. REUTERS

The proposed changes cover three pension schemes and the National Social Assistance Programme under the rural development ministry.
NEW DELHI: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Wednesday approved the renaming of the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) and several of its sub-schemes, including those named after former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.The Cabinet also approved the continuation of NSAP for five years, from 2026-27 to 2030-31, with a total outlay of Rs 53,428 crore.Here are the approved name changes and details of the schemes:
National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana. Launched on August 15, 1995, the programme provides social security assistance to poor and vulnerable households.
Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Vridhavastha Pension Yojana. The scheme provides monthly financial assistance to eligible elderly people from below poverty line (BPL) households.
Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme (IGNWPS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Vidhawa Pension Yojana. It provides financial assistance to eligible widows from BPL households.
Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme (IGNDPS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Divyangjan Pension Yojana. The scheme provides monthly pension assistance to eligible persons with disabilities from BPL households.
National Family Benefit Scheme (NFBS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Parivar Labh Yojana. The scheme provides financial assistance to eligible households following the death of the primary breadwinner.
Alse read: Diwali bonanza for railway staff: 78-day bonus cleared for 11.4 lakh employeesChanges to disability pensionAlongside the renaming, the Cabinet approved changes to the disability pension scheme. Monthly assistance will increase to Rs 375 for beneficiaries aged 0-79 years and Rs 625 for those aged 80 and above.The minimum benchmark disability requirement will be reduced from 80% to 40%, while the minimum age criterion will be removed, making individuals eligible for assistance from birth, subject to the scheme's other conditions.The Cabinet said the old-age and widow pension schemes, along with the family benefit scheme, would continue in their existing form.
A total of 3.20 crore beneficiaries across all 36 states and Union territories are expected to benefit from the approval.
Guidelines covering the revised eligibility criteria, beneficiary coverage and assistance under the disability pension scheme will be issued and implemented within three months.The programme was launched to fulfil the Central government's responsibility under Article 41 of the Constitution's Directive Principles of State Policy, which concerns public assistance in cases including old age, sickness and disability.Also read: IDBI Bank stake sale; Rs 53,428 crore welfare package- key decisions by Union cabinet

Western sanctions increase risk of satellite collisions — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:03:55 UTC
19:03:55 KST

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. The sanctions regime imposed by the European Union and the United States on Russia and other nations is increasing the risk of spacecraft collisions as satellite constellations expand, Yelena Pavlova, Chief Designer of a component of the Russian Automated Warning System on Hazardous Situations in Outer Space (ASPOS OKP), told TASS.
"Large low-Earth orbit satellite constellations are being expanded primarily by the Americans and the Chinese. While the Americans ensure collision safety for their own and European spacecraft (Starlink performed over 350,000 collision-avoidance maneuvers last year), they do not coordinate satellite trajectories with the Chinese or with the operators of the Rassvet satellites. This is a direct result of the sanctions policy pursued by the US and EU against 'unfriendly' Eastern states. Consequently, the simultaneous growth of these constellations significantly raises the probability of collisions due to the absence of universally accepted space traffic management rules," Pavlova noted.
According to her, the "layers" of the US military constellations Starshield and SDA pose a distinct threat. The US Space Command does not publish their orbital data, which also creates conditions for potential collisions with other space objects, the expert believes.

Poroshenko named opposition leader, European Solidarity rated least negatively among Rada factions – KMIS poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:02:32 EEST
19:02:32 KST

The European Solidarity party faction in the current 9th convocation of the Verkhovna Rada holds the highest public performance ratings among Ukrainians, although negative evaluations outweigh positive ones across all parliamentary political forces, according to the results of a nationwide public opinion poll conducted by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KMIS) between September 12 and 21. Commissioned by Forum NGO, the survey included questions assessing the performance of parliamentary factions and identifying perceived opposition leaders.
Some 38% of respondents believe the European Solidarity faction's activities benefit Ukraine, compared to 43% who believe they hinder development. In September 2025, 38% considered the faction's activities beneficial and 36% viewed them as a hindrance.
The Holos party faction follows in the rankings: 30% of respondents consider its activities beneficial to Ukraine, while 31% hold the opposite view. Ratings have slightly worsened compared to September 2025, when 33% noted benefits and 27% cited hindrances.
Meanwhile, 22% of respondents consider the Servant of the People faction's activities beneficial, while 66% believe its actions hinder state development (compared to 52% last year).
Similar negative trends are evident for the Batkivshchyna All-Ukrainian Union faction, whose activities are deemed beneficial by 21%, while 68% view them as hindering state development (up from 48% in September 2025).
Regarding Platform for Life and Peace group, 16% believe its activities benefit Ukraine, while 43% disagree. This represents no significant change compared to September 2025.
Overall, a majority of respondents (64%) positively evaluate the performance of at least one faction from the list, up from 59% in September 2025.
Respondents were also asked to identify the leader of the opposition in Ukraine; a majority (68%) were able to select a public figure from a list of six politicians. The largest relative share pointed to European Solidarity leader and MP Petro Poroshenko (30%). He is followed by MP Dmytro Razumkov (11%), volunteer and public figure Serhiy Prytula (8%), and Batkivshchyna leader and MP Yulia Tymoshenko (6%). MPs Yuriy Boiko and former Presidential Office advisor Oleksiy Arestovych were each named by 3% of respondents.
An additional 11% believe there is no genuine opposition in Ukraine (down from 16% in February). Compared to February, the shares of respondents naming Poroshenko (previously 24%) and Razumkov (previously 7%) increased, while metrics for other figures remained unchanged.
Commenting on the survey results, KMIS Executive Director Anton Hrushetsky noted that the crisis of trust in parliament among Ukrainians persists. "In effect, Ukrainians believe the parliament is more of a hindrance than a contributor to the country's development. Naturally, the critical attitude of Ukrainians toward the Verkhovna Rada and parliamentary political forces is not new... But during wartime, this situation is particularly alarming. It is especially critical that in the case of the Servant of the People faction—which forms the basis of the coalition and the current government—those who believe its actions hinder development outnumber those who see it as contributing by a factor of three," he stated.
Hrushetsky emphasized that the Verkhovna Rada is expected to pass necessary legislation to secure funding from Western partners and demonstrate Ukraine's fulfillment of European integration obligations, noting that opposition MPs must also demonstrate their responsibility.
The survey was conducted via telephone interviews (CATI) using a random sample of mobile phone numbers across all government-controlled regions among 1,002 respondents aged 18 and older. Under normal conditions, the formal statistical margin of error for such a sample (with a 0.95 probability and design effect of 1.3) does not exceed 4.1% for indicators near 50% and 1.8% for indicators near 5%, though wartime conditions introduce additional systematic deviation.

Nearly 200 high schools across France were expected to remain closed Wednesday amid continuing student blockades, as the government pledged proposals to improve university admissions.

Several schools remained blockaded in Paris, including Voltaire, Helene-Boucher, and the Balzac school complex. Balzac’s administration suspended in-person classes, citing access difficulties and safety concerns. 
Geffray said Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste would submit proposals to improve Parcoursup, France’s university admissions platform, to the prime minister by the end of October.

Despite Middle East war, Egypt remittances hit record $33.9bn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:01:21 UTC
19:01:21 KST

Breadcrumb
Despite Middle East war, Egypt remittances hit record $33.9bn
Remittances from Egyptians working abroad reached a record $33.9 billion in the first eight months of 2026, according to the Central Bank of Egypt.
The figure was 27.2% higher than the $26.6 billion recorded during the same period last year, an increase of about $7.3 billion.
The total between January and August has already exceeded the $29.6 billion received during the whole of 2024 and is approaching the $41.5 billion recorded across 2025.
Remittances reached about $4.2 billion in August alone, up 21.7% from $3.5 billion in the same month last year.
However, the monthly figure was about $300 million lower than in July, when inflows reached approximately $4.5 billion.
The latest figures continue a sharp recovery in money sent home by Egyptians overseas.
During the first eight months of 2025, remittances had risen 47.2% year-on-year, from $18.1 billion to $26.6 billion.
The increase followed a period in which Egypt's foreign currency shortage and a large gap between official and parallel exchange rates had pushed some overseas Egyptians away from formal banking channels.
Egypt moved to a more flexible exchange-rate regime in March 2024, allowing the value of the pound to be determined more closely by market forces.
The International Monetary Fund said remittances rose 62% year-on-year during the second quarter of 2024 and 85% in the third quarter after the official and parallel foreign exchange markets converged.
The currency shift formed part of a wider $8 billion IMF programme agreed in 2024.
For the whole of 2025, remittances reached $41.5 billion, up 40.5% from the previous year.
They totalled $36.5 billion during the 2024-25 financial year, according to Central Bank balance-of-payments figures.
The remittances surplus stood at $36.3 billion during that financial year, while Egypt's current-account deficit fell to $15.4 billion.
Remittances are a major source of foreign currency for Egypt, alongside exports, tourism, Suez Canal revenues and investment.
The Central Bank did not provide a breakdown of the countries from which the latest transfers were sent or the channels used to send them.

EU proposes delaying methane rules for oil and gas imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:01:15 UTC
19:01:15 KST

Concerns over Europe’s energy supplies have prompted the European Commission to seek a one-year postponement of new environmental requirements for foreign fuel suppliers, Reuters reported.
The rules, originally scheduled to take effect January 1, 2027, would require companies supplying oil and gas to the European Union to monitor and report methane emissions.
Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas and the second-largest contributor to climate change after carbon dioxide.
Under the proposed changes, importers would have until May 31, 2029, to demonstrate that their 2028 imports complied with EU methane monitoring and reporting requirements.
Suppliers outside the EU would be responsible for providing the necessary emissions information.
“This one-year postponement of the import-related rules is designed to help avoid further pressure on the security of supply of imported fossil fuels in the current geopolitical context,” the Commission said in a statement.
The proposal follows pressure from the United States and France, which have raised concerns about possible disruptions to Europe’s energy supplies.
The war in Iran has already affected global energy markets, increasing uncertainty about fuel availability ahead of winter.
In June, the United States, Europe’s largest supplier of liquefied natural gas, warned that the regulations could interfere with deliveries.
French President Emmanuel Macron also raised concerns in September, writing to Commission President Ursula von der Leyen about potential legal risks for European importers.
Supporters of the delay argue that foreign suppliers are not prepared to meet the requirements and could avoid the European market rather than risk financial penalties.
The postponement still requires approval from EU member states and the European Parliament.

Millions of European households could face greater difficulty paying their heating bills in the coming months as fuel prices remain high, European Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen warned.
Europe is not facing an energy supply shortage, but rising prices are placing significant pressure on household finances, he said.
Diesel prices have doubled since February, when U.S. strikes on Iran prompted Tehran to close the Strait of Hormuz. Gas prices have increased by 140 percent.
“It is a very serious situation we are in. And unfortunately, it will only become more serious in the coming months,” Jørgensen said.
He noted that even during an average winter, 47 million Europeans struggle to heat their homes adequately, sometimes having to choose between heating and food.
Energy costs are expected to feature prominently at this week’s EU summit in Brussels.
The European Commission has already proposed targeted financial support for vulnerable households and businesses.
Other measures under consideration include joint energy purchases, releasing oil reserves and delaying parts of EU methane regulations.
Germany, Spain and Italy are pushing for a common windfall tax on energy companies’ unusually high profits.
Although the Commission does not plan to propose an EU-wide tax, Jørgensen said it could help individual countries introduce one.
He also encouraged governments to lower electricity taxes, as Denmark has done, saying this could reduce household energy bills by an average of 14 percent.
Jørgensen said Europe’s long-term response must focus on reducing fossil fuel imports and expanding domestic renewable energy production.
“We must not backtrack on the green agenda. We need to secure more green energy,” he said.

Into the fire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:01:00 KST

In August 2014, ISIS swept into Sinjar, a town in northern Iraq and home to many of the country’s Yazidis, a Kurdish-speaking ethnic and religious minority long subjected to persecution. Regarding the Yazidis as infidels, ISIS killed thousands and enslaved thousands of women and girls, in what is now widely recognised as genocide.
The short documentary Into the Fire follows Hana Khider, a Yazidi woman who heads an all-female de-mining team. Khider works for the Mines Advisory Group, one of the founding members of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, which shared the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize with its coordinator, Jody Williams. The perilous work of Khider’s crew consists of searching for and deactivating hidden explosives left by ISIS, some disguised as everyday objects, including children’s toys. Directed by the British filmmaker Orlando von Einsiedel, the film moves between Khider’s job and her life as a wife and mother, showing two sides of caring for one’s community and rebuilding after the trauma of the genocide.
The film is part of von Einsiedel’s five-part series produced in collaboration with the Nobel Prize and National Geographic, with each instalment focusing on the continuing influence of a different peace laureate.
