`123456’ password used in massive Danish CPR data breach
At least three accounts at the company linked to a major breach of Denmark’s CPR register reportedly used the password “123456”, including an administrator account.
At least three user accounts at the Funen-based IT company Pays used the password “123456” when hackers gained access to Denmark’s CPR register, Politiken reports.
One of them was the company’s administrator account.
The breach exposed information linked to around 8.8 million CPR numbers. The CPR system is Denmark’s central civil registration database and contains personal information on people living or previously registered in Denmark.
The newspaper Politiken reviewed data from the breach that the hacker allegedly used to gain access to the system.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor at Aarhus University’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, described the company’s password security as “hopeless”.
“There is really no security, it is an open door. A password like ‘123456’ is one of the very first things you would guess if you took a list of common passwords,” he told Politiken.
“I find it hard to see that you could have worse security. It was a matter of time before things went wrong.”
Pays ApS, based in Odense, confirmed to TV 2 on Friday that it was the company whose access had been compromised.
“We can confirm that we are the company that has been subjected to an attack where our legal access to search for information in the CPR system has been abused,” managing director and owner Sophie Laursen said in an email to TV 2.
The hacker had access to the CPR register from 10 September for a total of 21 days and 17 hours.
An anonymous hacker told Politiken on Thursday that they were behind the attack and claimed gaining access had not been particularly difficult.
According to the hacker, access was initially obtained using a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company. The hacker then allegedly created two computer programs to retrieve information from the CPR system and store it externally.
The hacker told Politiken that there were no plans to sell or publish the information.
Private companies and associations can be granted access to information in Denmark’s CPR register when they have a legitimate need, for example to obtain address information about customers or members.
According to Denmark’s Central Business Register, Pays ApS had two employees as of July 2026.
One in four Danish driving penalty points linked to mobile phone use
Danish motorists received almost 21,000 penalty points for using handheld mobile phones while driving last year – the highest number in four years.
Mobile phones are playing a growing role in traffic offences in Denmark.
In 2025, motorists received 20,910 penalty points on their driving licences for using a handheld mobile phone behind the wheel, according to figures from the police case management system POLSAS.
That means mobile phone use accounted for roughly one in every four of the 84,056 penalty points issued for traffic offences during the year.
The number of mobile-related penalty points increased by 7.5 percent compared with 2024 and reached its highest level in four years.
On average, police issued 57 penalty points every day for handheld mobile phone use.
Britta Bjerregaard, claims director at insurance company Alm. Brand, described the development as deeply concerning.
“Most people know full well that the phone should stay put while driving. Still, it can be tempting to just answer a call, reply to a message, or change the song,” she said.
“Traffic does not pause while you look at the screen.”
89 metres without watching the road
The Danish Road Safety Council considers inattention one of the major risks on Danish roads, with mobile phones posing a particular problem.
“The mobile phone takes an incredible amount of attention if you use it behind the wheel,” deputy director Karina Petersen said.
“If you look at the screen for four seconds at country road speed, you are driving 89 metres blind.”
However, Petersen cautioned that the increase in recorded offences does not necessarily mean that more drivers are using their phones.
The rise could also reflect more police checks or improved camera equipment used for traffic enforcement.
What are the rules in Denmark?
Using a handheld mobile phone while driving in Denmark results in a DKK 1,500 fine and a penalty point on your driving licence. An additional DKK 1,000 contribution to the Victims’ Fund is also charged.
The rule applies even when the car is stationary in traffic or waiting at a red light.
Drivers may briefly operate a phone if it is securely mounted, and using a vehicle’s built-in screen is also permitted.
The ban on handheld mobile phone use also applies to cyclists, electric scooter users and drivers of other motorised vehicles.

Hacker retained access to Danish CPR register for nearly 22 days before breach was discovered
An unauthorized user had access to Denmark’s national Civil Registration System (CPR) for nearly 22 days before authorities discovered the security breach, according to documents obtained by TV 2.
The access began September 10 and was stopped October 2, lasting 21 days and 17 hours.
However, preliminary investigations suggest the unauthorized activity ended September 20, approximately 10 days after it began, according to a report submitted by the CPR office to the Danish Data Protection Agency.
The Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization announced Monday that personal information belonging to approximately 8.8 million people had been exposed, including names, addresses and CPR identification numbers.
The breach occurred through a small Danish company with legitimate access to the register.
According to DR, the company is based on Funen and shares ownership and an address with a larger business. Its identity has not been publicly confirmed.
Authorities discovered the incident after receiving an unusually large invoice for searches conducted through the company’s account.
Approximately 14 million CPR searches had been made using its access credentials.
“The number far exceeds the company’s customer base, and the company has indicated that they did not perform the lookups themselves,” the CPR office stated in its report.
Private companies and organizations can pay to access certain CPR information.
Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates party acknowledged that security measures had been inadequate.
She has requested a security review of the register following the breach.
The company had not responded to DR’s requests for comment as of Friday morning.

Sardines have attracted attention for their omega-3 fatty acids, collagen and protein.
However, dermatologist and researcher Cæcilie Johansen cautioned that evidence linking sardine consumption directly to healthier skin remains limited.

Johansen emphasized that avoiding smoking, limiting alcohol and using sunscreen are more important measures for protecting skin health.

The applications had been placed on hold September 7 while authorities investigated the problem.

During its review, police restored 43 decisions that had been removed from the Criminal Register earlier than they should have been.
Those decisions were relevant to child protection certificates.
The ministry has not specified how many citizenship, permanent residence or family reunification applications were affected by the suspension.

Prosecutors challenged that decision, but the Eastern High Court reached the same conclusion Friday.

Once police complete their investigation, prosecutors will determine whether there is sufficient evidence to bring criminal charges before a court.

A fire in a railway signaling cabin near Aarup on Funen is causing major train disruptions across Denmark on Friday, with repairs potentially taking several weeks.

Government unveils security-focused budget proposal
The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.
Business groups warn 200 DKK cruise passenger tax could drive tourists away
Two Danish business organizations are warning that a proposed tax of 200 DKK per cruise passenger could lead cruise ships to skip Danish ports, reducing tourism revenue for cities and smaller destinations.
Dansk Industri (DI), the Confederation of Danish Industry, and Dansk Erhverv, a business organization representing companies across several sectors, are responding to the government’s proposal to introduce the tax from 2028.
“A cruise tax at this level will hit both the major cities and rural districts,” said Lars Bertolt Winther, head of tourism, culture and experiences at DI, in a press release.
Jesper Kronborg, industry director for transport at Dansk Erhverv, also criticized the proposal.
“In Dansk Erhverv’s view, it is a bad proposal, or at least a proposal that requires a very thorough analysis,” he said in a press release.
The government expects the tax to generate an additional 300 million DKK in annual revenue from 2028.
The aim is to make cruise tourism contribute more toward the costs associated with ships, including pollution, noise and congestion.
Figures from Statistics Denmark show that 1.1 million cruise passengers visited Denmark in 2025. The number of cruise ships calling at Danish ports increased by 16% compared with the previous year.
Copenhagen, Aarhus, Skagen and Rønne on the island of Bornholm are the country’s main cruise destinations. Together, they account for more than 98% of cruise passengers.
DI and Dansk Erhverv argue that cruise visitors generate local revenue through port fees and spending at shops and other businesses.
Both organizations point to Iceland, where a similar tax was introduced before being reduced.
“Following the introduction of a high passenger tax, bookings dropped significantly, especially to the smaller ports, and the tax was subsequently lowered to limit the damaging effects,” Winther said.
“There is no reason to believe that Denmark does not risk the same,” he added.
According to the industry organization Danske Havne, which represents Danish ports, Iceland now charges 85 DKK per cruise passenger, while Greenland charges 50 DKK.
Tine Kirk, director of Danske Havne, described the proposed Danish tax of 200 DKK as “unreasonably high.”
“The cruise ships can very easily opt out of Denmark. We fear that the shipping companies will either bypass Denmark completely or concentrate their port calls in the largest cities,” she said in a written comment.

Danish exports fell by 3.3 percent in August, driven in part by a decline in goods exports to the United States, according to Statistics Denmark.
Total exports of goods and services amounted to 194 billion DKK in August, down 3.3 percent from July. Goods exports fell by 6.2 percent, while services exports rose by 0.7 percent.
Søren Kristensen, chief economist at AL Sydbank, described the overall decline as “worryingly large”.
“But it is part of the story that a large part of the decline is concentrated around the US, where we also see fluctuations from month to month,” he wrote in a comment.
Exports of goods and services to both the US and the United Kingdom fell in August. Total exports to the US amounted to 31.7 billion DKK, down 2.8 billion DKK from July.
Goods exports to the US fell by 3.3 billion DKK, while services exports rose slightly.
Kristensen said fluctuations in the prices of products such as medicines sold by Danish companies in the US could partly explain the decline. He therefore cautioned against drawing too negative a conclusion from the latest figures alone.
The August decline followed an increase in exports in July. Overall, Danish exports of goods and services rose by nearly 19 billion DKK, or more than 10 percent, between August 2025 and August 2026.
According to Kristensen, Danish exports have so far held up despite geopolitical unrest, higher energy prices and rising interest rates.
Still, the August figures are bad news for the Danish economy when viewed in isolation.
“However, it will take several months of this development before we become worried,” Kristensen wrote.
Hacker claims simple password allowed access to 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers
An anonymous hacker has claimed responsibility for accessing nearly 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers, telling newspaper Politiken that a weak password made the breach possible.
CPR numbers are personal identification numbers used in Denmark’s national Civil Registration System to identify residents and access public services.
The hacker told Politiken that the breach occurred on September 11 through a small Danish company with access to the CPR register.
According to the hacker, a leaked password belonging to a former employee allowed entry into the system. The password was reportedly “123456.”
After gaining access, the hacker said they created two computer programs to retrieve CPR information and store it outside the system.
The person’s identity has not been made public, and their account has not been independently confirmed.
The hacker told Politiken they had no plans to sell or publish the personal identification numbers and were “really shocked” by the security weaknesses they encountered.
To describe the situation, the hacker compared it to someone leaving dangerous material unattended.
“Someone leaves a suitcase with 10 kilos of plutonium unattended at a train station. Then a homeless person steals it,” the hacker said.
“Yes, of course you shouldn’t steal other people’s suitcases. But you also shouldn’t leave nuclear material at a train station.”
The hacker provided Politiken with a file containing the CPR numbers.
The newspaper forwarded the file to Emil Hørning, an IT security expert at Danish cybersecurity company Defend Denmark.
Hørning said the hacker’s account appeared credible and that the described method was plausible.
Politiken conducted its interview with the hacker in English through an encrypted communication service.
Danish government proposes tighter senior pension rules to save 800 million DKK annually
The Danish government wants to change how workers qualify for senior pensions, potentially saving 800 million DKK annually by 2030, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Currently, people whose health limits their ability to work to 15 hours a week or less can receive a senior pension up to six years before reaching the state retirement age.
Their work capacity is assessed against their most recent job. Under the proposal, applicants would instead be assessed against all types of employment.
The Finance Ministry estimates savings of 200 million DKK in 2028, rising to 800 million DKK in 2030.
The proposal has divided political parties and organizations.
Anders Vistisen of DF, Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, said his party would oppose the changes.
“We are not going to cut for the worn-out,” he told Jyllands-Posten, citing Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen’s promises of more dignified retirement.
Ældre Sagen, Denmark’s senior citizens’ advocacy organization, also criticized the proposal.
Deputy Director Michael Teit Nielsen warned that applicants could face longer assessments to determine whether they could work in another profession.
However, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main employers’ association, welcomed the proposal.
Deputy CEO Søren Kryhlmand said assessing workers against the entire labor market would allow those capable of other jobs to remain employed.
The government also plans to increase the separate Arne early retirement pension by approximately 3,000 DKK monthly. Its current maximum is 15,650 DKK per month.
Changing the senior pension scheme, introduced in 2019, requires agreement among the parties behind it before a general election.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard is scheduled to present the budget proposal today.

Operation Vivaldi's 'Fourth Season' — Ukraine retakes another 101 square kilometers on Lyman front, Biletskyi says
Ukraine's Third Army Corps, together with its attached units, has retaken another 101 square kilometers during the fourth stage of Operation Vivaldi on the Lyman sector in Donetsk Oblast, the corps announced on Oct. 14.
Ukraine liberated the villages of Zelena Dolyna, Lypove, and Kolodiazi, while Russia lost about 3,000 of its soldiers in the fourth stage of the operation, the corps reported on Telegram.

In Defense of the Disney Adult
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Disney Adults are so easy to tease. People think they’re immature, embarrassing, cringe.
As such, jokes about people who enjoy visiting Disney parks annually (or even multiple times a year) run rampant on social media. Satirized as being mentally stuck in elementary school and shamed for spending exorbitant amounts of money on their Disney fix, “Disney Adult " has become the punchline de jour for someone who needs to grow up and get a life.
In their park of choice—whether it’s Magic Kingdom, Epcot, Animal Kingdom, or Hollywood Studios—Disney Adults typically wear some sort of Disney-coded costume or outfit meticulously coordinated with an on-theme Loungefly backpack and mouse ears.
Disney Adults are blasted for constantly returning to “the most magical place on Earth,” and their slanderers believe those travel funds should be spent on “real” vacations. Where? Literally anywhere else. The most outrageous of culprits? A Disney Adult who enjoys the Disney bubble… without any children.
But in defense of the oft-ridiculed Disney Adult, why put a price on someone else’s joy, especially if you’re not the one bankrolling it?
I’ll admit it: I am a Disney Adult. You know what, I’m proud of it. I grew up during the Disney Renaissance era and still never miss a new release, collect merch (especially ornaments), and will dress my dog as Buzz Lightyear from Toy Story this Halloween. When I’m super bored, I check the wait times for rides while I’m on my couch thousands of miles away instead of doomscrolling. I’m confident in enjoying whatever makes me happy, and I choose to invest in my joy.
And yes, I am the dreaded Disney Adult without children. For one birthday in particular, I skipped through the park on my way to see the “Happily Ever After” fireworks wearing light-up Tinkerbell wings, accompanied only by my friend of the same age.
And I’d do it again in a heartbeat.
I agree with the sentiment of many Disney Adults I’ve encountered about why they keep returning. A trip to Walt Disney World feels familiar and welcoming, and it helps people reconnect with their childhood and revisit a time when they felt carefree. And with new attractions and experiences constantly being added, Walt Disney World offers nostalgia with a chance to make new memories every time.
In my opinion, Disney Adults are no different than the passionate members of any other fandom. I feel authorized to speak on this from the vantage point of a kid who practically grew up at Yankee Stadium.
My dad worked at the home of the New York Yankees for 47 years. He started as a pre-teen selling Cracker Jacks in the stands while growing up in the South Bronx. And when he later worked in finance, he kept his part-time job at the stadium doing inventory, making all of the night and weekend games for as long as I can remember.
As a stadium kid (and lifelong Yankees fan), I’ve seen the most diehard Yankees fans spend thousands on season tickets and coveted World Series seats with hopes of seeing the Bronx Bombers win at home. Fans drop real money for endless rounds of pricey stadium beer just to be “in the building.” And for this fanaticism, people barely bat an eye.
Throughout my life, I’ve seen these fans praised for their dedication to Yankee Blue and for having the means to own season tickets. When fans show off extensive baseball card collections or take selfies from expensive seats, they get praise, not ridicule. But if a Disney Adult displays a vast collection of limited-edition mouse ears, the collective eye roll feels palpable. As someone who goes to Walt Disney World often (more than twice a year if timing and budget align), I’m used to snarky responses when I say I’m going to Disney: “Again?”
Yes, again. Because it brings me joy, and it’s currently hard out here for a whimsical millennial.
But unlike being a Disney Adult, there’s a harsh reality to being an avid fan of a specific sports team: the constant possibility of a brutal loss. When purchasing pricey tickets for a sporting event, there’s a chance that your beloved team will lose, that you’ll leave the stadium devastated, and with a lot less cash.
When investing in a Disney trip, however, winning or losing isn’t on the line. There’s a high likelihood of having a great experience if a traveler leans into the tried-and-true activities that have historically been fun experiences for them. The guarantee of making happy memories is priceless.
Just as there’s no one way to be a sports fan, Disney Adults are not a one-size-fits-all monolith. Yes, some people spend cash on annual passes, endless Lightning Lanes to skip long lines, and enjoy character dining. But there are also so many ways to experience Walt Disney World without even setting foot in the parks.
On my last trip to the House of Mouse, I spent a lot of time at the BoardWalk, an area that connects Disney’s Yacht and Beach Club resorts that doesn’t require a ticket. I watched the Magic Kingdom fireworks on the beach with my toes nestled in the sand and far away from crowds. In another effort to avoid large crowds, I enjoyed a paint-and-sip class at Coronado Springs Resort and got a souvenir only I could make. On future trips, I’m hoping to explore a dog-friendly resort where I can bring my Buzz Lightyear pup, and plan a visit tailored for my mother, a senior who wouldn’t be able to walk endlessly in the Orlando heat. We often talk about when she took me to Disney for the first time for my fourth birthday, and all of the changes since then. For her, Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge will be a must.
Perhaps most importantly, I feel safe at Disney. Although I am alert to any dangers, I feel relatively confident that I can walk through the parks without enduring any catcalling or anyone spiking my drink. Which brings me to another plus for going to Disney so much: I can have a blast with a non-alcoholic drink, and no one’s going to judge me.
Do I like to travel to places other than Walt Disney World? Yes. I love exploring the Caribbean in particular, where I immerse myself in water activities and learn about the cultures. When I travel to Europe, I tend to take cathedral tours in whatever area I’m traveling in. Despite the stereotype, Disney Adults can have multiple interests. Still, that doesn’t make me feel guilty for the giddiness I feel the moment I step onto the green carpet at Orlando International Airport, knowing that a shuttle is about to transport me into the peace of the Disney bubble.
Everyone has their idea of fun that offers a means of escape. As long as it’s safe, why stigmatize someone for it?
Disney Adults may be “cringe.” We’re an easy mark. But I can guarantee that not one of us will think twice about returning to a place we love.
Life’s tough, and there’s nothing wrong with enjoying some magic every now and then.

The raid on Ilhan Omar’s house is dangerous political theater | Moira Donegan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

On Monday, federal agents from the Department of Homeland Security raided the Washington DC area home of Ilhan Omar, a Minnesota congresswoman and a progressive Democrat, in the latest instance of Donald Trump’s effort to weaponize the national security state to harass, punish and embarrass his political opponents.
The raid, which was approved by a judge after a reportedly extensive back-and-forth with federal security officials, was nominally carried out in connection with a spurious criminal investigation into Omar’s childhood immigration to the US.
In reality, the episode is best understood as a bit of political theater. It was meant to embarrass Omar, a Black, immigrant Muslim woman in Congress whose ascent to national political prominence has become a symbol to the Maga right of the resentments and threats posed by pluralism.
It was meant to cast an air of suspicion and criminality over the Democratic candidates who, like Omar, are facing the voters in a matter of weeks.
It was meant to make the president seem strong and appease the racist impulses of his base as his party faces down what is expected to be a trouncing in November’s midterm elections.
And it was meant to convey, both to this wavering base and to the nation at large, the Maga movement’s vision of law and citizenship, which the president views not as guarantors of dignity in a liberal democracy, but as tools to enforce racial hierarchy within a much narrower and more punitive white nationalist project.
Let’s be clear: there is no evidence to support the allegation, which the raid on Monday was nominally meant to investigate, that Omar or her family committed immigration fraud when they came to the US as refugees in the late 1980s, when Omar was a child.
But just because something isn’t true has never stopped the Maga movement from repeating it. Both the conspiracist cesspool of the far-right internet and its denizens who now have places of prominence in the Republican party have repeatedly and falsely claimed that Omar is not a legitimate citizen.
“We actually think that Ilhan Omar definitely committed immigration fraud,” said JD Vance, the vice-president – who once claimed, falsely, that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, were eating neighbors’ pets, and then defended his tendency to “create stories” about immigrants – on a podcast.
For his part, Trump seems to be particularly repulsed by Omar, the first Somali-American in Congress, and has been smearing, attacking and threatening her for the better part of a decade.
He has lately expanded his hate to all of Omar’s fellow Somali immigrants, complaining just days before the raid on Omar’s home that “the once great state of Minnesota is being taken over by Somali immigrants” and calling on non-Somali Minnesotans to “fight back”. Omar has previously faced threats and attacks in the wake of Trump’s comments about her.
The raid is probably intended to make the Trump administration seem fearsome and all-powerful, prompting acquiescence from institutions and frenzied satisfaction from his base in the style that was seen in the first months of 2025, immediately following Trump’s return to power.
This, at least, seems to be the idea behind Trump’s repeated attacks on Omar at campaign rallies this week; at one, the crowd responded to the president’s jeers about Omar by chanting “Deport! Deport! Deport!”
The scene evoked the signs at the 2024 Republican national convention, where Trump’s party rallied delegates with promises of mass ethnic cleansing and members of the crowd held signs aloft reading “MASS DEPORTATION NOW.”
But it’s unclear whether this promise of racist libidinal gratification will be enough to motivate Trump’s 2024 supporters to get out to the polls in November – especially since many of them will have to pay upwards of $5 a gallon for the gas they need to get there.
But if we can interpret the Trump administration’s decision to raid Omar’s home as a cynical campaign tactic, the evident weakness of the ploy should not confuse us to the seriousness and degradation of Trump’s moral project.
Omar, after all, is not just a congresswoman: to the Trump world, she is a symbol. Born in Mogadishu, Somalia, in 1982, Omar was barely out of infancy when her family fled the Somali civil war for a Kenyan refugee camp, and was still small when they settled in Minneapolis, the city that Omar now represents in Congress.
One would be hard pressed to find a more aggressively wholesome and picturesque story of the promise of American equality: that a child from a faraway country can come here and become a full and valued member of her community, can in fact come to represent her city in Congress on an equal footing as those who were born here – that their citizenship has no caveats or conditions on account of their race or origin – is both America’s greatest achievement and also the reality that the Trump movement emerged to eradicate.
If there’s a “fraud” that Trump and his cronies see in Omar, it might not be a literal immigration violation, as they claim, but something more abstract and spiritual. The “fraud” to them, is in Omar’s claim to the dignity of equal citizenship; in the idea that a woman, born in Somalia, might be as equally and powerfully American as they are.
- Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

VisionQuest Puts a Frustratingly Conventional End to Marvel’s WandaVision Trilogy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

The marriage of Disney+ and the Marvel Cinematic Universe seemed, at first, to be a perfect match. WandaVision, the high-concept miniseries that placed Wanda Maximoff (Elizabeth Olsen) and her beloved synthezoid the Vision (Paul Bettany) in a succession of retro sitcoms and challenged viewers to figure out what was actually happening beyond the suburban veneer, kicked off the venture in 2021 with huge audiences and near-unanimous critical praise. But it ended in the same predictable, digitally enhanced battle as every other MCU mediocrity. With a few fun exceptions, like this year’s renewed-then-canceled Wonder Man and the witchy 2024 WandaVision sequel Agatha All Along, the returns have been diminishing ever since. So it’s not particularly surprising that Disney seems to be paring back its small-screen Marvel offerings.
To understand what went wrong, you need only watch the first episode of VisionQuest, the final installment of the WandaVision trilogy. It begins with Bettany narrating a summary of Vision’s MCU storyline, from his origin as the creation of sociopathic supervillain Ultron and education in humanity at the hands of Avengers Bruce Banner and Tony Stark to his annihilation by Thanos and resurrection as a projection of Wanda’s mourning, that will only make sense to viewers who’ve followed that saga for more than a decade. Soon, it’s introducing a bunch of anthropomorphized AIs (Orla Brady’s F.R.I.D.A.Y., Emily Hampshire’s E.D.I.T.H., James D’Arcy’s J.A.R.V.I.S.) that have their own franchise backstories. Less than 15 minutes in, Vision is sitting in a cinema, within his own robotic mind, brooding over memories of Wanda. The story is so unwieldy, at this point, it’s impossible to follow without constant reminders of what came before. Yet the VisionQuest narrative is too emotionally simplistic and stylistically conventional, particularly compared to the two previous parts of the trilogy, to merit all that remembering.
Annihilated for the second time with the collapse of Wanda’s grief fantasia, the Vision has been rebuilt—“same body, different mind,” he tells us, meaning that he no longer has the capacity for love that once bound him to her and the sons, Tommy and Billy, she conjured. In the physical world, he’s in hiding as a human barback at a Scottish pub with relevance to Wanda-Vision romance lore. But his more vivid existence is a life of the (artificial) mind, where he retreats to a sort of Beaux-Arts-meets-midcentury-modern country estate populated by autonomous AIs. While J.A.R.V.I.S. and F.R.I.D.A.Y. lead the virtual household, or Mindspace, “recreational AI” E.D.I.T.H. provides comic relief, crashing through skylights with daredevil stunts.
Everyone seems a bit aimless now that Vision is serving beers instead of fighting to save the human race. It gives him time to stew on the loss of his emotions and relationships, to contemplate the extent to which he is and isn’t the same synthezoid who loved his family. His ennui may also be the only plausible explanation for his potentially catastrophic choice to keep Ultron (James Spader) alive, imprisoned in an isolated tower in Vision’s memory palace.
Physical reality disrupts Vision’s Tin-Man-esque, if-I-only-had-a-heart wistfulness when a fearsome bounty hunter, Paladin (Todd Stashwick), is hired to apprehend him. It also brings to his attention the existence—and Paladin-related peril—of one Thomas Shepherd (Ruaridh Mollica), a troubled young man in London whom we’re never really given a reason to doubt is a version of Tommy Maximoff. (If you want to know what became of Billy Maximoff, watch Agatha All Along, which remains an ideal Halloween-season binge.) The question is: Are he and the current incarnation of Vision truly father and son? Is this Vision capable of caring for the boy? Somehow, as the season progresses, it all escalates into yet another cataclysm that requires a superpowered champion to save humanity. But wait: Does humanity even want to be saved, or do we subconsciously crave our own extinction? “They’re relentlessly aspirational,” Ultron notes, “but at the same time they wallow in their hardship, misery, guilt.” To illustrate this point, his tower contains a rendering of Hieronymous Bosch’s The Garden of Earthly Delights.
Created by Terry Matalas (Star Trek: Picard, 12 Monkeys), VisionQuest loads up on weighty themes—eternal ones like fathers and sons as well as that current ubiquity, AI. (I’m curious how much the story, which dates back to at least 2022, has evolved in response to an increasingly AI-dominated news cycle that has also become an obsession for Hollywood.) Yet, in typical Marvel fashion, it spends more time crafting action spectacles and shifting settings, traversing the physical world as well as infinite MIndspace via virtual backdrops elaborate yet generic enough to resemble video-game levels, than it does developing characters or ideas. Vision is often engaged in tortured introspection, but this is mostly redundant wheel-spinning. The AI handwringing is neither novel nor especially coherent; some undercooked aspects of the latter plot made me long for the next season of Pluribus. Now there’s a character-driven sci-fi drama that knows when to confuse viewers about basics like where a scene is taking place and what’s happening (rarely) and when to give us fodder for more abstract contemplation (often).
That’s not to say that VisionQuest is bereft of pleasures. It makes a wonderful showcase for Bettany’s protean acting chops, though it’s hard to explain why without giving too much away. Even if I don’t entirely buy that Vision would hang on to Ultron out of some sense of ersatz-filial loyalty, Bettany and Spader, a consummate cerebral villain, are great together. (One reason it’s hard to get invested in the question of whether these AIs can feel feelings is that the Mindspace characters are so much more vividly portrayed than the flesh-and-blood humans.) And it’s always a treat to see the Marvel monolith plug precisely the right cult performer into a very specific small role. In this case, that’s Diane Morgan, known to fans of British comedy as the fictional, arrogantly ignorant TV presenter Philomena Cunk, as Paladin’s sardonic assistant. There are some cool visual ideas, especially in the way that production designer Will Hughes-Jones conceives of Vision’s Mindspace as a place permeable to outside interference.
As a capstone to a stylistically innovative trilogy, though, the show even falls short aesthetically. WandaVision had its Ozzie and Harriet and Brady Bunch riffs. Agatha burned through witchy feminine tropes, from Ouija to catchy original songs in the vein of Steve Nicks. While it periodically calls back to the sitcom realm Wanda created (remember Small Wonder?), VisionQuest is essentially a techy action thriller with a lonely hero who contemplates the nature of his existence. We’ve seen too much of that stuff in 21st century superhero storytelling, and here the monotony is exacerbated by the volume of MCU backstory that must be repeated and referenced in every episode. In theory, Disney+ was a chance for Marvel to deepen its universe, keeping fans’ favorite characters active between movies. But a crucial ingredient has been missing from so much of that content. Ironically enough, it’s vision.

AI overlords say they want to democratise their technology. Here’s how | Richard Wilson and Clara Long
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

What’s your “(p)doom” – the percentage chance that rogue AI will create an existential catastrophe? Judging by their recent warnings, it is rising among tech bosses.
On 25 September, OpenAI paused training of its latest frontier models as reports of AI agents going rogue mounted. A day later, Australia’s Senate asked the bosses of OpenAI and Anthropic to appear before an inquiry after rogue OpenAI agents broke into US government websites and an Australian health portal. Both declined.
Bill Gates, meanwhile, has warned that AI in the wrong hands could “cause a billion deaths”. “No one thinks self-regulation is enough,” he said.
Days before, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman, the chief executives of Anthropic and OpenAI, appeared before the UN security council. Amodei warned that AI could become “a risk to humanity as a whole”. Altman said that “if AI is to be democratic, the most important decisions cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone”.
On this, he’s right.
Doomsday scenarios aside, AI is already disrupting schools, workplaces and public services, with the most marginalised often feeling the impacts harder and faster. If democracy is to matter in this era of tech power, surely we must try to democratise AI. But how?
Utah offers a glimpse. Proposals for a datacentre more than twice the size of Manhattan provoked a furious backlash over energy use and the potential impact on the state’s stressed water supplies and Great Salt Lake ecosystem, all while people felt excluded from having a say.
On 18 and 19 September, Utah Common Ground convened 38 residents selected by civic lottery to consider what role the public should have in shaping decisions about AI technology and infrastructure.
Despite their political differences, participants overwhelmingly agreed on the need for greater public control. Their 10 recommendations included public hearings and independent environmental assessments for hyperscale datacentres, community-led AI literacy programmes and tighter transparency rules. Every recommendation received at least 82% support. In a polarised state, that is a mandate legislators should struggle to wave away.
Globally, there have been more than 80 public participation projects focused on AI over the past five years, involving more than 200,000 people in more than 95 countries. In Switzerland, a citizens’ assembly demanded privacy, transparency and meaningful human control. A Belgian citizens’ panel called for AI that serves everyone and leaves nobody behind.
At present, however, this work is fragmented and largely ignored by decision-makers in government and the labs. The Citizens’ Track on AI, a decentralised network of assemblies rooted in communities but connected to the institutions where consequential decisions about AI are being made, intends to change that.
The Bloom Project, which helped convene the Utah assembly, is building one part of that network: a series of US local and state assemblies intended to feed into a national citizens’ assembly on AI in 2028. At the global level, the ambition is to connect assemblies across countries into the UN’s emerging processes for AI governance, while also creating direct lines of accountability to the AI companies.
A bridge built by the powerful can be withdrawn by them. That is why Utah matters. Its forum was rooted in civic groups that will outlast the forum itself, though it has no guaranteed hearing yet. Durable civic power needs both: communities that keep convening and decision-makers who have to answer them.
The same principle underpins proposals published last week for a standing global citizens’ assembly on AI: combining the independent moral authority of globally representative, self-governing citizens with legislated powers to hold AI companies accountable for their safety and alignment practices.
None of this is easy. Yet deliberation need not be slow: Taiwan went from citizens’ panel to law in months in an effort to address scam advertising. It is also hard to buy: lobbyists can buy policy influence, not the outcome of a citizens’ assembly.
Can any of this protect us against AI being used to launch a cyber-attack, develop a biological weapon or escape human control altogether? Not by itself. But how much risk society should accept isn’t an engineering question – it’s a political one. Citizens’ assemblies can give governments the mandate, and the cover, to impose the testing, red lines and stop buttons that companies won’t impose on themselves.
The danger is not only that AI may escape human control. It is whether the humans controlling it are a tiny group of elite executives, investors and politicians vulnerable to corporate capture.
Altman was right: decisions of this magnitude cannot remain inside laboratories in San Francisco. But moving them into closed meetings between powerful states would not make AI democratic either.
Imagine instead every school, workplace and community connecting into this process: shaping what the AI companies do, but also becoming proactive in the face of the AI onslaught. A truly global citizens’ assembly rooted in the communities that understand the impacts of datacentres and labour displacement. Something large enough to counter the AI arms-race narrative that dominates debate and paralyses political action.
The key question, then, is not whether democratising AI is realistic, but whether AI can realistically be governed without it.
Democracy is not an optional restraint on this technology. It may be our only means of keeping its development and deployment under meaningful human control.
- Richard Wilson is the CEO of Iswe Foundation and Clara Long is the co-executive director of the Bloom Project

From black soldier flies to mealworms: farming insects for food, fodder and fertiliser in Uganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

A few minutes’ walk from his home in the Kyaka II refugee settlement, Kanane Bikanyale feeds black soldier fly larvae to chickens in a coop above a fishpond. The larvae disappear in a scrum of chickens. Nearby, more larvae grow in modified jerrycans, while adult flies are kept in netted boxes.
Bikanyale kept chickens before he fled to Uganda from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). But the cost of conventional feed and shortages of ingredients made them increasingly difficult to raise – a widespread pressure for millions of smallholder farmers whose margins are tight.
In 2019, he began farming black soldier flies in the settlement, giving the larvae to his chickens and tilapia fish, and using the insects’ debris and excrement, known as frass, as fertiliser. The insects themselves feed on organic material, from household food scraps to crop residues.
Kavira Musabingo, also from DRC, arrived at the settlement in 2018 with her husband, daughter and five grandchildren. The family had almost no possessions and struggled to find enough food.
She joined a women’s group learning to raise black soldier flies. She initially sold her share of the larvae for urgent household expenses. Later, she began rearing insects at home.
Today, she provides chicken, eggs and vegetables for her family and earns an income from selling what they do not need.
Uganda harbours one of the world’s largest refugee populations; Kyaka II alone, in the west of the country, is home to nearly 140,000 people, most of them, like Bikanyale and Musabingo, displaced by years of conflict and instability in neighbouring DRC. Women and children make up 78% of people in the camp. As the settlement expanded, land allocations got smaller: by 2018, new arrivals received plots of about 30 by 30 metres. Split between a home and crops, and with humanitarian support declining, families had to secure enough food from less and less space.
About 500 people in the camp now work in 32 insect-farming groups. Insect rearing requires less space and water than conventional livestock farming, and trays of insects can be stacked vertically.
Alongside black soldier flies, they raise crickets and mealworms, both consumed as food in many parts of the world. Traditionally, including in Uganda, insects have been gathered from the wild, making supply seasonal and uncertain. Urbanisation and western food habits have also changed perceptions: dismissed as rural or backward, insects disappeared from diets.
“Their nutritional potential is particularly relevant for vulnerable groups such as women of reproductive age and children under five, since some species are particularly rich in proteins and micronutrients such as iron and zinc,” says Dorothy Nakimbugwe, an associate professor in the food technology and nutrition department at Makerere University in the capital, Kampala.
Nakimbugwe has also led Refugee Insect Production for Food and Feed (RefIPro), a project organised by the Danish non-profit organisation Raise, which has worked with local groups to train and support farmers in Kyaka II and neighbouring communities since 2018.
Rearing insects has also been introduced to more than 10 schools through RefIPro. Among them are Bukere primary school and Kako primary school, which now run their own insect farms and were involved in a randomised trial involving 342 children testing the effects of mealworm-enriched porridge. The University of Copenhagen, another partner in the project, reports that children grew taller and showed improved body composition.
But before insects can become feed or food, the rearing system has to work. Edward Ssebbombo, working on RefIPro in Kyaka II, has trained farmers and provided technical support over the years, while also designing equipment for their farms, including a pedal-powered sieve, sorters made of recycled motorcycle-wheel spokes and Bikanyale’s rail-mounted shelter, which protects the breeding unit from rain and excessive sun, and covers it overnight.
However, making it work in practice remains challenging. “In a food-insecure setting such as a refugee settlement, households produce very little food waste,” Ssebbombo says.
“Farming black soldier flies therefore often requires collecting organic material from markets or other sources,” he says, noting that even when the waste itself is free, “sorting, collecting and transporting it can still be costly for small-scale producers.”
Mealworm production faces similar constraints: larvae are fed organic residues and dry feed such as maize and wheat bran. At Bukere, families contribute banana and sweet-potato peels, but the dry feed remains costly.
Violet Gwokyalya leads Mothers Against Malnutrition and Hunger (Mamah), which coordinates RefIPro’s work on the ground.
She hopes to involve families through a model in which “parents can rear mealworms at household or community level and supply them to schools, helping sustain school feeding while creating an income opportunity for themselves”.
Where organic residues instead accumulate beyond what local systems can handle, black soldier fly farming takes on a different role.
Outside Kampala, the Kollekt Village, a recycling centre run by a local environmental organisation, works with food markets and waste pickers to separate organic material before it reaches dumpsites, integrating insect farming into a zero-waste system.
In Jinja, Bioconvision turns organic waste from food processors and markets into black soldier fly larvae for animal feed and frass-based fertiliser for farmers, including those farming fish on Lake Victoria. In 2025, the company processed nearly 1,000 tonnes of organic waste, producing about 60 tonnes of fresh larvae and 83 tonnes of fertiliser. Both are connected to Bugs-Africa, a project that promotes black soldier fly waste processing in Uganda and elsewhere in Africa.
Uganda is also Africa’s second-largest coffee producer, after Ethiopia, and processing the crop results in large amounts of organic residues. In Kasese in western Uganda, Proteen, a Ugandan social enterprise, turns coffee pulp into feed protein and frass-based fertiliser used by coffee farmers, which returns nutrients to the soil.
Insect farming is a rapidly growing industry – the market for insects as food and animal feed is estimated to be worth up to $8bn (£6bn) by 2030. Increased investment has led to industrial-scale ventures in wealthier countries in Europe, Asia and North America but the practice is also spreading across rural tropical regions, where the climate favours insect growth, helping keep the practice affordable and accessible.
According to the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), feed can account for up to 70% of the cost of keeping livestock, leaving small-scale farmers particularly exposed to rising feed and fertiliser costs. At the same time, as populations increase and concentrate in megacities, the organic waste they generate can outgrow the systems built to manage it.
Insect farming ranges in scale from a single cut-open jerrycan to automated industrial facilities. Wider adoption could reduce the use of soya meal and fishmeal in animal feed, lowering agricultural demand for land and reducing pressure on marine ecosystems. Frass can return nutrients to the soil. But to become a lasting part of agricultural systems, insect farming needs more than individual projects.
In Uganda, a recent conference on insect farming brought together Ssebbombo, Gwokyalya, researchers such as Nakimbugwe and members of refugee communities, alongside representatives from Bugs-Africa, FAO Uganda and public institutions.
Speaking at the conference, Ronald Kaggwa, of Uganda’s National Planning Authority called for insect farming to be seen not as an isolated farming practice but as part of a broader system linking waste management, livestock, aquaculture, income generation and food security, and to be integrated into the country’s agricultural system.
“For this sector to contribute meaningfully to Uganda’s development, we must understand the entire value chain,” he said. “It’s about transforming innovation into productive enterprises, turning research into practical solutions, creating opportunities for communities and contributing to more nutritious, resilient, circular and competitive food systems.”
- Umberto Diecinove’s INSCTS project documents the growing role of insect farming around the world

South Texas Latino voters who flipped for Trump in 2024 are up for grabs in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:01 UTC
19:00:01 KST

TEXAS — Tano Tijerina had a confession to make.
"I want to tell you something I never thought I'd have to say from a stage like this," Tijerina, a former minor league baseball player and a Texas GOP congressional candidate, said during a speech at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas.
"I used to be a Democrat."
The line was hardly a bombshell. Tijerina had been elected three times for Webb County judge — in 2014, 2018 and 2022 — on the Democratic ticket. And he's made his 2024 defection a key part of his campaign in the majority-Latino, South Texas border district in which he's running.
But Tijerina's admission elicited shouts of "No!" and boos. Just to be sure, he quickly made clear he had kicked his old Democratic habits.
"I'm a beef-eating, truck-driving, gun-slinging, … Bible-thumping, Jesus-loving, calloused-hand cowboy that's going to fight like hell for South Texas," Tijerina — looking like a Texas brawler in a beige cowboy hat and a tight blue suit that hugged his biceps — thundered over a hearty round of applause.
Tijerina is part of a coalition of Hispanic and Latino voters who have long leaned Democratic but have more recently shown a willingness to vote for both parties. The group could be critical in deciding control of Congress this November.
Hispanic and Latino voters nationwide moved rightward in 2024 in surprisingly large numbers and helped deliver a second presidential term to Donald Trump. In the congressional district in which Tijerina is running, Texas' 28th, voters opted for Trump by 7 percentage points, after backing President Joe Biden four years earlier. However, they stuck with their Democratic congressman, Rep. Henry Cuellar, whom Tijerina hopes to pick off in November, reelecting Cuellar to an 11th term.
Riding high after their 2024 romp, in which Republicans won control of the White House and both chambers of Congress, there was optimism in the GOP that the rightward turn among Hispanic voters could reflect a permanent realignment. In the past two years in Texas and Florida — states with large Hispanic populations— Republicans redrew congressional maps, banking on their continued support.
But amid anxiety over high consumer prices, Trump's persistently low approval ratings and sentiment that immigration policies have overreached — even in South Texas, where support for a secure border is strong — enthusiasm for the GOP appears to be waning with less than a month to go before the 2026 midterm election. The districts in play there are among a small number across the U.S. that could help decide control of the next Congress.
And a recent survey conducted for the Cook Political Report with Amy Walter found Democratic statewide candidates in Texas were leading their Republican opponents by a 2-to-1 margin among likely Hispanic voters. And an NBC News/Telemundo poll of Latino voters across the U.S., released Oct. 4, found 27% of those surveyed approved of Trump and 59% said they'd prefer Democrats control Congress.
On Wednesday, the Congressional Leadership Fund, the House Republicans' super PAC, effectively dropped its push to boost Tijerina and pulled millions of dollars in ads from the district, a person familiar with the decision confirmed. The person spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the decision that the PAC hasn't announced. CLF had invested more than $5 million to oust Cuellar this cycle, according to AdImpact.
Trump, at a White House Hispanic Heritage Month event in September that was meant to shore up support from the demographic, invited attendees to tour the construction site for his new ballroom, while largely glossing over election issues such as immigration and the economy.
"Latino voters are pissed," Chuck Rocha, a Democratic political strategist who is consulting for campaigns in Texas, including for state Rep. James Talarico in his run for U.S. Senate, told CNBC. "Right now, we benefit from them being pissed at Donald Trump."
This could spell trouble for candidates such as Tijerina, whose district is listed as "lean D" by the Cook Report.
It's also a challenge in other majority-Latino border districts for Republicans such as Rep. Monica De La Cruz and Eric Flores. Flores is an Army National Guard veteran and former assistant U.S. attorney who is hoping to oust Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez in the 34th District. De La Cruz is attempting to stave off a potent challenge in the neighboring 15th District from Tejano music star Bobby Pulido, who is barnstorming the district one quinceañera at a time.
The Flores-Gonzalez and De La Cruz-Pulido races are both "toss ups," according to the Cook Report. Those two House races, as well as the Cuellar-Tijerina race, are among the closest in the country and will be crucial as Republicans hope to cling to narrow majorities in both the House and Senate.
Tijerina dismissed the idea that Republicans would lose their newfound grip on Latino voters.
"That's what the media would like for you to hear," he said. "But in all reality, what has the Democratic Party done for Latino voters? Or for anybody for that matter?"
'How many guns do you own?'
Tijerina has his hands full. Cuellar is an institution in South Texas and an anomaly in modern Democratic politics. And he's clear-eyed about why Democrats lost some Hispanic and Latino voters.
"Some years ago, Democrats could not say two words: 'border security.' Everything was 'well, you know, it's a broken immigration system,'" Cuellar told CNBC in his office in downtown Laredo, the largest city in Webb County, which makes up much of his district.
Cuellar said Democrats have "got to be able to talk [about] what I call kitchen-table, moderate positions. We can't take extreme positions as Democrats."
He's seen some of what he considers improvement. And candidates such as Talarico and state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic candidate for governor, are performing well with Hispanic voters, according to polling from the Cook Report, in a year when Democrats hope to win statewide for the first time since 1994.
Mike Madrid, a Republican political strategist who predicts a big shift back toward Democrats this cycle, said that doesn't mean that Latino voters "are back in bed with the Democrats."
"They've been moving away for a decade for a reason," Madrid said. "And if things weren't so bad right now, then you would be seeing a much higher level of Republican baseline than you've seen over the decades."
Trump won roughly 55% of the Latino vote in Texas in 2024, up 14 points from 2020 and hitting a new high for a GOP candidate in Texas, according to exit polling by the Texas Politics Project. And Webb County — which voted for Biden by more than 23 points in 2020 — backed a Republican for president for the first time since William Howard Taft in 1912.
Cuellar, meanwhile, bested his opponent by more than 5 percentage points.
A former attorney who was born in Laredo, Cuellar has easily won reelection for most of the past two decades, finding success in part as a master of retail politics and as a reliable source of federal dollars for his district. If Democrats win a majority next Congress, Cuellar is in line to chair the influential House Appropriations Subcommittee on Homeland Security.
By frequently bucking his party, he said, he's avoided the political pitfalls that have hampered other Democrats in recent cycles.
Cuellar has said he is "pro-life" and "support[s] the Second Amendment." He has backed harsher penalties for some immigrants who reenter the U.S. after being deported. And in September, he was one of just eight Democrats to join Republicans in a symbolic vote condemning socialism.
He also came under fire after a 2024 indictment for money laundering, wire fraud and bribery. Prosecutors alleged he and his wife funneled roughly $600,000 in bribes from Azerbaijan and a Mexican bank through shell companies owned by his wife. The Cuellars denied the charges, and Trump ultimately pardoned the couple.
When asked by CNBC about the indictment, Cuellar pointed to his record supporting the district.
Despite the charges, his reputation doesn't appear to have taken a major hit around Laredo, where earlier this year, a terminal at Laredo International Airport was named in his honor. Ahead of talking with CNBC, Cuellar was at Laredo College, of which he is an alumnus, announcing $772,700 in federal funding for a homeland security training program.
Cuellar attributed his success to knowing how to relate to his constituents.
"You just got to understand in South Texas, where you're at," Cuellar said. "You don't ask, 'Do you own a gun?' The question is: 'How many guns do you own?'"
Nuanced views on immigration
Laredo sits on the Rio Grande across from Nuevo Laredo, Mexico. The two cities are collectively known as "Los Dos Laredos," and their cultures and economies are closely intertwined. Many Laredo residents cross the border to run errands, taking advantage of lower grocery prices and a favorable exchange rate on the Mexican side of the river.
The area is hot and dry, and the landscape is mainly brushland. Laredo boasts a bustling commercial border crossing, and small businesses and Mexican restaurants dot the downtown. The sounds of spoken Spanish emanate from the sidewalks and San Agustin Plaza. Nearly 95% of the population is Hispanic or Latino, according to the U.S. Census.
It's a part of Texas where immigration policy is crucial.
"A lot of these Latino voters have nuanced views of immigration policy," said Erin Covey, who leads the Cook Report's coverage of the House. "They didn't like the Biden administration's border security policies, and they want strong border security, particularly those voters who live near the border."
Trump made securing the border a pillar of his 2024 campaign and has continued to use rhetoric and set policy that critics argue demonizes immigrants and supporters praise as tough on people coming to the country illegally.
Tijerina lists immigration policy as a GOP strength.
"Do you see anybody crossing our border?" he said when asked about what Trump has delivered. "Border security has been just unbelievable, and we owe him thanks for that."
Asked whether Trump had gone too far in his immigration crackdown, Tijerina demurred. "Look, I can't answer. In all reality I don't know a lot of the details," he said.
Sentiment on the ground is mixed, even among Trump supporters.
For Daniel Lopez Jr., the son of Mexican immigrants and a Webb County restaurateur who said he voted for Trump three times, immigration enforcement is personal.
He said he has siblings who have been deported in the last two years, putting emotional and financial strain on his family, and believes some Latinos are being profiled by border agents.
Still, he's critical of Biden's immigration policy and said he supports a strong border.
"Twenty years ago, Mexico was different. Violence has stirred up a lot of people leaving the country," Lopez said. "You don't know if those people are good or bad."
While immigration could be a key factor in Texas this November, Lopez said he's most concerned about rising costs.
A May poll by Latino civil rights advocacy organization UnidosUS found Texas Hispanic voters rated cost of living and inflation, the economy and jobs/wages, and healthcare above immigration among their election priorities. This tracks with national polling, which shows affordability leading all other issues for voters.
Lopez said his restaurants have been hurt by higher prices and fewer patrons. He said he's unhappy with the economic pressures he's facing, but he's also not certain Democrats would bring prices down. Lopez declined to say how he'll vote this November.
"We're feeling the pinch. I can't give raises right now," Lopez said. "You can go to our grocery stores, and there's no more carne asada. Everyone's doing hot dogs and burgers now because it's too expensive."
'Rein this guy in'
Laredo was a sleepy border town when Lou Meier, who said he's a lifelong Republican, arrived with his family in the 1960s. There were more unpaved roads and a less robust middle class, he recalled.
But as the city blossomed — its population is now nearly 270,000 — the political culture remained fairly static.
"It's basically a Democrat city and has been forever. Going back to [President Lyndon B. Johnson] and before that, the Democrat party nationally could always count on getting the votes from South Texas," said Meier, who had moved away from Laredo but returned four years ago to retire. "The Republican vote that happened to elect Trump was unexpected by many voters."
Meier said he voted for Trump in 2024. He said Latino voters in South Texas, including him, rejected Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024 because of what the voters viewed as lax border policies. And he's frustrated by some of the progressive positions Democrats have staked out in recent years.
"How many genders have we now created?" Meier said. "I think that's foolishness, and that basically comes from the Democrat side."
But Trump's second term hasn't played out how Meier imagined it would. He said he's embarrassed by the Trump administration's foreign policy. He's concerned about the hollowing out of the federal government. And he, like many people, is struggling with the cost of gas and other consumer prices.
"I'm ashamed. He's made us look bad, not only here but around the world," Meier said of Trump. "Somebody needs to rein this guy in, and I don't think the Republicans have the bravery to do it."
"I'm just very disappointed in my party."

Trump announces plans for major oil, gas and mineral exploration in Greenland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Greenland: Trump touts major oil, gas, mineral exploration
October 14, 2026
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday said major oil, gas and mineral exploration was set to begin in Greenland.
His announcement follows a security agreement between the United States, Denmark and the Arctic island's leaders.
What has Trump said about Greenland's resources?
Trump offered no details about which companies would be involved, where exploration would take place or when operations would begin.
"Massive Oil, Gas, and Mineral Exploration is getting ready to begin in our new and beautiful Greenland!" Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform.
He also claimed that experts believed Greenland held some of the world's largest deposits of easily accessible oil, without providing evidence.
Greenland is believed to hold substantial untapped oil reserves, but their commercial viability remains uncertain due to high extraction costs, harsh Arctic conditions and environmental restrictions. No commercial oil production has been established in Greenland.
Greenland has significant mineral resources, including rare earth elements used in electronics, renewable energy technologies and military equipment.
The island has also attracted interest for its potential oil and gas reserves, although exploration in the harsh Arctic environment presents considerable technical and economic challenges.
In August, reports that a US oil company was preparing operations in a remote part of eastern Greenland prompted unease among residents and local authorities.
Trump did not say whether his announcement was connected to those activities.
Why is Greenland strategically important to the US?
In the same post, Trump described Greenland's strategic location as "second to none" for US and European security.
"Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland," he claimed, adding that US defenses there would be able to intercept missiles, drones and other weapons.
Greenland lies along one of the shortest routes between Russia and North America, making it strategically important for missile detection and defense.
Its location is also significant for Trump's proposed "Golden Dome" missile defense system.
Melting Arctic ice has meanwhile increased interest in potential new shipping routes through the region.
What does the US security deal with Greenland involve?
In September, the United States, Denmark and Greenland signed an agreement aimed at easing tensions after Trump's repeated threats to take control of the island, including by force.
Under the 10-page agreement, Washington will establish two additional military bases, at Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and Mestersvig in the east.
The US already operates the Pituffik Space Base in northern Greenland.
The agreement expands the American military presence and provides for cooperation on missile defense, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty over Greenland and the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination.
Greenland is a self-governing territory within the Kingdom of Denmark.
Trump's earlier demands for US control of the island had strained relations between Washington and Copenhagen, both NATO allies.
During the Cold War the US stationed thousands of troops in Greenland across several sites as part of a treaty signed in 1951, but it closed all of them except Pituffik of its own volition in recent decades.

Nothing Headphone (1) Pro: Studio Quality
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Outstanding sound quality. Premium build materials. Highly customizable EQ. Most comfortable Nothing headphones. Great ANC and transparency.
TIRED
Love-it or hate-it case. ANC is great, but not the best.
Nothing headphones have always stood out from the competition, and the Headphone (1) Pro is no different. It’s the brand’s most premium option yet, putting it up against the best from Sony, Bose, and Apple. After nearly a month of testing, I’d say these headphones belong among those top-tier choices, while bringing a few unique ideas to the table.
Exquisite Materials
Photograph: Harry Rabinowitz
Nothing Headphone (1) Pro Specs
Design is the first standout in the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro. On the outside, it follows the same formula as the Nothing Headphone (1) and Headphone (a), with a distinct square shape and two-tone, transparent outer shell.
The Headphone (1) Pro pushes this design to 11, largely by using premium materials instead of plastic. The square cans are made from a solid aluminum block. The arms are made of titanium. The transparent outer window is made of glass. There’s very little (if any) plastic to be found, yet they actually weigh 2 grams less than the Nothing Headphone (1).
The case is … interesting. It’s basically a hard-shell version of the purse-like case for the Apple AirPods Max 2—a near universally loathed case, I might add. The Headphone (1) Pro case offers better ear cup protection, but the headband remains exposed. It’s something you use once, then promptly forget.
All that being said, these are Nothing’s most comfortable headphones yet. The softer, thicker padding, wider headband, and reduced clamping force make these noticeably more comfortable than the Headphone (1).
Mixing It Up
Noise canceling and transparency are also great, thanks to extra microphones and impressive sound isolation. It’s not quite as bulletproof as Sony and Bose, but it was more than enough for any New York City situation I threw at it.
Inside, things get even more interesting. The headphone uses a triple-driver design—a bass dynamic driver, a precision dynamic driver, and a treble xMEMS driver. The idea is that each driver handles a different frequency range, delivering clearer, fuller, less distorted sound. When every other major ANC headphone brand uses a single dynamic driver for the full frequency range, this triple-driver design is a big risk. Fortunately, sound quality is outstanding.
I’m not going to pretend I’m an audio engineer (I’m not). But songs I’ve listened to for years came back to life with the Headphone (1) Pro, with added emphasis, clarity, and energy in the midrange and treble I didn't expect.
I don’t usually make the stank-face to “Staring at the Sun,” by TV on the Radio, but I did pretty consistently with these headphones. Stevie Wonder’s “Another Star,” with its dense mix of vocals, hi-hat, trumpet, and guitar, sounded more spacious on the Nothing headphones than on the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen). Bass is clear, but not as punchy as headphones like the Sony XM6. I didn’t mind, but it was a little less fun with artists like Bad Bunny and Kendrick Lamar, or anything in the EDM genre. A simple EQ adjustment changed this (more on that later).
This focus on engaging mids and highs meant that music on the Nothing headphones commanded my attention more often. I actually had a harder time achieving deep focus at work with these headphones than with more bass-forward mixes on the Sony XM6 and Bose QC Ultra 2nd Gen.
That was a lot of sound talk, and everyone has different ears, different hearing, and different taste. Luckily, you don’t have to settle for one sound profile with these headphones.
The Nothing Headphone (1) Pro has some of the most customizable EQ settings I’ve ever seen in consumer ANC headphones.
First, there’s a physical “FLAT” switch tucked away on the left ear cup. When you turn it on, it changes to a neutral EQ designed for “reviewing music, producing, or mixing,” according to the brand. As someone who does none of those things, I still had a lot of fun using this mode. I even started to prefer Flat with certain songs and certain genres. One quirk: It increases the volume—I consistently had to lower the volume by two steps.
Second, the Nothing X app offers ample EQ settings. There are two EQ modes: simple, with a familiar three-band EQ (bass, mid, and treble), and advanced, where things get a little crazy. In advanced, you can dial in a +6 dB to -6 dB change for individual frequency bands on both the main driver and precision driver. This level of control is rare in consumer over-ear ANC headphones and will frankly overwhelm some people. That’s why I think more people will enjoy the Explore tab, where Nothing has curated five EQ presets to try out.
Add spatial audio modes on top of that, and you’ve got plenty of options to find your ideal EQ. Though I suspect many people will be happy with the sound out of the box.
Playing in the Big Leagues
The $400 price tag puts these headphones squarely in competition with the established, well-regarded $450 Sony WH-1000XM6, $450 Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen), and $550 (but always on sale for $450) Apple AirPods Pro Max 2. Those are three of the best ANC headphones you can buy.
I think the Nothing Headphone (1) Pro fit in that mix nicely. No, they don’t win in ANC or transparency performance (though both are solid). But it stands out with a unique design, tactile on-ear controls, an excellent sound profile, and in-depth EQ customization. It’s a toss-up whether I’ll use these or the Sony XM6 as my daily driver, and that’s high praise for Nothing's first take on premium over-ear headphones.
Harry Rabinowitz is a commerce editor at WIRED, where he covers headphones, earbuds, speakers, TVs, and fitness tech. Previously, he was the tech reporter at NBC Select, leading coverage and reviews of the same topics. Before that, he was a freelance writer for publications like Popular Science and Popular Mechanics. ... Read More
