cool kids are writing in all lowercase now. does that make you mad?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

the worst person you know probably writes in all lowercase.
they’ll tell you it’s an aesthetic choice, a testament to informality. they’re likely a twentysomething brooklyn resident like myself, bullish on being not the voice of their generation but a voice of a generation, and definitely guilty of posting performative notes-app screenshots and pseudointellectual, stream-of-consciousness “musings” that compare charli xcx to the pope.
what are they really up to, and do they know they’re participating in a long, exclusive, exclusionary tradition? the stylistic choice to write in lowercase is a dead horse that’s been beaten, flogged, and beaten again—what my generation calls ran through. and yet, it’s having a moment. i had to investigate.
for one side of the internet, lowercase writing is feminine.
it’s a “formal feature of how girls engage online,” says rayne fisher-quann, who’s 25 and lives (where else?) in brooklyn. known to the web for the all-lowercase personal essays she writes for her blog internet princess, fisher-quann insists that the offhandedness of lowercase “neutralizes” the self-importance of writing about oneself. it’s a way, fisher-quann says, “to avoid criticism.”
her feelings trace back to the digital spaces she occupied in her adolescence. “i got a lot of intellectual enrichment and influence from early 2010s feminist tumblr,” fisher-quann tells me. a decade-plus ago, incisive microblogs were on the rise on the platform, alongside the now-canonical page justgirlythings. justgirlythings pioneered the art of superimposing an all-lowercase serif-font sentence on a desaturated image (usually of a young woman wearing an oversized jumper and a messy bun sitting by a fireplace). it mostly covered cozy clichés such as “rainy days” and “lazy sundays.” becky campos, the blog’s author, says she wrote justgirlythings “because it almost felt like you were reading more of my diary instead of some polished copy. it showed that i’m more of a real person than some corporation making the posts.”
then there was rupi kaur, the instapoet of my generation. kaur’s work investigated the less manicured parts of the female experience, also through a lack of capitalization, except her words weren’t accompanied by stock imagery—they were the image. this performance of accessible vulnerability, akin to a live-laugh-love pillow, was kryptonite for millennial women: in 2016, kaur’s debut collection, milk and honey, sold more copies than the next-best-selling work of poetry, the odyssey, by a factor of 10. in homer’s defense, he didn’t have instagram.
while kaur describes her fixation on lowercase as an “ode to my identity as a diasporic punjabi sikh woman” (gurmukhi script only has one case) and a way to channel “equalness,” the virality of her work cemented the supple curves of the lowercase alphabet as an expression of femininity during the early days of social media. and the story might end there, if the internet were only populated by women.
but, to burst my own algorithmic bubble: behind every justgirlythings fan is a 4chan power user.
“i’m willing to believe that [using lowercase] is more deliberately aestheticized among young women on tumblr,” says adam aleksic, an internet linguist who goes by etymologynerd, “but none of the mega online communities use regular punctuation.” he and i are talking at a swanky coffee shop in soho, where he’s finishing up research on why the r-word is making a comeback.
to make his point, etymologynerd pulls up 4chan on his phone and starts scrolling. among the rancid all-lowercase musings, i notice a plethora of greater-than signs, angle brackets, and asterisks. because 4chan doesn’t support—has never supported—rich text (italicization, bolding, etc.), users also employ text-markup conventions: *yes* for yes, /i/hell no/i/ as hell no, etc.
while many may contend that writing in lowercase is a callback to one’s youth, sites like 4chan remind us that, at least within the digital sphere, the callback goes back much further and is part of a larger tradition. “lower case? it started with single-case tty model 33. now, it is habit,” ken thompson writes, in lowercase, in an email where he politely declines my request for an interview. (notice how thompson spells lower case as two words instead of one. before lowercase was a cornerstone of identity politics, it was just a lower case of the alphabet.)
ken thompson is 83 years old and, of course, one of the computer scientists to whom we owe the existence of the internet. he’s referring, in his email, to the teletype model 33, a popular terminal used for telecommunications that debuted in 1963. back in the ’50s, computers functioned on terminals that could support only 64 unique characters that—counting numbers, punctuation, and special characters—left no room for lowercase letters. this meant that most early programming languages (fortran, pascal, lisp) were written exclusively in uppercase. it was only between the ’60s and ’70s, when hardware manufacturing started to mature and memory costs started to plummet, that more characters became possible.
in early 1969, thompson got pulled from a project at bell labs, leaving him with nothing but time. so he decided to try to port a video game he had developed on company-owned equipment, space travel, to a more accessible pdp-7 computer he found unused in a neighboring department. he ended up reconfiguring the pdp-7’s operating system entirely and, alongside his colleagues dennis ritchie, douglas mcilroy, and bob morris, kickstarted the development of unix. unix made programming more ergonomic. with it, programmers no longer had to work with obscure machine code; there was no need to rewrite programs from scratch for every new computer model; and, perhaps most notably, it supported two cases.
soon, all the leading research institutions and corporations running on unix had to standardize how they capitalized in code: upper and lower case helped distinguish variables from constants (e.g., snake_case for variables, SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE for constants). these naming conventions, coupled with the increasingly collaborative culture of coding that unix established, evolved into a form of etiquette. capitalizing your code correctly was critical to how legible it was to other programmers, and excess capitalization was considered a faux pax. by the time this etiquette trickled down to the threaded text posts on usenet—the global network system created in 1979—the jargon file (better known as the hacker’s dictionary) had consecrated uppercase as SHOUTING.
point is, the internet used to be nerd country, reserved for those with technical expertise and written mostly in their idiom of programmatic lowercase shorthands. but everything changed in september 1993, when aol made usenet access a sign-on service, opening the floodgates to what the original usenet (then later irc and world wide web) users would call noobs. all of a sudden, an influx of digital non-natives started using proper grammar and correct capitalization, blissfully unaware of the rules that maintained the ecosystem they had just besieged. eventually, because there were just so many of them, the lowercase hacker vernacular became a marginalized quirk, and proper capitalization took over as the new norm.
i’m not saying the tumblr girlies stole from early-internet nerds destined for 4chan. but i am saying lowercase wasn’t invented by them, and perhaps has always been the hallmark of the outsider.
of course, maybe none of this matters. according to gretchen mcculloch, author of because internet: understanding the new rules of language, lowercase is a classic case of “resemanticization.” just look at something like “lol.” mcculloch’s theory is simple: first, a phrase is coined for a specific function (L.O.L. as laugh out loud). then, as more people use the phrase in different contexts (lol as an expression of nonchalance), its secondary meaning takes over. in just this way, the meaning of lowercase now bears no connection to its hacker associations, or even to its feminist co-optation.
today, lowercase can be clickbait—gong.io, an ai company that sells marketing data, analyzed over 85 million cold emails and concluded that those with lowercase subject lines get twice as many opens as properly capitalized ones do. i’ve heard of people my age who “become lowercase” because capital letters in texts and dating apps read as “too intense.” lowercase can also be a status symbol—when jack dorsey laid off 40 percent of his staff in february, he did so in an all-lowercase tweet. “the more senior you get, the less formal your emails are,” michelle liang, a tech growth investor, tells me. rarely were any of jeffrey epstein’s emails properly capitalized.
and yet, pockets of the internet still maintain that typing in lowercase is somehow antiestablishment, evident in the twitter trend of posting the phrase “i type in lowercase because i’m anticapitalist.” this could, perhaps, be a nod to the way writers like bell hooks used lowercase writing to “decenter” themselves from their writing; or to every college student’s favorite poet, e e cummings; or to the german bauhaus artists who deemed two cases aesthetically “inharmonic.”
aleksic, the etymologynerd, offers an alternative, more modern explanation: “people might be doing lowercase to signal that they’re not ai,” he says. obviously ai can write in lowercase, but you at least have to prompt it to do so, so there’s some inherent “friction,” etymologynerd says. after all, it’s not exactly easy to read an essay written entirely in lowercase.
the writer and self-diagnosed contrarian sam kriss sees beauty in how this tired, self-contradicting trope splits hairs: “writing enormous block paragraphs entirely in lowercase is the highest form of ‘respect’ i can render you,” he wrote recently on his substack. “reading my posts should be like scrubbing your eyeballs with sandpaper. i will keep attacking you until you are free.” etymologynerd goes so far as to insist that lowercase is the new normal.
or not. when i check back in on internet princess, fisher-quann’s substack, i notice she’s made a big change: she now writes with proper capitalization.
what say you?

Press review: Zelensky-Trump bad blood threatens US support and IMF updates GDP outlook
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Zelensky’s latest conflict with US President Donald Trump puts Ukraine at risk of losing American support; the IMF adjusts its 2027 economic outlook as the global situation is better than expected; and NATO's nuclear drills are causing tension on the European continent. These stories topped Wednesday’s newspaper headlines across Russia.
Media: Probability of Zelensky losing US support amid latest conflict with Trump
Although Vladimir Zelensky’s latest conflict with US President Donald Trump has European leaders feeling a little on edge, experts believe they are simply banking on waiting out the current Washington administration. Should the Republicans lose Congress in the midterm elections, it will make that strategy much more tenable, with Trump's powers potentially limited for the remainder of his current term. However, as long as Trump remains in power, Ukraine could lose US support: the White House has all the leverage it needs to cut off Kiev from intelligence, block arms deliveries via European funds, and even shut down Starlink satellite communications. Meanwhile, the UK and the European Commission are trying to derail the diesel agreement between Moscow and Washington.
Dmitry Suslov, deputy director of the Center for Comprehensive European and International Studies at the Russian National Research University Higher School of Economics, told Vedomosti that Trump's goal is not to force Kiev into a crushing defeat, so he is advocating a conflict settlement that makes both sides look like winners. The White House believes that "certain incentives" will persuade Russia to agree to a conflict freeze along the lines of engagement. The expert noted that the recently announced diesel deal is not an isolated instance of Russian-American cooperation, but rather a step toward Russia, in exchange for which Washington expects concessions from Moscow. "Russia should not agree to this framing of the issue. It should not be viewed as a precursor to mutual concessions or a settlement on Trump’s terms, but rather as practical, mutually beneficial cooperation between the two countries," Suslov pointed out.
According to expert Dmitry Novikov, Washington remains convinced that it can use economic incentives to persuade Moscow to make territorial concessions. "At the same time, the US aims to strengthen its influence here, since, for example, it could gain direct access to the gas transportation system. The plan is this: economics in exchange for politics, but the economics are controlled by the Americans," the expert said.
In turn, Bogdan Bezpalko, a member of the Russian Presidential Council for Interethnic Relations, told Izvestia that the White House could now announce new sanctions relief for Moscow that would benefit the US economy. Such a move would also put pressure on Zelensky and Kiev’s European allies, he stressed.
For now, however, European countries will try to push Ukraine toward steps that would derail the implementation of the Russian-American agreements on diesel fuel, Russian Foreign Ministry’s Ambassador-at-Large Rodion Miroshnik stated. According to him, the UK and the European Commission, led by Ursula von der Leyen, will be the main drivers of this push.
Vedomosti: IMF lists main threats to global economy
In 2026, global economic growth will be about 3.1%, while in 2027, that number is expected to rise to 3.4%, the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) World Economic Outlook report said. The organization has moderately raised its 2027 forecasts compared to its April projections, citing the world economy's better-than-expected ability to withstand the consequences of the Middle East war and other destabilizing factors. Nevertheless, the medium-term outlook for economic growth is disappointing compared to previous periods, the report noted. Key risks include the energy crisis, the AI bubble, and rising public debt in countries around the world.
According to the IMF, the secret to resilience lies in two key factors, economy expert Ksenia Bondarenko told Vedomosti. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz caused serious supply disruptions by cutting off the transit route through which nearly 20 million barrels of oil, or roughly a quarter of global maritime traffic, were transported daily prior to the war. The flexibility of the energy market made it possible to quickly reroute supplies and increase production outside the Persian Gulf. Thanks to countries such as the US, Brazil, Kazakhstan, and several others, production increased by up to two million barrels per day, the report pointed out.
Moving on to the second factor, Bondarenko stressed that global reserves were depleted in an effort to combat the energy crisis. This included the emergency release of strategic reserves under the auspices of the International Energy Agency, as well as the large-scale use of domestic reserves. These measures provided an additional four million barrels per day. Thanks to all of this, the shock caused by the closure of the Strait of Hormuz did not lead to a spike in oil prices to 110 dollars per barrel or a 0.9 percentage point decline in global growth. The net negative impact on global growth in 2026 was only about 0.3 percentage points. In addition, the investment boom around AI continued to support growth in business activity and trade, the expert emphasized.
For Russia, the IMF revised its GDP forecast to a growth rate of 0.9% for both 2026 and 2027, down from 1.1% previously. Rising commodity prices are supporting economic activity in Russia to some extent, despite a decline in total oil exports due to infrastructure damage, the IMF noted. The downward revision of the Russian forecast may be linked to a more cautious assessment of investment prospects, financial expert Alexander Abramov stressed. An unbalanced budget and increased spending amid the geopolitical situation could fuel high inflation, he emphasized. In this case, the Russian Central Bank’s key rate will also remain high, curbing investment and hindering economic growth, the expert concluded.
Izvestia: NATO drills causing tensions on European continent
Large-scale NATO nuclear exercises have begun in Italy, with 17 countries participating. Thousands of servicemen and dozens of aircraft capable of carrying nuclear weapons are involved. Russia has stated that these drills will not reduce regional tensions. The exercises are taking place at a time when the US seeks to deploy tactical weapons near Russia’s borders, and the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) has yet to be signed.
NATO troops are rehearsing scenarios involving dual-use aircraft: jets capable of carrying both conventional and nuclear weapons. According to military expert Dmitry Kornev, a key element of the Steadfast Noon drill is the practical testing of the Nuclear Sharing program for the use of American tactical thermonuclear bombs. "These special munitions are carried by specific types of aircraft, such as the German Tornado or the new-generation F-35 fighter jets used by the Netherlands, Denmark, Norway, Poland, Italy, and Finland," the expert told Izvestia.
Moscow’s official position on these exercises was articulated by the Russian embassy in Belgium, which maintains contact with NATO leadership. "We take note of statements by NATO officials that the drills are routine in nature and pose no threat to Russia. However, at a time when NATO is portraying our country as the main security threat, these exercises do not help reduce tensions on the continent and are part of the alliance’s nuclear policy, which is notoriously negative towards Moscow," the diplomats noted.
The New START Treaty officially expired on February 5, 2026. No new agreement was signed. For the first time since 1972, Moscow and Washington are not bound by a legal framework for controlling their nuclear arsenals. It is precisely in the absence of these deterrent mechanisms that the current drills are taking place. The expired START Treaty limited the delivery systems and nuclear warheads of Russia and the US, but it did not prohibit such exercises, Vasily Klimov, a senior research fellow at the International Security Center at the World Economy and International Relations Institute of the Russian Academy of Sciences, emphasized.
Vedomosti: Germany, Italy, and Belgium propose mechanism to opt out of cumbersome Brussels laws
The leaders of Germany, Italy, and Belgium have called for a new mechanism to be introduced among EU member states. The idea is to allow European governments to suspend laws adopted by Brussels if they deem the laws to be burdensome. According to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, and her Belgian counterpart Bart De Wever, the new mechanism would benefit small and medium-sized European businesses the most. The new initiative aims to ensure greater independence from Brussels and prevent unnecessary regulatory burdens, which could lead to irreversible losses of Europe’s industrial potential and further weaken investment and competitiveness.
It would be wrong to suggest that the initiative will weaken EU bodies. Germany, Italy, and Belgium have all benefited from European integration, and they have no interest in causing division at this time, Artyom Sokolov, a senior research fellow at the MGIMO Institute of International Studies, told Vedomosti. Rather, this is about rebalancing the EU as a possible way out of the current tense situation. This indicates that current EU leaders recognize the organization's problems with expansion, the expert noted.
For now, the mechanism mentioned by Merz, Meloni, and De Wever is "nothing but propaganda," Vadim Trukhachev, an associate professor at the Russian Financial University, pointed out. Such statements are made for domestic political purposes: Merz is concerned about his extremely low approval rating, Meloni faces elections next year, and De Wever is also trying to consolidate his position within Belgium. According to the expert, what’s more important is the ongoing debate within the EU over abolishing the veto and replacing it with the double-majority principle, when decisions are adopted if approved by 55% of member states (15 out of 27), representing 65% of the EU’s population, provided there is no blocking minority consisting of at least four countries.
Given that the EU is going through difficult times, leaders fear the collapse of consensus. Therefore, by transferring some powers to national capitals, they are trying to save the bloc, not dismantle it, political scientist Alexander Kamkin emphasized. If there is indeed a threat to Brussels in the form of the creation of some kind of parallel structure, the European Commission and its President Ursula von der Leyen may try to thwart the initiative of the three countries, the expert noted.
Nezavisimaya Gazeta: UK prime minister eyes external enemy, rapprochement with EU
The UK’s Labour Party will release evidence that Moscow allegedly interfered in British politics, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard told a media outlet. However, it is unclear exactly when this will happen. In this way, the Cabinet has backed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s virtually unsubstantiated accusation that Moscow attempted to influence the 2016 referendum on the UK’s exit from the EU. Burnham is now counting on a rapprochement with the EU. He even named the exact date when the groundwork for the country’s future reintegration will be laid: November 20, the date of the UK-EU summit.
"So far, Brussels’ reaction to the possibility of the UK’s return to the EU remains unclear. In theory, the EU return should please officials," political expert Alexander Tevdoy-Burmuli told Nezavisimaya Gazeta. He emphasized that London’s rapprochement with Brussels is driven by US President Donald Trump’s policies. "As one of the largest economies, as well as a country with nuclear weapons and permanent membership in the UN Security Council, the UK could once again become a welcome partner for the EU in this difficult situation," the expert explained.
However, it is true that reintegration is a complex process under current circumstances. "The UK has always been divided on the issue of EU membership. Brexit was an expression of this persistent division. In theory, the Burnham government could initiate talks on joining the EU. But that would require securing a majority in favor of reintegration within the country," Tevdoi-Burmuli emphasized.
This will not be easy. The British public associates the pro-European stance with failed immigration policies, which have become one of the country's central problems. "The UK has received a huge number of migrants, who are now a source of conflict. In addition, far-right forces advocating an end to migration are gaining ground in the country. In this context, joining the EU, where a left-liberal agenda is being implemented, could prove problematic," the expert noted.

Why are so many Americans forced to work standing up – unlike their president? | Arwa Mahdawi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Great news for everyone who is soon to fly via a US airport: the Trump administration has just elevated the travel experience. You still risk getting arrested by immigration agents and thrown into a detention centre, but never mind that! Instead, luxuriate in the fact that none of the poorly paid Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff with whom you interact will be sitting down. The government recently got rid of all the chairs at travel document checking stations, arguing that “maintaining a standing posture helps reinforce professionalism” and strengthens “our security posture and … commitment to hospitality”. Funnily enough, border patrol and customs officers have not adopted the same policy. Perhaps because their job tends to involve being as inhospitable as possible.
TSA agents aren’t the only US workers getting sore calf muscles during their shifts. Unlike their European and British counterparts, cashiers at US supermarkets have traditionally been forced to stand while working. The US’s upright obsession seems to be down to a Protestant work ethic and a lack of labour laws. Sitting apparently conveys laziness to the discerning American consumer. Over the years there have been numerous right-to-sit lawsuits pushing back on mandatory standing but, while things are shifting slightly, seated supermarket cashiers are still unusual. One exception is Aldi, which has been expanding aggressively in the US. Cashiers get chairs at Aldi because (surprise) it’s more efficient when your workers’ feet aren’t aching all the time.
While seated cashiers and TSA agents may be looked down on by the US establishment, it’s a different story for high-flyers. Rather than “maintaining a standing posture” to “reinforce professionalism”, the US president often looks as if he is snoozing at his desk. Which, to be fair, is probably because he regularly stays up all night posting extremely important memes on the internet.
Having their chairs seized isn’t the only indignity that TSA agents have faced recently: along with other federal employees, they had to work without pay for several weeks during government shutdowns in Trump’s second term. Members of Congress on the other hand? They could continue to collect their generous salaries during the shutdown unless they explicitly chose not to. Americans should not take this injustice sitting down.
Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Scientists simulated the light coming from these K-dwarf stars and found that some leaves grow faster under that type of light compared to our sun’s light. So what would life look like on these far-away planets? Scientists describe it as paradise: better weather, a smoother surface, water flowing everywhere and an abundance of plants and animals (or aliens, perhaps).

Could unity government offer way out of Israel’s electoral deadlock?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:57:38 UTC
18:57:38 KST

Two weeks ahead of Israel’s elections, the prospect of forming a unity government has returned to the forefront amid opinion polls indicating that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and the Jewish opposition bloc may both fail to secure the majority required to form a government, while the opposition rules out relying on Arab lawmakers to break the deadlock.
If neither bloc manages to secure 61 of the 120 seats in the Knesset, Israel could face two options: holding another election within months or forming a unity government bringing together Netanyahu’s Likud party and opposition parties.
The scenario under discussion excludes the far-right Jewish Power party, led by National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir, and largely excludes the far-right Religious Zionism party, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, as well as the religious Haredi parties and Arab parties.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has emphasized his efforts to avoid repeat elections.
“I am doing everything in my power to ensure that Israel has a stable government,” he said in an interview with the Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth on Monday.
“I will absolutely do everything I can to prevent repeat elections,” he added, warning that “Israel faces enormous national challenges and cannot afford the cost of repeated election cycles.”
However, Avigdor Liberman, leader of the opposition right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu party, rejected the idea of forming a unity government with Netanyahu on Tuesday.
“It would be a disgrace for generations to come, and it would be a paralyzed government,” he said at a conference organized by Yedioth Ahronoth.
“Netanyahu does not care about security or anything else, only power. A person who bears responsibility for a series of disasters cannot hold office,” he added.
Liberman said the opposition parties would decide on their candidate for prime minister after the elections if they win.
Meanwhile, Benny Gantz, leader of the opposition Blue and White party, expressed support for the idea of a unity government but ruled out the participation of Arab parties and the Haredim.
“Israel cannot afford another government that relies on Arab parties or Haredi parties,” he wrote on US social media platform X, adding: “Israel needs a broad Zionist unity government.”
Opposition leader Yair Lapid, however, rejected the proposal, expressing hope that Herzog would not push for what he described as “another fake unity government.”
He said Netanyahu would “deceive his partners” in such a government and called on the other opposition parties to declare in advance that they would refuse to join it.
The Israeli newspaper Maariv recently revealed a proposed formula for a unity government that would exclude Ben Gvir and Smotrich.
Under the arrangement, Netanyahu would serve as prime minister for a year and a half before being elected president of Israel by the Knesset.
Ben Gvir believes Netanyahu is planning to form a government that includes opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, head of the Yashar party, instead of him.
“All indications suggest that the prime minister is planning an alliance with Gadi Eisenkot,” Ben Gvir said Tuesday, urging Netanyahu to keep the bloc “purely and comprehensively right-wing.”
“Instead of taking seats away from me, go and take them away from Eisenkot,” he told Netanyahu.
Eisenkot has not officially addressed the possibility of joining a unity government.
Meanwhile, Israel’s consul general in New York, Ofir Akunis, called for the formation of a “broad national unity government,” saying, according to Maariv, that Israel “needed to demonstrate its unity to the world” and to those he described as “its enemies.”
Israeli commentator Yaron Dekel argued in an article published by Yedioth Ahronoth on Tuesday that an inconclusive election result could bring Israel back to the model of a unity government established in 1984.
He said this would require Netanyahu to “abandon Ben Gvir and Smotrich, freeze the judicial overhaul plan and agree to an independent investigation into the events of Oct. 7, 2023.”
These steps would give Eisenkot grounds to justify joining a government led by Netanyahu to his voters, he noted.
At the beginning of 2023, Netanyahu’s government advanced a judicial overhaul plan that it said would “balance the legislative, executive and judicial authorities.”
The opposition, however, viewed it as “a coup against democracy that would turn Israel into a dictatorship.”
Dekel noted that opposition leaders currently rule out cooperation with Netanyahu. However, their simultaneous refusal to rely on Arab parties, amid the possibility of a deadlock between the two blocs, could leave them “with no other choice.”
He explained that holding another election would not guarantee either bloc an improved position and could instead produce an even worse result.
In his view, one factor making a unity government conceivable is the absence of personal hostility between Netanyahu and Eisenkot, which could provide “a starting point for negotiations.”
Dekel stressed, however, that both sides would have to make “major concessions.”
Eisenkot could agree to Netanyahu serving as prime minister first under a rotation agreement, in exchange for clear political and security gains, he said.
He argued that “removing Ben Gvir and Smotrich from the government, appointing Eisenkot as defense minister, halting the judicial overhaul plan and establishing an independent commission to investigate the events of Oct. 7 could form a package of achievements that Eisenkot could present to his voters to justify joining the government.”
Netanyahu, for his part, would have to make the required concessions in advance if he wanted to serve as prime minister first, according to Dekel. Chief among them would be abandoning his far-right allies.
Elections for the Israeli Knesset are scheduled for Oct. 27. Opinion polls indicate that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the Jewish opposition bloc will be able to form a government.
Netanyahu has chaired the current government since late December 2022. It is described as the “most right-wing government in Israel’s history.”
Netanyahu also faces charges of corruption, bribery, and breach of trust in three cases.
In addition to the domestic corruption trial, Netanyahu has been wanted by the International Criminal Court since 2024 over war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in the Gaza Strip, where more than 74,000 people have been killed in a genocidal war since October 2023.

Nox Mobility’s first night train will link Hamburg and Munich via Bremen and Augsburg, with individual private ‘suites’ for all passengers.
A new night train in Germany linking Hamburg and Munich is set to launch on 23 March 2027.
Berlin-based Nox Mobility says its first service will run three times a week in each direction, with stops in Bremen and Augsburg.
With a new generation of night trains designed to make overnight rail “the most obvious alternative” to short-haul flights, Nox Mobility previously revealed that it plans connections between 100 European cities by 2035.
Its proposed network includes Paris, Barcelona, Amsterdam, Copenhagen, Warsaw, Budapest and Rome.
What will the new night train offer?
Passengers will travel in individual “Nox Suites”, each featuring a large seat, a table for working or eating, space for large luggage and power outlets.
At night, the seat unfolds into a lounge position, providing two metres of space to stretch out alongside the window.
However, travellers expecting the fully private bedrooms outlined in Nox’s original plans will have to wait. Its “Nox Rooms”, designed for one or two people, are scheduled to join the fleet from 2029.
As Euronews Travel reported in June 2025, the company initially envisaged launching in 2027 with private sleeping cabins. The latest announcement sets out a phased introduction, starting with the seat-based suites.
“With Nox, every passenger has their own space to work and rest in,” said Thibault Constant, Co-Founder of Nox Mobility. “A night on a Nox train should eventually bring together everything that used to take three bookings: getting there, staying the night and the morning at the destination.”
What time will the trains depart?
One-way fares start at €65. Southbound trains scheduled to leave Hamburg at 9:22 pm, calling at Bremen at 10:30 pm and Augsburg at 7:35 am before reaching Munich at 8:14 am.
In the opposite direction, departures from Munich are planned for 9:20 pm, stopping in Augsburg at 9:51 pm and Bremen at 7:20 am, with arrival in Hamburg at 8:27 am.

Large dogs age more quickly than small dogs at a molecular level
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:57:00 UTC
18:57:00 KST

Large dogs age more quickly than small dogs at a molecular level
- Large dogs age faster at a molecular level. A Science study found bigger breeds show quicker DNA methylation ageing and may die earlier.
- Researchers analysed 1,640 blood profiles from 894 pet dogs. They built an epigenetic clock with less than one year median error and linked older biological age to early death.
- The study also found sex differences on the X chromosome. It suggests breeding for rapid growth may shorten life, and slowing molecular ageing could help larger dogs stay healthy longer.
AI generated
Few animals show the link between size and lifespan as clearly as dogs. Within this one species, large breeds such as Great Danes typically die younger than small ones such as Chihuahuas. A new study indicates the reason may lie in how DNA changes with age in dogs.
Across mammals, bigger species like elephants usually live longer lives than smaller ones like mice, but within a species that pattern can reverse. Earlier comparisons across species linked certain biological mechanisms to exceptional longevity, but those are less suited to explaining differences among individuals within a species.
“We all know that big dogs usually don’t live as long as small dogs, but we have not known whether their cells actually age faster, or whether they simply hit certain diseases earlier,” said Noah Snyder-Mackler, a professor at Arizona State University’s School of Life Sciences and Center for Evolution and Medicine and one of the authors of the study published in the journal Science.
To find out, the researchers measured DNA methylation, chemical tags that help control which genes are switched on and off. Using age-related patterns in these tags, they built an epigenetic clock that estimated a dog’s age with a median error of less than one year.
Analysing 1,640 blood methylation profiles from 894 pet canines of various breeds, they found that larger dogs and male dogs showed signs of accelerated molecular ageing, while dogs whose biological age appeared older than expected based on the profiles faced a higher risk of early death.
“We found that large dogs show a faster-moving DNA methylation ageing signature in blood, and that this acceleration is especially strong in parts of the genome that normally help keep ‘jumping genes’ quiet,” Snyder-Mackler said.
Jumping genes, also called transposable elements, can copy themselves and insert into new spots in the genome. LINE1s are a type of jumping gene that is normally kept silent by DNA methylation, but their activation has been linked to genome instability, cancer and other age-related disease.
In large dogs, Snyder-Mackler said, “methylation at those regions appears to erode more quickly with age, as if the genome is losing some of the tape or clamps that keep these mobile elements suppressed”.
This suggests that the shorter lives of large dogs reflect a faster molecular ageing trajectory.
“If large dogs simply died earlier after following the same molecular trajectory, we would look for late-life triggers of disease or mortality. But if parts of the ageing programme move faster throughout adulthood, as our data suggest for the blood methylome, then there may be processes we can measure, follow over time, and potentially modify before disease appears,” Snyder-Mackler said.
Differences by sex
The researchers also found differences between male and female dogs, largely on the X chromosome – the sex chromosome that females carry in two copies and males in one. There, LINE1 elements showed higher methylation in males. Chromosomes are thread-like structures that carry genetic information inside cell nuclei.
“In our genome-wide analyses, the sex signal looked distinct from the body-size signal, so I would treat that as a separate biology that needs follow-up rather than the same mechanism in disguise,” Snyder-Mackler said.
The trade-off between large size and longevity may be a consequence of selective breeding rather than natural evolution. Humans bred dogs to grow quickly and reach large adult sizes for tasks such as guarding, hunting and herding.
“If selection strongly favours rapid growth or large adult size before old age, late-life costs can come along for the ride,” Snyder-Mackler added.
Previous explanations for why large dogs tend to have shorter lives focused on growth biology. Researchers have also suggested that larger dogs may undergo more cell growth, develop more quickly or face a higher risk of cancer.
“Our study does not replace those ideas; it gives us a molecular layer downstream of body size,” Snyder-Mackler said.
The findings raise the possibility that slowing molecular ageing could help extend healthy lifespan in larger dogs. Snyder-Mackler said, however, that lifespan is not governed by a single biological clock. Large dogs would still face breed-specific risks, meaning that slowing molecular ageing would not turn a Great Dane into a Chihuahua, in terms of lifespan, but could make one component of its ageing trajectory less compressed. Pope diagnosed with lung cancer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:56:46 UTC
18:56:46 KST

Pope diagnosed with lung cancer
Pope Leo XIV has had part of a lung removed after being diagnosed with cancer, the Vatican has announced. The diagnosis has exposed a gap in Vatican law, which has no clear procedure for transferring papal authority if the pontiff becomes too ill to govern.
The 71-year-old pope underwent surgery at Rome’s Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday after doctors discovered a small tumor. The Vatican confirmed that surgeons removed the lower lobe of his right lung and that tests identified the cancer as pulmonary adenocarcinoma, one of the most common forms of lung cancer.
“The surgery was completed successfully, within the expected timeframe and as planned,” the Vatican said in a statement. The operation lasted approximately 90 minutes, with the pope spending about three hours in the operating room. Doctors reported no complications.
Leo spent a calm night in the hospital, the Vatican said on Wednesday. His public engagements have been canceled through October 20, with doctors expecting him to remain hospitalized for about a week.
The pontiff, elected in May 2025, had previously said the lung nodule was small and detected at an early stage. Doctors have yet to say whether he will need further cancer treatment.
Pulmonary adenocarcinoma can affect both smokers and nonsmokers. While tobacco use is a major risk factor for lung cancer, exposure to secondhand smoke, radon and asbestos can also contribute. Leo has no known history of smoking, although cancer has affected several members of his family. His mother died of cancer in 1990, while the Vatican announced on Tuesday that his older brother is also battling the disease.
Under canon law, even a pope who is unconscious or permanently unable to govern remains in charge. Unlike secular heads of state, he has no deputy who automatically assumes his powers.
The Vatican’s day-to-day operations continue under senior officials, led by Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin, who was attending a conference outside the Vatican during Leo’s surgery.
“We were all struck by the serenity with which the pope announced this procedure,” Parolin told reporters on Tuesday. “Am I worried? Yes, because I certainly didn’t expect something like this.”
The problem has troubled the Vatican for decades. In 1965, Pope Paul VI prepared letters proposing his resignation in the event of serious illness. Pope Francis later drafted a similar letter to be invoked if he became medically incapacitated.
Neither document was ever used and their legal validity remains uncertain. Canon law requires a pope to resign freely, leaving no clear way to transfer power if he becomes permanently incapacitated.

A company source told Reuters earlier that a ballistic missile hit the Aramco headquarters complex. The source said an office tower in the complex was struck and that its top three floors were damaged.
Riyadh’s international airport has come under attack four times, including the attack on Oct 10 which was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia in a decade. Authorities have closed the airport until Oct 17, and airlines have canceled flights to Saudi Arabia.
Fearing the rise of Iranian influence and the prospect of chaos on its borders, Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in support of the government in 2015 after the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa.
The UN brokered a 2022 truce between the warring sides in Yemen that kept a fragile peace until 2026. REUTERS

How a radio glitch triggered a false hijack alert in Germany
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:53:54 UTC
18:53:54 KST

How a radio glitch triggered a false hijack alert in Germany
Authorities scrambled fighter jets to escort a plane on its way from Corfu to Nuremberg after a pilot sent a hijack alert.
German authorities briefly closed an airport and scrambled fighter jets to escort a passenger plane on Tuesday following an emergency alert indicating a hijacking was taking place on board. However, the alert had been accidentally triggered by a radio “malfunction”.
Corendon Airlines said its Boeing 737-800, which was en route from the Greek holiday island of Corfu to Nuremberg, Germany, sent out an emergency code while it was flying over Croatia “due to a brief malfunction in the radio communication system”.
In a statement, the airline said that “no emergency situation occurred”, and the 178 passengers, flight crew and aircraft had not been in danger at any point. The plane landed safely in Nuremberg.
What happened?
German police said Corendon Airlines flight XR456 “inadvertently” sent out an emergency “squawk” alert with the code 7500 while flying over Croatia on Tuesday.
A squawk is a four-digit code a pilot sends via the jet’s transponder to air traffic control. The code 7500 tells air traffic controllers that a hijacking is in progress.
However, air traffic controllers were unable to make contact with the pilots or crew, causing the alarm to be raised further. It is unclear why this happened.
“The aircraft could no longer be reached by radio to clarify the situation”, prompting warnings to be activated in several European countries, police said.
A Rafale fighter jet was scrambled from Croatia to intercept the Boeing passenger jet, while the German military also dispatched warplanes.
Police cordoned off the Albrecht Dürer airport in Nuremberg as a precaution until they knew the reason the pilot had sent the hijack alert.
Police spokesman Michael Petzold explained that authorities had “received a code directly from the cockpit that suggested a hijacking”.
“Since we were then unable to reach the cockpit, and the tower was also unable to contact the cockpit, we had to assume the worst – that it might indeed be a hijacking,” Petzold said.
The incident disrupted flights, with six flights delayed and two inbound flights diverted to other airports as a precaution, a Nuremberg airport spokesperson said.
Why are aviation authorities so concerned?
The hijack scare has come amid heightened concerns about aviation security after the copilot on board a Flydubai jet bound for Israel from Dubai attacked the captain with an emergency crash axe, forcing the flight to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia on September 30.
On Friday, the United Arab Emirates’ prosecutor general said the copilot was on a “suicide” mission to crash the plane at Ben Gurion airport in Tel Aviv and called the incident a “terrorist attack”.
Also, before the false hijack alert in the early hours of Tuesday, flights had been briefly disrupted at Nuremberg airport after pilots reported suspected drone sightings.
Authorities across Europe have already stepped up surveillance of the skies in recent weeks after a series of mostly mysterious drone incidents and concerns about Russian hybrid warfare.
Western nations, including Germany, have accused Moscow of launching a campaign of sabotage, espionage and disruption to undermine European support for Ukraine and destabilise the continent.
Several German airports have had to suspend operations for brief periods in recent months due to drone activity, with suspicion often falling on Russia.
Last month, the German government blamed Russia for an attempted attack at Leipzig/Halle airport in August using a drone laden with explosives. Berlin closed the Russian consulate among other measures.
Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed the allegations, saying Berlin “fabricated” the evidence. However, in light of the concerns, NATO’s top general told the Warsaw Security Forum earlier this week that the alliance has a new war plan for countering a Russian attack on its members, embedding lessons learned from the Ukrainian front lines.
How common are radio glitches and false hijack alerts?
Radio glitches are common, but incidents rarely escalate to major security events because pilots use back-up radios to communicate with air traffic controllers when they lose communication signals.
In 2019, a pilot flying an Air Europa jet from Amsterdam to Madrid accidentally transmitted hijack alert 7500. For half an hour, aviation authorities thought the alarm was a genuine emergency and followed safety protocols, which disrupted flights and led to the evacuation of part of Schipol airport in the Netherlands.
In 2011, a flight from Chicago to Germany was diverted to Toronto when a pilot spilled coffee and accidentally set off a hijack alarm. The spill caused distress signals to go out, including the 7500 transponder code.

Portuguese parliament backs extension of parental leave: what changes?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:50:00 UTC
18:50:00 KST

The new legal framework, arising from a joint proposal by PS and PSD, will give parents a more favourable regime than the one currently in force.
On Tuesday, MPs meeting in a parliamentary working group approved a joint proposal by the PS and PSD to extend parental leave. Under the proposal, parents would be entitled to fully paid leave for 180 days (six months) if it is shared, or 150 days (five months) if it is taken by only one of them.
In the first of these scenarios, each parent will have to take at least 30 consecutive days or two periods of 15 days in a row, in order to receive a benefit equal to their full reference wage, calculated by Social Security, for the period in which they are away from work. In single-parent families, the lone parent will be entitled to the full 180 days on 100% pay.
Alternatively, parents will be covered by a benefit worth 83% of their reference wage for six months (180 days) if the leave is not shared. They may also take up to 210 days of leave, paid at 90% if the father takes at least 60 consecutive days (two months) in addition to his 28-day exclusive parental leave, or at 86% if each parent stays at home with the baby, on an exclusive basis, for one of the last two months of leave.
The new legal framework will create more favourable conditions for parents than those currently in force. At present, fully paid leave only covers the first 120 days of the baby's life if there is no sharing, or 150 days if the father takes 30 days of leave on an exclusive basis. In both scenarios, parents can extend that period by a further month, although with a loss of income, as the benefit then corresponds to 80% and 83% of the reference amount respectively.
Following approval in the parliamentary working group, the text now moves on to the parliamentary Committee on Labour, Social Security and Inclusion and will then go to a final overall vote in the full chamber.
Even so, this extension of parental leave falls short of what was proposed in a citizens' legislative initiative submitted to parliament in 2023, which called for 100% pay during the baby's first 180 days of life, with the possibility of extending that period to 210 or even 240 days if the leave was shared. That initiative formed the basis for the joint amendment put forward by PS and PSD, a less ambitious proposal that has now been approved.
However, according to "Negócios" (source in Portuguese), this extension of parental leave will not affect leave that is already under way, as the measure approved by the working group will apply only to leave starting from next year.
The proposal also introduces the possibility for private-sector workers, as is already the case in the public sector, to opt for a continuous working day. This would allow employees with children under 12, or with dependants who have a disability or a chronic or oncological illness, to forgo their lunch or dinner break and work their hours in one stretch so that they can leave earlier. They will, however, retain the right to a break of up to 30 minutes.
How does Portugal compare with other European countries?
Even with the extension of parental leave, Portugal will still have a less generous system than, for example, neighbouring Spain (source in Portuguese). At present, in two-parent families, each parent is entitled to 19 weeks of fully paid leave, rising to 32 weeks in the case of single-parent families.
In France, until a few months ago, (source in Portuguese) maternity leave for a first child was just under four months on full pay, while fathers were entitled to 28 days of leave after the birth. New rules in force since July now allow parents to share an additional period of one or two months' leave on top of their existing entitlements. In such cases, they are paid 70% of their net salary in the first month and 60% in the second.
In Sweden, often cited as a benchmark in this field, the law provides for a total of 480 days (around 16 months) of paid leave, although the monthly benefit cannot exceed 80% of the recipient's salary. In Finland, (source in Portuguese) parents are entitled to 320 working days of leave per child (about 14 months): each parent has 160 working days, 63 of which can be transferred to the other parent. Parental benefit is calculated on the basis of the worker's income and paid by social security.

Korsaks' Museum of Contemporary Ukrainian Art damaged in Russian attack on Lutsk
The roof of the Adrenalin City cultural and entertainment centre in Lutsk caught fire on 13 October when debris from a Russian jet-powered drone fell on the building. Damage was caused to part of Cosmogony, an art project created by Petro Antyp at the Korsaks' Museum of Contemporary Ukrainian Art. The museum's other exhibition halls and artworks were unaffected.
Source: Viktor Korsak, the museum's founder
Details: Korsak said the ensuing fire had been contained. Part of Cosmogony, an art project he worked on with artist Petro Antyp for two years, was damaged. The project consists of six parts.
He described it as symbolic that this particular part of the work had been damaged in the Russian attack.
"The idea was to show humanity who we are, why we are here and where we are heading. And the sixth part, which is behind me, is about the future. It is perhaps symbolic that it was damaged, because this war has changed our future. Part of the future in the Cosmogony project has now been destroyed. And that raises the question of whether it is possible to destroy the future at all," the museum's founder said.
In his video address, Korsak also reflected on whether the sixth part of the project should be restored or left as it is, bearing the scars of the war and serving as a reminder of its consequences.
"In the end, I am left with this dilemma: should we restore this future, or leave it as it is for future generations, as a reminder of what war is and what it leads to – a reminder to those who start wars that war is a great tragedy," Korsak said.
He added that the decision would be made jointly with Petro Antyp.
Korsak said the other exhibition halls and the museum's artworks escaped damage. The museum will remain open and continue working on new projects.

Russia has accused Dutch authorities of denying visas to three of Russia’s leading female gymnasts for the World Championships in Rotterdam, which kick off this weekend, and jeopardizing their qualification path for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Reigning world all-around champion Angelina Melnikova, Tokyo 2020 team Olympic champion Viktoria Listunova and 2026 European silver medalist Anna Kalmykova have all reportedly been refused visas, the Russian Gymnastics Federation said Tuesday, citing the Dutch Embassy in Moscow.
The refusal notices apparently expressed diplomatic concerns, stating that “one or several Schengen member states consider the athletes a threat to their international relations.”
“We view the actions of the Dutch authorities as a deliberate elimination of the strongest gymnasts from competition for world medals and Olympic quotas,” the Russian Gymnastics Federation said.
The Dutch foreign and sports ministries declined to comment on individual visa applications, but clarified to local media that the refusals were unrelated to athletic performance.
The three denied athletes have faced scrutiny from Ukrainian sports authorities over their ties to the Russian military and public displays supporting the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Melnikova represents the military-affiliated CSKA sports club and has previously posted social media photographs featuring the pro-war “Z” symbol.
Listunova took part in a March 2022 pro-war rally with President Vladimir Putin and was previously denied neutral status by World Gymnastics over pro-military social media posts.
Kalmykova holds a sports contract with the Russian National Guard, according to Ukrainian officials.
Russia’s Ambassador to the Netherlands Vladimir Tarabrin said he personally visited the Dutch Foreign Ministry to demand visas, but was presented with “utterly unconvincing arguments that defy any reasonable criticism.”
Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov said the Russian Olympic Committee will lobby to strip the Rotterdam championship of its official Olympic qualifying status.
The Oct. 17-25 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam serve as the opening team qualifier for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games.
Out of 61 members of the Russian delegation, 47 were granted Dutch visas, including five male and three female gymnasts.
World Gymnastics and European Gymnastics lifted restrictions on Russian and Belarusian gymnasts after the International Olympic Committee provisionally lifted its ban on the countries’ Olympic committees in July.

"With today's 2.86 billion euro disbursement, we keep addressing Ukraine's most urgent operational needs," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The funding will go towards drones, air defense systems, missiles, radars, electronic warfare systems, and ammunition, reads a European Commission press statement.
"As Russia stalls on the front lines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks — cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies," von der Leyen said.

"These funds will strengthen us," Zelensky said.
The latest announcement follows a previous disbursement of 1.24 billion euros ($1.4 billion) in defense support on Oct. 7, and further disbursements from the EU are expected until the end of the year.
Within the EU's 90 billion euro loan, 28.3 billion euros ($31.7 billion) were earmarked for Ukraine's defense needs in 2026, of which 18.26 billion euros ($20.44 billion) have now been disbursed.
Ukraine's plans for how to spend the remaining 10 billion euros ($11.2 billion) have already been approved by the EU; all that is required is for Kyiv to send the receipts for sign-off by Brussels.

Residents’ preference for Turkish lira remains strong despite fund outflows: Central bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:46:40 UTC
18:46:40 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Fund outflows have not significantly weakened Turkish residents’ preference for lira-denominated assets, Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan said Wednesday.
Karahan delivered a presentation on Türkiye’s macroeconomic outlook and monetary policy during the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
“Fund outflows have not materially weakened residents’ preferences for TL assets,” Karahan said. “Residents’ preference for Turkish lira remains robust overall.”
Karahan said proactive measures had limited potential spillovers from funds subject to trading restrictions, while tight monetary policy supported demand for the lira.
He reiterated that the bank would maintain its tight policy stance until price stability is achieved, supporting disinflation through demand, exchange rate and expectations channels.
Interest rate decisions would take into account actual and expected inflation, alongside its underlying trend, to ensure the degree of tightness needed for a disinflation path consistent with the bank’s interim targets.
Decisions would remain cautious and be taken on a meeting-by-meeting basis, with further tightening if the inflation outlook deviated significantly from those targets.
 
Underlying inflation moderates despite energy pressures
Karahan said supply-side pressures had slowed disinflation, with energy prices exerting a major influence this year. Nevertheless, underlying inflation was moderating as weaker demand cushioned inflationary pressures.
Annual consumer inflation stood at 29.7% in September, down from 75.5% in May 2024. Monthly underlying inflation eased to 1.7% from 2% in June.
Seasonally adjusted monthly services inflation stood at 1.85%, its lowest level in five years.
Rent inflation was easing, with leading indicators pointing to further moderation. However, increases in transportation and communication prices partly offset declines in rent and education inflation.
Karahan said inflation expectations warranted continued caution, while high-frequency indicators confirmed weak domestic demand in the third quarter. Macroprudential policies also supported slower credit growth.
Despite weaker external demand prospects for 2026, the trade deficit remained moderate and tourism revenues were close to last year’s levels, helping contain the current account deficit.
Türkiye’s sliding-scale fuel tax mechanism had restrained fuel price increases, he said, adding that gold price fluctuations amplified volatility in reserve buffers.

Russia Gave Its Mi-28NM New Anti-Drone Defenses—A Ukrainian FPV Still Took It Down

- Category

Russia Gave Its Mi-28NM New Anti-Drone Defenses—A Ukrainian FPV Still Took It Down
A Ukrainian air-defense FPV drone shot down a modernized Russian Mi-28NM attack helicopter in midair, Ukraine’s 115th Separate Mechanized Brigade said after releasing footage of the interception on October 14.
The strike was carried out by pilots from the brigade’s “Pribultsi” air-defense unit, despite indications that newer Mi-28NM helicopters are being fitted with additional systems designed to protect them from drone attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“An anti-aircraft FPV drone intercepted the aircraft in midair, leaving no chance for either the machine or the crew,” the unit wrote.
The Mi-28NM is the most advanced production version of Russia’s Mi-28 attack helicopter family and represents a substantial modernization of the earlier Mi-28N.
The newer aircraft received improved sensors, weapons, avionics, and defensive systems after the baseline version demonstrated significant limitations during Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Recent Mi-28NMs have also appeared with previously unseen sensors marked with the abbreviation NVCh, referring to microwave frequencies in the 300 MHz to 300 GHz range. The devices have been observed on the helicopter’s wingtips, around the nose of the cockpit, and toward the tail.
Their exact function has not been publicly confirmed, but the positioning has fueled speculation that Russia is adding another layer of protection against Ukrainian FPV drones. The equipment may represent an upgrade to the Mi-28NM’s existing L-370 Vitebsk defensive suite or an entirely new anti-drone system.
Russia has separately developed the Multik electronic warfare system, produced by the Gradient research institute specifically to protect helicopters from FPV attacks. However, the equipment recently seen on Mi-28NMs does not visually match that system.
The Mi-28NM also carries significantly more capable weapons than earlier variants. Among them is the Izdeliye 305 light multipurpose guided missile, which Russian sources claim can engage targets at ranges of up to 25 kilometers.
Earlier, reports emerged that a Russian Mi-8 military transport helicopter that crashed in the Voronezh region was reportedly shot down by a Russian Su-35 fighter jet in a friendly-fire incident.
The incident occurred as Russian forces were responding to a large-scale drone attack. The Su-35 crew allegedly misidentified the Mi-8 helicopter as a hostile unmanned aerial vehicle and opened fire.

Ecology trail to Olor Waterfall opened near Putorana Plateau in Krasnoyarsk Region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:45:45 UTC
18:45:45 KST

KRASNOYARSK, October 14. /TASS/. An ecology trail leading to the Olor Waterfall in the Putorana Plateau foothills opened in Taymyr. While walking along the trail, visitors will be able to see various representatives of the northern flora and fauna, press service of the Expert Center at the Arctic Development Project Office (PORA) told TASS.
"The Five Ethnic Groups of Taymyr ecological trail has been opened," the press service said. "It leads to the Olor Waterfall on the Kharayelakh Range slopes, in the foothills of the Putorana Plateau."
"The name - Five Ethnic Groups of Taymyr - refers to the peninsula's five indigenous peoples - the Dolgans, Nganasans, Ents, Nenets, and Evenks," the press service continued. "Wooden sculptures about four meters high, created with traditional ornaments and symbols, are dedicated to their cultural heritage."
As the number of tourists has been growing over recent years, on the peninsula appeared natural trails, bonfires, debris and damage to vegetation - right in the direction to the Olor waterfall, the Expert Center said. The new ecology trail with an entrance group, navigation poles, information stands and themed art objects will guide visitors along an organized route.
According to the organizers, while walking along the new trail, visitors will be able to see rare representatives of the northern fauna, for example, gyrfalcon, peregrine falcon, white-billed loon and tundra swan. Special attention is paid to mosses, lichens and other plants that are sensitive to trampling.
"The development of tourism in the Arctic should not conflict with objectives to preserve its unique nature. Right on the contrary, a properly-organized tourist flow can reduce the burden on the fragile northern ecosystems, and at the same time it can make natural attractions more accessible. The ecology trail to the Olor Waterfall is a good example of this approach," Maxim Dankin, Director General of the PORA Expert Center and a member of the Russian Federation's Civic Chamber, said commenting on the event.
At the ceremonial opening of the trail, representatives of Taymyr's low-numbered indigenous peoples conducted the sacred Dolgan ceremony, dubbed "Alastyr", which included the symbolic purification of the sculptures with the smoke of rosemary and juniper - for good luck, they said.

PIKSI’s in Peril but You Can Help (guest post)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:45:00 UTC
18:45:00 KST

The Philosophy in an Inclusive Key Summer Institutes (PIKSI) in Boston aim to “broaden inclusion within professional philosophy.” In part because such efforts are currently unpopular with the powers that be, its primary funding, from MIT and Harvard, has been cut.
To cope with the cuts, its organizers say that “it is our plan to shrink it a bit and see what we can do to raise funds for 2027, with the hope that we can build it back up with other funding in 2028 and beyond.”
In the following guest post, Sally Haslanger (MIT) discusses what PIKSI Boston, which has been in operation since 2015, does, its impact on students, and how you can help with efforts to sustain the program.
PIKSI’s in Peril but You Can Help
by Sally Haslanger
PIKSI-Boston is a summer institute organized by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Harvard University, and the University of Massachusetts-Boston to address pipeline issues and broaden inclusion within professional philosophy.
Since 2015, we have supported 220 undergraduates or recent graduates (the Alain Locke Fellows) who have come to MIT for ten days in the summer to spend full-time studying philosophy—representing a broad range of traditions and areas—with visiting professors and graduate teaching fellows. Each Alain Locke Fellow is also paired with a mentor to assist them in the process of applying to graduate school.
The impact of this program is tremendous, not only for the fellows, but also for the faculty and graduate students involved. For instance, one fellow wrote: “Upon my return [home], I realized how transformative PIKSI-Boston was for me. I no longer feel like grad school is some far-off possibility and I feel that my ideas and experiences can create good philosophy.” Alums don’t all go into philosophy graduate school or pursue philosophy as a career, though many have. In a recent survey, of 31 respondents, 28 were pursuing philosophy or an adjacent field. Feedback suggests that the program has also empowered fellows to enter other professions with greater confidence.
PIKSI-Boston provides funds for round-trip travel, lodging, meals and social events for the Alain Locke Fellows as well as the visiting professors and teaching fellows. Funding also provides stipends for the co-directors of the Institute, course materials, and promotional items.
In the current climate, institutional efforts to address inclusion have been discouraged, and budget cuts in higher education have hit such programs hard. While the Philosophy Section at MIT remains committed to supporting PIKSI, their contribution falls well short of the funding needed and all other financial support has been eliminated. This is at a time when philosophy is of increasing public importance and careers that can benefit from an advanced degree in philosophy—such as philosophy of AI—are expanding.
Our aim, at PIKSI-Boston, is to reduce the size of the program for 2027 in order to maintain it during this financial crisis, and to spend the year seeking support to endow it.
We are asking colleagues to make a contribution to PIKSI-Boston using this link. (Once there, enter “Piksi” into the “search for a fund” field.)
The money goes to MIT and is earmarked for the PIKSI-Boston program. Because MIT is a non-profit, donations are tax-deductible. We also created a fundraising brochure (a “one pager”) that you should feel free to send to others:
Our goal is to raise enough to host ten undergraduates and two teaching fellows in 2027 or $40,000. If necessary, we will reduce the duration of the institute from ten to five days. Here are some examples of what your donation can provide.
Anything you can provide will be put to good use. This is an investment in the future of professional philosophy. You can donate here.
If you have questions, or if, by chance, you have leads for any major donors, please contact me.
Thank you for your support.

Yakutia's experts to study how regulated reindeer grazing affects permafrost preservation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:43:02 UTC
18:43:02 KST

YAKUTSK, October 14. /TASS/. Experts will study the role of reindeer grazing in permafrost preservation and in prevention of carbon dioxide and methane emissions in the Arctic. The study will be conducted under an agreement signed in Yakutsk at the Northern Sustainable Development Forum, Maxim Dankin, Director General of the Expert Center - Project Office for the Development of the Arctic (PORA), posted on Telegram.
"We are beginning our second voluntary climate project, for which we have chosen the Primorskiy reindeer breeding farm in the Bulunsky District," he wrote. "In August, together with the region's Arctic Research Center, we conducted an expedition and began preparations. The project is based on the idea of preserving permafrost through regulated reindeer grazing."
The project's goal, he continued, is to prevent carbon dioxide and methane emissions, additional carbon uptake by vegetation, and the task is to create a working model in Yakutia that could be replicated in other Arctic regions.
Animals affect the moss cover, contributing to the grassy vegetation development, and in winter they compact the snow, he said. This, in turn, allows the cold to penetrate deeper into the soil, slowing down the permafrost thawing and the stored carbon release. "The Arctic has been warming up 3-4 times faster than the rest of the planet. The permafrost degradation threatens infrastructures, leads to additional greenhouse gas emissions, and endangers the traditional way of life of the North's indigenous peoples," he explained. "Most revenues from the possible sale of carbon units will remain in the farm, to be directed to its development and to support for the indigenous people's traditional way of life."
The PORA Expert Center already has experience in implementing the first forest climate project in the Arctic, on the Yamal Peninsula. The project has been validated and right now it is at the stage of carbon units' registration.
The changing permafrost
According to Mikhail Zheleznyak, director of the Melnikov Permafrost Institute (the Russian Academy of Sciences' Siberian Branch), in Central Yakutia, the temperature varies depending on landscape conditions, and the soil temperature at a depth of 3-3.5 m varies towards warming at the depth of the seasonal thawing layer. In some woodlands, this difference over 50 years has reached 0.3 degrees, and there are areas where this temperature has changed by 2 degrees. "There are territories where the surface has thawed or sunk to almost three meters over 50 years," he told participants in a round table discussion - "From Yakutsk to Antalya: Forming a unified Arctic voice for COP31." "We are talking about a very complex system. Can it be predicted? Of course it can. What is missing? We need to know the trend."
The permafrost degradation process has points of no return, and permafrost has never been stable or permanent, the scientist said. "If we are talking about engineering structures for thousands of years to come, this is one aspect, but if we are speaking about a hundred years, then we can manage it. We must learn to manage it and to be building facilities properly. The problem is only with us. We need good design solutions and we need to know how the changes are developing. That is, we are missing an observation network."
About the forum
The 7th Northern Sustainable Development Forum took place in Yakutsk on October 7-10. Human capital development in the artificial intelligence era was the event's key topic. The forumfeatured participants from Russia's 20 regions and from twelve countries.
