Russian strikes leave 600,000 without power in Ukraine, as Starlink restrictions affect front line
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:42:08 BST
18:42:08 KST

Starlink restrictions in Ukraine war linked to political situation, Zelensky aide says
- Published
New restrictions on the speed at which some of Ukraine's weapons can travel and stay connected to the Starlink internet network have disrupted Ukraine's battlefield "missions", President Volodymyr Zelensky's adviser has warned.
Serhiy Beskrestnov said Ukraine had not been told about speed limits set overnight at 100mph (160km/h) by Elon Musk's SpaceX company.
Starlink is a vital tool allowing Kyiv to effectively guide drones to Russian targets and also protect Ukrainian skies.
Beskrestnov said SpaceX's move "cannot be a coincidence and is related to the current political situation". The firm has not commented.
In Wednesday's post on Telegram, Beskrestnov said that SpaceX had "implemented overnight a speed limit on Starlink terminals" and this had already resulted in "the disruption of a number of missions".
In a follow-up post, the adviser stressed that Starlink was the most effective tool for enabling interceptors to shoot down Russia's newly developed jet-propelled drones.
It comes as at least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes, Zelensky said. Pictures from Kyiv showed residents, some dressed in their pajamas, with bloodied faces.
He added that "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit in Kyiv and the capital region, and in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv – despite US President Donald Trump's claim on Sunday that an "energy ceasefire" was in place between Russia and Ukraine.
Three people were killed in Kyiv, local officials reported. Russia said its "massive" strikes had hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.
Later on Wednesday, at least six people were killed in a Russian drone strike on a warehouse in the north-western city of Lutsk, local officials said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and Moscow currently controls about 20% of Ukrainian territory.
A source in the Ukrainian defence ministry later told the BBC: "Last night, we detected restrictions affecting Starlink connectivity at speeds above 160 km/h." The source added that the "root cause" of the issue was being investigated.
Defence ministry sources later explained that "once a vehicle or asset exceeds this [160km/h] threshold speed, the terminal loses its connection".
They told the BBC that this made it more difficult to carry out drone operations, "specifically interceptors and middle-strike drones", and also degraded "capabilities for front line logistics, reconnaissance, and signal relaying".
In February, Musk's decision to deny Russian forces access to Starlink blunted Moscow's advance in Ukraine and caused confusion among Russian commanders.
Musk's SpaceX has not commented on the reported speed restrictions.
Zelensky has said that the US threatened to restrict intelligence sharing if he did not sign up to Trump's energy ceasefire. On Tuesday, Trump denied that Washington was withholding intelligence.
Ukraine relies on US satellite systems to track Russian missiles in order to issue alerts and to try to shoot them down. But over the past two nights, missiles have struck targets in the Ukrainian capital without any warning, before air raid sirens could be sounded.
According to Ukraine's air force, Russia launched 39 ballistic and cruise missiles and 128 drones overnight. Four of those missiles and 115 drones were shot down, it said.
It was the second night in a row that Kyiv was hit by Russian missiles, and came as Zelensky prepared to meet UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday to discuss accelerating air defence supplies to Kyiv.
Meanwhile, the Russian defence ministry said 902 Ukrainian drones had been shot down overnight over a number of Russian regions, including the capital Moscow and Crimea - Ukraine's southern peninsula annexed by Russia in 2014.
On Sunday, Trump wrote on Truth Social: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!"
Zelensky has since repeatedly said that Ukraine is ready to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow does the same.
But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. Under any truce, he added, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons", enabling it to continue the war.
For residents of Kyiv, the past two nights have been frightening.
Tetiana Storozhyk, 54, said a late night blast on Tuesday at her apartment block blew her from the kitchen into the hallway. The sirens sounded just as the missile hit the building, giving her no time to evacuate.
"It all happened in a fraction of a second. In that moment I lost everything" she said.
Storozhyk told the BBC that Ukraine needs weapons to protect its people, "but from the other side we need peace".
Without peace Ukraine is reliant on its air defences, but this wrecked neighbourhood is evidence of how ineffective they are without the right data.

INTERVIEW – Exemptions, inquiry, divisions: What matters in Israel’s election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:41:39 UTC
18:41:39 KST

As Benjamin Netanyahu fights to remain Israel’s prime minister in this month’s election, debate over his political future spans wars on multiple fronts, corruption allegations and accusations of authoritarianism.
But for Israeli-American activist and author Miko Peled, only two issues will “make or break” the vote: military service exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jews and demands for an inquiry into the failure to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks.
“Those are the two major issues that the campaigns are focusing on and the Israeli public is focused on,” he told Anadolu.
“All the other stuff is nonsense because people support the genocide. People support the attacks on Iran. People support the occupation of Southern Lebanon and parts of Syria.”
Exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, men have long divided the country. Many regard full-time religious study as their primary duty and oppose compulsory enlistment.
Peled estimated that close to 100,000 young ultra-Orthodox men were eligible for military service but refusing to enlist.
Netanyahu’s main opponents have pledged to end broad exemptions, while his ultra-Orthodox coalition partners have sought to preserve them.
Peled warned that efforts to compel enlistment could provoke massive unrest within Israeli society.
“They will never agree to serve. It's a very strong community. They follow the letter of the law of the Torah and they will not serve,” he said. “And the rest of the Israeli society will also not give up. They're not just going to let it happen.”
The second dividing line is accountability for the failure to prevent the October 2023 attacks.
Netanyahu’s main challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has pledged to establish an independent state commission of inquiry into the failures. Netanyahu has repeatedly resisted calls for such an inquiry.
Peled’s familiarity with Netanyahu stretches back to their childhood neighborhood in Jerusalem. The future prime minister attended school with Peled’s sister, Nurit.
In his memoir, The General’s Son, Peled recalled admiring Netanyahu, widely known as Bibi, as a young boy. That admiration faded when Netanyahu entered politics.
“He seemed insincere and opportunistic, and his views were uncompromisingly hawkish. It was obvious to me that no government under him was going to advance the cause of peace,” Peled wrote.
Netanyahu was prime minister when Peled’s niece, Smadar, was killed in a Jerusalem suicide bombing in 1997. Her death prompted Peled to seek encounters with Palestinians and helped shape his subsequent activism.
He argues that Netanyahu’s objectives have always been clear and that his continued political relevance reflects support for those objectives.
“His ideology was well known. He never hid what he wanted to do. And that's why he keeps getting elected, because the Israeli public likes what he says, and they like his ideology. They support his ideology.”
Peled accused Netanyahu of leading genocide and a broader campaign of ethnic cleansing against Palestinians, extending beyond Gaza.
“He is a war criminal … he should go to The Hague, and then go to jail for the rest of his life.”
But he argued that the outlook sustaining Israel’s wars extends beyond one leader. Israelis, he said, are educated to believe that perpetual conflict is necessary for survival.
“They know ‘we took the land from Palestinians, but we didn't have a choice. And they want to kill us because it's their land. And we have to fight them so that they don't kill us. And there's no solution,’” he said.
“Any of the major candidates, all of them say there is no solution.”
Peled said this belief permeated politics, education and public discussion, alongside demands for military strength and self-reliance.
He cautioned against assuming Netanyahu’s political career was ending, describing his coalition as “very comfortable” and predicting that its partners would perform well.
“Anybody who expects that for some reason he will disappear is not reading the map properly,” he said.
Peled’s political position also departs from that of his father, Matti Peled, an Israeli general who later championed peace and a two-state solution.
The younger Peled considers that solution unworkable, arguing that Israeli control over Palestinian territory has left no viable basis for it.
He said Israel would not stop taking Palestinian land “unless it is forcibly stopped by the international community.”
“Although it's not legally annexed yet. But it's in de facto, most of it is gone,” he said of the West Bank. “And you have these ghettos in which Palestinians live. And now they want to kick them out. So, the two-state solution is a myth.”
Peled described Zionism as a racist and genocidal ideology. To have two states, he said, the government would have to agree that Palestinians have rights, something he said “would never happen because the Zionist ideology says the whole land belongs to the Jewish people.”
Through the Palestine House of Freedom in Washington, which he founded, Peled advocates a democratic state across historic Palestine with a right of return for Palestinians.
“That option for peace is a free Palestine on all of historic Palestine with the right of return. That option will allow Israelis and Palestinians to live in peace.”
He said the organization sought to explain that alternative to elected officials and the public.
Asked whether outside powers could stop Israel, he said European countries and the US had the means but had failed to act.
“Of course, the Europeans and the Americans can stop it today. They could have prevented Oct. 7th. They could have prevented the genocide in Gaza … They could have prevented all of it.”
Peled urged countries to treat Israel as a “pariah” in sporting, academic and cultural life. He also expressed concern that countries traditionally supportive of Palestine were considering normalizing relations with Israel.
For him, changing government policy requires sustained public pressure.
“The constituents have to stand up and say no. The constituents around the world, citizens have to stand up and say no to normalization, no to trade, no to diplomatic relations,” he said.
“People have to do this. People have to demand of their governments that they do this. And then they also have to demand of the media to tell the truth.”
While the establishment of a Palestinian state seems distant and increasingly difficult, Peled said the state of Israel, particularly after the Gaza war began, “is crumbling from within.”
“Israeli society was ripped apart. Israeli society was never a cohesive society. It was a bunch of different groups tied together with scotch tape. Oct. 7 ripped off that scotch tape,” he said.
“So, when you hear the discourse in Hebrew between politicians, the journalists, people in the street, the vitriol is unbelievable. The hatred is beyond belief.”
He pointed to disruption at ports and airports and the continued displacement of residents from communities near Lebanon and Gaza as evidence of the strain.
He said the education and healthcare systems were “bankrupt,” called the police “corrupt,” and described the judicial system as “politicized.”
“So, what's left of the state?” he said. “Yes, they have big bombs. They've got the hardware to bomb everybody. But that's all there is. There's nothing else left. So, that state is crumbling.”
Peled argued that military power could not compensate for those weaknesses and warned that further pressure could precipitate a complete collapse.
“If there is no plan to replace the regime with a real democratic Palestine, the chaos that will ensue will be unfathomable, unimaginable,” he said.
“So our argument as Palestine House of Freedom is that we must have a plan in place so that when it does collapse, it's not chaos.”
He called for replacing what he described as an apartheid system with a democracy that “represents all the people there.”

Iran executes man accused of armed attacks during US-Israeli strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:40:38 UTC
18:40:38 KST

Ali-Sina Mostafavi, 38, a mountaineer and musician from Kerman, was executed on charges of “enmity against God” after being accused of firing on civilians and soldiers during the opening months of the war. He was also charged with participating in the January protests and sending footage
Iran executed a political prisoner in Kerman on Wednesday on charges of carrying out armed attacks during what the Iranian judiciary described as joint American-Israeli military operations on Iranian soil.
The Mizan news agency, the official outlet of Iran's judiciary, identified Ali-Sina Mostafavi, 38, as one of "the armed agents of the American-Zionist enemy" and accused him of opening fire on civilians in Azadi Square in Kerman on 24 March, wounding one person and a young girl.
According to Mizan, he also fired on conscript soldiers and passing vehicles on 21 April, injuring further civilians.
The judiciary additionally accused him of participating in protests in December 2025 and January 2026 — which the Iranian authorities call the "Dey protests" and describe as a coup attempt — and of sending footage to Persian-language media outlets based outside Iran, which Tehran brands as hostile.
Among the items seized from Mostafavi, said to be from the city of Bam, were a Brno rifle with telescopic sight, a shotgun, a second unlicensed shotgun, 246 rounds for the Brno and 30 Molotov cocktails, the judiciary said.
Mostafavi, who played the tar and had made a solo ascent of Island Peak in the Himalayas and attempted Ama Dablam, reaching 6,600 metres, was held in Shahab prison in Kerman. He was moved to solitary confinement in his final days and his family were summoned for a last visit.
Reza Pahlavi, the son of Iran's last shah, described Mostafavi on X as "a patriotic young man" condemned after forced confessions extracted under torture in what he called show trials, and urged others to speak out for political prisoners facing execution.
The charge Mostafavi faced, moharebeh, or "enmity against God," in Iranian law represents taking up arms against people's lives, property or honour in a way that creates insecurity.
Tehran has deployed the charge for decades to suppress opponents, critics and protesters.
Second execution this week
Two days earlier, the Mizan news agency confirmed the execution of Omar Dorastaran, 25, identified by the judiciary as a member of the Sunni militant group Jaish al-Adl.
He was accused of helping group members enter Iran, arranging accommodation and transport, and providing support for attacks on IRGC forces in Sistan and Baluchistan province, including the attack on the Paroud base and March 2024 assaults on military installations in Chabahar.
The 2024 attack on the Rask police post was among the deadliest carried out by armed groups in south-eastern Iran. Eleven security forces members were killed.
Dorastaran, single and from the village of Cheraghan in Rask county, was studying at a religious school in the city of Pishin at the time of his arrest, according to human rights organisations.
Halvash, a local media outlet in Sistan and Baluchestan, reported that he was arrested without a warrant and held for an extended period without access to visits or phone calls, and that security agents sought to extract forced confessions through torture.
Sistan and Baluchistan, one of Iran's poorest provinces, has long been the scene of armed clashes between security forces and Sunni militant and Baloch armed organisations. Fighting in the province has intensified in recent weeks.
Amnesty International on Tuesday condemned the execution of five men within a single week in Iran in cases linked to the January protests, and called for coordinated international pressure on Tehran to halt further executions.
The organisation said the Islamic Republic uses the death penalty systematically to intimidate opponents and raise the cost of protest. Iran executed at least 2,159 people in 2025, according to Amnesty.

In Mali, from the Wagner Group to Africa Corps: Will Impunity Continue?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:40:05 UTC
18:40:05 KST

When Africa Corps officially began operations in Mali in June 2025, few people held out hope that it would help alleviate the suffering of civilians in Mali, caused on the one hand by armed groups in Azawad and members from the Group for the Support of Islam and Muslims (GSIM), but also by the army and its auxiliaries from the Russian private military company known as Wagner.
Troops from Africa Corps, under the direct control of the Kremlin, had already begun deploying in the country as early as January 2025 and were gradually taking over Wagner’s role in support of the army’s military operations. Joint patrols by the army and Wagner between 2023 and 2025 were marred by serious violations which we recently detailed again in a report, some of which we believe amount to war crimes.
In particular, we document seven incidents in which 34 people were deliberately killed during these patrols. The victims – all civilians, according to the testimonies collected – were shot, had their throats slit, and were burned; some were even mutilated after death. Many of them were shot in cold blood while they were herding their livestock or after being apprehended.
Accounts of widespread torture
Deadly drone attacks in Ejdeir (without warning and on a market day, 16 dead) and Tangata (at night on a house, the day after a wedding, seven dead), in March and November 2025, also caused deaths and destruction. Both strikes were carried out without any apparent evidence of the presence of armed combatants or military targets at either location. If this was the case, these acts would constitute direct attacks against civilians and private property and should be investigated as possible war crimes.
Torture and ill-treatment were also commonplace during these operations. The same was true in the military camps at Léré and Nampala, where detainees could be held for months without being able to notify their families or appear before a judge – or could simply disappear.
Survivors of this torture – which was carried out alongside interrogations about the activities of armed groups – whose bodies sometimes still bear the scars, spoke with Amnesty International. Suspension by the arms, simulated drowning, electric shocks, beatings with boots, rifle butts, and iron bars, and detention in degrading conditions with unsanitary restrooms: the range of practices is wide. Some had been subjected to sexual violence, forced to undress, and made to remain naked for several days while in custody.
These abuses were committed primarily by Wagner Group members, but with the full knowledge of the Malian armed forces. According to the testimonies collected, at least five people died as a result of this torture. Members of the Fulani, Tuareg, and Arab communities living along the border with Mauritania were the main victims of the war crimes documented in this report.
The protection of civilians in the context of the conflict must be a priority for the Malian authorities and all parties to the conflict
Ousmane Diallo, Sahel researcher at Amnesty International
Because they are “suspected” by the army and members of the Wagner Group of colluding with or sympathizing with GSIM. Because they live in rural areas, in a zone of conflict between the warring parties. One crime followed another. These often-deadly military operations are accompanied by looting (money, livestock, jewelry, blankets, etc.) and the destruction of property, clearly calling into question the Malian authorities’ claims that they are targeting only members of armed groups.
Although Africa Corps has replaced Wagner, nothing has been done to change the situation. Impunity persists. To our knowledge, no legal proceedings have been initiated regarding the abuses committed by government forces against civilians since 2023. Victims do not dare to file complaints for fear of reprisals. Those who dare to criticize the conduct of military operations are subjected to repression. The military authorities exercise total control over information.
Allegations of abuses have already been levelled against members of Africa Corps, according to Human Rights Watch. On July 10, 2026, in Bombori, the village’s Fulani neighbourhood was raided: 80 men were rounded up outside before being beaten and interrogated about the activities of armed groups. Six people who tried to flee were shot dead, while three others were executed.
One atrocity must not follow another. The protection of civilians in the context of the conflict must be a priority for the Malian authorities and all parties to the conflict, in accordance with international humanitarian law. Military operations and camps must be monitored, and the justice system must be able to conduct independent investigations into all alleged cases of abuses.

Ukraine on Wednesday accused Russia of wilfully flouting Donald Trump's purported "energy ceasefire" and passing up an opportunity to ease hostilities, after a renewed wave of deadly strikes across the country that also hit vital power supplies.
Kiev in particular faced a barrage of powerful ballistic missiles and attack drones targeting energy facilities and critical infrastructure, despite the US president's surprise weekend announcement.
Four people were killed in the city and power to at least 600,000 people was cut after significant damage was reported to power facilities and equipment.
Power plants also came under ballistic missile attack in the eastern Kharkiv region, hitting electricity and heating infrastructure, Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky said.
Zelenskyy blasted the latest attack as "entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale", adding: "Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States".
"Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," he wrote on X.
Trump blindsided both Kiev and Moscow on Sunday by unilaterally announcing an "energy ceasefire", two days after enraging Ukraine's Western allies with news of a deal with heavily sanctioned Russia to supply diesel fuel.
The US leader has repeatedly lashed out at Zelenskyy — and even said he should be replaced as president — for Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries.
A senior Ukrainian official confirmed to AFP reports in recent days that Washington threatened to pull intelligence-sharing with Kiev that it relies on to detect incoming attacks.
The renewed signs of strain with Trump have cast doubt on those arrangements, as air raid sirens warning of approaching drones or missiles failed to sound on Monday night and Tuesday night before explosions were heard.
That has occurred only rarely in the past. Ukrainian officials attributed the issue to the Russian military's use of hard-to-detect missiles or potential technical issues.
But Zelenskyy on Tuesday evening said Ukraine had received "no early warning from our partners" about ballistic missile launches, calling it "absolutely unjust".
Starlink
An aide to Zelenskyy meanwhile said the operation of some Starlink internet terminals also appeared to have been restricted overnight, disrupting "a number of missions" by Ukrainian defence forces.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation," said Sergiy Beskrestnov.
A senior Ukrainian official told AFP that Starlink speeds had been "throttled", suggesting that it was done to Russia's advantage.
"What is important is that this has been ongoing since last night. Some restrictions were already being reported yesterday evening, so, in effect, it is happening in sync with this morning's Russian ballistic attack," they added.
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is prepared to hold off from striking Russian energy infrastructure, but accused the Kremlin of having "squandered the opportunity for de-escalation" in the nearly five-year conflict.
Russia has previously targeted Ukraine's power stations and heating infrastructure, crippling supplies before winter, when temperatures can plummet to as low as -20C.
Ukraine has been pushing its allies for more military support as Kiev increasingly comes under attack, particularly the supply of advanced interceptor systems to shoot down missiles and fast, jet-powered drones.
Russian ballistic missile attacks were also reported in the eastern region of Kharkiv and Zhytomyr in the northwest, and other strikes hit Sumy in the northeast and Chernigiv in the north.
Two people were killed in the central Dnipropetrovsk region and a further person in Zaporizhzhia in the southeast, the authorities said.
The governor of Russia's southwestern Saratov region, citing preliminary estimates, said a Ukrainian drone strike had killed one person in the city of Balakovo.
Moscow mayor Sergey Sobyanin said air defence forces had downed nearly 500 drones flying towards the Russian capital overnight.
Russian authorities said around 160 more were brought down over the Rostov region, while others targeted Moscow.
Russia says 902 Ukrainian drones shot down overnight
Russia's military said on Wednesday that it had shot down 902 Ukrainian drones overnight, 180 of them near the capital Moscow.
"Over the past night... air defence systems destroyed 902 Ukrainian drones" across around 20 Russian regions and annexed Crimea, the defence ministry said in a statement.
According to the capital's mayor Sergey Sobyanin, "180 drones were destroyed as they approached Moscow".
He posted on Telegram that it was among the biggest drone attacks to have targeted Moscow in recent weeks.
The attacks disrupted operations at Moscow airports, with flights at Vnukovo Airport suspended for more than eight hours, according to airport authorities.
Russia's defence ministry also said that it had carried out "a massive strike with high-precision weapons" overnight against "energy and communications infrastructure sites" in Ukraine's capital Kiev and the surrounding region as well as in the Kharkiv region, and that all the targets served military interests.

Tallinn roadworks overrun schedules, leaving commuters stuck in jams
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:39:00 UTC
18:39:00 KST

Tallinn roadworks overrun schedules, leaving commuters stuck in jams
Several roadworks in Tallinn are running longer than planned this year, with some set to continue into mid-November and closures causing significant congestion.
Deputy Mayor Kristjan Järvan (Isamaa) blamed unexpected circumstances, including a gas leak on Liivalaia tänav, and admitted procurement began too late this year.
Liivalaia tänav's resurfacing was due to finish on Sunday, October 18, while in nearby Kreutzwaldi tänav' the work was due for completion even earlier, on the Friday , but both have dragged on past that.
Liivalaia is a major through route in central Tallinn, while Kreutzwaldi already saw some disruption with the ongoing construction of the new ERR TV house even before the roadwork there started.
Other major works on Peterburi tee are is now nearing completion, but they have continued to cause traffic hold-ups on the major thoroughfare and many Tallinn residents have felt the cost of the construction personally.
The stretch of work is close to the Ülemiste City district, a major work and residential hub.
"The lane turning into Ülemiste City blocks that whole intersection. I think I lose about 20 minutes a day in this area," one Tallinn resident, Merle, told "Aktuaalne kaamera."
"I've been in traffic for an hour, certainly, maybe more," said another resident, Artur.
Deputy Mayor Järvan attributed the delays to unexpected circumstances. "The most striking of these is probably the Liivalaia Street repair, where a gas leak was identified and resurfacing work has been slightly postponed as a result. But they start next Monday. I would still like to get the whole project finished in the first weeks of November," he said.
Work on Peterburi tee is on schedule, Järvan said, and the Väo road section will be reached next year. The Kreutzwaldi tänav repair should be finished by the end of October.
Tanel Jairus, a mobility engineer at TalTech, noted that the duration of roadworks is difficult to predict, since it is not known what lies beneath the ground. The capricious nature of road repair also prevents large projects from being spread across the year.
"Installing all kinds of materials has separate conditions — what temperatures, what humidity, whether it's left until autumn rains or cold. Then the result of the work is worse as a result," Jairus said.
Jairus believes making major changes to how roadworks are organised would worsen the situation. "This current system, where each time a little better is done, is actually good," he said.
Järvan admitted that repair work only began at the end of summer because procurement started too late, and promised corrections on the city's part.
"This year we have worked very hard to get the procurement done this year, which means we will reach a contract at the beginning of next year, and that in turn means that next year roadworks can start in the spring, when the weather is warm enough," Järvan said.
Summer is the regular time for major road work in the capital but projects can often overrun well into the fall as here. Other major ongoing projects include the Hippodroom intersection, west of the city center.

IEA sees diesel supply squeeze lasting into 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:38:19 UTC
18:38:19 KST

A garbage truck drives past gas prices above $6 a gallon and diesel prices above $8 a gallon as they are displayed outside of a Shell gas station in Carson, California on September 22, 2026. (AFP / Getty Images)
Global diesel supplies are likely to remain tight into 2027 despite falling oil demand, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Oct. 14, citing conflicts in the Middle East and Russia.
Diesel markets were “under extreme pressure,” the Paris-based agency said in its monthly report. It expects the global oil market to remain in deficit through the end of this year.
High prices and supply restrictions are weighing on consumption.
World oil demand is forecast to fall by 2.6 million barrels a day in 2026 to an average of 102.4 million barrels a day, the largest annual decline since the 2020 pandemic.
Demand is expected to recover by about 2 million barrels a day next year but remain slightly below 2025 levels.
Crude exports from Gulf producers recovered to more than 75 percent of prewar levels in September. However, refined fuel shipments from the Middle East remained below half their prewar levels, and security risks left supply forecasts for the rest of the year largely unchanged.
Oil stocks tracked by the agency ended September 509 million barrels below prewar levels, with stocks held on land near their lowest levels in at least a decade.
The IEA said easing the diesel shortage depended on a recovery in Middle Eastern fuel supplies. Without that, further cuts in consumption, with high economic costs, could be needed to balance the market.
It warned of further turbulence before a possible oil surplus emerges in 2027.

U.S. Navy stocks up on spare parts for Aegis radars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:37:39 UTC
18:37:39 KST

- The U.S. Navy ordered $15.1 million in Raytheon spare parts for MK 99, SPY-1 and SPY-3 systems, citing its goal of 75 mission-capable ships.
- The order raises fleet stocking and forward-deployed stock levels, covering 419 requirements across 46 parts, with work running through December 2034.
The U.S. Navy is building up its stocks of spare parts for the radars and fire-control gear on its Aegis warships, ordering $15.1 million worth of components from Raytheon in a deal it tied directly to the surface fleet’s goal of keeping 75 mission-capable ships ready on any given day.
The Department of War contract announcement published on Oct. 13 describes a firm-fixed-price delivery order covering 419 requirements across 46 separate parts used on the MK 99 fire control system, the AN/SPY-1 radar’s transmitter group and the AN/SPY-3 multifunction radar. Each of the 46 parts carries its own National Item Identification Number, the code the U.S. military uses to track an individual item through its supply system.
By Pentagon standards the dollar figure is small, and the more telling detail is the reason the U.S. Navy gave for the purchase. According to the announcement, the requirements stem from the Naval Surface Force’s North Star goal of 75 mission-capable ships and include fleet stocking increases from remodeled allowances for operational availability and endurance supply, along with higher stock levels at forward-deployed sites. Allowance change requests and maintenance activity account for the rest of the demand.
An allowance is the quantity of a given part that a ship or support site is authorized to carry, so raising those levels means more spare radar and fire-control components kept aboard ships and at overseas depots closer to where the fleet operates.
All three systems sit at the heart of U.S. Navy air and missile defense. SPY-1 is the main radar of the Aegis combat system on Arleigh Burke-class destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers, while the MK 99 controls the illuminators that guide Standard Missile-2 interceptors onto their targets in the final seconds of flight. The X-band SPY-3 radar is fitted on Zumwalt-class destroyers and Ford-class aircraft carriers.
Vice Adm. Roy Kitchener, then commander of Naval Surface Forces, set the 75-ship North Star target in 2022 and aimed to reach it by fiscal 2024, a number that represented nearly half of the 164 surface ships in the fleet at the time. Under the surface force’s definitions, a mission-capable ship has completed basic certification and can deploy, though it may not yet be cleared for high-end combat. Surface force leaders said in early 2024 that the fleet had not yet reached the target, eighteen months into the two-year plan.
Raytheon already holds a larger slice of Aegis work this year, having received a $271.5 million contract on Aug. 3 for MK 99 fire control equipment, Aegis modernization hardware and engineering support, with options that could raise its value to $302.5 million.
Raytheon will perform 95% of the new order in Andover, Massachusetts, and the remaining 5% in Chesapeake, Virginia, with deliveries expected to run through December 2034. The U.S. Navy is paying with fiscal 2026 working capital funds that will not expire at the end of the current fiscal year, and Naval Supply Systems Command Weapon Systems Support in Philadelphia awarded the order on a sole-source basis after soliciting only Raytheon.

Feature: When Chinese moon goddess Chang'e speaks Kiswahili on Tanzanian stage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:37:20 CST
18:37:20 KST

by Xinhua writers Hua Hongli, Lin Guangyao, Lucas Liganga
DAR ES SALAAM, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- At the China Cultural Center in Tanzania's commercial hub of Dar es Salaam, Danifrida Ngonyani took to the stage as Chang'e, the legendary figure from Chinese mythology who flies to the moon.
This, however, was no ordinary retelling of an ancient tale: the characters spoke Kiswahili, while traditional Tanzanian instruments, including drums and marimba, accompanied the performance.
The play "Chang'e: Flying to the Moon" was part of celebrations marking the Mid-Autumn Festival, drawing diplomats, film industry stakeholders and other guests, who watched attentively and applauded the performance.
For the Tanzanian actress, who has been a member of the local organization African Film Arts and Social Revolution (AFASR) for about four years, playing Chang'e offered an opportunity to explore Chinese history and discover connections between the two countries' cultural traditions.
"Being given the role of Chang'e made me very proud and excited," she said, adding that the experience taught her about Chinese history and love.
The legend of Chang'e is deeply intertwined with the Mid-Autumn Festival, a cherished Chinese tradition when families reunite, gaze at the full moon, and share mooncakes.
According to one version of the legend, Chang'e drinks an elixir of immortality to prevent it from falling into the wrong hands. She then ascends to the moon, leaving her husband, Hou Yi, on Earth.
The festival, marked on the 15th day of the eighth month of the Chinese lunar calendar, is also associated with the harvest and symbolizes reunion and togetherness.
Bringing the story to a Tanzanian stage took more than language translation. The production incorporated local music and theatrical traditions, allowing Tanzanian performers to tell a Chinese story through artistic expressions familiar to their audiences.
Nyakwesi Silas Mujaya, founder and director of AFASR, said the approach sought to blend the two cultures, without allowing either to overshadow the other.
"When we take a Chinese story, we put it in a Tanzanian context and perform it in a way that allows both cultures to be represented," she said.
For Mujaya, the legend also carries themes familiar to Tanzanian audiences, including sacrifice, responsibility, protecting others, and the struggle between good and evil.
She said the story reminded her of Tanzanian historical figures who had made sacrifices for their people, as well as experiences within families and communities.
"Although the story comes from China, some of its values are similar to ours. We also celebrate our heroes and preserve stories about people who have done important things for society," she said.
The production was developed through cooperation between AFASR and the China Cultural Center in Tanzania.
A total of 14 artists took part, including stage performers and those responsible for music and visual elements. The one-hour play required about one month of continuous preparation, according to Mujaya.
The cultural center also provided support for production materials and costumes, helping the nonprofit organization meet some of the costs involved in staging the performance.
Founded in 2012, AFASR uses drama, theatre, music and dance to support women, children and young people, helping them develop artistic skills and find opportunities to participate in their communities.
"Arts and culture are not only a way of empowering people economically, but also a way of helping them understand their culture, develop skills and contribute to their communities and society," Mujaya said.
She noted that many participating artists still rely on other activities to support themselves between commissioned performances. AFASR hopes that wider cultural partnerships and more opportunities to perform will help make artistic work a more sustainable livelihood.
For Ngonyani, playing Chang'e has also deepened her interest in Chinese culture.
Preparing for the role introduced her to Chinese history and traditions she had not previously encountered. During activities associated with the production, she also learned about Chinese coffee-making practices, another experience that introduced her to unfamiliar cultural traditions.
"I like their culture. If I get the opportunity to visit China, I would like to learn many more things, including their cultural traditions and dances, because I also enjoy dancing," she said.
Mujaya shared that ambition, voicing hope for cooperation with the China cultural center to eventually enable AFASR artists to perform in China, introduce Tanzanian culture to Chinese audiences and learn from Chinese performers.
"I want to visit China not only to see the country, but also to learn about its culture. At the same time, I want Chinese people to learn about Tanzanian culture," Mujaya added. ■

Former Ukrainian military officer to stand trial in Germany over Nord Stream sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:37:08 UTC
18:37:08 KST

While some in the West were quick to accuse Russia of sabotaging its own gas export route, German investigators identified a cell of Ukrainians they say were the alleged perpetrators.
A former Ukrainian military officer is set to become the first person to stand trial over the 2022 Nord Stream pipeline bombings when proceedings begin in a German court on Wednesday.
In September that year, seven months after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a series of blasts under the Baltic Sea damaged three of the four Nord Stream pipelines designed to carry Russian gas to Europe.
While some in the West were quick to accuse Russia of sabotaging its own export route, German investigators identified a cell of Ukrainians they say were the alleged perpetrators.
Investigators allege Sergiy Kuznietsov, a former Ukrainian special forces officer, led a group of divers, an explosives expert, and a boat skipper that planted explosives on the pipelines.
Kuznietsov, who was arrested in Italy last year and extradited to Germany, will face charges including carrying out a "war crime," attacking civilian infrastructure and causing an explosion.
Ahead of proceedings getting underway in the northern city of Hamburg, a small group of pro-Ukrainian demonstrators staged a protest outside the court.
They held placards saying "Russia is a terrorist" and "What are war crimes? A blown-up pipeline? Or the bombing of buildings and the killing of people?"
According to the indictment, Kuznietsov entered Germany in early September 2022 using a forged Ukrainian passport and, together with the rest of the sabotage team, boarded a rented yacht in the German Baltic Sea port city of Rostock.
The yacht was allegedly loaded with large quantities of military-grade explosives and set sail for a spot where the pipelines ran under the Baltic Sea near the Danish island of Bornholm.
Divers then allegedly planted explosive charges equipped with timers on the pipelines, which blew up several days later.
Sabotage attacks
Kuznietsov's lawyers unsuccessfully tried to challenge the German court's jurisdiction over the attacks and have suggested they may argue that the pipelines were legitimate military targets in Ukraine's fight against Russia's invasion.
The defendant will refuse to testify during the trial as ex-members of Ukraine's special forces are banned from speaking publicly about their work when in the military, news magazine Stern reported on Wednesday.
The pipelines were built and owned by a corporate consortium led by Russian energy giant Gazprom.
At the time of the blasts, none were in operation.
Moscow had already suspended gas deliveries to western Europe through Nord Stream 1, comprising two pipelines, after the European Union imposed sanctions over the war in Ukraine.
Nord Stream 2, also made up of two pipelines, had only just been completed and never entered service.
When asked by AFP what Russia expected from the trial, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he expects "that those who carried it out will be named, along with those who ordered it."
"I don't think anybody has any doubt about who it really is," Peskov added.
A senior Ukrainian official, meanwhile, told the AFP news agency that Kyiv has "no expectations from the trial."
Sensitive subject
Kyiv has consistently denied orchestrating the sabotage.
But it has made no secret of its satisfaction with the results, saying that by rendering the pipelines inoperable, Moscow's ability to fund its war was weakened.
Another suspect, partially identified as Volodymyr Z. and accused of taking part in the sabotage as a diver, was arrested in Croatia in August.
A Croatian court has approved his extradition to Germany although he is appealing the decision.
According to media reports, Volodymyr Z. was advising the makers of a Hollywood film inspired by the sabotage, with Oscar-winning actor Adrien Brody tapped to portray the leader of the sabotage unit.
Volodymyr Z. had previously been arrested in Poland but was freed after a Polish judge refused to extradite him to Germany, ruling that the sabotage of the pipelines was justified as part of Ukraine's defence.
Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Germany has become Kyiv's leading military backer and regularly accuses Russia of sabotage and espionage on its soil.
But the Nord Stream sabotage remains a sensitive subject in Germany.
Some have blamed the attacks for helping to drive up energy prices and worsening a gas crisis that rocked Europe's biggest economy.

The Chinese pavilion features the theme "China: Where Business Meets Extraordinary Experiences," highlighting the country's modern convention and exhibition facilities, international hospitality services, and diverse cultural and tourism resources.

By combining natural landscapes with distinctive cultural attractions, the exhibitors aim to highlight the diversity of China's MICE destinations.
The China National Tourist Office in Los Angeles has organized more than 20 presentations to introduce China's latest MICE tourism destinations, products and developments to international industry professionals.
Wu Dawei, director of the China National Tourist Office in Los Angeles, said China's competitiveness in the international MICE market has strengthened in recent years as the country expands its opening to the world. Visa-free entry and transit policies have been further optimized, while international transportation links, mobile payment services and services for receiving inbound visitors have continued to improve.
China's participation in IMEX America is intended to deepen cooperation with international industry partners and encourage more international meetings and corporate incentive travel programs to choose China, Wu said.
Marta Pani, a lead project manager at Italy-based event management company Event Planet Group, told reporters that the company plans to hold an international medical conference in China next year.
"We always look for nice venues, nice cities that appeal to guests," she said.
She added that Beijing is certainly a popular tourist destination, but China has much more to offer beyond its major cities. "My knowledge of China is admittedly limited, but from what I've seen and heard, there's much more to explore beyond central Beijing."
IMEX America is one of the world's largest annual trade shows for the meetings and incentive travel industry. This year's event is expected to draw more than 17,000 professionals and feature more than 3,700 exhibitors representing destinations, venues, hotels, service providers and event planning companies worldwide. ■

China Focus: Drones rise over grassland the Red Army once crossed
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:36:30 CST
18:36:30 KST

A drone is seen in operation during an earthquake relief drill held in Tiebu Town of Ruoergai County, southwest China's Sichuan Province, May 12, 2026. (Xinhua)
CHENGDU, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- When Ngorcog was a child growing up on the vast grasslands of Sichuan Province in southwest China, she never imagined that barley and fruit would one day "fall from the sky."
For the young Tibetan woman, cargo transport used to rely on horses and yaks, and later, trucks. Today, the 25-year-old has a new role: pilot of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
"Learning to fly drones was difficult at first, but it was also fascinating," she said. Drone logistics services are becoming increasingly common in the Aba Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous Prefecture, where Ngorcog lives.
Ngorcog is from Baxi Town in Ruoergai County of Sichuan. In September 1935, during the Long March, the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China held the Baxi Meeting there, establishing the strategic policy of continuing northward.
The site of the meeting, Banyu Monastery, remains a place of regular worship for Ngorcog, who practices Tibetan Buddhism. In Tibetan culture, the sky holds special significance, with the mythical Garuda bird symbolizing good fortune.
Ngorcog's first encounter with drones came during her university years, when she and her classmates used one to take graduation photos.
"I felt both excited and nervous during takeoff," she recalled. "When the lens rose to the sky, offering a bird's-eye view of the surrounding world, the familiar scenery instantly looked different. My horizon was completely opened, and that sense of vastness was hard to describe in words."
However, it was not until after graduating in 2024 that she began professional training. Originally a music student, she decided to apply for drone training after seeing a recruitment notice from Ruoergai General Aviation Culture and Tourism Co., Ltd.
This company is the first low-altitude economy enterprise in Aba, a plateau region with an average altitude between 3,500 and 4,000 meters, and Ruoergai is China's first pilot county for the low-altitude economy on high-altitude plateaus.
Ngorcog was sent to a training and certification base in Jiande, east China's Zhejiang Province. "The hardest part was flying the 8-shaped route," she said. Three months later, she obtained her pilot license.
Her parents, both farmers, live 90 kilometers from her workplace. Having never seen a drone before, they were curious about their daughter's new job.
"They asked me if I could use the drone to spray pesticides on their vegetable plots," she said with a smile.
More than 90 years ago, the Red Army crossed the grasslands of Ruoergai and surrounding areas. In his book "The Long March: The Untold Story," American journalist and author Harrison Salisbury described the area as "untouched for 3,000 years." Filled with swamps, extreme cold and low oxygen, the treacherous terrain claimed the lives of many soldiers.
In recent years, Ruoergai has developed its low-altitude economy. So far, its low-altitude airspace covers 9,119 square kilometers, making it one of the largest contiguous low-altitude coordinated airspaces in China.
Located on a high-altitude plateau, Ruoergai is prone to extreme weather such as blizzards, and some areas face high risks of geological disasters. When roads are cut off by ice, snow or landslides, making them impassable for people and vehicles, drones can take off quickly to deliver urgent medicines, food and warm clothing to isolated areas.
In May this year, Aba held an earthquake relief drill in Ruoergai. The drill simulated a magnitude 6.6 earthquake that severed roads, paralyzed communications, and turned some villages into "isolated islands." During the exercise, compound-wing UAVs conducted aerial reconnaissance of the disaster area and airdropped first-aid kits, drinking water and communication equipment to the "stranded" zones, effectively addressing the communication and access challenges.
"When a sudden disaster occurs on the Ruoergai grassland, drones can fly immediately to areas inaccessible to vehicles, conduct reconnaissance and deliver emergency supplies," said Huang Peifeng, deputy head of Ruoergai County.
Meanwhile, Ruoergai is gradually incorporating drones into the monitoring and patrolling of grassland ecology and wetlands.
Including Ngorcog, the company established last year now has four local Tibetan female pilots who have successfully obtained licenses to operate medium-sized drones and officially started their jobs. Their main duties include aerial photography for tourism and resource data collection.
As a national strategic emerging industry, the low-altitude economy is rapidly gaining momentum. The Civil Aviation Administration of China predicts that the market size of China's low-altitude economy is set to exceed 3.5 trillion yuan (around 522 billion U.S. dollars) by 2035.
According to a report on education and industrial talent development in China's low-altitude economy this year, the shortage of core positions in the sector will reach 1.82 million in the next five years, with demand for technical roles surging by over 320 percent.
To enhance local children's understanding of drones, the company offers study tour courses.
According to Tsewang Lhamo with the Ruoergai General Aviation Culture and Tourism Co., Ltd., the company has collaborated with local schools for over a year, hosting 500 to 600 students. The curriculum includes aviation lectures, VR experiences, model aircraft making and drone soccer.
"Few people on the grassland had ever encountered drones before," Tsewang Lhamo said. "The children were very interested. I thought they might be afraid of the VR flying experience, but they weren't. During the lessons, they didn't even want class to end."
"Children here rarely have access to cutting-edge technologies. These drone study tours sow the seeds of the low-altitude economy on the grassland. The curiosity in their eyes is precious, and it shows us the unique potential of these grassland children," said Yang Rong, a teacher at a primary school in the Ruoergai county seat.
Tsewang Lhamo is also preparing to take her pilot license exam.
"I hope to master another skill," she said. "In the future, drones will be used in more places across the grassland." ■
Ngorcog (1st R) instructs trainees during a flight simulator training session in Ruoergai County, southwest China's Sichuan Province, July 15, 2026. (Xinhua)
A drone photo taken on Sept. 3, 2026 shows a monument to martyrs of the Red Army in Baxi Town of Ruoergai County, southwest China's Sichuan Province. (Xinhua)

Palestinian children’s rights lawyer Khaled Quzmar receives Amnesty Human Rights Award 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:36:17 UTC
18:36:17 KST

BERLIN, 13 October 2026 – This year’s Human Rights Award of Amnesty International Germany goes to the Palestinian lawyer Khaled Quzmar, in recognition of his longstanding commitment to defending the rights of children in the illegally occupied Palestinian territory. The award carries a prize of €20,000.
An internationally recognised expert on children’s rights, Khaled Quzmar has played a crucial role in exposing structural and systematic human rights abuses against Palestinian children and in placing demands for accountability and justice at the heart of public debate. He has documented human rights violations in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem for UN bodies and international courts, and has enabled countless children and their families to access legal assistance and psychosocial support.
Because of his work, Quzmar, who is based in Ramallah, has been subjected to considerable pressure, repression and smear campaigns by the Israeli authorities. Such instances include being summoned by Israel’s internal intelligence service, Shin Bet, and threatened with a lengthy prison sentence. As long-serving Director General of the human rights organisation Defense for Children International – Palestine (DCI-P), he was forced to dissolve the organisation in spring 2026, after more than 35 years, in the face of sustained harassment by the Israeli authorities. Since June 2026, he has served as Executive Director of the organisation Palestinian Center for Child Rights (PCCR).
Julia Duchrow, Secretary General of Amnesty International Germany, said: “For almost 40 years, Khaled Quzmar has worked tirelessly and against all odds to give a voice to the most vulnerable group in Palestinian society: its children. Their devastating living conditions are the direct consequence of structural human rights abuses and systematic oppression, which have intensified significantly in recent years. This state of affairs is depriving entire generations of a future. Allies of the Israeli government, including the United States and Germany, have contributed to this situation. They not only turn a blind eye to serious human rights abuses against Palestinians but facilitate them through arms deliveries. This must come to an end. Palestinian children need immediate and the fullest possible protection.”
Structural human rights abuses and systematic discrimination
For decades, Palestinian children have been subjected to grave human rights abuses as a result of Israel’s unlawful occupation and cruel system of apartheid against all Palestinians. Since the massive escalation of violence in October 2023 and the beginning of the genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, their situation has deteriorated dramatically.
“What is often portrayed as a humanitarian crisis is the result of political decisions by the Israeli government that are systematically destroying these children’s lives. This is not only about the lack of humanitarian aid for children across the unlawfully occupied Palestinian territory; it is about their right to life and physical integrity, to freedom and security, to education, health and housing – and ultimately about whether these human rights apply to Palestinian children at all,” said Julia Duchrow.
In the Gaza Strip, the Israeli military has killed at least 20,000 children since October 2023, and more than 17,000 have lost their families. Tens of thousands of children are living with severe injuries, hunger and disease, amid destroyed infrastructure and without access to basic services, schools and education. In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, children are affected by state-backed settler violence and displacement – with schools and infrastructure also being systematically destroyed there.
Repression of Palestinian civil society
Human rights defenders and human rights organisations in the Occupied Palestinian Territory face constant repression by the Israeli authorities and military. In October 2021, Israel designated the DCI-P – the organisation for which Khaled Quzmar had worked for many years – as a terrorist organisation, along with five other Palestinian civil society organisations, without providing any substantiated evidence. Amnesty International, the United Nations and numerous civil society organisations strongly criticised the designation. The German government and many other EU partners have also rejected Israel’s designation. Since the current ruling coalition took office – and particularly since 7 October 2023 – staff members of some organisations have increasingly been subjected to intimidation, smear campaigns, interrogation, arbitrary detention, imprisonment and ill-treatment, with some offices also being raided.
Amnesty International Germany’s Human Rights Award
Every two years, Amnesty International Germany honours individuals and organisations working for human rights under difficult conditions with its Human Rights Award. The award aims to recognise, support and protect their work and to raise public awareness of it. It carries a prize of €20,000. 2026 marks the 13th time the Amnesty Human Rights Award will have been presented. Previous recipients include Eren Keskin (Türkiye), Svetlana Gannushkina (Russia), Alice Nkom (Cameroon), Henri Tiphagne (India) and the Colombian organization Federation of Santander Fishers for Tourism and Environment (FEDESPAN).

Türkiye moves to speed fund repayments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:35:47 UTC
18:35:47 KST

Parliament’s Plan and Budget Committee discusses a bill setting out rules for the liquidation of 131 investment funds and repayments to affected investors. (AA Photo)
Türkiye aims to complete the liquidation of 49 more investment funds by the weekend, after 43,643 investors received 6.4 billion Turkish Liras in payments last week.
The Communications Directorate announced the target after an Oct. 13 Fund Board meeting chaired by Vice President Cevdet Yılmaz.
Ziraat Bank made the payments to investors in funds managed by A1, Bulls and Pardus. The remaining liquidation involves 34.1 billion liras in assets.
Completion would bring cash payments and asset transfers across the three companies’ 66 funds to 40.5 billion liras, covering 45,745 investors.
The board aims to complete interim payments for another 65 funds swiftly once legislation governing the process is enacted, the directorate said.
The nine-article bill, submitted on Oct. 9, was on the agenda of parliament’s Plan and Budget Committee on Oct. 14.
The wider liquidation covers 131 funds run by seven portfolio managers and more than 455,000 investors.
Ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) lawmaker Ersan Aksu, one of the bill’s sponsors, said no Treasury or budget funds would be used.
Payments would come from each fund’s assets and money recovered from those responsible for losses.
The bill would allow interim payments of up to 1 million liras per eligible investor, based on cash paid into the fund minus withdrawals, without inflation adjustment. These would be deducted from final payments.
Investors with less than 1 million liras in net investments could receive that amount in full if sufficient cash is available.
Where cash is insufficient, the Capital Markets Board (SPK) could prioritize those with the lowest net investments.
Where fund assets fall short, final settlement calculations would adjust cash inflows and outflows up to the liquidation date using the average change in consumer and domestic producer price indices.
The bill would also allow the Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (TMSF) to sell assets placed under its trusteeship before trials conclude.
Aksu said the affected funds accounted for 7.7 percent of total fund assets and that the problems posed no systemic risk.
Opposition lawmakers called for closer scrutiny, saying the bill’s impact assessment lacked sufficient information.
Separately, Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan said measures to contain risks spreading from funds under trading restrictions had limited the impact on the financial system.
In Bangkok on Oct. 14, he outlined increased repo funding, eased borrowing and collateral conditions and accelerated purchases of securities linked to the Turkish Lira Overnight Reference Rate.
The bank also raised the credit growth cap for small and medium-sized businesses from 4.5 percent to 5 percent.
Karahan said fund outflows had not significantly weakened residents’ preference for lira-denominated assets.

Breadcrumb
Far-right Colombian government opens embassy to Israel in Jerusalem
Colombia on Wednesday officially opened its embassy in Jerusalem, joining a small group of countries including the United States in taking the symbolic step of backing Israeli sovereignty in the contested holy city.
The vast majority of countries keep their embassies to Israel in Tel Aviv on the grounds that Jerusalemis under occupation and the status should be resolved through a diplomatic process.
"This is an important date for the State of Israel. It's also an important date for the city of Jerusalem," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said during a ceremony while signing the Colombian embassy's guest book.
Colombia's new hard-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella, in July announced that he would move his country's embassy to occupied Jerusalem, a sharp shift from his leftist predecessor who criticised Israel over its genocida of Gaza.
President Donald Trump shattered international consensus in 2018 during his first term by moving the US embassy to Jerusalem, which is home to Israel's parliament, prime minister and most other major governmental institutions.
Since Trump's move, only a handful of small, US-aligned countries have followed suit: Fiji, Guatemala, Honduras, Papua New Guinea and Paraguay.
Kosovo and Somaliland, which are not member-states of the United Nations, have also opened what they consider their embassies in Jerusalem.
Argentine President Javier Milei, another right-wing Latin American who is an outspoken supporter of Israel, has promised to move his country's embassy to Jerusalem.
Israel occupied east Jerusalem and annexed it in 1967, in a move not recognised by the vast majority of the international community or international law.
In August, Colombia's new hard-right government recognised Israel's claim over the Golan Heights, which it seized from Syria in 1967. The US was until then the only country to recognise Israel's annexation of the territory in 1981.
The United Nations and the rest of the world maintain that the plateau is Syrian territory under Israeli military occupation.

Swiss regulator fails PostFinance financial emergency plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:33:16 UTC
18:33:16 KST

Swiss regulator fails PostFinance financial emergency plans
The contingency plans of Switzerland's Postfinance bank in the event of severe financial difficulty have once again failed to impress the country's regulator.
Two other systemically important banks, Zurich Cantonal Bank and Raiffeisen, have, on the other hand, met regulatory requirements of the Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority (FINMA).
According to a statement issued by FINMA on Wednesday, PostFinance has met the requirements for additional loss-absorbing capital since the end of 2025 and has further developed its alternative strategy.
But the regulator stated that the options envisaged in the event that restructuring and the continued operation of the bank are not possible still need to be further specified.
In this context, Postfinance’s statutory universal service obligation must also be taken into account. The amendment to the Postal Services Act, which is currently under consultation, will reduce legal uncertainty in this regard.
All domestically focused systemically important banks require both an emergency plan and a stabilisation plan, which FINMA assesses annually.
Credit Suisse crisis
In its assessment of the plans submitted in 2025, FINMA noted progress in stabilisation planning at all three domestically focused banks. It had tightened the requirements following the Credit Suisse crisis.
+ Where did it all go wrong for Credit Suisse?
Certain elements of the revised requirements still need to be implemented. This concerns, for example, the documentation of crisis exercises and crisis communication plans. FINMA expects the identified gaps to be closed in a timely manner.
UBS assessment to follow later
However, according to FINMA, the assessment of the contingency plans does not mean that the continuation of systemically important functions is guaranteed without restriction in every conceivable crisis scenario.
The three domestically focused systemically important banks have smaller financial buffers to absorb losses, particularly when compared with globally active systemically important banks. In particularly severe crisis scenarios, this could limit their scope for action.
FINMA intends to provide separate information on UBS’s crisis planning in late autumn 2026.

Trump’s Phantom Ceasefires Are a National Security Problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:33:10 UTC
18:33:10 KST

On Sunday, Oct. 11, at 10:16 a.m., President Donald Trump announced on social media an immediate ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine covering attacks on energy infrastructure. He asserted that both parties had agreed. In the same post he issued an unmistakable warning: “Do not break it!”
Within half an hour of Trump’s announcement, a senior Ukrainian official told the press that Kyiv had no information about the purported agreement. Within the same hour, Zelensky’s own response was public: the announcement “was news for me.” He added that Ukraine would agree to a ceasefire if Russia did the same.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Exactly 59 minutes after Trump announced the purported ceasefire, Russia attacked Kharkiv’s CHP-5 power plant.
The alleged ceasefire was over.
Crickets from the White House.
Second time in a month
This was the second time in one month that the president issued a false claim about a negotiated ceasefire.
On Sept. 14, Trump declared: “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy Targets. Russia has agreed to do likewise!”
Yet a senior Ukrainian official made it clear that they had not heard of such a ceasefire. Zelensky expressed willingness to reciprocate if Russia halted its attacks, while saying Kyiv awaited details. Meanwhile, Russia continued to target Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
There are several possible explanations for President Trump’s repeated misrepresentations about ceasefires to the world:
Moscow, Washington vs. Kyiv: Can Trump Force Ukraine to Capitulate?
Does any of this matter?
Yes, and it is a matter of national security.
Repeatedly announcing ceasefires that have not been established is a grave failure of presidential responsibility. Such statements can shape military calculations, diplomatic decisions, financial markets, and the expectations of civilians whose lives depend on whether the bombing will actually stop.
When a president declares that both parties have agreed, he places American credibility behind that assertion. If the agreement does not exist, he undermines trust in future American commitments, creates confusion about who has promised what, and risks allowing continued aggression to disappear beneath a headline proclaiming peace.
Congressional leaders have a duty to call immediate hearings, establish what the president knew, identify who supplied his information, and determine what corrective action is required. Whether the explanation is deliberate deception, gross negligence, confusion, or something else, announcing an international agreement without establishing the consent of its participants raises serious questions about the president’s competence to oversee American foreign policy.
Congress must treat this as a matter of national security and demand an explanation. A president’s words about war and peace carry the authority of the United States; they cannot be excused as a salesman’s harmless exaggeration.
In the meantime, the world must respond advisedly to such claims by President Trump. “Fool me once, shame on you. Fool me twice, shame on me.”

Lockheed gets $117M for Apache radar-hunting sensors
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:32:34 UTC
18:32:34 KST

- The U.S. Army awarded Lockheed Martin a $117.1 million contract to support the Apache’s second-generation radar frequency interferometer through October 2031.
- Lockheed Martin is already developing a Generation 3 replacement sensor for the Apache fleet under a contract awarded in October 2024.
The U.S. Army has awarded Lockheed Martin a $117.1 million contract to keep supporting the second-generation radar frequency interferometer on its Apache attack helicopters, a passive sensor that lets crews find and pinpoint enemy radars without giving away their own position.
The Department of War contract announcement describes an indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity deal that mixes cost-no-fee, cost-plus-fixed-fee and firm-fixed-price terms for “post-production support services” on the Generation II system, with work running through Oct. 12, 2031. Lockheed Martin’s Owego, New York, business received the award after the Army solicited only one bid, and both work locations and funding will be set as individual orders are placed under the contract.
Known in military designation as the AN/APR-48B, the system listens for radar emissions on the battlefield rather than transmitting its own signal. It detects, identifies and locates enemy radars and then ranks them by priority for attack, while also cueing the Apache’s fire-control radar and warning the crew of radar-guided anti-aircraft threats. The same unit serves as the controller for the helicopter’s integrated survivability equipment, which ties it to the aircraft’s self-protection suite as well as its targeting.
Owego has supplied this family of sensors for decades. The first-generation AN/APR-48A flew on Apache Longbow helicopters in Desert Storm, Operation Iraqi Freedom and Operation Enduring Freedom, and the modernized second-generation version followed on the AH-64E Apache Guardian, the current production model flown by the U.S. Army.
The Generation II sensor also equips foreign Apache fleets, with Lockheed Martin delivering units to the United Kingdom, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and South Korea through Foreign Military Sales alongside those built for the U.S. Army.
Production of the current version has been winding down. An earlier $60.5 million award for AN/APR-48B production and related services scheduled work in Owego through Oct. 31, 2026, which places the new support contract right at the point where the Army shifts from buying the sensor to sustaining the fleet already in service.
A successor is already in development. In October 2024 the Army’s Apache program office hired Lockheed Martin to develop a Generation 3 radar frequency interferometer and radar warning receiver, promising better sensor performance in a smaller and lighter package built around a radio frequency system on a chip, and the new sensor is set to replace all Gen 2 systems across the Apache fleet.
That timeline explains the length of the new deal, since Generation II sensors will need spares, repairs and engineering support for as long as they remain on Apaches waiting for the upgrade. Neither the Army nor Lockheed Martin has said when Generation 3 will enter production or how quickly it will reach operational units.

As the US and China race ahead in AI, France carves its own path with Nvidia’s help
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:31:49 UTC
18:31:49 KST

Nvidia bets almost $10 billion in Europe as Paris pushes for AI sovereignty.
American Artificial intelligence giant Nvidia is spending big in France with a string of new investments in its technology and health companies, showing how Paris is safeguarding its technological sovereignty amid the AI race between China and the United States.
On Tuesday, Nvidia announced planned investments in medical booking website Doctolib, robotics company Genesis AI, chemicals and materials company Entalpic and enterprise software company Pigment.
The company says it brings its investments to Europe to nearly $10 billion (€9 bn) to the continent’s technology ecosystem.
Nvidia’s investments in France show how the country’s push, driven in particular by President Emmanuel Macron, to lead in technology has grown since the AI Action Summit in February 2025 and the ‘Choose France’ summits.
But AI sovereignty, which the European Commission defines as “Europe's ability to act independently in the digital world by developing and controlling key technologies,” depends heavily on infrastructure, which is currently being built in Western France.
The French AI structures
Taiwan’s Foxconn and French computing firm Bull announced in June they would partner to build powerful AI computers in Europe to power the continent's fast-growing network of AI factories, the large-scale computing centres that form the backbone of artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Foxconn initially manufactures or tests the components in its facilities in Czechia before final assembly, rack integration and validation take place at the newly opened Angers plant in Western France.
Foxconn will provide the AI factory infrastructure while Nvidia provides the latest AI chips.
Additionally, from 2028, Bull will manufacture systems based on the powerful NVIDIA Vera Rubin Ultra NVL72 rack-scale AI supercomputer in Angers.
Nvidia’s CEO and founder Jensen Huang said at Davos in January that AI is "exciting for Europe" because of its "incredibly strong manufacturing base" for building AI infrastructure.
Huang described this as Europe's moment to "leapfrog" the software era and also called robotics a "once-in-a-lifetime opportunity" for the continent.
The CEO describes AI as a five-layer cake that includes energy, chips, infrastructure, data centre servers and the AI models and applications.
“Nvidia is trying to help everyone across that cake, all the layers, work together and progress together,” Nat Ives, Nvidia’s director of enterprise for Benelux, France & Nordics, told Euronews Next in June.
He said that “comes home to roost in France in particular,” as France has nuclear renewable power, which is cheaper and more sustainable, as well as having the French multinational electric utility company EDF, which is owned by the French government.
The open weight debate
Another key announcement from Nvidia was its commitment to open-weight AI models, which means the numerical parameters are publicly released and allow anyone to download, run and modify them.
The race over open-weight AI, in which a model's parameters can be downloaded and run by anyone, has taken on a geopolitical edge.
Chinese developers have set the pace, while many American companies, such as OpenAI, keep their most capable systems closed. Meanwhile, the debate over safety has grown since AI agents have been found to go rogue and hack websites.
Nvidia said its own open models, called Nemotron, are now in production at French organisations that need “sovereign, trustworthy data”.
The company announced a big deployment in government. The workplace software platform called Twake.ai, built by French companies Linagora and Docaposte, has been chosen as the only officially recommended “sovereign” digital workplace for more than 2,500 French public organisations.
Here, sovereign will mean the data stays under French and European control rather than with foreign tech giants.
Additionally, in banking, a company called SBS is launching a platform that lets banks run AI tools, including AI agents that can carry out tasks on their own, inside their own systems. NVIDIA is working with SBS on the project.
It is not Nvidia’s first open-weight venture in France. In March, it partnered with French AI champion Mistral, which introduced its open-weight Mistral Large 4 in private preview last week.
France appears to be betting that sovereignty does not mean building everything alone, but rather with key partners across continents. With cheaper energy and its abundance of talent, it could forge its own path as China and the US battle it out.
