She brought Israeli agriculture to the world; October 7 changed everything
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:31:18 UTC
18:31:18 KST

For years, Danielle Abraham worked to bring Israel's agricultural expertise and innovation to countries struggling with water shortages, food insecurity and harsh climate conditions. After October 7, that mission took a new direction. Instead of taking Israeli expertise abroad, she sought to bring it home and put it to work for farmers whose livelihoods had been devastated.
Just days after the Hamas attack, Abraham launched ReGrow Israel, an initiative aimed at rebuilding farms and agricultural infrastructure in communities near the Gaza border. Initially, she envisioned it as a consulting service for farmers, with a team of experts assessing their needs and developing long-term recovery plans. But the reality on the ground was far more urgent. Farmers had been left without tractors, equipment or the infrastructure needed to resume operations. Before planning for the years ahead, they needed help getting their farms running again.
What began as an emergency response in southern Israel has since expanded to farms and communities affected by the war in the north. The initiative supports farmers by providing equipment, restoring infrastructure and bringing in professional expertise and technology, while also working to strengthen Israeli agriculture over the long term.
For this work, Abraham will receive the Nefesh B'Nefesh Sylvan Adams Bonei Zion Prize at a ceremony this coming Sunday, marking Aliyah Day. The event will be broadcast live on ynet. Now in its 12th year, the award recognizes immigrants from English-speaking countries who have made exceptional contributions to Israeli society across a range of fields. Abraham was selected in the Global Impact category.
Abraham's journey began more than 15 years ago in a lecture hall in London. An Oxford University music graduate working at Britain's Home Office, she was 23 when she attended a lecture by Israeli agronomist Yitzhak Abt. Abt, who had helped establish Israel's international agricultural assistance program through MASHAV, the Foreign Ministry's Agency for International Development Cooperation, spoke about immigrating to Israel from South Africa and his work advancing agriculture in Israel and developing countries.
When Abraham returned home from the lecture, she told her family: "When I grow up, I want to be him." The encounter changed the course of her life. Abraham left her job, sold her car and immigrated to Israel in 2010.
Israel was not entirely unfamiliar to her. She had visited during summer vacations as a child and had relatives living in the country. She grew up in a Zionist household, was active in a Zionist youth movement and had visited Israel at 16. At Oxford, she led a Jewish student society and defended Israel in public debates. Still, leaving a sought-after job in London to begin life as a new immigrant in Israel was a leap into the unknown.
'Just for a year'
When Abraham accepted a position at Israel's Foreign Ministry, she had not yet fully committed to building her life in the country. She told everyone back home that she was coming for just one year. "Only after six months did I start saying I was thinking about making aliyah," she recalled. "My family and friends said, 'We knew from the moment you got on the plane.'"
Her parents, she said, never told her what to do and supported whatever decision she made. But there was one moment when they realized she was not coming back. "When I bought a piano for my home, they said, 'Now that you have that, you're not coming back.'"
One of her first challenges in Israel was the language. She would write down unfamiliar words she heard and send text messages to a friend asking what they meant. On weekends, she went to the beach with vocabulary lists from her Hebrew classes and memorized them. She also taped the lists to cabinets in her office. "My vocabulary was mostly agriculture and developing countries," she recalled. "I couldn't order food in a restaurant, but I could talk about irrigation."
At the Foreign Ministry, Abraham joined MASHAV and later served as a senior policy adviser, representing Israel at the United Nations, the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) and the German Development Bank. In many ways, she had fulfilled the ambition sparked by Abt's lecture: using Israeli expertise to solve real-world problems around the globe.
In 2017, she began leading Volcani International Partnerships, an organization that draws on Israeli agricultural knowledge and innovation to address challenges such as food security, water scarcity and farming in difficult climate conditions. Agriculture, she explained, is one of the fields in which Israel is a world leader, combining the Zionist vision with practical benefits.
Bringing the expertise home
After October 7, Abraham decided to use the experience, experts and international connections she had accumulated to help Israeli farmers. "When the extent of the destruction in the Gaza border communities became clear, I saw that some countries facing similar situations turn to outside assistance," she said. "I told everyone, 'We have everything right here: researchers, agronomists, innovation and high-tech. We just need to bring it all together.'"
ReGrow Israel began by providing emergency assistance to farmers in communities near Gaza, including replacing agricultural equipment and repairing damaged infrastructure. The initiative later expanded to farms and communities affected by the war in northern Israel.
Since its establishment, it has raised tens of millions of dollars to help rebuild Israeli agriculture. But Abraham said the goal was not simply to repair what was destroyed. She wanted to use the recovery process to build a stronger, more advanced and more resilient agricultural sector.
For Abraham, agriculture is more than an economic industry. It is closely tied to Israel's food security, the livelihoods of residents in outlying regions and the ability to sustain communities along the country's borders. "If agriculture isn't strong there, we won't have communities on the border," she said. Yet she believes Israel still does not sufficiently recognize agriculture as a strategic asset. "I still don't see enough effort being made to use it to strengthen Israel, both at home and abroad."
Despite everything October 7 changed in her life and work, Abraham has no doubts about her decision to immigrate. "Of course," she replied when asked whether she would choose Israel again. "You have to be a little crazy to live here, but you have to believe."
Looking back at the young woman who arrived alone in 2010, barely speaking Hebrew, Abraham sees a quality she is still trying to preserve. "I see a brave young woman with a kind of naivety that's important today. Everything was possible. I wasn't willing to take no for an answer," she said. "That's the spirit I try to hold on to, even as reality changes. We need people with big visions and hope, who make decisions that aren't crazy but are a little courageous, and who start with small things."
Alongside Abraham, several other immigrants will receive the Nefesh B'Nefesh Sylvan Adams Bonei Zion Prize. Naomi Stuchiner, founder of Beit Issie Shapiro, will receive the award in the Community and Non-Profit category; Dr. Philip Klipstein, a senior researcher in science and technology, will be honored in the Science and Medicine category; Rabbanit Chana Henkin, founder and dean of Nishmat, the Jeanie Schottenstein Center for Advanced Torah Study for Women, will receive the Education award; and Ami Baran, president of the Israel Athletics Association and CEO of the Israel Softball Association, will be recognized in the Culture, Arts and Sports category.
Professor Marta Weinstock-Rosin, a neuropharmacologist who developed Exelon, a drug used to treat Alzheimer's disease, will receive the Lifetime Achievement Award. Barak Swarttz, a content creator and founder of GRIT for Good, will receive the Young Leadership Award, while former ambassador Ron Dermer, who served as Israel's ambassador to the United States and strategic affairs minister, will receive a special recognition award.
For Abraham, the honor provides a platform not only for her work but also for Israeli agriculture and for immigrants seeking to find their place in the country. She said she still feels like "a little girl from London who made a small effort." To her, the message behind the award is simple: "You can come here and make a contribution, whether big or small."

Austrian court grants former property tycoon Benko's request for house arrest
VIENNA, Oct 14 - An Austrian court on Wednesday granted former property tycoon Rene Benko's request to be released from prison to house arrest with an ankle monitor after he served two-thirds of a 30-month sentence for insolvency fraud.
Benko, 49, will now move from prison in his home city of Innsbruck to a roughly 60-square-metre (650-square-foot) apartment that his lawyer Norbert Wess has said has been rented for him in the city so he can better prepare for a fraud trial next month. Benko denies all wrongdoing.
Benko has been convicted of insolvency-related fraud in the two cases brought to trial so far stemming from a sprawling investigation into the collapse of the Signa property group he founded. The second conviction resulted in a suspended sentence.
He remains a suspect in the continuing investigation into a range of potential crimes including fraud, with prosecutors estimating the total harm caused by Benko and other suspects at €1.5 billion ($1.7 billion). His first two trials dealt with sums in the hundreds of thousands of euros.
At its peak, Signa controlled all or part of luxury properties including five-star hotels in Venice and Vienna and the Chrysler Building in New York, as well as high-end department-store chains such as Britain's Selfridges and Switzerland's Globus. Benko became a self-made billionaire.
"It was ordered that investigative detention be continued as electronically monitored house arrest," the court in Innsbruck said in a statement issued after the closed-door hearing on Wednesday, adding that conditions attached included having no contact with anyone related to Signa.
The next trial Benko faces is for aggravated fraud and insolvency-related fraud, with prosecutors accusing him of making a false guarantee causing harm of €5 million. The trial is due to be held in Innsbruck next month. REUTERS

Men Can’t Stop Faking How Much They Know About AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Say you’re a guy who reads WIRED—you know a thing or two about artificial intelligence. You recognize the names of well-known people developing AI, like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. But do you know who Mira Murati is? What about Susan Milner? Craig Dalton?
In a new survey of more than 5,400 Americans, 73 percent of male respondents told Harvard researchers they knew who Altman was. A little over half—53 percent—said they knew of Murati, Milner, and Dalton.
There’s one problem. Murati is a real person: she’s the former CTO of OpenAI and the current CEO of Thinking Machine Labs. Milner and Dalton, on the other hand, do not exist.
Compared to women, “we're seeing that men are more optimistic and more confident” across the board when it comes to AI, Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center executive director Laura Manley tells WIRED. Sometimes, that veers into overconfidence—like claiming to recognize fictional AI executives. (For context, 40 percent of women claimed to know who Milner and Dalton were; 38 percent said they recognized Murati.)
While Manley notes that men are more overconfident in general when surveyed, the report, published on Wednesday, digs into what the confidence gap on AI looks like, as well as the repercussions of gendered divides.
Researchers found that men use AI more frequently and are, on average, better able to correctly answer factual questions about AI. But men and women answer questions incorrectly at around the same rate. The discrepancy is based on how often women said they weren’t sure of an answer—an average of 3.3 questions out of 12 compared to 2.3 questions for men.
Researchers wondered if this predilection toward certainty colors coverage of AI. Across a year of media coverage, men were named in headlines about AI more than 14 times as often as women. Because top AI executives skew heavily male, researchers decided to reexamine coverage, looking solely at people who were quoted as subject experts. Three-quarters of these experts were men—a higher proportion than the actual AI talent pool, which is roughly 29 percent women.
“Maybe there should be more women prominently featured as experts or given the platform to express: not sure,” Manley says.
Besides intellectual bluster, Americans were generally in agreement that AI was freaking them out—men and women both rated “concern” as their top emotional response. However, female respondents were more concerned, fearful, and worried than their male counterparts. Men, meanwhile, rated every positive feeling—including curiosity, enthusiasm, and excitement—higher than women did.
In the current discourse, “there's so much confidence in either doom or abundance,” Manley says. “It just drowns out all of the voices that should be saying ‘not sure.’” There are many unanswered questions on proper uses for and the future of AI. One gender is simply less likely to acknowledge such uncertainty.
“We have to be able to be able to say ‘not sure’ more often,” Manley says.

In Odesa, nine members of Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center notification groups were convicted of abducting and torturing men
Kyiv • UNN
The court convicted nine military and civilian members of Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center groups of abducting and torturing men. Six received actual prison sentences.
In Odesa, nine employees of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers were convicted of unlawful deprivation of liberty, kidnapping, and torture. Among those convicted were military personnel and civilians involved in mobilization activities. This was reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, UNN reports.
Details
According to the available information, the court handed down the guilty verdicts in September–October 2026.
"Prosecutors from the Odesa Specialized Prosecutor's Office in the Defense Sphere of the Southern Region proved that in April–May 2026, they unlawfully detained men on the city's streets, forcibly put them into vehicles, and took them to the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers. During the detentions, the victims were beaten, exposed to tear gas, threatened, and humiliated. The men were also forced to provide personal data and information about other persons of conscription age. In one case, the victim was threatened with sexual violence; in another, a man lost consciousness after tear gas was used. In addition, during the forcible transportation of one of the men, a convicted person took UAH 5,200 from his wallet," the Prosecutor General's post says.
According to the available data, all nine men pleaded guilty and entered into plea agreements, which were approved by the court.
"The punishment depended on each person's role in the crimes. Six of those convicted were sentenced to actual imprisonment. The harshest sentence was 7 years and 1 month in prison. Two others were each sentenced to 2 years of restriction of service, with 10% of their monetary allowance deducted and transferred to state revenue, while one was sentenced to 5 years in prison with a 2-year probation period. Four of those convicted were also prohibited for three years from holding positions in district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers and from participating in mobilization activities," the post says.
The actions of those convicted were qualified under Part 1 of Article 28, Part 2 of Article 146, and Part 3 of Article 127 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. One of them was additionally convicted of robbery committed under martial law (Part 4 of Article 186 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
The trial of two more defendants is currently ongoing.
Reminder
Law enforcement officers reported suspicion to three heads of district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers—one incumbent and one former official in Zakarpattia, and one former official in Bukovyna. According to the investigation, from December 2025 to February 2026, the officials entered information on at least 857 fictitiously mobilized persons into the "Oberih" system, artificially inflating the reported performance of mobilization plans.

09:29:07 UTC
18:29:07 KST

Ukraine’s presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said SpaceX had imposed a 100 mph (160 km/h) speed limit on its military Starshield service overnight into 14 October, disrupting several missions without warning Ukraine’s defense forces.
Ukraine’s forces use Starlink-connected drones to strike Russian positions and logistics, including targets behind the front line. Unlike earlier restrictions introduced at Kyiv’s request to stop Russian forces from exploiting Starlink, the latest change reportedly targets the military Starshield service and was imposed without warning Ukraine’s military.
What the new restriction covers
Beskrestnov wrote that the restriction applies to the “military package” of Starshield services. He said the move “obviously cannot be a coincidence” and was connected with the “current political situation,” but did not explain what he meant.
Activist Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to Ukraine’s defense minister, reported that connections began disappearing at speeds above 160 km/h. He suggested SpaceX had acted at the Trump administration’s request but provided no evidence. Starlink does not work inside Russia, and the drones hitting Russia’s oil industry use other means of communication, Reuters noted. Sternenko added that the ordinary satellite terminals were still working.
Later on 14 October, Sternenko wrote that, according to military reports, restrictions had been tightened further, with connections starting to drop at 60–70 km/h. Beskrestnov later warned that the restriction also hits Starlink-linked interceptor drones, which he called Ukraine’s most effective current defense against jet-powered Shaheds.
Front-line units report dropped connections
Ukraine’s 7th Rapid Reaction Corps confirmed the disruptions in a statement to Reuters. The corps’ press service told Novynarnia that its units on the Huliaipole front began experiencing problems overnight. The corps said the change affected drones controlled through Starlink in flight and concerned Starshield’s data-transmission speed, which it said had previously been unrestricted.
The corps said connections could disappear for 10–20 seconds at movement speeds of 110–120 km/h, complicating drone control. Flying slower creates its own risk, it said, because “slower targets become more vulnerable to being hit by the enemy.”
Some high-speed drones, particularly mid-range strike models, must reach high speed quickly, the corps said. An unstable connection “will make it impossible to launch such aircraft or use them as intended.” Since the start of the day, one unmanned systems unit on the Huliaipole front had to cancel some missions because of connection problems, the corps said.
Earlier limits came at Kyiv’s request
In late January, SpaceX began restricting Starlink in Ukraine at Kyiv’s request after Russian forces started mounting terminals on strike drones. After Russian drones struck a passenger train in Kharkiv Oblast on 27 January, Beskrestnov, then an adviser to the defense minister, suggested one of them may have been controlled via Starlink. In early February, Ukraine introduced a whitelist under which only registered terminals could continue operating. Beskrestnov called the earlier countermeasures “temporary” and “emergency.”
SpaceX had not publicly commented on the restriction, and Ukraine’s Defense Ministry was looking into its cause, Radio Svoboda reported. Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski asked Elon Musk on X whether he was “playing politics with your products again,” adding: “As your European customers, we are watching you.”

Türkiye-EU Customs Union talks advance ‘case-by-case’ as bilateral trade hits $233B: Turkish trade minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:28:01 UTC
18:28:01 KST

Şerife Çetin, Ata Ufuk Şeker
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Türkiye-EU Customs Union talks to amend the agreement are progressing on a “case-by-case basis” to include areas such as e-commerce, public procurement, investments and agricultural products, the Turkish trade minister said.
Omer Bolat told reporters during his visit to Brussels that maintaining economic ties is just as important for the EU as it is for Türkiye, highlighting bilateral trade between Türkiye and the bloc, which has surged elevenfold over the past three decades to reach a record $233 billion.
He said the bilateral analysis had been completed, referring to the new Turkish public procurement law passed in late July, and that technical discussions with European counterparts were underway.
He noted that while the EU Council has yet to officially mandate the European Commission to launch Customs Union modernization talks due to the positions of certain member states, technical negotiations have begun.
“We’re making progress on a case-by-case basis since the relevant issues have come up and authorities of the European Commission are conducting negotiations with us,” he said.
Bolat also said intensive work has been underway for the past year to address the EU’s restrictive regulations proposed under the draft Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA).
The official warned that certain provisions in the draft could affect future investments and disrupt integrated supply chains, particularly in the electric vehicle (EV) and automotive sectors.
He also confirmed that communications were ongoing to convey Türkiye’s expectations and mitigate the potential economic impact of the proposed industrial regulations.
Bolat said the EU was coordinating with Türkiye in its legislative preparations on digital trade, as the country remains exempt from a newly implemented EU regulation imposing a fee of €3 ($3.36) per package.
He said political involvement by the European Parliament could have adverse effects, noting that many European officials also believe Türkiye should be included in the “Made in EU” origin framework. However, he added that the EU is ultimately a complex entity made up of diverse countries with differing economic interests, emphasizing the need to remain “calm and level-headed” on the matter.
Bolat added that he held intensive contacts in Brussels, making three official visits in the last three months following five visits last year, and said he expected positive developments from the talks.

3 Hong Kong taxi drivers banned for 3 months under demerit points system
In a first, transport chief reveals number of taxi drivers disqualified since points system took effect two years ago
Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said on Wednesday that since the mechanism took effect in September 2024, 229 taxi drivers had incurred demerit points as of October 2, with 125 cases involving a refusal to accept a hire.
In a reply to a question from lawmaker Chris Ip Ngo-tung, Chan said the three drivers had been disqualified for three months after incurring 15 demerit points or more on the Taxi-Driver-Offence points system - the first time authorities revealed this figure.
Under the system, taxi drivers will receive three, five or 10 demerit points for each of the 11 types of misconduct and can be disqualified from driving a taxi for three months if they accumulate 15 points or more within two years. Repeat offenders face a six-month suspension.

Latvia’s State Revenue Service (VID) has once again frozen the bank accounts of alcoholic beverage producer Amber Latvijas balzams following the termination of the company’s legal protection proceedings, according to a statement submitted to the Nasdaq Riga stock exchange.
The company said it is actively evaluating and discussing options to secure access to the funds essential for continuing its operations and to have the restrictions on its bank accounts lifted.
Amber Latvijas balzams representatives explained that the global downturn in the spirits market, declining export orders and other external factors had created significant cash flow difficulties, resulting in overdue excise tax payments.
Following prolonged negotiations over the outstanding excise tax liabilities, the State Revenue Service froze the company’s bank accounts.
To ensure business continuity and protect creditors’ interests, Amber Latvijas balzams filed an application for legal protection proceedings on the 30th of January, 2026. Riga City Court opened the proceedings on the 5th of February, 2026.
However, the legal protection proceedings were terminated in early October.
The company explained that the termination allows creditors to resume pursuing their previous claims, prompting the State Revenue Service to reinstate the freeze on its bank accounts.
According to VID data, Amber Latvijas balzams had outstanding tax debts of 28.28 million euros as of the 12th of October, 2026.
As previously reported by LETA, the legal protection proceedings involving Amber Latvijas balzams were terminated on the 9th of October, 2026 because the proposed restructuring plan had not received the support of the majority of creditors required under Latvia’s Insolvency Law.
An extraordinary shareholders’ meeting has been scheduled for the 3rd of November, 2026, during which the company will consider, among other matters, whether to initiate insolvency proceedings.
The meeting agenda includes an assessment of the consequences of terminating the legal protection proceedings
 and the company’s options for continuing operations, including the possibility of filing for insolvency.
Amber Latvijas balzams reported revenue of 74.464 million euros in 2025, a decrease of 4.8% compared with the previous year. The company’s profit fell by 31.5% to 836,359 euros.
Amber Latvijas balzams is part of Amber Beverage Group, an international alcoholic beverage production and distribution group headquartered in Luxembourg.
The group operates through manufacturing and distribution companies in the Baltic states and elsewhere around the world.
Amber Beverage Group is owned by billionaire Yuri Shefler.
Amber Latvijas balzams was registered in 1991 and has share capital of 10,495,660 euros.
The company’s shares are listed on the secondary list of the Nasdaq Riga stock exchange.

During the fourth phase of Operation Vivaldi, Ukrainian forces liberated three settlements in the Lyman sector of the Donetsk region: Zelena Dolyna, Lypove, and Kolodiazi.
Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, commander ofUkraine’s Third Army Corps, announced the operation’s results.
The Third Army Corps and attached units recaptured 101 square kilometers of territory and inflicted approximately 3,000 personnel losses on Russian forces.
“We prevented the enemy from outflanking the Sloviansk–Kramatorsk urban agglomeration and encircling it. We also secured the Kharkiv–Sloviansk highway. The enemy failed to cut off a key logistical artery supplying our forces in Donbas. We thwarted the offensive by the Russian ‘West’ grouping and forced it to redeploy some units of the 1st Tank Army, which eased the pressure on Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi,” Andrii Biletskyi shared.

They were supported by attached units, including the 66th Mechanized Brigade, the 3rd Border Guard Detachment, the 10th Dozor Mobile Border Guard Detachment, tactical groups from the 8th Special Operations Forces Regiment, the National Guard’s Lasar’s Group, the K-2 Unmanned Systems Forces unit, and unmanned systems units of the Security Service of Ukraine’s Special Operations Center “A.”
Throughout the operation, Ukrainian forces have regained full control of 16 settlements and liberated 277 square kilometers of territory. According to Biletskyi, Russian forces have suffered 8,000 personnel losses.
Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi said all four phases of Operation Vivaldi were complete, but the operation was far from over.
In September, the 3rd Army Corps told Militarnyi that its unmanned systems units had launched 36,000 strike missions during Operation Vivaldi, targeting Russian forces’ supply lines and logistics infrastructure.

renewed 1983 bathhouse in japan preserves tilework and curved interiors
shizunoyu fukushima is a renovation project that transforms enmeiyu, a public bathhouse designed by architect yoshiji takehara in 1983, into a bathing facility exclusively for men.
[FEATURED]
MABI ARCHITECTS preserves former bathhouse’s curves and tiles
MABI ARCHITECTS renovates Enmeiyu, a public bathhouse designed by Yoshiji Takehara in 1983, into Shizunoyu Fukushima, a bathing facility exclusively for men. The project retains elements of the original architecture while introducing new functions and spaces for relaxation and socializing.
The renovation preserves the building’s curved forms and distinctive tilework, which reflect its history. As many existing tiles as possible remain in the washing area, maintaining a connection to the former bathhouse. New facilities include a cold plunge pool, sauna, outdoor bathing area, indoor relaxation space, and bar counter, integrated alongside the original materials and spatial features.
Shizunoyu Fukushima brings new uses to neighborhood bathhouse
By combining retained architectural details with new uses, the project by MABI ARCHITECTS Studio carries forward the bathhouse’s role as a place for informal encounters and conversation. Shizunoyu Fukushima continues the former Enmeiyu’s connection to the local community, creating a setting where visitors can gather and interact across generations.

Finance minister says KMT's proposed NT$20,000 cash handout would require borrowing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

18:25:58 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Finance Minister Chuang Tsui-yun (莊翠雲) said Wednesday that doubling Taiwan's planned NT$10,000 (US$315) cash payout to NT$20,000 would require government borrowing, as most of the recent tax revenue increase went to local governments under a revised revenue allocation law.
During a Legislative Yuan Finance Committee session, KMT Legislator Lin Te-fu (林德福) said tax revenue in the first eight months of this year was NT$600 billion higher than in the same period last year, per Mirror Media. He called on the ministry to explain the basis for its borrowing estimates.
Chuang said national tax revenue rose by about NT$700 billion in the first nine months of this year compared with the same period in 2025, per Rti. However, the central government accounted for only NT$250 billion of the increase, while local governments received NT$450 billion.
The minister said the central government has allocated NT$235.7 billion in its proposed 2027 general budget to provide NT$10,000 to each eligible recipient, citing strong economic growth and rising tax revenue driven by the AI industry. She said increasing the payout to NT$20,000 would cost more than NT$470 billion and require government borrowing to cover the shortfall.
Chuang said local governments received most of the additional tax revenue partly because amendments to the Act Governing the Allocation of Government Revenues and Expenditures directed 95.5% of business tax revenue to local governments, Rti reported.
Lin also questioned why the payout was included in the general budget, suggesting the move was intended to coincide with an election year and pressure the Legislative Yuan into approving the spending, Mirror Media reported. Chuang said the NT$10,000 payout was included in the budget after careful fiscal assessment, without increasing net borrowing or affecting other government programs.
Chuang said the government hoped recipients could receive the money before Lunar New Year, but that would depend on the Legislative Yuan passing the 2027 general budget by Jan. 5 and President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) promulgating it by Jan. 20, according to Rti. If those deadlines are met, the ministry could complete the necessary system preparations in time to distribute the payments before the holiday, she said.

Analyst says Musk’s chip fab plan unlikely to threaten Taiwan’s TSMC

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Tesla CEO Elon Musk’s reported plan to build a semiconductor fabrication plant is unlikely to affect TSMC in the short to medium term, Kirkland Capital Chair Yang Ying-chao (楊應超) said Wednesday.
Speaking on the sidelines of a forum, Yang said building a chip fab is difficult and could take five to 10 years to materialize, even for an experienced company, per CNA. Musk reportedly plans to invest about NT$96.6 billion (US$3 billion) in an experimental fab dubbed Terafab.
Yang said many multinational companies have failed to enter chip manufacturing, citing IBM’s semiconductor division, which was eventually sold to GlobalFoundries. However, he said he is confident in Musk’s execution, citing his track record at Tesla and SpaceX.
Yang said chip shortages during the COVID-19 pandemic and escalating US-China trade tensions have strengthened US companies’ push for vertical supply chain integration. Companies are seeking to manage everything from integrated circuit design and manufacturing to packaging in-house, he explained.
US companies, including Intel, could be major partners in Musk’s project, Yang said, adding that Washington wants domestic companies to lead semiconductor manufacturing. He said TSMC could also benefit if Musk follows through on plans to sublease fab space or technical consulting.
Yang said closer cooperation could help TSMC gain a better understanding of Intel, which he believes could become a competitor, although that prospect remains unlikely in the short term.

Japan summons Russian ambassador

Those tensions heightened when Japan joined Western sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine, with Russia regarding Japan as an "unfriendly" country. But business ties remain with Japan a purchaser of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).
Then in August, Russian President Vladimir Putin visited one of the disputed islands, causing an uproar in Japan. On Tuesday, a delegation from a Chinese province visited the same island, in what appeared to signal closer coordination between Moscow and Beijing in their criticism of Tokyo.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said on Tuesday that Japan had refused to consider Moscow's concerns about what she called Tokyo's "remilitarization." She criticized Japan's alleged use of accredited journalists in Russia to gather information that could undermine Russian security.
"We have to note that what has occurred will become an additional factor clouding the atmosphere of Russian-Japanese relations," Zakharova said.
Asked whether improving relations between Russia and the U.S. and Japan's purchases of LNG from Russia made it difficult for Tokyo to take countermeasures, Kihara said: "It is true that there are many issues between Japan and Russia.
"From Japan's perspective, despite the difficult situation in Japan-Russia relations, Japan has taken resolute measures based on its position. At the same time, Russia is a neighboring country to Japan, and communication is necessary to resolve these issues."

U.S. Navy taps HII for $56M AUKUS submarine design work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:24:16 UTC
18:24:16 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Newport News Shipbuilding $56.2 million for AUKUS submarine engineering and design work, funded entirely by foreign partners.
- HII said its engineers will help design SSN-AUKUS, with an option that could raise the contract’s value to $91.1 million.
The U.S. Navy has awarded Huntington Ingalls Industries’ Newport News Shipbuilding a $56.2 million contract for engineering and design work on nuclear-powered submarines for America’s AUKUS partners, with foreign partner funds covering the full cost of the deal.
The Department of War contract announcement describes a cost-plus-fixed-fee deal covering engineering and technical support, along with design agent and design transfer activities for nuclear submarine capabilities and their sustainment. The work falls under Foreign Military Sales, the government-to-government channel Washington uses to sell defense equipment and services abroad, and an option, if exercised, would lift the total value to $91.1 million.
While the Pentagon notice leaves the foreign customer unnamed, HII filled in the gap on Oct. 13, saying in a company release that the award supports the trilateral Australia, United Kingdom and United States partnership known as AUKUS.
Signed in 2021, AUKUS is meant to give Australia a fleet of conventionally armed, nuclear-powered attack submarines. Canberra plans to acquire at least eight boats, including three to five Virginia-class submarines bought from the United States in the 2030s, followed by a new class designed with Britain and known as SSN-AUKUS.
According to HII, Newport News will keep supporting both the United Kingdom and Australia under the contract through technology insertion and engineering, as well as supply chain and workforce development. The award also funds an effort called United States Industry Support, under which Newport News engineers and designers will help design the SSN-AUKUS boat that Britain and Australia will build.
“Our longstanding nuclear experience at NNS directly benefits the AUKUS mission to support shared security objectives,” said Bryan Caccavale, Newport News Shipbuilding vice president of program management.
In submarine programs, the design agent is the yard responsible for a class’s technical design and for keeping it current over the boats’ service lives. Design transfer is the handover of that technical knowledge to another builder or navy, which Australia needs before it can maintain and eventually build nuclear submarines of its own.
Newport News will carry out 88% of the work at its Virginia shipyard, with the remaining 12% taking place at unspecified foreign locations. Work is scheduled to finish in September 2027, or in September 2028 if the option is exercised.
The contract carries no U.S. funding, and $19.1 million in foreign partner funds was obligated at the time of award without expiring at the end of the current fiscal year. Naval Sea Systems Command awarded the contract without competition, citing a statute that applies when only one responsible source can meet the requirement.
Newport News is one of only two American shipyards that build nuclear-powered submarines. It builds the bows, sterns and other modules for both the Virginia and Columbia classes, while General Dynamics Electric Boat in Groton, Connecticut, builds the central reactor section.
Electric Boat received a comparable award in April, a $196 million contract that Rep. Joe Courtney described as the first awarded by the U.S. Navy for AUKUS work. That deal used the same wording on engineering, design agent and design transfer support, and its options could raise its value to more than $930 million through April 2031.
On the Australian side, HII’s local operations won a 2025 contract to run the Australian Submarine Supplier Qualification Pilot Program, worth an initial A$9.6 million, which vets Australian companies for entry into the U.S. submarine supply chain.
Australia has pledged $3 billion to the U.S. submarine industrial base, paid in installments, and had delivered $2 billion of that amount as of April 23, according to Courtney.

The film’s title, "NAZA," refers to an acronym used by Israeli military intelligence to denote the number of civilians expected to be killed in an airstrike.
During the war, the Israeli army has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians and injured over 175,000 others since October 2023 in a brutal offensive that has left the entire enclave in ruins.
Netanyahu claimed that the film has presented a "false, misleading and biased narrative” that defames Israel and its military and damages the country’s international standing.
"There is concern that those involved in the defamatory film committed serious criminal offenses by exposing highly classified information and creating a breach in the information security of a highly sensitive intelligence unit,” he said in the letter.
The film, based on testimony from 24 Israeli soldiers and intelligence personnel, won the Special Jury Prize at the Venice Film Festival last month.
Following the award, Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar asked the Interior Ministry to consider revoking the citizenship of the film’s creators, describing the documentary as "vile” and accusing them of "treason.”
Zamir separately ordered Military Intelligence, the Military Advocate General’s Corps and the Israeli Air Force to identify the soldiers featured in the film and determine whether they were active-duty troops, career officers or reservists, according to Haaretz.
During discussions on the issue, Military Advocate General Itai Offir said that there would be no legal basis for criminal prosecution unless participants were found to have committed information-security violations or disclosed classified material.
He said disciplinary or command measures could, however, be taken if military orders were violated.
The Israeli army claimed that the documentary’s portrayal of its targeting procedures in Gaza contained "substantial factual errors.”
The Guardian, which produced the documentary, defended the film, saying the process used to assess the credibility of the testimonies was "rigorous” and included classified documents, verification of specific strikes and corroboration from additional confidential sources.
The newspaper said it had interviewed more than 100 people familiar with Israeli military systems used during the war in Gaza, including senior commanders involved in authorizing strikes.

US Embassy in Israel issues safety warning about unexploded ordnances after school trip explosion

The US Embassy in Israel issued a safety warning to American citizens on Tuesday about unexploded ordnance and munitions found across extensive areas of Israel, the West Bank, and the Gaza Strip, a day after a teenager was killed and 24 people were injured in an explosion during a school trip in northern Israel.
The warning followed the death of Elazar Yair Wilensky, who was killed when unexploded Hezbollah ammunition detonated during the school trip.
In its statement, the embassy warned that the danger was particularly great near border areas and that, in many cases, the locations of unexploded ordnance are unmarked, and the devices may be difficult to identify.
"Rain, flooding, agricultural work, and construction activities frequently bring buried munitions to the surface, making them more unstable," the embassy said.
The embassy stressed that unexploded ordnance can come in various shapes and sizes, including artillery shells, mortar bombs, rockets, grenades, landmines, and cluster munitions.
It warned particularly about small, round cluster bomblets, which may resemble balls or toys and attract children's attention.
"Assume that any unidentified object is dangerous," the statement said.
Embassy emphasizes three-step safety rule: Recognize, retreat, report
The embassy emphasized a three-step safety rule in its guidelines: recognize, retreat, and report.
Anyone who identifies a suspicious object should stop immediately and avoid approaching it to investigate. Instead, they should carefully retreat along the same route they used to reach the area, keep others away, particularly children, and report the object to Israel Police by calling 100.
The embassy also warned against physically touching unexploded ordnance, throwing objects at it, or using mobile phones and two-way radios nearby.
It further recommended against collecting ammunition casings, shell fragments, or war souvenirs, even if the items have reportedly been neutralized and are considered safe.
The embassy urged the public to avoid entering areas marked as minefields or contaminated by unexploded ordnance, and to remain on paved roads and familiar trails when hiking outside urban areas.
It also called on parents to explain to children that they must never touch unidentified metal objects and should immediately report any such discoveries to an adult.
In addition, the embassy recommended identifying the location of the nearest protected space, using Home Front Command warning applications, and keeping up to date with security guidance issued by the US State Department.

====================================================================================================

From Saddam Hussein to Israel: How Iran's wars have divided a nation - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:21:16 UTC
18:21:16 KST

On September 22, 1980, as Iraqi warplanes bombed Iranian airfields and Saddam Hussein's tanks crossed the Iranian border, Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini appeared remarkably unconcerned by what was unfolding in the fledgling Islamic Republic.
Iraq’s attack, he told the Iranian people, was little more than “a thief throwing a stone” before running away. There was no reason to panic, he insisted, and certainly no reason to believe that Iran had entered a major war. The country's armed forces were perfectly capable of dealing with the threat.
History, of course, would prove him spectacularly wrong as the war dragged on for eight long years and left an estimated half a million people dead.
Saddam's invasion brought together a deeply fractured Iranian nation
However, for all the destruction that followed, Saddam's invasion also achieved something that the Islamic Republic, barely a year and a half old, could scarcely have accomplished on its own. It brought together a deeply fractured Iranian nation, many of whose people had little affection for Khomeini or the clerical establishment that had seized power in Tehran.
Nearly half a century later, with Iran engaging twice in the space of one year against Israel and the United States, the question of how Iranians respond to an external enemy has returned to the fore. And while Iran's leaders have spent much of the past year insisting that the country stands united behind them, the events unfolding inside Iran tell a considerably more complicated story.
When Saddam launched his invasion, Iran was still struggling to come to terms with the revolution that had overthrown Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi in February 1979. The revolutionary government had barely established control over the country, while competing political factions were fighting for influence, and the military, once among the most powerful in the Middle East, had been weakened by purges of officers associated with the former monarchy.
There was unrest in the provinces and among different ethnic groups, opposition to clerical rule was growing, and the new Islamic Republic was still engaged in the bloody business of eliminating its political rivals.
From Baghdad, Hussein believed he had found his moment to strike and take, among other things, the Shatt al-Arab waterway and its key oil installations.
The Iraqi dictator calculated that Iran's internal turmoil would make a swift military victory possible, particularly if he could exploit the country's ethnic divisions. Hussein hoped that the Sunni-majority Arab population of Khuzestan, the oil-rich Iranian province bordering Iraq, would welcome his troops as liberators against their Shi’a oppressors.. He was very much mistaken.
Rather than embracing the invading Iraqi army, many Iranian Arabs joined their compatriots in defending their homeland. Political opponents of Khomeini, including supporters of the ousted monarchy, similarly recognized that whatever their differences with the new government, the country's territorial integrity was at stake. Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, a trained fighter pilot and son of the exiled Shah, even extended an offer to his country’s new rulers to return and fight for Iran.
Iranian patriotism, it turned out, extended considerably further than loyalty to the Islamic Republic.
"We are ready to send all our children to battle the thugs,” Khomeini stated just days after the invasion.
For Khomeini, the war provided an opportunity to harness that patriotism and place the defense of the nation at the center of his revolutionary government's struggle for survival. As the fighting dragged on, the regime more and more associated resistance to the Iraqis and Hussein with support for the Islamic Republic itself, while the demands of wartime offered further opportunities to silence domestic opposition and consolidate clerical rule. This was also the period of massive expansion in the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps - originally formed to safeguard the revolution domestically.
By the time the guns finally stopped in August 1988, the Islamic Republic had survived its greatest external challenge and emerged with a far stronger grip on power than it had possessed when Iraqi troops first crossed the border.
If the 1980-88 war, however, was relatively successful in its ability to get Iranians to “rally around the flag,” the wars of 2025 and 2026 proved more difficult for the Iranian regime to succeed in garnering nationalist fervor.
Unlike Iraq, American and Israeli military campaigns were conducted from the air
Unlike Saddam's invasion, which involved Iraqi ground forces attempting to capture and occupy Iranian territory, the American and Israeli military campaigns were conducted overwhelmingly from the air, targeting nuclear facilities, missile installations, military infrastructure, and senior figures within the Islamic Republic's security establishment.
Neither the US nor Israel attempted a comparable occupation of Iranian territory, and both countries repeatedly presented their military operations as directed against the regime and the threat posed by its military capabilities, rather than against the Iranian people themselves.
The reaction this time around, from Iranians, was very different.
There were, of course, civilian casualties, and considerable anger at the attacks, including among Iranians who have little sympathy for the government. The bombing of one's country by foreign powers is hardly a straightforward proposition, regardless of how deeply one despises those who govern it.
But Iran in 2026 is also a country that has endured almost five decades of Islamic Republic rule, successive waves of protests, deteriorating economic conditions, and increasingly brutal attempts by the authorities to suppress opposition.
The nationwide uprising that began in December 2025, and the massacres that followed in January, which left an estimated 40,000 people killed in two days, added another devastating chapter to that history. Security forces sought to crush demonstrations that had spread across the country, leaving families mourning their dead and an already profound divide between the population and the political establishment even deeper.
It is against this background that Iranians' response is even more powerful.
During Iraq’s invasion, Iranians from across the political spectrum rallied to defend their country against a foreign army. In 2026, footage emerging from inside Iran has shown people thanking the leaders of the very countries carrying out strikes against the Islamic Republic.
Graffiti appealing directly to US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu began appearing during the January uprising, including messages pleading with them to intervene as protesters faced the security forces. Following the American and Israeli military operations, other messages went considerably further, thanking Trump and Netanyahu for their actions.
In Karaj, west of Tehran, graffiti reading "We love you BB," a reference to Netanyahu, appeared on a wall, while videos circulated by Iran International showed Iranians expressing gratitude toward both leaders.
The sight of Iranians publicly thanking an Israeli prime minister and an American president for military action against targets inside their own country would have been almost inconceivable during the Iran-Iraq War.
Such expressions are not representative of the entire population, but the fact they are seen and they are there is crucial in understanding the standing of the Islamic Republic currently. Many Iranians oppose foreign military intervention, including those who are bitterly opposed to the Islamic Republic, and the continued appearance of pro-government rallies (however falsified their attendance numbers) demonstrates that the authorities retain a constituency prepared to mobilize in their support.
Nevertheless, the messages of gratitude, particularly those directed toward Netanyahu, offer an astonishing illustration of how far relations between sections of Iranian society and their rulers have deteriorated.
The Islamic Republic, meanwhile, sought to portray the wars as further proof of the country's enduring national unity.
Following the Twelve-Day War in June 2025, senior military and political officials repeatedly praised the solidarity of the Iranian people, with IRGC spokesman Brigadier-General Ali Mohammad Naeini declaring that Israel had encountered the "ironclad unity of the Iranian people."
Similar declarations accompanied the renewed conflict in 2026. In September, IRGC Aerospace Force commander Brigadier-General Majid Mousavi praised the nightly pro-government gatherings, describing them as a demonstration of the Iranian people's commitment to defending their country's identity, independence, and very existence, while urging continued support for the Islamic Republic and its armed forces. Later that month, President Masoud Pezeshkian accused the US and Israel of attempting to sow divisions within Iranian society, insisting that the country was experiencing "unprecedented unity and cohesion."
Such language would have been familiar to Khomeini, who spent much of the Iran-Iraq War portraying the sacrifices of ordinary Iranians as evidence of the nation's commitment to the revolution. But to proclaim national unity is one thing. Demonstrating that the population remains united behind those making the proclamations is quite another.
An incident in Tehran last Friday evening provided a particularly interesting example.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei, one of the Islamic Republic's most recognizable diplomatic voices throughout the conflict, was booed by members of an audience attending a performance of Arash, an orchestral theatrical production based on the legendary Iranian archer who sacrificed himself to protect his homeland.
According to footage circulated by Iranian media, Baghaei had taken a microphone to address the audience when some spectators began booing him.
Arash occupies a special place in Iranian mythology, a patriotic figure immersed in the defense of the nation's territorial integrity. That a senior representative of the Islamic Republic should encounter such a hostile reception at a production celebrating one of Iran's most enduring national heroes speaks to the complicated relationship between Iranian national identity and the clerical government that claims to represent it.
It also lets us see into a small window of the current feelings of the Iranian people compared to 1980.
Hussein invaded an Iran was still coming to terms with the upheaval of revolution
Saddam Hussein invaded a country that was bitterly divided, politically unstable, and still coming to terms with the upheaval of revolution. His expectation that those divisions would make Iran easy prey proved disastrous, as Iranians who disagreed profoundly about their country's future nevertheless found common cause in defending its borders.
Khomeini was able to capitalize on that national resistance, using the war to strengthen the very political system whose future had appeared so uncertain when the fighting began.
The Islamic Republic's present leadership has sought to draw upon much the same sentiment, invoking the nationalistic language of sacrifice, sovereignty, and resistance, while insisting that the nation stands firmly behind its armed forces. For those who know Iranians, love of their homeland is one thing that can bring them together.
But the Iran of 2026 is a very different country from the one Saddam invaded. Its people have lived under the Islamic Republic for almost half a century, and for a substantial section of the population, the government itself has become inseparable from the grievances that have repeatedly brought Iranians onto the streets.
Forty-six years ago, Saddam discovered that Iranians were prepared to put aside their differences to defend their country, allowing Khomeini to transform a war for national survival into a foundation for the Islamic Republic's consolidation. Today, the same government continues to invoke the patriotism of the Iranian people, but after decades of repression, revolution, and economic uncertainty, it can no longer assume that those who love their country are still loyal to those who rule it.

High Court hears petition demanding protection for lawyers from courthouse harassment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:20:52 UTC
18:20:52 KST

High Court justices questioned Wednesday whether the Courts Administration’s instructions adequately protect lawyers from courthouse harassment, pressing for clearer rules on conduct that guards should halt and how those rules are communicated to the public.
The case concerns lawyers representing Palestinians and human rights groups who say right-wing activists follow them through the Supreme Court’s corridors, film them at close range, and accuse them of supporting terrorism. The petitioners argue that preventing physical attacks alone is insufficient: Lawyers must be able to prepare for hearings, consult privately with clients, and represent them without intimidation.
Justices Dafna Barak-Erez, Gila Canfy-Steinitz, and Yechiel Kasher examined possible protections, including clearly defined areas where lawyers could work without interference. No ruling was delivered during the hearing, and a decision is due to be sent to the parties.
Guards instructed to intervene against harassment, humiliation, intimidation of lawyers
The Court’s Administration rejected the claim that its protection policy warrants judicial intervention. In an updated response submitted ahead of the hearing, it said security preparations had been strengthened, and guards were explicitly instructed to intervene against the filming aimed at harassing, humiliating, or intimidating lawyers.
During Wednesday’s hearing, state attorney Hadas Eran condemned interference with lawyers and said that courthouses were not places for demonstrations. She maintained that the instructions were implemented through training and briefings, with guards exercising judgment according to the circumstances.
The justices questioned whether that approach provided guards with sufficiently concrete guidance.
When Eran referred to a summary of a June 2023 meeting as the written basis for the instructions, Barak-Erez questioned whether it amounted to a comprehensive set of rules and asked when further work on instructions would be completed.
“These are very general instructions,” Canfy-Steinitz said, questioning whether they told a guard what to do in a particular situation.
Barak-Erez also asked how many people had been removed from courthouses over the past year for disturbing public order. Eran said she would have to obtain the figure, but the discussion exposed a further question: how visitors could be expected to comply with restrictions that were not clearly published. Barak-Erez used the example of a distance limit on filming, asking how someone would know they had breached an unwritten rule.
Filed in 2024 by the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel, HaMoked, Gisha, Yesh Din, and Physicians for Human Rights Israel, the petition challenges the policy of the Courts Administration and its director, Judge Tzachi Uziel.
No proposal was adopted during the hearing
The organizations, represented by attorneys Michael Sfard and Einat Gayer, proposed confining protests to a designated area inside the courthouse. Sfard argued that lawyers should not have to retreat to a separate room to work undisturbed.
The justices explored whether clearer protections for lawyers’ personal space would suffice or whether part of the lobby should be designated free of filming and harassment. They also questioned the scope of guards’ legal powers. No proposal was adopted during the hearing.
In a written update filed ahead of Wednesday’s hearing, the petitioners described confrontations during hearings concerning humanitarian aid to Gaza, prison conditions, punitive home demolitions, and other contested policies.
The update identified activists from Im Tirtzu in several incidents and argued that repeated involvement by the same individuals calls for measures to prevent further harassment.
Among the most serious allegations is an incident from March 30, 2026, during a hearing over displaced Palestinians’ return to refugee camps in the northern West Bank. According to the petitioners, an activist followed lawyers after they left the courtroom while the justices examined classified material, then violently pushed Association for Civil Rights in Israel (ACRI) attorney Oded Feller as he tried to enter another courtroom.
The filing said footage was provided to the court’s chief secretary and the incident was brought to the panel’s attention. Feller submitted an affidavit supporting the account.
The petitioners also described an October 29, 2025, hearing concerning Red Cross visits to detention facilities, after which a court security officer escorted lawyers and association staff out of the building. They said that the group had to crouch behind bushes while awaiting transportation to avoid attracting the hostile crowd.
These incidents, they argued, demonstrate the inadequacy of a policy that leaves lawyers retreating while those harassing them remain free to move around.
The dispute followed complaints dating back to 2020. Instructions developed after the June 2023 meeting with Sfard treated intrusion into lawyers’ personal space, curses, and incitement to violence as disturbances requiring intervention. The administration subsequently said guards had been instructed to maintain a three-meter distance to protect lawyers’ personal space.
Its December 2024 response defended the balance between lawyers’ safety, freedom of expression, and public access, and it pointed to a Bar Association room available for private work.
In an update submitted on Sunday, the administration cited additional training, advance planning for sensitive hearings, and inspections that it said found no departures from instructions. An internal directive clarifying responsibilities and coordination remains under review.
That update also cited a December 2025 Supreme Court decision permitting advance restrictions on courtroom attendance where serious disruption is reasonably anticipated, alongside live-streaming or screening in another courtroom.
Wednesday’s hearing ended with the practical questions unresolved: whether the existing instructions provide sufficient protection, whether clearer written rules are needed, and whether parts of the courthouse should be set aside to allow lawyers to work without interference.

Katz moves to ban a fiber-optic, SIM-operated drones from Israeli airspace amid growing threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:20:38 UTC
18:20:38 KST

Defense Minister Israel Katz plans to sign an order banning fiber-optic and SIM-controlled drones from flying in Israeli airspace on Sunday, Katz's office announced on Tuesday, in an effort to curb security threats posed by these drone types.
Among the varied threats mentioned were drone attacks, attempts to harm senior officials, usage of the drones by organized crime families, smuggling, and illicitly gathering intelligence.
The order will last six months from its signing and was approved in advance by both Katz and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at a cabinet meeting.
The order also includes exceptions for security force drones, fiber-optic drones tied to the ground, SIM-operated drones which had received prior authorization from the Civil Aviation Authority, and all non-fiber-optic or SIM-operated drones.
IDF establishing new drone-countering corps
Also on Tuesday, Walla reported that IDF Ground Forces Commander Maj.-Gen. Nadav Lotan is working to establish a new corps dedicated to countering low-altitude drone threats, as part of an effort to strengthen Israel's defenses against the growing threat posed by unmanned aerial vehicles.
The corps will initially be based on five battalions that routinely protect the borders with Jordan and Egypt, as well as the security barrier area in the West Bank.
Under the plan, these battalions will assume an additional mission alongside their existing responsibility for defending Israel's land borders: protecting against mobile threats operating in the airspace close to the ground.
Amir Bohbot contributed to this report.

Yemen hospitals overwhelmed by surge in war casualties, Red Cross warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:20:38 UTC
18:20:38 KST

Yemen fighting overwhelms hospitals, cuts aid to 800,000 people: Relief agencies
GENEVA – Hospitals across Yemen are struggling to cope with a sharp rise in war casualties, while intensified fighting along multiple front lines has cut off aid to around 800,000 people, humanitarian agencies said on Oct 14.
Front-line hospitals in areas including Marib, Taiz and Yemen’s Red Sea coast were seeing unprecedented numbers of weapon-wounded patients, with some facilities admitting more than 700 casualties in a single week, according to the Red Cross.
More than 200,000 people have been displaced from their homes since fighting in the country began in recent weeks, sparked by renewed fighting between the Iran-backed Houthi group and Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen, according to the United Nations’ International Organization for Migration.
“Trauma care staff are under enormous pressure,” ICRC health coordinator Feras Abusamra said in a statement.
Only a small proportion of Yemen’s functioning health facilities are capable of providing comprehensive trauma care, he said, while hospitals face large numbers of wounded people amid shortages of surgical supplies, anaesthesia, oxygen and medicines.
Yemen’s health services, battered by more than a decade of conflict, economic crisis, displacement and disease outbreaks, may have limited capacity to absorb a new surge in mass casualties if fighting intensifies further, the ICRC warned.
The fighting has also cut off life-saving humanitarian assistance for 800,000 people in Taiz – Yemen’s third-largest city, which currently hosts the largest number of people fleeing the fighting – and other areas impacted by the conflict, the UN World Food Programme said on Oct 14.
Some districts are now inaccessible because of fighting and road closures, the WFP said, adding that wheat flour stocks are nearly exhausted and remaining food in local markets may last only a short time.
“This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most,” said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP Representative and Country Director in Yemen, in a statement. REUTERS

 Listen
The head of the International Monetary Fund said on Wednesday that the US and other wealthy nations needed to urgently tackle mounting global debt levels that were weighing heaviest on low-income countries and straining the global financial system.
IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said that while US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other US leaders recognised that the federal deficit and national debt had grown too high, just trying to grow the US economy out of its more than US$40 trillion in national debt would not suffice.
“At the fund, we believe that, growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver fast enough the necessary adjustments,” Georgieva said at the autumn meeting of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.

Pope Leo XIV had peaceful night after lung cancer surgery Tuesday, the Vatican said Wednesday. The 71-year-old Chicago native had a malign tumour removed from his lung, To ensure the procedure was radical, the right lower lobe of the organ was removed, medical sources said. Democrats Party chairman Yair Golan sharply criticized President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday over a reported initiative to establish a national unity government if the October 27 election produces no clear winner, accusing the president of preparing the ground for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to remain in power before Israelis have even cast their ballots.
Golan's remarks followed a ynet report revealing Herzog's intention to pursue a unity government in the event of a post-election political deadlock. The Democrats leader argued that discussing such an arrangement before the vote risked undermining public confidence in the possibility of a change in government.
"Before we've even voted, before the people have had their say, Herzog and his mouthpieces are already laying the groundwork for 'unity' with Netanyahu," Golan said.
He accused supporters of such an arrangement of attempting to convince voters that Netanyahu's continued leadership was inevitable, regardless of the election results. Golan rejected that message, insisting that replacing the current government remained a realistic political objective.
"They're trying to demoralize you, to convince you that everything is lost, that Netanyahu will remain in power no matter what and that there's no point in fighting," he said. "It's a lie. We can win. We can replace this government. And we will."
Golan also framed the debate over national unity as a question of accountability for the October 7, 2023 Hamas massacre and the government's conduct during the ensuing war. He argued that entering a coalition with Netanyahu would mean setting aside responsibility for the security failures preceding the attack and the controversies that have marked his government's tenure.
The Democrats leader cited the handling of the hostage crisis, government support for ultra-Orthodox draft exemptions during wartime and what he described as damage to democratic institutions, public finances and national unity.
In a series of accusations directed at Netanyahu, Golan questioned whether advocates of a unity government expected Israelis to overlook those issues in the name of political stability.
He warned that allowing Netanyahu to remain in office for another four years would, in his view, deepen political divisions and threaten Israel's democratic character.
"And now they want us to give him another four years," Golan said. "Four more years of destruction, corruption and abandonment. Four more years that would endanger Israel's very future as a Jewish and democratic state."
His comments highlighted the resistance within parts of the opposition to any post-election arrangement that would leave Netanyahu as prime minister, even if the election fails to produce a clear parliamentary majority.

Ukraine Says SpaceX Limits Starlink Operations, Disrupting Military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:17:29 UTC
18:17:29 KST

Ukraine accused Elon Musk's SpaceX on Wednesday of limiting Starlink services, crippling its drones, as Russian missiles knocked out power stations in attacks President Volodymyr Zelensky called "ostentatious disrespect" to Donald Trump.
Kyiv's relationship with Washington has taken a sharp turn for the worse since U.S. President Trump abruptly lifted sanctions on Russian diesel last week and publicly turned on Zelensky.
Trump, under political pressure to lower fuel prices that have soared since he launched a war against Iran, has called on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian refineries, and said Ukrainians should replace their wartime leader.
The U.S. president also announced that Ukraine and Russia had both agreed to halt attacks on energy targets, although neither side confirmed this and the past two days have seen intensive Russian bombing, including of Ukrainian power stations.
No warning before Starlink cuts
Ukrainian military officials said Musk's SpaceX had without warning interrupted functioning of military-grade Starlink terminals moving at high speed, effectively preventing Kyiv from using them as onboard guides for drones.
"Our defense forces did not receive a warning about this limitation, and this led to the disruption of several missions," presidential adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.
The apparent suggestion that Musk's company might limit Ukrainian military capabilities drew a sharp response from Poland, which pays for Ukrainian Starlink subscriptions on Kyiv's behalf.
"Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski asked Musk on X. "As your European customers, we are watching you."
There was no immediate response from Musk, who in the past has called Sikorski a "small man." SpaceX did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside of U.S. business hours.
Musk is a close political ally of Trump, and the suggestion that SpaceX might limit Ukrainian capabilities reinforced wider Ukrainian concerns that Washington could withhold battlefield support to compel its onetime ally to make concessions.
Sources have told Reuters and other news organizations that the U.S. has threatened to cut off intelligence for early warning of missile strikes on Ukraine, to press Kyiv to suspend attacks on Russian oil refineries.
No warning ahead of missiles
Rescue workers in Kyiv were stretchering the injured from the wreckage of a blasted-out residential building overnight, while firefighters battled a huge blaze in the darkness. Officials said 2 people were killed and 21 wounded at the site.
Some 600,000 people were left without power as Russian missiles careened into power stations during hours of attacks that primarily targeted Kyiv and Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city. Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed it had struck four power plants in and around Kyiv and two in Kharkiv, among other targets. Zelenskiy said more than 30 power stations were damaged.
Ukrainian officials said late on Tuesday they had received no warnings from Western partners for a second day before the massive Russian attacks on the capital. Trump had insisted on Tuesday that Washington was still sharing intelligence.
Zelensky cast the latest attacks as a deliberate snub to Trump's declaration of a ceasefire on energy targets.
"Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong," Zelensky wrote on X. "The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale – Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
Zelensky has said Ukraine is willing to observe an energy ceasefire and has not targeted Russian refineries since Trump announced it, but will not continue to hold back if Russia ignores the purported truce. The Kremlin said on Tuesday that contacts were continuing about an energy truce.
Ukraine reported downing just four out of 39 Russian missiles, reflecting Kyiv's weakened air defenses against fast-moving ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones amid a shortage of weapons.
Starlink does not work inside Russia, and Ukrainian drones hitting Russia's oil industry use other means of communication, but Ukraine uses Musk's system to guide drones over its own territory, including parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia.
"According to our observations, during flights, the connection could drop for 10-20 seconds at speeds of just 110-120 km/h [68-75 mph]. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control," Ukraine's 7th Rapid Reaction Corps, deployed in the southeast, said in a statement to Reuters.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry said the limitations significantly complicate logistics and some drone operations.
Since being turned on over Ukraine in the early days of Russia's invasion in 2022, Starlink has been the lifeblood of Ukrainian battlefield communications.
Its resistance to electronic signal jamming has made it a crucial tool for flying long-range attack drones and drones used to drop supplies to frontline troops.

Italian premier says Trump's Russian diesel deal 'very risky'

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:17:02 UTC
18:17:02 KST

Melike Pala
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni on Wednesday described US President Donald Trump's agreement on Russian diesel as a "very risky" decision, ANSA news agency reported.
Speaking in the Senate ahead of the European Council summit, Meloni, who was considered a "Trump whisperer" before they fell out, said the surge in fuel prices was primarily driven by the war in Iran rather than Ukraine, questioning the rationale behind the US decision.
"Therefore, the outcome of this decision is uncertain, while the risks are clear: legitimization for Moscow," Meloni said, highlighting the potential risks of "additional revenues to finance its war and a weakening of Western sanctions leverage."
She said the agreement could send "contradictory" signals at a time when Western countries, including the US, have been seeking to pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, which continues since 2022.
The Italian premier also called for a stronger European role in efforts to end the war, urging EU member states to appoint an authoritative representative with a mandate from all 27 countries to ensure Europe has a unified voice in negotiations.
"We must ensure that Europe does not stand idly by," Meloni stressed.
She criticized the possibility of France, Germany and the UK pursuing diplomatic initiatives through the so-called E3 format without a collective EU mandate, saying any such efforts should be conducted on behalf of all member states.
Trump has urged Russia and Ukraine not to strike each other's energy sites, and last week announced that Moscow will supply diesel to global markets in an effort to lower fuel prices. His administration also temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel.
 
- EU budget priorities
Meloni identified high energy prices as the main challenge facing the Italian economy and business competitiveness, calling for a coordinated and rapid European response.
She reiterated Rome's position on the next EU budget, saying Italy would not accept an agreement that comes at the expense of the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), fisheries or cohesion funding.
Acknowledging the objective set by the bloc to reach an agreement by the end of the year, she said Italy would not support a deal simply to meet a deadline.
"We will only sign an agreement when it is right for Italy," Meloni said.
