Analysts in the commission's Division of Market Oversight submitted a formal enforcement referral after identifying participants, but Mel Gunewardena, senior advisor to Trump-appointed Chairman Michael Selig, reportedly ordered the supervisor to retract the document and froze career staff out of the inquiry.
A commission official told Blooberg that the original findings were US focused, explaining that leadership subsequently determined the agency needed a more comprehensive international market review covering futures, swaps, and over-the-counter activity instead of the initial referral.
The official said that the commission's enforcement division is continuing to examine trading activities, focusing specifically on March 23.
Democratic US Sen. Elizabeth Warren demanded that Selig and Gunewardena testify before Congress over allegations of derailing staff work, while the US Department of Justice has opened a parallel inquiry.

Court throws out CHF18m Swisscom fine in fibre-optic dispute
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:40:09 UTC
17:40:09 KST

Court throws out CHF18m Swisscom fine in fibre-optic dispute
The Federal Administrative Court has upheld an appeal by Swisscom to quash a CHF18 million Swiss fine due to the way in which it expanded its fibre-optic network.
The fine was imposed by the Swiss Competition Commission on the telecoms group.
The court justified its decision on the grounds that Swisscom did not hold a dominant position in the relevant market. The Competition Commission (Weko) had therefore wrongly assumed that there had been a breach of competition law.
The dispute centred on a new technology for expanding the fibre-optic network, which Swisscom had introduced in 2020. Under this system, a feed line is laid as far as the street manhole, where the signal is then distributed to households. This means that competitors can no longer lease end-to-end lines.
Weko had halted the roll-out with interim measures and imposed the sanction in December 2023. The judgement is not yet final and may be appealed to the Federal Supreme Court.

Drones attack Russia's most powerful data centre, over 650 km from Ukraine
Drones have struck Russia's most powerful data centre, owned by the country's largest bank and technology company, Sberbank.
Source: Reuters
Details: The facility is located in the city of Balakovo in Saratov Oblast, roughly 650-700 km from the border with Ukraine. It is Russia's primary data centre in terms of design power capacity, which stands at 82 MW. The site houses 3,000 server racks and up to 120,000 servers.
The Sberbank centre was also set to house Russia's largest supercomputer, which was scheduled for commissioning in 2027. It is not yet known whether it sustained damage in the attack.
However, the strike did not disrupt Sberbank's services, a senior company executive said.
"We confirm that the data processing centre was attacked. At the same time, all of Sberbank's systems and services are operating normally and without disruption," Sberbank First Deputy CEO Alexander Vedyakhin told reporters.
Along with Yandex, its main domestic competitor, Sberbank is a leading Russian developer of artificial intelligence. The Russian domestic AI market is split between Sberbank's GigaChat model and YandexGPT.
Background:
- Drones have previously attacked Yandex data centres several times. Strikes occurred on 8 October in Sasovo, on 9 October in Kaluga and on 11 October in Vladimir.
- Data centres in Sasovo and Vladimir were reported to have ceased operations following the attacks.
- Yandex would need at least six months to replace the damaged infrastructure of these three data centres.

Ryanair changes rules for passengers with luggage — what will apply from November 10
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

Ryanair changes rules for passengers with luggage — what will apply from November 10
Kyiv • UNN
From November 10, Ryanair check-in and baggage drop-off desks will close one hour before departure. The rules will not change for passengers traveling with hand luggage only.
The procedure for Ryanair passengers at airports is changing: from November 10, check-in and baggage drop-off desks will close 60 minutes before departure instead of the current 40 minutes. As stated in a press release, this should help avoid situations in which passengers miss flights because of security or passport control, reports UNN.
Details
Although only 20% of Ryanair passengers travel with checked baggage, the airline wants to give them more time. Travelers often face long queues at airports, especially during peak hours. For the vast majority of passengers, nothing will change. 80% travel with hand luggage only, check in online, and proceed directly to the departure gate. The new rules do not change anything for them.
Passengers will also be assisted by technical solutions: by the autumn, self-service kiosks are expected to be installed at more than 95% of airports. Passengers will be able to check in their baggage themselves, which will help reduce queues at the desks and save time.
Passengers who do not check in baggage and travel with hand luggage only must follow these Ryanair rules:
-  one small personal item. All Ryanair fares include the free carriage of one small personal item measuring no more than 40 × 30 × 20 cm. It must fit under the seat in front. For example, this may be a handbag or a laptop bag; 
-  priority boarding and two pieces of hand luggage. For an additional fee, passengers can purchase the Priority service, which allows them to bring one additional piece of hand luggage weighing up to 10 kg and measuring no more than 55 × 40 × 20 cm. It must be placed in the overhead luggage compartment above the seats. The service also includes priority boarding; 
-  for infants. Children aged from 8 days to 23 months may travel with two items of baby equipment free of charge per child. If an infant travels on an adult's lap, an additional baby bag weighing up to 5 kg and measuring no more than 45 × 35 × 20 cm may be brought on board. No separate free baggage allowance is provided for the child themselves. 
The following rule applies at the departure gate: if hand luggage does not fit into the baggage sizer, passengers may not be allowed to take it on board, or it may be carried in the aircraft's hold for an additional fee.

Tens of thousands of Israelis fly home to vote: ‘October 7 shook everyone’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:38:31 UTC
17:38:31 KST

With two weeks remaining until Israel's elections, tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad are planning to travel home, paying out of pocket to cast their ballots on October 27.
A special panel at the People of the State conference, the flagship event of ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth, brought together Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute; Yehonatan Bar Sadeh, president of FLY & VOTE, AID Coalition; and Yaron Deckel, a political commentator and former head of the Jewish Agency's delegation to Canada. The discussion focused on voting rights for Israelis living abroad, disagreements over the current system and the impact of October 7.
At the start of the discussion, Bar Sadeh was asked whether Israelis' willingness to spend significant sums of money to fly home and vote reflected a different attitude toward the upcoming election compared with previous ones.
"Israelis living abroad have always maintained a strong connection to Israel, and we saw that on October 8, 2023, when people boarded planes, returned home and reported for reserve duty," he said. "The average Israeli living abroad starts the morning by opening an Israeli newspaper, watches the news at night and, in between, lives and breathes Israel in real time."
Bar Sadeh said a survey conducted several months ago by his organization found that 84% of Israelis living abroad considered the upcoming election "critical."
"What you're actually seeing is a reflection of Israeli society and that same sense of urgency," he explained.
Deckel pointed to the reasons driving Israelis abroad to return home for the election.
"October 7 dramatically heightened people's sense of concern and involvement," he said. "What shook Israeli society and the State of Israel also shook Jewish communities abroad and Israelis living overseas, whether they've been there for four months or 40 years.
"Everyone has relatives, friends and acquaintances. That rupture, the massacre and the wars affected every Israeli, including those living abroad. The level of concern has risen dramatically, and that's why we're seeing this movement of people coming back to vote."
Deckel added: "I don't like headlines calling this 'the most fateful election in the country's history,' but I think we can all agree that this is a highly significant election, the first since October 7.
"We have the most right-wing government since the establishment of the state and the longest-serving prime minister, who is a controversial figure whether we like it or not. Combine that heightened concern with the legitimate sense that this is an important election, and you get the desire to come home and make a difference."
The discussion also addressed whether Israel should change its voting procedures to allow citizens to vote remotely rather than requiring them to appear at polling stations inside the country.
Bar Sadeh argued that the system needs to be updated.
"It made sense in the 1950s, when the law was passed," he said. "Today, people don't necessarily leave the country permanently. They travel abroad. Reality has changed, and we no longer look at these people as emigrants but as Israelis whose homes just happen to be abroad."
Recalling his time as a student in Jerusalem, Bar Sadeh called for a change in voting procedures.
"Nobody told me I couldn't vote in Tel Aviv," he said.
"Today, someone gets on a plane and goes abroad to study for a few years. You can't say that simply because a person has traveled overseas, they've lost their connection to Israel.
"Take someone who goes abroad for a 10-year professional training program but returns every year for reserve duty. Would anyone say that person doesn't deserve to vote?"
Plesner, asked about the Israel Democracy Institute's position, drew a distinction between two groups of Israelis living abroad.
According to available figures, he said, between 700,000 and 1 million Israeli citizens live outside the country.
"That's a very significant population, and we have an overriding national interest in strengthening our connection with them," he said. "But there's a big difference between that and granting blanket voting rights. I don't think that should be on the table."
Plesner argued that Israelis who have permanently relocated abroad should be treated differently from those whose lives remain centered in Israel.
"Even if they still feel emotionally connected to Israel, that's great. Let's maintain that connection," he said of those who have moved abroad. "But it's not right to grant them voting rights."
By contrast, he said, there are "Israelis who are currently abroad but whose center of life remains in Israel. Maybe they're on an extended trip after military service, studying abroad, undergoing professional training or doing postdoctoral research."
Those cases, he argued, warrant a different approach.
Plesner also said Israel is at one extreme of the democratic world when it comes to voting procedures.
"There's a whole range of systems around the world, and we're relatively far out on one end of the spectrum," he said. "We effectively require people to be physically present at the polling station."
Deckel agreed that Israel was lagging behind technologically.
"We're somewhat behind the times technologically," he said. "Other countries allow people to vote by mail or through computerized systems. They've moved forward, while Israel has remained stuck in 1948."
Plesner concluded: "There are ways to fix this. We need to allow Israelis who happen to be abroad to vote as well."
The discussion then turned to whether the law should be amended and how such changes could be implemented.
Deckel noted that lawmakers have the authority to determine eligibility and could have ruled that Israelis who severed their residency ties with the country — meaning they stopped paying taxes and National Insurance contributions — would lose their right to vote.
However, he said, lawmakers had chosen not to do so.
Any new legislation, Deckel argued, should be passed through broad agreement rather than by a narrow majority of "just 61 votes" in the 120-member Knesset.
Bar Sadeh warned against relying on seemingly objective criteria, such as the number of years someone has spent abroad, arguing that such measures do not necessarily reflect whether a person has genuinely severed ties with Israel.
He again cited the example of someone who spends a decade abroad pursuing professional training but returns annually for reserve duty.
Such a person should not lose the right to vote, he argued, raising the additional question of whether the same rules would apply to that person's spouse.
Plesner said the issue had always been politically sensitive, which explained why previous efforts to reform the system had failed.
He recalled that former lawmaker Shulamit Aloni attempted to advance such changes in the 1980s.
In 2015, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu included the issue in coalition agreements, believing that expanding voting access for Israelis abroad would benefit his Likud party.
A public committee was subsequently established and recommended allowing Israelis whose center of life remained in Israel to vote while abroad.
The committee also proposed setting up polling stations at Ben Gurion Airport two weeks before elections to accommodate soldiers and travelers.
Plesner cautioned against an overly broad expansion of voting access that would allow people "sitting by the water in San Francisco" to make decisions on matters of life and death affecting Israelis.
Deckel countered that someone living in San Francisco might have nieces and nephews in northern Israel or grandchildren in Ofakim.
"Then let them come here and vote," Plesner replied.
"That's exactly what they're doing today," Deckel noted.
The panel also addressed whether Israelis flying home to vote were likely to favor one side of the political spectrum.
Deckel said that, according to available data, the political distribution among Israelis living abroad generally resembles that of the population in Israel.
This time, however, he argued that those making the trip were predominantly liberal voters seeking to change the political landscape, a trend he said was causing concern within Likud.
In such a closely contested election, Deckel said, even one or one and a half Knesset seats could prove "extremely significant," particularly with polls showing the governing coalition and opposition blocs hovering near the threshold needed to secure a parliamentary majority.

Estonian Foreign Ministry: State cannot directly control company decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:38:22 UTC
17:38:22 KST

Although the Estonian Ministry of Foreign Affairs has pressured Silmet to stop purchasing rare-earth metals from Russia, the company has not yet ceased doing so, reports ERR News.
Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna stated that the ministry has pressured the chemical and metallurgical company Silmet, urging it to stop sourcing raw materials from Russia. The minister has now pledged to set a deadline by which the company must stop using Russian rare-earth metals. Tsahkna believes Silmet should end its cooperation with Russia starting early next year.
ERR asked the ministry what specific methods were used to secure a move away from Russian raw materials, why the company has not agreed to this, and whether the ministry (or the minister) bears responsibility for the fact that an Estonian company continues to cooperate with Russia while Russian aggression has been raging in Ukraine for five years.
In its response, the ministry noted that the company's reliance on Russian raw materials has long been a matter of public knowledge. According to the ministry, Estonian media reported on this issue as early as 1995. The ministry emphasized that dependence on Russian raw materials is not merely a business issue but also creates a strategic vulnerability that Moscow could exploit. Therefore, it is considered crucial to end this dependence as soon as possible. 
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs maintains contact with Estonian companies, including Silmet, regularly stressing the need to seek alternatives to supplies from Russia.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs explained that Silmet is a public limited company owned by an international group headquartered in Canada. Consequently, the state cannot directly influence business decisions or continuously monitor the nuances of its operations. Nor can the state verify whether the company has genuinely sought alternative raw material suppliers.
At the same time, the ministry emphasized that it is working to support Silmet in finding other supply channels and has cooperated with the European Commission, which is responsible for the European Union's common trade policy. According to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, a significant step toward change was taken on the 9th of October, when the European Commission selected the Silmet development project as one of 46 strategic EU projects. The project aims to modernize the company's facilities to enable the use of raw materials sourced elsewhere and to reduce European industry's dependence on Russia. The Ministry noted that the project would allow Silmet to grow and reduce its reliance on Russian raw materials.
Rare-earth metals potentially suitable for Silmet's operations can be found in Latin America, Asia, and Africa.
 The company itself is best positioned to assess the suitability of raw materials for its specific needs and technological processes. The Ministry emphasized that Silmet needs to explain to the public as soon as possible how it plans to end its dependence on raw materials supplied by Russia.
Increasing competition in the international market is making it more difficult to find alternative raw materials. Major industrial powers are actively competing for limited raw material supplies, thereby affecting availability and supply options. The ministry stated that Estonia aims to support Silmet's efforts to find alternative suppliers and reduce its dependence on Russia. Achieving this goal will require investment and technological changes within the company itself, as well as cooperation at the EU level to improve the availability of alternative supply channels.
Last week, at Estonia's request, a Russian company that supplies rare-earth metals to Silmet was removed from the EU's 22nd sanctions package.

Former U.S. Vice President Kamala Harris delivers a special lecture titled “American Leadership and the Future of Alliances” at the Asan Institute for Policy Studies in Seoul on Oct. 14, 2026. | Image: NK News

Interception rate for Russian jet-powered drones rises to 76% — Ihnat
Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, made the announcement during a televised broadcast, according to Ukrinform.
"Today, 128 UAVs of various types were deployed. These included Gerbera, Parody, and jet-powered UAVs. Of the 128 drones, 77 were jet-powered. That is a fairly large number. Naturally, the enemy is increasing the proportion of jet-powered UAVs in every attack. At the same time, the overall interception rate across all types of UAVs is 90%. In other words, 115 were shot down or suppressed, including 59 jet-powered drones. The figures are improving. I would emphasize that last month the interception rate for jet-powered UAVs was still around 60%; today, it has risen to 76%, based on the latest attack," he said.
Ihnat noted that it is impossible to intercept every drone.
The spokesperson also explained that jet-powered UAVs are relatively expensive to manufacture. According to him, a single engine costs approximately $40,000. Ihnat stressed the need to impose sanctions on Russia to reduce its capacity to manufacture such weapons.

Atlantic bluefin tuna spotted off the Flemish coast for the first time since 1960
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:36:57 UTC
17:36:57 KST

Atlantic bluefin tuna has been spotted off the coast for the first time since 1960. A technician working on the wind turbines off the Flemish coast saw them leaping out of the water whilst hunting. Later, researchers also caught three young rough-skinned sharks – the first such sighting since 1985. “Both species are making a comeback in our waters,” says Jan Seys of the Flanders Marine Institute.
Atlantic bluefin tuna spotted off the Flemish coast for the first time since 1960
The Atlantic bluefin tuna was observed off the Thornton Bank, used by the offshore wind farm off the Flemish coast. “A wind turbine maintenance technician saw around three tuna fish, measuring between 1.5 and 2 metres, leaping out of the water,” says Jan Seys of the Flanders Marine Institute, the VLIZ.
“Although no footage is available as evidence due to the speed at which the event took place, the sighting is reliable,” emphasises Seys. “The observer in question has eight years’ experience with all kinds of marine life and their behaviour, including porpoises, dolphins, seals and mackerel.”
‘They were clearly hunting,’ said the maintenance engineer, describing his extraordinary sighting. ‘They were just like torpedoes, shooting across the water at tremendous speed and disappearing again in an instant.’
The return of tuna
Until the mid-1960s, the Atlantic bluefin tuna was still a regular sight in our North Sea. Between 1950 and 1963, the west coast of Norway and the North Sea even had a fairly well-developed commercial fishing industry, after which the species disappeared quite suddenly.
Experts regard intensive tuna fishing in southern Europe and the Bay of Biscay as the main cause of the bluefin tuna’s disappearance from our regions. The collapse of herring stocks – the tuna’s favourite food – may also have played a part in this.
“The bluefin tuna was on the brink of extinction,” says Seys. “They are now making a comeback, thanks to better protection. There have recently been new sightings in the neighbouring countries. It was simply a matter of waiting for the species to reappear in the Belgian part of the North Sea. And that has now happened.”

Diesel squeeze expected to continue into 2027 despite Trump’s deal with Russia – business live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:36:20 UTC

Newsflash: US inflation jumped in September, and by more than expected, as the soaring cost of motor fuel pushed up the cost of living.
The US Consumer Prices Index roses by 3.7% in the year to September, up from 3.4% in August. Economists had forecast a smaller rise, to 3.6%.
Prices rose by 0.6% in Spetember alone.
Gasoline prices jumped by 9.1% in September, and were 34% higher tha a year ago, as motorists across America felt the impact of Donald Trump’s Middle East war at the pumps.
Those price pressures prompted Trump’s deal with Vladimir Putin last Friday – but as reported earlier, it’s not expected to unlock much extra supplies to the market.
Republicans are entering the midterm elections with the highest rate of inflation since the spring, according to a government report released today.
US price increases reached an annual rate of 3.7%in September, according to the latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, up from 3.4% in August. This final inflation report before the pivotal midterm elections comes amid polls showing widespread dissatisfaction with the Trump administration over the cost of living.
Price increases are the highest they have been since the annual inflation rate reached a three-year peak of 4.2% in May. Gasoline accounted for over half of overall price increases, up 34% from last year. Fuel oil, which is used to heat homes, increased by 74% from last year, a worrying sign for households heading into the winter. Air travel, which many Americans rely on during the holidays, also increased by 22.4%.
Overall, consumer prices went up 0.6% from August. Core inflation, which strips out volatile energy and food prices, also ticked up by 0.3% in September to 2.6% annually.
The outlook for US inflation largely hinges on what happens with the Strait of Hormuz, says James Knightley, ING’s chief international economist.
The AI boom is another factor pushing up prices, he points out:
Refined fuel prices continue to rise and run the risk of feeding through into a broader range of categories. At the same time, the tech/AI data centre roll out is adding to price pressures.
That said, Federal Reserve rate hikes will have limited impact on these two price drivers. In any case, the cooling housing market should translate into softer shelter inflation prints, while a less onerous tariff regime should also help. The key story though, is wage growth, which is the biggest cost input for corporate America. The low hire, low fire economy means there is little turnover in the jobs market, which is highly correlated with wage growth. Wages are currently running at just 3%, with the risk that we see a further slowdown coming through.
While bad news for households, this will help to dampen price pressures over the medium to longer term. Right now our forecast is for a December Federal Reserve rate hike before a long pause, but the risks to that view are skewed towards the Fed moving rates even higher before rate cuts come through.
The Fed’s next meeting, on 27-28 October, is just a week before the midterm elections.
Rogier Quaedvlieg, economist at ABN AMRO, predicts the Fed will avoid raising interest rates then – but will hit borrowers with a hike in December.
Quaedvlieg writes:
September CPI inflation was hotter than expected for the second consecutive month.
Core inflation rose by 0.34% m/m, while headline inflation increased by 0.649%, lifting the y/y rate to 3.7%. This was above consensus but in line with our forecast. The core reading was the key surprise, prompting markets to raise the implied probability of an October rate hike from less than 25% to more than 50%.
Energy prices are beginning to have a significant impact, including on airline fares. Prices of new and used cars also increased as new model-year vehicles entered the market. The AI buildout again added to price pressures, with large increases in computer software and accessories, as well as computers and peripherals. Although inflationary pressure was broader than in last month’s exceptionally concentrated report, the share of CPI components showing elevated inflation continues to decline.
We therefore still expect inflation to ease over the course of the year. We also continue to expect the Fed to hold rates in October before raising the policy rate by a further 25 bps in December.
US government borrowing costs are pushing higher, after today’s inflation report hardened expectations of interest rate rises from the Fed.
The yield on two-year Treasury bills has risen by 13 basis point (0.13 of a percentage point) to 4.92%, hitting their highest level since 29 September.
Ten-year US Treasury yields are up 9.5bps to 5.3% – towards the 24-year highs set earalier this month.
This adds to the fiscal mess facing the US (something the IMF warned about this morning); high bond yields push up the cost of servicing the $40tn US national debt, and makes issuing new debt more expensive too.
Congressman Brendan F. Boyle is blaming Donald Trump’s trade war, and his war with Iran, for driving up costs for Americans.
Boyle, a Democratic member of the House of Representatives, posted on X:
President Trump promised to lower costs on “day one,” but American families have already paid $3,500 more due to inflation since he took office. If he cared at all about working people, he would end his tariff taxes and his reckless Iran war.
This jump in inflation increases the chances that the US Federal Reserve raises interest rates later this month.
According to CMEFedwatch, a quarter-point Fed rate hike in October is now a 43% chance, up from 22% yesterday.
Stephen Brown, Chief North America economist at CapitalEconomics, says:
The upside surprise to core CPI in September was broad-based rather than due to any obvious temporary factors, therefore bringing an October rate hike back into play and presenting upside risks to our forecast for just two more 25 bp hikes from the Fed.
Quilter: 'Ugly US inflation data' is blow to Trump
Today’s higher than expected inflation reading is “a blow to Donald Trump ahead of November’s midterms”, says Richard Carter, head of fixed interest research at Quilter Cheviot.
It could also encourage the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates, which would not please Trump at all.
In a note headlined “Ugly US inflation data may shift Fed into more aggressive hiking mode”, Carter explains:
The President has been desperate to show he is getting inflation under control and providing the environment for rate cuts, even going so far as allowing Russian diesel back into the market, but those moves are proving too little too late as the war in the Middle East continues to have a grip on the global economy.
“CPI came in at 3.7%, slightly above expectations, and similarly core inflation was above predictions, suggesting that prices are feeding into the wider economy. Fuel and energy do remain the primary driver of inflation and certainly explains the actions of the US administration of late.
“This data is going to heap a whole lot of pressure on the Federal Reserve. Any chance of cuts to help with a stumbling labour market have essentially been vanquished with such elevated levels of inflation. The conflict in the Middle East will not be resolved any time soon, and as such, the current levels of inflation will likely remain well into 2027.
“Bond yields have been under scrutiny in recent weeks as those inflation concerns harden, and this will do little to appease the market. It is not inconceivable that ten-year treasury yields continue to march higher. Indeed, today’s data means another rate hike this year from the Fed cannot be ruled out as it may need to get more aggressive in its policy decisions in order to quell other inflationary trends.”
In a worrying sign, core inflation across the US has also risen.
The inflation measure which strips out food and energy costs rose to 2.6% in the year to September, up from 2.4% in August.
That could be a sign that inflationary pressures are broadening, which would concern central bankers.
George Brown, senior economist at Schroders, says:
“While energy prices might be grabbing the headlines, today’s report suggests the inflation problem runs much deeper. A stronger-than-expected core inflation reading adds to mounting evidence that domestic price pressures are becoming more entrenched, rather than easing.
“Markets are right to assume that policy will need to become much more restrictive to return inflation to target. The question is whether the Fed is prepared to tighten as much as the inflation outlook demands.”

Russia’s Krasnodar Region Raises Alert as Oil Washes Ashore on Black Sea Coast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:36:09 UTC
17:36:09 KST

Authorities in Russia’s southern Krasnodar region have raised the alert level in Gelendzhik and Novorossiysk over an oil spill after fuel oil washed ashore and satellite images showed pollution spreading along the Black Sea coast.
Governor Veniamin Kondratyev issued an order warning of a potential emergency in the two cities. He attributed the spill to “accidents” involving vessels targeted by Ukrainian naval drones on Oct. 6.
The order calls for increased environmental monitoring and surveillance of potential industrial hazards. It also recommends that the regional branch of Russia’s Marine Rescue Service take measures to prevent oil from reaching the shoreline.
Fuel oil has already been found along roughly 500 meters of coastline near Novorossiysk, the city’s chief rescue official, Alexei Oderov, said.
Local residents have also reported pollution on the shore. Olga Kotlyar, head of the Abrau-Dyurso rural district, appealed for volunteers to help municipal workers clean up a beach.
Birds with reported chemical burns from petroleum products have been found in Gelendzhik and the nearby resort village of Arkhipo-Osipovka.
The satellite monitoring project Transparent World earlier reported that an image taken overnight on Oct. 10 showed a large oil slick between Arkhipo-Osipovka and Novorossiysk.
Over the following two days, the slick broke into smaller patches and spread as far as Anapa, the project said. It also identified oil traces near Novorossiysk Bay and the Caspian Pipeline Consortium’s offshore loading facilities.
Transparent World linked the pollution to the Oct. 6 naval drone attack on the tanker Aframax Rio off Sochi. The vessel can carry up to 100,000 metric tons of oil, though its cargo at the time of the attack has not been independently confirmed.
The Mash Telegram channel, citing unnamed sources, reported that the tanker was fully loaded.
The attack triggered a major fire that blanketed Sochi in black smoke. The blaze was extinguished the following day.
Authorities closed beaches in Sochi and the neighboring federal territory of Sirius after the attack, but reopened them on Oct. 8, saying tests had found no oil contamination in local waters.
Russia’s consumer protection watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said seawater samples from all districts of Sochi met sanitary standards.

Glencore starts secondary listing on Australian stock exchange
Swiss commodities group Glencore has begun trading on the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) on Wednesday with a secondary listing.
There were no major price fluctuations shortly after trading began.
Following a brief rise in the share price, the shares were trading at the issue price of 11.25 Australian dollars again just under an hour after trading began, at around 12 noon local time.
So-called CHESS Depositary Interests (CDIs), each of which economically represents one Glencore share, are traded on the Australian stock exchange. Existing shareholders will be able to convert their Glencore shares into CDIs in future, provided the relevant regulatory and technical requirements are met.
According to Glencore, the company has been active in Australia for over 25 years. The secondary listing was undertaken for strategic reasons.
The market offers access to an experienced investor base with proven expertise in the commodities sector, said CEO Gary Nagle in the run-up to the listing. It also strengthens the company’s presence in one of Glencore’s most important markets and increases financial flexibility.
In the long term, trading volumes in Australia are expected to reach a similar level to those currently seen in South Africa.

The event is expected to take place in late May 2027 in one of Bulgaria’s most attractive destinations, the Valley of Roses, the Ministry of Tourism announced.
“Our international guests will experience the magic of the rose harvest and discover the cultural heritage we have preserved for centuries,” the minister added.
The forum programme could include a visit to the Rose Museum in Kazanlak, a presentation on the production of Bulgarian rose oil, and an opportunity for guests to explore the Thracian Tomb of Kazanlak, which is part of UNESCO’s World Heritage List, as well as the Valley of the Thracian Kings.

EU’s AI rules face first enforcement test over lab incidents
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:35:07 UTC
17:35:07 KST

The EU is investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over AI agents that hacked outside organisations, raising questions about whether the AI Act covers rogue models escaping the testing environment.
The European Commission is moving to enforce its new rules on leading AI labs after a string of incidents, EU digital chief Henna Virkkunen said. But applying the rulebook is far from straightforward, and these early cases will set important precedents.
The Commission’s AI Office is investigating OpenAI and Anthropic after AI agents autonomously hacked into other organisations, the first test of the limits of the EU’s AI rules.
“Our AI Office has started enforcing these rules, and sent requests for information addressing issues such as security, external evaluation and monitoring how models are used,” Commission Executive Vice-President for Technological Sovereignty Henna Virkkunen said at the International AI Summit in Dublin on Wednesday.
The investigations concern an “unprecedented” incident in which an OpenAI agent escaped its testing environment to hack rival Hugging Face, and one in which a recent Anthropic model gained “unauthorised access” to three outside organisations.
Both incidents happened over the summer. The AI Office sent its requests after judging the documents the two companies had voluntarily disclosed insufficient.
Since August, the AI Office has held enforcement powers under the AI Act, the EU’s comprehensive law on artificial intelligence, which also covers the most powerful models and requires their developers to implement risk-mitigation measures.
But legal experts are contesting the Commission’s power to investigate. The incidents occurred during testing, before the models were placed on the EU market, so they argue, the AI Act does not apply.
“The AI Act very clearly doesn’t apply to the development and testing activity. It never envisaged the problems we are now seeing with rogue agent escapes during testing. It’s a bit of a stretch to say that an agent was put into service if it escapes its testing environment during development,” Barry Scannell, a partner at the law firm William Fry, told Euronews.
The law does include an R&D exemption covering research, testing and development. The Commission is pushing a broader interpretation that would let the AI Office police the development phase too under certain circumstances.
“We won’t enforce in the testing phase. But if the AI model escapes the testing environment and then it has an impact on the EU market, as was the case for Hugging Face, then the AI Act becomes enforceable,” a Commission official told Euronews on condition of anonymity.
Hugging Face has global operations, hosting AI models and datasets that developers use globally. As a result, the OpenAI incident also impacted customers in the EU.
The Commission likens it to a virus escaping a lab: the company has clearly failed to put adequate risk-mitigation measures in place and is harming others.
Last week, Virkkunen met the Scientific Panel, an advisory group of independent experts, to discuss the technical developments behind the multiplication of such incidents in recent months.
The experts flagged worrying trends, Euronews has learned. Leading labs are investing in ever more powerful models with inadequate cybersecurity and safety practices, raising concerns that many incidents may go unreported.
Even more troubling, the more capable the models become, the more they tend to drift from their design objectives. Oversight mechanisms grow less effective, and models might even cheat when evaluated.
For parts of the AI safety community, the nightmare scenario is that models’ continuous self-improvement turns such temporary losses of control into permanent ones, with rogue agents escaping human control for good.
In short, the EU executive is determined to enforce its rules when agents escape their testing environment, in what could be Brussels’ first legal battle to force Silicon Valley’s labs to take safety into account already at the development stage.
“The Commission has been loud and clear: AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control and we stand ready to take all necessary steps to ensure that companies follow the AI Act rules,” Virkkunen said.

Auden opens global headquarters in Taoyuan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:35:02 UTC
17:35:02 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Taoyuan-based antenna manufacturer Auden launched its global headquarters on Tuesday to research low Earth orbit satellite connectivity and other next-generation networking technologies, CNA reported.
The building can hold 450 staff members and has a laboratory for satellite and 5G networking technologies. It can support performance tests for larger antenna platforms to maximize efficiency.
Auden Chair Chang Yu-pin (張玉斌) said the headquarters will lead research while the Hsinchu plant handles pilot and mass production. He added that a Vietnam plant opened on Oct. 6 to localize partial production and delivery.
Chang expects low Earth orbit satellite connectivity to drive strong demand for phased array antennas in two years, with Vietnam's production capacity expected to reach 60% of Auden's Kunshan plant in China. He added that the antennas support government, military, and maritime operations and should expand as low Earth orbit satellite as well as direct satellite connectivity matures.
A phased array antenna is a computer-controlled set of rods that can send multiple independent signal beams to its target in fractions of a second without bulky satellite dishes.
Low Earth orbit satellites are located closer to Earth at altitudes from 160 to 2,000 kilometers to support fast global internet access as offered by SpaceX’s Starlink or Amazon Leo. The satellites can also capture high-resolution maps and record environmental data like weather patterns.
Auden Vice-President Wen Wen-sheng (溫文聖) said the Hsinchu plant also covers antenna surface-mounting and component packaging. He noted that the facility has begun pilot production of radio frequency and other communication modules.
Wen said that although the firm is doing tests and small-scale production, it expects greater order volume in 2027. He added that Auden will first focus on low Earth orbit satellite connectivity and gradually expand to optical fiber technology.

Mozart opera ‘Cosi Fan Tutte’ puts romance to the test in Taichung
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:34:34 UTC
17:34:34 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart’s comic opera “Cosi Fan Tutte” unfolds in a recording studio in 18th-century Germany, bringing a tale of love and deception to the National Taichung Theater later this month.
French director Laurent Pelly reimagines the opera as a play within a play, bringing a fresh perspective to the opera’s tangled relationships. First staged in 2022, the production will run for four performances at the theater from Oct. 29 to Nov. 1, according to a National Taichung Theater press release.
Created by Mozart and librettist Lorenzo da Ponte, it centers on two young officers who put their fiancees’ loyalty to the test. Encouraged by a cynical philosopher, the men disguise themselves as wealthy foreigners and pursue each other’s partners, turning a wager into an increasingly complicated game of attraction and deception, according to Opera Guide.
What begins as a seemingly playful experiment gradually exposes the contradictions in human relationships. As the characters’ affections shift, the opera explores whether fidelity is a matter of principle or circumstance, and whether anyone can predict how they would behave when put to the test.
Conductor Lin Chin-chao (林勤超) said the opera’s extended ensemble passages allow audiences to hear several characters’ emotions unfold simultaneously. While one character lies, another may be falling in love, while a third remains unaware of what is happening.
First performed in 1790, “Cosi Fan Tutte” has long drawn debate over its treatment of love and fidelity, with its elaborate deception seeming implausible. Yet Mozart’s music gives the story greater complexity.
Extended ensemble passages allow several characters’ conflicting reactions to unfold at once, rather than focusing primarily on individual arias. Mozart’s shifting harmonies and use of woodwind instruments, including bassoons, clarinets, and oboes, further enrich these exchanges, revealing the emotions beneath the characters’ outward composure, Lin said.
The music also gives the comedy an emotional depth that extends beyond its playful surface. In “Un’aura amorosa,” a gentle melody conveys tenderness, while the demanding vocal runs in “Come scoglio” showcase the singer’s virtuosity. “Donne mie, la fate a tanti,” meanwhile, brings a wry edge to the opera’s treatment of romantic relationships, according to the National Taichung Theater.
Despite its comic moments, the opera offers no simple happy ending, said Lucio Gallo, who plays Don Alfonso. None of the characters can return to their former state of mind after the experiment, leaving a lingering sense of bitterness beneath the humor.
Executive Director Karine Girard said Pelly’s production places the singers and their music at the center of the experience. The recording studio provides a contemporary setting that can be understood by audiences around the world.
The singers initially appear in a recording session before gradually inhabiting their operatic roles. As the performance progresses, props and background elements recede, drawing attention to the singers’ bodies and expressions.
Beneath its lively surface, “Cosi Fan Tutte” portrays people caught between desire and uncertainty. More than two centuries after its premiere, Mozart’s creation still leaves audiences to decide whether the characters’ flaws are unique or universal.

Sofia will host Bulgaria’s First International Defense Tech Hackathon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:34:21 UTC
17:34:21 KST

Author
Vessela Krasteva
Interview
Sofia will host Bulgaria’s First International Defense Tech Hackathon
Students, military personnel and engineers develop technological solutions to today’s defence challenges
Interview with Interview with Vladislav Prelezov and Petar Kirkov
Wednesday 14 October 2026 10:20
Wednesday, 14 October 2026, 10:20
PHOTO eurodefense.tech
Font size
Sofia will host Bulgaria’s first international hackathon dedicated entirely to defence and dual-use technologies. The event will take place from October 16 to 18 at Tech Arena at the Technical University of Sofia and is part of the German initiative European Defense Tech Hub (EDTH).
Military drones, and particularly how to detect, identify and neutralise them, have become one of the most pressing issues facing Bulgaria in recent days. Can technology provide solutions to the challenges involved, and what might these solutions look like? These and other questions concerning national security will be explored at the event, where participants will seek to develop practical answers.
A hackathon is typically a short event, often lasting around 48 hours, during which programmers, designers, entrepreneurs and experts work in teams to create a functional software or product prototype. Over three days in the Bulgarian capital, more than 120 participants will come together, including students, cadets from military universities, engineers from high-tech companies in Bulgaria and abroad, and representatives of national institutions.
Petar Kirkov (left) and Dr. Vladislav Prelezov
PHOTO Vessela Krasteva
“I'm going to use the word ‘hackers’, although we’re not talking only about hackers. We’re bringing together people who will work in this field so that we can help build networks among them and develop new technologies for the defence industry in the broadest sense, from artificial intelligence to prototypes, drones and counter-drone systems,” Petar Kirkov, a lecturer and one of Bulgaria’s leading cybersecurity experts, told Radio Bulgaria.
The event is a joint initiative of the Technical University of Sofia, the European Defense Tech Hub, a European defence innovation community connecting engineers, start-ups, military personnel, investors and institutions, and Capital, a weekly publication covering politics, business and economics.
PHOTO @BabyPro.ming
The origins of this type of technology competition date back to the summer of 2024, when Munich hosted the first international EDTH hackathon. Bulgaria made its mark from the outset: a project developed by a team of school students won third place, with the organisers making a special exception to the age requirements.
Petar Kirkov was one of the mentors supporting four students from the Technological School of Electronic Systems (TUES) at the Technical University of Sofia. Their prototype, designed to detect anti-personnel mines by their thermal signature, impressed the jury in Germany.
The project finished among the top three at the 2024 European Defense Tech Hackathon, competing against 34 projects and nearly 150 participants from around the world.
Bulgarian students develop project for detecting anti-personnel mines
PHOTO eurodefense.tech
Over the past two years, EDTH has organised close to 100 hackathons worldwide. Around 40 of the teams that have taken part have since developed into companies, and approximately half have tested their technological solutions in real-world conditions during demo days in Europe, particularly in Ukraine.
Drawing on his professional experience and his impression of the talent available in Bulgaria, Petar Kirkov proposed earlier this year that the country host a similar hackathon. The idea was quickly embraced and brought to life with the help of the Technical University of Sofia.
PHOTO AFP
“For the Technical University, this is a major and very important event,” explained Dr Vladislav Prelezov, the university’s director of public relations, speaking in Radio Bulgaria’s studio.
“The defence industry is moving very quickly, just like every other industry in today’s world. IT technologies are becoming part of everything and are extremely important. Our university is preparing its students to become the engineers of the future, not only in the defence industry but across the wider world we are building.
I want to emphasise that we are open to precisely this kind of hackathon and to events where young people can demonstrate what they can do and appreciate the value of the education they receive. They are the future leaders in engineering, not only here in Bulgaria but anywhere in the global economy. This is extremely important to us as a higher education institution, because competition is everywhere. The global demand for talent is enormous, and as a small country of around six million people, we have to prove that we can compete with the larger nations.”
Prelezov takes pride in the fact that more and more graduates of Bulgaria’s largest technical university are continuing their research there and choosing to stay in Bulgaria. He is convinced that this is vital for the development of the country’s industry as a whole.
PHOTO Reuters
“What I see is that Bulgaria has many companies and talented people doing all sorts of things, but very often they don’t communicate with one another and instead look abroad,” Kirkov added. “That is precisely the philosophy behind the hackathon we are organising: to bring these people together in one place and encourage synergy between them. Great things are happening in Bulgaria. We have excellent specialists, and when we bring them together, the result is often much better than the sum of their individual ideas.
Let me add a little more about our 2024 project, because it is a very good illustration of this. When people hear ‘defense industry’, they tend to picture military vehicles painted green. But what earned these young men third place was an artificial intelligence technology capable of detecting anti-personnel mines. In other words, it was a technology designed to protect everyone’s safety.”
Petar Kirkov also points out with evident satisfaction that one of the members of Bulgaria’s “bronze-winning team” from two years ago, Kaloyan Miladinov, is now part of the organising team for the hackathon at the Technical University.
Modern warfare is more closely tied to new technologies than ever before, says Vladislav Prelezov, who knows the subject from his professional experience at the Bulgarian Ministry of Defense and his work as a military reporter for national media.
PHOTO eurodefense.tech
“A war, God forbid, could be fought simply by pressing buttons thousands of kilometres away from the battlefield. That is why I strongly support Petar Kirkov’s initiative. Military personnel may think in a particular way, but engineers can help prevent ideas that threaten human life. They provide protection. And that is precisely why this hackathon is so useful: it will teach us not only how to build a military drone, for example, but also how to counter such a drone.”
Another important aspect of the hackathon is that events of this kind create a valuable meeting point for ideas, funding opportunities and experts capable of identifying which technological concepts can actually work today, Kirkov explains.
Modern technologies bring together many complex elements. Unlike in the Middle Ages, when discoveries and ideas were often associated with individual achievements, innovation today depends on synergy between people with different skills and expertise, he adds. The programme planned for the Sofia hackathon reflects this approach.
PHOTO eurodefense.tech
“On October 16, there will be several working workshops where specific topics will be discussed, followed by what we call challenges. Each hackathon has a set of concrete challenges for the participants to work on. We will give them the opportunity to form teams by the following day. That is where networking comes in. We allow, and even encourage, participants to build teams, change their initial choices if they wish, and reorganise on the spot to create a team that can work effectively on the task at hand.
They will have until Sunday morning to work on their projects, after which we will help them prepare their presentations for the jury. The presentations will be followed by demonstrations of prototypes or whatever the teams have developed, and finally the results will be announced".
The three highest-ranked teams, as selected by the jury, will be presented at the Regional Defence and Security Summit 2026. This platform connects the regional ecosystem with Europe, bringing together politicians, military leaders, industry representatives, technology companies, innovators and investors in Sofia on October 21.
The Sofia hackathon organised by the European Defense Tech Hub will take place shortly after  drone attacks targeted commercial vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone in the Black Sea. Kirkov believes that the incidents may motivate participants to come up with ideas in this particular field. After all, he says, a good engineer’s instinct is to look at a problem and think: “This is something I can solve, and I can do it more effectively.”
PHOTO eurodefense.tech
Detecting and identifying all kinds of drones is one of today’s most pressing technological challenges.
“With the technologies we have, we know very well how to detect large aircraft hundreds of kilometres away and determine what type of aircraft they are, where they are heading and so on. But a small plastic drone flying 50 metres above the ground is extremely difficult to detect using existing technology. Solving this problem requires an entirely different class of technology, as well as new approaches and a different way of thinking.
“I expect this to be one of the most topical subjects at the Sofia hackathon,” Petar Kirkov says.
PHOTO eurodefense.tech

The foreign ministers of Australia, Canada, France and the United Kingdom have expressed deep regret over Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas’s decision to postpone presidential and legislative elections until September 2027, urging the Palestinian Authority to reverse the decision and organize elections without further delay.
In a joint statement issued on Tuesday, the ministers noted that nearly two decades had passed since the last Palestinian Legislative Council elections and five years since the postponement of elections scheduled for 2021.
They said an entire generation of Palestinians had reached adulthood without an opportunity to elect their political representatives.
The ministers described the latest postponement as a major disappointment that further denied Palestinians the exercise of their electoral rights and risked undermining public confidence in democratic institutions.
They acknowledged the significant challenges involved in organizing elections that meet international standards and ensure the participation of all eligible Palestinian voters.
READ: UN pledges technical support for Palestinian elections amid vote delay
The statement also commended the Palestinian Central Elections Commission for its efforts to establish practical arrangements to address those obstacles and facilitate voter participation.
The ministers emphasised that credible elections were an essential component of the Palestinian Authority’s reform commitments, including democratic renewal and accountable governance, as outlined in the 2025 New York Declaration.
They said strengthening Palestinian governance was necessary to establish the institutional foundations for implementing the two-state solution, which they described as the only viable path to lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians.
“As staunch supporters of the Palestinian right to self-determination, we call on the Palestinian Authority to reconsider the decision to postpone elections and to take the necessary steps to hold legislative and presidential elections without further delay,” the ministers said.
The four countries reaffirmed their willingness to support efforts to organise the elections and called on Israel to refrain from measures that could obstruct the process, including interference with arrangements intended to ensure the participation of all eligible Palestinians.
The statement concluded by reiterating the four governments’ opposition to any role for Hamas in the future governance of Palestine.

US President Donald Trump announced on Friday that he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin on diesel shipments and a temporary easing of US sanctions against Russia. Europe’s media discuss wider implications and the impact on the US’s credibility as an ally.

US companies need Ukraine as testing ground

Shocking and senseless

Latvia’s Constitutional Court refuses to open case over timber industry support decisions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:31:06 UTC
17:31:06 KST

Latvia’s Constitutional Court has refused to initiate proceedings following an application submitted by Prosecutor General Armīns Meisters in the so-called timber industry case, explaining that the prosecutor general is not legally entitled to bring the specific claim before the court, the Constitutional Court told LETA.
The court concluded that the contested decisions are legally binding on a single institution within a public-law entity and do not directly require any actions to be taken outside public administration.
Furthermore, the decisions do not regulate an indefinite number of situations and are not intended for repeated application.
Consequently, they do not qualify as regulatory enactments that fall within the Constitutional Court’s jurisdiction to examine the compliance of legislation with higher-ranking legal provisions or the compatibility of Latvian national law with international agreements concluded by Latvia.
The court explained that the contested Cabinet meeting decisions are individual legal acts of the Cabinet of Ministers and do not meet the criteria for administrative acts.
The Constitutional Court noted that reviewing the legality of such acts falls within its jurisdiction.
However, the Constitutional Court Law allows only a specific group of institutions and officials to submit applications concerning these decisions. These include the President of Latvia, the Saeima, at least 20 members of parliament, the Cabinet of Ministers and the Judicial Council within its legally defined competence. The prosecutor general is not among those authorised to submit such applications. The court emphasised that lawmakers deliberately established an exhaustive list of eligible applicants and relevant legal acts in the Constitutional Court Law. This list cannot be expanded through legal interpretation.
Accordingly, the Constitutional Court concluded that the prosecutor general had no legal standing to submit the application concerning the disputed decisions.
As previously reported, Prosecutor General Armīns Meisters had asked the Constitutional Court to declare two provisions of Cabinet meeting decisions invalid from the moment they were adopted.
The decisions instructed the Ministry of Agriculture to introduce price adjustments in 2024 and maintain them for one year
 under long-term contracts concluded by the state-owned company Latvijas valsts meži (LVM) for the supply of second-grade softwood sawlogs.
“This is a legal avenue used by the Prosecutor’s Office to ensure compliance with the law. It is important to recognise that there has been no such precedent before, and we are using all the possibilities provided by law to ensure that the actions of state institutions comply with the Constitution and legislation. “Applying to the Constitutional Court in this case is the next legal step towards having the matter assessed by an independent court,” Meisters previously stated.
In his application, the prosecutor general argued that the contested Cabinet decisions were incompatible with Latvia’s Constitution, national legislation and the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.
According to the Prosecutor’s Office, the Cabinet adopted the decisions without the necessary statutory authorisation to dispose of public property at prices lower than those established in legally binding commercial contracts.
Following its investigation, the Prosecutor’s Office concluded that the Cabinet led by former Prime Minister Evika Siliņa (New Unity) had acted unlawfully
 by instructing LVM to change its timber pricing arrangements. As a result, the Prosecutor General’s Office submitted a formal protest to the government on 16 June, demanding that the decisions be revoked.
However, the government led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) decided not to comply with the request and informed the Prosecutor General’s Office of its decision on the 27th of July.
Following the government meeting, Kulbergs claimed that his government could not revoke the previous administration’s decisions concerning support for the timber industry because doing so was not legally possible. According to the prime minister, ministers were unanimous on the matter.
After reviewing the arguments presented in the Cabinet’s response, the Prosecutor’s Office concluded that the government’s position was unjustified.
 Consequently, in accordance with the Prosecutor’s Office Law, the prosecutor general submitted an application to the Constitutional Court seeking the annulment of the contested decisions.
In June, Meisters told LETA that the criminal investigation into the so-called timber industry case was progressing, with investigators identifying increasing amounts of evidence and additional lines of inquiry. “This will certainly not take years to reach a result,” the prosecutor general said at the time. He added that the procedural status of those involved in the criminal proceedings had not changed. No additional individuals had been included in the case, and none had been removed.
The ten individuals against whom criminal proceedings have been initiated and in relation to whom investigative actions were carried out on 14 May are Armands Krauze (ZZS) (former Minister of Agriculture and current Saeima deputy), Raivis Kronbergs (former State Secretary of the Ministry of Agriculture), Ģirts Krūmiņš (State Secretary of the Ministry of Agriculture), Ilze Silamiķele (Deputy Head of the Ministry of Agriculture’s Forest Sector Strategy and Support Division), Pēters Putniņš (former Chairman of the Management Board of Latvijas valsts meži), Zane Driņķe (Chairwoman of the Supervisory Board of Latvijas valsts meži), Valdis Lūks (Adviser to the Chairwoman of the LVM Supervisory Board), Kristaps Klauss  (Vice-President of the Latvian Federation of Woodworking Industries), Reinis Muižnieks (employee of the timber company Pata Strenči and Valmiera Municipality Council deputy representing the party Valmierai un Vidzemei) and Uldis Mierkalns (owner and head of Pata).
No preventive measures have been imposed on any of these individuals, as such measures can only be applied to persons who have been formally designated as suspects or accused.
The criminal proceedings, initiated in March, are examining two main lines of investigation. The first concerns officials at the Ministry of Agriculture who may have abused their official positions to unlawfully secure support for the timber industry. The second concerns possible negligence by officials at Latvijas valsts meži.
According to investigators, these officials may have had opportunities to prevent financial damage to the state but allegedly failed to act in accordance with the law.
The suspected inaction of LVM officials may have caused losses of approximately 50 million euros to the Latvian state.
Mierkalns and other individuals who are not public officials are being investigated for allegedly assisting in the abuse of official positions.

Ukrainian Drones Hit Sberbank Data Center After Yandex Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:30:36 UTC
17:30:36 KST

Ukrainian drones targeted a major data center under construction for Russian state lender Sberbank in the Saratov region overnight, First Deputy CEO Alexander Vedyakhin said Wednesday, as attacks on Moscow disrupted more than 500 flights.
Vedyakhin said all banking systems and online services continued to operate normally and no employees were injured in the attack in the Volga River city of Balakovo, according to the state-run news agency TASS.
Users across Russia nevertheless reported disruptions to Sberbank and its GigaChat artificial intelligence service, as well as several other major online platforms, according to outage tracker Detector404. The reports did not establish a link between the disruptions and the drone attacks.
NASA’s satellite fire-monitoring system showed multiple fires in Balakovo.
Saratov region Governor Roman Busargin said “all infrastructure facilities” were operating normally, without identifying Sberbank’s data center as a target. He said one woman was killed and several homes were damaged in the drone strikes.
The attack on Sberbank follows three consecutive Ukrainian drone strikes that disabled half of tech giant Yandex’s data centers. Ukraine says it is responding to Russian attacks on its own data sites.
“You didn’t think it would stop with just Yandex, did you?” Ukraine’s Fire Point arms company said in a social media post Wednesday morning.
Sberbank began construction of the 55,000-square-meter (592,000-square-foot) facility in 2021, promoting the 122.2 billion ruble ($1.4 billion) project as one of Europe’s largest data centers, with completion expected in 2030.
Sberbank and its main domestic rival, Yandex, are leading Russian developers of artificial intelligence, with their respective GigaChat and YandexGPT models. State media reported in 2024 that Sberbank’s Balakovo center would host Russia’s biggest supercomputer, which was scheduled to go into operation in 2027.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defense systems destroyed 902 Ukrainian drones over 19 Russian regions and annexed Crimea between Tuesday evening and Wednesday morning.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said “most” of the 493 Ukrainian drones flying toward the region were neutralized, 180 of them on direct approach to the capital.
The attacks on Moscow prompted civil aviation authority Rosaviatsia to restrict arrivals and departures at all four Moscow airports after 10 p.m. Tuesday, in the second prolonged shutdown of Moscow’s airports in less than a week.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces struck seven Ukrainian energy infrastructure facilities and a data center with ground-launched missiles and long-range strike drones overnight.
Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak later accused Ukraine of attacking two oil refineries in the Saratov and Ryazan regions Wednesday, saying Kyiv was showing no signs of moving toward an energy ceasefire announced by U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ukrainian presidential adviser Dmytro Lytvyn denied those statements, telling reporters that Ukraine struck a data center and another unnamed target but not refineries.
Reuters contributed reporting.

China chip exports jump 136% to US$45b as AI frenzy jacks up prices
ICs among the fastest-growing categories in September, underlining country’s growing influence in semiconductor supply chain
China’s integrated circuit (IC) exports surged 136 per cent year on year in September to US$45 billion, exceeding the 108 per cent growth rate in the first nine months of the year in a sign of the country’s rising influence in the global semiconductor supply chain.
In September, China exported 32.7 billion units of ICs, according to customs data released on Wednesday, a 1 per cent year-on-year increase in volume. But higher prices fuelled the 136 per cent jump in value amid a memory chip shortage stemming from the global building spree in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The first three quarters as a whole saw exports of 275.2 billion IC units worth nearly US$302 billion, according to the General Administration of Customs.

In Hong Kong, accountability must be more than a slogan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:30:06 UTC
17:30:06 KST

Advertisement
Opinion
In Hong Kong, accountability must be more than a slogan
The Anderson Road, One Stanley and Queen Mary Hospital cases suggest that the city remains better at talking about accountability than ensuring it
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Mike Rowse is an independent commentator. 
When news broke last week that three newly completed housing blocks were to be demolished without ever having been occupied, I suffered an immediate attack of deja vu. In early 1974, I was in the first wave of recruits to the Operations Department of the newly established Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC).
As luck would have it, my first posting was to the team dealing with the old Public Works Department. That was my introduction to the wide world of corruption and shoddy work in the local construction industry. The terrible thing is that some practices seem to have hardly changed at all despite half a century of efforts to eradicate them.
Common problems we found in those days were foundations not dug deeply enough or concrete not up to strength. There seemed to be a particular issue with steel reinforcement bars: there were not enough of them, or they were too short, too thin or in the wrong place. Sometimes they were deficient in all four aspects.
The Anderson Road project is a classic example of the genre. A CK Asset subsidiary was successful in the tender for a residential site in Kwun Tong. There were to be six blocks comprising 2,930 flats for starter homes, at least 1,000 of which were to be sold at a significant discount to eligible buyers as required by the Housing Bureau.

Police hold 11 in raid on Turkey pro-opposition Halk TV
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

Breadcrumb
Police hold 11 in raid on Turkey pro-opposition Halk TV
Turkish police raided the headquarters of the pro-opposition Halk TV, halting its live broadcasts and arresting 11 people, the channel and prosecutors said early Wednesday.
"Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee (manager) has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted," the channel wrote on X shortly before 7:00 am (0400 GMT).
Halk's news channel and the live broadcasts on its YouTube site were both offline.
It was the latest crackdown on the pro-opposition media and came just two weeks after the authorities shut down the website and social media accounts of T24, a leading digital news website, citing its "LGBT propaganda".
In a statement to Turkish media, prosecutors said they had issued a warrant for 17 people, 11 of whom had been detained as part of an investigation into Halk's chairman Cafer Mahiroglu on suspicion of "bribery", "rigging tenders," and "money laundering."
It said companies co-owned or managed by Mahiroglu had been seized and that the authorities put a government-appointed trustee in charge of them.
Of the remaining six people named in the warrant, four were abroad, one was in a correctional facility, and the last was still being sought for, it said.
Mahiroglu was not among those detained as he lives abroad.
'We're under a blockade'
In several posts as dawn was breaking, Halk journalists said they were unable to get into the building.
"The police have sealed off the entrance to our building. That's the situation... There's nothing left to say," wrote Onur Dalar on X, his words echoed by a colleague.
"At Halk TV, the management is now under a trustee. Broadcasting systems have been seized. Our channel is literally under blockade. I still can't get into the institution where I've worked for 5 years—none of us can. The police haven't left the building," wrote Gamze Altunay.
The move came just hours before the start of the defence's arguments in the sprawling corruption trial of jailed Istanbul mayor Ekrem Imamoglu and some 400 other defendants.
The move drew a furious reaction from the main opposition Yeni Parti and the Turkish Journalists' Union (TGS)
"In recent years, the lawlessness used by the political authorities to overcome every problem has once again struck freedom of the press today... We do not accept this tyranny!" wrote TGS on X.
And opposition leader Ozgur Ozel also lashed out against a TV channel "watched by millions" describing the government's action as "weak and cowardly".
"Storming a TV channel with a police raid at dawn and appointing a trustee is something only dictators do. Unfortunately, they have brought our country to this state," he wrote.
He said it was no coincidence the raids came just hours before the start of the defence arguments in Imamoglu's trial.
"They did this on the very day the defence was to begin in Turkey's biggest political trial. Those who appoint trustees to municipalities and usurp the will of the people have now appointed a trustee to Halk TV, watched by millions. Because they are WEAK and COWARDLY!"
Last year, Halk TV—which has faced repeated sanctions from Turkey's broadcasting regulator—was threatened with possible closure over its critical tone towards the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
