Lithuanian minister proposes to ban self-employment for foreign students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:56:00 UTC
16:56:00 KST

Lithuania’s interior minister has proposed banning foreign students from working under self-employment certificates, arguing that some use student visas primarily as a way to obtain temporary residence permits rather than pursue their education.
Tanjid, a student from Bangladesh in his second year at Vilnius College, says he balances work and studies in Lithuania.
“I know my class schedule – I have one or two lectures a day, so it’s easy to fit everything in,” he says.
However, finding work under an employment contract while pursuing a bachelor’s degree is difficult, he adds.
“I worked full time in a warehouse over the summer, but once classes started, it became difficult to balance everything, so I quit. But I came here to study – that’s what I’m focused on, and I work only to support myself,” he says.
According to the Migration Department, more than 230,000 foreigners currently hold temporary residence permits in Lithuania. Only about 5%, or 12,000 came to the country to study. The largest groups of international students come from Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Morocco and Belarus.
Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas argues some students seek to enter Lithuania primarily to work, rather than study. He said foreign students exploit the system by attending classes only when necessary to maintain their residence status.
He said employers and universities also benefit from the current arrangement, as higher enrolment brings additional funding to educational institutions.
“The lecturers themselves say that migrants come only to take exams and ask for passing grades so that their residence permits based on studies are not revoked,” Katelynas said.
The minister wants to eliminate the option for foreign students to work under self-employment certificates (individuali veikla), which offer a more flexible arrangement than standard employment contracts.
He said European Union directives prevent Lithuania from banning foreign students from working altogether, but that regulating self-employment falls within national competence.
Last year, the Migration Department inspected higher education institutions and found cases in which students were absent from classes they were scheduled to attend. The department also found that institutions had failed to report when foreign students took academic leave, which could have triggered the revocation of their residence permits.
Katelynas declined to name the institutions involved, saying they were mostly colleges.
Eugenijus Gentvilas, a member of parliament from the Liberal Movement faction, questioned whether restrictions on foreign students were justified when the number of international students remained relatively small compared with the overall immigrant population.
“Please tell us which higher education institutions, which colleges, failed to learn from the observations made,” Gentvilas said. “Talking about restricting the number of foreign students when there are 12,000 of them among 220,000 migrants sounds excessively harsh toward other higher education institutions, which are being asked to internationalise their studies.”
Migration Department Director Indrė Gasperė said institutions are now more responsive to reporting requirements.
“Any change concerning a student must be reported to the Migration Department: if the student has discontinued their studies or is not earning enough credits,” she said. “Failure to report this information carries a fine under the Code of Administrative Offenses. Universities are listening to us.”
Universities also say the situation has improved.
At the private Kazimieras Simonavičius University, about two-thirds of students are foreign nationals. University representative Edgaras Genys said attendance had improved and cases of abuse had declined after rules were tightened.
“In previous years, the rules were more liberal and the admission criteria were somewhat lower, so such things could happen,” he said.
However, Genys warned that restricting employment options could make Lithuania less attractive to international students choosing where to study.
The Conference of Rectors of Lithuanian Universities also opposes the proposed restrictions.
“We would not want our students to be disadvantaged compared with students in other countries,” representative Alvidas Šarlauskas said. “Spending half the week on additional work alongside one’s studies is reasonable.”
Katelynas insists foreign students would still be able to work under standard employment contracts if the proposed restriction on self-employment is introduced. In practice, however, that would be near-impossible, since employers are generally reluctant to offer contracts to student and part-time employees.

From scientific discovery to real-world impact: What researchers should know about entrepreneurship
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:55:10 UTC
16:55:10 KST

Turning a scientific discovery into a successful business requires more than innovative technology. Researchers must learn to identify real-world problems, work with experts from different fields and understand what it takes to bring a product to market. At Tehnopol’s DeepTech Coffee Morning on 8 October, Tanel Mahlakõiv, Director of Translational Research at Icosagen Cell Factory, shared practical lessons from his career in science and biotechnology.
Having studied and worked in Estonia, France, Germany and the United States, Mahlakõiv has experienced both academic research and the commercial biotechnology sector. His career has taken him from genetics and virology to immunology and personalised cancer treatments, with one central question guiding his work: how can scientific knowledge make a meaningful difference beyond the laboratory?
Start with the problem, not the technology
One of the key differences between science and business lies in the questions they ask. Scientists seek to understand how something works, discover new knowledge and demonstrate results. Businesses, however, must determine whether that knowledge solves a meaningful problem and whether the solution can be delivered reliably and economically.
According to Mahlakõiv, researchers often begin with an interesting discovery and then look for potential applications. In business, the process should frequently work in the opposite direction: first identify an important problem, then determine what a successful solution would need to look like.
A technology may be scientifically impressive without having a viable commercial application. For example, a promising drug candidate might prove impossible to manufacture at scale, face regulatory obstacles or lack a sufficiently large market.
This is why commercial potential, customer needs and practical feasibility should be considered from the beginning rather than after years of development.
Scientists already have valuable business skills
Moving from academia into entrepreneurship does not mean abandoning scientific thinking. Researchers already possess many skills that are valuable in business, including analytical thinking, systematic problem-solving, experimentation, managing uncertainty and learning from failure.
Mahlakõiv’s own career demonstrates how knowledge can be transferred between disciplines. Experience gained in virology and immunology has proved valuable in his current work on cancer treatments. Similarly, collaboration with experts from other scientific fields has allowed him to apply technologies in new contexts and make discoveries that would otherwise have been difficult to achieve.
However, researchers entering business must also develop additional skills, including understanding costs, communicating with customers, negotiating and making decisions with incomplete information.
Mahlakõiv encouraged scientists to view entrepreneurship as a skill that can be learned, rather than an identity they must adopt. Commercialising research does not necessarily mean prioritising profit over science. It can also be motivated by the desire to create meaningful impact, develop new solutions and contribute to society.
Equally important is recognising that no founder needs to know everything. Deeptech companies require multidisciplinary teams bringing together scientists, engineers, regulatory specialists, intellectual property experts and business development professionals.
Particularly in deeptech, where specialised equipment and infrastructure can require substantial investment, collaboration with universities, research institutions and established companies can help startups access the resources they need.
Personalised cancer therapy demonstrates the journey from research to impact
To illustrate how scientific knowledge becomes a practical solution, Mahlakõiv introduced a project currently underway at Icosagen Cell Factory: developing the capability to manufacture personalised CAR-T cell therapy in Estonia.
CAR-T cell therapy uses a patient’s own immune cells, which are genetically modified to recognise and attack specific cancer cells. The treatment has shown significant potential for patients with certain blood cancers, including leukaemia and lymphoma.
However, access to commercial CAR-T therapies in Estonia has been limited by the country’s small market, high treatment costs and lack of local manufacturing infrastructure.
To address this problem, Icosagen Cell Factory joined forces with Tartu University Hospital and North Estonia Medical Centre. Their initial objective is to establish local manufacturing capabilities for CD19 CAR-T cell therapy for approximately 20 patients per year.
The project follows a clear commercialisation logic: problem > solution > evidence > product > customer > impact.
While the scientific evidence supporting CAR-T therapy already existed, making the treatment available locally required considerably more than scientific expertise. The partners needed to establish manufacturing facilities, develop and validate production processes, introduce quality control systems, train personnel and address regulatory requirements.
After approximately two years of development, the team completed three manufacturing process validation runs during summer 2026. At the time of the presentation, the project was progressing through the necessary regulatory approval procedures.
The experience illustrates that scientific discovery is only a small part of bringing an innovation to market. Much of the work lies in transforming that discovery into a reliable, safe and economically viable product.
Importantly, the project is also establishing infrastructure and expertise that could support future personalised cancer treatments. By building a technological platform rather than focusing solely on one product, the team is creating opportunities to develop therapies targeting other types of cancer.
Understand the obstacles and know when to stop
Mahlakõiv also highlighted two challenges that researchers can underestimate when commercialising their ideas: regulation and intellectual property.
Drawing on his own experience with a startup concept involving the preservation of an individual’s healthy gut microbiome, he explained how regulatory requirements can make an otherwise promising idea commercially difficult to pursue.
Conversely, Estonian healthtech company Better Medicine provides an example of navigating regulatory challenges successfully. The company has developed AI-powered software supporting radiologists in detecting and assessing kidney tumours, demonstrating the importance of bringing innovative technology into compliance with medical device requirements.
Another essential business skill is knowing when to stop. While scientists often respond to unexpected results by designing further experiments, businesses must consider the resources required and the likelihood of commercial success.
Mahlakõiv recommended approaching development through a structured process: hypothesis > experiment > evidence > decision. Before committing significant resources, teams should define not only what success looks like, but also what results would justify abandoning or changing their approach.
This does not mean avoiding failure. Rather, it means learning from experiments early enough to make informed decisions before investing further time and money.
Turning knowledge into solutions
Mahlakõiv’s central message was that scientists can become successful entrepreneurs without giving up their scientific identity. However, turning research into real-world impact requires a broader perspective.
Customer needs, intellectual property, manufacturing capabilities, regulations, financing and market potential should all be considered early in the development process. These are not isolated steps to be addressed one after another, but interconnected questions that influence whether an innovation can ultimately succeed.
Scientific discoveries create opportunities. Turning them into solutions that people can actually use requires the right expertise, effective collaboration and a willingness to approach research from a business perspective.
The DeepTech Coffee Morning also introduced the DeepTech Accelerator, delivered by Tehnopol and Sparkup Tartu Science Park. The 18-month accelerator supports science-based startups and research teams in developing their technologies, validating business models, finding customers and preparing for investment. Selected teams can receive up to €170,000 in business development support.
Applications for the second round are open until 8 November. Learn more about the DeepTech Accelerator and apply here.

12th Kyiv International Economic Forum to Take Place on October 26, Focusing on Business and Economic Resilience Amid New Challenges
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:53:42 EEST
16:53:42 KST

Kyiv will host the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) on October 26, bringing together more than 500 participants, including owners and executives of Ukrainian and international companies, government officials, investors, diplomats, and experts. This year’s theme, “People. Business. Economy. What’s Next?”, will guide discussions on how businesses and Ukraine’s economy can withstand mounting challenges, adapt to changing conditions, and return to growth.
Now in the fifth year of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s economy faces growing pressure. Russian attacks continue to target industrial facilities, energy infrastructure, ports, railways, logistics hubs, and other assets critical to business operations. According to Ukraine’s Ministry of Economy, direct damage from destruction could reach approximately $10 billion annually. Combined with the blockade of seaports, these losses have already cost Ukraine an estimated 1.5 percentage points of GDP in 2026.
In its October forecast, the World Bank projects that Ukraine’s economic growth will slow to 1.2% in 2026 and reach just 1.5% in 2027 if active hostilities continue. The Bank previously projected 4% growth in 2027, assuming hostilities would end by late 2026.
“While discussions previously focused on Ukraine’s reconstruction, the priority today is how to strengthen economic resilience here and now. Businesses need solutions that will help them protect their assets, maintain production, and continue investing even during wartime”, says Vasyl Khmelnytskyi, KIEF initiator, founder of UFuture holding.
Participant Registration
KIEF 2026 will feature 14 panel discussions addressing the most pressing challenges facing Ukraine’s economy. Key topics will include protecting business facilities, maintaining operations during air raid alerts, decentralizing logistics and energy supply, ensuring reliable communications, insuring against war-related risks, securing compensation for lost assets, accessing finance, and maintaining macroeconomic stability.
Discussions will also explore how Ukraine can adapt its industrial development strategy and energy policy to new realities, redefine national economic priorities, strengthen international cooperation, and advance European integration amid emerging challenges. Special attention will go to frontline cities and the practical solutions they have already implemented to keep their economies functioning.
Confirmed forum speakers include:
- Oleksandr Komarov, CEO and President of Kyivstar Group;
- Ruslan Shostak, President of TERWIN Corporation, founder of EVA and Varus;
- Francis Malige, Managing Director, Head of Financial Institutions, EBRD;
- Yuliia Svyrydenko, President of KSE Business School;
- Vyacheslav Klymov, Co-owner of NOVA Group;
- Dominykas Tuckus, Managing Director of the Amber Infrastructure Fund;
- Igor Nikonov, Founder of the Ukrainian development company KAN Development;
- Tomas Fiala, Founder of Dragon Capital;
- Inga Andreieva, Country Manager, Ukraine and Moldova, Mastercard;
- David Godfrey, Board Member, British-Ukrainian Economic Future, Former Chief, Executive, UK Export Finance (UKEF) | CBE.
Ukraine’s economy has already demonstrated its ability to adapt rapidly to major disruptions. In 2022, following the destruction of the Kremenchuk oil refinery and the resulting fuel shortages, the country rebuilt its fuel supply chains, while thousands of businesses relocated from frontline regions to safer areas further inland.
In 2023, Ukraine launched its own maritime corridor after traditional shipping routes were blocked. Following large-scale attacks on the power grid last year, businesses and the government also accelerated the development of distributed power generation.
Media Accreditation
“Today, any discussion about the future must start with practical decisions that businesses, the government, and international partners can make right now to sustain economic resilience and restore growth. This is precisely what KIEF 2026 is about”, says Yuriy Pyvovarov, CEO of KIEF.
Title Partners: UFuture, Mastercard, AEQUO, PrivatBank, Kyivstar
Forum Partners: Sense Bank, NEQSOL Holding, FUIB, DTEK, Ajax Systems, Uklon, TERWIN, Eclectic Talents Group, BALEX, CEO Club Ukraine
Interfax-Ukraine is the forum's media partner.

Ukrainian drones hit Russia's biggest data centre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:50:38 UTC
16:50:38 KST

Ukrainian drones hit Russia's top data centre in attack on AI ambitions
MOSCOW, Oct 14 - Ukrainian drones hit Russia's biggest data centre on Wednesday, part of a series of attacks appearing to target Moscow's ambitions to develop Russian artificial intelligence capabilities on a par with those from the US and China.
The strike on the Balakovo data centre, owned by Sberbank, the country's largest bank and technology company, followed three attacks in the past week on data centres owned by Russian technology group Yandex.
"We confirm that the data processing centre was attacked. At the same time, all of Sberbank's systems and services are operating normally and without disruption," Sberbank First Deputy CEO Alexander Vedyakhin told reporters.
President Vladimir Putin held a previously unannounced meeting on Wednesday with top officials on "information security", in which Sberbank CEO German Gref took part. The Kremlin said that the meeting was not linked to the attacks on data centres. Russia's state RIA Novosti news agency reported in 2024 that the Sberbank centre hit on Wednesday would host Russia's biggest supercomputer, which is scheduled to go into operation in 2027.
The Yandex data centres, hit earlier, hosted all three of that company's operating supercomputers. Neither Yandex nor Sberbank has said whether supercomputers, used to train the AI models, were damaged in the Ukrainian attacks.
Along with Yandex, its main domestic rival, Sberbank is Russia's leading developer of artificial intelligence. The domestic market is shared between Sberbank's GigaChat model and YandexGPT.
DIFFICULTIES PURCHASING CHIPS
Both companies have invested heavily in the development of their models but lag global leaders in the United States and China by up to nine months, according to Sberbank's own estimates, partly due to Western sanctions which hinder Russia's access to the most advanced hardware.
"It's clear what difficulties we face when purchasing modern graphics processing units. Both we and Yandex suffer from this," Gref said on September 29, calling it the biggest reason why Russia lags behind the US and China in AI.
Sberbank is in talks to buy chips from Chinese makers, but in an interview with Reuters on June 3, Vedyakhin said that US chipmaker Nvidia's monopoly on its CUDA software platform, which has become an AI industry standard, is an even greater problem.
Yandex said previously that its supercomputers operated on Nvidia A100 chips, a model launched in 2020 and since then succeeded by more advanced H100 chips.
Sberbank has two functioning supercomputers. The most advanced one, called Christofari Neo, ranked 167th in the Top 500 list of the world's most powerful supercomputers, is located in Moscow and is based on Nvidia A100 chips.
Yandex's most advanced Chervonenkis supercomputer is ranked 101st in the same list.
IT expert Mikhail Klimarev told Reuters it could take a long time to replace the chips due to Western sanctions, while damage to the supercomputers could set back the Russian AI industry, which already suffered from sanctions.
"The equipment is being imported, but it's done at a high cost, through indirect routes. First, you need to negotiate so that someone is willing to sell it to you and is not afraid of sanctions," he said.
PROTECT ASSETS
Some commentators compared the lack of reported disruption at state-controlled Sberbank with Yandex — whose taxi and food delivery units had reported disruptions — saying it showed that Sberbank's centres are better protected.
"This is a great example of what a business owner can do to protect their assets," wrote military blogger Alexander Kots. Under an August decree by Putin, the state can take over administration of poorly protected facilities.
The Sberbank site is located close to the Balakovo nuclear power plant, which the data centre uses as an energy source, and the Saratov hydroelectric power plant. No damage was reported to either plant from the attack.
Ukraine says it is responding to Russian attacks on its own data sites. Both countries have attacked each other's refineries, power stations, ports and e-commerce companies.
Russia's digital development ministry said this week it was in talks with the military on protecting the data centres, while some lawmakers called for them to be moved underground where the hardware will be out of reach for drones.
"We need a so-called Doomsday data vault," Valery Yermakov, deputy CEO of state-controlled Rostelecom, another major data centre operator, told a conference in Moscow. REUTERS

Poll: Center head Mihhail Kõlvart becomes most popular choice for prime minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:50:00 UTC
16:50:00 KST

Poll: Center head Mihhail Kõlvart becomes most popular choice for prime minister
Center Party Chairman Mihhail Kõlvart has knocked Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu off the top spot in the Delfi and Turu-uuringute AS poll on preferred prime minister candidates.
Reinsalu had already matched his lowest approval rating in three years last month, at 18 percent, but his support fell further in October, with just 16 percent of voters now preferring him as prime minister, Delfi reported Wednesday.
Kõlvart, meanwhile, saw a surge in support, with 20 percent of respondents now preferring him as prime minister, his highest rating ever in the survey, Delfi noted. In May this year, Kõlvart's rating climbed to 19 percent, putting him level with Reinsalu at the time, before falling back to 16 percent.
Commenting on the results, Turu-uuringute AS CEO Tõnis Stamberg told Delfi that Kõlvart's rise was driven by increased support among ethnic Estonian voters. Kõlvart is backed by 13 percent of ethnic Estonians and 50 percent of ethnic Russians, compared with 18 percent and 6 percent, respectively, for Reinsalu. As recently as August, Kõlvart had the support of 11 percent of ethnic Estonians, compared with 22 percent for Reinsalu, indicating that Kõlvart has gained ground among ethnic Estonian voters while Reinsalu has lost support.
Kõlvart's support increased among both rural and urban residents, while Reinsalu lost ground among urban voters. However, Reinsalu managed to maintain his support among rural residents at 21 percent for a month. In October, Kõlvart gained support among respondents with the lowest and highest levels of education, while Reinsalu saw his biggest losses among those with the lowest levels of education, with smaller declines among university-educated respondents.
Asked whom they would prefer to see as prime minister, 20 percent of respondents in October named Kõlvart, 16 percent Reinsalu, 13 percent Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) Chairman Martin Helme, 10 percent Eesti Parempoolsed leader Lavly Perling, 7 percent Social Democratic Party Chairman Lauri Läänemets, 5 percent Reform Party Chairman and incumbent Prime Minister Kristen Michal, and 2 percent Estonia 200 leader Kristina Kallas. Another 27 percent were unable to say.
Turu-uuringute AS conducted the survey for Delfi online and by telephone from October 1 to 3, with 899 Estonian citizens ages 18 and older responding.

Saudi employee arrested for allegedly bugging OpenAI office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:49:58 UTC
16:49:58 KST

Breadcrumb
FBI arrests Saudi employee for allegedly bugging OpenAI office
A Saudi employee of OpenAI was arrested after allegedly planting a recording device in one of the company's San Francisco offices, the AI firm and federal prosecutors said Tuesday.
"We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices" and "referred the matter to the FBI," OpenAI told AFP in a statement.
OpenAI's security team found the device late last month and the employee, Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested on 9 October, the US Justice Department said.
Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer who had worked for OpenAI since July 2025, allegedly wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and inserted it into a television located in an "executive conference room," according to a Justice Department statement.
He was allegedly caught on camera "near" the conference room multiple times but was not authorised to participate in meetings located there.
He used a "productivity tool" to search for more information about OpenAI's office buildings, meeting rooms, calendars, schedules and people's locations, according to the statement.
A chatbot account connected to Alfozan's spouse also allegedly contained queries related to remote audio recording and encrypting memory cards.
"This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said in the statement.
"The intelligence community remains committed to safeguarding America's cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats," Clayton added.
The arrest and allegations come amid a fierce global race to dominate in artificial intelligence, which the Trump administration has pushed to be rebranded as "superintelligence."
Saudi Arabia's state-backed AI firm Humain invested $3 billion in Elon Musk's xAI shortly before the American billionaire's space company, SpaceX, acquired the AI division in February.
Now known as SpaceXAI, the division announced last year that it was teaming up with Humain to build a 500-megawatt data center in Saudi Arabia.
Multiple devices
It was not immediately clear what, if any information the recording device was able to collect.
"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI told AFP in a statement.
A second device was found by OpenAI's security team when they searched an unattended bag that belonged to Alfozan, according to the Justice Department.
Alfozan was caught on security footage from inside the restricted conference room where he appeared to look behind the television where the recording device had been placed, the Department said.
A LinkedIn account matching Alfozan's name and resume show that he previously worked at Facebook-owner Meta, as well as an AI startup and a venture capital firm.
He was also a student at University of California at Berkeley and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
The Justice Department said Alfozen had been charged with "using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications," for which he could face up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
It did not accuse Alfozan nor Saudi Arabia, which is a close US ally, of spying activity in its statement on Tuesday.
Alfozan is expected to appear at a federal court hearing on 19 October.
In 2022, a former Twitter worker, Ahmad Abouammo, was found guilty of spying for Saudi officials keen to unmask critics on the platform.

U.S. moves leave Ukraine less able to defend itself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:49:49 UTC
16:49:49 KST

- Ukraine received no partner warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches for two straight nights, the Ukrainian Air Force said, detecting missiles only minutes before impact.
- Starlink also stopped working above 160 km/h for Ukraine’s military, hitting tactical drones used in defense, as Russia’s strike left 600,000 without power.
Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian strikes has been limited by two U.S. moves in a single night: the country went without early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches from its partners for a second time in a row, and Starlink, the U.S. satellite service its frontline units depend on, was cut back for the Ukrainian military just as Russia launched one of its heaviest missile attacks on Ukraine’s power grid.
The Ukrainian Air Force said Russia launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv at about 10:40 p.m. on Oct. 13, and that once again no information about the launches had come from Ukraine’s partners before the missiles were in the air. The Air Force said the reasons were being investigated.
“The situation is similar to yesterday’s. No information regarding launches from enemy territory had been received from our partners. The reasons are being investigated,” the Ukrainian Air Force said in an official statement.
Ukraine has relied heavily on early warning from the United States, whose satellites can spot the heat of a missile launch deep inside Russia within moments, giving Ukrainian air defense crews time to prepare and giving cities time to sound air raid sirens. Without those alerts, Ukrainian forces only detected the incoming ballistic missiles once they came within range of ground radars, a few minutes before impact, and tried to shoot some of them down. The lost minutes shorten the reaction time for interceptor crews and hit civilians hardest, leaving people in Kyiv and other cities less time to reach shelters and metro stations.
The attack that followed was massive. Zelenskyy said Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions overnight into Oct. 14 at energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and Kharkiv, damaging 26 facilities in the power system and four in the oil and gas sector and leaving at least 600,000 people without electricity. He said there were dead and injured and warned that outages could spread.
Zelenskyy said the missile salvo deliberately targeted the energy infrastructure covered by the ceasefire President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11, which Moscow never confirmed accepting.
“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” said Zelenskyy.
During the same night, Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military began losing their connection whenever they moved faster than 160 km/h (100 mph). Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy who is widely known by his call sign “Flash” and who has tracked Russian attempts to jam Starlink along the front, said the restriction hit the military StarShield package of the SpaceX service and that units received no notice before it took effect.
“Our defense forces did not receive any warning about this restriction, and it led to the disruption of a number of missions. It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation,” said Serhii Beskrestnov.
The restriction falls on Ukraine’s defense, not on its strikes inside Russia. SpaceX has never allowed Ukraine to use Starlink for strikes on Russian territory, and Zelenskyy said earlier this month that Kyiv was still asking for that permission, so Ukraine’s long-range drones and cruise missiles that hit targets in Russia do not rely on the service. Starlink has also been unavailable to Russian forces since February, when SpaceX and Ukraine’s Defense Ministry introduced a whitelist that cut off unregistered Russian terminals. Inside Ukraine, Starlink is used on tactical drones and uncrewed ground vehicles that operate over Ukrainian and Russian-occupied territory, so a speed cap above 160 km/h cuts the links of fast tactical strike and interceptor drones fighting Russian troops and drones along the front.
Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko, who first reported the change, said ordinary satellite terminals kept working and suggested SpaceX may have acted at the request of the Trump administration, while British analyst Jimmy Rushton noted that the limit does nothing to protect the Russian oil refineries Trump has criticized Ukraine for striking.
Ballistic missiles are the hardest part of Russia’s strike packages for Ukraine to stop, because they fly too fast and too high for most of its air defense systems, and Ukraine relies mainly on U.S.-made Patriot batteries to intercept them. Zelenskyy asked Washington and other partners for more Patriot interceptors and called on Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia under the law sponsored by Sen. Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed in September.
“We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine,” said Zelenskyy.
The Ukrainian Air Force warned that further Russian attacks cannot be ruled out. Neither the White House nor SpaceX has explained why the missile launch warnings stopped or why the Starlink speed limit was introduced, or said whether either change is temporary.

Ukrainian OSINT channel: Russia turned a bare field into a Geran-5 launch site in a month—and drones are already arriving
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:49:28 UTC
16:49:28 KST

Russia has nearly finished the first section of a new launch site for jet-powered Geran-5 attack drones near the town of Millerovo in Rostov Oblast, anonymous Ukrainian OSINT channel Absolutely Reliable Source reported on 13 October. The channel’s bio says it covers Ukraine’s deep strikes and that its author belongs to a larger, unnamed structure. It says Russia rushed the build to scale up attacks after its September strikes on Kyiv.
The site is meant for the kind of drone Ukraine stops far less often than the older Shaheds. Ukraine downs 55% of jet-powered Shaheds, the class that includes the Geran-5, and more than 90% of the older propeller-driven ones, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 26 September. Russian industry makes about 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month, Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) told Militarnyi in August. A new launch site is how Russia plans to fire more of them, the channel argues.
Built in weeks, by the channel’s count
The channel’s images from 1 September show no construction at the site. The latest ones show eight prepared positions for launchers and 32 places for preparing drones for launch, the channel wrote. Imagery from the day before its post shows drones being unloaded in one zone, it said.
The channel’s headline says the work took a month. Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi, comparing the channel’s own images from 1 September and 12 October, put it at about six weeks. Both readings rest on the same images, which have not been independently verified.
Built like Tsymbulova
The construction style is very similar to Tsymbulova, Russia’s jet-drone base in Oryol Oblast, the channel wrote. That base has separate positions for storing, preparing, and launching jet drones, Militarnyi said. By late May, less than a month into an expansion of Tsymbulova, Russia was already building 10 more launchers there.
Ukrainian drones have hit Tsymbulova repeatedly, though most of the damage imagery comes from Absolutely Reliable Source. Militarnyi reported strikes on the base’s bunkers and hangars in September. Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck it again overnight on 1 October, damaging two ground shelters and drone preparation areas, Absolutely Reliable Source said. On 10 October, OSINT channel Exilenova+ reported another drone strike there, saying several bunkers, one jet-drone launcher, and a drone storage area were hit.

“They are doing nothing other than carrying out acts of terror in Europe, seeking to spread fear in our societies and targeting civilian infrastructure,” he said. “If that is not terrorism, what is?”
Budrys urged European Union member states to take action against the GRU at a meeting of the bloc’s Foreign Affairs Council in Luxembourg this week.

Total hydrocarbon production grew by 3.3% to 514.4 million barrels of oil equivalent (boe), including 10.71 million tonnes of liquid hydrocarbons (up 2.6%). In the third quarter, hydrocarbon production totaled 168.2 million boe--an increase of 4.2% compared to the previous year.

Bolat presses EU to include Türkiye in industrial plans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:45:54 UTC
16:45:54 KST

Trade Minister Ömer Bolat spoke at the Türkiye-EU Business Summit in Brussels on Oct. 13. (AA Photo)
Trade Minister Ömer Bolat has said Türkiye and the European Union have made progress on parts of a customs union update, while Ankara continues to seek inclusion in the bloc’s industrial plans.
Speaking to reporters in Brussels, Bolat said talks were advancing on e-commerce, public procurement, investment and agriculture.
The EU Council has yet to authorize formal modernization negotiations, he said, citing the stance of some member states.
“We are moving forward issue by issue,” he said.
Technical talks on a bilateral public procurement agreement have begun, he added.
Bolat said Ankara was seeking changes to the proposed Industrial Accelerator Act to address restrictions affecting automotive investment and electric vehicles.
The European Parliament and EU Council have yet to decide on the proposal, including its “Made in EU” requirements.
At the Türkiye-EU Business Summit on Oct. 13, he called for a “Made with Europe” approach that includes Türkiye as an equal partner and protects production ties.
He said concerns over imports from third countries should not lead to excluding trusted partners.
Bolat said bilateral trade reached $233 billion in 2025, including $62 billion in automotive trade.
At a separate dialogue with EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic, the two sides announced the removal of a barrier involving Türkiye’s TAREKS import controls.
They also agreed to advance implementation of mutual recognition arrangements for trusted traders and begin technical work on recognizing each other’s electronic signatures.
Bolat met Belgian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot on Oct. 14 to discuss raising bilateral trade to $15 billion and expanding investment ties.
The next bilateral Joint Economic and Trade Committee meeting is expected in Brussels in 2027.

Americans say Trump misusing presidency for personal wealth

More than half of Americans believe US President Donald Trump is placing his personal wealth ahead of the country’s interests, while roughly six in 10 think he is profiting from the presidency in ways they consider illegal or unethical.
According to a new survey by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research, 56% of US adults believe Trump has placed “a lot” of emphasis on his personal business interests since returning to the White House.
By comparison, only about one-quarter said he had given the same level of attention to the interests of the country as a whole, while roughly one in 10 said he had focused heavily on people like them.
The survey also found that around 60% of Americans believe Trump is either illegally profiting from his presidency or engaging in unethical behavior that does not necessarily break the law.
About 40% said they believe he is doing something illegal, while approximately 20% considered his conduct unethical but not illegal. Only about one-fifth said he was doing nothing wrong.
“His wealth increases,” said Barbara Thaxton, an 87-year-old independent voter from Florida. “But the people in the country are just barely getting by.”
The findings come as Trump’s family business expands into new ventures, including cryptocurrency and overseas real estate deals, raising renewed questions about potential conflicts of interest between his private financial activities and his public responsibilities.
Trump has relaxed restrictions on his family’s overseas business activities that were in place during his first term and launched several cryptocurrency ventures since returning to office.
In a financial disclosure filed in June, the president reported receiving more than $1 billion from new cryptocurrency businesses, according to the report, according to Press TV.
One major venture received a $500 million investment from a United Arab Emirates business linked to the country’s royal family after Trump’s election victory.
The Trump Organization has also pursued eight foreign real estate deals during the first year of his presidency, including projects in countries where governments exert considerable influence over private business.

Kazakhstan reveals key spending priorities for 2027
Kazakhstan’s Minister of Finance Madi Takiyev presented the draft law on the republican budget for 2027–2029 to members of the Qurultay, outlining the Government’s key spending priorities for the coming year, Qazinform News Agency reports.
According to the minister, the draft budget was developed in line with the Budget Code and the country’s socioeconomic development forecast through 2030.
For 2027, Kazakhstan projects budget revenues of 25.4 trillion tenge and expenditures of 30.2 trillion tenge, with a planned deficit of 4.6 trillion tenge, or 2.3% of GDP.
“In 2027, 6.9 trillion tenge will be allocated to social assistance and social security, while healthcare will receive 2.5 trillion tenge to fund guaranteed free medical services, medicines, and health insurance,” Takiyev said.
The Government also plans to allocate 60.4 billion tenge to scientific research projects in 2027, up 18.4 billion tenge from 2026.
Regional development is another key priority, with around 7.4 trillion tenge, or nearly a quarter of the annual budget, allocated to this area.
The funds will primarily go toward improving social and public utility infrastructure to enhance living standards.
Meanwhile, 3.7 trillion tenge has been earmarked for the real sector of the economy in 2027, with most of the funding directed toward transport infrastructure, agriculture, industry, entrepreneurship, and digital development.
“Another priority is security, public administration, and reserves, for which 4.9 trillion tenge has been allocated in 2027. The largest share, 3.3 trillion tenge, will go to law enforcement and security agencies, while 787 billion tenge is earmarked for public administration,” the minister said.
Earlier, Qazinform News Agency reported that Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Economy Serik Zhumangarin had presented Kazakhstan’s socioeconomic development forecast for 2027–2029 during a plenary session of the Qurultay.

- VAT refund amount reduction - 1.1 trillion tenge
- Other factors - 0.5 trillion tenge
At the same time, a revenue decline of 0.5 trillion tenge is expected.

Watch again: NATO chief Mark Rutte holds press conference in Estonia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:43:00 UTC
16:43:00 KST

NATO chief in Tallinn: Estonia a benchmark for what a member state should be
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said Estonia does not merely meet the alliance's defense spending requirements — it sets the standard on it and other contributions.
Rutte was on an official visit to Estonia Wednesday. Speaking at a press conference in Tallinn, Rutte said "You don't just rely on the alliance – Estonia strengthens it," Rutte said.
"Estonia doesn't just meet its commitments, it sets the standards," he went on noting Estonia's defense spending at 5 percent of GDP is among the highest of member states, and its "exceptional leadership" in support for Ukraine.
The NATO Secretary General also called Russia's hybrid attacks, such as the Milrem Robotics arson attack, an attempt to force attention onto Putin and his problems rather than onto Ukraine's fight.
"Putin is trying to weaken our resolve and stop our support for Ukraine, but Russia is failing – it is failing on the battlefield in Ukraine, and we will not be intimidated."
"These hybrid attacks … are a sign of weakness. What they love us to do is to talk about it all day, and to be rattled, and to have press conferences on it. We're not going to do that. We will react where we need to react," noting that while some high profile responses to Russia's hybrid attacks, for instance Baltic Sentry, is highly publicly visible, other responses are not.
In response to a journalist's question, Rutte said NATO is a defensive alliance and there is no evidence Russia would attack a NATO ally.
"We don't think so, and we so no imminent threat against NATO territory. If we would see a build up, we will react to it."
Also appearing at Wednesday's press conference was Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform), who said Ukraine's NATO membership would in the long term be Estonia's strongest security guarantee, and that NATO itself would benefit.
Michal said supporting Ukraine represents a part of Estonia's own security, as Russia's aims have not changed. He said Russia is testing allied unity with hybrid attacks and trying to draw attention away from Ukraine — to make allies focus on their own problems and tire of supporting Kyiv.
Michal said Estonia will continue its military support, with aid this year amounting to 0.28 percent of GDP, down from 0.35 percent last year. He said Estonia has contributed €21 million to NATO's PURL initiative, and announced a new €10 million contribution.
The Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative is a NATO-coordinated scheme under which allies and partners pay for weapons bought from the U.S. and sent to Ukraine. The U.S. itself has largely paused weapons donations to Ukraine under President Donald Trump, though it continues to share intelligence with Kyiv — as General Secretary Rutte pointed out in response to a question Wednesday.
The Estonian prime minister added Ukraine needs more weapons and, above all, more effective air defense, and that Estonia learns from Ukraine daily. He said Ukraine's experience is invaluable for developing Estonia's own defense capability and defense industry, whose revenues are growing at around 44 percent per year.
Ukraine's NATO accession is not currently on the table, largely due to opposition from several countries, chiefly the U.S.. Membership would also require Article 5 to apply, obliging all allies to come to the defense of an attacked member, and also requires a new member not be in a state of conflict at the time of joining, a condition which Russia has ensured cannot be fulfilled.
Asked about the claim that NATO could close Russia's access to the Gulf of Finland, and even the whole Baltic Sea, in the event of a conflict, Michal said that when it comes to the Baltic Sea, everyone can look at the Strait of Hormuz to imagine what would happen here if Russia attacked.
Rutte is visiting Estonia as part of his tour of NATO's eastern flank.
Wednesday's press conference can be rewatched by clicking on the video player above.

John Healey ‘targets tax crackdown on online marketplaces’ in first budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:42:48 UTC
16:42:48 KST

A tax crackdown on online marketplaces such as Amazon and eBay that could raise up to £1bn more for the Treasury is reportedly being drawn up for John Healey’s first budget.
The chancellor is said to be preparing to announce that online marketplaces will be made responsible for collecting tax owed by all retailers selling on their platforms.
Marketplaces have been required to collect VAT for overseas businesses selling into the UK since 2021 but some foreign operators have posed as British retailers, using shell companies or other techniques to avoid this rule.
Under the proposed change, websites would be made responsible for collecting VAT at source for retailers on their platform who have an annual turnover of more than £90,000, no matter where they are based.
Healey is expected to announce this change will be made to fund cuts to business rates for high street shops, the Times reported.
The government ran a consultation over the summer on changing the “deemed reseller” rules, saying “non-compliance persists among both overseas and UK-based businesses, distorting competition and disadvantaging compliant firms online and on the high street”.
It consulted food delivery platforms as well as retail marketplaces, suggesting it was considering drawing them into the system.
Amazon said it welcomed the prospect of a change to deemed reseller rules. “Closing this loophole will raise significant revenue for the exchequer and simplify compliance for both HMRC and legitimate sellers,” the UK’s biggest online marketplace said.
The development comes as pressure continues to grow on Andy Burnham and Healey to relieve struggling small businesses on the high street before the budget on 28 October.
Before he was elected in Makerfield, Burnham said he would increase the threshold for business rates so that 140,000 small high street retailers would not pay the tax.
The government is facing calls from many factions to cut tax, with large retailers pushing for changes to national insurance to boost youth employment, for example.
However, this week the Institute for Fiscal Studies warned Healey that his budget risks being a “work of fiction” unless he sets out plans to cover £35bn in spending pressures.
The IFS said the damage from higher inflation meant the chancellor would need to either top up funds for his current government spending plans or impose deep real-terms cuts by the end of the decade.
In a boost for the Treasury, this week the International Monetary Fund upgraded its GDP growth forecast for the UK this year to 1.3%, up 0.3 percentage points from its previous update in July.
However, the IMF also cautioned that Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances. Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit.
A spokesperson for the Treasury said: “As has always been the case, decisions on tax are a matter for the chancellor to set out at fiscal events rather than routinely commenting on rumour, speculation or proposals.”

Wildlife photographer of the year 2026 winners – in pictures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:41:54 UTC
16:41:54 KST

Wildlife photographer of the year 2026 winners – in pictures
A selection of the winning images from this year’s competition across topics ranging from underwater to urban wildlife, and photojournalism to mammal behaviour. The overall winner is Federico Veronesi of Italy for his powerful image of an elephant carrying a dead calf
Wildlife photographer of the year 2026 | The Aftermath by Federico Veronesi, Italy | Winner, Behaviour: Mammals
Veronesi witnessed a powerful moment of an elephant carrying a dead calf, a rare glimpse into complex animal behaviours. He was tracking elephants when he came across an unusual pattern of drag marks in a dry riverbed in Namibia. A female emerged with the calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk. Behaviours centring on death have been observed in Asian and African elephants, including vocalisations, guarding the dead, inspecting and handling bones and carrying the deceasedPhotograph: Federico Veronesi/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Escape Artistry by Michał Michalski, Poland | Winner, Natural Artistry
Michalski uses a slow shutter speed to create the illusion of trees still swathed in autumn foliage. A field of unharvested sunflowers had attracted mixed flocks of birds, especially goldfinches and bramblings. As they took to the sky, startled by a sparrowhawk, Michalski blurred the movement against a backdrop of leafless birches. There is evidence that flocks containing multiple species forage more efficiently, partly because each brings different skills to the groupPhotograph: Michał Michalski/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
The Great Divide by Alex Visbal, Colombia | Winner, Wetlands: The Bigger Picture
Visbal documents how a single engineered line can reshape an entire wetland. The distinctive pink colour on the left is caused by microbes that thrive in extremely saline water, which happens when an area is cut off from a supply of fresh water. The ecology of the lake in Utah is in sharp decline due to industrial use, upstream diversions and climate change. Since this image was taken, the state has brought the area under conservation managementPhotograph: Alex Visbal/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Shedding Light by Agorastos Papatsanis, Greece | Winner, Plants and Fungi
Papatsanis uses ultraviolet light to reveal the glowing yellow stems of ‘beautiful bonnet’ mushrooms growing from a decaying log. On the lower slopes of Greece’s Mount Olympus, he experimented with UV illumination until it revealed the strongest fluorescent response from the mushroomsPhotograph: Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Night-Time Catch by Alex Lindbloom, US | Winner, Oceans: The Bigger Picture
Lindbloom finds a whale shark investigating the catch of a bagan, or mobile net-fishing platform, in the inky waters off Papua. He started searching for sharks around dawn when the nets were still in the water. Initially lacking natural light for his drone’s camera, he found these sharks illuminated by the bagan’s bright lightsPhotograph: Alex Lindbloom/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
A Watchful Eye by Aaron Sanders, UK | Winner, Animal Portraits
Sanders glimpses a common octopus behind a curtain of kelp in the waters off Cornwall. Aaron had been diving off Porthkerris Beach when he noticed the footprints of octopus suckers through a thin blade of kelp, and a single eye slowly emerging. ‘We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity,’ he saysPhotograph: Aaron Sanders/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Shifting Sand by Sitaram Raul, India | Winner, Behaviour: Invertebrates
Raul encounters a scorpion burrowing into one of the shifting dunes of the Thar desert. Exploring the dunes at night, he saw many scorpions searching for prey. But as sunrise approached, they started burrowing to avoid the intense heat. Raul timed the exposure so that the excavated sand was suspended in mid-airPhotograph: Sitaram Raul/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
The Meeting Place by James Lewin, UK | Winner, Animals in their Environment
Lewin watches a young bull elephant spray a group of zebra as they congregate in Kenya’s Chyulu hills. While there was no shortage of subjects and action around this waterhole, he had to deal with the harsh, unforgiving light. He chose to soften the light using a camera converted to infrared, creating this dream-like scenePhotograph: James Lewin/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Afternoon Snack by Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas, Germany | Winner, Rising Star Award
Tinker-Tsavalas reveals the exquisite beauty of the tiniest of animals in the finest of detail. When he spotted this robber fly, it had already impaled the flesh fly with its needlelike mouthparts. The bubbles forming in the victim’s eyes indicate that the robber fly has injected digestive enzymes that liquefy its internal tissues before they are sucked outPhotograph: Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Secret Worlds by Kutub Uddin, Bangladesh/UK | Winner, Portfolio Award
Kutub Uddin reveals a magical and often surreal world of slime moulds that can barely be seen with the naked eye. In this image – Tiny Dancers – an immature Cribraria aurantiaca is at a tiny and often overlooked stage in its life. Uddin became interested in slime moulds in 2024, and devotes much of his time to revealing this hidden world – exploring his local woodlands in West Sussex, where fallen logs and damp forest floors provide opportunities for discovering these fascinating organismsPhotograph: Kutub Uddin/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Warning Sign by Francisco Negroni, Chile | Winner, Photojournalism
Negroni recorded this scene of a dead puma amid the rugged, windswept beauty of Patagonia – tied to the fence and presented as a hunting trophy. The province of Santa Cruz in Argentina banned the hunting of pumas in 2025, but illegal persecution continues. Livestock predation is one of the major causes of human–puma conflict, and it’s suggested that enclosing sheep at night and using guard dogs can significantly reduce the loss of livestock without resorting to huntingPhotograph: Francisco Negroni/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Birdsong Painted in Light by Konrad Gräeter, Germany | Winner, 15-17 Years
Gräeter highlights a male blackbird singing in a vineyard early one April morning. He had to crouch down low on the steep slope of the vineyard and point his camera through a gap in the foliage to frame the blackbird within its landscape. Blackbirds can be heard singing at different times of day, but their songs have the most complex compositions at dawnPhotograph: Konrad Gräeter/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Protective Pose by Anton Sorokin, US | Winner, Behaviour: Amphibians and Reptiles
Sorokin finds a California newt laying its eggs as it clasps vegetation that already holds another newt’s egg clutch. He waded along the edge of the pond, carefully dipping his camera and lighting beneath the surface to record this remarkable view of parental care. The newts interlock their back feet to protect the clutch, which is vulnerable to predation by other newts. They will stay like this until the gelatinous mass around the eggs has swollen too large to be eaten and has solidified on to the stemPhotograph: Anton Sorokin/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Young wildlife photographer of the year 2026 | Labour of Love by Oscar Whitfield, Zimbabwe/UK | Winner, 11-14 Years
Whitfield notices the arduous exertion of this dung beetle pushing its precious cargo. Using a fast shutter speed and high light sensitivity, he lay flat on the ground to photograph the beetle at eye level, with the sunshine and heat creating dry dust all around him. Breaking up dung and burying it prevents the conditions required for methane production, reducing the quantity of greenhouse gas emissions. Burying dung also helps it decompose fasterPhotograph: Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Making Morays by Tony Wu, USA/Japan | Winner, Under Water
Wu provides a first-time glimpse into the mating ritual of two Abbott’s moray eels at the apex of their spawning arc. On the verge of swimming back down to safety, the larger male in the foreground has already released a diffuse cloud of sperm, while the female in the background has just commenced ejecting a stream of eggs. This is likely the first time the courtship and spawning have been documented, and observations from Wu’s work with biologists are feeding into published scientific studies. Kagoshima Prefecture, Kyushu, JapanPhotograph: Tony Wu/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Scenes from the Swamp by Isak Pretorius, South Africa Winner | Behaviour: Birds
Pretorius chanced upon two elusive shoebill storks among wetland vegetation, while exploring the swamp in a narrow canoe with a guide. The birds pulled out vegetation, dropped it and then repeated the process several times. It is likely this is a breeding pair gathering nesting material. Though often called the shoebill stork, these large birds are more closely related to pelicans, herons and ibises. Fewer than 5,300 mature shoebills survive across their entire range and their numbers are decreasingPhotograph: Isak Pretorius/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Wily Coyotes of San Francisco by Loren Elliott, US | Winner, Photojournalist Story Award
Elliott opens a window into the lives of the often-misunderstood coyotes living in the environs of San Francisco. About 100 of these urban-adapted wild canines live alongside more than 800,000 human inhabitants, and attitudes towards them are mixed. Coyotes sometimes prey on domestic animals, but they also bring benefits such as controlling disease-carrying rodentsPhotograph: Loren Elliott/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Urban Jungle by Seth Forestson | UK Winner, Urban Wildlife
Forestson spots a common water monitor carrying its fish supper in a Bangkok park. The challenge wasn’t finding the lizards, but catching them in action, as they spend most of the day basking in the sun. Common water monitors have successfully adapted to living in cities across south and south-east Asia. They will take whatever food source is available, such as the plentiful supplies of catfish and koi in the lakes of Bangkok’s Lumphini ParkPhotograph: Seth Forestson/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026
Flight of the Bumblebee by Amelie Davis, UK | Winner, 10 Years and Under
Davis highlights a common carder bee suspended in mid-air as it flies in to land and feast on a flower in Surrey. On this August afternoon the garden was ‘teeming with bees’. Without her camera, she borrowed her dad’s smartphone and was able to record the delicate detail of a single wingbeat. Bees perceive plants and flowers in many ways. Distinguishing one colour for nectar and another for pollen helps them make rapid decisions when foragingPhotograph: Amelie Davis/Wildlife photographer of the year 2026

More than 1,300 Taiwanese gain Siraya identity

2026-10-14
07:41:32 UTC
16:41:32 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — As of the end of September, 1,336 Taiwanese have obtained Plains Indigenous status as members of the Siraya people.
The Plains Indigenous Peoples Status Act passed its third reading in the Legislative Yuan on Oct. 17, 2025, and was promulgated by the president on Oct. 23, taking effect on the same day, per CNA.
The Cabinet officially recognized the Siraya as one of Taiwan’s Plains Indigenous peoples on July 31. Applications to be included in the official list of Siraya group members and Plains Indigenous status registration opened on Aug. 13, according to CNA.
The law aims to protect Plains Indigenous peoples’ demand for formal recognition and their right to identity.
According to a Council of Indigenous People’s (CIP) report, the council has accepted applications for recognition from nine Plains Indigenous peoples since the law took effect: the Siraya, Taivoan, Makatao, Taokas, Kaxabu, Pazeh, Papora, Babuza and Ketagalan, CNA reported.
The CIP said a panel of experts and scholars will soon review applications from the Pazeh, Kaxabu, and Taokas peoples. A draft proposal outlining membership requirements for the Taivoan people will be announced soon.
The council said it would expedite the procedures for official recognition and identity registration.

Alexander Yui: Taiwan is shoring up defenses to make China invasion difficult
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:41:19 UTC
16:41:19 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan is strengthening its military and civilian defenses to deter a Chinese invasion, Taiwan Representative to the US Alexander Yui Tah-ray (俞大㵢) said Wednesday.
Speaking on the BBC World Service program "The Interview," Yui said Taiwan aims to make any Chinese attack difficult and costly. He said the country does not need to defeat China's military, but must prevent its forces from landing and taking control.
Yui said Taipei has spent decades preparing for a possible conflict with China. However, Russia's invasion of Ukraine has raised public awareness of the threat and increased support for stronger defenses.
The war has also amplified public favor for higher military spending, longer military service, and better civilian readiness, Yui said. Taiwan has extended compulsory military service from four months to one year and increased its defense budget.
Yui said Taiwan is also learning from Ukraine's use of drones in combat. The war has shown how low-cost drones can damage far more expensive military equipment, including warships.
Taiwan is expanding production of aerial, surface, and underwater drones to strengthen its defenses. Yui said local firms are also working to replace Chinese-made parts and build partnerships with US and European companies.
Yui also discussed a proposed NT$439 billion (US$14 billion) US arms sale to Taiwan that is awaiting approval. He said Taiwan hopes the Trump administration will approve the deal soon, as weapons can take years to arrive after an order is placed.
Yui said Taiwan needs better systems to detect and counter drones as it faces China's much larger military. However, he declined to identify the specific weapons Taiwan is seeking.
Yui also addressed concerns that US President Donald Trump could make concessions on Taiwan to improve relations with Chinese leader Xi Jinping. He said Washington has repeatedly stated that its Taiwan policy remains unchanged and expressed confidence that the country would not become a bargaining chip in talks with Beijing.

"Our defence forces did not receive a warning about this limitation and this led to the disruption of several missions," Beskrestnov wrote on Telegram.
Ukrainian volunteer Serhiy Sternenko also reported the disruption, suggesting that SpaceX might have introduced the restrictions at the request of US President Donald Trump's administration.
There is, however, no independent evidence that the White House ordered the change, and the reason for the reported restrictions remains unclear.
Another potential source of US leverage?
The development has raised concerns that access to critical American satellite communications could become another source of leverage over Kyiv, alongside reported US threats to suspend intelligence-sharing unless Ukraine halts its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
According to media reports the Trump administration warned that intelligence cooperation could be curtailed, although Washington has denied suspending intelligence-sharing and Ukrainian officials maintain that cooperation continues.
The timing has also attracted attention following public criticism of Zelenskyy by Elon Musk, the billionaire owner of SpaceX, which operates Starlink.
On Saturday Musk responded to a White House video of Trump criticising Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil facilities, writing on X: "Zelenskyy has gone too far."
The comment came amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Washington and Kyiv, following Trump's agreement with Moscow to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports and his demands that Ukraine suspend attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
No connection has been established, however, between the reported Starlink restrictions and the diplomatic dispute.
Russia continues strikes despite Trump's 'energy ceasefire'
The reports come amid fresh questions over the reliability of advance intelligence-sharing after Zelenskyy said Ukraine had received no warning from its partners ahead of Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv for a second consecutive night.
The attacks continued despite Trump's declaration of an energy ceasefire, which Kyiv says Moscow has failed to observe.
According to Zelenskyy Russia launched 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions against Kyiv, the surrounding region and Kharkiv overnight, damaging 26 electricity facilities and four oil and gas installations and leaving at least 600,000 people without power.
"Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States," Zelenskyy wrote on X, accusing Moscow of deliberately targeting infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by Trump.
Despite the growing tensions with Washington Zelenskyy appealed directly to the US president to impose tougher sanctions on Russia and provide additional Patriot missile interceptors.
"We ask America and EVERYONE in the world who does not turn a blind eye to reality to respond and to respond forcefully," he wrote.
The latest developments underscore Ukraine's continued dependence on American intelligence, military technology and air defence support at a time when relations with Washington have become increasingly uncertain.

welcome to the new designboom! all you need to know about our redesigned website
from bookmarking your favorite articles to more space for beautiful visuals and entirely new sections, our new website is built to let you get pleasantly lost. we’ve cleared out the digital noise, turned up the soundtrack, and opened up 27 years of designboom archives for you to explore. dive in and see what’s new!
[FEATURED]
DESIGNBOOM UNVEILS NEW WEBSITE
Since we first hand-coded our way onto the internet in 1999, designboom has never really sat still. If you have been reading us for a while, you know we’ve completely rebuilt our digital home multiple times over the last 27 years. And in between six major website iterations, we’re always tinkering, introducing intuitive new tweaks and optimizing features. But a couple of years ago, we realized we didn’t just need another visual refresh, we needed to completely rethink how our community interacts with our content.
After months of planning, we are excited to introduce our brand new website! We wanted to build a space where beautiful images and video have generous room to breathe, where our 27-year archive unfolds like a living network, and where editorial content, sound, maps, and community ideas take center stage. The result is a sharper, more interactive designboom, uncluttered, intuitive, and built for curiosity. Here is what’s new.
save stories, BUILD YOUR OWN ARCHIVE
Finding a brilliant architectural pavilion from last week or a forgotten chair design from 2007 is only half the experience; holding onto it is the other. You can now create a free account on designboom to bookmark articles, build your own permanent visual library, and easily track the status of your project submissions all in one place.
NO MORE PROGRAMMATIC ADVERTISING
The most radical change to the site is what you won’t see. We have completely removed programmatic banner advertising. Instead of filling our pages with automatically placed advertisements, we’re reserving commercial space for direct brand partnerships that actually make sense for our audience. This allows us to have greater control over what appears alongside our editorial content, and to create a more beautiful browsing experience with less visual interruptions.
For us, this decision goes beyond cleaning up the interface. We want architecture, design, art and technology to occupy the space they deserve, without irrelevant ads competing for attention. It doesn’t mean commercial partnerships will completely disappear from designboom. Quite the opposite: we believe in building thoughtful collaborations and tell brand stories that matter to us and to our community.
SOUND, MAPS, AND INTERACTIVE GUIDES
A visual platform doesn’t have to be silent. We’ve launched designboom listens, embedding curated Spotify playlists directly into our guest portraits. Now, you can actually listen to the exact tracks architects and artists play while they work in their studios. We are also expanding our interactive guides and maps, making it much more intuitive to navigate physical events and exhibitions around the globe.
A NEW EDITORIAL RHYTHM: CHAPTERS
Rather than relying solely on a chronological news feed, we introduced designboom Chapters at the beginning of this year. These are curated editorial arcs that cluster our stories around a central theme, spanning from Play and Craft, to Spectacle and how we live together. They now get their much deserved prime spot on the new homepage, as well as an expansive Chapters archive page for readers to explore all themes we’ve covered so far, chronologically.
MORE SPACE FOR READERS and GUEST submissions
With over 200,000 readers actively contributing to designboom, community is the foundation of our platform. The new homepage gives reader-submitted projects a much clearer, dedicated space alongside our daily editorial stream. Furthermore, we have completely revamped the homepage look of our design-directory, competitions, courses and shop.
A MORE VISUAL AND CONNECTED DESIGNBOOM
We’ve given images and video a more prominent role throughout the website, while refining typography, spacing and the overall visual language. The idea was to let projects speak for themselves, whether they involve an entire building, an experimental material or an object small enough to fit in your pocket. We’ve kept the interface deliberately restrained, allowing the work we publish to provide most of the color. Less digital ‘clutter’, fewer places for the eye to trip over it.
We’ve also brought our archive closer to the surface. Stories now connect more naturally through designers, architects, locations and subjects, turning tags into possible routes through more than two decades of publishing. You might arrive looking for a building completed last week and end up discovering a table from 2009. We rather like that possibility. After all, the internet should occasionally allow us to get pleasantly lost.
Taken together, these changes reflect what we want designboom to be today: a place to discover what’s happening now, explore what came before, save what matters to you and, every so often, stumble upon something you didn’t know you were looking for.
Welcome to the new designboom. Have a look around, and let us know what you think! 💛

Fenerbahçe opened the league phase with a 1-1 home draw against Roma, while Villa earned a 3-2 victory at Club Brugge. The Istanbul side enters Matchday 2 in 19th place with one point; Villa is ninth with three.
The visit presents a steep challenge for Fenerbahçe. Unai Emery’s Villa is unbeaten in its past 13 European home games and has won the past 10. The English side drew 2-2 with Brentford in the Premier League on Oct. 10 after an encouraging run before the international break.

Also on Oct. 14, Manchester City and Paris Saint-Germain, which have reshaped football with the financial backing of Gulf state owners, clash in their latest Champions League meeting.

The triumph over Inter Milan in Istanbul that completed a treble of Champions League, Premier League and FA Cup was the pinnacle of City’s rise since a 2008 takeover fronted by Sheikh Mansour, the vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.
But a cloud now hangs over City’s haul of silverware from the past 15 years unless it can overturn the findings of an independent commission on appeal.
City was found to have used “sham” commercial deals with Emirati companies to inflate revenue and reduce costs to the tune of over 900 million pounds ($1.2 billion) between 2009 and 2018.
No sanction has yet been meted out, but a severe points deduction or even expulsion from the Premier League are among the potential punishments.

Australian court overturns Aboriginal heritage order blocking billion-dollar gold mine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:38:42 UTC
16:38:42 KST

Faisal Mahmud
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
An Australian court has overturned a government order protecting an Aboriginal heritage site that halted a billion-dollar gold mine project in New South Wales, ruling that the decision was legally invalid.
The Federal Court ruled in favor of mining company Regis Resources, which challenged a 2024 protection order covering 400 hectares of its McPhillamys Gold Project near Blayney, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) reported Wednesday.
The order, issued by then-Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek, prevented construction of a tailings dam intended to store mining waste, rendering the project financially unviable, according to the company.
Justice James Stellios ruled that procedural requirements had not been followed when considering an Aboriginal heritage protection application involving a culturally significant area associated with the Wiradyuri people.
The original application, lodged in 2020 by Wiradyuri elder Aunty Nyree Reynolds, sought protection for an area linked to the Blue Banded Bee Dreaming story.
Stellios stressed that the ruling concerned procedural errors rather than the merits of the Aboriginal heritage claims.
The matter will return to Environment Minister Murray Watt for reconsideration.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the government was examining the judgment, while Watt pledged continued engagement with Indigenous communities and industry.
Regis Resources welcomed the ruling, describing it as a significant step toward reviving one of Australia’s largest undeveloped gold projects.
