Brazil in Focus: This Month in Architecture, Housing, Learning Spaces, and Urban Life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

This month's Brazil in Focus looks at how architecture and urban development intersect with questions of housing, education, public space, and mobility across the country. This month's selection includes an indigenous settlement in Maricá recognized by UN-Habitat for its approach to adequate housing, editorials examining university campuses and planned cities as frameworks for collective life, and projects ranging from a timber-structured airport expansion to a commercial building that engages São Paulo's public realm and a residence shaped by its landscape. Also on the radar are the winning proposal for Itaú Cultural's new headquarters on Avenida Paulista, international recognition for two Brazilian landscape architecture projects, and a national diagnosis highlighting persistent gaps in pedestrian infrastructure and road safety.
UN-Habitat Recognizes an Indigenous Settlement in Brazil for Its Approach to Adequate Housing
The 2026 UN-Habitat Scroll of Honour Award has recognized Aldeia do Espraiado – Tekoa Ara Hovy, in Maricá, Rio de Janeiro state, as part of its international selection of initiatives addressing adequate housing and sustainable urban development. Established as Brazil's first Indigenous village created by a municipality, the settlement provides a permanent home for a Guarani Mbyá community whose 13 families relocated there in early 2025. Previously living within a state park without secure land tenure or access to several basic services, the community now has access to traditional homes, a bilingual school, a health post, a cultural center, a community kitchen, and water infrastructure. Developed with community participation, the initiative combines municipal investment with traditional building practices, connecting housing provision to land security, cultural continuity, and access to essential services.
Related Article
Latin America in Focus: This Month in Architecture, Inhabitation, Memory, and Cultural Exchange
From Learning Spaces to the Planned City
From the Classroom to the Courtyard: How 10 Brazilian Universities Rethink the Learning Space examines how university architecture in Brazil extends beyond the classroom to shape relationships between learning, collective life, and the city. Taking the Faculty of Architecture and Urbanism at the University of São Paulo, designed by Vilanova Artigas and Carlos Cascaldi in 1961, as a point of departure, the editorial looks at ten projects that approach the campus as a space for interaction and urban integration. Examples range from AT Arquitetura's Unisinos campus in Porto Alegre, which occupies an entire city block, to Lins Arquitetos Associados' educational pavilions at Unileão in Juazeiro do Norte, where new buildings connect existing structures through gardens and communal spaces.
Drawing a New City: Brasília, Fordlândia, and Ciudad Guayana explores how planned cities across Latin America embody ambitions to reshape society and establish new ways of living. The article considers two contrasting Brazilian examples: Fordlândia, Henry Ford's late-1920s attempt to reproduce an American industrial town in the Amazon, and Brasília, the new capital conceived as part of a national modernization project. While Fordlândia's imported building models and imposed routines struggled to accommodate local environmental conditions and workers' lives, Brasília's monumental plan by Lúcio Costa and civic architecture by Oscar Niemeyer gave physical form to a vision of Brazil's future.
Featured Projects
Doutor Leite Lopes State Airport / Bacco Arquitetos Associados
In Ribeirão Preto, Bacco Arquitetos Associados reimagines the Doutor Leite Lopes State Airport through an expansion that combines industrialized construction, timber engineering, and passive environmental strategies. The 10,840-square-meter intervention envelops the existing terminal with a new structure made primarily from glued laminated timber (glulam), introducing a material rarely used in airport infrastructure in Brazil. The prefabricated components enabled rapid assembly while limiting disruption to the terminal's ongoing operations, and the exposed timber structure reduces the need for additional finishing materials. Cross-ventilation, natural lighting, water features, and vegetation also help address the region's hot climate. Beyond the terminal itself, the project includes an urban plan for the airport's surroundings, anticipating future hotel and commercial development while retaining the existing runway.
Jeronimo Faria Lima Building / Perkins&Will São Paulo
Located at the intersection of Brigadeiro Faria Lima Avenue and Jeronimo da Veiga Street in São Paulo, the 20,500-square-meter Jeronimo Faria Lima Building by Perkins&Will São Paulo explores how a commercial development can engage with the surrounding public realm. Differing from a conventional office tower, the project introduces a sunken plaza with cafés, social spaces, and collaborative areas at the first basement level, extending pedestrian activity into the building. A pedestrian bridge connects the plaza to the main lobby, creating a gradual transition between public and private spaces. The building's two stacked volumes are separated by a landscaped garden level that interrupts the tower's vertical profile, while vegetation continues across its terraces and arrival areas.
Rouxinol House / Sergio Sampaio Archi + Tectônica
Set on a steep site in Jacareí, in São Paulo state's Paraíba Valley, Rouxinol House by Sergio Sampaio Archi + Tectônica responds to a 50-meter slope, views of the Jaguari River reservoir, and more than 300 surveyed trees. The 440-square-meter residence is organized across three overlapping levels, letting rooms open to the surrounding landscape while minimizing disturbance to the terrain and existing vegetation. The building's cubic form follows a 3.80-meter structural span arranged on a 9-by-9 modular grid, using glued laminated timber beams and columns supported by steel pilotis. The design also incorporates plans for photovoltaic energy generation, solar water heating, and underground biodigesters.
On the Radar
Estúdio Módulo Wins Competition for New Itaú Cultural Headquarters in São Paulo
Estúdio Módulo has been selected to design the new headquarters of Itaú Cultural on Avenida Paulista, one of São Paulo's main cultural and public corridors. Developed by partners Marcus Vinicius Damon, Guilherme Bravin, and Érica Tomasoni, the proposal brings together exhibition galleries, a theater, an auditorium, studios, and educational facilities within a sequence of interconnected spaces, gardens, and terraces. A public plaza organizes access to the building, while terraces frame views of the avenue. The façade combines white brise-soleils with colorful interior surfaces, filtering daylight and creating a changing appearance as visitors move along the street. The design draws on Brazilian Concrete Art while exploring the relationship between cultural institutions and public life.
Two Projects by Licuri Receive Recognition at the CITY'SCAPE Award 2026
Brazilian landscape architecture studio Licuri received two distinctions at the 2026 CITY'SCAPE Award in Milan for projects that approach landscape as both ecological infrastructure and shared public space. Parque Viva Energia, located within Vivapark Porto Belo in Santa Catarina, received a joint first prize. Designed around two constructed lakes that support water retention and flood control, the park combines preserved vegetation, native Atlantic Forest species, pedestrian paths, gardens, and recreational areas. Its landscape design also introduces dedicated play spaces that encourage interaction with natural elements. Clube Náutico de Araraquara, in São Paulo, received a special mention and the FSB Forum Italy Sport&Play Special Prize. Its 664-hectare grounds feature diverse gardens, preserved Cerrado vegetation, and more than 400 tree and shrub species.
New National Diagnosis Highlights Gaps in Brazil's Pedestrian Infrastructure
The Walkability and Pedestrian Mobility Diagnosis in Brazil 2026, published by the Caminhabilidade Institute, compiles data on pedestrian infrastructure, road safety, urban planning, and social inequalities to inform public policy. Produced in partnership with the National Secretariat for Urban Mobility at Brazil's Ministry of Cities, the report finds that nearly four in ten daily trips are made exclusively on foot. However, 14.8% of the population lives on streets without sidewalks, and 64.6% on roads where sidewalks have obstacles. The diagnosis contributes to the development of Brazil's National Urban Mobility Plan (PlanMob Brasil), advocating for walkability as a strategic component of urban mobility policy.
This article is part of our Regional Focus series, bringing together recent architecture news, projects, and emerging developments from across Brazil. Explore more architecture news and projects from the region on ArchDaily.

European Security Council: New idea or a repackaged hybrid toolbox?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:29:56 UTC
15:29:56 KST

The European Commission wants a European Security Council to counter sabotage and cyberattacks. Critics say it repackages the EU’s existing hybrid toolbox without addressing the unanimity rule that limits its power. Watch the video!
The European Commission wants to create a European Security Council to better prepare the bloc for sabotage and external threats. In her State of the Union speech, President Ursula von der Leyen supported the plan as the EU’s answer to sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions from Russia. “Europe needs its own counter-hybrid playbook,” she said.
The idea is not new. French President Emmanuel Macron floated it in 2017, and France and Germany backed it in a 2018 declaration.
The plan bundles three proposals: a leaders’ forum for strategy, an Emergency Security Protocol to respond quickly to hybrid threats, and a Strategic Enablers Instrument to invest in shared military capabilities.
The Council would sit alongside NATO and is expected to include the EU’s 27 members plus the UK, Norway, Ukraine and Canada. The emergency protocol, modelled on NATO’s Article 4, would allow a country hit by an attack to trigger a meeting of all 27 to coordinate attribution, sanctions and diplomatic response.
Brussels insists the plan is not a rival to NATO, which focuses on collective defence.
Experts and critics say the problem is a lack of decision-making power, not meeting formats. The EU already has a Hybrid Toolbox, Rapid Response Teams and the IPCR crisis mechanism. Without reform of the unanimity rule, they warn the Council risks becoming another forum without real power.
For now, it has no legal basis, membership rules, voting system, budget or start date. More detail is expected in the EU’s upcoming Security Strategy.

UN warns EU against cutting international aid in next budget

The United Nations headquarters building in New York City, U.S., June 8, 2021. (AFP File Photo)
The U.N.’s refugee agency has warned the European Union against “short-sighted” cuts to international aid, as Germany spearheads a push to slash the size of the bloc’s next joint budget.
“It’s an easy target. It’s much more easy to explain to the taxpayers that we are going to spend less money abroad,” Jean-Nicolas Beuze, the UNHCR’s representative to the EU, told AFP in an interview on Oct. 13.
“There is a short-sighted view of saying we are going to make savings by spending less abroad, but of course this will have negative consequences on our prosperity and our stability and security.”
EU leaders will wrangle over the 2028-2034 budget at a summit in Brussels from Oct. 15 as they push to reach a deal by Christmas.
Ireland, which holds the EU’s rotating presidency, last week suggested shaving some 140 billion euros ($156 billion) off an earlier 2-trillion-euro proposal for the overall budget.
But that failed to satisfy a group of so-called “frugal” countries led by Germany, who are arguing for deeper cuts at a time that national budgets are under strain.
Foreign aid already looks like it could be on the chopping block.
Ireland has put forward cutting the part that covers international aid by 17 percent, while largely leaving sensitive areas like funding for EU farmers untouched.
The UNHCR representative warned against cutting both humanitarian aid and broader development funding.
“Cutting the humanitarian aid would have an immediate and visible impact. It means that parents won’t be able to put food on the table, and children won’t go to school,” he said, pointing to a potential increase in refugees heading to Europe as a consequence.
“But we need the same efforts and focus on development if we want to get out of this vicious circle of creating dependency.”

With Yemen-Saudi war, Palestinians question Iran's goals

While some Palestinians supported Houthi attacks in the Red Sea during the Israeli genocidal war, others question their impact, especially as the latest round of fighting in Yemen that erupted since mid-September, and spread to Saudi airports and other civilian facilities.

Operations at the complex in eastern Saudi Arabia have continued normally but some employees have been asked to work from home, according to two of the people.
A fourth person said some functions had been shifted to global offices, adding that the fire was still burning into the early hours of Wednesday.
The facility hosts an operations centre which helps the world's largest oil company oversee onshore and offshore oil rigs, refineries, export terminals and thousands of kilometres of pipeline.
Saudi Arabia's energy ministry said in a statement that Tuesday night's attack, which came as fighting between Yemen's Iran-allied Houthis and the kingdom intensified, had caused a limited fire.

Washington reinstated its blockade of Iranian ports in July and launched "Operation Economic Outcast" on August 24, a campaign aimed at severing Iran’s remaining financial and commercial links with the global economy.
According to energy intelligence platform Vortexa, Iran’s seaborne crude exports fell to zero in the second week of September from a 14-day average of 230,000 barrels per day at the start of the month, and remained there as of October 5.
In September, Washington expanded the campaign to target Iranian airlines, further isolating the country and making links to the outside world more limited and costly.

Iran to step up attacks on shipping before US vote
Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.
Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.
Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit.
The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.
The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.
"The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices," one of the two officials said.

The latest round of fighting was triggered by Houthi strikes on Riyadh's international airport at the weekend that left 13 people dead and operations suspended in the worst attack since 2015.
The escalation compounds fears about the impact of the Middle East crisis on global growth, with crude prices sent soaring since Iran effectively shut the crucial Strait of Hormuz after it was attacked by the US and Israel in February.
"The Saudi economy is important for the region and the world," IMF managing director Georgieva said at a news conference during the Annual Meetings of the Fund and World Bank in Bangkok.
"In that sense, these developments have potentially negative spillovers for everybody, everywhere," she said.

France’s Only 155mm Artillery Shell Casing Factory Faces Possible Shutdown
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:28:21 UTC
15:28:21 KST

France’s only factory producing 155mm artillery shell casings has been ordered to fix safety issues with its industrial equipment.
If Forges de Tarbes fails to meet the requirements by the end of 2026, some of its equipment will have to be shut down, potentially affecting ammunition production, French media outlet BFM reports.
The prefecture of the Hautes-Pyrénées department issued the order.
The factory must bring its pressure equipment into compliance with current safety regulations.
The issues involve components used to operate hydraulic presses, which are essential for forging artillery shell casings.
According to the report, five pieces of equipment used to operate the hydraulic presses failed to undergo mandatory re-inspections on time. Another nine pieces were due for inspection by mid-August.
The authorities have set December 31, 2026, as the deadline for resolving the violations. By that date, all pressure equipment must undergo the required inspections.
If the requirements are not met, the affected equipment will have to be shut down.
The company could also face administrative penalties for failing to comply with the order. Criminal proceedings may also be launched if there are legal grounds to do so.
This is not the first time production at the factory has been halted this year. The plant was already shut down from mid-August to mid-September.
The problems at Forges de Tarbes extend beyond the condition of its equipment. In early October, employees told BFM Business that the factory relies on outdated machinery that is difficult to keep operational.
According to one employee, the equipment has long needed modernisation, despite the factory’s strategic importance to the defence industry.
Concerns have also been raised about raw material supplies and the factory’s financial situation. Employees fear that material shortages could threaten continued production.
French media have also reported difficulties in securing the metal needed to manufacture artillery shell casings.
The factory employs around 60 people. In 2021, it came under the control of the Europlasma Group after facing the threat of court-ordered liquidation.
The group specialises in acquiring struggling industrial companies in France. However, its takeover has not resolved all the problems at Forges de Tarbes.
The situation at the factory is significant for France’s defence industry, as it is the country’s only manufacturer of 155mm artillery shell casings.

Good morning, I’m Mared Gwyn. Today: European leaders close ranks with Zelenskyy, drones keep raining on the Black Sea, and an exclusive interview with the Spanish Foreign Minister.
But first: On Tuesday evening, a Russian ballistic missile hit a power plant in Kyiv without Ukraine having received advance warning from its Western allies and despite US President Donald Trump's claims of an "energy ceasefire", President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Alarm bells: Such intelligence gaps have been rare in the past, and naturally raise questions over whether the Trump administration has limited intelligence-sharing with Kyiv amid a recent fallout following the US-Russia diesel deal. Trump denied that Washington had cut off intel when asked by reporters last night. More in our top story below.
Back on the front foot: Meanwhile, Zelenskyy will meet Prime Minister Andy Burnham in London today, as European leaders begin rallying behind him following a bruising weekend of tensions with the White House.
It’s a marked shift in approach from the UK leader, whose predecessor was all too careful to avoid alienating Donald Trump in his foreign policy.
Burnham is expected to pledge tighter sanctions and increased military and financial support for Ukraine in the coming weeks, according to a statement by 10 Downing Street. The UK has also promised to accelerate deliveries of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs) to help counter jet-powered Russian drones.

"Our team has sent the American side proposals for possible next meetings and further talks. We are ready to meet in the coming days, and I sent this proposal to Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner," Zelenskyy said on Tuesday.
Shoring up support: Zelenskyy will also join EU leaders in person on Friday this week, on the second day of the European Council summit. He's preparing several additional meetings while he’s in town, in a sign of how badly Kyiv needs political support at this precarious moment, my colleague Jorge Liboreiro reports.
Zelenskyy could also hold his first bilateral meeting with Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, sources told Euronews, following a breakthrough over minority rights that has paved the way for further progress in Ukraine's EU accession negotiations.
Jorge also hears that the European Commission is preparing new disbursements under the €90 billion support loan this week.
EU officials and diplomats are confident that the 27 leaders will close ranks and rally behind Zelenskyy in a show of unity against Trump’s go-it-alone diplomacy. The summit conclusions may even express displeasure over the diesel deal, though this will depend on consensus between the leaders.
“We think the deal is regrettable. It’s against the strategy that we’ve been following for the past four years to put pressure on Russia and disconnect from Russian energy sources,” a senior EU official said.
“We have seen that dialogue with the US doesn’t always lead to full agreement in the way the EU and the US see things, but it's always better than not having dialogue,” the official added. “This is what needs to continue to be done.”
The pressure is also on for European nations to provide Kyiv with the air defence missiles it desperately needs, with Spain and Greece, both of which have the missiles in their stockpiles, so far resisting that pressure.
Speaking to our EU editor Maria Tadeo at the Warsaw Security Conference, Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said: “I can guarantee you that we have done as much as we can every time and we will continue to do it.”
Bring back the frozen assets: Albares also said he believes the EU should revive the debate around channeling immobilised Russian state assets into a loan for Ukraine, months after it was struck down due to predominantly Belgian opposition.
"Why should we put our taxpayer money when there are frozen assets and we know that there will have to be reparations at the end of the war?" Albares questioned. Watch.

Moldovan warning: The Moldovan National Army’s Chief of Staff, Vitalie Micov, told my colleague Angela Skujins that the drone threat is also having a marked impact on his small landlocked country, which borders Romania and Ukraine. He estimates that a drone enters Moldova’s skies almost once every two or three days, some laden with explosives.
“They are also having a significant impact on the morale of the civil society and impacting the safety and security within the region,” Micov added.
The EU response: The issue is expected to feature at Thursday and Friday’s EU summit in Brussels, where leaders are set to endorse measures to bolster Europe’s eastern flank and advance counter-drone infrastructure projects.

President declines comment on US-Russia diesel deal, cites lack of facts
President Ülle Madise declined to comment directly on the US-Russia diesel deal, saying she lacks the facts, but added that anything which strengthens Russia is bad.
Madise was inaugurated on Monday. She made Latvia, Estonia's nearest neighbor, her first official foreign trip the next day. She said she was expecting a call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy "within hours."
U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Friday that Russia would immediately release more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel onto American and global markets, with further shipments to follow. The US has lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.
"I can honestly say that the information about this so-called diesel deal is relatively new to me. And I have learned from experience that before taking a firm position, you should get your facts straight. At the moment, I don't have those facts," Madise said at a press conference following a meeting with Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs.
"Speaking in abstract terms, it is undoubtedly clear that anything that helps the aggressor to wage war is bad. Anything that harms Ukraine, which is fighting against the aggressor, is also bad. But that is speaking in abstract terms, as I do not currently know the specific facts," Madise reiterated.
Madise also stressed the importance of allied relations and NATO's functioning. "We all need a strong NATO, we need strong defense capabilities of our own, we need the United States as our partner in NATO, and we also need our partners' military personnel in both Latvia and Estonia. This is exceptionally important."
Madise said she expected to speak by telephone with Zelenskyy later on Tuesday, or on Wednesday. "And I hope to hear from him in greater detail how he views the situation you are asking about."
Madise also spoke about the close relations between Estonia and Latvia at the joint press conference. The Estonian flag was flying at the Latvian presidential palace on Tuesday. The new president arrived in Riga barely 24 hours after taking office — a gesture Latvia sees as highly significant.
Latvian President Rinkēvičs noted that Madise had visited Latvia very frequently in the past. "She knows our country very well, as well as all the areas in which we are developing bilateral cooperation," the Latvian head of state said.
Madise also addressed artificial intelligence and its role in Estonian and Latvian societies, including in relation to their respective languages. "I believe President Rinkēvičs and I also agree that now, as artificial intelligence plays an increasingly influential role in our lives, it is important that the languages and cultures of small nations — Latvian, Estonian and others — are properly and accurately represented in AI models," Madise said.
Rail Baltica and support for Ukraine were also on the table. Neither put forward ideas for accelerating the high-speed rail project.
Madise is due to travel to Finland today, Wednesday, for her second foreign trip.
Trump said Friday Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, with another 500,000 tons in November and a further 1 million tons after that — less than four days' demand for US transport. The US lifted sanctions on Russian diesel exports, though it remains unclear which tankers could be used given sanctions on many, and what condition Russian refineries are in after Ukrainian strikes. Zelenskyy said the deal would embolden Moscow's attacks. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the U.K .would be strengthening its sanctions on Russia.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,557,350 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:24:07 UTC
15:24:07 KST

Russia has lost 1,557,350 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 14.
The number includes 1,650 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,414 tanks, 25,535 armored combat vehicles, 162,789 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,195 artillery systems, 2,212 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,704 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,951 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

IMF urges action on debt as borrowing costs rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:23:10 UTC
15:23:10 KST

IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva holds a tablet device during the Managing Director briefing on the Global Policy Agenda during the 2026 IMF-World Bank Group Annual Meetings at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center (QSNCC) in Bangkok on October 14, 2026. (AFP Photo)
International Monetary Fund chief Kristalina Georgieva urged governments on Oct. 14 to repair public finances as rising bond yields increase the cost of servicing debt.
“Make urgent repairs to the fiscal house before the cracks widen,” she told a news conference at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
She called for higher revenues, more efficient spending and stronger public financial management, warning that the global economy’s resilience was reaching its limits.
Global public debt is on course to exceed 100 percent of economic output, the IMF said, as governments face growing costs for defense and aging populations.
The U.S. war with Iran has pushed up energy prices and inflation expectations, adding to pressure on central banks to raise interest rates.
Era Dabla-Norris, deputy director of the IMF’s Fiscal Affairs Department, said countries with high debt needed to act now.
Bond yields had risen by an average of around 110 basis points since late February, she said.
Greater reliance on short-term borrowing meant interest rate rises fed into government financing costs more quickly, she warned.
IMF research projects average government interest payments will rise from 2.3 percent of GDP in 2021 to 3.7 percent in 2031.
In low-income countries, interest already absorbs an average of 15 percent of tax revenues.
Georgieva also called for action to address growing global economic imbalances.
“To put it very simply, China needs to spend more, the U.S. has to save more and Europe has to invest more,” she said.

Ukrainian forces report restrictions on military version of Starlink
Ukrainian forces have reported that they encountered restrictions on Starshield, the military version of the US satellite communications system Starlink, on the night of 13-14 October. The service offers higher speeds and is critical to drone operations.
Source: Serhii Sternenko, a Ukrainian volunteer and founder of the Sternenko Community Charitable Foundation (a charity that supplies FPV drones to the Ukrainian military), on X (Twitter); four Ukrainska Pravda sources on the front line
Quote from Sternenko: "Last night, the operation of Starlink terminals in Ukraine was restricted. Connectivity began to drop when moving at speeds exceeding 160 km/h. As a result, a number of critical missions were disrupted. SpaceX likely took these measures at the request of the Trump administration."
Quote from Source 1: "Our Unmanned Systems Battalion commander reported at the morning briefing that the speed of Starshield has been restricted by partners."
Quote from Source 2: "Yes, this specifically applies to Starshield, the high-speed Starlink. It has been restricted to 100 mph, which is approximately 160 km/h. Our guys say this happened during the night."
Details: A commander sent UP a video clearly showing two Ukrainian drones flying above cloud cover losing connection and failing to continue their mission.
Sources in the defence forces explained to UP that standard Starlink (Starlink Mini), which is installed on drones, has a speed limit of up to 160 km/h. This is insufficient for executing certain missions. For an aircraft to fly faster, access to the military version of Starlink – Starshield – is required.
According to publicly available data, Ukraine began using Starshield in 2024.

Yasin Gungor
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella signed a security decree empowering authorities to block street barricades, ban road closures, and counter disorder ahead of planned nationwide demonstrations on Wednesday.
"In Colombia, the right to protest is respected, but there is no right to destroy, to block roads, to attack security forces, to commit assault, or, of course, to sow chaos," Espriella said in a video address. He said the measure grants the government "the teeth it needs" to defend citizens and "combat vandalism and urban terrorism disguised as protest."
The order comes after mobilization calls by major labor unions, including the teachers' federation Fecode and the Central Union of Workers, alongside left-wing organizations planning rallies across Bogota, Medellin, Cali, and Barranquilla.
Former President Gustavo Petro announced plans to join demonstrators marching from Parque Nacional to Plaza de Bolivar in the capital over demands concerning education, healthcare, labor protections, and living costs.
Espriella maintained that authorities will establish unified command posts to coordinate police, military, and municipal leadership, pledging that security forces will document disruptive acts while preventing demonstrators from stopping cargo transport or blocking emergency vehicles.

Russia launches 39 missiles, 128 UAVs at Ukraine; 4 missiles, 115 drones downed or suppressed – Air Force
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:21:50 EEST
15:21:50 KST

Russian forces on Wednesday overnight deployed 39 missiles and 128 drones of various types against Ukraine, of which air defense forces shot down or suppressed four missiles and 115 UAVs, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"On the night of October 14 (from 18:00 on October 13), the enemy launched a massive combined strike against Ukraine using strike UAVs and 39 missiles of various types approaching targets on a ballistic trajectory," the Air Force said in a message on Telegram.
In total, the radio-technical troops of the Air Force recorded 167 air attack weapons – 39 missiles and 128 drones of various types.
According to preliminary data as of 09:00, air defense shot down or suppressed four missiles and 115 enemy UAVs, including 59 jet-powered drones. According to the Air Force, this accounts for 90% of the total number of strike UAVs.
Russian forces used Iskander-M, KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Oniks missiles, as well as Shahed strike drones, including jet-powered ones, Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera, Italmas, and Parodiya-type decoy drones.
The main directions of the strike were Kyiv, Kyiv region, and Kharkiv region. According to the Air Force, a key feature of the attack was the simultaneous deployment of various air attack weapons from multiple directions, along with a large number of ballistic missiles targeting energy infrastructure facilities.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile troops, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, as well as mobile fire groups of the Ukrainian Defense Forces.
According to preliminary information as of 09:00, impacts of missiles and strike UAVs were recorded at 22 locations, with falling debris from intercepted targets recorded at eight locations. Some Russian missiles failed to reach their targets.
As of the time of publication, the attack was ongoing, with Russian strike drones remaining in Ukrainian airspace.

Pressured at home, EU leaders weigh China trade steps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:20:51 UTC
15:20:51 KST

Pressured at home, EU leaders weigh China trade steps
BRUSSELS, Oct 14 - European leaders gather in Brussels on Thursday to weigh up the future of trading ties with China, whose surging exports of cars and other manufactured goods are threatening to harm local industry and cause mass layoffs across Europe.
Other topics for the two-day meeting range from Ukraine - including US President Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia - to the Middle East, defence, migration, the EU's long-term budget and moves to enlarge the 27-country bloc.
For some, the summit may mark a welcome break from domestic troubles. French President Emmanuel Macron is facing student protests and sharp bond losses over a budget deadlock, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is struggling to get his coalition on track after regional vote defeats, and Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez trails in polls before an election.
Across Europe, mainstream politicians are under pressure from far-right and nationalist parties buoyed by a sense among many voters that the economy is not generating enough wealth to fund the levels of public services they expect.
Twin challenges of cheap Chinese exports and higher US tariffs are putting further pressure on the region's industrial base and leading in some cases to job losses - such as the 100,000 to go at Germany's Volkswagen.
GROWING TRADE DEFICIT WITH CHINA
Against that backdrop, EU leaders will start on Thursday by discussing whether a preliminary deal sketched out with Beijing to stem a surge of hybrid car imports is a good enough first step to keep talking to China about a wider trade understanding, rather than envisaging tougher restrictions.
Franco-German proposals have already been presented for possible measures to rein in a goods deficit with China that hit €360 billion ($402 billion) last year and was already €200 billion in the first six months of 2026.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said such a deficit was "unsustainable" and promised the EU would use every possible means to reduce it.
The EU executive's focus has shifted away from improving access for European companies to Chinese markets and towards allowing China to sell less into the bloc. Trade deficits exist in many sectors, including machinery, textiles, basic metals, chemicals and cars.
European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic called the EU-China deal last week a "very good result" but cautioned that it was only a first step in the wider process of rebalancing.
EU leaders are likely to tell the Commission to keep up its dialogue with Beijing, while determining whether to take further measures. But a senior Commission official said on Monday that dialogue alone was unlikely to complete the job.
Last week's Franco-German paper said there was an urgent need for measures to deal with imports of chemicals and PET - the plastic widely used in packaging. It also called for measures to limit companies' reliance on single sources for critical supplies and to strike back quickly against countries that harm the bloc.
The Commission is likely to propose the first such measure in December, even if leaders this week decide to keep talking to China in the meantime.
GERMAN U-TURN
The joint paper marks a U-turn for Germany, which only two years ago was a vocal critic of EU plans to impose tariffs on China-built electric vehicles. Now, it has signed up to France's protectionist stance.
"It is significant that a policy switch that had been boiling under the surface in Berlin for the last few weeks and months, is now official," said Sander Tordoir, chief economist at the Centre for European Reform. "And it is significant that the two most important EU member states clearly see eye to eye on how to deal with the second China shock."
Macron lost his parliamentary majority in 2024, so European policy is one of the few remaining levers through which he can still exert political influence and try to shape his legacy - he has to step aside next year when his presidential term ends.
Sanchez, who has pressed for a softer line towards Beijing as his country welcomes Chinese investment, could meanwhile be out of office after a snap election he called for November 29 as polls show the centre- and far-right could win enough votes to form a government.
By contrast, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni enter the summit from positions of relative political strength, although rising inflation and energy costs are hampering Italy.
The government's agenda in Poland has been stymied by the nationalist president and weariness towards refugees and fears of war in Ukraine spilling across the border have pushed voters towards far-right parties. REUTERS

Nvidia plans to announce $2 billion in new European investments within the next week, chief executive Jensen Huang said, as the U.S. chipmaker expands its backing for the region’s artificial intelligence industry.
Speaking at an event in Paris on Oct. 13 at the start of a tour that also includes London and Berlin, Huang said the planned deals would add to the $8 billion Nvidia invested in Europe over the past year.
He also announced new funding for four French startups: Doctolib, Genesis AI, Pigment and Entalpic.
Doctolib develops digital healthcare services, while Genesis AI focuses on robotics. Pigment provides AI-powered business planning software, and Entalpic uses AI to develop advanced materials, Nvidia said.

“Europe needs to get in the race,” he said, arguing that AI could drive economic growth and be developed safely.
He rejected calls to slow the technology’s development as concerns grow over AI systems operating beyond human control and the environmental impact of energy-intensive data centers.
European governments have sought a role in developing international safeguards against the technology’s potential risks.
Huang said open-source models could help Europe narrow the gap with advanced AI technologies in the United States. Such models can be cheaper to use and more easily adapted to different languages and local needs, he said.
Nvidia has invested in Mistral AI, the French developer of open-source models, and supplies AI chips for the company’s data centers.

China's factory-gate inflation quickens on increased energy prices
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:19:08 CST
15:19:08 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's producer price index (PPI), which measures costs for goods at the factory gate, rose 5 percent year on year in September, with the growth rate accelerating by 1.2 percentage points from August, official data showed on Wednesday.
This pace marked the fastest growth since June 2022. On a monthly basis, the PPI increased 1.2 percent, with the growth rate widening by 0.8 percentage points from the previous month, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
The faster growth was mainly driven by rising international crude oil and non-ferrous metals prices, changes in supply and demand in certain energy and raw material industries, and growing demand from emerging sectors such as artificial intelligence (AI), NBS statistician Dong Lijuan said.
Prices in petroleum extraction, refined petroleum product manufacturing and organic chemical raw material manufacturing rose 14.5 percent, 7.4 percent and 5.4 percent, respectively, from the previous month.
Prices in non-ferrous metals mining and processing, and non-ferrous metals smelting and rolling, increased 1.6 percent and 1.5 percent, respectively. Together, these five industries contributed approximately 0.63 percentage points to the monthly PPI increase.
Changes in supply and demand in certain energy and raw material industries also drove prices higher. Coal mining and washing prices surged 9.5 percent month on month, while coal processing prices jumped 13.6 percent, amid increased coal stockpiling ahead of the winter heating season, temporary supply tightness in major coal-producing regions, and expectations of higher international coal prices.
Meanwhile, recovering demand for construction materials like steel and cement, coupled with rising raw material costs, lifted prices in related industries.
Accelerated development in AI and coordinated computing-power as well as electricity infrastructure also boosted demand and resulted in higher prices in certain manufacturing sectors.
Prices in both electrical machinery and equipment manufacturing, and computer, communications and other electronic equipment manufacturing, rose 0.4 percent month on month, together contributing roughly 0.07 percentage points to the PPI increase, the data revealed.
Wednesday's data also showed that China's consumer price index (CPI) rose 0.9 percent year on year in September on higher energy and industrial consumer goods prices. ■

Pacific bluefin tuna confirmed in waters off southern Australia
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:19:02 CST
15:19:02 KST

CANBERRA, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- DNA testing has confirmed the first records of Pacific bluefin tuna caught by recreational fishers in Victoria, southeastern Australia, after two large fish caught off the state's coast in July were initially assumed to be southern bluefin tuna.
The fish were caught in Bass Strait, between the Australian mainland and the island state of Tasmania, off Western Port Bay, weighing about 165 kg and 131.6 kg, respectively, according to a statement released Wednesday by the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organization (CSIRO), Australia's national science agency.
Fishers noticed unusual features on the fish and arranged for muscle samples to be collected for genetic testing. DNA screening at CSIRO laboratories in Hobart, the state capital of Tasmania, followed by further sequencing analysis, confirmed both fish were Pacific bluefin tuna.
Among the world's largest and most powerful tuna species, Pacific bluefin tuna are more commonly found in the Northern Hemisphere but are also caught in New Zealand waters. They can grow to nearly three meters in length and weigh close to 450 kg.
Months later, anglers caught large numbers of tuna weighing between 130 and 217 kg off Lakes Entrance, on Victoria's eastern coast. Preliminary assessments suggest they may also be Pacific bluefin tuna, with genetic testing underway.
The discovery suggests the species may occur in southern Australian waters more regularly than previously recognized, according to the CSIRO statement. ■

Indonesia's Minister of Higher Education, Science and Technology Brian Yuliarto speaks in an interview with Xinhua in Jakarta, Indonesia, Oct. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Cen Yunpeng)
JAKARTA, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Indonesia and China are accelerating cooperation in technical and vocational education and training (TVET) to align with Indonesia's national development goals and rising industrial demands, Indonesia's Minister of Higher Education, Science and Technology Brian Yuliarto told Xinhua in an interview on Tuesday.
Collaboration between institutions from both countries is expanding rapidly, providing targeted capacity building for Indonesian students, Brian said.
"Several of our vocational universities have strong collaborations, both with industry and also with the universities in China," he noted, adding that this synergy allows students to receive training tailored to international benchmarks.
This educational and industrial alignment directly supports the Asta Cita (Eight Aspirations) national agenda outlined by Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, which prioritizes food security, energy security, electronics, semiconductors, and downstream mineral processing.
As the presence of Chinese enterprises in Indonesia grows, the country hopes these industries will actively employ alumni from local vocational institutions, he said.
Talking about the upcoming 2026 World Vocational and Technical Education Development Conference, which will open on Thursday in China's Tianjin Municipality, Brian said Indonesia aims to expand institutional partnerships and upgrade student capacity to meet Chinese industrial standards.
"When we fulfill the China standards, of course, we can fulfill the world standards," said Brian, noting the global footprint of Chinese industries.
Addressing global technological shifts such as artificial intelligence, robotics, machine learning, and green energy, Brian highlighted China's leading role on the technological frontier, adding that partnering with Chinese institutions helps Indonesia adapt its educational system to fast-changing global trends.
Chinese enterprises have already supported Indonesian universities by donating advanced equipment and constructing joint laboratories. Moving forward, Indonesia plans to expand double-degree programs, student and faculty exchanges, and visiting professorships, he said.
In line with the Golden Indonesia 2045 vision, high-quality economic development must rely on science and technology. Combining Indonesia's natural resources and large population with China's technological expertise offers a solid foundation for joint industrial progress starting from university-level research, said Brian. ■

Economic Watch: Tourists staying for more than the view in China's counties
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:18:31 CST
15:18:31 KST

NANNING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Five-star hotels had long been Li Na's default choice when traveling with her family. But on a recent road trip through Daxin County in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, she took a chance on Nali, a semi-secluded retreat surrounded by rice paddies and jagged karst peaks.
After just one night, her children were playing beside the irrigation ditches while Li was already planning a return trip with friends this winter.
When asked whether she had discovered a hidden gem, she laughed. "It's already quite well known."
Nali lies within Mingshi scenic area near the Vietnamese border. Mingshi is hardly a secret, and neither are the celebrated rice terraces of Longsheng County in the city of Guilin. Both are part of a broader tourism pattern in Guangxi, where county-level destinations have drawn travelers for decades.
Where visitors once snapped a photo and left, what has changed is what they do once the obligatory social-media photo has been posted. They can linger over a meal, try local crafts or make their accommodation part of the experience. For rural tourism operators, the challenge is to turn that stay into steady local income, rather than depend on peak holiday business.
Many urban visitors are simply drawn to the slower pace of rural life. Zhong Wei, for example, drove with his family from Shenzhen to Daxin County a couple of days before the National Day holiday began. Instead of a packed itinerary, he wanted "a place for a cup of coffee and a view of the rice fields."
Local tourism official Wei Wen said multi-day visits were becoming increasingly common, with some travelers staying as long as a week. High-end boutique resorts have helped raise service standards while supporting the growth of smaller, family-run guesthouses, Wei said.
The economic benefits are also increasingly remaining within local communities. In 2018, Chen Junming joined a pioneering group of entrepreneurs who began converting old village homes and vacant plots into rural inns.
Many businesses now weave agriculture into their offerings. During planting and harvest seasons, guests can wade into the paddies and try their hand at farm work, while restaurants and bars serve rice-inspired dishes and novelty drinks, including rice-flavored Americanos.
Nali alone now employs more than 100 people, with local residents accounting for about 70 to 80 percent of its workforce. Other villagers earn income from land rentals or dividends.
Across Mingshi, the holiday program featured concerts in the rice fields and evening bonfire parties. Where visitors once arrived and departed on the same day, "the new offerings are giving them a reason to stay after dark," said a local resort operator.
For this year's National Day holiday, five-star hotel bookings across Guangxi rose 59 percent year-on-year on Meituan, a major online lifestyle platform in China, while Fliggy, Alibaba Group's online travel platform, reported a nearly 50 percent jump in bookings for private-car tours in the region.
The trend is not limited to Daxin. At the Longji Rice Terraces in Longsheng County, guesthouse operators are also developing activities around a landscape that visitors have long come to photograph. Families can catch fish in flooded paddies, cook traditional bamboo-tube rice or join local residents in farm work.
Official figures show that in 2024, 282 households in Dazhai Village, at the heart of the Longji Rice Terraces, shared about seven million yuan (1.04 million U.S. dollars) in tourism revenue.
This August, a national policy directive encouraged counties to re-purpose vacant village properties rather than build new ones.
Despite the holiday boom, sustaining demand outside peak season remains a challenge. That concern resonates with local innkeepers such as Li Hongxi. "A room may be fully booked during the long holiday periods, but it still has to generate income for the rest of the year," Li said.
For Cao Shiwu, a tourism scholar at Nanning Normal University, the real test is not how many visitors come during a holiday, but how many come back.
For now, Li Na's return to Daxin remains only an intention. If she does book that winter stay, it will say more about the county's lasting appeal than another crowded day in October. ■

Netanyahu says he didn't meet Egyptian spy chief during pre-Oct. 7 visit to Israel. So who did?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:18:29 UTC
15:18:29 KST

"Egypt's intelligence minister was here. He spent 59 minutes on the ground. I'm turning to the security and law enforcement authorities. I want to know whom he met. Someone who met with him is trying to pin this on me." With those remarks Tuesday evening, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed that Abbas Kamel, Egypt's former intelligence chief, had visited Israel shortly before the October 7, 2023 massacre. According to reports, Kamel had arrived with a warning that Hamas was preparing a major attack.
Netanyahu's acknowledgment, delivered during an interview with Channel 14, has raised more questions than answers. On Wednesday morning, Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana told Kan public radio that Kamel had arrived in Israel 11 days before the massacre and had apparently met a senior security official. "He met someone here. The question is whom," Ohana said. "My assessment is that he met one of the heads of the security establishment. The prime minister is calling for an investigation, and so am I. We have no answer to that question."
The reported Egyptian warning is not new. Just two days after the massacre, ynet's Smadar Perry reported, following an Associated Press report about an Egyptian warning, that Kamel had conveyed a message to Netanyahu's office concerning "something unusual, a massive operation" that was being prepared in Gaza. The Prime Minister's Office denied receiving such a warning. Yet three years later, it remains unclear whether any serious effort was made to establish whether Egyptian officials had delivered information to Israel's security establishment, even if it had not reached Netanyahu personally.
According to previously published flight records, an aircraft associated with Egyptian intelligence landed at Ben Gurion Airport shortly before 10 a.m. on September 26, 2023. It departed for Cairo 67 minutes later.
Netanyahu insists that he neither spoke with nor met Kamel during the visit. But identifying who did meet him would appear to offer a relatively straightforward starting point for an investigation. The prime minister could, for example, ask Transportation Minister Miri Regev to have airport officials examine any available security camera footage or records from that day. Whether he has taken such a step remains unclear.
The episode also raises a broader question about Netanyahu's oversight of the security establishment. If Egypt's intelligence chief held a meeting with senior Israeli security officials less than two weeks before the massacre, how could the prime minister have been unaware of it? At the very least, the possibility of such an encounter taking place without his knowledge raises questions about the management of sensitive security and intelligence matters.
Netanyahu also offered an explanation for why he would not have met Kamel himself. "He didn't speak to me. Since when does an intelligence chief speak to a head of state? It's never happened to me. There's no such thing. He would always come with someone," he said.
Yet just two years earlier, Netanyahu had hosted Kamel at the prime minister's residence in Jerusalem. Footage released by the Prime Minister's Office in 2021 showed the two shaking hands and speaking during a visit by a delegation of senior Egyptian officials led by Kamel. While that meeting does not establish that Netanyahu met him in September 2023, it contradicts his broader claim that such encounters do not take place.
For now, Netanyahu's demand for answers has been made publicly on television. On previous occasions, the prime minister has issued formal announcements stating that he instructed security agencies to investigate particular matters. This time, however, it remains unclear whether he has issued such instructions or sought to examine the airport's security records.
'We do not underestimate any threat'
The controversy resurfaced last month when The Atlantic published an investigation revealing details of Kamel's brief September 26, 2023 visit. According to the magazine, the Egyptian intelligence chief warned Israeli officials that Hamas appeared to be preparing a major attack and urged Israel to introduce economic concessions in Gaza to prevent an escalation. The warning did not specify a date or provide detailed operational information. Flight records cited in the investigation showed that the aircraft carrying Kamel remained in Israel for just 67 minutes before returning to Cairo.
A former Israeli official interviewed by The Atlantic said the extraordinary nature of the visit should itself have made the urgency of Kamel's message clear. The fact that the head of Egyptian intelligence had traveled to Israel for such a brief meeting was significant. "The messenger was the message," the official said. About two hours after the Egyptian aircraft landed, Netanyahu attended a ceremony in Jerusalem marking the 50th anniversary of the Yom Kippur War. Reflecting on the lessons of that surprise attack, he declared: "We do not underestimate any threat."
The Wall Street Journal separately reported that Kamel called Netanyahu in early October 2023 to warn him of an impending attack from Gaza, after two earlier Egyptian warnings had reportedly gone unheeded. According to the newspaper, Kamel was growing increasingly anxious about the situation. The report reinforced the account first published by Smadar Perry in ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth in the days following the massacre. Netanyahu continues to deny that he spoke with Kamel or personally received the reported warning.

China heads for record trade surplus as exports surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:18:24 UTC
15:18:24 KST

China’s exports surged in September, putting the country on course to exceed last year’s record trade surplus as the United States and European Union press Beijing to rebalance trade.
Exports rose 36.3 percent from a year earlier, General Administration of Customs data showed on Oct. 14, well above the 25.7 percent forecast in a Bloomberg survey. Imports climbed 31 percent, leaving a monthly surplus of $133.5 billion.
That brought the January-September surplus to $938.1 billion, compared with a record $1.2 trillion for the whole of 2025.
Shipments to the U.S. rose 39.6 percent, compared with a low base last year when trade fell sharply as Washington and Beijing imposed steep tariffs on each other’s goods.
Exports to the EU increased 25.3 percent, while imports from the bloc barely changed.
EU officials have called the bloc’s trade deficit with China, which exceeds 1 billion euros a day, “unsustainable.”
Talks last week produced an initial agreement to curb Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the EU, though analysts say these account for only a small share of bilateral trade.
Beijing is relying on exports to meet its annual growth target of 4.5 to 5 percent as domestic demand remains weak. Retail sales rose just 0.4 percent in August.
Separate data showed factory-gate prices rose 5 percent year-on-year in September, up from 3.8 percent in August and the fastest increase since June 2022, as the Middle East conflict drove up energy and commodity costs.
Consumer inflation remained subdued at 0.9 percent, compared with 0.8 percent in August, the National Bureau of Statistics said.
Capital Economics economist Nguyen Hoang Nam said electronics prices had also risen because of the global AI boom and memory chip shortages. But falling prices in other consumer goods suggested weak domestic demand continued to weigh on underlying inflation, he added.
The International Monetary Fund cut its 2026 growth forecast for China to 4.5 percent on Oct. 13. The economy grew 4.3 percent in the second quarter.

Ex-EU commissioner Kadri Simson returns to politics as a Social Democrat
Former European commissioner and Center Party veteran Kadri Simson is returning to Estonian politics, this time as a member of the Social Democratic Party (SDE).
Simson, who served as European commissioner for energy from 2019 to 2024, plans to run for election to the Riigikogu in Tartu next March, marking a return to the city where she grew up and where her late father, longtime Center Party politician Aadu Must, chaired the city council.
Nearly two years after leaving the Center Party, Simson said she joined the Social Democrats because they offer Estonia a positive direction, not just simply opposition to others.
"Our voice in Europe has clearly grown weaker in recent years," she said, stressing that Estonia needs a stronger presence in the EU. "We must do more to advance Estonia's interests and support Ukraine."
Simson cited these among the factors motivating her decision to run for election as MP. The former EU energy chief also called for changes in energy policy, saying Estonia must reduce its dependence on imported fuels.
She said her decision had been nearly two years in the making, stubbornly turning down calls to return to politics in the meantime.
"But as the president said yesterday, you can't just stand by and do nothing," Simson recalled. "I couldn't remain indifferent either."
SDE chair: I wouldn't rule out a win
The former commissioner believes the Social Democrats can win next spring, crucially offering "stability, positive progress and European values."
SDE chair Lauri Läänemets noted that Simson's leadership experience would strengthen the party's credentials, adding that more politicians from all levels are expected to join their ranks as well.
He said the SDE, which has previously earned one seat in the 101-member Riigikogu in Tartu, is now aiming to win two. "I wouldn't rule out the Social Democrats winning the elections in Tartu either," he added.
While the Social Democrats will certainly benefit from Simson's energy expertise, the party chair stressed their ambitions go beyond just energy policy.
"The key question this election," Läänemets said, "is whether we choose a stronger, more democratic and unified European Union or turn our backs on the values that have made Estonia successful."
Kadri Simson was a member of the Center Party from 1995 to 2024, served as MP across four Riigikogu terms and was Estonia's minister of economic affairs and infrastructure before joining the European Commission.
As a Center Party member, she previously ran for the Riigikogu in Pärnu.

There's also returning luminaries such as Kyiv-based DakhaBrakha who blend Ukranian folk and contemporary sounds, and Indian violin virtuoso Dr. L. Subramaniam, who played the first-ever WOMADelaide.
"To have stood the test of time and become one of Australia's longest running and most cherished festivals is an enormous honour," festival director Ian Scobie said in a statement.
"But what makes it truly special is that the spirit of discovery, connection and celebration that sparked WOMADelaide in 1992 is as alive today as ever."
In that spirit, you can investigate Japan's ex-punks Seppuku Pistols, India's first all-female hip hop collective Wild Wild Women, Irish folksters The Haar, Afro-psychedelic Soweto seven-piece BCUC, the empowering dub of Jamaica's Hempress Sativa, and innovative accordion player Yegor Zabelov from Belarus.
There's plenty more for adventurous ears to unpack next March, and in WOMADelaide's upcoming artist additions.

'Blown out of proportion' — Domestic politics at the core of South Korea's rift with Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:16:27 UTC
15:16:27 KST

'Blown out of proportion' — Domestic politics at the core of South Korea's rift with Ukraine
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung listens to a journalist during a news conference at the presidential Blue House in Seoul, South Korea, on Sept. 18, 2026. (SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Seoul's diplomatic spat with Kyiv continues to deepen, but experts say it is less about Ukraine than about South Korea's own politics.
The East Asian country, traditionally counted among Ukraine's partners in the region, announced on Oct. 8 that it is recalling its ambassador from Kyiv amid a dispute over North Korean prisoners of war (POWs).
The rift started on Sept. 23 with President Volodymyr Zelensky telling the U.N. General Assembly that Kyiv had transferred two North Korean POWs, captured while fighting on Russia's side, to Seoul.
The move angered South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who accused Ukraine of violating a confidentiality agreement. Ukraine initially claimed that there was no such deal, with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha later downplaying the situation as a "diplomatic misunderstanding."
In a matter of days, the row turned into a never-ending tit-for-tat war of words: on Oct. 6, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said that Ukraine had privately apologized for the incident but that the apology was, apparently, "insufficient."
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry responded that Sybiha had merely expressed regret that the situation had escalated to this level, noting that diplomatic correspondence should remain confidential.
While there is no end in sight to the diplomatic stand-off, experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent argued that none of this was likely to affect the strategic side of relations between Ukraine and South Korea.
“Even now, (South Korea’s) Foreign Ministry says cooperation with Ukraine will continue, so hopefully a cooling-down period will come, and both countries can get back to what is really important.”
Instead, the feud says more about the politically tense situation of President Lee — and about South Korea's piling geopolitical challenges.
read also
An ambiguous partner
After the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, South Korea has officially joined Western-led anti-Russian sanctions, notably by restricting strategic exports and helping cut Moscow off from the international financial system.
In practice, the sanctions regime is not fully respected. For instance, the Guardian has found that Seoul is now exporting diesel by sea to Russia, after heavy Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries caused shortages across the country.
"South Korea joined the sanctions, but is partially circumventing them, and is not ready to openly supply Ukraine with weapons," explained Leonid Petrov, a Korea researcher at the Australian National University.
Seoul maintains this ambivalent approach because authorities want to be able to normalize ties with Moscow if the war in Ukraine ends, said Sydney Seiler, a researcher and former U.S. national intelligence officer for North Korea.
On the other hand, South Korea remains a donor — albeit a relatively minor one — of humanitarian and non-lethal military aid to Ukraine, with commitments totaling approximately $627 million since 2022, according to the Kiel Institute.
"And when it comes to arms deliveries, South Korea doesn't support Ukraine openly, but it can do this indirectly, for instance, by selling arms to (an intermediary like) Poland," explained Chun In-Bum, a retired South Korean lieutenant general and expert affiliated with the Institute for Security and Development Policy, a Stockholm-based think tank.
Another issue is intelligence cooperation, where South Korea is seriously interested in learning from Ukraine's wartime experience, Chun said.
"Even now, (South Korea's) Foreign Ministry says cooperation with Ukraine will continue, so hopefully a cooling-down period will come, and both countries can get back to what is really important," he added.
read also
Unstable politics in a country surrounded by autocracies
Ultimately, the Ukraine-South Korea feud was mainly about Kyiv's announcement seemingly getting in the way of potential talks between Seoul and Pyongyang, according to Seiler.
"Lee is interested in warming up relations with North Korea and ultimately in holding a summit with (North Korean dictator) Kim Jong Un," noted Fyodor Tertitskiy, an international relations scholar at Korea University in Seoul.
On the North Korean side, though, there is absolutely no interest in rapprochement with Seoul, experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent agreed. In any case, Seiler doubts the POW transfer would have much bearing on whether Kim decides to engage.
But since Lee cares deeply about this initiative, his administration is particularly sensitive to it, Chun explained.
On top of the diplomatic issues, Zelensky's announcement also raised some worry about the security of the transferred North Korean soldiers.
"It's quite well-known that South Korea is full of North Korean spies, many of whom disguise (themselves) as people who defected from the North," Petrov explained. "So, it makes sense that these kinds of exchanges should be done quietly."
But Chun believes that Zelensky's announcement at the U.N. General Assembly did not change much in terms of the soldiers' safety, as North Korea would have found out about the exchange anyway.
The development came at a particularly sensitive time for Lee, whose ratings fell for a second week in a row to 35.2%, an Oct. 12 poll showed.
According to Petrov, these ratings were also one of the reasons why Zelensky's move became "a scandal deliberately blown out of proportion" by Seoul.
Finally, South Korea's changing geopolitical situation also plays a role. With China, Russia, and North Korea in the immediate vicinity, authorities in Seoul are increasingly wary of the strengthening alliance of the three countries.
"Lee Jae Myung is mainly just trying not to irritate any of these countries," Petrov said.
But Lee's administration might not be "fully comprehending" the geopolitical shifts going on in the region, Seiler said, by insisting on attempts to appease North Korea, which "aren’t working," rather than prioritizing cooperation with partners like Ukraine and the U.S.
"In any case, Zelensky did the right thing" by transferring the North Korean soldiers to Seoul, Chun said.
"This was a courageous move, especially (since) they could have just sent them back to Russia — as a Korean, I am just personally thankful to Ukraine that they did not."

North Korea building military deployment, logistics capabilities through Ukraine war: US general
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:15:59 UTC
15:15:59 KST

North Korea is gaining valuable experience in long-distance troop deployments and military logistics through its involvement in Russia's war against Ukraine, the commander of US Forces Korea said on Tuesday.
Gen. Xavier Brunson told a discussion hosted by the Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington that Pyongyang's support for Moscow had strengthened its operational capabilities, according to Yonhap News Agency.
"They've learned how to go from North Korea to find themselves in Russia to move men, weapons and equipment there," Brunson said.
He said North Korean forces had gained experience in establishing supply chains, moving troops and equipment over long distances and mobilising military resources, extending their capabilities beyond battlefield tactics.
Brunson warned that Pyongyang's ability to incorporate wartime experience into its military operations could complicate deterrence efforts by Washington and Seoul.
He also said Russia had provided North Korea with military equipment, including electronic warfare jammers, in exchange for its support.
Turning to the proposed transfer of wartime operational control from the US to South Korea, Brunson reiterated his support for a conditions-based transition, cautioning against proceeding before critical military requirements were met.
He also proposed expanding cooperation with South Korea's defence industry to establish regional maintenance and repair capabilities for US military equipment.
In July, South Korea was monitoring reports of additional North Korean troop deployments to Russia, while Japan condemned growing military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang.
The two countries strengthened their military partnership after North Korean leader Kim Jong-un and Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a mutual defence treaty in June 2024.

Russia launches massive ballistic missile strike on energy grid: air defence brings down 4 out of 39 missiles and 115 drones
Russia attacked Ukraine with 39 ballistic missiles and 128 drones on the night of 13-14 October, mainly targeting Kyiv and Kyiv and Kharkiv oblasts. Ukrainian air defence forces shot down or jammed four missiles and 115 drones.
Source: Ukraine's Air Force; President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on X (Twitter)
Quote from the Air Force: "The key factor was simultaneous use of offensive aerial weapons of various types from different directions and a large number of ballistic strikes against energy facilities."
Details: The Air Force noted that since 18:00 on 13 October, the Russians have launched 39 missiles and 128 drones on Ukraine. Iskander-M, KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Oniks missiles were launched from Russia's Kursk, Bryansk, Voronezh and Rostov oblasts.
The Russians also used Shahed, Banderol/Dan-T, Gerbera and Italmas drones and Parodiya decoy drones. Of the UAVs launched, 77 were jet-powered.
The drones were launched from the areas of Russia's Millerovo and Oryol and temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in Crimea and from the waters of the Sea of Azov.
Early reports indicate that as of 09:00, air defence forces had brought down or jammed four missiles and 115 drones, including 59 jet-powered ones.
Hits by some of the missiles and drones have been recorded at 22 locations. Intercepted aerial assets and debris crashed at eight locations. Some of the Russian missiles failed to reach their targets.
Aircraft, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare assets, unmanned systems units and mobile fire groups from Ukraine's defence forces have been involved in repelling the attack. As of 09:00, several strike drones were still in the sky over Ukraine.
Quote from Zelenskyy: "Overnight, the Russians used 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast and Kharkiv. A targeted Russian ballistic missile strike specifically against energy infrastructure – the very infrastructure covered by the ceasefire announced by the American president."
Details: Zelenskyy said that the Russian attack has left at least 600,000 people without electricity, and blackouts could affect even more consumers.
The president added that the Russians have significantly damaged facilities and equipment at 26 energy sites and four oil and gas facilities. He emphasised that some people are reported to have been killed and injured, although he did not specify their numbers.
Zelenskyy called the strike deliberate and demonstrative, stating that Russia has squandered an opportunity to de-escalate the hostilities.
He called on the US and Kyiv's other partners to respond decisively to the attack, urging Donald Trump to introduce tough sanctions against Russia. He also asked partners to supply Ukraine with additional interceptor missiles for Patriot systems.
Background: On the night of 13-14 October, three people were killed in a Russian attack on the city of Kyiv. First responders are continuing to deal with the aftermath in three districts in the capital.

Moscow’s Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports suspended operations amid the drone threat. Vnukovo remained closed for more than eight hours, and passengers were reportedly asked to leave their aircraft.

One killed, residential buildings damaged in Balakovo
One person was killed and several residential buildings were damaged in Balakovo, Saratov Oblast, following an overnight drone attack, Oblast Governor Roman Busargin reported.
On Oct. 14, Russia’s Defense Ministry warned of a Ukrainian drone attack on the city. Busargin later said the attack had damaged several residential buildings and caused one death.

The area includes a Sberbank data center and a metallurgical plant, although the specific sites affected have not been independently confirmed.
One possible target identified by monitoring channels was Sberbank’s large data center complex in Balakovo. Construction of the facility is ongoing, with sections being commissioned in stages, meaning parts of the complex may already be operational.
The project, valued at 122.2 billion rubles (more than $1 billion), is intended to become one of Russia’s largest data centers. It is designed to accommodate around 3,000 server racks and up to 120,000 servers, with a planned power capacity of 82 megawatts. Shortly before 7 a.m., Exilenova+ published footage it described as evidence of an attack on the data center.

The plant specializes in steel and rolled metal products, including reinforcing bars and merchant bars. It has its own steelmaking facilities and produces more than 1 million tons of rolled steel annually.
Russian authorities have not publicly confirmed damage to either the data center or the metallurgical plant, and Ukraine has not commented on the reported attack.
Russian data centers reportedly targeted in recent attacks

On Oct. 8, another attack struck Yandex’s largest data center in Ryazan Oblast, reportedly triggering a major fire. The same day, the company removed the locations of its data centers in four Russian Oblasts from online maps.
