ICC judge calls US pressure ‘most blatant attack on the court’ – interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Almost immediately after former International Criminal Court (ICC) judge Navi Pillay was announced as this year’s Nobel Peace Prize laureate, Donald Trump’s administration struck the Court with sweeping sanctions. For ICC judge Kimberly Prost, however, the pressure from Washington is nothing new: the Canadian judge has been under personal US sanctions for nearly two years. “This is a pretty extraordinary attack on the court,” she tells LRT.lt in an exclusive interview.
When sanctions were imposed on her in February last year, Canadian judge Prost felt their impact immediately: her payment cards issued in the Netherlands and Canada were blocked. Although she managed to retain access to a few bank accounts, banking services remain very limited, and even small transfers are often blocked. The judge also lost access to paid services provided by Apple, Google, and Amazon, as well as the ability to travel to the United States. Even a French company distanced itself from the sanctioned judges and decided to stop paying their health insurance claims.
The latest blow from the United States is the imposition of sanctions on the ICC itself, aimed at financially paralysing the court.
“We're working to be resilient, but it's a very serious matter, which is why it's so important that everyone understands what's going on,” she stresses.
In an ironic twist, Prost, who recently visited Vilnius, was participating in the #Disinfo2026 conference, for which Lithuania also reportedly withdrew its support following pressure from the United States, according to media reports.
Nevertheless, despite the US attack on the ICC, Prost insists that it will neither break the judges’ resolve nor bring their work to a halt.
“The court will continue its important mandate to render justice,” she emphasizes.
You were sanctioned by the US a little over a year ago. What was your first reaction when you learnt about this?
We all – all of the judges, the elected officials and staff – knew that the executive order was there and they had always indicated that individuals would be added to the list as they were going along. It wasn't totally unexpected in the sense that I broadly knew that.
But I think I was taken aback because I didn't particularly see the basis where I was concerned, given my work. I just sort of processed it for a few minutes and then realized, okay, I'm going to have to adjust to this new reality.
Ironically, I worked for five years as the ombudsperson for the Security Council Al-Qaeda Sanctions Committee, so I was very familiar. I interviewed a lot of people subject to UN sanctions, but as it went along, it became clear that until you really experience it yourself, you don't have the entire perspective on what it's like.
How it has affected you personally and in your daily life?
It really does permeate your daily life because it affects things that are so average and sort of assumed.
First of all, all your credit cards are immediately canceled no matter what country they are issued. So, my cards were in Canada and in the Netherlands were immediately canceled, because of the influence of the United States in the financial and the SWIFT system.
Then there's the panic about banking services because literally banks can decide they don't want to do business with you, that could be a business decision even if they're, not American banks. <…>
Then there's all these services that are so permeating in our lives: computers, so “Apple”, “Apple Wallet” was gone obviously. “Google”, any services that are paid for. And you don't know what's going to be canceled and what's not, there's been a variation between the judges. So, the randomness also makes it even worse in some ways because there's no predictability. I make bank transfers, my bank will assist me, but will other banks receive the money or can people send from their banks to me? <…>
Then there's just the whole psychological effect of this, which is I've been in criminal justice work for pretty well all of my life, my colleagues – in human rights, criminal justice, and you're suddenly on a list with those purported to be involved in human rights violations, terrorism, and organized crime. You're put in the same category, that's very hard.
That just gives some of the idea of what we're dealing with. Obviously, I can't go to the United States. For some of my colleagues who have, for example, children in the United States, their visas get canceled or it's very complicated if you have a spouse or a child who happens to be American. I don't have those factors, although my siblings in Canada are very nervous about crossing the border. So far, they've made it.
The US say that you were sanctioned for your role in authorizing the ICC's investigation into US personnel in Afghanistan. Could you explain your this decision, and why do you think the sanctions were imposed?
I'm not really sure to tell you the truth.
My involvement is very limited. Six years ago, before this administration even took power, I sat on the appeals chamber temporarily, I'm a trial judge, replacing a judge, and we were faced with an appeal by the prosecutor of a pretrial decision refusing the authorization for the investigation in Afghanistan.
Why I was sanctioned six years after that, I have no idea.
This was at the very beginning, all of the allegations of a horrific crime by Taliban, ISIS, various military forces, and including a component of US officials and their activities in Afghanistan.
We unanimously, on the basis of what I consider overwhelming evidence and clear law, authorized the prosecutor to conduct the investigation, including the US portion. Now, the footnote to that is that about two years after, the prosecutor, who's faced with many competing areas of varying situations, decided to deprioritize the American component and focus on the other crime in Afghanistan and other situations.
So there is no investigation into the American component of Afghanistan, and I have no other involvement in anything, any of the investigations into the Israel-Gaza situation or Afghanistan.
And so why I was sanctioned six years after that, I have no idea.
I want to talk a bit about the broader pressure. President Trump and members of his administration have been highly critical of the ICC. At the UN he even described the court as “out of control”, you – “evil group of people,” and urged countries to leave the court. Has the ICC ever faced this level of political pressure?
Well, this is a unique angle. The ICC has long had issues that can involve geopolitics, if you put it that way, and these kinds of pressures. The United States, for example, at the early days under the Bush administration, was carrying out a campaign to have states who were parties, sign these, what we called Article 98 agreements, that they would never turn over US personnel. So that was a part of the same objection. But I would say this is pretty extreme.
I do have colleagues though, who are also subject to arrest warrants from the Russian Federation and have been convicted in absentia for their work related to the file in Ukraine. <…>
But this is a pretty extraordinary attack on the court. And what I emphasize here it's not because, “woe is me with what's happened in my life”. I can tell you, I sat on the Srebrenica trial, and I've sat on trials at the ICC, and what I see in people's lives by comparison, this is annoyances. But it's the purpose (and this is what makes this distinct), it's the most blatant attack rendered against the independence of judges and the rule of law – you must decide the cases the way we want or you must not do your job, or we're going to impose these measures.
That's a pretty shocking position for the government of the United States to take, in my view.
It's the most blatant attack rendered against the independence of judges and the rule of law
Following from that, when judges become targets of sanctions, and when the US appears to be actively and very openly devaluating the court's work, how significant of a risk is this, as you say, attack on the court, and how it affects the court's judicial independence?
I can assure you that it doesn't affect the court's judicial independence, and I think I've been very clear in every interview to say we will continue. We will continue to look at the evidence, the facts, apply the law, and do so objectively. Objectively, either way, not in favor, not in fear.
We will continue to do our job that way, and the court will continue its important mandate to render justice in these situations. I have no concern that that's ever going to stop. I don't see this as the end of the ICC, the Rome statute system or international law.
But we have to understand the seriousness of this attack. The secretary of state Marco Rubio said, “We want to tear down the ICC brick by brick,” in addition to the comments of the president in the General Assembly.
So their aim here is now no longer even a matter of speculation, and that's what we need to address. And these measures that they're using can be very crippling. They're not going to affect our core work, but all of the energy resources that have to be sent away from other measures we could be taking, are directed towards trying to protect the court, and now that's the threat – that they're going to hit the institution, which obviously has all sorts of implications for contracts and salary payments and all of those matters.
We're working to be resilient, but it's a very serious matter, which is why it's so important that everyone understands what's going on.
One of the biggest criticisms of international justice is that it struggles to reach the most powerful. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Yet it is quite difficult at the moment to imagine either of them appearing before the court. What do you think needs to happen for such political figures to eventually stand a fair trial?
I'll answer that question sort of in the abstract.
I will say about the process: we have issued those arrest warrants for those individuals. Arrest warrants carry a lot of meaning in and of themselves. There are legal determinations made not just by the prosecutor, but by a chamber, that there's sufficient evidence to warrant the issuance of these arrest warrants. And all of our states' parties are under an obligation to arrest. So that's the process.
More broadly, though, I think if you look at the overall history of international criminal justice, we are not the first court to issue arrest warrants implicating sitting heads of states. Obviously, there was the case of The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia of Slobodan Milošević and in addition, Charles Taylor in the Sierra Leone court was the subject also of proceedings.
What will happen in the ICC cases, only time will tell. But in those cases, it became a question of a long process. And ultimately, both Mr. Taylor and Mr. Milošević were tried. Mr. Milošević died before verdict, and Charles Taylor was convicted.
But I think it evidences that it is possible. It's certainly possible that arrest warrants will be executed, that the law will apply equally to everyone. And that's what the Rome Statute says – disregard official title capacity. So, I still believe that is always possible, and I hope that is possible as well in the context of the ICC. I know it is.
What we will see factually, only time will tell.
Lithuania has been one of the strongest advocates for accountability for crimes committed during Russia's war in Ukraine. We play an important role in a Special tribunal for the crime of aggression against Ukraine. I don't know if you saw, in Vilnius there is a large sign addressed to Russian president, which reads, “Putin, The Hague Is Waiting For You.” So again, I want to come back to this question that it is hard to imagine that he will appear there. How you personally view justice in such cases?
It's a great question. Ask me that on March 10th, 2027, at 5:00 PM, when I'm no longer a sitting judge.
I'm happy to speak to my vision of international criminal justice and the execution of these warrants. And I would say that, for example, back when I was at The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia and Milošević had already been arrested, but I know people who were there at the very beginning who expressed the view that Mr. Milošević would never appear in the Tribunal.
Again, we look at the whole process, what international justice can do and we'll have to wait and see.
But the specific case, I'll just not comment on that.
And we do have Rodrigo Duterte. He's no longer head of state, but he arrived, and those warrants were also issued when he was still a sitting head of state. So time will tell.
Lithuania is a very important and has been a very active supporter of the ICC throughout the life of the court. Very committed, and I hope that that will continue.
Lithuania is so invested in the ICC because of our strong support for Ukraine. Lithuania in general shows very strong support for the ICC, but at the same time, we are receiving some signals from Washington. It has been said to Lithuania that the question of the ICC is particularly relevant for the countries hosting the US troops. As you know, with geopolitical and war threats, it is a very disturbing question for us. Although, I have to say that the US have not said explicitly yet that they will withdraw the troops, if we remain the member of the court.
What would you say to such countries as ours, which strongly support the ICC and international justice, but also face geopolitical pressure?
I would be simply taking that to a very high level. Lithuania is a very important and has been a very active supporter of the ICC throughout the life of the court. Very committed, and I hope that that will continue.
Every country has to manage their relationships with states. My country has to manage a relationship with United States, for example. I simply hope that every country will prioritize what is for me so fundamental to, as I like to refer to it, our global village, which is the rule of law, justice for victims and an end to impunity for atrocity crime.
And I hope that they will find other ways, I hope all our states will find ways through diplomacy, through support, through statements send a very clear message that they're always willing to engage and to consult, but those are our values and principles that have to be maintained. I very much hope that, and I am pretty confident that Lithuania will continue with that path.
To echo what the Prime Minister of the Netherlands Rob Jetten said in the General Assembly, which we're all quoting now quite a bit, “Hands off the ICC”.
So that's my hope.

Beyond the Box: What Shipping Container Architecture Gets Right and Where It Falls Short
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Using shipping containers as the basis for a structure—also known as "cargotecture"—seems like a simple approach to building. Perhaps deceptively so. While it's true that containers are a quick, cost-effective, and often low-effort building material, and that they're durable and customizable, container conversions also bring their challenges. Without careful planning, the build process can be painful and the results underwhelming.
To understand whether containers are the right choice for a construction project, it's important to look past their industrial allure to the realities and constraints of steel boxes as a building material.
"Cargotecture" Challenges and Limitations
The use of shipping containers for architectural projects is an exercise in creating a beautiful and functional structure while overcoming an array of rigid constraints.
The most obvious is the width: at 2.44m, intermodal containers are only slightly wider than a caravan or motorhome. Side-opening containers can mitigate this constraint, or you can remove entire walls and connect two or more containers, though this brings engineering challenges, as will any alteration to the container's structure.
Another key hurdle is thermal conductivity. Containers are made from weathering steel, which gets cold in winter and hot in summer. Insulation and ventilation are critical, particularly for living and working spaces, but installing thick batts eats into the already limited space within the container.
There are a wealth of other challenges to navigate, from foundations to utility connections to the long-term mitigation of rust. Each, however, can be addressed through careful design and planning.
Overcoming Confines: Scandinavian-Inspired Tiny Home With Terrace
Despite a footprint of less than 14m², this tiny home uses a smart design to feel far larger. A clever internal layout creates distinct bed, kitchen, and bathroom spaces, while French doors open onto an outdoor terrace, extending usable space and bringing more natural light into the interior.
From Cramped to Open Plan: District 10 Container Building
Need more space than a container offers? Joining two or more containers can create a larger footprint, as demonstrated by this Dundee development, which uses more than 30 containers. Carefully removing internal walls and reinforcing the structure allows the individual units to function as a larger, more open-plan space.
Easy Access: Private Garage for Vehicle Preservation
Traditional containers feature doors at their ends, which can make access awkward, not just for home and workspace conversions, but for storage too. A car enthusiast faced this issue and solved it by converting a side-opening container that protects the vehicle while providing direct access.
Comfort in Extreme Temperatures: Dual-Layer Insulation
The thermal conductivity of steel means insulation is a must for any living or working space conversion. But extreme temperatures demand thick insulation, which can quickly eat into the limited space within a container. One approach is to combine internal insulation with external cladding, adding another layer of protection without taking up too much internal room.
Where Conventional Construction Still Wins
While shipping containers offer a range of advantages as a building material, for certain projects the cost-benefit analysis will still lean toward a traditional build. It's important to recognize the point at which extensive container modifications negate the financial and time advantages of modular steel.
This typically occurs when a build features complex geometries, wide-span clear spaces, or local zoning constraints that govern aesthetics. Container conversions can also have multi-decade lifespans, but they typically won't last as long as a traditional build.
Ultimately, containers shine in architecture when their intrinsic benefits—prefabrication, modularity, rapid assembly, the industrial look—are preserved, rather than modified beyond recognition.

Iran expanding attacks on ships beyond Hormuz to keep oil prices high; official vows full closure coming - report
A US military official said Iran has started using unarmed spotters in small boats to find targets, including US naval vessels, after much of its radar was destroyed
Iran is deploying new tactics against ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz in a bid to keep oil prices high and influence the outcome of the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials said.
Tehran has tried to control the strait since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on February 28, restricting passage through a waterway that carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war. The officials declined to detail the new strategy, but one said Iran began using different offensive tactics in recent weeks against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions.
Attacks on those ships have increased since, the official said. The shift covers both the type and pace of attacks and, they said, was approved at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership.
“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one official said. The other said Tehran would not let President Donald Trump lower prices before the November vote. “Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the official said.
The officials said operations would also expand beyond the strait into the Gulf of Oman and farther afield. “Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz,” the second official said. Both said Tehran is moving toward a point where no vessel violating its restrictions could pass. “It will be complete closure soon,” one said.
Shipping data points to an escalation. There were at least five incidents involving tankers and other commercial ships around Hormuz in the past 48 hours, including drone strikes, according to maritime security sources and reports to UK Maritime Trade Operations.
Suggested articles
- Iran fortifying nuclear sites; warns of land incursions into Gulf states if the US launches new strikes - report | i24NEWS
- Britain accuses Iran's IRGC of directing foiled RAF Fairford terror attack | Yuval Barnea
- After the deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia, Iran offers to open dialogue between Riyadh and the Houthis | i24NEWS
Attacks have surged to their highest level since the war began, according to independent data. “There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said. Ships have also been hit off the coasts of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates in recent days.
A US military official said that after the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, the Revolutionary Guards began using spotters to identify targets. Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran has been unable to stop a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official added.
The war, which costs about $3 billion a month, has become a key issue on the campaign trail. Trump is weighing next steps against Iran but has said he will not attack before the vote, while the US presses its naval blockade of Iranian ports. The Pentagon and Iran’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

US federal agents arrested a Saudi national who was an OpenAI engineer and charged him with installing a hidden audio recording device in an executive conference room at the AI company, the Justice Department said on Tuesday.
The case highlights growing security concerns around sensitive AI research as companies and governments compete fiercely for the talent and technology that could confer economic and strategic advantages.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, had worked as an engineer at OpenAI since July 2025, the Justice Department said in a statement. An email sent to an address associated with that name got no response, and it was not immediately clear who his lawyer was.
OpenAI discovered the recording device plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room at one of its San Francisco buildings on September 30, according to the department.
The thumb-sized device, which had a microphone and could connect to a camera, was concealed in toilet paper, according to an FBI complaint. It was installed on or about September 28, while its stored data was encrypted and inaccessible. Investigators later found a similar customized device in Alfozan's personal bag.
OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its internal AI models to identify the person responsible for planting the device and trace its origins.
OpenAI says employee intended to place additional recording devices in sensitive areas of its offices
The company said it had evidence that the employee intended to place additional recording devices in sensitive areas of its offices to secretly record meetings.
"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was terminated," the company said.
OpenAI referred the matter to the FBI, which is continuing to investigate. The Saudi embassy in the United States did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.
"Abdulrahman Alfozan allegedly concealed a covert recording device inside his employer's executive conference room to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology," FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed in an interview with Channel 14's The Patriots on Tuesday that he had never met with a foreign intelligence chief in his capacity as prime minister, despite official records showing that he hosted Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel at his Jerusalem residence in May 2021 and discussed security and diplomatic matters with him.
"When does an intelligence chief come and speak to a head of state? It hasn't happened to me once, OK? There's no such thing," Netanyahu said during the interview.
The remarks came after the prime minister confirmed that an Egyptian aircraft had landed in Israel in September 2023, just days before the October 7 Hamas attack.
Netanyahu denied meeting with the Egyptian intelligence chief on that occasion, saying he had been attending a memorial ceremony for fallen IDF soldiers at the time.
He also demanded to know whom the senior Egyptian official had met during his visit to Israel.
"I want to know who he met. I don't know," Netanyahu said, claiming that whoever had met the official was trying to "pin it on me."
However, in attempting to explain why it would be unlikely for an intelligence chief to meet with a prime minister, Netanyahu made a sweeping assertion that contradicts the documented history of his own meetings.
The official statement and photograph from May 2021
On May 30, 2021, the Prime Minister's Office published a statement titled "Prime Minister Netanyahu meets with Egyptian General Intelligence Chief Abbas Kamel and a delegation of senior officials headed by him."
The statement explicitly said: "Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met today with Egyptian General Intelligence Chief Abbas Kamel and a delegation of senior officials headed by him at the Prime Minister's Residence in Jerusalem."
According to the statement, the two discussed strengthening cooperation between Israel and Egypt and regional issues, and welcomed the ties between the countries and their joint efforts on security and diplomatic matters.
The statement also said Netanyahu raised Israel's demand for the return of the soldiers and civilians who were being held in the Gaza Strip at the time.
The meeting also addressed mechanisms to prevent Hamas from building up its capabilities and from using resources intended for the civilian population.
The meeting was also attended by then-intelligence minister Eli Cohen and then-national security adviser Meir Ben-Shabbat, who had previously held an extended meeting with Kamel.
The statement was accompanied by an official photograph of Netanyahu and Kamel shaking hands, taken by Government Press Office photographer Amos Ben-Gershom.
A video of the meeting was also published on the prime minister's official YouTube channel.
In other words, this was not a meeting revealed retrospectively through anonymous sources, but a diplomatic event that Netanyahu himself chose to make public through his office.
Netanyahu also met with the CIA director
The meeting with the Egyptian intelligence chief is not the only instance that calls into question Netanyahu's sweeping claim.
In February 2024, Walla reported that then-CIA director William Burns had arrived in Israel and met with Netanyahu and former Mossad chief David Barnea as part of efforts to advance a deal to release the hostages being held in Gaza.
Netanyahu and Burns met again in Jerusalem in May of that year, against the backdrop of negotiations over a ceasefire and hostage deal.
Such meetings are a routine part of diplomatic and security relations between national leaders and the heads of foreign intelligence agencies, particularly when those officials are involved in sensitive negotiations or serve as envoys for their governments.

Polls show a tight race.

A settlement reached last week requires the NGO to stop selling additional flights as part of the programme, while allowing previously purchased tickets to remain valid.

Israel could leave Syria but needs buffer zones in Gaza and Lebanon, ex-national security chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
04:52:36 UTC
13:52:36 KST

Retired Maj. Gen. Giora Eiland, former head of Israel's National Security Council, spoke Tuesday at the People of the State conference, the flagship event hosted by ynet and Yedioth Ahronoth. Eiland discussed what he described as Israel's fundamental mistake in 2007 that ultimately led to the October 7 massacre, as well as the differences between Israel's buffer zones in Gaza and Lebanon and the territory it holds in Syria.
"The great mistake always begins with an incorrect description of reality," Eiland said, referring to the Gaza Strip. "From 2007, through October 7 and to this day, the State of Israel has continued to make the mistake of mischaracterizing the reality in Gaza. The description is that there are two million unfortunate people there, and one day a terrible terrorist organization called Hamas came along, forcibly took over the Strip, and therefore it is right for us to fight Hamas, but we have nothing against the two million unfortunate people who found themselves in this situation."
"This naive description has nothing to do with reality," he continued. "In 2007, Gaza became a state in every sense, with clearly defined borders, an effective central government capable of collecting taxes, managing all the health care, education and sanitation systems, and so on. It has a completely independent foreign policy and its own army. The correct way to define what happened on October 7 is that the State of Gaza launched a war against the State of Israel."
Eiland argued that this flawed understanding of reality also shaped the IDF's assessment of Hamas. "For years, it was known that on the other side of the border there was a Nukhba force of at least 3,000 men, well-equipped and well-trained, with extremely high religious motivation, and just 10 minutes away from reaching any Israeli community or IDF base. Their clear and defined mission was to raid the State of Israel."
"In all IDF situation assessments over the years, from the division and command levels to the General Staff, when they discussed what might happen, they defined the worst-case scenario as a simultaneous attack by 60 terrorists. Wait a minute, you know they have 3,000, and you're saying the worst case is 60? How did such a huge gap emerge?"
"The answer is very simple. It is entirely philosophical," Eiland explained, arguing that the military's assessment was shaped by its definition of Hamas as a terrorist organization conducting guerrilla warfare through individual terrorists.
The sin of belief
According to Eiland, the same mistake was evident along Israel's northern border on October 7. "In 2014, Hezbollah established the Radwan Force, numbering 6,000 terrorists. Gradually, they moved closer to the border, building bunkers and infrastructure. The formal mission of the 91st Division is to defend the Galilee, but it did not prepare for defense."
"To do that, you need to implement the principles of defense: depth and reserves. What did the Galilee Division actually have at 6:30 a.m. on October 7? A thin line of outposts, no depth, no second line, no reserves and, most importantly, no available firepower capable of effectively delivering a large volume of fire against points of infiltration."
Eiland argued that the series of failures was not the result of a mistaken strategic conception, but something more fundamental.
"You first adopt a belief about what will happen and what will not happen, and from that moment you arrange the facts to fit that belief," he said. "Your brain is flexible enough to adapt reality to the belief instead of the other way around."
"That is worse than a mistaken conception, because a conception at least supposedly reflects a flawed thought process, but still a thought process. I'm talking about belief. Belief that has no rational basis, whose entire foundation is emotional and is built on many false assumptions that I developed over the years and never even examine."
Despite his criticism, Eiland identified two areas in which he believes the IDF has improved over the past three years. The first is basic military discipline, which he described as "appalling on October 7."
"The army has learned, and I think the improvement is real," he said.
The second improvement, he argued, is the recognition that Israel needs buffer zones along its borders. "In both Lebanon and Gaza, Israel cannot defend itself when there are communities along the border and, on the other side, an enemy 200 meters away with offensive intentions," he said.
However, Eiland argued that the situation along the Syrian border is significantly different. "There are many operational and tactical differences, and the need to hold territory in Syria is lower than in Lebanon," he explained.
He stressed that he was not proposing a unilateral Israeli withdrawal from the territory. "Israel can return to the border line provided there is an American plan guaranteeing that advanced weapons manufactured in Turkey or Russia will not enter Syria," he said.
"We can give up that particular enclave inside Syria. It is a risk worth taking, provided the strategic benefit we receive in return is far more important."

Over half of Amaha clients live with mental health concerns for a year before seeking help; 56% report self-harm thoughts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
04:51:15 UTC
13:51:15 KST

Many people struggle with mental health issues for over a year before seeking professional help
NEW DELHI: Mental health concerns can persist for months, sometimes years, before people seek professional help. By then, the distress may be affecting their relationships, work and ability to manage everyday tasks. More than half of people who eventually sought care had lived with their concerns for over a year, while 56.2% reported thoughts of self-harm before reaching professional support, according to the Amaha Mental Health Report 2026.The report is based on responses from 13,825 people who answered questions before beginning care with the mental healthcare provider between October 2025 and September 2026. Only 11.3% sought help within a month of experiencing mental health concerns.Dr Amit Malik, psychiatrist, founder and CEO of Amaha, said, “India’s progress in mental health must be judged by whether people can get timely, effective care, not simply by how openly we talk about it. These are the accounts of people who reached us; they should make us ask who is still unable to access care.”He added that friends, families and communities were vital to helping people recognise their needs and find care, and said finding treatment should not become “another test of a person’s resilience”.
Nearly 95% of respondents reported at least two concerns, averaging five each. Anxiety was most common (72.1%), followed by stress (67.5%), low mood (58.3%), relationship difficulties (55.6%) and sleep disturbances in over a third. The report also found a gap between self-reported distress and clinical diagnosis: 33% of those initially reporting stress were later diagnosed with depression, while among those reporting repetitive thoughts and behaviours, 32% were diagnosed with depression and 11% with obsessive-compulsive disorder.Before approaching a professional, many respondents relied on informal support or tried to manage their concerns on their own. More than half (54.5%) had spoken to friends or family, while 44.6% had turned to self-help resources such as books, apps, videos and online communities. Nearly a third had tried therapy previously, and 19.4% had used prescribed medication.Avoidant coping strategies, including excessive screen time, oversleeping and overworking, were reported by 82.7%. Another 15.4% said they had turned to alcohol or other harmful substances instead of professional support.The impact extended to everyday functioning. Only 12.3% said they could manage all their daily tasks, while 27.3% said they could not manage most tasks or any at all.
Young adults and working professionals formed the bulk of the cohort. Those aged 25–34 accounted for 51.3% of respondents, followed by 26.9% aged 18–24. Working professionals made up 64.3%, while students accounted for 15.3% and unemployed people 7.9%.Friends were the most frequently named contact in a mental health crisis (33.9%), followed by spouses (20.5%) and siblings (18.1%), underscoring the role of family and social networks in recognising distress and helping people access care.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Chief technology officers gathered for a panel at TIME’s Executives of the Year Impact Dinner: Tech & Data on Tuesday night in New York City and discussed the ways that technology has shifted how their companies operate.
Speaking on the panel at the TIME forum were Franziska Bell, CTO and executive vice president of The Home Depot; Fiona Tan, CTO of online marketplace giant Wayfair; and Sam Dozor, CTO of global e-commerce company Rokt, which sponsored Tuesday’s event.
Bell emphasized “always being grounded in the consumer experience” when thinking about how to adapt to new and emerging technologies, or what she described as “the art of the possible.”
One new AI tool that The Home Depot has deployed is Magic Apron, an “AI empowered home improvement expert,” Bell explained, that can help customers locate items in store, answer how-to questions about products, and respond to images uploaded by users.
Applications like Magic Apron, which Bell says has been rolled out in 2,000 U.S. stores, result from Bell assessing the “friction” involved in customer experiences and working to reduce it with technological tools.
She did not, however, discount the crucial roles that humans play alongside tech.
“I’m a huge believer in human-AI teams,” Bell said. “That’s really where the magic happens.”
Tan also spoke about the customer experience at Wayfair and how technology has been leveraged to help consumers figure out what they want from the company’s wide selection of products.
“A lot of times people don’t know what they’re looking for, they can’t describe it, and so perhaps we offer you a journey that will resonate,” she said. “We have to also innovate and provide them an experience that speaks more to them.”
When it comes to hiring new employees who can tackle consumer experience goals and integrate AI into their work, Tan stressed the importance of “adaptability” in young candidates who can seamlessly adjust to the quickly changing tech landscape.
Tan also said that it’s important to pair younger generations with older ones who have more experience at their companies.
Dozor said that the moment is prime for companies to invest in technology.
“The time is here,” he said. “The time is now, and all of us need to live it.”
One of the ways Rokt does this is by expanding the variety of work its employees can do using AI. “It’s amazing to see engineers lean into building product specs and designers writing code,” he said.
In that spirit, Rokt, he explained, takes a forward-looking approach to its work, always thinking about what’s next for its employees and what they can accomplish.
“Times are changing quickly,” Dozor said, and people can choose to live in the past, present, or future. “We’ve chosen to live six months from now.”

Three executives at very different companies gathered in New York on Tuesday evening for TIME’s Executives of the Year Impact Dinner: Tech & Data, during which they reflected on their leadership roles in the current technological age.
Giving toasts at the event were David Griffiths, the group head of artificial intelligence at Citi bank; Selena Deckelmann, the chief technology and product officer at Wikimedia Foundation, the non-profit organization that houses Wikipedia; and Gary Brantley, senior vice president and chief information officer at the National Football League.
Griffiths acknowledged the uncertainty that comes with rapidly developing tech, but he said that human decision-making will determine the impact of that advancement—for good or ill.
“Many of us have spent our entire careers waiting for this moment. Technology is finally catching up with our ambition. The future is so incredibly exciting. Yet, if we’re honest, it’s also unsettling,” he said. “Most of the choices about what comes next won’t feel historic when we make them. They’ll be quiet: who we listen to, what we fund, when we decide to wait, and when we decide to act. And the people who will live with those choices mostly are not in this room.”
Our “accountability,” he said, “that stays with us.”
Deckelmann also spoke about the enduring role humans will play as technology continues to affect companies like her own.
“Technology can’t decide how to live a good life or give our lives meaning. Our people and communities do,” she said.
Deckelmann explained that a typhoon had led her parents to meet, and thanks to Wikipedia allowing users to create, edit, and share public information pages, she was able to reach out to the New York-based musician who had written the page about the storm.
“I was able to do that because this technology that is behind Wikipedia encourages these very human connections,” she said. “And it’s these human connections and the sharing that comes from them that are essential to creating a future where we live good lives together.”

“Together, they taught us one of the most important lessons I have ever learned: You show up each and every day even when you are tired, even when you are discouraged, and especially when you do not feel like it,” he said. “None of us arrived where we are on our own.”

- The case adds to Trump’s wider clash with the media, as the outlets argue the ban was retaliation that breached First Amendment and due process rights.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – A US federal judge has extended access to the White House for CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists, deciding on Oct 13 that President Donald Trump likely broke the law when he tried to ban them, in the latest ruling against him in a press freedom dispute.
US District Judge Timothy Kelly issued a written decision elaborating on his Sept 24 emergency order that reinstated access for the journalists.
The news organisations and press freedom groups have accused Trump of unconstitutional retaliation against journalists for coverage he does not like.
Kelly’s order in September gave CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists access to the White House grounds on a temporary basis.
The judge issued a ruling called a preliminary injunction on Oct 13 that will remain in effect until he makes a final judgment in the lawsuit brought by the news organisations, unless an appeals court lifts his order.
Kelly wrote that Trump’s public remarks made clear that he banned the news outlets because he considered their reporting biased and inaccurate, and not because of national security concerns, as government lawyers later asserted in court.
“Simply put, that is unlawful viewpoint discrimination,” the judge wrote, adding that “no one should read this decision as suggesting that President Trump’s complaints are meritless”.
Trump appointed Kelly in 2017 during his first presidential term.
Past presidents have battled with the press, but Trump’s campaign against the media has been unprecedented.
He has upended decades of tradition by denying basic access to many major news organisations, launching personal attacks on journalists for their reporting and elevating media outlets seen as more sympathetic to his administration.
He has also filed lawsuits against multiple news outlets.
Trump announced the ban in September on his social media platform, saying CNN, Politico, and MS NOW “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report fiction and lies when they’re covering the President of the United States”.
The Justice Department has emphasised Trump’s contention that the ban is legally justified on national security grounds.
The outlets have said the revocation of their White House passes was unlawful retaliation for their news coverage and have accused the Trump administration of manufacturing meritless national security concerns to justify the ban.
The outlets said in their lawsuit that the ban violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for freedom of speech and a free press, as well as their rights to due process, meaning fair treatment from the government.
The White House on Sept 24 reinstated the CNN, MS NOW and Politico journalists after Kelly decided the ban “likely violated their constitutional due process rights”, and ordered their access immediately restored.
‘Coerce better coverage’
The judge held a hearing on Oct 8 to hear arguments from the news outlets and the Justice Department on whether to extend the protection for the journalists against being barred from the White House.
The Justice Department defended the bans as fair and justified.
“Here we have the unusual situation where the President himself has said he wants to chill speech. He wants to coerce better coverage,” Theodore Boutrous, an attorney for the outlets, told Kelly during the hearing.
“CNN, MS NOW and Politico engaged in apparently indefensible conduct,” said Justice Department lawyer Michael Velchik.
The legal battle is being waged just weeks before the Nov 3 US midterm elections in which Trump’s fellow Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress.
Trump’s job approval ratings are at record lows in opinion polls amid concerns over issues such as inflation and the Iran war. REUTERS

The Federal Court ruled that then-Environment and Water Minister Tanya Plibersek's decision in 2024 to grant an Aboriginal protection order over part of the site of a gold mine project located about 180 km west of Sydney was invalid.
Regis Resources, the Australian gold producer developing the 1.1 billion Australian dollar (about 769.3 million U.S. dollar) McPhillamys Gold Project, challenged Plibersek's ruling in the courts, declaring that the protection order meant the site was no longer financially feasible.
The protection order, which related to a river considered significant to the local Aboriginal people, prevented Regis Resources from building a tailings dam to store mining byproducts near the river's headwaters.
Handing down his decision on Wednesday, Federal Court Justice James Stellios made no ruling on the merits of the heritage protection claim, but said Plibersek's declaration was invalid due to a material process failure.
"Consequently, the declaration made by the minister was made without authority," he said, adding that the proposal would be sent back to the current federal environment and water minister for consideration.
Speaking ahead of the ruling being announced, NSW Premier Chris Minns said he wanted the mine to go ahead.
Regis Resources said in its annual report for 2026 in August that it was advancing a strategy aimed at developing the project as soon as possible.
"We remain committed to McPhillamys, which has the potential to become not only a long-life, low-cost operation but also the core of a significant new mining hub," it said.
According to the company, the mine will produce 190,000 ounces of gold per year on average. ■

World Insights: Germany's CDU recalibrates strategy amid economic woes

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:40:40 CST
13:40:40 KST

BERLIN, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Germany's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) concluded a two-day closed-door leadership meeting on Monday, vowing to regain voter trust through a renewed focus on economic affordability, social justice and security.
The meeting took place amid mounting domestic political pressure, with Germany facing economic anxieties, rising living costs and growing voter dissatisfaction.
At a press conference following the meeting, German Chancellor and CDU leader Friedrich Merz said the party must work its way out of a "crisis of trust."
"Life has become more expensive in recent years. People notice this and simultaneously feel a growing sense of injustice," Merz said, stressing that the country is facing pressure to change.
To address the immediate cost-of-living crisis, the CDU leadership pledged to push for financial relief, specifically targeting energy costs.
The party plans to use budgetary room to lower the electricity tax to the European minimum.
According to Merz, if Germany's economic growth consolidates at the projected level, tax revenue at the federal level could provide the 5 billion euros (5.58 billion U.S. dollars) needed for the tax cut.
Last week, the German government sharply raised its economic growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3 percent from 0.5 percent, noting that exports and government consumption were the main impetus for strong growth in the first half of the year.
However, the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry warned last week that despite the improved economic outlook, private investments and domestic demand are failing to gain momentum.
"What companies need now is a determined reform agenda, including reducing costs, cutting bureaucracy, speeding up processes and modernizing infrastructure," said Helena Melnikov, the chamber's chief executive.
"In all these areas, the federal government must shift up three gears," Melnikov said.
Merz and CDU Secretary General Franziska Hoppermann both noted that the party's new approach is built on affordability, justice and security.
The three keywords have captured "the general mood of the people," said Hoppermann.
President of the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce Peter Adrian said reducing the electricity tax is long overdue.
"Germany has some of the highest electricity prices in Europe," Adrian said, noting that what matters now is "swift action following these words."
"Given the cost burden on businesses, every month counts," he said.
The CDU's recalibration comes as Germany's political landscape grows increasingly fragmented.
Merz expressed concerns over the recent election of the first far-right Alternative for Germany state parliament president in Saxony-Anhalt, noting that it is particularly alarming that the candidate received votes from lawmakers outside his own party.
The CDU leadership meeting also coincided with a sudden shake-up in the federal government.
Baerbel Bas on Monday announced her resignation as federal minister of labor and social affairs and as co-chair of the Social Democratic Party. Alexander Schweitzer, former state premier of Rhineland-Palatinate, will succeed her.
Despite the abrupt cabinet change, Merz signaled a commitment to legislative continuity to push forward the reforms. ■

Takaichi says Japan, U.S. in talks on tightening rules for U.S. troops' off-duty conduct
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:40:37 CST
13:40:37 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said at a House of Representatives committee session Tuesday that Japan and the United States have launched senior working-level consultations following the alleged murder of a local woman by a U.S. Marine stationed in the southern prefecture of Okinawa, public broadcaster NHK reported.
During questioning at the session, ruling Liberal Democratic Party lawmaker Masahisa Miyazaki pointed out that similar incidents keep occurring despite Japan's repeated requests that the U.S. side enforce discipline.
In response, Takaichi said the Japan-U.S. senior working-level consultations launched last week would discuss effective preventive measures, and that the Japanese government would do everything possible to address the case.
Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi told the same session that some matters need further review, and concrete measures should be put forward as soon as possible.
On Oct. 3, a 39-year-old Japanese woman was found dead at a hotel in Naha, the capital of Okinawa. A 20-year-old U.S. Marine stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma, identified as Devin Ballard, was arrested by Okinawa police the following day on suspicion of murdering the woman and stealing her wallet and other belongings. Ballard has denied the allegations.
The incident prompted the Okinawa prefectural government to call for a fundamental review of the Japan-U.S. Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA), which has long been criticized as overly protective of U.S. base service members. However, the central government has not yet announced any plan to revise the agreement.
Signed by Japan and the United States in 1960, the SOFA governs the legal status of U.S. forces stationed in Japan. Under the agreement, the United States has the primary right to exercise jurisdiction over offenses allegedly committed by U.S. service members in the performance of official duty. For off-duty offenses, Japan generally has the primary right of jurisdiction, but if the suspect is already in U.S. custody, U.S. authorities in principle retain custody until Japan files charges.
This means that once a U.S. service member suspected of an offense returns to a U.S. base in Japan, whether the suspect is handed over to Japanese police rests largely with the U.S. military, and many cases involving U.S. military personnel in Japan have gone unresolved. ■

Economic Watch: From crop planting to dental health: China's AI taking root in ASEAN
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:40:35 CST
13:40:35 KST

NANNING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- "Can blueberries grow on my land?" For many farmers, introducing a new crop is an appealing opportunity, but taking the risk on untested soil can be daunting.
Now, Landy AI, an agricultural large language model developed by a Chinese company, is helping more than one million farmers across China and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) explore new possibilities lying beneath their feet.
By marking out the location of the farmland on a GPS map and entering the crop they want to grow, users can instantly get a report assessing the suitability of the candidate crop for the area and their potential returns.
This is only one of many functions supported by the model developed by JJR Science & Technology Group Co., Ltd., a smart agriculture company based in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.
The model is among products displayed at the China-ASEAN Artificial Intelligence Application Cooperation Center in Nanning, the regional capital. The center was founded last year, when China-ASEAN bilateral trade exceeded 1 trillion U.S. dollars for the first time. Since then, the center has cataloged more than 1,000 potential AI scenarios, opened 279 to developers, set up offices in Vietnam, Laos, and Malaysia, backed more than 30 cross-border projects, and assembled an alliance of 55 companies.
Guangxi, a key gateway of China to ASEAN, is leveraging its geographical advantages, technological strengths and shared characteristics with ASEAN markets to develop AI solutions tailored to local needs and meet the region's growing demand for AI applications.
JJR is one example of a company embracing the AI trend. Established in 2008, it began developing Landy AI in 2024. Since then, the firm has collected a vast amount of data, which includes temperature, precipitation and sunlight across different areas, as well as characteristics, production processes and marketing strategies for various crops.
Together, they enable the model to support farmers' decision-making on pre-production investment, in-production technique and post-production sales.
Two years after its launch, Landy AI now supports six languages: Chinese, English, Lao, Thai, Khmer and Malay. The company has also developed an AI-powered orchard inspection system that can collect real-time weather, pest and soil data through different sensors, as well as an AI vision system that monitors crop growth and identifies risks from pests and diseases.
In Cambodia's Kampong Chhnang Province, JJR's AI helps arrange equipment, such as sprinkler and drip irrigation systems in vegetable greenhouses. In Pakse, Laos, more than 4,000 mu (about 267 hectares) of banana plantations are managed with greater precision through the company's new tech.
The popularity of AI agricultural applications in ASEAN markets is no coincidence. "Many Southeast Asian countries grow tropical crops such as bananas, dragon fruit and durian, which align well with Guangxi's planting strengths," said Lin Zhongda, head of the international business department at JJR. Guangxi alone produced nearly one-seventh of China's fruit in 2025.
Applied across more than 2 million mu of farmland in China and ASEAN countries, the company's smart agriculture solutions are expected to reduce labor costs by more than 20 percent, said Chen Xiujuan, director of JJR's management center. She added that the age of Landy AI's users ranges from 20 to 60, which aligns with the product's original purpose.
"Seasoned farmers are showing strong interest and demand for professional agricultural knowledge and AI assistants to help them grow new opportunities," Chen said. "Young people committed to rural revitalization can use our AI to make up for their lack of experience."
From Guangxi, AI is also playing a stronger role in healthcare, benefiting ASEAN countries. At Guangxi Medical University College of Stomatology, a multilingual AI interpretation system developed by its affiliated hospital enables real-time translation between Chinese and more than 10 Southeast Asian languages, with a focus on dental terminology, according to Kuang Hai, deputy Party secretary of the hospital.
Meanwhile, a system combining AI with VR allows dentists from ASEAN countries to practice clinical procedures in immersive virtual environments without having to travel across borders.
Kuang, who specializes in cleft lip and palate treatment and has led multiple surgical missions in Laos, said the hospital is also using AI to develop a speech assessment and rehabilitation platform for patients suffering from the condition. The platform is now being used by some in Laos.
Many patients continue to have speech difficulties after surgery due to poor coordination of their lip muscles, but speech rehabilitation is often overlooked, said Kuang. "The platform uses AI to analyze patients' speech, identify problems and provide targeted guidance and exercises online. This saves patients the time and expense of traveling to the hospital for therapy and improves rehabilitation outcomes," Kuang added.
So far, the platform has served more than 2,000 patient visits, including those from remote mountainous areas of Guangxi. In addition to Mandarin, it also supports Lao.
Beyond the applications, Guangxi is also working on the computing power needed to support real-world AI deployment.
In Nanning, RunDo, a platform operated by Runjian Co., Ltd., monitors almost 300 megawatts of solar capacity across nearly 3,000 sites in Malaysia remotely, with drones and AI replacing manual inspections. The platform has boosted maintenance efficiency by over 30 percent and cut labor costs by more than 20 percent, according to the company's data.
Runjian's token factory in Nanning can generate up to 200 billion tokens per hour. "We package computing power into standardized token services that users can access on demand, much like electricity or water," said Huang Haijiang, executive vice president of Runjian's token business division.
This allows users to avoid the costs and complexity of building their own computing infrastructure and fine-tuning AI models, while paying only for what they use, Huang added.
Guangxi's efforts are part of a broader national push to expand AI applications and explore overseas markets.
Guidelines issued by the State Council last week to accelerate the development of new quality productive forces highlighted the need to advance the "AI Plus" initiative and promote high-standard opening up. This points to new opportunities for AI cooperation between China and ASEAN, as the two sides have remained each other's largest trading partner for six consecutive years.
At the 23rd China-ASEAN Expo held last month, 296 AI companies participated, up 48 percent from the previous edition.
Xie Zhujun, deputy director of the information center at the Guangxi Academy of Social Sciences, said China-ASEAN digital cooperation is geared toward long-term coordination, has broad potential to drive the real economy and will bring lasting benefits to people across the region. ■

Russian strikes hit key power plant in Kyiv, Zelensky says
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher

Russian strikes hit key power plant in Kyiv, Zelensky says
- Published
A key energy facility supplying Kyiv with heating and electricity has been hit in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
Darnytska CHP-4, or CHPP-4, and a residential building were hit in a strike the president said came with "no early warning from our partners".
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said two people had been killed and 21 injured in the missile strike on the apartment block late on Tuesday. He said "several energy facilities" in Kyiv had been hit without giving more detail.
Kyiv has reported multiple Russian strikes since US President Donald Trump said an energy ceasefire had been agreed by Russia and Ukraine two days ago.
In the early hours of Wednesday, Klitschko said the "massive missile attacks" had knocked out power to parts of Kyiv.
Kyiv officials have urged residents to stay in shelters after declaring a red alert due to a "missile threat".
Following the strikes on Tuesday, Zelensky said: "Ukraine supported an energy ceasefire. Russia is targeting yet another power plant and the lives of our people.
"This is absolutely unjust: when they are destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches," he added.
"It is important that the world does not stay silent about this. And it is important that the United States really see what is happening and who is responsible for this war continuing."
It is the second night in a row Kyiv has been hit by Russian missiles, and comes as Zelensky prepares to meet UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at Downing Street on Wednesday to discuss accelerating air defence supplies to Kyiv.
Following strikes on Monday night, there was speculation America had cut off access to key intelligence enabling Ukraine to track incoming threats.
Earlier on Tuesday, Trump denied that was the case.
"We are helping them and we are sharing intel," he said.
"We want the war to end. So we're working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end."
Asked about Russian strikes on Ukrainian energy sites, Trump said: "Ukraine hit many sites the day before."
But he demurred when asked if Russia had broken a ceasefire. He said both countries want the war to "come to an end" but "just don't know how to get there".
It comes after Zelensky said on Sunday that a 60-day ceasefire would allow his country to hold presidential elections, following comments from Trump that "it's time for Ukraine to get a new president".
Following Trump's announcement on Sunday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said Ukraine doesn't deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.
Lavrov added that under any ceasefire, Europe would be able to "pump [Ukraine] with new weapons" for it to continue the war.
CHPP-4, which provides heating and electricity to the Dniprovskyi district and parts of the Darnytskyi district, has been hit multiple times during the war.
It was severely damaged in a separate Russian missile attack in February this year, which forced it to shut down.
That strike left more than 1,000 residential buildings without heating and hot water, along with 47 schools, 72 kindergartens and 18 medical institutions, according to Reuters.

Danish supermarkets review cyber risks after attacks on French grocery chains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

A hacking incident affecting refrigeration systems in hundreds of French stores has prompted Denmark’s major grocery retailers to emphasize their digital security measures.
The attack struck supermarkets operated by Intermarché and Coopérative U on Monday, causing refrigerated display cases to increase their temperatures.
The affected cooling systems were supplied by Danish industrial company Danfoss. Food stored in the compromised units had to be discarded.
Danish supermarket groups Coop, Dagrofa and Salling Group confirmed that none of their stores were affected.
“We are naturally aware of cyberattacks, and we are continuously focused on both maintaining and adapting our security level,” Coop spokesperson Jacob Lassen told Ritzau.
Salling Group, which operates several Danish supermarket chains, said it does not use the refrigeration systems involved in the French incident.
However, the company expressed concern about the wider threat facing grocery retailers.
“We do not use the mentioned systems, but regardless, it is disturbing to hear reports of hacker attacks against the grocery industry in France,” Salling Group said in a statement.
The three Danish groups declined to provide figures on the number of cyberattacks or attempted intrusions they experience.
Nevertheless, they acknowledged that digital threats have increased in recent years.
Salling Group said it regularly faces attempted cyberattacks, similar to other large companies in Denmark and internationally.
Coop said it has established procedures and emergency plans for responding to potential incidents.
The retailer also maintains contact with authorities and industry organizations to strengthen its cybersecurity.
Danfoss confirmed to Ritzau that a “limited number” of its refrigeration control systems were affected by Monday’s attack.
The identity of those responsible remains unknown.

Kirsten Schwalbe becomes Denmark’s oldest person ever at 112

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.

More than 5,500 vehicles in Denmark are affected by a global safety measure involving the Swedish automaker’s EX30 electric SUV, according to Volvo’s Danish division.
The recall covers 234,000 cars worldwide, including 5,542 EX30 and EX30 Cross Country vehicles in Denmark from model years 2024 through 2027.
Volvo said the problem involves cushions attached to the front headrests, which could become detached during a sufficiently severe collision.
The defect could increase the risk of injury to the driver or front passenger.
“The recall concerns the front headrests, where a cushion in rare cases can detach in a collision of sufficient severity,” Volvo told news agency Ritzau.
The company emphasized that it has received no reports of injuries linked to the problem and is taking preventive action.
Affected Danish customers will receive direct notifications through e-Boks, Denmark’s digital mailbox system for official communications.
Volvo said it has also informed the relevant authorities.
In Sweden, where Volvo is based, slightly more than 15,000 vehicles are affected, the company told Swedish automotive publication Carup on Tuesday.
The automaker plans to strengthen the attachments securing the front headrest cushions in the affected vehicles.
The announcement follows another EX30 recall earlier this year.
In February 2026, Volvo recalled 40,323 electric EX30 SUVs because of concerns that their high-voltage battery packs could overheat.
According to Reuters, the company planned to replace the affected batteries.
Until the replacements could be completed, owners were advised to limit charging to 70 percent of battery capacity to reduce the risk of fire.

U.S. authorities say the country’s second-largest bank failed to report more than 5 billion USD in suspicious transactions, including some linked to national security concerns.
The Treasury Department announced penalties exceeding 1.2 billion USD, approximately 8 billion DKK, over alleged failures to comply with anti-money laundering and sanctions regulations.
According to officials, some transactions were connected to suspected Chinese money laundering networks and illegal financing activities near the southwestern US border.

That settlement concerns apparent violations of several U.S. sanctions programs involving Iran, Russia, narcotics trafficking and global terrorism.
A Bank of America spokesperson said the company was committed to addressing the problems identified by regulators.
“We will continue to support federal and local law enforcement authorities in thousands of investigations and report hundreds of thousands of suspicious activities each year,” the spokesperson said.
Under an agreement published by U.S. regulators, the bank must work with an independent third party to identify and report suspicious transactions that were previously missed.
The bank must also undergo an independent review of its systems for monitoring and reporting suspicious financial activity.

Rising numbers of serious traffic injuries have prompted Moderaterne, the Moderates, to call for stricter safety rules for people using electric bicycles.
Sten Larsen, the party’s health spokesperson, told regional broadcaster TV2 Østjylland that helmets should become a legal requirement for e-bike riders.
“E-bikes are both heavier and faster than regular bicycles,” Larsen said.
He pointed to an increase in serious injuries and deaths involving electric bicycles as justification for the proposal.
Currently, Denmark does not require helmets for ordinary bicycles or standard e-bikes, whose motors provide assistance at speeds of up to 25 kilometers per hour.
However, helmets are already mandatory for speed pedelecs, which can provide motor assistance up to 45 kilometers per hour.
According to the Danish Road Directorate, 200 e-bike riders were injured in traffic accidents in 2025, including 133 who suffered serious injuries. Another 11 riders died.
The number of seriously injured e-bike riders was the highest recorded in six years.
Larsen wants to discuss the proposed legislation with Transport Minister Signe Munk of Socialistisk Folkeparti, the Socialist People’s Party.
Ritzau sought a comment from Munk, but her ministry said she was unavailable.
Cyklistforbundet, the Danish Cyclists’ Federation, opposes making helmets compulsory, arguing that such a measure could discourage cycling.
“Our purpose is to get more people to cycle. So every measure that pulls in the opposite direction, we will oppose. But we warmly recommend that people use a bicycle helmet,” federation chair Jens Peter Hansen told TV2 Østjylland.
The proposal would introduce a helmet requirement for standard e-bikes, bringing their rules closer to those already applying to faster electric bicycles.

International trains, InterCityLyn express services and InterCity trains have continued to run as normal, but at reduced speeds on parts of the route between Odense and Middelfart or Fredericia.

Three Danish films shortlisted for Europe’s Oscars
Three Danish films have been shortlisted for the European Film Awards, often described as Europe’s equivalent of the Oscars.
The films are the dramas Kvinde ukendt by May el-Toukhy and Gæsten by Mads Mengel, and Sine Plambech’s documentary Rescue, the Danish Film Institute announced on Instagram.
A total of 45 films have been shortlisted in the fiction category.
May el-Toukhy’s Kvinde ukendt has already received international recognition. The drama was selected for the Venice Film Festival in September, where it won the main prize, the Golden Lion. Its lead actress, Mathilde Arcel, was named best actress.
The film has also been selected as Denmark’s entry for the Academy Awards in the Best International Feature Film category.
Set during the liberation of Denmark in May 1945, the drama follows a woman who has worked as a maid in the home of an elderly, respected widower she is now preparing to marry. She struggles to hide the fact that she has had a relationship with a German soldier.
Mads Mengel’s Gæsten has also attracted international attention. In July, the film received two awards at the Karlovy Vary International Film Festival in the Czech Republic.
It won the Special Jury Prize in the festival’s main competition, known as the Crystal Globe Competition, while Mengel was named best director.
The film follows Karl and Emilie, a couple preparing to host a naming ceremony for their son. Their plans are disrupted when an uninvited guest arrives: Karl’s mother, played by Trine Dyrholm, with whom he has not spoken for years.
The third Danish film on the shortlist is Rescue, a documentary by anthropologist Sine Plambech. It had its world premiere at the Toronto International Film Festival in September.
The documentary follows people fleeing across the Mediterranean and examines how the European Union’s border policies affect the lives and conditions of refugees.
Rescue is one of 15 films shortlisted in the documentary category.
Producers, distributors and other rights holders can submit films for consideration by the European Film Academy. The academy’s board and invited European experts then select films for the shortlist.
Members of the academy, which includes professionals from across the European film industry, watch the shortlisted films and vote to determine the final nominations. They vote again to select the winners once the nominations have been announced.
The final nominations will be announced on November 14. The awards ceremony will take place in Athens, the Greek capital, on January 16.
