TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — A Taiwanese nurse who traveled to Tibet said Chinese security agents questioned him about his personal background, political views, and military service.
The nurse, surnamed Lin (林), said the approximately one-hour interview took place shortly after he checked into a hotel in Tibet, per FTV News. Authorities questioned three of the eight Taiwanese members of his tour group separately, including two nurses and an aircraft maintenance technician.
Lin described the experience in a post on Threads on Monday. Because he had worked at two public hospitals, they also asked whether he had treated military personnel and had contact with Taipei City Government officials.
He said that his tour guide called him out shortly after he checked into the hotel, and a man escorted him to a private room with a balcony where two women were present. None of the three identified themselves, and Lin later learned they were national security personnel.
They did not confiscate his phone or ask him to sign a confidentiality agreement. The interviewers asked where he completed his military service, which branch he served in, what he learned, and why he served for only four months.
They asked whether the DPP's proposed NT$10,000 (US$311) cash payment was real, which countries Lin had visited, and whether he liked the US. When asked about his political affiliation, Lin said he did not support any particular party and voted based on candidates’ platforms, an approach the interviewers appeared unable to understand.
The interviewers also asked whether he would support unification with China in exchange for a higher salary and whether he knew he could change his nationality to become Chinese.
Lin told CNA that the interviewers tried to create a relaxed atmosphere but appeared displeased when he described China as “relatively unfree,” citing the questioning itself as an example. One interviewer seemed unable to understand his criticism, insisting that they were merely chatting and that Lin had not been detained.
He believed the questioning was intended to influence his thinking or gauge Taiwanese people's genuine views. “I felt he often asked irrelevant questions, but many of them were attempts to test my position,” Lin told CNA.
Lin said the experience, along with the attention his social media post received, had made him reluctant to visit China again in the near future, according to CNA.

As of June 30, the outstanding BNPL financing balance among this age group stood at 2.4 billion ringgit, it said. Some 96.8 million ringgit, or 4 per cent of the outstanding balance, was classified as non-performing or unpaid.
The ministry said that industry regulator the Consumer Credit Commission strictly required BNPL providers to conduct creditworthiness checks and affordability assessments before extending lines of credit to young customers.

New York City horse carriages set to be banned in 2028 after deal

New York City horse carriages set to be banned in 2028 after deal
- New York City will vote on a deal to ban horse-drawn carriages. If passed, the ban starts on 1 June 2028 and ends a 150-year Central Park tradition.
- The plan follows the death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan and rising safety concerns. Supporters say it is about public safety, while operators warn of job losses and horse care costs.
- The bill includes job support plans for drivers and workers, and stronger horse protections. It also bans horse sales for slaughter and sets a US$10,000 penalty for breaking the ban.
AI generated
NEW YORK – Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the New York City Council speaker reached a deal on legislation to ban horse-drawn carriages, potentially putting an end to a Central Park staple and tourist magnet that began operating more than 150 years ago.
The legislation is set for a vote on Oct 22 and, if passed, the ban would take effect June 1, 2028.
It would require “humane disposition” of the animals, forbidding the horses’ sale for slaughter or transfer to other carriage companies.
Sixty-eight horse cabs currently operate in Central Park, employing roughly 150 drivers and more than 180 horses, according to industry spokesperson Christina Hansen.
The new legislation lists 29 sponsors in the City Council, which is enough support for the measure to pass the 51-member body.
The agreement was confirmed by council speaker Julie Menin’s office.
It was first reported by POLITICO.
Horse-drawn carriages in the city have long faced opposition from animal rights activists who argue that forcing the animals to work in urban conditions undermines their long-term health and is unsafe.
While on the campaign trail in 2013, former Mayor Bill de Blasio promised to shut down the industry on his first day in office, though he ultimately failed after his plan failed to secure support from City Council.
But after a carriage-related death last summer, concerns over the industry proved impossible to ignore.
On June 17, 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan fell off a carriage and died while on a family trip to the city.
His death prompted carriage services to shut down for six days while drivers reviewed safety protocols.
A poll from the Central Park Conservancy, which advocated for the ban, found that 68 per cent of New Yorkers supported prohibiting the carriages after Mahajan’s death.
“This is fundamentally about public safety,” said David Saltonstall, the CPC’s vice-president for government relations.
“It’s about mitigating a known and growing risk that we have watched build for years, which very sadly culminated in the death of Romanch Mahajan.”
Saltonstall cited a growing list of carriage-related incidents.
At least seven people – including drivers and tourists – have been injured since May 2025, according to the conservancy.
Mahajan’s death is believed to be the first fatality resulting from carriage accidents in Central Park’s history.
Carriage operators say the rate of horse-related injuries is still much lower than other permitted park activities, like riding e-bikes or scooters.
They also say that without carriage revenue, they’ll likely struggle to care for their horses and pay fees to relocate them after the ban goes into effect.
The deal announced on Oct 13 includes some changes from legislation proposed this summer, including a framework intended to help horse carriage drivers find new jobs and compensation after the ban takes effect.
The amended Bill would require agencies chosen by the mayor to deliver a plan to support carriage drivers, owners and stable workers by April 1, 2027.
That support could include financial compensation but the legislation requires only that the city consider compensating carriage owners, and does not promise payments.
Transport Workers Union International President John Samuelsen pushed back against the Bill in a statement, calling it “political opportunism.”
He added that the Bill provides “no meaningful economic relief for workers.”
Hansen, the industry spokesperson, said taking care of her horse, Sherman, costs roughly US$10,000 (S$12,805) per year.
“There is no pool of money set aside for the future, the next 20 years of Sherman’s life,” she said.
The Bill also includes what Menin’s office described as stronger protections for horses – barring owners from selling or transferring licensed horses for slaughter or to other carriage businesses.
Owners would have to notify the Health Department and the Mayor’s Office of Animal Welfare at least 10 business days before getting rid of a horse, and anyone caught running a horse-drawn carriage after the ban takes effect could face civil penalties of US$10,000.
“The tragic and preventable death of 18-year-old Romanch Mahajan made clear that the status quo is no longer acceptable,” Menin said in a statement about the deal.
Roughly 140 carriage horses are in the city at any given time, according to Conor McHugh, who manages the Clinton Park Stables, one of the three locations where most of the animals are housed.
McHugh said in an interview last summer that if a ban passes, the stable – which has been open for more than 150 years – would be forced to shut down.
McHugh said he has been approached by groups in the past interested in acquiring the land Clinton Park Stables was on.
He said those real estate groups were likely using safety as a cover to put them out of business.
“They’re just happy to have some incident or accident to latch onto to try and make the case,” he said. BLOOMBERG

Commentary: Bass vs. Raman: Here's who won the L.A. mayoral debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
04:03:22 UTC
13:03:22 KST

Bass vs. Raman: Here’s who won the L.A. mayoral debate
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Karen Bass and Nithya Raman faced off Tuesday night in a debate hosted by NBC4 and Telemundo52 in Universal City. It was the L.A. mayoral candidates’ last head-to-head before the Nov. 3 election.
Times columnists Lorraine Ali, Gustavo Arellano and Steve Lopez weigh in on the highlights and lowlights.
Arellano: Raman had the line of the night at the very beginning, channeling — of all politicians — Ronald Reagan, one of the last people you’d think of as an Angeleno, even though he absolutely was.
“Are you better off than you were four years ago?” she asked while looking directly into the camera.
For the vast majority of L.A. residents, the answer is a resounding no.
Up until tonight, Raman has done a good job of communicating a message of hope and change, while Bass, as the incumbent, has repeatedly tripped on her record over the biblically bad four years of her first term.
But I didn’t hear that Raman tonight — partly because Bass made her play defense, from her first answer to her closing statement.
The mayor won the debate, if we’re judging by forensics. She rarely looked down at her notepad, unlike Raman. It’s something I’ve never noticed about Raman before — either a new nervous tic, or an indication that the City Council member can’t seem to speak with conviction, which has been a frequent critique against her.
Bass’ barrages got to Raman more than a few times, leading her to talk over the NBC and Telemundo moderators or even shush them. A whining Raman is not a good Raman, which her advisors need to drill into her sooner rather than later.
But Raman’s answers never meandered and weren’t too elliptical, even when she was pressed by the able moderators. Since she’s ahead in most reputable polls, Raman’s job for the night was not failing — and she cleared that low, low hurdle.
Bass, meanwhile, needed to deliver a knockout punch. Instead, as a politico friend who cares for neither candidate texted me after the debate, she won one round. There are only so many more rounds before election day for her to catch up — and Bass can’t rely on just winning on points anymore, especially with an opponent who’s now running like she’s ahead.
During closing remarks, Raman hearkened back to her Reagan shout-out, stating, “We cannot afford another four years of decline, of mismanagement, of excuses.” She then pivoted to her positivity message, smiling while proclaiming, “We can be joyful and ambitious again.” The more she sticks to that upbeat vibe, the better she comes off to a voter base tired of the doom and gloom that has fallen over L.A. under Bass.
Bass, meanwhile, came off as funereal, beginning with, “It has been the honor of a lifetime to serve in the city that I was born and raised.” That’s how you start a retirement announcement, not another four-year term. Let’s see what the voters say on election day.
Lopez: After watching the debate, I don’t think this thing is over.
Yes, Raman has been ahead in polling, and Bass is saddled with high negativity ratings, the baggage of the Palisades fire and the continued challenge of homelessness.
But this debate could have been a knockout punch for Raman, and instead, I think Bass won the night, not just by touting her achievements and responding sharply to criticism but by seeming to have a better command of the moment.
My colleague Lorraine Ali made a good point — how many people were actually watching this debate? Probably not many, so it’s not like this one-hour back-and-forth tips the scale.
But as has been noted, a huge percentage of likely voters remain undecided. Maybe that’s because they’re not in love with either candidate. Or maybe they’re ready to move on from Bass but aren’t sure about who Raman really is. If they watched tonight, looking for an answer, I’m not sure they got one.
Raman came into elected office as a darling of the Democratic Socialists of America and was a high-profile member of that wing on the City Council. But even the council’s DSA members didn’t endorse her bid for mayor. In fact, Bass has gotten support from 13 of the 15 council members.
So how will Raman build a coalition in a city where mayoral power is shared with the council, and matters like homelessness are the joint responsibility of the city and the county, and any progress is stymied without strong mayoral relationships in Sacramento and D.C.?
It’s possible that the council will come around to her if she’s elected, because just as the mayor needs the council to get much done, the council needs the mayor.
But I’d like to know more about who Raman is and why she’s flip-flopped so much (on support for the LAPD, on the mansion tax, on the Inside Safe homeless initiative, etc., etc.), as my colleague David Zahniser reported just the other day.
Learning and evolving can be a good thing. But voters need to know who Raman is, what her vision is for the city and how she expects to lead.
I didn’t get that in this debate. Bass, whose first term works against her as much as for her, is still hanging on and hanging in.
It may come down to whether older voters, who are likely to favor Bass, turn out in greater numbers than younger voters, who are likely to favor Raman.
But from where I sit, it ain’t over. Except maybe for the Dodgers.
Ali: Raman was ahead in the polls headed into tonight’s mayoral debate, so her job wasn’t quite as hard as Bass’, who is fighting for her political life. Raman just needed to knock the mayor off balance — then keep her there for an hour. But that didn’t happen.
Bass came off composed, confident and in command of the conversation, while Raman appeared less sure of herself, frequently looking down to check her notes while defending her work on key concerns such as homelessness (until recently, she was chair of the city’s housing and homelessness committee) and attacking Bass for leaving the city “leaderless” during crises such as the Palisades and Lineage fires.
The overall tone of the debate was less heated than when the two candidates met in August to battle it out sans Spencer Pratt, the former reality TV personality and Republican contender who lost in the primary.
But there were moments Tuesday when the women’s history as colleagues — and onetime allies — informed their attacks on one another.
Bass said that Raman was “not ready for prime time” and that she had a “contemptuous” relationship with her constituents. Raman continually pointed out that Bass had failed to remedy L.A.’s homelessness crisis, and did so from the perspective of someone who had worked closely with the mayor.
There’s still a question around how many folks actually watched the debate, and if the candidates’ points will resonate in subsequent clips or memes. Neither contender has the charm or spark of, say, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and as vapid as it may sound, charisma matters.
Three weeks out from the election and there still isn’t a lot of excitement over the mayoral choices on the ballot. This debate didn’t help that cause, or juice the race.
Lucky for Bass, she has the presence of a leader, and that gave her the edge over Raman tonight. But was anyone watching beyond my fellow columnists Gustavo Arellano and Steve Lopez?

What we know about Pope Leo’s lung cancer operation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

What we know about Pope Leo’s lung cancer operation
- Pope Leo XIV had a cancerous tumour removed from his right lung on Oct 13 in a 90-minute operation, which the Vatican said was “successful”.
- Experts told AFP the tumour was pulmonary adenocarcinoma, a common non-small cell lung cancer, and early detection gives a much better chance of recovery.
- Doctors said more tests will decide if he needs chemotherapy or radiation, but surgery alone suggests a very early stage and a good prognosis.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Pope Leo XIV had a cancerous tumour surgically removed from his right lung on Oct 13 in a 90-minute operation described as “successful” by the Vatican.
Here are what several medical experts told AFP about the surgery and diagnosis.
What is pulmonary adenocarcinoma?
Pulmonary adenocarcinoma, the type of tumour removed from the Pope, generally comes from “a primary cancer”, said Dr Juanita Mora, a medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association.
She told AFP that “is a good thing” because it means the tumour is from lung cancer instead of generating from the spread of another cancer.
There are two main types of lung cancer: “small cell” cancers, which spread aggressively and make up about 10 to 15% of diagnoses, and “non-small cell” cancers, which make up the vast majority.
“Adenocarcinoma is the most common kind of what’s called non-small cell lung cancer,” David Spigel, a medical oncologist specialising in lung cancer research at Nashville’s Sarah Cannon Research Institute, told AFP.
Promising outlook
David Carbone, director of the Oncology Center at Ohio State University, noted that while smoking is the most well-known risk factor for a lung cancer diagnosis, “most lung cancers that we diagnose today are in people who haven’t smoked, or (stopped) many years ago”.
Lung cancer is the top cause of cancer death worldwide, according to the World Health Organization (WHO), but the prognosis can vary significantly depending on the type of lung cancer and how advanced it is when first detected.
“When we look at five-year survival rate from lung adenocarcinoma, and it’s nicely localised, the rate is approximately 63% to 67%,” Mora said.
“But if we catch it early, it becomes 80% to 98%, especially after surgical removal.”
In such a case, the patient “will achieve a cure and never have their life threatened by cancer”, Spigel added.
A standard procedure
Pope Leo XIV announced the presence of the lung nodule on Oct 11, saying it had been “detected at a very early stage” and was localised.
The Vatican said “the lower lobe of the right lung was removed” during the Oct 13 operation to remove the mass.
“He had part of his right lung taken out, which is the standard procedure,” Carbone told AFP.
“There’s a lot of reserve in the lung, and people can have an entire lung removed and live a normal life,” he added.
“I would expect that he’d be back to completely full level of activity very soon.”
What now?
The question now is whether Pope Leo XIV will need additional treatment such as chemotherapy or radiation.
According to the experts consulted by AFP, the answer will depend on several factors, such as the size of the cancerous mass removed, how aggressive it was, its genetic characteristics, and whether or not it has spread.
A Vatican source indicated that additional testing is underway.
For Carbone, the fact that the Pope has already undergone surgery is encouraging.
“Because if it had spread to, for example, the lymph nodes in the centre of the chest, he would have had some treatment before surgery, which he didn’t have,” he explained.
“They really do go straight to surgery only for the earliest stage tumours, which makes me think this was a very early stage tumour, and has a quite good prognosis.”
He stressed that treatment for lung cancer has improved considerably over the past few decades, “and the prognosis is better than ever. So I would be hopeful for a full recovery”. AFP

Making Room for Water: Floodable Parks in Latin America
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

Walk along a river in almost any Latin American city and you will find stretches that have been straightened, lined with concrete, buried beneath roads, or pushed behind industrial areas and residential neighborhoods. Throughout the twentieth century, urban expansion gradually occupied riverbanks and former floodplains, while waterways were redirected or confined within infrastructure intended to control them. Yet the water continued to return. For decades, flooding has been the most frequent natural disaster in Latin America and the Caribbean, according to the Inter-American Development Bank.
Some cities have begun to reconsider what happens along these edges. Across Chile, Mexico, and Brazil, parks are being developed within riverbeds, drainage channels, and other territories exposed to flooding. These spaces accommodate water during heavy rainfall while providing areas for recreation, circulation, and gathering throughout much of the year. Their design also changes how surrounding neighborhoods access territories previously associated with flooding, pollution, or limited public use.
Reopening the City's Relationship with Water
In Santiago, the Zanjón de la Aguada was once a boundary between different parts of the city. Rainwater, irrigation runoff, and sewage shared the same channel, while industry and informal settlements developed along its banks. For decades, recurring floods and pollution affected the surrounding neighborhoods, reinforcing the area's separation from the rest of the city.
The Parque Inundable Víctor Jara, developed by Chile's Ministry of Public Works, is gradually transforming approximately 4.7 kilometers of this corridor into a linear park. Built in stages since 2013, it brings pedestrian and cycling paths, playgrounds, sports facilities, and green areas to neighborhoods that have historically had limited access to public space. The park retains its role in managing floodwater, incorporating recreational areas alongside drainage infrastructure. Later stages include water-retention areas, extending the possibilities for public use along the Zanjón.
Further north, in Copiapó, the relationship between the city and its river is shaped by a different condition. Located near the southern edge of the Atacama Desert, the Copiapó River can remain dry for extended periods, making its wide bed appear available for other uses. Yet occasional floods continue to affect its banks.
As the city expanded on both sides of the river, the riverbed became a barrier between neighborhoods. Aggregate extraction, mining waste, and debris disposal contributed to its deterioration, leaving a large stretch of centrally located land neglected and difficult to use.
When Teodoro Fernández Arquitectos developed Kaukari Urban Park, the challenge was to accommodate the river's changing conditions while giving residents access to its banks. Fernández described the importance of learning to live with the river's veleidades, or unpredictable behavior.
The design reorganizes the riverbed into areas that respond to different water levels. Lower ground remains available for the river and vegetation, intermediate terraces accommodate walking and gathering, and higher areas contain civic spaces, recreational facilities, and sports activities. During dry periods, residents can use parts of the river corridor while the landscape retains space for rising water.
The park also establishes connections between neighborhoods on opposite banks. Straight pedestrian paths extend the existing street layout along the northern side, while the southern bank follows a more irregular arrangement. What had long functioned as a physical division becomes part of the city's everyday circulation and public life.
A different relationship between water, landscape, and public use appears in Temuco, in southern Chile. Located between the Cautín River and the Pichicautín stream, Isla Cautín occupies land historically exposed to flooding. The 28-hectare Parque Urbano Isla Cautín, designed by Osvaldo Moreno and Martínez & Asociados, incorporates these conditions into a landscape that also responds to the cultural and social history of the site.
The park is organized around a large central meadow, with wetlands, channels, and planted areas that collect and absorb rainwater. A surrounding network of paths and public facilities accommodates sports, recreation, education, and cultural activities.
The intervention also gives particular attention to the communities connected to the territory. Its public programs include a ceremonial area for Mapuche traditions and a Human Rights Memorial associated with the site's history during Chile's military dictatorship. Water management becomes part of a larger public landscape where environmental restoration, cultural practices, and collective memory occupy the same territory.
Bringing Public Life into Flood-Prone Infrastructure
In other projects, architects work with existing infrastructure or land already designated to receive floodwater, introducing public activities into spaces that have traditionally served more limited functions.
In Nogales, near Mexico's border with the United States, an earthen dam built during the 1960s gradually became surrounded by housing. Some homes were constructed directly against its slopes, while wastewater collected in the reservoir and recurring floods threatened nearby residents. The dam continued managing runoff from the surrounding hills, but the neighborhood had few public facilities.
When Taller Capital, led by Loreta Castro Reguera and José Pablo Ambrosi, was commissioned to design a park beside the reservoir, the architects reconsidered the dam itself. Their Colosio Embankment Dam project introduces stepped terraces made of gabions (wire cages filled with stones) that stabilize the slopes and create pedestrian paths around the water.
Platforms designed to accommodate flooding contain sports courts, gardens, and playgrounds. A triangular roof provides shade and a gathering place for residents while making the intervention visible from the nearby avenue.
For the surrounding neighborhood, the dam becomes a place people can enter and use. The public facilities form part of the infrastructure itself, allowing recreation to occupy an area that continues to manage runoff during heavy rainfall.
A similar concern with neglected urban land shaped Rachel de Queiroz Park in Fortaleza, Brazil. In the Presidente Kennedy neighborhood, the Cachoeirinha stream crossed an area affected by illegal dumping and wastewater pollution. As surrounding neighborhoods became more densely developed, the reduction of open ground also contributed to increasingly frequent flooding.
Designed by Architectus S/S, the park addresses these conditions through nine interconnected ponds that collect water from the stream and surrounding drainage systems. Aquatic vegetation helps filter pollutants, while the ponds provide additional space to hold water during heavy rainfall. The designers integrated this system into a public landscape with walking and cycling paths, sports facilities, playgrounds, and gathering areas.
The intervention has also changed how people use the area. A site previously affected by pollution and informal waste disposal now accommodates daily recreation alongside the restored watercourse. The planted ponds have begun supporting local vegetation and wildlife, extending the park's contribution to the surrounding environment.
The Changing Role of Flood-Prone Land
These projects reconsider how cities occupy territories shaped by water. Areas previously associated with flooding, pollution, or restricted access now accommodate pedestrian routes, recreational facilities, and cultural activities, allowing surrounding communities to use spaces that had long remained disconnected from everyday urban life.
Their design also requires accepting that the conditions of these places will change. Different elevations, floodable surfaces, and water-retention systems allow public activities to take place within landscapes that continue to receive water during heavy rainfall. Maintaining these spaces and managing their changing use become part of their long-term operation.
As cities continue to expand along rivers and flood-prone territories, these interventions raise questions about how much land should remain available for water and how it can be used between flood events. They also show how architecture can extend the public value of these territories, bringing new activities and connections to places historically defined by their environmental constraints.

UN official says ‘window of opportunity’ for peace in DR Congo
The envoy lauds the progress in diplomatic efforts despite the worsening security and humanitarian situation.
A senior United Nations official has told the Security Council there is a “window of opportunity” for peace in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, a mineral-rich region plagued by decades of conflict.
Huang Xia, the UN special envoy for the impacted Great Lakes Region, on Tuesday said that both US- and Qatar-led peace processes have achieved “notable progress”.
However, “despite this sustained diplomatic effort, the security and humanitarian situation in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo has continued to worsen”, he added.
Several parties, including the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group and the Congolese army, have clashed in the territory, prompting a series of international diplomatic efforts.
Huang stressed the “urgency of seizing the window of opportunity, which is currently offered by the increased alignment of peace efforts”.
“Such a window does not remain open indefinitely,” he said.
“I therefore urge all parties to translate commitments into verifiable actions, and to place their trust in confidence built through deeds rather than through declarations.”
The Congolese government and the M23 signed a commitment towards a ceasefire in Doha in July 2025. The DRC and Rwanda also formalised a US-brokered peace deal in December in Washington, DC.
However, fighting has continued on the ground.
New talks were held in August in Switzerland, involving representatives from the United States, Qatar and the African Union.
Huang said the UN would facilitate a meeting on October 18 in Zambia’s capital, Lusaka, between the defence ministers of Burundi, the DRC, Uganda, Rwanda and Tanzania.

Economic Watch: Uncertainty grows in September for U.S. small businesses
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:47:00 CST
12:47:00 KST

WASHINGTON, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- U.S. small business uncertainty is growing amid high interest rates and inflation, according to data published Tuesday by the National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB).
The group's monthly small business optimism index declined 0.8 points in September to 97.9, one-tenth of a point below the 52-year average of 98.0. At the same time, the organization's uncertainty index rose 1 point to 90, remaining well above the historical average of 68.
"Small business optimism stayed near the long-term average in September as Main Street owners remain uncertain about business conditions," said NFIB Chief Economist Bill Dunkelberg. "Small business owners are proceeding with caution as they interpret how rising costs, interest rates, and the difficulty in finding qualified employees are impacting their business."
Some economists said both the war in Iran and the cost of energy are major issues impacting small businesses.
Dean Baker, a macroeconomist and co-founder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, told Xinhua: "High energy prices and the war are the big issues. With the stalemate continuing, businesses are becoming more pessimistic about the war ending any time soon."
One top issue of concern for small businesses was inflation, with 20 percent of owners reporting it as their single most important problem, up 4 points from August.
Only 7 percent of owners reported that it was a good time to expand their business, down 5 points from August.
Small business owners' self-evaluation of the health of their business turned more negative in September, with substantially more owners rating their business as "fair" -- 35 percent, up 7 points -- and fewer rating them as "good" -- 48 percent, down 9 points.
A net 8 percent of owners reported paying a higher interest rate on their most recent loan, up 4 points from August and the highest level since June 2025. The average interest rate on short-maturity loans was 8.2 percent in September, up 0.7 points from August and close to the historical average of 8.3 percent.
The findings come less than a month before the U.S. midterm elections, in which Republicans, the party in power, are widely expected to lose seats and even cede control of Congress to Democrats.
One factor weighing on Republicans is that President Donald Trump had campaigned on promises to tamping down inflation, which had surged under the previous administration.
Trump has so far not delivered on those promises, and experts said there is very little that any politician, Democrat or Republican, can do to reduce inflation. Bringing down persistently high prices often requires the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates to levels that could trigger an economic downturn, a move few politicians would want to support.
Some experts said uncertainty is bad for economic growth.
Brookings Institution Senior Fellow Darrell West told Xinhua: "Small businesses (account for) many of the American jobs, so uncertainty in that sector due to energy costs and supply chain risks is very problematic just a few weeks before the election."
"Uncertainty generally means businesses slow their hiring and spending, which is bad for economic growth. This is part of the affordability challenge facing Republicans in the midterm elections," West said.
Other experts said Republicans are having a tough time creating economic relief before the midterm elections.
Clay Ramsay, a researcher at the Center for International and Security Studies at the University of Maryland, told Xinhua: "Employees in small businesses can't help but know when their owners and managers are under strain. Republicans are groping for ways to create relief, but there is no time left before the midterms for such measures to take effect." ■

WASILLA, Alaska/TAIPEI – Taiwan said on Oct 14 it was making progress in talks to buy LNG from Alaska and would invest US$4.4 billion (S$5.64 billion) in the project after US President Donald Trump told a rally in the state that Taipei would buy 30% of its output.
Taiwan’s economy ministry said state-owned energy firm CPC Corp has made significant progress with the project developer after nearly a year and a half of negotiations and evaluation.
Alaska LNG, which would produce 20 million tonnes annually, has been discussed for decades, but many in the industry are sceptical about its commercial viability given that it requires a lengthy pipeline and capital that mean it would cost more than double a comparable US Gulf Coast plant, analysts have said.
Under the plan, CPC would purchase 6 million tonnes of Alaska LNG per year once production begins, in line with a letter of intent signed in 2025, and participate in the project’s development with an estimated investment of up to US$4.4 billion, the ministry said.
“Specific investment arrangements, equity stakes and related terms will be determined through subsequent negotiations and commercial contract procedures,” it said.
The ministry did not say whether a binding sale-and-purchase agreement had been signed.
Trump was in Alaska campaigning for Republican Senator Dan Sullivan, who is in a tight race against Democratic candidate Mary Peltola ahead of the Nov 3 congressional elections.
Taiwan officials said in February they would ramp up purchases of US natural gas to constitute about a third of the island’s imported supply in 2026, and reduce purchases from other countries.
Push to supply Asia
In 2025, Taiwan Presidential Office secretary-general Pan Men-an visited the site of the proposed LNG project in Alaska that the Trump administration has been pushing hard to allies in Asia as a supply option.
So far, Alaska LNG it has lined up agreements covering 13 million tonnes a year from buyers in Asia and French major TotalEnergies. It needs agreements for another 3 million tonnes and must turn them into binding deals in order to line up financing for the project.
It would open direct access for US-made LNG to Asian markets including Taiwan without having to go through the Panama Canal or around the Horn of Africa, reducing transit time and costs.
The project’s developers aim to take a final investment decision on the 1,287km pipeline in 2026, followed by the export facility in 2027, with first LNG exports targeted for 2031.
Trump said last month that South Korea had agreed to invest in the US$54 billion pipeline for the Alaska LNG project, but Seoul said it was not yet set in stone.
Taiwan was the No. 5 LNG importer in 2025 behind China, Japan, South Korea and India, shipping in 23.8 million tons of the super-chilled fuel, mostly from Australia and Qatar, according to Kpler data.
Taiwan’s economy ministry said on Oct 14 that if the project proceeded on schedule, it could begin supplying additional natural gas to Taiwan as early as 2032. REUTERS

Fair Friend Group has order visibility through the first quarter of 2027, with domestic orders mainly coming from the semiconductor and AI sectors. Its energy-sector customers are primarily involved in the US shale oil industry.
Quaser Machine Tools Inc. has an order backlog worth at least NT$2 billion, mainly from the aerospace and defense industries. Orders extend beyond the second quarter of 2027.
The company has also secured an order from a customer in the solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) industry. Certification is expected to be completed in November, and the first set of equipment is scheduled to ship from the company’s UK plant by the end of the year.
At Shieh Yih Machinery Industry Co., orders related to AI server manufacturing have surpassed those for high-end household appliances this year. The company expects its order visibility to extend through the end of 2027.
Taiwan Takisawa Technology Co. has received orders mainly from manufacturers of AI server cooling systems, hydraulic pipe fittings, and drone components. Its order visibility extends through the second quarter of 2027.
Machine tools are used to process metal and other materials into precision parts through operations such as cutting, grinding, and drilling, making them essential to manufacturing across industries. As demand for AI servers and robots grows, manufacturers are investing in the equipment needed to produce their components, according to Gugu Fund and UDN Money.

Judge indefinitely blocks Trump from banning 3 media outlets from White House
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
03:25:39 UTC
12:25:39 KST

A federal judge late Tuesday night indefinitely extended his block on the White House from enforcing a ban on three media outlets that President Donald Trump announced in mid-September.
The preliminary injunction by Judge Timothy Kelly replaces his temporary restraining order against Trump's ban of MS NOW, CNN and Politico from the White House complex as a lawsuit challenging the ban plays out.
"President Trump's own comments suggest that he intended the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes to alter their reporting on him," wrote Kelly, who was nominated by Trump for his seat in U.S. District Court in Washington.
In his written opinion, Kelly said the three outlets were likely to succeed on their claim in their pending lawsuit, which argues they were denied due process when Trump summarily barred them without giving them a chance to argue against it.
The judge cited two existing opinions by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which establish a due process right to journalists whose White House passes are targeted for revocation. Those appellate opinions are binding on federal District Court judges in D.C.
The judge also said, for the first time in this case, the outlets were likely to succeed on two First Amendment claims in their civil suit, which allege retaliation and viewpoint discrimination.
Kelly's order Tuesday is not a final ruling on the merits of the suit. And it does not compel the White House to restore access to the Oval Office and Air Force One to the outlets.
Kelly brushed aside the Department of Justice's claim that in addition to concerns about inaccurate news stories, Trump decided to revoke the outlets' access to the White House on national security grounds.
"There is no evidence in the record that President Trump made the decision to revoke Plaintiffs' hard passes on national security grounds from the get-go, nor at any time has he directly stated that national security was the reason for his decision," Kelly wrote.
The judge said the DOJ's national security argument appears to be "merely a post-hoc justification for the decision" after the outlets sued.
MS NOW reported Wednesday that the DOJ declined to comment on the ruling.
"Still, no one should interpret the Court's decision to suggest that President Trump's concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media's reporting are unfounded, or that the government is powerless when its true aim is to protect national security when classified information is unlawfully disclosed," Kelly wrote.
"That said, for the reasons explained below, the Court will extend the relief it already ordered, which will continue to preserve the status quo while this case proceeds," Kelly said, referring to his prior order that restored access by the outlets to the White House.
The judge said that without the preliminary injunction, the outlets were "likely to suffer irreparable harm."
His ruling came on the heels of a court hearing last Thursday, when the DOJ defended the ban, which reportedly led to 78 journalists having their so-called hard passes to the White House revoked before Kelly ordered them restored with his previous temporary restraining order.
Trump last month said he would appeal any decision by Kelly blocking his ban. CNBC has requested comment from the White House and DOJ.
Theodore Boutrous Jr., an attorney for the outlets, said in a statement, "We are grateful that the Court ruled in favor of our clients."
"When the President issued his 'ban on the free press,' he blatantly and explicitly violated due process and the First Amendment," Boutrous said. "Since then, the President has repeatedly, candidly, and consistently admitted in public that he banned our clients from the White House to punish reporting he doesn't like and to try to force journalists to cover him in ways he prefers."
"The harm this ban did to our clients, the First Amendment, and the public as a whole is profound," the attorney said. "The Court was right to enjoin the White House from enforcing this "unconstitutional ban on the free press" for the foreseeable future."
Trump on Sept. 18 said that he was banning the three outlets because of how they have covered him.
In a Truth Social post that day, Trump wrote that the outlets "shouldn't be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they're covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America."
Trump later said that same day that he had become "sick" of "cumulative stories" by the outlets.
The ban took effect on the following day, Sept. 19, when journalists from the outlets were denied access to the White House grounds and had their permanent passes confiscated by Secret Service officers.
The outlets sued Trump on Sept. 21 in a civil complaint that said, "This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles."
Kelly, two days later, issued a restraining order that temporarily reversed the ban for at least 14 days. Journalists from the three outlets on Sept. 24 were allowed to return to the White House, and since then Kelly extended the restraining order to allow him time to consider whether to issue Tuesday's preliminary injunction, which has no set expiration date.
— Justin Papp contributed to this report.

Israel returns 22 stolen ancient artefacts to Greece
The cultural exchange comes amid strengthening ties between the two countries.
Israel has returned 22 ancient artefacts stolen from Greece, a cultural exchange that comes as the two countries strengthen ties.
Greek and Israeli officials did not provide details on Tuesday on how the artefacts were discovered in Israel or the circumstances surrounding their illegal removal from Greece.
The Israel Antiquities Authority’s Theft Prevention Unit had located the items, Pninat Yanay, Israel’s ambassador to Greece, said.
Greek Minister of Culture Lina Mendoni accepted the objects from the Israeli Antiquities Authority at a ceremony held at the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.
“It is the first time that Israel has returned antiquities to Greece, marking the starting point of closer cooperation between the two countries for the protection of cultural heritage,” Mendoni said.
“Every return of a cultural object to its place of origin has a broader symbolic and moral dimension.”
The collection includes 15 Attic vases, six Corinthian vases, and a bronze female statuette.
The objects are dated between 700 BC and 320 BC.
Yanay said the return of the antiquities created “the conditions for further strengthening cooperation between Greece and Israel”.
Greece-Israel relations
Greece and Israel have strengthened energy and defence ties in recent years.
In August, Israel signed a $3.5bn defence deal to build a multi-layered air defence system in Greece, called the Achilles Shield. It is the largest defence deal between the two countries, and one of the most significant export agreements in Israel’s recent history.

Ukrainian ex-officer goes on trial in Germany over Nord Stream blasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
03:06:42 UTC
12:06:42 KST

Ukrainian ex-officer goes on trial in Germany over Nord Stream blasts
The trial is expected to run into February and could test Germany’s political stance on Ukraine.
A Ukrainian former military officer is standing trial in Germany, accused of organising the secret operation that blew up the Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022 and cut Western Europe off from its biggest source of Russian natural gas.
The trial opened on Wednesday at the Hamburg Higher Regional Court and is expected to run into February next year.
It is the first public hearing of the evidence in a years-long investigation.
The defendant, a 50-year-old identified under German privacy rules only as Serhii K., is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents – including divers and an explosives expert – in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times.
He denies any involvement and is the only person on trial.
Reporting from the German city of Hamburg, Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane said the case is tied to the broader geopolitics of Europe.
“Germany was dependent to a large extent on Russian gas for all sorts of energy uses. It clearly isn’t using Russian gas anymore,” said Kane.
The prosecution
Serhii K. was arrested in Italy in August 2025 and extradited to Germany that November.
Prosecutors accused him of working with other members of the military to plan the operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.
They allege he travelled to Germany through Poland on a forged Ukrainian passport about three weeks before the attack.
They say the group used a sailboat hired in the northern city of Rostock to reach an area near the Danish island of Bornholm, where they attached military-grade explosives with timers to the pipelines on the seabed.
German prosecutors say attacking civilian targets and destroying infrastructure in this way would amount to a war crime.
Joachim Weber, senior fellow for strategic foresight and risk analysis at the University of Bonn, told Al Jazeera that the case has put the German government in a difficult position because it supports Ukraine in its fight against Russia, including with over 100 billion euros ($112bn) in aid.
“The (German) government is not very happy, probably, that this court case is in court now. It took four years,” Weber said.
“German governments have not really commented on this case. Why? Because it’s politically difficult for them,” added Weber.
The blasts and the fallout
On September 26, 2022, Swedish seismologists detected several blasts, some 17 hours apart.
Three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines ruptured, sending huge plumes of methane into the atmosphere.
Nord Stream 1 had supplied about half of Germany’s natural gas imports. Its twin, Nord Stream 2, was built but never opened, after Berlin cancelled approval shortly before Russia invaded Ukraine.
Moscow denied blowing up its own pipelines and had already cut supplies in response to European sanctions.
Ukraine’s government denies involvement.
Russia said on Monday it expected a “just verdict” naming the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.
Another suspect, Vladimir Z., a trained scuba diver who prosecutors say was one of the divers on the team, was arrested in Croatia in August.
Last month, a Croatian court approved handing over the wanted man to Germany.
The Nord Stream case has strained ties between Berlin and Kyiv, even as Germany remains one of Ukraine’s strongest backers, with Russia and Ukraine still trading strikes.

Wang Xinyu's firmer step against bigger ups and downs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:00:31 CST
12:00:31 KST

WUHAN, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- After a straight-sets loss to Wang Xiyu saw her exit the WTA Wuhan Open in the first round for the second straight year on Monday, China's Wang Xinyu hugged her compatriot, shouldered her bag and walked off in silence.
A day before the match, Wang Xinyu told Xinhua about her approach to winning and losing. "Everyone wants to win. But sometimes failures and setbacks can teach us more. The key is to keep an open mind, so you can learn from them and keep getting better."
During the same tournament in 2025, she described that year as a "wave-shaped" one full of ups and downs. This year, she said, "the waves got even bigger."
Her season began brightly. In Auckland in January, she won four straight matches to reach the final, where she lost to top seed Elina Svitolina. At the Australian Open, she knocked out No. 24 seed Jelena Ostapenko and No. 13 seed Linda Noskova to reach the last 16 for the first time in her career.
The clay-court season proved more difficult, with a series of early exits during what she called "the most frustrating stretch of the year," marked by self-doubt.
The French Open brought a turning point when she battled through a three-set victory.
"I remember when I won it, I felt so many emotions," said Wang, who usually appears calm. She called that moment "an explosion of pent-up emotion."
"Winning that match gave me a lot of confidence, and a lot of determination to keep going and keep challenging myself."
On grass, a surface on which she feels more comfortable, Wang gradually rebuilt her confidence. In late June in Bad Homburg, she fired 15 aces in a straight-sets opening win before reaching the semifinals, where she lost to four-time Grand Slam champion Naomi Osaka. At Wimbledon, she advanced beyond the first round for the fourth consecutive year.
Then came the North American swing. In Cincinnati, she came from a set down to beat Donna Vekic before losing to top seed Aryna Sabalenka. At the US Open, she fell in three sets to No. 21 seed Anna Kalinskaya in the second round.
"Although I didn't win that match [against Kalinskaya], I've been building up little by little through experiences like that, and I can see myself getting better," she said.
In Singapore in late September, Wang met Vekic again and won 6-1, 6-2 before beating a qualifier to reach the quarterfinals.
Back home, however, Wang suffered consecutive first-round exits at the China Open and Wuhan Open.
"I'm still trying to balance the excitement and expectations of playing at home," she said.
Now in her eighth year as a professional, Wang continues to learn and refine her technique and playing style. "You have to keep learning new things. In tennis, there's no such thing as 'holding' your level or your form. If you're not learning, you're going backwards," she said.
"I think the most important thing in learning is to treat yourself as if you know nothing. You need to let go of what you think you already know, and learn new things with a completely open mind."
"It won't be smooth at the start. But a lot of the time, you need that determination, that belief and confidence to believe you can do it," Wang said. "I know my goal is to win a Grand Slam, and I know that I'm on the road, walking toward my goal."
Looking ahead, Wang remained optimistic about what the rest of the season might bring. "2026 is not over yet, and I hope the next few weeks will continue to surprise me." ■

UN Human Rights Council elects 15 members in uncontested vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
02:55:15 UTC
11:55:15 KST

UN Human Rights Council elects 15 members in uncontested vote
Rights groups say uncontested vote undermines accountability as countries with poor human rights records win seats.
Human rights groups have sharply criticised the uncontested election of 15 members of the United Nations’ premier human rights body, saying it let countries with poor rights records win seats.
The 193-member General Assembly held the vote on Tuesday.
Positions on the 47-nation Human Rights Council are allocated to the UN’s regional groups to ensure geographical representation. And for the second year in a row, all regional groups put forward the exact number of candidates for available seats for the three-year term, resulting in uncontested races.
“This uncompetitive vote makes a mockery of the word ‘election’,” said Louis Charbonneau, UN director at Human Rights Watch.
“No one should have a seat on this crucial body handed to them on a silver platter”, Charbonneau said.
He called on UN member nations to “insist on competitive slates so they can reject candidates with poor human rights records”.
In Tuesday’s vote, the Africa group’s Zambia, Ghana, Nigeria and Burundi were elected.
The Asia-Pacific group’s Kuwait, Nepal, Jordan and Japan won seats, as did Brazil, the Dominican Republic and Uruguay from the Latin America and Caribbean group.
Ireland and Germany from the mainly Western group, and Moldova and Ukraine from the Central and East European group, will also join the Human Rights Council.
The Geneva-based council reviews the human rights records of all countries periodically, appoints independent investigators to report on issues such as torture and situations in countries such as North Korea, Iran and Myanmar, and sends fact-finding missions to investigate rights violations. These include missions in Ukraine, the occupied Palestinian territories and Israel, and Sudan.
The council was created in 2006 to replace a human rights commission discredited because some members had poor rights records. But the new council soon faced similar criticism, including that countries sought seats to protect themselves and their allies.
Soon after starting his second term, US President Donald Trump announced the withdrawal of Washington from the Human Rights Council, accusing it of anti-Israel bias. He also pulled the US out in his first term.
UN spokesman Stephane Dujarric, responding to a question about the UN position on the uncontested vote, said it was a matter for the 193 member nations.
“But what we’ve always said is that member states who are elected to this organisation’s highest human rights body have an added responsibility to protect human rights,” he said.

China's factory-gate inflation rises 5 percent
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
02:45:09 UTC
11:45:09 KST

China's producer prices rose at their fastest pace in more than four years in September while consumer inflation edged up, as higher oil and commodities lifted factory-gate costs.
The producer price index (PPI) rose 5 percent from a year earlier, new data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed, up from 3.8 percent in August. That marks the fastest pace of factory-gate inflation since June 2022.
Higher oil and commodity prices, driven by transport disruptions, adverse weather and geopolitical tensions, have increased cost pressures for manufacturers.
"Much of the upward pressure still came from commodity supply disruptions caused by the Middle East conflict, with prices rising particularly sharply in fuel processing, chemicals and non-ferrous metals," said Nguyen Hoang Nam, China economist at Capital Economics.
The consumer price index (CPI) gained 0.9 percent year-on-year, up from a 0.8 percent increase in August.
Gasoline prices soared 16.6 percent from a year earlier and contributed about 0.47 percentage points to headline CPI growth, the statistics agency said.
Beijing has stepped up support for the economy, approving an additional 550 billion yuan in unused local government bond quota for infrastructure and other spending, adding to measures such as mortgage subsidies. 
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was up 1 percent on year, unchanged from August. (Xinhua, Reuters)

Cho says Taiwan monitoring suspected plague case in Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
02:39:52 UTC
11:39:52 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Premier Cho Jung-tai (卓榮泰) said Monday that Taiwan is closely monitoring reports of a suspected plague-related death in Russia and has strengthened epidemic surveillance as authorities seek to verify the cause of the illness.
Cho said the government was “highly concerned” and had instructed the Ministry of Health and Welfare to maintain close contact with international health organizations and monitor developments, per UDN.
During a question-and-answer session at the legislature, DPP Legislator Wang Ting-yu (王定宇) raised concerns about reports of a possible pneumonic plague case in Siberia and speculation about a second case, questioning whether authorities could obtain reliable information from Russia and China.
Health Minister Shih Chung-liang (石崇良) said Taiwan had contacted the World Health Organization to verify the reports. The cause of the Russian patient's death has not been confirmed, and no evidence has established that plague was responsible.
The WHO said Russian health authorities reported that no plague cases have been recently registered in the Irkutsk Oblast, following the death of a laboratory worker from severe pneumonia. An epidemiological investigation was underway, and testing of people who had contact with the deceased had not detected high-threat pathogens, according to the WHO's Saturday update.
The agency said there was no evidence of ongoing transmission linked to the case, although the available information was insufficient to draw firm conclusions about the potential public health risk.
Shih said plague has three main forms: bubonic, pneumonic, and septicemic. Pneumonic plague affects the lungs and can spread between people through infectious respiratory particles. Although it can be fatal if treatment is delayed, antibiotics are effective when administered promptly, per UDN.
Cho said the Health Ministry had briefed the Cabinet on the issue about two weeks earlier. He subsequently instructed the ministry to continue monitoring the situation and coordinate with international health organizations.
The premier also ordered enhanced monitoring of travel and transportation associated with Taiwan's “Mini Three Links,” which connect Taiwan with China through designated routes involving trade, postal services, and passenger transportation.
Mainland Affairs Council Minister Chiu Chui-cheng (邱垂正) said his council was coordinating with the Health Ministry and preparing information for Taiwanese businesspeople living in China and people traveling between the two countries.
The Centers for Disease Control said Taiwan had recorded no plague cases since 1953 and was strengthening border health measures, including fever screening at airports and seaports. According to WHO data, 10 countries reported 2,646 confirmed plague cases between 2019 and 2025, per a press release.
Of these, 423 deaths were recorded. About 98% of confirmed cases were reported in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar. China reported 19 confirmed cases during the period, while Mongolia reported 17.
The CDC said Taiwan has established laboratory testing capacity and a network of medical facilities for infectious disease control. Antibiotics used to treat plague are available in Taiwan and can also be used for preventive treatment following exposure when medically indicated.
The agency urged the public not to panic while authorities continue to monitor international developments.

Trump’s Republican Party faces an uphill fight in the November midterm elections to retain control of the House of Representatives and the Senate.
With just three weeks to go before the crucial vote, the US leader is campaigning to shore up support for his party, including by holding rallies in traditionally Republican states facing unexpectedly competitive Senate races.
Affordability worries have emerged as a key voter concern as global oil prices rocketed in 2026, driving up costs at US petrol pumps as well and squeezing American households.
The flare-up with Yemen comes months after Tehran blocked the Strait of Hormuz – a vital shipping route for oil and gas – in retaliation against US and Israeli attacks in late February.
That sparked a conflict that has engulfed the Middle East. AFP

Bipartisan US senators urge Trump to scrap Russian diesel deal

- They said the diesel would do little to cut fuel prices, but would give the Kremlin more money and hurt US and allied security interests.
- The letter, led by Richard Blumenthal and backed by six Republicans, pressed Trump to revoke the licence and use tougher sanctions on Russia and its supporters.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - Republican and Democratic US senators joined forces on Oct 13 to urge President Donald Trump to scrap his diesel deal with Russia, calling it a “betrayal” that would bankroll Moscow’s war in Ukraine while doing little to ease soaring fuel prices.
The 12 lawmakers – including six members of Trump’s Republican Party – called on the president to reverse his agreement with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to allow the country’s diesel onto global markets.
“Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin’s murderous, illegal war,” they wrote in a letter spearheaded by Democrat Richard Blumenthal.
“This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded.”
The senators acknowledged the urgent need to reduce energy costs, which have surged amid the US war with Iran, but argued that the Russian supplies would have a negligible effect on prices.
Instead, they said, the deal would provide the Kremlin with additional revenue to finance its invasion of Ukraine, now in its fifth year.
The Republican signatories included former Senate majority leader Mitch McConnell and other senators with decades of experience, putting prominent members of Trump’s own party at odds with the president ahead of November’s midterm elections.
Trump announced on Oct 9 that Putin had agreed to release more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, with another 500,000 tons to follow in November, in an effort to curb fuel prices.
The US Treasury Department subsequently issued a temporary license allowing transactions involving Russian-origin diesel, including its sale and import.
The senators urged Trump to revoke the license and use new sanctions powers approved by Congress in September to increase economic pressure on Moscow and countries helping sustain its war, particularly China.
“Putin is a tyrant,” they wrote, demanding that Trump instead pursue a settlement that protects Ukraine’s sovereignty and security.
The senators’ scepticism over the economic benefits of the deal was echoed on Oct 13 by European Union economy chief Valdis Dombrovskis.
The proposed Russian diesel supplies were “not of any macroeconomic significance,” he told AFP, also questioning whether Moscow could deliver the promised volumes.
The agreement has added to tensions over Trump’s approach to the Ukraine war, with the US president repeatedly criticising Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.
On Oct 10, Trump warned Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that he “better damn well stop” the attacks.
Blumenthal accused Putin of exploiting the diplomatic impasse while seeking to inflict further hardship on Ukraine as winter approaches.
“Once again, he’s playing Trump for a fool,” he wrote on X. AFP

What is celebrated on October 14 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
05:23:26 EEST
11:23:26 KST

What is celebrated on October 14 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
October 14 marks World Standards Day, Environmental Education Day, World Spine Day, and Occupational Safety Day. According to church calendars, saints and the Intercession are commemorated.
On October 14, the world observes World Standards Day and World Environmental Education Day. According to the church calendar in the new style, the holy martyrs Nazarius, Gervasius, Protasius and Celsus, the venerable Paraskeva of Serbia and the venerable Nicholas Sviatosha are commemorated, while according to the old style, the great feast of the Protection of the Most Holy Theotokos is celebrated, UNN writes.
World Standards Day
The official date was established in 1970 to commemorate October 14, 1946, when the first conference of national standards organizations opened in London, laying the foundation for the creation of the International Organization for Standardization.
The event unites the efforts of ISO, IEC, that is, the International Electrotechnical Commission, and ITU, the International Telecommunication Union, to highlight the role of unified technical standards, protocols and quality requirements in global trade and consumer safety.
World Environmental Education Day
The date was established in 1972 during the United Nations Conference on the Human Environment in Stockholm and formalized at the UNESCO and UNEP conference in Tbilisi in 1977.
The main goal of the day is to raise public environmental awareness, implement sustainable development programs in educational institutions, preserve biodiversity, and foster a caring attitude in society toward natural resources and the planet's climate.
World Spine Day / World Back Day
A medical initiative under the auspices of the World Federation of Chiropractic, supported by international orthopedic organizations. The event draws attention to the widespread prevalence of spinal diseases, musculoskeletal disorders and chronic back pain.
The day emphasizes the importance of physical activity, correct posture in the workplace, ergonomics and the prevention of a sedentary lifestyle.
International Safety Officer Day
A professional observance dedicated to specialists who ensure compliance with safety regulations, protect workers' health and prevent occupational injuries at enterprises and construction sites around the world.
Remembrance Day of the Holy Martyrs Nazarius, Gervasius, Protasius and Celsus
According to the new calendar, Orthodox and Greek Catholic believers commemorate the holy martyrs Nazarius, Gervasius, Protasius and Celsus, who suffered for the Christian faith in Milan in the 1st century during the reign of Emperor Nero.
This day also commemorates the venerable Paraskeva of Serbia — an ascetic who practiced her spiritual life in the Jordan Valley, known for her prayerful silence and miracles, and the venerable Nicholas Sviatosha, who renounced the princely throne and wealth and took monastic vows at the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra.
According to the old calendar, believers celebrate the great great feast of the Protection of the Most Holy Theotokos. The feast was established to commemorate the apparition of the Mother of God in the Blachernae Church in Constantinople in the 10th century, when She spread her omophorion over the praying people and protected the city from an enemy siege.
According to the old style, the venerable Romanos the Melodist is also commemorated — a prominent Byzantine church hymnographer and author of many kontakia.

PARIS - Tens of thousands of people joined rallies across France on Oct 13 to support protesting high school students demanding better conditions in a major challenge to President Emmanuel Macron as his term winds down.
Some 161,500 people turned out in the rallies, according to the interior ministry – more than double the 71,500 estimate it gave for demonstrations on Oct 8.
Although most of the demonstrations were peaceful, violence erupted on the sidelines of one of two Paris marches that the interior ministry said drew 41,500 people.
AFP journalists saw some cars set on fire and police fired tear gas in the Invalides square as masked youths tried to erect barricades across roads and threw objects.
Tear gas was also fired during a demonstration in Lyon.
Swedish activist Greta Thunberg took part in one demonstration in the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis.
She said she had joined the protests because “our future is being robbed”.
French unions said 480,000 people took part in the rallies and the numbers suggested increased street opposition to the government just six months before a vote for a successor to Macron, who is completing his maximum second mandate.
The latest agitation came as the centrist government launched a debate in Parliament on a cost-cutting budget, facing fierce opposition from the left and right, while France’s worsening debt has spooked the bond market.
Pressure will increase as on Oct 17 national demonstrations against the cost of living are to take place, and unions and student groups see the two protest currents merging.
The students have been given strong backing by the far-left opposition France Unbowed (LFI) party whose leader and presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Melenchon was seen among crowds in Paris.
Dialogue, ‘not repression’
Thousands also marched in the cities of Nantes, Lyon, Lens, Strasbourg, Toulouse, Bordeaux and Marseille, according to police and AFP reporters.
“We stand in solidarity with the high schools that are worse off. We need real measures and proper dialogue, not repression,” said 16-year-old Emeline, outside a Marseille school.
“We’re here because we really feel we’re not being heard by the government,” said Nina, 17.
The student movement sprang up in September at lycees – high schools for those aged 15 to 18 – with students blocking the entrances to many schools to demand better classroom conditions.
Perceived heavy-handed police action against the students drove many to join Oct 13’s demonstrations.
One teen lost his hand when he picked up a police stun grenade during the protests, while another lost an eye, and another teeth when an officer fired a tear gas canister in his face.
Police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of violence against demonstrators, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nunez who said nearly 900 police had suffered injuries during the protests.
Some 147 teaching staff have been injured, the education ministry said.
‘Not budging’
“We’re not giving up the fight, whether it’s for the high school students who were hit with a harsh crackdown, or for denouncing police violence,” said Patricia, a 20-year-old university student in Paris who did not give her last name.
Some Indian tourists who wandered into the Paris demonstration said they were unnerved.
“Initially we were terrified,” said Snehil Jain, a 45-year-old visiting Paris for a week with his wife.
“We had seen the media images of violence around these protests. But then we saw it was a peaceful protest, so we were OK then.”
France’s education ministry said 214 schools, mostly high schools, were closed on Oct 13.
University student union l’Union Etudiante reported 90% of universities had closed nationwide to show support.
French students say they are determined to press their demands over absent teachers, dilapidated buildings, overcrowded schedules and other grievances.
They have dismissed a government pledge – made after last week’s demonstrations – to send 3,000 substitute teachers to the 114 worst-affected schools.
“We are continuing the blockades. We are not budging,” said Naouel, a high school student in Brest. She said she hoped the protests would continue after the half-term holidays, in late October.
On Oct 12, Macron had urged restraint from protesters, saying the issues “deserve time, consultations, discussion and respect”. AFP

inflatable pavilion by pneuhaus mimics dragonfly’s vision through 221 camera obscuras
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
02:10:51 UTC
11:10:51 KST

inflatable pavilion by pneuhaus mimics dragonfly’s vision through 221 camera obscuras
compound camera no. 3 creates a tactile viewing environment where hundreds of live images appear at once across a translucent surface; a construction of glass lenses, urethane-coated nylon, and air that allows visitors to adjust individual projections by hand.
[FEATURED]
Compound Camera No. 3 inflatable pavilion mimics dragonfly vision
Pneuhaus creates Compound Camera No. 3, an inflatable pavilion composed of 221 camera obscura cells that project multiple views of the surrounding environment onto its translucent inner surface. Inspired by the compound eyes of dragonflies, the installation explores how different perspectives can coexist within a single structure.
Each cell contains a glass double-convex lens, with its proportions and focal length determined by optical calculations. The pavilion combines concave and convex surfaces to direct views outward and inward, referencing the arrangement of a dragonfly’s ommatidia, which are oriented to observe different parts of its surroundings.
Touchable Camera Obscuras Allow Visitors to Change Lens Focus
Made from urethane-coated nylon, glass lenses, and air, the structure requires no rigid frame. A baffle layer separates and aligns its inner and outer membranes, while the soft surface allows visitors to press individual cells and adjust the focus of the projected images by hand. The result is an immersive viewing environment in which hundreds of images form without screens or digital sensors.
Covering more than 700 sqft, the pavilion can be installed in a few hours and withstands winds of up to 40 mph. Its curved entrance leads into a larger atrium, creating a sequence of spaces that expands and contracts as visitors move through the installation.
‘Today, most imagery reaches people through flat, backlit screens,’ shares Pneuhaus’ design team, ‘Compound Camera no.3 offers a quieter, more physical counterpoint: vision one can walk into, touch, and adjust by hand; a reminder that seeing can still be soft and playful rather than solely high-tech and mediated.’ The project builds on Pneuhaus’ earlier Compound Camera, created nearly a decade ago with 109 cells projecting views from a single point. The third iteration moves beyond the original dome to explore a more distributed, insect-like form of vision.

He faces a charge of using or attempting to use an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications.
According to the complaint, the recording device was found on September 30, concealed in toilet paper and plugged into a USB port at the back of a television in an executive conference room.The conference room did not have a security camera when the device was installed. However, CCTV footage from other parts of the office showed Alfozan near the room on nearly a dozen occasions last month, despite having no authority to access the space or attend meetings there, the complaint said.
OpenAI later installed a camera in the room. According to the FBI, footage recorded last week showed Alfozan entering the room and checking behind the television where the device had been placed.The complaint also alleges that Alfozan used a productivity tool to make multiple inquiries about the company's building addresses, meeting rooms, room capacities and calendars.Days before his arrest last week, Alfozan allegedly left an unattended bag in another room.
