====================================================================================================

Man charged over fatal shooting of child in northwest Sydney
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:05:06 CST
11:05:06 KST

SYDNEY, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Police said on Wednesday that a man has been charged with murder over the September shooting of a child in northwest Sydney.
The 12-year-old boy died in hospital days after he was shot in the face and neck at a unit in Sydney's northwest suburbs on the evening of Sept. 21.
A police statement on Wednesday said that nine other people who were in the home at the time of the incident were not injured. Three 18-year-old men were arrested at the time, with two released by police and the third charged with concealing a serious indictable offense.
Following an investigation, homicide squad detectives on Tuesday arrested a 19-year-old man, who was 18 at the time of the incident, at a prison in western Sydney and charged him with murder.
Superintendent Naomi Moore said at the time of the shooting that people who were present at the home were known to police for organized crime links, but that the incident was not believed to be related to ongoing conflicts between Sydney organized crime gangs. ■

====================================================================================================

Sweetness left by Red Army soldier in SW China's Guizhou
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:04:57 CST
11:04:57 KST

Song Guangping, son of late Red Army soldier Song Jiagtong, checks the growth of a pomelo tree in Lintan Village of Xishui County, southwest China's Guizhou Province, Sept. 10, 2026. The Chishui River winds through the mountains, with its waters murmuring as they flow past Lintan Village in Xishui County of southwest China's Guizhou Province.
Beside the former site of a Party Branch set by the Red Army in Lintan Village, a leafy pomelo tree stands quietly. Locals call it the "Red Army Pomelo."
For 77-year-old Song Guangping, the tree carries a lifelong memory. Standing before the tree near his old home, he often recalls the afternoon when his father, Song Jiatong, brought back the pomelo seedlings. To him, it is more than a tree. It is a living link between the Long March, the deep bond between the Red Army and the people, and a village's journey from poverty to revitalization.
Song Jiatong arrived in Guizhou with the Central Red Army during the Long March, the historic military maneuver in modern Chinese history. He was seriously wounded during the Four Crossings of the Chishui River and was rescued by local villagers.
After recovering, he chose to stay in Lintan, where he married and raised a family. In the early 1980s, Song Jiatong returned to his hometown of Ningdu, east China's Jiangxi Province, and brought back several honey pomelo seedlings. Four were planted, but only one survived.
No one has imagined that the single surviving seedling would take root by the Chishui River, bloom, and bear fruit, or that through villagers' grafting, it would eventually grow into more than 300 mu (20 hectares) of pomelo groves along the river valley.
"My father always kept the people in his heart," Song Guangping said. "Bringing the pomelo seedlings to Lintan was his way of helping the villagers live a better life."
Because the tree embodies the memory of unity between the Red Army soldiers and the people, locals affectionately call it the "Red Army Pomelo."
It soon became the village's "fruit of prosperity." From the 1980s into the early 2000s, more than 100 households in Lintan grew the fruit. At that time, they were the only pomelo growers for miles around. One pomelo sold for 5 yuan (about 0.75 U.S. dollars), and a single tree could produce two or three hundred fruits, earning a family several thousand yuan.
The income helped cover school fees for children across the village. Over the years, more than 100 students from Lintan went on to college.
The influence of the "Red Army Pomelo" has spread beyond Lintan. Villagers in Qinggangpo Village of Xishui County also transplanted and grafted trees from the original pomelo, introduced more varieties, and established a pomelo industry demonstration base.
"Qinggangpo Village is known for the Battle of Qinggangpo during the Long March," said Yi Song, Party secretary of the village. "We receive 200,000 visitors a year, and the tourism has been boosting our fruit farming. Since we began developing the pomelo industry, we have planted 1,800 mu (120 hectares) of honey pomelo, and total output is expected to reach 1.2 million yuan (about 180,000 U.S. dollars) this year."
From a single pomelo seedling to the industry of pomelo planting, the red legacy has never left this land. It has simply taken on a new form that is rooted in the soil and bringing sweetness to everyday life. (Xinhua/Wang Jingqiang)
People visit a museum themed on the Four Crossings of the Chishui River, one of the key events during the Red Army's Long March, in Tucheng Town of Xishui County, southwest China's Guizhou Province, Sept. 11, 2026. From a single pomelo seedling to the industry of pomelo planting, the red legacy has never left this land. It has simply taken on a new form that is rooted in the soil and bringing sweetness to everyday life. (Xinhua/Wang Jingqiang)
Song Guangping, son of late Red Army soldier Song Jiagtong, checks the growth of a pomelo tree in Lintan Village of Xishui County, southwest China's Guizhou Province, Sept. 10, 2026. The Chishui River winds through the mountains, with its waters murmuring as they flow past Lintan Village in Xishui County of southwest China's Guizhou Province.
Beside the former site of a Party Branch set by the Red Army in Lintan Village, a leafy pomelo tree stands quietly. Locals call it the "Red Army Pomelo."
For 77-year-old Song Guangping, the tree carries a lifelong memory. Standing before the tree near his old home, he often recalls the afternoon when his father, Song Jiatong, brought back the pomelo seedlings. To him, it is more than a tree. It is a living link between the Long March, the deep bond between the Red Army and the people, and a village's journey from poverty to revitalization.
Song Jiatong arrived in Guizhou with the Central Red Army during the Long March, the historic military maneuver in modern Chinese history. He was seriously wounded during the Four Crossings of the Chishui River and was rescued by local villagers.
After recovering, he chose to stay in Lintan, where he married and raised a family. In the early 1980s, Song Jiatong returned to his hometown of Ningdu, east China's Jiangxi Province, and brought back several honey pomelo seedlings. Four were planted, but only one survived.
No one has imagined that the single surviving seedling would take root by the Chishui River, bloom, and bear fruit, or that through villagers' grafting, it would eventually grow into more than 300 mu (20 hectares) of pomelo groves along the river valley.
"My father always kept the people in his heart," Song Guangping said. "Bringing the pomelo seedlings to Lintan was his way of helping the villagers live a better life."
Because the tree embodies the memory of unity between the Red Army soldiers and the people, locals affectionately call it the "Red Army Pomelo."
It soon became the village's "fruit of prosperity." From the 1980s into the early 2000s, more than 100 households in Lintan grew the fruit. At that time, they were the only pomelo growers for miles around. One pomelo sold for 5 yuan (about 0.75 U.S. dollars), and a single tree could produce two or three hundred fruits, earning a family several thousand yuan.
The income helped cover school fees for children across the village. Over the years, more than 100 students from Lintan went on to college.
The influence of the "Red Army Pomelo" has spread beyond Lintan. Villagers in Qinggangpo Village of Xishui County also transplanted and grafted trees from the original pomelo, introduced more varieties, and established a pomelo industry demonstration base.
"Qinggangpo Village is known for the Battle of Qinggangpo during the Long March," said Yi Song, Party secretary of the village. "We receive 200,000 visitors a year, and the tourism has been boosting our fruit farming. Since we began developing the pomelo industry, we have planted 1,800 mu (120 hectares) of honey pomelo, and total output is expected to reach 1.2 million yuan (about 180,000 U.S. dollars) this year."
From a single pomelo seedling to the industry of pomelo planting, the red legacy has never left this land. It has simply taken on a new form that is rooted in the soil and bringing sweetness to everyday life. (Xinhua/Yang Wenbin)

China ‘robot trainers’ fold clothes, wash dishes 200 times a day for up to US$900 a month
Some view this as deeply ironic: humans are teaching robots to work, yet these machines will one day replace their trainers
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
Across China, a new breed of freelance “robot trainers” are wearing motion-capture gear to turn everyday household chores – picking up cups, opening bottle caps and washing dishes – into data that will teach tomorrow’s machines.
The data is later converted into training sets to help robots work in settings ranging from kitchens and factories to supermarkets.
Such roles are increasingly advertised on mainland social media and job platforms. They reportedly pay trainers between 4,000 yuan and 6,000 yuan (US$600 and US$900) a month and attract unemployed workers and young people seeking flexible jobs.

IMF warns higher borrowing costs are straining public finances worldwide
Higher bond yields raise debt-servicing costs and increase fiscal pressure across advanced and emerging economies, global lender says
2-MIN READ2-MIN
1
 Listen
Rising sovereign debt and borrowing costs have prompted a fresh warning from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) about risks to the fiscal health of member countries, with 24-year highs in US Treasury yields expected to become one of the focal topics for central bankers and finance ministers gathering in Bangkok this week.
The average yield on 10-year government bonds across the Group of Seven economies increased by more than 1 percentage point between February and September this year, reaching its highest level in nearly two decades, according to an IMF blog post on Wednesday.
The US, France, Japan and other advanced economies have drawn attention in recent weeks as government bond yields climbed to multi-year highs, fuelling concerns about rising debt and spillover effects on emerging markets, a theme likely to feature at the IMF-World Bank annual meetings.
“Higher borrowing costs are adding to fiscal pressures at a time of high debt, making credible consolidation more urgent,” wrote Rodrigo Valdes, chief of the IMF’s fiscal affairs department, and deputy head Era Dabla-Norris.

US to drop charges against ex-CIA analyst over aid to South Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
02:00:00 UTC
11:00:00 KST

US to drop charges against ex-CIA analyst over aid to South Korea
Santul Nerkar and Michael S. Schmidt
- The US Justice Department will drop charges against former CIA analyst Sue Mi Terry over alleged secret work for South Korea.
- Prosecutors said she took luxury gifts and helped South Korean intelligence, but her lawyer said she acted in US interests and denied wrongdoing.
- Terry will avoid jail, must not speak with South Korean intelligence for one year, and the case has raised free speech and foreign influence concerns.
AI generated
NEW YORK – The US Justice Department has agreed to drop criminal charges against a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) analyst who was accused of covertly working for the South Korean government and receiving luxury gifts in return.
As part of a deal with federal prosecutors in New York City, Sue Mi Terry, who was a senior fellow for Korea studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, will not face jail time.
The deal, which amounts to the government walking away from a high-profile case involving foreign influence, is an unexpected development.
It comes just weeks before Terry was set to go on trial in the US District Court in Manhattan on charges of working as an unregistered foreign agent of South Korea.
She has maintained her innocence, while her lawyer said she was being prosecuted for doing the typical work of a prominent scholar of international relations in Asia.
In a statement, Lee Wolosky, a lawyer for Terry, said she had served her country “loyally for many years” and was pleased with the outcome.
“We have consistently maintained that her interactions with South Korean officials were conducted in furtherance of US interests and her work as a leading American specialist on North Korea and East Asia,” Wolosky said.
In a two-page letter filed on Oct 13, federal prosecutors in the Southern District of New York did not provide an explanation for reaching a deferred prosecution agreement with Terry, other than that the interests of the US and Terry would be “best served” by such a deal.
When Terry was arrested in 2024, prosecutors said she received luxury goods, dinners at Michelin-starred restaurants and other perks from the South Korean government in exchange for doing its bidding.
That work, prosecutors said, ranged from writing opinion articles that promoted South Korea’s stance on North Korea to arranging meetings between US government officials and South Korean intelligence agents.
By making the deal, Terry admitted to aiding South Korean intelligence officers in a number of ways, including by providing them with her notes from a meeting with the US secretary of state. She also admitted to receiving lavish gifts.
Terry is also barred from speaking to South Korean intelligence officials for the next year.
The case against Terry was one of dozens the Justice Department has brought in recent years to combat foreign influence in the US government.
The prosecutions have included efforts to rein in the Chinese government’s suppression of overseas dissidents, as well as the bribery conviction of former New Jersey senator Robert Menendez.
Terry’s prosecution drew criticism from some organisations.
In 2025, lawyers from the American Civil Liberties Union and the Knight First Amendment Institute filed a brief in Terry’s case, arguing that the indictment “threatens to punish her for constitutionally protected speech on a matter of public concern”.
Terry had also worked at the National Security Council and the National Intelligence Council and was called to testify before Congress about North Korea. Prosecutors produced instances of Terry’s work that they said were secretly promoting South Korean policy priorities, spanning the world of diplomacy, journalism and national security.
She is married to Max Boot, a Washington Post columnist, with whom she wrote a 2023 article about the improving relations between South Korea and Japan. The article, South Korea Takes A Brave Step Toward Reconciliation With Japan, was written at the behest of South Korea, prosecutors said. Boot was not accused of wrongdoing.
According to the indictment, Terry first started working as a foreign agent in 2013, five years after leaving the CIA.
The work began when she was contacted by a South Korean agent who was posing as a diplomat at the UN in New York City, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors said Terry worked with multiple handlers from South Korea, who bestowed gifts that included a Dolce & Gabbana coat worth US$2,845 (S$3,700), a Louis Vuitton handbag worth US$3,450 and at least US$37,000 to a gift account at her think-tank, which she controlled.
By 2014, she was on the FBI’s radar, which brought her in for a voluntary interview where she was “visibly nervous” as agents questioned her about her connections with South Korean intelligence officers.
Nine years later, Terry was interviewed again by the FBI. She admitted to agents that she had resigned from the CIA instead of being fired because the agency had “problems” with her contacts with South Korean officials. NYTIMES
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

Global deforestation slowed in 2025 but surged in Congo basin: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
01:57:00 UTC
10:57:00 KST

Global deforestation slowed in 2025 but surged in Congo basin: Study
- Global deforestation fell 15% in 2025 to seven million hectares, but experts say this is not enough to meet the 2030 pledge to end deforestation.
- Latin America improved, led by Brazil’s action plan and stronger Amazon enforcement, but progress is fragile because elections could reverse gains.
- The Congo basin worsened sharply, and a strong El Nino may bring more drought and fires, making future forest loss harder to stop.
AI generated
PARIS - Deforestation slowed worldwide in 2025, but the improvement is unlikely to last as the situation deteriorates in Central Africa and an exceptionally strong El Nino weather pattern intensifies, a new study said on Oct 14.
Seven million hectares of forest – roughly the size of the Republic of Ireland – were permanently destroyed in 2025, a 15% drop from the previous year, according to the annual Forest Declaration Assessment.
The slowdown, however, is not enough to keep the world from missing a pledge to end deforestation by 2030, according to the report, which was drafted by a coalition of research groups and non-governmental organisations.
The 2025 figure is “encouraging but so far it’s the exception, not a new trajectory”, Erin Matson, the study’s co-author and lead consultant at advisory group Climate Focus, said in a media briefing.
To meet the target, agreed at the United Nations’ COP26 climate talks in 2021, deforestation would have to fall by around one million hectares per year.
Clearing forests for agriculture or mining operations remains the leading drivers of deforestation.
2025’s improvement was due in part to progress in Latin America, with a 33% drop in what has historically been the world’s deforestation “hot spot”, according to the study.
The authors pointed particularly to Brazil’s deforestation action plan and increased enforcement in the country’s Amazon.
‘Irreversible’
Progress in the region, however, “rests heavily on the choices of a small number of governments and remains highly vulnerable” to recent and upcoming elections across the Amazon basin.
Brazil’s left-wing leader, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva – who has vowed to end illegal deforestation by 2030 – faces populist right Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in a runoff presidential election on Oct 25.
Deforestation had surged under the administration of Bolsonaro’s father, far-right former president Jair Bolsonaro.
Progress could also be threatened in Colombia and Peru, where hard-right presidents were recently elected, according to the experts.
Across the Atlantic in Africa, the situation deteriorated in the Congo basin, where rainforest loss reached 2.4 million hectares – near the same level of deforestation as the Amazon for the first time.
“Losing such a size of forest every year is a disaster,” said Sam Nguiffo, a lawyer and founder of the Centre for Environment and Development in Cameroon.
“As humanity, we clearly cannot afford that because it will be totally irreversible,” he said.
Logging for timber or felling trees for agriculture or mining appear to prevail in forest management in Central Africa, Nguiffo said.
Deforestation has a “massive impact on the cultural identity and on the livelihood of local and indigenous communities”, he said.
“The erosion of the forest, both in size and in number of species, reduces the space available for communities and fuels conflicts,” the lawyer added.
El Nino effects
El Nino, the warming phase of a natural climate cycle, also threatens progress because its effects include droughts, creating conditions for wildfires.
The current El Nino event, which emerged in June, is expected to peak later in 2026 but is already shaping up to be the strongest ever observed.
El Nino has been associated with strong drought in Indonesia, where tracts of forest and plantations have been burning in biodiverse Borneo and South Sumatra for months.
“If projections of the historically strong 2026-27 El Nino materialise, drought and fire risks will intensify further across tropical forest regions,” the deforestation report said.
Matson, of Climate Focus, noted that there was a “huge spike” in tree cover loss during the last “super” El Nino event in 2015-2016.
“We can’t fully predict the future but it’s unlikely, I would say, that in 2026 we’ll see the same kind of reductions (in deforestation) that we saw last year,” she said. AFP

Reading a book exposes us to the experiences of another person. Sometimes we are given these…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
01:45:29 UTC
10:45:29 KST

Reading a book exposes us to the experiences of another person. Sometimes we are given these experiences directly, as when we read a memoir or an autobiography. More often, we receive them indirectly, through the content and form of the book, which are shaped by the knowledge and intuitions the author has developed throughout their life.
Not only do we gain new knowledge as we read, we also add to our awareness. Our awareness expands through the experience of reading what the author has created through their own awareness. Such an experience is enormously valuable, for the experiences we can have directly in our own lives will always be a tiny subset of the total experience of humanity. By compressing experience into the medium of language, a book allows us to experience much more than we otherwise could.
We might then conclude that we can fully understand life by reading widely and that the awareness we gain from books is sufficient to living well. But while the awareness gained by reading is valuable, it does not follow that it replaces the awareness developed through other kinds of experience.

Jamaica accepts first flight of third-country deportations from US
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
01:44:09 UTC
10:44:09 KST

Jamaica accepts first flight of third-country deportations from US
Opposition leaders in Jamaica have questioned why the deportation deal with the Trump White House has not been made public.
The Caribbean country of Jamaica has received its first third-country deportations from the United States, as part of an expanding set of international agreements under President Donald Trump.
On Tuesday, 22 deportees from the US arrived at Norman Manley International Airport in Kingston, Jamaica.
Media reports indicate they were subsequently boarded onto a bus and taken to an undisclosed location.
Such deportations – which often involve non-citizens who have no ties to their destinations – have faced widespread condemnation from human rights groups and advocates who have questioned their legality.
But Jamaica is among a growing number of countries to accept third-country deportations, as part of Trump’s effort to implement the largest mass deportation campaign in US history.
At least 35 countries have entered into third-country deportation agreements with the US, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, an advocacy project affiliated with the groups Refugees International and Human Rights First.
The Washington Post reported last month that the Trump administration has earmarked roughly $410m to support such efforts.
Jamaica signed a bilateral memorandum of understanding in June to receive third-country deportations. Under the plan, Jamaica will transfer any deportees to their home countries or other destinations after their arrival.
The country’s government has also pledged not to accept any deportees with criminal records.
“The government reiterates that this is a transit arrangement intended to facilitate the return of Third Country Nationals to their country of origin or other receiving countries,” Jamaica’s Ministry of National Security and Peace and its Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade said in a joint statement.
It added that care for the deportees will be supported by the International Organization for Migration, a United Nations organisation.
“The arrangement will not be funded by the Government of Jamaica,” the joint statement added.
Opposition leaders in Jamaica, however, spoke out against the deportation, framing the deal as a threat to the island’s security. They also questioned why the agreement had not been debated publicly.
“Jamaicans are being asked to trust a secret document that touches their security, their communities and their public services,” said Fitz Jackson, the opposition spokesperson on national security.
In response to Jackson’s statement, Foreign Minister Kamina Johnson Smith argued that any questions about the deportation deal “have all been answered”. She also indicated that the US has not agreed to make the deal public.
“As I explained before, some countries have agreed to receive criminals, we have not,” she wrote on social media.
“Some countries have had their agreements made public, but our partner has not agreed for this one to be.”
Legal challenges against the third-country deportations are ongoing in the US, where advocates have argued that deportees are being removed from the country without due process of law, the constitutional right to a fair hearing.
Critics have also argued that third-country deportations sometimes send immigrants to countries where they may face danger.
Some of the recipient countries, such as South Sudan, are in the midst of ongoing conflict or have faced accusations of serious human rights abuses.
Opponents have even said the third-country deportations are being used as a backdoor method for circumventing court protection orders.
Such orders may prohibit the US government from returning certain immigrants to their home countries, for fear of violence and persecution.
But by sending immigrants to third countries, critics say the Trump administration avoids violating such protection orders – though in some cases, the third country has then returned the deportee to the country identified in the US protection order.
In a February report by Democrats on the US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, one official said anonymously that the purpose of such far-flung deportations was to instil fear.
“The point is that the administration can threaten people that they will literally be dropped in the middle of nowhere,” the official said. “The point is to scare people.”

Colombia peace tribunal charges ex-FARC members with anti-Indigenous crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

01:43:56 UTC

Colombia peace tribunal charges ex-FARC members with anti-Indigenous crimes
The former rebels are accused of abuses such as torture, murder and the displacement of Indigenous leaders during Colombia’s civil conflict.
Colombia’s transitional justice system, established to address crimes committed during the country’s decades-long civil conflict, has indicted several former members of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), formerly the country’s largest rebel group.
A group of 10 ex-rebels were charged on Tuesday with alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity between 1996 and 2016.
The Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP), the transitional justice tribunal, said that the accused had carried out crimes of torture, murder and forced displacement against five Indigenous groups in southeast Colombia.
“Today we are delivering justice to the most forgotten peoples of a segregated Colombia,” JEP magistrate Catalina Diaz said.
She explained that FARC commanders had ordered subordinates to plant landmines on Indigenous territory and ruin ecosystems the tribes relied on for survival.
“These people have had their basic right to exist compromised,” Diaz added.
The indictment is the latest example of Colombia’s efforts to reckon with the abuses and violence of a civil conflict that lasted for more than half a century, resulting in severe rights abuses.
Since the 1960s, left-wing rebels, government security forces, criminal networks and government-aligned right-wing paramilitaries have clashed over efforts to control territory and shape the country’s power structure.
Indigenous communities and activists continue to face violent attacks in Colombia today. Continued fighting has also led to an ever-growing death toll.
A 2022 report from Colombia’s Truth Commission found that 450,664 people were killed between 1985 and 2018 as a result of the conflict. An additional 121,768 people were forcibly disappeared.
Indigenous activists and community leaders hailed JEP’s decision on Tuesday as an acknowledgement that their communities were targeted.
“For the first time, the Colombian state recognises that [armed groups] did not just kill individuals,” said Yhon Jairo Figueroa, a leader of the Koreguaje tribe. “But they attempted to kill the knowledge, the language, the territory.”
Three of those accused are also former members of the last secretariat of the FARC, which reached a peace deal with the government in 2016 that included disarmament.
Critics of the deal and its implementation say that many of those responsible for abuses have escaped accountability. Some FARC fighters who refused to accept the agreement have since formed splinter groups that continue to fight in the conflict.
The 2016 deal ultimately granted the former rebels 10 seats in Colombia’s Congress to address the FARC’s political concerns.
One of the suspects indicted Tuesday was Julian Gallo, who served eight years as a senator under that deal.
The JEP, for its part, can impose only non-prison penalties. Last year, for instance, it sentenced seven ex-FARC members accused of kidnapping to eight years of reparations, including landmine clearing and helping to find missing persons.
Separately, JEP also sentenced former military members to reparation work for their involvement in the killing and disappearances of civilians, who were then tallied as rebels in government records. Those systemic misrepresentations became known as the “false positives” scandal.
But critics warn that threats to JEP’s existence loom under Colombia’s newly inaugurated far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella.
Allies of de la Espriella have proposed a nearly 17 percent cut to JEP’s funding for fiscal year 2027. Such budget reductions are set to be weighed by Colombia’s Congress this month.
Before taking office in August, de la Espriella served as a defence lawyer, in some cases representing right-wing paramilitaries. He has criticised the JEP, accusing it of issuing lenient sentences.

AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
01:41:55 UTC
10:41:55 KST

AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
- Summary:
- A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.
- Share:
Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?
New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness
Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.
"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.
"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."
To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.
Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.
A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness
The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.
However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.
The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.
"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."
Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.
Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI
The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.
Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.
Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.
The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.
"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Louis Longin, Jurgis Karpus, Nadine Meertens, Bahador Bahrami, Ophelia Deroy. AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems. Cognition, 2027; 278: 106733 DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106733

Anthropic is asking a federal court in Washington, D.C., to rehear its appeal in a case concerning the Pentagon's blacklisting of the company's AI models.

Does Hong Kong’s economy serve the people or profit?
While mainland China might not have a Nobel Prize-winning economist, its lifting of millions out of poverty offers an example worth reflecting on
4-MIN READ4-MIN
3
 Listen
C. K. Yeung is a former associate vice-president of Hong Kong Baptist University and professor of practice at Chinese University of Hong Kong
 
China has lifted nearly 800 million people out of extreme poverty, arguably the greatest achievement in poverty reduction in human history. Even so, no mainland Chinese economist has won the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences.
Across the Pacific, the United States has produced about 75 per cent of Nobel economics laureates, even as its economy staggers under mounting public debt, chronic fiscal deficits, and recurring financial crises and government shutdowns.
Of the 99 economics laureates ever awarded, only two are from Asia. Amartya Sen was honoured for his contribution to welfare economics and Abhijit Banerjee for his work in alleviating global poverty. Both are from India, not China. Why such an anomaly?
The short answer strikes at the heart of the matter: economics in the West and economics in China serve different purposes and recognise different kinds of achievements.

FBI disrupts Pyongyang revenue stream: North Koreans in US tech jobs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
01:25:00 UTC
10:25:00 KST

FBI disrupts Pyongyang revenue stream – North Koreans in US tech jobs
Dustin Volz
- The FBI disrupted a North Korean IT job network that used US facilitators and laptop farms to fund Pyongyang’s nuclear and ballistic weapons programmes.
- US officials said more than 40 laptop farms were dismantled in Texas, nearly 200 devices were seized, and indictments were unsealed against 12 suspects over a US$3 million fraud.
- The scheme used stolen identities, AI tools and Western accomplices to trick US firms, and the FBI warned the threat is growing and highly serious.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) in September disrupted a widespread network of American facilitators accused of aiding the North Korean government in securing remote information technology jobs that helped fund the reclusive country’s nuclear and ballistic weapons programmes, US officials said Oct 13.
The operation included the dismantling of more than 40 so-called laptop farms across Texas and the seizure of nearly 200 computer devices, the officials said, marking one of the largest efforts to date by the US authorities to block a key revenue stream that has helped North Korea evade harsh international sanctions and generate billions in cash in recent years.
The Justice Department separately unsealed indictments in Ohio on Oct 13 against two US nationals and 10 China-based North Koreans accused of committing identity theft to earn pay cheques from unwitting US companies that hired them.
Prosecutors said that scheme bilked 70 companies out of more than US$3 million (S$3.84 million) and ran from 2019 to 2025. The identities of two additional defendants remained under seal.
The moves were the latest by the US in an intensifying campaign to try to cut off a stealthy and evolving digital threat from North Korea whose scale is not entirely clear but likely vast.
US intelligence officials in the Biden and second Trump administrations have said the information technology worker scams are a primary method of funding Pyongyang’s weapons programme, alongside thefts of cryptocurrency.
North Korea is deploying “thousands of state-controlled IT workers to infiltrate companies in the United States and allied countries”, Brett Leatherman, the head of the FBI’s cyber division, said in an interview.
“Every one of these jobs is funding a stream for a nuclear and ballistic missiles programme obtained with the stolen identity of an American and the trust of an American employer.”
The bureau worked closely with the US-based cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike to identify and disrupt the network, Leatherman said.
He added that the coordinated actions were an early example of the FBI’s new cyber strategy, which was unveiled in September and promised closer collaboration with the private sector to target hackers in ways that impede or thwart malicious activity.
The strategy is part of a broader effort across the Trump administration to work more closely with US companies to strike hackers with cyberattacks, a pivot cautiously welcomed by some security experts.
US officials and cybersecurity analysts have said the North Korean IT worker scheme is among the most serious ongoing digital threats facing businesses today and that it remains underappreciated as a risk.
Adam Meyers, who oversees counter-adversary operations at CrowdStrike, said the North Korean schemes to get hired for jobs have been “increasing both in prevalence and complexity”.
It is difficult to know how widespread laptop farms are in the US, Meyers said, but noted that CrowdStrike identified an average of two new cases per day throughout September – which is likely only the tip of the iceberg.
For more than two years, US intelligence officials and cybersecurity researchers have warned that North Korea has been using stolen American identities – often acquired from compromised private information, like Social Security numbers, on the dark web – and artificial intelligence tools to get hired for remote IT jobs at companies across the US, Europe and elsewhere.
Experts have said companies ranging from small start-ups to Fortune 500 firms have been victimised.
A crucial aspect of the fraud campaign is support from people in the US who are recruited by North Korea to help bypass corporate security measures that detect fraudulent hires, according to investigators.
Facilitators help enable the fraud by receiving and setting up work laptops at addresses that appear like legitimate residences to corporate human resources teams.
North Korean operators then use software to remotely tunnel into those laptops and work on them, posing as Americans to the companies that hired them.
The appeal for facilitators is simple: Jobs that look like easy cash and, at least at first, might not require much of them. “They get kind of hooked on it initially, and then more gets asked of them, and they’re kind of in too deep at that point,” Meyers said.
Leatherman said that the Texas sweep did not include any arrests of facilitators but that the authorities warned them they could face criminal penalties should they continue to assist with remote fraud.
The decision stemmed in part from a desire to move quickly to upend the network rather than wait for prosecutors to file charges, he said.
Leatherman said the laptop farms often operate like a “mini data centre” for the North Koreans, where one facilitator hosts dozens or even hundreds of laptops used to fill scores of jobs.
A woman in Arizona sentenced in 2025 to more than eight years in prison was accused of hosting dozens of laptops at her home to help North Koreans connect to more than 300 US companies.
The tactics of North Korea’s IT worker army have steadily evolved to evade detection.
That includes increased reliance on artificial intelligence to create fake resumes, videos and photos, and to navigate virtual job interviews, officials said.
The fraudsters are also relying more on sub-contractors in places like Pakistan and Nigeria to further obscure North Korean involvement, Leatherman said.
In an advisory released on Oct 13, the FBI said the North Koreans were paying Americans and other Western accomplices to “perform a growing variety of identity and location obfuscation tasks” that included appearing on camera, participating in job interviews or meetings, verifying fraudulent identities, shipping packages, and even completing urinalysis tests or fingerprint submissions. New electrode design could improve green ammonia production: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:17:44 CST
10:17:44 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Researchers in Australia have developed a new electrode design that could improve the energy efficiency of producing ammonia using renewable electricity.
The new approach has overcome a fundamental energy limitation of the technology, opening new possibilities for cleaner and potentially more cost-effective production of one of the world's most important chemicals, according to a recent statement of Australia's Monash University.
Researchers have developed a new type of lithium-alloying electrode that significantly reduces the energy required to convert nitrogen gas into ammonia, a breakthrough that could help advance the transition away from fossil-fuel-based ammonia production, the statement said.
Instead of producing lithium metal on a conventional electrode, the researchers used gallium-based materials that combine with lithium, allowing the reaction that converts nitrogen gas into ammonia to occur at substantially more favorable electrical potentials.
Ammonia is vital for nitrogen fertilizers and is increasingly explored as a carbon-free fuel, but conventional production relies on large, centralized facilities that cannot readily use dispersed or stranded renewable energy, according to the study published in Cell Press Blue.
Under optimized experimental conditions, the researchers achieved a faradaic efficiency of 96 ± 6 percent, meaning almost all the electrical current was directed towards producing ammonia.
The findings could support future electrochemical ammonia production with an estimated energy efficiency of at least 22 percent, although further improvements are required to reach proposed commercial targets, the researchers said.
The next step is to integrate the new lithium-alloying cathodes into electrolyzer prototypes, scaling up the materials and demonstrating long-term ammonia production at competitive energy efficiency, they said. ■

CAIRO, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Norway's Jeanette Hegg Duestad won the women's 50m rifle three positions gold at the International Shooting Sport Federation (ISSF) World Cup Rifle/Pistol in Cairo on Tuesday, returning to the city where she claimed the world title last year.
The reigning world champion scored 362.7 points to secure gold, ahead of the Czech Republic's Veronika Blazickova, who took silver with 358.9, while Denmark's Rikke Maeng Ibsen claimed bronze with 349.1.
Duestad topped the qualification round with 592 points before taking an early lead in the final. She scored 208.9 points across the kneeling and prone stages and maintained her advantage through the standing stage, where shooters were progressively eliminated, eventually winning by 3.8 points.
The eight-woman final featured four of the world's top five shooters, including world No. 1 Seonaid McIntosh of Britain, who finished eighth. Switzerland's Chiara Leone, the reigning Olympic champion, placed fourth.
Despite the victory, Duestad said she had not felt technically at her best.
"It feels really good. I haven't felt at my best technically today, but I managed to actually fight every single shot," she told Xinhua. "In the end, it ended up really good."
Duestad also highlighted the strength of the competition, saying, "We have world champions here, Olympic champions, World Cup winners. I think actually all eight of us could have won this final."
For 23-year-old Blazickova, the silver marked her first World Cup medal after four previous appearances in finals.
Blazickova said she was pleased with her performance in the prone and standing positions, but considered kneeling her weakest stage and an area she needed to improve, adding that she had not expected to win silver against such strong competition.
Ibsen, a former European champion, secured her first World Cup medal of the season with bronze.
The ISSF World Cup Rifle/Pistol, held from October 8 to 16 at Egypt International Olympic City in the New Administrative Capital, east of Cairo, brings together hundreds of shooters from 51 countries and regions. ■

US fines Bank of America $1.2bn for money laundering, sanctions violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
01:15:30 UTC
10:15:30 KST

US fines Bank of America $1.2bn for money laundering, sanctions violations
The second-largest US bank faces record penalties for failing to comply with sanctions and money laundering laws.
The US Treasury Department has imposed more than $1.21 billion in penalties against Bank of America, the second-largest bank in the US, for violating anti-money laundering and sanctions laws.
The fines announced on Tuesday include the third-largest penalty in the department’s history, the US Treasury said in a statement.
“When a bank of this size fails to meet its anti-money laundering and sanctions obligations, the consequences extend far beyond its own walls, exposing the entire US financial system to significant illicit finance risks,” US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said.
He added that these “actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institutions are not above the law”.
Enforcement actions
According to the Treasury Department, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed a $1.2 billion penalty over the bank’s failure to mitigate and report “priority national security risks, including Chinese Money Laundering Networks and illicit finance along the southwest border”.
The failures identified by FinCEN involved deficiencies related to the bank’s suspicious transaction identification and reporting and customer due diligence processes. According to the statement, “the Bank effectively outsourced to third parties a substantial portion of its proactive detection and reporting obligations”.
“Bank of America failed to timely report to FinCEN over $5 billion dollars in suspicious transactions”, the Treasury said in the statement.
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) assessed a $750 million fine, the largest in its history, for the bank’s deficient and ineffective anti-money laundering compliance programme. FinCEN’s $1.2 billion penalty includes credit for the OCC fine.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) also announced an $11.6 million settlement agreement over apparent violations of numerous sanctions programmes, including on Iran, Russia, narcotics and global terrorism.
Bank of America agreed to settle 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programmes, and the settlement includes “significant compliance commitments regarding training, testing and audit, and future communication and cooperation with OFAC”.
In the statement, the Treasury said the actions “underscore the importance of effectively complying” with US anti-money laundering and sanctions requirements.
In response, Bank of America said in a statement: “Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right.”
“We have invested billions of dollars in technology and dedicated thousands of employees to combat financial crime, and our team is far along with and committed to completing the work required to address the issues raised by our regulators.”

Namibia battles cattle disease outbreak as EU suspends several meat imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
01:07:46 UTC
10:07:46 KST

Namibia battles cattle disease outbreak as EU suspends several meat imports
Foot-and-mouth disease threatens livestock farmers’ livelihoods and disrupts meat supplies as authorities impose curbs.
Windhoek, Namibia – “We had to close the market for several days. It was just before the weekend and month’s end. That’s when we need the money the most,” says Francisco, a vendor at Single Quarter, Windhoek’s largest open meat market.
He pours vinegar and cooking oil into a tomato and onion salsa, a traditional accompaniment to kapana, a popular grilled-meat street food. Around him, many stalls and grilling stations sit empty. Instead of the crowds that typically fill the market during business hours, only a handful of customers move between the stalls.
Recent closures and concerns about meat supplies have disrupted business.
“Our business is slow. We are struggling to buy meat, but without it, we cannot survive,” says another kapana vendor, who asked to remain anonymous. “This is our livelihood. The meat is much more expensive now, so we are making less money altogether. If this continues for three months, it is going to be very bad for us.”
In Katutura, Windhoek’s largest township, uncertainty over beef supplies is adding to residents’ financial concerns.
“If we don’t eat meat, what are we going to eat? We are Namibians,” one resident says, describing meat as a staple of the local diet. Another worries about rising prices and the wider consequences for Namibia, where livestock exports are an important part of the economy.
At a supermarket in the Okuryangava suburb, the butchery has already run out of some premium beef products. Store manager Enrico De Azevedo, 23, says consumer behaviour has also contributed to the pressure.
“We saw people panic-buying like they did during the COVID-19 pandemic with toilet paper. Now, they can go and stack their meat next to their toilet paper,” he says.
De Azevedo also recognises the wider economic risks. “For those in the export business, this will have grave implications.”
Outbreak threatens Namibia’s export market
Namibia’s Directorate of Veterinary Services (DVS) confirmed an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) on a commercial farm in the Karasburg State Veterinary District, in the southern //Kharas Region, on September 23, 2026.
In an address on October 5, President Netumbo Nandi-Ndaitwah said surveillance teams had recorded 127 positive cases across 15 farms. Teams had inspected 29,313 animals across 68 farms. The government had also established 20 surveillance teams and 10 roadblocks in the region as part of its response.
In an update covering the situation as of October 6, the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform reported that 129 animal samples had tested positive and 17 farms had been confirmed infected. Veterinary teams had inspected 72 of 81 targeted farms.
The outbreak was subsequently confirmed in a second region. On October 7, laboratory tests confirmed FMD in cattle at Kalala Island, in the Kabbe constituency of the Zambezi Region, in northern Namibia.
Veterinary officials from the Katima Mulilo State Veterinary Office investigated the suspected outbreak on October 5 after observing clinical signs in 20 cattle. Twelve samples were collected and submitted to the Central Veterinary Laboratory in Windhoek on October 6. All 12 tested positive for the virus the following day.
In a public notification issued on October 10, the ministry outlined restrictions across the Zambezi Region following confirmation of the outbreak.
These include suspending the movement of cloven-hoofed animals and their raw products, cancelling previously issued movement permits, and halting livestock auctions, informal markets and other animal-gathering events. Slaughter at local abattoirs, informal markets and social events has also been suspended.
Slaughter at export abattoirs may continue for eligible cattle under the commodity-based trade system, provided the animals meet quarantine requirements and pass traceability checks.
Emergency vaccination has begun in the affected area, while roadblocks and intensive surveillance are intended to prevent further spread.
FMD is a highly contagious viral disease affecting cloven-hoofed animals, including cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. It can disrupt livestock production and trade, particularly when it affects areas recognised as free of the disease.
Following confirmation of the //Kharas outbreak, Namibian authorities notified the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and introduced restrictions on the movement and export of cloven-hoofed animals and their products.
The European Union subsequently amended its import rules for Namibia’s previously authorised export zone, known as NA-1, following the outbreak.
The Zambezi detection has added to the challenge facing veterinary authorities, who are working to contain the disease and prevent further infections. The available information confirms outbreaks in both regions but does not establish that the disease spread directly from //Kharas to Zambezi.
“The outbreak has been a heavy blow to our country,” Marianne Pretorius, head of communications at the Namibia Agricultural Union (NAU), told Al Jazeera by email. “The restrictions are painful, but they are necessary, and the NAU supports them.”
On October 5, the European Union announced a temporary suspension of entry into the bloc of specified fresh meat products from cattle, sheep and goats, as well as certain products from other farmed and wild hoofed animals, from Namibia’s previously authorised export zone. The restrictions also cover specified processed meat products, including biltong and jerky.
The measure is not a blanket suspension of all Namibian meat imports. According to the EU, certain processed products that undergo the prescribed risk-mitigating treatment remain eligible for entry. Qualifying fresh-meat consignments certified by Namibian authorities before September 23 may also enter during a 90-day transitional period, subject to the applicable EU rules and border-control requirements.
The restrictions apply to the specific products covered by the EU measure. It remains unclear whether the Zambezi outbreak will affect exports to other markets or under other trade arrangements.
For the country’s livestock industry, the restrictions add to the uncertainty created by domestic movement controls and the loss of access to some export markets.
“For farmers in the //Kharas region, the impact is immediate and severe, but this is not only a //Kharas problem,” Pretorius said. “When export markets close, every livestock producer in the country feels it.”
She warned that the consequences could continue even after domestic trading resumes.
“Even when domestic trade resumes, prices may remain under pressure until export markets reopen,” she wrote. “That is why we are calling for market recovery to be treated with the same determination as disease control.”
Containment measures expand as economic costs mount
Namibia has stepped up efforts to contain the disease, including plans to strengthen veterinary fencing in high-risk areas.
Construction of a veterinary cordon fence along the Orange River in the //Kharas Region began in October. The barrier is intended to strengthen controls along the border with South Africa. The government has also pursued additional fencing and containment measures in high-risk areas.
The containment measures are intended to limit animal movement and reduce the risk of further infections. Their effectiveness will depend on surveillance, compliance with movement restrictions and the ability of veterinary authorities to identify and contain new cases.
The outbreak is also affecting the country’s meat-processing sector. The Namibian reported on October 12 that Meat Corporation of Namibia (Meatco) had placed about 400 production workers on three weeks of special leave with full pay. The situation was due to be reviewed on October 23, with workers’ return depending on guidance from veterinary authorities.
The Namibian also reported that Meatco had paid farmers N$31 million (about US$1.8 million) for cattle delivered to its Windhoek abattoir between August 29 and September 11. The payments cover cattle already delivered, while uncertainty remains over future sales and export access.
Farmers and meat vendors count the cost
For livestock producers, the outbreak threatens immediate income and the longer-term viability of their businesses. Restrictions on moving and selling animals can interrupt cash flow even for farmers whose herds have not been infected.
Gert Engelbrecht, a 40-year-old farmer from Aranos, said the restrictions had created financial and emotional strain for producers.
“Our livestock is not simply a business to us; it is our livelihood and something we have invested our lives in,” he told Al Jazeera. “Being able to move and sell livestock is fundamental to keeping the farming operation going. It affects farmers across Namibia when movement and markets are restricted. Ultimately, we need to regain our disease-free status.”
The DVS has intensified surveillance and is tracing livestock movements that took place before the outbreaks were detected.
For farmers, restoring market access is essential to keeping their operations running. Meat vendors, meanwhile, depend on reliable supplies to sustain their businesses.
“Farmers are fighters,” Engelbrecht said. “We understand why restrictions are necessary, but we are not sitting back and waiting for somebody else to solve this. We are working with the veterinary authorities to see this disease controlled, regain our status, and restore access to our markets.”

50 DAF Battle Network Programs Rolled into Single, $4.5B ‘Megatron’ Contract Vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
00:46:43 UTC
09:46:43 KST

The Department of the Air Force is consolidating more than 50 programs supporting its efforts to create a vast battle network into a single $4.5 billion contract vehicle to streamline software and technology integration.
The contract, dubbed “Megatron” in reference to the lead villain in the Transformers toy and movie franchise, is a multiple award, indefinite delivery, indefinite quantity vehicle to get technology now and in the future into the DAF Battle Network.
Brig. Gen. Joshua Williams, the department’s new portfolio acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management, highlighted the Megatron program at AFA’s Air, Space, & Cyber conference in September.
“The DAF Battle Network depends on an industrial base that can innovate, integrate, and deliver at the speed of relevance, and we need to build business mechanisms to enable their ability to do that,” Williams told reporters at the conference.
The contract vehicle will cover software delivery, commercial solutions to Battle Network challenges, and other tech needs, Williams said.
The draft notice for Megatron was posted in August, with a final request for proposals expected to be released this quarter. Multiple contract awards are planned for fiscal 2027 under the new “master plan,” Megatron Contracting Officer Julianne Payne told Air & Space Forces Magazine, “which span from sensor integration and connectivity to applications and secure data processing.”
“Key efforts include maturing our digital architecture, fielding secure processing at the edge, and delivering applications that put the operator at the center,” Payne added.
Merging Efforts
Past contract vehicles often created multiyear contracts tied to fixed requirements and hardware delivery. That doesn’t work in a world of rapid software updates, new sensors, and modes of communication needed for the DAF Battle Network.
“When a specific mission need arises, we can quickly compete delivery or task orders within this pool, compressing our acquisition timeline from over a year to a matter of months to get critical capabilities to the field faster,” Payne said. “For years, our sensors, command and control nodes, and warfighters have operated in stovepipes, making it difficult to share information quickly.”
The C3BM office’s decision to take this new contract approach isn’t happening in a vacuum. Payne noted that adversaries such as China are already building highly sophisticated capabilities to disrupt U.S. military networks. The larger effort to connect all operational capabilities via the battle network and ultimately to the larger Combined Joint All Domain Command and Control network must happen faster.
Soliciting, buying, and implementing standalone platforms for a single aircraft or satellite, common practice for decades, won’t cut it.
“If our systems do not integrate, they do not fight. That realization is what led to the creation of C3BM in 2022 to bring all those fragmented authorities under one roof,” Payne said. “Ultimately, that’s what drove us to the DAF Battle Network concept, and Megatron is the vehicle that is going to deliver it.”
Megatron combines two current IDIQ contracts: the Advanced Battle Management System IDIQ and the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center’s architecture and integration directorate’s XA IDIQ.
The ABMS contract launched in 2020 and was planned for an initial five-year run, allowing the Air Force to award multiple contracts for ABMS work across the force. The Air Force used the ABMS IDIQ to conduct live operational demos for real-time hardware and software testing in field conditions. Contractors participating ranged from small software companies to large defense primes.
The XA IDIQ was a planned 10-year effort from 2022-2032 to bring together early-stage concepts for the network’s architecture and integration.
But even with two large IDIQs, the Air Force had a problem. A company might bring a great concept to AFLCMC via the XA IDIQ but not have a contract under the ABMS IDIQ, creating a bottleneck between capability growth and deployment.
A New Approach
PAE C3BM intends to use the new Megatron contract to find the “best-of-breed” option across six lines of effort for the Battle Network:
- Digital Architecture & Standards
- Sensor Integration
- Secure Data Processing (including Cloud, AI, and Machine Learning)
- Network Connectivity (Line-of-Sight, Beyond-Line-of-Sight, and anti-jamming)
- Software Applications
- Synthetic Environments (computer-simulated training and development)
Staying Relevant
With rapid upgrades across the tech industry, the Megatron contract, and larger C3BM efforts, the goal is to bring the best tech into the system while keeping it secure and standardized across the network.
The PAE’s secure processing strategy works across multiple security classification levels, Payne said.
“This capability applies to form factors ranging from enterprise data centers to tactical edge hardware,” Payne said. “The contract mandates that vendors deliver compatible, mission-tailorable solutions, utilizing bare metal, virtualization, or cloud-based services.”
Across the Department of Defense, information technology managers and decision-makers face the burden of maintaining legacy technology and software while merging old but sometimes linchpin systems with new software and hardware.
With Megatron, officials seek to prevent “technical debt,” or the continued use of legacy systems that can’t be upgraded, and avoid future “vendor lock,” which allows a single vendor to control vital software or hardware because of proprietary constraints.
“If a contractor’s solution becomes obsolete or creates technical debt, we can recompete future delivery orders or task orders among the other qualified vendors in our pool. This continuous competition at the order level incentivizes contractors to deliver open, modern, and cost-effective solutions,” Payne said.

Israeli attacks kill one in Gaza, wound journalists in occupied West Bank
Nearly two-thirds of Gaza is under Israeli control a year into a ceasefire, and Netanyahu vows control of the West Bank.
An Israeli air strike on a vehicle in Gaza City has killed one person and wounded several others, emergency services told Al Jazeera, as Israeli attacks continue a year into the ceasefire.
The strike hit the Tuffah neighbourhood, in the city’s northeast, on Tuesday.
In az-Zawayda, central Gaza, a four-year-old boy, Osama Ahmed Abed, died of wounds from an Israeli attack three weeks ago, the Palestinian news agency Wafa reported.
His death brought the number of Palestinians killed in Gaza since October 7, 2023, to more than 74,382.
Gaza’s Civil Defence agency said it was deeply concerned about repeated forced displacement near the “Yellow Line”, the boundary to which Israeli troops withdrew under the October 2025 ceasefire.
It said “massive explosions” and “indiscriminate gunfire” by Israeli forces had damaged hundreds of displaced people’s tents and weakened homes hit earlier.
It appealed for urgent intervention to “halt this war against the civilian population”.
A shrinking Gaza
Al Jazeera’s maps show nearly two-thirds of Gaza is now under Israeli military control or subject to access restrictions. The “Yellow Line”, set under US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan to end the war, was meant to mark where Israeli forces first pulled back, with further withdrawals to follow.
Israeli forces have instead seized more territory.
The US-backed Board of Peace marked the ceasefire’s anniversary with a post saying Trump’s leadership “ended a war that had no end in sight”.
At least 1,400 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks since the truce began, and no Palestinian technocratic administration is in place.
More than 80 percent of Gaza’s buildings have been destroyed or damaged.
Raids in the occupied West Bank
In the occupied West Bank, Israeli attacks in Ramallah and el-Bireh wounded a child with live ammunition and left several Palestinians suffocating from tear gas, the Palestinian Ministry of Health said.
Palestine TV correspondent Khaled Mattawa was wounded in the hand by a sound bomb, and Sky News Arabia correspondent Firas Lutfi in the leg by shrapnel, Wafa reported.
Israeli forces also raided the offices of several Palestinian non-governmental organisations and the courtyard of the Palestine Medical Complex.
Al Jazeera’s Nida Ibrahim, reporting from Ramallah, said the attacks were “yet another step to undermine the Palestinian Authority”.
Human rights lawyer Muhammad Dahleh said Israel uses laws and military orders to shut down Palestinian rights groups, naming them “terrorist organisations based on privileged evidence” that is withheld from the groups and their lawyers.
Several were outlawed in 2021, and legal objections were rejected by Israeli military authorities, he said.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said in a video on X that Israel was “preparing for a scenario in which Palestinian Authority forces turn their guns against Israel in the West Bank”.
“There will be no Arab army west of the Jordan River. There will be the [Israeli military],” he said, adding that Israel would extend its control across the territory.

Space Force Activates Component Under Special Operations Command
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
00:30:45 UTC
09:30:45 KST

Editor’s note: This story has been updated to include a statement from an Oct. 14 Space Force release.
The Space Force has officially established its component to U.S. Special Operations Command, creating a ninth component charged with presenting space expertise to commanders in the field.
The service activated the component Oct. 7, according to a Sept. 29 memo confirmed to be authentic by Air & Space Forces Magazine, and it plans to hold a formal ceremony Nov. 2. The Space Force has had a special forces element operating at SOCOM headquarters at MacDill Air Force Base, Fla., but not a formal component field command.
The announcement comes more than 18 months after U.S. Special Operations Command revealed plans to create a space component. Congress pressed pause on that process in the fiscal 2026 National Defense Authorization Act, blocking funding for the move until the Space Force provided more details on its plans.
“While space capabilities are already integrated into [SOCOM] missions, this activation institutionalizes how the Space Force organizes, trains, equips, and presents forces for the special operations enterprise,” the service said in an Oct. 14 statement. A spokesperson did not address questions about the organization’s leadership and structure.
Space capabilities and forces have played a critical role in recent operations, according to senior defense officials. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff Gen. Dan Caine identified space forces as a “first mover” during the early days of Operation Epic Fury. And in a speech last month at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Chief of Space Operations Gen. Douglas Schiess highlighted electronic warfare operations performed by Guardians deployed with the Space Force’s 42nd Electronic Warfare Detachment, which supports U.S. Central Command and Space Forces Central.
Standing up components under every unified combatant command has been a focus of the Space Force since its establishment in 2019. Along with Space Forces Special Operations, or SPACEFOR-SOC, the service has component field commands within U.S. Northern Command, Southern Command, Pacific Command, Space Command, and Central Command. It also has a combined component for European Command and Africa Command, and sub-unified components in Japan and Korea.
Axios first reported on SPACEFOR-SOC’s activation.
As the Space Force looks to more than double its number of uniformed Guardians over the next five years—increasing its ranks from about 11,000 to 25,000 by fiscal 2031—officials have said the size of its component organizations must increase to meet operational demand.
“As we walked forward and stood up U.S. Space Force components—now with almost every combatant command around the planet—each one of those was sized to get off the ground and start doing the integrated work that we’ve seen,” Lt. Gen. Dennis Bythewood, commander of U.S. Space Forces-Space, the service’s SPACECOM component, told reporters in March. “But we already see that in stressing times, we’re having to surge people forward.”
To support future surge needs, Bythewood said at the time, components must grow to make sure that Guardian deployments don’t disrupt regular operations. He noted that his component has growth plans “already laid in” over the next few years.
