A planet 320 light-years away confirms what scientists long suspected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
00:24:40 UTC
09:24:40 KST

A planet 320 light-years away confirms what scientists long suspected
A scorching-hot planet 320 light-years away has confirmed a long-held assumption about planet formation, offering a powerful new clue in the search for habitable worlds.
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA)
- Summary:
- Astronomers have discovered that a scorching-hot planet 320 light-years away shares a striking chemical similarity with its host star, providing the first direct evidence for a fundamental assumption about planet formation. The breakthrough could help scientists predict what distant rocky planets are made of and identify worlds with conditions favorable for life.
- Share:
A scorching hot planet nearly 320 light-years from Earth has provided the first direct evidence for a fundamental assumption about how planets form. Astronomers discovered that WASP-189b shares an important chemical characteristic with its host star, supporting a long-standing idea that also helps scientists investigate potentially habitable worlds. The breakthrough came from the first simultaneous measurement of gaseous magnesium and silicon in an exoplanet's atmosphere, using the Gemini South telescope, part of the International Gemini Observatory, which is partially funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and operated by NSF NOIRLab.
Located nearly 320 light-years away in the Libra constellation, WASP-189b belongs to an extreme category of planets called ultra-hot Jupiters (UHJ). These enormous worlds reach temperatures so intense that even materials normally found in solid rock can turn into gas. Elements such as magnesium (Mg), silicon (Si), and iron (Fe) can therefore be detected in their atmospheres. Astronomers identify these substances through spectroscopy, a method that separates light into different wavelengths to reveal the chemicals present.
An international research team led by Jorge Antonio Sanchez, a graduate student at Arizona State University (ASU), investigated WASP-189b with the high-resolution Immersion GRating INfrared Spectrograph (IGRINS). At the time, the instrument was installed on the Gemini South telescope in Chile.[1]
For the first time, researchers were able to measure magnesium and silicon together in the atmosphere of a planet beyond our Solar System. Their observations revealed that the proportion of magnesium to silicon on WASP-189b closely matches the ratio found in its parent star. This result provides the first direct observational support for a widely used assumption about the chemical relationship between stars and their planets, offering a valuable new way to investigate planetary origins and evolution.
"These discoveries show Gemini's ability to help us understand the characteristics of the remarkable zoo of exoplanets in our solar neighborhood," says Chris Davis, NSF Program Director for NOIRLab. "Such discoveries are only possible because of Gemini's cutting-edge instruments."
A Long-Suspected Connection Between Stars and Planets
Astronomers believe that giant planets such as WASP-189b formed within enormous disks of gas and dust surrounding young stars. These structures, called protoplanetary disks, provide the raw materials from which planets develop. The chemical makeup of a giant planet's outer atmosphere is thought to retain clues about the environment where it originally formed.
Because stars and their surrounding disks originate from the same cloud of material, scientists have long assumed that they contain similar proportions of rock-forming elements. In particular, the ratios of these elements in a disk are expected to resemble those measured in its central star.
This relationship has become an important tool for predicting the composition of rocky exoplanets. Until now, however, the assumption was supported primarily by evidence from our own Solar System. Astronomers had not directly measured the same relationship in a planet orbiting another star.
The discovery involving WASP-189b provides that missing observational evidence, strengthening the scientific basis for using stellar chemistry to understand the materials from which distant planets form.
"WASP-189b gives us a much-needed observational anchor in our understanding of terrestrial planet formation since it offers a measurable quantity that validates the presumed resemblance of stellar composition and the proportion of rocky material around host stars used to form planets," says Sanchez.
What Planetary Chemistry Could Reveal About Habitability
The implications reach beyond understanding how planets are assembled. This chemical relationship is also important in astrobiology, which investigates the possibility of life beyond Earth and the environmental conditions that could support it, including habitable environments within our Solar System.
By studying the elements present in a star, astronomers may be able to estimate the relative amounts of rock-forming materials available to its planets. These materials influence a planet's internal structure, geological activity, and chemical environment, all of which can affect whether conditions suitable for life might develop.
Earth provides a familiar example. The elements that make up our planet help determine processes such as plate tectonics, the generation of its protective magnetic field, and the movement of essential chemicals into the atmosphere, oceans, and soil. Together, these processes contribute to the environment that allows life to thrive.
As researchers work toward studying smaller, rocky exoplanets in greater detail, establishing a reliable connection between stellar chemistry and planetary composition becomes increasingly important. The WASP-189b findings provide a significant step in that direction.
Powerful Telescopes Open a New Window Into Alien Atmospheres
Obtaining these measurements requires instruments capable of distinguishing extremely fine details in the light collected from distant planetary atmospheres. According to the researchers, the necessary spectral resolution for this kind of analysis is currently available only through ground-based telescopes.
"Our study demonstrates the capability of ground-based, high-resolution spectrographs to constrain critical species like magnesium and silicon, which are two elemental building blocks from which rocky planets form," says study co-author Michael Line, Associate Professor at ASU. "This advancing capability opens an entirely new dimension in our study of exoplanet atmospheres."
The team expects future observations using multiple wavelengths and similarly precise instruments to uncover a wider range of elements in exoplanet atmospheres. Building a more complete picture of their chemical compositions could reveal additional clues about how planets form, how they change over time, and which conditions might favor habitability.
By connecting the chemistry of a distant planet to that of its star, astronomers now have new evidence supporting a principle that could help guide the search for potentially habitable worlds throughout the galaxy.
Notes
- IGRINS operated as a visiting instrument at Gemini South between 2022 and 2023 before returning to its home institution. Its successful performance led to the development of an updated version, IGRINS-2, which was subsequently commissioned as a permanent facility instrument for the Gemini North telescope in Hawai'i.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Jorge A. Sanchez, Peter C. B. Smith, Krishna Kanumalla, Luis Welbanks, Michael R. Line, Stefan Pelletier, Steven Desch, Patrick Young, Jennifer Patience, Jacob Bean, Matteo Brogi, Dan Jaffe, Gregory N. Mace, Megan Weiner Mansfield, Vatsal Panwar, Vivien Parmentier, Lorenzo Pino, Arjun Baliga Savel, Lennart van Sluijs, Joost P. Wardenier. RIYADH/SANAA, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthi group exchanged threats of retaliatory attacks on Tuesday as cross-border strikes on major cities and oil facilities continued.
THREATS EXCHANGED
During a cabinet meeting on Tuesday chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia warned that Yemen's Houthis would face consequences for its repeated attacks on the kingdom.
The Saudi Council of Ministers praised the Coalition to Support Legitimacy in Yemen for its military operations against the Houthis and pledged to protect freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Also on Tuesday, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea warned that any attack on the Houthi-held capital would trigger what he described as a "harsh and painful" response against Riyadh.
The group later warned of several sites in Saudi Arabia, including facilities belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
SAUDI ARAMCO, RIYADH TARGETED
The Saudi Civil Defense announced early Wednesday that four people, including two women and one child, were injured and 15 residential homes sustained damage after debris from two intercepted cruise missiles fell in the capital Riyadh on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, a Saudi Aramco administrative building in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, was targeted Tuesday evening, causing a limited fire, the Saudi Press Agency reported early Wednesday.
On Tuesday night, the coalition said that it had intercepted multiple missiles and drones over eastern and southern Saudi Arabia. It also reported intercepting a ballistic missile targeting an administrative center in Al-Ahsa Governorate in the Eastern Province.
COALITION WARNING BEFORE STRIKES
The Saudi-led coalition on Tuesday urged civilians to evacuate the Yemen Petroleum Company's Al-Sabaha Central Station in Houthi-held Sanaa ahead of what it described as a "qualitative operation."
Coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Malki issued the warning on X and posted a map marking the site, describing the targeted facilities as vital resources used by the Houthis to support their military operations in Sanaa, Hodeidah and Dhamar.
The Houthis said Tuesday that Saudi warplanes and missiles carried out 104 strikes across areas held by the group over the past 24 hours.
Sarea said on X that F-15 and Typhoon fighter jets took off from Saudi air bases in Khamis Mushait and Taif, while missiles were launched from Najran in southwestern Saudi Arabia.
The Houthi spokesperson claimed the attacks caused civilian casualties without giving specific figures.
In Sanaa, the strikes hit the Yemen Petroleum Company's Al-Sabaha Central Station, a fuel storage and distribution facility west of the city.
In Hodeidah, strikes targeted fuel storage facilities in the Red Sea coastal area of Ras Isa and fuel supply warehouses in Bajil, east of the provincial capital. Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported that two people were killed in the strikes.
DIPLOMATIC EFFORTS GATHER PACE
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Tuesday told Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in a phone call, that Türkiye strongly supports Saudi Arabia and would continue to stand by Riyadh.
Also on Tuesday, Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan bin Abdullah held separate phone calls with his Qatari, Kuwaiti and UAE counterparts who condemned the Houthi attacks and reaffirmed their solidarity with the kingdom.
Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi discussed regional de-escalation with his Turkish, Iraqi and Egyptian counterparts, emphasizing the need to return to negotiations. Tehran had reiterated on Monday its readiness to help facilitate dialogue between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis. ■

UN experts slam Turkey’s ‘crackdown’ on LGBTQ organisations

- The experts said authorities raided bars, clubs and activists’ homes, and launched judicial action against more than 160 people and 20 groups and businesses.
- Turkey’s “My Family is Safe” operation also shut T24’s website and social media, while officials said it was part of Erdogan’s “Decade of the Family” to protect children, family and social order.
AI generated
GENEVA – UN human rights experts on Oct 13 slammed what they called the “severe crackdown” on LGBTQ organisations in Turkey, saying legitimate rights work was being unduly restricted.
Turkey’s LGBTQ community has increasingly come under pressure from the authorities, with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan describing it as a “deviant movement” of “perverts”.
The authorities recently launched a major clampdown on the LGBTQ community, raiding gay bars, nightclubs and the homes of activists and community members.
“Turkey must end the harassment of LGBTI human rights defenders and organisations and ensure a safe and enabling environment in which they can exercise their rights to freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association and continue their legitimate work without fear of arrest, intimidation, stigmatisation or criminalisation,” the UN experts said in a statement.
Although same-sex relations are legal in Turkey, hostility towards LGBTQ people remains widespread.
The UN experts said Turkey’s justice ministry has announced judicial measures against more than 160 individuals and 20 associations and businesses.
On Sept 30, as part of its “My Family is Safe” operation, Turkey shut down the website and social media accounts of T24, a leading independent digital news website, citing its “LGBT propaganda”.
“We are concerned that investigations reportedly invoke offences relating to ‘obscenity’, ‘morality’ and prostitution, alongside official statements describing associations as promoting ‘LGBT and immorality’ and the framing of LGBTI persons as a threat to families,” the UN experts said.
“We demand an immediate end to the so-called ‘My Family Is Safe’ operation.
“We demand the immediate release of persons detained solely for their legitimate human rights work.”
The experts included the special rapporteurs on human rights defenders, the independence of judges, freedom of expression, and freedom of peaceful association.
The statement was also penned by the expert on protection against violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity.
UN experts are independent figures appointed by the Human Rights Council. They do not, therefore, speak for the United Nations itself.
The experts said they were in contact with the Turkish government on the matter.
Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek has said the “My Family is Safe” operation was launched as part of Erdogan’s “Decade of the Family”, which is aimed at “protecting our children, the institution of the family and social order”. AFP

AI to cut headcount at more than half of British firms, CFOs say

- The trend adds to Britain’s jobless growth and rising youth unemployment, creating pressure for Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Labour government and AI Minister Kanishka Narayan.
- A Multiverse report says firms are buying AI tools without enough worker training. It warns spend may be wasted, while only a third of CFOs expect higher margins next year.
AI generated
LONDON – Many of Britain’s large businesses are ready to replace staff with artificial intelligence over the next year, according to a prominent survey of chief financial officers.
Deloitte said on Oct 14 that 52% of CFOs expect to cut headcount due to the technology, with AI adoption still in its early stages. More than two thirds – 67% – said they have achieved just a quarter of the changes they ultimately expect from AI.
The report adds to evidence of Britain’s jobless growth revival, which poses a political dilemma for Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s Labour government.
AI adoption and high employment costs are encouraging firms to expand with fewer roles. As a result, long-term unemployment is rising and youth joblessness is at its highest in over a decade – an anomaly in an economy that is whizzing past European peers.
It underscores the challenge facing AI Minister Kanishka Narayan, who pledged to “never leave working people to bear the cost” of the AI revolution, in a speech on Oct 12.
“I understand why people are naturally anxious about their jobs and what artificial intelligence means for their children’s future,” Narayan said. “I feel that concern, that anxiety too.”
While firms are using AI to cut costs, the impact on profits is less certain. Only a third of CFOs believe AI will help increase margins in the next year, according to the Deloitte report.
Deloitte surveyed 66 CFOs between Sept 17 and Oct 1. Of those, 12 were from FTSE 100 companies and 25 from FTSE 250 companies.
A separate report published this week by Multiverse, the London-based training platform founded by Euan Blair, suggested firms are struggling to join up AI investments with their existing workers.
“Almost none of them know what their people can do with AI, and that is where their spend is going to waste,” Blair said. The report said firms are spending more on AI tools without training their workers how to use them. BLOOMBERG

Ukrainian ex-officer stands trial in Germany over Nord Stream bombing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
00:10:53 UTC
09:10:53 KST

Nord Stream may have been lawful target, argue lawyers for Ukrainian accused of bombing
HAMBURG, Oct 14 - Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany on Wednesday that "an aggressor's infrastructure" may have been a lawful target.
Serhii Kuznetsov is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents including divers and an explosives expert that blew up Russia's largest gas pipeline to Europe in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times.
The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the bombing.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Kuznetsov's lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany's imports of natural gas before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a "Russian weapon".
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked.
RIGHT TO REMAIN SILENT
Prosecutors have alleged that Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant in Italy last year, worked with members of the Ukrainian military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.
Kuznetsov, 50, who prior to Wednesday was referred to publicly only as Serhii K. under German legal rules, has denied any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200-km (750-mile)-long Baltic Sea pipeline.
Wearing a grey suit and with a shaved head, he exercised his right to remain silent in court but did not cover his face. His lawyers said he could not mount a proper defence because he was obliged to withhold Ukrainian state secrets.
The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military aid. Russia said on Monday it expected a "just verdict" that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.
Kuznetsov's legal team had tried reaching out to Ukraine for information that might assist the defence but heard nothing, according to another defence lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp.
ATTACKING CIVILIAN TARGETS IS CONSIDERED A WAR CRIME
German prosecutors say the actions Kuznetsov is accused of — attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services — would amount to a war crime.
Kuznetsov is the only person on trial, but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers.
The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's longstanding dependence on Russian natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Nord Stream's supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, already built, but Berlin cancelled approval to open it just prior to Russia's invasion.
PLUMES OF METHANE GAS
The trial, expected to continue into February next year, could have domestic political implications.
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in opinion polls for more than a year, has called for an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ties with Moscow.
Although German state parliaments have no role in foreign policy, the AfD filed a motion in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Wednesday calling for an end to support for Ukraine, noting the "historical parallel" with the start of the trial.
The Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 metres under the Baltic and built by Russian gas concern Gazprom to supply up to 110 billion cubic metres of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries.
The September 26, 2022 blasts that ruptured three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines created a giant whirlpool at sea as huge plumes of methane gas rose into the atmosphere.
Prosecutors allege that Kuznetsov travelled to Germany through Poland some three weeks before the attack, using a forged Ukrainian passport. He and his group then used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialised military-grade explosives to the sea floor.
The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on September 6 and returned on September 23, 2022. REUTERS

Iran shifting tactics to step up attacks on shipping before US vote, officials say

AI generated
DUBAI/LONDON/WASHINGTON – Iran is deploying new tactics to target ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz as it seeks to keep oil prices high and influence the US midterm elections, two senior Iranian officials told Reuters.
Tehran has tried to exert control over the Strait of Hormuz since the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran on Feb 28. It has restricted passage through the waterway, which carried about a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war, in an effort to gain leverage over Washington.
Its threats and attacks have severely curtailed traffic through the strait, driving up oil prices, though some oil has continued to transit.
The two officials declined to provide details of the new strategy, but one said that Iran had started using different offensive tactics against vessels it considered in violation of its restrictions about 10 days ago, adding that this had led to an increase in attacks on such ships.
The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.
“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one of the two officials said.
The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials said.
Iran using spotters
A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Iran had changed tactics in one significant way: after the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including US naval vessels, the official said.
Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said.
Unwilling to risk its remaining fast boats, Iran had been unable to prevent a ramp-up in oil exports through the strait, the official said, particularly after US strikes devastated its navy.
The war – and its US$3 billion (S$3.8 billion) monthly price tag – has become a key issue on the US campaign trail for November’s midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress.
US President Donald Trump has been weighing next steps against Iran, but has said he will not attack again before the vote.
The US has meanwhile been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports and extending sanctions as it tries to pile economic pressure on Tehran to reach a deal to end the conflict.
The stand-off over Hormuz has left global energy markets exposed to further disruption, with the threat of attacks and high shipping and insurance costs complicating efforts to restore normal traffic.
In recent days, attacks on commercial ships still sailing through the strait have surged to their highest level since the war began, according to independent data.
There have been at least five incidents in the past 48 hours involving tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area, including drone strikes, according to data analysis from maritime security sources and incidents reported to British navy-affiliated agency United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
That approximately mirrored the rate of attacks on Oct 3-5, pointing to a new escalation, according to data from the UN shipping agency, the International Maritime Organization.
“There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said.
Attacks over an expanded area
As part of the new strategy, Tehran will also expand the geographical scope of its operations beyond the Strait of Hormuz to the Gulf of Oman and waters further afield, the officials said.
Analysis by maritime security sources based on attacks reported to UKMTO and maritime security companies in the region suggest this may already be happening. They show Iran targeting ships in areas beyond the Strait of Hormuz, including waters off the coast of Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, in recent days.
The second Iranian official added that Tehran would not allow Trump to bring down oil prices before the November elections.
“Just when they think they are getting close to the point where prices will fall, we will push them away from it. This is a game of chess,” the second official said.
“Such vessels would be safe nowhere, even outside the Strait of Hormuz.”
The Pentagon and Iran’s Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Complete closure of Hormuz soon, says Iranian official
Both Iranian officials said Tehran is moving towards a situation in which no vessel violating its restrictions would be able to pass through the strait. “It will be complete closure soon,” one of the officials said.
In its latest report on Oct 11, the US Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) said the threat to merchant shipping in the Strait of Hormuz remained “severe”, the second-highest level.
“IRGC attacks, attempted attacks, and/or harassment activity persisted including UAV overflight, targeted surveillance of merchant shipping, and occasional VHF hailing,” JMIC said. REUTERS

AI reveals a hidden chemical shortcut that could turn CO2 into fuel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
00:01:11 UTC
09:01:11 KST

AI reveals a hidden chemical shortcut that could turn CO2 into fuel
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Indian Institute of Science (IISc)
- Summary:
- Scientists used artificial intelligence to uncover nearly 10,000 chemical reactions involved in transforming carbon dioxide into fuels and chemicals, revealing crucial pathways that traditional models had missed. The discovery dramatically improved predictions of CO2 conversion and uncovered a surprising hydrogen reaction that could inspire more efficient catalysts.
- Share:
Scientists have uncovered thousands of previously overlooked chemical reactions that could help improve the conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) into valuable fuels and industrial chemicals. By combining machine learning with advanced computer simulations, researchers at the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) identified 9,389 individual reactions occurring on a copper catalyst, revealing unexpected chemical pathways that conventional models had missed.
The findings, published in Nature Communications, could help scientists develop more effective catalysts for transforming CO2 into useful products such as methanol. The research also uncovered a surprising way hydrogen can participate in these reactions, challenging established assumptions about how the process works.
One promising approach to recycling carbon dioxide is hydrogenation, which uses a catalyst to help CO2 react with hydrogen and form chemicals such as methanol. However, the process involves an enormous number of individual reactions taking place across the catalyst's surface. Simulating every possible step using quantum mechanics would require immense computing power, so researchers typically focus on a limited selection of reactions believed to be the most important. This simplification can leave hundreds of potentially critical reactions out of the picture.
"We began with a worry familiar to anyone who does mechanistic modeling: How do you know that your reaction network has not omitted the one step that matters?" says first author Anand Mohan Verma, who conducted the research as a CV Raman Postdoctoral Fellow at IISc and is now an Assistant Professor at the Motilal Nehru National Institute of Technology Allahabad (MNNIT Allahabad).
AI Reveals Thousands of Overlooked Chemical Reactions
To overcome this limitation, the research team began by using quantum mechanics simulations to build a detailed database containing 152 chemical reactions. They then trained machine learning models to quickly estimate the energy barriers that additional reactions would need to overcome.
Using automated computational tools, the scientists examined the possible reactions involving 105 chemical species present on the catalyst surface. They also determined which transformations could take place in a single reaction step. This approach expanded their original network from just 152 reactions to 9,389.
The difference was significant. When the researchers relied on the smaller network, their model incorrectly identified formic acid as the main product rather than methanol. It also predicted substantially less CO2 conversion than experiments indicated.
"When we modeled the process using the 152 reactions considered initially, the network wrongly predicted formic acid, not methanol, as the major product, and underestimated how much CO2 gets converted. Only when we expanded the network to include thousands of additional, previously overlooked reactions did the predictions fall in line with what we and others see experimentally," explains corresponding author Ananth Govind Rajan, Associate Professor in the Department of Chemical Engineering, IISc.
Expanded Model Predicts 40 Times More CO2 Conversion
When the scientists incorporated the larger reaction network into a model of how quickly the chemical processes occur, the predicted amount of CO2 conversion increased by approximately 40 times compared with the original model.
The expanded model also correctly identified methanol and carbon monoxide as major products, bringing its predictions into agreement with experimental findings.
Experimental validation was carried out by G Valavarasu and Santhosh Kotni at Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited's Green Research and Development Centre, along with Amol Amrute and colleagues at the Agency for Science, Technology, and Research in Singapore. Ambedkar Dukkipati, Professor in the Department of Computer Science and Automation at IISc, also contributed to the machine learning models.
A Surprising Hydrogen Pathway Challenges Conventional Chemistry
Beyond improving the predictions, the much larger reaction network exposed an unexpected mechanism involving hydrogen.
In several important reaction steps, hydrogen could be transferred to intermediate chemical compounds directly as molecular H2, rather than only through separate hydrogen atoms. Additional quantum mechanics calculations confirmed that this pathway can be especially favorable when hydrogen is transferred to intermediates containing oxygen.
This finding challenges a long-standing assumption about how hydrogen participates in catalytic reactions and could provide valuable clues for designing better catalysts.
"The idea that hydrogen can transfer as an intact molecule, without first splitting into atoms, runs against what most of us were taught," says co-author Shivam Chaturvedi, PhD student in the Department of Chemical Engineering, IISc. "This surfaced only because the network was large enough to allow for it, and the observation held up when we went back and computed those steps explicitly. This also suggests that catalysts that interact more strongly with H2 could potentially enhance pathways leading to methanol."
The researchers believe this unexpected mechanism could guide the development of catalysts that interact more effectively with molecular hydrogen, potentially improving the chemical pathways responsible for producing methanol from CO2.
The broader computational framework may also prove useful well beyond carbon dioxide hydrogenation. By integrating quantum mechanics simulations, machine learning, automated identification of chemical reactions, and models of reaction rates, the approach could help researchers investigate other important industrial processes.
Potential applications include CO2 reduction using different catalysts, nitrogen reduction, and water splitting. By revealing chemical steps that simpler models might miss, the technique offers scientists a more complete picture of complex catalytic reactions and new opportunities to improve processes used to produce fuels and chemicals.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Indian Institute of Science (IISc). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Anand M. Verma, Shivam Chaturvedi, Swastik Paul, Srinibas Nandi, Rahul Sheshanarayana, Kotni Santhosh, G. Valavarasu, Ambedkar Dukkipati, Chuandayani Gunawan Gwie, Pei Ying Moo, Chun Qi Joy Ng, Amol Amrute, Ananth Govind Rajan. Data-driven massive reaction networks reveal mechanistic pathways underlying catalytic CO2 hydrogenation. Nature Communications, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77080-4

An e-mail sent to an address associated with that name did not elicit a response, and it was not immediately clear who his lawyer was.
OpenAI discovered the recording device plugged into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room at one of its San Francisco buildings on Sept 30, according to the department.
The thumb-sized device, which had a microphone and could connect to a camera, was concealed in toilet paper, according to an FBI complaint.
It was installed on or about Sept 28, while its stored data was encrypted and inaccessible. Investigators later found a similar customised device in Alfozan’s personal bag.
OpenAI said in a post on X that it used its internal AI models to identify the person responsible for planting the device and trace its origins.
The company said it had evidence that the employee intended to place additional recording devices in sensitive areas of its offices to secretly record meetings.

Alfozan also used an AI productivity agent to seek information about meeting-room calendars and capabilities for about a month through Sept 16, according to the FBI complaint.
He has been a legal permanent resident of the US since September 2020.

He previously worked at Meta and Microsoft, it said.

Ex-gang leader gets 40 years to life for rapper Tupac Shakur’s 1996 murder
A 30-year hunt for justice ends with the sentencing of Duane ‘Keffe D’ Davis, who has written about his role in Shakur’s shooting death.
A former gang leader accused of masterminding the 1996 drive-by shooting of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison.
Tuesday’s sentencing capped a 30-year-long cold case that rattled the golden era of rap music in the United States.
In August, Duane “Keffe D” Davis, a former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, had been found guilty of first-degree murder with the use of a deadly weapon.
Davis, 63, is the sole person charged in the death of Shakur, who died at the peak of his fame at age 25.
Judge Carli Kierny announced Davis’s sentence at a hearing in Las Vegas, Nevada, where she chided him for the murder.
“You don’t get to take a man from his family, you don’t get to take his very life, his whole future from him and just walk away from it, especially when that man is Tupac Shakur,” Kierny said. “The world never forgot about him and his death, and neither did Las Vegas.”
During the hearing, prosecutor Marc DiGiacomo said that whatever sentence the court imposes, Davis is “guaranteed to die” behind bars.
For nearly three decades, Shakur’s death remained one of the music industry’s most notorious unsolved mysteries, prompting endless debate over who did it and why.
Davis had long been a suspect, but investigators lacked evidence to pursue an indictment.
The investigative deadlock shattered after Davis publicly boasted about his involvement in media interviews. He also recounted his role in the murder in his 2019 memoir, Compton Street Legend.
Previously, Davis entered into a 2008 proffer agreement with federal law enforcement officers, granting him limited immunity for statements he made privately to investigators.
But by repeating his statements outside his meetings with investigators, prosecutors said Davis had effectively voided the agreement’s protections.
DiGiacomo said that Davis was trying to profit from a killing that he committed, and for that, he deserves the maximum possible sentence.
Shakur had been in Las Vegas for a Mike Tyson heavyweight fight on the night of September 7, 1996, when he was shot.
Investigators said the shooting took place roughly two hours after a confrontation between Davis’s nephew, Orlando Anderson, and Shakur’s entourage.
In his memoir, Davis accused Shakur and his friends of assaulting his nephew. He explained he then sought to retaliate, and he admitted to handing the murder weapon to two alleged accomplices, seated in the backseat of a white Cadillac, who then fired the fatal shots.
Shakur had been in the passenger seat of a black BMW, stopped at a red light, when his vehicle came under fire. He died six days later.
Davis is the only person who was in the Cadillac that evening who is still alive.
Members of Shakur’s family spoke at the sentencing, including his siblings Maurice “Mopreme” Shakur and Sekyiwa “Set” Shakur.
“This man’s life mattered,” Sekyiwa Shakur told the court, while her brother called the murder “devastating, heartbreaking and sad”.
Following the verdict, Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal described the Shakur family as having to endure years of Davis “bragging about killing someone they loved”.
“They loved that man. And the arrogance that Mr Davis had in expressing his joy in killing that man ultimately was his undoing,” Palal said.
The ex-gang leader briefly addressed the court on Tuesday, asking the judge to order the return of property seized from his residence, including personal photographs.
When the judge asked if he wished to make any additional statements, Davis declined, stating, “No, I’m good.” He added that he would “appeal this case for sure”.

Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
00:42:22 BST
08:42:22 KST

Germany puts Ukrainian on trial accused of blowing up Nord Stream pipelines
- Published
A Ukrainian man has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany, four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history.
Prosecutors say Serhii Kuznetsov played a leading role in a team of saboteurs that destroyed the pipelines, accusing him of a war crime. His defence has called for the case to be dismissed.
The case is highly sensitive in Germany, one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place.
Extradited to Germany last year, Kuznetsov denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia.
Kuznetsov became the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts on Wednesday morning, and a packed public gallery looked on as he entered the courtroom, appearing relaxed.
He even smiled at times, including during initial exchanges where he spoke to confirm personal details such as his name and place of birth.
He had previously only been identified by German prosecutors as Serhii K and pictured with his face blurred, but a court spokeswoman said he had now waived his anonymity.
Kuznetsov, 50, wore a pair of headphones and appeared to listen intently to a translation of proceedings in Ukrainian, as the prosecution read out the charges against him of ordering divers and an explosive expert to attack civilian infrastructure.
The defence outlined their case, telling the court that only circumstantial evidence had emerged in the four years since the Nord Stream blasts.
"[Prosecutors] made a thorough investigation of four years," Italian defence lawyer Nicola Canestrini told the BBC outside the courtroom. "They did not find one single witness, they did not find no forensics, no DNA, no fingerprints - nothing!"
Canestrini and his colleagues argued that as a soldier the defendant was bound to secrecy, and therefore he could not have a fair trial as he was unable to defend himself.
"Let's say he has an alibi, he was on another secret operation, how can you prove that if he's [not able] to tell us as defence attorneys where he was and which witnesses we could summon?"
Prosecutors argue the case falls under Germany's code of crimes against international law as a war crime, as an "attack by military means against civilian objects".
The defence told the court his extradition to Germany was flawed as no mention had been made at the time of the war crime allegation.
In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame.
Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts.
As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied.
Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock.
They said later that "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat".
Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025 the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction, external and prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security".
Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies".
- Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine 
  - Published4 days ago
The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin.
Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war".
He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions."
However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case.
"They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained.
In August 2025, Kuznetsov was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany.
After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, when his surname emerged in court documents, Kuznetsov was transferred to Germany late last year.
German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army, external, and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert.
While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court.
In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just".
Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage.
Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial.
Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".

New White House spokeswoman Katie Zacharia heavy on Trump praise, light on questions in debut
- Katie Zacharia made her White House debut by praising Trump and taking only three questions in 15 minutes, unlike the usual long press briefing.
- She said her job is to “amplify, multiply and expand upon” Trump’s agenda, while Trump and aides praised her performance and media critics called it weak.
- She announced Trump had fired the US ambassador to Greece over a bribery scandal, as she stepped into the role during falling poll numbers and legal fights with news outlets.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – New White House Press Secretary Katie Zacharia made her briefing room debut on Oct 13 by taking remarkably few questions from journalists while leaving no doubt who she believes has all the answers – US President Donald Trump.
“I get to do what I was doing on the outside already, which was hoping to amplify, multiply and expand upon President Trump’s incredible agenda for the American people,” she said, describing her vision for the job.
Zacharia, a 41-year-old devotee of Trump’s hard-right MAGA movement, is taking over the White House communications role just as Republicans face warnings of heavy defeat in upcoming midterm elections.
She is also replacing the combative but skilled former press secretary Karoline Leavitt at a time when polls show the 80-year-old president becoming ever more unpopular.
Little known to the general public, Zacharia opened her first session at the famous briefing room podium by reading – at a notably slow pace – a lengthy list of what she said were achievements under the “energetic” leader.
These types of initial round-ups, dubbed “toppers” in White House press lingo, are usually followed by a long question-and-answer session in the packed room – often extending to dozens of questions.
But Zacharia took questions from just three reporters, starting with right-wing website Breitbart, an outlet frequently accused of spreading conspiracy theories.
The next questions went to Fox News, one of the key pillars of Trump’s media support, and to the Daily Mail tabloid website.
With that, after just 15 minutes, Zacharia declared the briefing finished and walked out, pursued by the sound of reporters shouting unanswered questions.
“I thought she was very good,” Trump, known to enjoy watching his staff members’ performances on television, later told reporters.
‘My president’
Up to now, Zacharia has been working as a commentator on Fox News and right-wing Newsmax, as well as advising Trump Media and Technology – the group behind the president’s Truth Social platform.
She did not indicate whether she will aggressively pursue Trump’s unprecedented attempts to punish US media outlets that he does not like.
Most recently, the administration has plunged into a legal dispute with CNN, MSNOW and Politico over attempts to bar them from the White House.
White House’s communications director Steven Cheung praised Zacharia’s performance, saying she “commanded the room” and reminded Americans of Trump’s “great work”.
But liberal commentator Brian Krassenstein predicted she will “be a disaster”. The New York Post tabloid described her as “visibly nervous”.
Zacharia did make one piece of news, announcing that Trump had sacked his ambassador to Greece after a bribery scandal.
The bulk of her messaging, however, solely aimed at polishing the image of the Republican leader, who nearly halfway through his term faces plummeting opinion polls over his war against Iran, economic hardship and a long list of domestic controversies.
“This is a president and administration that is looking out for you, the American people,” she said, declaring herself “thrilled to officially be part of this incredible journey”.
Asked if the demanding job would impact her personal life, Zacharia described how her family of four children was adapting.
But she slipped up, triggering ripples of laughter, when she referred to “my president, excuse me, my husband”. AFP

From no cards to many: Europe warns Trump not to waste Ukraine’s leverage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
23:29:00 UTC
08:29:00 KST

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky (L) and Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha (R) listen to US President Donald Trump address the 81st United Nations General Assembly at United Nations headquarters in New York, USA on September 22, 2026. | Angela Weiss/AFP via Getty Images
WARSAW — Ukraine has more leverage than a year ago — and European leaders are warning Donald Trump not to squander it by pressuring Kyiv to ease up on Russia.
"In less than two years we went from the stage of no cards to the stage of don't play your cards," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told an audience at the Warsaw Security Conference. "That's a true achievement."
Last year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was ambushed in the Oval Office by Trump, who ridiculed him for having "no cards" to play against Russia.
Advertisement
Trump’s recent demand that Zelenskyy “better damn well stop” Ukraine’s refinery attacks, and his call for Ukraine to install a new leader, amount to a recognition that Kyiv does indeed have significant leverage in the fight.
Kyiv’s refinery campaign is helping create a growing fuel shortage across Russia and is also harming the Kremlin's ability to finance the war. But European leaders fear that Trump's desperation to lower fuel prices ahead of next month's U.S. midterm elections by pressuring Kyiv to stop its attacks could weaken Ukraine’s hand without persuading Russia to end the war.
Sybiha’s comments drew loud applause at the Warsaw conference and underscored growing tensions among Kyiv, Washington and Ukraine's European allies after Trump said the U.S. had agreed with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel.
The dispute between Washington and Kyiv overshadowed a Warsaw event that is normally strongly pro-American, given Poland's status as a key U.S. ally.
"Ministers and heads of state won’t say so outright what they think about the Americans, but they certainly think a lot of things — the negotiations with Putin are yet another stab in the back for the Ukrainians," said a French lawmaker, speaking on condition of being granted anonymity.
"You end the war by persuading the aggressor to limit his level of ambition, not by asking the victim to capitulate," said Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski.
Advertisement
His German counterpart Johann Wadephul underlined that Berlin is pushing the Trump administration to fully impose energy sanctions approved by the U.S. Congress.
On Sep. 18, Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Russia and Iran Sanctions Act of 2026, codifying existing US sanctions against Russia and expanding the scope for applying secondary sanctions, tariffs and restrictions, including against the energy sector.
"This is not the time to lower the sanctions regime, but to strengthen it," Wadephul said.
U.K. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband echoed that call, saying Trump should exert pressure on Russia to agree to an energy ceasefire under which both warring nations would stop hitting each other's oil, gas, electricity and other assets.
Russia has so far refused to take such a step.
"Let us take seriously this issue of the energy ceasefire that President Trump has talked about, not simply a refinery ceasefire but a broad energy ceasefire, because in the last week alone we've seen 200 Russian attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure," Miliband said.
Advertisement
Trump pressures Ukraine
The U.S. president said on Monday that Putin is keener to end the fighting than Zelenskyy — despite the Kremlin not agreeing to any ceasefire.
"I think actually Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelenskyy," Trump said.
Since Trump announced an energy ceasefire — blindsiding both Kyiv and Moscow — Ukraine has paused bombing Russian refineries even as Russian attacks continue.
While Trump wants the attacks to stop, Ukraine's European allies are keen to cripple Russia's war effort.
"Ukraine is attacking refineries, which is having an effect, and data centers, which is also having an effect," Sikorski said. He also called on Poland's MAGA-aligned President Karol Nawrocki to use his influence with Trump "to explain to him that Putin is the aggressor and Zelenskyy is the victim of aggression."
Wadephul added that he had talked to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov during the U.N. General Assembly in New York last month, and saw no interest from him in ending the war.
Advertisement
"A lot of people in Europe and especially in Germany were asking us and me, 'Why don't you talk to the Russians?' So now I had that conversation, and you saw the result," he said. "It's a very dire result. And it shows that Russia right now is not ready for ceasefire."
During the same Warsaw event, Sybiha was forced to deny rumors that Washington may have stopped sharing intelligence with Kyiv in retaliation for its campaign of deep strikes against Russian oil refineries.
"You are asking me if we are getting intelligence data from the American side. Yes, we continue this cooperation," he said.
Concerns about a potential cut-off in U.S. intelligence grew on Tuesday after Ukraine's threat detection system failed to detect ballistic missiles that battered Kyiv overnight. Sybiha said the failure was due to a "special type of weaponry which was used by the Russian side."
Zelenskyy also underlined the need for continued intelligence sharing. "There was also a rather treacherous ballistic missile strike on Kyiv — five missiles that hit civilian infrastructure. Unfortunately, there was no warning from our partners regarding this strike. Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives."
Sybiha stressed that Kyiv needs to continue strengthening its ability to fend off Russia's constant air attacks while Ukraine's troops push back against Russian forces on the front lines.
Advertisement
"The future of Europe and the global security architecture is now being decided in Ukraine," he said.
Chris Lunday and Laura Kayali contributed to this report.

NEW DELHI/MUMBAI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman Tuesday said the govt was open and keen to "hear" discussions around the long-term capital gains (LTCG) tax as it was "healthy" to have the debate.The minister, however, declined to be specific on the matter as preparations for the Union Budget in Feb are already underway.The FM's comments raised investors' hopes of a reduction in LTCG tax and securities transaction tax (STT), a longstanding demand among foreign funds who have been big sellers in the Indian market in the last two years.As a result, after a steady start, stock prices jumped with the sensex finally settling 1.5% or 1,109 points up at 73,034 points while Nifty closed 1.6% or 359 points up at 22,722 points.RBI steps to check rupee volatility: FM While responding to an observation that investors, especially foreign funds, were keen on removal of capital gains tax and streamlining of taxation before they started investing in India, Sitharaman said, "Two years ago, we had bought all the asset classes similarly and people thought that I was increasing the tax. I was not increasing the tax, I was bringing all of them at par, so that an investor is not speculating as to which one gives them greater leverage.
So, these are the things on which there is a lot of debate. It's healthy to have this debate and I will be keen to hear them."At a Bloomberg event, FM acknowledged that investors, both within and outside, were commenting on LTCG and the question of treating all asset classes similarly has been a widely discussed topic.So far this year, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have bet sold Indian stocks worth a little over Rs 3 lakh crore, NSDL data showed. In 2025, the corresponding figure was a net outflow of nearly Rs 1.7 lakh crore and just Rs 427 crore in 2024. Since Sept 2024, sensex has lost about 13%.At the same event, Sitharaman also noted that rupee has depreciated "significantly" over the past year and a half, and RBI will continue its efforts to prevent excessive volatility. "RBI is not trying to fix the rupee, it is trying to stop the volatility, and for that there is a lot of effort from their side. I am sure RBI will take further steps to make sure that rupee does not become too volatile," she said in response to a query on capital outflows, especially in the equity market due to currency depreciation.
FM stressed that govt has kept the economy on a sound footing and been careful with its spending and borrowings, helping investors looking to diversify away from China. "Fiscal discipline is not going to be a matter which should worry investors," she said, adding that domestic private capital is moving in and is attracting private capital from elsewhere as well.
At a time when foreign funds are taking money out of India at a fast clip, a relook at the taxes related to the markets is a welcome move.According to Hitesh Sawhney, partner at Price Waterhouse, against the current backdrop of sustained foreign investor selling, elevated global yields and capital moving towards competing markets, revisiting LTCG taxation may be timely."A (zero) tax rate on LTCG, linked to a relatively longer holding period, could reward patient capital, encourage investors to remain invested in India and strengthen India's relative capital market attractiveness. It would also reduce foreign investors' dependence on treaty-based exemptions and the resulting uncertainty over treaty eligibility."

"In many states you have not been able to win election for decades," Shah said, citing Congress's barren electoral performance in a number of states, including in Gujarat, Tripura, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal, while SIR had started only after 2024.This is the first time Shah has taken on the opposition, which has been trying to ratchet up pressure for CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation through its street campaigns in the national capital, and signalled a determined intent of the BJP brass to challenge its opponents' allegation that Election Commission (EC) is working to benefit the party in polls.The framing of opposition's protests as an attempt to cover "infiltrators" is significant, as BJP has for long accused its opponents of helping illegal immigrants from Bangladesh as well as Rohingya from Myanmar getting registered as voters as part of their "votebank" politics.
With opposition parties coming together, BJP and JD(U) held a joint press conference where Union minister Piyush Goyal dared opposition-run govts in different states to quit if it considered polls following SIR rigged.Union minister and JD(U) functionary Lalan Singh said the entire campaign is not for saving democracy but weakening it by targeting constitutional institutions and trying to stoke anarchy through street protests. The two ministers echoed Shah on Congress's poor show in UP, Bihar and Tamil Nadu for decades, and said it is not even a key party in vast swathes of the country.Shah: BJP victories in ballot paper civic polls lesson for RahulUnion home minister Amit Shah's sharp comments came after BJP notched up another facile win in three local body polls in Gujarat, leaving Congress far behind. Aam Aadmi Party lost deposits in all 32 seats it contested in Gandhinagar Municipal Corporation, he noted.This win coupled with BJP and its allies' similar impressive show in local body polls in Tripura and Rajasthan, besides in the recent assembly and LS bypolls, demonstrated that people of the country are standing with PM Modi, BJP, and NDA like a rock, Shah said.
Many of these polls were held through ballot papers, he said, as the opposition has often blamed EVMs for its losses. "These elections are a lesson for Rahul Gandhi... You (Rahul) cannot win the confidence of people by fabricated media events, 'jhooth ki goonj'," Shah said, riffing on Rahul's "Chhatron ki Goonj" outreach to students in different cities.Mocking the opposition's march in New Delhi on Monday, he said Rahul Gandhi cannot become the voice of the people by mobilising cadres of 14 parties to collect a crowd of 8,000 through a distance of 1.5km. They have no reach in the vast hinterland, he added. "Your negative politics will not benefit you. You should connect with people," he added.

An OpenAI Employee Allegedly Used a Chatbot to Help Plant a Recording Device at the Office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
23:17:59 UTC
08:17:59 KST

An engineer at OpenAI allegedly concealed an audio recording device in a piece of toilet paper and attached it behind a monitor inside an executive conference room at one of the company’s San Francisco offices, according to a criminal complaint unsealed on Tuesday.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, whom federal prosecutors describe as a 35-year-old Saudi Arabian national and US permanent resident, allegedly spent several weeks querying an unspecified “productivity agent” and an “AI chatbot” to plan his alleged surveillance operation. He used an internal OpenAI tool to ask about meetings scheduled in the targeted conference room.
He also appears to have used a chatbot account associated with his spouse to ask various technical questions about setting up a covert audio recording device, according to prosecutors and the court filing.
OpenAI’s security team also allegedly found an additional recording device in Alfozan’s bag at the office.
Alfozan couldn’t be immediately reached for comment. He made an initial appearance in US District Court in San Francisco on Tuesday on one charge of “use of an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications.” If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison. He joined OpenAI in July 2025 and was fired last Friday to coincide with his arrest.
FBI director Kash Patel said in a statement that Alfozan aimed “to secretly capture sensitive communications about the company’s super intelligence technology,” but neither prosecutors nor OpenAI have offered any information so far about a potential motive.
“At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data,” OpenAI said in a statement on X. “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance.”
OpenAI discovered the bug—which was allegedly “concealed in toilet paper” and “inserted into a USB port on the back of a television” in the conference room—on September 30 during a countersurveillance sweep.
Alfozan previously worked at a cargo logistics startup and at Meta, according to a purported LinkedIn profile for him. In a recent podcast interview, Alfozan said he was also part of a group of Saudi engineers in Silicon Valley who offered consulting services to Saudi organizations.
The LinkedIn profile lists Alfozan as a part-time “venture partner” at RAED Ventures, a venture capital firm based in Saudi Arabia. Neither RAED Ventures nor Meta immediately responded to WIRED’s request for comment.
Last year, the Trump administration signed a pact with Saudi Arabia granting the kingdom access to advanced chips and AI technologies that might otherwise be restricted over national security concerns. Saudi investment firms remain a major source of capital for US tech companies.
Executives Only
According to the complaint, Alfozan allegedly planted the listening device “no later than on or about September 28, 2026.”
The conference room Alfozan targeted “can be reserved only by executives and executive assistants,” and is typically used “for internal leadership meetings,” “technical and product sessions,” and “external briefings” with business partners and government officials, according to the complaint. It is frequently used for discussions involving “highly confidential” information, including about research, products, business strategy, and government relationships, the complaint stated.
OpenAI’s statement called the recording device “sophisticated.” Authorities allege that the device Alfozan planted was called Seeed XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense, “a thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage.” It currently retails on Seeed’s website for $13.99. OpenAI’s security team tried to export the data stored on the microSD card, but were unable to review it because it was encrypted.
After discovering the device, OpenAI says it notified the FBI and was able to connect it to Alfozan after reviewing chat logs and surveillance footage, and searching a bag he left unattended at the office. The company then gradually disabled his access to company systems as the investigation was ongoing.
According to the complaint, OpenAI security personnel discovered the bag that Alfozan left unattended in a printer room on October 5. The security team went through the bag, which contained a second encrypted Seeed listening device and other personal items connected to Alfozan, including his wallet. Prosecutors say Alfozan later reported the bag as missing to OpenAI and subsequently recovered it from the company’s lost and found.
He followed up with unnamed personnel at OpenAI to say that some of the items that were supposed to be in the bag were still missing—including a credit card, about $500 in cash, and two AirPods—but neglected to mention the second listening device, which had been removed from the bag by OpenAI security.

What Do Brazil’s Elections Mean for its Foreign Policy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

What Do Brazil’s Elections Mean for its Foreign Policy?
Whether Lula or Flávio Bolsonaro wins Brazil’s presidential run-off, a right-leaning Congress and pressure from China, the US and Europe will constrain its foreign policy.
‘Brazil is not for beginners’. The mantra coined by Brazilian songwriter Tom Jobim in the 1960s is more valid than ever. As we approach the second round of the 2026 presidential election, everyone – from financial analysts in Faria Lima (the financial heart of Brazil) to the residents of the small town of Ubaíra (home to large rare-earth deposits) – is waiting for Brazil’s electoral results. Whatever the outcome of the ballot, it promises deep changes to their lives.
Two Projects, Shared Pragmatism
At the centre, there are two political, economic, institutional and social projects starkly different at first glance. On one side, there is President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, turning 81 years old and running for his fourth term. Lula is an experienced and skilful politician, having co-founded the Workers’ Party (PT) in 1980. Before being elected president in 2002, Lula was defeated in the 1989, 1994 and 1998 elections. Lula’s reputation is based on his capacity to build pragmatic alliances and reinvent himself while being able to communicate with the wide spectrum of Brazilian society. His administrations have been embraced by progressive sectors who advocated for economic development together with inequality reduction and advocacy for minority rights. Lula’s foreign policy sought to diversify partnerships and strengthen regional ties through regional organisations, such as the establishment of UNASUR (Union of South American Nations), working together with Hugo Chávez and funding infrastructure projects in Venezuela and Cuba through the Brazilian Development Bank (BNDES).
On the other side, there is Flávio Bolsonaro, 45 years old. He was four times elected a legislative representative in Rio de Janeiro and was elected a senator in 2018, being the fourth most voted in the country. Similarly to his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio had numerous partisan affiliations. He was affiliated to the Partido Progressista (PP) for most of his legislative years. PP is a traditional and centre-right party that was in coalition with PT from 2003 to 2016, being directly involved with corruption scandals. Flávio left PP in 2016 for the Partido Social Cristão, when he ran for Mayor of Rio de Janeiro. In 2018, he affiliated to the Partido Social Liberal for his election to the Senate. After failing to establish their own party, Flávio and Jair Bolsonaro had short periods in Republicanos (2020-21), and Patriota (2021), until they joined the Partido Liberal (PL) in 2021. In similar terms to PP, PL used to be a centre-right party from the centrão (‘big centre’) and joined PT’s administrations’ supporting base. Brazil has been known for its ‘coalition presidentialism’, where incumbents need to have legislative support to be able to govern. This supporting base represents a group of ‘physiologic’ parties, as they exchange their support to incumbents for larger budget allocations and strategic positions in ministries.
The partisan configuration in 2027 reveals a divided country that has, since 2018, progressively leaned toward a right-wing conservative agenda – or, at the very least, distanced itself from the left progressive
Therefore, there is an interesting common element between Lula and Flávio: their political pragmatism. Lula’s administration made coalitions with the big centre whereas Flávio and his father have been part of the big centre for many years of their political careers. Nevertheless, their differences seem to count much more to the markets and other foreign leaders, such as the US president, Donald Trump. Flávio’s leading results in the first round of the 2026 elections was celebrated by Trump, describing results as ‘a very, very big victory. Amazing, actually’. In US case, a potential victory for Flavio would confirm a Brazilian closer alignment to the US foreign policy and a progress of the ‘Donroe Doctrine’ in Latin America. For markets, there was also a striking optimism: Ibovespa, Brazil’s benchmark stock index, had an increase of 7.7% on the following day and broke a historical record, surpassing 200,000 points. Governability can explain this market enthusiasm, which stem from what Flávio Bolsonaro’s potential victory means for Brazil, the region and the world.
A Stronger Right
PL (Flávio’s party) transformed itself in 2021 when it welcomed the Bolsonaro family to its ranks. From the centre, PL became the institutional representation of Bolsonarismo, turning to a far more conservative political agenda. The party had an impressive performance in the 2022 election, moving from 33 to 99 representatives in the Chamber of Deputies. In 2026, PL moved to 121 of 513 seats. In the Senate, they secured 28 of 81 seats, meaning the party alone now has almost a quarter of the Chamber of Deputies and a third of the Senate. As other right and centre-right parties declared support for Flávio Bolsonaro in this upcoming second round, his potential administration could benefit from majorities, allowing far more governability than Lula, with the latter risking facing a complete deadlock in his administration.
Supporting governability, there is favourable popular mood. As Lula seeks a fourth term, fatigue with PT’s political project progressively grows – a sentiment that traces its origin back to the 2013 protests against the cost of living. Lula’s administrations from 2003 to 2010 inherited economic stability after years of hyperinflation and internal and external debt. A strong economic performance produced by favourable commodity prices together with a thriving Chinese economy to consume them elevated Brazil’s status as an ‘emerging economy’. A new middle class was eager to occupy spaces and consume products that were once out of reach. This alignment of the stars gave Lula the political capital to elect his successor, Dilma Rousseff (2011–14).
However, Dilma Rousseff’s administration suffered from the worsening of Brazil’s economic performance. Poor economic results compounded by corruption scandals led to a disassociation between the country’s aspirations and its real performance, not only by society but also in international forums. Popular discontent was quickly channelled by emerging civil society organisations, such as Movimento Brasil Livre and Vem Pra Rua, which not only forged an anti-corruption movement, but also provided new political figures to the Brazilian right-wing landscape based on a direct antagonism to PT and Rousseff’s administration. She won the second round by a slim margin, securing a fragile second mandate that immediately suffered from the lack of legislative support. Rousseff did not complete her mandate, being impeached in 2016.
The ideological fracture deepened throughout the years. Lula was barred from running in 2018 following convictions that were later annulled. His political capital could not secure PT’s victory through Fernando Haddad either and Jair Bolsonaro won as an anti-system candidate. Once in power, he quickly built his legislative support and elevated the judiciary as his new nemesis. His mandate (2019–22) was marked by political clashes with the Supreme Federal Court and challenges to the electoral system. Internationally, Lula and Dilma sought to increase Brazil’s influence in the main international forums as the Global South’s leading voice by participating in UN peace operations (MINUSTAH in Haiti and UNIFIL in Lebanon), and engaging with the BRICS since 2006 to counterbalance Western institutions. By contrast, Bolsonaro’s government was marked by a retreat of Brazil’s participation in international organisations, direct alignment with the US (during Trump’s administration) and strong support for Israel. Therefore, the partisan configuration in 2027 reveals a divided country that has, since 2018, progressively leaned toward a right-wing conservative agenda – or, at the very least, distanced itself from the left progressive.
But the main question that lies ahead is: would a potential mandate from Flávio Bolsonaro differ significantly from his father’s? Or can Lula still pursue his agenda in the face of such an adverse governing framework in 2027? If Flávio wins, he will enjoy much more goodwill from markets and the legislative houses (Chamber of Deputies and Senate) for his projects. He is clear about seeking the annulment of his father’s 2025 judicial conviction for plotting a coup whilst allies foresee a pardoning for those involved in the invasion of Congress on 8 January 2023. Some experts raised concerns about the future of the judiciary’s independence as the Senate could impeach Supreme Court justices and PL now has a third of the house. Regionally, Flávio will also enjoy a much more favourable ideological environment, as most countries in South America are now led by right-wing governments.
International Constraints
Internationally, the scenario is more blurred. China is in direct technological, resource and trade competition with the US, especially in Latin America, becoming Brazil’s main trade partner in 2009. Recently, China has expanded its focus to mining, infrastructure and energy China’s MMG agreed to acquire Anglo American’s nickel operations in 2025, and China Nonferrous Metal Mining Group acquired Mineração Taboca for tin and niobium extraction. In terms of infrastructure, China’s CRRC in a consortium with a Brazilian company will build an intercity railway between São Paulo and Campinas. Therefore, reducing the Chinese influx of investments in favour of the US (especially in critical minerals) will be a tough task in case of a victory for Flávio. Likewise, an expansion of Chinese investment in case of Lula’s victory could also be quite difficult, as he will face the widest opposition to his government. The relationship with Europe will be marked by the implementation of the EU–Mercosur trade agreement and by how environmental protection is championed by the future administration, as deforestation is a non-trade barrier for the EU. With the US, organised crime and tariff negotiations might dominate bilateral dialogues. In 2025, Trump imposed 50% tariffs on several Brazilian exports alleging unbalanced trade and political persecution of Jair Bolsonaro. Although the US Supreme Court annulled Trump’s presidential order, tariffs returned in 2026 and both countries agreed to create a working group to negotiate a relief deal.
The strong dominance of right-wing parties in legislative houses and a potential reduction of judiciary counterweight will not stop the advance of a conservative agenda, regardless of who occupies the Alvorada Palace. If a Flávio victory might make legislative–executive relationships much less convoluted in comparison to a Lula victory, the expectation is that clashes with the judiciary will be the main source of tension. In any scenario, Brazil’s following years promise breathtaking events with local and global repercussions.
