Pope Leo XIV’s surgery to remove a lung nodule has been completed, according to the Vatican, which added that a surgical procedure confirmed he has lung cancer.
Earlier, the Vatican said in a statement that the pope’s operation was "successfully completed, on time and as planned," and that the pontiff has returned to his room.
The nodule was discovered during routine checks and was well localised and in its early stages, according to the Vatican, during the operation at Rome's Gemelli hospital.
The surgical team was led by Stefano Margaritora, head of the hospital’s thoracic surgery unit.
The Vatican later said the pope, 71, has been diagnosed with lung cancer.
"An intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, as suspected from the preoperative examinations," Vatican News reported, citing doctors.
No complications
Lung adenocarcinoma is known as the most common subtype of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), accounting for roughly 40% of all lung cancer cases.
The pope was in the operating room for approximately three hours, while the operation itself lasted about 90 minutes.
"The doctors said it was successful and there were no complications," according to the report.
About 1 in 5 lung cancer diagnoses occur in people with no smoking history.
Causes in non-smokers can include genetic factors, radon exposure, or other environmental/occupational risks — no specific cause has been identified in Pope’s case, and the nodule was found incidentally (not because of symptoms).

US lawmaker introduces bill to dismantle DHS and abolish ICE
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
21:25:25 UTC
06:25:25 KST

A member of the US House of Representatives has introduced legislation to dismantle the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) alongside Customs and Border Protection (CBP), and establish a new federal Department of Community Safety.
Democratic Representative Delia Ramirez stated that the proposed Reimagining Safety Act is designed to replace the post-9/11 cabinet department with a community-centred agency focused on public safety, civil rights, and direct support for working families.
The bill would formally repeal the statutory authorities underpinning DHS, redirect federal funding towards community-level initiatives, and place strict prohibitions on government surveillance, the unlawful utilisation of personal data, and militarised border enforcement.
"DHS was founded out of a profound national trauma, established to violate our rights under the pretence of securing our safety," Ramirez said, pointing to the department's creation following the September 11, 2001, attacks.
"But we cannot add new pains to old ones."
Restructuring civil immigration
Under the legislative proposal, several established federal components would remain operational, including the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), and core customs administration functions.
In contrast, ICE and CBP would be completely dissolved.
The legislation would simultaneously inaugurate a dedicated civil immigration system removed from criminal and militarised law enforcement structures.
Ramirez explained that the measure is prompted by systemic concerns over immigration enforcement, fatal incidents inside detention facilities, family separations, third-country deportations, armed confrontations involving immigration officers, and documented failures in emergency disaster management.

The Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center tested its new intercontinental ballistic missile reentry vehicle Oct. 9, launching the developmental vehicle atop a Minotaur I rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif.
The Mk21A reentry vehicle, mated to the Sentinel ICBM, will eventually replace the Minuteman III as the land-based leg of the nation’s nuclear triad. Carrying the new W87-1 nuclear warhead, it will launch atop the Sentinel’s three rocket stages, blasting into space before reentering the atmosphere to strike its target.
The Oct. 9 test launch carried no warhead and was the first announced test of the new vehicle since June 2024.
“The Mk21A is crucial to modernizing our ICBMs in response to the rapidly changing global threat picture posed by our adversaries,” said Maj. Gen. William Rogers, the Air Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for ICBMs, in a statement. “The reentry vehicle’s development will ensure a safe, secure and effective deterrent for generations to come.”
The Mk21A is based on the Mk21 reentry vehicle used on the Minuteman III, and is being developed by Lockheed Martin. The Minotaur I launch vehicle, provided by Northrop Grumman, is based on the Peacekeeper and Minuteman rocket motors. The Space Force helped oversee the test through its Rocket Systems Launch Program, which provides commercial launch systems and excess ballistic missile assets for government payloads.
The Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center awarded Lockheed a $996 million contract for the Mk21A in October 2023 and followed with an additional $453 million contract modification in November 2025.
According to an April acquisition report released by the Pentagon in September, the latest contract modification was part of a new baseline for the program intended to “decouple its schedule from external programs and continue development with an updated, more resilient plan.”
The LGM-35 Sentinel program office is still working to overcome the cost and schedule problems that triggered a mandatory Pentagon review, and while officials claim progress, the program is undergoing a restructuring before it can meet Milestone B, which would authorize it to move into engineering and manufacturing development.
The acquisition report offers scant details on the Mk21A rebaseline effort, beyond noting that it includes a new “alternate flight test strategy” and additional test assets. It does note, however, that the June 2024 test successfully flight-tested the vehicle’s heatshield, and that Lockheed was working on integrating the arming and fuzing subsystem in February 2026. Air Force budget documents released in April projected “flight test of heatshield test vehicle and W87-1 environmental flight test unit” in fiscal 2026 and 2027.
A critical design review for the entire Sentinel system is planned by March 2027. The Air Force asked for almost $540 million to fund Mk21A reentry vehicle development in the fiscal 2027 budget request, up $184 million from 2026 as Sentinel ramps up integration and test activities.

A federal magistrate judge in Virginia ruled that Elon Musk engaged in "state sanctioned intimidation" of ex-FEMA CFO Mary Comans when he posted falsehoods on X last year accusing her of "criminal action" and of "funneling $58 million to illegal migrant hotels in Manhattan."
Musk, the world's richest person, was working for the Trump administration as the head of DOGE when he shared those posts on Feb. 11, 2025. The Department of Homeland Security said the next day it was firing Comans and three colleagues, and labeled them "deep state activists."
In Tuesday's order, U.S. Magistrate Judge William Fitzpatrick cleared Comans' name.
Comans served as FEMA CFO from around January 2018 until February 2025, and was also FEMA's operating chief from 2020 to 2021.
Fitzpatrick wrote in the order that, "The facts establish that high-ranking government officials," including Musk, then a special government employee, had "engaged in a coordinated public relations campaign to impugn the personal and professional integrity of Ms. Comans."
"Mr. Musk was the head of DOGE, he knew or should have known that any payments made to state or local governments through a FEMA grant in February 2025 were approved by his subordinates," the judge wrote.
He added that Musk posted a picture of Ms. Comans "to his millions of followers while falsely characterizing her government service as a 'criminal action,'" an act Fitzpatrick described as "little more than state sanctioned intimidation."
CNBC has reached out to Musk and White House attorneys involved in the case for comment.
Democracy Defenders Fund, which was involved in Comans' case, said in a statement that it was pleased with the decision.
"Mary Comans served in the federal government for 21 years," said Craig Becker, the group's head of affirmative litigation. "Career public servants are people, not pawns, and no one who has devoted their life to serving the American public should have their good name destroyed for partisan, political gain."

B-2 Stealth Bomber Returns to Base After Depot Maintenance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:59:50 UTC
05:59:50 KST

One of the Air Force’s critical B-2 Spirit stealth bombers has returned to Whiteman Air Force Base, Mo., after an extensive course of maintenance to restore its stealth coating and preserve its structural integrity.
The B-2, which bears the tail number 93-1086 and is nicknamed the Spirit of Kitty Hawk, underwent programmed depot maintenance at Air Force Plant 42, a highly secure facility in Palmdale, Calif., the Air Force said in an Oct. 10 statement. Northrop Grumman, which originally built the B-2 when it was called the Northrop Corp. and today builds B-21 Raiders at Plant 42, managed the Spirit’s depot maintenance.
Programmed depot maintenance is a regularly scheduled, labor-intensive process for thoroughly inspecting, overhauling and repairing Air Force aircraft. It becomes increasingly important as aircraft age and more maintenance troubles emerge.
The Spirit of Kitty Hawk touched down Oct. 7 at Whiteman, which is home of the 509th Bomb Wing. But it’s not returning to service just yet—it will now move to the 509th’s modification line to receive advanced stealth and communications upgrades.
The Air Force officially records 20 of the stealthy long-range B-2s in its inventory. But another B-2, called the Spirit of Hawaii, had a fiery crash in 2022 after its landing gear collapsed, which sparked a fire that ignited the bomber’s fuel tanks. The Air Force later said it planned to retire the Spirit of Hawaii, which would leave the service with 19 B-2s.
With so few B-2s in its fleet, the Air Force said, returning even one bomber responsible for some of the service’s core functions back to the field “represents a significant boost to readiness.”
“The B-2 is a small fleet,” Lt. Col. Jeffrey Lembrick, air vehicle and systems management materiel leader for the B-2 program office, said in the statement. “Every time we return a jet to the field, it represents an additional strategic option available for the President of the United States. When you talk about aircraft availability, one thing we know is that a jet can’t be used if it’s sitting at PDM. So, completing PDM and returning to the field is a big deal.”
Depot maintenance for the B-2 typically involves restoring its low-observable stealth coating, inspecting its fuel system for leaks, and maintaining its blade seals, which are strips of metal that seal gaps when doors for weapons bays, landing gear, or other compartments close. In recent years, B-2s have taken about 15 to 16 months to go through programmed depot maintenance, although in 2024, one B-2 finished the process a little more than a year after it began.
This time, the Air Force said, the Spirit of Kitty Hawk’s depot maintenance included replacement of its hot trailing edge, “a critical structural assembly designed to withstand the extreme thermal and acoustic fatigue generated by the bomber’s four engines.”
Maintainers also spotted and fixed several unexpected maintenance problems while the B-2 was going through the depot. This included carrying out “a strategic part swap” with another B-2 that was coming into the Palmdale depot, and manufacturing another replacement part on-site, a B-2 program office official said.

The World Cup was bad for some businesses in Los Angeles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:57:10 UTC
05:57:10 KST

The World Cup was bad for some businesses in Los Angeles
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
The surge in soccer fans this summer was bad for some businesses in Los Angeles.
World Cup host cities had lofty economic expectations for the summer tournament. But the city’s hotels only got a 1% bump in occupancy, according to a report published this week by Hospitality Education and Research Organization, a project of the Hotel Assn. of Los Angeles.
Seventy-two percent of surveyed hotels said the tournament hurt their 2026 finances, and 48% called the impact “extremely negative.” Just 2% said it met projections.
Downtown occupancy reached 66% in June, down from 71% a year earlier, the report says. Room nights fell between 10% and 12%.
Ahead of World Cup tournaments, FIFA holds large blocks of rooms. But FIFA canceled or released up to 70% of the hotel room blocks it had reserved in host cities, including Los Angeles.
“We understood that we were maybe going to be disappointed with attendance going into the World Cup simply by the volume of cancellations that came out of the room block agreement,” said Jackie Filla, president and CEO of the Hotel Assn. of Los Angeles.
The disappointing turnout led to staff reductions. Of the hotels surveyed 82% reduced seasonal staff and more than six in 10 reported reducing employee shifts, scheduled hours, or permanent staff.
Hotels did raise prices, with the average daily rate hitting $228, the highest of any comparable L.A. event in three years. But occupancy was 71%, well below the 83% recorded during Taylor Swift’s Eras Tour.
The survey drew 58 responses from 210 hotels, and the analysis was done by travel-data firm Rove using CoStar and AirDNA data. International visitors were also scarce, with Los Angeles welcoming 700,000 international arrivals in June and July — roughly 80,000 visitors below 2024 levels for the same period, the report says.
“We particularly didn’t see a lot of foreign visitors and that’s something that was disappointing,” Filla said. “Foreign visitors do spend three times the amount of money as the average domestic traveler.”
Short-term rentals, meanwhile, gained. Their demand rose 23% and revenue 21% versus July 2024, while hotel revenue fell 3.3%. Airbnb, the tournament’s official fan accommodation, offered new hosts $750 incentives.
The city is currently weighing a temporary proposal to ease its short-term rental rules through the end of 2028 to accommodate tourists. “That will really, truly undercut the business of hotels,” Filla added. “We saw some of that with the World Cup.”
The worry is carrying over to the Olympic Games, set to be hosted in Los Angeles in 2028. Six in 10 surveyed hoteliers expect an Olympic rental surge to hurt their bookings and rates, the report says.
The World Cup “gave us false hope to recover from a negative year,” one Los Angeles hotelier said, according to the report. “I also feel [the] same thing will probably happen for [the] Super Bowl and Olympics.”

Most Americans Think Trump Is Profiting From the Presidency Illegally or Unethically, Poll Finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:49:15 UTC
05:49:15 KST

Most Americans think that Donald Trump is profiting off the presidency either illegally or unethically, according to a new AP-NORC poll. The findings, published Tuesday, also illustrate that the President is perceived as prioritizing his business ventures above the country.
According to the poll, which surveyed 2,140 adults from Sept. 24 to 28, 4 in 10 respondents believe he has done something illegal and another 18% see his actions as unethical but not illegal.
A majority of respondents (56%) also said Trump has prioritized his personal business interests “a lot,” while only 23% said he has prioritized the country overall. Just 11% say he has prioritized “people like them,” while half of respondents said Trump has not prioritized people like them at all.
Republicans were much more likely than Democrats or Independents to say that the president prioritized the country overall; however, they were not without criticism. Only about 1 in 10 Republicans said Trump had done something illegal; most said he had done nothing wrong or that they did not know enough to judge.
“It's fairly unprecedented how much wealth increase this President has gotten in the past two years,” Raymond La Raja, a professor at University of Massachusetts Amherst and the co-director of the UMass Poll, tells TIME.
He points to last year, when a business tied to the royal family of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) invested half a billion dollars into Trump’s crypto ventures, raising conflict-of-interest questions from watchdog organizations and lawmakers. According to his latest annual financial disclosure from June 30, Trump earned more than $1.4 billion from these ventures last year alone.
“It's really a structural conflict-of-interest that he is regulating policies that directly benefit his family—and it's also incentivizing not just Americans, but foreign entities, like the United Arab Emirates, to invest in his family's projects,” he says. “So that's really worrisome.”
A separate UMass Amherst poll, conducted in August, points to broader concerns about government corruption. It showed that 75% of respondents noted a “great” amount of corruption in the federal government. Another 53% ranked the presidency as the “most corrupt institution in government”—above the Supreme Court, Congress, and the federal bureaucracy as a whole.
A majority of respondents (54%) said it was “definitely” corrupt for a public official to use their office to benefit themselves or their family financially, even if doing so was legal. Another 29% said it was “probably” corrupt.
Why Trump’s wealth and the economy could matter in the midterms
La Raja argues that the amount that constituents care about a politician’s enrichment or find it “unethical” often depends on how the country is doing overall.
“If you look at other countries when there's some time when there's somebody who's perceived as corrupt, people are more likely to tolerate it if the economy is booming,” he says, pointing to countries like Hungary. “But when the promise of prosperity is not showing up for the electorate, then they start to say, ‘What's going on?’ And that's when corruption looms larger.”
Just 28% of 2,275 respondents approved of Trump’s handling of jobs and the economy, according to a Financial Times/Focaldata poll released Tuesday. Consumer prices were up 3.4% in August from a year earlier, the latest figure available from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Two sources of price pressure have been Trump’s tariffs and the U.S. war with Iran. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York estimates that tariffs added 2.9 percentage points to consumer goods inflation by February 2026. The war has also driven up fuel prices, raising costs for industries that rely heavily on diesel.
“[Trump] promised a better economy, and now inflation is up,” La Raja says. “There’s a war, and importantly, the war is linked to inflation.”
The AP-NORC poll comes less than a month before the midterm elections, where the Republican Party is looking to hold onto its majorities in the House and the Senate. Experts are viewing the midterms not just as a referendum on Trump, but whether Republican candidates’ connections to Trump will help—or harm—them on Election Day.
“Presidential approval often serves as a political anchor in midterm elections—meaning dissatisfaction with Trump could extend to Republican candidates down the ballot, particularly among independents and suburban voters,” Brandon Rottinghaus, a professor of political science at the University of Houston, tells TIME. “Even Republicans who are personally popular may find it difficult to separate themselves from perceptions of the President.”
According to Rottinghaus, concerns around “presidential self-enrichment” are not unique to Trump. In fact, a 2023 AP-NORC poll asking respondents about former President Joe Biden’s handling of his son’s overseas business deals invoked similar concerns about conflict-of-interest that fell along partisan lines.
“But Trump's extensive business interests have made the issue particularly visible,” Rottinghaus continues. “Historically, voters have often judged presidential ethics through a partisan lens, with supporters more willing to excuse questionable conduct and opponents more likely to interpret it as evidence of broader problems with presidential accountability.”
How much income did Trump report in 2026?
Supporters are being told that the President took a financial hit by returning for a second term.
“There’s no financial gain like the past Presidents have had. It’s cost him to be in office,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told attendees at an Oct. 1 rally in Durant, Oklahoma.
According to his 927-page financial disclosure for 2025, Trump’s total reported revenue was $2.2 billion. In comparison, his total reported revenues for 2024 were closer to $622 million.
That spike can largely be attributed to the $1.4 billion windfall he received from his family’s crypto venture, including more than $550 million from World Liberty Financial token sales—nine times the amount he earned from the same token sales in 2024.
Trump’s family business, the Trump Organization, has also capitalized on his second term by expanding its real estate, golf, and licensing footprint in the Middle East, including in Saudi Arabia and Qatar—two countries that have become crucial to U.S. foreign policy, especially amid the war with Iran. These deals alone garnered around $14 million, according to filings from July 2026.
The overlap between Trump’s business interests and the presidency could extend beyond his time in office.
His representatives have proposed building a retreat for future presidents on land beside Trump International Golf Club in West Palm Beach. The club would pay for the lodging and provide government access free of charge, while Trump’s family business would continue to operate the adjoining golf course. Local officials are considering the plan, which could make the private club a destination for influential political visitors long after Trump leaves the White House.

‘the body is my canvas, tool, and medium’: lucy mcrae discusses identity and the spaces we carry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:35:36 UTC
05:35:36 KST

‘the body is my canvas, tool, and medium’: lucy mcrae discusses identity and the spaces we carry
the artist and designer uses worldbuilding to make emerging technologies tangible, asking how they might reshape our bodies, identities, and relationships with the future.
[FEATURED]
Lucy McRae on body futurism
The body is both the starting point and the testing ground for Lucy McRae’s speculative practice. Through sculpture, film, conceptual fashion, and experimental design, the artist explores how technology might change the way we inhabit ourselves and relate to others. Her work treats the human body as a medium through which possible futures can be experienced and questioned.
McRae leads Future Sensitive, an art-led speculative lab that brings together scientists, artists, and designers to explore body futurism and post-nature futures. Her interest in the subject developed through a combination of physical training, design research, and technological experimentation. After studying interior design at RMIT, she led a far-future design research lab at Philips from 2006 to 2010, where she worked on wearable technologies, including emotional-sensing dresses and electronic tattoos. The experience established a recurring question in her work: what happens when technology becomes inseparable from the body? ‘I’ve been investigating complex science for two decades. We can’t un-invent technology, and it all lands on the body,’ McRae shares with designboom. ‘The body has been my canvas, tool, and medium.’
from speculative technology to lived experience
For the British-born Australian artist, the body is a way to make complex technologies easier to understand and imagine. This idea informed Compression Cradle, a project presented at the 2019 Milan Triennale exhibition Broken Nature, curated by Italian author and critic Paola Antonelli. The work later inspired a visual reference in Blade Runner 2099, for which Lucy McRae designed a crèche and birth bags for replicants. It shows how ideas developed through her art can also find their way into the worlds of film. Her work also questions where the body ends and technology begins. In Swallowable Parfum, developed with synthetic biologist Sharef Mansy, McRae imagined a cosmetic pill that would make the body produce its own fragrance. Conceived as a fictional beauty commercial, the project attracted interest from pharmaceutical brands, turning an invented product into a point of contact with the real market. ‘After leaving Philips I kept looking at technology through an art and worldbuilding lens. What happens when technology becomes the size of a blood cell, and we can eat it? I was also exploring pheromone excretion, and how the smell of our immune system is body odor. With Sharef Mansy, a synthetic biologist, we created Swallowable Parfum, a cosmetic pill that makes the body produce its own fragrance from the inside. We made it as a fictional beauty commercial, and it drew real responses from pharmaceutical brands. The fiction became a market signal,’ Lucy McRae tells us. ‘So does the body become tech when we eat it?’ she asks. ‘Maybe the better question is what far greater things could exist if technology is swallowable.’
This interest also shapes the artist’s approach to fashion. Lucy McRae has recently completed a collection for Future Sensitive, drawing inspiration from costumes in films and artworks to create clothes for everyday wear. Set to launch in Los Angeles in 2027, the collection explores how clothing can express ideas about the future and change how we feel about ourselves.
clothing as an invisible architecture
 McRae’s background in interior design informs her understanding of wearable objects as more than garments. Her interest lies in the relationships between things: a room and a body, a machine and a building, or the person and the space immediately surrounding them. These boundaries become less stable when clothing is understood as something that can alter not only appearance but also perception and behavior.
‘I think objects we wear create architectures, but they’re invisible,’ Lucy McRae explains. ‘They’re fields of feeling, or of psyche.’ The effect, she suggests, can be subtle but consequential. Wearing a particular outfit may change how someone carries themselves or how they are perceived by others, creating a temporary social space without any physical construction. McRae is testing her forthcoming collection in public, where the clothes become a way of projecting an identity that might otherwise remain unspoken. ‘It says “I am cooler than you think,” or really, “I am cooler than I think.” It pumps up identity without words,’ she tells designboom.
Lucy McRae’s work shows how clothing can shape the way we see ourselves and how others see us. For the body architect, what we wear can change how we feel and how we interact with people around us, an interest that comes from her own experience growing up. McRae recalls feeling like an outsider and making her own clothes to fit in. The desire to belong, she says, is something everyone understands, and it continues to influence her work.‘The estrangement you sense might be a trace of that: a yearning, a trying, a squeezing into something. Wanting to belong is universal,’ she notes.
making futures that can be inhabited
The science fiction artist describes her work as a way of developing possible scenarios, using the physical experience of a project to make its implications more immediate. A future becomes more persuasive when people can imagine themselves inhabiting it, but that immersion should not prevent them from questioning what they encounter. ‘Powerful stories are felt more when you can imagine yourself as the character, lie down in them, and embody a future,’ she highlights. ‘Just as important, you have to be able to refute it, argue with it, or offer alternatives.’
McRae also wants people to take part in her work rather than simply look at it. One idea she hopes to explore is an artwork in a swimming pool, using wearable flotation pieces and activities in water. ‘I dream of designing artwork in a pool: wearable flotation pieces, rituals in water, buoyancy to relax, immerse and transcend. Maybe the whole thing gets filmed, and it becomes the campaign for the fashion launch!’ she adds with a laugh.

artist: Lucy McRae | @lucymcrae

Lawmakers Argue Trump's Russia Diesel Deal 'Violates' the Law. Here's What Legal Experts Say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:31:53 UTC
05:31:53 KST

President Donald Trump is facing growing backlash over his plan to import diesel from Russia, with some Republican and Democratic lawmakers insisting that the controversial deal “violates” the law.
Congress four years ago passed the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act, which prohibits U.S. imports of Russian-origin energy products covered by Chapter 27 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule, including diesel. Democratic Rep. Lloyd Doggett of Texas, the bill's chief sponsor, argued Monday that Trump is “directly violating that law” by “lifting sanctions to permit the first Russian diesel imports into the United States since the law took effect, without satisfying the specific legal conditions it requires.”
He suggested the lack of congressional oversight on Trump’s deal with Putin renders it unlawful, and noted how the plan showcases a sharp turn from Washington, as it comes just weeks after Trump signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill intended to target the country's financial institutions and the energy industry, which has largely financed the assault on Ukraine. The sanctions bill was named after Lindsey Graham, the late Republican Senator who spent the final year of his life building support for the measure.
“Russia can [now] export fossil fuel to the U.S. after Trump violated the specific provisions of a federal statute,” Doggett said on Tuesday in a statement to TIME. “While offering little benefit for Americans, this unlawful action will provide substantial new funding for Putin‘s war machine to continue murdering Ukrainian civilians.”
Doggett’s concerns match those of Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, who told NBC’s Meet the Press over the weekend that he believes “there’s a legitimate case for saying the President’s not following the law.”
Tillis was one of seven Senators who publicly urged the Administration on Sunday to “immediately reverse course” on the agreement announced Friday, arguing that it goes against the 2022 law.
“Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine,” read the statement co-signed by Republican Senators Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Susan Collins of Maine, Thom Tillis of North Carolina, and John Curtis of Utah, alongside Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Ron Wyden of Oregon, and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut.
“President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law. The Administration has also failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute,” they said.
In a letter sent to Trump on Tuesday, Tillis, Collins, and Murkowski, were joined by fellow Republican Senators Mitch McConnell of Kentucky, John Cornyn of Texas, and Alan Armstrong of Oklahoma alongside six Democratic Senators as they told the President the deal “is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies [and] should be rescinded.” The letter came a day after Trump publicly dismissed the criticism stemming from within his own party.
"Well, I think these are Republicans that can't really be serious," he told reporters at the White House. “Anything that could help our farmers, our ranchers, I like.”
Trump’s deal to "immediately" supply 300,000 tons of diesel to American and global markets comes as he faces growing political pressure ahead of the November midterms. Spiraling energy costs have become a key concern for voters, threatening to undermine Republican efforts to maintain their majorities in Congress. The financial upheaval has meant that Trump risks losing his hold on farm country. However, experts are skeptical that an influx of Russian fuel will bring relief to struggling Americans, given how short the supply is due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz.
While some lawmakers also predict the impact on American consumers will be slight, the key sticking point for many centers on whether Trump’s diesel deal with Putin violates the 2022 law, with some Republicans and Democrats insisting that Trump is pushing the limits of presidential authority. Here’s what to know about the debate—and where legal experts stand on the matter.
According to the 2022 law, what must happen for the import ban on Russian diesel to be lifted?
While Presidents typically have broad authority to waive sanctions, Congress placed specific limits on that power in the April 2022 legislation, says Kristen Eichensehr, a professor of law at Harvard Law School.
“In many sanctions authorities, the President has broad authority to waive imposition of the sanctions or to issue licenses that basically provide an exception to the sanctions,” she tells TIME. “The [2022 act] is an unusual law, given how careful and specific Congress was in providing that the President lacks that flexibility.”
Under Section 3 of the legislation, the President must first consult with the House Ways and Means and Foreign Affairs Committees, along with the Senate Finance and Foreign Relations Committees, and submit a report at least 45 days before providing the required certification.
Lawmakers have argued that the Administration has failed to follow this process.
“The President has to provide a certification to Congress in advance before lifting the prohibition,” says Eichensehr, pointing to the specific criteria set out in the wording of the law.
The law requires a determination by the President to Congress that the Russian Federation has withdrawn and ceased hostilities accepted by Ukraine; poses no immediate threat to any NATO member; and recognizes the right of the Ukrainian people to freely and independently choose their own government.
But Eichensehr insists that these are “not certifications that the President could make at the current moment” because “none of those things have happened, and that's the main restriction in the law.”
Even if all these conditions were met, the legislation would still require the President to wait an additional 90 days before the termination of the import ban could take effect, during which, Congress could enact a joint resolution of disapproval.
“On the substance, the President cannot, as a factual matter, make the certifications because Russia is still attacking Ukraine,” says Eichensehr. “As a procedural matter, [because he reportedly has not consulted Congress], he hasn't followed the process that the law sets out.”
Edward Swaine, a research professor at George Washington University Law School, suggests these restrictions were put in place to ensure that “when the President and the Treasury Secretary decide that circumstances have changed, they go back and explain this to Congress, and give it notice so that it can disagree.”
“The President is supposed to make this determination that Russia has withdrawn its forces and doesn't pose any further threat of aggression. These are fairly high standards,” he tells TIME, noting that the statue provides “Congress with adequate notice to allow it to generate a joint resolution of disapproval.”
“They don't want the President to be able to change this regime on a whim, and so I imagine Congress looking at this action and justifiably thinking that this is inconsistent,” he adds.
Treasury says the diesel deal is being carried out within the legal authorities
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has defended the legality of the agreement, insisting that the Trump Administration is acting within its existing legal authority to help bring energy prices down.
“We’re doing it with all the legal authorities we have, so anyone in Congress who says that—whether it’s an old bill or the current Lindsey Graham bill—prohibits us from doing it, is wrong,” he told Fox News on Sunday, without elaborating on which legal authorities he was referring to.
On Friday, the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued a temporary general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel fuel, including its importation, until April 7, 2027.
Swaine says that the Administration could argue that “the general license isn't [a] termination of the statutory prohibition; it's a suspension.”
“The [Treasury] Secretary could say this isn't the same thing as ending the prohibition on imports, it's just suspending it until April,” says Swaine. “The second thing [the Administration] could say is that it doesn't apply to all affected products, just a subcategory concerning diesel fuel, so there's [potentially] a difference between the actions that are required for the President to terminate the entire program and the actions that the Secretary is taking here.”
Responding to claims on social media that Bessent and the White House had broken the law, the Office of the Under Secretary for Terrorism and Financial Intelligence, part of the Treasury, insisted that the Administration had followed established procedures.
“The granting of this general license is consistent with similar actions previously taken by OFAC and is in compliance with all applicable laws,” the office said over the weekend.
The OFAC permitted transactions involving Russian oil and petroleum products already loaded on vessels, including from vessels previously under U.S. sanctions, to Indian ports in March; the office had also allowed the entry of specified diamonds in August that had been outside Russia before set cutoff dates under a previous Executive Order.
TIME has reached out to the White House and Treasury Department for comment.
How Congress could challenge Trump's diesel deal
Lawmakers could pursue congressional oversight and other political measures to challenge the Administration’s decision.
Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania has already announced plans to introduce “bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil” under the proposed “Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act.” Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, a Republican who has clashed with Trump on other high-profile issues, said he has agreed to co-sponsor the bill, because “Congress must make a stand.”
However, experts tell TIME what Congress is able to do may be limited to more of a symbolic display rather than anything that can move the needle.
“There's limited ability of Congress to do much besides pass legislation and politically enforce that,” says Swaine, suggesting that methods such as “withholding money, appropriations, and hearings” could be used if the situation escalated to that point.

What the Ukrainian Strikes on Yandex Tell Us About Central Asia’s Digital Infrastructure
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:31:00 UTC
05:31:00 KST

Over the last weekend, three Yandex facilities in Russia have been struck by Ukrainian drones, with Russian users subsequently reporting outages across Yandex’s services. After the third strike, on a data center east of Moscow in Vladimir, Central Asian users of Yandex’s superapp Yandex Go began reporting outages too.
Yandex is one of Russia’s largest technology companies, with a portfolio that resembles a hybrid of Google and Uber, but for the русский мир, the Russian world. Yandex Search holds an estimated 72 percent of market share in Russia while maintaining an estimated search engine market share in Kazakhstan of just under 30 percent. It is with its superapp, Yandex Go – which combines ride-sharing with food delivery and other services – that Yandex dominates in Central Asia.
In 2017 Uber effectively ceded Central Asia to Yandex, agreeing to merge operations in Azerbaijan, Armenia, Belarus and Kazakhstan, where the two companies had previously competed. Yandex Go expanded to Kyrgyzstan in 2017 and to Uzbekistan in 2018. A 2023 effort to enter the Tajik market was defeated by Dushanbe. In 2023, Yandex bought Uber out of the joint venture, becoming the undisputed ride-sharing and food delivery leader in the Central Asian region.
On October 11, following the strike on Yandex’s Vladimir facility, Yandex customers in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan began reporting trouble booking rides, ordering food and accessing their accounts. The press services of Yandex Qazaqstan, Yandex Kyrgyzstan, and Yandex Uzbekistan all acknowledged technical issues to local media outlets and said they had teams working to restore services.
Although services have reportedly resumed, at least in Kazakhstan, Russian media reports stated that it could take months to restore operations at the affected data centers. And that doesn’t factor in possible future strikes.
Kazakhstan’s Agency for the Protection and Development of Competition reportedly issued a warning to inDrive, an alternative ride-sharing app which operates in the country, after its prices spiked during the Yandex outage. As users shifted from the inoperable Yandex Go app to inDrive, prices went up dramatically. The agency claimed that in some cases the cost of rides tripled.
According to RFE/RL’s Kazakh Service, InDrive founder Arsen Tomsky “attributed the price hike to a sharp increase in demand and a shortage of available vehicles.”
This is just another way in which the Russian war in Ukraine has had knock-on effects in Central Asia. While complicating deliveries of KFC, plov or lagman late at night may not rank as the most critical of issues, this incident does underscore that Central Asia’s digital infrastructure remains closely linked with Russia’s. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development stressed that the personal data of Kazakh users of Yandex is safe because it is stored on servers in Kazakhstan. But the overarching architecture – the technical bits that connect a person to a driver – is not, and therefore risks posed to Russia’s digital infrastructure will continue to spill over into Central Asia.
Ukraine, for its part, positioned its attacks on Russian data centers as retaliation for Russia’s strikes against Ukrainian data centers. Kyiv also claimed that its attacks targeted centers that provide revenue streams to Moscow. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said at the Warsaw Security Forum on October 12 that “everyone noticed” a drop in Russian bot activity on social media after the strikes. The reality of that claim is, as these things tend to be, far more complicated.

380,000 LEGO flowers transform shanghai’s concrete oil tank into botanical landscape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:30:40 UTC
05:30:40 KST

380,000 LEGO flowers transform shanghai’s concrete oil tank into botanical landscape
the 30-meter-long installation spills across the west bund waterfront, bringing together monumental sculpture, artist collaborations and interactive experiences where visitors can grow their own digital gardens.
[FEATURED]
EGO BOTANICAL WAVE TAKES OVER TANK SHANGHAI
More than 380,000 LEGO flowers are spilling out of a former oil tank in Shanghai, forming a colorful wave that stretches 30 meters across the city’s West Bund waterfront. The monumental installation is the centerpiece of the LEGO Bloom Exhibition at TANK Shanghai, where the Danish toymaker has transformed an industrial landmark into an oversized botanical landscape. Covering approximately 800 square meters, the temporary intervention brings together roses, sunflowers, tulips, and other brick-built plants in a spectacle that gives the familiar plastic pieces an entirely different sense of scale.
The installation, titled LEGO Botanical Wave, appears to burst through the concrete structure before spreading across the surrounding ground. Thousands of individual flowers merge into sweeping bands of red, yellow, orange, and white, creating the illusion of movement despite their rigid construction. The contrast with the cylindrical oil tanks is particularly striking: an architecture once associated with heavy industry becomes the backdrop for an improbable garden, one where every petal has been assembled by hand.
LEGO BLOOM EXHIBITION BRINGS ART AND PLAY TOGETHER
The floral takeover continues inside TANK Shanghai, where 18 installations by artists and LEGO enthusiasts explore the possibilities of the Botanicals collection beyond conventional flower arrangements. Combining plastic elements with materials including metal, textiles, and mirrors, the works move between sculpture, experimentation, and decorative design. An immersive space surrounded by a 360-degree digital display adds another dimension to the exhibition, extending the botanical imagery beyond its physical components.
Elsewhere, the outdoor Bloom Gallery presents 18 LEGO botanical arrangements in everyday settings, suggesting how the artificial flowers might find a place in domestic interiors. A pop-up shop completes the experience, offering visitors the opportunity to take home smaller versions of the floral compositions. The exhibition also reflects LEGO’s growing interest in adult audiences, presenting the act of building as a creative pastime rather than something to be left behind with childhood.
VISITORS CAN ADD THEIR OWN LEGO FLOWERS TO A DIGITAL GARDEN
Participation is another important part of the LEGO Bloom Exhibition. In the interactive areas, visitors can assemble their own botanical creations before scanning them into a digital flower field, where their designs become part of a collective, continuously expanding landscape. The experience connects the physical act of putting bricks together with a shared virtual environment, allowing visitors to contribute something of their own to the exhibition rather than simply admire the finished installations.
Running from October 1 to 29, 2026, the exhibition is free to visit, with advance reservations required for the indoor spaces through LEGO’s WeChat Mini Program. The outdoor installation remains accessible without booking, turning part of Shanghai’s waterfront into a temporary garden of plastic flowers. It is a fittingly playful transformation for a former industrial site: the tanks have lost their original purpose, but one of them is overflowing again, this time with something considerably more colorful.

Cornell bans fraternity parties for rest of academic year after alleged gang rape
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:25:43 UTC
05:25:43 KST

Cornell bans fraternity parties for rest of academic year after alleged gang rape
NEW YORK – Cornell University will ban parties and social events at fraternity houses until the end of the academic year, its president said on Oct 13, responding to the outcry over an alleged gang rape on campus in 2024.
The measure is the strongest reaction yet from Cornell’s leadership to a lawsuit filed by a former undergraduate, Jane Doe, alleging that seven men sexually assaulted her at a party two years ago.
Over the past several weeks, the Ivy League school in Ithaca, New York, and its president, Michael Kotlikoff, have come under heavy criticism from students, faculty and donors over the response to allegations.
The suspension of parties and social events will apply to Interfraternity Council houses. The council website says Cornell currently has 34 fraternity houses.
“These measures will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue,” Kotlikoff said in a statement.
The Cornell Interfraternity Council did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Prosecutors reopened an investigation into the alleged gang rape after the lawsuit was filed.
New York Governor Kathy Hochul appointed New York Attorney-General Letitia James as an independent special prosecutor in the case, citing the earlier failure to protect the alleged victim.
US President Donald Trump repeated on Oct 13 his call to take James, his long-time critic and an elected Democrat, off the case.
“The Governor should take James off this case immediately,” Trump posted on his Truth Social platform.
Trump first questioned James’ appointment in early October, but his comments did not prompt any action by officials.
The offices of Hochul and the attorney-general did not immediately reply to requests for comment.
Since the lawsuit against seven fraternity members, the university and others was filed in September, the Cornell administration has faced student protests, a pending no-confidence resolution from faculty, criticism by alumni and a public assembly where students blamed university officials for tolerating what they described as a culture of sexual violence.
None of the men named in the lawsuit has been criminally charged.
“I have spent the past weeks listening to students, faculty, staff, parents, alumni and trustees, who have shared their feelings of deep connection and sympathy with Jane Doe, anger and frustration that this could happen at Cornell,” Kotlikoff said.
“Women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe,” he said, adding that additional staff would be hired to support survivors of sexual assault.
Cornell will also work with New York State Police to investigate incidents, he said, and accelerate previous recommendations put forward by a task force on sexual violence.
A total of 35% of undergraduate women reported experiencing non-consensual sexual contact involving force or incapacitation since entering Cornell, according to a university survey conducted in 2025 and published on its website.
“We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action,” Kotlikoff said. REUTERS

Pope Leo diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:23:18 UTC
05:23:18 KST

Pope Leo recovering "as expected" after surgery and lung cancer diagnosis, Vatican says
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery on Tuesday to remove a nodular lesion from his right lung, the Vatican announced.
The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican said in a news release following the surgery, describing the operation as "successful" and with "no complications." It said the diagnosis of lung cancer was confirmed during the surgery, which lasted 90 minutes.
In an update shared Wednesday by the Vatican, doctors leading the pope's care at Rome's Gemelli Hospital said he had undergone blood tests and a chest X-ray as scheduled following the surgery and that the results "confirm a normal post-operative course: the values are within the expected range for the type of procedure performed."
"The Holy Father has carried out respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking around his room," they added. "He has resumed a regular diet, having both breakfast and lunch. His recovery is proceeding as expected."
A Vatican spokesperson said Wednesday that the pope was expected to remain hospitalized for a week from the point of his admission on Tuesday.
In its earlier statement on the surgery, the Vatican said that, "to ensure a radical resection, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique," and "intraoperative histological examination confirmed the diagnosis of pulmonary adenocarcinoma, as suspected from pre-operative tests."
According to the Vatican, Leo "regained consciousness normally" following the procedure and was then taken back to his room on the 10th floor of the Gemelli Hospital, which has long provided medical care for popes.
"The Vatican tends to keep these things under wraps, so there'll be a lot of reading between the lines to try and detect what is the state of the pope's health," Candida Moss, the Edward Cadbury professor of theology at the University of Birmingham in England, told CBS News.
"We're going to need to get more information on his pathology," Dr. David Jones, chief of thoracic surgery at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, told CBS News. "Were lymph nodes involved? What's some of the molecular pathology that's going to be done that can help dictate what therapy, if any, is indicated?"
Leo, who was born in Chicago, is known for living an active and healthy lifestyle, including swimming and playing tennis, all factors that likely worked in his favor going into the surgery. He has maintained a busy schedule since becoming pope a year and a half ago.
Leo entered the Gemelli Hospital in the Italian capital through the main entrance earlier in the day and waved to dozens of well-wishers who had gathered to greet him. According to the Vatican, the team that performed the surgery was led by Dr. Stefano Margaritora, Gemelli's chief thoracic surgeon.
The Vatican on Monday canceled all Leo's audiences through Oct. 20. There was no word on whether Leo would be able to keep his planned trip to South America next month.
The typical recommendation for a procedure of this kind is to avoid air travel for about three weeks, which would put the pope right up against the start of that trip, which is scheduled for Nov. 6.
Moss told CBS News that Vatican protocol calls for the pope's cardinals and aides to step in and take up many of his duties as needed.
"We should also expect that, inasmuch as is possible, Pope Leo is going to continue to work," Moss said. "We have a long tradition of popes — not just Pope Francis, but also Pope John Paul II, who had Parkinson's for 10 years — who continued to remain as active as they could, and as active in Catholic liturgies as they could, right up until the end of their tenures."
While Gemelli has a specific papal apartment that past popes have used, complete with a private chapel on the 10th floor, Leo will actually be staying in a nearby room since the papal apartment is undergoing renovations, according to the Vatican press office.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post that he and his wife were "united in prayer" for the pope.
"May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father," Rubio wrote.
The Vatican had announced on Sunday that Leo would undergo surgery after a nodular lesion was found in his lung. According to the American Thoracic Society, a lung nodule usually measures less than half an inch in size and is discovered using a CT scan. Fewer than 5% turn out to be cancer, according to the thoracic society. If a nodule is determined to be cancerous, it is usually a sign of early-stage lung cancer.
"The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I've decided to have surgery to remove it," Leo said in remarks during his Sunday noon blessing. "Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers."
Lung adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer in the United States, according to the Lung Cancer Foundation of America, and makes up about 40% of all diagnosed lung cancers.
It forms in glandular cells on the outer parts of the lung and is likely to be diagnosed earlier than other lung cancers because it spreads more slowly, the LCFA said. Symptoms can include fatigue, shortness of breath and upper back and chest pain. Treatments can include surgery, chemotherapy, immunotherapy and radiation.
One of Pope Leo's 2 brothers also battling cancer
Louis Prevost, Pope Leo's older brother who resides in Florida, has multiple myeloma and is undergoing treatment, his wife, Deborah Prevost, told CBS News on Tuesday.
Multiple myeloma is a form of blood cancer, according to the Mayo Clinic. It forms in plasma cells, which are a type of white blood cell, and then builds up in the bone marrow.
Deborah Prevost did not share what stage her husband's cancer is in, but said he is currently in a clinical trial at a local hospital where he is being treated.
She said her husband was first diagnosed with multiple myeloma in 2017 but was able to maintain it at a "very low level" after undergoing treatment in 2019 that included stem cell treatment and a clinical trial. He "fell out of remission" three months ago, she said.
Deborah Prevost could not comment on the specifics of Pope Leo's condition, but said her husband and his brother spoke last week before Louis Prevost went in for his clinical trial. Pope Leo also informed his brother of his own situation.
"He [Pope Leo] called to let us know what would be happening," Deborah Prevost told CBS News. "We keep praying, keeping spirits up for both of them."

Dispatchers initially dismissed reports of failed US execution as prank: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:19:16 UTC
05:19:16 KST

Ahmet Salih Alacaci
13 October 2026•Update: 13 October 2026
Emergency dispatchers in the US initially questioned whether a call reporting the failed execution of death row inmate Christa Pike was a prank, delaying medical assistance, according to a media report on Tuesday
The first 911 emergency call came around 8.40 pm on Sept. 30, about an hour after Pike's execution by lethal injection began at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, Tennessee, Fox News reported, citing call recordings.
The caller reported that Pike was alive and was having difficulty breathing but could not provide a code verifying the emergency.
A dispatcher questioned whether the report was genuine or a prank call. At 9.03 pm, another dispatcher said supervisors had determined the call was false and no medical assistance was needed.
Pike's attorney, Kelly Gleason, called 911 around 9.08 pm, explaining that her client had survived the execution procedure and urgently needed medical care.
Recordings also revealed confusion among prison personnel, who initially denied making an emergency call.
Separately, a first responder reported that a person identifying themselves as a state official was outside the prison gate, insisting the emergency was genuine.
Emergency personnel were eventually allowed into the prison, and Pike was transferred to a hospital.
Pike survived two doses of the execution drug pentobarbital and remained unconscious for six days before regaining consciousness on Oct. 6, according to her attorneys.
She returned to prison Oct. 10 for continued medical care.
Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee has suspended additional executions pending a review of the failed procedure.

Peru governor touts Chinese interest in deep-water port pitched as Chancay alternative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Peru governor touts Chinese interest in deep-water port pitched as Chancay alternative
Scaled back to US$844 million from a US$7 billion plan, Corio terminal in Arequipa has yet to secure an investor or operator
A planned US$844 million port in southern Peru has drawn interest from several foreign investors, including Chinese companies, a regional governor said on Monday, as the government began promoting the project abroad.
“Several companies have approached us. We have investors from the US, China and India who are very interested,” Rohel Sanchez, the governor of Arequipa, told reporters after signing an agreement with the state investment agency Proinversion.

Duane 'Keffe D' Davis gets 40 years to life for orchestrating Tupac Shakur's murder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:00:50 UTC
05:00:50 KST

A former gang leader has been sentenced to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the 1996 drive-by shooting death of hip-hop star Tupac Shakur in Las Vegas, capping the prosecution of a long-unsolved murder that shaped the golden age of rap music.
Duane "Keffe D" Davis, 63, found guilty of first-degree murder in August, received the sentence during a hearing in a Las Vegas courtroom on Tuesday.
In tearful testimony before Judge Carli Kierny, Shakur's younger sister Sekyiwa Shakur said their mother had raised him to be a human rights activist and treated him as if he had the potential to change the world.
"He believed her," said Sekyiwa Shakur, wearing a black shirt. "He went out in the world to do that. And I believe he would have done it."
Until Davis' 2023 arrest, the killing of Shakur, shot dead in the passenger seat of an SUV driven by his record executive, Marion "Suge" Knight, had stood for nearly three decades as one of America's most notorious cold cases.
The murder, which silenced one of rap's most commercially successful and influential artists, heightened the image of violence permeating 1990s hip-hop culture while stoking the infamous East Coast-West Coast "gangsta" rap feud of the era.
Despite Davis' conviction, the question of who pulled the trigger in the fatal shooting of the 25-year-old rap legend has never been conclusively decided.
Davis was tried and convicted for masterminding the murder to avenge the beating of his nephew by Shakur and members of the rapper's entourage inside the MGM Grand casino on the Las Vegas Strip on September 7, 1996.
Davis has said he would appeal his conviction.
'The world never forgot about him'
Authorities said they long believed Davis was involved in Shakur's killing but lacked sufficient evidence to charge him.
That changed when he went public with his story in media appearances and a memoir that, along with tapes of his secret meetings with investigators, formed the bulk of the prosecution’s murder case.
In his book, "Compton Street Legend," Davis himself wrote that he was considered a suspect in the murders of both Shakur and Christopher Wallace, a rival rapper.
Addressing Davis on Tuesday, Kierny said his assertions that he had changed since the 1990s fell short.
"You don't get to take a man from his family," Kierny said, referring to Shakur. "The world never forgot about him."
The clash at the casino stemmed from hostility between two Los Angeles-area street gangs — the South Side Compton Crips, of which Davis was the self-described leader, and Mob Piru, which was associated with Shakur, Knight, and their music label, Death Row Records.
Members of both groups were in Las Vegas to see a world heavyweight title boxing match that night between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon.
Within hours of the casino brawl, Davis ushered his nephew and two other associates into a white Cadillac and went looking for Shakur and Knight, determined to settle scores, according to an account Davis later gave police in an unrelated investigation and that prosecutors cited during his murder trial.
Davis said he passed a gun to the two men seated behind him in the Cadillac, one of whom opened fire through the window when they caught up with, and pulled alongside of, Knight and Shakur’s vehicle in traffic.
Shakur was struck four times and died in a hospital six days later. Knight, who suffered a minor injury from a bullet fragment that grazed his head, is now serving a 28-year prison term on an unrelated voluntary manslaughter conviction.
While Davis was never accused of actually firing the shots that killed Shakur - Nevada law allows someone to be charged with murder as a participant in the crime - prosecutors have never named a suspected gunman.
All three other men in the Cadillac with Davis that night have since died.

Scientists urge tighter AI controls to prevent global cyber risks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
20:00:32 UTC
05:00:32 KST

Scientists urge tighter AI controls to prevent global cyber risks
The call comes as polls cast doubt on political leaders’ ability to manage AI risks amid US midterm elections.
A group of more than 300 scientists from around the world is calling for urgent changes to how artificial intelligence is developed and deployed amid growing concerns about its unpredictable behaviour.
The letter, released on Tuesday and signed by researchers representing universities and research institutes in 32 countries, warned that failures to follow basic cybersecurity practices could lead to damage to critical infrastructure.
Many recent incidents in which AI models escaped secure environments could have been prevented with stronger security systems, the scientists said.
They recommended that organisations developing and testing advanced AI systems capable of carrying out cyberattacks do so in more tightly controlled environments, including “air-gapped” systems that are not connected to the internet.
Growing concerns
The letter comes amid growing concerns about AI’s capabilities and its potential impact on everyday users. On Monday, Anthropic warned that its AI models could soon be capable of creating self-spreading malware that could affect everyday internet-connected devices, including smart TVs, security cameras and smart appliances such as ovens.
The report found that AI systems could identify unfamiliar devices without human intervention. The company, led by Dario Amodei, warned that smaller AI models could be capable of carrying out autonomous attacks by the end of the year.
The malware could also be difficult to contain because it might take days to infect a device and could spread across multiple machines rather than remain concentrated in a single, controlled location.
Taking control of internet-connected devices can have immediate consequences. In France, for example, hackers compromised cooling systems across hundreds of supermarkets, raising temperatures and causing more than $220,000 in damage.
Meanwhile, Axios news organisation reported on Friday that Anthropic, OpenAI and other major AI company executives are privately preparing for the possibility of a catastrophic AI-related incident that could disrupt access to major financial services, the internet and potentially critical infrastructure such as water and power systems. Several industry insiders believe a major incident could occur within the next six months to a year, it said.
The scientists also called for more safeguards, including the creation of an international organisation to establish a set of best practices for AI alignment and containment along with timely reporting of incidents.
One of the signatories, David Lie, a professor at the University of Toronto’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, said his concerns began after OpenAI’s AI agents bypassed controls and hacked into servers at the tech company Hugging Face.
“One is that OpenAI, in setting up its test environment, didn’t appreciate how capable its agents were,” Lie said.
“These were the AI agents that they were designing. Second is that the AI agents independently found each other and chose to collaborate on this attack, and third is that they also intentionally tried to deceive and mislead their human creators.”
Political pressures
The letter underscores growing public concern about AI, including in the lead-up to the US congressional midterm elections. A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 57 percent of voters said President Donald Trump’s administration was not taking AI risks seriously enough, while 54 percent said the same of Congress.
An AP-NORC poll echoed those findings, with about 80 percent of respondents saying the government should keep AI under human control. Respondents also expressed little confidence in either party’s ability to manage the technology: 39 percent said neither Republicans nor Democrats could be trusted to do a good job of reining it in, while 23 percent expressed greater confidence in Democrats and 21 percent in Republicans.

DR Congo Ebola cases pass 9,000 as efforts to curb transmission falter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:39:01 UTC
04:39:01 KST

DR Congo Ebola cases pass 9,000 as efforts to curb transmission falter
The Bundibugyo strain fuels deadliest Ebola outbreak in DR Congo’s history as health workers face mistrust from communities.
Confirmed Ebola cases have surpassed 9,000 in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) outbreak, according to Health Ministry data, as efforts to stifle transmission falter.
The ministry reported 9,066 confirmed cases and 4,381 deaths on Tuesday – a death toll of nearly half the known cases.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, has become the largest and deadliest in the DRC’s history. Globally, the toll is only second to the 2014 to 2016 West African epidemic, which saw 28,600 confirmed cases and more than 11,000 deaths across Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The Bundibugyo strain currently has no approved vaccines or treatments and has raised concerns over cross-border transmission.
Last week, Kenya reported its first imported case in which a Kenyan national who lived in the DRC travelled through Uganda before reaching Nairobi, where he died.
Uganda also reported 20 cases and two deaths earlier in the year, but the country was declared Ebola-free in August.
The current outbreak in the DRC was announced in mid-May, but some experts suspect it began as early as February. The virus, which is transmitted through contact with bodily fluids, has spread to seven provinces in the north and east.
Efforts to contain the virus face obstacles as health workers and other responders in the DRC face mistrust in local communities, with many believing the disease is a ruse for officials to siphon off money. The outbreak is also occurring amid an ongoing conflict between the M23 rebel group and government forces, making transport of healthcare resources to remote regions difficult.
A local politician in eastern DRC was beaten to death in September after he defended the government’s Ebola response on the radio, according to his political party.
A clinical trial to evaluate vaccine efficacy against the Bundibugyo strain is being prepared for the DRC in the coming weeks, WHO Health Emergencies Programme Executive Director Dr Chikwe Ihekweazu said on Tuesday.

====================================================================================================

OpenAI and Anthropic Tell British Lawmakers: Regulate Us
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:35:29 UTC
04:35:29 KST

Representatives for OpenAI and Anthropic told a British parliamentary hearing that voluntary pledges were no longer enough to ensure safety and that new laws should be introduced, deepening a public schism with Google DeepMind and Meta, both of which declined to back new legislation.
The Business, Innovation, Science, and Trade Committee, comprising a cross-party panel of MPs, held an evidence session on Tuesday with appearances from four frontier AI firms, four former staff of the firms turned whistleblowers and senior British civil servants.
“The rules should be binding,” Anthropic’s head of Europe Liam Booth-Smith told the committee, when asked if the company’s view was that AI safety now needs a statutory framework. The company, he said, has “consistently believed that there should be binding rules on companies and that voluntary commitments are not enough.”
OpenAI vice president Tom Duff Gordon was more cautious but still supportive, backing a statutory framework and an international convention. Duff Gordon said “there should be some elements that should be mandatory,” starting with incident reporting. “We don’t think basing everything on voluntary commitments for frontier risk is a good long-term plan,” he said.
However, their rivals would not follow. Asked directly whether he supported a statutory framework, Google DeepMind’s Owen Larter said: “Focus on the standards is what we would be doing.” Meta’s Rob Sherman pointed to Britain’s existing regulators, telling MPs they were “not writing on a blank page.”
The hearing exposed an existing divide on the subject of regulation, putting the conflicting approaches of AI leaders on the British parliamentary record. Exposing this divide in a second jurisdiction was the point, according to select committee chair Liam Byrne. The committee set out “to light up the wide differences in opinions between some of the wealthiest firms on Earth,” he told WIRED after the hearing, and to show “that you couldn’t rely on voluntary self-regulation.”
While the four executives gave evidence to the committee on AI safety, only a few hundred meters away, Britain’s security service director issued a warning about the dangers of AI.
MI5 director Ken McCallum used his annual threat update to warn of bioweapon misuse as a significant threat from AI. “Not yet realized, but the misuse case to which I’d attach greatest weight, is AI’s potential to change the stakes on existing or even new bioweapons,” McCallum said.
Responding to this comment, Byrne told WIRED: “The fact that the head of MI5 is warning about incredibly dangerous capability uplifts for bioterrorists in one part of Whitehall, and then in another part of Whitehall the permanent secretary of the Cabinet Office is basically admitting that our regulatory regime for AI is voluntary, tells you everything you need to know.”
In the final part of the evidence session, civil servants conceded to the committee how little the current system compels. Britain’s AI Security Institute (AISI) tests frontier models before release, but only when companies choose to hand them over.
Henry de Zoete, director of AISI, acknowledged that the institute was entirely reliant on the cooperation of the companies and foreign governments in order to gain access. Cat Little, the top civil servant at the Cabinet Office, which houses AISI, was pressed on whether the whole regime was voluntary. “At the moment, yes, it is,” she said.
When asked what would happen if AISI judged a model to be too dangerous, but it was released by a company anyway, de Zoete acknowledged AISI had no ability to prevent them from doing so.
“What we’re not doing is kite marking,” de Zoete said, using the British term for a safety certification. “We’re not saying yes or no to any sort of model.” He added: “These companies are either American or Chinese who are building at the frontier … There’s only so much we, as the UK, can do in that kind of context.”
The frontier executives also made plain that British access runs through Washington. “We provide our models predeployment to CAISI,” OpenAI’s Duff Gordon said, referring to AISI’s US counterpart. “We will continue to provide our models pre-deployment to AISI in the UK … and as long as we’re able to do that under the US government, we will continue to do it.”
The tension of the existing arrangement was made clear to British officials by Anthropic’s Booth-Smith. “We unfortunately were not able to provide full unrestricted access to [Mythos 5.1] to UK AISI at that time ... That’s a question for the US government,” he said before adding that AISI now had access.
The session also heard from four former lab researchers, among them ex-OpenAI staffer Daniel Kokotajlo. “I don’t think the companies can be trusted to self-regulate,” he told MPs. Steven Adler, who left OpenAI in late 2024, said he was “not confident in the safety culture across the industry.” Geoffrey Irving said the labs believe they are locked in a race that governments will not interrupt and that they cannot leave. “Both of those are false,” he said. “They could just stop.”
Following the hearing Byrne told WIRED that his committee would now dedicate a lot of time examining the UK’s path forward as a middle power on AI. He wants ministers to use Britain’s coming G20 presidency, alongside South Korea, which follows it in the chair, to broker an international convention that does not depend on the current White House. “The G20 presidency will outlive the US presidency of Trump,” he said.
“The risks,” he added, “are multiplying faster than our safety regime can control.”
