Apple on Tuesday announced a home hub called HomeView, marking CEO John Ternus' first launch outside of iPhones since he took over from Tim Cook at the start of September.
Apple said the device with a 7-inch screen was designed to be mounted on a wall or placed on a table. It's designed for multiple people in a household, and will recognize the user by their face to display pertinent information. It starts at $299 and ships on Nov. 13.
Tuesday's launch event is the second under Ternus, who was the company's longtime hardware boss before being promoted to CEO. Last month, Apple announced new models of its most important product, the iPhone, including a foldable model called the Duo that retails for nearly $2,000.
Apple also announced new Apple TV and HomePod hardware on Tuesday. The new Apple TV 4K costs $299 and has a redesigned remote that can play a sound if it is lost. Apple's HomePod Mini speaker comes in new colors and costs $149, a slight increase over its previous $129 price.
The products announced Tuesday are less critical for Apple than the iPhone, and investors remain focused on iPhone sales, but the accessories were positioned on Tuesday as a showcase for the company's new Siri abilities released last month.
Apple said HomeView features Siri AI, which can answer a broad range of questions. Users will be able to converse with Siri, and their conversations will continue on their iPhone or iPad. It has a built-in speaker for playing music.
"It recognizes your face to shift from a household screen to your own experience, fills the room with incredible sound, keeps you connected to the people who matter most with FaceTime, and makes it easy to control your smart home," Apple's marketing head Greg Joswiak said in a statement.
Apple said that HomeView will show information from the Messages, Photos, Calendar, and Reminders apps based on who is using the device, powered by Apple Intelligence. It can also be used to make FaceTime calls and as a digital photo frame. It's equipped with an Apple A18 chip. It supports up to six users.
Apple TV, HomePods, and HomeView are included in Apple's Wearables, Home, and Accessories category, which reported $7.88 billion in sales in the most recent quarter ended June, which was about 7% of the company's total revenue. The category also includes wireless headphones like AirPods and the Apple Watch.
But while Apple has dabbled in home products and platforms in the past, Tuesday's announcement shows Apple is making its home products a higher priority under Ternus.
"Apple always waits for an ecosystem to develop first until they are positive they can provide a stellar user experience," said Jennifer Kent, principal analyst at Parks Associates, which conducts research on the connected home.
Apple said its new products, including HomeView, can be used as a smart home hub, coordinating notifications and actions in the home and working with a range of products, including new locks, doorbells, and cameras from LG Electronics and Schneider Electric.
Apple is emphasizing privacy, and said on Tuesday that its Apple Home Collection accessories encrypt data so that only the user and people they share with can see it. Other smart home cameras, for example, maintain limited access to user video, or store it on servers.
"They are going above and beyond what a lot of other companies do when it comes to privacy and security protections," Kent said.
Apple's integration with the smart home is not just about sales, but also helps further lock customers into its ecosystem. People who use multiple Apple products and connections are less likely to switch to an Android phone.
HomeView can also become a smart home dashboard, Apple said. It can be used to view camera feeds, adjust the thermostat, or lock connected doors around the house.
Apple said that setting up a new smart home device takes one tap from the user's iPhone.
Tuesday's launch shows Apple's confidence as it launches new product categories. But the broader consumer electronics industry has been dealing with price increases and demand deterioration related to component shortages in memory and storage. It also comes as Ternus has reportedly pushed the company to release products faster.
Apple's new Apple TV 4K got a price hike from $199 to $299, and follows a similar price increase earlier this year, after Cook said that memory costs for Apple were unsustainable.

Cornell Halts Fraternity Parties After Jane Doe’s Lawsuit
Unknown

2026-10-13

Cornell University said on Tuesday that it is barring fraternity houses from hosting parties for the remainder of the academic year in an effort “to strengthen campus safety” after the school faced widespread backlash over its handling of an alleged gang rape by fraternity members in 2024.
Cornell President Michael I. Kotlikoff announced the news in a letter addressed to the campus community, which said that the ban will be effective immediately. He also outlined ways that the university would work to improve how it handles allegations of sexual assault in the future. In addition to strengthening campus safety, he addressed the need to provide better support to survivors—which involves allowing the New York State Police to independently investigate sexual assault allegations—and change the social culture at the university.
Cornell did not respond to questions about how the new measures would be implemented or tracked, but referred TIME to its FAQ page regarding the 2024 incident.
The announcement comes about a month after a woman, known as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit against several entities, including Cornell, the Chi Phi fraternity, and seven members of Chi Phi that she alleges sexually assaulted her in 2024. The case has made national headlines, and many people have criticized how Cornell and local authorities handled the incident. Hundreds of students and staff members held a protest on campus earlier this month, with some calling for Kotlikoff to resign and others chanting phrases like “Ban the frats!”
In his letter on Tuesday, Kotlikoff addressed the backlash, saying that his conversations with various members of the campus community and the campus protests “have underscored my deep conviction that we must do better: that the time for meaningful and lasting change at Cornell, and at campuses across the country, is now.”
“I am deeply sorry for the harm Jane Doe suffered in 2024, and appalled that this act of sexual violence occurred within our Cornell community,” Kotlikoff said. “It is clear that women on our campus continue to question whether they are safe. We must meet this moment by acknowledging where we have fallen short and taking meaningful action.”
Amid mounting pressure, Cornell’s Board of Trustees announced earlier this month that Sally Yates, a former acting U.S. attorney general, will lead an independent review into how the school handled the case. Kotlikoff also addressed the review in his letter, but said “it is clear that we cannot wait for these findings to take action.” Cooperation with the New York State Police would coincide with the independent review; Kotlikoff said in his letter that investigators will interview survivors who decide to pursue criminal charges and “prepare comprehensive investigative summaries for the appropriate law enforcement agency.”
Kotlikoff said that Interfraternity Council houses will be barred from holding parties and social events, which “will provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue.” He added that the university will have a “zero tolerance” policy if fraternities violate the new rule, and that any fraternity that hosts “an in-house party or social event will receive an immediate emergency suspension.” Cornell has previously said that the Chi Phi fraternity on campus "was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus."
Other measures that Kotlikoff announced include strengthening support for survivors, such as by adding staffers to the Cornell Office of Civil Rights, and “changing the social culture at Cornell” through several initiatives, such as enhancing “existing education and programming to address the bystander effect.”
“These are first steps toward systemic change on our campus,” Kotlikoff said. “We will take all necessary steps to address the conditions that led to Jane Doe’s experiences, and those of other survivors. Cornell must be a place where safety is not an open question.”

Why You Should Do Toe Raises, Not Just Calf Raises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:12:57 UTC
04:12:57 KST

Here’s a workout tip that sounds like it belongs in a nursery rhyme: Bring your toes toward your nose. That’s how physical therapist Joseph Hribick reminds patients to do toe raises. Fortunately, it’s not a flexibility test: Your toes don’t have to get anywhere near your face. Keep your heels on the floor, lift the fronts of your feet, and you’ll work the muscles along your shins.
“Each time we step, we need to be able to clear our toes from the ground,” says Hribick, a clinical assistant professor of physical therapy at Lebanon Valley College in Pennsylvania. Otherwise, your toes could snag on the carpet or catch as you walk through a doorway, making you more likely to trip.
If you’ve ever done calf raises, you know the opposite move: lifting your heels and rising onto the balls of your feet. Toe raises give the other side of your lower legs some attention. They require no equipment, you can do them while you’re sitting at your desk, and they can make your shins burn (in a good way) after surprisingly few reps.
What are the benefits of toe raises?
The star of the toe raise is the tibialis anterior, a muscle that runs along the front of your shin. It helps lift your foot as your leg swings forward—and then controls how your foot lowers after your heel touches the ground, Hribick says.
Your calves do the opposite job: They help push you forward. Daniel Safford, an assistant professor of physical therapy at Arcadia University in Pennsylvania, suggests giving both sides of your lower legs some attention. “You’re covering a lot of your bases if you do just those two things,” he says of calf raises and toe raises.
That can be especially useful if the muscles that lift your feet are weak. But will adding toe raises to your day make you a faster runner or keep you from falling? “That’s a little bit more of a question mark,” Safford says. Those muscles matter for walking and balance, but studies haven’t established that toe raises alone deliver those bigger benefits. Still, they’re a useful addition to a routine that also works your calves and challenges your balance.
How to do toe raises correctly
You can do toe raises sitting or standing; if your balance isn’t what it used to be, choose the chair. Plant both feet on the floor and lift the fronts of your feet while keeping your heels down. The balls of your feet should come up along with your toes—wiggling your toes alone doesn’t count. Take one to two seconds to lift, pause briefly, then two to three seconds to lower. “If you just bring your toes up and let them slam down, you’re not getting as much of a benefit,” Hribick says.
For a bigger challenge, try them standing. That means your legs are supporting your weight, and staying steady adds a challenge, so hold on to a sturdy counter. Lift the fronts of both feet at once. It’s fine to shift a little weight onto your heels, Safford says, but don’t lean your whole body backward to get your feet off the floor. Lift as high as you comfortably can; even if your feet barely budge, the muscles are still working.
Shoes or bare feet? Whichever you prefer. Barefoot, you may even get a glimpse of the exercise in action: Safford says the tendons can “kind of pop out on the top of the foot” as you lift, a bit like the tendons on the back of your hand.
How many toe raises should you do—and how often?
Start with five to 10 repetitions a few days a week, Safford suggests. That might sound almost too easy, but try a set before you decide. “You might feel more fatigued than you’d expect,” Hribick says.
As your shins get used to the exercise, add a few reps. Safford says you could eventually work up to 20 repetitions on most days of the week, but give yourself a couple of months to get there. “You don’t wanna go for broke,” he says. Mild soreness is possible when you start; if you have pain that’s severe or won’t go away, stop and get it checked out. The same goes for a new problem lifting your foot or toes that keep catching on the floor.
The best part about toe raises is that you can do them almost anywhere. Try a set at your desk, or do them standing at the bathroom sink. “You could do it when you’re brushing your teeth,” Safford says. “Just hold on to the counter.”

He, along with Kharge, was in Delhi on Monday to protest against SIR.Activists welcomed the assurances but said the govt must address the restrictions that, they argue, make it difficult to protest at the site of an issue or draw public attention to local grievances.“The Licensing Order, 2021 by the commissioner of police restricting protests to Freedom Park must be withdrawn, just as any restriction to designated venues for protests in any city. Protests cannot be caged in Freedom Park; holding placards and shouting slogans cannot be criminalised; peaceful marches cannot be met with police violence,” advocate and activist Clifton Rozario said.He added that police power could not be used against legitimate struggles in defence of the Constitution.My Vote, My Right, which had organised Monday’s protest march, welcomed Kharge’s decision to review the police handling of protesters and journalists, but urged the govt to withdraw the 2021 licensing order and restore the “2009 assemblies order”. The organisation also questioned Shivakumar over what it saw as a contradiction between his participation in a protest in Delhi and the action against demonstrators in Bengaluru, asking: “One law for you, one law for us — why?”A woman protester who was forcibly dragged away by police on Monday said restricting demonstrations to Freedom Park curtailed citizens’ rights. “This rule is what allows the police to deem any protest outside the said venue, even if it is barely a kilometre away, illegitimate,” she said.Activists under the Horatada Hakkigagi Janandolana said the restriction had also affected people seeking to raise local issues. A protest over a neighbourhood grievance, they argued, loses its immediate relevance when residents must travel to a central venue to be heard. They have cited workers, farmers, pourakarmikas, Dalit activists and residents protesting civic issues among those whose demonstrations have been affected.The coalition was, as of late Tuesday, preparing a fresh memorandum to the govt. On the same as the CM and Kharge’s assurances, Bengaluru police commissioner Seemanth Kumar Singh said KR Circle was a heavily congested junction and police had asked protesters to shift to Freedom Park. He said the protesters refused and blocked the road, following which police removed the blockade and made preventive arrests.Acknowledging a confrontation involving protesters, police and media personnel, Singh described it as unintentional and said officers had been instructed to exercise utmost care. He maintained that the right to protest in Bengaluru was, under the court’s order, limited to Freedom Park, and said police were prepared to provide protection when informed in advance.
Activists insist that reviewing Monday’s police action must go hand in hand with changing the rules governing where people can demonstrate. They want the govt to withdraw the 2021 order and restore the 2009 framework, under which they say protests could be held at different locations after informing the police.
Chethan Kumar is a Senior Assistant Editor with the Times of India. Aside from specialising in Space & Science, he has reported extensively on varied topics, with special focus on defence, policy and data stories. He has covered multiple elections, too. As a young democracy grows out of adolescence, Chethan feels, there are reels of tales emerging which need to be captured. To do this, he alternates between the mundane goings-on of the Common Man and the wonder-filled worlds of scientists and scamsters, politicians and soldiers. In a career spanning nearly 18 years, he has reported from multiple datelines — Houston, Florida, Kochi, Hyderabad, Chennai, Sriharikota (AP), NH-1 (J&K Highway), New Delhi, Ahmedabad, Raichur, Bhatkal, Mysuru, Chamarajanagar, to name a few — but is based out of Bengaluru, India’s science capital that also hosts the ISRO HQ.

Three Syrian road security personnel were killed Tuesday when unidentified assailants attacked their patrol in the countryside of Hama province in central Syria, the Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) reported.

EU watchdog urges smart glasses to clearly signal when recording
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:11:09 UTC
04:11:09 KST

EU watchdog urges smart glasses to clearly signal when recording
Advisory comes amid growing concern about the devices being used to secretly record girls and women.
The European Union’s data watchdog has called for smart glasses to clearly show when they are recording, saying bystanders have the right to know when they are being photographed or filmed.
The European Data Protection Board (EDPB) issued the non-binding recommendation on Tuesday, amid mounting concern about the devices being used to secretly record girls and women.
It said the use of smart glasses – which can resemble ordinary glasses but also take photos and videos, make phone calls and translate text when connected to the internet – raises “serious privacy concerns”.
EDPB chair Anu Talus said the glasses should have clear signals when they are recording, such as “bright LED lights, audio signals or voice activation cues, privacy-friendly smartphone notifications, or unique designs”.
“These warnings need to be reliable, hard to ignore, and always up to date,” said Talus. “Even in public spaces, bystanders should clearly understand that someone is filming or photographing them.”
The devices carry greater risks in “sensitive” spaces like schools and hospitals, as well as public spots like beaches, and raised concerns about children who are “more vulnerable to covert or intrusive processing of their personal data”, the EDPB warned.
The advisory comes amid campaigns in several European countries to ban or restrict smart glasses over privacy concerns.
Norway’s government said last week it was also worried about privacy invasions and wants a temporary ban on the use of smart glasses in certain public places. The capital Oslo already opted to ban glasses equipped with cameras in schools.
France’s e-Enfance association, which operates the national hotline for victims of online abuse, has also sounded the alarm about videos recorded with camera-equipped glasses and shared online.
Last month, French prosecutors said they had opened a criminal probe following sexual harassment complaints related to a social media trend of using smart glasses to film women on the street, without their consent, and posting the videos online.
In the United Kingdom and Ireland, a “Stop Smart Glasses” campaign has launched a petition and call for supporters to contact stores to stop their sale. It reached more than 10,000 signatures, which means the UK government must respond.

African resources 'belong to Africa': China's Xi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:06:15 UTC
04:06:15 KST

Chinese President Xi Jinping has said that African mineral resources "belong to Africa", offering Beijing's support for the industry and warning against "geopolitical rivalries" that could harm it.
China, through state-owned and private businesses, is a key player in Africa's valuable mining sector, particularly in extraction. It is one of several major powers vying for access to resources.
Accepting "the principle that African resources belong to Africa must be a prerequisite for any cooperation", Xi said during a meeting in Beijing on Tuesday with Botswana's President Duma Boko, whose country has a vast mining industry.
"Africa has been relegated to the bottom of the industrial chain and of the value chain by an unjust international division of labour. This is a historical injustice that requires urgent remedy," Xi said, according to official news agency Xinhua.
The Chinese leader called for balance between "moral principles and economic interests", while offering his country's assistance in drawing up development plans.
African countries hold around 30 per cent of the world's critical mineral reserves, including cobalt, copper, lithium, nickel and rare earths, according to the United Nations, making it a focus of competition between the United States and China for strategic resources. European nations and other actors are also competing for influence.
Xi, in his remarks, said that "African resources must not become instruments of geopolitical rivalries", calling for all foreign powers involved to "contribute sincerely to Africa's development" and help maintain a "stable" environment for cooperation.
China is Africa's largest trading partner and a major source of financing for infrastructure projects across the continent.
On May 1, Beijing extended a zero-tariff policy to all African countries except Eswatini, with which it has no diplomatic relations, under a policy announced last year.
Some critics accuse foreign actors including China of exploiting African resources without allowing the countries and their people to truly benefit from them.
Hailing his country's commitment to "African development", Xi said Beijing seeks to steer Sino-African mineral cooperation towards greater "industrial added value".

DOJ arrests two, seizes 187 devices in North Korean laptop farm crackdown in Texas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:05:38 UTC
04:05:38 KST

DOJ arrests two, seizes 187 devices in North Korean laptop farm crackdown in Texas
Oct 13 - The US Department of Justice on Tuesday announced the arrests of two Americans accused of helping North Korean IT workers to steal identities and obtain fraudulent employment at US companies to earn money for the North Korean government.
The agency announced the arrests of Michael James Bostelle, of Pennsylvania, and Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo, of Texas, on charges of wire fraud, money laundering and identity theft as part of the alleged scheme, the DOJ said in a statement.
• As part of the crackdown, the DOJ announced that the FBI conducted searches and took other action between September 21 and September 25 at more than 40 residences in Texas thought to be operating as “laptop farms” for North Korean IT workers, the DOJ said. The FBI seized roughly 187 laptops and other devices used to carry out the scheme.
• The indictment also charged Sun Sheng Ming, Pei Li Guang, Weng Shou Cheng, Han Guo Bin, Wang Jian Jun, Sheng Zhang Kun, Zhang Wei Ping, Zhang Li Ping, Yu Yang and Jin Long, all based in China, for their roles in the operation, according to the statement.
• According to an indictment unsealed on Tuesday, the Chinese-based operators directed Pena and Tey Michael Nolte, along with at least four other Americans, in the scheme. Nolte was named in the indictment but not charged.
• Nolte and attorneys for Pena and Bostelle could not immediately be reached for comment. Emails sent to addresses that the DOJ alleged were used by the Chinese-based participants went unanswered.
• Nolte allegedly recruited, managed and trained Bostelle and other Americans, who allowed their names and personal information to be used to permit the North Korea-directed operation to function, in exchange for proceeds from the scheme, the DOJ said. The Americans’ actions included receiving and hosting laptops belonging to US victim companies at their homes, to make it appear as if the North Koreans were legitimate employees operating in the US.
• The “massive” fraud impacted more than 70 U. companies, compromised the identities of 25 Americans, caused false information to be sent to multiple US government agencies, and generated at least $3 million in revenue for the overseas IT workers, the DOJ said.
• The US government has for years warned of North Koreans surreptitiously gaining employment at US companies to raise money for the North Korean government, access company networks and steal data.

Pope Leo’s lung operation ‘successfully completed’: Vatican
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-13
19:05:30 UTC
04:05:30 KST

Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer as doctors remove part of lung, Vatican says
- Pope Leo, 71, was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma after doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during surgery at Rome’s Gemelli hospital.
- The Vatican said the 90-minute operation was successful with no complications, and Leo is waking normally and expected to stay in hospital for about a week.
- His public events are cancelled until Oct 20, and the illness comes as he prepares for a busy papal schedule, including an 11-day South America tour in November.
AI generated
ROME – Pope Leo was diagnosed with a common form of lung cancer after surgeons removed a part of his right lung on Oct 13, the Vatican said in a medical bulletin, marking a significant health setback for the 71-year-old pontiff.
The Pope has lung adenocarcinoma, a common form of cancer, with tissue tests conducted during the operation confirming what doctors had suspected from preparatory examinations, the bulletin said.
He was admitted to Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Oct 13 for surgery to remove the growth that doctors had discovered in a recent routine health check.
The Pope’s lead surgeon,Stefano Margaritora, and his personal physician, Luigi Carbone, said in a statement that the procedure lasted about 90 minutes and was successful, with no complications.
“In order to make the procedure curative, the lower lobe of the right lung was removed using a video-assisted technique,” they said, making clear that the aim was to eliminate all cancerous tissue.
Human lungs have five lobes – three in the right lung and two in the left.
A medical expert said that in order to assess the pope’s case they would need to know the size of the tumour and whether the cancer had spread to his lymph nodes, information the Vatican did not immediately provide.
“While we have the diagnosis, we do not yet have the stage. This is critical to prognosis and treatment,” said Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown University in Washington and division chief of hematology-oncology at MedStar Georgetown University Hospital.
“If this is a small lung cancer with no lymph nodes involved, surgery itself is likely to be curative,” he told Reuters. “But if final analysis reveals a greater extent of cancer involvement, this indicates a poorer prognosis.”
Resting in his hospital room
The Pope regained consciousness normally after the operation and later returned to his hospital room, where he was resting, the medical bulletin said.
The Vatican said earlier this week that he was expected to remain in hospital for about a week and all his public events have been cancelled until Oct 20.
Leo left the Vatican ahead of the surgery shortly before 1pm in Rome and was seen waving from the back of a black SUV as his convoy drove about 9km north of the Vatican to the Gemelli.
Upon arrival at the hospital, Leo shook hands with several officials, walked in front of a waiting crowd of well-wishers, some of whom shouted “Auguri” (best wishes), and headed in via the main entrance.
Leo, elected by the world’s cardinals in May 2025, is relatively young for a Church leader. He enjoys sports, including tennis, and is not known to be a smoker or to have had recent health issues.
The late Pope Francis, Leo’s predecessor, was hospitalised several times as he grew frail in his later years. He died aged 88 in April 2025.
Leo, who spoke in a firm, clear voice at his only public event on Oct 12, keeps a very busy schedule. He is due to make an 11-day tour of Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from Nov 6 to 17, but it was not clear if this trip would still go ahead.
Typhoid fever
The Pope is the ultimate earthly authority for the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics and does not have a deputy who steps in when he is sick. When a pope is incapacitated, the business of the Vatican’s vast bureaucracy carries on as usual, holding off on any decisions that require papal approval.
Leo, born in Chicago in 1955 as Robert Prevost, served for decades as a missionary and bishop in Peru before becoming pope. In 1985, when he was a young priest, he came down with typhoid fever in Chulucanas, Peru and was hospitalised.
He recounted the experience in his only major interview given as Pope, in a book for Penguin Peru.
Leo said the pain was so bad that he asked God to die rather than continue suffering. He took his survival as a sign from God that “We need you here (on Earth),” he said.
“I never looked back,” said Leo. REUTERS

Israel’s former security chief sues Netanyahu for October 7 defamation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:39:03 UTC
03:39:03 KST

Israel’s former security chief sues Netanyahu for October 7 defamation
Ronen Bar accuses Netanyahu of being warned before Hamas attacks, as elections loom.
The former head of Israel’s domestic security agency Shin Bet has sued Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for defamation over claims of his responsibility in the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack.
Coming just before Israel’s close-fought October 27 election in which Netanyahu is fighting for his political life, the case filed on Wednesday is set to ramp up the country’s political drama.
Ronen Bar, the former director of Shin Bet, accused Netanyahu of “lying to cover himself” and said it was slanderous of the prime minister to have accused him of “criminal failures” over the attack, in a 134-page court document.
Bar said he telephoned the prime minister’s military secretary as soon as signs of a possible attack became apparent, but that he did not have Netanyahu’s direct number.
Netanyahu has said he was not alerted by Bar on the morning of the Hamas-led assault, insisting that he could have stopped the attack had the Shin Bet’s then-director or military leaders called to wake him up the day of the early-morning attack.
Bar’s lawsuit says Netanyahu made accusations “that he knew to be false, with the aim of diverting the debate from his own responsibility for the events of October 7”.
Instead, it was Netanyahu’s policies over several years that had “increased the dangers posed by terrorist organisations in Gaza”, it said.
Likud response
On Wednesday, Netanyahu responded to Bar’s accusations in a statement issued by his Likud party saying, “Ronen, are you serious?”
“You had my number on the red line and could have called me immediately, as all security chiefs do,” Netanyahu asked, adding, “How many lives could we have saved if only you had called in time?”
Bar resigned as head of Shin Bet in June 2025 amid recriminations over the deadliest attack in Israel’s history, while insisting he had informed Netanyahu of the threat in advance.
He is seeking three million shekels (about $968,500) in damages from Netanyahu.
Warnings, lies, manipulation
The allegations in Bar’s lawsuit come days after Netanyahu’s former military secretary, Avi Gil, told Israel’s Channel 12 that the prime minister’s office had “falsified records related to October 7, 2023”, including altering the recorded time of a key phone call.
Gil, who served as Netanyahu’s military secretary from July 2021 to May 2024, said a stenographer in the prime minister’s office approached him in January 2024 with instructions from Netanyahu’s chief of staff to change the time of a four-minute call from 6:40am local time (03:40GMT) to 6:29am (03:29 GMT).
“She told me, I’m not allowed to change it,” said Gil, accusing the head of Netanyahu’s office of manipulating telephone records, adding, “Those are facts, and there is no dispute about them.”
Last month, the Wall Street Journal reported that Netanyahu had been warned of the attack by Egypt’s intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel.
In a rare move, Kamel reportedly phoned the prime minister just days before the attack, underscoring previous warnings in September 2023, when he is said to have flown to Israel to warn security officials in person that Hamas was planning an attack.
Polls show Netanyahu is in a tight race to stay in power in the October 27 election, after being hammered by former staff and government officials as well as the opposition for failing to prevent the bloodshed.
At least 1,221 Israelis were killed on October 7, 2023, after Hamas broke through the fence separating Israel and Gaza, according to Israeli official figures.
Also, 251 Israelis were taken captive, including the bodies of 44 Israelis killed that day.
In the three years since, Israel has killed more than 74,300 people in Gaza, according to the Health Ministry in the enclave.
More than 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed in Israeli attacks since a tentative “ceasefire” backed by the US was reached last year.

Jewish teachers cancel Italy trip over ‘antisemitic pressure’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:10:19 UTC
04:10:19 KST

Educators from Jewish schools across the US canceled a study trip to Reggio Emilia, Italy, over whether the hosts would require participants to formally distance themselves from Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank.
The controversy has drawn accusations of antisemitism from Jewish educators and from Italian Jewish community leaders. It has also sparked a political dispute in Italy.
In an email sent to participants on October 9, the American organizers, the Paradigm Project, said they canceled the trip because of “antisemitic pressure being placed on the group.” In a Zoom call with the participants, the organizers also cited safety concerns amid the scrutiny of the Jewish school educators’ personal profiles by pro-Palestinian activists who were agitating for the declaration, a participant said.
Reggio Children considered asking for declarations distancing themselves from 'genocide'
In a leaked audio recording broadcast Monday evening by Italy’s Tg3 TV news program, the president of the host organization Reggio Children, Maddalena Tedeschi, discussed asking participants to sign declarations distancing themselves from the “occupation of territories and genocide.” The recording is of an October 6 meeting of the city’s early childhood education council.
In an interview with the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, Reggio Children spokesperson Francesca Severini said the request, intended to appease local pro-Palestinian activists, had never become an official participation requirement, but acknowledged that the additional wording had been discussed.
The Paradigm Project, a professional development network for Jewish early childhood educators, organized the trip for 68 Jewish educators. A separate delegation of 22 educators from Israel arrived in Reggio and was participating in the program this week.
“Now, more than ever, we must bring back the light and keep the bridge between us strong,” the Israeli educators said in opening remarks Monday.
Reggio Children, an educational organization partly owned by the municipality, promotes the city’s internationally influential approach to early childhood education and provides training for educators. Reggio Emilia Mayor Marco Massari and the city’s education official Marwa Mahmoud did not respond to requests for comment.
Pro-Palestinian activists protest ties to Israel
The cancellation, which came in a phone call from Paradigm to Reggio Children on October 7, follows months of tensions in the city, where pro-Palestinian activists had protested the participating schools’ ties to Israel. During the weeks preceding the trip, activist Cosimo Pederzoli had publicly accused some of the schools of supporting the Israeli military.
At the Oct. 6 meeting, Reggio Children presented a charter, titled “For a Democratic and Participatory Education,” asking visiting groups and partners to uphold human rights, oppose discrimination, reject war, and condemn genocide. The charter, which was approved and is now on the organization’s website, also opposes violations of human rights in occupied territories worldwide, without naming Israel or Gaza.
Severini, the spokesperson, said that activists, teachers and parents had pressured Reggio Children and the municipality to take the charter one step further and require participants to agree to the statement: “I … hereby declare that I distance myself from the occupation of Gaza and the violation of children’s and human beings’ rights in occupied territories as well as every place in the world.”
Severini said that the wording was included as “material for discussion” in a private WhatsApp group. The American organizers were not in the chat, she said, and subsequently received the wording without the context that it would not, in the end, be official language.
Her account contradicts Reggio Children’s earlier public statements. On October 7, the organization acknowledged that the educators had been asked to explicitly distance themselves from the policies of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government in response to concerns raised in the city. Mayor Marco Massari also acknowledged the additional commitment in a public statement, which says, “This Charter will be signed by all delegations visiting Reggio Emilia in the coming months and years.”
In an email to parents, leaders of Wilshire Boulevard Temple’s early childhood centers in Los Angeles said seven of their educators had been scheduled to join the trip and expressed support for Paradigm’s decision to cancel.
“Paradigm, on behalf of our educators and dozens of others, rightfully refused and canceled participation in the study tour and conference, due to the refusal to sign and other security considerations,” read the email. “All participants were notified on October 7, 2026.”
Pesha Kletenik, head of Manhattan Day School, had planned to join the trip. “This was one of the most painful experiences I’ve had,” Kletenik told JTA. “I never felt so targeted as a Jew before in my life. I’m an American citizen. I have one passport. I’ve lived here my entire life.”
Kletenik said she had hoped to adapt the Reggio approach to Jewish teaching and practice, including their model Passover seder, because “it aligns so beautifully with Jewish values.”
Steve Freedman, head of Schechter Bergen in New Jersey, said his school withdrew an educator from a separate trip planned for November. In a letter to families, he criticized the demand for a political declaration while affirming the school’s commitment to the Reggio approach.
The council of the Jewish Community of Modena and Reggio Emilia, a single institution based in nearby Modena that serves both cities, condemned efforts to boycott educational and cultural initiatives involving Jews. It described the conflation of diaspora Jews with Israel’s government as antisemitic.
The Reggio Emilia approach, developed after World War II by educator Loris Malaguzzi and local families, places children’s exploration, expression, and participation at the center of early childhood learning. It gained wider international recognition after Newsweek named one of the city’s preschools among the world’s 10 best schools in 1991.
Severini said Reggio Children’s relationships with American Jewish and Israeli educators stretch back roughly three decades. The Israeli liaison first visited in 1996, she said, and educators from Reggio have also traveled to the United States and Israel.
The organization has hosted educators from all over the world, Severini said, including China, Russia, and Iran. She said she knew of no comparable controversy involving other visiting groups, including previous delegations from Jewish schools.
Reggio Children, she said, hoped to continue its dialogue with the American educators. For Manhattan Day School’s Kletenik, the cancellation stood in stark contrast with the educational values that had drawn her to the approach.
“How are we to navigate rejection by the very experts we collectively idealized, the gatekeepers of the sensitive worldviews and teachings we trusted to nurture our most tender children?” she wrote in a message to her school’s board.

Where should Canadian Jews go? Where is the Promised Land? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

A recent article in the Canadian newspaper The Globe and Mail by Marsha Lederman, titled “The Promised Land,” deals with Jewish Canadian concerns over the marked increase in antisemitism in Canada, particularly after October 7.
Anti-Jewish experiences have included the intimidation of Jewish students at all educational levels, harassment at Jewish events, physical assaults, arson attacks on Jewish businesses, and drive-by shootings at synagogues.
Very recently, a mass shooting on Yom Kippur at a small synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, was only prevented because of the presence of an armed police officer, a fixture at all synagogues and Jewish facilities in Canada. The shooter died, and the officer suffered serious wounds.
Lederman’s focus is a program called Lech L’Tulsa, initiated by the Jewish community of Tulsa, Oklahoma, to attract Canadian Jews to the city. It includes some financial help for those making the move. A description of the program also appeared in a December 2025 issue of the National Post, another Canadian newspaper.
Lederman points out that antisemitism is common in the US, as well as in Canada, and many American universities and cities are hostile environments for Jews. However, she also refers to “pockets of respite,” such as Tulsa and Florida, and this made me realize how little the Jewish world has changed over the centuries.
For much of the Middle Ages, and well into the Renaissance, the uppermost question for European Jews was, where to flee? Where could they be safe?
It is not a coincidence that the legend of the Wandering Jew, a Jew said to have taunted Jesus on the way to the Crucifixion, and was then condemned to wander the Earth until the Second Coming, originated in the 13th century.
England has the dubious honor of having been the first European country to expel all of its Jews, in 1290. The first blood libel also originated in England, in 1144. Other countries followed suit: France on three occasions (1182, 1306, and 1394), and Spain in 1492.
Germany was different because German unification did not happen until 1871. Until then, Germany was a patchwork of small kingdoms, principalities, duchies, and free cities. Jews expelled from one place could find sanctuary in a friendlier territory nearby.
For example, Glikl, the Yiddish memoirs of a late 17th-century Jewish woman, edited by Chava Turniansky and published in English in 2019, describes how the Jews of Hamburg were periodically banished from the city, but they could live in nearby Altona, which was under the more welcoming jurisdiction of the King of Denmark.
Similarly, Jews were banned from living in the city of Nuremberg, in Bavaria, for hundreds of years, but they could do business there, then return every evening to their homes in the nearby town of Fürth. In fact, Jews benefited from the first German railroad, a six-kilometer line built in 1835 to join Nuremberg and Fürth.
Moving toward the Promised Land
Lederman's article was interesting and timely, but I was surprised there was no mention of Israel. While it is true, as she notes, that Canada and the US share a common language and culture, Canada and Israel are a closer match when it comes to social support in areas like health and education, not to mention, for Jews, history, and religion.
She does mention that her maternal grandparents obtained visas to go to British Mandate Palestine, but did not go and were murdered in Treblinka.
However, many of the Jews who had to go did, and are still going. In fact, about half of the more than 7.5 million Jews living in Israel today are either immigrants or descendants of immigrants, most from either the post-war DP camps of Europe, the Arab/Muslim world, or the former Soviet Union.
A small but steadily increasing stream of immigrants has also arrived from North America. The Israel Central Bureau of Statistics indicates that about 16,000 Canadians have made aliyah since the establishment of the state in 1948.
Israel’s Aliyah and Integration Ministry reported that 440 Canadian Jews moved to Israel from September 2025 to September 2026. Another 1,000 Canadian Jews have opened new aliyah files. This is a formal process, including an interview with a representative of the Jewish Agency and the submission of documents, including birth certificates and marriage records.
While the Tulsa initiative has received a significant number of inquiries from Canadians, the number of families who have actually made the move so far is quite small, according to an article in The Forward by Benyamin Cohen.
It quotes Jewish Canadian journalist Jesse Brown: “There’s a sadness,” he said about the Jewish exodus from Canada. “I’m not enthused or compelled by what I see as a ‘re-shtetling.’”
The Canadian Jewish population, about 400,000, is almost as large as that of France, the third largest Jewish community in the world. Antisemitism is a serious problem there as well. This year, 4,000 French Jews made aliyah, about 10 times the Canadian number.
A 2026 Canadian survey cited by Lederman indicates that one quarter of Canadian Jews are planning to leave Canada or are thinking seriously about it, and there are no signs that the antisemitism experienced by Canadian Jews is abating. While I don’t think we will see a stampede of Jews leaving Canada, I do think the numbers leaving will gradually increase.
As in the French example, Israel will be their primary destination. After all, in the final analysis, it turns out that America is not the Promised Land.
The writer, a Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada, is a retired professor at the University of Waterloo, Ontario, Canada.

====================================================================================================

Beneath the surface: What Palestinians think about themselves and their future - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:00:00 UTC
01:00:00 KST

After 48 years of living and working with Palestinians, there is a good chance that I know more Palestinians personally than almost any other Jewish Israeli.
I have spent much of my life in Palestinian homes, offices, universities, refugee camps, villages, and cities. I have known presidents, prime ministers, political leaders, academics, businesspeople, students, activists, and militants. I have negotiated with Hamas leaders and worked closely with Palestinians devoted to peace with Israel.
What follows is not scientific research. These are impressions accumulated over nearly five decades, shaped by thousands of conversations, personal relationships, and attempts to understand what lies beneath Palestinian political statements, slogans, and opinion polls.
Understanding what Palestinians think
My most important observation is that there is often a considerable gap between how Palestinians speak politically and how they live their lives. There is also a gap between the political identity Palestinians feel obligated to project and the questions they privately ask about their society, leadership, and future. I noticed this contradiction decades ago.
In Palestinian political discourse, words such as compromise and concession often imply weakness, surrender, or betrayal. Leaders who speak defiantly and insist on every Palestinian right without qualification may attract greater admiration than those who speak the language of moderation.
Yet many of the same Palestinians demonstrate remarkable moderation in their personal lives. They negotiate, compromise, and cooperate every day. Some of the harshest statements against Israel I have heard came from Palestinians who welcomed me into their homes, treated me as family, and maintained genuine friendships with Israelis.
This is not hypocrisy. For a people who have lived for generations without freedom, resistance is also the language of dignity. Compromise can sound like accepting injustice. Political defiance declares that Palestinians have not surrendered their national rights.
But the language protecting collective dignity can also prevent honest political discussion. Repeating familiar slogans becomes easier than questioning whether they still serve Palestinian interests.
I believe this is where Palestinian society finds itself today.
Traditional political strategies have failed to deliver their promises. Fatah promised diplomacy and negotiations would bring independence, yet its logo still displays rifles and a grenade, hardly symbols of peace. Hamas promised armed resistance would liberate Palestine.
Neither has delivered freedom. The Palestinian Authority has failed to establish accountable democratic government. Gaza has suffered catastrophic destruction, while the West Bank remains occupied and settlements continue expanding.
Palestinians know these realities better than anyone. But acknowledging failure is difficult when national identity has been built around the strategies being questioned.
Beneath the surface, many Palestinians are reassessing their political thinking. They are not questioning whether they deserve freedom but how freedom can be achieved. They are questioning the competence, honesty, and effectiveness of those claiming to represent them.
Consider armed resistance. Palestinian opinion polls have frequently shown substantial support for armed struggle. Israelis often interpret this as evidence that Palestinians prefer violence to peace.
But I wonder about the questions pollsters often do not ask. Would you personally pick up a gun and fight? Would you send your son to fight? Would you risk losing your home, your family, and everything you have built? I believe that support would decline dramatically, perhaps to only a few percent.
The difference between endorsing resistance as a principle and personally accepting its consequences is fundamental.
For generations, Palestinian political culture has celebrated sacrifice, steadfastness, and resistance. These values preserved national identity under extraordinarily difficult circumstances. But there is a difference between honoring sacrifice and asking whether further sacrifices will bring freedom closer.
Gaza has made that question unavoidable. The devastation following October 7 has forced a painful confrontation with political and military choices. Israel bears responsibility for its decisions and actions, but Palestinian leaders must also be accountable for theirs. If Palestinians deny that responsibility then they themselves are denying the political agency they demand.
I believe growing numbers of Palestinians recognize that killing Israelis will not bring liberation. Yet understanding what has failed does not automatically produce agreement about what should replace it.
There is also a profound crisis of representation, made worse by President Mahmoud Abbas's decision to postpone Palestinian elections for another year. The last legislative elections took place in January 2006 and the last presidential elections took place in 2005. An entire generation has reached adulthood without choosing its national representatives. Millions who were children or not even born when Hamas won are still judged for a political choice they never made. They have been denied the opportunity to choose differently.
The official explanations cite Israeli restrictions and difficult circumstances in Gaza, Jerusalem, and the West Bank. These are real obstacles, but if Palestinians must wait for ideal conditions before exercising their democratic rights, they may wait forever.
New political initiatives have begun emerging outside the Fatah-Hamas divide. Samer Sinijlawi's New Path electoral list collected 9,200 endorsement signatures when only 3,000 were required. The New Path is a Palestinian political party with peace with Israel at the top of its agenda. This demonstrates a willingness to organize around alternatives.
Young Palestinians want freedom from occupation but also want freedom from corruption, authoritarianism, and unaccountable leadership. They want to choose, challenge, and replace their representatives rather than inherit their parents' political loyalties. Palestinians cannot renew their national movement while mechanisms for political renewal remain closed.
Palestinians take enormous pride in their steadfastness, attachment to the land, and refusal to surrender their national identity. Remaining on the land, educating children, building businesses, developing institutions, and preserving communities are also forms of resistance. They may establish stronger foundations for independence than another cycle of violence.
Most Palestinians I know do not aspire to become permanent symbols of heroic sacrifice. They want ordinary lives with rights denied for generations: freedom of movement, personal security, political representation, economic opportunity, and national self-determination. They want normality without surrender.
This requires Palestinians to ask difficult questions. What kind of society do they want? What leadership do they deserve? What strategy can achieve independence? How can their national movement serve the people rather than political organizations?
Palestinians must answer these questions themselves. But their political thinking does not develop in isolation. Israeli policies and statements constantly influence Palestinian choices. When Israeli leaders declare that Palestinians will never have independence and that Israel will permanently control their land, they strengthen those arguing that moderation is useless. A Palestinian advocating negotiations must explain what those negotiations could achieve.
Imagine instead an Israeli leader saying: If Palestinians elect leaders genuinely committed to peace with Israel, they will find a genuine partner in Israel. Such a statement would not transform Palestinian society overnight. But it could strengthen Palestinians searching for alternatives to violence, failed negotiations, and the leadership of the past.
After 48 years, I remain convinced that Palestinian society possesses far greater capacity for pragmatism, moderation, and political change than its public rhetoric suggests. Political changes often begin quietly, in private conversations, family discussions, and questions younger generations ask their parents. But those changes must eventually find political expression.
The central question facing Palestinians is not whether they will continue struggling for freedom. It is whether they are prepared to redefine what that struggle should look like, what it should achieve, and who should lead it.
But there is another question: Will Palestinians be allowed to make those choices themselves? Palestinian freedom cannot mean only freedom from Israeli occupation. It must also mean freedom to choose, challenge, and replace Palestinian leaders.
Without both, there can be no genuine Palestinian political renewal. And without that renewal, the prospects for a different future between Israelis and Palestinians become even more distant.
The writer is the Middle East director of the International Communities Organization and the co-head of the Alliance for Two States.

Convened under the theme "Public Trust, Transparency, and Collective Action in the Ebola Response," the two-day workshop aims to deepen collaboration between public health institutions and media organizations to ensure transparent, evidence-based reporting.

She commended Kenyan authorities for their swift notification to international health bodies regarding the country's first imported Ebola case on Oct. 6.
Kenya confirmed its second Ebola case on Wednesday. The patient, a relative of the first patient who died last week, is under quarantine, according to the Health Ministry.
Highlighting the continued risk of regional transmission, Kimambo underscored that transparent data sharing is paramount to contact tracing and community containment, emphasizing the urgent need for enhanced epidemiological surveillance, rapid diagnostics, and clinical case management.
Wessam Mankoula, director of the Center for Public Health Emergencies and lead of the Continental Incident Management Support Team at the Africa CDC, said that delivering verified and accurate information is crucial for encouraging communities to adopt protective behaviors against the Ebola virus.
Mankoula noted that factual public messaging drives necessary behavior change, helping populations understand transmission dynamics and effectively disrupt infection chains. ■

UN Security Council renews Haiti sanctions regime
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
02:58:01 CST
03:58:01 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The Security Council on Wednesday adopted a resolution to renew the sanctions regime on Haiti for another year.
Resolution 2831 extends the sanctions regime, which includes an arms embargo, travel ban and assets freeze measures, for one year from the date of the adoption of the resolution.
It reaffirms the Security Council's decision that UN member states shall take appropriate steps to prevent the illicit trafficking and diversion of arms and related materiel in Haiti.
The resolution calls on member states that transfer firearms, ammunition and related materiel to relevant Haitian authorities, either by sale or donation, to support those authorities in strengthening physical security, stockpile management, and post-delivery controls to mitigate the risk of diversion.
It calls on the Haitian authorities to strengthen their weapons and ammunition management and to reinforce border and customs controls.
In addition, it confirms that the multinational Gang Suppression Force (GSF) in Haiti should support the Haitian National Police and the Haitian armed forces to record and dispose of illicit arms, ammunition and other materiel, seized as part of offensive operations or in the course of carrying out its mandate.
It further calls on the GSF to report any diversion of weapons and ammunition, including through loss and theft, to the Panel of Experts that assists the Sanctions Committee.
The resolution also extends the mandate of the Panel of Experts for a period of 13 months from its date of adoption.
It requests the panel to provide an interim report to the Security Council by March 28, 2027, and a final report no later than Sept. 1, 2027.
Resolution 2831 was adopted with 14 votes in favor among the 15 Security Council members. Russia abstained.
The Security Council introduced sanctions against Haiti in October 2022. ■

China, Pakistan begin first-ever joint army training exercise

Trump’s war on Iran is poised to sink his party in the midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:55:56 UTC
03:55:56 KST

The experts love to say that Americans don’t vote based on foreign policy, but it doesn’t take much digging to conclude that isn’t always true.
Sure, U.S. voters are probably thinking primarily about domestic issues when they go to the polls, but there have been a number of big elections in which war has undoubtedly been a major factor.
The Iraq War was the definitive issue of the 2008 Democratic primary, when then-Senator Barack Obama (who opposed the war) beat then-Senator Hillary Clinton, who voted for it. In 2016, Trump generated support by railing against “endless wars” and calling the U.S. invasion of Iraq “a big, fat mistake.” Most recently, Kamala Harris’s refusal to oppose the Gaza genocide helped seal her 2024 loss.
It’s hard to believe that foreign policy won’t be a major factor in November’s midterms, as Trump’s disastrous war on Iran continues to spin out of control with no discernible signs of an exit strategy.
At the beginning of the summer, it seemed that the administration was on the verge of securing an agreement, but its inability to restore the Strait of Hormuz to its pre-war status simply generated a series of botched negotiations and idle threats.
Americans are enduring astronomical gas prices, but they’re also seeing another “Forever War” potentially take shape, and although the Trump team has sought to censor details on the war, news about the scope of the conflict has inevitably trickled out.
A recent Congressional Research Service report reveals that 81 U.S. military aircrafts have been destroyed or damaged in the war. The Intercept’s Nick Turse points out that the Pentagon quietly raised its official count of U.S. casualties to 21, a full six months after Maj. Sorffly Davius died while “conducting operations” at Camp Buehring in Kuwait. According to estimates by Moody’s Analytics’ chief economist Mark Zandi, the war has cost U.S. consumers $265 billion so far, which is roughly $2,000 for every household.
An extensive Drop Site News investigation into the February 28 attack on a Minjab school revealed that at least 156 people were killed, 120 of them children.
“Why is [Trump] saying Iran may have bombed their own people when we can see the wreckage of Raytheon cruise missiles in the photos that we obtained that were taken from under the rubble?,” journalist Jeremy Scahill, who led the report, told NPR. “There were two direct hits on a school filled with children and teachers. It’s not that there hasn’t been reporting on this. It’s that reporting has not been translated into a very robust, aggressive investigation of what I would say is one of the worst single war crimes committed by the United States since Vietnam.”
Polling shows that war was unpopular with the U.S. population from the beginning, but recent surveys show that approval has continued to plummet. According to the Pew Research Center, just 34% of Americans believe that attacking Iran was the right decision, down from 38% in March. That shift has come entirely from Republican voters. 63% of them now believe it was the right call, compared to 69% who believed that in March.
This reality has forced some Republicans, like Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers and Ohio Sen. Jon Husted, to walk a tightrope between calling for an end to the war and remaining loyal to the President.
“The war can no longer be treated solely as a matter of executive decisions and geopolitical calculations,” writes political scientist Brian Hudson. “Responsibility extends beyond the White House to lawmakers who have supported its continuation, remained silent, or used party unity as a substitute for public debate. Accountability is no longer simply an external demand imposed on the party; it has become an internal issue affecting its credibility and cohesion.”
It’s also become an issue that Democrats can pin on the opposition party.
“It’s less Iran in particular than it is this notion of never-ending conflict and war in the Middle East, which Americans are so done with,” declared Rep. Jason Crow, who is demanding answers on a U.S. airstrike that killed at least 5 people attending a wedding in Iran. “It is very salient.”
This week, Democratic challenger Troy Jackson hammered GOP Senator Susan Collins (D-ME) on the issue during a debate, pointing out that the longtime incumbent voted for the war multiple times, despite currently expressing a desire for it to end.
“The reason why our fuel prices is going through the roof, and the way our — the reason why our electricity costs are going through the roof is because the cost of fuel, cost of oil is so high, because she wouldn’t stop President Trump with the Iran war,” he told the crowd.
Conservative W. James Antle III, Executive Editor of The Washington Examiner Magazine, writes that Republicans were always expected to lose some seats as an extension of being in power, but that anger over the war could sustain a massive electoral shellacking.
“Thanks to the Iran war and its fallout, there is a potential for a midterm election more like 2006. Twenty years ago, as Cook Political Report’s Amy Walter pointed out earlier this year, we had an unpopular president waging an unpopular war while Republican congressional incumbents were beset by assorted scandals,” he writes in Responsible Statecraft. “Today, the public has even less patience for the current war than in 2006.”
The reality is that the GOP is headed for a potential disaster in a few weeks, thanks in no small part to Trump’s terrible war.

Members of the public who tried to submit their views on a proposed change to the National Institutes of Health’s grant funding system say they found themselves locked out after the system shut down ahead of schedule.
The proposed change has been criticized as potentially reducing transparency. It seeks to revise how grant application scores—averaged measures of a research project's predicted outcomes—are communicated to both funding applicants and NIH program officers.
Under the change, applications would be sorted into three broad categories of merit, while their overall score, as determined by a panel of experts, would remain a secret. Some researchers have said this could open up the grant approval process to undue political influence.
On supporting science journalism

Spain’s Socialists widen lead in state poll as housing dominates election debate

Alyssa McMurtry
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Spain’s ruling Socialists widened their lead over the conservative opposition in a state poll released Wednesday, contrasting with other surveys that favor the right ahead of a snap election dominated by the housing crisis.
The Center for Sociological Research (CIS) put Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s party at 34%, nearly 12 percentage points ahead of the Popular Party (PP), compared with a 5.5-point lead last month.
The Socialists gained three points while the PP fell to 22.2%. Far-right Vox remained third with 17.1%, followed by the Socialists’ coalition partner Sumar at 6.1% and left-wing Podemos at 3.1%.
Together, the three left-wing parties would receive around 43% of the vote, roughly four points more than the PP and Vox combined.
The survey comes amid public anger over the eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman forced out of the home she had rented for seven decades who died two weeks later.
Her case sparked protests and encampments in Madrid and other cities, intensifying demands for action over housing costs and evictions.
Sanchez announced the Nov. 29 election after parliament rejected two government housing decrees.
Spain’s largest unions, CCOO and UGT, have also called a general strike for Nov. 11 to demand better wages and affordable housing, two days before the official election campaign begins.
Wednesday’s survey underscored the scale of concern, with a record 55.7% naming housing among Spain’s main problems, far ahead of immigration and the economy.
Anomalous poll
However, the CIS findings contrast sharply with other polls suggesting the conservatives and far right could win enough seats to govern together.
A 40db survey for El Pais and Cadena SER conducted after the election announcement gave the PP and Vox a combined lead of about 15 points over the Socialists, Sumar, and Podemos.
Public broadcaster RTVE’s polling average likewise projected a comfortable parliamentary majority for the PP and Vox, with a combined 202 seats in the 350-seat lower house.
The divergence is not new. An El Pais analysis of 44 elections since 2018 found that CIS surveys overestimated support for the left in 43 of them.
Its final poll before the 2023 general election came close to the Socialists’ actual vote share, but incorrectly predicted they would finish ahead of the PP.
The latest CIS survey was based on 5,025 interviews done in early October.

In Ukraine, civilian casualties were already rising. Restrictions on Starlink will only worsen the death toll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:54:34 UTC
03:54:34 KST

In Ukraine the situation was already jittery enough. Donald Trump has been inventing ceasefires and buying Russian diesel to shore up his flagging popularity, while a sinister new wave of faster, jet-powered drones are breaking through Kyiv’s stretched air defences. Casualties are rising as the weather turns.
Overnight, Russia bombed three power plants that supply Kyiv, aiming to cut off heating and electricity to the city. According to the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, for a second night in a row no warning came from Ukraine’s western allies of the incoming ballistic missiles – and so no air raid alert was issued.
Then, on Tuesday night, and without warning, Ukraine’s military found that Elon Musk’s Starlink mobile internet system, on which it heavily relies, had stopped working on its drones flying faster than 160km/h (100mph).
Or at least that was the official limit: in practice, drones flying over 80km/h could no longer communicate.
The immediate assumption in Kyiv is that the White House is once again trying to bully Ukraine into accepting an unattractive deal with Russia.
However, on Tuesday Trump did say that no intelligence-sharing had been paused, and similar comments were made by Mark Rutte, the secretary general of Nato on Wednesday. It is possible the lack of ballistic warning is coincidental.
Even Serhii Beskrestnov, Zelenskyy’s high-profile military technology adviser, has expressed public doubts about whether the US had paused the sharing of missile detection. “Friends, this is not the first time that the launch of an S-400 has not been detected,” he posted on Monday. “We should not jump to conclusions.”
However, there has now been an absence of incoming warnings for two days in a row. The second of these was in tandem with the unexpected throttling of Starlink, a system supplied by Musk with the approval of the US military.
So it is hardly reassuring against the backdrop of White House threats, which have emerged every time a flailing Trump has tried to end the war in Ukraine.
The last time Trump paused intelligence-sharing – which is, in effect, valuable information about Russian positions and movements – was in March 2025, shortly after Zelenskyy’s infamous dusting down in the Oval Office.
“You don’t have the cards,” Trump said, as he took another away. Ukraine rapidly lost a chunk of territory it had occupied in Russia’s Kursk region before sharing was restored.
A confirmed pause this time would mark a serious breach when Ukraine is more than holding off its larger neighbour on the frontline, even as the situation on the home front is worsening.
Russia has bombed two bridges in Kyiv, gas stations, city centre buildings and out-of-town warehouses, showing little restraint as it aims to harm Ukrainian civilians while it struggles to win the conventional war.
The effect of a more permanent halt to Starlink for Ukrainian drones or anything military that moves faster than 50mph is a little more complex. Starlink is how Ukraine directs many of its mid-strike (or mid-range) drones accurately towards their targets into occupied areas behind enemy lines, critical for helping the defenders maintain the rough balance on the front.
Yet, ironically, Starlink is not used for the long-range missions that target the Russian oil refineries about which Trump is so concerned, because it has long been disabled by the company inside Russia’s internationally recognised borders.
“There’s no meaningful effect on deep-strike operations,” one Ukrainian soldier said, while conceding there could be as much as a 30-fold drop in mid-strike operations because the alternatives are 30 times more expensive. Commanders are “replanning everything”, the soldier added, and aiming to find ways to carry on missions using different technologies and techniques.
Starlink is also, more importantly – as Beskrestnov emphasised on Wednesday – used by air-defence interceptors in the most effective system to down Russia’s deadly new jet-powered Shahed drones. These are at least twice as fast as traditional piston-engined Shaheds, and Ukraine’s rate of interception had dropped to 60% in September, before recovering to 75% according to the country’s air force.
The reality, then, is that the Starlink manoeuvre may not have much impact on oil prices, and only a limited effect on Ukraine’s frontline position, while putting the country’s civilians in greater danger.
As the Ukrainian human rights activist Oleksandra Matviichuk put it: “Without that protection, Russian drones will strike residential buildings, hospitals and schools like targets in a shooting gallery.”
Meanwhile, diplomatically, the situation is more finely poised. It was already the case that the Trump White House had proved to be a difficult and unreliable partner. What Zelenskyy, on a visit to London on Wednesday, needs from the likes of the UK prime minster, Andy Burnham, is pressure on the US to ensure the Starlink pause and whatever is happening with intelligence-sharing does not metastasise into a deeper crisis.

Florence’s ‘Maricarmen’: 94-year-old faces losing her home of 60 years as rent nearly triples
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:43:01 UTC
03:43:01 KST

The elderly widow, almost blind and using a walking frame still does not know about the eviction; her daughter says her story echoes Maricarmen, a symbol of Spain's fight for housing.
A 94-year-old woman in Florence faces losing the home she has lived in for more than 60 years after her landlord said her rent would rise from €450 to €1,200 a month.
Franca’s contract expires in February, and her family says she will not be able to afford to renew it on the new terms. Her case closely echoes that of María del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, the 87-year-old who became a symbol of the fight for housing in Spain after a steep rent rise led to her eviction in Madrid. She died in hospital a few days later.
"My mother gets a minimum pension and my father’s survivor’s pension. If she had to pay €1,200 in rent, she would be left with practically nothing to live on, not even enough to eat," her daughter told Corriere Fiorentino (source in Italian).
She has asked not to be named because she has not yet been able to bring herself to tell her mother.
The 70-square-metre flat has been Franca’s home since the early 1960s. She lived there with her husband, and her daughter was born there. According to her daughter, it is the only place her mother feels truly at home, filled with photos of her grandchildren, paintings of Florence’s narrow streets and mementoes from her daughter’s wedding.
The building contains several flats, all owned by the same landlord. It was once home mainly to Florentine families, many of whom had lived there for generations, but the tenants have changed over the years.
As far as her daughter knows, the flats are not being turned into holiday lets and remain ordinary residential tenancies. She believes, however, that the new management wants to squeeze far higher returns from the properties.
"They phoned me to tell me they would not renew the contract for my mother," she told the newspaper. "The contract was renewed every two years. They let me know that, for her to stay there, the rent would have to go up to €1,200 a month. But how can you ask for that kind of money from a 94-year-old pensioner?"
The family accepts that the rent cannot stay the same forever, and her daughter says she would help cover an increase so her mother could spend her final years at home.
"We could manage a small increase, I could help her out. But going from €450 to €1,200 is something else altogether. It is an impossible amount. And what pains me is that there was not even any chance to open a proper negotiation, to try to meet halfway."
She has since turned to the tenants’ union Sunia for help.
Franca’s case comes amid a wider squeeze on tenants in Tuscany, where 2,427 eviction orders were issued in 2025. Florence accounts for around 35% of all enforcement requests filed in the region.
