====================================================================================================

The Australian species turning up where no one wants it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:39:52 UTC
03:39:52 KST

In brief
- A familiar sight in Australian waterways could be wreaking havoc far from home.
- There are concerns its surging appearance across the world could create problems.
Every year, the upper Zambesi River breaks its banks and spreads across the wide Barotse floodplains in Zambia.
These seasonal wetlands are famed for their exceptional richness of species, from birds to unique cichlid fish.
But there are signs of profound upheaval. Native fish and invertebrate populations have fallen, river plants are being devoured and river banks hollowed out from within.
Every Australian knows common myna birds are bad, rabbits are worse and feral cats kill native animals unchecked.
But how do we decide what makes an introduced species "good" or "bad" — and will we ever concede that some species are here to stay?
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The culprit will be familiar. As the flood eases and the dry season begins, the shallow muddy pools left behind teem with redclaw crayfish (Cherax quadricarinatus), a freshwater crayfish native to the tropics in northern Australia and Papua New Guinea. Many Australians call these “yabbies”, as they do other medium-sized Cherax crayfish.
It might seem bizarre that an Australian species has become an invasive pest overseas. The flow of introduced species usually goes the other way. But these yabbies were forged in the intense crucible of the Australian climate. Unfortunately, they may be all but unstoppable in the Zambesi — and many other water bodies around the world.
Built for a harsh landscape
Over 100 species of freshwater crayfish are found in Australia. Many are remarkable. The giant Tasmanian crayfish (Astacopsis gouldi) is the largest crayfish in the world across both fresh and salt water, while burrowing crayfish species spend most of their lives in burrows, marked by chimneys of clay.
Of Australia’s ten freshwater crayfish genera (groups of species), the Cherax species are arguably the toughest.
They evolved to survive in Australian billabongs, ephemeral lakes left behind when a river changes course. These lakes can dry up and refill at times, causing a brutal wet-dry cycle.
Cherax species became adapted to survive in deeply inhospitable habitats, such as water with virtually no dissolved oxygen. They can burrow deeply and enter a dormant state for months to years before better weather arrives. A single female can produce several broods a year, with up to 1000 eggs in each brood.
They are aggressive generalists, eating everything from detritus and aquatic plants to fish, invertebrates and even each other.
As climate change brings more extreme weather, tough species such as the redclaw are better equipped to survive than local species who may have evolved in a kinder climate.
How did redclaws get to southern Africa?
Throughout the 1980s and 1990s, redclaws were exported to aquaculture facilities across Africa, Europe, Asia and South America. Farmers liked them for their hardiness, adaptability and rapid growth.
Their striking blues and reds made them popular in the global aquarium trade, creating a second major pathway for their spread.
It was all but inevitable that redclaws would escape containment and make it into local rivers. Some escaped aquaculture ponds during hurricanes or by being accidentally released. Others were pets released into waterways.
In the wild, the humble redclaw multiplied. Soon, there were signs of devastating shifts in local waterways.
We don’t know exactly how redclaws got into the Zambesi. During the 1990s, redclaws began to be spotted in the river. Their numbers soon surged – and native plant, fish and invertebrate species suffered.
Redclaws are now on the doorstep of pristine, highly sensitive ecosystems such as Botswana’s famous Okavango Delta. They are already present in South Africa’s famous Kruger National Park. Fishers in Zambia report significant falls in their catch. They can spread 6 kilometres in an average year — and up to 49km/year during flooding seasons.
Escapee redclaws are also moving through Central America and parts of Southeast Asia. Amazingly, redclaws are also considered an invasive species in parts of Western Australia.
Many Australians think fondly of yabbies (likely derived from “yabidj/yapitj”, the name used by several First Nations groups in southern Australia). How could they become pests?
Australia’s long geographic isolation meant its unique species evolved in a closed system. They often lack the competitive edge to survive against aggressive invaders from other continents. As a result, it’s rare for Australian wildlife to become invasive pests overseas.
But as our freshwater crustaceans show, there are exceptions.
Common yabbies pose another threat
The redclaw isn’t alone. Australia’s common yabby (Cherax destructor) has also escaped aquariums and aquaculture farms to quietly colonise rivers and lakes in parts of Europe and Southeast Asia. Endemic to the rivers of the Murray-Darling basin, it can tolerate water temperatures between 1C and 35C and survive in many habitats. This helps it outcompete many native crayfish.
Worse, Cherax destructor is susceptible to and can carry strains of lethal crayfish plague, meaning it can spread the pathogen to highly susceptible species in Europe. The plague is an aquatic mould native to North America, which infects the host’s cuticle (shell) and can lead to mass mortality events.
In Australia, Cherax species co-evolved with native predators such as Murray cod, platypus and rakali who naturally keep their populations in check.
Overseas, local predators are not always able to provide these checks and balances. Australian yabbies find it easy to bully and outcompete smaller, less aggressive native crustaceans and fish. They do particularly well in degraded rivers or lakes where native species are already struggling.
What can be done?
It’s nearly impossible to eradicate redclaws and yabbies once they are breeding in a major river system.
Traps often catch the larger adults, which can inadvertently trigger a population boom by freeing up food and territory for juveniles left behind.
In response, ecologists and conservationists are shifting tactics. In southern Africa, community harvesting programs train locals to catch and sell “redclaws” for food, suppressing numbers while.
In Europe, aquaculture hatcheries are deploying more effective physical barriers to halt escapes, alongside biological controls such as stocking waterways with large, predatory native fish.
Efforts like these, may keep redclaw numbers down in the Zambesi. But the yabbies are likely there to stay.
What the story of Australia’s pest yabbies tells us is that an organism that seems harmless or even struggling in its home habitat can sometimes become an environmental super-weapon when dropped into an ecosystem unequipped to fight it.
Moving species across borders has long been done for short-term economic gain. But as the plague of yabbies in the Zambesi shows, it’s ecological roulette.
For the latest from SBS News, download our app and subscribe to our newsletter.

Israel’s former security chief sues Netanyahu for October 7 defamation

Israel’s former security chief sues Netanyahu for October 7 defamation
Ronen Bar accuses Netanyahu of being warned before Hamas attacks, as elections loom.
The former head of Israel’s domestic security agency Shin Bet has sued Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for defamation over claims of his responsibility in the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack.
Coming just before Israel’s close-fought October 27 election in which Netanyahu is fighting for his political life, the case filed on Wednesday is set to ramp up the country’s political drama.
Ronen Bar, the former director of Shin Bet, accused Netanyahu of “lying to cover himself” and said it was slanderous of the prime minister to have accused him of “criminal failures” over the attack, in a 134-page court document.
Bar said he telephoned the prime minister’s military secretary as soon as signs of a possible attack became apparent, but that he did not have Netanyahu’s direct number.
Netanyahu has said he was not alerted by Bar on the morning of the Hamas-led assault, insisting that he could have stopped the attack had the Shin Bet’s then-director or military leaders called to wake him up the day of the early-morning attack.
Bar’s lawsuit says Netanyahu made accusations “that he knew to be false, with the aim of diverting the debate from his own responsibility for the events of October 7”.
Instead, it was Netanyahu’s policies over several years that had “increased the dangers posed by terrorist organisations in Gaza”, it said.
Likud response
On Wednesday, Netanyahu responded to Bar’s accusations in a statement issued by his Likud party saying, “Ronen, are you serious?”
“You had my number on the red line and could have called me immediately, as all security chiefs do,” Netanyahu asked, adding, “How many lives could we have saved if only you had called in time?”
Bar resigned as head of Shin Bet in June 2025 amid recriminations over the deadliest attack in Israel’s history, while insisting he had informed Netanyahu of the threat in advance.
He is seeking three million shekels (about $968,500) in damages from Netanyahu.
Warnings, lies, manipulation
The allegations in Bar’s lawsuit come days after Netanyahu’s former military secretary, Avi Gil, told Israel’s Channel 12 that the prime minister’s office had “falsified records related to October 7, 2023”, including altering the recorded time of a key phone call.
Gil, who served as Netanyahu’s military secretary from July 2021 to May 2024, said a stenographer in the prime minister’s office approached him in January 2024 with instructions from Netanyahu’s chief of staff to change the time of a four-minute call from 6:40am local time (03:40GMT) to 6:29am (03:29 GMT).
“She told me, I’m not allowed to change it,” said Gil, accusing the head of Netanyahu’s office of manipulating telephone records, adding, “Those are facts, and there is no dispute about them.”
Last month, the Wall Street Journal reported that Netanyahu had been warned of the attack by Egypt’s intelligence chief, Abbas Kamel.
In a rare move, Kamel reportedly phoned the prime minister just days before the attack, underscoring previous warnings in September 2023, when he is said to have flown to Israel to warn security officials in person that Hamas was planning an attack.
Polls show Netanyahu is in a tight race to stay in power in the October 27 election, after being hammered by former staff and government officials as well as the opposition for failing to prevent the bloodshed.
At least 1,221 Israelis were killed on October 7, 2023, after Hamas broke through the fence separating Israel and Gaza, according to Israeli official figures.
Also, 251 Israelis were taken captive, including the bodies of 44 Israelis killed that day.
In the three years since, Israel has killed more than 74,300 people in Gaza, according to the Health Ministry in the enclave.
More than 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza have been killed in Israeli attacks since a tentative “ceasefire” backed by the US was reached last year.

Le Pen vows to downsize EU as she brings contribution cut fight to Brussels
The front-runner in France’s presidential reiterated her campaign promise to pare back payments to the EU by billions of euros ahead of a critical summit on Thursday.
BRUSSELS — Far-right leader Marine Le Pen pledged to turn the European Commission into a “secretariat” in the service of its member countries as part of her plan to slash the size and power of the European Union should she win France’s presidential election next year.
“Over the past 10 years, France has seen the implementation of a European vision that is the exact opposite of the one I will champion,” Le Pen told reporters at a press conference in Brussels after a meeting with fellow European far-right leaders. “They wanted a powerful Europe. We got a powerless Europe. They wanted European sovereignty. All we’ve gotten is the dilution of national sovereignty.”
Asked by POLITICO what downsizing the EU would look like in practice, the front-runner in the race to replace term-limited President Emmanuel Macron next year said the EU should pare back its operations in areas it has expanded in recent years such as foreign policy, security and public health.
Advertisement
Le Pen also promised to “stop” the bloc’s Green Deal, which she claimed was harming economic growth, and eliminate institutions like the European Committee of the Regions and the European Economic and Social Committee.
“I’m not fooled by what the European Commission wants to do. The European Commission wants to turn itself into a state; we do not. And so we will stand in its way,” Le Pen said.
Though Le Pen has abandoned her calls for France to leave the European Union, she remains deeply skeptical of the bloc and its ambition.
She and her National Rally party last week said they would unilaterally slash France’s annual contribution to the EU budget by €11.1 billion as early as next year if Le Pen wins the presidency.
Le Pen is in Brussels the day before EU leaders meet for key discussions over the bloc’s next seven-year budget, which Council President António Costa had hoped to get finalized before elections in France, Italy and Poland in 2027 that could derail the talks.

But EU countries have weakened their commitment to wrap up negotiations by year-end amid a major split between frugal countries such as Germany, which want to further shrink the budget, and countries like France that support more EU spending.
Le Pen once again reiterated her accusations that Brussels’ attempt to speed up budget talks — which would prevent France’s next government from having a say in the matter — is “a democratic scandal.”

The $2.9 trillion corner of Australia's economy at the centre of a tax war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:35:28 UTC
03:35:28 KST

Key Points
- Small business groups warn 350,000 family firms face higher taxes or costly restructures.
- Coalition vows to repeal changes as compliance costs top $1 billion.
A multi-billion-dollar gap and a reignited political divide has opened up between small businesses over a new policy taxing trillion-dollar trust schemes.
The government plans to close a tax advantage many workers can't access by imposing a minimum 30 per cent tax on the income of 840,000 trusts that allow wealthy investors and family businesses to spread income across their family or obscure asset ownership in bankruptcy and family-court proceedings. Australian trusts have combined assets of $2.9 trillion with annual income of $600 billion.
The changes are projected to raise $4.47 billion in 2029/30 after they begin on 1 July 2028. Treasury data shows trusts are overwhelmingly used by Australia's top 10 per cent of income earners who receive about two-thirds of distributions, while the bottom 10 per cent receive one per cent.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the reforms affect fewer than 10 per cent of small businesses.
"Small businesses and others using discretionary trusts can access rollover relief from 1 July 2027 if they want to restructure, or can make an election for tax purposes to be exempt from the minimum tax, for as long as they continue to make distributions to pre-nominated beneficiaries in line with an upfront nomination," Chalmers said on Wednesday.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Senior economist at the left-wing thinktank the Australia Institute, David Richardson, told SBS News the changes plug a tax-dodging loophole used by wealthy people to spread income across their family or obscure asset ownership in bankruptcy and family-court proceedings.
"The ambiguity of who owns what in the trust means they become a vehicle for putting assets away, where it's very hard for bankruptcy proceedings to access them," Richardson said. "It's hard for the Family Court to know what's going on. So, generally, family trusts, even when they're taxed at 30 per cent, will still be useful for somebody on very high incomes, where the marginal tax rate is 47 cents."
That small businesses, and others are unhappy with the change, "shows you that they're presently doing well out of a trust structure", he said.
"They wouldn't be complaining unless they were genuinely avoiding what they would have to pay as either an individual sole trader or as the principal of some sort of corporate structure."
Australian Council of Social Service (ACOSS) CEO Dr Cassandra Goldie said the reforms restore some "basic economic fairness".
"It is not fair that someone earning $200,000 or more, who would usually pay 47 per cent tax on extra income, can bring that rate down to 30 per cent or less by passing income through a discretionary trust to their adult children or a private company, while an average worker pays tax at a rate of 30 per cent of the next dollar earned," Goldie said.
Why are small businesses unhappy?
The Council of Small Business Organisations Australia (COSBOA) CEO Skye Cappuccio said after months of consultation "fundamental problems" remain, forcing 350,000 family and small businesses structured this way to choose between "a substantial tax increase", or restructuring costs in the thousands of dollars for professional fees, duties and administration.
"These are not genuine choices. They are bad options that will make operating a small family business harder and more expensive," Cappuccio said.
"These are small family businesses that have legitimately used trusts for decades to protect assets, manage succession and plan for the future," Cappuccio said.
"This policy targets a business structure rather than the conduct the government is concerned about. There are more targeted ways to address tax integrity without imposing unnecessary costs on genuine small businesses.
"Queensland and Western Australian enterprises will be hit hardest by the changes because stamp duty may apply if a business there restructures its assets."
What's the political divide and controversy?
The Coalition failed to stall the laws on Wednesday, but opposition leader Angus Taylor said the Coalition will go to the election with a "policy of axing the tax".
Opposition treasury spokesman Tim Wilson said, "small and family businesses face a bill of up to $13.3 billion for the cost of valuations, advisers and stamp duty because our taxaholic treasurer broke his election promise and can’t kick his spending addiction".
"The treasurer has rewritten this tax again and again since budget night because he doesn’t understand his own policy or the damage it does. Every backdown is an admission it should never have been proposed in the first place," Wilson said.
Trusts excluded from the changes include deceased estates, disability, superannuation, charities, farms and fixed trusts.
The Housing Industry Association warned this is a new tax on tradies, and builders that diverts their attention from building the homes Australia desperately needs."
Greens leader David Shoebridge said on Wednesday there are too many concessions being made and will refer the bill to a Senate inquiry and that claims about restructuring costs should be supported by detailed modelling.
"We want to make sure that we don't, in passing this legislation, create that additional loophole," Shoebridge said. "This is about ensuring that there's a fair level playing field across business, but also across society, and that's our focus.
"If the Coalition is going to put a figure out like that ($13 billion), they need to back it up with numbers (and modelling)."
Will this really cost businesses $13 billion?
Treasury estimates the cost to businesses will be $141.5 million annually plus $940 million during an implementation phase.
But the Coalition and Wilson say the cost will be up to $13.3 billion based on a Wilson Asset Management estimate.
Wilson ran a successful campaign against changes to franking credits by coordinating with Wilson Asset Management in 2019.
But CPA Australia Tax Lead Jenny Wong told SBS News the Coalition’s figure includes stamp duty, and Treasury’s doesn’t. But there is no source or method listed as to how they arrived at their number.
"Our estimate is $2 billion to $2.8 billion, for advice alone (and) covers the cost of working out what to do across roughly 850,000 trusts, before anyone restructures or elects (beneficiaries)," Wong said. "The bill leaves 12 rules to be made later by the minister, up from 10, and ATO guidance won’t come until after the law passes."
The government has given families a way to avoid restructuring, and "that deserves credit", she said.
"But for those who still have to restructure, nothing in this bill makes it cheaper. Stamp duty can be most of the bill, and the Commonwealth can’t waive it,” Wong said.
"We support dealing with inappropriate income splitting (done) simply, fairly and in proportion," Wong said. "On that test, there is still work to do."
Treasury's analysis estimates that restructuring a family business can cost between $9,536 and $23,436 and that restructuring could cost family businesses more than the tax itself.

Reservists lose municipal-tax discounts after wartime protection expires, petition says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:35:20 UTC
03:35:20 KST

Low-income reservists who spent months in IDF reserve service are losing municipal property-tax discounts because their reserve payments push them above income limits, according to a petition Jerusalem’s Hitorerut movement says it submitted to the High Court of Justice on Tuesday.
The movement is seeking to restore a protection that expired at the end of 2025, leaving some students facing full property-tax (arnona) bills after previously receiving discounts of 80%. It argues that the government failed to renew the arrangement despite advance warnings and assurances that it would continue.
One case concerns a Hebrew University medical student who served 425 reserve days from the outbreak of the war through August 6, 2026, including 118 days in 2025. According to the petition, he received an 80% arnona discount in 2025 but was billed the full NIS 5,705.45 for 2026.
His wages from work in October 2025 amounted to just NIS 788, the petition says. Reserve payments and related supplements nevertheless helped bring his recorded annual income to approximately NIS 73,977, averaging NIS 6,165 a month - above the NIS 5,857 ceiling for a single-person household to qualify for an income-based discount in 2026.
Hitorerut argues that the payments did not reflect a lasting improvement in his earnings. After returning to his limited part-time work alongside his medical studies, he faced a full year’s municipal tax without the relief he previously received.
'Reservists should not have to fight twice'
“Reservists should not have to fight twice - once at the front and once against the bureaucracy,” Jerusalem Deputy Mayor and Hitorerut chairman Adir Schwartz said in a statement accompanying the petition.
The dispute concerns income-based discounts, rather than the separate arnona discount available to active reservists. Eligibility depends on household income and size, with national regulations setting the maximum discounts municipalities may grant.
Ordinary reserve compensation counts as income under those rules. For students and other low-paid workers, the minimum payment for military service can substantially exceed their usual wages. Months of service can therefore push them into a lower discount bracket or beyond eligibility altogether.
A temporary regulation allowed municipal councils to exclude those payments when assessing discounts for 2024 and 2025. Jerusalem adopted the arrangement. Hitorerut says its expiration left municipalities without authority to continue excluding the payments in 2026.
The filing describes two further cases. A married reservist and his wife saw their discount fall from 80% in 2025 to 20% in 2026, according to the petition. Another medical student, whose ordinary monthly wages were approximately NIS 2,600-3,000, received a full annual bill of roughly NIS 5,878 after previously receiving an 80% discount.
The movement argues that the result is unequal treatment of students earning comparable wages: those who did not serve can retain their discounts, while reservists lose relief because their previous year’s military compensation is counted against them.
Hitorerut, represented by attorney Matan Gutman, first petitioned over the issue in June 2024. The temporary regulation was published that November.
Extension requested, asks for overpayments to be refunded
In January 2025, the High Court closed that case and awarded the movement NIS 15,000 in costs. Justice Yechiel Kasher found that bringing the petition had been justified from Hitorerut’s perspective and appeared to have contributed to the amendment. He expressly avoided deciding whether the petition would have succeeded had it proceeded to a final ruling.
Schwartz requested an extension in September 2025. Hitorerut says the then-acting interior minister’s office subsequently conveyed approval, but the necessary regulation was never issued. The petition says further demands in August and September 2026 produced only an acknowledgment from the Interior Ministry, with no substantive response from the government offices approached.
A separate change has compounded the problem: An Interior Ministry notice attached to the petition confirms that 2026 eligibility is calculated using average income over 12 months. Applicants can no longer rely on the previous year’s final three months, an option that could help reservists whose service payments fell outside that period.
The movement seeks to restore the exclusion for 2026–2027, retroactive to January 1, 2026, or establish an alternative protecting affected reservists. It also asks for eligibility to be recalculated and overpayments refunded once an arrangement is adopted.
With Jerusalem’s October 31 deadline for discount applications approaching, Hitorerut is also seeking an extension so reservists do not lose the opportunity to apply while the issue remains unresolved. It further asks the government to consider a standing arrangement while emergency reserve call-ups continue.

Morocco opens first state-funded museum dedicated to Jewish culture in Arab world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:35:11 UTC
03:35:11 KST

The new Museum of Moroccan Jewish Culture opened its doors in the city of Fes on Monday, marking the first time in history that an Arab-Muslim country has allocated public funds to establish a museum entirely dedicated to Jewish culture.
According to Morocco's National Foundation of Museums, the 1,700 square meters space invites visitors on a journey into the heart of Moroccan Jewish life and Judaism through a rich and diverse collection of ritual and everyday objects, archaeological, ethnographic and artistic artifacts, archives and rare manuscripts, crafts, traditions, as well as practices and testimonies handed down through the 2500 of Jewish history in the country.
Exhibition galleries display Jewish religious artifacts from Arab World
Local media said the exhibition galleries explore communal institutions, including synagogues, Hebrew schools and rabbinical courts, as well as traditions associated with birth, bar mitzvahs, weddings, funerals and religious holidays. Objects on display include Torah scrolls, prayer shawls, marriage contracts, circumcision chairs, bridal costumes and jewelry.
Traditional crafts also feature prominently, including a reconstructed jeweler’s workshop, tools, silver ornaments, textiles, regional clothing and musical instruments. Audiovisual and digital installations complement the collections, while dedicated spaces will host educational activities for children and school groups.
The front of the building features a brass inscription in four languages: Arabic, Amazigh, Hebrew, and French.
The museum was designed with the involvement of the Moroccan Jewish community, represented in particular by Serge Berdugo, Founding President of the Foundation for Moroccan Jewish Cultural Heritage.
Construction of the museum was initiated by King Mohammed VI during his visit to Fez in April 2019, as part of a program to rehabilitate and showcase the old medina.
The Museums Foundation said the museum "forms part of King Mohammed VI's vision," which places "great importance on preserving and promoting all components of Moroccan identity, in their diversity and complementarity."
The work, completed in March 2023, was carried out by ADER-Fez in consultation with the National Foundation of Museums.
The opening of the Museum of Moroccan Jewish Culture on Monday was attended by Ahmed Toufiq, Minister of Endowments and Islamic Affairs; Khalid Aït Taleb, Wali (regional governor) of the Fez-Meknes region and governor of Fez Prefecture; Serge Berdugo, Founding President of the Foundation for Moroccan Jewish Cultural Heritage; Mehdi Qotbi, President of the National Foundation of Museums; and several other prominent figures, including ambassadors, directors and university presidents.

Alleged Chinese spies targeted former premier and AFP commander via LinkedIn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:34:59 UTC
03:34:59 KST

Alleged Chinese spies targeted former premier and AFP commander via LinkedIn
In short:
The alleged Chinese spies that targeted businessman Alexander Csergo, the first person to be convicted under Australia's foreign interference laws, also approached dozens of other Australians.
The AFP obtained records from the LinkedIn accounts used by the alleged spies as part of its investigation into Csergo.
What's next?
An expert on Chinese intelligence says the approach signals a "fundamental shift" in China's espionage tradecraft.
Two LinkedIn accounts connected to suspected Chinese spies amassed thousands of connections worldwide and approached dozens of Australians working in government, policing and trade with offers of paid consultancy, an ABC investigation has found.
The alleged spies posed as employees of a think tank, offering their targets competitive pay in return for "valuable advice".
Between 2016 and 2025, the alleged spies targeted more than 100 individuals linked to Australia, including former Queensland premier and now opposition leader Steven Miles, an Australian Federal Police commander and several senior federal government officials.
Their LinkedIn profiles appeared in the connection records of two LinkedIn accounts presenting themselves as think-tank representatives. The accused foreign agents reached out to 58 of those connections, and some recipients shared their personal contact details.
The ABC can reveal the Australians were targeted by the same alleged Chinese spying network that groomed Australian businessman Alexander Csergo, who has been jailed as the first person convicted of reckless foreign interference.
LinkedIn records obtained by the Australian Federal Police (AFP) during the investigation into Csergo show the accounts approached other Australians, including those who worked at government agencies and state trade and investment bodies.
The AFP alleged the operation was conducted by China's Ministry of State Security (MSS), the country's principal civilian intelligence agency. It said the MSS used fake LinkedIn profiles to contact and cultivate potential foreign sources, before requesting information from them.
The Chinese Embassy in Canberra rejected the AFP's claims as "entirely groundless".
"We firmly reject unwarranted accusations and vilification against China and hope that the Australian media will observe professional ethics and report in a fair and objective manner," a spokesperson told the ABC in an email.
In June, the Five Eyes alliance, an intelligence-sharing partnership consisting of the USA, the UK, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, issued a rare joint warning about Chinese intelligence using online job platforms for recruitment "that can provide China with a strategic and tactical advantage over the Five Eyes".
Asked by the ABC if it's aware of or investigating the alleged spying operation, a spokesperson for Australia's domestic spying agency, ASIO, said: "Consistent with long-standing practice, ASIO does not comment on — or confirm — investigations."
Inside the recruitment pitch
In November 2021, while Csergo was living in Shanghai, a LinkedIn account using the name Vera Su offered him part-time work.
The sender introduced herself as being from Nesa Consulting and said the organisation wanted experts to advise on trade between China and Australia.
According to the prosecution case, Csergo subsequently met two people known to him as Ken and Evelyn, prepared reports and received cash payments.
He was convicted in March of reckless foreign interference, an offence introduced under Australia's 2018 national security laws.
The prosecution case was that his conduct involved secrecy or deception and that he was reckless as to whether it supported a foreign principal's intelligence activities.
But an analysis by the ABC of Vera Su's communication records, first obtained by the AFP as part of its investigation into Csergo, revealed how the same LinkedIn accounts sought other people with useful expertise and contacts.
Among those directly approached were people whose profiles listed employment at Austrade — the federal agency that promotes Australian trade and investment — the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, Investment NSW, Invest Victoria and Tourism Australia.
The accounts' pitches also sought access to people inside government.
"I wonder if you have special source of information… for example: from important people in the government," one message asked.
Some recipients declined.
One Austrade employee said he could not accept money because he worked for the Australian government, although he offered to introduce people in his professional network.
Former Queensland premier Steven Miles was also connected with the same Vera Su account in April 2021 while he was deputy premier.
The ABC has seen no messages between Mr Miles and the account, and the connection alone does not establish that he received a consultancy offer or provided information. The ABC understands that Mr Miles did not respond to any message from Ms Su.
'Honey traps'
Data reviewed by the ABC shows some Australia-linked targets shared contact details or discussed continuing the exchange outside LinkedIn, including through WeChat, phone calls or meetings.
Business consultant Nick Coyle was dealing with the arrest of his former partner, Cheng Lei, in China on espionage charges when he was approached by the alleged Chinese spies.
"During that time, I was getting many strange approaches," he said. Some were "honey traps", people trying to become "friends", both online and in person.
"I just took the approach — if I don't know them from prior — I would steer clear," he said.
Australian life coach Adrian Cahill also exchanged contact with Vera in 2021. He suspects his background as a former soldier made him a more attractive target.
"I would get those a fair bit," he said. "People write to me saying, 'we've got a job, we've got money, we've got a budget.'"
He said his training helped him recognise those tactics, but people without security experience could be gradually drawn into providing "more and more information".
A 'fundamental shift' in tradecraft
Chinese intelligence expert Nicholas Eftimiades described the state-sponsored fishing expedition as a "fundamental shift".
Professor Eftimiades said China's growing AI capabilities may be playing a role, making mass outreach more efficient and safer for Chinese intelligence officers.
"They can reach out to hundreds of thousands at a time, it's a less expensive proposition to try and get people to work for you," he said.
"We can't keep up with that type of onslaught."
Former US federal prosecutor Vikas Didwania, who has run cases involving Chinese intelligence operations for the US government, said LinkedIn was a "goldmine" for intelligence gathering.
"We have seen on LinkedIn, people post information about what kind of classified information they have access to, what kind of clearances that they have."
Didwania said information obtained from LinkedIn recruits may not be classified, or even useful, but could be part of a process of cultivating sources.
"Over the course of that relationship, you can start to push a little more."
Delicate balance for Australians working with China
In recent years, ASIO director-general Mike Burgess has warned the threat of foreign interference in Australia had reached an "extreme level" and was likely to intensify.
Csergo is the first person convicted of reckless foreign interference under the new threat environment.
During Csergo's trial, the court heard he did not disclose any confidential information. His reports were compiled from publicly available material.
At a sentencing hearing last month, District Court Judge Craig Smith described Csergo as "an otherwise decent man" who had committed "a most serious offence".
He sentenced him to three years and six months in jail.
Judge Smith said it was "fundamental and important" to deter people from becoming involved in activities that could harm Australia's national security.
For Australians working with China, however, the verdict has also redrawn the perilous line between legitimate work with a foreign entity and state-sponsored interference.
Some experts have noted a complicating factor is that China has about 2,000 think tanks, with varying and often opaque ties to the Communist Party and the government.
China's 2017 national intelligence law requires organisations and citizens to support national intelligence work. Some experts argue its practical reach can also affect foreign companies operating in China.
Mr Coyle said Australians working in China had to become adept at "walking and chewing gum".
Mr Didwania said efforts to counter China's spying operations needed to be balanced against the risk of creating a chilling effect.
"How do we differentiate between the great kinds of collaboration versus the collaboration that's really part of an MSS recruitment," he asked.
"It becomes a real challenge."

Construction costs rose by 25% over the year: will apartments and reconstruction become more expensive for Ukrainians?
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
21:15:46 EEST
03:15:46 KST

Construction costs rose by 25% over the year: will apartments and reconstruction become more expensive for Ukrainians?
Kyiv • UNN
In August, construction work became 25.4% more expensive year-on-year, while volumes for January–August fell by 9.9%. This is increasing pressure on housing prices and reconstruction.
In Ukraine, the rise in construction costs has accelerated significantly. According to the State Statistics Service of Ukraine (the State Statistics Service), in August 2026, construction prices increased by 25.4% compared with the same month last year. The construction of non-residential buildings and engineering structures became the most expensive.
This situation creates additional risks for developers, investors, and the implementation of state reconstruction projects. Rising construction costs may affect apartment prices in newly built developments, as well as the cost of repairs and the reconstruction of housing damaged by Russian attacks.
Why construction work is becoming more expensive faster than overall inflation, how real estate prices are changing, and whether Ukrainians will have to pay more for square meters was examined by UNN.
How construction prices have changed in Ukraine
According to data from the State Statistics Service published on October 12, the construction price index in August 2026 was 101.7% compared with July. This means that the cost of construction work increased by 1.7% in just one month. The increase was even more significant year on year. Compared with August 2025, construction became 25.4% more expensive. For comparison, the annual increase was 23.7% in July and 23.1% in June.
As we can see, prices in the sector are rising at an accelerating rate. Moreover, this is a general trend covering residential, non-residential, and engineering construction.
Which construction segments became the most expensive
Price increases were recorded in all major areas of construction. Over the year, the cost of work on the construction of non-residential buildings rose the most—by 26.4%. In engineering construction, prices increased by 26.1%, while in residential construction they rose by 21.5%. Over the month, prices for the construction of non-residential facilities increased by 2%, engineering structures by 1.6%, and residential buildings by 1.3%.
Among individual types of facilities, transport infrastructure construction became the most expensive in August, rising by 2.1%. The cost of work on the construction of pipelines, electronic communications network lines, and power transmission lines increased by 1.8%.
At the end of January–August 2026, prices for construction and installation work were generally 18% higher than during the corresponding period last year. In the residential segment, the increase was 15.5%; in the non-residential segment, 18.7%; and in the engineering segment, 18.4%.
For comparison, construction prices rose by 5.8% over the whole of 2025 and by 7.9% in 2024, which, according to the vast majority of analysts in the sector, indicates increased price pressure on an industry that simultaneously provides new construction, repairs, and the reconstruction of damaged infrastructure.
Why construction work is becoming more expensive
Construction price growth is significantly outpacing consumer inflation. In August 2026, annual inflation was 8.1%, while construction work became 25.4% more expensive.
Several factors may currently affect the cost of construction projects at the same time:
-  Construction materials. Changes in the cost of metal, cement, concrete, thermal insulation materials, and other resources affect the overall construction budget. 
-  Energy. Electricity and fuel are necessary for the production of materials, the operation of construction machinery, and the transportation of cargo. 
-  Logistics. War-related risks, damage to transport infrastructure, and more complicated supply routes may increase transportation costs. 
-  Labor costs. Higher wages and competition for skilled workers increase the expenses of contracting organizations. 
At the same time, the State Statistics Service did not specify exactly what share of the August price increase was attributable to each of these factors.
The situation in the labor market deserves special attention. According to OLX Jobs, the median salary offered by employers in vacancies in the "Construction and tiling work" category amounted to UAH 38,125 in July 2026. This was approximately 22% more than a year earlier.
For construction companies, the increase in all these costs — for personnel, materials, and the execution of works — entails the need to revise estimates. Such an upward revision may be particularly significant for long-term projects whose budgets were based on previous prices.
Why prices are rising while the volume of work is declining
Despite the substantial increase in costs, the construction sector has not demonstrated a corresponding increase in production volumes. According to the State Statistics Service, in January–August 2026, the output of construction products decreased by 9.9% compared with the same period last year. The value of construction products produced during this period amounted to UAH 156.5 billion.
The largest decline occurred in the construction of engineering structures — 13.7%. Residential construction decreased by 3.8%, while non-residential construction fell by 6.3%. In August, construction volumes were 3.7% lower than in August 2025. At the same time, compared with July, they increased by 12.9%.
Moreover, the situation differed across individual segments. Year on year, August residential construction volumes decreased by 2.3%, while engineering construction fell by 12.2%. By contrast, non-residential construction demonstrated growth of 9.8%.
Will apartments become more expensive for Ukrainians?
The rising cost of construction work creates the preconditions for further increases in housing prices on the primary market. However, the relationship between construction costs and the sale price of an apartment is not direct. A developer may partially pass the additional costs on to buyers, reduce its own profitability, or revise the project’s implementation timeline. But the extent to which the price per square meter will rise will depend on demand, competition, and the financial condition of the particular company.
The situation in Kyiv’s new-build market is illustrative here. According to LUN statistics, as of October 13, 2026, the median starting price per square meter in economy-class new-builds was about UAH 40,500. Over the year, it increased by just 2%. In the comfort class, a square meter cost approximately UAH 56,300, 17% more than a year earlier. In the business class, the median price was UAH 83,300, demonstrating annual growth of 12%. Thus, even within a single city, different real estate segments demonstrate different trends.
Another example is Dnipro, where, according to LUN data as of early October, the median starting price per square meter in economy-class new-builds decreased by 5% over the year, while in the comfort class it increased by 15%.
Therefore, a 25.4% increase in the cost of construction work does not automatically mean that buyers already have to pay a quarter more for apartments. However, persistently high construction costs may create additional pressure on prices in new projects. It is worth noting that the impact on the secondary market will be even less direct, as apartment prices there are largely determined by demand, the condition of the housing, and its location.
How rising construction costs will affect Ukraine’s reconstruction
Rising prices in the construction industry matter both to commercial developers and to state and local authorities implementing recovery projects. These include the reconstruction of damaged residential buildings, schools, hospitals, roads, bridges, heating and water-supply systems, and energy infrastructure.
If a project budget was prepared earlier but the actual costs of carrying out the work have increased, the estimate may need to be revised. With limited funding, this creates a risk of delays or the need to change the sequence in which the work is carried out. For example, if a community planned to restore several facilities within a specified budget, rising construction costs may reduce the number of works that can be financed within the initial budget.
The need to ensure transparency in spending remains an additional challenge. Amid significant price fluctuations, reviewing estimates, substantiating the cost of materials, and monitoring the use of budget funds become particularly important.
Construction has become more expensive in Ukraine: how this will affect people rebuilding their own homes
The rising cost of construction work may also affect households that are repairing damaged apartments or rebuilding private houses. In such cases, additional expenses arise due to changes in the prices of materials, equipment, delivery, and construction workers’ labor.
This issue is particularly sensitive for homeowners who use the state єВідновлення compensation program. According to the program’s official portal, compensation for damaged housing may amount to up to UAH 200,000 for minor repairs, up to UAH 350,000 for major repairs to an apartment, and up to UAH 500,000 for major repairs to a private house. The specific amount is determined according to an established procedure, depending on the nature of the damage. If the actual cost of the necessary work exceeds the approved compensation amount, owners may face the need to seek additional financing.
Therefore, when planning housing restoration, it is important to rely on up-to-date cost estimates and the actual cost of the specific work.
What to Expect from the Construction Market in the Near Future
Experts are currently unanimous: future price dynamics in the construction sector will depend primarily on the cost of materials and energy resources, the availability of qualified workers, logistics, the security situation, and financing opportunities. If contractors’ costs continue to rise, this will sustain pressure on the budgets of new projects and may gradually be reflected in housing prices. However, it is also worth remembering that limited demand does not always allow developers to pass additional costs on to buyers in full. Under such conditions, companies may restrain price increases, offer installment plans, or postpone the launch of new projects.
For state-led reconstruction, the key issue will remain the balance between the amount of available financing and the actual cost of the work. Currently, Ukraine’s construction industry is in a difficult situation: the cost of carrying out work is rising, while overall construction volumes are declining. For the economy, this creates an additional burden on investment and reconstruction projects. For Ukrainians, it poses the risk of a gradual increase in the costs of purchasing new housing and carrying out renovations.

Balsio launches Workspaces, bringing team chat and WhatsApp contacts into one app

2026-10-14
18:15:45 UTC
03:15:45 KST

The €1.7 million-backed European work messenger now allows small teams to manage and organise internal conversations while staying connected with external contacts, including through WhatsApp interoperability for users in the EEA.
Balsio, the European work messaging app formerly known as BirdyChat, has launched Workspaces, expanding from professional messaging into a shared communication environment for small teams.
The new feature gives teams a Slack-style way to organise conversations around projects, clients, business areas and other parts of their work. But unlike workplace communication platforms built primarily around conversations inside a company, Balsio is designed for teams that are also actively communicating with clients, candidates, freelancers, suppliers and other external contacts.
Interoperability addresses an existing workplace habit
A 2025 study by researchers at Ghent University and Boston University found that, among employees using consumer messaging apps for workplace group chats, 65% used WhatsApp, with nearly four in five checking their work-related chats every day. This illustrates how deeply professional communication can become embedded in personal messaging apps. Balsio was originally designed to address this problem by giving professionals a separate space for work conversations without cutting them off from the external contacts they already communicate with on WhatsApp.
Balsio’s own usage data now shows that around 30% of messages sent by its users go to WhatsApp contacts, suggesting that interoperability is becoming a meaningful part of how the app is used rather than simply a feature users try once.
“Team communication software has traditionally been built around internal comms, but that is only one part of how many small businesses actually work,” said Rolands Mesters, co-founder and CEO of Balsio. “For an agency, recruiter or consultancy, some of the most important conversations are with people outside the company. Balsio brings those conversations together, so teams don’t have to keep switching between apps and losing focus just to stay connected with the people they work with.”
Workspaces without the enterprise complexity
Within a Workspace, teams can create shared chats for different areas of work, functioning similarly to channels in established workplace communication platforms. The feature is designed primarily for small teams and non-technical users, with an emphasis on keeping communication straightforward rather than building another large enterprise collaboration suite.
Workspaces are used for internal team conversations, while external contacts remain in direct chats. Eligible WhatsApp contacts can continue communicating via WhatsApp rather than joining the Balsio workspace.
Alongside Workspaces, Balsio is now available as a Windows desktop app, adding to its existing mobile, Mac and web availability. The app is available in nine European languages.
About Balsio
Balsio is a European messaging app for professional communication, founded and developed in Latvia. Formerly known as BirdyChat, it launched across Europe in May 2026 after raising €1.7 million from European investors and attracting more than 50,000 waitlist sign-ups. The app is built for small teams and professionals who want to separate work conversations from personal messaging while staying connected to colleagues and external contacts.
Balsio was the first third-party messaging service to implement interoperability with WhatsApp under the EU’s Digital Markets Act. Balsio users in the EEA can exchange one-to-one messages with WhatsApp users who have enabled third-party chats, without requiring those contacts to leave WhatsApp.

SpaceX rocket launch causes stunning ‘jellyfish cloud’ visible off US east coast
Unknown

03:15:25 KST

A SpaceX rocket provided a stunning pre-dawn display over Florida as a massive, luminescent “jellyfish cloud” spread for miles, caused by an expanding plume of fuel exhaust crystalizing in the sky and reflecting sunlight off the frozen particles.
The phenomenon occurred shortly after Tuesday’s 6.33am ET launch of the Falcon 9 rocket carrying cargo to the International Space Station.
The timing of the blastoff, 48 minutes before sunrise at Florida’s Cape Canaveral space force station, provided a perfect example of the colorful effect only fully visible from Earth during dusk and dawn launches.
The rocket’s north-eastern trajectory over the Atlantic also allowed residents of eastern states from Georgia to New York to enjoy the spectacle.
Nasa posted photographs of the jellyfish cloud on X, the social media platform owned by SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk. Among the hundreds of replies were images taken by sky watchers across multiple states.
Those who missed Tuesday’s dazzling celestial show have another opportunity to view one next Monday, 19 October, when another SpaceX Falcon 9 is scheduled to lift off from the same space force station pad.
An hour-long launch window for the satellite-deployment mission opens at 6.30am ET, little more than a half hour before the 7.01am sunrise.

AI Came for Math. Now It’s Chasing the Rest of Science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:15:00 UTC
03:15:00 KST

Last week, I attended a talk at MIT by Neil Thompson, who studies progress in computing and artificial intelligence. Over the course of just half an hour, Thompson made a convincing case that several scientific fields are about to be upended by AI.
As mathematicians reel from the way AI is automating their field, Thompson’s latest study suggests that probability, statistics theory, economic theory, high-energy theory, gravitation and cosmology, and quantum physics may be next, thanks to the rapidly evolving capabilities of frontier models. Between mid-2024 and mid-2026, the study shows, the best AI models went from being able to correctly solve about 2 percent of theoretical problems in these fields to about 35 percent of such problems. And there are no signs that this progress will slow down.
“Within just a few years, we expect a lot of theory questions to be totally transformed in terms of AI's ability to do them,” says Thompson.
Broadly, Thompson’s lab digs into how advances in computer science impact society and affect innovation. This study—which Thompson conducted alongside Gabriel Manso, a PhD student, and Claudio Mayrink Verdun, a research scientist—took problems stated in research papers posted online between December 2025 and May 2026, and then tested whether different OpenAI models—o1, o3, GPT-5, GPT-5.1, GPT-5.4, and GPT-5.5—could solve them.
Crucially, solutions to these problems were found in papers published after the training cutoff for GPT-5.5 and preceding models. This means that the models they tested had to work out solutions for themselves, rather than relying on answers fed in as training data. (Such papers served as ground truth for testing the models’ solving skills.) The researchers also blocked internet access, which prevented the models they tested from looking up solutions online.
The areas covered by the study were limited—the trio focused on fields in which AI models could figure things out without needing to run simulations or experiments. But the work suggests that the kinds of shock waves currently being felt in math are likely to ripple out to other math- and theory-heavy areas of scientific inquiry.
Last month, OpenAI rocked the math world by announcing that an unreleased model had solved a long-standing, grand challenge in mathematics known as Navier-Stokes, which concerns equations that explain the behavior of fluid motion. The episode proved extra controversial after a mathematician at NYU— who had been working with another academic associated with Anthropic—accused OpenAI of gazumping them after learning of their progress.
OpenAI and others have since announced hundreds more solutions to longstanding math problems, triggering something of a crisis in the field. Some mathematicians have called for limits on the use of AI, warning that the process of solving problems is often as useful as having the final answer.
As with math, Thompson says we should expect advances in other areas to have both positive and negative effects. He notes that theoretical advances sometimes drive practical advances in science and suggests that greater use of AI may mean that more progress happens this way.
Some prominent AI researchers have already founded new labs focused on AI for science, and the big AI labs are all ramping up scientific research. These efforts explore how AI could be empowered to conduct real experiments alongside theoretical analysis. AI may mean that theorists are no longer required to solve key problems, but the researchers say that doesn’t mean that experts won’t be needed to make sense of solutions and to make sure they’re sound.
“We are still going to need people to generate good ideas to connect the dots,” says Manso. He adds that for very complex problems, it’s possible that AI might make mistakes. (OpenAI, in fact, withdrew several solutions in its latest dataset post-publication.) “We also need ways to verify what was done, because it's very easy for a model to tell you ‘this is the right answer,’ and when you look at the entire solution, you start to see maybe it is not.”
This is an edition of Will Knight’s AI Lab newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Ties with Washington quickly turned sour
The interview came amid escalating tensions between Kyiv and the US, following several months of successful cooperation.
For much of the past year, Trump avoided casting Russia as the aggressor and repeatedly pressured Kyiv to make concessions. His tone shifted over the summer, when he praised Zelensky as “courageous” and said he was “holding his own” against Russia, though he stopped short of saying Ukraine was winning.

Washington then stepped up its push to end the war.

On Oct. 9, Trump struck a diesel deal with Putin that eased US sanctions on Russian fuel, which 12 senators from both parties called “a betrayal of Ukraine.”
A day later, Trump criticized Zelensky and said it was “time for Ukraine to get a new president.”
The US President then announced an energy truce on Oct. 11 that neither Kyiv nor Moscow confirmed, insisting the two sides agreed “because I said, ‘You agree.’”
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, Russia launched 39 missiles and 128 drones at Ukraine, leaving at least 600,000 people without power, according to Zelensky’s estimates.
Although Ukraine abided by the abrupt ceasefire announcement, Russia continued striking Ukraine nationwide. On Wednesday, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that Trump’s energy truce was never defined, so Russia cannot be accused of breaking it.
Around the same time, SpaceX imposed unannounced speed limits on Starshield terminals used by Ukraine’s military, disrupting drone missions, presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said.
Ukraine has also received no early warning of incoming ballistic missiles for two nights in a row, following reports that US envoys threatened to cut intelligence sharing over Kyiv’s refinery strikes.
NATO and EU, as well as Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said they had seen no sign that sharing had stopped, although recent reports by other senior Ukrainian authorities appear to suggest otherwise.

Ukraine’s Warships Join Forces With Britain’s Powerful HMS Dauntless in Major Naval Drills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:13:08 UTC
03:13:08 KST

- Category
- World
Ukraine’s Warships Join Forces With Britain’s Powerful HMS Dauntless in Major Naval Drills
Five Ukrainian Navy minehunters completed a seven-day training exercise off the southern coast of England, conducting live-fire drills, underwater mine disposal operations, and coordinated maneuvers alongside the British Royal Navy destroyer HMS Dauntless.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Royal Navy on October 12, the training marked the final phase of Exercise Lion Protector, a multinational military exercise organized by the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF) to strengthen maritime security and protect critical infrastructure across northern Europe.
The Ukrainian vessels—Henichesk, Mariupol, Melitopol, Chernihiv, and Cherkasy—are currently stationed in Portsmouth as part of Britain’s ongoing military assistance to Ukraine.
Training operations took place in waters near Dorset, Hampshire, and the Isle of Wight, where Ukrainian crews practiced naval gunnery, formation sailing, and the detection and neutralization of underwater explosives.
One of the principal components involved the SeaFox mine-disposal system, a remotely operated underwater vehicle designed to identify and destroy naval mines.
The system uses sonar and onboard cameras to examine suspected explosive devices. Its mine-disposal variant carries an explosive charge, allowing operators to destroy identified threats remotely through a fiber-optic control connection.
The Ukrainian minehunters Chernihiv and Cherkasy conducted live SeaFox operations, successfully destroying simulated mine threats through controlled underwater explosions.
The exercise concluded in the eastern Solent, where all five Ukrainian vessels sailed in close formation with HMS Dauntless, a Type 45 air-defense destroyer. The maneuver tested the Ukrainian crews' ability to coordinate movements and operate safely alongside a significantly larger warship.
The naval training formed the fifth and final stage of Lion Protector, which ran from August through October 2026 and involved forces from the 10-member Joint Expeditionary Force. The training also supports Ukraine’s preparations for future mine-clearance operations in the Black Sea.
Earlier, Ukraine considered deploying its UK-based minehunters to help clear naval mines from the Strait of Hormuz as part of a potential British-French-led operation. The proposal emerged as Ukraine’s warships remained unable to enter the Black Sea due to restrictions under the Montreux Convention.

IDA Türkiye defense, aviation summit kicks off with focus on global expansion, civilian tech integration
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:12:41 UTC
03:12:41 KST

Fuat Kabakci and Emir Yildirim
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The IDA Türkiye Defense and Aviation Industrial Cooperation Days summit kicked off in Ankara on Wednesday, gathering global sector representatives to facilitate industry partnerships.
The event was organized by the Ostim Defense and Aviation Cluster (OSSA), with support from the Turkish National Defense Ministry and the Defense Industries Agency (SSB). Anadolu serves as its global communications partner.
Ibrahim Yarsan, chair of OSSA, said at the event’s opening that the event has been rebranded since its 2013 launch to reflect its expanding global mission.
He said the cluster currently includes 359 firms, most of them small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that form the key supply chain powering major defense firms.
“This event is not just a trade show but a business development gathering,” he said, noting that IDA has facilitated over 8,000 one-on-one business meetings over the years.
“We’re taking it to the next phase, with the first step being IDA Spain,” he added. “We want Turkish firms to work more closely with Spanish firms and we have a key collaboration that began in Valencia, where we will hold the event next year.”
Orhan Aydin, chair of the Ostim Organized Industrial Region, said that Türkiye’s successful domestic defense production model is now being adapted to civilian sectors.
Aydin said that enforcing domestic contribution requirements similar to the SSB’s model enhanced Turkish industries’ capabilities to produce homegrown light rail vehicles, metro cars and high-speed trains with the participation of defense contractors such as Aselsan.
Seyit Ardic, president of the Ankara Chamber of Industry, said that the technological know-how gained through innovations in artificial intelligence (AI), autonomous systems and advanced materials can be brought to the civilian economy to improve efficiency.
“We must look at the success of Turkish defense and benefit from the technological and efficiency gains it brought across the entire industrial sector,” he said.
He suggested establishing a healthcare industries directorate to transfer strategic know-how gained in the defense sector to help accelerate domestic production in healthcare.
He added that efforts are underway to integrate more firms from the machinery, electronics and software sectors into high-value defense projects.
Gursel Baran, president of the Ankara Chamber of Commerce, said that Türkiye’s defense industry reached a domestic content rate of 80% as of this year, while defense and aerospace exports rose from $248 million in 2002 to $11 billion as of August 2026.
He noted that some 4,000 firms active in the sector manage over 1,400 ongoing projects and employ 100,000 workers, while annual research and development (R&D) spending in the sector reached $3.5 billion.
“A technology developed in the defense industry is used in many fields, ranging from automotive to healthcare, from communications to energy, and from transportation to space exploration,” he said. “Defense industry investments are also invested in the country’s scientific knowledge, production capacity, skilled workforce, and economic future.”
The IDA Türkiye 2026 summit will conclude on Friday.

UN peacekeeping chief says talks on future of Lebanon mission must begin soon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
18:10:52 UTC
03:10:52 KST

UN peacekeeping chief says talks on future of Lebanon mission must begin soon
BEIRUT, Oct 14 - UN peacekeeping chief Jean-Pierre Lacroix on Wednesday urged the UN Security Council to begin negotiations on the future of peacekeepers deployed in Lebanon, as Beirut campaigns for an extension to the mandate set to expire at the end of this year.
A UN peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL has been deployed in southern Lebanon since 1978 but the Security Council last year ordered the mission to begin withdrawing at the end of 2026.
Since a new war erupted in March between Israel and Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah, the Lebanese government has campaigned for an extension to UNIFIL's mandate, citing its role in monitoring hostilities and facilitating aid deliveries to villages in Israeli-occupied zones.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres earlier this year presented proposals for a continued uniformed UN presence in Lebanon but no action has been taken yet, Lacroix told Reuters in Beirut.
"These proposals are on the table of the Security Council. There has been no movement in the Security Council until now, but I believe that the negotiations will begin ... shortly, in earnest," he said.
"I think it would be better to have a decision soon rather than later, right? Because that would clarify also the horizon for us, certainly from the more limited point of view of our own planning," he said.
FORCES OPERATE HOTLINE TO EASE TENSIONS
Diplomats say the US is not supportive of an extended mandate for UNIFIL, but Lacroix said it was important to focus on Lebanon’s request and that negotiations at the Security Council could yield a constructive outcome.
Some 7,500 UNIFIL peacekeepers are still deployed at about 50 positions in southern Lebanon, which would be expected to be handed over to Lebanese army troops if no new UN force is agreed.
But since most of those posts lie in territory now occupied by the Israeli military, it remains unclear how Lebanese soldiers could deploy to take over the positions.
Lacroix said that clarity on whether a new UN force would deploy to southern Lebanon would help UNIFIL make sure it does not "leave those positions prematurely before we know what could come next".
In addition to facilitating aid deliveries and monitoring hostilities, the force operates a hotline to ease any tensions between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries.
Lacroix said the deconfliction role was particularly crucial given the presence of Israeli troops in a self-declared security zone deep in Lebanese territory.
He said that Israeli and Lebanese troops in the same geographic area presented "the risk of escalation, the risk of incidents getting out of control" and that "there is a need for a third party to de-escalate". REUTERS

TIRANA — Student demonstrations in Tirana spiraled out of control Wednesday as protesters clashed with police for over 10 hours, setting buildings on fire, entering government institutions and looting.
While Albania has seen daily protests since the end of May over opposition to a Jared Kushner-linked resort in the south of the country, on Tuesday, students took to the streets over conditions in universities and dorms, the cost of living, and grievances over governance.
“The right to peaceful protest is a foundation of democracy and the state’s obligation to guarantee it. But violence cannot be a means of expressing dissatisfaction, nor should the use of force by the police exceed the limits of the law and proportionality,” President Bajram Begaj said in a public statement Wednesday. Advertisement
Starting outside the Ministry of Education on Wednesday morning, masked individuals threw stones, paving slabs, bottles and improvised pyrotechnics at the institution. They ripped up metal railings from the side of the road and used them to batter the iron gates of the building. After several hours, police with batons, tear gas guns, water cannons, and riot gear moved in, forcibly removing protesters and citizens from the vicinity.
Over the following hours, the situation escalated further as protestors set fire to benches, trees, and several buildings. They breached the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Justice, and the Ministry of Finance, damaged several private businesses and billboards, then moved to the main boulevard and encircled the prime minister’s office. They later broke into shopping centers and banks.
Economy Minister Delina Ibrahimaj condemned the “burning and destruction of institutional premises,” calling them “unacceptable acts.”
As of Wednesday evening, at least 40 demonstrators had been arrested and dozens of injuries had been reported by protestors, civilians, and the police. Several journalists reported being prevented from conducting their work by police who physically blocked them or seized their equipment. On Tuesday evening, one young man had his legs broken and required emergency surgery following an altercation with police.
The situation remains tense as protestors, mostly in masks, and police continue to battle it out on the city’s main boulevard, home to several parliament buildings, the president’s office, and the prime minister’s office.
The U.S. Embassy in Tirana warned its citizens to be vigilant and avoid areas impacted by the protest, noting that it could spread. Explosions and sirens continue to be heard throughout the city center on Wednesday evening.
Meanwhile, the delegation of the European Union to Albania stated it has taken note of allegations of excessive violence by police against protestors and journalists and expects the police to prioritize full investigations. The EU delegation also called for de-escalation from both sides.

How Trump's diesel deal with Russia will impact the US and Ukraine
October 14, 2026

And later Trump announced an allegedly agreed "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia. Kyiv said the idea had not been discussed with Ukraine, but that it was prepared to halt attacks on Russia's energy infrastructure if Moscow did the same.
'Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine'
Security expert Carlo Masala of the Bundeswehr University Munich said the developments showed that "Trump is not interested in supporting Ukraine at all, but that domestic US politics and relations with Russia are far more important to him than supporting Ukraine."
He added that the president aims to sway the outcome of the US midterm elections on November 3 through an agreement with Russia.
All seats in the House of Representatives and a regularly scheduled portion of the Senate will be contested in the midterm elections. Polls suggest that Trump's Republican Party could lose its majority in the House. A loss of the Republicans' Senate majority is also possible. Surveys indicate that American voters are unhappy with high fuel prices, and the US president apparently hopes to influence prices through diesel shipments from Russia.
Observers, however, consider Trump's hopes that Russian diesel shipments could affect prices in the US illusory.
"The volume is so small that it will have absolutely no effect on prices," Thomas Jäger of the University of Cologne told German public broadcaster ARD.
The political scientist added that shipments planned before the midterm elections would not even cover US diesel demand for a single day.
"The same applies to any shipments that may arrive afterward, if they materialize, they will have no effect on prices either," he said.
Trump's goal, Jäger said, is simply "the story" — showing voters that he is trying to solve a problem that matters to them.
'No concrete military benefits for Russia'
The main criticism from Kyiv and EU countries is that Russia will use the revenue from diesel sales to finance its war against Ukraine.
Carlo Masala, however, does not foresee the agreement with the US having "any concrete positive military effects" for Russia.
He points out that Washington had already temporarily suspended sanctions on Russian oil exports in March this year, shortly after the US and Israel launched attacks on Iran.
"Despite the money Russia has and has received, it has no military strategy for making further advances in the Donbas. The issue is more about the political impact and the symbolism of the Americans striking separate deals with the Russians at Ukraine's expense," the expert said.
Another cause for concern in Kyiv could be US threats to suspend intelligence sharing with Ukraine and block the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) program unless Ukraine halts its attacks on Russian oil refineries. Under the PURL program, European countries procure US weapons for Ukraine.
European alternatives to US intelligence
A possible US decision to stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine for strikes on Russian territory would have "dramatic" consequences for Kyiv, Masala said, but European intelligence, particularly from France, could help mitigate the impact.
While French intelligence is "not as comprehensive as American intelligence," the Ukrainian military already uses it to carry out strikes in Russia with French weapons systems.
As for the weapons European countries procure from the US for Ukraine under the PURL program, Masala noted that the program's most important component — interceptor missiles for air defense — has barely been available to Ukraine since the start of the war with Iran.
Support for Ukraine across both US parties
Ahead of the US midterm elections, experts point out that Ukraine enjoys broad support not only among Democrats but also among Republicans. One example is the bipartisan passage this summer of legislation to tighten US sanctions against Russia, known as the "Lindsey Graham Act," named after its Republican congressional sponsor, who has since died.
Signed by Trump in September, the law gives the president a broad range of tools. He can impose sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions and Russia's shadow fleet, which is used to circumvent restrictions on oil exports. He can also impose punitive tariffs on buyers of Russian energy products.
"Trump may resist, but political forces, particularly after the US midterms, may push the administration in the direction of trying to seek an end to the war by using the tools available," former US diplomat Daniel Fried told DW.
He added that the "Lindsey Graham Act" and the 2022 law banning US imports of Russian oil are "not absolute, but strong barriers against dumb ideas like a unilateral unrequited diesel deal with Russia."
Several Democratic and Republican senators cited this legislation in a joint statement in which they described the diesel deal with Russia as illegal, calling on the US government to "immediately correct" its decision.

The destruction of the logistics centre followed a series of attacks on the retailer’s stores throughout the week. Earlier, Russian forces virtually destroyed a new shopping centre in Chernihiv - a facility the company had painstakingly rebuilt, larger and more modern, after it was completely destroyed in 2022, according to press secretary Yulia Chundovets’s Facebook post. Shortly afterwards, a strike hit one of the chain’s oldest shopping centres in Dnipro, a site that had been in operation for almost 20 years and was of particular importance to local residents, she wrote.
Two Veterans With Prosthetic Legs Conquer 6,476-Meter Himalayan Peak in Tribute to Ukraine’s Defenders

Founded by Oleksandr and Halyna Hereha in 2003 with the opening of their first home improvement store in Kyiv, Epicentr K has grown into a major national retail network. The chain currently operates 72 shopping centers across Ukraine, with a total retail area of more than 2 million square meters (21.5 million square feet) and around 38,000 employees.
