Helsinki Celebrates Grazia Deledda 100 Years After Her Nobel Prize
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:53:22 CEST
02:53:22 KST

One hundred years after Grazia Deledda was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, a seminar hosted at the University of Helsinki traced the work and success in Finland of the Sardinian-born writer, the first and only Italian woman to receive this highest literary honor, and the second in the world after the Swedish author Selma Lagerlöf.
                                    
At the heart of the event—which inaugurated the program of initiatives in Helsinki for the 26th Week of the Italian Language in the World—was Deledda’s original poetic style, which allowed the self-taught author to establish herself among the great female voices of 20th-century Italian and European literature. Her popularity in Finland dates back to the 1920s, when the Nobel Prize and Jalmari Hahl’s translations introduced her novels to the public of the young Finnish nation.
                                    
Organized by the Helsinki committee of the Dante Alighieri Society, with the support of “La Dante - Roma” and in collaboration with the Italian Cultural Institute and the University of Helsinki, the seminar featured presentations by Professor Giovanni Capecchi, an associate professor of Italian literature at the University for Foreigners of Perugia, in dialogue with Professor Outi Merisalo, full professor of Romance philology at the University of Jyväskylä, and with linguist Professor Enrico Garavelli of the Department of Italian at the University of Helsinki.
                                    
“Grazia Deledda’s greatness lies in her extraordinary ability to transform the ancestral roots of her homeland’s civilization into a universal narrative capable of deeply resonating with the imagination of the Nordic peoples, thereby contributing significantly to the dialogue between Italian and Finnish cultures.” These were the words of the Italian Ambassador to Finland, Nicola Todaro Marescotti, as he kicked off the celebrations at the historic Italian Residence, which was acquired as part of the national heritage in 1926.

Israeli Bedouin infiltrated IDF as spy for Gaza terror group linked to Bibas murders

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

The Beersheba District Court on Wednesday sentenced Shahadeh Abu Alqian, a resident of an unrecognized Bedouin community in the Negev, to 24 1/2 years in prison after he was convicted under a plea agreement of assisting the enemy in wartime, terrorism offenses and weapons violations. Abu Alqian acted on behalf of a terrorist organization based in the Gaza Strip and even enlisted in the Israel Defense Forces on his handlers' instructions to gather intelligence. He also stole a weapon from an IDF soldier and later transferred weapons to the West Bank for the terrorist organization.
According to the amended indictment filed by attorney Hofit Kantrowitz of the Southern District Attorney's Office, Abu Alqian decided in 2019 to take revenge against Israel and harm its security after an administrative demolition order was issued for his father's home. In September of that year, he stole an M4 assault rifle, a magazine and a laser sight from an IDF soldier in the Yatir area, then buried them near his home.
Beginning in 2021, Abu Alqian contacted terrorist operatives in the Gaza Strip through social media and Telegram, expressed support for the struggle against Israel and sought to join Hamas' military wing. He later began operating on behalf of the terrorist organization Kataib al-Mujahideen, providing his handlers with information and photographs of IDF bases, train stations, government-owned companies and shopping centers. He also reported on the movements of soldiers and helicopters near his home.
In March 2022, an operative from the terrorist organization known as "Abu Suleiman" contacted him and asked to purchase weapons. Abu Alqian offered to sell him the rifle he had stolen from the IDF and insisted on delivering the weapons directly to the West Bank. In May 2022, he recruited his cousin to help him, and the two loaded an M4 rifle, thousands of rounds of ammunition and five hand grenades into a vehicle and drove to the West Bank. There, they left the weapons in a hiding place for the terrorist organization.
At the same time, acting on his handler's instructions, Abu Alqian enlisted in the IDF on May 22, 2022, intending to gather information from within the military about Bedouin soldiers, army bases and military positions and pass it to the terrorist organization. About eight days after enlisting, he was arrested by Israeli security forces, thwarting his activities.
In December 2025, Abu Alqian was convicted after admitting to the charges in an amended indictment as part of a plea agreement. The offenses included assisting the enemy in wartime, active membership in a terrorist organization, aggravated theft, weapons offenses involving carrying and transporting firearms and handling weapons for terrorist purposes.
During sentencing arguments, prosecutors sought a lengthy prison term, a suspended sentence and a substantial fine. They also emphasized the severity of Abu Alqian's ties to Mujahideen Brigades, which was involved in the murder of members of the Bibas family during the war that began with Hamas' October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.
A three-judge panel consisting of Daniel Ben Tolila, Tal Lahiani Shoham and Yoav Atar sentenced Abu Alqian to 24 1/2 years in prison, a suspended sentence and a fine of 25,000 shekels.
Kantrowitz, who prosecuted the case, said after the hearing: "This is an exceptionally serious case in which an Israeli citizen chose to act against his country, maintain ties with a terrorist organization and even enlist in the IDF on behalf of a terrorist organization, with the aim of gathering information from within the military and harming national security.
"It is worth noting that, alongside the criminal proceedings, the defendant's details were also forwarded to the interior minister for consideration of revoking his citizenship. The sentence reflects the severity of his actions, the harm to national security and the need for significant deterrence," she added.
"The prosecution will continue to pursue the full extent of the law against those who choose to act on behalf of and assist terrorist organizations, endangering the security of the state, its soldiers and its citizens."

Germany puts Ukrainian on trial over Nord Stream sabotage
Ukrainian citizen Serhii Kuznetsov went to trial in Hamburg on Oct. 14 on suspicion of involvement in the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines.
A series of explosions rocked the controversial Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines in September 2022, destroying three out of four key gas pipelines linking Russia and Germany via the Baltic Sea.
Kuznetsov, a former soldier, was accused of leading the sabotage group, involving six other people. German investigators claim that he commanded the yacht "Andromeda," from which a team of divers allegedly carried out the attack against the pipelines.

Another Ukrainian suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravliov, was detained in Croatia in August 2026 and awaits extradition. Zhuravliov was first detained in Poland in September 2025, but a Polish court refused to extradite him to Germany and instead released him a month later.
The Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never became operational, had long been a flashpoint in European energy politics.
Even before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, critics said it deepened Germany's dependence on Russian gas and undermined European energy security.

Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) has detained an 18-year-old man in Kyiv suspected of working for Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). According to investigators, he attempted to register 148 Starlink terminals for use by Russian forces.

The suspect remains in custody without the possibility of bail. If convicted, he faces life imprisonment and confiscation of property.

Hezbollah exploits EU terror distinction to launder money through human trafficking, JCFA claims
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:39:58 UTC
02:39:58 KST

Hezbollah has exploited the European Union’s failure to designate its political wing as a terrorist organization to launder money raised through human trafficking in South America and Africa, according to a new analysis published by the Jerusalem Center for Security and Foreign Affairs (JCFA).
Ella Rosenberg, a senior research fellow at the JCFA and a member of the Dvorah Forum, argued in her analysis that the EU’s failure to designate Hezbollah’s political wing has allowed the Iran-backed group to operate more freely in its fundraising activities.
She said the distinction between Hezbollah’s political and military wings has enabled proceeds from human trafficking in Latin America, Africa, and the Middle East to be laundered through front companies, charitable organizations, and trade networks in Europe.
Hezbollah's documented fundraising through crime
Although Hezbollah, as an Iranian proxy, receives much of its weaponry and resources from Tehran, it also maintains a documented criminal network that relies heavily on human trafficking to finance its activities.
Although Lebanon criminalized human trafficking in 2011 under Law 164, enforcement has frequently been undermined by state corruption and Hezbollah’s influence, Rosenberg argued. The law covers the sexual exploitation of women, yet reports dating back to 2016 have highlighted prostitution rings allegedly operated in cooperation with Hezbollah-affiliated officials.
The terrorist organization has reportedly protected these rings, using its influence to prevent state security agencies from intervening in their illicit activities in exchange for an unknown share of the profits.
According to Rosenberg, the protection money generated by the sex trafficking rings was reportedly directed toward Hezbollah’s social welfare programs and used to cover the living expenses of terrorists killed in action.
Outside Lebanon, Hezbollah-affiliated logistical hubs have become deeply entwined with human traffickers, she continued. In Latin America, particularly Argentina, Brazil, and Paraguay, cartel members have reportedly supported Hezbollah operatives.
Victims trapped in debt bondage are coerced into forced labor or illicit activities to repay exorbitant transit fees charged by Hezbollah-aligned facilitators. Reports also indicate significant cooperation with violent drug cartels, including Los Zetas, generating substantial proceeds that are subsequently laundered through trade-based mechanisms.
Questions over the origins of Hezbollah's funds
In West and Central Africa, Hezbollah has a “deep financial footprint,” Rosenberg wrote. Hezbollah operatives are said to systematically exploit both the Lebanese diaspora living in the region and local populations.
Rosenberg also described Hezbollah’s alleged involvement in trafficking blood diamonds and narcotics across Africa. The group can reportedly organize bulk-cash smuggling operations and use schemes involving real estate and vehicles to facilitate transactions that leave little trace and transfer funds to Beirut while circumventing sanctions.
The origins of Hezbollah’s funding have come under increased scrutiny in recent weeks after reports that the group received $200 million from Iran to support people displaced by its war with Israel. The US State Department dismissed the initial report as a fabrication. However, days after Reuters reported on the alleged transfer, Hezbollah announced financial assistance of up to $14,000 for displaced families.
The origins of the funds have seemingly caused some confusion in Beirut. Lebanese MP Fouad Makhzoumi said that there were “serious questions about the sources of these funds, how they were brought into Lebanon, and how they were transported and distributed outside official financial frameworks.”
“Assisting our affected people is a national duty, but their suffering cannot serve as a cover for parallel financial systems or a pretext for circumventing Lebanese laws…,” he said.
“There can be no sovereignty for a state that does not monopolize arms nor assert its authority over the movement of money. Nor can we accept a state within a state, neither militarily nor financially. Lebanon needs one state, one legitimate weapon, and a law applied to all without exception.”

Fire damages Starlink ground station in Bulgaria that is used in part by the Ukrainian military
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:38:54 UTC
02:38:54 KST

An unidentified group set fire to Starlink satellite communications antennas in Bulgaria. Ivaylo Mirchev, a local lawmaker from the Yes, Bulgaria! party, was the first to report the incident.
Mirchev said 11 of the site’s 17 Starlink antennas were damaged at the facility, which is located near the Bulgarian capital, Sofia. On his Facebook page, Mirchev published a video of the fire. The footage shows a facility resembling a Starlink ground station — a key piece of terrestrial infrastructure that links satellites in orbit with the internet network.
It is unclear exactly when the fire was set. The first post about the incident was published on the evening of Oct. 12.
Mirchev said two unidentified people set the station on fire. He accused Bulgarian authorities of keeping quiet about the incident.
“It is obvious that these antennas were not chosen as a target by chance, because they provide the main communications link with the satellites. In late September, similar Starlink antennas were also attacked in Poland. How did the Polish state respond? It informed citizens and the public and took swift action.”
The exact location of the incident was not initially disclosed. Mirchev said only that the fire occurred at a “secret facility” near Sofia. Surveillance footage he posted shows a distinctive antenna and a sign reading “Plana Earth Station.”
The site appears to be the Plana satellite communications station, located south of Sofia. Satellite imagery reviewed by The Insider shows spherical structures at the site characteristic of Starlink ground stations.
Bulgaria’s parliament held a hearing about the incident on Oct. 14. Prime Minister Rumen Radev confirmed the incident and said an investigation was underway, though he declined to comment on the details.
Plamen Tonchev, head of Bulgaria’s State Agency for National Security, said the Starlink antenna site had been scheduled for expansion and that part of the fencing had therefore been removed. That appears to have made it easier for the perpetrators to gain access to the facility.
The station also provides service used by the Ukrainian military.
It remains unclear who was behind the fire. Mirchev suggested Russian intelligence services could have been responsible, though there is currently no evidence to support that claim.
A similar incident occurred in Poland in late September. Two suspects in that arson attack were detained in Germany earlier this week. Polish authorities have said they suspect Russian intelligence services of organizing the attack.

The event is Tajikistan's primary international film festival. The festival is organized by the state institution Tojikfilm with support from the Government of Tajikistan and timed to coincide with Tajik Cinema Day, celebrated annually on October 16.
The third edition is scheduled for October 15 to 20, marking the 35th anniversary of Tajikistan's independence. The 2026 theme is "Celebrating True Art." The second edition, held October 15 to 20, 2025, screened more than 40 films from 15 countries under the theme "The History of the Development of the Tajik People."
The festival is part of the Cinema Development Program of the Republic of Tajikistan for 2023 to 2027, a state-backed initiative to strengthen the national film industry, support young creative talent, and expand international cooperation in filmmaking.

====================================================================================================

The Guardian view on Spain’s snap election: high stakes for Europe as Pedro Sánchez gambles again | Editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:25:08 UTC
02:25:08 KST

When it comes to risk-taking, Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, has a formidable track record. In 2018, the Socialist party leader swept to power by triggering a no-confidence vote that unexpectedly ousted his centre-right predecessor Mariano Rajoy. He held on to it against the odds after calling a snap election in 2023, at a time when the popularity of his own party had plummeted and the far right was on the rise.
As he endures another rocky period in office, Mr Sánchez has once more rolled the dice. Last week, he announced a snap poll for November after his minority government was blocked from passing measures to ease Spain’s chronic housing crisis. The eviction of 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal from her Madrid home sparked nationwide protests over soaring rents and prices. The outrage grew with news of her death last Wednesday. Mr Sánchez clearly hopes that campaigning on a national cause célèbre gives him a chance of winning a stronger progressive mandate next month.
It would be rash to bet against one of Europe’s great political survivors. But the wider context suggests an uphill struggle and a potentially disastrous outcome. The poll lead enjoyed by the conservative Partido Popular (PP) over the Socialist party is substantial, while the far-right Vox party is polling close to 20% – enough to make it an indispensable partner in a PP-led coalition.
Both parties have exploited public anger at a damaging wave of corruption allegations involving senior Socialist figures in Mr Sánchez’s inner circle. The recent border chaos in Ceuta, when an influx of tens of thousands of migrants temporarily overwhelmed the Spanish exclave, has also damaged the government’s reputation.
The stakes for Spain and the rest of Europe are alarmingly high. A PP-Vox government would hand national power to the far right for the first time since the return of democracy after Franco’s death. As well as making life more difficult for migrants and minorities, that could have significant and destabilising constitutional implications. One achievement of Mr Sánchez’s tenure has been the defusing of tensions in relation to the Catalan separatist movement, albeit through agreeing a controversial amnesty deal in exchange for parliamentary support. Vox’s ultranationalist programme includes incendiary proposals to outlaw regional governments and parties, and centralise power in Madrid.
More broadly, defeat for Mr Sánchez would end a period in which Spain has acted as a much-needed counterweight to the rightwards lurch in European politics. His Socialist-led government has resisted Fortress Europe rhetoric and made the necessary case for the benefits of migration, while presiding over an economy that has comfortably outperformed France and Germany. Madrid has also stood apart from the continental rush to prioritise defence at the expense of social spending, while forthrightly opposing Donald Trump’s reckless war in the Middle East and the conduct of Israel’s war in Gaza.
During his eight years in power, Mr Sánchez has proved a master at spotting political opportunities in the midst of crises. By going to the polls as the issue of affordable housing dominates political debate, he has given his party the chance to play to its traditional social democratic strengths. But against strong headwinds, political brinkmanship may not be enough this time round. European progressives can only wait and hope that the prime minister’s biggest gamble yet comes off.

Why your cat is the best philosopher
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:24:09 UTC
02:24:09 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
A young girl looks out of the classroom window. It’s the end of the day, and she’s bored. She spots a goldfinch land on the ground outside. It hops about and twitches for whatever reasons goldfinches do that, and then takes off. It swoops and dives around the playground, as if doing it all for the girl. Oh, how she would like to fly.
Humans have long looked to the animal kingdom for inspiration. We envy their skills and talents: flight, speed, strength, sociability, and so on. Religions almost always feature animal imagery, and flags will often blazon a lion, an eagle, a wolf — something bold or heroic. And philosophers are in on the game as well.
Even in the earliest historical records, people were exploring the philosophical side of animals. What can this animal teach me? What virtues does it embody? What can I learn about myself by studying this creature?
Joining in an ancient line is John Gray’s book Feline Philosophy. In the book, Gray examines what we can all learn about life from spending more time around cats. His conclusion: We should all be a bit more feline.
Mo the Philosophical Cat
A cat does not do philosophy, and that makes it a better philosopher than anyone else. Gray argues that for humans, philosophy acts as a kind of medicine. We are full of doubt and anxiety about how to live, yes, but most of all we are filled with the existential dread that comes from knowing that we will die.
To combat this, we create systems like religions and ideologies. We try to soothe our death-terror with stories. We become obsessed with “the good life,” “the examined life,” and “time well spent.” We have turned the word “happiness” into a multi-billion-dollar industry, but as a species we are no happier than we ever were. We are sick, craving a cure, but the medicine we have isn’t working.
Cats, though, have no such sickness. Imagine a cat called Mo. Mo does not search for meaning in her life, and she is not trying to become a better cat. She does not experience her life as a project that could fail, and she doesn’t wake up with the imagined burden of a thousand cats’ expectations.
Mo hunts, she sleeps, and she sits in the sunlight. When she suffers, she does not add to her suffering by asking why. She does not need to invent systems or stories because the world is as the world is. Gray’s point is not that Mo is wise; Mo wouldn’t write books even if she could. The point is that Mo is not sick. Humans are.
Be more cat
Gray starts his book by saying that we cannot become a cat. We can try to transfigure if we want, but you’re mostly running up against the immovable wall of cellular biology. Still, we can mimic a cat. We can do more cat things and try to see things like a cat. Gray leans on a point that Blaise Pascal makes about ritual and religion: If you do something enough, it changes you. If you force your mind a certain way, it stays like that.
As the philosopher Mark Vorobej pointed out, it’s not entirely clear why Gray has singled out cats. What’s true here of cats is true of dogs, birds, rats, squirrels, moles, badgers, or mongooses. Should we be more mongoose? It’s a fair critique, but it is somewhat pedantic. I’m sure Gray is not some feline exceptionalist. I take his book to be a lesson in intentionality. We can try to become more like a cat, rat, or badger, and I think he chose cats because they’re both cute and far more present in our lives. We see cats at home or on social media. All over social media. It’s just much easier to talk about something so available. Yes, he could have chosen dogs, but hey — take your pick.
So, how can we be more cat? Well, we need to distance ourselves from this sick and broken human way of seeing things. Stop seeing your lives in terms of some huge, overarching metanarrative. Don’t try to find meaning in your suffering. Stop seeing the world in terms of puzzles to solve. Don’t try to persuade other people to be more reasonable. Recognize that you are who you are, and it is what it is. Sometimes life just happens. So climb trees, play with a ball, sleep a lot more, and lie by the fire when things get cold and dark. Cherish life and think only as much as you want.
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.

British Premier Andy Burnham on Wednesday ruled out a partnership between the Labour Party and the Green Party following the Greens' controversial motion declaring that "Zionism is racism."
Burnham was asked during the Prime Minister's Questions whether he would rule out a pact with the Greens.
"Can I condemn the motion that was passed unequivocally. It is wrong. It is antisemitic, and this side of the House will have nothing to do with it," Burnham responded. "We cannot support a partnership with a party that holds a position that has recently been adopted."
The Green Party passed a motion defining Zionism as "a political ideology which called for the creation – and, now it exists, the continuity – of an ethnonationalist Jewish State in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population."
In response to the controversy, a Green Party spokesperson said, "The motion at the Green Party conference has provoked strong debate and there are different views on aspects of the motion, but for Andy Burnham to conflate criticism of Israel, with antisemitism is disappointing and wrong."
Green Party leader Zack Polanski also criticized Burnham's remarks, highlighting his position as the only Jewish leader of a political party.
"I'm the only Jewish leader of a political party. I'm a victim of antisemitism every day and I've made it clear Jewish people are welcome in my party," Polanski wrote on US social media company X. "You're a prime minister who arms a genocide and locks pensioners up for opposing it."
Polanski described Burnham's comments as a "dangerous and irresponsible blurring of challenging Israel and antisemitism," which he called "deeply revealing."
"A Labour government who apologized over their actions over Gaza is demonstrating that it was all performative," said Polanski. "Andy Burnham still stands with Israel whilst it kills innocent people."

Estonia Backs Finland’s Call for EU-Wide Ban on Russian Tourist Visas
Estonia has joined Finland’s call for the European Union to suspend tourist visas for Russian citizens and impose broader entry restrictions while Russia continues its war against Ukraine, Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna stated in a post on X on October 13.
Tsahkna was responding to Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen, who called on EU member states to support a letter to the European Commission seeking a complete ban on Russian tourist visas for the duration of Russia’s war.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia has also intensified sabotage, espionage, cyberattacks, and other hybrid operations across Europe since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In October, Ukraine’s military intelligence warned that Russian intelligence services were preparing further operations across EU and NATO countries aimed at undermining support for Ukraine and weakening allied capabilities.
“Estonia joins Finland’s call to suspend tourist visas for Russian citizens across the European Union,” Tsahkna wrote.
“As Russia continues its relentless assault on Ukraine, bombing cities, destroying civilian infrastructure, and killing innocent people, it is unacceptable that Russian citizens can still enjoy unrestricted leisure travel within the Schengen area,” he added.
Tsahkna argued that EU visa policy should reflect the scale of Russia’s aggression and called for further pressure on the Kremlin.
“Visa policy must reflect the gravity of Russia’s ongoing aggression. The EU should continue to strengthen pressure on the Kremlin through all available means,” he wrote.
The Estonian foreign minister also urged the EU to adopt the measures needed to establish what he described as “a comprehensive entry ban on Russian combatants.”
In her original post, Valtonen called for a complete EU-wide ban on Russian tourist visas, noting that Finland had already stopped issuing visas for non-essential travel to Russian citizens in 2022.
“We must stop issuing tourist visas for Russian citizens across the EU,” Valtonen wrote. “I am calling for a complete EU ban on Russian tourist visas for as long as Russia continues its war of aggression.”
“It is not right that Russians can travel to Europe to enjoy the way of life and freedoms here while their country bombs the homes of Ukrainians,” she added.
Valtonen also called for a Schengen visa ban targeting the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin’s inner circle, tighter restrictions on Russian athletes, and stronger enforcement of existing visa restrictions on Russian combatants.
Finland has maintained stricter visa rules for Russian citizens since 2022, and Valtonen is now seeking to extend that approach across the EU. Her proposal would require coordinated action by member states and the European Commission.
In September, US prosecutors charged five alleged members of a Russian intelligence network accused of recruiting operatives for assassinations, arson attacks, and other violent plots in the US and Europe. Investigators linked the network to planned operations in Lithuania and Prague, while stating that countries supporting Ukraine were among its targets.

Russia’s Newest Drones Are Still Full of Western Tech—Ukraine Just Put the Evidence on Display
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:22:54 UTC
02:22:54 KST

- Category
- World
Russia’s Newest Drones Are Still Full of Western Tech—Ukraine Just Put the Evidence on Display
Ukraine displayed a captured Russian Geran-2 drone and Western-made components recovered from Russian UAVs at the Warsaw Security Forum, highlighting how foreign technology continues to reach Russia’s weapons industry despite years of sanctions and export controls.
The exhibition was organized by Ukraine’s Independent Anti-Corruption Commission, or NAKO, with support from the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry, the organization told UNITED24 Media on October 14.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The display was intended to show that Russia’s dependence on Western technology has not disappeared as its weapons production expands. Experts continue to identify electronics from the US, Switzerland, Germany, the UK, Japan, and Taiwan inside Russian drones, including newer jet-powered models that Moscow began deploying on a much larger scale in 2026.
According to NAKO, the components cannot simply be explained as old inventories accumulated before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Investigators are finding relatively recent electronics, indicating that Russia continues to acquire restricted technology through sanctions-evasion networks and third countries.
“Why should Western countries reconsider their approach to sanctions policy? This is a matter of Ukraine’s survival and the security of the entire democratic world. And we want to raise it to the political level,” NAKO Executive Director Olena Tregub said.
NAKO also organized a panel at the Warsaw Security Forum focused on sanctions and export controls. Opening the discussion, former US presidential special envoy Gen. Keith Kellogg said Western technology remains one of the factors sustaining Russia’s war effort.
Every foreign component that reaches a Russian defense factory, he argued, represents a failure somewhere in the supply chain and raises questions about enforcement.
EU sanctions envoy David O’Sullivan acknowledged that there is no simple solution.
Russia continues obtaining Western components through third countries that are not required to follow EU sanctions, making cooperation with those governments increasingly important if Europe wants to close the remaining routes into Russia’s defense industry.
Russia’s dependence is also not limited to microelectronics. Its military-industrial complex still relies on imported raw materials, machine tools, and other industrial equipment needed to manufacture advanced weapons.
“Even despite its rich natural resources, Russia still purchases a great deal of raw materials abroad, including rare-earth metals. It also purchases machine tools and other equipment. We have to approach this problem comprehensively,” Ukraine’s Presidential Commissioner for Sanctions Policy Vladyslav Vlasiuk said.
The Warsaw Security Forum brings together government officials, international institutions, and security experts from roughly 90 countries each year.
Previously, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence Directorate revealed new details about Russia’s Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile, identifying 58 Russian companies involved in its production, 22 of which remain outside international sanctions.

SARAJEVO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The "Immediate Response 26" external evaluation exercise for declared units of the Armed Forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina (AFBiH) will be held on Oct. 19-23 at the Manjaca Main Training Ground, the Ministry of Defense of BiH said on Wednesday.
The exercise aims to assess and enhance the operational capabilities of AFBiH declared units and reevaluate their training and equipment levels in line with NATO standards, the ministry said.
A total of 881 AFBiH personnel will take part in the exercise, while an additional 330 personnel from the AFBiH and NATO's Allied Joint Force Command Naples will participate in the exercise directorate and evaluation structure.
Conducted under NATO's Operational Capabilities Concept Evaluation and Feedback, the exercise will assess seven areas, including preparation, planning and design, operations, sustainment, command, control and communications, force protection, and information flow.
The exercise will include computer-assisted simulation and field training with opposing forces to enhance the capabilities of AFBiH command structures and units in planning and conducting peace support operations.
The ministry described the exercise as the largest and most complex AFBiH exercise in 2026 in terms of scale, organizational complexity and international cooperation, and one of the key priorities for operational capability training and evaluation. ■

DR Congo Ebola outbreak slows as hotspots shift: Africa CDC

02:13:20 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) shows early signs of slowing, but new hotspots are complicating response efforts, authorities said Wednesday.
"For the past two weeks, we have seen the curve starting to decline," said Jean Kaseya, director-general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), at a press briefing in Kinshasa.
The outbreak's epicenter was gradually shifting from Ituri Province, where the epidemic is believed to have first emerged in the country's east, toward neighboring North Kivu Province, Kaseya noted.
Despite the encouraging trend, Kaseya stressed that significant gaps remain in disease surveillance and contact tracing, hampering efforts to break chains of transmission.
International pledges to support the Ebola response have reached 3.045 billion U.S. dollars, up from 1.656 billion dollars in June, figures presented by Kaseya showed. However, only 962.66 million dollars, or 31.6 percent of the total pledged, has been disbursed.
Kaseya also called for greater transparency in the use of the funds.
Declared on May 15, the outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo ebolavirus, is the deadliest ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak worldwide, after the epidemic that struck West Africa between 2014 and 2016.
According to the latest epidemiological report released Wednesday by Congolese health authorities, the DRC had recorded 9,144 confirmed cases, including 4,410 deaths, as of Oct. 12, representing a case fatality rate of 48.2 percent. ■

Roundup: Chinese green technologies revitalize South African cement plant
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
01:13:08 CST
02:13:08 KST

DURBAN, South Africa, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- In South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal Province, a cement plant that has operated for more than four decades is taking on a new look.
At the Simuma cement plant, acquired by Huaxin Building Materials Group Co., Ltd. in December 2023, aging equipment is being upgraded, waste heat is being turned into electricity, and electric mining trucks are replacing diesel ones. At the same time, local employees are gaining technical skills through training and hands-on exchanges with Chinese colleagues.
TARGETED UPGRADES
Simuma was previously a major production base of Natal Portland Cement (NPC), one of South Africa's established cement producers. While the plant had an established production system and distribution network, some equipment had been operating for decades, pushing up production costs and limiting efficiency and capacity.
After acquiring NPC, Huaxin made Simuma a key site for technological upgrading and capacity expansion.
"The operations here started in 1984, which is quite a while back. And so it was in dire need to be upgraded, modernized and made efficient," said Simuma Plant Manager Rory Govender. "When Huaxin took over the plant and started the expansion and upgrading, we were very excited. It is something that we wanted for a long time."
Rather than replacing the entire equipment of the plant, Huaxin has focused on targeted upgrades, making use of existing infrastructure while addressing key production bottlenecks.
"We are not simply taking a solution from China and applying it here. We are looking at the existing equipment and the actual conditions in South Africa and carrying out targeted upgrades," said Wang Dongdong, the plant's maintenance manager.
Key facilities, including the preheater tower and clinker cooler, have been upgraded, alongside improvements to the limestone quarry and other parts of the production line, Wang added.
According to Govender, daily clinker output from Kiln 2 has risen from about 1,500 tons to 4,000 tons, while Kiln 1, which has been operating for more than four decades, has increased from about 1,500 tons to 2,200 tons a day.
"The plant now has an annual clinker production capacity of about 1.8 million tons and annual cement production capacity of around 2.5 million tons," said Govender, adding that this gives the plant a much stronger ability to supply the cement market not only in KwaZulu-Natal, but across South Africa.
GREEN TRANSFORMATION
The production-line upgrades have been accompanied by changes in how the plant uses energy.
Cement production is an energy-intensive industrial process that generates substantial amounts of heat. At Simuma, waste heat that would otherwise be lost is now recovered and converted into electricity.
The waste heat recovery system, introduced as part of Huaxin's efforts to improve energy efficiency and reduce greenhouse gas emissions, has allowed the plant to generate part of its own power, Govender said.
"At the moment, around 30 percent of our power is generated internally," Govender said, adding that the system reduces the plant's dependence on the national electricity grid while improving energy efficiency and helping cut emissions.
The green transition has also reached the limestone quarry. Huaxin has introduced electric mining dump trucks using new-energy equipment technologies from China, gradually replacing conventional diesel-powered vehicles.
NPC is the first cement company in South Africa to use electric mining trucks at its quarry, said Govender. "Compared with traditional diesel trucks, the electric trucks reduce operating costs, noise and carbon emissions."
BUILDING SKILLS
The transformation is not only visible in machinery and production figures. It is also changing the skills and career paths of local employees.
Following the acquisition, Huaxin retained the plant's local management structure while sending Chinese technical specialists to work alongside local teams on the plant's expansion and upgrade. On-site guidance, job-specific training and day-to-day technical exchanges have become part of the process.
Eugene Bray, the plant's expansion project manager, said the training had strengthened local employees' technical capabilities and confidence.
The company's mentor-apprentice approach, introduced in 2024, pairs Chinese technical specialists with South African employees and provides opportunities for employees with potential to advance into technical and management positions, he added.
"Chinese experts are paired with local employees according to their different positions," said Lungelo Mthalane, who was paired with Wang as mentor. He has risen from frontline worker to deputy maintenance manager after six years at the plant.
Some local employees have also had opportunities to travel to China and to Huaxin's operations in Tanzania and Zambia for further training and exposure to different production and management practices, he added.
"Through continuous learning, our technical skills and our ability to solve problems ourselves have improved," Mthalane said.
GROWING TOGETHER
Huaxin's investment also offers the opportunity for the surrounding communities to grow together along with the company.
Bray said the expansion and upgrade project created about 800 temporary jobs, benefiting communities within five to 50 kilometers of the plant.
Local contractors and small businesses have also gained new opportunities through their involvement in the project, Bray said. "Local contractors are also able to work very hands-on with the Chinese skills and experience, and they gained from that."
The transformation of Simuma offers a glimpse of how existing industrial assets can be upgraded through new investment and technology rather than replaced entirely.
By combining existing infrastructure and local expertise with Chinese technology, management experience and green solutions, the project is improving productivity while creating opportunities for skills development and local businesses.
For South Africa, which is seeking to revitalize manufacturing and strengthen industrial competitiveness, the experience shows how technological upgrading can help renew traditional industries. ■

Feature: 84 years on, Doolittle Raiders' descendants and Chinese volunteer researchers honor wartime friendship
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-15
01:12:54 CST
02:12:54 KST

HANGZHOU, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Holding a photo frame embedded with a fragment of a bomber, Beverly Daigle wiped away tears. The piece of metal came from the B-25 flown by Crew No. 13 of the Doolittle Raid -- the plane her father, Sergeant Robert Bourgeois, served aboard as bombardier.
"Getting a piece of the plane has really touched me," said Daigle, standing beside Zheng Weiyong, vice president of the Quzhou Doolittle Historical Research Association, in whose home the emotional handover took place on Wednesday.
"I'm so thankful for the gentleman who found this. The history is very important. Our journey is very important on both sides."
On April 18, 1942, a group of 16 U.S. bombers carried out a surprise raid on Japan in retaliation for the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor. After the mission, 15 planes heading to a friendly airport in Quzhou in China's Zhejiang Province ran out of fuel and crashed in various localities in east China. Of the 75 airmen aboard, 64 were rescued by the Chinese people.
Their rescue came at a tremendous cost. Some locals were tortured or killed by the Japanese soldiers who came to hunt for the Americans. After the rescue, the airport in Quzhou was subjected to intense bombing by the Japanese, who also waged biological warfare by spreading cholera, plague and other diseases.
In China, the Doolittle story has long been regarded as a symbol of the friendship forged between the Chinese and American peoples during their joint fight against fascism.
All members of Crews No. 13 and No. 14 came down in east China's Jiangxi Province. With help from Chinese civilians and military personnel, they eventually regrouped in Quzhou and arrived safely at the home front. Daigle's father was one of them.
On Tuesday, Daigle and four other representatives of the Children of the Doolittle Raiders arrived in Quzhou.
At the air-raid shelter where her father had once rested, she fell silent. She reached out and touched the shelter's stone wall, where the names of two Doolittle Raiders remained legible after more than 80 years.
"Luckily, they're still here," she said, her fingers tracing the carvings.
Since World War II, and particularly since the 1990s, descendants of the Doolittle Raiders have visited Quzhou repeatedly to trace where their fathers once stayed. In Quzhou, a group of volunteer researchers has worked to preserve this history. They have dug through archives and trekked through mountains and villages to help the Doolittle Raiders' descendants retrace their fathers' footsteps.
Zheng Weiyong is one of them. In his study, a hand-drawn map, 1.2 meters high and 2.4 meters long, records about 20 years of his fieldwork, with more than 100 crash sites and villages where pilots landed marked on it.
Zheng has visited the United States four times at the invitation of surviving Doolittle Raiders and their families. "We need to tell the world clearly how the Chinese rescued them," he said. "If the Chinese don't dig into these good deeds, who will?"
The descendants stood before the map for a long time, trying to read from the markings where their fathers' planes fell, where parachutes drifted, and the difficult routes they took under the protection of Chinese civilians.
"You need to understand the geography of the entire flight route -- where these pilots jumped and where the planes landed," said John Thomas Johnson, son-in-law of John Hilger, commander of Crew No. 14. "Without that geographic information, you can't tell the full story."
The markings on the map helped bring the fragments home. This time, Zheng returned five pieces from Crews No. 13 and No. 14 to the descendants. The fragments are mounted in frames noting the discovery location, finder and date, along with the following text:
"This fragment witnessed the Sino-American joint fight against Japanese militarists. The bravery, humanitarianism and selflessness demonstrated by the American and Chinese people during the Doolittle Raid and the rescue operations will be eternally remembered by posterity."
In return, Johnson Kimberly Jane, granddaughter of commander John Hilger, presented a model plane to the association. The inscription said her grandfather owed his long and fulfilling life to the Chinese people's "courage, kindness, and sacrifice," and that his family would be "forever grateful."
John Thomas Johnson, a journalism professor at the University of San Francisco, said the full story of the Doolittle rescue owes much to the dedication and collaboration of many people in both countries.
He hopes to do more research on the selection, formation and training of the crews after returning to the United States to "add more detail to that aspect of the story."
Hugs were the most common gesture between the descendants and members of the Quzhou research association, suggesting that, after more than 80 years, the bond between the Chinese and American peoples is still going strong.
Before leaving, John Thomas Johnson wrote a line for the journey: "Friendship today and tomorrow." ■

After he developed a fever, fatigue and joint pain, the quarantine response team isolated him and collected clinical specimens for laboratory testing.
According to the Ministry of Health, diagnostic evaluations returned matching positive results from both the National Virology Reference Laboratory and the Kenya Medical Research Institute-CDC facility, confirming the infection.
"He is now in a designated treatment center where trained teams are giving him supportive care. Because he was already in quarantine, his illness was detected early," the ministry said in a statement issued in Nairobi.
"Early supportive care improves his chances of recovery, and isolating him at the first symptom limits the chance of passing the virus to others. This is the response working as designed," it added.
The latest case comes after Kenya confirmed on Oct. 6 its first case of Ebola linked to the ongoing outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).
The index case, a Kenyan citizen who had resided in the DRC for seven years, recently returned to the country via regional transit routes.
The World Health Organization said the individual had sought medical evaluation at healthcare facilities in the DRC before traveling by road on Oct. 2 through Beni to Kampala, Uganda.
On Oct. 3, he boarded a commercial flight operated by Jambojet to Nairobi, where he initially underwent standard health screening upon arrival at the airport. He was then transported by a family member to Nairobi Hospital, where attending medical personnel immediately placed him in isolation.
Despite receiving supportive care, the patient died on Oct. 5 and was buried the following day in accordance with the country's safe and dignified burial protocols for viral hemorrhagic fevers. ■

CAIRO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- For Egyptian young actor Omar Sherif, playing Seif in the Chinese film "Once Upon a Time in the Middle East" was more than an acting experience. It was an opportunity to draw attention to the suffering of children caught in war and remind the world that they deserve to live in peace and choose their own futures.
"When I read the script, what touched me the most was how it talked about children caught up in war and showed care for them," Sherif said in a recent interview with Xinhua.
At the time, the war in Gaza was raging, making the story particularly meaningful to him.
"I wanted to play this role to show people that children of war struggle just to survive and live their own lives," he said.
Against the backdrop of continuing conflicts across the Middle East, the film's message carries particular weight. Beyond the destruction and displacement that dominate news coverage, it draws attention to the ordinary needs of children whose lives have been disrupted by violence: food, safety, someone they can trust, and the freedom to decide who they want to become.
"I wish this film makes people care more about war children and stop seeing them as just numbers," he said.
In the film, Seif is a kind-hearted person who sometimes struggles with anger. For Sherif, however, the character's real strength lies not in his ability to fight, but in his capacity to control his anger and prevent it from destroying his future.
The character's needs, the actor said, are universal, transcending nationality, language and political boundaries. His Egyptian background helped him connect emotionally with the story of conflict in the Middle East, even though he had never personally experienced war in Egypt.
Much of his understanding of war came from television and social media. To portray Seif convincingly, he relied on the script and the director's guidance, drawing on his own emotional responses to the suffering he had witnessed from afar.
For Sherif, the film's most moving moment comes when Seif bids farewell to Xu Fu, a character who has become especially important to him.
Having lost his colleagues, Seif faces the departure of one of the few remaining connections in his life. The farewell captures the loneliness and emotional loss that accompany conflict, reminding audiences that the consequences of war extend far beyond physical destruction.
"It was the most emotional scene for me," Sherif recalled, adding that he cried so intensely that it took him some time to return to himself even after the director called "cut."
The experience also left a lasting impression on the young actor personally. After spending months working with the cast and crew in China, he found it difficult to say goodbye to the people with whom he had built close relationships and shared unforgettable memories.
His journey to China had begun long before the film. With Chinese roots on his father's side, he had grown up watching Chinese action films featuring actors such as Bruce Lee and Jackie Chan.
But his first visit to China came when he was barely a teenager, after he was selected for the role from a huge pool of young actors who auditioned for the film.
Preparing for the role required him to learn Chinese and cook in Egypt for three months before continuing his training in China.
"I thought it would be easy to speak Chinese, but it was so hard and required a lot of practice," he said.
Yet the difficulties also brought him closer to the film and the people behind it. Returning to Egypt, he felt that China was no longer simply a country he had known through movies, but a place associated with people and personal memories.
Sherif hopes Seif's story will resonate with audiences far beyond the screen. For him, the character's name carries a final, deeply personal message: Seif means "sword" in Arabic, but he would rather use his hands to cook than to fight.
"I want children to live their lives, become what they want to be and choose their own futures," he said. "I want them to live in peace." ■

Families of Iran's terror victims call on Pakistan to act against militants
TEHRAN — Families representing Iran's 23,000 victims of terrorism have sent an open letter to the government of Pakistan urging decisive action against terrorist groups operating along the southeastern border, following a recent escalation of attacks in Sistan and Baluchestan Province.
The letter, issued Tuesday by the Habilian Foundation, which represents families of terror victims in Iran, specifically names the Takfiri group Jaish al-Adl, now operating under the title People's Strugglers Front. It accuses the group of exploiting border conditions to move freely into Pakistan, reside and find shelter in some areas.
Such a sustained pattern, the families wrote, could not occur without the knowledge of some local and central officials in Pakistan, citing Pakistani media reports and interviews with members of the groups.
The letter frames the issue not only as political and human rights concern but as a matter of legal obligations. It cites the Island of Palmas arbitration of 1928 and the International Court of Justice ruling in the Corfu Channel case of 1949 on the duty of states not to knowingly allow their territory to be used against the rights of other states.
It also invokes U.N. Security Council Resolution 1373 (2001), adopted under Chapter VII and binding on all members under Article 25 of the U.N. Charter, which requires states to refrain from supporting terrorists, deny them safe haven, prevent use of territory against other states, bring perpetrators to justice and ensure effective border controls, as well as to exchange operational information and cooperate bilaterally. It further cites Resolution 1566 (2004) on full cooperation with victim states and the principle of extradite or prosecute.
The families also refer to the General Assembly's 1970 Friendly Relations Declaration, its 1994 Declaration on Measures to Eliminate Terrorism and its 2006 Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy, while distinguishing those instruments from binding Council decisions.
On bilateral frameworks, the letter cites the 1960 Iran-Pakistan border administration agreement, the 1960 extradition treaty noted in the April 24, 2024 joint statement, and that statement's pledges on cooperation against terrorism, hostage-taking and kidnapping.
The families, acknowledging these are duties of due diligence rather than absolute guarantees, say the continued, open movement of militants is incompatible with any reasonable standard of care. They call on Islamabad to dismantle safe havens, secure the border, share intelligence, prosecute or, where treaty conditions are met, extradite suspects, establish a joint security and judicial mechanism, issue a formal written response, and create a permanent channel to receive documents from victims' families and inform them of proceedings.
The letter stresses that Iran-Pakistan ties have been uniquely fraternal since Pakistan's independence and warns that terrorists seek to undermine that bond.

Kyiv • UNN
The President of the United States was ready to offer Ukraine expanded security guarantees. The talks reached an impasse over territorial concessions and a deal with Putin regarding diesel.
US President Donald Trump was ready to offer Ukraine expanded security guarantees as part of a new peace plan. However, the territorial issue brought the negotiations to a deadlock, UNN reports, citing The Telegraph.
In addition, further dialogue became impossible after the unexpected agreement between the American leader and Russian dictator vladimir putin on easing restrictions on the export of Russian diesel fuel
Details
According to the publication, on October 9, during six-hour negotiations in Miami, the US president’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed an updated plan to end the Russian-Ukrainian war with representatives of Ukraine and European countries. One of the key issues at the meeting was providing Kyiv with enhanced security guarantees that would prevent another Russian invasion.
In particular, the American side made it clear that Trump was prepared to consider more extensive security commitments than those discussed previously. This involved potentially expanding support for Ukraine beyond the patrolling of its airspace by American aircraft and the provision of satellite intelligence data. At the same time, official Washington expected that strengthened security guarantees would help persuade the Ukrainian side to agree to a compromise on the territories (in particular, the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the Donetsk and Luhansk regions) as part of a future peace agreement.
Ukrainian representatives generally viewed the discussion of additional guarantees positively. However, Kyiv and European capitals immediately began to fear that Ukraine would be asked to make territorial concessions to russia in exchange for support and guarantees.
The situation became more complicated after Trump announced an agreement with putin to ease US restrictions on the export of Russian diesel fuel.
According to the publication, the US president’s decision came as a surprise to some participants in the negotiation process. In particular, Björn Seibert, head of the office of the President of the European Commission, told European diplomats during a closed briefing that the announcement of the diesel deal had been unexpected for the meeting’s participants. As a result, the negotiations in Miami ended without final agreements on security guarantees and the terms for ending the war.
Context

According to Washington’s plan, economic concessions were intended to demonstrate to the kremlin the potential benefits of ending the war. However, the Ukrainian side was skeptical of this approach, as russia continues to put forward territorial demands and shows no readiness to end the hostilities.
What preceded this

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the agreement, calling it unfair, and stressed that easing sanctions against russia would be possible only if moscow took genuine steps toward ending the war.

Access to Public Lands Should Unite All Americans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:00:26 UTC
02:00:26 KST

Experiencing wild, open, and natural spaces is part of what it means to me to be American, and I know I'm not alone in that belief.
Our shared connection to nature crosses geography, generations, and political beliefs. From a neighborhood trail to a national park or a stretch of open desert, the outdoors gives us places to come together, find perspective, and experience something larger than ourselves.
At a time of growing loneliness, division, and stress, being outside can improve physical and mental well-being, strengthen community, and reconnect us with one another. For millions of Americans, public lands make that possible.
But the places that sustain that connection are under growing pressure due to decisions made by elected leaders. That is why, as we head into this year’s midterm election, voters must ask every candidate a simple question: How will you protect our public lands?
The answer will help determine what we leave future generations.
Consider Bears Ears National Monument in Utah. A presidential proclamation issued this summer reduced the monument’s boundaries from roughly 1.36 million acres to about 131,000, removing monument protections from more than 90% of the landscape. Bears Ears is a living cultural landscape and sacred ancestral homeland of deep significance to Tribal Nations.
Similar decisions are unfolding across the country. Congress rolled back protections for the Boundary Waters, opening the door to mining in its headwaters. The Trump Administration is also considering transferring a parcel of Yosemite National Park to a private developer. Pristine roadless backcountry may also be opened to development and extraction. These decisions will have lasting consequences.
There is room for honest debate about how public lands should be managed. Recreation, conservation, grazing, timber, energy development, and local economies all deserve consideration. Responsible stewardship requires balancing those interests while protecting the places that generations of Americans have worked to preserve.
That debate matters because public lands are not only a conservation legacy—they are also an economic engine.
Outdoor recreation generates $1.3 trillion in economic output and supports 5.2 million American jobs. Communities and businesses across the country depend on the forests, rivers, trails, parks, and open spaces that draw people outdoors.
The meaning runs deep. Public lands are among the few places in American life that connect all of us. The rock climber in Yosemite and the hunter in Montana may not share the same politics, but they share a stake in keeping these places healthy, accessible, and protected. Public lands remind us that our common ground is more than an idea—they’re real places beneath our feet.
The decisions made today will outlast this administration and this Congress. Once public lands are permanently altered, fragmented, or developed, there’s no going back.
One of the best ways to protect these places is to help connect more people to experience them. People protect what they know. They fight for places that become part of their lives. The future of our public lands will be decided by whether Americans still believe they are worth protecting, and whether we elect leaders who believe it too.
As candidates ask for our vote, we should ask where they stand. Look at the choices they have made. Look at the policies they support and listen carefully to their answers. For generations, Americans of every political persuasion have chosen to safeguard extraordinary places for everyone who would come after them. The forests, rivers, and mountains we enjoy today exist because of those choices.
Now, the choice is ours.
We can treat public lands as another political issue, or we can recognize them for what they are: places that make us healthier, bring us together, and connect us to something larger than ourselves.
This November, we must elect leaders who believe that public lands are worth protecting.

Can math stay human in the age of AI?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Can math stay human in the age of AI?
When AI companies value competition over collaboration, we may lose out on understanding
“Exponentially exploding,” mathematician Thomas Bloom told me by phone, describing the flood of new results in his field. Little did he know that hours later, OpenAI was going to post 722 mathematical manuscripts an unreleased AI model had produced.
The firehose of new work lends new urgency to the question: How is AI changing mathematical discovery? In their race for headline-grabbing breakthroughs, AI companies typically do not disclose their methods and data. That competition among AI companies threatens to overwhelm human collaboration and understanding.
This tension had been playing out in miniature on a website Bloom runs that tracks progress on more than 1,000 problems originally posed and collected by Paul Erdős, one of the 20th century’s most prolific mathematicians. Here, people used to collaborate to discuss open problems, or ones for which the best solution either hasn’t been found or isn’t known to the greater math community. But increasingly, visitors were competing to close open problems with AI proofs that they often didn’t understand. Bloom, a mathematician at the University of Manchester in England, doesn’t want to spend his days refereeing AI-generated work. So, soon after we spoke, and before he knew that OpenAI would be announcing its latest results, Bloom posted that he’d no longer tag problems as open or solved, and he also closed comments.
It’s definitely exciting that AI can tackle so many open problems so quickly. But can it help mathematicians understand the answers and build on them?
Just two days after OpenAI’s deluge of results, the peer-reviewed edition of a Google DeepMind study became public. First reported in a preprint earlier this year, it offers an inside look at how one AI system tackles open math problems. The system called AlphaProof Nexus solved 9 Erdős problems and made a number of other interesting mathematical advances, researchers report October 8 in Science.
The report includes a detailed description of how the results were obtained. Plus, human mathematicians vetted many of the proofs. That’s “quite different” from how OpenAI and Anthropic are handling their math results, Bloom says.
“The ultimate objective of any AI for math research,” says research scientist and study co-author Swarat Chaudhuri of Google DeepMind in London, should be “to advance mathematics as done by human mathematicians.”
A look inside an AI math machine
In the recently published study Chaudhuri and his colleagues tested different configurations of their system. To tackle a collection of 353 open Erdős problems, they used multiple agents powered by the Gemini language model. These could call on AlphaProof, an AI model specially trained to do math, and the inspiration for the name of the overall system, for difficult steps. The agents also relied on Lean, math software that identifies steps that remain unproven, to check their logic. The agents shared their work, circulating promising proof attempts and discarding ones that weren’t going well.
The team also tested a simpler setup on the nine problems the full system solved. Independent Gemini agents worked through proofs using Lean’s feedback, without sharing attempts or consulting AlphaProof. That setup solved all nine, too. It was cheaper—using fewer computing resources—than the full system on easy problems and more expensive on the two toughest ones. The team did not establish whether the simpler setup would solve any of the problems the full system had missed.
The fact that the simpler setup could solve the same nine problems as the full system surprised Chaudhuri. It suggests that increasingly capable language models can tackle research mathematics with relatively simple checking tools.
But computer-checking comes with a caveat. Lean checks only the statement it’s given, as it is written in its code. And a mathematical statement may be incorrectly translated to or from Lean code. An October 6 preprint shows why this translation matters. In the paper, the researchers pinpoint mismatches between parts of OpenAI’s written Navier–Stokes proof and its Lean counterpart. The mismatches do not mean the written proof is wrong, the team writes, but they note that a valid Lean proof does not automatically validate an AI-generated math paper.
That’s why the vetting human mathematicians did for the DeepMind publication is so important. “The human mathematician has to really think through the problem and set goals for the system,” Chaudhuri says. And even if the system failed to finish a proof, its checked steps helped mathematicians focus on the remaining gaps. “Math is ultimately a human art,” Chaudhuri says. “The system enhances the human user’s insights, and the human user is able to guide the system with new ideas.”
With math ability comes responsibility
The mathematical results that the AlphaProof Nexus system achieved are “not really at the top level of importance,” says Bloom, who wasn’t involved with the work. But that underscores the team’s more measured approach. Google DeepMind, he says, is “trying to be more responsible with the science,” while companies like OpenAI are using math to showcase their software. OpenAI’s papers and accompanying Lean proofs were entirely AI-generated, leaving it up to the math community to work out what’s useful or useless.
OpenAI says they worked with an independent advisory group to develop best practices on how to share their AI math results. But that group has said their advice was to not test unreleased AI models on advanced math, guidance the company clearly ignored.
The company’s fast-moving, competitive approach continues to alienate mathematicians such as Bryna Kra of Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill. She says the company made some improvements in their efforts to cite past literature. And she’s excited about AI’s potential to solve important problems in math. But there is widespread concern, she says, that AI models have accessed people’s unpublished work. “We had a healthy, collaborative, sharing culture that is being destroyed,” she says. “Now, people are wary of sharing their ideas.”
Not all mathematicians feel this way about AI. The technology is “making math more accessible,” says Andrew Turner, who wonders why a small group of mathematicians should get to decide how we solve problems. Turner, who studied math and physics and is Now CTO of the company Plasma AI, based in New York City thinks “math is becoming engineering.” And doing math with machines will allow people to “answer questions previously unfathomable.”
A few days after Bloom shut down the competition on his website, Plasma AI announced a new website to track progress on Erdős problems. They will welcome AI results.
Bloom doesn’t see math as a Silicon Valley–esque move-fast-and-break-things competition. I agree, and hope that curious people will continue to explore problems they care about, with AI helping rather than taking over. At the end of his post announcing the changes to his website, Bloom wrote something that makes me tear up every time I read it. I hope everyone, even the most enthusiastic AI users, can find the time for this type of work: “Be confused, be stuck, be inspired. Find a messy proof, then find a better one,” he wrote. “Get tired, get hungry, get into a flow state. Argue, laugh, give up, drink some coffee and attack it again. Be human. Let your brain be open.”

Ukrainian DELTA combat system tested during maritime operations at NATO exercise
Ukrainian military personnel have practiced maritime operations using the DELTA battlefield situational awareness system during international NATO exercises, transmitting data in accordance with Alliance standards.
Source: Ministry of Defence of Ukraine
Details: The combat system was tested at the annual REPMUS 2026 (Robotic Experimentation and Prototyping with Maritime Unmanned Systems) international exercise, led by the Portuguese Navy.
Unmanned aerial, surface and subsurface systems, as well as radars, were integrated into the Ukrainian combat system.
Quote: "During the exercise, partners and Allies practised the joint employment of unmanned aerial, surface, and subsurface systems and tested interoperability within multinational forces. It is the largest international exercise focused on employing unmanned systems in maritime operations."
Details: According to the Defence Ministry, the Ukrainian team, participating in the exercise for the third time, coordinated its activities through DELTA. In particular, the military and their allies practiced maritime operations, namely reconnaissance, maritime area monitoring, manoeuvring, and escort and simulated engagement exercises.
The Defence Ministry noted that assets transmitting telemetry in line with NATO STANAG 4817 had already been integrated into the Ukrainian combat system.
Quote: "During the exercise, Ukrainian service members also shared combat experience with partners, particularly in the employment of unmanned systems in the maritime domain."
Details: The DELTA system is a Ukrainian situational awareness platform that ensures the collection, processing and display of information regarding enemy and friendly forces in real time, creating a single digital picture of the battlefield. It is an ecosystem of digital military products, which notably includes the Army of Drones.Bonus ( e-points E-points are earned by Ukrainian units for confirmed strikes on Russian soldiers and equipment ) programme, where strikes on enemy targets carried out by units using UAVs are recorded and confirmed.
In early 2026, the Mission Control module was introduced into DELTA, recording data on mission execution, the employment of unmanned systems and the results of combat operations.
Background: Earlier, Ukrainska Pravda reported that all DELTA users had been granted access to an AI assistant to work within the interface.
