Turkey: Government raids, takes over top news channel
October 14, 2026
Turkish authorities took control of Halk TV on Wednesday — raiding the outlet's Istanbul studios, cutting all broadcasts and appointing a government trustee to oversee the company during an investigation into alleged corruption.
"Police raid at Halk TV headquarters! A trustee [manager] has been appointed, broadcasts have been halted," posted the popular news channel on X as police guarded the building, financial crimes agents searched offices and computers, and technicians cut live news channel feeds and YouTube broadcasts.
Footage posted online showed the moment the channel's live broadcast feed was cut — during an interview about a huge investment-fund scandal — and replaced with a classic Turkish film from 1973.
In a statement, the Istanbul Prosecutor's Office announced that Halk TV owner Cafer Mahiroglu is under investigation for "bribery, tender-rigging, and laundering of assets derived from crime."
Government trustees were installed at Halk TV and other companies owned by Mahiroglu.
In all, prosecutors say 17 detention warrants were issued, with 11 individuals taken into custody.
Mahiroglu, who lives abroad and is being sought by authorities, decried what he called "a dark day for Turkey" and blasted the allegations against him as "baseless" in a video posted on X. The pro-opposition broadcaster said seven of his relatives had been detained by authorities.
"The public's right to information is being seized for political reasons," he said. "Using the judiciary as a weapon is the greatest harm inflicted on Turkey."
Erdogan smothering all press dissent in Turkey
Press freedom groups and opposition parties joined Mahiroglu in condemning the government takeover as the latest step by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan to silence his critics.
Ozgur Ozel, leader of the main opposition New Party, said the raid was an abuse of government power.
Ozel called the raids "weak and cowardly," saying it was no coincidence they occurred just as jailed Erdogan opponent, Istanbul Mayor Ekrem Imamoglu, was set to make headlines delivering his defense in a sprawling graft trial.
"Raiding a television channel at dawn and appointing a trustee is an act only dictators would commit," Ozel wrote on X. "Unfortunately, this is the state to which they have reduced our country."
Press freedom has suffered dramatically during Erdogan's 22 years in power.
In the most recent Reporters Without Borders world press freedom index Turkey ranked 163 of 180 countries.
Similar pattern as Erdogan government eats up one media outlet after another
Ankara-based Contemporary Journalists Association decried the action against Halk TV, stating: "The appointment of a trustee at Halk TV and the suspension of its broadcast constitute a grave intervention against press freedom and freedom of expression. This decision, which disregards constitutional rights and the public's right to access information, is unacceptable."
Halk TV's takeover made it the fifth major Turkish news outlet forcefully put under trusteeship, following similar situations at Flash TV, Eko Turk, Haberturk and Tele1.
Veysel Ok, co-director of media-rights watchdog MLSA, said the intervention against Halk TV was "one of the most significant steps in the government's efforts to monopolize the flow of information."
"Halk TV's position as the most-watched news channel also reveals the real target of this intervention: Depriving the public of its right to access news from different sources," Ok told French news agency AFP.
"Defending press freedom means defending the public's right to learn the truth, hold the government to account and freely decide its own future."
The European Parliament's Turkey rapporteur Nacho Sanchez Amor criticized the move on X, saying the government was clearly "not happy with controlling 90% of media" and was instead "aiming for the 100%."
"Amidst detentions of journalists & broad online censorship, freedom of media & expression will soon be just a memory."

India: Release CJP leaders arrested after attempting peaceful protests at Jantar Mantar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:07:00 UTC
01:07:00 KST

The Delhi authorities must immediately release Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, who have been remanded to five days of judicial custody after trying to protest at Jantar Mantar on Tuesday. Their arrests, following the removal of the site’s designation as an authorized protest venue, raise serious concerns about shrinking space for peaceful protest and dissent in India.
According to a post on X by CJP’s legal head, Ratna Singh, Das and Ranka were remanded to judicial custody on Wednesday. Party member Ajinkya Shinde, who was also detained, was released on a personal bond of INR 5,000 (USD 55). A First Information Report (FIR) was registered against Das and Ranka under provisions relating to breach of bond, criminal trespass and disobedience of orders, among other charges. Shinde was also placed under preventive arrest before being released.
“The authorities cannot claim to protect the right to protest while denotifying established protest sites and arresting people who attempt to use them. Peaceful assemblies should not be limited to a few designated sites. Rather, public spaces must remain available for people to peacefully assemble, challenge those in power, demand accountability, and make their grievances heard. Authorities cannot use the criminal justice system to punish people for exercising their right to peaceful assembly. We call for the immediate release of the CJP leaders and an end to the crackdown on peaceful dissent,” said Aakar Patel, Chair of Board, Amnesty International India.
Public spaces must remain available for people to peacefully assemble, challenge those in power, demand accountability, and make their grievances heard
Aakar Patel, Chair of Board, Amnesty International India
Jantar Mantar has long provided people from all walks of life, including workers, students and activists, a platform to bring grievances directly to public attention. Its importance lies not only in its capacity to accommodate gatherings, but in its accessibility and proximity to political institutions like the Parliament house.
On 12 October, Delhi Police officially removed Jantar Mantar from the list of legal, permitted areas for public protests and demonstrations. According to the Delhi police, this was done after a Supreme Court direction concerning alternative protest venues. Authorities identified venues like Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground as alternatives. However, naming replacement venues does not adequately guarantee the effective exercise of the right to peaceful assembly. Their accessibility, location, and ability for protesters to assemble within sight and sound of their intended audience are essential considerations. Moreover, as the UN Human Rights Committee has emphasized, “peaceful assemblies may in principle be conducted in all spaces to which the public … should have access.”
Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b) of the Indian Constitution protects freedom of expression and the right to assemble peacefully and without arms. Although reasonable restrictions are permitted on specified grounds, including public order, authorities do not have unrestricted discretion to exclude peaceful demonstrations from public spaces.
In Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018), the Supreme Court recognized the need to balance protesters’ rights with the interests of residents and other users of public space. Regulation must seek to accommodate competing interests, not impose arbitrary or blanket prohibitions.
International human rights law reinforces these protections. Articles 19 and 21 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) safeguard the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly.
The prohibition of protests at Jantar Mantar comes amid a broader police crackdown on demonstrations over electoral-roll revisions and demands for accountability from Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
Over the weekend of 10–11 October, police detained thousands of protesters and imposed restrictions affecting access to protest sites, public transport, and mobile internet, according to media reports and human rights organizations. Demonstrations were prevented from proceeding freely, with people detained as they attempted to gather in public spaces, and some detained from their homes even before they left for protest sites. Protesters who were travelling from Gujarat and Maharashtra to Delhi to participate in the protests were also detained by the authorities and prevented from continuing their journey to the capital.
Journalists covering the protests reported detention, physical mistreatment, confiscation of equipment, and obstruction despite displaying press credentials. Women journalists covering the protests have alleged that they were sexually harassed by Delhi Police. Lawyers seeking access to detainees faced also faced restrictions. These incidents raise concerns about journalists’ ability to document police conduct and lawyers’ ability to safeguard detainees’ rights.
“When protesters cannot assemble, journalists are harassed and cannot report freely, and lawyers face obstacles in reaching detainees, the entire system of public accountability suffers. By closing Jantar Mantar and restricting peaceful gatherings, the authorities are making dissent increasingly difficult to exercise. A right that exists only on paper, while people are denied places to assemble and face arrest when they try, is a right hollowed out in practice. These restrictions display strong authoritarian tendencies and risk turning public spaces into places where dissent is unwelcome,” said Aakar Patel.
Background
CJP, a youth-led movement that grew out of online satire, emerged as a protest force in June 2026, mobilizing students and young people against alleged examination irregularities and paper leaks. Its demonstrations at Jantar Mantar demanded the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
The current crackdown on peaceful protests was not only confined to Delhi. Police detained protesters in Mumbai and Bengaluru.
In Bengaluru, on 12 October, police detained at least 100 people who were marching towards the Karnataka Chief Electoral Officer’s office. In Mumbai, police detained more than 600 people on 10 October as they tried to gather at August Kranti Maidan.

Le Pen and Melenchon gain momentum ahead of French 2027 election, poll shows
PARIS, Oct 14 - French far-right leader Marine Le Pen and hard-left rival Jean-Luc Melenchon are gaining momentum ahead of next year's presidential election, a poll showed on Wednesday, with political polarisation widening as Emmanuel Macron's era draws to a close.
• Le Pen would top the first-round vote with either 37% or 38% depending on the scenarios tested by pollster Odoxa in a survey carried out among 12,000 people between September 24 and October 7.
• Melenchon would come second with 18% or 18.5% in each of the two scenarios.
• Both were tested against one centrist candidate comprising either Edouard Philippe or Gabriel Attal, both of whom are former Prime Ministers of Emmanuel Macron. Philippe is seen getting 17% of the votes, while Attal would get only 11%.
• Le Pen is seen beating Melenchon easily in a run-off and also winning, albeit with a more narrow margin, if she faced Philippe.
• The growing unpopularity of Macron, as he comes to the end of his two terms as president, has hollowed out France's centrist political ground.
• Melenchon has already run three times for president in 2012, 2017 and 2022 but has never managed to reach the second round. Le Pen has also run these same three times. She made it to the run-off in 2017 and 2022, but lost to Macron.

Pilgrims caught up in Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia

Pilgrims caught up in Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia
RIYADH - Pilgrims in Saudi Arabia to visit Islam’s holiest sites may not have anticipated being caught up in an air war, but some experienced an attack by Yemen’s Houthis first hand and others have been forced to change their plans.
Footage of the massive blast that killed 13 people and wounded 300 in a Riyadh airport departure terminal struck by a Houthi missile on Oct 10 showed many passengers attired in the simple white clothes of Muslim pilgrims travelling to Mecca.
Saudi media reported that a Bangladeshi imam leading a group of dozens of pilgrims was killed and others wounded in the attack.
While the Houthis have promised not to attack either Mecca or Medina, the two holiest places in Islam that attract millions of pilgrims each year, they are targeting other Saudi airports in what they call retaliation for Saudi attacks on them.
“I feel deeply worried for my family and myself,” said Fadi Anwar, a Jordanian living in Mecca sitting in the courtyard of the main mosque in Mecca who was wearing the pilgrim’s robes. “We constantly receive warnings (phone alerts from the authorities) and it causes us great anxiety.”
Saudi officials have said the kingdom is safe and that the security of visitors is valued above all else, an offer of reassurance even as Western governments have warned against using most Saudi airports.
Pilgrims visit Mecca throughout the year
Although most international pilgrims fly directly into Medina or Jeddah airports, many others travel via Saudi Arabia’s other main air hubs, including the many pilgrims who already live in the kingdom.
Al Amin Hassan Mohammed from Sudan, who was visiting Saudi-based family members before a pilgrimage to Mecca, said he had been in Riyadh during the Oct 10 attack, which sent him and neighbours onto the street.
“We were tired and worried. We went out of the houses and we talked with each other,” he said.
Mohammed, who has a married daughter in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province city of Dammam, close to Dhahran where the Houthis targeted a Saudi Aramco building on Oct 13, has made the pilgrimage to Mecca before.
Like Anwar and others visiting the holy city now, outside of the annual hajj that is a requirement for all able-bodied Muslims in their lifetime, he is making a lesser pilgrimage known as umrah that can take place at any time of year.
The vast courtyard of the enormous main mosque in Mecca was a swirl of pilgrims in their white robes on Oct 13, as they circled the black cube of the Kaaba, the point towards which all Muslims face to pray.
Mecca draws millions of people each year, both during hajj and for umrah, from both inside Saudi Arabia and overseas, and the attacks have made some nervous.
“May God keep this away from us and from all Muslims, both in Saudi Arabia and elsewhere,” Anwar said.
Travel disruption hits businesses, embassies and tourism
The strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-allied Houthis, resulting from the reignition of Yemen’s civil war as a spillover from the US-Iran conflict, have caused Saudi Arabia to ground many flights.
Schools in Riyadh have been switched to online learning this week and some offices have told staff to work from home.
The disruption has been particularly acute for those trying to travel, a group that includes pilgrims, business figures attending Saudi Arabia’s many high-profile conferences, Saudi tourists wishing to go on holiday and foreign residents wanting to fly home.
“We’ve had some trips postponed. We had friends who were travelling; it was delayed, they didn’t travel,” said Mohammed. His friends had been planning to fly via Riyadh but in the end they took a boat back to Sudan from Jeddah, he said.
Many people who had planned to fly from Riyadh are reviewing their options, with some making the four-hour trip to Bahrain, the seven-hour drive to Qatar or the 10-hour drive to Dubai.
A senior executive Reuters spoke to on Oct 14 was busy arranging transport for foreign employees, sending them by road to Doha in Qatar for onward flights.
A diplomat in Riyadh said several embassies had also used Doha for trips to and from Saudi Arabia over recent days, including for staff temporarily leaving with their families.
The representative of a company organising transport to Doha and Dubai said fares to those destinations had doubled.
Being prepared to pay is no guarantee of travel - in the early phases of the US-Iran war, Iranian fire grounded many flights around the Gulf and that direct conflict may erupt again with US President Donald Trump threatening to resume strikes. REUTERS

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:05:22 UTC
01:05:22 KST

Palantir and the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, have called off their legal fight over claims the Labour mayor was blocking the US tech company from signing a contract with the Metropolitan police because of its values and ethics.
Palantir and the mayor’s office for policing and crime (Mopac) announced on Wednesday they had withdrawn allegations against each other, heading off a high court trial scheduled for January.
Palantir sued Mopac in June after Khan stepped in to block it from awarding Palantir a two-year, £50m deal for Scotland Yard to use AI to process intelligence in criminal investigations in a system called unified operational analytics (UOA), citing a “clear and serious breach” of procurement rules.
With Palantir also working for the Israeli military and for the Trump administration in its immigration crackdown, Khan has previously said Londoners only wanted to see public money being paid to companies that “share the values of our city”.
Louis Mosley, who heads Palantir in the UK and Europe, responded by accusing Khan of politicising procurement and said he was “putting politics above public safety”. He said: “What Londoners value is not being mugged, not being raped by a serving police officer.”
The agreement to drop the claims against each other comes a month after Palantir hired Tom Watson, the former Labour party deputy leader, as a full-time lobbyist. The firm was concerned that if public authorities were able to block it from winning contracts due to objections over the values of its senior leadership, it would undermine its ability to operate in the UK.
Palantir is facing a battle to retain its £330m NHS medical data contract amid a vociferous campaign from parts of the public and some MPs for it to be replaced by a less controversial company.
Palantir and Mopac said in a joint statement that Mopac’s decision in May to block the contract “was not based on Palantir’s values or ethics or any wider reporting about the company”.
“Mopac recognises Palantir’s concerns that media reporting of a statement from the mayor’s spokesperson before the decision was taken could have incorrectly created the impression that an assessment of the company’s values had been a factor in that decision,” it said.
“Mopac’s consideration was based upon its statutory role of examining spend proposals, against the appropriate legal tests and the relevant guidance on procurement, governance, affordability and ensuring value for money for Londoners.”
Khan said: “London is the technology capital of Europe, and I am proud that leading software firms choose the city as their home. Palantir makes a significant contribution to jobs and investment in the capital, employing a large number of Londoners whose services have been procured legally by organisations across the UK and beyond.”
Watson said: “The mayor and his team have recognised their actions could have created the impression that the decision to block the UOA contract was based on Palantir’s values. I’m very pleased that they have today corrected any such impression, and that even in the face of extreme provocation from highly organised pressure groups, decisions about deploying technology can still be made on their merits and in the public interest.”
A new procurement process for the £50m police tech deal is under way and Mopac has agreed to treat Palantir “fairly and equally” if it bids, as expected. Equally, Mopac is not bound to agree to Palantir’s appointment.
Each side is covering its own legal costs, no admissions of liability are made and no damages have been paid.

Norway to provide over US$78m in additional economic aid to Ukraine
Norway will provide Ukraine with an additional 750 million Norwegian kroner (about US$78.5 million) to support the functioning of the state amid the full-scale war.
Source: European Pravda, citing a statement by Norwegian International Development Minister Åsmund Aukrust in an interview with VG
Details: Aukrust stated that the funds will help finance the salaries of public sector workers, social payments and infrastructure recovery.
The funding will be directed to the World Bank's SPUR 2 programme to support Ukraine. The Norwegian contribution will increase the amount of credit funds available to Ukraine.
Aukrust noted that every Norwegian krone contributed could secure approximately three kroner in loan financing for Ukraine. Thus, 750 million kroner (about US$78.5 million) could help raise over 2 billion kroner (about US$209 million) in loans.
The mechanism involves Norway providing the initial funding, with the World Bank using its credit capacity to raise funds on the financial markets, which are subsequently provided to Ukraine as loans.
The minister added that the war is being fought on the front line, but it is also fought every day by ensuring the functioning of society, guaranteeing that children can go to school, and ensuring that nurses treating the wounded receive their salaries.
Background:
- At the end of September, it emerged that Norway was increasing its financial support for humanitarian activities regarding Ukrainian children abducted by Russia, arbitrarily detained civilians and prisoners of war, announcing a new contribution of 25 million kroner (€2.3 million).
- It was also reported that Norway will allocate €90 million to the Ukraine Facility programme to promote reforms in the anti-corruption and energy sectors.

Palestine said Wednesday that Colombia’s opening of an embassy in West Jerusalem violates international law and UN resolutions.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry said the opening constituted “a flagrant violation of international law and relevant UN resolutions, and an assault on the Palestinian people and their just and legitimate national rights.”
It stressed that all measures and decisions to change the legal and historical status of Jerusalem are “null and void and have no legal effect.”
It said that “opening an embassy to Israel in occupied Jerusalem violates international legitimacy resolutions, particularly UN Security Council Resolutions 476 and 478.”
The two resolutions that were adopted in 1980 affirm the illegality and invalidity of Israeli measures intended to alter the character and legal status of Jerusalem, amid Israel’s enactment of a law annexing East Jerusalem.
The ministry said Colombia’s move also “undermines the international consensus on the city’s legal status and infringes on the Palestinian people’s inalienable rights.”
It warned that the step encourages Israel to continue its “colonial policies and attempts to impose illegal realities on the ground.”
In addition to Colombia, the US, Guatemala, Honduras, Kosovo, Papua New Guinea, Paraguay, Fiji, Nauru and Somalia’s breakaway region have moved their embassies to West Jerusalem or opened embassies in the city, a move that runs counter to international resolutions concerning the status of Jerusalem.
The Palestinian Foreign Ministry urged Colombia to comply with international law and respect relevant UN resolutions, calling on it to “reverse this step to preserve prospects for achieving a just and comprehensive peace.”
Earlier Wednesday, Colombia opened the embassy in West Jerusalem. The move follows the restoration of its diplomatic relations with Israel in August, after Colombia severed ties with Tel Aviv in May 2024 under a previous government.
Jerusalem remains at the heart of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and is widely regarded as one of its most sensitive issues.
While Israel claims the entire city as its capital, Palestinians view East Jerusalem, occupied by Israel since 1967, as the capital of a future Palestinian state, in line with longstanding international consensus and UN resolutions.

Hidden for 7,000 years: the enigmatic skeleton from Großköllnbach
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:51:07 UTC
00:51:07 KST

Was the Stone Age teenager laid to rest in a twisted pose on purpose, or did the body slip in a sloping grave?
Sometimes a dark discolouration in the soil is enough to open a window onto a long-forgotten world. In the Lower Bavarian village of Großköllnbach (Dingolfing-Landau district) just such a clue led to a discovery that is posing new questions for archaeologists: in a pit they uncovered the remains of a person who lived around 7,000 years ago.
But it is not just the great age of the find that makes it remarkable. Above all, it is the unusual position of the skeleton: unlike the burials that were customary at the time, the body lies in a striking, twisted posture. The condition of the cervical spine is also puzzling researchers.
A burial that breaks the mould
The discovery came to light during archaeological investigations in the future Steigäcker IV development area. The excavation team had been examining the site for five weeks when what initially appeared to be a nondescript change in soil colour turned out to be a pit containing human bones.
For district archaeologist Dr Florian Eibl, it is above all the type of burial that is unusual. The people of the Linear Pottery culture (Linienbandkeramik), one of the earliest farming cultures in Central Europe, often buried their dead in crouched burials. The deceased were laid on their side with their legs drawn up, in a posture resembling a sleeping person.
In Großköllnbach, however, the picture is different: the dead person's right leg was bent up extremely sharply, while the left leg was angled outwards. This posture clearly departs from the usual burial practices.
The pit itself also raises questions. Its base was uneven and sloping. In the archaeologist's view, the body may have slipped down the incline after being laid to rest. Individual bones could therefore have shifted or been pressed into the soft clay.
Was the unusual posture therefore intentional? Or did it only arise because of the conditions in the grave?
A young person with striking bones
One thing is clear from the initial examinations: the dead person was an adolescent, as shown by the growth plates on the bones, which had not yet completely fused.
Bones can also provide clues to diseases, injuries and physical strain. The experts are currently paying particular attention to the cervical spine, where a pronounced deformation can be seen. Whether this is due to an illness or a physical peculiarity during life, or only arose because of the position in the grave and after death, still has to be clarified.
A detailed anthropological analysis is expected to provide further clues.
Discovery among clay ovens and age-old longhouses
The skeleton is not the only remarkable find on the site. The excavations are bringing to light an extensive settlement landscape of the Linear Pottery culture. This culture emerged in the 6th millennium BC and marks the spread of the first farming way of life across large parts of Central Europe.
After five weeks of excavation the archaeologists had documented around 150 features. The traces of three large longhouses can be seen in the ground, although at most two of them are likely to have stood at the same time.
Particularly revealing are several preserved hearths and cooking areas, including domed clay ovens whose floors were insulated with tightly packed pebbles. This is where food was cooked, grain was processed and, in all likelihood, an important part of communal life was organised.
Grinding slabs were also discovered. In the archaeologists' view, the stone used for them may have come from areas beyond the Danube or the Bavarian Forest. If this origin is confirmed, the finds would indicate that even the early farmers were procuring and transporting materials over considerable distances.
What happened 7,000 years ago?
The excavation site is not open to the public. The skeleton has now been completely recovered and taken to the district archaeology department for further examination. There the bones are to be studied anthropologically. Only then will it be possible to say in more detail what traces this young person’s life has left, and which questions may never be answered.
Once the scientific investigations have been completed, the district archaeology service intends to share further findings.
Until then Großköllnbach remains a place where the soil reveals not only the traces of an ancient settlement but also the story of a person whose final resting place still poses riddles even after seven millennia.

Europe risks triggering major war if it accepts Russia’s terms, expert warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

00:50:00 KST

Europe risks triggering major war if it accepts Russia’s terms, expert warns
Olena Davlikanova, an expert in democratic governance, security policy and strategic forecasting and a senior associate analyst at the Sahaidachnyi Security Center, said this in a comment to Ukrinform.
In her view, the lack of a coordinated and consistent European position toward Moscow remains one of the key risks.
“Europe does not have a common, fully coordinated, rock-solid position on Russia. There are too many forces that want to restore cooperation and return to business as usual, and the risks of this are very high,” she said.
Davlikanova believes European countries must be prepared for Russia to test NATO’s ability to act under Article 5 – not necessarily through a large-scale military invasion, but through a series of coordinated hybrid attacks, including sabotage, cyberattacks and “massive aerial terror.”
She also did not rule out a limited incursion into the territory of a NATO member state, most likely one of the Baltic countries, and the seizure of one or two cities. Moscow could use such a scenario to try to demonstrate that the Alliance is incapable of acting in accordance with the principle of collective defense.
In her view, the main danger is that Ukraine could become a bargaining chip in such a situation. Under this worst-case scenario, Russia would play the “nuclear card,” and some European governments might then say, “Let us talk to Russia; let us negotiate.” Russia, in turn, could respond: “Fine, we can withdraw our troops, but then you must stop helping Ukraine.”
“At that point, if this happens, Europe will open the door to a major war itself,” Davlikanova said.
She stressed that the war is not about Donbas, or even Ukraine or Kyiv. It is about restoring Russian influence in Europe.
Davlikanova also noted that although NATO has significantly evolved in its understanding of modern warfare since 2022, changes to military doctrines, training approaches and exercises are progressing slowly.
She cited the experience of Ukrainian military personnel who take part in exercises and play the role of the simulated adversary. Their experience indicates that some NATO units are still not fully prepared for “War 5.0” – warfare involving integrated systems and technologies. The expert added that instructions written behind a desk and experience gained on the battlefield are two different things.
She also pointed to the slow pace of decision-making in European institutions, describing it as “the greatest vulnerability.”
As reported, Swedish Defense Minister Pål Jonson recently said that Europe had little time left to prepare for a new war with Russia.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Wednesday she would sign a decree requiring social media and streaming platforms to protect children and teenagers from violent, sexual and other potentially harmful content.

Mexico's move follows a broader global push to protect minors online, with governments in Europe and Australia tightening oversight of digital platforms and US states pursuing a range of child-safety measures.
Brazil has also moved to strengthen protections for children online. Such measures have raised questions over how to protect minors while safeguarding privacy and freedom of expression.

That Kemi is spectacularly wrong about almost everything is a big help to the PM | John Crace
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:36:12 UTC
00:36:12 KST

Little things please little minds. And minds don’t come much smaller than some of those in Westminster. If a researcher had come up with a study that showed one element two points higher in value than countless other experiments, it would almost certainly be marked down either as an outlier or “within the margin of error”. At the very least, no conclusions would be drawn until many other experiments had been conducted which had produced similar results. Serious scientific journals would just laugh at you if you asked them to publish your findings.
And yet. In one – just one out of many – recent opinion poll, the Tories have increased their ratings by a couple of points and are now for the first time in years in second place, ahead of Reform. And all of a sudden, Kemi Badenoch is insisting this is incontrovertible proof that the Tories are back in business. All the sins of its 14 years in government have been wiped clean. All hail to Kemi, the new chief. She is the chosen one. And the Conservatives are a government-in-waiting.
You need a certain amount of self-confidence to make it as a party leader. Not to say a touch of the Panglossian. The ability to insist all is well when it is turning to shit. But you can have too much of a good thing. You must at least be within touching distance of reality. And it appears that once again Kemi has jumped the shark. The one good poll has gone to her head and she now believes she is invincible. Nothing can touch her narcissism.
In her early days as Tory leader, Kemi used to crash and burn every week at prime minister’s questions. She considered preparation and research to be beneath her. Instead, she peddled the latest conspiracy theories she had seen on X with a series of scattergun questions. She only started to improve when her minders tried to get her to concentrate for 10 minutes of sustained questions on one subject. Yet over the conference break, Kemi has undergone a brain wipe. She is back in her happy space of making it up as she goes along. No one knows better than Kemi.
Sadly for the Tory leader, Kemi’s approach is also Andy Burnham’s happy place. Much more of this and the prime minister is going to look forward to his Wednesday lunchtime encounters in the Commons. Never look an easy win in the eye. Not because he’s word perfect – there are still a lot of unanswered questions about his involvement with the Manchester City owners – but because there’s an engaging openness to him you seldom find in other politicians. A willingness to answer the questions and to appear as if he’s listening. Mr Congeniality.
It’s also a big help to Andy that Kemi is spectacularly wrong about almost everything. Arguments are always so much simpler when your opponents are deluded. Indeed you couldn’t escape the irony of her insisting that it was Burnham who was consistently mistaken about everything. Even the head of MI5, Ken McCallum, had slapped the prime minister down for suggesting hostile actors had interfered with the Brexit referendum. Kemi can’t bear the fact she might have had the backing of the Russian state in 2016.
Burnham chose to respond to Kemi in the most hurtful way. With kindness. No anger. Just a gentle reiteration of the facts. It was incontrovertible that Russia had tried to influence both the 2019 general election and the EU referendum. The evidence was in front of our eyes. Russian bots selling misinformation all over social media. It was a non-story. And far from correcting him, McCallum had gone out of his way to confirm this.
What the MI5 boss had gone on to say was that it would be better for everyone concerned if we all just dropped the story as it would only give the Russians further encouragement. And who had been keeping the story alive for a third day by bringing it up at PMQs? Take a bow, Kemi. The Tory leader seemingly content to carry on doing the Russians’ dirty work for them. At least Nathan Gill, Reform’s former leader in Wales, had the sense to get paid for this. Kemi was doing it for free. Andy ended by saying he would be delighted to debate whether Brexit had done more harm than good. Kemi shook her head. This isn’t an argument the Tories are keen to have. Their feeling is Brexit is something we all just have to suck up.
After that, Kemi looked a bit lost. Clueless. Scouring her file for something to ask. Instead she just wasted her own and everyone else’s time. First by asking about the budget. As if Burnham was ever going to say: “You know what? Since you’ve asked I might as well give you a heads-up two weeks early.” All Kemi achieved was to make herself look half witted. She ended up sounding a bit hurt. She had hoped that Andy would have spent more time problem-solving than point-scoring. There are days with Kemi when even giving a straight answer comes across as point-scoring.
Earlier in the day, Dominic Cummings had been giving evidence to a Lords select committee on how to prevent rogue actors from entering No 10. That should have been a very short session. Just stop morons like Boris Johnson from appointing people like Dom as his special adviser. Curiously this hadn’t occurred to Dom, nor to the dopey peers interrogating him.
It was a bizarre hour and a half. The sort that gives you mild PTSD. Your mind goes back to all the damage he did to the country during the Brexit referendum and during his year in No 10 and suddenly the horror floods back. Just when your brain has done its best to forget all about him. To consider him a footnote in history. For the record, Dom is as deluded as ever. His main thesis seemed to be that Boris was right to allow him to do whatever he liked but no one else in No 10 should ever be allowed to do what he did. Some things never change. We are well rid of him.

Campaigners decry slow progress in repaying victims of carer’s allowance crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:35:51 UTC
00:35:51 KST

Campaigners have urged Andy Burnham to step in after it emerged just a handful of the tens of thousands of unpaid carers who unknowingly racked up huge debts when welfare officials unlawfully changed benefits guidance have been repaid.
The first official update on the carers allowance reassessment exercise launched by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) in April confirms that progress in cancelling wrongful overpayments has started slowly.
Only 2,400 cases (1.04%) of an estimated caseload of 233,300 had been reviewed in the first five months of the £75m three-year scheme, with just 100 carers receiving a total of £40,000. The average repayment to individual carers was £342.
Campaigners said the slow progress was “deeply disappointing” and warned that at current rates it would take about 40 years for the exercise to be completed.
“After years of waiting for justice, only a small number of carers have had their cases reviewed five months into this exercise,” said Helen Walker, chief executive of Carers UK.
“The vast majority still face a lengthy and uncertain wait for resolution, all whilst enduring the ongoing financial hardship caused by these delays.
“There there must be a clear and realistic plan to accelerate progress. With 230,900 identified cases still awaiting review, these figures raise serious questions about whether DWP is on track to deliver within the funding period.”
Sir Ed Davey, the leader of the Liberal Democrats, who has long campaigned on unpaid carer injustices, said: “The carer’s allowance scandal didn’t start on his watch, but the failure to put things right is fast becoming a scandal of its own. The prime minister needs to step in and speed things up now.”
The DWP is understood to have prioritised accuracy over speed in its approach and remains confident it will complete the reassessment exercise on schedule by March 2029. It plans to double the number of staff on the project to 250 by next April.
The reassessment exercise followed an official review by the disability rights expert Liz Sayce published last year which concluded systemic DWP shortcomings had caused hundreds of thousands of carers to unwittingly to run up benefit debts as high as £20,000.
The Sayce review was triggered by an award-winning Guardian investigation, which revealed how hundreds of thousands of unpaid carers were pushed into financial hardship and emotional despair as a result of years of official neglect and failure.
Sayce told the Guardian on Wednesday: “Today’s statistics show that reassessments have started slowly and it’s vital that DWP shares both a robust plan for speeding them up, so people trust they will not have prolonged waits for justice.”
The figures show that DWP has made full repayments to 100 carers totalling £40,000, and reduced overpayment debt incurred by a further 100 carers by a total of £20,000. The amount returned to carers is 41% lower than initially estimated.
The reassessment exercise covers cases where the DWP breached the law by failing to allow carers with irregular wages from part-time work to average their incomes over a year, unfairly exposing them to being penalised for breaching earnings limits.
The Sayce review revealed that the “averaging earnings” problem arose in 2020 after DWP officials quietly changed existing guidance without advising carers or taking legal or policy advice. Many carers who believed they were allowed to average earnings over a one-year period were, as a result, issued with overpayment demands.
Campaigners praised the government for taking action to put right carer’s allowance injustices. But they are also frustrated at the lack of progress on other Sayce review recommendations, including overpayments caused by universal credit faults, and debts caused by officials failing to act on earnings information given by carers.
A DWP spokesperson said: “We are on track to complete the carer’s allowance reassessment exercise within the three years previously announced.
“To support the exercise we have been recruiting and training new decision makers in a rolling programme, ensuring we take the time to assess cases with the accuracy that carers deserve.
“We have plans in place to increase resource at a steady pace over the course of the exercise.”

Two container ships near the strait of Hormuz have sunk after being struck by missiles, amid the sharpest rise in Iranian attacks on shipping since the start of the US-Israel war with Iran.
The increase in attacks suggests Iran is trying to fully close the strategic waterway in an attempt to frustrate Donald Trump’s efforts to bring down fuel prices before the US midterm elections on 3 November.
The Trump administration has been attempting to deflect attention from the economic impact of the war on Iran by blaming Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries for increased fuel prices.
On Wednesday, UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) reported at least five incidents including drone strikes in the previous 48 hours targeting tankers and other commercial ships around the Hormuz area.
“There is a tempo increase in strikes, which looks deliberate,” one maritime security source said.
The Singapore-flagged container ship GFS Pride sank on Wednesday after an attack the previous day. Hours later, the Antigua- and Barbuda-flagged Cape Dao sank close to the strait, having been hit by a projectile on 23 September, according to data from the International Maritime Organization.
Apparently referring to the GFS Pride, Iran said a cargo ship had sunk after hitting a naval mine while making an unauthorised passage through the strait.
State television quoted a statement from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that said the ship was travelling on an “illegal and dangerous route” when it hit the mine.
The ship, which was shown tilted in the water and spewing a thick plume of smoke, was carrying 2,500 containers, the broadcast said.
However, UKMTO suggested that both ships had been hit by unidentified projectiles, raising questions over Tehran’s account.
Iran has repeatedly warned ships against trying to transit through the strait without its approval. The US military has been guiding ships through the waterway on a route nearer to Oman’s coast.
Ships in the area were reporting an intense series of attacks in recent days, with six vessels attacked on Sunday alone, according to UKMTO’s monitoring.
Analysis by the Financial Times said 24 ships were hit in the two weeks to 11 October. Of the vessels hit, three were refined energy product tankers and two others were crude oil tankers.
The increased tempo of Iranian attacks appears to have caused a dramatic drop-off in oil shipments through the strait, as Tehran appears determined to demonstrate its ability to strike ships before the US midterms that will decide control of Congress.
US fuel prices have surged by almost 70% since Trump launched his war on Iran, and the Republican party is bracing for punishment at the polls.
According to two Iranian officials, Iran has recently begun using new tactics against vessels it considers to be in violation of its restrictions. The strategy included a change in the type as well as the pace of attacks, with one goal being to influence the outcome of the US vote, they said.
“The aim is to frustrate efforts by the United States and its allies to bring down global oil prices,” one of the two officials told Reuters.
The decision to adopt the new strategy had been taken at the highest levels of Iran’s leadership and was fully coordinated across the country’s ruling system, the officials added.
A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed that Tehran had changed tactics in one significant way. After the US destroyed much of Iran’s radar capabilities, the IRGC had started using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, including American naval vessels, the official said.
Last week, in a previously unreported incident, the US military determined that Iranian spotters were operating from a dhow, calling in targets to the IRGC, the official said. US forces confronted the vessel, told its occupants to abandon ship and then destroyed it. There were no casualties, the US official said.

Futureless Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:34:13 UTC
00:34:13 KST

Futureless Russia
People walk along the Floating Bridge over the Moskva River against the backdrop of a Kremlin tower and St. Basil's Cathedral in the evening twilight, in Moscow, Russia, on June 29, 2026. (Contributor / Getty Images)
Nina L. Khrushcheva
Professor of international affairs at The New School
On Sept. 25, a Moscow court sent the political analyst Alexander Kynev to pretrial detention for "large-scale illegal drug production, sale, and trafficking" — a charge that could land him in prison for 10–20 years. But no evidence of Kynev's involvement in illegal drugs has been made public.
A leading expert on regional political processes and electoral systems, Kynev has long reported on election fraud in Russia, though he openly supports the New People party, which was launched in 2020 as a sort of Kremlin-backed project to absorb "protest votes," particularly from young people. He previously worked at the independent vote-monitoring organization Golos, which was named a "foreign agent" and shut down under pressure from the Kremlin last year.
Last month, Kynev — himself a "foreign agent" — publicly criticized the Duma elections, in which the ruling United Russia party won an unprecedented — and highly improbable — 349 seats of 450. A few days later, he was arrested and reportedly beaten so badly in custody that he ended up in a prison hospital with a fractured tibia.
The arrest of a Kremlin detractor on trumped-up charges is nothing new. But Kynev is not the regime's typical nemesis: his analysis has long been an accepted barometer for public sentiment.
Some sources report that the arrest surprised key officials in President Vladimir Putin's administration. To them, Kynev was a critic, but a useful one, capable of giving them a glimpse into what is really happening in Tver or Tomsk. Silencing him amounts to smashing the thermometer because the fever is inconvenient.
The main job of Russia's apparatchiks has long been to insulate Putin from anything deemed to be beneath him. He wants to think about NATO, Ukraine, and his place in history, not potholes, regional budgets, and provincial elections.
The bureaucrats oblige by cultivating a false reality to please him.
The result is politics in vitro, with Putin effectively leading from within a glass jar, where Russia is united behind the Ukraine war, the economy has shrugged off sanctions, and every election reaffirms support for the status quo.
Outside the jar, however, the economy is under severe strain. Growth has slowed to a crawl, businesses struggle to generate profits, and borrowing costs are high. Social spending is increasingly consumed by bonuses for new contract soldiers and payouts to the families of dead ones. Holes in regional budgets are growing. Soviet-era pipes and power plants are falling apart.
Comparisons with the 1930s no longer sound like exaggeration.
It is impossible to know exactly what about the real world, if anything, has gotten through to Putin.
What is known is that virtually every institution through which reality was once transmitted to the Kremlin has been suppressed or dismantled. Elections have become farcical. Courts have lost any semblance of independence. Independent media have been muzzled. Even once-tolerated critics are being jailed and beaten.
Comparisons with the 1930s no longer sound like exaggeration. An analyst in a cast, days after criticizing an election, is the handiwork of a ferocious security state. The question is whether anyone will — or even can — contain it.
Past periods of Russian terror, as brutal as they were, were subject to a hard brake. In the 16th century, Ivan the Terrible allowed his oprichnina (private army) to ravage the country for seven years, but then realized it was achieving little, abolished it, and executed many of its leaders.
Stalin halted the Great Terror a little over two years after it began and removed the chief of the People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs (NKVD), Nikolai Yezhov (whom Stalin later had shot).
Unchecked terror eventually starts eating its own managers.
These were not acts of mercy: leaders realized that unchecked terror eventually starts eating its own managers. But, from inside his glass jar, Putin cannot see this. Nor can he fully control the state apparatus that is carrying out the terror. Ivan's oprichniki were a tool of the state; today, the state itself behaves like the oprichnina.
Such a system does not dismantle itself.
On the contrary, it leverages every resource and capability to fortify itself. As under Stalin, the best engineers and the scarcest materials now go to the war effort in Ukraine, and science survives mostly where it serves the front.
Foreign companies also pay: those that want to leave Russia must sell at a steep discount and make a "voluntary contribution" to the state budget; others are placed under "temporary management" so they can be quietly pillaged.
In recent months, the Ministry of Justice has run an online exhibition called "Defense of the Sovereignty of the Russian State: History and the Present."
The timeline begins with the Smuta, or Time of Troubles (1598–1613), when Russia endured a violent succession crisis, with numerous usurpers and impostors, including Polish invaders, attempting to claim the title of czar.
For Russia today, it is the ultimate warning: a divided elite plus foreign meddling equals disaster. Repression is meant to prevent this outcome.
And yet, the tumultuous Smuta eventually gave way to a new dynasty and three centuries of Romanov rule, under which Russia gradually turned toward the West.
Today, as the Russian state does everything in its power to prevent collapse, it precludes such a renewal by overseeing the gradual erosion of the capabilities that could drive dynamism.
For example, the state is pushing young people toward vocational training, rather than the kind of education that would prepare them to thrive in high-tech fields. This is not a country that is preparing for the future. As North Korea has shown, a sclerotic state can endure for decades.
Russia has known invasions, revolutions, and internal chaos. It has had ruthless leaders who engaged in severe repression and clung to power. But there was generally a sense that Russia was headed somewhere — that the brutality served some end, however unjustifiable the means.
Even Stalin's terror brought factories, dams, and a vision of the future. In this sense, today's terror is unique in Russian history: its only aim is to perpetuate the state that is executing it.

Mont Blanc, the ‘roof of Europe’, loses more than a metre of height in a year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:33:52 UTC
00:33:52 KST

Western Europe’s highest mountain shrank by more than a metre last year. The peak of Mont Blanc in France now stands 4,807.47 metres above sea level, a team of surveyors said on Wednesday, putting “the roof of Europe” 1.29 metres lower than in 2025.
The mountain is about 4,792 metres tall but the summit constantly shifts as heat, wind and precipitation change the thickness of snow and ice on top. The height scientists recorded during an expedition last month was 1.88 metres greater than it was in 2023, when it reached the lowest levels in recent memory.
Chartered surveyors from the Union Nationale des Géomètres-Experts (UNGE) and the Ordre des Géomètres-Experts, who have regularly monitored the peak since 2001, used precise satellite technology to measure the mountain, and drones to create a detailed model of the snow and ice cap.
The summit has shrunk back by 3.43 metres since a high of 4,810.90 metres in 2007, the data shows.
The experts cautioned against linking fluctuations in height from year to year to the rapid loss of Alpine ice being caused by fossil fuel pollution.
“Regarding ice mass, it is essential to distinguish between changes in surface altitude and changes in the total volume or mass of ice,” a UNGE spokesperson said. “An increase in summit altitude does not necessarily mean that the mountain has gained ice mass, nor does it contradict the documented retreat of Alpine glaciers.”
Climate breakdown was a factor in western Europe’s hottest summer on record this year, scarring Alpine regions and melting ice at dizzying speed. Earlier this month, Swiss glaciologists warned of an “explosion of melt rates” after confirming that one-fifth of the country’s ice had been lost in the past five years, and 5.5% of volume was lost between 2025 and 2026.
Jean des Garets, the president of the Haute-Savoie departmental chamber of surveyors and the leader of the Mont Blanc expedition, said the warming trend could be seen with the naked eye in the rest of the Alpine massif but that “for the moment, climate change doesn’t seem to have the same impact above 4,000 metres”.
“When we climb, we pass by the Brigade Blanche hut before the Tête-Rousse glacier,” he said in comments reported by the French television channel TF1 on Wednesday. “We’ve seen that the glacier has moved up. It has literally melted before our very eyes and now in some places we’re crossing a stream instead of a glacier.”

UNIFIL was first established in 1978 to confirm Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon. U.S. Air Force AI fighter jet draws 30+ test proposals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:22:14 UTC
00:22:14 KST

- The U.S. Air Force sought three X-62 VISTA test concepts for fiscal 2027 and 2028 but received a final proposal of more than 30.
- The AI research jet also flew an IBM NorthPole chip and third-party autonomy software during HAVE HOLIDAYS tests at Edwards Air Force Base.
The U.S. Air Force went looking for three new flight test ideas for its AI-controlled X-62 VISTA research jet and came away with more than 30, after the first research symposium built around the aircraft drew over 80 participants to Edwards Air Force Base, California, in August.
The three-day meeting at the U.S. Air Force Test Pilot School brought together people from industry, academia and the joint force, according to the 412th Test Wing, which released details on Oct. 13. Organizers set out to define three test concepts the X-62 could fly in fiscal 2027 and 2028, but participants submitted a final proposal of more than 30, which the service described as substantial and previously untapped demand for the aircraft.
“We were awed by the level of positive responses and interest,” said Col. Maryann Karlen, commandant of the Air Force Test Pilot School. “This demonstrates, without a doubt, the demand for testbeds like the X-62.”
The X-62, short for Variable In-flight Simulator Test Aircraft, is a heavily modified two-seat F-16D that can mimic the handling of other aircraft and host software that flies the jet while safety pilots sit aboard. It became the first X-plane flown by artificial intelligence in combat-style maneuvering, flying against a crewed F-16 in a 2023 dogfight under the DARPA Air Combat Evolution program.
Briefings at the symposium came from DARPA, the Air Force Research Laboratory, MIT Lincoln Laboratory and the Air Force Institute of Technology, among others. Aircrew from an Air Combat Command fighter squadron also shared recent operational experience on getting pilots to trust machine-learning systems.
The jet is now in the middle of a Mission Systems Upgrade funded by the Test Resource Management Center, which adds an advanced radar, more computing power and room for additional sensors. Lockheed Martin Skunk Works, Calspan Corporation, the Air Force Research Laboratory and RTX are working on the upgrade through the Air Force Test Center. Once finished, the X-62 is meant to work alongside VENOM, the U.S. Air Force’s fleet of F-16s converted for autonomy testing at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, and to try out new AI uses for high-priority programs.
Ahead of the expected surge in test work, the school flew a series of short missions it named HAVE HOLIDAYS to work out how to integrate and fly new software quickly. They ran in parallel with HAVE HEAT, an April campaign in which an AI agent on the X-62 autonomously intercepted an airborne target using live infrared sensor data.
One of the HOLIDAYS tests, HAVE BALLDROP, put an autonomous agent from a third party outside the usual prime contractors onto the jet for the first time, drawn from an Air Force Research Laboratory program called xFACTOR. Another, HAVE THANKS, flew BirdBox, an open-architecture laboratory software framework that helps sensors recognize targets at the tactical edge.
HAVE DREIDEL tested commercial runtime assurance software from 3Laws Robotics, which acts as a set of guardrails to stop an autonomous aircraft from breaking limits set by its operators. In HAVE SANTA, engineers put IBM’s NorthPole chip, a low-power processor modeled on the way the brain handles information, inside the VISTA’s computers, where it ran Lockheed Martin Skunk Works’ “Supermassive” simulation and calculated parallel flight trajectories in the air.

WingXpand unveils swappable brain for drones and rovers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:11:27 UTC
00:11:27 KST

- WingXpand unveiled xPAIR, a swappable control module that runs the company’s aircraft, ground vehicle and watercraft with shared AI and payloads.
- The company says xPAIR has been demonstrated with U.S. Special Forces teams and at U.S. Army events, but has named no customer or price.
U.S. drone maker WingXpand has unveiled xPAIR, a removable control unit that the company says can be moved between its small fixed-wing aircraft, a ground vehicle and a small boat, letting one set of AI software and sensors run uncrewed systems in the air, on land and on water.
The Schaumburg, Illinois, company introduced the system on Oct. 13 and described it as patent-pending. Operators click the xPAIR module into the xRAI aircraft to watch a wide area from above, into the xTRAIL ground vehicle to get closer without sending a soldier, or into the xSAIL watercraft to reach places accessible only by water. WingXpand calls it the first such system in the world, a claim The Defence Blog could not independently verify.
All three platforms share the same threat-detection AI library, communications and payloads, and are run from one user interface. WingXpand says operators can therefore add vehicle types without buying separate control equipment or retraining for each domain, and that the module can fuse data from different vehicles in real time to give a single picture of the area.
“Our military doesn’t need another autonomous system built for one narrow mission,” said James Barbieri, co-founder and CEO of WingXpand.
The company has not released specifications for the xTRAIL or xSAIL, nor said how long it takes to move the module between vehicles in the field or how much a set costs. It also has not named a military customer for xPAIR itself. A company representative told The Defence Blog the technology is already being adopted by the U.S. Department of War, state governments and Fortune 50 companies, and the release says xPAIR and the company’s other systems have been demonstrated with several U.S. Special Forces teams and at U.S. Army events.
WingXpand is best known for the xRAI, a fixed-wing drone with telescoping wings that packs into a backpack and expands for flight. The company added a vertical takeoff and landing kit in 2024 and has worked with Raytheon under a U.S. Army contract to integrate infrared sensors and AI threat detection into the aircraft. It also won the U.S. Army’s xTechSpecialForces competition and has announced contracts with U.S. Special Operations, the U.S. Army and the U.S. Navy, as well as approval for use by Montana state agencies. The company has listed prices for its xRAI aircraft starting at $14,900.
WingXpand says xPAIR is built in the United States and compliant with the National Defense Authorization Act, which bars federal buyers from drones and components made by Chinese manufacturers. The company also pitches the shared core as a way to scale production, arguing that building one common module lets it adjust the mix of air, ground and maritime vehicles as customer demand changes.

Republicans face expanding midterm backlash over Iran war, living costs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:11:00 UTC
00:11:00 KST

Republicans face expanding midterm backlash over Iran war, living costs
TEHRAN — Donald Trump says the approaching U.S. elections will not change his position regarding Iran. Republican candidates are already changing theirs.
With three weeks remaining before the November 3 midterms, an unpopular war and its economic consequences are forcing the president’s party to defend Senate seats in states he carried comfortably in 2024, while Democrats press toward control of the House.
The retreat is visible in campaign spending and candidates’ language.
Republican money has been redirected from North Carolina to Kansas. Iowa Senate nominee Ashley Hinson has called for an “immediate end” to the war on Iran, despite repeatedly voting against House resolutions seeking that outcome.
Republicans are spending heavily in Texas, where Democrat James Talarico threatens Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Washington’s military decisions have become liabilities in places far removed from West Asia. Fuel, transportation, and agricultural costs give voters a daily measure of a war Trump continues to promise will end soon.
His party now has to answer for the difference between those assurances and household bills.
Trump’s economic argument undermined
Pew Research Center’s October 8 findings show how sharply public expectations have changed.
Among 5,062 adults that were surveyed between September 28 and October 4, 65 percent disapproved of Trump’s handling of military action against Iran; only 33 percent approved.
Republican and Republican-leaning approval fell from 69 percent in March to 63 percent. Democrats remained overwhelmingly opposed.
The public has also abandoned expectations of a short operation. In March, 43 percent believed the war would end within six months. Now, 47 percent expect it to continue for more than another year, and another 30 percent anticipate six to 12 additional months. Trump’s promises are running against an increasingly skeptical electorate.
Economic concerns help explain that skepticism. 73 percent expressed strong concern about higher gasoline and fuel prices caused by the war. 61 percent of Republicans shared that concern. Fear of American military casualties was almost as widespread, at 71 percent overall.
On October 9, the University of Michigan reported that consumer sentiment had fallen to 46.3, from September’s 48.1. Expected inflation over the next year reached 4.7 percent, compared with 3.4 percent in February before the U.S.-Israeli war began.
These are expectations, not measured inflation, but they show households anticipating further pressure. Lower-income consumers reported particularly steep declines in confidence.
Trump has promised that oil prices would “drop like a rock” once the war ended. For candidates approaching November 3, promised relief offers less protection than prices voters can actually see.
Republicans defend an expanding Senate map
Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority. Democrats need a net gain of four seats for outright control, which requires breakthroughs in states Trump won by double digits as well as successful defenses of their own seats.
The opportunity has widened, but the arithmetic remains difficult.
North Carolina provides one of the clearest Democratic openings. Former governor Roy Cooper faces former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley for retiring Senator Thom Tillis’s seat.
Polls published October 13 placed Cooper ahead by eight to 14 points. A major Republican super PAC has shifted resources toward Kansas, where Senator Roger Marshall faces Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton.
Texas demands a far larger Republican investment. Paxton defeated incumbent John Cornyn in the Republican contest with Trump’s backing.
Republicans have spent approximately $210 million on the Senate race, against Democrats’ $39 million, Reuters reported. Yet a ReconMR/Siena survey conducted October 5-8 put Talarico ahead 48-44 percent.
That result deserves attention without being mistaken for a victory. Texas has not elected a Democrat statewide since 1994. Paxton’s difficulties have given Democrats an opening, but Republicans retain enormous resources and a long-established advantage.
In Maine, Susan Collins faces former state Senate president Troy Jackson. A recent Washington Post-Schar School survey placed Jackson ahead 50-46 percent.
Alaska’s Dan Sullivan is defending against former representative Mary Peltola under ranked-choice voting.
In Ohio, former senator Sherrod Brown challenges Jon Husted, appointed after JD Vance became vice president.
Democrats need to protect Georgia and Michigan. Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff entered July with nearly $43 million available against Republican challenger Mike Collins’s $2.1 million.
Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed faces former congressman Mike Rogers for retiring Senator Gary Peters’s seat, with recent surveys showing a competitive race despite Democratic leads.
Israel policy and money pouring in
Michigan brings the foreign policy dispute into an unusually direct view. During their debate on October 8, El-Sayed said Israel has lobbied Washington into the Iran war and challenged Rogers’s support for the war. “I don’t want to be pushed into a war by Israel, and I don’t want to be in a war with Iran,” he said.
His argument, which has become increasingly popular, confronts a longstanding assumption in Washington that close military alignment with Israel serves American security regardless of its regional consequences. It also gives anti-war voters a position more specific than general dissatisfaction with Trump.
The fight extends to campaign financing. Senator Bernie Sanders, who for years has tried to create a daylight between the current Netanyahu government and the Israeli regime in general, said in an October 2 post on X that AIPAC planned to spend $233 million "against candidates criticizing Benjamin Netanyahu’s government."
El-Sayed won his primary despite extensive pro-Israel spending supporting opponent Haley Stevens.
Republicans have another powerful financial backer. Reuters reported on October 12 that Elon Musk had spent roughly $366 million during the election cycle, including $276 million since July, to help preserve Republican control.
His interests are tangible: House Democrats have called for investigations into his government contracts and work leading Trump’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency.
Offering accountability without a guaranteed reversal
Republican vulnerability reaches beyond the Senate. Analysts estimate that only 40 to 50 House districts are genuinely competitive, despite all 435 seats being contested.
Redistricting and partisan sorting limit the gains available even in a favorable Democratic year.
In 2018, Democrats gained 41 seats; analysts interviewed by Reuters now anticipate a considerably narrower majority if the party wins. State contests reinforce the uncertainty.
Texas Governor Greg Abbott faces Democrat Gina Hinojosa in a race, producing sharply different surveys. YouGov’s poll, conducted between September 28 and October 5, put Hinojosa ahead 48-47 percent; an earlier Fox News survey favored Abbott 52-47. Neither establishes a decisive advantage.
The October 12 raid of Representative Ilhan Omar’s Washington home added another dispute to the campaign.
U.S. federal agents, this time under Homeland Security Investigations, executed a court-approved warrant in a criminal investigation whose details remain limited.
Omar characterized the raid as a calculated effort to target political enemies and weaponize law enforcement, declaring that state intimidation would not silence her.
Ultimately, while a Democratic victory may yield incremental opportunities for limited oversight, it does not guarantee an immediate or automatic end to the war.
The House’s September 15 demand that Trump stop military action or obtain congressional authorization passed 220-204, with seven Republicans joining Democrats, but remains nonbinding.
American electoral discontent is measurable. However, enforceable restraint on American military aggression is still unproven and looks unlikely.
Although domestic electoral discontent can be readily documented, effective and enforceable restraint on U.S. military action remains elusive and improbable.

Netflix is laying off 6% of its workforce, or roughly 1,000 employees, in its biggest cuts since 2022, according to an internal memo seen by Reuters, as the streaming pioneer faces tough competition for viewers from legacy rivals and YouTube.
The bulk of the job cuts would be in Netflix’s product, tech, legal and human-resources teams, the email co-CEOs Greg Peters and Ted Sarandos sent to employees on Wednesday showed.
“Our mission – to entertain the world – is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritize our people and resources,” they said in the memo.
“Our business is strong and growing, and we remain on track to deliver our full-year forecast.”
Netflix shares, down about 25% so far this year, rose 0.7% on Wednesday. The company had about 16,000 employees at the end of last year.
This year, the streaming company faced doubts about its ability to sustain the growth that disrupted the US media industry by putting pressure on cable TV businesses.
Engagement, or the amount of time users spend on Netflix, has become a key concern for investors as platforms such as YouTube and TikTok attract viewers with free-to-watch, user-generated content that gives them a cost advantage over Netflix.
A failed pursuit of Warner Bros Discovery’s streaming and studio assets earlier this year deepened doubts about Netflix’s strategy. Paramount completed its $110bn Warner Bros acquisition earlier this month to form Skydance.
“They haven’t been able to find like another line of major revenue,” said Ross Benes, a senior analyst at eMarketer, adding the company remained reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a ceiling.
“Eventually, because they’ve kind of nearing a ceiling with that, they’ll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that’s where it’s been more of a struggle.“
Netflix has been trying to expand beyond its subscription business by investing in an ad tier, live programming and gaming.
Its last major round of layoffs came in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs in two rounds after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade.
The Wall Street Journal first reported on Wednesday’s memo.
