Retrouvez le compte rendu du Conseil des ministres du mercredi 14 octobre 2026 :
14 octobre 2026 - Compte-rendu
Compte rendu du Conseil des ministres du 14 octobre 2026.
PROJETS DE LOI
DISPOSITIONS RELATIVES AU SECTEUR NUCLEAIRE
La ministre déléguée auprès du ministre de l’économie, des finances et de la souveraineté industrielle, énergétique et numérique, chargée de l’énergie, a présenté un projet de loi visant à accompagner la relance du nucléaire français. Complémentaire de la loi adoptée en 2023, ce texte va faciliter la réalisation des grands projets de la filière, notamment le renouvellement des installations de traitement et de recyclage des combustibles nucléaires, tout en préservant les plus hauts standards de sûreté.
Le 10 février 2022, dans son discours à Belfort, le Président de la République fixait un cap ambitieux : faire de la France la première grande nation à sortir de sa dépendance aux énergies fossiles, en réduisant sa consommation d'énergie tout en accroissant sa production d'électricité décarbonée. Au cœur de cette stratégie figure la relance du nucléaire français, avec la prolongation des réacteurs existants lorsque les exigences de sûreté le permettent, la construction de nouveaux réacteurs EPR2 et le renforcement de l'ensemble de la chaîne industrielle. Cette orientation a été confirmée et confortée par la troisième programmation pluriannuelle de l'énergie (PPE3) présentée par le Premier ministre le 12 février dernier.
La loi d'accélération du nucléaire du 22 juin 2023 a permis de simplifier et d'accélérer les procédures nécessaires à la construction de nouveaux réacteurs EPR2, notamment sur les sites existants.
Un peu plus de trois ans après son adoption, l'avancement des projets et les premiers retours d'expérience ont mis en évidence la nécessité de compléter ce cadre législatif. À l'approche du lancement formel du programme de nouveau nucléaire français, le Gouvernement s’engage pour lever les derniers obstacles identifiés et donner à la filière les moyens de concrétiser ses projets.
Le projet de loi présenté en conseil des ministres a été construit autour de quatre objectifs :
- Accélérer la modernisation des installations du cycle du combustible nucléaire.
Les mesures de simplification prévues par la loi de 2023 seront étendues aux installations de l'aval du cycle, notamment au projet « Aval du futur » porté par Orano. Ce programme vise à renouveler les installations industrielles de La Hague, essentielles au traitement et au recyclage des combustibles nucléaires.
- Clarifier les règles applicables aux installations nucléaires pour garantir la priorité à la sûreté.
Le texte vise également à assurer la primauté des exigences de sûreté nucléaire et de radioprotection lorsque l’application de certaines dispositions du code de la construction et de l'habitation aggraverait des risques en matière de sûreté ou de radioprotection ou s’avèrerait techniquement impraticable.
- Faciliter l'organisation des grands chantiers industriels, sans réduire les exigences de contrôle.
Sous réserve d'une autorisation préalable de l’Autorité de sûreté nucléaire et de radioprotection (ASNR), les exploitants pourront confier la surveillance d'intervenants extérieurs à certaines sociétés de leur groupe. Cette organisation resterait placée sous la responsabilité, la direction et le contrôle de l'exploitant nucléaire.
- Faire de la relance du nucléaire une réalité industrielle et économique.
Avec ce nouveau texte, le Gouvernement donne les moyens à la France de passer des orientations stratégiques à la réalisation concrète des projets, en donnant aux industriels un cadre adapté à l'ampleur des investissements et des chantiers à venir.
RATIFICATION DE L’ORDONNANCE DU 27 JUILLET 2026 PORTANT DIVERS AJUSTEMENTS DU CODE DES IMPOSITIONS SUR LES BIENS ET SERVICES
Le ministre de l’économie, des finances et de la souveraineté industrielle, énergétique et numérique et le ministre de l’action et des comptes publics ont présenté un projet de loi ratifiant l’ordonnance n° 2026-671 du 27 juillet 2026 portant divers ajustements du code des impositions sur les biens et services (CIBS).
Cette ordonnance prolonge le chantier de modernisation et de simplification du droit fiscal engagé par le Gouvernement en 2019. Ce travail a conduit à la création du CIBS au 1er janvier 2022, puis à son enrichissement progressif, notamment avec l’intégration de plusieurs taxes au 1er janvier 2023 et, par une ordonnance du 17 décembre 2025, avec le transfert des dispositions relatives à la taxe sur la valeur ajoutée (TVA).
Une entrée en vigueur du nouveau régime de TVA reportée au 1er janvier 2027
À la suite de la consultation publique menée sur la recodification de la TVA dans le CIBS, le Gouvernement a pris en compte les attentes exprimées par les entreprises et les praticiens du droit.
L’entrée en vigueur du transfert des dispositions relatives à la TVA dans le CIBS est ainsi reportée au 1er janvier 2027, afin de permettre aux acteurs concernés de préparer plus sereinement la transition vers ce nouveau cadre juridique, notamment dans le contexte de la mise en œuvre de la réforme de la facturation électronique à compter du 1er septembre prochain.
L’ordonnance répond également à une demande importante de simplification : elle regroupe désormais, au sein d’une subdivision unique du livre II du CIBS consacré à la TVA, l’ensemble des dispositions relatives au droit à déduction de la TVA pour améliorer la lisibilité du droit applicable.
L’ordonnance intègre par ailleurs les mesures relatives à la TVA adoptées depuis l’ordonnance du 17 décembre 2025, notamment celles issues de la loi de finances pour 2026. Elle prend ainsi en compte plusieurs évolutions récentes du droit fiscal, comme l’harmonisation à 5,5 % du taux de TVA applicable aux services liés à la gestion des déchets.
L’ordonnance met également à jour les références rendues nécessaires par l’entrée en vigueur de la partie législative du nouveau code des douanes au 1er mai 2026.
Elle poursuit aussi l’harmonisation des catégories fiscales utilisées pour identifier les régimes de contrôle, de recouvrement et de contentieux : les « taxes sur le chiffre d’affaires » deviennent par exemple les « taxes sur les biens et services ».
Une sécurité juridique renforcée pour les opérateurs
L’ordonnance confirme explicitement que la doctrine administrative opposable aux redevables demeure inchangée lors de l’entrée en vigueur du CIBS. Cette garantie, déjà prévue par l’ordonnance du 17 décembre 2025 et précisée dans un rescrit publié le 18 février 2026 au Bulletin officiel des finances publiques – Impôts, est ainsi réaffirmée.
L’ordonnance prend également en compte plusieurs demandes de clarification formulées lors de la consultation publique, notamment afin de rapprocher certaines formulations de la jurisprudence et procède enfin à diverses corrections d’erreurs matérielles identifiées dans l’ordonnance du 17 décembre 2025.
DECRET
ACCELERATION DES PROCEDURES LIEES A LA CONSTRUCTION DE NOUVELLES INSTALLATIONS NUCLEAIRES A PROXIMITE DE SITES NUCLEAIRES EXISTANTS ET AU FONCTIONNEMENT DES INSTALLATIONS EXISTANTES
Le ministre de la ville et du logement a présenté un décret relatif à la détermination des modalités d’application de l’autorisation d’urbanisme spéciale pour les constructions, installations ou aménagements temporaires nécessaires au logement, à l’hébergement ou aux déplacements des personnes participant aux travaux de construction d’un nouveau réacteur électronucléaire ou à la logistique et aux activités de préfabrication du chantier de ce même réacteur. Il est pris pour l’application de l’article 9-1 de la loi n° 2023-491 du 22 juin 2023, créé par la loi n° 2025-1129 du 26 novembre 2025 de simplification du droit de l’urbanisme et du logement (« Huwart »).
Ce décret vient préciser ce régime spécifique des autorisations d’urbanisme qui permet, compte tenu du caractère temporaire des constructions, installations ou aménagements concernés, de les autoriser à déroger aux règles d’urbanisme, tout en les soumettant à une autorisation délivrée par le préfet après accord du maire de la commune concernée. L’autorisation fixe le délai, qui ne peut excéder vingt ans, à l’expiration duquel le terrain doit être remis en son état initial.
Le décret détaille la liste des pièces supplémentaires à fournir dans les dossiers de demande d’autorisation et les modalités particulières d’instruction de ces demandes.
En outre, il fixe les modalités relatives aux garanties financières qui peuvent être exigées lorsque les caractéristiques du terrain d’assiette ou l’importance du projet le justifient. Il précise les critères permettant au préfet d’en fixer le montant, ainsi que les conditions de consignation et de déconsignation. Sont également précisées les conditions de remise en état des terrains à respecter, ainsi que les mesures permettant d’en assurer le respect.
Enfin, le décret prévoit que lorsque l’autorité compétente pour délivrer l’autorisation ne répond pas à la demande dans les délais qui lui sont impartis, son silence vaut décision implicite de rejet. En effet, compte tenu de l’objet de l’autorisation, qui doit notamment mentionner la durée d’implantation temporaire et, lorsque cela se justifie, le montant des sommes à consigner, le décret prévoit qu’une décision expresse de l’administration doit intervenir.
Ces mesures, particulièrement attendues par les acteurs du secteur nucléaire et ciblant des projets déjà identifiés, notamment sur le chantier EPR2 de Penly (76), seront applicables aux demandes d’autorisations d’urbanisme déposées à compter du lendemain de la publication du texte au Journal officiel.

Pope Leo recovering well after cancer surgery, Vatican says
Unknown

Pope Leo recovering well after cancer surgery, Vatican says
The 71-year-old pontiff is recovering in Rome’s Gemelli hospital after surgery to remove a cancerous growth on his lung.
Pope Leo XIV is out of bed, walking, eating and has undergone respiratory physiotherapy, according to a doctor’s note published by the Vatican a day after his lung cancer surgery.
A blood test and chest X-ray revealed “normal post-operative” progress, doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora said, adding that values were “within the expected range for the type of procedure performed”.
“The Holy Father underwent respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking in his room”, they said, adding that “he resumed his regular diet and had breakfast and lunch.”
“Recovery is proceeding as planned,” the doctors said.
Part of lung removed
The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with cancer after an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, according to a medical bulletin published by the Vatican on Tuesday.
Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican added, noting the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests. It did not provide details on the recovery outlook or course of treatment.
The Vatican said the procedure lasted 90 minutes and that the surgery “was successful, and there were no complications”.
A medical statement shared by The Holy See’s press office, following the surgery, noted the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in the hope of eliminating any lingering traces of the cancer.
After the procedure, Pope Leo returned to his room at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where he is expected to recover for a week, with all his audiences through October 20 cancelled.
The Vatican said doctors are not currently discussing chemotherapy or other therapies pending the results of other tests.

Internationals lose right to IND payouts under new asylum law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:09:47 UTC
00:09:47 KST

Internationals lose right to IND payouts under new asylum law
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
International workers, students and family migrants will no longer be entitled to penalty payments when the immigration service IND misses its deadlines, the asylum ministry has said after a new law was passed by the senate on Tuesday.
The change was presented as an asylum measure, but a ministry spokesperson told Dutch News the law applies to applications for regular residence permits, including highly skilled migrants, students and family members.
The IND is supposed to make a decision on a residence application within 6 months. If it misses that deadline, applicants can go to court to demand a payment for every day it remains late. Once the new law takes effect, judges will only be able to order the IND to reach a decision within a set period.
The government abandoned plans to axe penalty payments for regular residence applicants in 2024, saying it could conflict with EU law. The ministry told us it could not yet say what had changed.
Asylum minister Bart van den Brink told MPs in September the IND had paid out close to €100 million in penalties, noting that some asylum applicants had ended up receiving over €100,000. The IND also insists these penalties do nothing to speed things up.
A spokesperson from the IND told Dutch News the service does not currently know how much in penalty payments is paid for regular permit applicants, but it will calculate the figures in the coming weeks.
D66, which voted against the asylum package in April, backed the new law. In April, D66 senator Boris Dittrich told Dutch News the party opposed the package because it would have made living in the country without valid papers a criminal offence. That measure is not part of the new law.
A D66 spokesperson acknowledged that the IND’s failure to meet deadlines “is not resolved by this amendment”, but told us on Tuesday the penalties “no longer provide an incentive to work more efficiently and have therefore outlived their purpose”.
“In our view, abolishing the penalty payments must go hand in hand with measures aimed at the ultimate goal: faster procedures, so that everyone who comes here receives clarity as quickly as possible,” the spokesperson said.

The suspect was identified as employee Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, who was arrested on October 9, about a week after OpenAI discovered the surveillance device. He made an initial appearance in a US court on Tuesday.
He was charged with using or endeavouring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. Alfozan joined OpenAI as an engineer in July 2025.
Prosecutors said the device was wrapped in toilet paper and inserted in a USB port on the back of a TV in an executive conference room.
He was allegedly spotted near the executive conference room in CCTV footage on multiple dates before the device was discovered, according to the Justice Department.
Conversations in the conference room "frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information," the Justice Department said.
The allegations come as the US and China race to become the leader in AI, which the Trump administration has pushed to be rebranded as "superintelligence".
“We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices. We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier,” OpenAI said in a statement posted on X.
The ChatGPT maker said it had “no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data”.
If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (€200,000) fine, followed by three years of supervised release.

Tiny implants can use the body itself to talk to each other
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Tiny implants can use the body itself to talk to each other
The network could let tiny implants sense symptoms and trigger treatments
Medical implants are getting smaller and smarter. But getting them to talk to each other remains tricky.
Now, researchers have developed a way for tiny implantable devices to send electrical signals through the body’s own tissues. The approach could offer a low-power way for implants to work together, with one detecting a symptom and another delivering treatment, the team reports September 24 in Science.
Currently, getting devices to communicate through tissue comes with trade-offs. Some medical devices, such as insulin pumps linked to glucose monitors, use Bluetooth, which relies on radio signals. Receiving those signals requires power even when a device is only listening, increasing the need for battery power and making devices harder shrink. Radio signals also weaken as they travel through body tissue, limiting how far apart communicating devices can be.
The new network called SWANS, the Smart Wireless Autonomous Networking System, works differently. A wearable external hub or implant generates an electric pulse that produces a small current in the surrounding tissue. Tiny implants can detect those electrical signals while using almost no power when they are only listening. And without large batteries, those implants can be small enough to inject through a syringe.
To demonstrate how the network works, the team attached motion sensors to the front legs of rats. When the animals moved their front legs, the system’s external hub sent signals through their bodies to neurostimulator implants in the sciatic nerves, causing muscles in the back legs to contract.
The synchronized limbs weren’t really the point. The experiment was designed to show that signals could travel through the body, linking different kinds of devices, says Alex Abramson, a biomedical engineer at Georgia Tech in Atlanta. It was “a proof of concept showing that you can really connect this system to anything.”
Abramson says a network of smart implants could automatically deliver a drug or stimulate a neuron exactly when needed to treat complex conditions like Parkinson’s disease. Simple signals can be sent from one implant to another, while an external hub can coordinate more complex networks of sensors and devices, possibly using artificial intelligence.
Before the new network can be used in humans, researchers will need to show that the electrical signals do not cause unintended problems like heart rhythm disruptions. Such issues have not turned up in the experiments in rats yet, but the technology will need to be tested over longer periods of time and in larger animals, Abramson says.
Materials engineer Amir Alavi says the network’s potential could grow as other technologies improve, including wearables, AI systems and miniature, battery-free implantable sensors like those his lab is developing. “There are now several really interesting directions converging,” says Alavi, of at the University of Pittsburgh’s Swanson School of Engineering. “If those pieces eventually come together, you could have implants that are much smaller, simpler, longer-lived, and more connected than what we have today.”

Rising inequality, diesel deal and another execution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Rising inequality, diesel deal and another execution
Welcome to our press review of events in the United States. Every Wednesday we look at how the Swiss media have reported and reacted to three major stories in the US – in politics, finance and science.
With the midterm elections getting closer, the political stakes – and decisions – are heating up in the US. The knock-on effects are being felt elsewhere in the world.
Help us improve the press review
As a reader of our weekly press review, your feedback is important to us. Please take two minutes to answer a short survey and help us improve our journalism. This survey is anonymous and all data is confidential.
👉 [Take the surveyExternal linkExternal link]
Rising inequality and income disparity may well play a big part in the forthcoming US midterm elections, according to the Neue Zürcher Zeitung.
“The feeling among some voters of having been left behind economically helped Donald Trump win his first term as president in 2016,” says the newspaper. “Economic factors played a decisive role in his 2024 re-election as well. Now, voter dissatisfaction is likely to take a toll on Trump’s Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections.”
Since the turn of the Millennium, wealth has quadrupled for the top 20 earners, but much less so for middle-income groups, states NZZ. And a similar picture has emerged regarding wages.
This may come back to haunt the current administration, the newspaper observes. US voters also feel more disconnected from politics, which is also dominated by the wealthy.
“The growing influence of large donations contributes to the popular narrative that big business can exert undue influence on politics – something ordinary wage earners have little power to counter,” says the NZZ. Rising rents, food and fuel prices in recent months have only added to voter frustration. The situation clearly points to a resounding loss for the Republican Party as voters will likely “vent their anger over the rising cost of living at the ballot box”.
How the cost of living may influence votersExternal link – NZZ (German, paywall)
President Donald Trump has rolled the dice once again to win votes next month. Having threatened to restrict supplies of US diesel to the world, Trump then lifted sanctions on Russian fuel exports.
The end game is clearly to bring down the price of diesel to win back disaffected domestic voters in time for the midterm elections. The Russian deal has been criticized for allowing Russia to make more money to spend on waging war in Ukraine.
Diesel prices in the US have risen by an average of 70%, and gasoline prices by 40% since the start of the year, states the Neue Zürcher Zeitung.
“[Trump’s] reasons for once again undermining Europeans while accommodating Russia remain baffling,” says the newspaper. “While he alienates the US’s staunchest allies and exacerbates the suffering in Ukraine, the anticipated volume of Russian diesel exports is unlikely to significantly alter global market prices.”
Le Temps also questions the rationale. “At best, the figures cited amount to barely a week’s worth of US consumption. Yet, evidently, that is enough for Donald Trump to abandon Kyiv once again.” “The White House incumbent contributed to this situation by launching a war against Iran,” the newspaper points out.
Opinion of Trump’s diesel deal by Le TempsExternal link (French, paywall) and NZZExternal link (German, paywall)
Americans were still reeling from the botched execution of Christa Pike when Secretary of War Pete Hegseth announced the livestreaming of the execution of a former army officer.
Ex-major Nidal Hasan has been condemned to death by firing squad after killing 13 people in a mass shooting at an army base in 2009. Hegseth said he would livestream the execution for public consumption on December 3.
The backlash has been fierce, leading to suggestions that the White House could intervene to reverse the decision. But Swiss public broadcaster SRF believes Hegseth’s comment is part of his long-standing strategy of communicating to the public in direct, and often shocking, style.
“Hegseth knows how to make headlines. He regularly tackles topics that offend parts of society,” says SRF. “The planned execution [of Hasan] is indicative of how Hegseth manipulates public attention.”
Previous efforts at tapping into public opinion include a purge of ‘woke’ ideology in the armed forces. “No fat guys, no trans people, no beards, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals.” “Hegseth has evidently developed a strategy for packaging messages in a way that is easy to understand,” says SRF. “His ability to communicate in a way that resonates with Trump’s electorate was crucial in Trump’s decision to bring him into his administration in the first place.”
SRF’s summary of Hegseth’s communications strategy (German)

Ex-UK army chef jailed for nearly four years over homemade gun, explosives
LONDON, Oct 14 - A British army chef who was motivated by an extreme right-wing ideology was jailed for nearly four years on Wednesday after he was arrested with a homemade gun and explosives.
Mark Broadhurst, 28, was arrested at his barracks in September 2024 after police discovered online messages espousing racist views, his desire to form a militia and his intention to create homemade firearms and sell them to right-wing groups.
He was in a Telegram group with three other men who last year were jailed for a combined total of 29 years for planning to carry out a terrorist attack at mosques or synagogues as part of what they believed to be a coming "race war".
When Broadhurst was arrested, police found knives and crossbows, black powder, 9mm ammunition and air pistols at his home address, as well as what police described as "an improvised homemade cannon".
Broadhurst pleaded guilty to possession of a firearm and making or possessing an explosive under suspicious circumstances, though he denied he possessed them for the purposes of terrorism.
But a judge ruled that Broadhurst's offences were connected to terrorism and he was sentenced at Sheffield Crown Court to three years and 10 months in prison.
"Mark Broadhurst was clearly interested in violence and developing weapons that had the ability to cause untold harm to innocent people," Frank Ferguson, head of the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said.
"He was immersed in extremist material and maintained close contact with three now-convicted terrorists inspired by SS tactics and supremacist ideology over a prolonged period." REUTERS

Norwegian police arrested five people Wednesday as part of an international investigation into suspected fraud and bribery involving NATO procurement contracts, with authorities estimating losses of at least 1 million euros ($1.1 million).
The suspects were detained in the western Norwegian region of Bergen over allegations that a company and its subcontractors inflated invoices for services provided to NATO vessels visiting ports in northwestern Europe between 2021 and 2025.
Norway's national economic crime unit said the alleged overbilling targeted the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA), which provides procurement and logistical support to the alliance's 32 member states and their partners.
The investigation also prompted coordinated searches in Germany and Romania, according to Eurojust, the European Union's agency for criminal justice cooperation.
Investigators suspect that the company submitted fraudulent invoices for shore-based services supporting vessels and their crews during port visits. The company is also accused of using an intermediary to bribe public officials in exchange for favorable treatment in contracts involving the NSPA.
Eurojust estimated that NATO member states suffered losses of approximately 1 million euros, although investigators have yet to determine the full financial impact of the alleged scheme.
Authorities searched the company's premises and several residences in Romania, while German investigators conducted raids at two businesses and a private residence.
The company at the center of the investigation has not been publicly identified.
Marianne Bender, a senior public prosecutor at Norway's economic crime unit, warned that rising global defense spending could create greater opportunities for financial misconduct.
"Defence sector budgets are increasing worldwide, which entails an increased risk of economic crime. This is an area we are monitoring closely," Bender said.
"If NATO has been defrauded, there will be a tough crackdown," she added.
The NSPA coordinates purchases of defense equipment, security systems and logistical services for NATO members and partner countries. The alliance itself does not own military assets such as ships, tanks or weapons.

====================================================================================================

AI adoption more than doubles in almost every EU strategic sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:42:34 UTC
23:42:34 KST

Summary
· The share of firms using AI in EU strategic sectors grew from 7% in 2021 to 18% in 2025: media, energy and electronic sectors lead, while mobility, tourism and agri-food lag behind
· The analysis and the methodology developed by the JRC allow to measure and monitor AI uptake and barriers to use in the strategic sectors, covered by the Apply AI strategy
· The growth of AI use is mainly driven by LLMs as they have become more accessible and available at lower cost
· Sector-specific measures for AI adoption are essential for a deeper integration of AI into core processes
The share of firms using AI in EU strategic sectors grew from 7% in 2021 to 18% in 2025, according to a new JRC analysis. While each of the 10 sectors advanced in use of AI, the growth was uneven, driven mainly by accessible, general-purpose AI — systems that analyse or generate text, code, images, sound and video.
The analysis and the methodology developed allow to measure and monitor the levels and development of AI usage, types of deployments and barriers to its adoption in the strategic sectors covered by the Apply AI Strategy.
Launched a year ago, the strategy aims to boost AI uptake and encourages organisations to consider the opportunities and risks posed by AI solutions to improve processes, efficiency and competitiveness. It proposes specific actions to support the adoption of relevant AI use cases in strategic sectors. The 10 strategic sectors are essential for EU economic security, green and digital transitions, and defence readiness.
They include agri-food, climate (climate and environment); defence (defence, security and space); electronic (electronic communications); energy, manufacturing (manufacturing, engineering and construction); media (cultural and creative sectors, and media); mobility (mobility, transport and automotive); pharma (healthcare, including pharmaceuticals) and tourism.
Considering the whole EU economic areas besides the strategic ones, the share of firms adopting the use of AI is slightly higher: it grew from 8% in 2021 to 20% in 2025.
The analysis drew on the Eurostat’s ICT enterprise survey data collected between 2021 and 2025, based on the EU classification of economic activities (NACE). It assesses adoption levels, technologies, applications and adoption barriers across them. The results are published in the report AI adoption across European strategic sectors.
What are the AI adoption trends in strategic sectors?
Firms in the cultural and creative sectors, media, energy, and electronic communications are leading the AI adoption with respectively 38%, 34% and 30 % of firms using AI. In these sectors, AI is used for a variety of business functions, from ICT security to R&D and production, demonstrating a broader diffusion of the technology.
In contrast, mobility, tourism and agri‑food are the sectors presenting the lowest uptake. In these, AI applications are still confined to marketing, sales, and other accessible tasks. Manufacturing and climate industries show a mixed pattern, combining ready-to-use AI tools with a modest shift towards using AI in production processes.
In general, the increased AI adoption is mainly driven by AI systems analysing and generating written or audio output for marketing and sales purposes, technologies which have become more accessible and are available at a lower cost.
From tools to core processes, different adoption patterns across strategic sectors
While the overall adoption curve is positive, the analysis highlights that in many cases AI still needs to be embedded into core business processes, such as production, where the greatest productivity gains are possible. Firms that tailor AI and integrate it into their production, workflows or infrastructure tend to achieve higher value-added outcomes, leveraging data and expertise.
The differences between capital-intensive industries, typically requiring sophisticated computing infrastructure, and labour-intensive sectors, based on people and skills, play also a role for understanding AI adoption. The data show that the capital-intensive sectors, such as energy and electronics, are experiencing a stronger growth in AI uptake than sectors more balanced in terms of capital and labour. Between 2021 and 2025, AI-uptake of energy firms grew from 18% to 34%, while electronics from 12% to 30%.
A sector-specific approach is needed to support AI adoption
The analysis highlights three key components when looking at how firms adopt AI: how much a company has reorganised its way of working to take full advantage of AI, how much it uses AI in production, and to what extent it is adopting ready-to-use AI solutions vs custom made ones, the level of AI commoditisation.
The ranking of strategic sectors along these key components shows a positive correlation between organisation and production. The firms investing more in structural organisational changes to integrate AI are more likely to use AI in production, suggesting that organisational changes must be prioritised. This is the case of energy, electronic communications or defence industries.
The analysis reveals that the use of ready-to-use AI solutions vs custom-made ones depends on the specificities of each sector. For instance, the climate sector, despite having a medium AI uptake, displays a low uptake of off-the-shelf AI solutions, as it requires a higher degree of customisation compared to other strategic sectors.
At the same time, the manufacturing sector, overall displaying a low AI uptake, ranks higher than climate for adopting off-the-shelf solutions. This indicates that using accessible ready-to-use AI solutions does not necessarily increase integration of AI into production processes.
Overall, the analysis suggests that policy measures aimed at increasing AI integration into core processes need to be tailored to the specificities of the strategic sector.
Bottlenecks to AI adoption
The data show that the lack of relevant expertise is widely indicated as the main obstacle to AI adoption across the vast majority of strategic sectors. In particular, two factors emerge as the dominant bottlenecks: the scarcity of specialised skills and the regulatory uncertainty, including concerns about data protection and privacy. The report suggests that digitalisation initiatives, skills development, and organisational change can support AI uptake and close the gap between tool uptake to deeper integration.
The results of the study will support policy makers with setting targets and create new sector-specific measures on how to increase AI adoption in the strategic economic areas.

Breadcrumb
Azerbaijan school hijab ban spark protests and rupture with Turkey
New school dress rules introduced across Azerbaijan’s primary and secondary schools this week, which effectively ban the Muslim hijab, have led to 37 arrests and triggered class boycotts, and a nationwide social media campaign while causing a row with the country's longtime ally Turkey.
The newly implemented rules, approved last month, prohibit clothing that the government says violates the “principle of secularism”.
Although the regulations do not explicitly state that they target the Muslim headscarf, videos circulating online have shown girls in hijabs crying after being denied entry to schools under the new uniform requirements.
The amendment to the Descriptions of Uniforms for Students of State General Education Institutions aimed to establish a unified dress code reflecting the country’s “secular principle”, according to the state-run Azerbaijani Press Agency (APA).
Clothing reflecting the “history, culture, and national and moral values of the Azerbaijani people” may be worn during celebrations, subject to approval by the Pedagogical Council, which operates under the Ministry of Science and Education, APA said.
However, this decision to effectively ban the hijab has sparked an outcry.
Local Azerbaijani media outlets reported that students at at least two schools boycotted classes in protest against the restrictions, while pupils also reportedly demonstrated outside schools on Monday.
Azerbaijan’s Interior Ministry told APA that people in Baku had confronted school staff over the uniform requirements, damaged school property and attempted to disrupt lessons.
It said that “37 people were arrested as a criminal investigation had been opened into disturbing public order”.
Meanwhile, social media users based in Azerbaijan have reported difficulties accessing platforms such as Instagram and TikTok, claiming that the sites only work when accessed through virtual private networks (VPNs).
Protests against the uniform policy are ongoing, with critics accusing the authorities of restricting access to social media to suppress dissent.
Azerbaijani authorities have not officially commented on the reported social media outages.
Rupture with Turkey
The controversy has also attracted attention beyond Azerbaijan.
Oktay Saral, an adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, described Azerbaijan’s move as “unacceptable”.
“Leaving a student who covers her head for reasons of faith at the school gate – how can this fit into any conscience, any sense of justice?” he posted on X.
Turkey has been a key ally of Azerbaijan, supporting it in its 2020 war with Armenia, which ultimately led to Azerbaijan regaining control of the Nagorno-Karabakh region.
The ruling Yeni Azerbaijan Party (YAP) hit back on Tuesday, saying Saral’s “irresponsible” comments risked damaging Azerbaijan’s closest relationship on the international stage.
Azerbaijan is a predominantly Shia Muslim country but, after decades of Soviet rule, emerged as one of the most secular states in the Muslim world.
The authorities have imposed restrictions on religious worship and arrested individuals accused of "extremism" in efforts to prevent radicalisation.
Critics have accused the Azerbaijani government of persecuting devout Muslims.
Restrictions on headscarves previously sparked demonstrations between 2010 and 2012, with police dispersing protests and making arrests.
Meanwhile, Azerbaijan’s close relationship with Israel, particularly amid its genocidal war on Gaza, has prompted criticism of the government from Turkish social media users.
Baku’s decision not to leave the UN General Assembly hall during Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s address last month drew a wave of condemnation.

frame to folly transforms from carnival gateway to neighborhood teahouse in pittsburgh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:35:50 UTC
23:35:50 KST

frame to folly transforms from carnival gateway to neighborhood teahouse in pittsburgh
frame to folly, a collaborativde project between architectural crafts collective, partlab, and neighborhood allies, is a modular timber pavilion developed for different sites and community uses in pittsburgh.
[FEATURED]
modular pavilion shifts from carnival gateway to public furniture
Frame to Folly is a modular timber pavilion designed to be disassembled, transported, and reconfigured for different sites and community uses in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Developed by Carnegie Mellon University’s student-led Architectural Crafts Collective and Pittsburgh-based PARTlab (Laboratory for Radical Participatory Design), the project forms part of a year-long partnership with local nonprofit Neighborhood Allies.
The structure uses a system of vertical timber frames connected by interchangeable infill panels that double as seats, tables, backrests, and awnings. Initially assembled as a gateway for Pittsburgh’s annual Spring Carnival, the pavilion was prefabricated at a shared fabrication space, flat-packed, and transported to the festival site. The frames were joined on the ground and raised into place using a communal technique that required no heavy equipment. Bright orange infill panels were then secured with removable hardware, providing seating, shade, and other amenities for festival visitors.
Reusable timber components adapt to new community setting
After the three-day event, the pavilion was disassembled and moved to the backyard of a neighborhood tea shop, where the same components were reconfigured as flexible public furniture and an open-air teahouse. Built collaboratively by the Architectural Crafts Collective, a student-led design-build collective at Carnegie Mellon University, and Pittsburgh-based PARTlab, the modular system adapts to the new setting while retaining its original components.
At the end of its use at the tea shop, the structure will either be gifted to another community for reconfiguration or disassembled and donated to a material bank operated by the neighboring public library. Through its successive forms and uses, Frame to Folly demonstrates design for disassembly and material reuse, treating architecture as an adaptable system that can respond to changing community needs.
project info:
name: Frame to Folly
architect: Carnegie Mellon University’s Architectural Crafts Collective and PARTlab (Laboratory for Radical Participatory Design)
design team: Sydney Mansavage, Emma Phelps, Tai Le, Gaetan Pelletey, Hazel Buonopane, Jason Asiedu, Neal Lucas Hitch, Kristina Fisher
location: Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, US

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. Russia has to build a transparent and clear system for the life and work of foreign specialists, taking into account the needs of all those arriving in the country, CEO of the Agency for Attracting Foreign Talent to Russia Irina Korotkova said.
Earlier, Korotkova said that since the launch of the Time to Live in Russia program, people from 97 countries had submitted 842 applications, with the first seven candidates from China, Jordan, Syria, Canada, Iran, Mexico and Spain already approved.
According to the CEO, interest in the program exceeded the organizers’ expectations. She noted that participants share Russia’s values and are willing to benefit the country.
“Over the past six months, we have observed that the mechanism [of the Time to Live in Russia program] really works and interest in the program has even exceeded our expectations. These are people that share our values and want to benefit our country. For this mechanism to work, we have to create a transparent and clear system for foreign specialists to live and work here. People should consider our country their home, a place where they can realize their potential and where their families will live. Scientists have certain needs, while representatives of creative professions or athletes have others. So each person needs a personalized approach,” the press service of the Agency for Strategic Initiatives (ASI) quoted Korotkova as saying.
Support from day one
Once foreigners receive the special status, they can get a temporary residence permit outside the quota or immediately apply for a residence permit, bypassing the temporary residence stage. The processing of applications will be fast-tracked. The program also helps with relocation, finding a job and settling in Russia.
According to First Deputy Head of the Citizenship and Foreign Citizens Registration Service under the Russian Interior Ministry Konstantin Bukreyev, the ministry helps foreigners who have chosen to move to Russia, including under a decree that streamlines the procedure for obtaining temporary residence permits for those sharing traditional Russian spiritual and moral values. "The Interior Ministry also provides them with advisory and other assistance with paperwork on a priority basis, in a one-stop shop," Bukreyev said.
Program participants’ stories
One participant, Mexico’s Domingo Garcia Martinez Surita, has already been living in Moscow for several years. He worked for big international pharmaceutical companies and is now developing the business for the Russian pharmaceutical firm R-Pharm in Latin America.
"Russia is a wonderful country, it is very safe here. Traditional values resonate with me. I am a Christian, a rather conservative person and I like how Russia values family," he said.
Another participant, Jordanian bioinformatics scientist Tarek Faruni, returned to Russia after working at leading research centers abroad, including Harvard Medical School, McGill University and ETH Zurich. "Russia is a great country. I have lived here before and decided to return, I like Russian culture. My wife is Russian, my son speaks Russian and we want to raise him here," he said.
About program
The Time to Live in Russia program was launched in April 2026, following an initiative to streamline the relocation of foreigners who share traditional Russian values. It is run by the Agency for Attracting Foreign Talent to Russia, a subsidiary of the ASI.
Apart from this program, Russia also has a relocation mechanism under Presidential Decree No. 702, which streamlines the procedure of obtaining temporary residence permits for foreigners who share traditional Russian spiritual and moral values.

Google has defended its decision to clear hundreds of hectares of forest for data centres in Finland before completing environmental assessments, claiming it believed authorities had agreed to the work. The dispute has also reached local government, where a senior building inspector has taken leave after alleging that she faced dismissal over comments to the media.
The company cleared approximately 330 hectares in Muhos, northern Finland, and carried out work at another planned data centre site in Kajaani.
Add Helsinki Times as a preferred source on Google (opens Google in a new tab)
Finland's Licensing and Supervisory Agency, LVV, ordered both projects to halt work last week because their environmental impact assessments remain unfinished.
In a written response submitted to LVV on Wednesday, Google said discussions with authorities had led it to believe the work complied with Finnish legislation.
According to Finnish broadcaster Yle, Google began logging in Muhos in March and informed municipal building authorities about the scale of its operations in June.
The company said municipal officials approved preparatory work under Section 109 of Finland's Building Act and confirmed on 23 June that operations could proceed.
Documents examined by Helsingin Sanomat, however, show that LVV had warned in May that forest clearance of this scale required an environmental impact assessment. Finnish legislation requires such assessments when permanent forest removal exceeds 200 hectares in a continuous area.
Google had also applied for a landscape work permit, which the municipality rejected while the assessment remained incomplete.
The dispute has raised questions about municipal oversight.
Muhos building inspector Eero Airaksinen, who approved preparatory work in June, previously told HS that he had faced pressure from several directions and was uncertain about the legal requirements. He is now on sick leave.
Meanwhile, chief building inspector Jultuz Änwär has taken leave following a dispute over her employment, according to HS.
Änwär told Yle that municipal officials threatened to terminate her employment after she criticised the handling of Google's project in an interview. She joined the municipality in August and said she would not have approved the work while permit procedures remained incomplete.
Municipal technical director Mikko Kari denied any connection between the interview and discussions about terminating her employment during probation.
Municipal committee chairman Jaakko Pellikka confirmed to HS that Änwär had requested leave but did not disclose the reason. No dismissal decision has been announced.
Google said it intends to complete the environmental assessments within six weeks for Kajaani and ten weeks for Muhos.
The company also requested permission to undertake limited stabilisation work, including drainage management, erosion prevention and water quality monitoring.
Residents have raised concerns about muddy runoff flowing from the cleared land towards the Oulujoki River, according to HS.
The dispute concerns projects forming part of Google's €13 billion investment plans for Finnish data centres over two years.

Saudi Arabia/Yemen: Civilians must not pay the price of escalation in hostilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:32:28 UTC
23:32:28 KST

Responding to the dramatic escalation of armed hostilities between the Huthi de facto authorities, the Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia in recent weeks and the growing toll on civilians amidst ongoing attacks, Amnesty International’s Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, Heba Morayef, said:
“The risks to civilians in Yemen and Saudi Arabia are rapidly increasing each day this conflict escalates. All parties to the conflict must ensure civilians are protected and abide by their obligations under international humanitarian law.
“Over the past week, deadly Huthi attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia have caused significant civilian harm, including a 10 October attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that killed 13 people and wounded hundreds more- the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in over a decade. The attack came amidst the return of full-blown armed hostilities to Yemen with devastating consequences for civilians there, particularly on the coast and around Ta’iz, Yemen’s third largest city.
Civilians are never legitimate targets. They must not pay the price of further escalation.
Heba Morayef, Amnesty International
“Civilians are never legitimate targets. They must not pay the price of further escalation. The deliberate targeting of civilians or civilian infrastructure, including civilian airports, is prohibited under international humanitarian law and can amount to a war crime.
“All warring parties must immediately refrain from carrying out direct attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as indiscriminate or disproportionate attacks.
“In Yemen, where civilians are already grappling with a severe humanitarian crisis and the impact of years of sporadic bouts of fighting, the conflict will further compound the suffering of the civilian population. It is critical that parties to the conflict take all feasible precautions to avoid or, in any event, minimize harm to civilians and civilian objects, and provide unfettered access to humanitarian aid for civilians in need.”
Background
Recent weeks have seen a dramatic escalation in hostilities between the Huthi de-facto authorities in Yemen, the internationally recognized Yemeni government and Saudi Arabia. The renewed conflict in Yemen is linked to the regional conflict involving the US, Israel, and Iran. The Huthis are supported by Iran and the Yemeni government by Saudi Arabia.
The escalation in Yemen follows the breakdown of a UN-brokered ceasefire in July 2026, following air strikes on Sana’a airport claimed by the internationally recognized government. Between 2015 and 2022, Amnesty International documented gross human rights violations and serious violations of international humanitarian law, including likely war crimes, committed by parties to the conflict, including the Huthi armed group and Saudi-led coalition.
The escalation has been accompanied by intensified ground fighting between the Huthis and Yemeni government forces inside Yemen, including deadly attacks by Huthi forces on civilian areas. While the real death toll is significantly higher, the UN human rights office reported in late September that it had documented at least 32 civilians, including 15 children, killed since August.
Huthi forces have also carried out attacks targeting airports, military installations and oil facilities across Saudi Arabia, as well as ships at sea. Between 5 and 11 October, Huthi attacks on civilian airports across Saudi Arabia damaged passenger terminals and civilian aircraft and killed at least 20 people and injured more than 350 people, according to the National.
Saudi Arabia has also resumed its air strikes in Yemen. According to the Yemen Data Project, at least 66 civilians have been killed and 90 injured.
The latest escalation is exacerbating an already severe humanitarian crisis in Yemen where, according to UN figures, at least 18.3 million people are acutely food insecure and more than 2.2 million children under five and 1.3 million pregnant and breastfeeding women are acutely malnourished. Access to food and healthcare have repeatedly worsened due to the conflict, warring party conduct and humanitarian funding cuts.

Ethiopian troops mass heavy weapons near Eritrean border amid war fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:22:29 UTC
23:22:29 KST

Andrew Wasike 
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Ethiopian government forces have deployed tanks and heavy weapons toward the Eritrean border after advancing through northern Tigray, according to the latest conflict-monitoring reports on Wednesday.
The move has raised fears that renewed fighting could escalate into a confrontation between the neighboring countries, said the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), an independent organization that monitors armed conflicts worldwide.
“Eyewitnesses observed a substantial convoy of tanks and heavy weaponry advancing from Adigrat toward Fatsi and Zalambessa,” according to ACLED, referring to two key strategic towns on the Eritrean frontier.
ACLED reported that the movement began overnight Monday and continued Tuesday, following the capture of the towns by Ethiopian troops and allied Tigray Peace Force (TPF) fighters.
Eritrea has rejected Ethiopian accusations of military incursions, with Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel accusing Addis Ababa of pursuing “an unprovoked war of aggression.”
The Eritrean government has also urged international intervention, with Foreign Minister Osman Saleh urging the UN Security Council to “take the requisite deterrent measures against it in accordance with Chapter VII of the UN Charter.”
The Critical Threats Project, a US-based security research organization, said in its Tuesday assessment that Ethiopian troops had advanced approximately 37 kilometers (23 miles) north from Adigrat to Zalambessa without encountering substantial resistance.
It also reported that Eritrean troops had established defensive positions north of Zalambessa, citing open-source military monitoring, although the extent of Eritrea's deployment could not be independently confirmed.
ACLED said Eritrean forces previously stationed along the Zalambessa-Fatsi corridor withdrew across the border Monday, while rival Tigrayan fighters retreated toward Debre Damo and Irob.
The withdrawal does not establish that all Eritrean troops have left Ethiopian territory, with the situation along other sections of the border remaining unclear.
The military advances are part of an Ethiopian counteroffensive against forces linked to the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), whose renewed campaign has destabilized northern Ethiopia.
The TPF is aligned with Ethiopia's federal government, while the rival Tigray Defense Forces are associated with the TPLF.
The latest fighting has also brought Ethiopia and Eritrea into an increasingly hostile diplomatic confrontation.
Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of sending troops into Tigray and supporting armed opposition groups, allegations Asmara denies.
In a letter to the UN Security Council, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos warned that his country had "no option but to defend itself against Eritrea."
Eritrea responded by accusing Ethiopia of threatening its sovereignty and attempting to justify military action against its territory.
The dispute is further complicated by Ethiopia's longstanding demand for access to the Red Sea, which Eritrea views as a potential threat to its territorial integrity, particularly regarding the strategic port of Assab.
Landlocked since Eritrea gained independence in 1993, Ethiopia has repeatedly described maritime access as essential to its economic development.
The two countries fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 before restoring diplomatic relations in 2018. Eritrean troops later supported Ethiopia's federal government during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, but relations deteriorated after the Pretoria peace agreement.
The renewed military buildup threatens to undermine that agreement and raises concerns that fighting inside Ethiopia could spread across the border.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu responded Wednesday afternoon to the detailed defamation lawsuit filed by former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar, addressing just one of the allegations. "Ronen Bar, who saw the warning signs on the night of October 7 and didn't call me, now says he didn't have my phone number. Ronen, are you serious?" Netanyahu wrote in response to the lawsuit.
"You had my red phone number, and you could have called me immediately, as all the heads of the security establishment do," he continued. "The Shin Bet security guards, your subordinates, who are with me 24/7, could have reached me within minutes. How many lives could we have saved if you had only called in time?"
Responding to Netanyahu's remarks, associates of Bar said no one takes the matter more seriously than he does, adding that the loss of so many lives was an extremely serious matter.
"If the prime minister is serious, he should waive his immunity, face the allegations and provide explanations for the policies he established, the communication procedures he put in place, which the military secretary described, and the recommendations to eliminate senior Hamas officials that he never acted upon," an associate said.
Former military secretary Avi Gil, who held the position on the eve of October 7, explained in an interview last week that the prime minister does not ordinarily carry the red phone with him but goes to it when requested.
The retired major general also confirmed a report published by journalist Nadav Eyal in August 2024 concerning a warning about the possibility of war that Bar delivered to Netanyahu in July 2023.
Earlier Wednesday, the former Shin Bet director filed a defamation lawsuit against Netanyahu after the prime minister accused him of "crimes" related to his conduct before the October 7 massacre and amplified conspiracy theories alleging that Bar "knew about a real threat on the night of October 7."
Bar is seeking 3 million shekels in damages, demanding the disclosure of documents and calling on Netanyahu to waive his immunity. "In the absence of a state commission of inquiry, the truth will be established in court," the lawsuit states.
In the detailed filing, Bar outlined a timeline of the warnings he says he delivered to Netanyahu. He claimed that he repeatedly warned the prime minister about the possibility of a security escalation and that, contrary to Netanyahu's assertions, intelligence gathered by the Shin Bet was passed to the relevant authorities on the night of October 7.
The documents describe warnings conveyed to Netanyahu around Ramadan and the spring holidays in 2023, as well as between July and September of that year.
Bar alleged that he warned of the erosion of Israeli deterrence and challenged assessments that Hamas had been deterred. According to Bar, he also presented operational options targeting senior Hamas leaders, but the plans were never approved for implementation. He claimed Netanyahu dismissed or ignored the proposals.
According to the lawsuit, from late July through the Jewish High Holidays, Bar repeatedly warned that Israeli deterrence was weakening and disputed the prevailing assessment that Hamas was deterred. In fact, Bar maintained the opposite: He warned that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar had become increasingly messianic and called for a military strike, alongside a broader set of operational recommendations.
On Tuesday, Netanyahu acknowledged for the first time that Abbas Kamel, Egypt's intelligence chief at the time and one of President Abdel Fattah el-Sissi's closest associates, had landed in Israel about a week and a half before the October 7 massacre.
In an interview with Channel 14, Netanyahu said Kamel "did not meet with me because I was at a memorial ceremony for fallen IDF soldiers." According to reports, Kamel warned during the visit of "a major attack being planned by Hamas."
Netanyahu also claimed he did not know whom Kamel had met during the secret visit on September 26, 2023. "Egypt's intelligence minister was here. He spent 59 minutes on the ground. I'm turning to the security and law enforcement authorities. I want to know whom he met. Someone who met with him is trying to pin this on me," Netanyahu said. He also questioned, "Since when does an intelligence chief speak with a head of state?"
However, years earlier, Netanyahu had hosted Kamel at the prime minister's residence in Jerusalem. A video released at the time by the Prime Minister's Office showed Netanyahu and Kamel shaking hands and speaking, while Kamel was heading a delegation of senior Egyptian officials visiting Israel.
Two days after the October 7 massacre, Ynet journalist Smadar Perry reported, following an Associated Press report about an Egyptian warning, that Kamel had conveyed a message to Netanyahu's office warning of "something unusual, a massive operation" expected to originate from Gaza.
The Prime Minister's Office denied the report at the time.

Poland’s Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski has publicly criticized SpaceX chief Elon Musk over the latest disruptions in Starlink's operation in Ukraine. Poland is the largest supplier of Ukraine’s terminals, having provided about 29,500, roughly half the network. It also has a Starlink ground station in Wola Krobowska that provides connectivity for much of Central and Eastern Europe, including Ukraine, RMF24 reports.
On 13 October, SpaceX imposed a 100 mph (160 km/h) speed limit on the StarShield military package that Ukrainian forces use, disrupting drone missions without warning. Poland, which pays about $50 million a year for Ukraine’s Starlink terminals, told Musk it is watching.
“Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again? As your European customers, we are watching you,” Sikorski wrote on X.
The “big man” jab echoed their 2025 clash, when Musk told Sikorski to “be quiet, small man” after the minister noted that Warsaw, not SpaceX as charity, pays for the service.
Meanwhile, presidential adviser Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov said that this could not be a coincidence and was most likely tied to the current political situation.
When a drone outruns its own signal
The cap bites exactly where Ukraine’s drones do their work. The StarShield package had previously carried no data speed limit, and the change directly affected drones that use Starlink to steer in flight, the 7th Air Assault Corps said.
“During flights, the connection could drop for 10 to 20 seconds at speeds of just 110 to 120 kilometers per hour. The drones kept moving, but these interruptions made them harder to control,” the corps said, describing problems that now start well below the new ceiling.
A dependence Kyiv has feared for years. The limit revives an old worry. Ukraine neither owns nor controls Starlink, and the restriction follows fresh fears of a shutdown after Musk backed US President Donald Trump’s call for Zelenskyy to resign.

Strait of Hormuz traffic plunges once again amid new wave of Houthi attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:21:01 UTC
23:21:01 KST

Nuran Erkul Kaya
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
- Middle East crude oil, petroleum, and LNG exports collapse amid sharp escalation in maritime attacks
- Strait of Hormuz traffic down to 6 vessels on Monday
- Low of 6.7M barrels of crude transited per day this week
Crude oil and petroleum exports from the Middle East sharply dropped over the past week as Iranian-backed Yemeni Houthi militias intensified their attacks on commercial vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz, disrupting regional shipping lanes.
Maritime transit in the region suffered drastically since the US and Israel’s pre-emptive joint strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, followed by Tehran’s effective closure of the vital waterway and a subsequent American naval blockade.
Attacks on commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz reached a new peak this year over the past week.
At least 14 incidents of attacks, attempted strikes, and obstructions were recorded in and around the Strait of Hormuz on Oct. 5-12, while six ships were attacked on Monday alone, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations and global maritime security sources.
Commercial vessel traffic via the strategic chokepoint fell to its lowest since July 22, affecting outward energy flows.
Oil, petroleum, and liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports from the Middle East plummeted in the wake of the war, and while there have been signs of partial recovery, intensifying security risks sparked concerns.
Houthis increased their attacks on Saudi Arabia, threatening transit through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. 
Vessel transits through Bab el-Mandeb, Hormuz hit new low
Middle Eastern crude oil, petroleum, and liquid chemical exports — including shipments from the Gulf of Oman and the Red Sea — fell from 21.1 million barrels per day on Oct. 8 to 6.7 million barrels on Oct. 11, 10.4 million barrels on Monday, and 8.3 million barrels on Tuesday, according to Kpler.
The weekly average of 17 million barrels remained below the pre-war volume of around 23.3 million barrels per day.
Only six commercial ships were able to transit the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, while previously 32 ships passed through on Oct. 8, 24 on Oct. 9, 11 on Oct. 10, and 12 on Oct. 11.
Meanwhile, vessel transit through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait also dropped, with 35 vessels passing through on Oct. 8, 39 on Oct. 10, 46 on Oct. 11, and 32 on Monday.
The attempts by the Houthis to establish a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia to seize control of the Bab el-Mandeb corridor added a new volatile dimension to the wider conflict.
Large-scale supply disruptions across both the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait could pressure global energy supplies and market stability even further, analysts say.

The former mayor of Groningen, Koen Schuiling, has lost his appeal against a conviction for offending public decency that led to him being forced to take early retirement two years ago.
Judges upheld a €250 fine imposed by a court in Zwolle after he was found guilty of masturbating in his car on the A7 motorway in the city.
He was reported to police by a passing lorry driver, but insisted when questioned that he had stopped to relieve stomach complaints caused by a medical condition.
The court found that the driver had a clear view of Schuiling’s car and had given an detailed and consistent account of what he saw. His testimony was corroborated by an audio recording made in the cab in which he could be heard angrily challenging Schuiling about his behaviour.
Schuiling stepped down from his post in September 2024, a year before his term of office was due to end. At the time he said he lacked energy after an “extraordinarily intense period” that included the coronavirus lockdowns and the rollout of compensation to homeowners in Groningen who were affected by earthquake damage.
But it soon emerged that home affairs minister Judith Uitermark demanded his resignation after she was briefed by the police and public prosecutor about the allegations against Schuiling, arguing it exposed him to blackmail.
Police had received two earlier complaints in the previous six months about the mayor behaving inappropriately at the wheel of his vehicle.

In his view, Ukraine needs to ramp up its domestic production of air defense systems. The expert believes Ukraine will be able to do so faster than European countries can develop the industrial capacity needed to meet Ukraine’s needs.
As Ukrinform reported, Serhii Beskrestnov (“Flash”), a freelance adviser to the President on technology, said SpaceX had imposed speed restrictions on Starlink terminals while in motion overnight without notifying Ukraine’s Defense Forces.

Colombia inaugurates embassy to Israel in Jerusalem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:08:45 UTC
23:08:45 KST

Colombia inaugurates embassy to Israel in Jerusalem
Palestinian officials condemn move by Colombia’s new government that marked a major shift after former President Petro had severed ties with Israel.
Colombia has opened its embassy to Israel in Jerusalem, joining a small group of countries in taking the controversial step of backing Israel’s claim to sovereignty in the contested city.
Palestinian officials swiftly denounced the inauguration on Wednesday that came as Israel is facing mounting international pressure over the genocidal war on Gaza, where three years of attacks have killed more than 74,000 people.
The move by the administration of new Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella is a major shift from his left-wing predecessor Gustavo Petro, who in 2024 severed ties with Israel over the war on Gaza.
De la Espriella, who was sworn in in August, has also restored a free trade agreement between Israel and Colombia that Petro terminated.
Colombian Minister of Foreign Affairs Omar Bula Escobar said on Wednesday that relations between the two countries “should never have been broken” and that Bogota was taking “taking a concrete step towards restoring diplomatic relations”.
“Israel is a strategic partner. It always has been, and from now on, it will be an even stronger one,” he said during a ceremony that marked the embassy’s opening.
The opening made Colombia the 10th country to establish its embassy in Israel in Jerusalem – most countries keep their formal diplomatic missions in Tel Aviv.
Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar welcomed the move during the ceremony. “This is an important date for the State of Israel. It’s also an important date for the city of Jerusalem,” he said while signing the Colombian embassy’s guest book.
Colombian Ambassador Tania Gilinski said Israel had always been a “strategic partner” and that moving forward it “will be so with even greater determination and strength”.
‘Violation of international law’
The Palestinian Authority condemned Colombia’s embassy move, calling it “a violation of international legitimacy resolutions” that undermines “the international consensus on the legal status of the holy city”.
Jordan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs also criticised the move as a “violation of international law and relevant international resolutions”.
United States President Donald Trump moved the US embassy to Israel from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem during his first term in 2018, angering Palestinians and sparking international condemnation. Previous US presidents, as well as nearly every other country, refrained from opening embassies in Jerusalem, arguing that the city’s final status should first be resolved in negotiations between Israelis and Palestinians.
The status of Jerusalem remains one of the core unresolved issues of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, with Israel claiming the undivided city as its capital while Palestinians view occupied East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state.
Israel occupied East Jerusalem and annexed it in 1967, in a move not recognised by the vast majority of the international community.
Since Trump relocated the US embassy to Jerusalem, only a handful of small, US-aligned countries have followed suit, namely Fiji, Guatemala, Honduras, Papua New Guinea, Paraguay and Nauru. Kosovo and Somaliland, which are not member-states of the United Nations, have also opened what they consider their embassies in Jerusalem.

‘English nationalist’ content creators film themselves in asylum seekers’ house
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:08:24 UTC
23:08:24 KST

A Home Office accommodation provider has launched an investigation after “English nationalist” content creators posing as contractors filmed themselves entering a property housing asylum seekers.
The video, titled “HMO Hunting in Leicestershire”, was posted to the Truthhurts101UK YouTube account, which describes itself as being run by an “English nationalist citizen journalist” and claims to cover “immigration, demographic change, policing and stories others overlook”. The footage was also posted to the associated TH101UK’s X account, where is has been viewed more than 300,000 times.
The video shows three men accessing the back entrance of a house in Leicestershire accommodating asylum seekers. The men enter via an unlocked back door and move through several rooms of the house, including the kitchen, where they examine the contents of the fridge. They repeatedly claim to be looking for “paperwork”, searching through a pile of letters near the front door and boxes discarded in the back garden. The man filming, who narrates the video, claims he is the first to “document” this property.
When the men filming encounter three men, who are believed to be asylum seekers living at the property, in the kitchen they tell them they are contractors sent to assess the property for repairs. They ask one man living at the property whether the property is run by Serco, a Home Office contractor used for asylum seeker accommodation, which the man confirms, and whether he has “paperwork”, which he says he does not.
When the man living at the property asks the man filming for his ID he briefly shows him a lanyard. It is unclear what information it shows.
In the footage, the man filming specifically names the street and the village where the house is located, and shows the exterior of the property and its surroundings, making it clearly identifiable.
A Serco spokesperson said: “We are aware of this post. We take issues of this nature extremely seriously and are investigating.”
A Home Office spokesperson said: “The safety and security of those housed in asylum accommodation, staff who work there and local communities are of the upmost importance to the government. We engage extensively with contractors, local authorities and the police and expect any instances of criminality to be taken seriously.”
A TH101UK spokesperson defended the footage, accused the asylum seekers of being “ticking timebombs” and questioned why the Guardian, which they described as “irrelevant” and a “rag”, was “scrutinising independent journalism”.
They added: “Don’t worry, I’ll keep asking the questions you should be.”
In recent years, there has been an increase of self-styled “auditors”, and far-right activists have attempted to gain access to hotels and other forms of accommodation housing asylum seekers, sometimes under the guise of wanting to carry out “inspections”.
When challenged, often by private security outside hotels, some have attempted to confuse the issue by quoting supposed “common law” principles, which have been taken up by members of the far right as a legal recourse that supersedes statutory laws.
However, the increasing use of houses of multiple occupancy (HMOs) as part of the government’s plans to phase out the use of hotels to house asylum seekers has given some of these activists a new target, with some obtaining addresses from publicly available documents and sharing details with one another in online groups.
TH101UK entered another asylum seeker property in Norfolk several months ago and posted footage online.
After the Guardian brought the footage to the attention of YouTube, a spokesperson confirmed that it breached its standards, and said that it had been removed from the platform.
A YouTube spokesperson said: “Harassment and cyberbullying are not allowed on YouTube and as part of this, we do not allow content that reveals someone’s personally identifiable information. Upon review, we have removed the flagged video for violating our harassment and cyberbullying policies.”
Louise Calvey, the executive director of Asylum Matters, expressed concern about the video. She said: “This is a premeditated invasion into someone’s home for clicks and attention. The people that court this are the very worst of us, they’re the ones the pose a threat – barging into people’s homes, filming in people’s private spaces. The audacity and sense of entitlement is breathtaking.
“Government must urgently take steps to improve protections, remove the details of shared accommodation sites of all descriptions from the public domain, support people accommodated as victims of crimes, and escalate quicker police responses.”
