The end of UNIFIL: What next for south Lebanon?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:07:46 UTC
23:07:46 KST

Breadcrumb
The end of UNIFIL: What next for south Lebanon?
Beirut, Lebanon - As the UN's longest-serving presence on the Blue Line between Lebanon and Israel counts down to its exit, a European replacement is being floated as the answer.
The real choice facing Beirut, however, is between a security arrangement written in Washington and one it builds itself.
For 48 years, the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL) has been deployed across the country's southern border villages.
It never deterred the wars fought across the Blue Line - a 120-kilometre (75-mile) temporary demarcation boundary established by the United Nations on 7 June 2000 to confirm the withdrawal of Israeli forces from southern Lebanon.
What they did, consistently, was watch, record, and report, and in a region where every side contests every account, that act of witnessing carried weight of its own.
Few in Lebanon expect the UN body's exit to change the balance of force. “UNIFIL was merely an eyewitness,” retired Brigadier General Saeed Qazah, a military expert, told The New Arab.
Operating under Chapter VI of its mandate, it could only record violations and report them to the UN. Its absence, he argued, “will not change the military reality on the ground as much as it will leave a logistical and economic vacuum”.
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun's push for an extension was blocked by a US-Israeli veto, and he had welcomed a French-Italian idea for a European Union force to take UNIFIL's place. On Monday, the contours of that EU role took a more concrete shape.
European Union foreign ministers agreed to establish a new support mission in Lebanon to advise and train the country's military and internal security forces. It would have an initial mandate of three years.
But the European option still lacks the mandate, consent, and the American backing it would need.
UNIFIL's real successor is being negotiated elsewhere, and what awaits Lebanon after December is less a handover than a test of whether the state can do alone what it has long outsourced.
A European force without a shape
The new European mission "will advise and assist the Lebanese Armed Forces and Internal Security Forces to strengthen territorial control, border security, and internal security," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said in a statement on Monday.
Over 10 EU members are reportedly willing to contribute people and resources to it, but more operational planning is required before it is launched. An EU official told Reuters this week that the mission hoped to deploy personnel in the coming months.
But retired Brigadier General Saeed Qazah sees a deeper flaw.
“UNIFIL could not prevent the Lebanese-Israeli conflict or control the land and the border, and European forces will have no effective role there either,” he said.
Enforcing peace would require a Chapter VII mandate, which a Russian and Chinese veto would block. “No country is willing to send its soldiers to fight or sacrifice their lives on behalf of the Lebanese army,” he added.
Consent is the other wall. Political analyst Ali Sbeiti says Israel refuses to give Paris any role, given their disputes over regional files and the Gaza war. Qazah agrees that no foreign force can deploy on the border without the approval of both Lebanon, Israel, and a UN resolution.
The one exception, he said, “is a mission limited to training and logistical support for the Lebanese army, away from the border. The only feasible European mission, in other words, is the one that does least of what UNIFIL did”.
UNIFIL's real successor is being negotiated elsewhere
Writer and political analyst Nader Hijaz points to the "third party" under discussion in talks between Beirut and Israel, a body that would verify implementation of the framework agreement.
“That is, in practice, the field replacement for UNIFIL,” he said. Whether it would merely monitor or hold broad powers, such as searching homes and seizing weapons, is unresolved, and a deal has been deferred until after Israel's elections.
On one point, Hijaz is categorical. “Washington will never accept any force that is not under direct American command,” he told The New Arab. The US and Israel, he said, are open to a specific Italian role but not a French one.
Sbeiti adds that the Europeans lack the nerve to act in the south without explicit American blessing. The successor, in short, is being decided in a US-brokered process, on a timetable set by Israeli politics.
Beirut and Hezbollah's calculations
The Lebanese state and army would welcome almost any arrangement that averts a vacuum, and President Joseph Aoun immediately expressed backing for the EU’s announcement this week of a security support mission.
Hijaz notes that military cooperation with France and Italy is already established, and Sbeiti describes an official welcome for any friendly presence, even as a mere eyewitness.
Hezbollah, however, is harder to read. Its secretary-general, Naim Qassem, has called the US-sponsored framework agreement a red line and a surrender of sovereignty, holding up instead the US-Iranian memorandum signed in Islamabad.
Qazah expects the party to reject any foreign force, since it does not want a witness to its breaches, “just as Israel does not want neutral forces bearing witness to its violations”.
Sbeiti, however, disagrees. “Hezbollah can no longer block a plan the state backs, and has no fundamental problem with France, given shared understandings between Paris, the party and Tehran,” he told The New Arab. “The main knot remains with the American and Israeli sides,” he noted.
Hijjaz, meanwhile, says the party's stance will hinge on whether a force operates south of the Litani or beyond it, and whether it pursues the group's weapons. Either way, the decisive veto lies outside Lebanon.
What south Lebanon loses
The mission is exiting in its worst hour. It has recorded a sharp escalation between Israel and Hezbollah, with hundreds of projectiles on some days. It still fields more than 7,400 troops from 46 countries, its backbone European, and seven peacekeepers have been killed in hostile attacks in 2026 alone.
Ceasefires have collapsed in succession, from April's arrangements to the US-sponsored Trilateral Framework in June, and Israeli forces still hold positions inside Lebanon that Beirut says block the army's full deployment.
Washington led the push to end the mission, favouring arrangements outside the Security Council, as in Gaza. Prime Minister Nawaf Salam warned of a vacuum, arguing the UN offers a neutrality no other actor can match, and more than two-thirds of parliament petitioned for UNIFIL to be strengthened, not withdrawn.
Since 1978, and especially after its reinforcement following the 2006 war, UNIFIL has been an economic engine for the border villages.
At its peak, Qazah said, more than 15,000 soldiers in a narrow area drove spending, services, and procurement. Their departure will cut “a vital economic artery” in a region already devastated by Israeli strikes.
Three roads after December
The first is direct military coordination between the Lebanese and Israeli armies, favoured by Washington and Israel and signalled by US envoys' talk of opening crossings once the weapons file is closed. Lebanon rejects it as security normalisation.
The second is a multinational force with European troops under American command, which depends on a wider regional deal and US-Iranian understandings and Israel's elections.
The third is self-reliance: Qazah argues the government can declare the border villages a military zone under National Defence Law No. 102 of 1938, placing all security forces under army command and allowing curfews, closures and searches.
A European coalition will remain ink on paper without a UN mandate, the consent of both parties and an American guarantee against escalation. None of these is in Beirut's gift. The world is not handing the south to a new guardian; it is handing it back to the Lebanese state. Lebanon can assert its sovereignty through its own army or risk a vacuum that turns the border strip into an open front once more.
For Qazah, the choice is already clear. Imposing security, he said, is the exclusive responsibility of Lebanon's political leadership, which must give the army firm orders “to impose security by military force, not by begging for it or imposing it by consensus”.
Alaa Sarhal is a Lebanese journalist

The Best Way to Respond to Passive-Aggressive Comments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:07:29 UTC
23:07:29 KST

Have you ever left work at 5 p.m., only for a colleague to not-so-sweetly ask, “Going home already?”
If so, you’ve probably been the target of a passive-aggressive comment. The two halves of the very phrase “passive-aggressive” spell out the familiar dynamic, says Laurie Weingart, a professor of organizational behavior at Carnegie Mellon University who has studied how people express conflict at work. Someone is expressing opposition or anger—the aggressive part—but doing so indirectly. The words leave room for an innocent interpretation. The tone? Not so much.
That ambiguity puts you in an awkward position: Do you respond to what was said or what you think the other person meant—or give in to the urge to snip right back? We asked experts what to say when someone seems to be taking a dig at you but won’t quite say what they mean.
Why people default to passive-aggressive communication
Sometimes it feels safer to hint at a feeling than to say it directly. Admitting you feel some sort of way calls for a kind of vulnerability that a sarcastic remark does not. “Some people just haven’t learned how to say or don’t feel comfortable saying, ‘I’m hurt. You hurt my feelings,’” says Melissa Gluck, a psychologist in New York City. If you grew up around people who rarely said what they meant, the indirect approach might even feel normal.
There can also be something more specific behind a partner’s pointed comment. In research on romantic relationships, Levi R. Baker, a psychology professor at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro, found that people sometimes express displeasure indirectly because they’re unsure how much their partner cares. “People are really doing this to kind of test their partner,” he says. They’re signaling, “I’m upset with you, I’ve got some hurt feelings,” then waiting to see whether their partner notices and tries to find out what’s wrong. Underneath it all, Baker says, they may be wondering: “Do they care about me? Do they value me?”
Still, understanding where a comment might come from doesn’t make it feel any better to hear. It can leave you wondering whether you’ve been insulted—and how to answer an accusation the other person never quite made.
How to respond to a passive-aggressive comment
Weingart’s advice is to make your response “more direct and less intense” than the comment you just heard. Start by giving your friend a chance to be direct. If someone says, “Must be nice to have that much free time,” Brook McKenzie, a licensed chemical dependency counselor in Dallas who often helps families work through indirect communication and resentment, suggests responding: “I’m not sure how you meant that. Can you say it another way?” Another option: “It sounds like there might be something you want to say to me directly. Is there?”
The question should be an invitation, not an accusation. “Why are you being so passive-aggressive?” may be tempting, McKenzie says, but you’ll likely end up arguing about their tone instead of whatever is actually bothering them. Returning the sarcasm tends to cause the same problem, with two people annoyed instead of one.
If you’re talking to someone you’re especially close to, Gluck suggests a gentle opening: “I feel like something’s off. Do you want to talk about it?” That lets them tell you what’s wrong without requiring you to guess. If they say everything’s fine, you can take them at their word for the time being. “It’s not our job to become the feelings detective,” Gluck says.
If you have a good idea of what's underneath the comment, you can acknowledge that, too. Say your partner responds to your plans with friends by remarking that you certainly have time for everyone else. Baker suggests reassuring them that you want to spend time together and proposing a plan: “I’m going out tonight, but I’d really like to have dinner with you tomorrow.” You don’t need to cancel your plans to show that you care.
At work, clarity may serve you better than a conversation about feelings. If your boss says, “Leaving already?” when your workday is over, Weingart suggests asking: “Is there something else you need me to do before I leave?” A coworker’s jab may warrant even less: “Yep, the workday’s over. Have a great weekend.” Either response avoids assuming you know what the other person meant.
And sometimes the best response is no response. If a friend makes one out-of-character comment on a rough day, Gluck says, you can let it pass. If it keeps happening, that’s a different conversation.
What to do when someone is repeatedly passive-aggressive
A pattern deserves a more direct approach. If a friend repeatedly jokes that you never make time for them, Gluck suggests naming both what you’ve noticed and how it lands: “This isn’t the first time you’ve made that comment. It’s starting to hurt my feelings, and I’d like to know if something’s bothering you.”
The same pattern can emerge in families. Say you tell your mother it upset you when she criticized you in front of relatives, and she replies, “I guess I’m just a bad mom.” Gluck suggests saying: “That’s not what I said. I was trying to tell you how I feel, and it hurts when you put those words in my mouth.” That brings the conversation back to what she said in front of your relatives, instead of turning it into a debate about whether she’s a good mother.
What if they insist they were just joking? Weingart recommends separating their intention from the effect: “You may not have meant it to be hurtful, but that’s how it sounded to me.” You don’t have to prove what was in their head to explain what happened on your end.
It’s also fair to be clear about what you’re willing to do next. Consider borrowing McKenzie’s go-to line for recurring comments: “I’m willing to have difficult conversations with you. I’m not willing to keep guessing what you mean.”

Documents
Details
If consultation is to be undertaken on an amendment to the regulations or the implementation of new regulation, the MAA will issue an NPA. The NPA will explain the rationale behind the amendment, the possible impact on the regulated community (developed into an impact assessment (IA)) and set the deadline for comment/feedback. Feedback is important to further develop the IA.
Comments or enquiries on any NPA are to be sent to DSA-MAA-MRPEnquiries@mod.gov.uk by the date stated in the NPA. Please use the NPA Response Form template provided below to return your consolidated comments.
After the comments closure date, the NPA will be removed from the website.
NPA comment response sheets contain the collated MAA responses to individual NPA publications.
In the final preparation for publication similar Regulated Community comments have been consolidated into one response.
Some of the MAA responses to the Regulated Community comments may have been superseded by further internal review prior to the official publication of the new issue.

France records 4% rise in women killed by partners or ex-partners in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:06:47 UTC
23:06:47 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The number of women killed by their current or former partners in France rose 4% in 2025, reaching 111 victims, according to figures released Wednesday by the Interior Ministry.
Police and gendarmerie recorded 136 violent deaths involving current or former partners last year, compared with 138 in 2024, a decrease of 1%, the ministry said in its annual study.
Of the victims, 25 were men, down 19% from the previous year.
On average, one person died every three days in a case involving a current or former partner, according to the report.
Authorities also recorded 445 attempted homicides involving current or former partners in 2025, accounting for 10% of the 4,365 attempted homicides recorded nationwide.
The share was up from 9% in 2024, the study said.
The northern department of Nord recorded the highest number of victims, with eight, followed by Bouches-du-Rhone with seven.
Alpes-Maritimes and Herault each recorded five victims, while Aisne, Gironde and Marne each reported four.
In France’s overseas territories, Reunion recorded three victims, while French Guiana and New Caledonia each recorded two, according to the ministry.

Louvre could be forced to close without major overhaul, director warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:06:40 UTC
23:06:40 KST

A year after thieves made off with €88 million of crown jewels that have never been found, the new man in charge says leaking pipes and crumbling galleries mean security fixes alone won’t save the Paris landmark.
The Louvre could eventually have to shut its doors to the public unless France’s next government backs a sweeping transformation of the world’s most-visited museum, its director has warned.
Christophe Leribault told Le Figaro on Wednesday that the museum would seek private funding for the work, but that a major injection of public money would have to be approved after France’s national elections next year.
“Whoever forms the next government must keep in mind that if the Louvre is not repaired, updated, and transformed, it will very quickly fall behind and will eventually have to close its doors to the public. That would be a disaster,” he said.
Successive minority governments have struggled for years to pass annual budgets, and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is trying to rein in public spending to reduce France’s vast deficit.
A year on from the heist
Leribault, an art historian who previously ran the Musée d’Orsay, took over in February after Laurence des Cars resigned in the fallout from last year’s jewel theft.
On 19 October 2025, a four-man gang used a lorry-mounted lifting platform to break into the Apollo Gallery and, in broad daylight, took eight pieces of the French Crown Jewels worth an estimated €88 million. A Senate inquiry later found that only one of two cameras covering the break-in point was working. The jewels have never been recovered.
Speaking to AFP ahead of the anniversary, Leribault said an €83 million security masterplan was “moving forward at speed”. Measures include a new head of security post, an upgraded camera network – found to have old cameras and major gaps – and better surveillance around the perimeter and at access points.
No ‘miracle’ solution
Leribault argued that lasting improvements could only come as part of a wider overhaul of the museum, which welcomed around nine million visitors last year.
"The operations needed to secure the museum require work on the historic building and its infrastructure," he wrote. "There is no easy, miracle ‘surface’ solution. Everything is interconnected, everything is linked."
The museum first opened its doors the public in 1793 and celebrated it 233rd birthday this summer.
The museum’s problems include old plumbing, badly insulated galleries and cramped public areas. A leaked memo from des Cars in January 2025 said some areas "are no longer watertight" and that "visiting the Louvre is a physical ordeal". In February, a burst heating pipe damaged a ceiling painted by Charles Meynier in 1819.
The scale and cost of the work have become highly political. President Emmanuel Macron has championed the "Louvre – New Renaissance" project, which includes a new entrance and has been estimated by the government at €700–800 million over ten years, partly funded by a 45% rise in ticket prices for most non-European visitors.
Trade unions have criticised Macron and des Cars for prioritising grandiose plans for an architectural overhaul instead of more modest changes that would improve the visitor experience.

Happiness, not awe, may be the better emotional lever for openness to diversity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:00:14 UTC
23:00:14 KST

Feeling happy might do more to open people’s minds to social diversity than experiencing a sense of awe. New research published in the International Journal of Psychology indicates that a brief burst of joy leads to more positive attitudes toward inclusion, while awe has little effect. The findings challenge the expectation that awe would outperform other positive emotions in fostering acceptance of others.
Awe is an emotional response typically triggered by perceiving something vast and extraordinary that challenges a person’s usual understanding of the world, like a starry night sky or a towering mountain range. This feeling tends to diminish attention to oneself and make people view their surroundings as interconnected and meaningful.
Because awe encourages people to feel part of something larger than themselves, researchers have wondered whether it could help foster more positive attitudes toward diversity. The research, led by Jens Agerström, a professor of psychology at Linnaeus University, set out to test whether experiencing awe could encourage greater openness toward different social groups.
“Previous research has shown that people who are exposed to awe-inducing stimuli (e.g., vast and beautiful landscapes, moon landings) are more likely to act more prosocially (e.g., help another person),” Agerström told PsyPost. “We wanted to extend the research literature by examining whether awe can also make people more diversity oriented by, for instance, expressing more positive attitudes toward ethnic minority groups.”
Prior work provided reason to think awe might bridge social divides. For instance, a 2015 study found that awe shifts attention away from the self and promotes generosity: in one experiment, adults who watched an awe-inducing nature clip gave away more raffle tickets than those who watched a happiness-inducing one. Building on this, an experiment covered by PsyPost in 2023 found that experiencing awe, rather than joy, made children more likely to donate to members of an outgroup.
Happiness served as the comparison. Like awe, it is a positive emotion that tends to broaden people’s outlook and encourage helping and cooperation, which made it a solid benchmark. But the researchers expected awe to come out ahead, because awe is more strongly tied to a sense of a smaller self and a connection to others. Happiness also has a more mixed record: a 1994 study found that happy moods can lead people to rely more heavily on social stereotypes.
To test this, the researchers recruited 3,196 adults through the online research platform Prolific. The participants, who averaged about 40 years old, were randomly assigned to one of three groups, and each group watched a 28-second video designed to evoke a specific emotional response.
The awe group viewed majestic images of the universe, vast landscapes, and the Apollo 11 moon landing accompanied by sweeping music. The happiness group watched cheerful scenes of children playing and birthday parties paired with joyful music. A third, neutral control group saw everyday images of people studying or taking a coffee break with ambient background noise.
Immediately after watching the clips, the participants completed three questionnaires assessing their orientation toward diversity. The first survey measured general attitudes toward diversity, asking respondents if they value getting to know people from different racial or cultural backgrounds. The second survey measured diversity fatigue, which captures feelings of weariness or annoyance toward societal inclusion efforts. The third survey assessed social dominance orientation, which captures how much a person believes some social groups are simply inferior to others and that inequality between groups is acceptable.
The researchers found that the awe video did not measurably change how participants answered the surveys. On all three measures, the awe group’s responses did not differ statistically from those of the neutral control group.
Happiness, on the other hand, consistently shifted responses in a more inclusive direction. The neutral group’s average diversity attitude score was about 4.6 on a 6-point scale, and the happiness group scored about 0.08 points higher. The happiness group also scored 0.10 points lower on diversity fatigue (neutral group average: about 2.1 on a 5-point scale) and 0.15 points lower on preference for group hierarchy (neutral group average: about 2.4 on a 6-point scale).
When the two emotions were compared directly, the happiness group reported more positive attitudes toward diversity than the awe group and showed a slightly lower preference for social hierarchy, a difference that fell just short of statistical significance. The two groups did not differ reliably in diversity fatigue. The results held when the researchers excluded participants who finished unusually quickly or slowly and when they accounted for age and gender.
These shifts are small, but the authors note they emerged after a 28-second video and on measures thought to be fairly stable. The researchers suggest that happiness may promote social bonding, cooperation, and concern for others, which could carry over into more welcoming attitudes, though the study did not test this explanation.
“Brief inductions of awe do not seem to make people more diversity oriented,” Agerström noted. “Somewhat unexpectedly we found that happiness, which we used as a contrasting emotion, resulted in more positive diversity-related attitudes. Perhaps most interestingly, happiness seems to reduce social dominance, an individual difference characteristic capturing preferences for inequality and discrimination.”
The team’s biggest surprise, Agerström said, was “that happiness seems to triumph over awe when it comes to diversity.”
The lack of an effect for awe is in tension with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that evoking awe through science fiction increased people’s identification with all of humanity. However, that earlier study measured a broad sense of global connection rather than specific attitudes toward demographic diversity and social equality.
“The main takeaway is that even a brief experience of happiness can make people more positive toward diversity and reduce diversity fatigue and social dominance orientation. Interestingly, the researchers did not find similar effects for awe,” said Ewa Palikot of the Institute of Psychology at the Polish Academy of Sciences, who was not involved in the study. “Like the authors, I expected awe to have a positive effect on attitudes toward diversity, especially since previous research suggests that awe can make people feel more connected to others and encourage prosocial behavior.”
As with all research, there are a few things to keep in mind. The study relied on a very short video clip to spark emotion. A 28-second video can easily lift a person’s mood, but it might not be intense enough to trigger the profound, transformative sense of awe that comes from standing at the edge of the Grand Canyon. It is possible that a stronger, real-world experience of awe would yield different results.
The researchers note, however, that in a pretest with 125 people, the awe video produced about as much awe as the happiness video produced happiness, so a weaker emotional jolt does not obviously explain the difference. The main study itself did not check how participants felt after watching.
The researchers offer a few possible explanations for why awe fell short. Awe is a complex emotion, and although their awe video produced very little fear, it did produce some surprise, which the authors suggest could prompt a disorienting search for order rather than curiosity and openness. It is also possible the video did not create the “small self” feeling thought to drive awe’s social benefits, something the study did not measure.
“The size of the observed effects of happiness was small and it is important to examine whether happiness has the potential to shape diversity-oriented behavior in real-world settings,” Agerström said. “For example, can a more joyful workplace reduce prejudice?”
Palikot cautioned against generalizing the experimental findings to everyday life. “It is important to remember that these findings do not mean that happier people are necessarily more open to diversity in everyday life,” she told PsyPost. “The researchers looked at how a brief feeling of happiness affected people’s reported attitudes right after watching a video. We still don’t know how long these effects last or whether they influence people’s actual behavior.”
The participants in this study also started out with relatively low preferences for social hierarchy, which left less room for their scores to drop, although the happiness effect still emerged.
“As is always the case, findings need to be replicated before strong conclusions are drawn,” Agerström emphasized. “Also, other awe-inducing methods (than those we tested) may have the potential to increase diversity. Future research needs to look into this.”
Looking ahead, Agerström said the team’s long-term plan is “to unobtrusively study effects of awe and happiness on diversity behavior.” Unobtrusive studies observe what people actually do without making the measured behavior obvious, which can reduce the pull to give socially desirable answers.
“From a cross-cultural perspective, I would be curious to see whether happiness and awe have similar effects across cultures,” Palikot said. “Previous research shows that happiness and positive emotions are not viewed in the same way in different cultural contexts. For example, in some East Asian cultures, emotional balance is more valued, and strong positive emotions like happiness can also be associated with negative consequences. This does not necessarily mean that these emotions have different effects on social attitudes, but I think it would be interesting to explore.”
The study, “Happiness, Not Awe, Makes People More Diversity-Oriented,” was authored by Jens Agerström, Magnus Carlsson, and Towe Nilsson.

ASML’s chip equipment sales to China soar 109% despite US export curb push
The Dutch firm expects China to account for 20 per cent of its total sales this year, even as the US pushes for tighter export restrictions
Dutch semiconductor equipment giant ASML expects China to account for about 20 per cent of its total sales this year, after seeing shipments to the market more than double during the previous quarter despite mounting US pressure for tighter export restrictions on less advanced chipmaking machinery.
The company’s sales to China surged 109 per cent in the third quarter compared with the previous three months, according to financial results released on Wednesday. That took China’s share of ASML’s machine sales to 23 per cent, up from 14 per cent in the second quarter.
The revenue jump comes as Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten faces pressure from Washington to tighten restrictions on sales of chipmaking machines to China.

14:00:03 UTC
23:00:03 KST

The climate is warming up faster than we can respond. According to a new report published Oct. 14 in the journal BioScience, “Earth’s climate system is moving deeper into uncharted territory.”
The State of the Climate, an annual report that tracks the Earth’s “vital signs,” monitors several climate related indicators—ranging from greenhouse gas concentrations and temperature changes to tree cover loss due to wildfire. The researchers found that, of the 16 planetary vital signs, seven are currently at record extremes. This includes sea levels and greenhouse gasses in the atmosphere. Meanwhile several others, such as areas burned during wildfires and ocean heat levels, show evidence of acceleration or abrupt shifts.
The researchers warn that the rate of global warming appears to have accelerated, from about 0.05°C per decade between 1880 and 1970 to roughly 0.36°C per decade between 2010 and 2024—and the 2°C threshold meant to limit planetary damage could be reached before 2050 they warn. These accelerating and intensifying changes could raise the risk of reinforcing feedback loops and crossing tipping points—critical thresholds that, when crossed, can lead to accelerating and often irreversible environmental changes. In 2025, the Earth passed its first climate tipping point, as rising ocean temperatures, acidification, overfishing, and pollution are combining to cause coral bleaching and mortality.
"Earth’s life-support systems are being pushed beyond stable limits," the report states, "with changes unfolding faster than our ability to respond."
This year, a number of extreme weather events made the impacts of an acceleratingly warming planet impossible to ignore. July 2026 was the hottest month on record for the contiguous United States, with ocean temperatures also reaching a record high that month. Back-to-back heat waves in Europe lead to an estimated 35,000 excess deaths, preliminary reports show. A number of regions—including Utah in the U.S., Ontario, Canada, along with France, Spain, Britain, and Belgium have either experienced their worst wildfire years in history or are on track to do so. While we don’t yet know enough to link these individual weather events to climate change, research shows that it is supercharging extreme weather events.
Concentrations of greenhouse gases—including carbon dioxide, methane, and nitrous oxide—all reached record levels in 2026, the researchers say. In May 2026, atmospheric carbon dioxide exceeded 428 parts per million, roughly 50% above pre-industrial levels and generally higher than any time in the last 2 million years.
The authors of today’s report also tracked indicators of the human activities driving these planetary changes, like energy use, food production, and economic growth. Fossil fuel consumption remains the dominant driver of these changes. Fossil fuel consumption rose by 0.9% in 2025, the report found, with oil, coal, and gas all reaching record highs, and annual energy-related carbon dioxide emissions surpassed 41 gigatons for the first time—the equivalent of emissions released by over 10,800 coal-fired power plants in one year.
There have, however, been some signs of progress, the report notes. Low-carbon sources provided roughly 43% of global electricity generation in 2025, and solar and wind energy consumption grew by approximately 18%. That was before the war in Iran laid bare the world’s reliance on fossil fuels, and triggered a global green energy boom.
But cutting carbon emissions will no longer be enough on its own, the report states. Adaptation measures—ranging from shifts towards plant-based diets, to restoring mangroves to better protect against storm surges—will be key to adjusting to a changing climate.
The report underscores an unavoidable truth. "We are witnessing the rapid destabilization of the Earth’s climate system,” it states. “This is no longer a warning for the future; it is a diagnosis of the present.”

Earth’s Condition Is ‘Serious and Getting Worse’ as Climate Change Intensifies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

The climate just got its annual checkup, and the results aren’t looking so hot.
“If Earth were a patient coming in for an annual physical, I would say its condition is serious and getting worse,” Oregon State University researcher Bill Ripple says.
Ripple is the lead author of a new paper chronicling the state of the climate, published on Wednesday in BioScience. The findings show that seven of the 16 planetary vital signs tracked by the researchers have never been in a more extreme state.
That includes the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, which is 50 percent higher than preindustrial levels due to burning fossil fuels, as well as symptoms of burning all that oil, coal, and gas. Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets have shrunk to record lows, while ocean heat has soared to record highs.
Climate change has already quickened the pace of warming from about 0.05 degrees Celsius per decade from 1880 through 1970 to 0.36 degrees Celsius per decade since 2010, according to the analysis. While the global average temperature, including land, isn’t at a record extreme, that may change by the end of the year as El Niño strengthens. The natural climate pattern is characterized by a hotter-than-normal Pacific Ocean, but it also boosts global heat levels by pouring more energy into the atmosphere. This year’s El Niño is shaping up to be one for the record books.
“A strong El Niño could temporarily push global temperatures even higher, while bringing additional heat and drought to vulnerable regions,” says Ripple. He adds that “El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it's now occurring on top of a much warmer planet. That makes its impacts potentially more dangerous.”
Of particular concern are ecosystems such as coral reefs and tropical forests. The spread of ocean heat is likely to fuel a mass coral die-off, known as coral bleaching. With each successive wave of bleaching, reefs become less resilient. Corals are among the ecosystems most threatened by climate change; if the planet warms beyond 1.5 degrees Celsius, most of the world’s coral will be unlikely to survive.
Tropical forests also face pressure from El Niño. This is especially true of the Amazon, which tends to see dry weather during this climate pattern. The timing couldn’t be more dire: The region, dubbed “the world’s lungs,” is already under intense pressure from logging and mining interests and the possible return of a right-wing government in Brazil that prioritizes extraction and land clearing over conservation.
The new report also warns that the Amazon is among the ecosystems at risk of crossing a tipping point—that is, reaching a threshold where it shifts from a tropical rainforest into something more resembling savanna. It’s highly unlikely that crossing that tipping point is imminent, let alone something that will happen this year. But this year’s blast of El Niño–influenced weather will edge it closer.
“Warming, drought, and deforestation could push the Amazon toward widespread forest degradation,” Ripple says. “My concern is that these changes could interact, making them increasingly difficult to stop.”
The report is an avalanche of bad news for the climate, though it does note that carbon-free forms of energy are playing a bigger role in the power grid. The report calls it a sign we’re in the “Age of Electricity.” Despite that, annual greenhouse gas emissions are at record highs. In other words, the world is still smoking a pack a day, even at the risk of losing a lung.
“There are some encouraging signs, especially the growth of renewable energy, but they aren't yet enough to reverse the overall deterioration,” Ripple says. “The climate emergency is not something waiting for us in the future. We are already living through it.”

Ukrainian Il-76 spotted leaving Saudi airport near Yemen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:53:03 UTC
22:53:03 KST

- A Ukrainian Air Force Il-76MD flew from Sharurah, near Saudi Arabia’s border with Yemen, toward Istanbul on Oct. 12, flight-tracking data shows.
- Neither Ukraine nor Saudi Arabia has explained the flight, which follows Ukraine’s deployment of counter-drone specialists to Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states.
A Ukrainian Air Force Il-76MD heavy transport aircraft was tracked on Oct. 12 flying out of Sharurah, a Saudi town in Najran Province near the border with Yemen, in a rare appearance of a Ukrainian military cargo plane in the south of the kingdom.
Flight-tracking data shared by the open-source account Egypt’s Intel Observer shows the four-engine jet, registration 76661, heading north over the Red Sea at about 10,350 m (33,975 feet) at 17:28 UTC on its way from Sharurah to Istanbul’s Sabiha Gökçen airport, roughly an hour and 48 minutes after takeoff. The account said the aircraft had earlier flown to Sharurah from Lviv in western Ukraine, a leg not visible in the published screenshot.
Neither Kyiv nor Riyadh has said what the aircraft carried or why it landed at Sharurah. The open-source account speculated that it may have delivered Ukrainian interceptor drones or military specialists, possibly to support Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces, and described Sharurah as their main supply hub, a claim that has not been confirmed by any government.
Sharurah’s airport serves both civilian and military traffic and sits close to the Yemeni frontier. It was one of seven southern airports Saudi Arabia shut to civilian flights in March 2015, when the kingdom began its air campaign against the Iran-aligned Houthi movement in Yemen.
Ukraine already has a documented military footprint in the Gulf. After Iran launched drone and missile strikes on Gulf states during the war that began in March 2026, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had sent more than 200 counter-drone specialists to the region, and later put the number at 228 across five partners, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Kuwait and Jordan. Zelensky signed a defense agreement with Saudi Arabia during a Gulf visit in the spring, and Ukrainian officials have offered partners interceptor drones built to bring down Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones.
According to information obtained by The Defence Blog, Ukrainian specialists are helping Saudi Arabia and other countries in the region defend against hostile drone strikes, and are also training local forces in new tactics for employing attack drones.
That work has drawn threats from Tehran. In March, an Iranian member of parliament said Ukraine’s support to Gulf states made it Iran’s “legitimate war target.”
The Il-76MD is a Soviet-designed strategic airlifter able to carry about 40 tonnes (88,000 pounds) of cargo, and the Ukrainian Air Force operates only a small number of them. Ukrainian military Il-76 flights abroad are usually tied to cargo pickups, equipment deliveries or the movement of personnel.
The routing through Istanbul fits a flight path north over the Red Sea and Turkey back toward Ukraine, though the tracking data does not show the aircraft’s final destination after Sabiha Gökçen or whether it returned empty.
What the aircraft unloaded or picked up at Sharurah, and whether the flight was linked to Ukraine’s counter-drone mission in Saudi Arabia or to the conflict in Yemen, remains unconfirmed.

South African opposition party cancels major rally
South Africa’s opposition uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party has called off a major rally ahead of next month’s local elections, as party leader and former President Jacob Zuma remains under medical care in the hospital.

However, there was speculation that the party’s finances were in disarray and it was unable to pay for the function.

MK Party spokesperson Sifiso Mahlangu said the party would conduct an urgent and independent investigation into reported discrepancies in the final councillor candidate lists published by the Electoral Commission of South Africa (IEC).
The party’s 2026 local government election manifesto, referred to as the People’s Mandate, would be distributed electronically to party structures and members on October 15, Mahlangu said.
Zuma was admitted to Netcare St Anne’s Hospital in Pietermaritzburg last week after reportedly falling ill during an MK Party election campaign in uMsinga, KwaZulu-Natal. The party described his hospital visit as a routine medical check-up. However, speculation about his condition continued after reports suggested he had been discharged and returned to his Nkandla home.
On Tuesday, the Jacob Zuma Foundation dismissed the reports, saying he remained under medical care at the hospital. Foundation spokesperson Mzwanele Manyi said the former president was in good spirits, based on information from someone who had spoken to him and spent time with him. The foundation has appealed for Zuma’s privacy and dignity to be respected while he receives medical care.

Its leadership would engage directly with affected ward candidates who had been nominated through community meetings. The party also resolved to establish proportional representation (PR) councillor deployment committees at national, provincial and regional levels to finalise the deployment of councillors from its PR lists.
The MK Party announced the launch of its national Molo Makhelwane campaign, which will run until midnight on November 3, the eve of the elections. The campaign would involve party structures, councillor candidates and volunteers visiting households, engaging churches and listening to residents’ concerns across cities, townships, farms and villages.
The party said its candidates and volunteers must be visible in communities as it seeks to strengthen its relationship with residents. “The streets must now be green!” said Mahlangu.

Russia’s internet shutdowns push state firms back to landline phones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:52:44 UTC
22:52:44 KST

State procurement of landline telephones tripled in the first eight months of 2026 as mobile internet outages hit nearly 80% of the country. Rostelecom’s chief urged Russians to keep one at home “like a fire extinguisher".
Russian state-owned companies spent more than three times as much on landline telephones in the first eight months this year as in the same period in 2025, as mobile internet shutdowns affecting nearly 80% of the country push ministries and businesses to seek alternatives to disrupted networks.
Procurement data cited by the Russian business daily Vedomosti show spending at 118 million roubles (€1.26 million) from January through August, with the number of purchase tenders up 12.5%.
Purchases are concentrated in the country’s largest business and infrastructure hubs.
Market participants told Vedomosti that the surge was driven by the restrictions, a shift by Russian ministries and companies to domestically produced software-based PBX systems after Western vendors withdrew from the Russian market following the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, and demand for secure communications channels.
Russia began systematically shutting down mobile internet access in May 2025, when services went offline in more than 40 regions ahead of Victory Day celebrations. What were initially episodic outages quickly became routine.
An independent monitoring project recorded 655 mobile internet outages in June 2025, rising to 2,099 in July, a figure that exceeded the worldwide total for the entire previous year, according to analysts.
The disruptions have hit banking, taxi services, food delivery and navigation, particularly in rural areas.
The authorities have justified the shutdowns as a defence against Ukrainian drones, which they say are guided via mobile internet signals.
Experts have disputed this, saying drones can fly preset routes without a network connection, and the shutdowns have reached regions far from the front line.
In March, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the presidential administration “uses landline telephones” when asked how restrictions in central Moscow affect the work of the president’s office.
Shortly after, head of state telecoms company Rostelecom Mikhail Oseyevsky urged Russians to return to fixed lines.
“Like a fire extinguisher, there should be one in every home," Oseyevsky said.
Russia has approximately 12.2 landline telephones per 100 residents. In Moscow, around 2 million households use fixed lines provided by MGTS, the city’s main telephone operator.
Across the country, there are about 17.4 million urban household landline connections.
The Ministry of Economic Development forecasts that the number of all landlines will fall to between 8.2 and 8.5 per 100 residents by 2029.

BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- At Robot Mall in Beijing, when music was playing, Melissa Valarezo and two of her friends raised their phones to record a robot performing Chinese martial arts, amazed by how smoothly it moved.
"This is incredible. I never expected a robot to do kung fu so well, almost like a real person," the university student from Ecuador told Xinhua in an interview.
Valarezo and her friends also planned to have afternoon tea at a nearby restaurant, where nearly 20 robots of different types work together to provide services, from greeting guests to cooking, serving and cleaning up after meals.
"We just couldn't wait to try," Valarezo said. "Everything here feels so futuristic!"
The three were among a growing number of global tourists drawn to China not only by the country's ancient wonders and culinary delights, but also by its futuristic intelligent robots, as the country's artificial intelligence (AI) boom turns cutting-edge technology into a new tourist hook.
During the week-long National Day holiday in early October, multiple Chinese cities rolled out robot-themed events and AI-powered experiences that became unexpected hits among visitors.
In east China's Shanghai, a street fair dedicated to embodied AI drew crowds, with foreign tourists seen posing for photos with humanoid robots. In tech hub Shenzhen in south China, the Huaqiangbei electronics market attracted overseas shoppers eager to try AI translation glasses and flying devices. Similar scenes played out in Chengdu, southwest China's Sichuan Province, where robot shop managers greeted customers and introduced products.
Official data shows that foreign nationals made almost 61.29 million border crossings in the January-August period this year, up 19.5 percent from the same period in 2025. Over the National Day holiday week, visits by foreign tourists also maintained an upward trend, increasing 5.4 percent from last year.
For Anna Seferta and Thomas Drayton, a young couple from the United Kingdom aged 24 and 29, Robot Mall in Beijing was a must-stop. Drawn by online clips of humanoid robots running a half marathon in Beijing in April, they decided to see it for themselves.
"We think it's very advanced. We've never seen anything like this in the U.K.," Seferta said, highlighting that she was mostly impressed by the hospital section. "The robot arm helps cut surgery down by five hours, and the exoskeletons for old people would be very good. All these applications are rewarding."
Launched in 2025 in the Beijing Economic-Technological Development Area, also known as E-Town, the mall is the world's first 4S store for embodied AI robots.
It displays more than 100 of China's most advanced robot products across fields like medical care, elderly care, entertainment, logistics and industry, turning sci-fi fantasy into an experience within arm's reach.
Inside the mall's exhibition hall, visitors can interact with a wide range of robots. They can grab a cup of robot-made latte with their own image printed in the foam, ask a humanoid robot resembling Albert Einstein questions about almost any topic, or join a tabletop drift car race in which speed depends on their brainwaves.
"International visitors are a common sight here," said Yang Song, an on-site technical supporter at the mall. "They enjoy robot boxing and soccer the most. Many find it interesting to control robot players in competitive games."
The mall did not land in E-Town by chance. Home to over 300 leading robotics companies, E-Town has put the whole district to work as a testing ground: self-driving cars, robot restaurants, robot elderly care stations and the world's first humanoid robot half marathon have all taken root there, alongside Beijing's largest public AI computing platform.
The area is working to build a global AI hub, with its core AI industries projected to surpass 200 billion yuan (about 29.74 billion U.S. dollars) in scale by 2030.
E-Town's rise mirrors the country's broader momentum. China's robotics industry has developed a complete industrial chain covering key chips, components and complete machines. By the end of June, China had completed or brought into operation more than 70 robot training facilities, with over 40 others under construction or on the drawing board.
This growing network is preparing more machines for roles beyond the factory floor, and beyond the country's borders. In the first half of 2026, Chinese manufacturers accounted for 97 percent of humanoid robot shipments worldwide, according to a report released at the 2026 World Robot Conference.
Among the visitors to E-Town was Phillip Sepulveda, a 34-year-old photographer from New York. The young man has since childhood suffered from a neurological condition caused by a tumor. Touring the exhibition hall in a wheelchair, he was drawn to a hiking exoskeleton on display.
"The exoskeleton is the sort of thing that would help me a lot," he said. "There are many products now, devices for the hips, for the knees, but we are looking for something for the whole leg."
His father, Jorge Sepulveda, a physician, photographed the product information and said the family was interested in further research.
"We came to see medical devices for mobility, like exoskeletons. It seems China is investing a lot in AI," the father noted, stressing the importance of global cooperation in this rising industry. "AI could be dangerous, as agreed by the CEOs of some AI companies. But if governments and the world cooperate, maybe we can prevent the dangers of it and use it to benefit more people."
For the family, the visit was about more than sightseeing. They left the mall hoping that somewhere in China's expanding robotics industry, they might find a device that could help Phillip walk more easily.
It is a hope that speaks to something broader. Technology is ultimately about changing lives for the better. ■

Two scenarios for the Yemen war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:50:28 UTC
22:50:28 KST

Two scenarios for the Yemen war
What comes next is either a retreat for the Houthis or a war of attrition.
The attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi Arabia have pushed the war in Yemen to a new level. The targeting of civilian infrastructure, including airports, which has killed at least a dozen people and injured hundreds, has left no room to maintain the “red lines” that previously outlined the limits of escalation.
This is a reckless gamble by the Houthis which is not in their interest. They are aware that the retaliation will be fierce, yet they continue to attack Saudi Arabia to fulfil Iran’s agenda that seeks heightened tensions before the United States midterms.
Given the motivation to escalate, the present situation has the potential to develop into two scenarios: A major region-wide operation against the Houthis or a war of attrition.
Scenario one: A united front against the Houthis
In response to the Houthi escalation, Saudi Arabia is striving to garner maximum international support while deepening its regional and international alliances. The aim is to come up with a united front capable of taking on what has become a regional threat.
Riyadh is certainly looking to its Gulf neighbours who, themselves, are impacted by the continuing conflict in the region. There is a collective realisation that everyone is in grave danger, not just Saudi Arabia.
Therefore, Gulf states – perhaps with the exception of Oman – will support Riyadh both directly and indirectly in the fighting in Yemen.
Pakistan and Turkiye are also likely to join the front, having signed with Saudi Arabia a defence agreement known as the Mecca Pact. The pact is to be ratified by the Turkish parliament in the next few days, opening the way for Turkish military deployment in support of Saudi Arabia. Meanwhile, indirect involvement by Turkiye and Pakistan, along with logistical and intelligence support, appears to be already well under way.
A US intervention is also possible, although it seems unlikely before the US midterms, as military engagements in the Middle East remain unpopular among US voters.
A region-wide coalition can help support the counteroffensive of the forces loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government already under way. This could give the necessary push to retake the western coastal region, including areas beyond Bab al-Mandeb and Dhubab.
Such gains could ease pressure on Red Sea shipping and potentially shift the military balance in favour of the government. The opening of additional fronts across other Yemeni cities and governorates could stretch Houthi forces, disperse their resources, and increase the likelihood of further government advances.
Retaking Sanaa could also be on the horizon. The primary obstacle delaying the Yemeni government’s recapture of the city is internal discord among the various factions within the government itself, compounded by negative external interference that exacerbates these rifts and weakens the collective effort to confront the Houthis.
Recent measures taken by the government, specifically efforts to unify its decision-making and consolidate its military operations command, have yielded noticeable progress on the ground. However, achieving the ultimate objective of retaking Sanaa requires sustained effort and focused determination.
If government forces make substantial gains, that could force the Houthis to offer concessions in exchange for a pause in fighting. They have done that before. Their purpose would not be to seek peace but to get enough breathing room to regroup and eventually go back to fighting. Negotiators should keep that in mind when approaching talks with the Houthis.
Scenario two: A war of attrition
If the Saudi-led coalition and the Yemeni government succumb to internal divisions and disagreements, this may slow progress against the Houthis. This would allow the Houthi fighters to hold on to their positions while increasing their pressure on the strategic town of Taiz and maintaining the campaign against civilian targets in Saudi Arabia.
Such a development could further complicate the conflict, increase civilian casualties and displacement, and prolong the war without producing a decisive military outcome.
This will have a significant economic impact on Saudi Arabia and complicate the implementation of its development goals, as it would have to prioritise defence spending.
The rest of the Gulf economies will also be negatively impacted because Saudi Arabia plays such a central role in the region. What is more, losing ground to the Houthis would mean that the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz would also continue, disrupting energy exports from the region.
In this scenario, there will be “no victor, no vanquished” deadlock in Yemen, but Iran would emerge as winner. A war of attrition along the Red Sea coast would provide Tehran with significant breathing room, allowing it to alleviate pressure on its own war efforts.
This would enable Iran to use the Houthi card as leverage in the intermittent negotiations it conducts with the international community, emboldening it to raise the bar regarding its conditions and demands during those talks.
This means that the only way to resolve the crisis in Yemen is decisive military action led by the Yemeni government and supported by a region-wide coalition. For that to happen, the government has to get its internal affairs and its relations with allies in order.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Chinese Premier Li Qiang delivers a keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the 140th China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province, Oct. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Ding Haitao)
GUANGZHOU, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Wednesday emphasized that China will continue to promote high-quality development, expand high-standard opening up, and take proactive and practical actions to add more impetus to the world economy.
Li made the remarks while delivering a keynote speech at the opening ceremony of the 140th China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong Province.
Noting this year marks the 70th anniversary of the establishment of the Canton Fair, Li said that President Xi Jinping specially sent a congratulatory letter, fully affirming the achievements made by the Canton Fair and reaffirming China's determination to expand high-standard opening up.
Through the Canton Fair, the world has witnessed the tremendous vitality in China's economy and society, seen the magnificent journey of hundreds of millions of Chinese people striving forward all the way, and felt the increasingly deep connection between China and the world, Li said, adding that an increasingly open, continuously innovative and trustworthy China brings new opportunities, provides new impetus and injects certainty into the world.
Li pointed out that the Canton Fair has stood the test of shifting international circumstances and kept brimming with fresh vitality, embodying plain yet profound inspirations.
"Market connectivity is not a tool for playing games, but an effective means to generate incremental growth. China is committed to promoting the continuous integration and common growth of its domestic market and the international market, and building an open world economy," the premier said.
Li said China is willing to import more high-quality products, especially high-value-added products. "We hope that more countries will work with China in the same direction, lift restrictions and actively promote the optimized and balanced development of trade," he added.
"As the largest developing country, China has always been committed to promoting common development," said the premier. "China will always be a trustworthy and reliable good friend of developing countries, and is willing to join hands with the vast number of developing countries on the journey to modernization," he added.
He said China stands ready to share more market opportunities, expand more mutually beneficial cooperation, and firmly safeguard the international economic and trade order with all parties.
WTO Director-General Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala delivered a video address, noting that China has achieved remarkable development and provided rare opportunities for the world.
Noting that the Canton Fair is an important platform connecting China with the world, Okonjo-Iweala said that against the backdrop of increasing global uncertainties, it is hoped that all parties will jointly advance WTO reform and build an open, rules-based global trading system.
More than 700 representatives from nearly 90 countries and regions attended the opening ceremony.
This edition of the Canton Fair brought together more than 30,000 exhibiting companies and about 340,000 overseas buyers. ■

Dublin hotel cancels 70 rooms booked for antisemitism conference delegates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:45:57 UTC
22:45:57 KST

The Herbert Park Hotel in Dublin canceled a reservation for 70 rooms intended for delegates attending an international conference on combating antisemitism after learning the purpose of their visit, according to Maurice Cohen, chairman of the Jewish Representative Council of Ireland.
In his speech at the opening event at the Irish Foreign Ministry – sent to The Jerusalem Post – Cohen recalled meeting with hotel management after the booking was completed, and being questioned about whether the gathering was connected to the Israel Defense Forces.
Cohen also remembered the manager’s demeanor changing and becoming tense after he mentioned that the delegates would be Jewish leaders.
“There is an uncomfortable irony in organizing an international conference to discuss antisemitism and finding that, before the conference has even begun, you have already encountered something that forces you to ask exactly the questions the conference was created to address,” he said.
“How quickly does the word ‘Jewish’ change a conversation? How easily does a gathering about antisemitism become associated with the Israeli army?”
He noted that the question about the IDF was not an innocent misunderstanding, as it instead “revealed how quickly Jewish identity can be collapsed into Israel, how quickly Israel can be collapsed into suspicion, and how quickly suspicion can become discrimination because contemporary antisemitism does not always arrive wearing the language of the past.
“It does not always announce itself with a slur, a threat, or a placard. Increasingly, it can present itself as a question, a precaution, a policy, a request for clarification. It begins by treating Jewish identity as evidence of political allegiance,” he said.
Resetting the conversation between Jewish groups and governments
The European Jewish Congress called the incident “deeply disturbing.”
“That a hotel would cancel accommodation for participants in a conference dedicated to combating antisemitism, while raising questions about supposed links to the Israeli military, reflects precisely the kind of prejudice and suspicion that such gatherings seek to confront,” the EJC noted.
“It is profoundly troubling that those working to combat antisemitism should themselves encounter such treatment. Jewish organizations and those standing against hatred must never face exclusion or discrimination because of their work,”
Israel’s Foreign Ministry said. “The Irish government cannot use the fight against antisemitism as a diplomatic PR exercise while failing to confront it at home.”
The conference in question was the 15th meeting of the Special Envoys and Coordinators Combating Antisemitism (SECCA) Forum, organized by the World Jewish Congress in partnership with the European Commission, and convened as an Associated Event under Ireland’s rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union.
Jewish community leaders from across the world joined government envoys, representatives from international organizations, and technology company executives in Dublin from October 12 to 14.
Leaders representing the J7 Large Communities’ Task Force Against Antisemitism – connecting the Delegación de Asociaciones Israelitas Argentinas, Executive Council of Australian Jewry, Canada’s Center for Israel and Jewish Affairs, the Representative Council of French Jewish Institutions, Central Council of Jews in Germany, and Board of Deputies of British Jews, alongside the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) and the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations from the United States – also joined the forum following a series of high-level meetings in London earlier in the week.
Statements, condemnations only go so far
The gathering included a meeting with Ireland’s Taoiseach or government leader, Micheál Martin; visits to the European headquarters of TikTok and Meta; and other discussions.
“Our meeting in Dublin is a much-needed opportunity to reset the conversation between Jewish organizations, governments, and technology companies,” Maram Stern, WJC executive vice president, said. “Statements and condemnation of antisemitism only go so far. Practical solutions must urgently be put in place to protect Jewish life globally.”
The delegates were officially welcomed by Irish ministers despite the current Ireland-Israel tensions.
At the start of Tuesday’s agenda, Colm Brophy, a member of the Irish parliament, said he was “very pleased to welcome Jewish community leaders” and was particularly happy to see that the event has a focus on AI and on the regulation of online platforms, given the “troubling increase in antisemitism and other forms of racism online in recent years.”
The incident comes amid a sharp deterioration in relations between Ireland and Israel, with Jerusalem accusing Dublin of fostering an increasingly hostile environment toward the Jewish state.
Tensions have escalated following Ireland’s recognition of a Palestinian state, its legal and diplomatic moves against Israel, and controversy over Dublin City Council’s proposal to remove the name of former Israeli president Chaim Herzog from Herzog Park in Rathgar and replace it with “Free Palestine Park.”
The attempt was eventually condemned by Irish officials, and the J7 representatives visited the park for a photo-op this week during the conference.

INTERVIEW - ‘You’re not alone, the truth will come out’: Nobel winner Navi Pillay on global support for Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:45:10 UTC
22:45:10 KST

Nobel Peace Prize laureate Navi Pillay said Palestinians seeking justice are not alone and the truth will emerge, urging the international community to draw lessons from the collective action and economic sanctions that helped end apartheid in her native South Africa.
In an exclusive interview on Wednesday, Pillay, judge at the International Court of Justice and a former UN human rights chief, reflected on her experience fighting apartheid and the importance of international support for Palestinians amid continuing concerns over accountability for violations in the Gaza Strip.
"I imagine I'm correct in saying that even though Palestinians are struggling for their freedom for more than 90 years now, attention by the international community and support by the international community would be of great significance for them," she told Anadolu.
"The message being, you're not alone. That with information and correct information, the truth will come out."
Pillay, 85, who was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize for her contributions to international justice, chaired a UN commission of inquiry, which concluded last year that Israel committed genocide in Gaza.
Recalling her experience under apartheid, she said South African lawyers fought a lonely struggle with little international attention. "We really had very little relief. And honestly, the rest of the world didn't pay attention to us," she said.
The rights lawyer said a UN commission gathering evidence and presenting its findings internationally would have greatly helped Black South Africans at that time.
Pillay stressed the importance of identifying the root causes of Palestinian suffering, and reiterated her commission's finding that Israel's unlawful occupation was the root cause of the longstanding conflict.
She criticized governments for increasingly prioritizing their political and regional interests over their responsibilities to maintain international peace and justice.
She said the UN Security Council already possessed mechanisms to respond to violations, including peacekeeping operations, investigative commissions, mediation and economic sanctions.
"The principal tool they have is to impose sanctions, economic sanctions against governments that are violating international human rights law, international humanitarian law, they've used this before," she said.
Questioning the international community's response to Gaza, Pillay said: "So, the question that civil society is asking: 'Why are you sitting back and doing nothing in the face of huge violations that we, the people, can see daily? We can see genocide being committed on our television screens'."
"And I am as unhappy as most people that there has been so little action," she added.
Drawing on South Africa's experience, where apartheid ended in 1994, Pillay emphasized the decisive role of international economic pressure.
"Apartheid came to an end mainly because of the economic sanctions imposed by the Security Council, by the United Nations against the apartheid government," she said.
"I never thought apartheid will end in my lifetime, but it's this collective action by governments, by businesses, and civil society all over the world that brought an end to apartheid."
Pillay said she had been hoping for similar international cooperation in response to the situation in Gaza.
"I've been hopefully looking for and calling for that level of cooperation, that level of condemnation of the huge violations and killings of Palestinians," she said.
Asked whether Israel's growing international isolation and sanctions targeting settlers in the occupied West Bank could help end its impunity, Pillay said such developments could contribute to broader collective action.
"The one thing we cannot accept is doing nothing," she said.
Recalling Nelson Mandela's position that South Africans could not fully enjoy freedom while Palestinians remained oppressed and occupied, she said Palestinians were seeking measures similar to those used against apartheid.
"Palestinians are calling for the kind of action that was taken to end apartheid. They see the value of economic boycotts," she said.
She also referred to protests by Israelis against efforts to weaken the country's Supreme Court, urging governments to respect civilians' right to protest and cooperate with international criminal investigations.
She stressed that international legal principles must be applied consistently, without selectivity or bias, particularly when civilians are suffering.
Pillay emphasized that governments, rather than international organizations alone, bear responsibility for preventing genocide.
"The Genocide Convention is very clear. The duty is on every state to prevent genocide," she said. "That's a purpose; it's not to react to genocide and to punish the alleged perpetrators. The main reason is to prevent, because it's an intolerable crime when a whole group is being destroyed in whole or in part."
About the potential legal responsibility of governments supplying weapons, intelligence or political support despite warnings of serious violations, Pillay said the states themselves established international conventions and treaties.
"They set the standards. Now they must implement them without selection," she said, arguing that governments were failing to apply their own commitments because of political interests.
Pillay recalled that her UN commission had urged the General Assembly to seek an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice (ICJ) concerning Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory.
She welcomed the court's opinion in 2024, which found Israel's continued presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful, and outlined obligations concerning Palestinian rights.
She, however, acknowledged that legal proceedings offered limited immediate relief to people suffering on the ground.
"I agree; they're not very helpful to relieve their immediate dire situation," she said. "Let's use international law to assert and realize the rights of people who are oppressed everywhere in the world."
On shortcomings of the international system and its eroding credibility, Pillay pointed to the dominance of governments within the UN and the shrinking space for civil society.
"Certainly, the system is very skewed. Who controls the United Nations? It's member states, it's governments," she said, urging UN members to conduct their affairs in closer cooperation with civil society organizations.
Turning to Washington's measures against the International Criminal Court (ICC), Pillay called on governments, including those outside the Rome Statute, to oppose the campaign.
"I would like to see states of the world, the member states, whether they're parties to the Rome Statute or not, to condemn the unlawful measures and sanctions that the United States is imposing on this court," she said.
"We should say roundly that it's unacceptable, and then we all have the responsibility to help the court to overcome these obstacles."
The former ICC judge expressed confidence that the court's staff would continue their work despite mounting political pressure.
"They're not going to stop doing what they are doing because they are working out of commitment. They believe that it is possible to realize justice for all," she said.
Reflecting on receiving the Nobel, Pillay described the recognition as unexpected and deeply meaningful. "This award was a huge surprise to me, but a wonderful surprise," she said.
She expressed gratitude that the Nobel Committee had recognized different aspects of her decades-long career, from challenging apartheid to advancing international justice.
"You don't win a case all the time. You win some. You lose many, especially under apartheid South Africa," she said.
Pillay described the committee's recognition of her work as a "memorable moment," saying she appreciated its efforts to examine her contributions to international peace and justice.
