Prosecutors accused Russell Brand of rape and sexual assault against six women. He denies all the charges.
Actor and comedian Russell Brand, who was once one of the United Kingdom’s best-known television presenters, acted as a ruthless predator: to satisfy his insatiable sexual appetite, he raped women or sexually assaulted them, ignoring their protests. Prosecutors said this, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
The 51-year-old Brand, the former husband of American singer Katy Perry, is on trial on charges of three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of engaging in sexual activity without the complainant’s consent; the charges concern six women and events that took place between 1999 and 2009.
He denies all the charges and will present his defence later in court.
"Today I feel blessed," he said as he arrived at London’s Southwark Crown Court. "Of course, I am nervous, but I hope this trial will lead to positive outcomes for everyone involved."
Opening the case, prosecutor Riel Karmi-Jones said that some of the six women who brought the allegations had resisted, while others had been unable to respond to his advances. According to her, this made no difference to Brand.
"His appetite — a strong desire for sexual contact — was indiscriminate and insatiable," the prosecutor said.
Although he could be funny, charming and pleasant to talk to, when he wanted something he also displayed a childish conviction that any desire of his should be satisfied, she added.
"He was ruthless, calculating, manipulative and, the prosecution contends, a sexual predator," Karmi-Jones said.
According to her, the alleged offences were committed over a decade while he was building his career — from performing stand-up comedy to working as a television presenter, actor and star of Hollywood films.
In addition
The first of these incidents allegedly occurred in 1999, when he was performing a show on the sidelines of a Labour Party conference in Bournemouth. The first complainant, who watched the show and believed Brand was gay, said that he raped her in a hotel room; she had invited him there because she thought he was interested in the matter she had discussed with him.
According to the prosecutor, one of the fellow performers who appeared with him at that show said that Brand boasted of wanting to sleep with 5,000 women over the course of his life.
He is accused of trying to drag a woman into a toilet cubicle at the MTV Europe office where she worked in 2001. Three years later, another woman said that he pulled her into a toilet cubicle in a bar and then committed an act of oral rape.
Around the same time — in 2004 or 2005 — a woman who worked for a media company reported that he engaged in sexual activity with her without her consent in her office.
The fifth complainant — one of his fans — said that in 2009 she had consensual sex with him at his home, but that he then raped her anally, the prosecutor said. The sixth complainant, who worked for Channel 4, alleges that Brand demanded a massage from her that same year and then pressed his face against her groin.
During police questioning, Brand refused to answer questions but provided a written statement in which he said that he did not remember the incidents and had never engaged in sexual activity without his partner’s consent, although he admitted having sex in toilet cubicles during parties, Karmi-Jones said.
According to the prosecutor, the women involved in the case did not know one another and had not reported the matter to police at the time for various reasons, but decided to make their complaints after a television programme aired and a newspaper article was published in 2023, in which other women made anonymous allegations.
Brand sat in the dock wearing a dark suit and a thin white scarf, staring intently ahead.
The trial, which is expected to last around six weeks, has attracted enormous media attention: an additional courtroom was opened to accommodate more journalists, and numerous media outlets launched daily podcasts.
The comedian, known for his outrageous style and appearance, rose to popularity in Britain before he began appearing in films—including the 2010 movie "Get Him to the Greek"; that same year, he married Perry. They divorced in 2012.
Recently, Brand has taken part in online broadcasts discussing U.S. politics, religion, and freedom of speech.

Louvre boss warns of closure risk without major renovations
- The Louvre risks closure unless lawmakers approve major renovations, as boss Christophe Leribault warns the museum is “creaking and over-capacity” and needs urgent repair.
- Leribault wants private funding too, but says major public money may only come after the 2027 elections. He warned delay would be a “disaster”.
- The museum is also upgrading security after a 2025 jewel heist worth US$100 million. Plans include new security leadership, better cameras and stronger perimeter checks.
AI generated
PARIS – The Louvre Museum risks having to close its doors to the public unless lawmakers approve a major overhaul of the creaking and over-capacity institution, its head told a French newspaper on Oct 14.
Speaking to Le Figaro, Christophe Leribault said that the museum intended to tap private sources of funding for its transformation, but that a major injection of public money would need to be approved after national elections in 2027.
“Whoever forms the next government must keep in mind that if the Louvre is not repaired, updated and transformed, it will very quickly fall behind and will eventually have to close its doors to the public. That would be a disaster,” he said.
Successive minority governments in France have struggled for years to pass annual budgets and current Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is struggling to rein in public spending to reduce the country’s vast deficit.
Leribault was appointed in February in the aftermath of an embarrassing Oct 19 heist in 2025 which saw a gang of thieves raid the Louvre to steal crown jewels worth an estimated US$100 million (S$128.3 million).
He has made tackling the problems highlighted by the theft a priority, with the roll-out of an €83 million (S$118.9 million) security masterplan “moving forward at speed”, he told AFP ahead of the one-year anniversary of the crime.
Measures include creating a new head of security position, upgrading the security camera network – which was found to have old cameras and major gaps – as well as improved surveillance around the perimeter and at access points.
No ‘miracle’ solution
Leribault argued that long-term improvements could only be made as part of the larger overhaul he has planned for the institution, which welcomed around nine million visitors in 2025.
“The operations needed to secure the museum require work on the historic building and its infrastructure,” he wrote.
“There is no easy, miracle ‘surface’ solution. Everything is interconnected, everything is linked,” he added.
The world’s most-visited museum is widely seen as facing structural problems from its old plumbing, badly insulated galleries and cramped public areas.
The extent of the work and the cost have become extremely political, with President Emmanuel Macron championing a €600 million overhaul that would include a new entrance.
Trade unions criticised Macron and Leribault’s predecessor, Laurence des Cars, for prioritising grandiose plans for an architectural overhaul instead of more modest changes that would improve the visitor experience. AFP

Colombia opens embassy in Jerusalem
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:57:32 CST
21:57:32 KST

JERUSALEM, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Colombia inaugurated its embassy in Jerusalem on Wednesday as its new president Abelardo de la Espriella moved to restore full diplomatic relations with Israel, reversing his predecessor's decision to sever ties over Israel's military operations in Gaza.
The ceremony was attended by Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa'ar and his Colombian counterpart, Omar Bula Escobar.
Under de la Espriella, the two countries reached an agreement on July 15 to restore full diplomatic and economic relations, which took effect after the new Colombian president took office in August. On Tuesday, Colombia and Israel formally reinstated their free trade agreement.
In May 2024, then-Colombian President Gustavo Petro announced that Colombia would sever its ties with Israel, accusing its government of committing genocide in Gaza, an allegation Israel rejects.
In October 2025, after Israel intercepted a Gaza-bound flotilla and detained two Colombian nationals, Petro expelled Israel's remaining diplomats and terminated the free trade agreement between the two countries.
Colombia's embassy, previously located in Tel Aviv, is the tenth foreign embassy in Jerusalem.
The Palestinians see East Jerusalem as the capital of their future state. Israel annexed East Jerusalem after the 1967 Middle East war and declared the whole city as its "eternal and indivisible capital" in 1980.
The United Nations Security Council declared the move "null and void" in Resolution 478 in 1980, stating that it violates international law and does not alter the status of East Jerusalem as occupied territory under the Fourth Geneva Convention.
The United States recognized Jerusalem as the capital of Israel in December 2017 and relocated the U.S. embassy in Israel to the city in May 2018.
As the city's status remains disputed, most countries maintain diplomatic relations with Israel but keep their embassies in Tel Aviv or elsewhere. ■

WINDHOEK, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Namibia has launched a compulsory vaccination drive in the Karasburg State Veterinary District, the epicenter of an ongoing foot and mouth disease (FMD) outbreak, a government official announced Wednesday.
In an update, Romeo Muyunda, deputy director for public relations at the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries, Water and Land Reform, said the exercise will begin on Wednesday and run in three rounds over three months.
"Animal owners must present their animals as instructed by the District State Veterinary Office, at the time and place to be communicated by the Office," he said, noting that the campaign covers all farms south of the B3 and C10 roads up to the Orange River, plus a band of two farms north of those roads.
Veterinary officials will conduct the campaign and livestock owners are not allowed to vaccinate their animals.
To further contain the virus, Muyunda said that authorities will construct a new animal disease control fence stretching from Klein Manasse to Naute Dam and onward to the Fish River Canyon. Construction will commence after the official notification to affected landowners, in accordance with the Animal Health Act.
Surveillance figures indicate that a total of 63,011 animals have been inspected, with 131 testing positive for FMD across 18 confirmed infected farms. The outbreak in the Kharas Region remains confined to the Karasburg State Veterinary District, he highlighted.
Addressing the recent detection of FMD in the northern Zambezi Region on Oct. 11, Muyunda stressed that there is no epidemiological link between the southern outbreak in Kharas and the northern cases.
As of Oct. 13, active surveillance had detected no new clinical cases or additional lesions in the Zambezi Region since the 12 positive cases reported on Oct. 7.
"The Zambezi Region remains at high risk of FMD introduction due to the presence of resident buffalo populations in protected areas, which are known carriers of the FMD virus, as well as ongoing FMD outbreaks in neighboring countries," Muyunda said.
He said the ministry is monitoring the situation closely and urged the public and the livestock industry to report any suspected unauthorized movements of meat and meat products violating containment measures. ■

EU proposes one-year delay to methane import rules
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:57:18 CST
21:57:18 KST

BRUSSELS, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- The European Commission on Wednesday proposed postponing certain obligations for fossil fuel importers to ease pressure on them due to high energy prices and supply concerns.
The obligations under the European Union (EU) Methane Regulation would be postponed for one year, it was announced.
The proposal came as the conflict in the Middle East has put further strain on global energy markets, driving up prices and raising the risk of reduced availability of oil and gas, the Commission said.
The proposed amendment to the regulation would delay monitoring, reporting and verification obligations for importers of natural gas, oil and coal, as well as methane-intensity reporting requirements for both importers and EU producers.
The Commission said the postponement would give importers additional time to comply with the rules, while helping avoid further pressure on security of supply of imported fossil fuels.
Nevertheless, it added that the amendment would not change the overall ambition, integrity or scope of the regulation, reaffirming the bloc's commitment to reducing methane emissions.
The proposal will now be submitted to the European Parliament and the Council of the EU for adoption.
Adopted in 2024, the EU Methane Regulation introduced phased requirements to increase transparency on methane emissions. It covers domestic energy production, transportation and processing, as well as imports of oil, gas and coal.
According to the Commission, methane is the second-largest source of greenhouse gas emissions after carbon dioxide. ■

The alleged $840,000 scheme involved funds allocated by the central government to the Lviv regional administration.
In another case reported by the National Police in June, a former deputy mayor of Kharkov was accused of involvement in a scheme that resulted in $340,000 in losses through inflated prices for construction materials used in fortifications.
Zelensky’s government has faced a series of corruption scandals involving people close to him since last November. A recent opinion poll suggests that Ukrainians rank government corruption as a greater concern than Russian missile and drone strikes.
The Ukrainian leader is facing additional pressure after President Donald Trump accused him of harming US interests by attacking Russian oil refineries amid the global fuel crunch. Trump suggested that Ukraine should replace Zelensky with someone willing to compromise.
Zelensky has since complained that the US has stopped providing early warnings of incoming Russian ballistic missile strikes. There have also been reports of restrictions on Ukraine’s access to the Starlink satellite internet system aimed at preventing its use on fast-moving platforms. Starlink is owned by Trump ally Elon Musk, who has backed the US president’s call to replace Zelensky.

Cheap weapons, growing fears: Inside the Taliban’s drone campaign against Pakistan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:52:44 UTC
21:52:44 KST

Cheap weapons, growing fears: Inside the Taliban’s drone campaign against Pakistan
Pakistan says it intercepted 23 suicide drones launched from Afghanistan into Pakistani airspace in September alone. Since the conflict began in February 2026, the Taliban have increasingly used drones to attack Pakistan, raising concerns in Islamabad.
The Pakistani army on September 23 said it had shot down at least eight fixed-wing drones in Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, less than 1,000 metres from the Afghan border. It was the latest reported attempt by the Taliban to target Pakistani forces using this type of drone.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Since the conflict between Pakistan and the Taliban began in February of this year, the Taliban have deployed armed first-person-view (FPV) drones – small quadcopters carrying munitions such as mortar shells – to attack Pakistani positions near the border. They have also used larger, fixed-wing suicide drones equipped with more powerful engines, potentially capable of flying hundreds of kilometres.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
On September 28, Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry said it had delivered a diplomatic protest note to the Taliban over what it described as "provocative incursions", citing 23 drones launched from Afghanistan into Pakistani airspace since the beginning of the month.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
From friends to foes
Once close allies, Pakistan and the Taliban entered into open conflict about eight months ago when Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Mohammad Asif publicly declared that “relations with the Taliban had deteriorated into an ‘open war’.”
The conflict escalated after Pakistan began targeting positions of the Pakistani militant group Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) inside Afghanistan. Also known as the Pakistani Taliban, the TTP is officially recognised as a terrorist organisation by multiple countries and international bodies, including the United Nations, Pakistan and the European Union.
The TTP has carried out attacks in Pakistan for nearly two decades and has long-standing ties with the Afghan Taliban, which Pakistan accuses of sheltering and supporting the group.
When Pakistan, which has aerial military superiority over Afghanistan, has struck suspected TTP positions deep inside Afghanistan, the Taliban has retaliated with ground attacks and drones.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
'Making a fixed wing drone is not that complicated anymore'
UAV expert Mark Grozel explains:
 These drones are roughly two metres in size and could carry between half a kilogram and one kilogram of explosives. They have a very limited military effectiveness and are easy to intercept. They are slow and fly at low altitude. The difficulty is detecting them: they are hard to spot, but once detected, they are easy to shoot down.
There are multiple scenarios. One is that a foreign government supplies them. Or they could be, to some extent, homemade. Today, making a fixed-wing drone is not that complicated anymore.
Autopilot software that controls a drone’s trajectory is widely available.
On [the e-commerce site] Alibaba, you can easily buy components such as the engine and battery. The body could be made with a 3D printer, or from polystyrene or even balsa wood…
After examining photos and videos of drones that Pakistan’s army said it had intercepted, FRANCE 24 identified what appear to be DLE55 engines fitted to each of the suicide drones shown. These 55cc single piston engines and are commercially available online.
Despite their basic engines, small explosive payloads and simple radio navigation systems, these drones have a heavy psychological impact.
'Their main power is their psychological impact'
According to Grozel:
 The strength of this kind of fixed-wing drones is that they are cheap to make. Any group with the resources, including the Taliban, can now produce them.
They allow you to tell your adversary: ‘I can threaten your infrastructure at any moment.’ If one hits a school or a fuel facility, the consequences could be catastrophic. Their main power is their psychological impact.
The Taliban’s drone attacks come amid a broader conflict between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban, fueled by the activities of the TTP.
Direct engagements between the TTP and Pakistani security forces have increased significantly since the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, rising from 98 incidents in 2021 to 470 in 2024. Throughout 2025, regular clashes along the border reportedly resulted in approximately 4,000 deaths.
On September 18, 2026 a TTP suicide car bomb attack on a mosque killed 21 people in the Pakistani border city Kohat .
The roots of the Taliban–TTP alliance
Mukhtar Wafaei, an expert on the Taliban who specialises in Afghan affairs, explains how relations between Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban deteriorated into military conflict.
 To understand the current situation, we have to go back to the Soviet-Afghan war in the 1980s.
During those years, Afghan and Pakistani fighters were sent from religious schools in Pakistan to participate in the “jihad” against Soviet forces in Afghanistan.
These relationships were forged during that period and remained largely unquestioned until the September 11 attacks and the subsequent US invasion of Afghanistan.
After the collapse of the Taliban’s first government in 2001, Taliban leaders and members dispersed, with many seeking refuge in Pakistan’s border regions, including Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Waziristan and Balochistan.
To display this content from Telegram, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
 They maintained these long-standing cross-border relationships. In 2008, the Afghan Taliban expanded their presence across various parts of Afghanistan. Around the same time, several jihadist organisations operating in Pakistan, originating from the same tribal regions and carrying out violent attacks, came together under the TTP.
Another turning point came in 2021, when the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan. Taliban leaders who had been sheltered in safe houses in Pakistan belonging to the TTP, left for Afghanistan. Their Pakistani friends, allies and associates accompanied them to Kabul and also took refuge there.
Between late 2021 and mid-2022, Pakistan attempted to negotiate with the TTP. But after the group refused to disarm or accept Pakistan’s constitutional framework, it ordered its fighters to launch nationwide attacks on November 28, 2022. The Taliban claim the TTP is a Pakistani internal issue and deny any responsibility.
When diplomatic ultimatums failed to halt cross-border militant operations, Pakistan resorted to air strikes inside Afghanistan, prompting the Afghan Taliban to retaliate with attacks on Pakistani territory.
To display this content from , you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Pakistan also launched a mass expulsion campaign, with 2.39 million Afghans returning from Pakistan to Afghanistan over a period of more than two years.
To display this content from , you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
 There is a very deep ideological relationship between the Afghan Taliban and the TTP rooted in the extremist Islamist religious schools in Pakistan. They share the same ideology, come from the same religious tradition and follow the same teachings. They can no longer be separated. They are effectively one group.
A few months after the Afghan Taliban returned to power, the TTP leader stated very clearly in Pashto that Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan and the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, meaning the Afghan Taliban, were one group. He said: “We are not two groups. We are one group, following one programme, one ideology and one method.”
This is particularly revealing because the TTP leader himself explicitly described the two movements as one.

Returning to Gaza after two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:52:18 UTC
21:52:18 KST

When I entered Gaza through the crossing, I was shocked and stunned by what I saw. Looking to my right and left, all the houses were destroyed, leaving no trace. The streets were unrecognizable. Every street had a name, but I couldn’t identify them, there were no landmarks. The destruction was utter and unnatural.
I returned to Gaza in May after two years of living in Egypt. I don’t regret going back to Gaza. But I’m still in shock, unable to accept life and the situation people are living in. The situation is terrible, unnatural.
Since the genocide began in October 2023, things have been extremely difficult. We were deeply shocked by the reality of what was happening in Gaza: the destruction, the displacement, and the killing of people.
This war, of course, had a grave impact on us and changed the course of our lives. This also affected our work and changed the nature of our role as women leaders and advocates in the field of women’s rights.
Carrying out our work in Rafah at the beginning was difficult. During the first three months, I refused to ask the social workers and lawyers to work inside the shelters out of fear for their safety. But little by little, we began working, knowing this war could last a long time. It is extremely difficult to be responsible for your team, to ask your own team to put themselves at risk, when, at any moment, they could be exposed to bombardment or death.
Then our office was destroyed, and its assets and resources were lost, so I had to start managing and directing the association from my home. I lived in a two-storey house in Rafah and I hosted between 35 and 40 displaced people there, yet I still managed to use part of the ground floor for work. We were able to continue providing services from my home despite the serious risks, because the Israeli occupation was targeting us, targeting anyone trying to help people, whether through offices, warehouses, or vehicles used for humanitarian response.
The area where I lived in Rafah was sheltering almost 1.2 million people, due to the mass displacement from the north to the south. We distributed hygiene and food assistance packages to displaced families in tents and UNRWA school shelters at a time when government shelters were not yet operating. At the time, we had a kitchen in Rafah allowing us to cook regularly for people. That was an important part of our work in addition to distributing fresh water to the tents. We also built women’s restrooms among the tents in informal shelters.
I had two main reasons for going to Egypt. I was scheduled for surgery in November 2023, but I ignored it. I thought that being in the middle of a war was not the right time for surgery. But eventually, my condition worsened, and I became more ill and exhausted. I decided I had to undergo treatment.
It was also because I felt I was in real danger. I had a feeling that Rafah was nearing its end. I was terrified for my children. I was having nightmares that made my fear for them even stronger and that led me to decide to go to Egypt.
It was not an easy decision. It is not easy to leave your home, your family, and your work, and even my entry into Egypt was not guaranteed.
I was not granted a medical referral for medical evacuation. If I had waited for medical evacuation for my turn to come and had been lost in the bureaucracy, only God knows whether I would have survived. So I decided to pay for my treatment out of pocket. I paid $7,500 (£5,580) to be able to leave and that was only for me to pass through the Rafah crossing into Egypt. I also paid $3,000 (£2,230) for my daughter to be allowed to leave with me.
Thankfully, I was financially able to afford leaving and receiving treatment. Sadly, most people in Gaza were not and this left many patients, especially women and children, at risk of death.
It was a very difficult journey. All my children were with me when I was at the Rafah crossing. I was crying so hard, thinking I might never see them again, afraid that while going to Egypt, I might lose them, because the possibility that I or they may die or never seeing each other was real.
I thought I would go for a couple of months and register my children so they could come to Egypt while I received treatment, and then I would return to Gaza, to my home, my husband, and my work. I wanted to return to my life in Gaza once I knew my children were safe.
Then what I feared most happened. I travelled on the 29th of April 2024, and on the 5th of May, the Rafah crossing was permanently closed. It remained closed until February 2026.
I found myself stranded, separated from my kids. Those were two very difficult years for me. I was constantly trying to ensure their safety, as they were in danger while I was safe and this was an agonizing guilt. I was given sedatives so I could sleep, instead of staying awake with worry. Whenever there was shelling near them in Al-Mawasi, Khan Yunis, my daughter and I were gripped by terror. We couldn’t enjoy life, we couldn’t feel any sort of safety or mental peace. We lived in a state of constant tension.
Then came the news that my home had been completely destroyed. I hadn’t even finished paying for it yet; I still owed the half amount in installments and outstanding checks and I had lived there for less than two years. All the toil and hardship of a lifetime spent building a home for ourselves and our children to settle down, it vanished in the blink of an eye. It was devastating news; I fell ill for a week after hearing it and seeing the images of the house’s total destruction.
Things were extremely difficult; the suffering and hardship were very real. Yet I remained fully engaged in my work on a daily basis, around the clock. Sometimes I worked normal hours, other times, the internet was so poor in Gaza that I had to communicate at night. We spoke whenever possible, at any time, even on weekends. I did not have a single day off to rest. God helped Wefaq remain standing, continue working, and keep helping people.
The decision to return to Gaza was inevitable. What should I do in Egypt? Just live in a safe house? Of course not. I had to return to my Homeland, to my children, my family, my home, my work, my friends, my colleagues, and everyone.
Honestly, as soon as the crossing opened, I registered on the embassy’s website to return. What delayed me a bit was completing my medical treatment to ensure my health. I didn’t feel safe in Egypt, and I did not feel joy in Egypt during my two years because, truly, the land, the homeland, and the family are the only safe havens.
The days leading up to my return were filled with anxiety. My name was on the lists, but no one knew when the approval would come. I was in a terrible hurry and wanted to go back and see the children. I was afraid the crossing might close again before I could return. I was constantly stressed, anxious, and making calls, desperately wanting someone to help me get back quickly.
Then I returned to Gaza on May 13th, 2026. The journey back was incredibly tiring, it’s inhumane. We sat in the sun for three or four hours to be checked waiting for the Israelis to tell the Europeans and the Palestinian side that “it’s ok, send their group”. There are no toilets. It was very hot that day and you could not drink water, so that you would not have to go to the bathroom and in the end when I arrived at the [Israeli crossing] and we were searched and we got on the buses, I got dizzy from sunstroke, where I fainted.
At the Israeli crossing there was humiliation and inspection. I saw people who were harassed and had many of their belongings confiscated. There was disrespect. We remained on the bus waiting after we were searched and checked, sitting in the bus, locked up and suffocating, and there was no air conditioning. We remained waiting on the bus from 5:30 PM until 2:30 AM, when the buses finally set off.
It was a shock to me after I entered Gaza and the bus started moving. People began to cry at the sheer scale of the devastation we had witnessed in Rafah city and along our route from the crossing to Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis.
I now live in a tent in the Al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis in the Sultan Mahmoud camp, which houses no fewer than 200 families. The situation is terrible, unnatural. I’m still honestly in shock and I can’t accept life at its natural rhythm
Imagine living in a tent, just a tarpaulin, on sand. I am considered much better than others: I have a large tent for my children and a room roofed with corrugated zinc. I have a bed, and I bought a wardrobe. I’m trying to cope. Other people’s situation is extremely bad. I’m still in shock at how people can bear this and live normally.
Daily life in Gaza is very difficult. There’s no water and people have to wait for a water tanker to come so they can fill up. Goods are available now, but it’s very expensive and not everyone can afford it; most people rely on charities but even many charities have stopped operating.
The health situation is dire; garbage is everywhere and basically there’s no sewage system. The pipes could burst in some streets, making them impassable. There’s also a widespread infestation of rodents and fleas in most of the tents and not everyone can afford pesticides or rodent control products, which could lead to the spread of epidemics. Most people go to hospitals knowing beforehand that there is no treatment, no medicine, and no equipment. The most important thing Gaza needs now is the rehabilitation of hospitals and the establishment of various medical points to provide health services.
We at the Wefaq Foundation are working on a humanitarian response to meet people’s needs, providing hygiene kits, dignity kits, food parcels, vegetable baskets, hot meals, children’s clothing, women’s clothing, and tents. We are also doing our basic work of providing multi-sectoral services to women who are victims of violence, and women and children at risk. We provide psychological support, consultations, psychotherapy also, health services, social services, legal services, and consultations, even representation through referrals. We have also implemented many economic empowerment projects to develop businesses such as bakeries, mills, spice shops, restaurants, food products, and sweets.
Buthaina, pictured back in Gaza this month
Gaza needs everything. But first, Gaza needs an end to the Israeli occupation and its reconstruction, so that people can live a dignified, protected, and honorable life, far from the humiliation and degradation that people are currently living in and the restoration of rights to their owners.

Failure to activate Hormuz fertilizer plan could trigger food crisis, UN official says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

Failure to activate Hormuz fertilizer plan could trigger food crisis, UN official says
BANGKOK, Oct 14 - A failure by the United States and Iran to agree within weeks on a UN-backed plan for moving fertilizer through the Strait of Hormuz could cause a food security crisis in parts of Asia and Africa, an official overseeing the proposed scheme said on Wednesday.
The United Nations set up a taskforce in March to facilitate passage of fertilizers through the strait. It is yet to implement the mechanism it drew up, but United Nations Under-Secretary-General Jorge Moreira da Silva said this could be activated within 7-10 days of an agreement between Washington and Tehran.
"It's absolutely crucial to get the deal in the next few weeks. Otherwise, we will miss the planting season," he said in an interview in Bangkok, on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings.
The White House, US State Department and Iran's Embassy in Bangkok did not immediately reply to a request for comment.
Iran has sought to tighten its grip on the Strait of Hormuz since US and Israeli strikes on February 28, using the chokepoint to pressure Washington, which has been pressing its own naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Before the war, the waterway handled roughly a third of globally traded urea — the world's most widely used fertilizer — and nearly half of seaborne sulphur, a key input. It is also a major conduit for global oil supplies.
Fertilizer shipments out of the Gulf region remained largely halted more than six months after the start of the conflict, the Washington-based International Food Policy Research Institute said in a note last month. Fertilizer products accounted for a "very negligible" share of the resumption of some shipping during a ceasefire between mid-June and mid-July, it said.
FIVE VESSELS A DAY
If the Hormuz disruption continues, commodity prices could rise by up to 81% for cereals, 66% for oil crops and 30% for animal products, according to an August report by the International Chamber of Commerce.
"If we miss that planting season, the productivity of agriculture would significantly drop and the impact on prices will significantly increase," Moreira da Silva said.
The proposed operation would use a coordination centre in Oman to register vessels and coordinate safe passage, with UN monitors working alongside local authorities at Gulf ports to verify cargo loading.
The passage of only five vessels per day through Hormuz could keep fertilizer supplies flowing to countries in critical need, Moreira da Silva said.
Ships would be tracked during transit, and additional inspections could be carried out if countries raised concerns about a vessel or its cargo, he added.
MULTIPLE SHIPPING CHOKEPOINTS
Iran and the United States have exchanged proposals through intermediaries since a June interim ceasefire collapsed, but efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have stalled over Tehran's conditions and Washington's insistence on addressing Iran's nuclear programme from the outset.
The proposed UN mechanism could operate alongside negotiations on a comprehensive deal aimed at securing lasting peace and freedom of navigation, Moreira da Silva said.
"What we are telling them is, while you continue your discussions towards a comprehensive deal, let us work, let us do our job," he said, declining to specify the exact bottlenecks to a deal as discussions continue with both sides.
Beyond the Hormuz crisis, a deteriorating situation in the Black Sea region, where cargo vessels have come under attack, and an offensive by Iran-backed Houthi militants along a key Red Sea shipping route are compounding the threat to global food security.
"What we are witnessing now is a concentration of factors," Moreira da Silva said. "Climate crisis, simultaneous disruption of maritime chokepoints on the Black Sea, on the Red Sea and on Hormuz." REUTERS

Netherlands denies visas to 3 Russian athletes, barring them from world championships
Dutch authorities refused to grant visas to three Russian gymnasts, preventing them from taking part in world gymnastics championships held in Rotterdam later this month, the Russian Gymnastics Federation said on Oct. 13.
Angelina Melnikova, Viktoria Listunova, and Anna Kalmykova were denied entry as "one or more Schengen area member states consider the athletes a threat to their international relations," the federation said on its Telegram channel.
Participation of Russian athletes in international competitions remains controversial and, in some sports, restricted due to Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
At the same time, Dutch authorities approved visas for five other gymnasts, the Russian Gymnastics Federation said later on Oct. 13, noting that 47 of the 61 members of the Russian delegation had been granted entry so far.
Listunova publicly expressed support for Russian aggression in Ukraine and was previously denied visas for a gymnastics competition in Croatia in August.
Melnikova has also voiced backing for Russian President Vladimir Putin and even ran as a candidate for the ruling United Russia party in local election primaries last year.
Both Melnikova and Listunova are Olympic gold medalists.
Kalmykova, in turn, holds a sports contract with the Russian National Guard, according to Kyiv.
The Russian Gymnastics Federation denounced the decision and said it would appeal to the International Olympic Committee and World Gymnastics.
Rotterdam will host the World Artistic Gymnastics Championships from Oct. 17 to 25, serving as the first stage of team qualification for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.
World Gymnastics imposed sanctions on Russian and Belarusian gymnasts at the outbreak of the full-scale war in 2022, but allowed them to compete as "neutral athletes" two years later.
The international association finally lifted its ban in May 2026, allowing Russian and Belarusian gymnasts to compete under their national flags, as part of a broader loosening of restrictions on Russian athletes.
Kyiv continues to urge global sports organizations to maintain sanctions against Russian and Belarusian athletes.
Russia's all-out war has taken a heavy toll on Ukraine, with hundreds of Ukrainian athletes and coaches killed and hundreds of sports facilities destroyed by Russian missile and drone attacks.

US annual inflation rises to 3.7% in September as gasoline prices surge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:47:09 UTC
21:47:09 KST

Mücahithan Avcıoğlu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
US annual consumer inflation accelerated to 3.7% in September, exceeding market expectations of 3.6%, as surging gasoline prices drove a sharper monthly increase, official data showed Wednesday.
The annual inflation rate rose from 3.4% in August, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
On a monthly basis, the Consumer Price Index (CPI) increased 0.6% in September, up from 0.4% in August.
Gasoline prices jumped 9.1% over the month, accounting for more than half of the overall monthly increase. Energy prices rose 5.2%, accelerating from a 2.1% gain in August.
Shelter costs also contributed to price pressures, increasing 0.4% after rising 0.3% the previous month.
Food prices were unchanged overall, as a 0.1% decline in grocery prices offset a 0.2% increase in the cost of eating out. 
Core inflation also accelerates
Core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, rose to 2.6% annually in September from 2.4% in August.
Monthly core inflation remained at 0.3%.
Prices increased across several categories, including recreation, used cars and trucks, education, airline fares, and apparel.
Used vehicle prices rose 0.7% over the month, while airline fares increased 1.2% and recreation costs climbed 0.5%. Communication prices fell 0.2%.
On an annual basis, energy prices surged 20.4%, with gasoline up 34.2% and fuel oil rising 74.2%.
Electricity prices increased 4.4% from a year earlier, while natural gas prices rose 5%.
Food prices climbed 2.5% annually, and shelter costs increased 3.2%.

Clash between security personnel and protesters during Delhi protests
NEW DELHI: The Delhi Police is investigating social media handles allegedly spreading rumours and inflammatory content during protests demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation in the national capital. "Delhi Police’s IFSO unit has a dedicated cyber patrolling team that monitors such posts to verify their authenticity and compliance with legal provisions. If we find a post to be factually incorrect, false, a rumor, a threat to public order, defamatory, or likely to incite anarchy, we take action in accordance with the law," he said.Bhatia said the investigation into the Pakistan-linked account was ongoing, along with other cases registered over social media content.
"When we sought registration details for one such specific handle, the IP address traced back to Pakistan; we are currently investigating that case. The process is ongoing, and we have registered other cases as well; investigations are underway, and we will share further details and evidence with you as they emerge," he said.Giving details of a post that allegedly claimed police were firing at demonstrators, Bhatia said the claim was false and could have heightened tensions."We found a post intended to incite chaos; the handle registered in Pakistan."He further claimed that the handle alleged that the police were opening fire on the demonstrators. "It was a deliberate attempt to whip up a volatile atmosphere based on falsehoods. Since the claim was untrue, we immediately requested the post's removal and registered a case; further action is underway," he said.
The Delhi Police had also recently debunked a viral social media video claiming that Rahul Gandhi's residence had come under attack and that gunfire had been reported.According to the police, the footage was from December 2019 and was unrelated to current events. The investigation comes amid police action against three Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) activists over alleged attempts to disturb public peace and instigate others through social media. Sourav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were remanded to five days of judicial custody, while Ajinkya Shinde was bound down for six months to maintain peace and good behaviour.According to a Delhi Police statement, the action followed an incident on October 13 in which the three activists and 11 other CJP members allegedly entered the denotified Jantar Mantar protest site through private premises and obstructed police personnel. CJP has maintained that it will continue to demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and challenge the denotification of Jantar Mantar.

Three people were seriously injured in a blast at an Intel factory in Kiryat Gat on Wednesday, caused by what Israel Police suspect to be a gas cylinder explosion.
Israel's Fire and Rescue Authority initially warned that hazardous chemicals may have leaked following the explosion. Firefighters worked to identify the source of the chemicals and extinguish the ensuing fire, which has since been put out.
The Fire and Rescue Authority said the incident involved nitrogen trifluoride (NF3), a non-flammable gas with oxidizing properties.
Following the explosion, Mayor Kfir Suissa said, "After an on-site assessment of the situation in cooperation with all relevant parties, the fire at the factory was completely extinguished. As of this time, there are no special instructions for residents, and there is no danger to the public. We ask that you not come to the area of the incident, in order to allow the security and rescue forces to complete their work at the scene without interruption."
Intel’s Kiryat Gat factory, also known as FAB 28, manufactures semiconductor chips used in the company’s processors. The facility is one of Intel’s key manufacturing sites in Israel and plays a role in the company’s global semiconductor production operations.
Three in serious condition after Intel blast in Kiryat Gat
United Hatzalah medical teams treated three people who suffered burns across their bodies following the incident in Kiryat Gat, the emergency medical service said.
Yanaki Weinberg, deputy head of United Hatzalah’s Kiryat Gat branch, and paramedic Moshe Winfeld said they treated a man around 45 who was critically injured and suffered burns across his body. He was transported by a United Hatzalah ambulance to meet an intensive care ambulance while resuscitation efforts were underway. The team delivered two electric shocks using a defibrillator during the journey, and the man's heart miraculously began beating again. He was then transferred to Soroka Medical Center by intensive care ambulance.
Hila Rinkoff and Zvi Levin, paramedics with a second United Hatzalah ambulance team at the scene, said they evacuated another man, around 30, who was also critically injured, to meet an intensive care ambulance while resuscitation efforts were underway.
A third man, around 25, was treated at the scene and evacuated in moderate-to-serious condition, they added.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu spoke with MDA director-general Eli Bin to inquire about the condition of those injured in the explosion, the Prime Minister’s Office said later on Wednesday.
The prime minister wished the injured a speedy recovery and thanked the emergency responders for acting quickly and decisively, the statement added.

Germany news: Merz attacks extremes for fueling division

- A man has gone on trial accused of playing a role in the 2022 explosion at the Nord Stream gas pipelines
Here is a roundup of all the headlines across Germany on Wednesday, October 14:

Two men violently free prisoner in Essen while he was out on a doctor's visit
Police have launched a major search in the western city of Essen after two masked men attacked prison officers taking an inmate to a doctor's appointment and freed him.
They overpowered and tied up the prison staff in the building lobby leading into the doctor's office on the Kennedyplatz in the city center, shortly before 1 p.m. local time (11 a.m. UTC).
The assailants and the inmate then split up and fled in different directions using e-scooters, police said. The prisoner was serving a custodial sentence for drug offenses and assault charges.
"The 34-year-old inmate with German citizenship and the two men suspected of freeing him are on the run. Police are searching for the men with numerous officers and has published a photo of the prisoner," Essen police wrote in a statement.
Police warned that it "could not be ruled out" that the suspects were armed, and asked anybody who thought they saw them not to approach or speak to them, but to call the emergency services immediately.
The operation also briefly involved a bomb scare that turned out to be a false alarm. Specialists deployed after a call from a concerned member of the public but it transpired the item was a wooden mock hand grenade.
Police did not immediately comment on whether the prisons officers accompanying the prisoner sustained injuries in the attack. 
Nord Stream trial draws supporters and media attention
There is huge interest in this court case. No sooner had the court doors opened at 07:30 local time in Hamburg than the first journalists, observers and protesters began arriving.
A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist." One participant from Germany told me they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."
Inside, a Ukrainian student told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii Kuznietsov.
"Serhii Kuznietsov is a hero," the student said. In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, Kuznietsov faces a lengthy prison sentence.
Nord Stream defendant's lawyers challenge war crime charge
Lawyers for the Ukrainian man accused of organizing the Nord Stream pipeline attack have challenged the evidence and the war crime charge as his trial opened in Hamburg.
Serhii Kuznietsov, a 50-year-old former Ukrainian special forces officer, is accused of planning and supervising the September 2022 sabotage. Prosecutors say the attack targeted civilian infrastructure using prohibited methods of warfare.
Defense lawyer Jes Meyer-Lohkamp said there were no fingerprints, DNA traces or witness statements placing his client aboard the Andromeda, the yacht allegedly used in the operation.
Prosecutors allege Serhii Kuznietsov boarded the vessel on the German island of Rügen with six accomplices: a skipper, an explosives expert and four divers. The group allegedly attached four explosive devices fitted with timers to the pipelines.
His lawyers argued that Russia used the pipelines as a weapon of economic pressure, making them a legitimate target. They also said Italy had approved his extradition on sabotage allegations, rather than a war crime charge, and sought dismissal of the case.
The defense sought to have the case dismissed, also arguing that military secrecy obligations prevented Serhii K. from discussing potentially exonerating evidence, even with his lawyers.
The explosions ruptured three of the system's four pipelines near Denmark's Bornholm island. Russia had already halted supplies through Nord Stream 1, while Nord Stream 2 had never entered service.
Wadephul warns against economic 'gifts' to Russia
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has urged allies to maintain pressure on Russia following attacks on civilian ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast.
"Gifts embolden Putin to continue on his course. Only firmness creates a willingness to talk," he said after meeting his Bulgarian counterpart in Berlin. He did not explicitly mention US President Donald Trump's recent diesel supply deal with Russia.
Wadephul said Europe must end its dependence on Russian energy to sustain economic pressure on Moscow.
He also urged Russia to agree to a ceasefire covering grain shipments, warning that further attacks threatened people facing hunger, particularly in Africa.
Fat-fingered cockpit error likely triggered Nuremberg hijack alert
A pilot's apparent mistake when entering a transponder code triggered the hijack alert that led to a major police operation at Nuremberg airport, German police said.
Investigators believe the pilot intended to report a radio failure but accidentally entered 7500, the code signaling a hijacking.
The Boeing 737-800's radio was defective, leaving the crew unreachable after takeoff from the Greek island of Corfu, police said.
Police spokesperson Michael Petzold said the pilot apparently did not realize the mistake. The pilot is not under investigation because police believe he acted unintentionally.
Military aircraft accompanied the plane in Croatian airspace, and Austrian interceptors were alerted. Two German Eurofighters then escorted it to Nuremberg.
A police team trained to negotiate with hijackers and a Bavarian support unit were deployed at the airport during the alert.
Officers had less than an hour between the emergency signal and landing to prepare, Petzold said. Police later gave the all-clear.
Lufthansa wins bid for stake in Portugal's TAP
Germany's Lufthansa has won the contest to buy a 44.9% stake in TAP Air Portugal with an offer of €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion), Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said.
Lufthansa beat rival Air France-KLM after months of efforts to privatize the state-rescued airline, Montenegro told journalists following a cabinet meeting.
Social justice and Christian references: DW's Berlin bureau chief weighs in on Merz's speech
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's overriding message was one of justice, especially between generations.
That was for the home crowd, trying to explain the governing coalition's reform plans of the social systems. Interestingly he also sprinkled in some Christian references, something he seems to be doing more recently.
Most likely the German chancellor is trying to show more empathy and a more positive vision of the future.
His own conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party colleagues have increasingly been demanding this after losses in three state elections this fall.
Merz warns of growing injustice between generations
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned that Germany faces a growing gap in fairness between generations unless it undertakes major reforms of its social security systems.
"A justice gap has opened up between the generations in our country, and this gap will grow unless we act," Merz told the Bundestag.
He said children and young people risked being forced to shoulder a greater burden than could reasonably be justified under principles of fairness.
Merz acknowledged that successive governments had paid insufficient attention to the long-term consequences of their decisions, explicitly including governments led by his own center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
The chancellor said his government had developed a broad reform program covering pensions, care, the labor market, economic competitiveness and the modernization of the state.
He argued that justice should mean equal opportunities, fair rewards for achievement and fairness between generations, rather than redistribution at the expense of those contributing to the economy.
Merz said the reforms were necessary to preserve Germany's prosperity and ensure that younger generations were not left carrying an unfair share of the costs.
Merz accuses political extremes of seeking chaos
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has accused political forces on the far left and far right of deliberately dividing society, spreading disinformation and downplaying the threat posed by Russia.
Speaking in the Bundestag, Merz said he could not understand why politicians at both ends of the political spectrum continued to minimize Russian aggression.
"One gets the impression that you want chaos because you hope to gain political advantage from it," he told lawmakers.
Merz warned that extremism was increasingly making its presence felt in Germany's national and regional parliaments, as well as everyday life.
However, he acknowledged that extremist movements could draw support from legitimate dissatisfaction and feelings of injustice, arguing that constructive political action was the only effective response.
"Justice for us does not come through the exclusion of minorities," Merz said, calling for policies that promote equal opportunities and fairness between generations.
He contrasted what he described as the destructive politics of division and exclusion with the responsibility of democratic parties to address genuine grievances and govern for everyone in Germany.

Merz says Ukraine aid does not come at welfare's expense
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has rejected accusations from the far right and far left that support for Ukraine comes at the expense of social spending.
"Not a single euro is missing from social spending," he told parliament, speaking ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.
Merz said an exemption from Germany's constitutional borrowing limits allows spending on defense and assistance for Ukraine to be financed through additional credit.
He accused the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the socialist Left Party of seeking to divide Germany
AfD and BSW join forces against Ukraine support
In the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany Party (AfD) won recent elections in a landslide, a new alliance has flexed its muscle.
The AfD put forward a motion to halt arms deliveries to Ukraine and lift sanctions against Russia. Instead, they argue, peace talks with Russia should be initiated.
The Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), which holds five seats in the state parliament, again teamed up with the AfD to ensure a majority for the motion. The BSW combines left-leaning economics with right-wing populist positions on immigration and relations with Russia.
AfD and BSW also called for an immediate halt to financial support for Ukraine, to the extent that it goes beyond humanitarian aid.
The motion by the AfD and BSW has no more than symbolic value, as decisions regarding sanctions against Russia and aid to Ukraine are made not by the federal states, but by the federal government and the European Union.
But the new alliance of AfD and BSW has a wider significance. It is seen by observers as a sign of longer-term and closer cooperation between the two parties, which originate from very different ideological camps.
Although the AfD emerged as the clear winner of the state elections in September 2026, it lacks a majority to form a government. It has been searching for partners in the state legislature. So far, the BSW is the only party officially negotiating with the AfD on forming a government.
Merz to set out EU priorities after urging reforms
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is expected to outline Germany's priorities on Ukraine, European defense and economic competitiveness in a parliamentary address ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.
His government statement is scheduled for 14:05 local time (12:05 UTC), followed by a 90-minute debate. EU leaders meet on Thursday and Friday, with the Middle East, the bloc's next long-term budget and EU enlargement also on the agenda.
After the speech, the opposition Greens are set to put forward two motions calling for faster bloc enlargement and stronger measures to counter economic coercion and protect the bloc's market.
Merz's address follows a more domestic-focused speech on planned reforms at an employers' conference in Berlin on Tuesday. There, he said he would press ahead with changes to Germany's welfare system even at the expense of his own popularity, arguing that younger generations stood to benefit.
Energy prices push German inflation to 3.3%
Germany's annual inflation rate rose to 3.3% in September, its highest level since December 2023, as fuel and heating oil prices surged.
The Federal Statistical Office confirmed its preliminary estimate, up from 2.9% in August and 2.8% in July.
The increase was again driven by energy prices, said the office's president, Ruth Brand, highlighting higher costs at gas stations and for heating oil.
Energy prices rose 14.9% compared with September last year, their steepest annual increase since February 2023. That followed increases of 10.5% in August and 8.3% in July.
Motor fuel prices jumped 37.1%, while heating oil rose 74.9%. Firewood, wood pellets and other solid fuels became 15.6% more expensive.
However, electricity prices fell 5.5%, natural gas prices dropped 2.8% and district heating cost 1% less.
The office attributed those declines partly to government measures implemented since the start of the year.
Nord Stream sabotage trial met with demonstrations
The trial of a Ukrainian man accused of leading the operation that blew up the Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022 has begun in Hamburg.
The 50-year-old, Serhii Kuznietsov, faces charges including a war crime, causing explosions, destroying structures and disrupting public services.
DW correspondent Matthew Moore was there as court doors opened at 07:30 local time in Hamburg.
A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist." One participant from Germany told DW that they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."
Inside, a Ukrainian student also told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii Kuznietsov.
"Serhii Kuznietsov is a hero." In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, Kuznietsov faces a lengthy prison sentence.
Prosecutors allege that he planned the attack with other Ukrainian military personnel on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state bodies. They say the aim was to prevent Russia from using gas export revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.
Serhii Kuznietsov, who was arrested in Italy last year, denies involvement. Ukraine's government has also denied any role in the attack.

"The 34-year-old inmate with German citizenship and the two men suspected of freeing him are on the run. Police are searching for the men with numerous officers and has published a photo of the prisoner," Essen police wrote in a statement.
Police warned that it "could not be ruled out" that the suspects were armed, and asked anybody who thought they saw them not to approach or speak to them, but to call the emergency services immediately.
The operation also briefly involved a bomb scare that turned out to be a false alarm. Specialists deployed after a call from a concerned member of the public but it transpired the item was a wooden mock hand grenade.
Police did not immediately comment on whether the prisons officers accompanying the prisoner sustained injuries in the attack. 
Nord Stream trial draws supporters and media attention
There is huge interest in this court case. No sooner had the court doors opened at 07:30 local time in Hamburg than the first journalists, observers and protesters began arriving.
A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist." One participant from Germany told me they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."
Inside, a Ukrainian student told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii Kuznietsov.
"Serhii Kuznietsov is a hero," the student said. In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, Kuznietsov faces a lengthy prison sentence.
Nord Stream defendant's lawyers challenge war crime charge
Lawyers for the Ukrainian man accused of organizing the Nord Stream pipeline attack have challenged the evidence and the war crime charge as his trial opened in Hamburg.
Serhii Kuznietsov, a 50-year-old former Ukrainian special forces officer, is accused of planning and supervising the September 2022 sabotage. Prosecutors say the attack targeted civilian infrastructure using prohibited methods of warfare.
Defense lawyer Jes Meyer-Lohkamp said there were no fingerprints, DNA traces or witness statements placing his client aboard the Andromeda, the yacht allegedly used in the operation.
Prosecutors allege Serhii Kuznietsov boarded the vessel on the German island of Rügen with six accomplices: a skipper, an explosives expert and four divers. The group allegedly attached four explosive devices fitted with timers to the pipelines.
His lawyers argued that Russia used the pipelines as a weapon of economic pressure, making them a legitimate target. They also said Italy had approved his extradition on sabotage allegations, rather than a war crime charge, and sought dismissal of the case.
The defense sought to have the case dismissed, also arguing that military secrecy obligations prevented Serhii K. from discussing potentially exonerating evidence, even with his lawyers.
The explosions ruptured three of the system's four pipelines near Denmark's Bornholm island. Russia had already halted supplies through Nord Stream 1, while Nord Stream 2 had never entered service.
Wadephul warns against economic 'gifts' to Russia
German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has urged allies to maintain pressure on Russia following attacks on civilian ships off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast.
"Gifts embolden Putin to continue on his course. Only firmness creates a willingness to talk," he said after meeting his Bulgarian counterpart in Berlin. He did not explicitly mention US President Donald Trump's recent diesel supply deal with Russia.
Wadephul said Europe must end its dependence on Russian energy to sustain economic pressure on Moscow.
He also urged Russia to agree to a ceasefire covering grain shipments, warning that further attacks threatened people facing hunger, particularly in Africa.
Fat-fingered cockpit error likely triggered Nuremberg hijack alert
A pilot's apparent mistake when entering a transponder code triggered the hijack alert that led to a major police operation at Nuremberg airport, German police said.
Investigators believe the pilot intended to report a radio failure but accidentally entered 7500, the code signaling a hijacking.
The Boeing 737-800's radio was defective, leaving the crew unreachable after takeoff from the Greek island of Corfu, police said.
Police spokesperson Michael Petzold said the pilot apparently did not realize the mistake. The pilot is not under investigation because police believe he acted unintentionally.
Military aircraft accompanied the plane in Croatian airspace, and Austrian interceptors were alerted. Two German Eurofighters then escorted it to Nuremberg.
A police team trained to negotiate with hijackers and a Bavarian support unit were deployed at the airport during the alert.
Officers had less than an hour between the emergency signal and landing to prepare, Petzold said. Police later gave the all-clear.
Lufthansa wins bid for stake in Portugal's TAP
Germany's Lufthansa has won the contest to buy a 44.9% stake in TAP Air Portugal with an offer of €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion), Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro said.
Lufthansa beat rival Air France-KLM after months of efforts to privatize the state-rescued airline, Montenegro told journalists following a cabinet meeting.
Social justice and Christian references: DW's Berlin bureau chief weighs in on Merz's speech
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's overriding message was one of justice, especially between generations.
That was for the home crowd, trying to explain the governing coalition's reform plans of the social systems. Interestingly he also sprinkled in some Christian references, something he seems to be doing more recently.
Most likely the German chancellor is trying to show more empathy and a more positive vision of the future.
His own conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party colleagues have increasingly been demanding this after losses in three state elections this fall.
Merz warns of growing injustice between generations
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has warned that Germany faces a growing gap in fairness between generations unless it undertakes major reforms of its social security systems.
"A justice gap has opened up between the generations in our country, and this gap will grow unless we act," Merz told the Bundestag.
He said children and young people risked being forced to shoulder a greater burden than could reasonably be justified under principles of fairness.
Merz acknowledged that successive governments had paid insufficient attention to the long-term consequences of their decisions, explicitly including governments led by his own center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).
The chancellor said his government had developed a broad reform program covering pensions, care, the labor market, economic competitiveness and the modernization of the state.
He argued that justice should mean equal opportunities, fair rewards for achievement and fairness between generations, rather than redistribution at the expense of those contributing to the economy.
Merz said the reforms were necessary to preserve Germany's prosperity and ensure that younger generations were not left carrying an unfair share of the costs.
Merz accuses political extremes of seeking chaos
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has accused political forces on the far left and far right of deliberately dividing society, spreading disinformation and downplaying the threat posed by Russia.
Speaking in the Bundestag, Merz said he could not understand why politicians at both ends of the political spectrum continued to minimize Russian aggression.
"One gets the impression that you want chaos because you hope to gain political advantage from it," he told lawmakers.
Merz warned that extremism was increasingly making its presence felt in Germany's national and regional parliaments, as well as everyday life.
However, he acknowledged that extremist movements could draw support from legitimate dissatisfaction and feelings of injustice, arguing that constructive political action was the only effective response.
"Justice for us does not come through the exclusion of minorities," Merz said, calling for policies that promote equal opportunities and fairness between generations.
He contrasted what he described as the destructive politics of division and exclusion with the responsibility of democratic parties to address genuine grievances and govern for everyone in Germany.

Merz says Ukraine aid does not come at welfare's expense
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has rejected accusations from the far right and far left that support for Ukraine comes at the expense of social spending.
"Not a single euro is missing from social spending," he told parliament, speaking ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.
Merz said an exemption from Germany's constitutional borrowing limits allows spending on defense and assistance for Ukraine to be financed through additional credit.
He accused the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) and the socialist Left Party of seeking to divide Germany
AfD and BSW join forces against Ukraine support
In the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany Party (AfD) won recent elections in a landslide, a new alliance has flexed its muscle.
The AfD put forward a motion to halt arms deliveries to Ukraine and lift sanctions against Russia. Instead, they argue, peace talks with Russia should be initiated.
The Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), which holds five seats in the state parliament, again teamed up with the AfD to ensure a majority for the motion. The BSW combines left-leaning economics with right-wing populist positions on immigration and relations with Russia.
AfD and BSW also called for an immediate halt to financial support for Ukraine, to the extent that it goes beyond humanitarian aid.
The motion by the AfD and BSW has no more than symbolic value, as decisions regarding sanctions against Russia and aid to Ukraine are made not by the federal states, but by the federal government and the European Union.
But the new alliance of AfD and BSW has a wider significance. It is seen by observers as a sign of longer-term and closer cooperation between the two parties, which originate from very different ideological camps.
Although the AfD emerged as the clear winner of the state elections in September 2026, it lacks a majority to form a government. It has been searching for partners in the state legislature. So far, the BSW is the only party officially negotiating with the AfD on forming a government.
Merz to set out EU priorities after urging reforms
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is expected to outline Germany's priorities on Ukraine, European defense and economic competitiveness in a parliamentary address ahead of an EU summit in Brussels.
His government statement is scheduled for 14:05 local time (12:05 UTC), followed by a 90-minute debate. EU leaders meet on Thursday and Friday, with the Middle East, the bloc's next long-term budget and EU enlargement also on the agenda.
After the speech, the opposition Greens are set to put forward two motions calling for faster bloc enlargement and stronger measures to counter economic coercion and protect the bloc's market.
Merz's address follows a more domestic-focused speech on planned reforms at an employers' conference in Berlin on Tuesday. There, he said he would press ahead with changes to Germany's welfare system even at the expense of his own popularity, arguing that younger generations stood to benefit.
Energy prices push German inflation to 3.3%
Germany's annual inflation rate rose to 3.3% in September, its highest level since December 2023, as fuel and heating oil prices surged.
The Federal Statistical Office confirmed its preliminary estimate, up from 2.9% in August and 2.8% in July.
The increase was again driven by energy prices, said the office's president, Ruth Brand, highlighting higher costs at gas stations and for heating oil.
Energy prices rose 14.9% compared with September last year, their steepest annual increase since February 2023. That followed increases of 10.5% in August and 8.3% in July.
Motor fuel prices jumped 37.1%, while heating oil rose 74.9%. Firewood, wood pellets and other solid fuels became 15.6% more expensive.
However, electricity prices fell 5.5%, natural gas prices dropped 2.8% and district heating cost 1% less.
The office attributed those declines partly to government measures implemented since the start of the year.

The trial of a Ukrainian man accused of leading the operation that blew up the Nord Stream gas pipelines in 2022 has begun in Hamburg.
The 50-year-old, Serhii Kuznietsov, faces charges including a war crime, causing explosions, destroying structures and disrupting public services.

A small pro-Ukraine protest held up a banner saying, "Russia is a terrorist." One participant from Germany told DW that they wanted to remind the world of "the war crimes taking place against the Ukrainian people."
Inside, a Ukrainian student also told DW that he and others had made the journey from Kyiv to show support for the defendant, Serhii Kuznietsov.
"Serhii Kuznietsov is a hero." In the eyes of the German prosecutors, it is another matter. They accuse him of carrying out a war crime. If found guilty of his part in the gas pipeline bombing, Kuznietsov faces a lengthy prison sentence.
Prosecutors allege that he planned the attack with other Ukrainian military personnel on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state bodies. They say the aim was to prevent Russia from using gas export revenues to finance its war against Ukraine.
Serhii Kuznietsov, who was arrested in Italy last year, denies involvement. Ukraine's government has also denied any role in the attack.

Russians have struck Kyiv's two combined heat and power plants almost 50 times this year, mayor says
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
