Russians have struck Kyiv's two combined heat and power plants almost 50 times this year, mayor says
Russian forces struck Kyiv's two combined heat and power plants, CHPP-5 and CHPP-6, with 12 missiles and drones in 2022, seven in 2023, none in 2024, 19 in 2025 and almost 50 so far this year.
Source: Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko during an address to the Verkhovna Rada (Ukrainian parliament)
Details: "Throughout this time, experts have been working, repairing equipment and preparing the facilities for winter every year. And Kyiv has stood firm," Klitschko noted.
He said the city authorities are doing everything in their power to keep the capital running, despite "the spiteful slaps that the central government constantly tries to deliver".
"Kyiv is functioning under difficult wartime conditions, under constant devastating attacks by the enemy. These attacks target infrastructure, the energy sector, industry, businesses and every resident of the capital," the mayor stressed.
He noted that preparations this year have taken place under Russian attacks and amid "the show the authorities put on around the Resilience Plan".
Klitschko said Kyiv has prepared almost 700 generators of various capacities for heat and water supply facilities, as well as 70 mobile boiler houses. Three diesel power stations have been built, along with a backup water intake facility.
Kyivvodokanal, the capital's water utility, currently has 103 generators. The utility is also expecting high-capacity generator systems for water supply that are being manufactured for Kyiv abroad.
More than 6,000 pieces of equipment, including generators, inverters and batteries, have been purchased for residential buildings under municipal energy resilience programmes.
According to Klitschko, all educational institutions have generators of various capacities, including 285 high-capacity units. The capital's hospitals are equipped with backup power sources and currently have 480 generators.
He also noted that 15 hospitals have their own wells, with another six under construction. Eleven medical facilities have autonomous heating supplied by their own boiler houses. By the end of the year, 21 hospitals are expected to have such heating, Klitschko said.
Quote: "Kyiv is working, rebuilding and repairing, and keeping the city running. This is happening amid staff shortages at municipal utilities and suspended payments, while the enemy is tearing the city apart every day and every night."
Background:
- Russian forces carried out a combined attack on Ukraine. Several air-raid warnings were issued in the city of Kyiv and some oblasts on the night of 13-14 October. The capital is experiencing power cuts.
- Following problems caused by Russian attacks, water pressure has been reduced in Kyiv's Shevchenkivskyi, Solomianskyi and Pecherskyi districts.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that the city of Kyiv is the least-prepared region in Ukraine according to the country's resilience plans. He has therefore begun consultations on "security and management steps".
- On 9 October, Zelenskyy accused Kyiv's city authorities of failing to take the necessary steps to implement the resilience plans.
- Since the beginning of autumn, Russian attacks have repeatedly brought the capital's transport infrastructure to a virtual standstill. In particular, the Kyiv metro stopped operating on 8 October due to a drop in voltage.
- Klitschko has stressed that amid intensified Russian attacks, the situation in Kyiv is now a matter of survival. Residents who have friends or relatives outside Kyiv have been advised to consider temporarily moving out of the capital.
- On 13 October, members of the Ukrainian parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, summoned Klitschko to the session of parliament on 14 October.

Michal at Meeting with Rutte: Estonia to Support Ukraine with €10 Million Through NATO’s PURL Initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:29:20 UTC
21:29:20 KST

The meeting with the NATO Secretary General focused on the future of the Alliance, increased defence spending, the development of defence capabilities, deterring Russia, and supporting Ukraine.
“Our security environment has become more unpredictable, and the rules-based world order is under serious pressure. But the most important thing has not changed: NATO works. NATO has the capabilities, plans and will to defend every Ally and the entire NATO territory,” Michal said.
According to Michal, all Allies should meet the commitment to spend 5% of GDP on defence as soon as possible, so that the necessary defence capabilities can be developed rapidly using these resources. This is a challenging task, but a fairer sharing of the burden within NATO is a necessary effort, and Estonia is setting a good example in this regard.
“Over the next ten years, we will invest €26 billion in national defence. Half of that amount will go directly towards armaments and military capabilities. Estonia’s defence industry turnover has grown by an average of 44% annually over the past three years. Last week, the Estonian government decided to establish a new defence industry park, which will enable the production of military explosives and additional ammunition,” Michal said.
Strengthening NATO’s deterrence and defence capabilities sends a clear message to Russia: the Alliance takes threats seriously and is committed to ensuring its security and defence. According to Michal, Russia’s increasingly risky behaviour and its growing number of hybrid attacks are intended to divert attention from supporting Ukraine. We will respond to Russia’s actions collectively and continue providing robust assistance to Ukraine.
“This year, our military assistance to Ukraine amounts to 0.28% of GDP. Last year, it was 0.35%. We have also supported Ukraine through NATO’s PURL initiative with €21 million, and we will soon contribute a further €10 million to this mechanism,” Michal said. He expressed hope that all other Allies would also find opportunities to increase their contributions.
Michal stressed that Ukraine’s experience is invaluable for developing the defence capabilities and defence industries of NATO Allies as well. NATO membership would provide Ukraine with the strongest long-term security guarantee, benefiting everyone.
During the visit, the NATO Secretary General also met with Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna and delivered a public lecture at Tallinn University of Technology. He will also meet with President of the Republic Ülle Madise. In the evening, he will visit Ämari Air Base, where he will be welcomed by Defence Minister Martin Herem and Commander of the Estonian Defence Forces, Lieutenant General Andrus Merilo.

Guinea-Bissau denies it has approved controversial vaccine trial in newborns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:21:16 UTC
21:21:16 KST

Guinea-Bissau has not approved the controversial hepatitis B study in newborns that would be funded by the US government and private partners, the African country’s minister of health said on Tuesday.
The study, which would not investigate the safety or effectiveness of vaccines but would instead track “nonspecific” health outcomes like overall mortality or neurodevelopmental conditions, has been championed by Robert F Kennedy Jr, secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime anti-vaccine activist.
Members of a Danish research ethics committee were informed that officials in Guinea-Bissau had approved an updated design of the study, which influenced some committee members’ votes to proceed with the trial last week.
But the health ministry never agreed to or authorized the trial, said Quinhin Nantote in Portuguese at a press briefing, where he referred to the study as “tests”.
“The ministry did not authorize the tests under the terms presented in the publications currently in circulation,” the health minister said. He said officials in Guinea-Bissau were “surprised” to see media reports that the country had given approval to the study.
“Any scientific research initiative involving human beings, particularly children, must strictly comply with applicable national legislation, international ethical principles, competent evaluation and approval mechanisms,” Nantote said.
He spoke after convening an emergency meeting in Guinea-Bissau with the Bandim Health Project, the local ethics committee, the National Institute of Public Health (Inasa) and the Expanded Vaccination Program (PAV).
The Bandim Health Project is run by the Danish researchers Peter Aaby and Christine Stabell Benn, whose decades of research have been called into question in the past year.
The claims made in nearly all of their papers are “highly misleading”, said Charlotte Strøm, a Danish researcher who has co-authored research showing that Aaby, Stabell Benn, and their co-authors had no significant findings in 24 out of 25 studies and that they’ve chosen not to publish research that may not support their viewpoints.
“When researchers operate like this and abandon proper methodological rigor, they literally decide on the results themselves, and that is not science,” Strøm said, calling it “problematic, questionable [and] unethical”.
She added: “I believe there is serious cause for concern.”
Kennedy has repeatedly praised their work, which he says shows that after vaccination, “you can have mass injuries, and catastrophic injuries, and they’re hiding in plain sight”.
Aaby, Stabell Benn and Frederik Schaltz-Buchholzer did not respond by press time to the Guardian’s questions about why the Danish ethics committee members were told the trial had been approved by local authorities and why it could not be held in Denmark.
In Denmark, infants born to hepatitis B-negative parents do not receive the shot, there is widespread testing for and low incidence of the virus, and the robust healthcare system can track health outcomes and provide timely and comprehensive medical care – making it an ideal location for such a study.
“It’s completely unethical that this trial is even proposed,” because a safe and effective vaccine has been available for decades, said BK Titanji, a researcher at Emory University.
It’s “reassuring” to see Guinea-Bissau pushing back on the trial, Titanji said, adding: “A study like this one needs the highest level of ethical scrutiny. You are going to be conducting a study on the most vulnerable population, which is newborn babies, in a country that is resource-constrained.”
When Titanji recently applied for approval of a collaborative study in Cameroon, she had to include extensive documentation in her application – and it was a survey, not medical research on human subjects, she said. “I can’t come to Emory’s [institutional review board] and just be like: ‘I got permission from Cameroon.’ I have to provide the document.”
The researchers should release these documents and an updated protocol showing how the study would be conducted, she said.
Experts have decried the African experiment as “horribly unethical and cruel”, “neocolonialist” and “damaging”.
“For the government of Guinea-Bissau to stand up against the United States and Denmark exploiting its children is no small statement,” said Colette Delawalla, a researcher and founder and CEO of the non-profit Stand Up for Science. “We absolutely must respect their sovereignty as a nation.”
It would cost approximately $13,200 to buy enough vaccines through Unicef and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance, to immunize all newborns in Guinea-Bissau each year, Delawalla pointed out.
Everyone involved should work together to ensure that every baby in Guinea-Bissau receives the birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccination, she added. “This is not muddy water: we can use Black babies to further pseudoscience or we can save children’s lives with a 20-cent shot.”
It is unclear whether the US plans to move forward with the study, even after reporting indicated that the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has again set aside $1.6m for funding for the trial this year, to be matched by private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation and the Bluebell Foundation.
“The study has not been approved,” the HHS told Reuters in a statement. The agency has not responded to the Guardian’s questions about the trial.
At least four members of the Danish committee resigned after approval for the trial was fast-tracked. The rules of the committee had to be changed because randomized controlled trials were outside of its purview. When committee members requested more information about the Guinea-Bissau approval, no further details were provided.
The study would enroll 14,000 newborns in Guinea-Bissau, half of whom would be vaccinated at birth and half of whom would be denied the immunization for the first six weeks of life. Hepatitis B is widespread in the country, and infection in children can have serious lifelong effects.
Guinea-Bissau, which currently has a transitional military government following a coup in November, requested in January a team of experts from the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) to help evaluate the study. In the meantime, Nantote said at the time, it was “canceled or suspended”.
Other officials in Guinea-Bissau also pushed back on the research. “It’s not going to happen, period,” the foreign minister, João Bernardo Vieira, said in February.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has offered support in rolling out the hepatitis B vaccine at birth to all newborns in Guinea-Bissau. “WHO stands ready to support Guinea‑Bissau as it considers its way forward and in accelerating the introduction of the birth dose and strengthening implementation,” the organization said in a February statement pushing back on the trial.

Tunisian journalists fear jail again as freedoms erode
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:20:49 UTC
21:20:49 KST

Tunisian journalists fear jail again as freedoms erode
TUNIS, Oct 14 - Journalists in Tunisia who enjoyed a burst of press freedom after the 2011 Arab Spring are once again looking over their shoulders in the knowledge their work may land them in prison.
The 2011 overthrow of autocrat Zine El-Abidine Ben Ali unshackled Tunisia's media, but a decade later President Kais Saied's seizure of sweeping powers began eroding those gains.
Now, independent media face a full-on crackdown, rights groups say, and Tunisia has tumbled more than 50 places in the past five years to 137th in Reporters Without Borders' press freedom index.
"We are living in a grey area, as if we were in a shifting minefield, and we pay the price every day," said Aymen Rezgui, editor-in-chief of independent outlet Nawaat, reflecting on how at least limits were clear pre-2011 versus current uncertainty.
Around him, in a small garden in Tunis, about half a dozen colleagues sit smoking, trading jokes and discussing investigations they plan to publish on subjects ranging from the quality of drinking water to conditions of prisons.
They know that any of the stories could lead to prosecution.
Some 20 journalists face criminal charges over their reporting or social media posts, with four already imprisoned, according to Zied Dabbar, head of the National Syndicate of Tunisian Journalists, who called the situation unprecedented.
Saied has said he is not a dictator and that journalists are free to criticize authorities and frequently do.
Authorities say prosecutions are impartial judicial matters and that no one is above the law.
The Tunisian prime minister's press office did not respond to requests for comment.
Rezgui said Nawaat regularly receives threats — anonymously or from government supporters on social media branding him a traitor — over reporting on issues ranging from prisons to power cuts and water shortages.
The outlet has also faced judicial restrictions, including a government order suspending activities for a month last year.
Many other journalists report similar pressures.
Last month, Mohamed Yousfi, editor-in-chief of independent news website Al-Qatiba, was arrested on his way to a private radio station for a live programme. A judge has charged him with illicit enrichment, which he says is a fabrication.
Other jailed journalists and media figures include prominent broadcasters Mourad Zeghidi and Borhen Bsaies, who were first convicted of spreading false news and insulting the president, and later of tax evasion. They deny the charges and say they have been framed.
SOME CHOOSE EXILE
For some, leaving Tunisia has become the only option to avoid a similar fate, despite the personal cost.
In December 2025, Khaoula Boukrim, founder of independent website Tumedia and a prominent critic of the president, left for France fearing imminent arrest.
Months later, she was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison over writings critical of the judiciary and a system of governance she described as authoritarian.
Journalist Haythem Mekki has also left Tunisia after receiving a prison sentence following public comments he made denouncing conditions in a hospital morgue.
Saied’s supporters say such cases have nothing to do with freedom of expression.
Press freedom groups argue, however, that prosecutions are increasingly being used to intimidate and silence critical voices.
Beyond prosecutions, journalists are frequently prevented by police from working in public and are sometimes detained for hours, the journalists' syndicate says.
Most ministries no longer have press offices, while several international correspondents have been denied accreditation, further restricting independent coverage.
Political and critical programmes have disappeared from many private radio stations. State media has increasingly marginalised dissenting voices, the syndicate says, though the TAP state news agency remains a rare exception, continuing to cover protests, opposition activities and civil society initiatives.
The pressure reverberates beyond newsrooms.
A photograph of Zied Heni, a radio journalist sentenced earlier this year to a year in prison after criticising a judicial ruling, hangs in the living room of his Tunis home.
His wife, Thouraya Zouari, said she and their three daughters have struggled to cope with his detention.
"We cannot accept that Zied is in prison," she said. "We are living through a nightmare."
But she said that the family was determined to carry on the struggle for freedom of expression in his absence.
"He has instilled in his daughters the resolve not to remain silent in the face of injustice and oppression," she said of the daughters who still criticise Saied on social media and take part in street protests. REUTERS

Russia Could Test NATO Regardless of How War in Ukraine Ends, Estonian Defense Minister Says
Russia is likely to test the security of a NATO member state regardless of how its war against Ukraine ends, Estonian Defense Minister Martin Herem warned, suggesting that Moscow could seek to undermine the Alliance by exploiting divisions between its members.
In an interview with European Pravda published on October 13, Herem said Russia would begin strengthening its military capabilities as soon as the war in Ukraine came to an end, potentially creating conditions for further aggression against European countries.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Estonian defense minister, the threat would persist regardless of whether Ukraine successfully liberated its occupied territories or the conflict ended with a freeze in hostilities.
“If I take into account the attitude of the Russian state [towards its neighbours], and if I look at what they are producing right now for military purposes, then I think when they stop here [in Ukraine]—it doesn't matter how, whether you kick them out beyond the border, or the war is frozen. And given their attitude, they will definitely test somebody,” Herem said.
While acknowledging the possibility of Russian aggression against Estonia, Herem emphasized that Moscow could choose another country, including neighboring Latvia, as its next target.
He argued that Russia's primary objective would not necessarily be territorial occupation but rather the expansion of its political influence through actions designed to weaken trust within targeted countries and among NATO allies.
“Whether their first attack will be against Estonia, I'm not sure. It could be Latvia or somewhere else. What they want to achieve is influence. They need power… They need to harm us and make us distrust each other, both in Estonia and among the Allies.,” he explained.
Herem suggested that Russia could deliberately provoke a confrontation with NATO to undermine the Alliance's unity, potentially conducting operations either below the threshold for invoking Article 5 or through actions that trigger the collective defense provision.
He also warned that Russia could exploit divisions within NATO even if the Alliance successfully defended itself under Article 5. He argued that a costly military victory could trigger criticism among member states over their failure to prevent the conflict, allowing Moscow to propose a return to normal relations and gradually expand its influence over the Alliance.
Asked whether future Russian attacks could be prevented, Herem expressed skepticism about the effectiveness of deterrence alone, arguing that NATO countries must prioritize military preparedness.
“I'm not sure if we can deter the mad person. But what we have to do is to prepare. And that's the only thing. We have to prepare very seriously [for an attack] and if we do that, we may prevent it. We have to be ready,” the minister stated.
Herem's warning comes as NATO continues developing its military strategy to counter a potential Russian attack, drawing on lessons from Ukraine's experience defending against Moscow's invasion.
According to The Wall Street Journal on October 12, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, General Alexus Grynkewich, presented a new defense strategy known as the “Theory of Victory” during the Warsaw Security Forum. Its classified version had been finalized three months earlier.
The strategy focuses on stopping an initial Russian offensive, preventing further advances, and systematically weakening attacking forces. Drawing on Ukraine's battlefield experience, it also emphasizes what Grynkewich called “affordable mass,” prioritizing relatively inexpensive drones to complement NATO's advanced weapons systems and strengthen the Alliance's defensive capabilities.

Russia Scrambles to Hide Its Strategic Bombers From Ukrainian Drones, Builds 16 Giant Shelters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:19:10 UTC
21:19:10 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Scrambles to Hide Its Strategic Bombers From Ukrainian Drones, Builds 16 Giant Shelters
Russia is building 16 massive aircraft shelters at its Engels-2 air base in the Saratov region in an apparent effort to conceal and protect its strategic bombers from Ukrainian drone strikes. The construction follows repeated Ukrainian attacks on the facility, which houses Tu-160 and Tu-95MS bombers used to launch cruise missiles against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Defence Blog on October 13, satellite imagery published by open-source intelligence group AviVector shows that Russia has nearly completed the steel frameworks for the first three shelters.
Images captured by Airbus Defence and Space on October 12 reveal three large structures standing on newly constructed concrete platforms, each connected to the airfield by paved taxiways.
Construction began in early September, when AviVector first identified preparations for the 16-shelter project.
Each shelter measures approximately 63 by 63 meters (207 by 207 feet), with walls reaching 7 meters (23 feet) and a maximum height of around 17 meters (56 feet).
The structures are large enough to accommodate Russia’s Tu-160 supersonic strategic bombers, which measure approximately 54 meters in length, as well as the smaller Tu-95MS aircraft.
Satellite imagery also shows earth barriers behind the shelters, apparently designed to redirect engine exhaust. Their positioning suggests that Russian bombers could start their engines inside the structures before taxiing directly onto the airfield.
The project could significantly change how Russia conceals its strategic aviation assets at Engels-2, where bombers have traditionally remained exposed on open parking areas.
The new shelters would make it more difficult for satellite surveillance to determine which aircraft are stationed at the base while potentially offering protection against Ukrainian drone strikes and debris.
However, the structures currently consist only of steel frameworks, and their ability to withstand attacks will depend on the materials used for their walls and roofs.
Engels-2, located approximately 600 kilometers (370 miles) from the Ukrainian front line, is one of Russia’s primary strategic aviation bases and has repeatedly been targeted by Ukrainian long-range drones since December 2022.
In July 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) had destroyed a Tu-95 strategic bomber at Engels. Satellite imagery released afterward appeared to confirm the aircraft’s destruction.
Another Tu-95 was damaged during an August 28 drone strike conducted by the SBU’s Alpha unit.
The Tu-95 is no longer in production, meaning Russia cannot replace destroyed aircraft with newly manufactured bombers of the same type.

World’s oldest shipwreck off Turkey: 4,700-year-old amphorae discovered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:18:12 UTC
21:18:12 KST

The shipwreck found near Antalya’s Kekova Island, dated to roughly 4,400–4,700 years ago, sheds light on maritime trade in the eastern Mediterranean.
Underwater excavations carried out off the island of Kekova in Antalya have brought to light amphorae dating back around 4,400–4,700 years. The finds, which are said to belong to a wreck from the Early Bronze Age, are expected to shed light on Anatolia's maritime history and trade links in the Eastern Mediterranean.
Turkey's Minister of Culture and Tourism Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, in a post on his social media account, underlined the importance of the ancient vases recovered during the excavations, saying: "In our 'Blue Homeland', we are bringing to light traces of the world's oldest shipwreck."
Clay analyses carried out on the amphorae, which are thought to have been used to transport olive oil or wine, indicate that the jars were probably produced in workshops in the Jordan Valley. The discovery of similar examples in Egypt, Troy and Crete reveals traces of trade and cultural interaction between different regions.
Ersoy stated that they would continue to illuminate Anatolia's maritime history with new findings and to preserve the underwater cultural heritage for future generations. The minister also congratulated Associate Professor Hakan Öniz, who's leading the scientific excavations, and the team involved in the work.
How was the wreck off Kekova found?
Amphora samples taken from the remains of a wreck identified off the island of Kekova during underwater surveys carried out in previous years by Akdeniz University showed that the ship may date back to the Early Bronze Age.
Acting on permits from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, excavations in the area began in 2026 under the leadership of the Antalya Museum Directorate.
The fact that similar vessels have been found near the pyramids of Giza, Saqqara and Abusir in Egypt, as well as in Troy and Crete, suggests that the cargo carried by the wreck may have been linked to an extensive trade network. Researchers believe that the ship set sail from a port on the Levantine coast and headed towards Troy or Crete.
An amphora marked with nine signs sheds light on sailors' lives
One of the amphorae found in the excavations stands out with two holes in its body and nine distinct marks on it. Initial examinations suggest that the jar may have been a churning amphora used in the production of cheese or butter.
This possibility raises the prospect that sailors of the period may have carried goats on long voyages, milked them on board and produced their own dairy products. The finds therefore contribute not only to research into the transport of commercial goods, but also to studies on the everyday conditions of sea journeys and eating habits.

AI generated
PARIS – French President Emmanuel Macron believes students waging three weeks of protests that have closed many schools have “legitimate” grievances but are also being “exploited” by political forces, a government spokeswoman said on Oct 14.
The leader, who is in his final six months of office, has asked the government to come up with “concrete responses” within weeks to the unrest by high school pupils, spokeswoman Maud Bregeon told reporters.
She spoke after Macron held his weekly meeting with his Cabinet, a day after nationwide solidarity demonstrations showed significant support for the students.
The interior ministry said 161,500 people turned out for demonstrations on Oct 13 held in Paris and other cities. Unions organising the rallies put the figure at 480,000.
Some violent scenes erupted on the sidelines of marches in Paris and Lyon, with police firing tear gas in response.
In his Cabinet meeting, Macron “stressed that young people have legitimate concerns, but said these are being exploited for political purposes and turned into urban violence”, Bregeon said.
With French presidential elections due in April and May 2027, some opposition parties have seized upon the demonstrations.
Jean-Luc Melenchon, the presidential candidate for the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) party, participated in one of the Paris demonstrations.
The far-right National Rally (RN) party of Marine Le Pen, whom surveys give as the frontrunner for the elections, has voiced support for police deployed to the protests and blamed students for violent episodes.
Alleged police brutality
Students, unions, rights groups and parents have accused the police of brutality against the students, with some of the young protesters maimed.
The family of one 15-year-old high school student who lost his hand when a police stun grenade exploded said on Oct 14 they had started legal action to demand an “impartial” investigation.
One of the family’s lawyers, Bertrand Wattez, said the boy, Evan, denied the police account, relayed by prosecutors, that he had tried to pick up the grenade when it went off on Oct 5. He also denied participating in the student protests in his city of Lens.
The lawyer said that Evan not only lost his left hand as a result of the blast but also several fingers on his right hand.
In another violent incident, a 16-year-old student was blinded during a Sept 30 protest outside his school in Tours. His family blamed the police.
Late on Oct 13, the prosecutor for Tours said the officer involved had been charged with aggravated battery.
Police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of officer violence against demonstrators, according to the interior ministry.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said nearly 900 police officers had also suffered injuries during the protests. AFP

THE HAGUE, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Dutch semiconductor equipment maker ASML said Wednesday it is exploring ways to expand production capacity beyond the previously announced 30 percent increase planned for 2028, as growing investment in artificial intelligence (AI) drives stronger demand for its equipment.
ASML President and Chief Executive Officer Christophe Fouquet said in a statement that customers continue to raise their short- and medium-term equipment demand forecasts, driven primarily by their expectations for the scale and duration of AI-related investment. Given the improved visibility into future demand, some customers are expressing interest in placing orders for 2029 and even 2030.
"With such strong visibility and an order book momentum that continues to increase quarter on quarter this year, we now expect that our supply as currently planned for both 2027 and 2028 will not fully meet the demand of our customers," Fouquet said.
"So we have to do more and we are looking basically at ways, especially in 2028 and beyond, to further extend our capacity," he added.
ASML reported total net sales of 11.7 billion euros (13.09 billion U.S. dollars) in the third quarter of 2026, up 25 percent from the previous quarter. Net income reached nearly 5 billion euros (5.6 billion dollars) in the third quarter.
The company expected full-year 2026 net sales of between 44 billion (49.24 billion dollars) and 45 billion euros (50.36 billion dollars), with a gross margin of around 56 percent, Fouquet announced.

Feature: Impaired but unbroken, China's disabled build a living
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
20:08:37 CST
21:08:37 KST

Liang Kaiyu improves his artificial leg at his studio in Liangshan County, Jining City of east China's Shandong Province, July 7, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Liyuan)
JINAN, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- After losing most of his left leg in an accident, Liang Kaiyu spent so much time perfecting his prosthetic that it eventually became his livelihood.
The prosthetic he first ordered frequently buckled mid-stride and needed constant charging. So Liang set to work, modifying it until it fit him like a glove.
Since then, he has made or refitted more than a dozen artificial legs. One has a mountain bike shock absorber at the ankle. Another has a thruster for swimming. Some of them have electronic knees and ankles he programmed himself.
Going by "Steel Leg" online, Liang posts videos of his work, repairs prosthetics for other amputees and makes a living from it. "Every day there's something I want to do," he said. "I tinker with a part, solve a problem, and when it works I'm happy."
Liang is among more than 2 million registered residents with disabilities in east China's Shandong Province. Late last year, the province announced a three-year plan running through 2027, with targets for job training, self-employment and supported work. At least 45,000 disabled people will receive vocational training.
The plan encourages local governments to reserve space for disabled entrepreneurs in government-funded business incubators and startup parks. Eligible entrepreneurs can apply for guaranteed startup loans of up to 300,000 yuan (44,828 U.S. dollars).
The province is also promoting a "community micro-business" model that requires government-run convenience service outlets to set aside at least 10 percent of their stalls for disabled workers.
WHERE THERE IS A NEED, THERE IS A WAY
Like Liang, people with reduced mobility sometimes become entrepreneurs, driven by needs that aren't otherwise met.
Gong Yuben runs an online shoe store in the port city of Yantai that sells shoes one at a time, not in pairs. He lost his right leg in a traffic accident in 2012, when he was a teenager. Because shoes are sold only in pairs, he accumulated too many new but useless right shoes over the years.
This year, he began working with suppliers to split pairs and sell them individually. His store soon drew a small group of clients who also recommended it to friends with similar needs. Sales are modest, but they answer a real need. "To someone who actually needs it, one shoe is a complete pair," Gong said.
Zou Jiahao's entrepreneurship was driven by a different need: a good cup of coffee from his wheelchair. His wheelchair-accessible cafe in his home city of Qingdao has a ramp at the entrance, a wide doorway for wheelchairs, and a lower counter set at the ideal height for customers on wheels and for him on the other side.
Zou said the initial investment for the 60-sqm shop was about 100,000 yuan, spent mostly on coffee machines and furniture. The local federation for people with disabilities helped negotiate favorable rental fees.
"Equal employment means having the chance to learn a skill, use it, and earn the life you want," Zou said, adding that he is betting on customers, with disabilities or not, to keep coming back for his coffee and service.
China has an estimated 86 million people with disabilities as of 2023, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. In 2025, more than 8.9 million were employed, the China Disabled Persons' Federation (CDPF) reported earlier this year.
China's plan for the protection and development of people with disabilities during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) outlines a wide range of priorities and initiatives to enhance social protection, life-cycle care and rights protection for disabled citizens.
A major target is to create a million new jobs for people with disabilities in urban and rural areas, said Cheng Kai, chairman of the CDPF.
BUILDING ON WHAT THEY CAN DO
Guangming Experience Hall, a darkness exhibition in Jinan, Shandong's provincial capital, hires visually impaired people exclusively as guides, turning their navigation skills into a new profession. Though "Guangming" means "light," the museum invites visitors to make their way around in the dark, simulating experiences like a bus ride or a shopping trip -- relying only on touch, sound, and smell.
When it opened in early 2024, only six of the about 60 visually impaired applicants were hired. They became familiar with every corner of the hall and learned to "read" visitors' moods from their voices.
Chang Wanxiu, 29, said the job has boosted her confidence and made her feel like everyone else. "With this job, I need to leave home, take the bus, and talk to different people," she said. "At first I was nervous. But after walking through it again and again, I found my footing."
A government-backed program also trains visually impaired therapists for community health centers and helps them open private clinics. "People with disabilities have their own strengths and potential," said Tang Jianquan, head of the Shandong provincial association for the visually impaired. "Once put in the right place, they can prove to be valuable workers for their enterprises as well as for their personal fulfillment."
Despite being hearing impaired, Xiao Wei (not his real name) is as well-prepared as any seasoned food deliveryman. When a customer calls, his smartwatch buzzes, an AI assistant answers and converts the conversation to text, and he quickly replies with one of dozens of pre-edited messages stored on his phone.
The delivery service center trained him and paired him with veteran riders. "I don't feel like a disabled person on the job," he typed in response to Xinhua. "I can feel my own sense of value."
A Starbucks outlet in Qingdao's Shibei district began recruiting and training hearing-impaired workers in 2021 with the municipal disabled persons' federation. Training usually takes a month, but at least twice as long for a hearing-impaired employee, said store manager Lyu Yan. "It's important to slow down the training but keep the same standard, so that all our employees are treated as equals."
To help them, the store installed screens that convert speech to text in real time and lower counters that make it easier to read customers' lips.
Lu Lin, chairman of the China Association of Persons with Physical Disability, said helping people with disabilities find work is a complicated project and one needs to get every step right, from their leaving home to settling into a job.
These often involve infrastructure such as accessible roads and transport, as well as fair wages, social insurance, adequate labor protections and personal development opportunities. "We want more job opportunities for them and every support they need, so that they can live with independence and dignity." ■
Zou Jiahao brews coffee for customers at his wheelchair-accessible cafe in Qingdao, east China's Shandong Province, July 21, 2026. (Xinhua/Zhang Liyuan)

Russia Announces Visas for Citizens of Montenegro in Reciprocal Move
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:08:32 UTC
21:08:32 KST

Russia will introduce visa requirements for citizens of Montenegro in retaliation to Podgorica’s decision to end its bilateral visa-free travel agreement with Moscow as it seeks to join the EU in 2028.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova confirmed that Montenegro’s foreign ministry notified Moscow of its intent to cancel the 2008 mutual travel agreement on Sept. 28.
“In practice, this means that starting Nov. 1, our citizens will only be able to enter and remain in Montenegro with visas. Accordingly, citizens of Montenegro will also have to obtain visas for trips to Russia,” Zakharova said.
Montenegro announced in July that it would end visa-free access for citizens of Russia, Belarus, China, Saudi Arabia and Turkey to align with EU standards.
Zakharova argued the decision would curb Russian tourism, harm local businesses and degrade Montenegro’s investment climate.
Montenegro has for years remained one of the few European countries to offer visa-free entry to Russians for up to 30 days and absorbed a large wave of anti-war Russian emigres after the invasion of Ukraine.
Local media reported earlier this year that two-thirds of registered Russian residents had left Montenegro in anticipation of the new visa rules.
“It’s pointless for Montenegro to expect Brussels to compensate them for their inevitable losses,” Zakharova said.
She warned that EU accession would require prospective members among the Balkan nations to adopt a “confrontational anti-Russian course” that would go against their national interests.
The subject of tightening border controls recently drew the attention of the founder of the popular pro-war Telegram channel Rybar, who was detained and deported from Montenegro on claims that he was seeking to film a documentary portraying EU integration as an externally imposed process.
Russian-Montenegrin relations have been strained since 2016, when Podgorica accused Russia of plotting a failed coup with Serbian ultranationalists. The Kremlin denied that claim.
Ties worsened further after Montenegro joined NATO in 2017 and aligned with EU sanctions over Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Montenegro has also banned Russian state media and expelled Russian diplomats for espionage, prompting Moscow to add the country to its list of “unfriendly” states.
Reuters contributed reporting.

Ukraine-NATO AI built to forecast Russia’s front-line drone attacks from past data and weather is ready to plug into the army
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:07:38 UTC
21:07:38 KST

Ukraine and NATO have unveiled two artificial intelligence (AI) tools in Vilnius, Lithuania, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported on 13 October. One forecasts Russian drone attacks near the front and is ready to join the Armed Forces’ situational awareness systems. The other helps plan artillery fire and is still in testing.
A forecast of where, when, and which drones will fly targets the main source of losses near the front. In March, Ukraine’s military put the share of front-line casualties caused by FPV drones at up to 80%. In May, Ukraine’s drone forces commander Robert Brovdi said Russia was copying Ukraine’s model to grow its drone forces. A month earlier, Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov wrote that adding more drones no longer fundamentally changes the battlefield. The next stage, he said, is full integration of AI.
Forecasting Russian drone attacks
The NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Center (JATEC) presented both at a three-day seminar in the Lithuanian capital. NATO’s Allied Command Transformation and Ukraine’s Armed Forces built the tools with JATEC’s support.
“The solution has already been validated using real-world datasets. It has been refined and is ready for integration into the Armed Forces of Ukraine's situational awareness systems,” the ministry said.
Model No. 13 works from past data, weather, and the current battlefield situation. The ministry said it can identify the intensity of attacks, the areas, the time windows, and the types of drones with a high probability.
Ranking artillery options
Model No. 32 is a decision-support module. It tests whether artillery plans can be generated automatically. It weighs the mission’s requirements and current operational data, including available weapons, ammunition, firing positions, and constraints.
Ukraine’s new military AI does more than watch the battlefield—it helps commanders plan what comes next
First, it applies logistics, ballistics, and impact-zone parameters to throw out unworkable options. Then it scores and ranks the rest. That means less hand-based comparison, faster decisions, and a more efficient fire loop, the ministry said. The prototype is now with the Ukrainian military for trials. If the trials succeed and it is validated, it could be expanded to other units that strike Russian forces.

Remains of Ukrainians killed in 1944 attack by Polish Home Army found in Poland – photos
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:07:00 EEST
21:07:00 KST

Remains of Ukrainians killed in 1944 attack by Polish Home Army found in Poland – photos
A Ukrainian expedition has discovered around 30 sets of human remains belonging to Ukrainians killed in the village of Łasków in Poland. The remains were found in individual and mass graves at an Orthodox cemetery. Residents of Łasków were killed in an attack by units of the Polish Home Army (Armia Krajowa) and Peasants' Battalions in March 1944.
Source: Ukrainian Institute of National Remembrance on Facebook
Details: The expedition is being conducted in the Lublin Voivodeship with the permission of the Polish authorities as part of the implementation of agreements reached by the Ukrainian-Polish Working Group on Matters of Dignified Burial.
Search operations are underway in Łasków based on historical records of the mass killing of Ukrainians on 10 March 1944. Historians estimate that more than 300 people were killed at the time.
Experts from Ukraine and Poland have so far established information about 327 residents of Łasków who were killed. However, some historians believe the death toll was higher, at around 350. Further research is expected to establish the number of victims.
"The preliminary findings confirm accounts given by former residents of Łasków who managed to survive the horrific events of March 1944. We plan to continue searching for burial sites, with the next stage involving exhumations, the reburial of the victims and a dignified commemoration of their memory," said the head of the Dolia municipal company, which is conducting the work in Łasków.
This is the second expedition by Ukrainian experts to Poland since a lengthy break that began in 2016. The last similar work, during which human remains were discovered, took place that year. The expeditions resumed in autumn 2025 in the village of Jureczkowa.
Background: Earlier, a search for the remains of Polish Army soldiers who died in September 1939 during a battle with the German Wehrmacht was completed at the old Holoskiv Cemetery in Lviv. The search uncovered 113 complete sets of remains of Polish Army soldiers, as well as the remains of 17 Wehrmacht servicemen.

Leonardo DRS wins $500M slot to supply counter-drone radar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:06:53 UTC
21:06:53 KST

- Leonardo DRS won a three-year counter-drone contract with a $500 million ceiling from Joint Interagency Task Force 401.
- The company can now compete for orders for its tactical radars, but it disclosed no initial task order or funding.
Leonardo DRS has won a spot on a Pentagon counter-drone contract worth up to $500 million, giving the company a path to sell its tactical radars to Joint Interagency Task Force 401, the U.S. Department of War organization set up last year to speed anti-drone gear to troops.
The company announced the three-year indefinite-delivery/indefinite-quantity award on Oct. 14 in a press release, saying it will be eligible to compete for task orders covering integrated counter-drone sensing for force protection and low-altitude air defense. The $500 million figure is a ceiling for orders rather than money committed, and Leonardo DRS did not report any initial task order or say how much has been obligated.
“Our counter UAS and air defense radars have demonstrated proven detection, tracking, and force protection performance in operational environments,” said Max Cohen, senior vice president and general manager of the Leonardo DRS RADA Technologies business unit.
That business traces back to Israeli radar maker RADA, which merged with DRS in 2022 and builds compact tactical radars designed to spot small drones, rockets and mortar rounds. Its Multi-mission Hemispheric Radar flies on the U.S. Army’s Stryker-based Maneuver Short-Range Air Defense vehicle, for which Leonardo DRS also integrates the mission equipment package. According to the company, the same family of sensors supports counter-rocket, artillery and mortar missions as well as short-range air defense for deployed forces.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth ordered JIATF-401 created in August 2025 to replace the Joint Counter-small Unmanned Aircraft Systems Office. The task force reports to the deputy secretary of war, is run under the U.S. Army, and has a director who can approve up to $50 million per counter-drone effort without going through the usual acquisition chain.
Leonardo DRS is one of several companies to receive a JIATF-401 contract with an identical $500 million ceiling this year. The first went to Perennial Autonomy in May, covering Merops interceptors and Bumblebee quadcopters among other drone-killing systems. Since then, CACI, AeroVironment, Digital Force Technologies, DroneShield and SRC have announced similar vehicles, most of them tied to Domestic Shield, the task force’s push to protect military bases and other sites inside the United States.
Radar maker SRC is the closest comparison, having received a $10.24 million first order for its Gryphon radars alongside its own $500 million vehicle earlier this month. Leonardo DRS framed its award around expeditionary and deployed forces, and its release does not mention Domestic Shield.
“This JIATF IDIQ positions DRS to accelerate the delivery of integrated C-UAS sensing technologies through rapid fielding of operationally relevant capabilities that help protect forces and strengthen low-altitude air defense as new threats emerge,” said John Baylouny, president and chief executive officer of Leonardo DRS.

Yemen: WFP warns of potential ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ as fighting blocks aid delivery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Yemen: WFP warns of potential ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ as fighting blocks aid delivery
Intensifying fighting in Yemen has cut off life-saving assistance to 800,000 people as shifting frontlines, blocked roads and growing insecurity severely restrict access to the city of Taiz and other conflict zones, the UN World Food Programme (WFP) said on Wednesday.
“We are critically concerned about the escalating conflict, but even more so about the growing number of people we can no longer reach because of it,” said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP country director in Yemen.
He noted that many of the affected families have been displaced multiple times and were already struggling to afford even basic food items.
“This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe if assistance cannot move safely and reach those who need it most,” he warned.
Trapped families, rising needs
Taiz is Yemen’s third largest city and capital of an eponymous governorate in which some districts have hosted the largest numbers of people displaced by the mounting violence between Saudi-supported Government troops and Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
Many of the displaced are now inaccessible due to ongoing fighting and imminent road closures around the governorate.
WFP said the situation is especially alarming as Taiz has some of the highest levels of food insecurity, with 10 out of 16 districts already classified at emergency levels.
Dwindling food stocks
The latest monitoring indicates that wheat flour stocks are nearly depleted while local markets are running out of food, according to the UN agency.
WFP and partners cannot access more than 600,000 people in Taiz who depend on humanitarian assistance, including more than 200,000 women and children.
Some 800,000 people are now out of reach nationwide, taking into account communities affected by access losses on the West Coast.
Millions going hungry nationwide
The UN continues to sound the alarm over the crisis in Yemen, where more than 18 million people face acute food insecurity. Some 2.2 million children under five are acutely malnourished, including 500,000 suffering from severe acute malnutrition, the most life-threatening form of the condition.
Recent WFP monitoring in accessible areas found that nearly 75 per cent of households were unable to meet their basic food needs – a record number for this year and a sign that food security is significantly deteriorating.
WFP said the escalation has also severely disrupted its operations, with offices breached, assets and food stocks lost and critical supply chain routes cut off.
Disrupted operations, detained personnel
Meanwhile, 37 of its staff are among 72 UN personnel who remain detained by Houthi de facto authorities. WFP has joined UN Secretary-General António Guterres in repeatedly calling for their immediate and unconditional release.
The agency continues to uphold the critical need for safe and sustained humanitarian access in Yemen along with immediate funding. Teams have provided emergency assistance to more than 115,000 newly displaced people are preparing to expand to include 1.5 million people when access is restored.
WFP stressed that it requires $268 million to sustain operations through 2027, which include emergency food assistance, nutrition programmes, school meals, resilience activities and critical humanitarian logistics services.

Artist of the month: Steph Huang
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:58:56 UTC
20:58:56 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – When picking up a bottle of olive oil at the supermarket, few consumers consider the complex geographic landscapes and global capital networks it crossed before reaching the table.
For London-based Taiwanese artist Steph Huang (黃麗音), food serves as a primary lens through which to dissect the globalized economy and contemporary labor systems. Following prestigious accolades including top honors at the Taipei Art Awards in 2022 and the Mark Tanner Sculpture Award in 2023, alongside exhibitions at Tate Britain and Perrotin, this year marks another career pinnacle for the 1990-born artist.
In October, Huang teams up with curator Liao Chuan-ya (廖釧雅) for her solo exhibition, "The Glittering Grove," at TKG+ gallery in Taipei. Meanwhile, a British iteration of her signature project, "Lili Deli," debuted at Frieze London.
As the featured artist of the month, Huang reflected on her creative path, tracing global food systems from memories in Taiwan to the olive groves of southern Spain.
Huang’s practice frequently centers on micro-objects from everyday life. In "Grafting," presented at Art Basel Hong Kong, she layered mangoes, shoji screens, and Taiwan’s colonial histories to explore family memory and identity.
In "The Glittering Grove," her field research shifted to olive groves and industrial assembly lines in southern Spain. Huang explained that while both projects started with specific agricultural products, olive oil operates on a planetary scale that shapes our fundamental relationship with food and nature.
Immersing herself in Spanish olive orchards, Huang witnessed the stark realities of agricultural economics firsthand. She was surprised by how small a fraction of the market price actually returns to the farmers for their fruit.
She said that while advertisements promote ultra-processed foods, fresh produce rarely receives such attention because it carries no brand and generates no outsized profit margins. The remote, off-grid experience also reshaped her personal outlook, leading her to realize that much of the modern convenience people pursue is not strictly necessary.
Inside the exhibition space, visitors hear the subtle sounds of olive harvesting, while wallpaper featuring field photographs of fallen olives and branches frames the room.
Blown glass plays a crucial role in Huang’s material vocabulary, where its delicate, translucent, and fluid quality contrasts sharply with mass-produced olive oil. Huang explained that the fragility of blown glass serves as a metaphor for the vulnerability of the global food system.
For Huang, using readymades is an act of assemblage rather than a desire to provoke. She said that readymades carry their own history and weight, allowing her to utilize their material forms and textures to reveal hidden social relations.
By highlighting discarded olives and branches, Huang elevates systemic remnants into visual focal points. Unharvested pods, fish bones, fallen figs, discarded shells, and old shoji screens have all taken center stage in her recent work as part of an effort to subvert conventional perspectives and flip hierarchical relationships.
"The Glittering Grove" observes that while an olive's economic value shifts across production stages, the fruit itself remains unchanged while the surrounding institutional framework transforms.
When asked if this mirrors the market fate of artworks, Huang offered a candid view on the dual reality of art.
She explained that while a piece accumulates layers of commercial value and class signifiers upon entering art fairs and collections, art ultimately exists for the public to engage with, criticize, and view. She added that when standing in front of a work with friends, the discussion revolves around personal affinity rather than market value.
Huang’s cross-cultural experience living in London sharpens her view of global supply chains. She attributed her curiosity about food systems to her Taiwanese background, saying that being an outsider makes it natural to question local dining habits and cultural traditions.
Looking ahead, Huang remains eager to explore new media, including an upcoming project incorporating a collection of vintage ties. Through poetic assemblages, Huang translates global capital into tangible form, encouraging viewers to look at everyday items on supermarket shelves with a renewed sense of awareness.

CNA reported that a groundbreaking ceremony was held at the port in the Changhua Coastal Industrial Park. Changhua County Magistrate Wang Hui-mei (王惠美) said the county will fund the project, which is expected to take about 900 days and be completed in 2029.

The county government said the broader development plan will cost more than NT$2.5 billion and include a new fish market and additional docks. Despite the county's NT$1.4 billion investment, the plan still faces a funding gap of nearly NT$1.2 billion, per CTS News.
The county has asked the central government to help cover the shortfall. Officials said the support would allow further development to proceed without placing more financial pressure on the county.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The upgraded Hai Lung submarine will be the focus of joint sea-air anti-submarine warfare exercises in waters southwest of the country from Oct. 28 to Nov. 27.
The Navy’s surface fleet and 256th Submarine Squadron will conduct the exercises in three phases, per Liberty Times. The surface fleet’s portion will involve joint sea-air anti-submarine operations, with Air Force P-3C anti-submarine aircraft and Navy S-70C(M) anti-submarine helicopters also taking part.
The Hai Lung has completed a combat system upgrade and test-fired a US-made MK-48 heavyweight torpedo. Its sister submarine, the Hai Hu, is undergoing a separate combat system upgrade at a shipyard.
The upgrade gave the Hai Lung a new combat management system designed to improve target tracking and its ability to engage multiple targets simultaneously, Liberty Times reported. The submarine can also fire US-made MK-48 Mod 6 Advanced Technology heavyweight torpedoes and submarine-launched Harpoon anti-ship missiles.
Military sources said the exercises are strategically important for securing the southwest maritime corridor. Waters are deep and have complex currents, making them a key area for submarine operations and a potential route for Chinese submarines seeking to pass through the First Island Chain and enter the Pacific Ocean.
Frequent exercises in the area allow surface ships and submarines to practice defensive tactics under realistic conditions and build a database of local underwater conditions, according to Liberty Times. This knowledge could help Taiwan improve its underwater warfare capabilities and deter Chinese submarines from infiltrating nearby waters or imposing a maritime blockade, the sources said.
The exercises will also test coordination among naval and air force units, which must share information to detect and track underwater threats. During the drills, the Hai Lung is expected to serve as a simulated adversary or a key component of underwater defense scenarios involving P-3C aircraft, S-70C helicopters, and Navy surface vessels.

About six weeks passed between the start of site preparation and the appearance of the main elements of the launch infrastructure.

Ukrainian long-range strikes have repeatedly targeted Tsymbulova.

Following another strike on October 1, storage areas and launch infrastructure at the site were again damaged.

Researchers use genome sequencing to study tuberculosis transmissions in Kaohsiung
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:58:27 UTC
20:58:27 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Researchers have used whole-genome sequencing to trace how tuberculosis bacteria spreads in Kaohsiung and understand the role of older adults in the chain of transmission.
“As many countries face rapidly ageing populations, reading the genetic code of TB bacteria can show us where the disease is really spreading and help us act earlier,” said Lin Hsien-ho (林先和), a co-corresponding author of the study and the director of the Institute of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine at National Taiwan University.
In a study published in The Lancet Microbe, researchers read the complete genomes of tuberculosis bacteria collected from close to 4,000 patients diagnosed over five years in Kaohsiung and compared the samples to identify links between infections.
Taiwan recorded 5,742 tuberculosis cases last year, the lowest number on record, but more than half of the patients were aged 65 or older, according to data from the health ministry. The study sheds light on the role older adults may play in transmission, suggesting they are not only vulnerable to the disease but may also contribute to its spread.
“We often think of older people with tuberculosis as patients who need treatment, not as part of the chain of transmission,” Lin said. “Our results suggest they may be both.”
The researchers found that adults aged 65 and older accounted for about four in 10 patients whose samples were genetically linked to those from at least one other patient, suggesting relatively recent transmissions.
The study also identified distinct patterns of transmission among different strains of tuberculosis bacteria. One strain spread readily in rural and mountainous areas but did not reach urban areas, where another group of strains predominated.
“Combining bacterial DNA with information about patients and where they live can reveal where tuberculosis is spreading and which groups of people need closer attention,” according to a press release.

Royal Caribbean cruise passenger who went overboard rescued after she spent 20 hours at sea, Greek coastguard says

The incident occurred early on Friday when the Royal Caribbean Cruises ship Odyssey of the Seas was sailing southwest of the island of Zakynthos, the coastguard said.
The 44-year-old Salvadorian woman subsequently told her rescuers she had jumped because "she wanted to disembark," a coastguard spokesperson told AFP.
"She was 20 hours at sea," the officer said.
After an alert went out early on Friday, two coastguard boats and a navy helicopter were dispatched to the area and other nearby ships were rerouted.
The Odyssey of the Seas also joined the search, the officer said.
 A passing freighter eventually located the woman, fully conscious, in a life ring early on Saturday and she was picked up by a Greek coastguard patrol boat.
A video released by the coastguard shows a crew throwing a rope to a woman floating inside an orange life ring in the water in the dark.
She was taken to the port of Katakolo and then to hospital in the nearby city of Pyrgos for health tests that include a psychiatric evaluation ordered by a local prosecutor, the coastguard officer said.
According to Royal Caribbean, Odyssey of the Seas is 1,138 feet long and can accommodate 4,198 guests. The ship offers seasonal cruises to the Greek Isles.
Last year, a man jumped off a Royal Caribbean cruise ship near the Port of San Juan — allegedly to avoid paying off more than $16,000 in gambling debt to the cruise line. ‘A big responsibility’: Clifton Suspension Bridge master hails £7.6m renovation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:46:23 UTC
20:46:23 KST

The job does not give the holder age-old perks such as the right to drive sheep across the great structure, but the title “bridge master” does have a certain ring to it.
“I don’t tend to say I’m the bridge master when I’m at a party,” said Tristan Ralph, the current holder of the title. “But people do seem to know and bring it up. It’s a job less ordinary, isn’t it? It’s a Victorian sounding title and people are really, really interested.”
There is, however, nothing ceremonial about the title. Ralph is in charge of maintaining and running the Clifton Suspension Bridge, a UK feat of engineering, without any public money.
“It does feel a big responsibility,” said Ralph. “When the chairman of the trustees rang to say we’d like you to do it, you suddenly feel the pressure. It’s so famous and people in Bristol, quite rightly, are proud and almost possessive of it. Bristolians think: ‘It’s our bridge.’”
The bridge master – and the not-for-profit charity the Clifton Suspension Bridge Trust – have the task of maintaining the bridge “in perpetuity”. “I’m a temporary custodian,” Ralph said. “When I’m finished, I have to make sure it is handed on in just [as] good a condition or better than I inherited it.”
Ralph, a bridge engineer by profession, was speaking to mark the conclusion of a large refurbishment project that has taken two and a half years and involved hand-painting more than 4,000 original iron chain links and installing an energy-efficient lighting system. It has cost about £7.5m. “It’s been a big job,” he said. “But it’s come pretty much bang on budget, which is rare these days.”
That is important because, to many visitors’ surprise, the bridge does not receive public funding. “The upkeep of the bridge, the running of it, the salary costs and everything are all paid only by our toll money,” said Ralph. “People think that we might get something from local or central government. But, no, it’s just the toll money.”
Motorised vehicles – including motorcycles – pay £1 to cross the bridge. There is no charge for pedestrians, cyclists or horse riders. As well as being a beautiful structure, it is also a vital part of Bristol and North Somerset’s transport system.
Ralph said: “It draws the tourists in. We get visitors from hundreds of countries every year but primarily, it’s still a vital piece of local infrastructure. If the bridge wasn’t here, the difference it would make to Bristol traffic would be incredible. We average over 8,000 vehicles a day still. Maintaining it as a transport link is utterly vital.”
The end of the refurbishment does not mean Ralph can rest on his laurels and spend more time hobnobbing with members of the Bridge Owners Forum.
“In a few years, we’ll need to paint the underside of the bridge. The under-bridge gantry unit itself will be replaced over the coming years. So there’s always something. We need to keep on top of things. It’s like your house or your car. If you just ignore it, don’t do things for a couple of years, they start breaking down.”
As in most walks of life, the climate emergency is a challenge Ralph and the trust are having to face. “We were monitoring the bridge daily in the summer with the very hot weather. And maybe if the bridge was being designed today, there would be a little bit more robustness around wind.”
The prevailing south-west wind is not usually a problem and the bridge rarely has to close but if it blows directly through the Avon Gorge it can be more difficult. “We need to keep an eye at both the magnitude of any wind events but also their frequency,” Ralph said.
The engineer admires the bridge’s designers, including Isambard Kingdom Brunel. “It’s remarkably advanced for its time.”
And there is no sign that its days are numbered, largely because the Victorians did not skimp. Ralph said: “There are three layers of chains. The original Brunel design only had two, but because it went from a timber design to a cast-iron deck, they upped it to three.
“There’s a little bit of comfort in there. Today there might be pressure to say, well, can you keep it to two, but in Victorian times they did like to add a little bit of meat on the bones.
“It doesn’t have a finite life. There’s no end date in our plans. We all just keep it going in the highest standards as we can. It’s in really good condition as long as we keep doing what we need to do, keep our attention on it and don’t let things drift. Forever is a long time but there’s no reason why we have any need to worry at the moment.”

Israel now treats US as ‘declining power’ and war as permanent condition, says former intelligence chief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:46:15 UTC
20:46:15 KST

A former head of Israeli military intelligence has said that since 7 October 2023, Israel has been run by an unwritten security doctrine that writes off the US as a declining power, rejects peace as a strategic goal and makes war a permanent feature of national life.
Major General (res.) Tamir Hayman, who now heads Tel Aviv’s Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), sets out the doctrine in a paper the think tank published this week.
Hayman says the new concept has never been written down or presented to the public. Even so, it now “inform[s] decision-making and dictate[s] Israel’s approach to security”. He argues the shift goes beyond military planning and points to “a change in Israel’s national identity”.
The most striking principle is the doctrine’s view of Washington. Hayman says it treats the US as a “declining power” and holds that “excessive adherence to restrictions imposed on Israel by a US administration is dangerous”.
Under this thinking, the US, “given its ongoing social and political shifts, will soon abandon Israel in any event”. Dependence on Washington is also seen as exposing Israel “to the influence of a progressive American value system that is incompatible with Israel’s Jewish character”. Cutting ties with the US is therefore “not only inevitable, but essential to Israel’s independence and the resilience of its Jewish national identity”.
Hayman rejects that view. He points out that Israel is a small country with few natural resources and depends heavily on trade with the rest of the world. For that reason, he says, the country’s security chiefs have always believed it needs a major power on its side, because Israel “cannot sustain an autarkic defence economy isolated from the world”. In other words, Israel is incapable of producing everything it needs for its own defence.
Hayman questions whether a relationship with Washington based only on mutual interest would be enough to protect Israel. He also asks whether cutting Israeli science and arms industries off from international partnerships, such as the EU’s Horizon research programme, would leave Israel facing “technological stagnation and diplomatic isolation”.
Throughout the Gaza genocide, Israel has relied on American weapons and on US diplomatic protection at the UN.
READ: Axios: Netanyahu discussed joint strike on Iran with Trump before Israeli election
Hayman identifies four other major principles behind the new doctrine. Taken together, they describe a state that puts ethnic identity before democracy, sees peace as a trap and treats war as normal.
The first is that Israel’s Jewish identity comes before its democracy. Under the doctrine, the state must stay Jewish “even at the cost of eroding its democratic values”. Hayman asks whether Israel can still call itself “Jewish and democratic” if it pursues a policy of curbing the civil rights of its Palestinian citizens, who make up about a fifth of the population.
The second principle rejects peace altogether. The doctrine holds that “a meaningful peace agreement is unattainable in the Middle East” and assumes that “any arrangement with Arab actors is temporary and deceptive”.
The doctrine treats peace deals as “merely technical and temporary arrangements”. Peace has no value of its own and is only “a means of achieving other policy objectives”. Peace itself is dismissed as “a naive concept” belonging to the left-wing “peace camp”, and set against “security”, which belongs to the right.
The third is contempt for Israel’s Arab neighbours as states. The doctrine views most of them as “not genuine nation-states, but collections of tribes and ethnic groups lacking a shared history”. It therefore sees their collapse as “a natural process” that Israel can manage and “should even encourage”.
The fourth is that war is Israel’s normal condition, not an exception. Preventive war is preferred, and the “constant presence” of war is considered “an asset to national security”. The paper quotes the slogan “Silence is filth” to sum up the view that seeking peace is a sign of weakness.
The doctrine goes further on territory. It calls for “forward defence” zones and civilian settlements in the occupied West Bank and in security zones inside Syria, Lebanon and the Gaza Strip. It rules out a Palestinian state and dismisses the Palestinian national movement as “an inauthentic Western narrative”.
Hayman says the doctrine draws its power from never being stated openly. It works “as an unwritten concept revealed through practice, rather than as a government’s declared policy”. He calls for a public debate on whether it is “a necessary adaptation” to Israel’s security situation or “an expression of a fundamental, unchecked shift in the state’s identity”.
