Peacekeeping and dividing: The US intervention in Sudan takes a familiar path
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:41:32 UTC
20:41:32 KST

Peacekeeping and dividing: The US intervention in Sudan takes a familiar path
At the end of September, the US refused to issue a visa to Sudanese Armed Forces leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, just days before his scheduled speech at the UN General Assembly in New York City. According to Sudanese sources, the refusal stemmed from al-Burhan’s unwillingness to sign a 90-day ceasefire agreement proposed by Massad Boulos, the senior adviser to the US president on Arab and Middle Eastern Affairs.
When civil war broke out in Sudan on April 15, 2023, the US refused to support either side of the conflict. Washington officially maintained a neutral stance toward both the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), and pushed for a transfer of power to a civilian-led government.
However, US policy has recently become tougher with regard to the SAF and al-Burhan, who also heads the Transitional Sovereignty Council recognized by most countries. Besides denying al-Burhan a visa, Washington is also pushing the UN to expand the existing arms embargo (which currently targets only the Darfur region, largely controlled by the RSF) to encompass all of Sudan.
Visa scandal
The US decision to deny al-Burhan a visa drew sharp criticism from the UN and various international observers. A spokesperson for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, Stephane Dujarric, said Guterres is “deeply concerned that a visa has reportedly not yet been issued to the President of the Transitional Sovereign Council of Sudan.”
A few days before the planned trip, Sudan’s permanent representative to the UN, al-Harith Idriss al-Harith Muhammad, sent a letter requesting UN intervention to allow al-Burhan to attend the meeting.
The US State Department, however, declined to comment on the visa controversy. Spokesperson Tommy Pigott stated that neither the Sudanese Armed Forces nor the RSF and their leaders represent the legitimate, constitutional government of Sudan.
“The United States and President Trump stand ready to work with anyone who is a serious partner for peace in Sudan,” Pigott added.
In accordance with the 1947 UN Headquarters Agreement, the US is committed to facilitating visa issuance for representatives of UN member states, including political opponents. However, the US has frequently deviated from these obligations in practice. Notably, the Obama administration denied entry to former Sudanese President Omar al-Bashir in 2013, preventing him from attending the UN General Assembly.
Al-Burhan, who was scheduled to speak at the General Assembly on September 24, ultimately canceled his trip to New York City. Instead, the Sudanese delegation was led by the foreign minister.
The Boulos plan
Massad Boulos’ proposal, initially presented in February, consists of five key elements: establishing an immediate humanitarian ceasefire, ensuring access for humanitarian organizations and protecting civilians, establishing a permanent ceasefire, transitioning to a civilian government, and post-war reconstruction.
As part of the American initiative, a nationwide 90-day humanitarian ceasefire is meant to facilitate the delivery of humanitarian aid and safeguard civilian populations; a coordinating committee will also be created to oversee the implementation of the ceasefire. The plan also calls for establishing a UN mechanism involving the African Union and the League of Arab States in order to monitor a limited withdrawal of troops and deploy international observers.
In July, the Sudanese government expressed doubts regarding the political aspects of this plan but generally supported the humanitarian initiatives. The RSF, on the other hand, agreed to a three-month humanitarian ceasefire but rejected the demand for troop withdrawals from captured territories.
In September, Boulos confirmed that the US continues to collaborate with partners – including the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Qatar, Türkiye, and European nations – to achieve a humanitarian ceasefire in Sudan. Nevertheless, both sides remain skeptical: The army fears that a pause would allow the RSF to regroup, while the Rapid Support Forces are reluctant to lose ground in Darfur and Kordofan.
US sanctions and allegations of the use of chemical weapons
In Washington, many view al-Burhan as the more favorable partner compared to his rival, RSF commander Muhammad Hamdan Daglo. However, despite the numerous war crimes committed by the RSF – especially following their takeover of El Fasher, the capital of North Darfur State – Washington has officially maintained an equidistant stance toward both sides and positioned itself as a mediator.
The US has repeatedly imposed sanctions on both the armed forces and the RSF, but the primary focus has been on Sudan’s Armed Forces and General al-Burhan. The first round of sanctions was announced on June 26-27, 2025. At the time, the US State Department declared that the armed forces used chemical or biological weapons (reportedly chlorine) against their own population during clashes with the RSF in 2024. Washington called this a violation of the Chemical Weapons Convention and international law.
The Sudanese government adamantly rejected the accusations, calling them baseless and politically motivated, asserting that Sudan neither produces, stores, nor uses chemical weapons, and expressed willingness to cooperate with the US in a technical investigation of the claims.
The sanctions severely restricted the export of sensitive American goods and technologies to Sudan, and imposed an outright ban on Sudan’s access to loans, guarantees, and any form of financial assistance from the US government.
A second package of sanctions was implemented in June-July 2026, further restricting the government’s access to international financing, banning the export of certain American goods to Sudan, and preventing Sudanese airlines from using US airspace. According to the US State Department spokesperson, these sanctions will remain in effect until Sudan eliminates “all chemical weapons and production facilities under international verification.”
In regard to the RSF, the US has applied individual measures. In April, at Washington’s initiative, the UN Security Council imposed sanctions on four RSF leaders, including Muhammad Hamdan Daglo’s brother, citing war crimes and crimes against humanity in El Fasher. Nevertheless, the main economic pressure points are directed against Sudan’s Armed Forces.
Critics argue that while the aim of these sanctions is to penalize violators of international law, they could exacerbate the humanitarian crisis by limiting supplies not only of arms but also of essential goods, as all resources will be diverted toward military operations, leading to the worsening of living conditions.
Does US policy legitimize the divide?
Following the fall of El Fasher – the last stronghold of the army in Darfur – the RSF solidified control over the entire region. In July 2025, they announced the formation of a parallel government in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur State. The presidential council, made up of 15 members, was headed by RSF commander Muhammad Hamdan Daglo himself.
The US has not officially recognized the structure, but is effectively engaging with it as a legitimate political actor, even in the wake of UN sanctions against its members. Washington continues to view the RSF as a potential participant in peace talks; however, this stance inadvertently legitimizes Sudan’s fragmentation by acknowledging the RSF as a parallel political entity with its own administration and agenda. The proposals risk leading to a de facto division of the country, with the Sudanese Army controlling the north, east, and center of the country, and the RSF controlling Darfur and parts of the south.
Russia’s veto
On September 11, 2026, the UN Security Council unanimously voted to extend the existing arms embargo on the Darfur region for another month, a measure initially implemented in 2004 amid the brutal ethnic War in Darfur. However, US efforts to broaden these restrictions to encompass all of Sudan have met with strong opposition from Russia and China. Russian Deputy Permanent Representative to the UN Anna Evstigneeva questioned why the council was being asked to expand the embargo at this particular moment, pointing out that similar concerns were not raised in 2023 when the Rapid Support Forces posed a threat to Khartoum and other major cities.
“The Sudanese government and its armed forces now have an undisputed advantage on the ground and serve as guarantors of state institutions, national unity, and civilian protection,” she said, noting that all available resources are necessary for achieving these goals.
The US argues that the current sanctions framework is outdated and no longer reflects the realities of the ongoing conflict. Russia’s potential veto has effectively blocked a US resolution aimed at extending the embargo to all of Sudan and increasing sanctions pressure on both sides of the conflict.
However, the US is not backing down. On October 8, the UN Security Council extended the arms embargo on Sudan’s Darfur region for another two months, until December 11, unanimously adopting a draft resolution tabled by the US. Once again, the renewal period is as short as possible – essentially a technical rollover. Over the course of these two months, member states will continue negotiations on broader amendments to the sanctions regime. China, Russia, as well as the DR Congo, Somalia, Liberia, and Pakistan, oppose the US initiative, favoring instead a sanctions regime strictly limited to Darfur without expanding its scope.
Campaign in the US media
Just days before the Security Council vote, the US media again started talking about the Sudanese Army’s alleged use of chemical weapons – a key factor influencing the US initiative to broaden the embargo. In early September, The New York Times and Washington Post published findings from a joint investigation based on a supposedly leaked confidential dossier, which included videos, photographs, blueprints, and intercepted communications – totaling around 150 files.
Massad Boulos, while presenting his initiative to the UN Security Council, explicitly cited the use of chemical weapons as one of the justifications for the need to extend the embargo.
Russia and China oppose this proposal, even though there was no formal vote on the US resolution. According to Evstigneeva, Moscow “will not allow even a hint of broadening the restrictions.” China’s representative to the UN, Sun Lei, stated that expanding the embargo could worsen the humanitarian situation and lead to the further fragmentation of Sudan.
The Boulos initiative comes amid an apparent shift in the dynamics of the war in Sudan. The Rapid Support Forces have been affected by a new wave of desertions; meanwhile, the Sudanese Army is ramping up operations in Darfur and the Blue Nile region. It has also achieved significant gains in North Kordofan by capturing several strategic locations in recent months. This offensive ensured the safety of the National Export Highway linking Khartoum (via Omdurman) to El-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan, and intensified pressure on RSF supply lines.
The risks of US intervention
Despite its stated peacekeeping intentions, US involvement in Sudanese affairs risks complicating an already challenging situation. Firstly, tying visa issuance to specific ceasefire conditions sets a dangerous precedent for using access to international institutions as leverage.
Secondly, US initiatives effectively reinforce Sudan’s division by recognizing the RSF as a legitimate power alongside the official army. This could drive both sides toward a permanent split rather than fostering compromise within a unified state.
Lastly, expanding sanctions and embargoes without considering local realities may trigger an even greater humanitarian disaster, limiting supplies of not just weapons but also essential goods. History shows that unilateral pressure seldom leads to peace; more often, it prolongs conflict and fuels radicalization. The US policy toward Sudan risks deepening the country’s divisions and extending the conflict, potentially turning Sudan into yet another ‘frozen’ hotspot on the African map.

Russia’s Supreme Court on Wednesday outlawed the Batal Hajji brotherhood, a closed Sufi Muslim order originating from the North Caucasus republic of Ingushetia.
The court granted a request from state prosecutors to designate the order as an “extremist” organization for “providing material support for bandit insurgents of the North Caucasus.”
The Prosecutor General’s Office said Batal Hajji members were linked to numerous attacks on Russian police and military in the North Caucasus and orchestrated the deadly 2009 Nevsky Express train bombing claimed by Chechen rebel leader Doku Umarov.
The prosecutor also said that Batal Hajji affiliates aided the deadly March 2024 attack on the Crocus City Hall concert venue near Moscow and the assassination of Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov the same year by selling weapons and ammunition to the perpetrators.
“More than 100 members of the order have been convicted of the illicit trafficking of means for committing acts of terror. Leaders and members of the community organized illegal channels to supply foreign-made firearms from abroad,” the prosecutor’s office said in a statement published Wednesday.
Russian authorities designated the brotherhood’s so-called “military wing” a “terrorist” organization in 2023.
The Batal Hajji brotherhood was founded in the 19th century by Ingush Sheikh Batal Hajji Belkhoroev, a pupil of the Chechen Muslim mystic Kunta-Hajji (Kunta Kishiev).
Membership in the closed order, which numbers around 20,000 members, is passed down strictly by birthright.
The order’s members held a handful of key government roles and a near monopoly on Ingushetia’s construction industry in the 1990s and early 2000s before a clash with the republic’s new Kremlin-appointed leadership led to their fall from power.
Around 100 of its members allegedly joined the Russian military in 2022 as part of the Batal Hajji Rapid Response Unit, a part of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov's Akhmat military unit within the Russian army, according to the exiled news website Meduza.

Andy Lord appointed Interim Chair of NAD Group Advisory Board

Andy Lord has been appointed Interim Chair of the National Armaments Director (NAD) Group Advisory Board.
Andy is currently Commissioner of Transport for London, responsible for the delivery of safe and reliable transport services across the capital.

Andy has been appointed by Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, until April 30, 2027.

National Armaments Director Rupert Pearce said of the appointment:
  I am delighted to welcome Andy as Interim Chair of the NAD Group Advisory Board. Andy brings extensive experience both within our organisation, having served as a DE&S Board member and trusted critical friend for eight years, and in leading large, complex organisations.
His insight, challenge and independent perspective will be invaluable as we continue to build the NAD Group into an integrated, mission-focused organisation.
The new Advisory Board’s role is to provide independent support and challenge to the NAD and senior leadership, helping to ensure that the Group is well run and manages its strategy, performance and risks effectively.

‘Heartbreaking’ elephants and wily coyotes: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 – in pictures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:32:49 UTC
20:32:49 KST

‘Heartbreaking’ elephants and wily coyotes: Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026 – in pictures
This year's winners showcase powerful stories from the natural world and the urgent need to protect it.
A poignant photo of a female elephant carrying a deceased calf has won the Wildlife Photographer of the Year competition 2026.
Titled ‘The Aftermath’, it was taken by Italian wildlife photographer Federico Veronesi while he was tracking elephants in Huab River Valley in Namibia.
After noticing an unusual pattern of drag marks in the sand of a dry riverbed, he caught up with a family of elephants, one of whom had the calf wedged between her tusk and trunk.
It isn’t the first time possible displays of grief have been witnessed in elephants, with previous behaviours including vocalisations, guarding the dead, and inspecting and handling bones.
The black-and-white image has been described by Kathy Moran, Chair of the Wildlife Photographer of the Year Jury, as an emotional “gut punch” and “heartbreakingly poignant” proof of the animals’ consciousness.
As well as the Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, a further 19 category winners were selected from a record-breaking 65,403 entries from 121 countries and territories.
Who won Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026?
Oscar Whitfield, who was 14 when he captured his prize-winning photo, took home the main youth award this year for a shot of a dung beetle at work in Zambezi National Park, Zimbabwe.
Though small, these powerful insects play their part in curbing the Earth’s greenhouse gases by breaking up and burying dung, preventing it from producing planet-heating methane. This also helps it decompose faster, reducing the number of pests affecting livestock and wildlife.
There are more than 5,000 species of dung beetle found around the world.
Prize-winning photographers capture urban wildlife
From coyotes roaming the hills of San Francisco to giant lizards hunting in Bangkok, this year’s winning photographs also revealed how animals are adapting to life alongside humans.
In his award-winning portfolio, ‘Wily Coyotes of San Francisco’, US photographer Loren Elliott documents a resident pack living among the city’s more than 800,000 inhabitants.
Around 100 coyotes are thought to live in the city, where attitudes towards the animals are mixed. While they sometimes prey on domestic animals, they also help control populations of disease-carrying rodents. Elliott’s photographs invite viewers to reconsider these often-misunderstood animals and their place in an increasingly urban world.
Another urban encounter by UK photographer Seth Forestson won the Urban Wildlife category.
Capturing a common monitor lizard carrying its prey through Bangkok’s Lumphini Park, Seth lowered himself onto the muddy ground to frame the creature against the city skyline.
Common water monitors have successfully adapted to the Thai capital’s urban environment, taking advantage of readily available food, including catfish and koi in Bangkok’s park lakes.
Underwater encounters reveal what’s hidden in the depths
Human impacts on wildlife are not confined to land. Beneath the surface, photographers are documenting both intimate animal encounters and the growing pressures on marine ecosystems.
Animal Portrait-winner Aaron Sanders had been diving off a Cornish beach when he noticed the footprints of octopus suckers through a thin blade of kelp. As a single eye emerged, “We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity,” he recalls.
The encounter is a glimpse of a wider story brewing in the waters off southwest England, where sightings of common octopuses have increased dramatically. While the carnivorous predators are more commonly found in the Mediterranean, above-average spring sea temperatures have expanded their territory, with devastating impacts on local fishing industries.
In another show of humans’ impact on marine life, US photographer Alex Lindbloom snapped a whale shark investigating the catch of a ‘bagan’, or mobile net-fishing platform, in the inky waters off Papua, Indonesia.
The species has declined sharply over the past 75 years mainly due to ship strikes, fishing gear entanglements and illegal fishing.
A watering hole brings wildlife together
Some of the winning images reveal the unexpected interactions that take place when different species gather in the same habitat.
In ‘The Meeting Place’, UK photographer James Lewin captures a young bull elephant spraying a group of zebras as they congregate around a waterhole in Kenya’s Chyulu Hills. Lewin used an infrared-converted camera to soften the harsh light, giving the scene a dreamlike quality.
Waterholes can become vital lifelines during severe droughts, bringing together animals that might otherwise keep their distance.
Wildlife Photographer of the Year is developed and produced by the Natural History Museum, London. The winning photographs will be on display at the Natural History Museum from 16 October 2026 until July 2027.

Amateur astronomer harnesses AI to find a possible hidden exoplanet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:32:26 UTC
20:32:26 KST

An amateur astronomer harnessed artificial intelligence agents to find a previously undiscovered exoplanet lurking in publicly available data.
Pavel Rabtsevich, a Spain-based product manager and a space science hobbyist, was poring over data collected by NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), an exoplanet-hunting space telescope, when he noticed something odd.
TESS looks for the subtle dimming caused by planets transiting, or passing in front of, their stars. Of the more than 126,000 target stars that Rabtsevich was examining with a custom-built AI algorithm, his machine-learning assistant directed its focus toward one in particular: TIC 4206066. The star was located around 116 light-years away from Earth in the Orion constellation, and the data indicated it dimmed for about two hours every three days.
With his curiosity piqued, Rabtsevich dug through the TESS archives for more data on the same star and found an additional 22 instances of dimming. If the signal were to be confirmed to represent an exoplanet, that world would a super-Earth with a radius around 1.4 times as large as that of our planet. Although such an exoplanet would likely be a rocky world, its three-day orbit of TIC 4206066 would mean it had an estimated surface temperature of 1,000 degrees Fahrenheit (540 degrees Celsius).
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
But stars can dim for many other reasons. In this case, for instance, Rabtsevich noticed the dips in TIC 4206066's light in 2018 tended to align with moments where TESS fired its thrusters, which may have skewed the results. For now, while Rabtsevich hopes this may be a new exoplanet, he acknowledges that all that can be confirmed is a “repeating transitlike signal in open data, with a plausible planetary explanation and alternatives that aren’t yet ruled out.”
“Models agreeing with each other isn’t evidence,” he says. “What I rely on is a signal anyone can measure, calculations anyone can rerun, control samples and rules published before the next [datasets] arrive.”
The search couldn’t have been done without AI, Rabtsevich adds, noting that he used multiple agents and that the models “wrote the code, ran it and checked each other's work.” Even so, he maintains, “the research itself was mine: the question, the plan, the rules, the computing, the decisions on every candidate and what to publish.”
The potential for at least one exoplanet orbiting TIC 4206066 seems “solid,” says astronomer Greg Laughlin of Yale University, who now works in the AI industry. Rabtsevich’s analysis is “a great example of human-AI teamwork,” he adds: large language models such as Claude and Codex have proven effective at combing astronomical literature for overlooked discoveries.
If there is indeed an exoplanet circling TIC 4206066, Rabtsevich may not actually be the first to have seen it. Pablo Mercader Perez, a Ph.D. student at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and a member of the TESS team, says the signal was picked up by a detection filter in 2020 but was ultimately rejected because of a lack of conclusive evidence. Since then TESS has conducted many more observations of that part of the sky.
“Thanks to this, we got much more data than we had before for this particular star system, and the signal became a lot clearer,” Mercader Perez says. In terms of statistical significance, “this planet candidate became effectively detectable only in January of this year.”
A deep-learning model developed by Mercader Perez’s team has also flagged the potential exoplanet, he says.
“Independently but also not public yet, a search performed by [astronomer] Michelle Kunimoto using her software called LEO-Vetter had also selected this planet candidate already back in early 2026, which is another way in which it would almost certainly have been alerted in the official list in the next few months,” Mercader Perez says.
Other amateurs, either acting entirely independent of or taking cues from Rabtsevich's exciting candidate, are now pursuing additional AI-assisted dives into public datasets from TESS and other NASA missions. And some have reported promising early results.
In the meantime, Rabtsevich's calculations have prompted NASA’s TESS team to reexamine the star once the spacecraft’s orbit around the sun brings the target into position in November. He’s also recruited several other astronomers to look at the star and critique his findings, which include a speculative additional exoplanet in a more distant orbit around the star.
Regardless of who might claim the discovery, “it’s exciting that the parent star has been put on TESS’s high-cadence list, which should elevate the confidence in the detection,” Laughlin says. “There’s every reason to expect that this candidate super-Earth will pass further tests and make it into the official census.”

French viewers shocked by Israeli soldiers’ accounts of Gaza in ‘NAZA’ documentary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:31:41 UTC
20:31:41 KST

French viewers who attended screenings of “NAZA,” a documentary exposing Israel’s killing of civilians in Gaza, said they were shocked by Israeli soldiers’ accounts that reduced Palestinian victims to numbers rather than recognizing them as human beings.
Produced by British newspaper The Guardian and directed by Oscar-winning filmmaker Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, the documentary was screened in French cinemas on Oct. 12-13.
The film drew considerable interest in Paris on its opening day, with most tickets sold.
French viewers who watched “NAZA” at two cinemas in the capital shared their reactions with Anadolu. 
‘I think the filmmakers are very courageous’
A French viewer, Kenzi, said the documentary explained the meaning of NAZA, a term referring to civilian casualties, and left him deeply shocked.
He said Israeli soldiers repeatedly discussed numbers and calculations, almost all of which represented people killed in Gaza.
“We know what is happening, we talk about it, we see it, but not to this extent. And here, it was really shocking to see Israeli soldiers talking about it. Sometimes you could sense regret, sometimes not so much. They spoke quite coldly. So, it really disturbed me. And, I think it was very well made. It went by very quickly,” he said.
Noting that the soldiers compared their actions in Gaza to a video game, Kenzi said: “They talk about artificial intelligence to identify people to kill. At a certain point, you see that they no longer measure the number of people they are going to kill, the collateral damage, the NAZAs.”
He said the soldiers frequently referred to a “system.”
“It seemed as though they had been brainwashed and made to believe that they were on the right side, until they realized for themselves that what they were doing was vile,” he said.
Kenzi recalled the soldiers repeatedly saying they “just wanted to eliminate the enemy.”
“They clearly said that the enemy was children aged 3 to 6, women who had done nothing to deserve this. Often, they wanted to eliminate an enemy leader, and in the end, they killed his entire family except that person,” he said.
Praising the Israeli directors, he added: “I think the filmmakers are very courageous to have initiated a project like this.” 
‘It affected everyone in the theater’
Iona, a 23-year-old French viewer, said: “I think the film is extremely important. It is extremely important to have this perspective because we often hear testimonies from victims, but here we have testimonies from the attackers, who put the situation into concrete words.”
She said the documentary could help people understand what was happening and stand on the right side of history, adding that the language used and the questions asked deeply affected her.
“He was not afraid to use the word ‘genocide.’ He asked directly whether it was genocide, and they said yes,” she said, referring to the interviewer.
Iona said she found it shocking that the soldiers did not regard the victims as people.
She also highlighted scenes showing people living normally in Tel Aviv while people in Gaza were dying.
“Everything was extremely striking,” she said.
Emphasizing the importance of making such films and allowing everyone to speak, she added: “There was everyone in the theater — young people, older people. You could see that it affected everyone in the theater. There was silence at the end. It was extremely moving.”
She urged people to watch the documentary, ending her remarks with: “Free Palestine.” 
‘Reducing human beings to numbers shocked me the most’
Adam, a 27-year-old French viewer, said the documentary left him speechless throughout.
“I was aware of the history and the political issues behind it, of the massacre and genocide taking place in Palestine,” he said.
But hearing testimony from people within the system was still shocking, he added, saying it gave concrete substance to the atrocities.
“Overall, I think the documentary is very well made and presented, because it raises several questions, particularly about the dehumanization of victims through the term NAZA.
Ultimately, the victims, the ‘collateral damage,’ as they like to call them, become nothing more than numbers. Reducing human beings to numbers was what shocked me the most,” he said.
Adam said the massacre in Palestine did not begin in October 2023 and praised the directors’ courage despite pressure from the Israeli government.
‘An interviewer who recognized the disastrous situation in Gaza’
Another French viewer, Yacine, said the repeated emphasis on numbers was among the documentary’s most striking elements.
“They had an interviewer who appeared objective, who had some distance and recognized the disastrous situation unfolding in Palestine and Gaza,” he said, referring to Abraham.
By contrast, he said, the soldiers interviewed appeared conditioned by war.
“There is a real contrast between the images we saw of Tel Aviv, where people seem safe and appear to lead fairly peaceful daily lives, and the images of Gaza at the end of the film, which embody war and destruction themselves,” he said.
“When you see the images, you get the impression that there is almost no life left. People are surviving.”

Zelensky arrives in UK as London vows to speed up anti-drone missile deliveries for Ukraine
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in the U.K. on Oct. 14 to meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III, as London pledges missiles to help Ukraine counter Russia's jet-powered drones.
The visit comes at a tense moment for Ukraine, with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration pressuring Kyiv to halt strikes against Russian oil refineries and threatening to cut off intelligence sharing and arms shipments.
Ahead of Zelensky's visit, Burnham vowed that the U.K.'s support for Ukraine remains "rock-solid."
The Ukrainian president was first welcomed by King Charles at Buckingham Palace before meeting Burnham.
"I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience. It is important for me to have the opportunity to personally thank him for his unwavering support for Ukraine," Zelensky said on X.
The British prime minister then welcomed Zelensky at 10 Downing Street in the company of a military ceremonial guard, the first such honor granted to a foreign leader, according to the BBC.
The British government has announced an air defense missile package worth 45 million pounds (around $60 million) for Ukraine, as the country faces an intensifying onslaught of Russian missiles and drones.
"The U.K. will accelerate deliveries of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), which have proven extremely effective against jet-powered drones that are being used to strike far beyond the front lines in Ukraine, including Kyiv and beyond," the British government said in a press release on Oct. 13.
Russia has been increasingly deploying jet-powered drones that are faster and more difficult to intercept than older Shahed models, posing a new threat as Ukraine braces for massive strikes against energy infrastructure in winter.
Of the 45-million-pound package, the U.K. will expedite the delivery of 10 million pounds ($13 million) worth of LMMs to meet the most urgent winter needs.
"I’m announcing that we're accelerating the delivery of British-made air defenses for (Ukraine)," Burnham told the press while meeting Zelensky. The British leader also said he would seek to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the U.S.
Burnham's office said earlier that he had instructed his cabinet to prepare additional military and financial assistance packages for Ukraine, as well as fresh sanctions against Russia.
The U.K. further reiterated that it stands by its plans to ban maritime services for Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.
London said last year it would implement the phased ban over 2026 "in lockstep with our European partners."
The EU plans to ban Russian LNG imports by January 2027 but has failed to agree on a full ban on maritime services, with Greece securing a carve-out for Russian LNG exports to non-EU countries.

She Remains a Stranger: Motherhood, memory and the loss of home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:31:09 UTC
20:31:09 KST

Breadcrumb
Rasha Hilwi's She Remains a Stranger: On motherhood, inherited exile and the meaning of home
In the opening pages of her recently published literary memoir Dhalat Gharibeh (She Remains a Stranger), Palestinian author, storyteller and journalist Rasha Hilwi offers a lexicographical meditation on the word ghurba.
"Ever since I crossed those seas, I’ve tried to translate the word ghurba into other languages. I came to the same conclusion as others before me: some things cannot be translated.
Ghurba derives from the root gharaba.
Ghurba (noun). The verbal noun of gharuba.
“His ghurba lasted long”: his separation from his homeland and family lasted a long time.
Ghurba is nawā or being far away.
“He lived for a long time in ghurba”: he lived for a long time in lands of displacement.
“I found him in a state of ghurba”: he was found in loneliness and desolation.
“The loss of loved ones is itself a ghurba”: whoever loses someone dear becomes like a stranger among people, even if they have never left their homeland."
Published in July 2026 by the Berlin-based Arabic bookshop and publisher Khan Al Janub, She Remains a Stranger is an intimate autobiographical narrative about motherhood, Palestine, and what it means to inhabit several forms of ghurba all at once.
For Hilwi, the impulse to write this book was an old one. But it was motherhood, and the estrangement born of it, that ultimately gave form to the story.
"Before motherhood, writing about culture was a major part of my life. Then motherhood came and severed me from that world. This is characteristic of how motherhood functions more generally: It imposes a particular kind of isolation, separating you not only from your former self, but also from the outside world," Hilwi tells The New Arab.
"But more than that, motherhood put me face to face with so much I had left unresolved: my relationship with myself, with places, with my family’s heritage, and that of my ancestors. It forced me to deal with feelings of pain, loss and, above all, ghurba," she adds.
Together with the realisation that she was battling postpartum depression, this confrontation set Hilwi on a journey of healing.
So, in 2022, she returned to her most familiar form of expression: writing.
She began chronicling her life as a new mother of twins in Amsterdam, far from her first home, Palestine, and the coastal city of Akka, where she grew up.
Writing became a way of making sense of it all.
"It shielded me from a heaviness I hadn’t yet realised I was carrying," she asserts.
Hilwi writes of the weight she was carrying, which was never hers alone. It comprised the histories of the women who had moulded her, particularly her mother and grandmother, and all they had passed down to her.
It was an inheritance imbued with both pain and love.
She also writes of the weight of becoming a mother abroad: of her attempts to root her children in a heritage that is geographically remote yet intimately present.
Sometimes, this means something as ordinary as encouraging them to enjoy her familiar spreads of labneh, za’atar and olive oil on their Amsterdam dining table.
At other times, it means insisting they pronounce helwe properly with the Arabic ‘ḥ’ rather than the ‘h’ of a foreign accent.
As Hilwi navigates everyday life, the book's bigger question begins to take shape. What can a mother give her children of a home they have not known as she has?
But just as writing offered Hilwi a way through this question, the devastation unfolding in Gaza rendered the very act of writing meaningless.
For Hilwi, motherhood made the distance between Amsterdam and Gaza unbearable.
She found herself comparing her children’s safety against the reality of Palestinian mothers struggling to keep theirs alive, or "how one child could be playing on an actual slide while another slides down the wall of a destroyed house in Gaza."
Yet, with time, Hilwi realised she could not abandon writing. However modest, it was a contribution she could make, "a small piece in a much larger mosaic through which Palestinians continue to affirm their continued existence, whether in academia, theatre, cinema, literature, or elsewhere."
Making a home from fragments
Hilwi’s She Remains a Stranger contributes to that mosaic, her act of remembering offering some relief from a deepening sense of ghurba.
As she takes the readers with her through the daily rhythms of motherhood in Amsterdam, Hilwi journeys back through memory, revisiting the life she once shared with her family in Palestine, from Haifa, where her grandparents rebuilt their lives after being forcibly displaced from their village of Iqrit in the Upper Galilee in 1948, to Akka, her hometown, where she was born and raised.
As a third-generation Nakba woman, she imagines the life that might have been. She writes of a ghurba that did not begin with her departure from Palestine to Berlin, or her subsequent move to Amsterdam.
It is a ghurba that was already part of her inheritance.
"There is a ghurba that I know: that of Palestinians in their own country, in their own cities, especially those who stayed. I am one of them. I did not witness the Nakba, but I have lived with its direct impact on my grandparents, who became strangers on their own land, constantly reminded by an entire system that they were strangers and refugees in their own country."
But if ghurba can be inherited without ever leaving home, what happens when one does leave? This question also runs through Hilwi’s account of her journey from Akka to Berlin, a city she sought out in search of a life she had been denied.
"I did not go to Berlin for Berlin. I went for Arab Berlin, a city that had taken in so many of our people because of our catastrophes."
There, she found glimpses of the life she might have known in Akka had the Nakba never happened. Surrounded by friends from Beirut and Cairo, she could eat Syrian food, attend an Egyptian show, or listen to Lebanese music.
In Berlin, she found a home assembled from fragments of other homes, brought together by people whose different journeys had directed them to the same city.
"There was still alienation, of course, much of it arising simply from being in a new city, with a new language and a new way of life. Despite all that, Berlin gave me a sense of home. I needed it because I had been denied that in my own hometown. Israel had taken that right from me."
But finding something of home elsewhere did not mean that Hilwi’s ghurba disappeared. When she eventually moved from Berlin to Amsterdam, to be with her husband and raise her family, it followed her, taking on new meanings.
"It was in Amsterdam that motherhood truly put me face to face with all these forms of estrangement: from Palestine, from the experience of creating a life in two new cities; and from the heritage I was carrying."
With time, however, Hilwi came to see that her ghurba was not necessarily something to overcome, but something to understand.
"I don’t think there will ever be a moment when I stop feeling estranged. Ghurba will always accompany me, and perhaps that is important because it gives rise to questions as well as a constant search for meaning."
As it acknowledges the persistence of ghurba, Hilwi’s text is equally concerned with the life that remains possible after rupture, whether after motherhood, displacement or the devastation of genocide.
For Hilwi, this possibility materialised in motherhood, which offered "a sense of home" and, as she writes in the book, became "the vital force that stirs the muscle of imagination."
For her, motherhood was not only another site of estrangement, but a way of imagining life beyond it. And storytelling, in turn, became Hilwi’s way of insisting on that life’s continuation.
"The fact that we are still able to tell the story, that the story continues to be told, is itself an answer to genocide."
A Dutch Translation of She Remains a Stranger, titled Ze blijft een vreemde and translated by Djuke Poppinga, is scheduled for publication in November 2026 by Uitgeverij Jurgen Maas in Amsterdam.
The book excerpt featured at the beginning of this article was translated from Arabic by Nourhan Tewfik.
Nourhan is a London-based arts journalist specialising in the Middle East. She is also an Arabic TV/film consultant and researcher
Follow her on Instagram: @nourhantewfik

Bank of America Fined $1.21B Over AML Failures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:29:00 UTC
20:29:00 KST

Reported by
U.S. authorities imposed more than $1.21 billion in penalties on Bank of America on Tuesday over failures in its anti-money laundering controls and apparent violations of U.S. sanctions, in what the Treasury Department called the third-largest enforcement penalty in its history.
The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) assessed a $1.2 billion penalty, saying the bank failed to adequately detect and report financial activity involving priority national-security and illicit-finance risks, including Chinese money-laundering networks and activity along the U.S. southwestern border. Regulators said Bank of America failed to report more than $5 billion in suspicious transactions, including more than $1 billion linked to such priority risks.
As part of the FinCEN resolution, Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act, including by failing to maintain an adequate anti-money laundering program, conduct required due diligence on correspondent accounts for foreign banks, and file suspicious activity reports. The bank must also use an independent third party to identify and report suspicious activity its systems previously missed.
Separately, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) imposed a $750 million penalty — the largest in the regulator’s history. That amount is credited toward FinCEN’s $1.2 billion penalty rather than added to it. The OCC said the bank’s compliance program remained “deficient and ineffective” despite a 2024 cease-and-desist order and that weaknesses in transaction monitoring caused late suspicious activity reports involving billions of dollars.
The Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) also reached an $11.66 million settlement with the bank over 475 apparent violations of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Myanmar, Somalia, narcotics trafficking and global terrorism. OFAC cited payments involving blocked banks, failures to properly prioritize sanctions alerts and delays in updating watchlists.
Bank of America said it worked with regulators to resolve the cases and was addressing the deficiencies.
“Financial crime compliance is serious, and we are responsible for getting it right,” a spokesperson said, adding that the bank has invested billions of dollars in technology and assigned thousands of employees to combat financial crime. The bank said its remediation work is well advanced and that it remains committed to completing the measures required by regulators.

Hundreds of generators, mobile boiler houses and backup power plants: Klitschko spoke about how Kyiv will get through the most difficult winter
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:28:32 EEST
20:28:32 KST

Hundreds of generators, mobile boiler houses and backup power plants: Klitschko spoke about how Kyiv will get through the most difficult winter
Kyiv • UNN
Kyiv has prepared nearly 700 generators, 70 mobile boiler houses and three diesel power plants. The capital's hospitals have 480 generators.
Kyiv’s city authorities have prepared hundreds of generators, mobile boiler units, and other backup power sources to ensure the operation of critical infrastructure. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko stated this from the parliamentary rostrum after being invited to the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine on October 14, reports UNN.
Details
The mayor said that throughout the full-scale war, the capital had been increasing the number of backup power sources intended to ensure the operation of critical infrastructure in the event of possible prolonged power outages.
In particular, nearly 700 generators of various capacities and 70 mobile boiler units have been prepared for heat and water supply facilities. In addition, three diesel power plants have already been built in the capital, and a backup water intake has been arranged.
Currently, Kyivvodokanal has 103 generators. At the same time, the utility is awaiting additional high-capacity generator systems being manufactured abroad for Kyiv
According to him, the mayor’s office paid particular attention to providing residential buildings with backup power. Under the city’s energy resilience programs, more than 6,000 pieces of equipment have been purchased for residential buildings, including generators, inverters, and batteries.
Ensuring the provision of hospitals and educational institutions
According to the mayor, all educational institutions in the capital are equipped with generators of various capacities. Among them are 285 high-capacity generators.
In the medical sector, additional capabilities are also being created to enable institutions to operate autonomously in the event of disruptions to centralized electricity, water, and heat supplies. In particular, hospitals in the capital currently have 480 generators
He added that their own wells for water supply had already been installed at 15 medical institutions, while six more are under construction.
In addition, eleven hospitals have autonomous heating supplied by their own boiler houses. By the end of 2026, the city authorities plan to increase the number of such medical institutions to 21
Klitschko emphasized that these measures are aimed at maintaining the operation of vital institutions even if centralized networks are damaged.
We remind you
A little earlier, the Kyiv City State Administration explained how preparations for winter are progressing at medical institutions.

====================================================================================================

French students continue school blockades ahead of talks with officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:27:57 UTC
20:27:57 KST

Nearly 200 high schools across France were expected to remain closed on Wednesday amid continuing student blockades, as the government promised proposals to improve university admissions.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told French broadcaster BFMTV that 96 percent of high schools were open, with no disruptions reported in three-quarters of the country’s departments. His remarks came a day after the fifth round of nationwide protests.
Several schools remained blockaded in Paris, including Voltaire, Helene-Boucher and the Balzac school complex. Balzac’s administration suspended in-person classes, citing difficulties accessing the site and safety concerns.
Geffray said Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste would submit proposals to improve Parcoursup, France’s university admissions platform, to the prime minister by the end of October.
He said he was open to “adjustments, possibly substantial ones”, while questioning what would replace the platform if it were abolished.
According to Geffray, fewer than 20 percent of the 90,000 contributions submitted through a government platform collecting students’ complaints concerned Parcoursup.
He ruled out immediate changes to the baccalaureate, France’s school-leaving examination, saying: “I’m not going to change the baccalaureate six months before a presidential election; we need to stop constantly reforming.”
Students demand investment
Student representatives are scheduled to meet Geffray and Baptiste on Thursday afternoon as they press for €10 billion ($11 billion) in investment.
Pierre Sourzat, president of the organisation Les Lyceens!, told Franceinfo that students expected concrete measures after receiving “only crumbs”.
Although protest organisers have not called for a sixth round of demonstrations on Thursday, the Union of High School Students urged demonstrators to maintain their blockades.
Union President Ryad Rani and other student representatives also called for participation in a “yellow vest” demonstration scheduled for Saturday.
Meanwhile, classes resumed at Kleber High School in Strasbourg, where clashes between students and police had occurred in recent weeks.

Sri Lanka Customs exceeds 2026 annual revenue target ahead of schedule
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:22:45 CST
20:22:45 KST

COLOMBO, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Sri Lanka Customs has surpassed its annual revenue target for 2026 with more than two months remaining in the year, the Customs announced Wednesday.
It said it had collected 2.208 trillion Sri Lankan rupees (about 6.69 billion U.S. dollars) in revenue as of Tuesday, exceeding its full-year target of 2.207 trillion rupees.
The latest figures indicate that Customs has exceeded its annual target by 1 billion rupees, reaching the milestone nearly 11 weeks before the end of the year.
The achievement means that any additional revenue collected during the remainder of 2026 will further increase the department's collections beyond its original annual target. ■

China's finance ministry outlines key agenda items for APEC Finance Ministers' Meeting
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:22:39 CST
20:22:39 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Finance has introduced the key agenda items and expected outcomes of the APEC Finance Ministers' Meeting scheduled on Oct. 20 and 21 in Hong Kong.
A ministry official said China will put forward four major topics -- fiscal policies to support people's livelihoods, financing of digital infrastructure, promoting inclusive finance tailored to local conditions, and fostering exchanges and cooperation among young finance professionals across APEC.
Economies urgently need to strengthen macroeconomic policy coordination and adopt appropriate fiscal and financial policies to better support innovation and inclusive development, the official said.
At the same time, the rapid advancement of digital technologies and artificial intelligence has generated new demand for digital infrastructure investment and financing, and highlighted the importance of improving exchanges among young finance professionals and strengthening future policy-making capacity, the official said.
Finance ministers or their representatives from 21 APEC economies, along with senior representatives from relevant international organizations and partner institutions, will attend the meeting.
At the meeting, representatives of APEC economies will hold in-depth exchanges and work toward consensus documents and deliverables on major topics, the official said.
"Through these outcomes, we hope to pool useful experience from all parties, promote policy exchanges and experience sharing, and provide support for deepening Asia-Pacific financial cooperation and sustaining Asia-Pacific economic growth," the official said.
The official said the meeting in Hong Kong will build up financial sector outcomes ahead of the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, scheduled in Shenzhen in November.
China stands ready to work with all APEC economies to uphold multilateralism, deepen macroeconomic policy coordination, maintain the stability and smooth functioning of regional industrial and supply chains, and jointly promote long-term sustainable economic growth in the Asia-Pacific to advance the building of the Asia-Pacific community, the official added. ■

Yemen's Houthis claim large-scale missile, drone attack on Saudi airport, oil facilities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
19:22:37 CST
20:22:37 KST

SANAA, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Wednesday it had launched a large-scale missile and drone attack targeting an airport and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia, vowing to continue strikes against Saudi targets in the coming days.
In a statement broadcast by Houthi-run al-Masirah TV, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the group targeted Saudi energy giant Aramco in Dhahran in the Eastern Province, as well as King Khalid International Airport and an Aramco refinery in Riyadh.
According to Sarea, the operation involved "a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones," which accurately hit their targets, causing damage and fires.
The Houthi spokesperson said the operation was carried out in retaliation for Saudi Arabia-led strikes on the Houthi-held capital of Sanaa and other areas under the group's control. He said Saudi-led forces had carried out 2,281 air and missile strikes since the latest escalation began.
Sarea vowed that the group's attacks "deep inside Saudi Arabia" would continue in the coming days, targeting airports and oil facilities. He also renewed a warning to international airlines, civilians and employees to stay away from airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia that the group had designated as targets.
The Houthi claim came after the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said it intercepted six Houthi missiles and three drones heading towards Saudi Arabia on Tuesday. An Aramco administrative building in Dhahran was targeted Tuesday evening, sparking a limited fire, while debris from two cruise missiles intercepted over Riyadh injured four people and damaged 15 homes, Saudi authorities said Wednesday.
The latest Houthi operations followed a series of Saudi-led coalition strikes on Tuesday targeting the Yemen Petroleum Company's Al-Sabaha fuel storage and distribution facility west of Sanaa, as well as fuel facilities in the Red Sea province of Hodeidah.
Cross-border hostilities have intensified sharply in recent days. A Houthi attack on a passenger terminal at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Saturday killed 12 people and injured 309 others, according to the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation. The Saudi-led coalition subsequently vowed a firm response to the attack.
Yemen has been mired in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. Major hostilities had largely subsided following a UN-brokered truce in 2022, before the latest fighting led to a sharp escalation in ground battles and cross-border missile, drone and air attacks. ■

JAKARTA, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Supply disruptions and surging consumption have triggered fuel supply bottlenecks across Indonesia's resort island of Bali, causing long queues at gas stations, state-owned oil and gas firm Pertamina said Wednesday.

Pertamina and the Bali provincial government assured the public that overall fuel stocks are sufficient, with new shipments arriving and round-the-clock deliveries underway to ease congestion and restore normal supply. ■

Vietnam's Party official calls for urgent actions to achieve over 10 pct economic growth
China
Unknown Publisher

HANOI, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Tran Cam Tu, permanent member of the Secretariat of the Communist Party of Vietnam Central Committee, on Wednesday urged Party organizations and local authorities to take decisive actions to achieve the country's economic growth target of over 10 percent this year, local media Nhan Dan reported.
Speaking at a conference with Party organizations of localities and state agencies in Hanoi on the day, Tu called for stronger implementation of Party resolutions, improvement in administrative reform and tougher actions against corruption, wastefulness and negative phenomena, the report said.
Tu underscored the need to accelerate public investment disbursement, resolve stalled projects and develop domestic businesses, particularly those in supporting industry and with strong technological capacity and supply chain linkages.
He called for measures to address unemployment among more than 1.6 million young people, describing it as a critical issue affecting social stability and long-term development.
Vietnam's gross domestic product grew 9.95 percent year on year in the third quarter and 9.01 percent in the first nine months, the report added.
The country is seeking to achieve an average economic growth rate of at least 10 percent in the 2026-2030 period under the resolution of the 14th National Party Congress, according to the Vietnam News Agency. ■

Russia seeks to strip Dutch event of Olympic status over gymnast ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:22:35 UTC
20:22:35 KST

Russia seeks to strip Dutch event of Olympic status over gymnast ban
Russia will seek to strip an upcoming gymnastics championship in the Netherlands of its Olympic qualifying status after the Dutch authorities denied visas to three of its top athletes, Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev announced.
The Netherlands refused entry visas to Angelina Melnikova, Viktoria Listunova, and Anna Kalmykova, the Russian Gymnastics Federation (RGF) revealed on Tuesday, barring them from the World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam in three days, a qualifying event for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. According to the RGF, official refusal notices said “one or more Schengen member states” considered the athletes “a threat to their international relations.”
In a statement later that day, Degtyarev said the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC) will demand that the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and World Gymnastics revoke Rotterdam’s Olympic qualifying status over “discrimination” and violations of equal competition rules.
“The politically motivated refusal by the Netherlands to issue visas to the leaders of Russia’s artistic gymnastics team once again shows that Europe is no place for high-performance sport,” Degtyarev said, warning: “Today, Europeans have disregarded the decisions of international organizations and denied Russians visas, tomorrow they will refuse entry to someone else.”
Only four gymnasts from the Russian squad have so far obtained visas; five others are still awaiting decisions.
Melnikova was set to defend her women’s all-around world title after winning gold at last year’s championships in Jakarta. She also won all-around gold at this year’s European Championships in Zagreb. Listunova won Olympic team gold alongside Melnikova at the Tokyo Games, where she was Russia’s youngest gymnast at just 16. Kalmykova, 18, is among the youngest members of the squad. She helped Russia win the team title in Zagreb and claimed individual all-around silver.
Missing Rotterdam will hurt the trio’s chances of reaching the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics but won’t rule them out. The championships are the first stage of the qualification process, with individual berths still available through later World Cup events and continental championships in 2027 and 2028.
‘Inhumane’: Visa snub sparks outrage
The move drew criticism from Russian athletes and sports officials. The RGF called it “direct discrimination against Russian athletes” and a “a flagrant violation of the principle of equal conditions for Olympic qualification.” RGF Vice President Nikita Nagorny called the situation “disgusting.”
Two-time Olympic gymnastics champion Lidia Ivanova accused the Dutch of deliberately sidelining Russia’s strongest competitors.
“With this decision, they are demonstrating their weakness,” she told Match TV. “They did this knowing full well that they were denying visas to top Russian gymnasts... It’s sheer nastiness.”
Olympic speed skating champion Svetlana Zhurova also accused the Dutch of shutting out strong rivals, telling RT that politicizing sports is destroying it.
Reacting on social media, Melnikova said she “felt like crying” and called the actions “inhumane.”
“If they keep mixing sport with politics to such an extent, it will become a complete nightmare,” she said, posting a team photograph with the caption: “This is what the Netherlands considers a threat to international relations.”
Western bans and Russian medals
Russian and Belarusian athletes were excluded from numerous international competitions following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022, after an IOC recommendation and bans imposed by individual federations. Earlier this year, the IOC provisionally lifted its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee, opening the way for a broader return. Several federations, including World Gymnastics, have since eased their restrictions.
The shift has met resistance in the EU, a strong supporter of Ukraine. Nine member states, including the Netherlands, urged Brussels in an open letter to cut funding for international sporting bodies that readmit Russian and Belarusian athletes. On Monday, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas promised proposals to “sustain Russia’s isolation in global sports.”
Russia has called the bans on its athletes politically motivated and “cowardly.” Despite the restrictions, Russian athletes have continued to win titles wherever they are allowed to compete.
Last week, Inal Tasoev won gold in the men’s over-100 kg division at the 2026 World Judo Championships in Baku. In August, Russian artistic swimmers swept all three golds awarded on the opening day of the World Junior Aquatics Championships in Budapest. In July, Pavel Graudyn won the men’s individual saber title at the World Fencing Championships in Hong Kong, and Russian junior figure skaters swept all four disciplines at an ISU Junior Grand Prix event in China in August, returning after a four-year ban.

Exhibition of pioneering Hong Kong school for national talent in early 1940s opens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Exhibition of pioneering Hong Kong school for national talent in early 1940s opens
Showcase of Ta Teh Institute and its legacy will be presented at Hong Kong Museum of History from Wednesday to February 15 next year
A new exhibition about a pioneering school that nurtured talent for the country has opened at a Hong Kong history museum as part of the government’s efforts to promote national education, with many exhibits shown in the city for the first time.
“National Development and Achievements Series: Cultivation and Renewal – The Education Legacy of Hong Kong’s Ta Teh Institute”, a free exhibition presented by the Leisure and Cultural Services Department, will run at the Hong Kong Museum of History in Tsim Sha Tsui from Wednesday to February 15 next year.
Ta Teh Institute was a liberal arts university established in Tuen Mun in 1946 during the Chinese Civil War. It was the second university to be established in the city after the University of Hong Kong. The institute closed down in 1949.

Syria accuses Israel of arming Druze militias in Suweida
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
11:21:01 UTC
20:21:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria says Israel funding Druze militias to fuel chaos
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani has accused Israel of supplying weapons and financial support to armed militias in the southern province of Suweida, alleging that Israel is seeking to destabilise Syria and undermine its sovereignty.
Speaking at a press conference in Damascus on Tuesday, al-Shaibani said Israel was supporting armed groups operating outside the authority of the Syrian state, amid continuing tensions over the future of the predominantly Druze province.
"Israel supports armed militias operating outside the law in the city of Sweida, providing them with weapons and funding to pursue an agenda of chaos in the region," he said, according to Syria's official SANA news agency.
The accusations come amid mounting concerns over Israel's involvement in southern Syria, where Israeli forces have expanded their military presence since the overthrow of Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
Al-Shaibani accused Israel of pursuing a wider campaign to destabilise the country through attacks on infrastructure, the occupation of additional Syrian territory and the displacement and detention of Syrian civilians.
He said the fate of dozens of Syrians detained by Israeli forces remained unknown, calling on the international community to intervene and prevent further escalation.
Suweida has remained largely outside central government control following deadly clashes in July 2025 involving Druze armed factions, Bedouin groups and Syrian government forces.
The violence, which included abuses against Druze civilians by government-linked fighters, deepened mistrust between Damascus and sections of the Druze community.
Israel subsequently launched airstrikes against Syrian government positions, including targets in Damascus, claiming that its intervention was necessary to protect Syria's Druze minority.
However, Israeli involvement has also raised concerns about efforts to encourage the fragmentation of Syria by supporting armed groups opposed to the central government.
Much of Suweida is now controlled by factions associated with Druze religious leader Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, who has openly advocated separating the province from Damascus and establishing an independent Druze entity under Israeli protection.
In January, al-Hijri told Israeli newspaper Yedioth Ahronoth that his movement considered itself closely aligned with Israel and viewed the country as a guarantor of its political future.
"We see ourselves as an inseparable part of the existence of the State of Israel. This relationship is international and of critical importance," he said.
He also called for Syria's partition, arguing that independent or autonomous territories represented a possible future for the country.
In August, al-Hijri went further, declaring during a gathering in Suwayda that his supporters were an "integral part of the State of Israel" and shared its ideology.
His position has nevertheless faced opposition from other Druze religious figures, activists and armed factions who reject Israeli intervention and support maintaining Suwayda within a unified Syrian state.
The New Arab has previously reported on allegations that Israel has provided financial and military assistance to Druze militias operating in Suweida, including the Military Council, an armed faction associated with al-Hijri.
According to a Washington Post investigation published in December 2025, Israeli officials acknowledged providing support to Druze armed groups through the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF).
The report detailed financial transfers, weapons supplies and military assistance, including an alleged payment of $24,000 to help establish the Military Council.
It also described cooperation involving military training and the provision of weapons, including anti-tank missiles, to strengthen Druze factions opposed to Damascus.
The allegations have added to concerns that Israel is seeking to cultivate armed allies in southern Syria as part of a broader effort to prevent the re-establishment of strong central government authority.
Israel has repeatedly demanded the demilitarisation of southern Syria and opposed the deployment of Syrian government forces near its borders, while continuing military operations inside Syrian territory.
Following Assad's overthrow, Israeli forces seized the UN-monitored buffer zone established under the 1974 disengagement agreement and expanded their presence beyond positions occupied before December 2024.
Israel has occupied most of Syria's Golan Heights since 1967, an occupation not recognised by the international community.
Despite the tensions, Damascus and Israel have engaged in several rounds of US-mediated negotiations aimed at establishing new security arrangements along their shared frontier.
In August, Syrian and Israeli delegations met in Jordan under American mediation to discuss Israeli military operations, the detention of Syrian civilians and the possibility of withdrawing Israeli forces to positions held before Assad's overthrow.
Al-Shaibani called for Israel to return to the 1974 disengagement agreement and allow the United Nations Disengagement Observer Force to carry out its responsibilities.
He also urged Israel to engage seriously in the US-sponsored negotiations, reiterating Damascus's commitment to reaching an agreement that respects Syrian sovereignty and territorial integrity.
The Syrian foreign minister's latest accusations come as the government of President Ahmed al-Sharaa continues efforts to consolidate its authority across the country, with Suwayda remaining one of the principal areas outside Damascus's control.

Preparing for winter: a home checklist to help retain heat and prepare for outages
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
14:11:29 EEST
20:11:29 KST

Preparing for winter: a home checklist to help retain heat and prepare for outages
Kyiv • UNN
These tips will help retain heat, check the heating system and electrical wiring, and prepare supplies of water, food, and medicine. Fire safety is also highlighted separately.
Against the backdrop of Russia’s aggressive attacks on Ukraine’s energy system, people are trying more actively than last year to prepare for winter, both in cities and in towns. All the more so because domestic and foreign politicians and experts unanimously warn that the winter of 2026–2027 could prove to be the harshest and most difficult in the entire history of our country.
UNN has compiled a practical checklist for residents of apartments and private houses that will help reduce heat loss in advance, make sure equipment is in working order, arrange a water supply, and plan what to do in case of power outages.
How to insulate windows and doors to avoid losing heat
It is worth starting with the simplest things: check whether there are drafts coming through the windows, balcony doors, or entrance doors. Worn-out seals should be replaced, gaps around frames should be sealed, and the fittings adjusted if necessary.
You can take thick-fabric curtains out of the closet or buy some. They help reduce the feeling of cold near the window and eliminate small drafts. However, they should be positioned so that the fabric does not cover the radiators. First, such an artificial barrier between the room and the radiator will inevitably prevent the room from warming up. Second, there is a risk that at some point the curtain could begin to smolder from the high temperatures and cause a fire.
Likewise, radiators should not be blocked by furniture or decorative screens, so as not to impede the distribution of heat throughout the room.
If you live in a private house, in addition to the windows and doors, you should обязательно inspect the roof and take care of insulating the attic. Without this, even continuous gas or stove heating will not create a feeling of warmth in the home, because heat losses will be enormous.
At the same time, you should not resort to the opposite extreme of completely blocking ventilation openings for the sake of warmth. Even in winter, rooms need to be aired, especially if condensation forms on the glass or mold appears. If the house is heated with firewood or food is prepared on a stove powered by a gas cylinder, properly functioning ventilation is an essential condition for safe living. Neglecting safety could ultimately end tragically for all the home's residents, who risk fatal carbon monoxide poisoning.
Why heating should be checked before the first frosts
Residents of apartments with centralized heating should inspect radiators, valves, and pipe connections. Traces of rust, moisture, or leaks are reasons to contact the building manager or a plumber.
Owners of gas boilers need to arrange maintenance in advance: checking the boiler, ventilation, and flue systems to ensure they are working properly. If the house has a stove or fireplace, its structure should be checked for cracks before the season begins, the chimney cleaned, and the dampers and doors checked to make sure they function properly.
A separate issue for apartment buildings is preparing the common property. Through the homeowners’ association or management company, it is worth finding out whether the heating substation has been inspected, pipes in the basement insulated, windows in the entrance stairwell glazed, and doors made to close tightly.
How to prepare the electrical system and backup lighting for the winter months
Before winter, it is also worth inspecting accessible sockets, switches, and cables. Hot sockets or a burning smell are good reasons to call an electrician.
In case of power outages, it is advisable to have flashlights, spare batteries, charged power banks, and cables for phones at home. You should ask your provider whether the internet will work without electricity and how to power the router.
If finances allow, you can purchase a power station. It should be selected according to the power requirements of the appliances you plan to connect. Such equipment must not be covered, placed near heat sources, used with damaged cables, or connected to the home electrical system with a homemade cable featuring two plugs. You should also avoid buying a power station "second-hand," from questionable sellers, or on Chinese marketplaces. In such cases, there is a possibility of encountering an uncertified, damaged, or defective product.
Water and food supplies in case of a blackout
One of the most important aspects of preparing for winter (especially in a city) is storing water. The guideline for an adult is about three liters of drinking water and 10–12 liters of utility water per day. It is advisable to calculate a minimum reserve for at least three days, taking into account children, pets, and the needs of people requiring care.
For storing drinking water, clean, tightly sealed food-grade containers are suitable. Utility water for hygiene and flushing the toilet can be kept in other large bottles or buckets, or the bathtub can be filled with it.
Among food products, it is better to choose those that can be stored for a long time without refrigeration and do not require heat treatment (boiling or frying): canned goods, crispbreads, nuts, dried fruit, ready-made cereals, or other long-storage products. Before arranging these supplies on the shelves of a kitchen cabinet, it is worth checking the expiration dates once again and placing a manual can opener nearby.
How to live in a home without heating and not freeze
In case the heat goes out, you should prepare thermal underwear, warm socks, several layers of clothing, blankets, and sleeping bags. For temporary accommodation, you can choose one room with the fewest drafts and close the doors to other rooms: one small room is easier to heat than a multi-room apartment or private house.
It is strictly forbidden to heat a room with a gas stove or oven, or to use barbecues and charcoal indoors. A generator must also not be started in an apartment, building entrance, garage, or on a balcony: it should be used only outdoors, at least six meters away from doors and windows, in accordance with the manufacturer's instructions.
In addition, it is important to know and understand from the outset that prolonged cooling of a home is especially dangerous for young children, older people, and people with chronic diseases. If the temperature in the residence becomes critically low, you should consider in advance moving to a heated building or the nearest Point of Invincibility.
How to ensure fire safety and prepare a first-aid kit in winter
Before the season begins, it is advisable to check the smoke detector, and in homes with gas or stove heating or other combustion appliances, install a carbon monoxide detector. Carbon monoxide has no smell, so it is impossible to detect its presence without a special device. The fire extinguisher must be in working order and easily accessible.
You should also review your home first-aid kit: check the expiration dates of medicines, replenish first-aid supplies, and stock up on medications that must be taken regularly, in accordance with the doctor's prescriptions.
It is also useful to keep a small bag with the most essential items ready in case of a temporary evacuation.
General advice is to keep some cash in small denominations in case of disruptions to communications and payment services. For pets, provide food, water, and a carrier.
Reminder
