Former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar sues Netanyahu over Oct. 7 accusations, reveals ignored warnings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:39:48 UTC
19:39:48 KST

Former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar filed a defamation lawsuit against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Tel Aviv District Court on Wednesday, accusing him of spreading false allegations about Bar's conduct before the October 7, 2023 Hamas massacre and promoting conspiracy theories suggesting that the security chief had advance knowledge of an imminent attack. Bar is seeking 3 million shekels in damages and wants the court to reject any claim of immunity by Netanyahu.
In the lawsuit, Bar argues that Netanyahu received repeated warnings about the risk of a major security escalation but continued pursuing a policy of restraint toward Hamas. He is seeking the disclosure of documents detailing intelligence assessments and security discussions in the months preceding the massacre, declaring that in the absence of a state commission of inquiry, the truth would have to emerge through the courts.
The lawsuit, filed through attorneys Reuven Behar, Yoram Bonen and Doron Kol of the FBC law firm, presents Bar's account of the warnings he delivered to Netanyahu throughout 2023 and the intelligence developments in the hours before Hamas launched its attack.
Bar acknowledges that the Shin Bet failed to provide the intelligence necessary to prevent the massacre. However, he maintains that Netanyahu is attempting to shift responsibility for the disaster onto the security agency while obscuring his own decisions and policies.
"As the head of the service, I bear responsibility for the Shin Bet's failure to provide the intelligence required regarding the October 7 attack and its timing," Bar wrote. "Accordingly, with my head bowed before the bereaved families, I resigned from my position."
Bar announced his departure after the government had dismissed him. At the time, an interim High Court order against the dismissal was in effect, and the court subsequently ruled that the government's decision had been unlawful.
The lawsuit argues that Bar's acceptance of responsibility for the Shin Bet's intelligence failure does not absolve Netanyahu of responsibility for the policies that preceded the massacre. It accuses the prime minister of pursuing a strategy of containment, maintaining quiet in Gaza and facilitating funding that ultimately strengthened Hamas, despite Bar's objections.
He said he had remained silent for three years while awaiting the establishment of an independent state commission of inquiry that would examine both the Shin Bet's achievements and its failures.
"We fought, eliminated senior Hamas figures in Gaza and Lebanon, and brought hostages home through daring Shin Bet operations and determined negotiations," he wrote, accusing Netanyahu of conducting a sustained campaign of false allegations against him.
"Given the prime minister's unrestrained outburst, I decided not to remain silent and to show the public the motives behind such improper conduct," he added.
Bar further accused Netanyahu of using his position to prevent the establishment of any commission of inquiry while attempting to shape public opinion through what the lawsuit described as baseless manipulation.
"The plaintiff had no choice but to ask the honorable court to restore truth to its rightful place as the preferred option in this kind of discussion," the filing states.
Warnings ignored, restraint maintained
A central element of Bar's lawsuit concerns the intelligence assessments and recommendations he says he presented to Netanyahu throughout the months preceding October 7.
According to the filing, Bar repeatedly warned of the possibility of a multi-front confrontation, particularly involving Gaza, and cautioned that Israel's deterrence was weakening. He says those warnings intensified between July and September 2023, as Hamas expanded its activities and Israel approached the Jewish High Holidays.
Bar disputes the assessment that Hamas had been deterred from launching a major confrontation. He maintains that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar had become increasingly ideological and unpredictable, and that the Shin Bet recommended offensive measures against senior Hamas figures and operatives directing attacks from Gaza.
The proposals included restricting the entry of workers from Gaza, conducting targeted operations against terror organizers in the West Bank and preparing strikes against senior Hamas leaders. According to Bar, several recommendations were dismissed, received no response or were never implemented.
The updated lawsuit account also includes an allegation concerning a July 9, 2023, security cabinet meeting. Bar says that, against the backdrop of the discussion, some government officials had floated the idea of allowing Hamas to control the West Bank. He says he insisted on making clear that Hamas was a fundamentalist religious movement committed to Israel's destruction and the murder of Israelis. The filing does not identify the officials who raised the idea or establish that it was adopted as government policy.
The lawsuit also challenges Netanyahu's broader policy toward Gaza, which Bar characterizes as an approach of "quiet at any cost." He alleges that the prime minister favored avoiding military confrontation, preserving relative calm and allowing Hamas to remain the governing authority in the territory.
Bar further claims that Netanyahu supported continued Qatari funding to Gaza despite Shin Bet warnings that some of the money was contributing to Hamas' military buildup.
According to the lawsuit, intelligence presented to Netanyahu indicated that funds ostensibly intended for civilian needs were also supporting activities such as tunnel construction and weapons procurement. Bar says he supported action against senior Hamas leaders and that the security agency had developed plans for targeted killings, but those plans were not approved.
The filing also describes disagreements over the Shin Bet's role in shaping national security policy. Bar alleges that Netanyahu told him strategic decisions were the government's responsibility rather than the intelligence chief's, even as the agency continued warning about the consequences of restraint.
What happened on the night of October 7?
Another central dispute concerns the intelligence available to Netanyahu during the hours immediately preceding the Hamas attack.
Bar rejects Netanyahu's allegation that the Shin Bet concealed information about an imminent threat. According to the lawsuit, the agency distributed an alert at 3:03 a.m. on October 7 to Israel's security organizations, including the military, police and National Security Council.
The warning identified indications of possible offensive activity along the Gaza border, although the exact nature and scale of the threat remained unclear.
Bar says he also instructed his staff to update Netanyahu's military secretary at the time, Avi Gil, in accordance with the communication procedures used by the Prime Minister's Office. The decision, he claims, was documented in the Shin Bet's computerized operations-center records before the attack began.
The lawsuit describes another obstacle to direct communication between the intelligence chief and the prime minister. Bar claims that, unlike former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, Netanyahu did not provide him with his personal cellphone number. Communications therefore passed through his military secretary or chief of staff Tzachi Braverman.
Bar alleges that Netanyahu neither returned his calls nor intervened after the attack began. He also claims that Netanyahu did not change the procedure requiring security agencies to communicate with the prime minister through his military secretariat even after October 7.
The filing also rejects claims surrounding the deployment of a Shin Bet tactical team known as Tequila during the night. According to Bar, such teams are dispatched many times a year, and their deployment does not require the agency director's personal authorization. He argues that the decision to send a team cannot, by itself, demonstrate advance knowledge of an impending large-scale assault.
Bar also denies speaking with the IDF chief of staff or the head of Military Intelligence before the attack.
According to his account, his first conversation with the chief of staff took place at 6:29 a.m., after rocket fire had already begun. During that conversation, he warned that the rocket barrage might be intended to divert attention from infiltrations into Israeli territory.
The lawsuit further alleges that Netanyahu had prohibited Bar from speaking with then-Defense Minister Yoav Gallant. It notes that senior military officials, including the head of Southern Command and the IDF Operations Directorate chief, returned from leave in response to the developing situation.
Bar argues that Netanyahu has repeatedly blamed the Shin Bet for matters outside the agency's operational responsibility, including the deployment of military forces, supervision of civilian gatherings and activation of local security teams.
The lawsuit describes those accusations as malicious and false allegations intended to conceal the truth from the public.
'The lies can no longer be allowed to spread'
Bar also links the deterioration in his relationship with Netanyahu to an affidavit he previously submitted to the High Court of Justice.
In that affidavit, he raised concerns about potential security risks involving advisers in the Prime Minister's Office and their alleged connections to Qatar, as well as allegations that the government sought to use the Shin Bet against political protests.
According to Bar, Netanyahu's subsequent statements amounted to a personal campaign of defamation that also damaged the reputation of the security service, its personnel and those killed in the line of duty.
He cites the continued absence of a state commission of inquiry, alongside reports of alleged attempts to alter official records and what he describes as efforts to establish misleading narratives about October 7, as reasons for taking legal action.
"It is no longer possible to allow the prime minister's stream of lies to continue seeping into public consciousness," Bar wrote.
He argues that attempts to conceal information, rewrite history and systematically spread conspiracy theories represent not only unacceptable leadership practices but also a danger to Israel.
As part of the proceedings, Bar intends to seek disclosure of intelligence assessments, meeting records and other documents relating to the warnings he says were delivered before the massacre.
His lawyers anticipate that Netanyahu could invoke immunity and say they are prepared to challenge such an argument. They acknowledge that the court would have to balance the public interest in examining the evidence against the need to protect national security.
"In an era of divisive leadership based on lies, only determined action will restore truth to the public discourse," Bar wrote.
He urged Netanyahu not to hide behind claims of immunity, adding: "In the absence of a state commission of inquiry, the truth will emerge in court. A little light will dispel much darkness."
The warnings Bar says Netanyahu received
The lawsuit includes a detailed chronology of meetings, written assessments and recommendations delivered to Netanyahu between November 2022 and October 2023. The following are the central developments, according to Bar's account.
November 7, 2022: At an initial working meeting before Netanyahu returned to office, Bar warned that Sinwar was directing attacks from Gaza into the West Bank without paying a price. He reiterated an earlier recommendation to target Sinwar and strengthen Israeli deterrence. The filing records no response from Netanyahu.
January 8, 2023: Bar warned that Sinwar was seeking a multi-front confrontation and that the absence of an Israeli response to attacks directed from Gaza was undermining deterrence. He recommended action in Gaza, including possible restrictions on workers entering Israel.
January 17: During a visit to the Shin Bet, Netanyahu called for managing the confrontation with Hamas in Gaza through measures that were not overly aggressive.
February 13: Bar sent Netanyahu an unusual personal letter warning of a "perfect storm." According to the lawsuit, he argued that Israel's internal divisions and instability in the Palestinian arena were creating an opportunity for its enemies. Netanyahu's response focused on the Shin Bet's responsibility to protect elected officials and their families.
March 7–22: Bar warned that Hamas was drawing encouragement from Israel's internal divisions and that intelligence warnings about attacks had increased threefold. He recommended targeting a senior Hamas figure in Gaza, but says the proposal received no substantive response.
April 3–19: A series of intelligence assessments warned of growing cooperation among hostile organizations and increasing attacks originating from the West Bank and Gaza. Bar advocated targeted offensive measures to reverse the deterioration in deterrence.
May 21: Following Operation Shield and Arrow, Bar presented intelligence suggesting Sinwar was undergoing what he described as a messianic transformation. He recommended expanding targeted killings across multiple arenas. According to the lawsuit, Netanyahu expressed concern that Israel's enemies could respond by attempting similar operations against him personally.
May 24: Bar warned that Hamas had interpreted Israel's reluctance to confront it as a sign of weakness. He called for a change in policy, but says his recommendation went unanswered.
July 6: In an annual strategic planning document, the Shin Bet outlined Hamas' military buildup and recommended renewed targeted operations. According to the filing, the document was delivered to Netanyahu through his military secretary and returned several days later with handwritten comments from the prime minister. Netanyahu wrote that the head of the Shin Bet was not responsible for setting Israel's national strategy.
July 9: Bar told a security cabinet meeting that Operation Guardian of the Walls in 2021 had marked a turning point toward multi-front confrontation. According to the lawsuit, the discussion took place against the backdrop of a proposal by some government officials to allow Hamas to control the West Bank. Bar says he demanded that it be made clear that Hamas was a fundamentalist movement committed to destroying Israel and killing Israelis.
July 23: Bar says he delivered a direct strategic warning of war, explaining that Israel's enemies viewed the country's internal divisions as an opportunity. He cautioned that intelligence could not necessarily predict the precise date or hour of an attack and recommended preventive action. According to the lawsuit, Netanyahu did not act on the warning.
August 2: An intelligence assessment warned of connections between Hamas and Iranian terror networks and the possibility of an escalation in Gaza. Bar recommended preparations for military confrontation and continued targeted operations.
August 20–22: Bar warned that Israel was entering a dangerous period ahead of the Jewish High Holidays. He argued that Hamas was no longer deterred and was intensifying its involvement in attacks, calling for offensive action and improved preparedness along the Gaza border.
September 3: Bar warned that Hamas was exploiting Israel's policy of maintaining calm to strengthen itself without consequences. He recommended targeting operatives directing attacks from Gaza.
September 12: At a cabinet discussion attended by Netanyahu, Bar warned that the security situation required a change in approach. According to the lawsuit, Netanyahu instead instructed officials to seek the quietest possible holiday period.
September 14–17: Bar reported an unusual message from an adversary that he interpreted as evidence of inadequate Israeli deterrence and an increasingly unavoidable confrontation. The updated account explicitly states that Bar immediately informed Netanyahu about the message. He recommended heightened alertness along the Gaza border.
September 21: A Shin Bet assessment recommended a preemptive strike to prevent further escalation. According to Bar, the proposed operation was postponed until after the holidays because of Netanyahu's instruction to maintain calm.
September 27: At a security discussion, Netanyahu said he did not want an escalation with Gaza and called for the judicious use of force.
October 1: Bar warned that the level of terrorist activity being directed from Gaza had reached a peak. He recommended a plan to target senior Hamas figures and those directing attacks, while warning that fighting could erupt before the holiday period ended. According to the lawsuit, Netanyahu authorized preparations for the proposed operations, but no follow-up meeting was convened and the measures were not implemented.

The SBU and police applied a new article of the Criminal Code against a fraudulent call center for the first time
Kyiv • UNN
The SBU and National Police exposed a fraudulent call center in the Lviv region and detained three participants. Victims were robbed through malicious files and crypto-assets.
The Security Service and the National Police have applied a new article of the Criminal Code of Ukraine for the first time. Law enforcement officers uncovered a covert call center in the Lviv region, the SBU press center reports, according to UNN.
Details
The investigation established that the suspects gained unauthorized access to the funds of citizens of Ukraine and EU countries and then appropriated them.
To find potential victims, the perpetrators created fake accounts of women on social media and dating platforms. After establishing contact, the perpetrators sent their interlocutors malicious files disguised as Google Photos of attractive girls. Once such a file was opened, software was installed on the victim’s device that provided hidden remote control over the gadget
They cashed out the stolen money through an illegal currency exchange office, using crypto-assets. Three suspects were detained "red-handed" on the premises of the call center.
They were notified of suspicion under the following articles of the Criminal Code of Ukraine:
-  Parts 1 and 2 of Article 255-4 (creation of an electronic-communications fraud organized group, leadership of it or its structural unit, as well as participation in such a group); 
-  Part 5 of Article 190 (fraud); 
-  Part 5 of Article 361 (unauthorized interference with the operation of information (automated), electronic communications, and information and communication systems, and electronic communications networks). 
Context
The Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine supported strengthening liability for electronic-communications fraud and the activities of fraudulent call centers. The relevant Law No. 10190 was adopted in its entirety on September 16.
Later, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed the law.

Scientists may have finally solved the mystery of the Moon’s two faces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:38:46 UTC
19:38:46 KST

Scientists may have finally solved the mystery of the Moon’s two faces
- Date:
- October 14, 2026
- Source:
- Science China Press
- Summary:
- Scientists may have solved a long-standing mystery about why the Moon’s two sides are so different, using samples collected from its farside for the first time. Their findings suggest that uneven heating from Earth's gravitational pull drove enormous flows of ancient magma, creating the dramatically different lunar landscapes we see today.
- Share:
Scientists investigating why the Moon's two sides look so different have uncovered new evidence that could help explain this long-standing mystery. A research team led by Professor Hejiu Hui of Nanjing University analyzed lunar rocks collected by China's Chang'e-6 (CE6) mission and found clues suggesting that enormous movements of molten rock shaped the Moon billions of years ago.
The researchers examined the chemical compositions of three types of lunar rock: anorthosites, Mg-suite rocks, and mare basalts. They compared these samples from the Moon's far side with material collected from the near side during the Apollo and Chang'e-5 missions. Their findings suggest that the Moon's striking differences emerged through large-scale heat-driven circulation within its ancient lunar magma ocean (LMO), after the Moon became tidally locked to Earth.
Why the Moon's Two Sides Are So Different
The side of the Moon facing Earth looks remarkably different from the hemisphere permanently turned away from us. The near side features vast plains of dark volcanic basalt and relatively high concentrations of potassium, rare earth elements, and phosphorus (KREEP). In contrast, the far side is dominated by ancient, heavily cratered highlands, with a much thicker crust and relatively few volcanic plains.
Scientists have debated the origins of this uneven structure for decades. Proposed explanations have included differences in how the Moon's original magma ocean circulated, a massive collision, heating caused by gravitational tides, and uneven development of the lunar crust. However, none of these ideas has gained universal acceptance.
Another important question has remained unanswered. Although the contrasts between the two hemispheres are clearly visible at the surface and within the crust, scientists have been uncertain whether similar differences extend deep into the lunar mantle.
Chang'e-6 Samples Reveal a Surprising Similarity
A major opportunity to investigate this mystery arrived in 2024, when Chang'e-6 became the first mission to return samples from the Moon's far side. For the first time, scientists could directly compare rocks collected from both lunar hemispheres.
The analysis revealed an important similarity beneath the Moon's contrasting surfaces. Basalts collected by Chang'e-6 show chemical signatures indicating that they originated from depleted mantle material, much like the low-Ti basalts brought back by Apollo astronauts. This suggests that the mantle cumulates, minerals that accumulated as the Moon's magma ocean crystallized, do not differ substantially in composition between the two hemispheres.
The researchers found additional support for this conclusion in Mg-suite rocks. These rocks form through interactions between the crust and mantle when portions of the accumulated mantle material partially melt. Their magnesium number (Mg#) provides an important indicator of the composition of the mantle material from which they originated.
Because Mg-suite samples from Chang'e-6 and Apollo have similar Mg# values, the researchers concluded that the mantle cumulates beneath both sides of the Moon share broadly similar chemical characteristics. In other words, the materials that crystallized from the Moon's original magma ocean show no significant compositional divide between the near side and far side.
The Moon's Crust Tells a Different Story
While the mantle appears relatively uniform in composition, the lunar crust reveals a much more pronounced contrast.
Anorthosite samples returned by Chang'e-6 have higher peak Mg# values than comparable Apollo samples, indicating that the far side's crust contains more magnesium-rich material. This agrees with earlier observations made by instruments studying the Moon remotely.
The researchers also identified important chemical differences in Mg-suite rocks. Samples from Chang'e-6 contain extremely low concentrations of rare earth elements and have lower thorium-to-samarium ratios, expressed as Th/Sm, than their Apollo counterparts.
These differences suggest two possible explanations. Either Mg-suite magmas formed on the far side without substantial involvement from KREEP-rich material, or the layer containing these elements developed unevenly across the Moon, leaving the two hemispheres with different chemical compositions.
How Earth's Gravity May Have Shaped the Moon
Combining these findings, the researchers developed a model that could explain how the Moon acquired its two dramatically different faces.
According to their proposed scenario, the Moon's early magma ocean initially cooled and crystallized in a relatively uniform manner. This process produced the first mantle cumulates and anorthositic crust, before the Moon became tidally locked to Earth.
The situation changed once the Moon settled into an orbit that kept the same hemisphere facing our planet. At that time, Earth and the Moon were much closer together, and gravitational tidal forces generated more heat on the lunar near side than on the far side.
This uneven heating created a temperature difference across the Moon's molten interior, setting off large-scale horizontal circulation. Hot magma moved from the near side toward the far side, carrying previously formed magnesium-rich anorthosite material with it.
Over time, this movement accumulated more crustal material on the far side, helping explain why that hemisphere developed a thicker crust with a higher magnesium content.
At the same time, the remaining molten material flowed preferentially toward the near side. As a result, the far side developed only relatively thin layers enriched in KREEP and ilmenite-bearing cumulates (IBC), while more of these late-stage materials became concentrated on the near side.
This model of heat-driven magma circulation provides a possible explanation for why the Moon has a chemically similar mantle but such dramatically different crustal compositions. By connecting the newly analyzed Chang'e-6 samples with the Moon's early thermal history, the findings offer fresh insight into the processes that shaped Earth's closest celestial neighbor.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Science China Press. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Yuantao Gu, Yue Zhang, Wenxin Ouyang, Hejiu Hui, Kai Zhao, Yongli Xue, Ziyan Han, Yuxin Chen, Zhuqi Yang, Yutao Lin, Yue Guan, Qiuli Li, Tao Yang, Gang Zeng, Huan Hu, Zongjun Yin, Suping Wu, Nan Zhang, Xiaolei Wang, Xiancai Lu, Rucheng Wang. Lunar farside-nearside asymmetry formation during magma ocean solidification. National Science Review, 2026; 13 (15) DOI: 10.1093/nsr/nwag424

What the science really says about Blue Zones and living past 100
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:36:25 UTC
19:36:25 KST

Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.
You’ve probably heard of the Blue Zones: a handful of locations around the globe where people supposedly live to be 100 at astonishingly high rates. That evocative notion has inspired best-selling books, at least one Netflix documentary series, and no small number of diet plans.
But how certain can we be that Blue Zones really exist? My guest today has spent years digging into that question, and let’s just say he’s not convinced.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Saul Justin Newman is a senior research fellow at University College London and the University of Oxford. His new book, Morbid: Debunking Modern Longevity Science, takes a skeptical, irreverent look at the booming business of lengthening human lifespans and finds the data wanting.
Thank you so much for coming on to chat with us today.
Saul Newman: It’s my pleasure.
Feltman: So why don’t we start with how you first got interested in studying longevity?
Newman: Well, it was almost by accident. I’ve compared it to all sorts of things. I think the most fun was: Imagine the janitor fell into the dungeon at the castle and, you know, had to fight the dragon with a mop and bucket, right? It’s just—I didn’t mean to get involved. But a friend had sent me this paper in Nature, and I’d had an interest in it. I’d written this doctoral thesis on the evolution of how long you live. And he sent me this paper, and it was awful. I mean, completely awful.
They had decided that there was this limit to human life, right? 115, 125 years. And their logic was essentially, well, human improvements in lifespan have stopped getting better at old ages. But the way they’d discovered this was to accidentally round off all the data at these old ages to zero and publish that in the best journal in the world. And I couldn’t let it go because it was such a terrible paper. And, you know, it’s now eight years later, and I’m still trying to get it retracted.
And so I became interested, you know, if the standards of evidence are this low, what is the answer? You know, is there this limit to human life? Is there not? And from there, I just kept getting more and more interested. It was like being an air crash investigator. It’s macabre. Something has gone drastically wrong. But I also just, I really wanna know: What has happened? You know, what is the answer here? And here I am, almost a decade later, still tugging at threads.
Feltman: Well, and for listeners who don’t spend a lot of time looking at the statistics section of papers in Nature, could you unpack for us a little bit about what it seemed had gone wrong in that study? And then why, if so, there’s been so much pushback to you raising those concerns?
Newman: Well, the things that had gone wrong ran to maybe a dozen pages. But the two key ones were first, that they’d picked the wrong column in a spreadsheet, and that column had got rounded down to zero, right? And it was like, how much longer do I expect to live at age 100? There’s two columns, one that says the real value, one that’s rounded off, and they’d used the rounded-off data.
The second thing they’d done, which is even more, sort of, high-school-failure-at-maths kind of logic, was that they had said the maximum age that humans had reached had gone up and then down. But the sample size they’d used had also gone up and then down, right? They’d started including countries in the study, then they’d started taking them away. And if you corrected for that, like, within each country, the maximum human lifespan was going up.
And I think the reaction was really interesting because one part of the reaction was to just pretend it never happened, and the other was an opposing team who effectively said, “Oh, no, no, no, there’s no limit to human lifespan. We’re gonna publish in Science.” And what they’d done is they had rounded up all the 105-year-old records in Italy and said, “Well, we’re gonna fit our model, and we’re gonna show that instead of reaching a limit that you can’t survive past, there’s this other situation, a situation called a late-life mortality plateau.”
And what that really is is a situation where effectively you’re playing Russian roulette every few months in terms of survival, right? There’s no limit to how long you can get a run of luck, but your odds of dying every year are about 50 percent. Now, this was published in Science, and it was more extraordinary because the model they fit treated midlife as age 65 to 80. Now, that’s not midlife, and if you change that assumption at all in any direction and use the same data, the same models, they didn’t get a result. The result ran away. So out of 861 possible inputs, theirs was the only result that gave you a significant outcome and the only thing that gave you a science paper.
So that’s, you know, that’s either research fraud or an extraordinary, extraordinary coincidence, right? And I think we can figure out which one, because if it was a coincidence, they would’ve retracted the paper.
Feltman: Mm. So tell us a little bit about your new book. You know, like you said, it’s been almost a decade, thinking about this, digging into it. So how has your thinking on it evolved?
Newman: Well, when you look at this field, you can either get angry, or you could do what I’ve done, which is make a sort of self-effacing comedy book about how pointless it all is. Because you get this long parade, this carnival parade of ideas, and none of them ever work in aging science. Like, there’s never been a single thing that’s worked in aging science, and yet you’re spending billions of dollars. You know, one of these researchers, just one of them, had sunk something like $8 billion worth of [other] people’s money into nothing. He turned it into house extensions, effectively. And so, you know, my thinking has evolved to be more cynical.
But, I’ve come at this from a very interesting perspective because my job when I started getting interested in longevity involved manipulating organisms’ lifespans. I was predicting flowering time, right? In plants. And in plants, we have a excellent understanding of how to change how long something lives. It’s trivial, right? We’ve been doing it for century and a half at least. And yet those systems don’t look anything like the supposed longevity cures we’re being pitched. They have absolutely nothing to do with, you know, someone selling me pills on YouTube. And that contrast was remarkable to me because it enabled me to pull apart many of these core ideas that people in aging science have been pitching.
You know, one of them was this idea of telomeres, the idea that this little clock on the end of your chromosomes that gets shorter and shorter as you age is what makes you get older, effectively, is what makes you age. And this is an incredibly popular idea.
And it’s junk, because the core idea of the telomere hypothesis is that if clockwork shortening of these things on the end of your chromosomes causes aging, well, why not just make the clock longer or wind it up? And the answer is, well, it prevents cancer growth. You know, the original idea was that telomeres get shorter and shorter and shorter, and when they get short enough, cancers stop growing. It completely halts cancer growth, and that’s the benefit. So you get this tug-of-war between cancer on one side and aging on the other, and somewhere in the middle you end up with a bit of aging and a bit of cancer.
But the core problem hiding in the open is that cancer doesn’t stop growing, right? And yet everyone ages. So you have this thing that happens to every single one of us always, and the mechanism that’s supposed to be holding it in balance has been observed nowhere, any—like, by nobody. Cancers, like, they don’t spontaneously cease growing. So one of the questions raised is: How did you have this idea in the public with tens of thousands of scientific papers for decades when it is so ridiculous that the idea that this occurs?
And, you know, I kept running across problems like this again and again and again. One of the most popular was pulling apart Blue Zones, but this was sort of, it’s almost an afterthought in the process of pulling down these, sort of, charlatan-driven narratives of aging research.
Feltman: Well, and since this is one that I think will be most familiar to listeners, I would love to hear a little bit about the Blue Zone thing. You know: How did we become so obsessed with Blue Zones, and what did you find when you started poking around at them?
Newman: Well, initially I just was interested in a theoretical process. But the Blue Zones was fascinating because it’s hugely popular, and the idea is that somewhere far away, there’s this exotic place where people live past 100 at an extraordinary rate.
Now, first of all, the data behind that either doesn’t make sense or is in terrible shape. So in Okinawa, for example, it turned out that if an American plane had bombed the place during World War II, especially destroying, like, the town hall with all the birth records, that’s where you got the 100-year-olds. And this very simple reason was that the American GIs working in a different calendar, different language, had replaced the birth certificates. And of course they made errors.
And the other reason is this remarkable problem that in Japan you have the head of the household register a death. Now, if the household gets hit by a firebomb and everyone dies, who registers the death? Nobody. So you had this remarkable case in 2010 where 236,000 people, roughly 82 percent of the 100-year-olds in the country, turned out to have been long dead, and nobody had noticed, especially not the Blue Zones demographers, despite the fact they’d been studying the place since 1976.
The data actually got worse from there because Loma Linda, you know, I pressured the discoverer of the Loma Linda Blue Zone—the only American Blue Zone. “Where is your data?” And he admitted, “Well, I got asked by my editor to find an American Blue Zone, so I found one.” On the drive between his house in LA and Las Vegas, there’s a turn, and beneath the eight-lane freeway, is Loma Linda, which apparently has a fountain of youth. And that’s it. That’s the evidence.
And, you know, it got worse and worse. The Greek one was amazing. There was recently an investigative report into the only 100-year-old named by the Blue Zones for Greece. Now, he was claimed to reach 102, and he was claimed to have survived lung cancer for 30 years. But if you looked at his private documents, his personal documents, he was in his 90s, and if you asked his personal doctor, he’d never had cancer.
Feltman: Wow.
Newman: And that was, published in the New York Times and a bunch of cancer patients loved it. And it was based on nothing.
Feltman: What do you think it is that makes this field so prone to this kind of, you know, sloppy work at best and, you know, potentially outright deception?
Newman: It’s very simple. No one wants to go to the gym, right? Nobody, nobody wants to do the hard stuff that’s like, “Well, how do I live a long time?” Like, go and ask a doctor who cares about you, “How do I live a long time?” They’ll say what I say. “Get some exercise, don’t drink, don’t smoke, and if you’re in doubt, like, come and talk to the doctor again.” Now, none of that can be sold. Like, there’s no YouTube profit to be made out of that. So if you wanna avoid all that stuff, then someone will sell you a magic pill.
And even more, sort of, troublesome is, if you do all this stuff, if you’re a weekend warrior, and you run the marathon, you’re an even better sales target because you’re easy to convince that there’s something else you have to do, right? It’s very easy to convince these people that you’ve got to go further than the marathon. It’s simply not the case, but it leads to this extraordinary set of sales pitches. And we’re seeing this come out in really toxic ways because billionaires are very susceptible to this. And, when the stakes are that high, when there is, you know, some of these people selling longevity cures are making tens of millions of dollars, then they will go to any length to sell it. Any length. You know, you’ve got clinics in Saudi Arabia, clinics in Honduras. They go there explicitly because there are no laws, in governing whether or not you get any after-clinical care, whether or not you die. It’s really remarkable.
But I think the best example of this was when I looked at the people who are supposed to be the world’s oldest people, and I love them because they’re all cheeky scamps, right? Like, there’s no way they’re this old, you just have enough bravery to pretend. America’s oldest man, Charlie Smith, he was amazing. Charlie Smith is essentially just some guy who was working in a field picking fruit, and his boss says, “Charlie, you gotta get some ID.” So he goes to the Social Security Administration, they tell him he’s 113, and then they immediately lose the file. So Charlie is now, as far as anyone is concerned, he’s 113. so he goes to meet the president. They take him to the Apollo launch. They put him in the New York Times. They’re like, “This man is incredible.” It’s like he’s completely making it up, and nobody cares. Everyone loves the guy, and I love the guy. Like, he’s fantastic because it’s clear he’s probably about 68, but he’s just going with it. [Laughs].
We’re so desperate to believe that this happens that we’ve got, like, the chain-smoking, whiskey-drinking guy in the White House. He has no business being there, but he’s wonderful. And it happens, again and again. It’s really funny.
Feltman: So what do you think longevity research would look like if we actually did it?
Newman: Well, we do actually do it, and it’s called medicine. That’s what medicine is, right? People are saying, “Oh, well, what if we tried to make people live longer and have healthier lives?” Like, you think no one’s thought of this before? You think this is a revolutionary, like, new idea? It’s what medicine is. [Laughs].
And so you just get this torrent of nonsense about, “Oh, well, what if we extended [lifespan]?” We already have been doing this for thousands of years in a way that, you know, has rules and results. So I think if you cleaned up longevity research, what you would do is you would close the National Institute [on] Aging, and you would take every single dollar, probably double it, and put it into actual fundamental research that works. That’s all you would do.
And everyone who was in the NIA that knew what they were doing would just change their job title. And everyone who was a charlatan could go down the road and sell mattresses or whatever is plan B.
Feltman: [Laughs]. Well, thank you so much for coming on to chat with us. This has been great.
Newman: It’s been a real pleasure.
Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. Tune in on Friday to hear about folks who are seeking sobriety from social media.
Science Quickly is produced by me, Rachel Feltman, along with Fonda Mwangi, Allison Rodgers and Jeff DelViscio. This episode was edited by Alex Sugiura. Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. See you next time!

Claude just found a CRISPR-like DNA pattern, but even Anthropic's scientists aren't sure what it does
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:36:16 UTC
19:36:16 KST

Artificial intelligence companies have been making waves in mathematics, but they are also turning their attention to other sciences, too—including molecular biology.
Late last month, Anthropic claimed it had discovered a curious stretch of DNA in a virus called a bacteriophage that repeats over and over again. This is a similar feature to that of CRISPR, the basis of the powerful gene-editing tool CRISPR-Cas9.
The newly discovered DNA repeats sit next to a gene for a reverse transcriptase enzyme, a type of enzyme that copies RNA into DNA—a hint that this discovery may have some useful properties. But Eric Kauderer-Abrams, Anthropic’s head of life sciences, and Nicholas Perry, a researcher at the company, are clear: it’s still unknown exactly what this enzyme and the neighboring repeating pattern of DNA actually do.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Claude, Kauderer-Abrams says, displayed intuition and persistence similar to that of a real biologist in the lab, showing “exactly the type of logic that the really talented computational biologists that we work with would go after.”
But much more work is needed to understand what this region of the genome does, and Claude is no replacement for biologists, the scientists say. “What this internal domain does, we’re still not sure,” Kauderer-Abrams adds.
Scientific American spoke to Kauderer-Abrams and Perry to find out how they got Anthropic’s AI model Claude on the hunt for these interesting bits of DNA in the first place and how it found this stretch of DNA.
[An edited transcript of the interview follows.]
When you decided to use Claude to search for patterns in DNA, what did you hope to find?
KAUDERER-ABRAMS: Our efforts in the life sciences are organized around two goals. The first is to dramatically accelerate the pace of basic science, and the second is to accelerate curing disease and extending health span. The first scientific problem that we decided to directly pursue ourselves was trying to find and systematize and scale up the process of finding useful new things that already exist in nature and turning them into tools that that have utility in science and medicine. We were inspired from how many great discoveries that went on to revolutionize science and medicine came about from looking around in nature and finding these odd things—PCR [polymerase chain reaction] tests, for example, or CRISPR. We believe that, with [an] AI agent collaborating in every step of the process, we would be able to increase the rate of making these sorts of discoveries.
I want to clarify one important thing: citing this amazing lineage of discoveries, we are by no means claiming that what Claude has discovered here is of that status. This was the first discovery in our lab that Claude made on its own, and we’re excited by it. But we’re very early; it’s the very beginning.
We know that it has these interesting properties that may be suggestive of having some potential as a tool, but we have no idea what its function is yet, and we’re at the very beginning of the research.
What training data and prompts made this possible for Claude?
KAUDERER-ABRAMS: Great question. We do a lot of work on each of those two things. On the training data, we have been putting a tremendous amount of energy into training Claude in biology—in the hardcore scientific tasks like bioinformatics and structural biology and organic chemistry and some of the softer things ... related to trying to have research taste and some level of strategic decision-making for things on the drug development side.
As for what prompts we use, in this case, we gave Claude a fairly generic prompt to go looking for particular patterns in DNA sequences that are associated with reverse transcriptase enzymes. We’ve run these sorts of searches through other families [of DNA polymerases], but it was a fairly generic prompt. Obviously, it’s not a prompt that an amateur biologist would have written.
What we asked Claude explicitly for in this prompt was to go and look for accessory proteins that might be hitching a ride along with these reverse transcriptase genes. And what Claude found was actually not that but this array of repeats in noncoding RNA. That’s what triggered Claude, realizing that that this might be a more interesting system that’s worth paying attention to.
Can you tell me about the DNA in which it found these patterns?
PERRY: One of the other things that Claude noticed was that these array of associated reverse transcriptases seem to be isolated to jumbo phages, which have very large genomes for bacteriophage. We have not seen this occur anywhere else, whether that’s other viruses or bacteria or humans. But in biology, the number one rule is to expect the unexpected. These genes have the ability to spread really widely in ways that you don’t expect. That’s another kind of beauty of this field: [it] is that there’s always something new to find, even with something like this. It’s completely possible that there are relatives or similar systems elsewhere.
Finding reverse transcriptases is something that’s been possible long before Claude. Is AI necessary to do this work, especially given how energy intensive large language models (LLMs) can be?
PERRY: The best thing that I can say about this is that the number of tokens and the compute time to do this analysis are actually fairly little. It’s actually affordable to the types of labs that are interested in doing this type of research. And as a comparison point, the time it would take for a human scientist to do the equivalent analysis that Claude did is on the weeks-to-months scale, and Claude was able to produce this analysis in a day.
The hardest part about doing biology is designing and performing all of the experiments that you need to actually prove what a biological system does, and so shrinking this up-front time of just finding something interesting to work on has really tremendous value for scientific efficiency. Even if there was a compute cost up front, you’re saving lots of human labor costs and effort.
Why use an LLM versus other kinds of machine learning?
KAUDERER-ABRAMS: There’s a distinction between general reasoning models, like LLMs, and the specialized AI biofoundation models like protein language models and protein structure prediction. We see these as today playing mostly complementary roles, in that you have the specialized tools that have been trained to do one thing, and you can’t interface them with them in natural language, but they’re very good at that one thing. The general reasoning models play a different role in that they can actually do all of the steps of the research process, including deciding which specialized tool models to call and in what context to use them.
Now that it’s been identified, where does the research go next?
KAUDERER-ABRAMS: There are two parts to this. The first is the research associated with this particular enzyme system, and the second is the research program that we’re running, generally, that extends far beyond this one enzyme system.
The first point, that’s exactly why we were excited to release this work so early.... [We want to open it up to the community and see what everyone can do with it. We’re excited for whoever is interested in participating to figure out what its function is, and I’ll stress that’s the important part. Finding these things is not quite a dime a dozen because [it’s] not every day that you find something with this set of properties. But the really impactful part is understanding the function and developing it into a tool. We’ll certainly be participating in that as well.
Then, separately, there are all sorts of other research projects that we’re starting. This is one shape of [a] research project of systematizing and scaling up searching for useful new tools in large databases and DNA sequences. But there are other kind of adjacent research projects that we’re just getting started, that all use the theme of seeing “How can we infuse AI into every step of the research process and use that to scale it up?”
As you mentioned, it’s one thing to identify interesting parts of DNA, but it’s another to turn that into something useful. How would Claude help close that gap?
KAUDERER-ABRAMS: We see Claude accelerating the process of turning a naturally occurring discovery into a tool by accelerating all of the cycle times of what’s happening in a research process.
When you look at Claude helping to draft the experimental protocols and analyze the data and debug things when you’re working in the lab, I think that that’s been one of the striking things. I think it’s obvious to people that AI is useful in computational work. What’s less obvious to people is that if you come to our lab, you’ll see Nick and our scientists that are at the bench, literally walking around with their computers, talking to Claude as they’re running the protocols.
How are you safeguarding against hallucinations?
KAUDERER-ABRAMS: That’s absolutely an important concern. And as a whole company, we’ve been putting a tremendous amount of technical effort into reducing hallucinations. As a whole field, we’ve made a lot of progress over the past few years. Beyond that, we have rigorous evaluations that we run that measure the reproducibility and Claude's capabilities in all these different areas.
But there’s no substitute, at the end of the day, for the human biologist. You have to use your judgment, and the model will sometimes say things that are incorrect, and that is part of what it means to be skilled at using AI is to recognize that that's the case and incorporate that awareness into how you work.
What applications do you think these sequences might have in the future?
KAUDERER-ABRAMS: It's really too early for us to speculate about the applications. I think I can say it is fairly uncommon to find this set of properties all together where you have some sort of base enzyme that already interacts with nucleic acids and you have a repeat array that is found up front with a certain structure that, in some ways, is reminiscent of the arrays that you find with CRISPR, and then you have an accessory protein. There’s certainly many of these systems that have been found in nature, but a good number of them have gone on to be developed into useful tools.

US Oshkosh Defense Begins Production of First DXPV Kaaiman Prototype for the Netherlands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:35:40 UTC
19:35:40 KST

US company Oshkosh Defense has begun production of the first prototype of the Dutch Expeditionary Patrol Vehicle (DXPV) Kaaiman military off-road vehicle for the Dutch Ministry of Defense.
The company announced this on October 13 in an official press release.
The DXPV is based on the American Joint Light Tactical Vehicle (JLTV) and adapted to the Dutch marines’ requirements for expeditionary operations, particularly in coastal areas.
Compared with the base JLTV platform, the new vehicle features an upgraded suspension for improved off-road mobility, enhanced corrosion protection for operation in marine environments, and the ability to fit modular armor.
In addition, the design incorporates enhanced systems for operation in various climate conditions, integrated onboard equipment, and a modular architecture that allows further upgrades to meet customers’ requirements.
The prototype is being built on an existing production line that also manufactures JLTV-based vehicles equipped with counter-drone systems.
Using a production platform helps shorten the development timeline and prepare the new version for manufacture more quickly.
Militarnyi previously reported that in April 2025, the Netherlands selected Oshkosh Defense to supply 150 DXPV vehicles under the Future Littoral All-Terrain Mobility – Patrol Vehicle (FLATM-PV) program.
In June 2025, the parties signed an agreement to supply the vehicles to the Royal Netherlands Marine Corps.
The vehicles were given the local name Kaaiman, with deliveries scheduled to begin in 2028.
In January 2026, the Netherlands also ordered an additional batch of DXPV vehicles worth $25–30 million. The number of vehicles in the order was not disclosed.
The new ORVs are expected to improve Dutch marines’ mobility during coastal operations and in challenging off-road conditions.

Ukrainian Ex-Officer Stands Trial in Germany Over Nord Stream Bombing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:17:05 UTC
19:17:05 KST

Lawyers for a Ukrainian ex-military officer accused of leading the bombing of Russia's Nord Stream pipeline in September 2022 argued at the start of his trial in Germany on Wednesday that "an aggressor's infrastructure" may have been a lawful target.
Serhii Kuznetsov is accused of leading a group of Ukrainian agents including divers and an explosives expert that blew up Russia's largest gas pipeline to Europe in one of the biggest infrastructure sabotage operations of modern times.
The case provides the first opportunity for a public hearing of evidence gathered during a years-long investigation, which has been diplomatically and politically awkward for a German government that remains staunchly supportive of Ukraine despite the investigative trail linking Kyiv to the bombing.
Moving to have the case dismissed, Kuznetsov's lawyer Nicola Canestrini argued that the pipeline — which provided half of Germany's imports of natural gas before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine — was a "Russian weapon."
"Is it unlawful to destroy an aggressor's infrastructure without harming any human beings?" Canestrini asked.
Right to remain silent
Prosecutors have alleged that Kuznetsov, who was arrested under an international warrant in Italy last year, worked with members of the Ukrainian military to plan the clandestine operation on behalf of unidentified Ukrainian state entities.
Kuznetsov, 50, who prior to Wednesday was referred to publicly only as Serhii K. under German legal rules, has denied any involvement in the blasts that ruptured the 1,200-kilometer (750-mile)-long Baltic Sea pipeline.
Wearing a grey suit and with a shaved head, he exercised his right to remain silent in court but did not cover his face. His lawyers said he could not mount a proper defense because he was obliged to withhold Ukrainian state secrets.
The government in Kyiv has also denied any involvement, a sensitive point in its relations with Germany, Ukraine's largest European supplier of military aid. Russia said on Monday it expected a "just verdict" that would reveal the names of the perpetrators and those who ordered the operation.
Kuznetsov's legal team had tried reaching out to Ukraine for information that might assist the defense but heard nothing, according to another defense lawyer, Jes Meyer-Lohkamp.
Attacking civilian targets is considered a war crime
German prosecutors say the actions Kuznetsov is accused of — attacking civilian targets and causing explosions that destroyed infrastructure and damaged public services — would amount to a war crime.
Kuznetsov is the only person on trial, but Croatian authorities have arrested another man, identified as Vladimir Z., who prosecutors believe was one of the divers.
The explosion of Nord Stream sealed the end of Germany's longstanding dependence on Russian natural gas, although Moscow had already cut supplies over Berlin's support for European sanctions following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Nord Stream's supply had been due to double with the opening of a twin pipeline, Nord Stream 2, already built, but Berlin canceled approval to open it just prior to Russia's invasion.
Plumes of methane gas
The trial, expected to continue into February next year, could have domestic political implications.
Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), leading in opinion polls for more than a year, has called for an end to military aid for Ukraine and a restoration of energy ties with Moscow.
Although German state parliaments have no role in foreign policy, the AfD filed a motion in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Wednesday calling for an end to support for Ukraine, noting the "historical parallel" with the start of the trial.
The Nord Stream system, lying at a depth of 80 to 110 meters under the Baltic and built by Russian gas concern Gazprom to supply up to 110 billion cubic meters of gas to Germany, was formerly at the core of economic ties between the two countries.
The Sept. 26, 2022, blasts that ruptured three of the four concrete-coated steel pipelines created a giant whirlpool at sea as huge plumes of methane gas rose into the atmosphere.
Prosecutors allege that Kuznetsov traveled to Germany through Poland some three weeks before the attack, using a forged Ukrainian passport. He and his group then used a sailboat hired in the northern German city of Rostock to reach an area close to the Danish island of Bornholm, where they rigged specialized military-grade explosives to the sea floor.
The weekly Der Spiegel magazine and ZDF public television have previously reported that five men and one woman were on the rented yacht Andromeda, which left Rostock on Sept. 6 and returned on Sept. 23, 2022.
A Message from The Moscow Times:
Dear readers,
We are facing unprecedented challenges. Russia's Prosecutor General's Office has designated The Moscow Times as an "undesirable" organization, criminalizing our work and putting our staff at risk of prosecution. This follows our earlier unjust labeling as a "foreign agent."
These actions are direct attempts to silence independent journalism in Russia. The authorities claim our work "discredits the decisions of the Russian leadership." We see things differently: we strive to provide accurate, unbiased reporting on Russia.
We, the journalists of The Moscow Times, refuse to be silenced. But to continue our work, we need your help.
Your support, no matter how small, makes a world of difference. If you can, please support us monthly starting from just $2. It's quick to set up, and every contribution makes a significant impact.
By supporting The Moscow Times, you're defending open, independent journalism in the face of repression. Thank you for standing with us.
Remind me later.

Daily: Silmet promises to drop Russian supplier by year's end
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:17:00 UTC
19:17:00 KST

Daily: Silmet promises to drop Russian supplier by year's end
Estonian rare earth metals producer Silmet plans to end its reliance on Russian raw materials by the end of the year, a move that will involve reduced production and temporary shutdowns at its existing facility.
Silmet's parent company, NEO Materials Group, has reportedly circulated information internally and to Estonian government agencies indicating that it is awaiting a final shipment from the Solikamsk Magnesium Plant, which should help it get through the coming winter, Postimees has learned. Silmet has pledged to sever its supply chain ties with Solikamsk by the end of this year.
In a statement published on its website, Neo said: "As part of Neo's preparations for Silmet 2.0, the facility is ending its current feedstock arrangement and will transition to new suppliers." Company spokesperson Vasileios Tsianos told Postimees in response to its questions that more information would be made public when the time was right.
Meanwhile, Neo is making changes to Silmet's existing production schedule that will result in reduced output and temporary production shutdowns at its existing light rare earth separation facility.
"It's good that our country's message got through — Russian raw materials pose a critical risk to production and buying them puts money in the hands of those who should not be profiting from the Western world," Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) told Postimees.
ERR News reported on Thursday that a Russian company supplying rare earths to Estonia's Silmet was removed from the European Union's proposed 22nd sanctions package at Estonia's request. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said on October 10 that Estonia had been pressuring the Sillamäe-based NPM Silmet and its owner Neo Group to find alternative suppliers and set a deadline for ending its dealings with the Russian supplier.

Indonesia wildfires choke Singapore, force East Timor schools shut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:16:00 UTC
19:16:00 KST

Air pollution in parts of Singapore reached "very high" levels Wednesday while East Timor closed schools, as haze from Indonesian forest fires triggered a regional crisis.
The blazes in Indonesia have burned through hundreds of thousands of hectares of forest and plantations on Borneo and Sumatra islands, sickened local residents and sent thick haze across the region.
Air pollution in western Singapore on Wednesday hit "very high" – the country's top level – the National Environment Agency said.
It recorded levels of tiny particulates capable of penetrating the bloodstream and lungs, known as PM2.5, at 288 micrograms per cubic meter, vastly exceeding the World Health Organization's recommended average annual exposure of 5 micrograms.
Indonesia regularly battles wildfires during the dry season, but has seen stronger-than-usual blazes this year as a powerful El Nino cycle brings drought.
Experts also point to slash-and-burn land-clearing practices that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape of Sumatra and Borneo.
The haze has drifted into neighboring Singapore, Malaysia and East Timor, which said it would shut schools nationwide for three days from Thursday, and as far afield as the Philippines.
The closures in East Timor were necessary "as a preventive measure to protect the health of students, teachers and other members of the educational community, given current air quality conditions", the government said.
It urged families to keep children indoors and to use "respiratory protection" if going outside.
Singapore rolled out subsidies for haze-related medical treatment from Monday, a measure last activated in 2015 when similar blazes in Indonesia cloaked Southeast Asia in toxic smoke for weeks.
The city-state has also begun distributing N95 masks to eligible residents when pollution reaches very unhealthy levels.
Singapore's National Trades Union Congress said Monday that public transport workers and delivery riders could receive free N95 masks, but AFP found uptake was slow.
"It's a little bit uncomfortable to wear a mask, and some orders we have to walk around blocks, or park outside," a delivery rider, who gave his name only as Daniel, told AFP.
"With the mask, I will have to breathe heavier," the 27-year-old said.
Ong Kwang Wei, 57, who has asthma, said he wore an N95 mask outdoors and carried his inhaler and medication with him at all times.
He was accompanying his 88-year-old mother – also masked – for a health check-up after a recent bout of flu.
"Once the flu kicks in my asthma is exacerbated ... I get breathless, I cough, I get phlegm, so I need to use my inhaler," Ong said.
In Indonesia, tens of thousands of people have sought treatment for respiratory illness linked to haze from fires burning in Borneo, South Sumatra and Papua regions.
On Sumatra island, a fire razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official said Tuesday.
Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps.
But the fire continued to smoulder underground in peatland and when the wind shifted, the flames moved toward their homes.
The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people fled the village.
"My house is gone," Leni, a 55-year-old villager now staying at a shelter with her family, told AFP.
"There's nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me ... I panicked and didn't have the time to grab anything," said Leni, who like many Indonesians has one name.
President Prabowo Subianto on Monday ordered the government to mobilize maximum efforts, with officials saying more than 60,000 personnel had been deployed to combat fires on the ground.
But efforts so far, including cloud seeding and water-bombing, have had limited success.
The haze has prompted Malaysia to request a meeting of regional body ASEAN and on Tuesday Malaysian parliamentarian Syed Saddiq Rahman urged a "diplomatic protest."
"We must send a diplomatic protest note, not just on behalf of Malaysia, but ASEAN. You need to treat them as an outcast in the region," he said.

EU proposes delaying methane obligations amid pressure on energy importers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:15:59 UTC
19:15:59 KST

Melike Pala
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
The European Commission proposed Wednesday postponing by one year the implementation of certain provisions of the EU Methane Regulation concerning fossil fuel importers, aiming to ease cost pressures on European industry amid rising energy prices.
The proposed amendment would delay monitoring, reporting, and verification obligations for importers of natural gas, oil, and coal, as well as reporting requirements related to methane intensity for both importers and EU producers, according to a statement.
The bloc said the move comes as the conflict in the Middle East puts additional pressure on global energy markets, driving up energy prices and potentially reducing the availability of gas and oil.
"This is driving up energy prices and may cause reduced availability of gas and oil, hampering the EU's competitiveness and security of supply," the statement said.
The proposed one-year postponement is intended to prevent additional pressure on the security of imported fossil fuel supplies while giving companies and national administrations more time to prepare for compliance with the regulation.
The proposal will now be submitted to the European Parliament and the European Council for consideration and adoption.
The EU Methane Regulation, adopted in 2024, is the world's first comprehensive legislation addressing methane emissions associated with imports of oil, natural gas, and coal.
The regulation covers domestic production, transportation, and processing, as well as imports, and introduces progressively stricter requirements to improve transparency and reduce methane emissions.
The commission stressed that the proposed amendment would not affect the regulation's overall ambition, integrity, or scope, reaffirming the bloc's commitment to reducing methane emissions.

Are US, Israel racing to deploy space-based lasers or orbital weapons first? - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:15:29 UTC
19:15:29 KST

In September, two consecutive top US military officials made public, for the first time, that America has offensive weapons already deployed in space.
That the US, China, and Russia have anti-satellite weapons available is no secret and has been assumed in recent years, with China unofficially demonstrating old space weapons in 2007, and Russia and China both demonstrating newer weapons since 2021.
But a public declaration by the US set off speculation about whether the deployed weapons are focused on the area of: either directed-energy weapons such as lasers; or kinetic anti-satellite weapons such as missiles; or platforms for disrupting or disabling satellites’ activity without actually destroying them, which is also known as rendezvous and proximity operations (RPOs).
A fourth method could be nuclear, but it is assumed that this was not the focus of the US announcement since the terrible consequences in space would impact the attacker as much as the defender.
In April, Unit 9900 officer Lt. Col. “S” and space-war expert Tal Inbar discussed Israel's efforts to defend its space assets against adversaries.
Also, on June 24, with the Post noting that Russia, China, and Iran have all worked on ways to attack, damage, jam, or drag satellites in space, IDF Brig. Gen. Yael Grossman responded, “There are threats from space. We work with the Defense Ministry with a lot of power; with the broader defense establishment, we can all bring forward achievements.”
Developments in space vehicles
Regarding the US announcement, so far those space experts who are commenting are leaning toward category 3 of RPO.
This is especially true for deploying RPOs, which can fight off other RPOs.
The reason is that RPOs have existed in one form or another since the US used multiple space vehicles to repair one another in the 1960s. In that sense, the largest jump was developing the technology and tactics for sending one space vehicle or satellite to match the orbit of another.
Once a country makes that major scientific jump, adding on a robot arm to attack or an additional system to jam is just a matter of time and energy.
Another reason RPOs may be favored would be to avoid the debris problem caused by using kinetic anti-satellite weapons, such as missiles.
The US has said it is hoping to make major advancements in stationing anti-missile physical interceptors in space that can protect satellites by 2028.
Despite all this focus on RPOs for the US, China, and Russia, Israel has expressed keen interest regarding space weapons in relation to lasers.
On June 29, Defense Minister Israel Katz told a briefing of military reporters that Israel is developing space lasers to carry out attacks above the Earth.
This was an expansion and more specific version of a statement which Katz made earlier in June, when he committed Israel to becoming the leading player with space attack capabilities.
“One of the central goals which the prime minister and I set is that we are recruiting the best minds,” since “as of today, no country has the ability to mount attacks in space. We must be the leading country in the world with this capability,” said Katz.
The defense minister continued, “If we achieve this, it will ensure the advantage of deterrence, of the ability to attack, destroy, and all of the other matters, versus our enemies with large resources.”
Lasers to be used to defend Israeli assets
But Monday was the first time that Katz specifically mentioned space lasers.
Israel is already a leading country in developing Iron Beam as a land-based space laser, and during a visit to Elbit earlier in the summer, The Jerusalem Post saw and heard about work on presumed future fighter-jet-based lasers.
Overall, it seemed clear that Katz on June 29 was referring to Iran.
This is especially true since during the 2026 war, Israel struck multiple Iranian space war-related facilities, including facilities working on developing capabilities to attack satellites in space.
It was unclear if he indirectly also wanted to deter Russia and China from assisting Iran in this and other spheres.
According to foreign reports, lasers might be able to destroy enemy satellites and also burn up any debris that an attack in space by other means might cause.
Some have already speculated that Israel could destroy enemy space satellites using the Arrow 3 missile system, given that it already strikes ballistic missiles in space.
Yet, due to the same issue that Russia and China already fell into regarding debris, many countries are working on other techniques, such as paralyzing, damaging, jamming, dragging, or using lasers against satellites in space.
While some Israeli officials have hinted at such efforts, Katz’s public statements on June 29 were the clearest one to date by a senior Israeli official.
Why the US's first focus is on RPOs
In contrast, if Iran or other enemies advanced past Israel in space, they could attack Israeli satellites and reduce its surveillance capabilities.
After all of this, why then do most experts believe that the US's first and current focus is on RPOs, and not lasers?
It is not that the US and the other countries with space programs are not working on developing space lasers. They are.
Also, Israel’s success with developing the Iron Beam for actual deployments as a ground laser has spurred other countries forward in the more general laser defense area.
But lasers in space or on aircraft are still a distant solution, as they involve a series of more complex physics and engineering problems, which invariably will take longer to solve than RPOs.
RPOs are thereby an immediate answer to help deter enemies from attacking, since they can be used to attack enemy satellites, as well as providing defense against other countries’ potential RPO attacks.
If enemies have existing and immediate weapons to attack an object, such as a satellite, the US and other countries, potentially even including Israel, are likely to focus on immediate solutions, with the focus on space lasers being a longer-term goal.
In that sense, the US statement in September was about immediately deterring China and Russia from attacking American satellites.
In contrast, Katz’s June statement was less about immediate attack, defense, or deterrence.
Rather, it was more about either bragging to the Israeli public about a future distant achievement, or psychological warfare against Iran to the extent that the Islamic Republic might believe it can work with Moscow and Beijing to go after Israel’s satellite advantage.
