Trump blamed Islam for France's protests. Students want teachers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:15:28 UTC
19:15:28 KST

Breadcrumb
France's students demand better schools as Trump turns protests into an Islam debate
At a demonstration in Paris’s 13th arrondissement on 10 October, high school students sang the national anthem and chanted "Macron démission." Their placards read "Nous avons besoin de plus de professeurs," "We need more teachers." Some urged others to stay calm and not to run, warning that this was what the CRS, France’s riot police, wanted. Before long, officers moved in to disperse the crowd.
For three students aged 16 to 18 from the 13th and 19th arrondissements, interviewed that day, the problems are concrete: overcrowded classrooms, no computer room, a shortage of teachers in their final year, and a canteen so packed that they have about 10 minutes to eat.
Meals must be booked in advance, and many end up buying food elsewhere. One week, they said, food had cost them €170. All three asked not to be named because of tensions around the protests.
When they sat their exams, the students said, they were sent to other sites, in rooms so stifling that some left for the toilets just to breathe. They took their concerns to a meeting at another high school with school leaders and officials, but the answers were disappointing.
Some issues were passed on to other authorities, including the education authority and Valérie Pécresse’s regional council, and the agreed changes won't take effect until next year. The students want them now.
On 6 October, as demonstrations spread across France, US President Donald Trump offered a different explanation.
"This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!" he wrote on Truth Social.
The students reject that. The protests have nothing to do with religion or immigration, they said. High school students come from every background, and there should be no shortcuts. None of them wanted their origins or religion mentioned. They wanted, they said, to be judged on what they were saying.
The movement began in September in disadvantaged suburbs of Paris and has since spread across the country.
More than 250,000 people took part in protests nationwide, according to the Interior Ministry, while organisers put the figure at 450,000.
'They tend to infantilise us'
A 23-year-old Arab medical student of North African heritage from Seine-Saint-Denis, the department north of Paris where the movement has deep roots, described classrooms not built for more than 30 pupils, broken furniture, and rooms that are hard to bear in winter. He asked to remain anonymous because of upcoming exams.
"Instead of trying to understand our difficulties and find solutions, they tend to infantilise us," he said. "We are capable of identifying the problems in our schools and saying what needs to change."
He is used to Trump’s provocations, he said, and pays them little attention. "What he said has, as usual, nothing to do with reality," he said, adding that he saw it as political point-scoring ahead of the US midterm elections.
What worries him more is that young people from immigrant families have their grievances read through assumptions about their identity, rather than their experience. "Our demands risk being reduced to questions of origin or religion," he said.
Many young people, he said, refuse to speak to channels such as CNews and BFMTV, which they see as portraying people from immigrant backgrounds in racist and Islamophobic terms.
"We want the media to talk about why we are mobilising, rather than turning our demands into a debate about our identity," the young student added.
A 21-year-old woman who went to school in Seine-Saint-Denis before moving to a Paris high school, and who also asked not to be named, said the protesters’ demands were legitimate.
She was stunned, she said, that students asking for better conditions had been met with violence. As for Trump, she said, "he should keep quiet."
The crackdown has been heavy. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted over alleged offences linked to the unrest, including 1,483 minors, according to the Justice Ministry.
Inequality built into the system
The staffing crisis is national. According to the Education Ministry’s statistics directorate, DEPP, 9.8 percent of teaching hours in public secondary schools went undelivered in 2024–2025: 7.5 percent because absent teachers were not replaced, and 2.3 percent because schools were closed.
In Seine-Saint-Denis, two-thirds of schools had unfilled teaching positions, according to a union survey cited by Reuters.
Louise Paternoster, a representative of the CGT education union in the department, told Reuters the area did not receive resources to match its needs.
"In a period of budgetary restraint, it is more difficult to reduce inequalities," said Clémence Cardon-Quint, a professor at Paul-Valéry University Montpellier who studies education funding.
The problems start long before high school. A primary school teacher in her fifties, who asked not to be named, said her biggest challenge was supporting pupils with autism, ADHD and dyslexia.
"Inclusion is a very good thing, but we need the resources to welcome these children properly," she said.
Teachers sometimes have to make or buy materials themselves, which multiplies preparation time, and other children get less attention.
"Unfortunately, the die is very often cast as early as the first year of primary school," she said. A child who struggles to read needs help from speech therapists or psychologists, or support through France’s disability service, the MDPH, and that depends on families pushing for it. Some children, she said, reach secondary school without the level they need.
A concession, not a solution
Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu acknowledged that young people’s anger did not come out of nowhere, while condemning violence and accusing outside groups of exploiting the protests. Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot rejected Trump’s reading, saying France should tell its own story.
On 8 October, Education Minister Édouard Geffray announced that around 3,000 qualified teachers who had not yet started work would be sent to schools facing staffing shortages.
It was a stopgap, not 3,000 new permanent posts. Student unions welcomed it as a first victory but vowed to keep mobilising.
Student unions have called a new national day of protest for 17 October. Asked about Trump’s claim that the protests were about Islam, the primary school teacher did not hesitate.
"It’s completely absurd and has absolutely nothing to do with it."

Iran executed mountaineer and musician Ali Sina Mostafavi, 38, on Wednesday, according to state sources, continuing the Islamic Republic’s use of executions as punishment against protesters. Mostafavi, from Bam in Kerman province, was executed after the Supreme Court upheld a death sentence handed down by a Revolutionary Court in Kerman, the judiciary-affiliated Mizan news agency reported.
Human rights groups had warned less than 24 hours earlier that he had been moved to solitary confinement and his family summoned for a final visit. Pahlavi’s communications team then issued an urgent appeal, saying he had been tortured into confessing and convicted in a sham trial.
Mizan said Mostafavi carried out a series of shootings in Kerman during the war, which Iranian authorities call the Ramadan War. It said he opened fire in Azadi Square on March 24, wounding a civilian and a young girl. On April 21, it said, he fired at conscript soldiers and passing vehicles, injuring several people. It also accused him of two failed shooting attempts targeting police on the Kerman-Mahan road.
Authorities said a search of his hideout turned up a scoped Brno rifle, two shotguns, 246 rounds of ammunition and 30 Molotov cocktails.
The judiciary also said Mostafavi sent photographs and videos of sites struck during the war to Persian-language opposition media abroad. It said he expressed willingness to carry out an operation at Kerman airport. According to the authorities, messages on his phone included exchanges with Persian-language broadcasters and messages to Israel’s official Persian-language account.
Mizan said he took part in the nationwide protests that began in December 2025 and continued into January, and sent footage of the unrest to media outside Iran.
The judiciary said the case was heard with a defense lawyer present. It said the conviction rested on investigative findings, security reports, and Mostafavi’s confessions. The public account did not include the defense’s arguments or independently verifiable evidence. Iranian authorities have not released evidence that he acted under the direction of Pahlavi or Israeli officials, while human rights groups have raised concerns about his treatment in detention and the circumstances of his conviction.
'A political prisoner and young athlete'
Pahlavi’s team described him as “a political prisoner and young athlete” in “immediate danger of execution.” The account said in Persian that he was a patriotic mountaineer and alleged his conviction followed “forced confessions under torture” and a “show trial.”
The League for the Defense of Human Rights in Iran said armed security officers arrested Mostafavi at his home in the early hours of April 25. The group alleged he was beaten during the arrest.
Branch 1 of the Kerman Revolutionary Court, presided over by Judge Hadi Aghaei, sentenced him to death on charges including moharebeh, or waging war against God, acting against national security, and gathering and colluding. Branch 41 of the Supreme Court upheld the sentence on September 28, according to human rights reports.
On Tuesday, rights groups reported his transfer to solitary confinement at Kerman prison.
Iran sees sharp rise in the use of the death penalty
Before his arrest, Mostafavi was an experienced mountaineer. IranWire and Human Rights for Sports said he climbed Island Peak in Nepal and attempted Ama Dablam, reaching about 6,600 meters. Records in Kerman mountaineering club archives show he joined a 2016 expedition to Alam-Kuh, one of Iran’s highest mountains. Human rights reports also describe him as a musician.
The execution follows a sharp rise in the use of the death penalty against people accused of involvement in the January protests, opposition activity and war-related security offenses.
On Tuesday, Amnesty International condemned the executions of five men between September 30 and October 5 who had been convicted in connection with the January uprising. “The arbitrary executions of these five young men serves as another chilling reminder of how the Iranian authorities weaponize the death penalty to render the cost of dissent so high that it terrorizes the population into silence,” said Diana Eltahawy, the group’s deputy regional director for the Middle East and North Africa.

Marrakech Airshow showcases building blocks of Israel-Morocco defense ties - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14

19:15:10 KST

The recent Marrakech Airshow showed that Israel and Morocco are moving toward closer defense ties. Israel’s Defense Ministry said last week that Israel has opened a national pavilion at the show and that the ministry had led an Israeli delegation to Morocco to participate.
“This marks Israel's first official participation in the defense exhibition held in Morocco since the signing of the Abraham Accords, and the first time the Israel Ministry of Defense (IMOD) International Defense Cooperation Directorate (SIBAT) has opened an Israeli national pavilion and headed a delegation of Israeli defense industries at the show,” the ministry said.
Eight Israeli companies came with the delegation, including ASIO Technologies, Orbit Communication Systems, SHILAT Optronics, UVision Air, and XTEND Systems. Israel’s big three defense giants, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, Elbit Systems and Israel Aerospace Industries, were also present.
This was an important opportunity for Israel’s large companies as well as the smaller and midsize ones to showcase various systems. The ministry highlighted “advanced, combat-proven technologies at the show, including loitering munitions, AI-powered robotic systems, autonomous navigation capabilities for UAVs, laser guidance for FPV drones, satellite communications, and more.”
The ministry is seeking greater defense cooperation with countries abroad. This includes numerous Israeli companies taking part in AUSA this week.
It also includes the recent major Israeli defense deal with Greece for Achilles Shield. In that deal, valued at around €3 billion, Israel will help Greece build a multi-layered air defense array based on Israeli systems. These systems include David’s Sling and Spyder, made by Rafael, as well as the Barak system, made by IAI.
As such, a trend is clear. Israeli ties with Morocco are not just about Morocco but part of a larger story of Israeli ties with Greece and the US. Morocco is seeking to acquire several Israeli defense systems, and reports indicate it has already acquired several. For instance, we reported in January 2026 that Morocco had deployed IAI’s Barak air defense system.
The Economist also reported last year that Morocco was producing drones in cooperation with an Israeli company. “Morocco is Africa’s new military tech hub,” an op-ed at The Jerusalem Post said in April.
Israeli-Moroccan friendship goes back years
The building blocks of Israel-Morocco relations include a friendship going back years. Morocco is part of the Abraham Accords. A small number of Israeli troops joined a US-backed exercise called Africa Lion in Morocco in 2025. Calcalist reported on October 12 that “Moroccan Military Industry (MMI) will begin delivering armored vehicle turrets to the Moroccan army in March 2027, the company's general manager said on the sidelines of the Marrakech Air Show.”
The report added that “sources at the air show and earlier media reporting have said MMI is closely linked to Israel's Elbit Systems and uses its technology. MMI itself told Reuters it is a Moroccan defense company, a characterization that leaves the precise nature of the relationship with Elbit unaddressed on the record.” A separate report at Calcalist also said that Morocco was interested in IAI’s Lora missile.
The Lora missile has been around for years. Back in 2020, IAI said that a “complex trial included two scenarios to test and demonstrate LORA’s advanced capabilities. The first scenario involved a short-range launch to 90 km and the second to a long range of 400 km.” The German Navy completed a successful dual operational firing trial with IAI's Naval Lora ballistic missile, IAI said in September.
On October 12, Morocco World News also noted: “Morocco and Israel are holding advanced talks over the possible integration of the Israeli David’s Sling air defense system into the Royal Moroccan Armed Forces, according to the German defense publication Europäische Sicherheit & Technik (ES&T).”
Several reports from the Marrakech show highlighted Morocco's search for more advanced defense equipment. For instance, Le360 reported that Morocco’s MMI unveiled a system called Spear, an “autonomous mortar system designed for light combat vehicles.”
The same site highlighted Israel’s pavilion at the air show. Le360 also noted that an Israeli officer “held a one-on-one meeting with the commander of the Royal Air Force. The two officials discussed strengthening strategic ties and continuing cooperation between the two air forces, according to reports.” The goal of these reports is to illustrate growing Israel-Morocco cooperation.
Morocco has been welcoming of Israel cooperation
The air show was a key part of publicly showcasing Israel-Morocco cooperation. At a time when Israel has sometimes faced challenges abroad and controversy, Morocco has been welcoming. It has been more welcoming than France, for instance. Morocco’s drive to increase its capabilities, especially in air defenses and precision fire, is important. It would knit Morocco into a regional defense architecture that brings together countries with advanced systems. These could include Israeli systems that are being sold in Europe, such as to Greece.
As such, one could imagine a link between Morocco, Greece, Israel, and other countries that share various advanced systems. This would also position Morocco as an advanced, capable military power at the head of the Mediterranean. This matters because Morocco and Algeria are rivals, and Algeria is hostile to Israel. A recent UAE-Algeria diplomatic crisis also adds to the complexity. Libya, divided by civil war, also plays a role.
With so much at stake in today's regional shifts from the Horn of Africa to the Sahel, Morocco-Israel ties likely matter more than ever. The recent air show symbolized these ties and showcased practical military technology.

Desire was indiscriminate, prosecutor tells court

Although he could be funny, charming and likeable when he wanted something, he also had a childlike expectation that his every desire should be met, she added.
“He was ruthless, he was calculating, he was manipulative and, the prosecution say, he was a sexual predator,” Karmy-Jones said.
The alleged offences took place over a decade as he progressed from gigs as a stand-up comedian to a TV presenter, actor and Hollywood movie star, she said.
Brand says never engaged in non-consensual activity
The first is alleged to have occurred in 1999 when he was performing in a show on the fringe of the Labour Party Conference in Bournemouth.

Around the same time in 2004 or 2005, a woman working at a media company said he indecently assaulted her at her office.

When interviewed by police, Brand declined to answer questions but provided written statements in which he said he did not remember the incidents, had never engaged in non-consensual activity and accepted that he had had sex in toilet cubicles during parties, Karmy-Jones said.
Woman came forward after TV programme
The women involved did not know each other and had not taken the matter to the police at the time for various reasons, but came forward with complaints following a TV programme and a press report in 2023 in which anonymous allegations were made by other women, the prosecutor said.
Brand sat in the dock wearing a dark suit and thin, white scarf, staring forward intently.

From 'Indira Gandhi' to 'PM': Cabinet takes up proposal to rename 4 pension schemes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:04:15 UTC
19:04:15 KST

The proposed changes cover three pension schemes and the National Social Assistance Programme under the rural development ministry.
NEW DELHI: The Union Cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Wednesday approved the renaming of the National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) and several of its sub-schemes, including those named after former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi.The Cabinet also approved the continuation of NSAP for five years, from 2026-27 to 2030-31, with a total outlay of Rs 53,428 crore.Here are the approved name changes and details of the schemes:
National Social Assistance Programme (NSAP): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Samajik Sahayata Yojana. Launched on August 15, 1995, the programme provides social security assistance to poor and vulnerable households.
Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Vridhavastha Pension Yojana. The scheme provides monthly financial assistance to eligible elderly people from below poverty line (BPL) households.
Indira Gandhi National Widow Pension Scheme (IGNWPS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Vidhawa Pension Yojana. It provides financial assistance to eligible widows from BPL households.
Indira Gandhi National Disability Pension Scheme (IGNDPS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Divyangjan Pension Yojana. The scheme provides monthly pension assistance to eligible persons with disabilities from BPL households.
National Family Benefit Scheme (NFBS): It will be renamed Pradhan Mantri Parivar Labh Yojana. The scheme provides financial assistance to eligible households following the death of the primary breadwinner.
Alse read: Diwali bonanza for railway staff: 78-day bonus cleared for 11.4 lakh employeesChanges to disability pensionAlongside the renaming, the Cabinet approved changes to the disability pension scheme. Monthly assistance will increase to Rs 375 for beneficiaries aged 0-79 years and Rs 625 for those aged 80 and above.The minimum benchmark disability requirement will be reduced from 80% to 40%, while the minimum age criterion will be removed, making individuals eligible for assistance from birth, subject to the scheme's other conditions.The Cabinet said the old-age and widow pension schemes, along with the family benefit scheme, would continue in their existing form.
A total of 3.20 crore beneficiaries across all 36 states and Union territories are expected to benefit from the approval.
Guidelines covering the revised eligibility criteria, beneficiary coverage and assistance under the disability pension scheme will be issued and implemented within three months.The programme was launched to fulfil the Central government's responsibility under Article 41 of the Constitution's Directive Principles of State Policy, which concerns public assistance in cases including old age, sickness and disability.Also read: IDBI Bank stake sale; Rs 53,428 crore welfare package- key decisions by Union cabinet

Western sanctions increase risk of satellite collisions — expert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:03:55 UTC
19:03:55 KST

MOSCOW, October 14. /TASS/. The sanctions regime imposed by the European Union and the United States on Russia and other nations is increasing the risk of spacecraft collisions as satellite constellations expand, Yelena Pavlova, Chief Designer of a component of the Russian Automated Warning System on Hazardous Situations in Outer Space (ASPOS OKP), told TASS.
"Large low-Earth orbit satellite constellations are being expanded primarily by the Americans and the Chinese. While the Americans ensure collision safety for their own and European spacecraft (Starlink performed over 350,000 collision-avoidance maneuvers last year), they do not coordinate satellite trajectories with the Chinese or with the operators of the Rassvet satellites. This is a direct result of the sanctions policy pursued by the US and EU against 'unfriendly' Eastern states. Consequently, the simultaneous growth of these constellations significantly raises the probability of collisions due to the absence of universally accepted space traffic management rules," Pavlova noted.
According to her, the "layers" of the US military constellations Starshield and SDA pose a distinct threat. The US Space Command does not publish their orbital data, which also creates conditions for potential collisions with other space objects, the expert believes.

Poroshenko named opposition leader, European Solidarity rated least negatively among Rada factions – KMIS poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
13:02:32 EEST
19:02:32 KST

The European Solidarity party faction in the current 9th convocation of the Verkhovna Rada holds the highest public performance ratings among Ukrainians, although negative evaluations outweigh positive ones across all parliamentary political forces, according to the results of a nationwide public opinion poll conducted by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KMIS) between September 12 and 21. Commissioned by Forum NGO, the survey included questions assessing the performance of parliamentary factions and identifying perceived opposition leaders.
Some 38% of respondents believe the European Solidarity faction's activities benefit Ukraine, compared to 43% who believe they hinder development. In September 2025, 38% considered the faction's activities beneficial and 36% viewed them as a hindrance.
The Holos party faction follows in the rankings: 30% of respondents consider its activities beneficial to Ukraine, while 31% hold the opposite view. Ratings have slightly worsened compared to September 2025, when 33% noted benefits and 27% cited hindrances.
Meanwhile, 22% of respondents consider the Servant of the People faction's activities beneficial, while 66% believe its actions hinder state development (compared to 52% last year).
Similar negative trends are evident for the Batkivshchyna All-Ukrainian Union faction, whose activities are deemed beneficial by 21%, while 68% view them as hindering state development (up from 48% in September 2025).
Regarding Platform for Life and Peace group, 16% believe its activities benefit Ukraine, while 43% disagree. This represents no significant change compared to September 2025.
Overall, a majority of respondents (64%) positively evaluate the performance of at least one faction from the list, up from 59% in September 2025.
Respondents were also asked to identify the leader of the opposition in Ukraine; a majority (68%) were able to select a public figure from a list of six politicians. The largest relative share pointed to European Solidarity leader and MP Petro Poroshenko (30%). He is followed by MP Dmytro Razumkov (11%), volunteer and public figure Serhiy Prytula (8%), and Batkivshchyna leader and MP Yulia Tymoshenko (6%). MPs Yuriy Boiko and former Presidential Office advisor Oleksiy Arestovych were each named by 3% of respondents.
An additional 11% believe there is no genuine opposition in Ukraine (down from 16% in February). Compared to February, the shares of respondents naming Poroshenko (previously 24%) and Razumkov (previously 7%) increased, while metrics for other figures remained unchanged.
Commenting on the survey results, KMIS Executive Director Anton Hrushetsky noted that the crisis of trust in parliament among Ukrainians persists. "In effect, Ukrainians believe the parliament is more of a hindrance than a contributor to the country's development. Naturally, the critical attitude of Ukrainians toward the Verkhovna Rada and parliamentary political forces is not new... But during wartime, this situation is particularly alarming. It is especially critical that in the case of the Servant of the People faction—which forms the basis of the coalition and the current government—those who believe its actions hinder development outnumber those who see it as contributing by a factor of three," he stated.
Hrushetsky emphasized that the Verkhovna Rada is expected to pass necessary legislation to secure funding from Western partners and demonstrate Ukraine's fulfillment of European integration obligations, noting that opposition MPs must also demonstrate their responsibility.
The survey was conducted via telephone interviews (CATI) using a random sample of mobile phone numbers across all government-controlled regions among 1,002 respondents aged 18 and older. Under normal conditions, the formal statistical margin of error for such a sample (with a 0.95 probability and design effect of 1.3) does not exceed 4.1% for indicators near 50% and 1.8% for indicators near 5%, though wartime conditions introduce additional systematic deviation.

French students continue school blockades ahead of talks with government officials
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:02:23 UTC
19:02:23 KST

Necva Tastan Sevinc
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Nearly 200 high schools across France were expected to remain closed Wednesday amid continuing student blockades, as the government pledged proposals to improve university admissions. 
Education Minister Edouard Geffray told French broadcaster BFMTV that “96% of high schools are open,” with no disruptions reported in three-quarters of the country’s departments, a day after the fifth round of nationwide protests. 
Several schools remained blockaded in Paris, including Voltaire, Helene-Boucher, and the Balzac school complex. Balzac’s administration suspended in-person classes, citing access difficulties and safety concerns. 
Geffray said Higher Education Minister Philippe Baptiste would submit proposals to improve Parcoursup, France’s university admissions platform, to the prime minister by the end of October. 
He expressed openness “to adjustments, possibly substantial ones,” while questioning what would replace the platform if it were abolished. 
According to Geffray, fewer than 20% of the 90,000 contributions submitted to a government platform collecting students’ complaints concerned Parcoursup. 
He ruled out immediate changes to the baccalaureate, France’s school-leaving examination. 
“I’m not going to change the baccalaureate six months before a presidential election; we need to stop constantly reforming,” he said. 
Student representatives are scheduled to meet Geffray and Baptiste on Thursday afternoon as they press for €10 billion ($11 billion) in investment. 
Pierre Sourzat, president of the organization Les Lyceens!, told Franceinfo that students expected concrete measures after receiving “only crumbs.” 
Although organizers have not called for a sixth round of protests Thursday, the Union of High School Students urged demonstrators to maintain blockades. 
Union President Ryad Rani and other student representatives also called for participation in a “yellow vest” demonstration scheduled for Saturday. 
Meanwhile, classes resumed at Kleber High School in Strasbourg, where clashes between students and police had occurred in recent weeks. 
French President Emmanuel Macron has acknowledged the “legitimate anxieties” of young people amid nationwide high school protests, while condemning violence during demonstrations, government spokesperson Maud Bregeon said Wednesday. 
Bregeon said Macron believed young people’s concerns had been “politically exploited and transformed into urban violence.” 
The president denounced what he called “unacceptable scenes” of violence during demonstrations, particularly on Tuesday, she said. 
Macron has asked the government to provide “clear and concrete answers” in the coming weeks, including measures to protect teachers and an assessment of school buildings. 
The government has assigned 2,000 of the 3,000 substitute teachers it had pledged to deploy, Bregeon said. 
Geffray said earlier Wednesday that more than one-third of the 3,000 substitute teachers had already been deployed to work with students. 
Meanwhile, the justice minister released an updated tally of cases linked to urban violence during the student movement. 
Since the blockades began, 7,950 people have been taken into police custody, including 6,773 minors and 1,177 adults, according to the minister. 
Of those, 2,735 people have been prosecuted, while 2,225 have been offered alternatives to prosecution. 
A further 1,263 cases were dismissed, and 26 people were placed in pretrial detention, the minister said.

Dowgielewicz expressed hope that the EU’s new multi‑year budget will include solid guarantees for continued financial support for Ukraine.
“We are working to convince EU governments to provide the necessary financing. If negotiations on the EU budget conclude successfully in the near future, we will make every effort to increase our support for Ukraine in the coming years,” he said.

He said the threat level along the border had not increased but that he expected people might try to seek asylum in Lithuania to avoid military service.
The Lithuanian military has said cooperation between institutions to strengthen border security is routine and helps ensure that joint tasks are carried out effectively.
Troops are patrolling areas around border guard stations alongside border officials. Depending on operational needs, the military may also deploy mobile patrols, mobile observation posts and military police crews.

Russia has accused Dutch authorities of denying visas to three of Russia’s leading female gymnasts for the World Championships in Rotterdam, which kick off this weekend, and jeopardizing their qualification path for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
Reigning world all-around champion Angelina Melnikova, Tokyo 2020 team Olympic champion Viktoria Listunova and 2026 European silver medalist Anna Kalmykova have all reportedly been refused visas, the Russian Gymnastics Federation said Tuesday, citing the Dutch Embassy in Moscow.
The refusal notices apparently expressed diplomatic concerns, stating that “one or several Schengen member states consider the athletes a threat to their international relations.”
“We view the actions of the Dutch authorities as a deliberate elimination of the strongest gymnasts from competition for world medals and Olympic quotas,” the Russian Gymnastics Federation said.
The Dutch foreign and sports ministries declined to comment on individual visa applications, but clarified to local media that the refusals were unrelated to athletic performance.
The three denied athletes have faced scrutiny from Ukrainian sports authorities over their ties to the Russian military and public displays supporting the 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Melnikova represents the military-affiliated CSKA sports club and has previously posted social media photographs featuring the pro-war “Z” symbol.
Listunova took part in a March 2022 pro-war rally with President Vladimir Putin and was previously denied neutral status by World Gymnastics over pro-military social media posts.
Kalmykova holds a sports contract with the Russian National Guard, according to Ukrainian officials.
Russia’s Ambassador to the Netherlands Vladimir Tarabrin said he personally visited the Dutch Foreign Ministry to demand visas, but was presented with “utterly unconvincing arguments that defy any reasonable criticism.”
Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyaryov said the Russian Olympic Committee will lobby to strip the Rotterdam championship of its official Olympic qualifying status.
The Oct. 17-25 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam serve as the opening team qualifier for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games.
Out of 61 members of the Russian delegation, 47 were granted Dutch visas, including five male and three female gymnasts.
World Gymnastics and European Gymnastics lifted restrictions on Russian and Belarusian gymnasts after the International Olympic Committee provisionally lifted its ban on the countries’ Olympic committees in July.

The EU disbursed 2.86 billion euros ($3.2 billion) in military support to Ukraine on Oct. 14 as part of the bloc's 90 billion-euro ($100 billion) support loan for Kyiv.
"With today's 2.86 billion euro disbursement, we keep addressing Ukraine's most urgent operational needs," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The funding will go towards drones, air defense systems, missiles, radars, electronic warfare systems, and ammunition, reads a European Commission press statement.
"As Russia stalls on the front lines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks — cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies," von der Leyen said.
The disbursement lands one day before EU leaders are set to meet for a two-day summit, which President Volodymyr Zelensky is also expected to attend.
"Ukraine will be front and center at this week's European Council," von der Leyen said after an Oct. 11 call with Zelensky.
The latest disbursement was also previewed as a result of that call, with Zelensky thanking von der Leyen for the payment in a Telegram post.
"These funds will strengthen us," Zelensky said.
The latest announcement follows a previous disbursement of 1.24 billion euros ($1.4 billion) in defense support on Oct. 7, and further disbursements from the EU are expected until the end of the year.
Within the EU's 90 billion euro loan, 28.3 billion euros ($31.7 billion) were earmarked for Ukraine's defense needs in 2026, of which 18.26 billion euros ($20.44 billion) have now been disbursed.
Ukraine's plans for how to spend the remaining 10 billion euros ($11.2 billion) have already been approved by the EU; all that is required is for Kyiv to send the receipts for sign-off by Brussels.

Residents’ preference for Turkish lira remains strong despite fund outflows: Central bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:46:40 UTC
18:46:40 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
Fund outflows have not significantly weakened Turkish residents’ preference for lira-denominated assets, Central Bank Governor Fatih Karahan said Wednesday.
Karahan delivered a presentation on Türkiye’s macroeconomic outlook and monetary policy during the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
“Fund outflows have not materially weakened residents’ preferences for TL assets,” Karahan said. “Residents’ preference for Turkish lira remains robust overall.”
Karahan said proactive measures had limited potential spillovers from funds subject to trading restrictions, while tight monetary policy supported demand for the lira.
He reiterated that the bank would maintain its tight policy stance until price stability is achieved, supporting disinflation through demand, exchange rate and expectations channels.
Interest rate decisions would take into account actual and expected inflation, alongside its underlying trend, to ensure the degree of tightness needed for a disinflation path consistent with the bank’s interim targets.
Decisions would remain cautious and be taken on a meeting-by-meeting basis, with further tightening if the inflation outlook deviated significantly from those targets.
 
Underlying inflation moderates despite energy pressures
Karahan said supply-side pressures had slowed disinflation, with energy prices exerting a major influence this year. Nevertheless, underlying inflation was moderating as weaker demand cushioned inflationary pressures.
Annual consumer inflation stood at 29.7% in September, down from 75.5% in May 2024. Monthly underlying inflation eased to 1.7% from 2% in June.
Seasonally adjusted monthly services inflation stood at 1.85%, its lowest level in five years.
Rent inflation was easing, with leading indicators pointing to further moderation. However, increases in transportation and communication prices partly offset declines in rent and education inflation.
Karahan said inflation expectations warranted continued caution, while high-frequency indicators confirmed weak domestic demand in the third quarter. Macroprudential policies also supported slower credit growth.
Despite weaker external demand prospects for 2026, the trade deficit remained moderate and tourism revenues were close to last year’s levels, helping contain the current account deficit.
Türkiye’s sliding-scale fuel tax mechanism had restrained fuel price increases, he said, adding that gold price fluctuations amplified volatility in reserve buffers.

Russia Gave Its Mi-28NM New Anti-Drone Defenses—A Ukrainian FPV Still Took It Down

Unknown Publisher

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Gave Its Mi-28NM New Anti-Drone Defenses—A Ukrainian FPV Still Took It Down
A Ukrainian air-defense FPV drone shot down a modernized Russian Mi-28NM attack helicopter in midair, Ukraine’s 115th Separate Mechanized Brigade said after releasing footage of the interception on October 14.
The strike was carried out by pilots from the brigade’s “Pribultsi” air-defense unit, despite indications that newer Mi-28NM helicopters are being fitted with additional systems designed to protect them from drone attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“An anti-aircraft FPV drone intercepted the aircraft in midair, leaving no chance for either the machine or the crew,” the unit wrote.
The Mi-28NM is the most advanced production version of Russia’s Mi-28 attack helicopter family and represents a substantial modernization of the earlier Mi-28N.
The newer aircraft received improved sensors, weapons, avionics, and defensive systems after the baseline version demonstrated significant limitations during Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Recent Mi-28NMs have also appeared with previously unseen sensors marked with the abbreviation NVCh, referring to microwave frequencies in the 300 MHz to 300 GHz range. The devices have been observed on the helicopter’s wingtips, around the nose of the cockpit, and toward the tail.
Their exact function has not been publicly confirmed, but the positioning has fueled speculation that Russia is adding another layer of protection against Ukrainian FPV drones. The equipment may represent an upgrade to the Mi-28NM’s existing L-370 Vitebsk defensive suite or an entirely new anti-drone system.
Russia has separately developed the Multik electronic warfare system, produced by the Gradient research institute specifically to protect helicopters from FPV attacks. However, the equipment recently seen on Mi-28NMs does not visually match that system.
The Mi-28NM also carries significantly more capable weapons than earlier variants. Among them is the Izdeliye 305 light multipurpose guided missile, which Russian sources claim can engage targets at ranges of up to 25 kilometers.
Earlier, reports emerged that a Russian Mi-8 military transport helicopter that crashed in the Voronezh region was reportedly shot down by a Russian Su-35 fighter jet in a friendly-fire incident.
The incident occurred as Russian forces were responding to a large-scale drone attack. The Su-35 crew allegedly misidentified the Mi-8 helicopter as a hostile unmanned aerial vehicle and opened fire.

Ukrainian forces have regained control of another 101 square kilometers (39 square miles) of territory and liberated three villages in the Donetsk region, bringing the total area recovered during Operation Vivaldi to 277 square kilometers (107 square miles).
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Ukrainian military says the offensive has disrupted Russia’s plans to encircle the strategically important cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
According to Ukraine’s Third Army Corps on October 14, the fourth phase of Operation Vivaldi resulted in the liberation of Zelena Dolyna, Lypove, and Kolodiazi near Lyman. Corps commander Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi reported that Ukrainian forces had restored full control over 16 settlements during the four-stage operation.

U.S. Navy stocks up on spare parts for Aegis radars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:37:39 UTC
18:37:39 KST

- The U.S. Navy ordered $15.1 million in Raytheon spare parts for MK 99, SPY-1 and SPY-3 systems, citing its goal of 75 mission-capable ships.
- The order raises fleet stocking and forward-deployed stock levels, covering 419 requirements across 46 parts, with work running through December 2034.
The U.S. Navy is building up its stocks of spare parts for the radars and fire-control gear on its Aegis warships, ordering $15.1 million worth of components from Raytheon in a deal it tied directly to the surface fleet’s goal of keeping 75 mission-capable ships ready on any given day.
The Department of War contract announcement published on Oct. 13 describes a firm-fixed-price delivery order covering 419 requirements across 46 separate parts used on the MK 99 fire control system, the AN/SPY-1 radar’s transmitter group and the AN/SPY-3 multifunction radar. Each of the 46 parts carries its own National Item Identification Number, the code the U.S. military uses to track an individual item through its supply system.
By Pentagon standards the dollar figure is small, and the more telling detail is the reason the U.S. Navy gave for the purchase. According to the announcement, the requirements stem from the Naval Surface Force’s North Star goal of 75 mission-capable ships and include fleet stocking increases from remodeled allowances for operational availability and endurance supply, along with higher stock levels at forward-deployed sites. Allowance change requests and maintenance activity account for the rest of the demand.
An allowance is the quantity of a given part that a ship or support site is authorized to carry, so raising those levels means more spare radar and fire-control components kept aboard ships and at overseas depots closer to where the fleet operates.
All three systems sit at the heart of U.S. Navy air and missile defense. SPY-1 is the main radar of the Aegis combat system on Arleigh Burke-class destroyers and Ticonderoga-class cruisers, while the MK 99 controls the illuminators that guide Standard Missile-2 interceptors onto their targets in the final seconds of flight. The X-band SPY-3 radar is fitted on Zumwalt-class destroyers and Ford-class aircraft carriers.
Vice Adm. Roy Kitchener, then commander of Naval Surface Forces, set the 75-ship North Star target in 2022 and aimed to reach it by fiscal 2024, a number that represented nearly half of the 164 surface ships in the fleet at the time. Under the surface force’s definitions, a mission-capable ship has completed basic certification and can deploy, though it may not yet be cleared for high-end combat. Surface force leaders said in early 2024 that the fleet had not yet reached the target, eighteen months into the two-year plan.
Raytheon already holds a larger slice of Aegis work this year, having received a $271.5 million contract on Aug. 3 for MK 99 fire control equipment, Aegis modernization hardware and engineering support, with options that could raise its value to $302.5 million.
Raytheon will perform 95% of the new order in Andover, Massachusetts, and the remaining 5% in Chesapeake, Virginia, with deliveries expected to run through December 2034. The U.S. Navy is paying with fiscal 2026 working capital funds that will not expire at the end of the current fiscal year, and Naval Supply Systems Command Weapon Systems Support in Philadelphia awarded the order on a sole-source basis after soliciting only Raytheon.

Feature: When Chinese moon goddess Chang'e speaks Kiswahili on Tanzanian stage
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:37:20 CST
18:37:20 KST

by Xinhua writers Hua Hongli, Lin Guangyao, Lucas Liganga
DAR ES SALAAM, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- At the China Cultural Center in Tanzania's commercial hub of Dar es Salaam, Danifrida Ngonyani took to the stage as Chang'e, the legendary figure from Chinese mythology who flies to the moon.
This, however, was no ordinary retelling of an ancient tale: the characters spoke Kiswahili, while traditional Tanzanian instruments, including drums and marimba, accompanied the performance.
The play "Chang'e: Flying to the Moon" was part of celebrations marking the Mid-Autumn Festival, drawing diplomats, film industry stakeholders and other guests, who watched attentively and applauded the performance.
For the Tanzanian actress, who has been a member of the local organization African Film Arts and Social Revolution (AFASR) for about four years, playing Chang'e offered an opportunity to explore Chinese history and discover connections between the two countries' cultural traditions.
"Being given the role of Chang'e made me very proud and excited," she said, adding that the experience taught her about Chinese history and love.
The legend of Chang'e is deeply intertwined with the Mid-Autumn Festival, a cherished Chinese tradition when families reunite, gaze at the full moon, and share mooncakes.
According to one version of the legend, Chang'e drinks an elixir of immortality to prevent it from falling into the wrong hands. She then ascends to the moon, leaving her husband, Hou Yi, on Earth.
The festival, marked on the 15th day of the eighth month of the Chinese lunar calendar, is also associated with the harvest and symbolizes reunion and togetherness.
Bringing the story to a Tanzanian stage took more than language translation. The production incorporated local music and theatrical traditions, allowing Tanzanian performers to tell a Chinese story through artistic expressions familiar to their audiences.
Nyakwesi Silas Mujaya, founder and director of AFASR, said the approach sought to blend the two cultures, without allowing either to overshadow the other.
"When we take a Chinese story, we put it in a Tanzanian context and perform it in a way that allows both cultures to be represented," she said.
For Mujaya, the legend also carries themes familiar to Tanzanian audiences, including sacrifice, responsibility, protecting others, and the struggle between good and evil.
She said the story reminded her of Tanzanian historical figures who had made sacrifices for their people, as well as experiences within families and communities.
"Although the story comes from China, some of its values are similar to ours. We also celebrate our heroes and preserve stories about people who have done important things for society," she said.
The production was developed through cooperation between AFASR and the China Cultural Center in Tanzania.
A total of 14 artists took part, including stage performers and those responsible for music and visual elements. The one-hour play required about one month of continuous preparation, according to Mujaya.
The cultural center also provided support for production materials and costumes, helping the nonprofit organization meet some of the costs involved in staging the performance.
Founded in 2012, AFASR uses drama, theatre, music and dance to support women, children and young people, helping them develop artistic skills and find opportunities to participate in their communities.
"Arts and culture are not only a way of empowering people economically, but also a way of helping them understand their culture, develop skills and contribute to their communities and society," Mujaya said.
She noted that many participating artists still rely on other activities to support themselves between commissioned performances. AFASR hopes that wider cultural partnerships and more opportunities to perform will help make artistic work a more sustainable livelihood.
For Ngonyani, playing Chang'e has also deepened her interest in Chinese culture.
Preparing for the role introduced her to Chinese history and traditions she had not previously encountered. During activities associated with the production, she also learned about Chinese coffee-making practices, another experience that introduced her to unfamiliar cultural traditions.
"I like their culture. If I get the opportunity to visit China, I would like to learn many more things, including their cultural traditions and dances, because I also enjoy dancing," she said.
Mujaya shared that ambition, voicing hope for cooperation with the China cultural center to eventually enable AFASR artists to perform in China, introduce Tanzanian culture to Chinese audiences and learn from Chinese performers.
"I want to visit China not only to see the country, but also to learn about its culture. At the same time, I want Chinese people to learn about Tanzanian culture," Mujaya added. ■

Former Ukrainian military officer to stand trial in Germany over Nord Stream sabotage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:37:08 UTC
18:37:08 KST

While some in the West were quick to accuse Russia of sabotaging its own gas export route, German investigators identified a cell of Ukrainians they say were the alleged perpetrators.
A former Ukrainian military officer is set to become the first person to stand trial over the 2022 Nord Stream pipeline bombings when proceedings begin in a German court on Wednesday.
In September that year, seven months after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a series of blasts under the Baltic Sea damaged three of the four Nord Stream pipelines designed to carry Russian gas to Europe.
While some in the West were quick to accuse Russia of sabotaging its own export route, German investigators identified a cell of Ukrainians they say were the alleged perpetrators.
Investigators allege Sergiy Kuznietsov, a former Ukrainian special forces officer, led a group of divers, an explosives expert, and a boat skipper that planted explosives on the pipelines.
Kuznietsov, who was arrested in Italy last year and extradited to Germany, will face charges including carrying out a "war crime," attacking civilian infrastructure and causing an explosion.
Ahead of proceedings getting underway in the northern city of Hamburg, a small group of pro-Ukrainian demonstrators staged a protest outside the court.
They held placards saying "Russia is a terrorist" and "What are war crimes? A blown-up pipeline? Or the bombing of buildings and the killing of people?"
According to the indictment, Kuznietsov entered Germany in early September 2022 using a forged Ukrainian passport and, together with the rest of the sabotage team, boarded a rented yacht in the German Baltic Sea port city of Rostock.
The yacht was allegedly loaded with large quantities of military-grade explosives and set sail for a spot where the pipelines ran under the Baltic Sea near the Danish island of Bornholm.
Divers then allegedly planted explosive charges equipped with timers on the pipelines, which blew up several days later.
Sabotage attacks
Kuznietsov's lawyers unsuccessfully tried to challenge the German court's jurisdiction over the attacks and have suggested they may argue that the pipelines were legitimate military targets in Ukraine's fight against Russia's invasion.
The defendant will refuse to testify during the trial as ex-members of Ukraine's special forces are banned from speaking publicly about their work when in the military, news magazine Stern reported on Wednesday.
The pipelines were built and owned by a corporate consortium led by Russian energy giant Gazprom.
At the time of the blasts, none were in operation.
Moscow had already suspended gas deliveries to western Europe through Nord Stream 1, comprising two pipelines, after the European Union imposed sanctions over the war in Ukraine.
Nord Stream 2, also made up of two pipelines, had only just been completed and never entered service.
When asked by AFP what Russia expected from the trial, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he expects "that those who carried it out will be named, along with those who ordered it."
"I don't think anybody has any doubt about who it really is," Peskov added.
A senior Ukrainian official, meanwhile, told the AFP news agency that Kyiv has "no expectations from the trial."
Sensitive subject
Kyiv has consistently denied orchestrating the sabotage.
But it has made no secret of its satisfaction with the results, saying that by rendering the pipelines inoperable, Moscow's ability to fund its war was weakened.
Another suspect, partially identified as Volodymyr Z. and accused of taking part in the sabotage as a diver, was arrested in Croatia in August.
A Croatian court has approved his extradition to Germany although he is appealing the decision.
According to media reports, Volodymyr Z. was advising the makers of a Hollywood film inspired by the sabotage, with Oscar-winning actor Adrien Brody tapped to portray the leader of the sabotage unit.
Volodymyr Z. had previously been arrested in Poland but was freed after a Polish judge refused to extradite him to Germany, ruling that the sabotage of the pipelines was justified as part of Ukraine's defence.
Since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Germany has become Kyiv's leading military backer and regularly accuses Russia of sabotage and espionage on its soil.
But the Nord Stream sabotage remains a sensitive subject in Germany.
Some have blamed the attacks for helping to drive up energy prices and worsening a gas crisis that rocked Europe's biggest economy.

LAS VEGAS, United States, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China showcased its tourism offerings at IMEX America 2026, which opened Tuesday at the Mandalay Bay Convention Center in Las Vegas.
The three-day trade show brought together tourism officials and industry representatives from several Chinese provinces and regions under the national tourism brand "Nihao! China." It marks China's third consecutive year of participation in the exhibition for the meetings, incentives, conferences and exhibitions (MICE) industry.
The Chinese pavilion features the theme "China: Where Business Meets Extraordinary Experiences," highlighting the country's modern convention and exhibition facilities, international hospitality services, and diverse cultural and tourism resources.
Tourism authorities and companies from Beijing, Hunan, Shaanxi, Jiangsu, Sichuan and the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region are showcasing their destinations and services through individual booths. By combining natural landscapes with distinctive cultural attractions, the exhibitors aim to highlight the diversity of China's MICE destinations.
The China National Tourist Office in Los Angeles has organized more than 20 presentations to introduce China's latest MICE tourism destinations, products and developments to international industry professionals.
Wu Dawei, director of the China National Tourist Office in Los Angeles, said China's competitiveness in the international MICE market has strengthened in recent years as the country expands its opening to the world. Visa-free entry and transit policies have been further optimized, while international transportation links, mobile payment services and services for receiving inbound visitors have continued to improve.
China's participation in IMEX America is intended to deepen cooperation with international industry partners and encourage more international meetings and corporate incentive travel programs to choose China, Wu said.
Marta Pani, a lead project manager at Italy-based event management company Event Planet Group, told reporters that the company plans to hold an international medical conference in China next year.
"We always look for nice venues, nice cities that appeal to guests," she said.
She added that Beijing is certainly a popular tourist destination, but China has much more to offer beyond its major cities. "My knowledge of China is admittedly limited, but from what I've seen and heard, there's much more to explore beyond central Beijing."
IMEX America is one of the world's largest annual trade shows for the meetings and incentive travel industry. This year's event is expected to draw more than 17,000 professionals and feature more than 3,700 exhibitors representing destinations, venues, hotels, service providers and event planning companies worldwide. ■

China Focus: Drones rise over grassland the Red Army once crossed
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
17:36:30 CST
18:36:30 KST

A drone is seen in operation during an earthquake relief drill held in Tiebu Town of Ruoergai County, southwest China's Sichuan Province, May 12, 2026. (Xinhua)
CHENGDU, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- When Ngorcog was a child growing up on the vast grasslands of Sichuan Province in southwest China, she never imagined that barley and fruit would one day "fall from the sky."
For the young Tibetan woman, cargo transport used to rely on horses and yaks, and later, trucks. Today, the 25-year-old has a new role: pilot of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
"Learning to fly drones was difficult at first, but it was also fascinating," she said. Drone logistics services are becoming increasingly common in the Aba Tibetan and Qiang Autonomous Prefecture, where Ngorcog lives.
Ngorcog is from Baxi Town in Ruoergai County of Sichuan. In September 1935, during the Long March, the Central Committee of the Communist Party of China held the Baxi Meeting there, establishing the strategic policy of continuing northward.
The site of the meeting, Banyu Monastery, remains a place of regular worship for Ngorcog, who practices Tibetan Buddhism. In Tibetan culture, the sky holds special significance, with the mythical Garuda bird symbolizing good fortune.
Ngorcog's first encounter with drones came during her university years, when she and her classmates used one to take graduation photos.
"I felt both excited and nervous during takeoff," she recalled. "When the lens rose to the sky, offering a bird's-eye view of the surrounding world, the familiar scenery instantly looked different. My horizon was completely opened, and that sense of vastness was hard to describe in words."
However, it was not until after graduating in 2024 that she began professional training. Originally a music student, she decided to apply for drone training after seeing a recruitment notice from Ruoergai General Aviation Culture and Tourism Co., Ltd.
This company is the first low-altitude economy enterprise in Aba, a plateau region with an average altitude between 3,500 and 4,000 meters, and Ruoergai is China's first pilot county for the low-altitude economy on high-altitude plateaus.
Ngorcog was sent to a training and certification base in Jiande, east China's Zhejiang Province. "The hardest part was flying the 8-shaped route," she said. Three months later, she obtained her pilot license.
Her parents, both farmers, live 90 kilometers from her workplace. Having never seen a drone before, they were curious about their daughter's new job.
"They asked me if I could use the drone to spray pesticides on their vegetable plots," she said with a smile.
More than 90 years ago, the Red Army crossed the grasslands of Ruoergai and surrounding areas. In his book "The Long March: The Untold Story," American journalist and author Harrison Salisbury described the area as "untouched for 3,000 years." Filled with swamps, extreme cold and low oxygen, the treacherous terrain claimed the lives of many soldiers.
In recent years, Ruoergai has developed its low-altitude economy. So far, its low-altitude airspace covers 9,119 square kilometers, making it one of the largest contiguous low-altitude coordinated airspaces in China.
Located on a high-altitude plateau, Ruoergai is prone to extreme weather such as blizzards, and some areas face high risks of geological disasters. When roads are cut off by ice, snow or landslides, making them impassable for people and vehicles, drones can take off quickly to deliver urgent medicines, food and warm clothing to isolated areas.
In May this year, Aba held an earthquake relief drill in Ruoergai. The drill simulated a magnitude 6.6 earthquake that severed roads, paralyzed communications, and turned some villages into "isolated islands." During the exercise, compound-wing UAVs conducted aerial reconnaissance of the disaster area and airdropped first-aid kits, drinking water and communication equipment to the "stranded" zones, effectively addressing the communication and access challenges.
"When a sudden disaster occurs on the Ruoergai grassland, drones can fly immediately to areas inaccessible to vehicles, conduct reconnaissance and deliver emergency supplies," said Huang Peifeng, deputy head of Ruoergai County.
Meanwhile, Ruoergai is gradually incorporating drones into the monitoring and patrolling of grassland ecology and wetlands.
Including Ngorcog, the company established last year now has four local Tibetan female pilots who have successfully obtained licenses to operate medium-sized drones and officially started their jobs. Their main duties include aerial photography for tourism and resource data collection.
As a national strategic emerging industry, the low-altitude economy is rapidly gaining momentum. The Civil Aviation Administration of China predicts that the market size of China's low-altitude economy is set to exceed 3.5 trillion yuan (around 522 billion U.S. dollars) by 2035.
According to a report on education and industrial talent development in China's low-altitude economy this year, the shortage of core positions in the sector will reach 1.82 million in the next five years, with demand for technical roles surging by over 320 percent.
To enhance local children's understanding of drones, the company offers study tour courses.
According to Tsewang Lhamo with the Ruoergai General Aviation Culture and Tourism Co., Ltd., the company has collaborated with local schools for over a year, hosting 500 to 600 students. The curriculum includes aviation lectures, VR experiences, model aircraft making and drone soccer.
"Few people on the grassland had ever encountered drones before," Tsewang Lhamo said. "The children were very interested. I thought they might be afraid of the VR flying experience, but they weren't. During the lessons, they didn't even want class to end."
"Children here rarely have access to cutting-edge technologies. These drone study tours sow the seeds of the low-altitude economy on the grassland. The curiosity in their eyes is precious, and it shows us the unique potential of these grassland children," said Yang Rong, a teacher at a primary school in the Ruoergai county seat.
Tsewang Lhamo is also preparing to take her pilot license exam.
"I hope to master another skill," she said. "In the future, drones will be used in more places across the grassland." ■

Palestinian children’s rights lawyer Khaled Quzmar receives Amnesty Human Rights Award 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:36:17 UTC
18:36:17 KST

BERLIN, 13 October 2026 – This year’s Human Rights Award of Amnesty International Germany goes to the Palestinian lawyer Khaled Quzmar, in recognition of his longstanding commitment to defending the rights of children in the illegally occupied Palestinian territory. The award carries a prize of €20,000.
An internationally recognised expert on children’s rights, Khaled Quzmar has played a crucial role in exposing structural and systematic human rights abuses against Palestinian children and in placing demands for accountability and justice at the heart of public debate. He has documented human rights violations in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem for UN bodies and international courts, and has enabled countless children and their families to access legal assistance and psychosocial support.
Because of his work, Quzmar, who is based in Ramallah, has been subjected to considerable pressure, repression and smear campaigns by the Israeli authorities. Such instances include being summoned by Israel’s internal intelligence service, Shin Bet, and threatened with a lengthy prison sentence. As long-serving Director General of the human rights organisation Defense for Children International – Palestine (DCI-P), he was forced to dissolve the organisation in spring 2026, after more than 35 years, in the face of sustained harassment by the Israeli authorities. Since June 2026, he has served as Executive Director of the organisation Palestinian Center for Child Rights (PCCR).
Julia Duchrow, Secretary General of Amnesty International Germany, said: “For almost 40 years, Khaled Quzmar has worked tirelessly and against all odds to give a voice to the most vulnerable group in Palestinian society: its children. Their devastating living conditions are the direct consequence of structural human rights abuses and systematic oppression, which have intensified significantly in recent years. This state of affairs is depriving entire generations of a future. Allies of the Israeli government, including the United States and Germany, have contributed to this situation. They not only turn a blind eye to serious human rights abuses against Palestinians but facilitate them through arms deliveries. This must come to an end. Palestinian children need immediate and the fullest possible protection.”
Structural human rights abuses and systematic discrimination
For decades, Palestinian children have been subjected to grave human rights abuses as a result of Israel’s unlawful occupation and cruel system of apartheid against all Palestinians. Since the massive escalation of violence in October 2023 and the beginning of the genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, their situation has deteriorated dramatically.
“What is often portrayed as a humanitarian crisis is the result of political decisions by the Israeli government that are systematically destroying these children’s lives. This is not only about the lack of humanitarian aid for children across the unlawfully occupied Palestinian territory; it is about their right to life and physical integrity, to freedom and security, to education, health and housing – and ultimately about whether these human rights apply to Palestinian children at all,” said Julia Duchrow.
In the Gaza Strip, the Israeli military has killed at least 20,000 children since October 2023, and more than 17,000 have lost their families. Tens of thousands of children are living with severe injuries, hunger and disease, amid destroyed infrastructure and without access to basic services, schools and education. In the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, children are affected by state-backed settler violence and displacement – with schools and infrastructure also being systematically destroyed there.
Repression of Palestinian civil society
Human rights defenders and human rights organisations in the Occupied Palestinian Territory face constant repression by the Israeli authorities and military. In October 2021, Israel designated the DCI-P – the organisation for which Khaled Quzmar had worked for many years – as a terrorist organisation, along with five other Palestinian civil society organisations, without providing any substantiated evidence. Amnesty International, the United Nations and numerous civil society organisations strongly criticised the designation. The German government and many other EU partners have also rejected Israel’s designation. Since the current ruling coalition took office – and particularly since 7 October 2023 – staff members of some organisations have increasingly been subjected to intimidation, smear campaigns, interrogation, arbitrary detention, imprisonment and ill-treatment, with some offices also being raided.
Amnesty International Germany’s Human Rights Award
Every two years, Amnesty International Germany honours individuals and organisations working for human rights under difficult conditions with its Human Rights Award. The award aims to recognise, support and protect their work and to raise public awareness of it. It carries a prize of €20,000. 2026 marks the 13th time the Amnesty Human Rights Award will have been presented. Previous recipients include Eren Keskin (Türkiye), Svetlana Gannushkina (Russia), Alice Nkom (Cameroon), Henri Tiphagne (India) and the Colombian organization Federation of Santander Fishers for Tourism and Environment (FEDESPAN).

Men Can’t Stop Faking How Much They Know About AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

Say you’re a guy who reads WIRED—you know a thing or two about artificial intelligence. You recognize the names of well-known people developing AI, like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. But do you know who Mira Murati is? What about Susan Milner? Craig Dalton?
In a new survey of more than 5,400 Americans, 73 percent of male respondents told Harvard researchers they knew who Altman was. A little over half—53 percent—said they knew of Murati, Milner, and Dalton.
There’s one problem. Murati is a real person: she’s the former CTO of OpenAI and the current CEO of Thinking Machine Labs. Milner and Dalton, on the other hand, do not exist.
Compared to women, “we're seeing that men are more optimistic and more confident” across the board when it comes to AI, Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center executive director Laura Manley tells WIRED. Sometimes, that veers into overconfidence—like claiming to recognize fictional AI executives. (For context, 40 percent of women claimed to know who Milner and Dalton were; 38 percent said they recognized Murati.)
While Manley notes that men are more overconfident in general when surveyed, the report, published on Wednesday, digs into what the confidence gap on AI looks like, as well as the repercussions of gendered divides.
Researchers found that men use AI more frequently and are, on average, better able to correctly answer factual questions about AI. But men and women answer questions incorrectly at around the same rate. The discrepancy is based on how often women said they weren’t sure of an answer—an average of 3.3 questions out of 12 compared to 2.3 questions for men.
Researchers wondered if this predilection toward certainty colors coverage of AI. Across a year of media coverage, men were named in headlines about AI more than 14 times as often as women. Because top AI executives skew heavily male, researchers decided to reexamine coverage, looking solely at people who were quoted as subject experts. Three-quarters of these experts were men—a higher proportion than the actual AI talent pool, which is roughly 29 percent women.
“Maybe there should be more women prominently featured as experts or given the platform to express: not sure,” Manley says.
Besides intellectual bluster, Americans were generally in agreement that AI was freaking them out—men and women both rated “concern” as their top emotional response. However, female respondents were more concerned, fearful, and worried than their male counterparts. Men, meanwhile, rated every positive feeling—including curiosity, enthusiasm, and excitement—higher than women did.
In the current discourse, “there's so much confidence in either doom or abundance,” Manley says. “It just drowns out all of the voices that should be saying ‘not sure.’” There are many unanswered questions on proper uses for and the future of AI. One gender is simply less likely to acknowledge such uncertainty.
“We have to be able to be able to say ‘not sure’ more often,” Manley says.

18:29:18 KST

In Odesa, nine members of Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center notification groups were convicted of abducting and torturing men
Kyiv • UNN
The court convicted nine military and civilian members of Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Center groups of abducting and torturing men. Six received actual prison sentences.
In Odesa, nine employees of the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers were convicted of unlawful deprivation of liberty, kidnapping, and torture. Among those convicted were military personnel and civilians involved in mobilization activities. This was reported by the Office of the Prosecutor General, UNN reports.
Details
According to the available information, the court handed down the guilty verdicts in September–October 2026.
"Prosecutors from the Odesa Specialized Prosecutor's Office in the Defense Sphere of the Southern Region proved that in April–May 2026, they unlawfully detained men on the city's streets, forcibly put them into vehicles, and took them to the Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers. During the detentions, the victims were beaten, exposed to tear gas, threatened, and humiliated. The men were also forced to provide personal data and information about other persons of conscription age. In one case, the victim was threatened with sexual violence; in another, a man lost consciousness after tear gas was used. In addition, during the forcible transportation of one of the men, a convicted person took UAH 5,200 from his wallet," the Prosecutor General's post says.
According to the available data, all nine men pleaded guilty and entered into plea agreements, which were approved by the court.
"The punishment depended on each person's role in the crimes. Six of those convicted were sentenced to actual imprisonment. The harshest sentence was 7 years and 1 month in prison. Two others were each sentenced to 2 years of restriction of service, with 10% of their monetary allowance deducted and transferred to state revenue, while one was sentenced to 5 years in prison with a 2-year probation period. Four of those convicted were also prohibited for three years from holding positions in district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers and from participating in mobilization activities," the post says.
The actions of those convicted were qualified under Part 1 of Article 28, Part 2 of Article 146, and Part 3 of Article 127 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. One of them was additionally convicted of robbery committed under martial law (Part 4 of Article 186 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
The trial of two more defendants is currently ongoing.
Reminder
Law enforcement officers reported suspicion to three heads of district Territorial Recruitment and Social Support Centers—one incumbent and one former official in Zakarpattia, and one former official in Bukovyna. According to the investigation, from December 2025 to February 2026, the officials entered information on at least 857 fictitiously mobilized persons into the "Oberih" system, artificially inflating the reported performance of mobilization plans.
