India remains a ‘natural partner’ for Russia – Jaishankar
India remains a natural partner for Russia as Moscow turns increasingly toward Asia amid its deteriorating relations with European nations, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar has said. Maintaining strong ties with Moscow serves the interests of both countries and the wider world, he added. 
Russia’s relationship with Europe has become “pretty much a broken, embittered relationship,” pushing Moscow to strengthen its ties with Asia, particularly China, Jaishankar told the Bloomberg New Economy Forum in New Delhi on Tuesday. 
He noted that Russia had historically considered itself a European country and valued its relationships with both Europe and the US, but that sanctions following the escalation of the conflict in Ukraine had pushed it toward Asia. 
The European Union on Monday adopted new sanctions targeting 826 Russian companies and 743 executives, saying the restrictions were intended to increase pressure on Moscow over the Ukraine conflict.
🇷🇺🤝🇮🇳 'India Is A Natural Option': Jaishankar On Russia’s Pivot To Asia The EAM asserted that it is in both 🇮🇳’s and the world’s interest that 🇷🇺 has other major options in Asia - framing New Delhi's 75-year partnership as an essential geopolitical stabilizer. https://t.co/vuzrW4JnXk
— RT_India (@RT_India_news) October 14, 2026
The Indian foreign minister said it is in New Delhi’s interest, and that of the wider world, for Russia to have multiple choices and maintain substantial partnerships with other Asian powers. “We are a natural option in that regard,” Jaishankar said, pointing to nearly eight decades of steady relations between New Delhi and Moscow. 
India has continued to assure Russia that despite changes in the international order and Moscow’s strategic calculations, the longstanding bilateral partnership remains intact, he said. 
The relationship has served both countries and contributed to the balance of power in Asia, Jaishankar added.
India and Russia have maintained close ties for decades, particularly in defense, energy, and space cooperation. The two countries formalized a strategic partnership in 2000 and elevated it to a Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership in 2010.
They are also targeting $100 billion in bilateral trade by 2030, compared with $68.7 billion in the 2024-25 financial year. Russian oil remains a major component of India’s imports, despite pressure from Washington to scale back purchases.
New Delhi has also stepped up its involvement in efforts to end the Ukraine conflict, which it has maintained should be resolved through dialogue and diplomacy.

China's foreign trade maintains sound momentum in first three quarters
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
16:00:06 CST
17:00:06 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on China's import and export of the first three quarters of 2026 in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 14, 2026. (Xinhua/Jin Liangkuai)
BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's foreign trade maintained sound momentum in the first three quarters of 2026, with both exports and imports growing rapidly and the overall growth rate reaching its highest level for the same period in five years, official data showed Wednesday.
The country's total imports and exports rose 18.8 percent year on year to 39.94 trillion yuan (about 5.94 trillion U.S. dollars) in the January-September period, according to the General Administration of Customs (GAC).
Growth accelerated through the year, with the expansion rate rising from 15.3 percent in the first quarter to 18.3 percent in the second quarter and 22.3 percent in the third quarter.
Foreign trade growth in the first three quarters was the fastest for the same period in the past five years, with both quarterly and monthly growth rates generally accelerating, said Wang Jun, GAC's deputy head.
"Latest international data show that such a growth rate ranks among the top among major economies, and China remains the world's largest trader of goods," the official told a press conference on Wednesday.
Exports increased 16.4 percent year on year to 23.2 trillion yuan, while imports expanded by 22.3 percent to 16.74 trillion yuan, GAC data showed.
In September alone, China's total imports and exports reached 5.16 trillion yuan, up 27.5 percent from a year earlier and crossing the 5-trillion-yuan mark for the first time. This figure also marked the sixth consecutive month of double-digit monthly growth.
Exports rose 29.6 percent year on year to 3.03 trillion yuan, while imports grew 24.6 percent to 2.13 trillion yuan for the month.
The country's trade with more than 180 countries and regions expanded during the first three quarters. Trade with free trade partners reached 19.55 trillion yuan, up 30 percent and contributing over 70 percent of the total trade increment. Meanwhile, trade with other APEC economies rose 23.9 percent to 24.07 trillion yuan.
Trade with ASEAN grew 22.7 percent to 6.84 trillion yuan, that with the European Union rose 8.4 percent to 4.78 trillion yuan, and trade with the United States increased 4.1 percent to 3.18 trillion yuan.
Exports continued to shift toward new and higher-quality growth drivers. The equipment manufacturing sector contributed nearly 90 percent of the export increment, while intermediate goods accounted for more than half of total exports, underpinning global industrial and supply chains, according to the GAC. ■

12th Kyiv International Economic Forum to Take Place on October 26, Focusing on Business and Economic Resilience Amid New Challenges
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:53:42 EEST
16:53:42 KST

Kyiv will host the 12th Kyiv International Economic Forum (KIEF) on October 26, bringing together more than 500 participants, including owners and executives of Ukrainian and international companies, government officials, investors, diplomats, and experts. This year’s theme, “People. Business. Economy. What’s Next?”, will guide discussions on how businesses and Ukraine’s economy can withstand mounting challenges, adapt to changing conditions, and return to growth.
Now in the fifth year of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine’s economy faces growing pressure. Russian attacks continue to target industrial facilities, energy infrastructure, ports, railways, logistics hubs, and other assets critical to business operations. According to Ukraine’s Ministry of Economy, direct damage from destruction could reach approximately $10 billion annually. Combined with the blockade of seaports, these losses have already cost Ukraine an estimated 1.5 percentage points of GDP in 2026.
In its October forecast, the World Bank projects that Ukraine’s economic growth will slow to 1.2% in 2026 and reach just 1.5% in 2027 if active hostilities continue. The Bank previously projected 4% growth in 2027, assuming hostilities would end by late 2026.
“While discussions previously focused on Ukraine’s reconstruction, the priority today is how to strengthen economic resilience here and now. Businesses need solutions that will help them protect their assets, maintain production, and continue investing even during wartime”, says Vasyl Khmelnytskyi, KIEF initiator, founder of UFuture holding.
Participant Registration
KIEF 2026 will feature 14 panel discussions addressing the most pressing challenges facing Ukraine’s economy. Key topics will include protecting business facilities, maintaining operations during air raid alerts, decentralizing logistics and energy supply, ensuring reliable communications, insuring against war-related risks, securing compensation for lost assets, accessing finance, and maintaining macroeconomic stability.
Discussions will also explore how Ukraine can adapt its industrial development strategy and energy policy to new realities, redefine national economic priorities, strengthen international cooperation, and advance European integration amid emerging challenges. Special attention will go to frontline cities and the practical solutions they have already implemented to keep their economies functioning.
Confirmed forum speakers include:
- Oleksandr Komarov, CEO and President of Kyivstar Group;
- Ruslan Shostak, President of TERWIN Corporation, founder of EVA and Varus;
- Francis Malige, Managing Director, Head of Financial Institutions, EBRD;
- Yuliia Svyrydenko, President of KSE Business School;
- Vyacheslav Klymov, Co-owner of NOVA Group;
- Dominykas Tuckus, Managing Director of the Amber Infrastructure Fund;
- Igor Nikonov, Founder of the Ukrainian development company KAN Development;
- Tomas Fiala, Founder of Dragon Capital;
- Inga Andreieva, Country Manager, Ukraine and Moldova, Mastercard;
- David Godfrey, Board Member, British-Ukrainian Economic Future, Former Chief, Executive, UK Export Finance (UKEF) | CBE.
Ukraine’s economy has already demonstrated its ability to adapt rapidly to major disruptions. In 2022, following the destruction of the Kremenchuk oil refinery and the resulting fuel shortages, the country rebuilt its fuel supply chains, while thousands of businesses relocated from frontline regions to safer areas further inland.
In 2023, Ukraine launched its own maritime corridor after traditional shipping routes were blocked. Following large-scale attacks on the power grid last year, businesses and the government also accelerated the development of distributed power generation.
Media Accreditation
“Today, any discussion about the future must start with practical decisions that businesses, the government, and international partners can make right now to sustain economic resilience and restore growth. This is precisely what KIEF 2026 is about”, says Yuriy Pyvovarov, CEO of KIEF.
Title Partners: UFuture, Mastercard, AEQUO, PrivatBank, Kyivstar
Forum Partners: Sense Bank, NEQSOL Holding, FUIB, DTEK, Ajax Systems, Uklon, TERWIN, Eclectic Talents Group, BALEX, CEO Club Ukraine
Interfax-Ukraine is the forum's media partner.

Complaints of nuisance behaviour on Hong Kong public transport hit 3-year high
Noisy and inconsiderate passengers who play loud music or put feet up on seats in the spotlight as government cites jump in complaints since 2023
Complaints about noisy and inconsiderate passengers on Hong Kong’s public transport have more than doubled over three years, with authorities recording a surge in reports of people playing loud music and putting their feet on seats.
“[Passengers] should be considerate and maintain mutual respect towards other passengers when using public transport services,” Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan said in a written reply to lawmaker Mark Chong Ho-fung.
Noise complaints, including those involving passengers playing audio at high volume on electronic devices, rose from 10 in 2023 to 11 in 2024, and then to 24 last year.
Complaints about improper or unhygienic conduct, such as placing feet on seats, also doubled from 21 in 2023 to 42 last year, with 33 recorded in 2024.

Ukrainian drones hit Russia's biggest data centre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:50:38 UTC
16:50:38 KST

Ukrainian drones hit Russia's top data centre in attack on AI ambitions
MOSCOW, Oct 14 - Ukrainian drones hit Russia's biggest data centre on Wednesday, part of a series of attacks appearing to target Moscow's ambitions to develop Russian artificial intelligence capabilities on a par with those from the US and China.
The strike on the Balakovo data centre, owned by Sberbank, the country's largest bank and technology company, followed three attacks in the past week on data centres owned by Russian technology group Yandex.
"We confirm that the data processing centre was attacked. At the same time, all of Sberbank's systems and services are operating normally and without disruption," Sberbank First Deputy CEO Alexander Vedyakhin told reporters.
President Vladimir Putin held a previously unannounced meeting on Wednesday with top officials on "information security", in which Sberbank CEO German Gref took part. The Kremlin said that the meeting was not linked to the attacks on data centres. Russia's state RIA Novosti news agency reported in 2024 that the Sberbank centre hit on Wednesday would host Russia's biggest supercomputer, which is scheduled to go into operation in 2027.
The Yandex data centres, hit earlier, hosted all three of that company's operating supercomputers. Neither Yandex nor Sberbank has said whether supercomputers, used to train the AI models, were damaged in the Ukrainian attacks.
Along with Yandex, its main domestic rival, Sberbank is Russia's leading developer of artificial intelligence. The domestic market is shared between Sberbank's GigaChat model and YandexGPT.
DIFFICULTIES PURCHASING CHIPS
Both companies have invested heavily in the development of their models but lag global leaders in the United States and China by up to nine months, according to Sberbank's own estimates, partly due to Western sanctions which hinder Russia's access to the most advanced hardware.
"It's clear what difficulties we face when purchasing modern graphics processing units. Both we and Yandex suffer from this," Gref said on September 29, calling it the biggest reason why Russia lags behind the US and China in AI.
Sberbank is in talks to buy chips from Chinese makers, but in an interview with Reuters on June 3, Vedyakhin said that US chipmaker Nvidia's monopoly on its CUDA software platform, which has become an AI industry standard, is an even greater problem.
Yandex said previously that its supercomputers operated on Nvidia A100 chips, a model launched in 2020 and since then succeeded by more advanced H100 chips.
Sberbank has two functioning supercomputers. The most advanced one, called Christofari Neo, ranked 167th in the Top 500 list of the world's most powerful supercomputers, is located in Moscow and is based on Nvidia A100 chips.
Yandex's most advanced Chervonenkis supercomputer is ranked 101st in the same list.
IT expert Mikhail Klimarev told Reuters it could take a long time to replace the chips due to Western sanctions, while damage to the supercomputers could set back the Russian AI industry, which already suffered from sanctions.
"The equipment is being imported, but it's done at a high cost, through indirect routes. First, you need to negotiate so that someone is willing to sell it to you and is not afraid of sanctions," he said.
PROTECT ASSETS
Some commentators compared the lack of reported disruption at state-controlled Sberbank with Yandex — whose taxi and food delivery units had reported disruptions — saying it showed that Sberbank's centres are better protected.
"This is a great example of what a business owner can do to protect their assets," wrote military blogger Alexander Kots. Under an August decree by Putin, the state can take over administration of poorly protected facilities.
The Sberbank site is located close to the Balakovo nuclear power plant, which the data centre uses as an energy source, and the Saratov hydroelectric power plant. No damage was reported to either plant from the attack.
Ukraine says it is responding to Russian attacks on its own data sites. Both countries have attacked each other's refineries, power stations, ports and e-commerce companies.
Russia's digital development ministry said this week it was in talks with the military on protecting the data centres, while some lawmakers called for them to be moved underground where the hardware will be out of reach for drones.
"We need a so-called Doomsday data vault," Valery Yermakov, deputy CEO of state-controlled Rostelecom, another major data centre operator, told a conference in Moscow. REUTERS

Poll: Center head Mihhail Kõlvart becomes most popular choice for prime minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:50:00 UTC

Poll: Center head Mihhail Kõlvart becomes most popular choice for prime minister
Center Party Chairman Mihhail Kõlvart has knocked Isamaa leader Urmas Reinsalu off the top spot in the Delfi and Turu-uuringute AS poll on preferred prime minister candidates.
Reinsalu had already matched his lowest approval rating in three years last month, at 18 percent, but his support fell further in October, with just 16 percent of voters now preferring him as prime minister, Delfi reported Wednesday.
Kõlvart, meanwhile, saw a surge in support, with 20 percent of respondents now preferring him as prime minister, his highest rating ever in the survey, Delfi noted. In May this year, Kõlvart's rating climbed to 19 percent, putting him level with Reinsalu at the time, before falling back to 16 percent.
Commenting on the results, Turu-uuringute AS CEO Tõnis Stamberg told Delfi that Kõlvart's rise was driven by increased support among ethnic Estonian voters. Kõlvart is backed by 13 percent of ethnic Estonians and 50 percent of ethnic Russians, compared with 18 percent and 6 percent, respectively, for Reinsalu. As recently as August, Kõlvart had the support of 11 percent of ethnic Estonians, compared with 22 percent for Reinsalu, indicating that Kõlvart has gained ground among ethnic Estonian voters while Reinsalu has lost support.
Kõlvart's support increased among both rural and urban residents, while Reinsalu lost ground among urban voters. However, Reinsalu managed to maintain his support among rural residents at 21 percent for a month. In October, Kõlvart gained support among respondents with the lowest and highest levels of education, while Reinsalu saw his biggest losses among those with the lowest levels of education, with smaller declines among university-educated respondents.
Asked whom they would prefer to see as prime minister, 20 percent of respondents in October named Kõlvart, 16 percent Reinsalu, 13 percent Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) Chairman Martin Helme, 10 percent Eesti Parempoolsed leader Lavly Perling, 7 percent Social Democratic Party Chairman Lauri Läänemets, 5 percent Reform Party Chairman and incumbent Prime Minister Kristen Michal, and 2 percent Estonia 200 leader Kristina Kallas. Another 27 percent were unable to say.
Turu-uuringute AS conducted the survey for Delfi online and by telephone from October 1 to 3, with 899 Estonian citizens ages 18 and older responding.

Saudi employee arrested for allegedly bugging OpenAI office

Breadcrumb
FBI arrests Saudi employee for allegedly bugging OpenAI office
A Saudi employee of OpenAI was arrested after allegedly planting a recording device in one of the company's San Francisco offices, the AI firm and federal prosecutors said Tuesday.
"We discovered a sophisticated recording device that was hidden inside one of our offices" and "referred the matter to the FBI," OpenAI told AFP in a statement.
OpenAI's security team found the device late last month and the employee, Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested on 9 October, the US Justice Department said.
Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer who had worked for OpenAI since July 2025, allegedly wrapped a USB device in toilet paper and inserted it into a television located in an "executive conference room," according to a Justice Department statement.
He was allegedly caught on camera "near" the conference room multiple times but was not authorised to participate in meetings located there.
He used a "productivity tool" to search for more information about OpenAI's office buildings, meeting rooms, calendars, schedules and people's locations, according to the statement.
A chatbot account connected to Alfozan's spouse also allegedly contained queries related to remote audio recording and encrypting memory cards.
"This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative," Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said in the statement.
"The intelligence community remains committed to safeguarding America's cutting-edge intellectual property from foreign threats," Clayton added.
The arrest and allegations come amid a fierce global race to dominate in artificial intelligence, which the Trump administration has pushed to be rebranded as "superintelligence."
Saudi Arabia's state-backed AI firm Humain invested $3 billion in Elon Musk's xAI shortly before the American billionaire's space company, SpaceX, acquired the AI division in February.
Now known as SpaceXAI, the division announced last year that it was teaming up with Humain to build a 500-megawatt data center in Saudi Arabia.
Multiple devices
It was not immediately clear what, if any information the recording device was able to collect.
"At this time, we have no indications of this individual inappropriately accessing or exfiltrating model weights, source code, or customer data," OpenAI told AFP in a statement.
A second device was found by OpenAI's security team when they searched an unattended bag that belonged to Alfozan, according to the Justice Department.
Alfozan was caught on security footage from inside the restricted conference room where he appeared to look behind the television where the recording device had been placed, the Department said.
A LinkedIn account matching Alfozan's name and resume show that he previously worked at Facebook-owner Meta, as well as an AI startup and a venture capital firm.
He was also a student at University of California at Berkeley and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
The Justice Department said Alfozen had been charged with "using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications," for which he could face up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.
It did not accuse Alfozan nor Saudi Arabia, which is a close US ally, of spying activity in its statement on Tuesday.
Alfozan is expected to appear at a federal court hearing on 19 October.
In 2022, a former Twitter worker, Ahmad Abouammo, was found guilty of spying for Saudi officials keen to unmask critics on the platform.

U.S. moves leave Ukraine less able to defend itself
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:49:49 UTC
16:49:49 KST

- Ukraine received no partner warnings of Russian ballistic missile launches for two straight nights, the Ukrainian Air Force said, detecting missiles only minutes before impact.
- Starlink also stopped working above 160 km/h for Ukraine’s military, hitting tactical drones used in defense, as Russia’s strike left 600,000 without power.
Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian strikes has been limited by two U.S. moves in a single night: the country went without early warning of Russian ballistic missile launches from its partners for a second time in a row, and Starlink, the U.S. satellite service its frontline units depend on, was cut back for the Ukrainian military just as Russia launched one of its heaviest missile attacks on Ukraine’s power grid.
The Ukrainian Air Force said Russia launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv at about 10:40 p.m. on Oct. 13, and that once again no information about the launches had come from Ukraine’s partners before the missiles were in the air. The Air Force said the reasons were being investigated.
“The situation is similar to yesterday’s. No information regarding launches from enemy territory had been received from our partners. The reasons are being investigated,” the Ukrainian Air Force said in an official statement.
Ukraine has relied heavily on early warning from the United States, whose satellites can spot the heat of a missile launch deep inside Russia within moments, giving Ukrainian air defense crews time to prepare and giving cities time to sound air raid sirens. Without those alerts, Ukrainian forces only detected the incoming ballistic missiles once they came within range of ground radars, a few minutes before impact, and tried to shoot some of them down. The lost minutes shorten the reaction time for interceptor crews and hit civilians hardest, leaving people in Kyiv and other cities less time to reach shelters and metro stations.
The attack that followed was massive. Zelenskyy said Russia fired 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 attack drones and loitering munitions overnight into Oct. 14 at energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, the Kyiv region and Kharkiv, damaging 26 facilities in the power system and four in the oil and gas sector and leaving at least 600,000 people without electricity. He said there were dead and injured and warned that outages could spread.
Zelenskyy said the missile salvo deliberately targeted the energy infrastructure covered by the ceasefire President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11, which Moscow never confirmed accepting.
“Russia has never before shown such ostentatious disrespect toward the United States,” said Zelenskyy.
During the same night, Starlink terminals used by Ukraine’s military began losing their connection whenever they moved faster than 160 km/h (100 mph). Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy who is widely known by his call sign “Flash” and who has tracked Russian attempts to jam Starlink along the front, said the restriction hit the military StarShield package of the SpaceX service and that units received no notice before it took effect.
“Our defense forces did not receive any warning about this restriction, and it led to the disruption of a number of missions. It is obvious that this action cannot be a coincidence and is linked to the current political situation,” said Serhii Beskrestnov.
The restriction falls on Ukraine’s defense, not on its strikes inside Russia. SpaceX has never allowed Ukraine to use Starlink for strikes on Russian territory, and Zelenskyy said earlier this month that Kyiv was still asking for that permission, so Ukraine’s long-range drones and cruise missiles that hit targets in Russia do not rely on the service. Starlink has also been unavailable to Russian forces since February, when SpaceX and Ukraine’s Defense Ministry introduced a whitelist that cut off unregistered Russian terminals. Inside Ukraine, Starlink is used on tactical drones and uncrewed ground vehicles that operate over Ukrainian and Russian-occupied territory, so a speed cap above 160 km/h cuts the links of fast tactical strike and interceptor drones fighting Russian troops and drones along the front.
Ukrainian volunteer Serhii Sternenko, who first reported the change, said ordinary satellite terminals kept working and suggested SpaceX may have acted at the request of the Trump administration, while British analyst Jimmy Rushton noted that the limit does nothing to protect the Russian oil refineries Trump has criticized Ukraine for striking.
Ballistic missiles are the hardest part of Russia’s strike packages for Ukraine to stop, because they fly too fast and too high for most of its air defense systems, and Ukraine relies mainly on U.S.-made Patriot batteries to intercept them. Zelenskyy asked Washington and other partners for more Patriot interceptors and called on Trump to impose strong sanctions on Russia under the law sponsored by Sen. Lindsey Graham, which Trump signed in September.
“We ask for additional packages of Patriot missile interceptors for Ukraine,” said Zelenskyy.
The Ukrainian Air Force warned that further Russian attacks cannot be ruled out. Neither the White House nor SpaceX has explained why the missile launch warnings stopped or why the Starlink speed limit was introduced, or said whether either change is temporary.

An Indonesian domestic helper in Hong Kong has been remanded in custody after being charged with killing her 93-year-old employer at the weekend.
Kharsina, 52, was brought to the Kwun Tong Court on Wednesday to face a count of murder.
Police arrested her in the early hours of Monday after her 93-year-old employer was found unresponsive in her flat at Long Yiu House in Kai Tak’s Tak Long Estate on Sunday.
Paramedics rushed the elderly woman to hospital after administering emergency treatment at the scene, but she was pronounced dead shortly after.

Three more villages and 101 sq km: Ukrainian commander Biletskyi reports new gains in Operation Vivaldi
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:29:00 EEST
16:29:00 KST

Three more villages and 101 sq km: Ukrainian commander Biletskyi reports new gains in Operation Vivaldi
The 3rd Army Corps and attached units have liberated Zelena Dolyna, Lypove and Kolodiazi on the Lyman front, bringing another 101 sq km of territory back under Ukrainian control during the fourth stage of Operation Vivaldi.
Source: 3rd Army Corps, citing an address by its commander, Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi; DeepState, a Ukrainian group of military analysts
Details: Biletskyi said the operation had begun with efforts to root out Russian infiltrators but developed into a rapid, large-scale offensive. He said that Russian forces have begun losing control of their units, where "real chaos has broken out".
Quote: "We have prevented the enemy from bypassing the Sloviansk-Kramatorsk urban agglomeration from the flanks and encircling it, while also protecting the Kharkiv-Sloviansk motorway. The enemy has failed to cut the key logistics artery of our grouping in Donbas.
We have disrupted the offensive by Russia's Zapad (West) Group of Forces and forced it to redeploy some units of the 1st Guards Tank Army, easing the pressure on Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi."
Details: The corps reported that Russian forces had suffered about 3,000 casualties during the fourth stage of the operation, bringing their total losses in Operation Vivaldi to 8,000.
Over the four stages of the operation, Ukrainian forces have liberated 277 sq km of territory and restored full Ukrainian control over 16 settlements.
DeepState also reported the liberation of Kolodiazi, Lypove and Zelena Dolyna. The analysts also said the defence forces have regained control of areas near Stavky and Shandryholove.
The corps said the operation involves the 3rd Assault Brigade, the 60th Mechanised Brigade, the 125th Heavy Mechanised Brigade, the 3rd Separate Reconnaissance Battalion, the 25th Anti-Tank Battalion and the 21st Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment, also known as Kraken.
Attached units are also taking part in the operation: the 66th Mechanised Brigade, the 3rd Border Guard Detachment, the 10th Mobile Border Guard Detachment (known as Dozor), tactical groups from the 8th Special Operations Regiment, the Lasar's Group unit of the National Guard, the K-2 unit of the Unmanned Systems Forces and unmanned units from the Security Service of Ukraine's Special Operations Centre A.
Background:
- On 15 September, the 3rd Army Corps reported that it had cleared 75 sq km and liberated another 10 sq km during counteroffensive operations in northern Donetsk Oblast.
- On 20 September, it emerged that the 3rd Army Corps had liberated the villages of Shandryholove and Derylove in Donetsk Oblast as part of Operation Vivaldi and established full control over Drobysheve.
- On 28 September, Biletskyi reported that Russian forces had lost 2,000 military personnel during the third stage of Operation Vivaldi, while more than 250 Russian soldiers had been taken prisoner.
- On 3 October, Zelenskyy told Reuters that 125-140 sq km had been liberated in Operation Vivaldi by that point and that Russian losses had risen significantly over the previous two to three months.

SJM urges Centre to block Starlink’s rollout
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:26:27 UTC
16:26:27 KST

Swadeshi Jagran Manch (SJM) urged the Centre to block Starlink’s commercial rollout
NEW DELHI: RSS-affiliated Swadeshi Jagran Manch (SJM) on Tuesday urged the Centre to block Starlink’s commercial rollout, questioning whether Elon Musk’s satellite broadband service could ensure that Indian traffic passes through domestic gateways and comply with orders to restrict connectivity in specified areas.SJM national co-convener Ashwani Mahajan said the concerns involved India’s capacity to monitor communications lawfully and enforce security restrictions. It argued that laser links between satellites could allow traffic to bypass Indian ground infrastructure and travel through foreign networks.“A key regulatory condition is that Starlink must be able to precisely restrict its services at the govt’s behest,” SJM said. It questioned whether the company could meet this requirement, citing terrorism, riots and protests as situations in which authorities may seek local shutdowns.At issue, in SJM’s argument, is whether Indian authorities can enforce security directives on a foreign operator whose network extends beyond the country’s physical borders. SJM contrasted this with incumbent telecom companies which, it said, cooperate with investigators and can suspend services in designated areas.
The group accused Musk of applying public pressure instead of addressing Indian security concerns. Its intervention follows his allegation that “certain oligarchs” were blocking Starlink to protect their businesses and his criticism of Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani.SJM also flagged potential misuse by insurgents and smugglers. Starlink equipment was recovered during a drug seizure in Andaman and Nicobar Islands and an army search operation in Manipur in 2024. Musk has maintained that Starlink’s satellite beams were never activated over India.Starlink received a telecom licence on June 6, 2025, and authorisation from space regulator IN-SPACe on July 8 that year. Its commercial launch awaits completion of security assessments and spectrum assignment.
On Oct 8, the communications ministry rejected the discrimination allegations as “baseless and misconceived”, saying Starlink, Jio’s satellite venture and Bharti-backed OneWeb were at broadly the same regulatory stage. Each must demonstrate security compliance before seeking spectrum, it said.Starlink has previously said Indian user data would remain within the country and its security controls would meet Indian requirements.Arguing for indigenous alternatives, SJM claimed blocking Starlink would accelerate domestic satellite broadband development and eventually deliver cheaper connectivity to remote areas. It said India’s growing space capabilities and private sector participation could support domestic alternatives, even if their rollout took some more time. It also invoked US trade restrictions, arguing India was entitled to withhold permission on national security grounds.
Manash Pratim Gohain is a seasoned journalist with over two decades at The Times of India, where he has built a rich body of work spanning education policy, politics, and governance. Renowned for his incisive coverage of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, accreditation reforms, and skilling initiatives, he has also reported on student politics, urban policy, and social movements. His political reportage—both reflective and news-driven—adds depth to his writing, bridging policy with public impact. Through his 2,500 articles and related outlets, he has emerged as a trusted voice in national discourse, particularly in linking education reform to broader societal change.

Ukraine outlines extent of damage from massive Russian attack on energy sector
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
10:26:00 EEST
16:26:00 KST

Ukraine outlines extent of damage from massive Russian attack on energy sector
Power outages have been recorded this morning for consumers in the city of Kyiv and in Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Sumy, Donetsk, Dnipropetrovsk, Khmelnytskyi and Zaporizhzhia oblasts as a result of the latest Russian attack on the energy grid.
Source: Ukrenergo, Ukraine's state-owned electricity transmission operator
Details: Repair work has begun in areas where it is safe to do so.
Blackout schedules will be in effect throughout the day for up to two queues Ukrenergo defines a "queue" as a group of consumers and businesses using a specific amount of megawatts. The Dispatch Centre sets the number of queues needed across oblasts to address energy deficits. Critical infrastructure and eligible industrial companies that import at least 60% of their energy cannot be disconnected, according to a Ukrainian Cabinet resolution – meaning electricity may be unavailable for up to eight hours a day.
Power engineers also urge the public to limit consumption during peak hours – from 16:00 to 22:00 – to avoid overloading the power system and prevent grid failures.
Background:
- On the night of 13-14 October, the Russians conducted a combined attack on Ukraine. Specifically, missile and drone air-raid warnings were issued several times in Kyiv and a number of oblasts. Power cuts were recorded in the capital.
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy noted that Russian strikes have caused significant damage to 26 energy sites. He wrote that at least 600,000 people currently remain without power and added that further blackouts are possible.

Pope Leo recovering in Rome hospital after cancer diagnosis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:25:18 UTC
16:25:18 KST

Pope Leo XIV spent a peaceful night in hospital after undergoing surgery for lung cancer, the Vatican said Wednesday, adding that further information about the 71-year-old pontiff's condition would be released later in the day. 
Leo was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer, after doctors removed the lower lobe of his right lung during an operation Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital. The diagnosis, suspected during preliminary examinations, was confirmed through tissue analysis performed during surgery.
The operation lasted approximately 90 minutes and was completed without complications, according to a statement issued by Stefano Margaritora, the surgeon who led the procedure, and Luigi Carbone, the pope's personal physician. Leo spent about three hours in the operating room before regaining consciousness and returning to his hospital room.
Doctors removed the entire lower lobe of the right lung in an effort to eliminate the cancerous tissue. The human lungs have five lobes, three on the right and two on the left. The Vatican has not disclosed the tumor's precise size or whether cancer cells were found in nearby lymph nodes, factors that could influence the pontiff's prognosis and any need for additional treatment.
Leo was admitted to the hospital Tuesday after a small, localized growth was discovered during routine medical examinations. He had publicly disclosed the finding Sunday, saying doctors believed it was best to remove the nodule because of its early detection.
The Vatican previously said the pope was expected to remain hospitalized for approximately one week. All his public engagements have been canceled through October 20.
Elected in May 2025, Leo is relatively young for a pontiff and has generally maintained an active lifestyle, including playing tennis. He is not known to smoke and had no previously disclosed major health problems during his papacy.

As US pursues mine deals, Xi warns African resources are not tools for ‘rivalry’
The long-term viability of China-Africa ties relies on the continent gaining more value from its resources, analysts say
“Africa’s resources belong to Africa,” Xi told Botswanan President Duma Boko in Beijing on Tuesday, according to Chinese state news agency Xinhua.
He said it was a “historical injustice” that an unfair international division of labour had left the continent at the bottom of industrial and value chains, and China would contribute to plans for greater added value for Africa’s mining sector, according to state broadcaster CCTV.
Xi said China would be glad to see other parties providing genuine support for Africa’s development, and would work to create more favourable conditions for business investment and operation, Xinhua reported.

‘Constitution, not convenience’: Harvard-affiliated Indians hit out at anti-EC protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
07:23:34 UTC
16:23:34 KST

Harvard-affiliated Indians flag attacks on constitutional institutions and alleged misuse of the university’s name
NEW DELHI: The crackdown on protesters in Delhi has triggered a sharp divide among members of the Harvard University community, with two groups issuing contrasting statements, one condemning alleged police excesses and the other cautioning against what it described as a campaign to undermine India's constitutional institutions.Disapproving the use of terms such as “siege” to describe the police deployment in Delhi and “thieves” or “compromised” to characterise constitutional authorities, a section of Harvard affiliates said such language raised concerns about attempts to undermine public trust in democratic institutions.
"Troubling are reports of the use of Harvard University’s name to lend credibility to a political campaign without appropriate authorisation. The language used to describe India as being under 'siege' and to characterise constitutional authorities as 'thieves' or 'compromised' raises serious concerns about the intent to undermine public trust in democratic institutions," the wider cross-section of the Harvard community, including lawyers, policymakers, civil servants, scientists and academicians, said in a statement.
‘Constitution, not convenience'
The latest statement signed by 44 individuals raised concerns over what it described as a “concerted campaign” against the country's constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission, the Supreme Court, the office of the Chief Justice of India (CJI) and Parliament.
"We are deeply concerned by the negative public discourse and concerted campaign against India’s constitutional institutions, including the Election Commission of India, the Supreme Court, the office of the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India, and Parliament," the statement released on Wednesday said.It also addressed the role of law enforcement agencies in maintaining public order, saying their actions should be subject to fair scrutiny but that allegations must be grounded in evidence and due process.“The actions of law enforcement agencies to uphold public order deserve fair scrutiny, but sweeping accusations and abusive rhetoric cannot substitute for evidence, due process or institutional accountability,” the signatories said.They also stressed the need to respect public officials and the offices they hold, adding that constitutional principles and civil liberties must not be applied selectively.“The Constitution, rule of law, and civil liberties must be respected at all times, not just when it suits our interests,” the statement said.Summing up their appeal, the signatories said: “Our commitment must remain to the Constitution, not convenience; to justice, not selective outrage; and to democratic institutions, not the politics of accusation.”
October 12 statement condemns police action
In a statement dated October 12, around 100 Harvard alumni, students, faculty and staff condemned what they described as the “unprecedented siege of Delhi by police and paramilitary forces” and alleged arbitrary, illegal and unconstitutional action against peaceful protesters across the country on October 10."We, as alumni, students, faculty, and staff of Harvard University, are deeply concerned by the unprecedented siege of Delhi by police and paramilitary forces and arbitrary, illegal, and unconstitutional police actions against peaceful protestors across the country on 10th October 2026. We strongly condemn police brutality, unlawful detention, and violations of constitutional rights of all peaceful protestors," the letter shared by Live Law read.
The signatories condemned alleged police brutality, unlawful detention and violations of protesters' constitutional rights, while expressing solidarity with fellow Harvard affiliates Shadan Farasat, a senior advocate in the Supreme Court and Harvard Law School alumnus from 2009, and Mehr Pasricha, a Harvard Kennedy School graduate from 2025.The signatories called on the government and law enforcement authorities to end alleged violations of constitutional rights, respect the right to peaceful protest and access to legal assistance, and ensure that those responsible for abuses are held accountable under the rule of law.
Aastha Jha is a writer at The Times of India, covering politics. She also writes on business, global affairs, social issues, with a focus on policy, governance and their impact on everyday lives. Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, meets with French President's Diplomatic Adviser Emmanuel Bonne at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 13, 2026. (Xinhua/Liu Weibing)
BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng met with French President's Diplomatic Adviser Emmanuel Bonne in Beijing on Tuesday.
The two sides exchanged views on practical economic and trade cooperation between China and France, and economic and trade relations between China and the European Union (EU).
He, who is also a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, said that there is broad room for improvement in China-France economic and trade cooperation.
He added that China is willing to continue to work with France to implement the consensus reached by the two heads of state, strengthen practical cooperation in all economic fields and achieve mutual benefit and win-win results.
Noting that China and the EU are important economic and trade partners, He said that China is willing to continue dialogue with the EU in the economic and trade field to inject more stability and positive energy into the development of China-EU economic and trade relations.
Bonne said that France attaches great importance to economic cooperation with China and is willing to work with China to continuously achieve positive results in the China-EU trade and investment consultations, and maintain the stable development of economic and trade relations between the two sides. ■

Forlan buoyed by Uruguay restart after World Cup
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:08:56 CST
16:08:56 KST

MONTEVIDEO, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- Diego Forlan has offered a positive appraisal of his first matches in charge of Uruguay's national team, applauding his players' attitude in a recent three-stop friendly tour of Asia.
The Celeste lost 3-1 to Japan in Miyagi on September 24 before beating South Korea 4-1 in Seoul four days later and then cruising past India 6-1 in Kolkata on October 6.
"The feeling was great," Forlan told a news conference on Tuesday. "The team showed its quality throughout. We were able to give debuts to several players and the established ones performed at a very high level. It was a pleasure to be a part of the group."
Forlan replaced Marcelo Bielsa as manager in August, weeks after the team's failure to reach the knockout stage of the FIFA World Cup.
The 47-year-old, who is also in charge of Uruguay's under-20 national team, said the players had helped him settle into the position.
"What gave me the most peace of mind was their backing, their desire to come [to the national team]," he said. "We had talks with them beforehand, and everyone wanted to be there."
The former Manchester United, Villarreal, Atletico Madrid and Inter Milan striker said he was particularly impressed with his team's performance against South Korea.
"Honestly, I believe it had been a long time since I'd seen Uruguay's national team play the way they did against an opponent of a high standard," Forlan said.
"We scored some high-quality goals and controlled the tempo from the start. In the second half we could have scored a fifth or sixth goal."
Forlan scored 36 goals in 112 games for Uruguay, winning the Golden Ball as the best player at the 2010 World Cup after scoring five goals to help Uruguay reach the semifinals.
Forlan's coaching experience includes spells in charge of Uruguayan clubs Penarol and Atenas. ■

RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct. 13 (Xinhua) -- A first-half goal from attacking midfielder Adson gave 10-man Vasco da Gama a 1-0 away win over Boca Juniors in the first leg of their Copa Sudamericana semifinal on Tuesday.
The visitors took the lead in the 25th minute at La Bombonera when Adson latched onto an Andres Gomez cross with a glancing header into the far corner.
But Gomez went from protagonist to villain in the 64th minute, receiving two yellow cards in quick succession. Despite its numerical disadvantage, the Brazilian side defended resolutely to secure a vital first-leg advantage.
"It's not easy to play here, especially when you go a man down, but we were able to absorb the pressure," Adson said after the match. "We haven't won anything yet. We still have plenty of work to do to win the next match and reach the final."
The decisive return match will be played in Rio de Janeiro next Tuesday. The winner on aggregate will play the victor of the other semifinal between Atletico Mineiro and Montevideo City Torque in next month's final in Barranquilla, Colombia. ■

Myanmar marks International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
15:08:40 CST
16:08:40 KST

YANGON, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- Myanmar held a ceremony in Nay Pyi Taw to mark the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction, the state-owned daily The Global New Light of Myanmar reported on Wednesday.
During the ceremony on Tuesday, Vice President U Nyo Saw said that, as Myanmar is highly vulnerable to natural disasters, the country places great emphasis on pre-disaster preparedness and disaster risk reduction activities in accordance with the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030 and the Disaster Management Law in Myanmar.
He highlighted that capability and inclusive participation are vital factors in building disaster resilience and that it is necessary to strengthen resilience step by step, starting from individual households up to the national level, as a national duty.
Observed annually on Oct. 13, the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction focuses this year on the theme "Resilience Starts at Home." The message emphasizes that everyone deserves a home that is safe, affordable and able to withstand the hazards around it. ■

Lee Ming-che warns Europe of China’s transnational repression
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:50:45 UTC
15:50:45 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Human rights activist Lee Ming-che (李明哲) highlighted the dangers of China's transnational repression during a visit to the European Parliament on Tuesday.
Speaking with lawmakers Bernard Guetta and Engin Eroglu, Lee said that transnational repression targets outspoken advocates and can involve threats against family members and local associates, CNA reported. Information manipulation is sometimes used to deter victims and their families from seeking help or revealing the truth, he added.
Lee was arrested by Chinese authorities in Macao in 2017 for allegedly threatening national security. He was released in 2022.
Drawing on his own experience in detention, Lee said the Chinese government used local associates to threaten his wife by invoking concerns for his safety, per CNA. They demanded that she stop speaking publicly and sever her ties with Taiwan’s government and civil society groups.
Lee said that after returning to Taiwan, family members of other people detained in China had also sought his help. In addition to worrying about their loved ones’ well-being, they feared that publicizing the cases or seeking assistance from the government could lead to adverse consequences for their relatives. Such tactics obstruct efforts to uncover the truth and isolate human rights defenders, he said.
The activist urged democracies to provide necessary protection through public authorities and work with NGOs. People facing threats should be able to seek help safely and continue participating in public affairs, he said.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan plans to purchase 6 million tonnes of liquefied natural gas (LNG) annually from a proposed Alaska project and invest up to NT$141.5 billion (US$4.4 billion) in its development, the Ministry of Economic Affairs said Wednesday.
State-owned CPC Corp. has made significant progress in negotiations with the US developer after nearly 18 months of discussions, the ministry said in a statement. The proposed deal would diversify Taiwan's natural gas supplies, improve delivery flexibility, and strengthen energy security while deepening US-Taiwan cooperation, it said.
US President Donald Trump said at a rally in Alaska on Tuesday that Taiwan had agreed to purchase 30% of the natural gas from the proposed Alaska LNG pipeline project, Reuters reported. Bloomberg News cited Trump as saying the agreement would cover purchases over 20 years.
CPC signed a letter of intent covering LNG purchases and investment in the Alaska project in Taipei in March 2025. Specific investment arrangements, ownership stakes, and other terms remain subject to further negotiations and company approval procedures.
The project could diversify Taiwan's LNG shipping routes, as shipments could reach the country directly across the Pacific, reducing exposure to geopolitical supply risks, the ministry said. If development proceeds on schedule, supplies could begin reaching Taiwan as early as 2032.
CPC will continue coordinating with its US counterparts, conducting project assessments, and seeking budget approval. The ministry said it would continue monitoring global natural gas markets and reviewing domestic demand forecasts to help ensure a stable energy supply.

‘To Be Ordinary’ brings Taipei family drama to Busan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:50:15 UTC
15:50:15 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Weber Yang (楊一展) admits he visited some dark personal places when building the character he plays in “To Be Ordinary,” the new film from acclaimed director Lee Yun-chan (李芸嬋).
But Yang did not really have much choice, given certain unmistakable similarities between himself and his character and the stages they are going through in life.
“Like this character I feel like I am now going through a midlife crisis,” Yang said. “I told the director this on the first day of shooting. It's actually very confusing.”
“There is a continuous loss of direction. You don't know if it's because of work, or because of your hormones, or the things around you.
“Simply from this perspective, I think if there is any inspiration at all from this movie, then I hope it is the message that you can still find a direction in life.”
“To Be Ordinary” — which made its world premiere in the main Competition section this past week at the 31st Busan International Film Festival — marks Lee’s return to feature filmmaking after a break of some 20 years.
It also reveals the filmmaker has not lost her ability to frame deep, sometimes unnerving family drama. The time away, including time spent making the series “Women in Taipei” (2022) for Disney+, seems to have simply sharpened it.
“To Be Ordinary” features Yang and Winnie Chang Shih-Ying (張詩盈) as a struggling couple whose son is hit by an elderly driver while riding his motorcycle — an accident that leads the guilt-ridden driver to offer various forms of compensation.
During the movie, the family’s fortunes and their individual relationships fall and rise as they move slowly toward some sort of acceptance of their lives and of each other.
“The whole story really wants to present the relationships between people in contemporary urban families in Taipei,” Lee said. “There are many unexpected events in a big city, and even the right decisions can have many incomprehensible results.”
The film is an almost immersive experience, bringing viewers up close and personal with the family in their trouble and grief as they slowly try to work their way through both. That the situations and dialogue feel so real comes down to the script Lee wrote and the strength of the central performances.
Both Yang and Chang said there were times when they struggled with the work and the characters they play, given the serious nature of the story. But there is no doubt their struggles were worth it.
“I think when you really encounter a major change, you have the opportunity to look back and see what it is that you have been moving towards in this lifetime,” Chang said. “Are you living for others or for yourself?”
For Lee, the film marks a welcome return to feature filmmaking, following the acclaim she received early in her career with “The Shoe Fairy” (2005), which starred Vivian Hsu (徐若瑄), screened at Busan and picked up two nominations at the Golden Horse Awards.
“When writing this script, I collected many stories from people around me because for the past 20 years, I have returned to family life,” the director said. “I have raised two children so I have insights into the different families living in Taipei.”
“You may face many sudden accidents and impacts and so having lived in Taipei my whole life, I wanted with this film to share my feelings about people's lives in general but especially in this city.”

Sigurd expands testing capacity with NT$2.2 billion Hsinchu acquisition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:50:12 UTC
15:50:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Sigurd Microelectronics Corp. is expanding its testing capacity with a NT$2.2 billion (US$68 million) acquisition in Hsinchu.
The company said Tuesday that its subsidiary, Sigurd UTC Corp., won the bid to acquire a factory in Hsinchu Science Park. The acquisition comes as major US customers seek more advanced testing services for increasingly complex AI and high-performance computing chips, according to CTEE.
The site covers about 26,000 square meters of land and is expected to boost Sigurd's testing capacity by about 25% once fully operational. It will focus on developing testing equipment and services for high-speed optical communication chips used in AI data connections and silicon photonics.
The site will also offer wafer testing for application-specific AI chips, as well as testing services for chips packaged using chip-on-wafer-on-substrate, or CoWoS, technology. Other services will include testing and backend processing for general-purpose chips.
Sigurd is also increasing its production capacity at other sites. Its second plant in Hukou began production in the second half of this year, while its third plant in the Zhongxing area is scheduled to begin operations early next year.
The company reported cumulative revenue of NT$17.3 billion in the first three quarters. The figure was up 21.15% from the same period a year earlier, reflecting continued contributions from AI-related and high-end chip testing.
Packaging and testing is a key stage of semiconductor manufacturing that follows wafer fabrication. Packaging protects individual chips and provides the electrical connections needed to power them and link them to other components, while testing verifies that they function correctly and meet performance requirements, according to Gugu Fund.
As AI chips become more powerful and incorporate more components to handle growing volumes of data, testing must meet stricter performance requirements. This has increased the need for verification at multiple stages of production, from wafer testing to post-packaging checks and high-speed signal testing.
Meanwhile, advances in silicon photonics and co-packaged optics which bring optical communication closer to computing chips, are adding to the technical challenges of testing high-speed semiconductors. Analysts say companies that develop their own testing equipment and offer integrated services may be better positioned to secure higher-value contracts as these technologies advance.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) said Wednesday that the country will speed up its green transition and strengthen energy security to support economic growth and keep local industries competitive.
Speaking at the opening of the net-zero sustainability exhibition, Lai said businesses face growing pressure to cut emissions as global supply chains tighten environmental standards. He said companies that fail to reduce emissions could lose orders and fall behind international competitors.
Lai said the government has set new targets to guide the country's green transition. He said Taiwan aims to cut carbon emissions by 26% to 30% from 2005 levels by 2030, and by 36% to 40% by 2035.
The president said the government is using carbon fees and investment programs to help businesses meet these targets. Lai noted that the country completed its first round of carbon fee payments in May, with all revenue set aside for green upgrades and innovation.
The government has also established a NT$10 billion (US$318 million) fund project to attract private investment in low-carbon industries, he said. Lai said it plans to invest another NT$100 billion over eight years to help small- and medium-sized businesses adopt digital tools and cut emissions.
Lai said a stable power supply is essential as artificial intelligence drives up electricity demand. He added that the country is expanding renewable energy, improving energy storage, and upgrading its power grid to strengthen energy security.
The government will also promote energy-saving measures to help meet rising power demand, Lai said. He added that these efforts would support industrial growth while keeping the country on track to reach its net-zero emissions goals.

The head of the International Monetary Fund on Wednesday called for countries to make "urgent repairs" to address fiscal balances as bond yields spike and pressure grows on governments to manage ballooning debt.
"What is our loudest call to policymakers right now? Make urgent repairs to the fiscal house before the cracks widen," managing director Kristalina Georgieva said at a news conference on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank in Bangkok.
"Now is the time to enhance revenues, to rationalise spending and improve public financial management," she said.
The global economy "remains resilient in the face of very frequent repetitive shocks and in the face of uncertainty", Georgieva said. "But this resilience is reaching its limits."
The IMF is "ringing the alarm bell on excessive global economic imbalances growing", she added.
"To put it very simply, China needs to spend more, the US has to save more and Europe has to invest more," Georgieva said.
Her comments come as officials and experts gather in the Thai capital to discuss challenges facing the global economy as higher energy prices arising from US attacks on Iran drive up costs.
In its closely watched World Economic Outlook released on Tuesday, the IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast by 0.1 percentage points to 3.1 percent.
However, it warned that while there is new economic activity sparked by rising investment in artificial intelligence, poorer countries are not benefiting as they deal with soaring energy costs.
On the United States, Georgieva said it cannot grow its way out of mounting public debt and needs to make other fiscal adjustments to put its debt on a more sustainable path.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, she points out, recognises that  US deficits and overall debt, now above US$40 trillion, are too high.
"The authorities very much rely on strong growth in the United States" to help reduce debt, Georgieva said. "At the fund,  we believe that  growth, of course, helps, but it cannot deliver  fast enough the necessary adjustments. So, some [fiscal] measures would be necessary. (Agencies)

China’s annual inflation edges up to 0.9% in September
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:47:34 UTC
15:47:34 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
14 October 2026•Update: 14 October 2026
China’s annual consumer inflation accelerated to 0.9% in September from 0.8% in August, slightly below market expectations of 1%, according to National Bureau of Statistics data released on Wednesday.
The reading marked the highest inflation rate since June, as increases in non-food prices were partly offset by a continued decline in food costs.
Non-food prices rose 1.5% from a year earlier, compared with a 1.2% increase in August. Prices for transport and communication climbed 4.3%, accelerating from 2.5% the previous month.
Healthcare prices increased 2.7% year-on-year, while education, culture and recreation costs rose 1.4%, both unchanged from August.
Clothing prices increased 1.2%, easing from 1.3% a month earlier. Housing costs fell 0.3%, matching the decline recorded in August.
Food prices declined for the sixth consecutive month, falling 1.7% from a year earlier after a 1.4% decrease in August. Pork prices dropped 10%.
Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, stood at 1% year-on-year.
On a monthly basis, consumer prices increased 0.2% in September, below expectations of 0.3% and slowing from August’s 0.4% rise.

New enforcement threshold and warning signs cut speed trap fines by €1 million a month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-14
06:46:00 UTC
15:46:00 KST

New enforcement threshold and warning signs cut speed trap fines by €1 million a month
Since warning signs became mandatory for mobile speed cameras, the number of fines issued has fallen by nearly 90 percent, while revenue from fines dropped by almost €1 million in September.
In September last year, police issued €1,256,318 in fines using mobile speed cameras. This September, following the installation of warning signs ahead of the cameras and an increase in the enforcement threshold, fines totaled just €199,052, a decrease of nearly €1 million.
The drop in fine revenue was driven by a 90 percent decline in the number of fines issued. Raising the enforcement threshold nearly halved the number of violations, while the introduction of warning signs reduced it by roughly half again. As ERR has previously reported, citing police statistics, mobile speed cameras issued 26,228 fines in September last year, compared with just 2,939 across Estonia in September this year.
However, police spokesperson Taavi Kirss said revenue from fines has never been a priority for the police and will not be in the future.
"Our only priority has always been to make Estonia's roads safer and ensure that drivers obey speed limits. Higher speeds make it harder to spot hazards and lead to more severe consequences and more serious injuries in the event of an accident," Kirss said.
MP: The goal is to slow down traffic, not fill the treasury
Madis Timpson (Reform), chair of the Riigikogu's Legal Affairs Committee, who pushed for mandatory warning signs ahead of mobile speed cameras, told ERR that short-term police statistics may not provide a complete picture and that a longer period and more thorough analysis are needed to assess the actual impact.
"I think it's a little too early to draw conclusions based on just one month. We really need to look at a longer period than one or two months," Timpson explained. However, he said the decline in fines was a positive sign. "If the police say the number of fines has fallen by 90 percent, that's a good thing."
Commenting on the fact that the sharp drop in fines has left the state budget nearly €1 million short in a single month, with the trend likely to continue in the coming months, Timpson said issuing fines should never be an end in itself for either local governments or the state, even if it means forgoing millions of euros in potential annual revenue.
"The police have always said that the goal is not to issue fines but to calm traffic. If traffic has become calmer, that's a success," he said. "I certainly wouldn't want to live in a country where we try to fill the state coffers by issuing as many fines as possible," he added.
Timpson: I have not seen senseless speeding
Timpson disagrees with observations by some road users that drivers only obey the speed limit in the immediate vicinity of warning signs. The politician said his assessment is based on extensive personal experience driving between Tallinn and Viljandi every week.
"I drive between Viljandi and Tallinn several times a week. I don't think the situation is that bad. In my opinion, the overall traffic situation has improved considerably over the years," Timpson said, adding that it is wrong to regulate the behavior of all road users because of a few offenders.
"There have always been speeders, although there seem to be fewer of them lately. I haven't even noticed anyone driving recklessly fast," Timpson said.
Timpson also described his own negative experience with a mobile speed camera.
"I was once caught by a speed camera myself, doing 56 kilometers per hour. It was midday on a straight stretch of road with speed limit signs showing 90, 70 and then 50. I know because I drive that road several times a week. I switched off cruise control and coasted into the 50-kilometer-per-hour zone at 56. There were no cars coming from either direction, no other road users and the road was straight for three kilometers. Of course, I paid the fine, but it still left a bit of a bad taste in my mouth," Timpson recalled.
According to Timpson, however, his own fine was not the main motivation behind the legislative amendment. Rather, his decision to initiate the bill was a matter of principle: to restore fairness after police initially promised to install warning signs themselves but subsequently failed to do so.
"The bill actually originated from the fact that the police came to the Riigikogu in late 2018 and said they wanted to install mobile speed cameras and that warning signs would be placed ahead of them. In 2019, when the law was passed, this was reiterated on the floor of the Riigikogu. The law was passed, but the signs were never installed. In other words, the Riigikogu was deceived. If you went to your employer and promised to do something but then failed to deliver, what do you think would happen to you? I'd fire you," Timpson said.
On July 1, the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) raised the enforcement threshold for mobile speed cameras on its own initiative. Mobile cameras now issue fines only when drivers exceed the speed limit by at least 6 kilometers per hour, up from the previous threshold of 3 kilometers per hour, to avoid penalizing momentary lapses in attention. The change applied only to the eight mobile speed cameras operated by the PPA across Estonia. Fixed speed cameras continue to enforce speed limits starting at 3 kilometers per hour over the limit.
In May, three Riigikogu members — Valdo Randpere, Madis Timpson and Marek Reinaas — introduced a legislative amendment requiring police to place warning signs ahead of mobile speed cameras. The amendment was passed despite police opposition and took effect on August 1.
A study published by the Estonian Transport Administration in September found that 77 percent of drivers exceed the speed limit on at least some types of roads, an increase from last year. Of those who speed, 22 percent have encountered a dangerous traffic situation as a result, a figure that has also risen.
